Ilse Rosenthal-Schneider, a student of Albert Einstein, Max Planck, and Max von Laue, once discussed some intricate questions about Kant and his interpreters with Einstein. Einstein illustrated his views in the following way. ‘Kant is a sort of highway with lots and lots of milestones. Then all the little dogs [his interpreters] come and each deposits his contribution at the milestones.’ Miss Rosenthal-Schneider indignantly said: ‘But what a comparison!’ Einstein, laughing loudly, remarked: ‘But what will you have? # Preface

This is the last volume of *The Historical Development of Quantum Theory*; the entire series has been in the process of research and writing for over twenty-five years. The writing of such a work was conceived by J. M. in his youth when he met Wolfgang Pauli in Zurich and, at Pauli’s suggestion, became a student of Werner Heisenberg’s at Göttingen. The first detailed outline for the writing of these books, which would keep on changing as the work progressed, was made jointly by us (J. M. and H. R.), when we became associated with Heisenberg’s encouragement at the University of Texas at Austin in April 1970, where J. M. then was; it was there that the actual plan of undertaking the research and writing of this work in its final form took shape. We spent several years in doing relevant research on different aspects of the historical development of quantum theory, but we only began to write it in January 1975 at the University of Geneva and continued it at the International Solvay Institutes of Physics and Chemistry at the *Université libre de Bruxelles*; at both places, excellent facilities were provided to us for performing our work. The research on and the writing of this work progressed further in Munich, and later in Brussels, Munich and Houston, and the first four volumes (five books) were published by Springer-Verlag New York in fall 1982. Volume 5 of this work (consisting of two parts), dealing with Erwin Schrödinger and the creation of wave mechanics, was published by Springer-Verlag New York on the occasion of the centenary of the birth of Schrödinger in 1987.

By that time, we had spent so much effort on this extensive work, and our collaboration had been so intense throughout, that we decided to take leave from it for some time and attend to some other projects that had been neglected on account of our preoccupation with this enterprise. J. M. became involved in editing (together with Arthur Wightman) *The Collected Works of Eugene Paul Wigner* (in eight volumes, Springer-Verlag, 1990–1999), wrote *The Beat of a Different Drum: The Life and Science of Richard Feynman* (Oxford, 1994) and *Einstein, Physics and Reality* (World Scientific, 1999), as well as completed the project (with Kimball A. Milton) of writing *Climbing the Mountain: The Scientific Biography of Julian Schwinger* (Oxford, 2000); he also remained engaged in numerous other historical–scientific research undertakings and professorial appointments in Europe and the United States. H. R. took the main responsibility (jointly with W. Blum and H.-P. Dürr) for editing *Werner Heisenberg: Gesammelte Werke/Collected Works* (four annotated volumes of the scientific papers were published by Springer-Verlag from 1984 to 1993); five volumes of Heisenberg’s general, scientific, philosophical, and political writings of *Gesammelte Werke/Scientific*

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0007 -->

viii

Preface

*Papers* were also edited by H. R. (together with W. Blum and H.-P. Dürr) and published from 1984 to 1989 by R. Piper-Verlag, Munich and Zurich. H. R. further completed a number of other scientific projects, such as a biography of Hermann von Helmholtz (VCH, Weinheim, 1994), a series of fundamental historical–scientific papers, and the book *The Origin of the Concept of Nuclear Forces* (with Laurie Brown), IOP, Bristol, 1996, besides being occupied with much administrative work at the *Max Planck-Institut für Physik* in Munich. However, the J. M.–H. R. collaboration on Volume 6 (in two parts), which would take the history of the development of quantum theory from 1926 until 1942, with an epilogue dealing with further developments until 1999, was resumed in 1994 and continued throughout by express mail, telephone, faxes, and personal contacts. It has now been completed. The long years during which this work has been in the process of research and writing are a tribute to our sustained loyal and deeply friendly collaboration and unusual compatibility of our scientific–historical approach. To a certain extent, we have devoted our mature academic and scientific careers to the writing of this work; it has not always been easy, but it certainly has been most rewarding.

We came into intimate personal contact with most of the great architects of quantum mechanics and quantum field theory, knew them well, and had the benefit of their continuous support and encouragement. We would like to dedicate this entire work to Niels Bohr, Max Born, Louis de Broglie, Paul Dirac, Werner Heisenberg, Friedrich Hund, Pascual Jordan, Oskar Klein, Wolfgang Pauli, Erwin Schrödinger, Gregor Wentzel, and Eugene Wigner. We, especially J. M., wish to express our deepest thanks for their kind support to John S. Bell, Hans Bethe, P. M. S. Blackett, Felix Bloch, David Bohm, Aage Bohr, Hendrik B. G. Casimir, Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, Leon N. Cooper, Freeman J. Dyson, Richard Feynman, Vladimir Fock, Murray Gell-Mann, Walter Heitler, Josef M. Jauch, Res Jost, Nicholas Kemmer, Willis E. Lamb, Jr., Evgeny M. Lifshitz, Robert E. Marshak, Christian Møller, Nevill F. Mott, Robert S. Mulliken, J. Robert Oppenheimer, Rudolf Peierls, Frederick Reines, Léon Rosenfeld, Abdus Salam, Julian Schwinger, John C. Slater, Ernst C. G. Stueckelberg, Charles H. Townes, Leon Van Hove, J. H. Van Vleck, B. L. Van der Waerden, Victor F. Weisskopf, Carl Friedrich von Weizsäcker, John A. Wheeler, and Chen Ning Yang. In addition, H. R. owes a special debt of gratitude to Friedrich Hund and Werner Heisenberg, who—until their respective deaths—greatly helped and encouraged him in this undertaking. Without their communication, constant interest, encouragement, and friendship, we would not have gained the insight into this vast and complex field and the determination to devote ourselves for such a long time to persist with it.

# Acknowledgments

In Volume 1, Part 1, we have already acknowledged most of the personal sources of support for this extensive work. In this final volume, we would like to acknowledge the unfailing assistance of the curator and staff of *The Jagdish Mehra Collection* at the University of Houston, Houston, Texas, and the staff of the library of the *Max Planck-Institut für Physik* in Munich, Germany, especially Mrs. Frieda Ohrmund. Mrs. Norma Cowley of the Space Physics and Astronomy Department at Rice University, Houston, Texas, undertook the daunting task of typing the manuscript of Volume 6, and she completed it with her usual grace and cheerfulness; we are very grateful for her devoted help.

J. M. would like to thank the Curatorium of the *Minna-James-Heinemann-Stiftung* of Essen (Bredeney), Germany, for grants in support of research and writing this volume. His gratitude and thanks are also extended to the *Alexander von Humboldt-Stiftung* of Bonn, Germany, for a reinivitation to spend three months in Munich in 1997, and to the John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation of Chicago, Illinois, for a grant for research on this volume.

H. R. thanks Karl von Meyenn for numerous illuminating discussions regarding Wolfgang Pauli’s role and personality in the whole history of quantum theory. We are both indebted to Manuel Doncel for a critical reading of the manuscript of the first two chapters, and similarly to Laurie Brown concerning discussions of the developments in the 1930s and for a critical reading of the manuscript of Chapter IV.

Finally, we would like to express our unfailing gratitude to our wives (Marlis Mehra and Martha Rechenberg) for putting up with us, and even encouraging us, in our constant involvement in the research and writing of this extensive work. Thanks.

# Prologue

In his fifth communication on irreversible radiation phenomena, submitted to the Prussian Academy of Sciences in Berlin on 18 May 1899, Max Planck completed his theoretical derivation of the law describing the temperature dependence of the radiation intensity emitted from a blackbody (Planck, 1899). The law, in agreement with the relations derived earlier by Willy Wien and Friedrich Paschen and known as ‘Wien’s law,’ was obtained by Planck by combining electrodynamical and thermodynamical considerations and expressed as

$$E_\lambda = \frac{2c^2b}{\lambda^5} \exp\left(-\frac{ac}{\lambda\theta}\right) \qquad \text{(i)}$$

(Planck, 1899, p. 475), with $E_\lambda$ denoting the radiation energy for the wavelength $\lambda$ at the absolute temperature $\theta$, and $c$ denoting the velocity of light *in vacuo*. The constants $a$ and $b$ in Eq. (i), like $c$, were considered by Planck as ‘natural constants,’ which assumed, respectively, the values

$$a = 0.4818 \times 10^{-10} \sec \times ^\circ\text{C},$$
$$b = 6.885 \times 10^{-27} \text{erg} \times \text{sec}. \qquad \text{(ii)}$$

On 19 October 1900, Planck was forced by new, improved measurements of several experimentalists working at the *Physikalisch-Technische Reichsanstalt* to abandon the law, Eq. (i), and to replace it with a different equation,

$$E_\lambda = \frac{2c^2b}{\lambda^5} \frac{1}{\exp\left(\frac{ac}{\lambda\theta}\right) - 1}, \qquad \text{(iii)}$$

containing the same natural constants [Planck, 1900c, p. 204, preserving the previous notations for the constants of Eq. (i)]. When, less than two months later, again at a meeting of the German Physical Society in Berlin, Planck offered the derivation of Eq. (iii)—afterward called ‘Planck’s radiation law’—he made use of the kinetic theory of matter besides the earlier electrodynamical and thermodynamical considerations (Planck, 1900f). In his presentation of 14 December 1900,

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0015 -->

xviii Prologue

Planck proposed to use the constant $b$—which was soon denoted by $h$—for determining the smallest *finite energy element* or *quantum* $\epsilon$ of radiation having the frequency $\nu$, namely,

$$\epsilon = h\nu, \qquad \text{(iv)}$$

which entered into the statistical mechanical part of his derivation of the law, Eq. (iii).
In the subsequent years and decades, this law withstood the critical test of all experiments. Planck’s procedure marked the beginning of the new age of quantum theory. As one of the two great theoretical schemes that characterized the physical sciences of the twentieth century (the other being the relativity theory), quantum theory revolutionized the views concerning the constitution of matter and created a genuine domain of ‘microphysics’ in contrast to the classical domain of ‘macrophysics.’ It thus opened the path to the understanding of numerous brilliant discoveries in the world of atomic physics—from the earliest phenomena discovered to the present ‘standard model.’ Hence, the historical development of quantum theory, as discussed in the six volumes of this series, also represents an essential portion of the foundations of physics in the twentieth century. In the previous five volumes, we have given detailed accounts of the story emerging from Planck’s discovery of the ‘elementary quantum of action’—as Planck himself named the constant $h$ (Planck, 1906, p. 154)—to the completion of the two schemes of modern atomic theory: quantum and wave mechanics. Volume 1 embraces the preliminary theoretical efforts, undertaken between 1900 and 1925, to describe an ever-increasing wealth of quantum phenomena detected in atomic physics and theory of radiation. Volumes 2 to 4 constitute *one* sequence of essentially consecutive events that led to a consistent theoretical scheme—quantum mechanics—especially in the hands of Werner Heisenberg, Max Born, Pascual Jordan, and Paul Dirac; their theory set forth to describe adequately a large range of quantum phenomena. Volume 5 outlines in detail the historical development of the alternative approach, as pursued by a much smaller (more isolated) group of quantum physicists; they started from quite different concepts than the above-mentioned ‘majority’ group (Heisenberg *et al.* had indeed followed closely in the footsteps of Niels Bohr), namely, Louis de Broglie’s idea of quantum-theoretical matter waves, and arrived at ‘wave mechanics.’ This theory of the Viennese Erwin Schrödinger in Zurich accounted immediately for an even larger range of atomic phenomena than the earlier quantum mechanics, and confirmed the results achieved by the latter. Though the partisans of both approaches agreed that the practical results turned out to be identical in their respective schemes, they profoundly disagreed about the interpretation of the atomic phenomena. In Sections 1 to 4 of this Prologue, we shall look back briefly on the contents of the previous volumes and comment on the principal episodes of how the two so different formulations of modern atomic theory evolved; in Section 5, the programme of the present volume will be outlined.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0016 -->

1. The Rise of Quantum Physics (1900–1913) xix

**1. The Rise of Quantum Physics (1900–1913)**

The first decade of quantum theory following Planck’s recognition of the fundamental importance of the quantum of action $h$ in blackbody radiation resulted—besides numerous other examples to incorporate energy quantization, Eq. (iv), into the framework of classical theories—especially in the application of the energy-quantum or ‘light-quantum hypothesis’ of Albert Einstein (1905b) to a variety of phenomena (Einstein, 1906g; Stark, 1907b, c, 1908a; Haas, 1910a, b, c; Nernst and Lindemann, 1911a, b; Sommerfeld, 1911a, b). These pioneering applications, together with several analyses of the theoretical basis of the blackbody radiation law by Planck himself (1906; 1910a, b) and others (Einstein, 1906c; Ehrenfest, 1906b, 1911; Lorentz, 1908a, b; 1909b), provided further insight into the consequences of the revolutionary step taken in 1900 for the scientific description of nature. Yet, the importance of Planck’s original procedure was challenged in an interesting study by the historian and philosopher of science Thomas S. Kuhn; in his book on *Black-Body Theory and the Quantum Discontinuity, 1894–1912* (1978), Kuhn arrived at what he claimed to be ‘extraordinary results,’ namely, (1) Planck’s theory up to 1906 ‘was still classical’ and (2) the ‘non-classical step’ provided by Planck’s law was not recognized before the investigations of Paul Ehrenfest (1906b) and Albert Einstein (1906c); hence, he would like to credit Ehrenfest rather than Planck with having ushered the new era of quantum theory.
One may argue about Kuhn’s first claim; indeed, the legend of Max Planck, an innocent classical physicist (who was not quite aware of what he had wrought in December 1900), has been upheld by certain physicists and historians, although it is contradicted by Planck’s activity in all of the revolutionary fields that arose around 1900. The second argument, however, rests on even poorer historical evidence and, furthermore, on a misjudgment of the main trends of the development of physics in the first dozen years of the twentieth century. Not only did Kuhn base his proof of Ehrenfest’s priority in the recognition of quantum discontinuity on a supposed—though not actually preserved—correspondence between the celebrated Planck and Ehrenfest, the young Viennese student of Ludwig Boltzmann (see, especially, Kuhn, 1978, Chapter VI), but this highly speculative procedure seems to be more sensational than factual. More importantly, however, Kuhn overlooked an essential aspect of the actual development of the physical theories after 1900. Against occasional claims to the contrary, we must stress here that the so-called classical theories were not completed, nor the consequences arising from them exhausted by December 1900, when Planck proposed to quantize the energy of the blackbody oscillators. Indeed, classical mechanics and classical electrodynamics were finally fully established only after 1905, when the relativity theory of Einstein, Hendrik Lorentz, and Henri Poincaré had been formulated; before then, no theoretician could rightfully claim that the blackbody radiation law and related phenomena lay outside the range of the classical theories; that is, for instance, they would not follow from some very queer behaviour of electrons in matter (and, indeed, even afterward, certain physicists tried to construct models in

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0017 -->

xx Prologue

which the observed quantum effects would be described without involving any quantum-theoretical hypotheses). The same situation existed with respect to classical statistical mechanics, which especially Einstein and James Jeans (independently) used with great care to derive a classical blackbody radiation law, a law not known until 1905 (see Einstein, 1905b; Jeans, 1905b—in contrast to Lord Rayleigh, 1900b); Jeans afterward desperately sought to establish Planck’s law, the only experimentally confirmed law for blackbody radiation, on the basis of the classical theory (Jeans, 1908, 1910).
Beyond any doubt, the path to a genuinely non-classical theory did not lie open for the physicists of the early twentieth century *before all of the consequences from classical theories had been settled*. Consistent with this task, one must consider the eager participation of Planck, besides Einstein, in working out the details of relativistic mechanics and thermodynamics, just to be sure that no classical explanation of his blackbody radiation law was overlooked (see, e.g., Planck, 1907). Like others, Planck did not succeed, and therefore modified his original quantum hypothesis to overcome, at least partly, the gap between the quantum-theoretical and classical description (Planck, 1911a, 1914a). However, after the completion of the first decade of the twentieth century, the concerned scientists seem to have recognized the crucial point of the quantum problem, and they began to discern more or less the direction in which one had to look for a solution. This assumption may be concluded from some clear statements made at two conferences around 1910, namely, the Salzburg *Naturforscherversammlung* in September 1909 and the *Conseil de Physique Solvay* at Brussels in fall 1911, which we shall repeat here.
On the first occasion, Albert Einstein (next to Planck, the decisive early pioneer of quantum physics) presented a detailed report on the status of the radiation problem, based on relativity theory and kinetic theory; after computing the fluctuation of the radiation momentum due to Planck’s relation (iii), he concluded:

*Besides the spatial irregularities in the distribution of the momentum of radiation emerging from the undulatory theory, there are still other irregularities in the spatial distribution of the momentum, which in the case of small radiation energy by far exceed in strength the first-mentioned irregularities.*
*As far as I know, one has not yet succeeded in establishing a mathematical theory of radiation, which satisfies at the same time the demands following from the undulatory theory and the quantum structure. . . . The difficulty lies in the fact that the fluctuation properties of radiation [due to Planck’s relation] provide few points to begin with in setting up such a theory.* (Einstein, 1909b, p. 824)

Two years later, in the general discussion of the problems of radiation and quanta at the first Solvay Conference on Physics, two French scientists (who had previously not been involved in these topics) commented on the results that had been presented mainly by their German colleagues. Thus, Henri Poincaré, the famous mathematician, said:

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0018 -->

xxi

1. The Rise of Quantum Physics (1900–1913)

The new investigations discussed here not only seem to question the fundamental principles of mechanics but have even shaken an aspect, which until now was taken as being completely interwoven with the very concept of the law of nature. We are dealing with the question: Can we still represent these laws in the form of differential equations? (Poincaré in Eucken, 1914, p. 364)

The physicist Marcel Brillouin then remarked:

> It seems to be certain that we have to introduce into our physical and chemical considerations a discontinuity, a stepwise changing quantity, of which we had no idea until recently. . . . Should one go still further and even throw away the basis of the electromagnetic theory and classical mechanics, instead of being satisfied with fitting the discontinuity into the old mechanics? (Brillouin, *loc. cit.*)

Later in the discussion, Brillouin stressed ‘that it is little satisfactory to obtain the discontinuity from seemingly continuous processes’—i.e., by accounting for the obvious quantum jumps existing in nature with the help of further, still unknown, dynamical laws of the old continuous type (*loc. cit.*, p. 367).

Again, two years after the Solvay Conference, Walther Nernst’s student, Arnold Eucken, reviewed the state of affairs in an article on ‘The Development of Quantum Theory from Fall 1911 to Summer 1913,’ a postscript to the German publication of the Solvay reports and discussions of 1911. Eucken stated that the basic question concerning the relation of the new quantum theory to the foundations of the traditional (classical) mechanics might admit the following three possibilities or questions to be answered:

1. *Does quantum theory lie within the up-to-now approved mechanics?*
2. *Vice-versa*, is the *present mechanics perhaps the special case of a more general mechanics* (preliminarily being articulated in quantum theory), which may still be expressed by differential equations and contains no discontinuities?
3. Does quantum theory deviate qualitatively from today’s mechanics by a particular feature—the *occurrence of discontinuities*? That is, does *quantum theory* lie *beyond mechanics*? (Eucken, 1914, p. 372)

Eucken concluded that already the material presented at the first Solvay Conference and shortly afterward would rule out possibility 1. ‘In principle,’ he continued, ‘the suggestion cannot be totally rejected that one may obtain the conventional mechanics as a special use of a more general *quantum mechanics* [our italics] working without discontinuities’ (Eucken, *loc. cit.*, p. 373). However, he added immediately, several experimental facts explicitly demonstrated the existence of *discontinuities* in the energy distribution of atomic systems; thus, apparently, possibility 2 was also excluded; consequently, only possibility 3 remained.

Exactly at the time when Eucken wrote his review of quantum theory, Niels Bohr proposed a new theory of atomic structure including the quantum concept and Einstein’s radiation quanta (Bohr, 1913b, c, e). At the Birmingham meeting of the *British Association for the Advancement of Science* on 12 September 1913,

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0019 -->

xxii

Prologue

James Jeans finally gave up his previous opposition against the quantum hypothesis, although at the *Conseil Solvay* in 1911 he had still presented a rather tricky, classical explanation of Planck’s radiation law. He now argued vigorously that the photoelectric effect and the phenomenon of fluorescence could only be accounted for by the Planck–Einstein relation, which associated the light of frequency *ν* with the energy quanta *hν*. Thus, he continued his report on the ‘Discussion on Radiation’ as follows:

> By following this principle implicitly Dr. Bohr has arrived at a most ingenious and suggestive, and I think we must add most convincing, explanation of the laws of series spectra. . . .
>
> The series of results obtained in this way are, I think, far too striking to be dismissed merely as accidental. At the same time it wont be futile to deny that there are difficulties, still unsurmounted, which appear to be enormous. I would mention in particular the difficulty of explaining the Zeeman effect and interference. (Jeans, 1914a, pp. 379–380)

Evidently, the first dozen years of the twentieth century firmly established the existence of quantum effects in nature and the demand for their adequate description, most probably involving some discontinuities.

## 2. The Triumph and Decline of the Bohr–Sommerfeld Atomic Theory (1913–1925)

The twelve years following Niels Bohr’s pioneering paper on atomic constitution may be divided into two sub-periods. In the first half, the theory—especially in its extended formulation obtained since 1915 by Arnold Sommerfeld and his disciples, the most effective researchers in atomic theory—scored new triumphs in dealing with the spectra of atoms and molecules. During the second period, however, the difficulties lurking initially only in a few exotic applications of the theoretical scheme accumulated increasingly to destroy eventually the entire basis of the so-called ‘semi-classical’ or ‘old quantum theory.’

As the bright starting point of this entire period, Bohr also solved—after explaining the origin of the usual hydrogen spectra (Bohr, 1913b)—the problem raised by the new ‘Pickering series of hydrogen,’ by attributing it to the ionized helium atom (Bohr, 1913d). Henry Gwyn Jeffreys Moseley then measured and organized the X-ray spectra of the chemical elements, especially the *K*- and *L*-spectra, with the help of Bohr’s concepts; he thus provided a substantiation of the nuclear-atom model proposed by Ernest Rutherford in 1911 and used by Bohr in 1913 (Moseley, 1913, 1914b). In December 1915 and September 1916, Arnold Sommerfeld generalized Bohr’s one-quantum-number scheme to include two or even three quantum numbers to describe the electron orbits in atoms having two or three degrees of freedom—i.e., Kepler orbits in the plane or in space, including relativistic corrections and the action of magnetic fields (Sommerfeld, 1915b, c;

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0020 -->

xxiii

2. The Triumph and Decline of the Bohr–Sommerfeld Atomic Theory (1913–1925)

1916d). His Russian visitor, Paul Sophus Epstein, in Munich and the astrophysicist Karl Schwarzschild in Berlin calculated the Stark effect of the hydrogen lines, i.e., their splitting in an electric field (Epstein 1916a, c; Schwarzschild, 1916b). The Bohr–Sommerfeld theory of atomic structure indeed seemed to account for all of the discrete radiation emitted and absorbed by atoms and molecules, when magnetic and electric fields were acting upon them. Moreover, the theory rested on classical dynamics with the addition of a few quantum-theoretical hypotheses, such as the existence of ‘stationary states’ (expressed by the so-called ‘phase integrals’); however, the radiation emitted by atoms did not obey the laws of classical electrodynamics, but had rather to be calculated with the help of the Planck–Einstein relation (iv), with *ε* denoting the energy difference between two stationary atomic states. Whether this atomic theory was compatible with Eucken’s possibility 2, however, still remained undecided.

Although many physicists hoped to avoid a radical change in the classical description (valid for macroscopic bodies) in the world of atoms, the difficulties of the original Bohr–Sommerfeld approach accumulated after 1920, when an increasing number of experimentalists and theoreticians became occupied in applying it to a variety of atomic and molecular systems. The difficulties centered especially on three domains: (1) the radiation phenomena, (2) the structure of molecules and two-electron atoms, and (3) the anomalous Zeeman effects and complex structure of many-electron atoms as well as the magnetic anomaly.

(1) *The Light-Quantum and Radiation Theory*: Ever since 1905, when Einstein (1905b) had expounded his light-quantum hypothesis, the majority of physicists held against it the successes of the (classical) electromagnetic wave theory. Thus, even Max Planck, the discoverer of quantum theory (when drafting with Walther Nernst in 1913 a proposal to the Prussian Academy for the membership of and a position for Albert Einstein in Berlin), wrote ‘that he [Einstein] may have missed the target in his theory of light-quanta’ (quoted in Clark, 1971, p. 215); and Robert A. Millikan, while experimentally substantiating Einstein’s formula for the photoelectric effect (obtained by involving the light-quantum concept), concluded that ‘the semi-corpuscular theory by which Einstein arrived at his equation seems at present to be wholly untenable’ (Millikan, 1916b, p. 383). The radiation problem not only consisted in explaining both the quantum *and* the undulatory interference phenomena of light, but also in the necessity of a correspondence limit when passing from the quantum-theoretical to the classical description of atomic systems. Thus, even Bohr was happy when, in 1921, he succeeded in deriving Adalbert Rubinowicz’s selection rules for atomic radiation (Rubinowicz, 1918a, b, 1921) *without* applying Einstein’s directed light-quanta that Rubinowicz had assumed (Bohr, 1921b). It was not before Arthur H. Compton discovered his effect of the frequency-shift of X-rays when scattered by atoms (Compton, 1923a, b), and Peter Debye (1923) and Adolf Smekal (1923c) treated this and similar effects with the help of the light-quantum, that the latter hypothesis achieved some respectability. Rather than accepting it, however, Bohr and his associates, Hendrik Kramers and John Slater, attempted to devise an entirely new and revolutionary radiation

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0021 -->

xxiv

Prologue

theory that exhibited, on the one hand, the proper correspondence limit between the quantum and the classical description, but, on the other hand, violated the fundamental energy and momentum conservation (Bohr *et al.*, 1924). At this moment, Sommerfeld intervened. In the fourth edition of his well-known *Atombau und Spektrallinien*, he stressed the simultaneous existence of the incompatible corpuscular and undulatory aspects of electromagnetic radiation and stated the ‘*non liquet* (i.e., it cannot be decided)’ between the light-quantum and the classical description (Sommerfeld, 1924d, p. 59).

(2) *The Hydrogen Molecule and Helium Structure*: Niels Bohr believed that his quantum theory of atomic structure of 1913 would also apply to molecules, and he immediately proposed a specific model for the hydrogen molecule, the simplest molecule existing in nature (Bohr, 1913e). However, subsequent evaluations of the latter’s specific heat and ionization potential did not fit the available data (Epstein, 1916f; Franck *et al.*, 1919). Then, in 1921, Bohr initiated a new approach especially to deal with many-electron atoms based on the correspondence principle and a ‘building-up (*Aufbau*) principle’ (Bohr, 1921a, d), the details of which he presented in seven lectures delivered at Göttingen in June 1922. At the same time, Max Born, one of his hosts in Göttingen, joined the group of atomic model builders with the intention of constructing in a systematic manner ‘less arbitrary’ models of atoms and molecules, which he tried to base on unambiguous quantum rules, and making computations with the help of the refined dynamical perturbation theory of periodic systems that had been developed by astronomers and mathematicians. He first turned to the problem of the hydrogen molecule, but could not propose any specific model to describe correctly the observed properties of this molecule (Born, 1922). Then, together with Werner Heisenberg, he attacked another atomic system of similar simplicity: the helium atom. By treating it mathematically in a most sophisticated manner on the basis of the standard Bohr–Sommerfeld quantization rules, they obtained wrong values for the energies of the excited helium-atom states (Born and Heisenberg, 1923b). Their negative result fitted well with two other, similarly unsuccessful, calculations of few-body systems: neither the ground state of the helium atom (Kramers, 1923a; Van Vleck, 1922b) nor that of the hydrogen molecule-ion (Pauli, 1922) seemed to come out correctly from the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory of atomic structure. It took two more years until the experts became convinced that even the behaviour of the hydrogen atom, when subjected to crossed external electric and magnetic fields, could not be described properly (Pauli, 1926b, p. 164).

(3) *Many-Electron Atoms and Magnetic Anomaly*: In 1916, the successful calculations of the Zeeman and Stark effects of the hydrogen atom seemed to open the door to a complete description of all atomic spectra. One of the first tasks in this direction was to consider the problem of the anomalous Zeeman effects, besides the standard triplet splitting (explained already on the basis of the classical theory by Hendrik Lorentz and confirmed in 1916 by the quantum theoreticians), other kinds of splittings were also observed. Although the treatments of Sommerfeld, Heisenberg, and Alfred Landé shortly after 1920 yielded formulae that apparently described the data, these authors involved in their calculations quite

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0022 -->

3. The Emergence of Quantum and Wave Mechanics (1923–1926)  
xxv

arbitrary extra assumptions that had to be satisfied (Sommerfeld, 1920a; Landé, 1921c, f; Heisenberg, 1922a). In 1923, Landé derived an ingenious formula for the so-called *g*-factor that made it possible to reproduce even the most complex Zeeman effects, namely,

$$g = 1 + \frac{J^2 - \frac{1}{4} + R^2 - K^2}{2\left(J^2 - \frac{1}{4}\right)}, \tag{v}$$

with $K$, $R$, and $J$ denoting the (quantized) angular momenta of the series electron, the atomic core, and the sum of both, respectively (Landé, 1923a, p. 200). However, this expression could not be made compatible with the (classical) dynamics underlying the Bohr–Sommerfeld atomic model, as Pauli demonstrated in two thorough theoretical investigations (Pauli, 1923a, 1924a). Even the simplified splitting, which showed up in the case of strong magnetic fields (agreeing again with the classical Lorentz triplet), would not follow from the theory; hence, Pauli wrote to Landé on 23 May 1923:

> The energy values for strong fields can be interpreted [only] by the assumption that the magnetic moment of the inner system [i.e., the atomic core] assumes twice the value it would have corresponding to its angular momentum in the classical electron theory of magnetism, while the outer [i.e., the series] electron creates a magnetic moment in agreement with the Biot–Savart law. Hence we suggest here that the Biot–Savart law fails, while the mechanical concept of the angular momentum remains valid. (Pauli, 1979, p. 87)

This schizophrenic handling of classical dynamics in the treatment of the anomalous Zeeman effects of many-electron atoms—part of which Pauli would later associate with the concept of a ‘non-mechanical stress (*nicht-mechanischer Zwang*)’ of the electron (Pauli, 1925b)—had been noticed already in connection with another effect, the gyromagnetic ratio for metal electrons, as observed in the Einstein–de Haas effect of 1915. Contrary to the classical result presented by Einstein and de Haas (1915), two experimentalists later found the ratio of magnetization over angular momentum of a metallic rod to assume the value $\frac{e}{m_e}$ instead of the classical value $\frac{e}{2m_e}$, with $e$ and $m_e$ denoting the charge and mass of the electron, respectively (E. Beck, 1919a; Arvidsson, 1920). The same factor-two anomaly now showed up in the description of the anomalous Zeeman effects.

### 3. The Emergence of Quantum and Wave Mechanics (1923–1926)

The development of quantum and wave mechanics—constituting the contents of Volumes 2, 3, and 4, on the one hand, and Volume 5, on the other—occurred

3. The Emergence of Quantum and Wave Mechanics (1923–1926) xxvii

$J, K$, and $R$). ‘One can say,’ Pauli commented, ‘that the two expressions [(vi) and (vii)] are related to each other like the differential quotient $\frac{d}{dj}$ to the difference quotient $\left( \frac{1}{j} - \frac{1}{j - 1} \right)$, which seems to hint at something non-mechanical.’ (Pauli to Sommerfeld, *loc. cit.*, in Pauli, 1979, pp. 105–106)

*10 September to 8 October 1923*: In three notes submitted to *Comptes Rendus* of the *Académie des Sciences (Paris)*, Louis de Broglie proposed the concept of ‘matter waves’; that is, he associated with each mass particle—even the light-quantum should have a tiny mass—moving with velocity $v$ a ‘fictive wave’ having the phase velocity $v_{\text{ph}} = \frac{c^2}{v}$, and, in the nonrelativistic limit, the wavelength
$$ \lambda = \frac{h}{m_{\text{o}}v}, \tag{viii} $$
with $m_{\text{o}}$ denoting the mass of the particle and $h$ Planck’s constant (L. de Broglie, 1923a, b, c; 1924b).

*9 October 1923*: In a letter to Pauli, Heisenberg explained the ‘new Göttingen theory of the anomalous Zeeman effect’ as follows: (1) Model considerations have only symbolic value in principle, as constituting the classical analogue to the ‘discrete’ quantum theory. (2) The quantum-theoretical energy expression $H_{\text{qu}}$ is derived formally by averaging the classical Hamiltonian function $H(j_1, \dots, j_n)$, expressed in the action variables $(j_1, \dots, j_n)$ of the $n$-fold periodic atomic system (according to the Bohr–Sommerfeld model), i.e.,
$$ H_{\text{qu}} = \Delta F \quad \text{with} \quad F = \int H(j_1, \dots, j_n) dj_1, \dots, dj_n. \tag{ix} $$

(3) The usual assumptions introduced previously to account for the anomalous Zeeman effects (i.e., the anomalous double magnetic moment of the core, in agreement with the anomalous gyromagnetic ratio) can be taken over. Heisenberg wrote to Pauli: ‘Born summarizes our task for the next stage in the phrase “discretization of atomic physics”.’ (See Pauli, 1979, p. 127) Evidently, the new Göttingen discretization programme coincided, at least partly, with Pauli’s reformulation of Landé’s *g*-factor formula, Eq. (vi), involving difference rather than differential quotients.

*25 March 1924*: Hendrik Kramers submitted his quantum-theoretical dispersion formula, describing the scattering of light by atoms and containing negative oscillator strengths $f_j^e$, which imply the emission-frequency denominators $(\nu_j^2 - \nu^2)$ (Kramers, 1924a).

*13 June 1924*: Among other quantum phenomena, Born derived from the Göttingen discretization programme Kramers’s new dispersion formula: the procedure was to replace the classical differential quotient (with respect to the action variable of the periodic system) of a quantity $\Phi$ by the quantum-theoretical dif-

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0025 -->

xxviii                                                                                                         Prologue

ference $[\Phi(n + \tau) - \Phi(n)]/\tau h$, where $n + \tau$ and $n$ denoted the quantum numbers of two stationary states of the system (Born, 1924b).

*2 to 10 July 1924*: Satyendra Nath Bose of Dacca, India, presented a consistent derivation of Planck’s blackbody radiation law by considering that the light-quanta obey a new type of statistics: in it, the phase cells of size $h^3$ can be occupied by arbitrary numbers of light-quanta (i.e., 0, 1, 2, 3, etc.). Einstein, who received, translated, and had Bose’s paper published (Bose, 1924a), made use of the new statistics to describe the behaviour of atoms in ideal gases (Einstein, 1924c).

*5 January 1925*: Kramers and Heisenberg extended the dispersion theory also to include the incoherent scattering of light by atoms, notably, the effect of frequency-shift predicted by Adolf Smekal (1923c); in the mathematical scheme, sums and products of single terms depending on two quantum numbers appeared (Kramers and Heisenberg, 1925).

*8 January 1925*: In his second paper on the quantum theory of ideal gases, Einstein hinted at a relation between de Broglie’s matter waves and the behaviour of atoms in ideal gases due to Bose statistics; in particular, he suggested the resolution of the old, classical Gibbs paradox concerning the entropy of gas mixtures (Einstein, 1925a).

*16 January 1925*: Pauli associated with the (bound) electrons a ‘classically indescribable duplicity (double-valuedness) of the quantum-theoretical properties,’ endowing each electron in the atoms four quantum numbers instead of the usual three (due to Sommerfeld) and assuming the ‘exclusion principle’: that is, no two or more electrons in an atom can occupy a given set of all four quantum numbers (Pauli, 1925b). Thus, he provided the basis for a new, namely the first consistent theory of the periodic system of chemical elements.

*3 June to 9 July 1925*: In continuing his previous guesswork of obtaining quantum-theoretical results from classical ones by means of what he called the ‘sharpened application of the correspondence principle,’ Heisenberg expounded in letters to his scientific friends (Kronig and Pauli) a new ‘quantum-theoretical reformulation of kinematic and mechanical relations’ in atomic theory. In doing so, he especially followed the philosophy of employing only observable magnitudes in the new theory. Thus, he rewrote the dynamical variables of periodic atomic systems as ‘quantum-theoretical’ Fourier series,

$$x = \sum_n a(n, n - \tau) \exp[2\pi i v(n, n - \tau)t], \qquad \text{(x)}$$

arriving at the puzzling conclusion that two such quantum variables did not commute in general, i.e.,

$$x \cdot y - y \cdot x \neq 0. \qquad \text{(xi)}$$

In order to solve the equation of motion in the case of the simplest non-trivial model, the anharmonic oscillator, Heisenberg assumed the existence of a lowest

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0026 -->

3. The Emergence of Quantum and Wave Mechanics (1923–1926) xxix

energy state and the reformulated Bohr–Sommerfeld phase integral, which now took on the form of a sum rule (similar to the ‘Thomas–Kuhn sum rule’ known from spectroscopy). In this way, he obtained the stationary energy rules of the quantum-theoretical anharmonic oscillator characterized by half-integral quantum numbers $n + \frac{1}{2}$, as observed in molecular spectra; also, some empirically substantiated intensity formulae (of Ralph Kronig and Helmut Hönl) followed from the new reformulation scheme (Heisenberg, 1925c).

*July–September 1925*: Upon studying Heisenberg’s manuscript before submitting it for publication, Born recognized in July 1925 Heisenberg’s non-commutative multiplication rule for quantum-theoretical variables (Fourier series) to be identical with the well-known mathematical multiplication rule for matrices; in particular, he suspected that Heisenberg’s reformulated quantum condition represented simply the fundamental commutation relation for the quantum-mechanical matrix variables, the momentum **p** and position **q**, i.e.,

$$ \mathbf{pq} - \mathbf{qp} = \frac{h}{2\pi i} \mathbf{1}, \tag{xii} $$

with **1** denoting the unit matrix of infinitely many rows and columns. Together with Pascual Jordan, Born developed in August and September 1925 the first consistent quantum-mechanical scheme; this ‘matrix mechanics’ constituted a Hamiltonian scheme for infinite Hermitean matrices (representing quantum-mechanical variables), which replaced the old semi-classical quantum theory of periodic atomic systems and satisfied the correspondence principle (Born and Jordan, 1925b).

*17 October 1925*: George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit in Leyden interpreted Pauli’s fourth quantum number as an ‘intrinsic rotation’ of the electron (later called ‘spin’); its half-integral value (in units of $\frac{h}{2\pi}$) explained the gyromagnetic ratio observed in metals and used in the earlier discussion of the models of anomalous Zeeman effects (Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, 1925).

*7 November 1925*: After studying the proof-sheets of Heisenberg’s pioneering paper of July 1925 (which Heisenberg had sent to Ralph Fowler), Paul Dirac in Cambridge developed his own formulation of the Göttingen quantum mechanics, based on non-commuting ‘$q$-numbers’ (a generalized form of matrices). As a fundamental relation in his Hamilton–Jacobi scheme of atomic dynamics, he found a reformulation of the classical Poisson brackets for two variables $x$ and $y$ by the quantum-theoretical commutator $\frac{2\pi}{i\hbar} [x \cdot y - y \cdot x]$. Dirac’s scheme also satisfied the correspondence principle (Dirac, 1925d).

*16 November 1925*: Born, Heisenberg, and Jordan submitted their monumental paper ‘*Zur Quantenmechanik. II* (On Quantum Mechanics. II),’ providing a detailed account of the complete matrix-mechanical formalism for periodic systems of arbitrarily many degrees of freedom plus the associated perturbation schemes,

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0027 -->

xxx                                                                         Prologue

which made it possible to treat both non-degenerate and degenerate cases (Born *et al.*, 1926).

22 *December 1925*: Starting from the Born–Jordan work on matrix mechanics, Cornelius Lanczos of the University of Frankfurt proposed a ‘field-like’ formulation of the theory in terms of linear integral equations, where the integral kernels represented Heisenberg’s quantum variables (Lanczos, 1926a). The equivalence of the matrix and the integral-equation schemes had been formulated already twenty years earlier by the Göttingen mathematician David Hilbert, Born’s teacher and colleague in Göttingen.

5 *January 1926*: During his leave of absence in Cambridge, Massachusetts, Born worked out with the mathematician Norbert Wiener of MIT a different—besides matrix mechanics, *q*-number theory, and

$$H\psi = E\psi, \tag{xiii}$$

where $E$ were the energy eigenvalues and the ‘Hamilton operator’ $H$ (acting on the wave function $\psi$) was obtained from the classical Hamilton function ($Hq_i, p_i$) by replacing the momentum variables $p_i$ by the corresponding operator expressions,

$$p_i = \frac{h}{2\pi i} \frac{\partial}{\partial q_i}. \tag{xiv}$$

29 *April 1926*: Dirac applied his $q$-number scheme to treat the relativistic scattering of radiation by atoms, the Compton effect (Dirac, 1926c).
10 *May 1926*: In his third communication on quantization as an eigenvalue problem, Schrödinger developed the wave-mechanical perturbation theory and calculated the Stark effect of Balmer lines (Schrödinger, 1926f).
11 *June to 24 July 1926*: In two papers, submitted to the *Zeitschrift für Physik*, Heisenberg (1926b) introduced the concept of ‘quantum-mechanical resonance’ or ‘exchange’ in many-body problems and solved the helium problem by applying wave-mechanical methods (Heisenberg, 1926c).

$$\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial t} = \frac{2\pi i}{h} E\psi, \tag{xv}$$

26 *August 1926*: Upon analyzing the ‘physical content’ of Schrödinger's theory, Dirac found, in particular, that wave functions were symmetrical with respect to the exchange of two sets of variables describing two particles if the particles obeyed Bose statistics, and that the correspondingly antisymmetrical wave functions were connected with particles obeying the exclusion principle and Fermi statistics (Dirac, 1926f).

## 4. The Conceptual Problems of the New Atomic Theory

The two methodically quite different forms of the new atomic theory, which were created between 1923 and 1926, were able to account properly for the observed

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0029 -->

xxxii                                                                          Prologue

quantum phenomena yielding identical results for the same problems. The slightly
younger wave mechanics provided most physicists with an easily manageable and
more conventional mathematical tool to calculate complex and, in particular,
aperiodic atomic systems. When Heisenberg presented a review of ‘*Quantenmechanik*’ on 22 September 1926, at the prestigious *Versammlung deutscher Naturforscher und Ärzte* in Düsseldorf, he was able to present already an impressive list
of successes obtained during the previous year by the Göttingen theoreticians, and
by Pauli, Dirac, Schrödinger, and their associates (Heisenberg, 1926d). Heisenberg also explained on this occasion the fundamental concepts of the new atomic
theory, stressing in particular ‘the typical element of discontinuity’ and the role of
Bohr’s correspondence principle, which had guided the physicists in Göttingen,
Hamburg, and Cambridge in their successes. Quantum mechanics, declared Heisenberg in Düsseldorf, avoided the use of the visualizable (*anschauliche*) concepts
that dominated the former semi-classical ‘old quantum theory,’ notably, the ‘Bohr
orbits’ of electrons and the like, and provided a consistent mathematical description
of the physical situations. Schrödinger’s theory, Heisenberg argued, started
from de Broglie’s concept of matter waves and formally seemed to allow a ‘continuous’ description by means of differential equations (i.e., it still seemed to be
compatible with Eucken’s possibility 2); however, the wave function could not be
interpreted in space and time like a classical object. Heisenberg stressed that ‘The
peculiar reality of the de Broglie waves lies in the interference phenomena which
repudiate every interpretation based on classical concepts,’ and continued: ‘The
exceptional significance of Schrödinger’s results consists in the statement that a
visualizable interpretation of the quantum-mechanical formulae exhibits typical
features of both a corpuscular and a wave theory’ (*loc. cit.*, p. 992). He felt that the
main strength of wave mechanics consisted in ‘that it allows a simple determination
of the transition probabilities, which is very difficult in general with the help
of the mathematical methods of [the alternative quantum mechanics]’ (*loc. cit.*,
p. 991).

In this speech, Heisenberg also enunciated perfectly the opinion of his colleagues in Cambridge, Copenhagen, Göttingen, and Hamburg, who formed the
majority of the pioneers of quantum mechanics. On the other hand, Schrödinger
felt and argued quite differently, and so did the partisans of the theory of wave
mechanics in their publications. Thus, for instance, the Viennese theoretician Hans
Thirring, a university mate and friend of Schrödinger’s, wrote the following in his
review article on ‘*Die Grundgedanken der neuen Quantentheorie* (The Fundamental
Ideas of the New Quantum Theory)’:

*Quantum mechanics*, the theory founded by Heisenberg, and then further extended by
Born, Jordan and Dirac, can be considered as a kind of phenomenological theory, as
it poses for itself the task of establishing relations only between quantities that are
*observable in principle*. Against this stands *wave mechanics*, the theory founded by
Schrödinger in connection with de Broglie’s ideas. It operates with new concepts and
abstractions, which cannot be observed in principle, as for instance waves having
unknown physical meaning in multi-dimensional spaces; hence it clashes deliberately

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0030 -->

4. The Conceptual Problems of the New Atomic Theory xxxiii

with the principles that had guided Heisenberg in formulating his theory. Nevertheless it leads finally to the same results as quantum mechanics, especially in a much more advantageous manner regarding the mathematical treatment; thus the introduction of the noted fictitious concepts turns out to be a very helpful and profitable tool. (Thirring, 1928, p. 385)

And about a year later, Henry Thomas Flint, a Reader of Physics at the University of London, characterized the new atomic theory developed by de Broglie and Schrödinger as even 'in fact a classical theory, for the methods are those which were familiar to physicists before the beginning of this century' (Flint, 1929, p. vii). In contrast to this declaration, Flint presented in the fifth chapter of his book, which he specifically entitled 'The Physical Significance of the Wave Equation,' Born's non-classical probability interpretation of the wave function.

Though Thirring and Flint did not belong among the active pioneers of either quantum of wave mechanics, one may ask the question whether their emphasis on the so-to-say 'classical' features of wave mechanics really did justice to its contents, and whether one could indeed circumvent the radical concepts formulated by the members of Niels Bohr and Max Born's circles since the early 1920s. Would one really be able, as Willy Wien wrote to Schrödinger in his letter of 23 June 1926, to abandon 'the quagmire of integral and half-integral quanta, of discontinuities and arbitrary use of the classical theory' to 'soon become used again to rigorous physical thinking?' By 'rigorous physical thinking' Wien, professor of experimental physics at the University of Munich and discoverer of the first law of blackbody radiation, meant the great tradition of nineteenth-century physics, as represented by his teacher Hermann von Helmholtz, whom he had praised in 1921 as follows: 'Since Helmholtz was the last and one of the greatest representatives of a closed epoch in the history of physics, in which causality and the logical setup constituted the firm basis, the contemporary and future physicists will have to return to him again and again' (Wien, 1921, p. 699).

Werner Heisenberg, whom Wien especially accused in 1926 of having abandoned the well-established tradition of Helmholtz, would not reply to such attacks nor turn the wheel back to classical concepts; he would rather continue to work on the completion of the physical interpretation of quantum mechanics and, many years later—in September 1934—deliver again a programmatic speech at a *Naturforscherversammlung*, which he entitled '*Wandlungen der Grundlagen der exakten Naturwissenschaft in jüngster Zeit*' (Changes in the Foundations of Science in the Most Recent Times)' (Heisenberg, 1934f). Although the old Willy Wien had taken refuge in the physics of the previous epoch—which Heisenberg called 'the edifice of classical physics'—he (Heisenberg) now unfolded in front of his large audience of scientists and physicians a broad scenario of 'closed systems' in science, consisting of a sequence of theories: next to the edifice of classical physics, he placed that of modern atomic physics, in which classical mechanics, electrodynamics, statistical mechanics, and the relativity theories were partly replaced by quantum mechanics and its relativistic extensions. In particular, Heisenberg

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0031 -->

xxxiv Prologue

claimed that the new system of atomic theories turned out to be as logically consistent and closed as the previous ones, and other such closed systems might be envisaged in future science.

## 5. Outline of the Developments Completing and Extending Quantum Mechanics (1926–1999)

This present volume (in two parts) of *The Historical Development of Quantum Theory* deals essentially with the main events of the almost fifteen years following the summer of 1926. During that period, 'the modern atomic theory,' as Heisenberg and his colleagues would call quantum mechanics, was completed and took on the shape of a mathematically and conceptually consistent theoretical scheme—just a 'closed system' in Heisenberg's words of 1934—well substantiated by thousands of experimental investigations, though certain problems, even of the nonrelativistic quantum physics—such as superconductivity—remained unresolved. The epistemological questions dealing with causality and reality in the new scheme were also clarified, though Albert Einstein and Erwin Schrödinger remained dissatisfied with the solutions proposed in the 'Copenhagen Interpretation' of Bohr, Heisenberg, and Pauli. The domain of 'microphysics,' which had been inaugurated at the end of the nineteenth century with the discovery of the first atomic constituent, the electron, was thus added to the former fields of physics, and has grown ever since, with new details and extensions added in the past decades.

In the period following the discovery of quantum and wave mechanics, the number of investigations and publications devoted to the completion, application, and extension of quantum physics grew immensely: the theory spread out not only in the traditional universities and research institutions, especially in Middle Europe and England, where quantum concepts had been fostered before, but also notably flourished in Russia, the United States, Italy, and France, and later in India, Japan, and beyond, gaining active contributors in all parts of the scientific world. We shall not be able to deal here, as in the previous volumes of this series, with even the majority of all of the important investigations, but rather have to restrict our attention to certain selected developments that assisted particularly in establishing the completion of quantum mechanics and adding new fields to the 'closed scheme' of microphysics.

Thus, the first two Chapters, I and II, in Part 1 of this volume will be devoted to the fundamental progress in the physical interpretation of quantum mechanics, achieved essentially between June 1926 and the end of 1927: first the complete formulation of the probabilistic scheme of quantum mechanics, especially by Max Born, Paul Dirac, and Pascual Jordan, but also with the valuable contributions of others, such as Gregor Wentzel, Hendrik Kramers, and Léon Brillouin; second, the detailed investigation and creation of a consistent physical interpretation of the unified system of quantum and wave mechanics—this so-called Copenhagen

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0032 -->

5. Outline of the Developments Completing xxxv

Interpretation demanded the extension of the theory into the domain of relativity, as only a relativistic quantum field theory could satisfactorily complete a finished, closed interpretation of the aforementioned unified scheme. Chapter III, which completes Part 1 of the book, discusses the decisive steps establishing the empirical and mathematical foundations of quantum mechanics up to about 1932. A host of individual experimental verifications, from the Auger–Meitner effect to the Raman effect, supported the underpinnings of the theory, whose mathematical foundation was explored by specialists like David Hilbert, John von Neumann, and Aurel Wintner. Von Neumann further produced a rigorous, though not unchallenged, theory of measurement in quantum mechanics, and the mathematician Hermann Weyl and the physicists Eugene Wigner and Werner Heisenberg pioneered the application of group theory in atomic and molecular physics. Three major fields of the applications of quantum mechanics were also created by 1932 and are included in Chapter III: molecular theory and quantum chemistry, the quantum theory of metal electrons and the solid state, and the beginnings of nuclear theory and of the description of high-energy processes.

Remarkably, in spite of the relatively large number of people working on quantum physics in those days, only a few distinguished theoreticians became decisively involved in the more fundamental items treated here. Hence, the stories told in Part 1 more resemble the old-fashioned historical accounts emphasizing the work of distinguished people ('kings' and 'heroes') and some of their intimate associates ('knights') than the now fashionable 'democratic' history—not to mention the 'externalistic' historical approaches to quantum theory. However, a natural explanation of the procedure chosen in our work should be sought in that the solution to the problems required the most experienced and audacious participants in the enterprize, the kings and not the pawns. The kings included mainly Bohr, Born, Dirac, Heisenberg, Jordan, Pauli, and Wigner among the physicists, and Hilbert, Weyl, and von Neumann among the mathematicians, supported by a few other first-rate scholars.

Part 2 essentially consists of the voluminous Chapter IV, which we have entitled 'The Completion and Extensions of Quantum Mechanics'; it exhibits a somewhat different character, although this may not be reflected in the first two sections dealing with the 'causality' and 'completeness' debates. Because of the radical break with important features of the classical description of nature in the previous centuries—which meant nothing less than renouncing the sacred Cartesian principle of separation between the observing subject and the observed object in nature—the philosophical discussion of the consequences derived from the quantum-mechanical formalisms intensified after 1925. This debate even split, as we have shown in Chapter II (and at times in the previous volumes of this series), the great initiators and protagonists of the quantum-mechanical revolution until 1920 into two opposing camps: apart from Bohr, Born, and Sommerfeld, all of the senior physicists, particularly Einstein, Planck, and Schrödinger, denied in particular the genuinely statistical nature of the microphysical phenomena, which the members of the Copenhagen and Göttingen centres of atomic theory and their

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0033 -->

xxxvi Prologue

colleagues constantly deepened and clarified farther. Thus, in Section 1 of Chapter IV, we tell the story of the causality debate that evolved from Heisenberg's uncertainty relations until about 1934; in Section 2, we then summarize the results of the epistemological debate initiated by Einstein in 1935, when he published with Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen a discussion concerning the problem of reality and completeness in relativistic quantum theory, in which Bohr, Heisenberg, and Schrödinger—the latter with the formulation of his famous 'cat paradox'—became involved.

In the early 1930s, quite serious doubts were also raised against the validity of quantum mechanics, and here especially Bohr, Heisenberg, Pauli, and their followers participated eagerly to clarify the question whether the new theory of microphysics could really describe the nuclear, elementary-particle, and cosmic-ray phenomena. In Sections 3 and 5, the successes and difficulties of these advanced topics at the forefront of modern physics are summarized, and in Section 4, we deal with the progress achieved in the quantum-mechanical treatment of a series of questions associated with solid-state, low-temperature, and high-pressure (relativistic) phenomena. Although quite a few fundamental problems did remain unsolved here, quantum mechanics provided encouraging results even in the topics of 'matter under extreme conditions,' as Friedrich Hund called the last-mentioned field. Hence, by the end of the 1930s, the general conviction among the majority of quantum physicists that the existing theoretical schemes of quantum mechanics, perhaps augmented and generalized by some new ideas or elementary constituents of matter, would eventually overcome all existing difficulties became firmly established. Again, a small group of particularly experienced pioneers, including Bohr, Dirac, Heisenberg, and Pauli, felt the limitations of the theory most severely.

The following six decades, sometimes called 'the age of nuclear physics'—characterized perhaps superficially by spectacular applications of nuclear phenomena—confirmed the rather optimistic hopes of the majority of quantum physicists. More details and properties of atomic nuclei and of elementary particles—forming the innermost structure of matter—became revealed through the use of large devices (like particle accelerators) and refined theories. On the other hand, the last puzzles that had been left unanswered in solid-state and low-temperature physics were essentially solved, and the applicability of quantum mechanics to a variety of condensed matter phenomena became evident. Indeed, with the discovery of the transistor in 1947, a microphysical revolution began in industry and daily life, connected with miniaturization and computerization, which has continued ever since. The recognition of new and more refined quantum effects also renewed the debate on the interpretation of quantum mechanics. In the Epilogue, which completes Part 2, we seek to sketch some of the main features of these exciting developments of quantum theory.

# Chapter I
## **The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory**

### Introduction

On 3 August 1914, a couple of days after World War I broke out, Max Planck, then rector of the University of Berlin, delivered the traditional speech on the foundation of this institution and its chief patron Friedrich Wilhelm III. He gave it the title ‘Dynamical and Statistical Laws,’ explaining in it in some detail to his audience—including professors, students, and state officials—two major and essentially different ways of formulating physical laws. Following a long introduction, he emphasized:

> Physics, too, like the social sciences already since a long time, has learned to appreciate the great value of a form of description which differs totally from the causal one, and has applied it since about the middle of the last century with steadily increasing success: this is the statistical method, with the development of which is connected most intimately the entire more recent progress of theoretical physics. (Planck, 1914c, reprint, p. 79)¹

Planck himself, perhaps more than any other contemporary theoretical physicist, had contributed to that ‘entire more recent progress of theoretical physics,’ and he now presented several characteristic examples to his auditors. In particular, he reported on the role of statistical laws in the theory of macroscopic phenomena, which thus became plagued by a sharp dualism in the description of physical facts. Planck then summarized:

> According to the foregoing presentation, the dualism between statistical and dynamical [physical] laws seems to be most closely connected with the microscopic and macroscopic worlds, which we have to accept as an experimentally established fact. Now facts cannot be denied by any theory, whether one finds the situation unsatisfactory or not; hence we cannot but concede to the statistical laws the position which they deserve in the whole system of theoretical physics. (Planck, loc. cit., p. 87)

This concession notwithstanding, Planck did not hide his opinion on what must be the final goal of theoretical physics, and he continued:

---
¹ A translation of this article has been given in Heilbron (1989), but we shall use our translation for the excerpts.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0036 -->

4 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

However, dynamics and statistics should be regarded by no means as something assuming the same level of description. The reason is that a dynamical law satisfies the causal requirement completely, and therefore possesses a simple character; every statistical law, on the other hand, represents a complex situation, which should not remain unresolved, for it always carries along with it the problem of reducing the situation to its simple dynamical elements. The solution of such problems constitutes one of the main tasks of the developing sciences: chemistry is engaged in working them out, as are the physical theories of matter and electricity. Also meteorology may be mentioned in this context, because we recognize in the efforts of V. Bjerknes an impressively conceived plan to reduce all statistical features of meteorology to their simple elements, i.e., the [dynamical] physical laws. Whether this attempt succeeds or not, it must be undertaken in view of the very nature of statistical description; though one often assigns to it the first word, it should never be the last one. (Planck, *loc. cit.*)

**Planck's opinion concerning the primacy of dynamical laws over statistical ones was, however, not shared by all contemporary scientists, as he admitted:**

One has tried to remove this [dualism], if one cannot do better, by denying the existence of any absolute certainty or impossibility altogether and admitting only greater or smaller degrees of probability. According to this view, no dynamical laws would rule in nature but only statistical ones, and thus the concept of absolute necessity would completely disappear from physics. Such a conception, however, should soon turn out to be an erroneous one, as shortsighted as fatal, even if we had completely ignored the fact that all reversible processes without exception obey dynamical laws and there exists no reason to abandon these laws. Just as other [exact] sciences and humanities cannot do without presupposing absolute laws, so also physics cannot. Indeed, even the consequences of statistical description, which have been mentioned earlier, would lack the basic foundation without them [i.e., without the existence of absolute dynamical laws]. (Planck, *loc. cit.*, p. 86)

One may somewhat superficially argue—and historians of science and physicists who came later have done so—that Planck already by 1914 belonged to the conservative generation that emerged from the earlier, nineteenth-century period of classical and causal physics; and one may further emphasize that Erwin Schrödinger, Planck's successor in the chair of theoretical physics at the University of Berlin, and younger by about thirty years, thought differently. As proof, one cites the latter's inaugural lecture, given on 9 December 1922, at the University of Zurich under the title '*Was ist ein Naturgesetz?*' ('What is a Law of Nature?') and published many years later (Schrödinger, 1929a). Like Planck in 1914, Schrödinger discussed several examples of physical theory—from the kinetic theory of matter to the theory of gravitation—but, in contrast to Planck, he argued in 1922 against the necessity of adhering to a strictly causal description of nature.
Actually, Schrödinger referred to older considerations, which his Viennese teacher Franz Exner had expressed repeatedly (e.g., Exner, 1919), and he concluded:

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0037 -->

# Introduction

5

The assertion put forward by Exner states the following: it is quite possible that natural laws *in toto* possess a statistical character. The existence of an absolute law of nature—which, as it is still generally postulated, provides the basis of the statistical law—*cannot be derived from experience*. Such a two-fold formulation [i.e., a statistical and a causal one] of the laws of nature is *per se* improbable. The burden of proof rests on the defenders, not on the sceptics, of an *absolute causality*. To doubt the latter appears to be by far the more natural position. (Schrödinger, 1929a, p. 11)

Schrödinger’s anticausal credo of 1922 thus contradicted Planck’s, and when he submitted his lecture for publication many years later—without any changes—he added the remark: ‘The later creation and development of quantum mechanics has put these [i.e., Exner’s] ideas in the focus of interest’ (Schrödinger, *loc. cit.*, p. 9). The development of quantum mechanics in the 1920s and the fact that ideas similar to Exner’s recurred in many public addresses of physicists, notably, in Germany, led the American science historian Paul Forman to suggest a close relation between these doubts about the causal laws of science, on the one hand, and the spiritual–sociological background of the early Weimar Republic, on the other. In his extended essay, Forman concluded:

> It seems difficult to deny that the shifts in scientific doctrine exposed in this paper were in *effect* adaptions to the Weimarian intellectual environment. Moreover, whatever similarities one may find in the mental postures of non-German exact scientists in the same period, there is one feature which cannot, I think, be found outside the German cultural sphere: a repudiation of “causality.” (Forman, 1971, p. 115)

Many arguments can be (and indeed have been) raised against the whole thesis or specific points of Forman’s article, which, on the other hand, has become something like a ‘cult’ paper among certain historians of science.$^2$ The line of arguments against it should begin with the reminder that Exner expressed his radical statistical ideas already in his rectorial address of 1909 in *Imperial* Vienna, and continue with the fact that the most influential partisan of acausal thinking, the Danish physicist Niels Bohr, cannot be considered as a representative of the German Weimer Republic at all. The detailed historical development of quantum theory, which has been presented in the previous volumes of this series, provides the most convincing arguments, *arising solely from the analysis of the physical phenomena* (without any interference from external influences). It was primarily this analysis of internal scientific reasons that fostered the discussion of statistical laws in this creative period, which resulted in the discovery and completion of the new atomic theory between 1923 and 1928, and we shall supply further convincing evidence for this fact in the present volume as well.

6 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

Still, we shall not completely ignore the role played by external—e.g., social and political—influences on scientific advance.<sup>3</sup> As a spokesman, let us again quote Schrödinger, who emphasized the influences of the ‘milieu’ on contemporary physics in a lecture delivered on 18 February 1932, before the Prussian Academy of Sciences.<sup>4</sup> Under the title ‘Is Science a Fashion of Time?’ and claiming the motto ‘Our civilization constitutes a whole,’ Schrödinger addressed the following topics:

1. What is called for in fine arts, especially in arts and crafts, but also elsewhere, is “pure practicality” (reine Sachlichkeit).
2. Desire for revolution. Preference for freedom and lawlessness.
3. Idea of relativity—theory of invariants.
4. Methodology of ruling masses [human masses and mass-production], partly by rational organization, partly by machine reproduction.
5. Statistics. (Schrödinger, 1932b, p. 43)

Among this wide spectrum of topics, which Schrödinger discussed in 1932, and where he emphasized the statistical aspects, he did not refer to the particular intellectual and cultural atmosphere of the Weimer Republic—in which he had now lived for nearly five years—as favouring this approach in science (or life in general). He rather drew attention to the applications of statistical methods in some areas of physics and astrophysics, to which scientists had become accustomed in the previous fifty years. Although in astrophysics, the methods in question served the purpose of deriving from the bulk of data, each connected with some uncertainty, strict causal rules—that is, the statistical element entered only via the human inability to take error-free data—Schrödinger argued that the recent applications in physics exhibited a different character: as in the humanities, say, in economics and sociology, the physical phenomena yielded only laws for averages, not for individual processes or the behaviour of individual objects. This observation led Schrödinger to conclude:

> May one perhaps also in those aspects see something in common with a characteristic of our epoch, which, though not yet achieved, is still desired? Because it appears to be the goal of a higher civilization to achieve the necessary order and legality in the social life (Zusammenleben) of human beings without any detailed interference in the conduct of the individual, but rather in the way of studying the average talents of

# Introduction

human beings and their statistical variation and then proposing suitable motives and presenting such goals to [achieve] human desires as to ensure, at least for a broad average, a bearable social life. (Schrödinger, *loc. cit.*, p. 62)

We conclude from Schrödinger’s talk that by 1932 he had forgotten the social and political turmoil of the revolutionary early postwar years in Germany.[^5] In physics especially, a new physical theory—quantum mechanics or wave mechanics—had been established in the years between 1925 and 1928, perhaps the most stable and optimistic period of the Weimar Republic. The new theory was indeed based crucially on statistical concepts, notably, on what one called ‘the statistical interpretation of quantum theory.’ The origin of this new interpretation and the first application to complete the proof of equivalence of the different mathematical schemes provided by the Göttingen–Cambridge quantum mechanics and Schrödinger’s wave mechanics, respectively, will be the main topic of this chapter.

In order to separate the particular statistical method employed in quantum mechanics from those used earlier in the classical theories or the old quantum theory, we shall give in Section I.1 a synopsis of the applications of statistical considerations in physics before 1925. The results achieved in the pre-quantum-mechanical period illustrate the power of a straightforward application of the probability concept, which had been formulated mathematically in the late seventeenth century for describing and computing accidental events in games of hazard, science, and other fields of human life and activity and, later in the nineteenth century, in the kinetic theory of matter. The kinetic theory dealt with the behaviour of a large number of particles, the atoms or molecules (supposed to constitute the smallest particles of matter), which could not be handled by even the most advanced dynamical methods. Since this particular theory—unlike the previous kinetic theories of matter (say of the Greeks or the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries)—employed statistical methods, it was eventually called ‘statistical mechanics’ (Gibbs, 1902); it served to explain on a microscopic, dynamical basis the characteristic observations described by macroscopic thermodynamics. At the turn of the twentieth century, new phenomena were detected that required an intrinsically statistical description. We refer, in this context, to the phenomena of blackbody radiation and atomic spectra, on the one hand, and to the properties of radioactive decay of certain chemical substances, on the other. The statistical methods employed for explaining the new empirical facts deviated somewhat from the conventional ones applied earlier in classical physics, because one had to take into account the apparent lack of individuality of atomic particles.

Before we can turn to the final statistical theory, which satisfied all requirements of the new, successful quantum-mechanical description, another method crucial for the problem of physical interpretation must be considered that has also
