8  Chapter I  The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

been employed already in classical dynamics: the theory of canonical transformations. As shown previously in many places, the adaptation of the theory of canonical transformations to the quantum-theoretical situation helped in establishing the necessary *correspondence*—in the sense of Niels Bohr’s principle—between the quantum and the classical description of atomic phenomena.$^6$ These efforts were continued even more systematically in the first half of the year 1926, when the wave-mechanical approach became available, because now the new task arose to relate the different quantum-mechanical schemes that seemed to provide equivalent descriptions of atomic phenomena.

Paul Dirac, who made the most effective use in quantum mechanics of the transformation-theoretical method, in his standard treatise on *The Principles of Quantum Mechanics*, stated:

> The growth of the use of transformation theory, as applied first to relativity and later to quantum theory, is the essence of the new method in theoretical physics. Further progress lies in the direction of making our equations invariant under wider and still wider transformations. This state of affairs is very satisfactory from a philosophical point of view, as implying an increasing recognition of the part played by the observer in himself introducing the regularities that appear in his observations, and a lack of arbitrariness in the ways of nature, but it makes things less easy for the learner in physics. The new theories, it looks apart from their mathematical setting, are built up from physical concepts which cannot be explained in terms of things previously known to the student, which cannot even be explained adequately in words at all. Like the fundamental concepts (e.g., proximity, identity) which everybody must learn on his arrival into the world, the newer concepts of physics can be mastered only by long familiarity with their properties and uses. (Dirac, 1930d, p. v)

However, for the active quantum physicist in 1926, the introduction of the methods of transformation theory assisted decisively in removing the strangeness of the new concepts involved in the quantum- and wave-mechanical schemes. Originally, that task appeared to be simpler in the case of the Göttingen–Cambridge formulations, which exhibited a direct correspondence-like connection with the previous (old) quantum theory of atomic structure, but the wave-mechanical approach abandoned this basis (and classical foundations) completely by renouncing such concepts as atomic particles or quantum jumps. Though Erwin Schrödinger and others (among them, especially, Wolfgang Pauli and Carl Eckart) succeeded in deriving mathematical equations relating quantum-mechanical matrices and wave-mechanical eigenfunctions, a deeper connection between the two conceptually so different schemes could be established only by a properly reformulated, general quantum-mechanical transformation theory. Before this systematic reformulation occurred later in 1926, however, two other developments occurred: first, the attempts of Wentzel, Kramers, and Brillouin to interpret aspects of the wave-mechanical theory physically by creating a specific approxxi-

mation method; second, the conceptually more fundamental statistical interpretation of the wave function by Born.

Léon Brillouin (born 1887), Hendrik Kramers (born 1894), and Gregor Wentzel (born 1897) all belonged to the generation of physicists who had grown up with the old quantum theory and its application to problems of atomic structure. Though actively participating in the endeavours to improve the standard Bohr–Sommerfeld model, they were surprised more or less by the rapid emergence of quantum and wave mechanics. Being well acquainted with the details of atomic phenomena and the previous problems of describing them, they now devoted their experience to contribute to the clarification of the questions opened by, or still remaining in, the new atomic theory. Wentzel began to ponder about the physical content of quantum mechanics in early 1926.$^7$ In a substantial paper submitted on 27 March 1926, he found a close—so to say, correspondence-like—relation between the matrix-mechanical perturbation theory (as developed by Born, Heisenberg, and Jordan) and the action-angle scheme of his former teacher Arnold Sommerfeld in Bohr’s quantum theory of atomic structure. Hence, the calculation methods of quantum mechanics, though they appeared entirely different from the corresponding classical methods, could nevertheless be closely connected: every classical operation, however tricky, had its counterpart in a slightly generalized matrix scheme. Independently of Wentzel, the junior Fritz London (born 1900) worked on a similar problem presenting his own matrix-mechanical action-angle scheme in spring 1926. In spite of some mysteries remaining in the interpretation of the formalism—especially, the frequencies of the multiply periodic atomic systems did not disappear, though they should according to the Born–Heisenberg–Jordan philosophy—these investigations convinced the experts about the consistency of quantum mechanics, mainly because of the correspondence to the ‘well-understood’ Bohr–Sommerfeld theory. No such correspondence seemed to exist in the case of wave mechanics; hence, the necessity arose in spring and summer 1926 to find such a relation. Wentzel first devised a method to approximate the solution of a Schrödinger eigenvalue equation by employing a series *Ansatz* in powers of the parameter $(h/2\pi i)$. Independently, Brillouin in Paris suggested the same approximation, which yielded (e.g., in the case of the Stark effect) an adequate connection for high quantum numbers to the ‘classical solutions’ (in the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory). A little later, Kramers in Utrecht examined the Wentzel–Brillouin method carefully and proposed several improvements. These efforts, which prepared the way for the interpretation of quantum and wave mechanics, will be discussed in Section I.2.

Section I.3 is devoted to the next, truly revolutionary step in the problem of interpretation. In June 1926, Max Born introduced a new probability concept, deviating totally from the one used previously: he identified the wave amplitude in the wave-mechanical description of atomic scattering and other processes with a

What he originally needed as a more or less technical device, in order to deal with the scattering problem, proved to be the crucial step in interpreting Schrödinger’s undulatory scheme and connecting this interpretation with the results derived from the alternative scheme of quantum mechanics. Although the full understanding—we now call it, with the pioneers, the ‘physical interpretation’—of both formulations of modern atomic theory, based on Born’s probability interpretation of the wave function, would only be reached by the further important steps taken by Werner Heisenberg and Niels Bohr in the following year, 1926 still brought major progress toward the final goal: Paul Dirac and Pascual Jordan, working independently of each other, completed in December the mathematical proof of the equivalence of quantum and wave mechanics, by using quite different (but equivalent) approaches.

Born’s concept of the probability amplitude entered crucially into the efforts of Pascual Jordan, his former student and assistant, when he built a quantum-mechanical transformation theory on a strict mathematically axiomatic basis, which then allowed the formulation of all atomic problems properly. Jordan started, so to say, from statistically generalized Schrödinger’s eigenfunctions and then showed how these could be specialized to serve as characteristic elements in Schrödinger’s wave mechanics, Dirac’s q-number theory, the Born–Heisenberg–Jordan quantum mechanics, or the Born-Wiener operator mechanics, respectively. A general transformation property implying the quantum-mechanical commutation relations made it possible to migrate among the different formulations. Jordan’s transformation theory is treated in Section I.4.

Dirac attacked the problem quite differently, showing far less interest in the usual mathematical formalism and technicalities. He also concerned himself with generalizing the wave function within a transformation-theoretical scheme that was wide enough to embrace all physical applications, but he preferred to choose his own language. By employing his ‘delta-function,’ which soon became well known, he was able to move easily between matrix and wave formulations. Dirac’s results turned out to be practically equivalent to Jordan’s; in contrast to Jordan, however, Dirac again displayed great simplicity and elegance, which had become the characteristic hallmarks of his ingenuity. In Section I.5, we treat Dirac’s transformation theory.

I.1 **Probability in Classical and Quantum Physics until 1925**$^8$

The probability calculus originated as a theory of games of hazard. Very soon it was applied, often without sufficient foundation, to investigate mass phenomena, say in insurance business, starting with the estimate of life expectancy and the evaluation of

$^8$ Extensive literature on this theme exists, from which we cite just a few publications that have appeared more recently (since our discussion of some of the major aspects of this theme in the earlier volumes of this series): Theodore M. Porter (1986), Lorenz Krüger *et al.*, eds. (1987), and Olivier Darrigol (1988).

I.1 Probability in Classical and Quantum Physics until 1925

11

death registers. During its classical period—i.e., in the eighteenth and nineteenth century—and until its “heroic period” 1925–1940, one studied in probability calculus the economic and social risks of all sorts; one suggested statistical predictions; one established the law of error in astronomical and other observations; and one finally discussed juridical problems, such as the composition and decisions of court juries, etc. Further, the calculus was applied in metaphysical questions, such as for deciding the existence of God (see Pascal’s bet), but also to phenomena in which accident does not play any role, e.g., the daily sunrise (Laplace). (Loève, 1985, p. 709)

This short account from a modern essay on the historical development of probability calculus indicates especially the various applications of a relatively young mathematical theory. It stresses, moreover, its special origin, not as a problem arising from other mathematical disciplines or as a problem posed by physics or other technical disciplines, but rather from efforts to describe situations in economics and sociology, if not politics.$^9$

During the eighteenth and nineteenth century, the foundations of the classical probability calculus were established in books, including the early treatises of Jacob Bernoulli (1654–1705) and Abraham de Moivre (1667–1754)—*Ars Conjectandi* (1715) and *Doctrine of Chances* (1718, 1740, 1756), respectively—and the later works of Pierre Simon de Laplace (1749–1827) and Pafnutij Lvovič Čebyšev (1821–1894). This classical theory also contained the ‘method of least squares’—i.e., the theory of errors of observation proposed by Adrien-Marie Legendre (1752–1833) and Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777–1855)—which we may consider, besides the theory of the games of chance, as the second important external motivation for developing the probability calculus.$^{10}$ The phenomenon of Brownian motion, named after Robert Brown, the Scottish botanist who discovered it in 1827, would finally provide a third physical motivation to develop the probability calculus, although its appropriate description arose only in the early twentieth century.

In the same period, i.e., from the middle of the seventeenth to the end of the nineteenth century, just as the mathematical theory of probability, also the disciplines of classical physics were established: namely, mechanics (from Isaac Newton’s formulation up to the final form given to it by William Rowan Hamil-

$^9$ Although the Renaissance mathematician Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), and later the great Galileo Galilei (1564–1642), had discussed some concepts and rules of probability calculus, its official history as a systematic discipline began in the middle of the seventeenth century, when the “problem of partition” was mentioned by the French Chevalier de la Méré to Blaise Pascal (1632–1662) and Giles Personne de Roberval (1602–1675). This problem is the following: in general, the participant who gathers the most points in a tournament of games of hazard wins the prize; however, how should the prize be distributed among the participants when the tournament is not finished yet? Pascal obtained the solution to this problem and corresponded about it with Pierre de Fermat (1601–1665) in 1654; their exchange of correspondence (published in 1679) and the later results of Pascal (also published posthumously, in 1675), together with the work of Christiaan Huygens (1629–1695)—*De ratiociniis in ludo aleae* (published in 1675)—constituted the first publications in the new field.

Although Legendre published the results first (in his book on the orbits of comets, 1806), Gauss is known to have invented and used the method already fifteen years before presenting it in his famous *Theoria motus* of 1809.

12  Chapter I  The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

ton and Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi), thermodynamics, and the combined theory of electricity and magnetism (including optics, up to its final shape in the scheme of James Clerk Maxwell and, even later, its relativistic extension). In all of these theories probability considerations played only a very subordinate role, which should not be too surprising, as the age of enlightenment—the central period (in the eighteenth century) that provided the philosophical and conceptual foundations of science—emphasized that most, if not all, natural phenomena are dominated by the causal principle (or the ‘principle of sufficient cause’ or ‘sufficient reason’). At the end of this formative period, the great philosopher Immanuel Kant (1724–1804) even forbade the use of ‘the game of probability’ (‘Spielwerk von Wahrscheinlichkeit’) in his critical philosophy, because:

> Nothing more illogical can be found than to establish in a metaphysics, a philosophy of pure reason, one’s judgments on probability and guesswork. ... One could, with the same right, found a geometry or arithmetic on guesswork. ... Only in empirical (descriptive) science may guesswork be admitted; however, in such a way that at least the possibility of what is assumed has to be completely certain. (Kant, 1783, p. 196)

Similarly, Laplace, in his philosophical essay on probability, insisted that all physical phenomena must be ruled by the strictest determinism, defined in the following way:

> The present events are connected with those of the past by the evident principle that nothing can come into existence without a generating cause. This axiom, known under the name of “principle of sufficient cause,” also extends to the actions which one considers to be irrelevant. ... We must therefore assume the present state of the universe to be the effect of the previous one, and also to be the cause of the following state. An intelligence that knows, at a given instant, all the forces acting in nature, as well as the relative positions of the elements composing them, and being comprehensive enough to subject to analysis [all] the given quantities, would incorporate the motions of the largest bodies of the universe, as well as those of the lightest atoms, in a single formula; nothing would be hidden to this intelligence, past and future would lie open before its eyes. (Laplace, 1825, German translation, pp. 1–2)

The human mind, Laplace continued, constitutes—regarding the perfection it has given to (Newtonian) astronomy—only a feeble image of this super intelligence (later termed ‘the Laplace demon’). Still, it tends to that perfection without ever reaching the goal, thus raising man above the level of an animal and letting him acquire ‘immortal fame in progressing along this path.’

In spite of his belief in an ultimate, perfectly causal description of nature, Laplace admitted the mathematical discipline of probability calculus to be useful in two aspects:

(1) It provides the possibility of eliminating unknown influences on observation (thus, for example, the scientist can approach the true result by averaging over repeated observations, etc.).

(2) It yields some results even in situations, in which the scientist does not know all necessary conditions to arrive at a perfectly deterministic solution of the problem.

Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution to be the only stable one, involved assumptions contradicting mechanical laws. That is, by no allowed means could Boltzmann derive the thermodynamical behaviour of gas molecules, including the fulfillment of the second heat theorem (increase of entropy), just on the basis of reversible particle dynamics. Only when Boltzmann required the gas molecules to obey certain rules of probability calculus, did he arrive at the desired goal that he had described in the introduction to his fundamental paper of 1877:

> that one can calculate the state of heat equilibrium by searching for the probability of the different possible states of the system. The initial state will be in most cases a very improbable one; starting from it, the system will rush to increasingly more probable states, until it finally has reached the most probable one, i.e., the one denoting the equilibrium of heat. (Boltzmann, 1877b, p. 374)

And, in order to proceed successfully, he had to ‘identify that quantity, which one is normally used to call entropy, with the probability of the state under consideration’ (Boltzmann, *loc. cit.*). From here, the real (often tragic) story of relating thermodynamics started, especially in the form of then developing ‘statistical mechanics’, to the old (classical) dynamics a story, in which after 1900 quantum dynamics—which replaced, to some extent, Newton’s scheme in atomic systems—also became involved.$^{12}$

Shortly before Boltzmann expounded the definition of probability, his Viennese friend and colleague Joseph Loschmid had argued in 1876 that the second heat theorem (the second law of thermodynamics) should not be considered to follow from mechanical laws, because the collisions between molecules were reversible. This objection, called the ‘reversibility argument’ (‘*Umkehreinwand*’), came up again in the discussions of Boltzmann’s ‘*H*-theorem’ (claiming that the entropy, $-H$, of the kinetic system can only increase) that occurred in England after 1890 (between Edward Culverwell, George Hartley Bryan, and Samuel Hawksley Burbury). Boltzmann, who joined this discussion in 1894 (at the Oxford meeting of the *British Association for the Advancement of Science*), however, stressed a little later (in February 1895): ‘It can only be deduced from the laws of probability, that if the initial state is not specially arranged for a certain purpose, but haphazard governs freely, the probability that $H$ decreases is always greater than that it increases.’ (Boltzmann, 1895b, p. 414). Similarly, he replied to another objection, the ‘recurrence argument’ (‘*Wiederkehreinwand*’), raised first by the French mathematician Henri Poincaré (1854–1912) and repeated in 1896 by Planck’s Berlin student Ernst Zermelo (1871–1953): it stated that ‘a bounded world, governed only by the laws of mechanics, will always pass through a state very close to its initial state.’ Boltzmann similarly countered this argument by saying:

$^{12}$ We have discussed these items in some detail in Volumes 1 and 5; here, we shall only summarize, at the end of this section, several important results.

**I.1 Probability in Classical and Quantum Physics until 1925**  
**15**

Poincaré’s [recurrence] theorem does not contradict but rather confirms the calculus of probability, since the latter teaches us equally well that there are, within aeons (long periods) also comparatively short time intervals, during which the probability of a state, say, the entropy of a gas mixture, again decreases considerably. Hence, there recur more ordered states, once in a while even those which closely approach the initial state. (Boltzmann, 1897b, p. 395)

That is, although the initial state of a system having smaller entropy can recur in principle, the probability for that is very small.

The statistical kinetic theory of Maxwell and Boltzmann soon received its, so to say, canonical form in the treatise of Josiah Willard Gibbs (1893–1903) on ‘statistical mechanics’ (Gibbs, 1902). Gibbs’s main contribution—besides giving a clear, mathematically elegant presentation of the dynamics of systems containing arbitrarily many objects—consisted in developing the theory of ensembles (the ‘microcanonical,’ ‘canonical,’ and ‘grand canonical’ ensembles) and defining the ‘coefficient of probability’ $P$, which denoted the ‘probability that in an unspecified system of the ensemble will lie within given limits of a canonical ensemble,’ as (see Gibbs, *loc. cit.*, p. 88)

$$P = \exp\left\{\frac{\psi - \varepsilon}{\vartheta}\right\}, \tag{1}$$

with $\varepsilon$ denoting the energy of the system, and $\psi$ and $\vartheta$, constants of the whole ensemble (the latter being, up to a constant, identical with the absolute temperature $T$). At the end of his book, Gibbs provided a particular illustration of the entropy problem, the so-called mixing paradox: if one takes two chambers containing different gases or liquids, and opens the valve between them, the contents mix and the entropy increases; does this also happen when the molecules in both chambers are the same? Gibbs explained the paradoxical situation by introducing his ‘generic phases,’ but his procedures gave rise to serious discussions in the next two decades.

The statistical mechanics of Gibbs did not answer the question of how far its principles violated the principles of classical mechanics. Paul Ehrenfest (1880–1933), Boltzmann’s student, attempted to throw light on this question in his *Encyklopädie* article, written jointly with his wife Tatyana (P. and T. Ehrenfest, 1911). Thus, for example, they found that the so-called ‘*Stoßzahlansatz*’ of Clausius and Boltzmann—that is, the assumption that the number of collisions between two oppositely moving groups of molecules is equal to the number of molecules per unit volume of one group multiplied by the volume of the molecules of the second (transverse) group—which the Ehrenfests called the ‘hypothesis of molecular disorder,’ and from which one can derive the $H$-theorem, contradicts both the reversibility of the dynamical equations and Poincaré’s recurrence property. Further, the authors analyzed what they called ‘the dubious ergodic hypothesis’ used by Boltzmann (1868) to derive the second heat theorem: it seemed that no mechanical system could satisfy this hypothesis, but perhaps certain systems satisfied

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0048 -->

16 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

a weaker ‘quasi-ergodic hypothesis,’ which might do the same job. In addition, the Ehrenfests criticized Gibbs’s derivation of the second law of thermodynamics, because the latter had failed to distinguish between what they called ‘fine-grained’ and ‘coarse-grained’ density in phase space.

In an appendix to their article, the Ehrenfests pointed out that a description involving the ‘hypothesis of probability’ (i.e., a genuinely statistical hypothesis) cannot be distinguished experimentally from other (deterministic) descriptions unless arbitrarily large deviations from the thermodynamical equilibrium, i.e., large fluctuations, are admitted to occur. These large observable fluctuations assumed an important role in the discussion of several similar phenomena discovered during the early years of the twentieth century, although the founding fathers of statistical mechanics had claimed them to be unobservable. Thus, Gibbs had written:

> It follows that human experience and observation with respect to such an ensemble as we are considering, when the number of degrees of freedom is of such order of magnitude as the number of molecules in the bodies subject to our observation and experiment, [the deviations] would be in general vanishing quantities, since such experiences would not be wide enough to embrace the more considerable divergencies from the mean values, and such observations not be nice enough to distinguish the ordinary divergencies. (Gibbs, 1902, p. 74)

But how large would the deviation from equilibrium actually turn out to be?

It was through his derivation of the blackbody radiation law that Planck established for the first time in December 1900 the value of the constant $k$ entering Boltzmann’s (1877b) relation between the thermodynamical entropy $S$ and the probability $P$ of microscopic states, i.e.,

$$S = k \log P. \tag{2}$$

From the data on blackbody radiation, he then obtained

$$k = 1.346 \times 10^{-16} \text{ (c.g.s. units)}. \tag{3}$$

This constant $k$ (later named after Boltzmann) not only yielded the number of atoms in a gram-molecule of the substance, but it also determined the size of fluctuations, as Albert Einstein showed a few years later (Einstein, 1904). In particular, he derived for the energy fluctuation $\varepsilon^2$ ($= \overline{E^2} - \overline{E} \cdot \overline{E}$, with $\overline{E}$ and $\overline{E^2}$ denoting the averages of the energy $E$ and its square $E^2$ of the system under investigation), the relation

$$\overline{\varepsilon^2} = kT^2 \frac{d\overline{E}}{dT}, \tag{4}$$

where $T$ is the absolute temperature. In the following year, Einstein explained with

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0049 -->

I.1 Probability in Classical and Quantum Physics until 1925

17

the help of kinetic fluctuations the well-known (since 1828) phenomenon of Brownian motion (Einstein, 1905c; see also Smoluchowski, 1906).

Between 1905 and 1910, besides the Brownian motion, a large number of fluctuation phenomena were discovered in kinetic systems, in particular: (1) fluctuations in radioactive decay (Schweidler, 1905); (2) fluctuations of the electric potential of condensers (Einstein, 1907e); (3) critical opalescence (Smoluchowski, 1908; Einstein, 1910a); (4) $\gamma$-ray fluctuations (Schweidler, 1910a, b). Their experimental evaluation allowed a fundamental determination of Avogadro’s number $N$ (the number of molecules in a gram-molecule, e.g., from Einstein’s fluctuation formula for the displacement of Brownian particles: see Perrin, 1914), which even convinced the physicochemist Wilhelm Ostwald (1853–1932), the old opponent of Boltzmann’s views, of the validity of the atomic hypothesis in nature. As Marian von Smoluchowski, besides Einstein (and Schweidler), the most eminent researcher in the field, could state in September 1912 at the Münster *Naturforscherversammlung*:

> These “automatic deviations from the state of ideal thermodynamic equilibrium” are not the offspring of fantasy of speculating theoreticians; we are rather dealing with real physical phenomena which assume a fundamental significance in microphysics, but also passing over, in many cases, into the domain of conventional macrophysical phenomena. (Smoluchowski, 1912, p. 1078)

When asked whether one might use the density fluctuation and other fluctuation phenomena for the purpose of violating the second law of thermodynamics (or constructing the *perpetuum mobile of the second kind*, as the German physicists used to call it), he replied that ‘at present it was excluded not only by purely technical difficulties, but by conditions of principle’ (Smoluchowski, *loc. cit.*, p. 1079).

How, then, does irreversibility arise in a statistical mechanical system? Again, Smoluchowski answered this question in a programmatic talk, presented in spring 1913 at the *Gaswoche*, organized by David Hilbert in Göttingen:

> As we realize, there exists, from the point of view of molecular statistics, no difference at all in principle between thermodynamical equilibrium and non-equilibrium states, or reversible and irreversible processes, respectively. All “microscopic states,” which are at all possible, possess given probabilities and the corresponding entropy values, as compared to the balanced normal state [of equilibrium or highest probability]. . . . In short, all molecular processes are reversible in principle. (Smoluchowski, 1914a, pp. 103–104)

Irreversibility, Smoluchowski continued, ‘is only a subjective concept of the observer, the applicability of which does not depend on the nature of the physical process but just on the position of the point of departure [of the system under investigation] and the period of observation.’ Rather:

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0050 -->

18 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

such processes appear to us as being irreversible, whose initial point lies far outside the average domain of fluctuations, and which can only be observed during periods of time that are short compared to the time of recurrence. (Smoluchowski, *loc. cit.*, pp. 112–113)

As a particular example, Smoluchowski treated the case of emulsions, and derived an expression for the recurrence time $\theta$ of a state $n$, notably,

$$\theta = \frac{\tau}{W(n)} \cdot \frac{1 - W(n)}{1 - W_n(0)}, \tag{5}$$

where $W(n)$ denotes the probability of the state $n$ and $W_n(0)$ the probability that this state occurs again in a period of time $\tau$ (Smoluchowski, 1915b). Evidently, Eq. (5) completes the consideration of the ‘irreversibility paradox’ in statistical mechanics.$^{13}$

Before his death in September 1917, Smoluchowski submitted an article ‘On the Concept and Origin of Probability Laws in Physics’ for the issue of *Naturwissenschaften* dedicated in honour of Max Planck’s 60th birthday (in April 1918). After analyzing the previous uses of probability calculus, he concluded: ‘Evidently, as far as the application in theoretical physics is concerned, *all those theories of probability*, which treat chance as an “unknown partial cause,” must be considered as *insufficient* from the very outset. *The physical probability of an event can only depend on the conditions which influence its occurrence, however, not on the degree of our knowledge.*’ (Smoluchowski, 1918, p. 254). We should add that Smoluchowski believed this conclusion to also hold in the case of radioactive decay. Indeed, he suggested for the latter phenomenon a mechanical model, consisting of spheres in a box, whose probability of leaving it is properly adjusted to the statistical radioactive decay constant; this model, he said, provided a ‘regulated chance.’ Hence, he claimed, no real conflict existed between statistical and deterministic (‘dynamical,’ as Planck would say) laws, as ‘chance—in the physical meaning of the word—can originate quite well from exactly defined, lawful causes’ (Smoluchowski, *loc. cit.*, p. 263: ‘*der Zufall in dem in der Physik gebräuchlichen Sinne—sehr wohl durch exakt definierte gesetzmäßige Ursachen definiert werden kann.*’).

So far, all of the considerations mentioned above remained in the field of classical mechanics, though some of the phenomena referred to belong, at least from today’s point of view, to the domain of quantum physics, notably, the blackbody radiation law of Planck, the statistical radioactive-decay law of von Schweidler, and the latter’s study of $\gamma$-ray fluctuations. Now, Planck’s derivation of the radiation law involved statistical assumptions at two places. The first seems to be only little known and occurred early, even in the prequantum-theoretical period: when, in 1898, Planck tried to prove the irreversibility of his model system, in which a

resonator placed in the centre of a spherically shaped, totally reflecting cavity absorbs and emits radiation, he found it necessary to introduce an additional hypothesis, namely, the concept of ‘natural radiation’ (*natürliche Strahlung*); this assumption also entered into the later quantum-theoretical derivation of the blackbody radiation law; hence, one must argue that, as in classical statistical mechanics, also in quantum-statistical mechanics, irreversibility does not arise without any additional assumption beyond (quantum) dynamical laws.

The second statistical hypothesis concerns Planck’s peculiar definition of the probability of the microscopic state in cavity radiation, and this definition deviates markedly from the classical one. Indeed, what the creator of quantum theory wrote already in his first paper (Planck, 1900f), and defended vigorously in all following presentations, did not at all satisfy—as the later analyses of Einstein, Hendrik Antoon Lorentz, Paul Ehrenfest, and others showed explicitly—the concepts of classical statistical mechanics.$^{14}$ Thus, Einstein proved that the classical wave theory leads to the so-called Rayleigh–Jeans law, and a classical light-quantum hypothesis yields Wilhelm Wien’s radiation law (Einstein, 1905b).

The core of this criticism may be seen in the following Planck procedure: in his expression for the probability of the states in the cavity, he used the division by the factor $N!$, with $N$ giving the number of the radiation (energy) quanta, arguing that identical (microscopic) objects—he later extended the idea to the case of gas molecules (Planck, 1916b)—cannot be distinguished. In early 1920, Ehrenfest and his collaborator Viktor Trkal called this division ‘obscure,’ claiming—in contrast to Planck’s opinion—that the thermodynamical entropy in physics could be determined only up to an additive constant anyway (Ehrenfest and Trkal, 1920). While, for instance, Erwin Schrödinger supported the claim of Ehrenfest and Trkal (Schrödinger, 1924a, and later), the Indian physicist Satyendra Nath Bose (1894–1974) showed that one obtained Planck’s original statistical expression by a counting method different from the classical method for particles: he thus introduced a new (‘Bose’) statistics for light-quanta, in which he not only assumed identical light-quanta (i.e., those of identical frequency) to be indistinguishable (as Planck had done), but also to have the peculiar property that they could occupy the cells of the quantum-theoretical phase space in arbitrary numbers (Bose, 1924a). Einstein then generalized Bose’s statistics to also hold in the case of material atoms of ideal gases (Einstein, 1924d). In a second communication on the same topic (Einstein, 1925a), he demonstrated especially how the new statistics seemed to be compatible with (or even follow from) the matter waves of Louis de Broglie (1895–1987), and that the latter concept resolved the classical mixing paradox of Gibbs (the matter waves of identical particles can interfere approximately to destroy mixing entropy). Indeed, already the lack of individuality of identical microscopic particles and light-quanta contradicted the initial assumptions that Laplace had proposed over a hundred years previously, when he approached the

20 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

problem of applying probability calculus to (mechanical) many-particle systems. Moreover, obviously, quantum mechanics even demanded further characteristic changes in the application of the statistical method.

Shortly before the advent of quantum mechanics, Niels Bohr, Hendrik Kramers, and John Slater proposed a completely new probabilistic method: they claimed that, in processes occurring between radiation and individual atomic particles (atoms, electrons, etc.), energy and momentum could be conserved only statistically, i.e., on the average (Bohr *et al.*, 1924). Their radical statistical theory, although gaining the support of some physicists (e.g., Schrödinger), was rejected finally in April 1925 as a result of the experiment of Walther Bothe and Hans Geiger (Bothe and Geiger, 1925a, b). Hence, the revolutionary statistical approach, different from all previous descriptions of nature (including those that Exner had had in mind earlier), died a year after its invention. Still, another probability concept, also radically different from the classical one, would emerge in quantum mechanics; and this new statistical theory would then solve, among other problems, the puzzle that gave rise to the unsuccessful Bohr–Kramers–Slater radiation theory of 1924.

## I.2 Early Quantum-Mechanical Transformation Theory and the Wentzel–Kramers–Brillouin Method

The first quantum-mechanical theory, proposed by Heisenberg, Born, and Jordan, possessed a close formal similarity to classical mechanics, i.e., to each quantity of the classical theory corresponded one in quantum mechanics, such that the physical relations (say, the equations of motion in the Newtonian or Hamiltonian scheme, the equations of perturbation theory, etc.) remained untouched. Hence, although the essential facts and aspects of interpretation in both theories were quite different—e.g., no electron orbits in atoms or, more generally, no space-time interpretation in microphysics seemed to exist anymore—one could still claim that quantum mechanics somehow described the behaviour of mass points. Undulatory or wave mechanics, the alternative form of quantum mechanics, as developed by Schrödinger, seemed to lack exactly this feature. In an early review of the ‘foundations of wave mechanics,’ Ludwig Flamm emphasized:

> The engaging feature of undulatory mechanics consists in the fact that it appears to be a natural development of the great physical traditions. Roughly half a century has passed since, by the establishment of Maxwell’s theory, electrodynamics and optics became united in one scheme. Now wave mechanics seems to put dynamics also on the same level as optics. Should this not lead eventually to a harmonious confluence of mechanics, optics and electricity into an all-embracing [field] theory? (Flamm, 1926a, p. 616)

Such a process, Flamm argued further, would improve the present state of (classical) electrodynamics, which had not yet—due to the fundamental role of the

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0053 -->

I.2 Early Quantum-Mechanical Transformation Theory 21

pointlike electron in it—really replaced the old physics of matter by a physics of fields. Now, however, ‘the phase waves seem to be called to pave the path towards a genuine field theory of matter.’ ‘From this point of view,’ Flamm concluded, ‘one might be inclined to recognize in wave mechanics already features of a future, more complete, state of development in physics’ (Flamm, *loc. cit.*).

Flamm’s enthusiastic plea for a purely wave interpretation of atomic phenomena—he also claimed (in the spirit of Schrödinger’s earlier prehydrogen work, Schrödinger, 1926b) that the ideal (Einstein) gas consisted of de Broglie waves in a closed volume—did not, however, impress the leading experts in the new atomic theory. In order to extract the

Jacobi procedure in classical mechanics. For that purpose, he identified the initially generalized transformation matrix **S** with the quantum-theoretical reinterpretation of the classical ‘action function’ $S$, and he took over from classical dynamics the differential equation defining $S$ (for systems of periodic degrees of freedom), namely,

$$dS = \sum_{k=1}^f p_k dq_k + \sum_{k=1}^f w_k dJ_k, \tag{7}$$

which he rewrote in quantum mechanics as the set of equations (we now drop with Wentzel the explicit matrix notation):

$$SJ_k - J_kS = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{\ell=1}^f [p_\ell(q_\ell J_k - J_k q_\ell) + (q_\ell J_k - J_k q_\ell)p_\ell]$$

and

$$Sq_k - q_kS = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{\ell=1}^f [w_\ell(J_\ell q_k - q_k J_\ell) + (J_\ell q_k - q_k J_\ell)w_\ell]. \tag{8}$$

Here, as in the classical case, the pair $p_k$, $q_k$ represents any set of canonical variables of the system, and the pair $J_k$, $w_k$ denotes the corresponding pair of action-angle variables. We have shown earlier (see Volume 3, Section IV.4) how Wentzel used Eqs. (8) effectively to write a general quantum-mechanical theory of multiply periodic systems, and succeeded in adapting the elegant classical method of solution, the ‘complex phase-integral’ of Arnold Sommerfeld (1916d), for the purpose of the new atomic theory.

Independently of Dirac, Pauli, Heisenberg, and Wentzel, Fritz London in Stuttgart thought about extending the Göttingen quantum mechanics to include a treatment of the general systems described in ‘classical’ (old) quantum theory by action-angle variables. In his note, entitled ‘Über die Jacobischen Transformationen der Quantenmechanik’ (‘On the Jacobian Transformations of Quantum Mechanics’) and signed on 19 May 1926, he attempted to resolve the dualism between the old and the new quantum theory, namely, the use of different pairs of canonical variables, i.e., the action-angle variables in the former and the libration coordinates in the latter scheme (London, 1926b). For that purpose, he introduced the matrix function **E**(**q**) of the position variable **q**,

$$\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{q}) = \sum_{s=0}^\infty \frac{\mathbf{q}^s}{s!}, \tag{9}$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0055 -->

23 I.2 Early Quantum-Mechanical Transformation Theory

which satisfies the ‘differential equation’

$$\frac{h}{i} \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial \mathbf{q}} = \mathbf{pE}(\mathbf{q}) - \mathbf{E}(\mathbf{q})\mathbf{p} \equiv h\mathbf{E}(i\mathbf{q}). \tag{10}$$

This equation also remained valid for the momentum **p** being a constant of time, i.e., being an action-angle variable **J**($= J_{kk}$), or formally,

$$h E_{k\ell}(iw) = (J_{kk} - J_{\ell\ell})E_{k\ell}(iw). \tag{11}$$

London then proved by complete induction the relation

$$\mathbf{F(p)E(niq) - E(niq)F(p)} = \mathbf{E(niq)[F(p + nh) - F(p)]}$$
$$\mathbf{\quad = [F(p) - F(p - nh)]E(niq).} \tag{12}$$

He now interpreted Eq. (12) as a *canonical transformation*, using the fact that **E**($ni\mathbf{q}$) represented the $n$-th power of the matrix function **E**($i\mathbf{q}$). When applied to the action variable **w**, it yielded the result

$$\mathbf{E^n(iw)F(J)E^n(iw)} = \mathbf{F(J + nh)}, \tag{13}$$

i.e., a transformation or a displacement of the elements of the diagonal matrix **F**(**J**)—**F** being a function of the (diagonal) quantum variable **J**—by $n$ units in the positive direction of the main diagonal. London further defined a matrix integration (inverse to the differentiation procedure) in the following way:

$$\frac{i}{h} \int \mathbf{F(p)} dp = \mathbf{Fq^{-1}} + \mathbf{qFq^{-2}} + \mathbf{q^{-2}Fq^{-3}} + \mathbf{q^{-3}Fq^{-4}} + \cdots. \tag{14}$$

Based upon the formulae (9)–(14), London developed his action-angle scheme. He concluded, in particular, that the equation of motion for the angular variable **w** led to the classical frequencies, not to Bohr’s frequencies of quantum jumps. On the other hand, he noticed that the equation

$$\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{E(inw)} = \mathbf{E(inw)} \frac{i}{h} \int_{\mathbf{J}}^{\mathbf{J}+nh} \nu_{k\ell}(\mathbf{J}) \, d\mathbf{J} \tag{15}$$

yielded the integral-averaging representation given in 1924 by Max Born (1924b) and Hendrik Kramers (1924b). He commented upon the results as follows:

> We therefore see that Heisenberg’s theory, which contains as frequencies only the “observable” frequencies of jumps, cannot be carried through in this narrow sense [of keeping only observable quantities in the theory]. The rotational frequencies are also

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0056 -->

24 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

contained as a consistent concept in his theory; in particular—and this I consider to be the essential fact—both quantities turn up as different modes of appearance of *one and the same thing* connected in a manner peculiar to the theoretical scheme, whose substantial content, however, still remains a complete mystery. (London, 1926b, p. 920)

Apart from this incomprehensible aspect, London encountered no other problem when writing the scheme analogous to the Jacobian transformation method in classical (Hamiltonian) mechanics, including the action function **S**($\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{P}$) and the corresponding partial differential equations for the variables $\left( \mathbf{P} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{S}}{\partial \mathbf{q}} \text{ and } \mathbf{Q} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{S}}{\partial \mathbf{P}} \right)$. Then, the Born–Jordan commutation relations for the pair of canonical quantum variables remained invariant (under the transformation of **p**, **q** into **P**, **Q**) if the position variable **q** and the transformed variable **Q** satisfied the (generalized) Jacobi equation,

$$\mathbf{q} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{S}}{\partial \mathbf{p}} \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbf{Q} = -\frac{\partial \mathbf{S}}{\partial \mathbf{P}}. \tag{16}$$

This scheme might be extended easily to quantum systems of several degrees of freedom, provided the separation of variables could be achieved. After demonstrating in two examples (the harmonic oscillator and the rotator) how his matrix formalism worked, London refrained from proceeding further, pointing to the fact that ‘meanwhile Schrödinger had succeeded, with the help of the eigenvalue [wave mechanical] method, in reducing matrix mechanics to widely developed analytic disciplines.’ ‘Hence,’ he concluded, ‘it does not appear to be suited for the moment to try to develop the mathematical tools [of matrix mechanics] further, so long as there exists the well-defined hope of getting along, with the already existing mathematics’ (London, *loc. cit.*, p. 924).

In a postscript, London mentioned the work of Wentzel (1926a)—about which he had learned after the completion of his paper—as having carried out some of the same programme that he himself had suggested to be treated in the future, but he commented: ‘Wentzel’s method, however, consists in an *elimination* of the generator of the transformation and does not lead, therefore, to an explicit representation of canonical transformations and thus to [a calculation of] intensities’ (London, *loc. cit.*, p. 925). Wentzel was well aware of that fact, and he struggled with the solution of that problem in the months following his March paper. After Schrödinger had demonstrated how to calculate Heisenberg’s matrices with the help of wave-mechanical methods (Schrödinger, 1926e) and subsequently evaluated the Stark effect amplitudes (Schrödinger, 1926f), however, Wentzel abandoned matrix mechanics and turned to wave mechanics, because: ‘One is for the first time in possession of a generally applicable method of calculating the intensities of spectral lines on the prescription of quantum mechanics’ (Wentzel, 1926b, p. 621). Notably, in a letter to *Naturwissenschaften*, he presented an evaluation of

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0057 -->

25 I.2 Early Quantum-Mechanical Transformation Theory

the intensities of discrete X-ray (*K*- and *L*-) lines of lithium and tungsten (Wentzel, *loc. cit.*). The further programme on line intensities, which Wentzel indicated at the end of this letter, was investigated by Erwin Fues (see, e.g., his paper on the intensities of band spectra of diatomic molecules: Fues, 1926b); hence, Wentzel, at that time in close contact with Schrödinger, Fues, and Pauli,$^{15}$ turned to a more fundamental problem and presented his results in a paper, entitled ‘Eine Verallgemeinerung für die Zwecke der Wellenmechanik’ (‘A Generalization of Quantum Conditions for the Purposes of Wave Mechanics’), which was received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 18 June 1926 (Wentzel, 1926d).

Wentzel wrote: ‘*Herr* Pauli drew my attention in a letter to the fact that, in the limiting case of classical mechanics, [the wave function] $\psi$ returns into itself after circling around a branching cut at $y_0[= \pm p]$, if and only if the modulus of periodicity of the action function $(\oint y_0 dx)$ assumes an integral multiple of [Planck’s constant] $h$.’$^{16}$ Thus, Wentzel characterized ‘one of the starting points’ of his new paper (adding also that Pauli had traced the idea to conversations with Oskar Klein). He knew, of course, his teacher Sommerfeld’s semiclassical approach to multiply periodic systems—he had just made use of it in his March paper referred to above—and was well acquainted with the analytic properties of the action integral, in which the momenta $p$ of separable systems appeared as square roots of expressions containing the conjugate position variables $q$. In classical theory then, the action integral assumed integral-multiple values of Planck’s constant; this corresponded to the fact that the ‘modulus of periodicity’ of the quantum-mechanical action function took on integral-multiple values of $h$ (Wentzel, 1926a, Section 2). That is, he had thus proved that two such different schemes as matrix mechanics and the old quantum theory led, at least in the simplest case of the hydrogen atom, to identical results. He hoped, of course, that the same occurred in wave mechanics, but somehow this scheme seemed to be further removed from the classical analogue than the Göttingen matrix scheme. On the other hand, Schrödinger had argued in his second communication on wave mechanics: ‘The point of phase agreement [of the waves] moves according to the same laws as the image point of the mechanical system’; further, he had claimed that ‘the superposition of these wave systems really produces a noticeable disturbance only in a relatively small region surrounding the point of phase agreement, and that everywhere else they practically destroy one another through interference’ (Schrödinger, 1926d, p. 505; English translation, p. 24). Evidently, this statement had to be read as Wentzel put it: ‘The vibration process mainly occurs in the region of the classical orbit’ (Wentzel, 1926d, footnote 1, p. 521). Hence, the wave-mechanical description should reproduce more or less the orbits of the old Bohr–Sommerfeld atomic model, and one had to relate the solutions of the wave-mechanical problem

---

$^{16}$ Wentzel, 1926d, footnote 2, p. 519. The letter of Pauli to Wentzel mentioned in his paper does not exist in the published Pauli correspondence.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0058 -->

26 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

somehow with those of the old quantum theory. Wentzel promised to do so, and more, in his June paper, whose contents he summarized in two sentences: ‘In this note a method shall be developed to solve the eigenvalue problem of Schrödinger’s “wave mechanics” by successive approximation starting with the limiting case of classical mechanics (or the previous [old] quantum theory, respectively). This [old] approximation method can in many cases be arranged such that it stops after a few steps.’ (Wentzel, loc. cit., p. 518)

Wentzel first presented the method for systems having one degree of freedom. In particular, he inserted into the time-independent Schrödinger equation,

$$\frac{d^2\psi}{dx^2} + \frac{4\pi}{h^2} p^2\psi = 0, \quad \text{with } p^2 = 2m[E - V(x)], \tag{17}$$

the substitution

$$\psi = \exp\left(\frac{2\pi i}{h} \int y \, dx\right). \tag{18}$$

Then, he arrived at a differential equation of the Riccati type, which had been used since the eighteenth century—e.g., by Jean le Rond d’Alembert (1717–1781)—to solve the boundary-value problem of the inhomogeneous vibrating string, namely,

$$\frac{h}{2\pi} \frac{dy}{dx} = p^2 - y^2. \tag{19}$$

Wentzel now noticed that, for the classical limit of vanishing quantum of action $h$, Eq. (19) reduces to an algebraic one. Or, if he identified the limiting value $y_0$ as

$$\lim_{h \to 0} y = y_0 = \frac{dS}{dx}, \tag{20}$$

he obtained formally Hamilton’s differential equation for classical dynamics, i.e.,

$$\left(\frac{dS}{dx}\right)^2 = y_0^2 = p^2. \tag{21}$$

Now, he proposed to solve Eq. (19) by treating the term on the left-hand side as a small perturbation and expanding the *Ansatz* for $y$ in a power series of the ‘small-perturbation’ parameter $(h/2\pi)$, i.e.,

$$y = \sum_{\nu=1}^{\infty} \left(\frac{h}{2\pi i}\right)^\nu y_\nu = y_0 + \frac{h}{2\pi i} y_1 + \cdots. \tag{22}$$

If inserted in the Riccati equation (19), this yielded a recursion formula for the

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0059 -->

I.2 Early Quantum-Mechanical Transformation Theory

27

coefficient $y_\nu$ of the power series (22), in particular,

$$\frac{dy_{\nu-1}}{dx} + \sum_{\alpha=0}^{\nu} y_\alpha y_{\nu-\alpha} = 0, \qquad (23)$$

and the first few coefficients were

$$y_0, \quad y_1 = -\frac{dy_0/dx}{2y_0}, \quad y_2 = -\frac{dy_1/dx + y_1^2}{2y_0}. \qquad (24)$$

Two particular solutions emerged from $y_0 = +p$ and $y_0 = -p$, respectively, corresponding to positive and negative (mechanical) momentum in the classical ($h \to 0$) limit; all other solutions of Eq. (19) are degenerate for $h = 0$ (which marks an essentially singular point).

The procedure applied here evidently stemmed from classical optics: there the *Ansatz* (22) initiated an asymptotic expansion in terms of small wavelengths as compared with the dimensions of the optical apparatus (diaphragms, slits, etc.). Wentzel could take over the idea into his wave-mechanical approximation method from Peter Debye (1909), to which Schrödinger had also referred in his second communication.¹⁷ To the important question that arose, namely, whether his series (22) converged, he answered: 'We need the solutions only in the vicinity of the singular points of the differential equation, where they provide at least asymptotic solutions of Eq. [(19)], expressed as semi-convergent power series' (Wentzel, 1926d, p. 519). Upon that, Pauli, to whom Wentzel had reported his results, raised doubts in a letter dated 11 June 1926 (replying to one of Wentzel that has not survived): 'I believe that your method of solving the Riccati equation by means of expansions in orders of $h$ is usable only to a limited extent. It may probably work for the Stark effect, but in general the series will not break off; and then it will be bad, because the single terms will be of the same order of magnitude' (Pauli, 1979, p. 331).

Not being too impressed by this objection for the moment, Wentzel proceeded to calculate the $k$-th eigenfunction $\psi_{(k)}$ from this scheme, obtaining

$$\psi_{(k)} = \exp \left( \frac{2\pi i}{h} \int y \, dx \right), \quad \text{with } y = \frac{h}{2\pi i} \frac{d\psi_{(k)}/dx}{\psi_{(k)}} \qquad (25)$$

under the condition: all integrals $\psi_{(k)}$ remain either finite or vanish at the singular points of the original differential equation (the latter belonging to the accessible values of the position variable $x$). On taking such a singular point, one obtains in its vicinity two particular solutions for the wave function, depending on which of the two solutions of the Riccati equation is inserted, $y$ either starting with $y_0 = +p$

¹⁷ See our discussion in Volume 5, Part 2, pp. 562–563.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0060 -->

28 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

or $-p$ [the $\psi$’s, Eq. (18), assume purely imaginary values, as they should, outside the classical orbit]. Approaching the limiting point, then, one of the functions (18) becomes exponentially zero, the other exponentially infinite; evidently, the former must be identified with the eigenfunction of the physical problem. Wentzel further demanded $\psi_{(k)}$ to be an analytic function in the complex plane. Because Schrödinger’s eigenfunctions are characterized by the numbers of nodes (zeros of $x$), this condition is satisfied, provided the integral $\int y \, dx$, when performed along a closed path including the poles, reduces to the sum of the residues of the functions $(d\psi_{(k)}/dx)/\psi_{(k)}$, or

$$ \oint y \, dx = \sum_{\nu=0}^{\infty} \left( \frac{h}{2\pi i} \right)^\nu \oint y_\nu \, dx = k \cdot h. \tag{26} $$

Eq. (26) finally determined, therefore, the eigenvalues $E_k$ of the original Schrödinger equation (17). Evidently, the limit $h = 0$ led to the previous quantization rule (i.e., $\int p \, dx = kh$), and Wentzel concluded: ‘The integral around the zone of zeros of $\psi$ corresponds to Sommerfeld’s integral around the branching cut of the two-valued function $y_0 = \pm p$, which characterizes the region of the classical orbit’ (Wentzel, 1926d, footnote 1, p. 521). All nodes of the wave-mechanical problem, however, can be recognized as lying close to the region of the classical orbit (where $y$ becomes an oscillating function; otherwise it converges to zero in accordance with Schrödinger’s observation). The new wave-mechanical method is actually applicable, Wentzel claimed further, beyond the range covered by the classical residue method of Sommerfeld (which failed, for instance, when two classical orbits were possible).

In Section 3 of his paper, Wentzel established the relation between his wave-mechanical approximation solution for eigenvalues and the matrix-mechanical solution, which he had proposed in his March paper (Wentzel, 1926a). By referring to the ‘Schrödinger–Pauli construction’ of matrices from wave functions, notably,

$$ (\mathbf{x})_{kl} = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} x \psi_k \psi_l \, dx \quad \text{and} \quad (\mathbf{p})_{kl} = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \psi_k \frac{d\psi_l}{dx} \, dx, \tag{27} $$

he found for the solution of $y$ corresponding to the $l$-th eigenfunction $\psi_l$ the values,

$$ (\mathbf{y})_{kl} = \frac{h}{2\pi i} \int \psi_k \left( \frac{d\psi_l}{dx} \right) dx = (\mathbf{p})_{kl}, \tag{28} $$

in agreement with the matrix solution of the Riccati equation.$^{18}$ In the last general

---

$^{18}$ The wave-mechanical approximation method proved not only to be equivalent to the matrix method in most cases, but also even superior to it, as it clearly fixed the sum of residues of $y$ to become $k h$ instead of $(k + \alpha)h$, with $\alpha$ an indefinite constant (see Wentzel, 1926a, p. 82).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0061 -->

I.2 Early Quantum-Mechanical Transformation Theory 29

section (§4), Wentzel finally extended his approximation method to separable systems having several degrees of freedom; these Riccati equations were obtained for each degree of freedom, exhibiting the more complex form,

$$ \frac{h}{2\pi i} \frac{dy}{dx} = g(x) - \frac{h}{2\pi i} f(x) y - y^2, \tag{29} $$

instead of Eq. (19) and allowing a recursion solution for the coefficients $y_\nu$ in the powers of $(h/2\pi i)$.

Before turning to the special applications given by Wentzel, the remarkable fact must be mentioned that less than three weeks after his paper was submitted, Marcel Brillouin, on 5 July 1926, presented a note of his son Léon Brillouin to the Paris Academy of Sciences, entitled ‘La mécanique ondulatoire de Schrödinger; une methode générale de résolution par approximations successives’ (‘The Undulatory Mechanics of Schrödinger; a General Solution Method by Successive Approximations,’ L. Brillouin, 1926a). Brillouin went through the same steps as had Wentzel—i.e., he made the *Ansatz* (18) for the Schrödinger equation of general systems of several degrees of freedom and arrived at the corresponding Riccati equation (with $q_k$ as position variables and $m^{kl}$ the ‘mass matrix’):

$$ \sum_{k,l} m^{kl} \frac{\partial W}{\partial q^k} \frac{\partial W}{\partial q^l} + 2(V - E) = -\frac{h}{2\pi i} m^{1/2} \sum_{k,l} \frac{\partial}{\partial q^k} \left\{ m^{-1/2} m^{kl} \frac{\partial W}{\partial q^l} \right\}, \tag{30} $$

with $W$ denoting the action integral and $m$ the determinant of the mass matrix $m^{kl}$. He assumed the residue of $W$ to have the value $I_k$,

$$ I_k = n_k \cdot h, \tag{31} $$

which arose ‘from Louis de Broglie’s resonance interpretation of the quantum conditions’ (L. Brillouin, 1926a, p. 25). Instead of the function of $y$ of Wentzel—corresponding to the derivative of the action function, $\frac{\partial W}{\partial q^k}$, in Brillouin’s paper—he (Brillouin) expanded $W$ in a power series in $(h/2\pi i)$, or

$$ W = W_{(0)} - \frac{h}{2\pi i} W_{(1)} + \left( -\frac{h}{2\pi i} \right)^2 W_{(2)} + \dots, \tag{32} $$

and then found the appropriate equations for the terms $W_{(0)}$, $W_{(1)}$, etc., obtaining in zero-th approximation the classical equation of Hamilton

$$ \sum_{k,l} m^{kl} \frac{\partial W_{(0)}}{\partial q^k} \frac{\partial W_{(0)}}{\partial q^l} + 2(V - E) = 0. \tag{33} $$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0062 -->

# 30 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

Looking at the higher-order approximations, e.g., the first-order one,

$$2 \sum m^{kl} \frac{\partial W_{(0)}}{\partial q^k} \frac{\partial W_{(1)}}{\partial q^l} = m^{1/2} \sum_{k,l} \frac{\partial}{\partial q_k} \left\{ m^{-1/2} m^{k,l} \frac{\partial W_{(0)}}{\partial q^l} \right\}, \quad (34)$$

Brillouin discovered them to be ‘linear equations, a novelty of Schrödinger’s mechanics’ (L. Brillouin, *loc. cit.*, p. 26). He added: ‘If there exists a separation of variables in the Hamiltonian, the first approximation is solved by quadrature in each variable, but the higher approximations establish a coupling between these variables, because in general one does not obtain separation.’ (L. Brillouin, *loc. cit.*) Only in the case of ‘complete separation’—i.e., the potential and the kinetic terms in the Hamiltonian are given by sums of terms, each depending only on the variables of one degree of freedom (especially then $m^{kl} = 0$ for $k \neq l$)—would one arrive at a set of equations of the type (19), which can also be solved in successive approximations by simple quadrature.

Although Brillouin, in his note, formulated Wentzel’s problem for more general systems, he essentially arrived at the results obtained earlier. He did so in a quite formal way without addressing the relations between the existing quantum-mechanical schemes, which had been Wentzel’s primary concern. Further, he did not pay particular attention to the function-theoretic arguments in the proposed approximation, on which Wentzel had placed particular emphasis. Still, these were the arguments, which Pauli—to whom Wentzel had written the details of the paper he had submitted in an (obviously) lost letter—strongly attacked in his response to Wentzel:

> In spite of the explanations given in your letter, I have still not understood the function-theoretic aspect of your procedure to calculate the eigenvalues with the help of the differential equation, $y = \left( \frac{h}{2\pi i} \right) \frac{\psi'}{\psi}$. Schrödinger’s (nonrelativistic) equation has—irrespective of whether $E$ is an eigenvalue or not—anyway other, always integer—transcendental functions $\psi$ as solutions, which assume real values on the real axis (as one can easily prove by trying a power-series *Ansatz*). The eigenvalues are only distinguished by the fact that these integer-transcendental functions $\psi$ then remain finite at infinity on the real axis. From *these* solutions $\psi$ one obtains at any rate—for eigenvalues and non-eigenvalues—unique functions $y = \left( \frac{h}{2\pi i} \right) \frac{\psi'}{\psi}$ having no branches, which possess poles for zero values of $\psi$. I do not see the connection between your non-unique solutions and Schrödinger’s unique solutions of the differential equation for the non-eigenvalues, and further, no connection between Schrödinger’s $\psi$ remaining finite on the real axis [as in the case for eigenvalue solutions] and your $\psi$ remaining unique (in any case there exist always, among others, also unique $\psi$’s). (Pauli to Wentzel, 5 July 1926, in Pauli, 1979, p. 334)

Although Pauli here hit, on first inspection, a not-so-important detail for the derivation of the new approximation scheme—Brillouin had not touched on this

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0063 -->

# I.2 Early Quantum-Mechanical Transformation Theory 31

aspect at all—his earlier warning concerning the consequence of the power series in $h$ deserved greater attention, for it threw doubt on the practical validity of the applications. Here, however, the experimental evidence apparently spoke in favour of the validity of the first approximations.

In his June paper, Wentzel employed his method in two cases: the free non-relativistic hydrogen atom and the associated Stark effects. In the first example, he reestablished the ‘classical’ Balmer formula. He found, in particular, that $y_0$, the first term in his perturbation series, already contributed an integral multiple of $h$ to the sum of residues for the radial degree of freedom,

$$\frac{1}{h} \oint y_0 \, dr = n. \quad (35)$$

However, the addition of the angular momentum-dependent residues yielded the Rydberg formula for the energy terms of the hydrogen atom with ‘half-integral azimuthal quantum numbers’ $l + \frac{1}{2}$. The behaviour of the approximated wave functions at the singular points $r = 0$ and $r = \infty$ agreed with that of Schrödinger’s exact solution.

For the Stark effect—whose first-order solution Schrödinger had treated in his third communication (Schrödinger, 1926f), which appeared before Wentzel’s paper—Wentzel also obtained the well-known and fully substantiated ‘classical’ formula. ‘On the other hand,’ he noticed, ‘the second term [in the electric field strength $F$] deviates from the result of Epstein [(1916e)],’ and he explained:

> Epstein found according to the old quantum theory, instead of the expression within the bracket [multiplying in the new calculation the constant of the second order in the field, $-h^6 F^2 n^4 / (2^{10} \pi^6 m^3 e^6)$, with $F$ the electric field strength, $n$ the principal quantum number, $m$ and $e$ the mass and the charge of the electron], i.e.,
>
> $[17n^2 - 3(n_1 - n_2)^2 - 9(n_3 - 1)^2 + 19],$
>
> the expression
>
> $[17n^2 - 3(n_1 - n_2)^2 - 9n_3^2]$.
>
> Both expressions coincide for large quantum numbers [$n_3$], but for small quantum numbers the new expression is markedly larger than Epstein’s. (Wentzel, 1926a, p. 527)

Wentzel pointed out that the latest experiments of the Japanese physicist Masazô Kiuti (1925) and the Canadian John Stuart Foster (1926) seemed to confirm his new calculations.$^{19}$ He even suggested that this result on the quadratic Stark effect,

$^{19}$ Pauli had drawn Wentzel’s attention to Kiuti’s results already in a letter dated 8 May 1926, in reply to Wentzel’s of 1 May, which contained first indications of the wave-mechanical approximation method and its possible applications (this letter of Wentzel has been lost).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0064 -->

# 32 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

which deviated so strongly from the classical result, threw light on the still unresolved helium problem (in early June 1926), but Heisenberg’s (1926b) paper, which provided a different key to that problem, was already on the way.

In summer 1926, besides Wentzel, Hendrik Kramers, another more experienced expert on atomic theory, became involved in studying the relation between the old, semiclassical quantum theory and the new quantum or wave mechanics. He had just left Copenhagen in May of that year to succeed W. H. Julius in the chair of theoretical physics at the University of Utrecht. After an absence of nearly ten years from Holland, Kramers had to establish himself back at home. In Holland, which had a great tradition in science and, especially, in the application of science to technology, Kramers not only had to represent the international school of modern theoretical physics, but also prove himself to be helpful to colleagues working successfully in experimental spectroscopy, solid-state, and low-temperature physics.$^{20}$ The first paper he submitted from Utrecht, entitled ‘*Wellenmechanik und halbzahlige Quantisierung*’ (‘Wave Mechanics and Half-Integral Quantization’), dealt with ‘a method of solving by approximation the Schrödinger eigenvalue and eigenfunction problem for an arbitrary [atomic] system of one degree of freedom’ (Kramers, 1926, p. 828). That is, just a couple of months after Wentzel and Brillouin, Kramers studied the same problem. Although he arrived eventually at the same, or very similar, results as the previous authors, he proceeded somewhat differently; in particular, he spent much effort on clarifying Wentzel’s problem of the uniqueness of solutions, and the entire method thus became later baptized as the ‘Wentzel–Kramers–Brillouin’ (WKB) method.

Of course, Kramers also began with the Schrödinger equation (17). He then introduced the quantum number $n$ as the number of zeros of the Schrödinger function between the points $x_1$ and $x_2$ (given by the position coordinates, where the quantity $\tilde{y} = p^2$ assumes zero values), and stated:

> For the case when $n$ is a large number, we can construct on account of an elementary consideration a function $\phi$, which represents in the domain $x_1 < x < x_2$ an approximate solution of [Eq. (17)].$^{21}$ Because of the wave-like character of $y$ in this domain and on the consideration that $y$ for large $n$ changes only little over a wavelength, we are led to propose the following *Ansatz* for $\phi$:
>
> $$\phi = g(x) \cos f(x), \quad [(36)]$$
>
> with $f(x)$ denoting a “smooth” function of the sort represented by $y(x)$, while $f(x_2) - f(x_1)$ assumes the order of magnitude of $\pi$. (Kramers, *loc. cit.*, p. 828)

$^{20}$ For Kramers’s scientific activity in Holland (first in Utrecht, and, after 1934, in Leyden as successor to Paul Ehrenfest) until his death in 1952, see Max Dresden’s biography of Kramers (Dresden, 1987, especially, Chapter 15).

$^{21}$ In order to avoid conflict with Wentzel’s notation, we have replaced Kramers’s original notation $y$ (denoting the square of Wentzel’s $y$) by $\tilde{y}$, and $\psi$ (again, not to conflict with Wentzel’s notation) by $\phi$. Kramers also called the wave function in the Schrödinger equation as $\phi$, which we convert into Wentzel’s $\psi$.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0065 -->

# I.2 Early Quantum-Mechanical Transformation Theory 33

For the function $f(x)$, Kramers derived the approximate expression

$$f(x) = \frac{2\pi}{h} \int^x y^{1/2} \, dx, \quad (37)$$

and $g(x)$, in first approximation—i.e., neglecting terms of second and higher order in $dy/dx$—became

$$g(x) = y^{-1/4}. \quad (38)$$

In order to determine the energy eigenvalues $E_n$ and the integration constant on the right-hand side of Eq. (37) in such a way that $\phi$ really approximates the Schrödinger eigenfunction $\psi_n$, Kramers emphasized the following observation: ‘It does not suffice to consider only the properties of [the approximate] $\phi$, already because of the fact that $\phi$ becomes infinite in $x_1$ and $x_2$ and assumes complex values for $x < x_1$ and $x > x_2$’ (Kramers, *loc. cit.*, p. 829). Therefore, he studied the exact solutions of $\psi$ of the Schrödinger equation (17) in the vicinity of turning points $x_1$ and $x_2$ (in the classical theory) and obtained the integration constants in both cases; thus, the correct approximation functions became, respectively,$^{22}$

$$\phi = y^{-1/4} \cos \left[ \frac{2\pi}{h} \int_{x_1}^x y^{1/2} \, dx - \frac{\pi}{4} \right]$$

and

$$\phi = y^{-1/4} \cos \left[ \frac{2\pi}{h} \int_{x_2}^x y^{1/2} \, dx - \frac{\pi}{4} \pm \frac{\pi}{2} \right]. \quad (39)$$

The functions $\phi$ are identical only if the condition holds that:

$$2 \int_{x_1}^{x_2} y^{1/2} \, dx = \oint p \, dx = \left( 2m + \frac{1}{2} \right). \quad (40)$$

Hence, Kramers concluded:

> From this we conclude that our approximative representation of the Schrödinger eigenfunction [Eqs. (36)–(38)] corresponds exactly to those energy values which, in the language of the old quantum theory, would be described by half-integral quantum numbers. The relative accuracy of the energy values will be of higher order in $1/n$ (in general, probably $1/n^2$), while the energy values calculated by integer [quantum number] quantization in general are different from the Schrödinger eigenvalues by the

$^{22}$ Although the exact value of the Schrödinger function at $x_1$ is always positive, at $x_2$ it may be positive or negative, in which case, the plus or minus sign in the second equation (39) applies.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0066 -->

**34** &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**Chapter I** &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

relative order $1/n$. Thus we arrive at a certain understanding of the fact known from several examples that the half-integer quantization provides a better approximation to the quantum-mechanical result than the integer quantization. (Kramers, *loc. cit.*, pp. 832–833)

Finally, in §2 of his paper, Kramers wrote explicit expressions for the approximate eigenfunctions for all values of the position coordinate $x$.
In comparing his method (in §3) with those of Wentzel and Brillouin, Kramers declared a close relationship to exist among the three schemes, but criticized the nonuniqueness of the results of his colleagues. ‘It appears . . . that the beautiful method of calculating the eigenvalues by considering the complex integral $\oint \frac{\psi'}{\psi} \, dx$ around the branching points, and using successive approximations, requires a closer justification,’ he admitted, but noted at once that: ‘The example presented seems to indicate that it is correct. If one uses it. . . , one immediately arrives at the prescription of half-integer quantization.’ (Kramers, *loc. cit.*, p. 836) He then applied his own method to problems of motion in a central field, especially to atoms of nonhydrogen type, in which the exact Schrödinger equation yields for the square of the radial momentum $p_r$ the expression,
$$
p_r^2 = y = 2m[E - V(r)] - \left( \frac{2\pi}{h} \right)^2 \frac{l(l + 1)}{r^2}, \tag{41}
$$
and the approximation (for large $n$)—in agreement with the half-integer quantization of the classical result—gives$^{23}$
$$
p_r^2 = y = 2m[E - V(r)] - \left( \frac{2\pi}{h} \right)^2 \frac{l(l + \frac{1}{2})^2}{r}. \tag{42}
$$
The difference between the two results ‘is hardly important (*fällt kaum ins Gesicht*),’ Kramers claimed and consequently hoped that his approximation method ‘might be of some use in the problem of calculating the transition probabilities of series and X-ray spectra’ (Kramers, *loc. cit.*, p. 839).
George Uhlenbeck recalled: ‘Kramers came and gave a speech [in Leyden]; this must have been 1926 or 1927—I was still assistant to Ehrenfest. In it he talked about the Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin method. He made the impression, so to say, that he knew everything which there was. He was a little bit pedantic, just the way he talked.’ (Uhlenbeck, AHQP Interview, 5 April 1962, pp. 17–18) Now, indeed, in order to put the limiting procedure from wave mechanics to classical mechanics of the old quantum theory, one had to be quite pedantic. One had to exert special care, as we have already indicated, at the so-called ‘turning points’ of the system

35 I.2 Early Quantum-Mechanical Transformation Theory

(where either one of the momenta $p$ or the time-derivative of a position coordinate $x$ becomes zero): there, classical mechanics had to break down, and the wave-mechanical inequality $\left|\frac{\partial \lambda}{\partial x}\right| \ll 1$ (with $\lambda$ the de Broglie wavelength) could not be satisfied.$^{24}$ In Wentzel’s procedure, there arose the mathematical task of combining the partial solutions of the differential equation for the approximate problem in such a way that it approaches the solution of the rigorous wave-mechanical equation. What Wentzel had done did not seem to be sufficient, either to Pauli or to Kramers. One had necessarily to consider the behaviour of the exact wave equation at least in the vicinity of the ‘turning point,’ and only the ‘pedantic’ Kramers attacked this task in his pioneering paper of 1926; it was later further investigated by some of his students—e.g., A. Zwaan in his Utrecht dissertation (1929)—or colleagues.$^{25}$ Kramers himself returned to the question in another paper, written with a student and dealing with the special case of the asymmetric top (Kramers and Ittmann, 1929b). In this context, we should also mention that Zwaan’s doctoral dissertation was criticized later by the American mathematician George David Birkhoff (1933) and finally corrected by physicists (Kemble, 1935b; see also N. Fröman and P. Fröman, 1965).

Three further remarks might be added to the discussion of the WKB method in quantum physics. First, the method is occasionally called, especially in Great Britain, the Jeffreys–Wentzel–Kramers–Brillouin (JWKB) method, because the English astronomer Harold Jeffreys (1891–1989) developed parts of the technique in 1923 (Jeffreys, 1925). Even he had precursors, however, both among the mathematicians and the physicists, whose occupation with the problem went back to the early nineteenth century.$^{26}$ The second remark concerns the later fate of the method, which may be summarized as: ‘The JWKB-method is of wide application not only in quantum mechanics but also in other branches of theoretical physics, e.g., in the theory of electromagnetic waves. It has been used for many years with great success, and it is well known that in several common applications the method gives very accurate results.’ (N. Fröman and P. Fröman, loc. cit., p. 2).

The last remark refers to the goal of the quantum physicists who proposed the WKB method: they were, in fact, mainly interested in investigating the (hopefully) close relations of classical to quantum mechanics, both for understanding the physical content of the new atomic theory and for using the successful (and often elegant) computational methods of the old quantum theory. However, the connections obtained exhibited a conceptual difficulty: on the one hand, the theo-
