36 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

reticians succeeded, by superimposing several eigenfunctions of the Schrödinger equation for certain systems as a wave group, in obtaining—in the case of large quantum numbers—a wave packet that describes a path close to the classical orbit (e.g., Debye, 1927; Darwin, 1927d). On the other hand, Pauli pointed out in his *Handbuch* article that ‘the previous quantum theory allowed only in the special case of multiply periodic systems statements about stationary systems, while the eigenvalue problem of wave mechanics always possesses a solution,’ and further:

> Also in this general case it is . . . always possible to construct wave packets (Schrödinger, 1926g; Kennard, 1927; Darwin, 1927d) which move along classical-mechanical orbits. In the course of time, however, a smearing out of the wave packets occurs in all cases; and therefore the fact that in the density [analysis] of such a packet only discrete frequencies occur cannot be connected directly with a simple periodic behaviour of the classical-mechanical orbits for long periods. This latter behaviour is, as has been known since a long time in the case of the three-body problem, rather complicated; the fact that it does not play a role in the application to atomic systems constitutes a [real] progress. (Pauli, 1933c, p. 176)

To sum up the individual merits of the three pioneers of the **WKB** method: Wentzel developed the relation between the quantum-mechanical schemes and the first approximation method; Brillouin, in rediscovering Wentzel’s scheme, recognized the fundamental linearity of wave mechanics; and Kramers delved deepest into the limiting connection between quantum and classical mechanics. All three contributed by their work to what finally became the physical interpretation of quantum mechanics. Before the quantum-mechanical transformation theory—toward which the **WKB** method represented an essential step—could be completed, another conceptual aspect of the theory had to be included: the statistical interpretation of Schrödinger’s wave function.

**I.3 Max Born’s Probability Interpretation of Schrödinger’s Wave Function**

Upon considering the relation between the intensity of spectral lines and the Fourier coefficients $c_{\tau}$ for the classical transition amplitudes of atomic radiation ($\tau\omega$), Niels Bohr declared in late 1917: ‘We must expect that for large (quantum numbers) $n$ these coefficients will on the quantum theory determine the *probability of spontaneous transition* for a given stationary state for which $n = n'$ to a neighbouring state for which $n = n'' = n' - \tau'$ (Bohr, 1918a, p. 15). In this important paper, which greatly stimulated the development of the quantum theory of line spectra in the following years, Bohr explicitly referred to recent work of Albert Einstein, who had based a new derivation of Planck’s blackbody radiation law by describing atomic transitions in a manner similar to radioactive decays: that is, by introducing the proper probability arguments into the quantum theory of atomic structure (Einstein, 1916d, 1917a). The probability argumentation of Einstein left

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0069 -->

# I.3 Max Born’s Probability Interpretation of Schrödinger’s Wave Function

37

a deep impression on Max Born, and one is tempted to conclude that it played a vital role in the final, and perhaps most important, step of marrying the physical atomic theory with the mathematical probability calculus: that is, Born’s probability interpretation of Schrödinger’s wave function.²⁷

Born, in his later years, tried on several occasions to trace the path that had led him to this fundamental concept in modern quantum mechanics. He made a few remarks about it in his 1954 Nobel lecture, and later gave some details in *My Life: Recollections of a Nobel Laureate* (written for his children) as well as in interviews in the early 1960s.²⁸ What Born recalled may be summarized as follows:

(1) In early summer 1925, Born and others in Göttingen learned about Louis de Broglie’s matter-wave hypothesis; Walter Elsasser, a student of Born and James Franck, applied this hypothesis to explain the Ramsauer effect and some irregular electron-scattering observations.

(2) In summer and fall 1925, Born developed, with Pascual Jordan and Werner Heisenberg, the latter’s new quantum-mechanical ideas. Born spent the following term primarily at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge, Massachusetts, where he worked with Norbert Wiener in developing operator mechanics, an extension and modification of matrix mechanics, which allowed one to treat aperiodic motions.

(3) Upon his return to Göttingen in April 1926, Born encountered Erwin Schrödinger’s first communication on wave mechanics. At the same time, he learned from Pascual Jordan: Pauli had informed him that wave mechanics and its earlier rival, the Göttingen–Cambridge quantum mechanics, yielded the same results in atomic problems.

(4) Schrödinger’s harsh critique of the matrix scheme of the Göttingen physicists and his quite distinct, apparently causal, interpretation of wave mechanics, aroused Born’s resistance.

(5) In analyzing Schrödinger’s interpretation of radiation phenomena, Born reminded himself of two ideas, which his friend Einstein had discussed earlier in this context: first, the use of light-quanta with appropriate statistical properties to account for the classical interference effects; second, the notion of the classical electromagnetic wave as a ‘ghost field’ (‘Gespensterfeld’) or ‘guiding field’ (‘Führungsfeld’) for light-quanta. Both of these ideas ultimately merged into his concept of considering the wave amplitude as a ‘probability amplitude.’

(6) After reflecting unsuccessfully about crucial confirmations in radiation problems, Born decided to prove his new concept in two unsolved problems of quantum mechanics: the scattering of matter waves (electrons, alpha particles) by atoms and the question of adiabatic invariance. He worked out the solution of the first problem in detail in June and July 1926.

(7) In a lecture presented in summer 1926 at the Oxford meeting of the *British Association for the Advancement of Science* (which Born remembered wrongly as having taken place in Cambridge), he spoke about his probability interpretation and the consequences for the physical description of atomic phenomena.

(8) In fall and winter 1926, Born worked out the details of the problem of adiabatic invariance and the scattering of alpha particles by hydrogen atoms.

²⁷ See also Born’s appraisal of Einstein’s statistical theories: Born, 1949.
²⁸ Born, 1978, and the AHQP interview with P. P. Ewald in June 1960.

38 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

Several authors have attempted to analyze Born’s narrative from the viewpoint of the critical historian or philosopher.<sup>29</sup> In this section, an even sharper reconstruction of the historical development leading to the probability interpretation is sought, using the available (mainly primary) sources. It is not our intention, however, to accuse the nearly eighty-year-old Born of having presented a wrong or distorted account, as has recently become occasionally the custom of the younger generation of historians of science. We shall rather show how additional facts, when combined with critically interpreted and mildly corrected parts of the ‘old caddy’s story,’ yield a consistent and quite thrilling episode in the intellectual history of modern science.<sup>30</sup> For this purpose, we proceed by first outlining the conceptual ideas of Born’s approach to quantum theory before 1926; then, we focus our attention on the situation in spring 1926, when Born responded to the new wave mechanics and especially to Schrödinger’s criticism of the earlier Göttingen–Cambridge quantum mechanics; third, we discuss the first formulation of the probability interpretation in connection with the scattering problem; fourth, Born’s lecture at Oxford then outlined the broad philosophy underlying the new statistical approach to quantum mechanics and pointed out other applications and confirmations, such as the proof of the ‘adiabatic principle’ in quantum mechanics; fifth, and finally, the formation of the Göttingen school of quantum mechanics, as a consequence of Born’s fundamental contributions to the theory, will be discussed.

### (a) **Born’s Conceptual Approach to the Quantum Problem (up to Spring 1926)**

As we have reported in Volume 1 (Section III.2), Max Born came to deal with the quantum theory only in 1912 (before that he had concerned himself with relativity, the other modern theory of the twentieth century), when he applied (together with Theodor von Kármán) the Planck–Einstein quantum-theoretical ideas to the kinetic theory of solids. Considered to be—by Einstein and others, including himself—rather as a theoretical physicist who specialized in performing formal, thorough, and systematic calculations than an inventor of new concepts, he had not pondered for many years (in the 1910s) about the meaning and significance of fundamental quantum concepts. However, he kept a sharp eye on the literature and interacted with Albert Einstein (at least since they had both been together in Berlin from 1915 to 1919) and later with Niels Bohr (especially after the latter’s Göttingen lectures in June 1922)—the official ‘philosophers’ of quantum physics—about the deeper physical interpretation of quantum phenomena. One of the earliest signs of this interest may be seen in a letter to Einstein, dated 4 June 1919,

<sup>29</sup> Although Max Jammer, in his book, followed largely Born’s account (Jammer, 1966, pp. 281–293), Abraham Pais corrected it carefully with information derived from published papers (Pais, 1982b). Nancy Cartwright, on the other hand, attempted to understand Born’s philosophical motivation and principles (Cartwright, 1987).
<sup>30</sup> For a harsh criticism of using the recollections of participating scientists in science history, see Heilbron, 1989.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0071 -->

I.3 Max Born’s Probability Interpretation of Schrödinger’s Wave Function 39

in which Born wrote: ‘Quantum theory creates in me similar feelings as yours. One should really be ashamed of its successes, because they are obtained according to the Jesuits’ principle: “One hand should not know what the other does”’ (*Einstein et al.*, 1969, p. 29). In a later letter of the same year, addressed to Wolfgang Pauli, Born gave hints about his thoughts concerning more fundamental questions in quantum theory; he wrote:

I have especially been interested in your remark at the end (of your paper) [Pauli, 1919b], that you regard the application of the continuum theory to the interior of the electron as meaningless, because one is then dealing with things which are unobservable in principle. I have pursued exactly this idea for some time, though up to now without positive success: that is, the way out of all quantum difficulties must be sought by starting from entirely fundamental points of view. One is not allowed to carry over the concepts of space and time as a four-dimensional continuum from the macroscopic world of experience into the atomistic world; the latter evidently demands another type of number-manifold to give an adequate picture. (Born to Pauli, 23 December 1919, in Pauli, 1979, p. 11)

However, he admitted at once that he did not have the slightest idea of how to proceed.

As the years went by, Born really plunged deeply into the quantum problems and, beginning in the early 1920s, he addressed notably the problems of atomic structure. Having convinced himself that the old quantum theory with its fundamental tool of phase integrals and the accompanying rules failed to describe the empirical facts (e.g., in the helium atom), he indeed tried approaches different from the usual semiclassical one: in 1923, he proposed to replace the differential equations of dynamics by difference equations, and in 1925, he expressed his assistant Werner Heisenberg’s new quantum-mechanical ideas in the form of discrete matrices. This Göttingen matrix mechanics seemed to satisfy all of the requirements of a new atomic theory, which he had emphasized for several years, notably: (1) that it should contain only observable quantities; (2) the particle structure of atomic systems should remain essentially unaltered.

In spite of such obviously straightforward procedures connecting the old Bohr–Sommerfeld theory of atomic structure with the modern quantum mechanics, two episodes played an important role in Born’s scientific life during the crucial period 1924–1925, which throw a different light on quantum phenomena. First, in early 1924, Niels Bohr, Hendrik Kramers, and John Slater proposed a revolutionary approach to the radiation problem (i.e., the existing puzzle presented by the dualistic nature of radiation as a wave phenomenon in the sense of classical electrodynamics and as light-quantum, respectively): they assumed a statistical connection governing the fundamental processes between matter and radiation, violating strict conservation of energy and momentum in the microphysical domain (Bohr *et al.*, 1924). Born, like other quantum physicists, though in contrast to his friend Einstein (and, later on, Pauli), welcomed the new Copenhagen radiation theory, basically because it did not disagree with his own programme of a discrete quan

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0072 -->

40 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

tum mechanics and was consistent with the spirit of Einstein’s statistical derivation of Planck’s law in 1916 (which he considered to be fundamental). Einstein argued against such consequences, however, and wrote to Born:

> But I do not want to be driven to give up strict causality, before one has not struggled quite differently than hitherto against this step. The idea that an electron exposed to a ray chooses, *out of free will*, the moment and direction, where it wants to jump off, I find unbearable. If so, then I would rather like to be a cobbler, or even an employee of a casino than a physicist. Admittedly, my attempts to provide quanta a sizable form so far have always failed, but I do not yet give up all hope. And, if ultimately it won’t work at all, then at least the consolation rests that it is only my own fault. (Einstein to Born, 29 April 1924, in Einstein *et al.*, 1969, p. 118)

However, in 1924, Born rated Bohr’s expertise in quantum theory higher than Einstein’s scruples, as did Erwin Schrödinger (though for different reasons).<sup>31</sup>

The other episode had to do with a certain acceptance of Louis de Broglie’s matter-wave hypothesis in Göttingen, and in this again Einstein played a role as mediator through his work on the Bose statistics of ideal gas atoms (Einstein, 1924d, 1925a). Einstein’s second paper (1925a) posed certain puzzles of understanding for Born and James Franck, as Born mentioned to Einstein in summer 1925:

> Fortunately Ehrenfest showed up here and has enlightened us (*hat uns ein Licht aufgesteckt*). Then I read the paper of Louis de Broglie and was gradually up to your tricks. Now I believe that the “wave theory of matter” will become a very important thing. The considerations of our Herr Elsasser are not yet o.k.; so far it turned out that he has been sadly mistaken—but I still believe that his remark, especially on the reflection of electrons, can be rescued. It appears to me that a connection (of quite formal nature) exists between this and that mystic[al] explanation of reflection, diffraction and interference by “spatial” quantization, as has been proposed by Compton and Duane, and studied more closely by Epstein and Ehrenfest. (Born to Einstein, 15 July 1925, in Einstein *et al.*, 1969, p. 120)

In spite of the initial attention these two episodes received, they seemed to influence only little the procedure of Born and his principal associates in quantum theory. Thus, he continued to work with Pascual Jordan on reformulating the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory of atomic structure in terms of the difference-equation method, a scheme based—as the authors declared—only on observable quantities in atomic physics (Born and Jordan, 1925a). Upon the completion of Heisenberg’s pioneering paper (Heisenberg, 1925c), the two of them joined forces again to put quantum mechanics into the garb of matrices (Born and Jordan, 1925b). They claimed, in particular, that their algebraic formulation displayed explicitly the main physical contents of atomic physics: the discreteness of stationary states, the transition amplitudes, and the ‘quantum jumps’ occurring in collision processes of

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0073 -->

I.3 Max Born’s Probability Interpretation of Schrödinger’s Wave Function 41

atoms with atomic particles or radiation. In the three-man paper, which completed the framework of matrix mechanics (Born *et al.*, 1926), and even more in the operator-scheme extension of quantum mechanics (Born and Wiener, 1926a), hope sprang that a more general atomic theory would emerge that would allow one to describe in a unified manner both periodic and aperiodic phenomena: e.g., the behaviour of ionized atoms and the scattering of atoms and their constituents.

In November 1925, Born went to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where he gave a series of lectures on the modern atomic theory, including the new methods developed by the local mathematician Norbert Wiener and himself. About the latter, he remarked:

> A more exhaustive treatment of the method is as yet unwarranted. Suffice [it] to say that it has been possible to show that, in the case of the harmonic oscillator, the operational calculus gives the [same result] as the matrix calculus. Moreover, treatment of uniform rectilinear motion is possible, a case where the matrix calculus breaks down completely. Investigations on the theorems of angular momentum, on hyperbolic orbits in the hydrogen atom and on similar problems are in progress. (Born, 1926d, p. 127)

At the same time, Born stressed the shortcomings of all existing schemes as follows:

> Our theory gives the *possible* states of the system, but no indication of whether a system is in a given state. It gives at most the probability of the jumps. However, the statement that a system is at a given time and place in a certain state probably has a meaning, which the present state of our theory does not allow us to formulate. This is also the case with regard to the problem of light-quanta. Here the Compton effect and the related experiments of Bothe and Geiger, Compton and Simon have shown that both the energy and momentum of light travel as [in a] projectile from atom to atom. But the existence of interference, that is the fact that light added to light can produce darkness, is just as certain. It cannot yet be seen how these two views can be reconciled or whether a matrix representation of the electromagnetic field will lead further [although the matrix treatment of cavity radiation, given in Born, Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926, had yielded certain aspects of the dualistic behaviour of radiation]. (Born, *loc. cit.*, pp. 128–129)

The situation in the questions enumerated here would change faster than Born envisaged in January 1926, basically on account of the emerging wave mechanics, which awaited him on his return to Germany.

### (b) **Wave Mechanics and Schrödinger’s Attacks on Göttingen Quantum Mechanics (Spring 1926)**

After some touring through the United States, Max Born returned to Göttingen early in April 1926, as Hedwig Born informed Einstein a few days later (H. Born

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0074 -->

42 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

to Einstein, 11 April 1926, in Einstein et al., 1969, p. 128). At that time, the quantum physicists there, as elsewhere, were excited about Schrödinger’s first publication on the ‘undulatory’ or ‘wave’ mechanics, which offered an alternative method of dealing with atomic problems (Schrödinger, 1926c). The astonishment grew even further, when Pascual Jordan received Wolfgang Pauli’s letter of 12 April (see Pauli to Jordan, in Pauli, 1979, pp. 315–320), explaining that the apparently completely different theories of Schrödinger and the Göttingen physicists yielded identical results, and a more or less perfect formal equivalence could be established between the two schemes. The easier handling of the wave-mechanical methods quickly stimulated Born’s hope to apply them to problems in which his mind had been engrossed for some time, such as the hyperbolic orbits of the hydrogen atom or the Compton effect, which he had not been able to treat by means of any extension or modification of the matrix methods. Several weeks later, Born could read all of the details of the demonstration of the formal equivalence of the two schemes (wave mechanics and matrix mechanics) given by Schrödinger himself (Schrödinger, 1926e). The same paper also greatly annoyed him, however, for it contained very negative, if not derogatory, remarks about the Göttingen quantum mechanics.

First of all, Schrödinger declared:

> I am not aware at all of any generic relation [of wave mechanics] with Heisenberg [’s matrix mechanics]. I naturally knew about the theory, but I was discouraged, if not repelled, by what appeared to me as very difficult methods of transcendental algebra, defying any visualization. (Schrödinger, 1926e, footnote 2, p. 735; English translation, p. 46)

Later on in the paper, Schrödinger explained a little what he meant by visualization in atomic physics:

> To approach the theoretical description of such problems, it is quite necessary to oversee clearly the transition between macroscopic, visualizable mechanics and the micromechanics of the atom. To me it seems extraordinarily difficult to tackle problems of the kind mentioned above, as long as we feel obliged on epistemological grounds to suppress intuition in atomic dynamics, and to operate only with such abstract concepts like transition probabilities, energy levels, etc. (Schrödinger, loc. cit., p. 753)

Born must have been shocked by these remarks. However, as was natural, Schrödinger not only preferred his own method of calculation, but he also wanted to renounce—in favour of a vague ‘intuition’ and understanding of the ‘transition from macroscopic to microscopic mechanics’—all concepts that had been essential to the previous quantum theory of atoms, concepts that had been advocated for a dozen years by Niels Bohr, notably, the existence of stationary states and the so

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0075 -->

**I.3 Max Born’s Probability Interpretation of Schrödinger’s Wave Function 43**

clearly observable quantum jumps.$^{32}$ Erwin Schrödinger—the same man, less than two years before, had pleaded so strongly in favour of the probabilistic Bohr–Kramers–Slater radiation theory—now directed a frontal attack against such a well-established concept as ‘transition probability.’

In his equivalence paper, Schrödinger also turned against a more specific application of the matrix calculus, namely, Born and Jordan’s proposal to represent the electromagnetic fields by matrices to establish properly the necessary coupling of atoms with radiation. ‘The undulatory mechanics shows,’ he argued, ‘that there exists at least no compelling reason to do so, because the mechanical-field scalar $\psi$ certainly possesses the property to enter even the untouched [classical] Maxwell-Lorentz equations between the electromagnetic field vectors as a “source” of the latter’ (Schrödinger, *loc. cit.*, p. 754). Evidently, he wished to renounce all of the consequences of Einstein’s light-quantum hypothesis, including the view often expressed by Einstein since 1905 that one should imagine the electromagnetic field as a ‘probability wave’ of an assembly of photons.$^{33}$ Schrödinger now wished to forget all of this well-grounded knowledge handed down from the previous decades, which meant that he was willing to abandon, among other things, the accepted explanation of the Compton effect and the collision experiments of Born’s colleague James Franck. Clearly, Born had every reason to react against such heretical views, in spite of a feeling of complete exhaustion after his strenuous visit to America.$^{34}$ But how should he begin?

In his later, more detailed paper on collision processes (Born, 1926b), Born explained his initial plan in the following way. He had recognized the necessity of finding a third ‘interpretation of quantum mechanics,’ somewhere in between

---
$^{32}$ In a letter to Arnold Sommerfeld, dated 28 April 1926, Schrödinger expressed his rejection of the Göttingen matrix mechanics even more drastically when he said:

‘As far as Heisenberg’s mechanics is concerned, it appears to me at the moment to be represented by the following picture. Think of a man, who has arrived accidentally in *such* a way upon the theory of functions that he takes a *function* to be identical with a countable set of constants, i.e., what *we* call the coefficients of their power series. In principle, one should be able to deduce the entire theory of functions on this basis, without taking any notice of the *visualization*, which we have of an analytic function. . . . However, in any case, the largest portion of *our* theory of functions would be accessible on this ascetic path only by utmost labour, because the ability for visualization, which we have obtained in normal life, would then be used to a totally insufficient extent.’

$^{33}$ Born referred in several interviews to Einstein’s remarks in that context. We may trace the latter back to Einstein’s first light-quantum paper, where he wrote: ‘The wave theory of light which operates with continuous functions in space has been excellently justified for the representation of purely optical phenomena and it is unlikely ever to be replaced by another theory. One should, however, bear in mind that optical observations refer to time averages and not to “instantaneous values”’ (Einstein, 1905b, p. 132; English translation, pp. 91–92). Also, in September 1909—at the Salzburg *Naturforscherver- sammlung*, in which Born participated and first met Einstein—the latter commented positively on a remark of Johannes Stark to the same effect, namely, that light-quanta add more less statistically together to yield interference phenomena.

$^{34}$ In the summer term Friedrich Hund, the newly appointed *Privatdozent*, relieved Max Born from some of his arduous duties by taking over the big lecture course on mechanics.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0076 -->

44 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

matrix mechanics—in which ‘an exact representation of the processes in space and time is impossible’—and wave mechanics, working with ‘wave groups having small extensions in all directions,’ i.e., a space-time localization. In order to establish it, he referred to:

> a remark of Einstein concerning the relation of the undulatory field to light-quanta; he [Einstein] said approximately that the waves serve only to direct the path of the corpuscular light-quanta, and he spoke in this connection of a “ghost field” (“*Gespensterfeld*”). This field determines the probability for the situation that a light-quantum, carrier of energy and momentum, assumes a certain path; the field, however, is not associated with any energy and momentum. (Born, *loc. cit.*, p. 804)

Based on this conception of Einstein’s,³⁵ Born (according to his recollections) began to consider the most obvious problem, namely, that of the scattering of photons, but he did not make much progress and turned to the scattering of matter waves of atomic [i.e., mass] particles. In the later paper, he offered a justification:

> To connect this idea [of the photon] with quantum mechanics, one should better postpone it until one has finished incorporating the electromagnetic field into this formalism. However, because of the complete analogy between the light-quantum and the electron, one may think of writing down the laws of electron motion in a similar form. And it appears obvious there to consider de Broglie-Schrödinger waves as the “ghost field” or better “guiding field” (“*Führungsfeld*”). (Born, *loc. cit.*)

That is, Born felt safer when treating first the nonrelativistic scattering problem of electrons colliding with atoms. For this purpose, he developed his own approximation method, whose lowest-order solution later came to be called ‘the Born approximation.’³⁶ Simultaneously, however, he thought of other scattering problems in which to apply his statistical interpretation, notably, the Rutherford scattering of alpha particles by atomic nuclei, and of a quite different problem: the demonstration of ‘adiabatic invariance’ in quantum mechanics. He would investigate all of these problems during the following half year or so, a remarkably heavy research load for an exhausted forty-four-year-old professor.

**(c) Quantum-Mechanical Scattering Phenomena**
**(Summer 1926 to Fall 1926)**

Early in summer 1926, Max Born embarked upon a systematic study of a quantum-mechanical scattering theory, i.e., the collision of electrons and other

³⁵ It is difficult to detect it explicitly in any of Einstein’s publications, but we may perhaps see an indication reflected in Schrödinger’s work on the ideal gas theory (immediately preceding his wave-mechanical solution of the hydrogen atom)—Schrödinger, 1926b—in which Schrödinger talked of atoms as being represented by ‘white crests’ (‘*Schaumkronen*’); this work arose from a close interaction with Einstein. (See Volume 5, Part 2, Section III.2; also, von Meyenn, 1984.)

³⁶ According to Born’s recollection, this name was first used in the book on atomic collisions by Nevill F. Mott and H. S. W. Massey (1933).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0077 -->

**I.3 Max Born’s Probability Interpretation of Schrödinger’s Wave Function 45**

atomic particles with atoms. Because we have treated the principal features of this theory earlier (in Volume 5, Part 2, pp. 723–735) as an application of Schrödinger’s wave-mechanical methods, we can focus here upon the essential conceptual aspects arising from the scattering theory and some of its subsequent developments. Born first submitted a note containing his main ideas and the results of a preliminary calculation to the weekly journal *Die Naturwissenschaften*; when it was not accepted there—because of ‘lack of space,’ as Born mentioned in a footnote in the actual publication—he sent it immediately to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, which received the short paper on 25 June 1926, and quickly published it in the following issue of 10 July under the title ‘Zur Quantenmechanik der Stofβvorgänge’ (‘On the Quantum Mechanics of Collision Processes,’ Born, 1926a.)

In this ‘Preliminary note,’ as he called it, Born expressed his main motivation as the desire to show that the *existing* quantum mechanics was a complete theory; i.e., it could also deal with quantum-theoretical transitions, in particular, the problem of collisions between atomic particles. Born evidently considered Schrödinger’s wave mechanics not only as being formally equivalent to the Göttingen–Cambridge schemes of quantum mechanics, but *also* as the same theory; he even regarded it as ‘the deepest formulation of the quantum laws’ (Born, *loc. cit.*, p. 864). He then applied it to the collision problem in an approximation, which avoided dealing with the complex situation arising from the coupling of particles at short distances: in that case, the asymptotic states of electron and atom (i.e., long before and after the act of collision) can be well defined (namely, both the uniform, rectilinear motion of the electron and the stationary state of the atom, which is considered to be very heavy, hence, at rest). The solution of the Schrödinger wave equation—Born was unable to handle the problem in the other schemes of quantum mechanics (including operator mechanics)—thus yielded the transition of the scattering electron from its initial state [momentum $p = (h/2\pi)k$ in the $z$-direction] into the final state, characterized by the direction cosines $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)$. Intuitively, a plane ingoing wave resulted in a scattered wave $\psi_{n\tau}$,

$$ \psi_{n\tau}(x, y, z; q_k) $$
$$ = \sum_{m} \iint_{\alpha x + \beta y + \gamma z > 0} d\omega \Phi_{n,m}(\alpha, \beta, \gamma) \sin k_{nm}^{(\tau)}(\alpha x + \beta y + \gamma z + \delta) \cdot \psi^0_m(q_k), \quad (43) $$

with $\psi^0(q_k)$ denoting the eigenfunctions of the unperturbed atom. The ‘unique’ interpretation of Eq. (43), according to Born, was the following: ‘$\Phi_{n,m}(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)$ determines the probability that the electron coming from the $z$-direction is thrown into the direction given by $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ (and a phase shift $\delta$), its energy $\tau$ increasing thereby by a quantum $h\nu^0_{nm}$ at the expense of the atomic energy’ (Born, *loc. cit.*, pp. 865–866).

In his lecture, delivered upon receiving the 1954 Nobel Prize for Physics, exactly for introducing the probability interpretation into quantum mechanics, Born described briefly how he arrived at his conclusion:

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0078 -->

46 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

I immediately took up his [Schrödinger’s] method since it held the promise of leading to an interpretation of the $\psi$-function. Again one idea of Einstein gave me the lead. He tried to make the duality of particles—light-quanta or photons—and waves comprehensible by interpreting the square of the optical wave amplitudes as probability density of the occurrence of photons. This concept could at once be carried over to the $\psi$-function: $|\psi|^2$ ought to represent the probability density for electrons (or other particles). (Born, 1964, p. 262)

We have shown earlier that the actual procedure was not all that straightforward, as it involved several intermediate steps (see Volume 5, Part 2, pp. 723–735). Here, we add only that, according to Born’s preliminary note, the probability assignment did not appear to be so definite: indeed, he claimed that the wave function (and not its absolute square!) had to be connected with the probability. Only in a footnote, added in proof (i.e., a little later), did Born say: ‘More accurate considerations show that the probability is proportional to the square of the quantity $\Phi_{nm}$’ (Born, 1926a, p. 865).$^{37}$ This uncertainty notwithstanding (which he would fully remove in the following detailed paper), Born finally clearly expounded his famous statement: ‘Personally, I tend to renounce determinism in the atomic world,’ though he immediately cautioned: ‘But that is a philosophical question which is not decided by physical arguments alone’ (Born, *loc. cit.*, p. 866).

The extended paper on ‘*Quantenmechanik der Stoßvorgänge*’ (‘Quantum Mechanics of Collision Processes,’ Born, 1926b), received four weeks later, again by *Zeitschrift für Physik*, then contained the details of the collision calculation, as well as the embedding of this physical problem into Born’s systematic working programme which included:

(1) periodic processes (already treated in matrix mechanics and wave mechanics);
(2) aperiodic processes (such as the collision problem treated in detail in the present paper);
(3) nonstationary processes (which should be attacked later).

For all of these different types of atomic problems, the probability interpretation suggested in the preliminary note had to be applicable and produce correct results or predictions. Now, in the case of periodic systems (e.g., atoms and molecules described by the time-independent Schrödinger equations), the completeness relation for an arbitrary solution,

$$\psi(q) = \sum_{n} c_n \psi_n(q), \tag{44}$$

$^{37}$ In later interviews, Born actually mentioned that he had at first made a mistake in the collision study, which was later corrected. From a logical point of view, and bearing in mind the above-mentioned reconstructed development of the interpretation, it appears to be a little surprising that Born made that mistake, but probably it was just a minor sloppiness that should not be weighed too heavily against him. [See also the paper of Alfred Landé (1926a), and especially an earlier study of Gregor Wentzel (1924a) on the problem of associating the light-quantum amplitude with probability.]

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0079 -->

I.3 Max Born’s Probability Interpretation of Schrödinger’s Wave Function 47

with $\psi_n$ being the $n$-th eigenfunction associated with $W_n$, the quantum-theoretical energy of the stationary state, allowed one to derive the relation

$$\int |\psi(q)|^2 dq = \sum_{n} |c_n|^2, \tag{45}$$

which immediately made it possible to establish the probability interpretation. Evidently, in the case of aperiodic systems, more computational work was necessary. Already, in the simplest case of the uniform rectilinear motion, Born had to introduce a special trick, namely, an ‘averaging’ definition of the completeness relation, because the plane-wave eigenfunctions $\exp(\pm ikx)$ could not be normalized as the usual eigenfunctions of the stationary atomic states.$^{38}$

Turning now to the case of aperiodic motions, which occur in connection with the emission of continuous spectra by atoms, Born applied his method of considering only the asymptotic behaviour of the wave function (following from a time-dependent Schrödinger equation) that satisfied the conservation law for the energy. As the most general solution, he obtained a wave scattered in all directions, whose amplitude and phase depended on the angle of deflection. In the case of elastic collisions, the expression for the probability became

$$\Phi d\omega = \pi^2 k^2 \left| \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} f_n^{\infty} (-\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{s}) \right|^2, \tag{46}$$

where $\mathbf{s}$ denotes the direction of deflection and the $f_n^{\infty}$ emerge from a sequence of successive approximations for the asymptotic amplitudes.$^{39}$ For inelastic collisions, on the other hand, the first-order approximation yielded

$$\Phi_{nm} d\omega = \pi^2 k_{nm}^2 \left| f_n^{\infty} (-\mathbf{k}_{nm} \cdot \mathbf{s}) \right|^2. \tag{47}$$

The results from the theory, Eqs. (46) and (47), agreed, as Born noted happily, with experimental observation—apart from the fact that in the case of noble gas atoms the elastic scattering must be described by higher order than the first ($f_0^{\infty}$) approximation. Hence, Born concluded that his collision theory, involving the probability interpretation as an integral part, indeed solved the problem of quantum-mechanical scattering completely within the wave-mechanical formulation. He further declared that, if one so wished, the usual concepts of space and time might be retained, but *not* the causal determination of single events. He finished with the remark:

$^{38}$ See our discussion in Volume 5, Part 2, pp. 728–729.
$^{39}$ Born’s approximate solution was built in analogy to the well-known perturbation theory of time-independent systems in matrix mechanics (discussed in Volume 3, Section III.2) or wave mechanics (Volume 5, Part 2, Section V.1). That is, the equation for the $n$-th-order perturbation arises from a differential equation with a “source”-term of $(n - 1)$-th order. (For a systematic review, see Wentzel, 1933a, p. 714 ff.)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0080 -->

48 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

I would like to believe that the laws of motion of light-quanta may be dealt with in an analogous manner, the difference being that already in the basic problem of free emission no periodic phenomenon—but a damping process (*Abklingungsprozeß*)—occurs; hence one has to deal not with a boundary-condition problem but with an initial-value problem for the coupled wave equations for the Schrödinger wave function and the electromagnetic field. (Born, 1926b, p. 827)

In the next two investigations of his programme, however, Born did not deal with this task—which he had called ‘one of the most urgent ones’—but with a couple of different problems: that of adiabatic invariance and an exact evaluation of the collision of an atomic particle (electron or alpha particle) with a neutral hydrogen atom. He submitted the result of the latter calculation to the Göttingen Academy in late fall 1926 (Born, 1926e). In it, Born proved the Rutherford scattering formula for large values of the incident momentum $p$ of the alpha particle,$^{40}$ or

$$a k_0 = a \cdot \frac{2\pi}{h} p \ll 1, \tag{48}$$

with $a$ denoting the Bohr radius of the ground state of hydrogen. Born later recalled an episode connected with this calculation:

When I published my paper ... I gave it to [J. Robert] Oppenheimer in order for him to check the involved calculations. He brought it back and said: “I couldn’t find any mistake—did you really do this alone?” The astonishment expressed by these words and visible in his face was rather excusable, for I was never good at long calculations and always made silly mistakes. (Born, 1978, pp. 233–234)

Born remembered still another story about his scattering theory. About two years later, Hans Bethe discussed the scattering of electrons in a crystal lattice and found that the probability amplitudes in that case reflected the periodicity of the lattice (Bethe, 1928a). After reading his paper, Born wrote the young physicist an ‘appreciative letter,’ upon which Bethe replied: ‘It is rather a pity that you did not see the connection between the collision problem of material particles and the well-known scattering of X-rays.’ (Born, *loc. cit.*, p. 234)

**(d) The Physical Interpretation of Quantum Mechanics and Adiabatic Invariance (August–October 1926, with a Later Addendum)**

At the end of the summer semester in Göttingen, Born again went on a trip, this time to England, where he attended the Oxford meeting of the *British Association for the Advancement of Science*, held from 4 to 11 August 1926. There, the British

$^{40}$ In the first quantum-mechanical derivation of the Rutherford scattering formula, Born was beaten by Gregor Wentzel (1926e).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0081 -->

I.3 Max Born’s Probability Interpretation of Schrödinger’s Wave Function 49

speakers of *Section A* (Mathematics and Physics), like Ernest Rutherford, William Henry Bragg, and Bragg’s son William Lawrence, were complemented by illustrious foreign guests, notably, from Germany; they included Niels Bohr, Konstantin Carathéodory, James Franck, Carl Runge, Manne Siegbahn, and Willy Wien. Thus, Born found himself in distinguished company; moreover, he had and took the opportunity of meeting two young contributors to quantum mechanics, both of whom would soon come and join him in Göttingen.$^{41}$ In addition, he had an encounter with an experimentalist, which would also obtain importance for the history of quantum physics: as Clinton Joseph Davisson, the discoverer of matter waves in 1927, recalled then years later (in his Nobel lecture): ‘The New York experiment was not at all, at its inception, a test of the wave theory. Only in the summer of 1926, after I had discussed the investigation in England with Richardson, Born, Franck and others, did it take on this character’ (Davisson, in *Nobel Foundation*, 1965, p. 390).

On 10 August 1926, Max Born read his paper on ‘Physical Aspects of Quantum Mechanics’ at Oxford, in which he discussed, from a very general point of view and without any mathematical detail, his new fundamental proposal of using statistics in quantum mechanics. In particular, he said:

> In classical dynamics the knowledge of the state of a closed system (the position and velocity of all its particles) at any instant determines unambiguously the future motion of the system; that is the form that the principle of causality takes in physics. Mathematically, this is expressed by the fact that the physical quantities satisfy differential equations of a certain type. But besides these causal laws, classical physics always made use of certain statistical considerations. As a matter of fact, the occurrence of probabilities was justified by the fact that the initial state was never exactly known; so long as this was the case, statistical methods might be, more or less provisionally, adopted. ...
> The physical assumption corresponds to this: we make an assumption about the initial distribution, if possible, one about equally probable cases, and then we try to show that our initial distribution is irrelevant for the final, observable, results. We see both parts of this procedure in [classical] statistical mechanics: we divide the phase space into equally probable cells, guided only by certain general theorems (conservation of energy, Liouville’s theorem); at the same time we try to translate the resulting space-distribution into a distribution in *time*. But the ergodic hypothesis, which was to effect this translation, and states that every system if left to itself covers in time its phase space uniformly, is a pure hypothesis and is likely to remain one. It thus seems that the justification of the choice of equally probable cases by dividing the phase space into cells can only be derived *a posteriori* from its successes in explaining several phenomena. (Born, 1927a, p. 354)

$^{41}$ J. Robert Oppenheimer, who had already spent a year in Cambridge (under the supervision of Joseph John Thomson), applied on 18 August 1926, to the *Board of Research Studies* at Harvard University to be allowed to continue his studies with the fellowship under Professor Max Born in Göttingen, because the latter ‘was particularly interested in the problems at which I hope to work’ (Oppenheimer, 1980, p. 98). Paul Adrien Maurice Dirac, on the other hand, split his year of absence from Cambridge (on two research grants) between Niels Bohr’s Institute of Theoretical Physics in Copenhagen (September to December 1926) and Born’s Institute in Göttingen (arriving there shortly after Christmas 1926).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0082 -->

50 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

After this introduction, Born turned to microphysics and noted that the situation gets more complicated there. Especially, 'microscopic coordinates are only introduced to keep the individual phenomena at least theoretically determinate,' but 'do not exist for practical purposes.' Thus, even the validity of Coulomb's law in alpha particle scattering could be shown by Ernest Rutherford only by applying (indirect) statistical methods, and one had to ask the question whether the Newtonian concept of force should not be replaced by a statistical definition. Passing on, finally, to a quantum-mechanical description of microphysical phenomena, Born argued, does change the situation even more drastically, as it provides no means for the determination of particles in space and time. Hence, 'this suggests that quantum mechanics ... only answers properly put statistical questions, and says nothing about the course of individual phenomena' (Born, *loc. cit.*, p. 355). Still, one has a wave function and forces that 'determine the vibrations of ... ψ that depends on the position of all the particles (a function in configuration space), and determine them because the coefficients of the differential equations for ψ involve the forces themselves' (Born, *loc. cit.*). The main lesson that can be learned from quantum mechanics is as follows:

A knowledge of ψ enables us to follow the course of a physical process insofar as it is quantum-mechanically determinate: not in a causal sense, but in a statistical one. Every process consists of elementary processes, which we are accustomed to call transitions or jumps; the jump itself seems to defy all attempts to visualize it, and only its result can be ascertained. This result is, that after the jump, the system is in a different quantum state. The function ψ determines these transitions in the following way: every state of the system corresponds to a particular characteristic solution, an *Eigenfunktion*, of the differential equation; for example, the normal state the function ψ₁, the next state ψ₂, etc. For simplicity we assume that the system was originally in the normal state; after the occurrence of an elementary process the solution has been transformed into one of the form

$$\psi = c_1\psi_1 + c_2\psi_2 + c_3\psi_3 \ldots,$$ [(49)]

which represents a superposition of a number of *eigenfunctions* with definite amplitudes $c_1, c_2, c_3, \ldots$. Then the squares of the amplitudes $c_1^2, c_2^2, \ldots$, give the probability that after the jump the system is in the 1, 2, 3, state. Thus $c_1^2$ is the probability that in spite of the perturbation the system remains in the normal state, $c_2^2$ the probability that it has jumped to the second, and so on. These probabilities are thus dynamically determined. But what the system actually does is not determined, at least not by the laws that are at present known. (Born, *loc. cit.*, pp. 355–356)

Born considered the situation in the new atomic theory as having been prepared more or less by the previous statistical approaches in classical physics; although in the latter the problem arises how to identify the two different concepts of force—as determining the dynamics of individual particles and being derived from the statistical analysis of experiments—in quantum mechanics, 'this problem has no longer, strictly speaking, any sense.' The classical dynamical definition of force,

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0083 -->

I.3 Max Born's Probability Interpretation of Schrödinger's Wave Function 51

Born claimed, is so useful for the description of phenomena, because it is the limiting case of the new quantum-mechanical definition. As he noticed:

Actually, it is usually the adiabatic case with which we have to do: i.e., the limiting case where the external force (or the reaction of the parts of the system on each other) acts very slowly. In this case, to a very high approximation

$$c_1^2 = 1, \quad c_2^2 = 0, \quad c_3^2 = 0, \ldots,$$ [(50)]

that is, there is no probability for a transition, and the system is in the initial state again after the cessation of the perturbation. Such a slow perturbation is therefore reversible, as it is classically. One can extend this to the case where the final system is really under different conditions from the initial one; i.e., where the state has changed adiabatically, without transition. That is the limiting case with which classical mechanics is concerned. (Born, *loc. cit.*, p. 356)

Upon his return to Göttingen, Born worked out the details of the 'adiabatic case,' and in mid-October, he submitted an investigation on *'Das Adiabatenprinzip in der Quantenmechanik'* ('The Adiabatic Principle in Quantum Mechanics'), whose abstract stated the result achieved: 'A theorem analogous to Ehrenfest's adiabatic principle can be formulated and proved on the basis of the statistical interpretation of quantum mechanics, developed recently in connection with collision phenomena' (Born, 1926c, p. 167). In his *Recollections*, Born explained the intention and goal of his paper as follows:

There were other ways of confirming the statistical interpretation. The simplest method seemed to me the action of an external force with given time dependence on an atomic system. A special feature of such processes, which interested me particularly, was the so-called adiabatic principle, which was formulated, during the Bohr-Sommerfeld period of quantum theory, by Paul Ehrenfest in the following manner. As an atomic system exchanges energy, according to Planck, only in quanta of finite energy *hν*, where *ν* is the frequency, *h* Planck's constant, a very slowly changing force (with only small frequency components) can produce no "quantum jump" between stationary states at all, but only a continuous modification of the properties of these states. This principle has been used to determine (or should one rather say guess?) the quantities which were characteristic for the stationary states (adiabatic invariants). Now the question arose as to how this adiabatic property could be derived from quantum mechanics.
This question was answered in several papers, the first by myself alone, later ones in collaboration with the very gifted Russian physicist V. Fock. (Born, 1978, p. 233)

The first work mentioned above treated the envisaged problem with great technical effort. The time-dependent Schrödinger equation is written for the motion of an electron in a potential plus a time-dependent perturbation, and the solution is calculated and discussed in all steps. Born recognized the central mathematical 'trick' in the following observation:

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0084 -->

52 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

If the system is transformed by a perturbation that lasts a finite time from one state to another, the constants of distribution, whose squares denote the probabilities for the state, undergo an orthogonal transformation

$$c_n = \sum_m b_{mn} c_m, \quad \sum_k b_{mk} b_{nk}^* = \delta_{mn}$$ [(51)]

The squares of the coefficients then are the transition probabilities

$$\Phi_{nm} = |b_{nm}|^2, \quad \sum_m \Phi_{mn} = 1.$$ [(52)]

(Born, 1926c, p. 176)

The general results derived from the intricate calculations may be summarized as follows:

(1) Quantum-mechanical transition processes are reversible like the classical ones, except that the reversibility is now expressed as a property of the transition probabilities (Born, *loc. cit.*, p. 178).
(2) Evaluating the probabilities for spontaneous emission requires higher-order calculations (Born, *loc. cit.*, p. 181).
(3) 'For infinitely slow perturbations the probability of a quantum jump is zero.' This theorem corresponds to the classical theorem of adiabatic invariance of action integrals.' (Born, *loc. cit.*, p. 182)
(4) The most general 'adiabatic theorem,' i.e., one with perturbing forces that do not vanish after a finite time period but retain a constant value, can be proved, at least up to the fourth order (Born, *loc. cit.*, p. 190).

The paper of October 1926 did not end Born's interest in the problem of adiabatic invariance. In summer 1928, he returned to it and treated, together with his Russian visitor Vladimir Fock, the particular case of systems with degenerate energy states, for which the earlier demonstration had failed. Born and Fock, after carrying through the necessary steps with more satisfactory and general mathematical methods (developed meanwhile by Paul Dirac, Fock, and others), concluded with the optimistic remark that 'the adiabatic theorem may even be valid in cases not substantiated here; probably the theorem remains true also for systems having, in addition to a point spectrum [i.e., discrete energy states], a continuous spectrum' (Born and Fock, 1928, p. 178).

(e) **Born's School of Quantum Mechanics (1926–1933)**

Max Born's lecture at the *British Association* meeting at Oxford in summer 1926 showed him as taking a leading role in the mathematical theory and physical interpretation of quantum mechanics. He became the first principal spokesman for the majority of quantum physicists, who felt uneasy, if not under attack, by Erwin

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0085 -->

I.3 Max Born's Probability Interpretation of Schrödinger's Wave Function 53

Schrödinger's quasi-classical continuum interpretation of wave mechanics. He stated his aim again quite sharply in October 1926:

This point of view consists in considering a fusion of mechanics and statistics in the following sense: The new mechanics, unlike the old one, does not answer the question: "How does this particle move?", but the question: "How probable is it that a particle moves in a given way?" Hence the existence of particles (point charges, electrons) is assumed, but, strictly speaking, only in the case when no forces are acting. The particles are always accompanied by waves; the de Broglie-Schrödinger waves depend on the forces present, and the square of their amplitude determines the probability that a particle is present in the state of motion corresponding to the wave. (Born, 1926c, pp. 167–168)

It was quite obvious to Born that quantum mechanics could not be understood as a continuity theory, as attempted by Schrödinger and welcomed by many, especially (but not only) older colleagues.⁴² He rather argued that one had to involve 'the fundamental ideas of the matrix theory created by Heisenberg,' which arise from 'a natural description of an atomic process by means of "quantum jumps"' and 'emphasize the character of these processes as inconceivable [on the basis of] the classical-geometrical description' (Born, *loc. cit.*). In particular, Born criticized the recent views of Schrödinger, expressed in his fourth communication (Schrödinger, 1926h), that in a single atom 'several eigenvibrations are excited simultaneously': this assumption would contradict the usual natural interpretation of continuous atomic energy states, like the orbits of electrons leaving ionized atoms (and being rendered visible in a cloud chamber). 'We shall, therefore, stick to Bohr's view that an atomic system always assumes only *one* stationary state,' he argued, or more generally: 'At a given instant of time, all we know is that—according to the prehistory and the existing physical conditions—a certain probability exists for the fact that an atom is in the *n*-th state. And we further claim that we have to select as a measure for this *probability of state* the quantity $|c_n|^2 = |\int \psi(x,t)\psi_n^*(x,t)dx|^2$ (Born, *loc. cit.*, pp. 170–171).
In spite of some initial opposition, the probability interpretation of the wave function was quickly accepted by most of the quantum physicists, except the most senior ones. Among the latter, Einstein, Planck, and Max von Laue reacted very skeptically to the abandonment of causality in the classical sense.⁴³ Einstein, in particular, disagreed with almost all statements in this regard in Born's papers and, already in the first expression of his lasting dissent, he wrote to Born: 'Quantum mechanics is very impressive. But an inner voice tells me that it is not yet the real thing [*der Wahre Jakob*]. The theory says a lot, but does not bring us closer to the secret of the Old One. I am at all events convinced that *He* is not

---
