<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0086 -->

54 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

playing at dice’ (Einstein to Born, 4 December 1926, in Einstein *et al.*, 1971, p. 91). Among the younger physicists, Adalbert Rubinowicz, an early contributor to the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory of atomic structure, noted: ‘I recall that Born’s paper did interest me so much that I took it [with me] on a walk. I stopped at a tramway stop to meet my wife and was studying it. Born’s point of view appeared to me to be quite a natural one, a continuation of the views of the older quantum theory’ (Rubinowicz, AHQP Interview, p. 18). Similarly, George Uhlenbeck—a young man and new contributor to quantum mechanics at Leyden at the time of the appearance of Born’s paper—recalled: ‘That was one of the papers which we discussed very much and which I had to study ... I accepted the probability interpretation very soon. It was probably in connection with that ... that Ehrenfest said, what we should do now was to see the consequences of all these things for statistics ... That was then the whole task which came in fall of 1926. It was until 1927 that we worked on that’ (Uhlenbeck, AHQP Interview, Session IV, p. 14).<sup>44</sup> Finally, Eugene Wigner, who, at that time, was in Berlin, where Einstein, Planck, and von Laue were skeptical, confessed: ‘I am sure that for me the physical content of Born’s paper was not a surprise’ (Wigner, AHQP Interview, p. 12).

Though Born’s statistical interpretation appeared to be obvious or ‘natural’ to many of his colleagues working in the field of quantum and wave mechanics, it augmented Born’s own reputation as much as his contributions to the fundamental theory itself. In particular, the clear lectures on atomic theory that he had delivered in the United States, his many brilliant publications in *Zeitschrift für Physik*, and finally his talk at Oxford, helped in attracting a considerable number of visitors to his institute at the University of Göttingen, where the new theory had been pioneered. In his *Recollections*, Born himself noted rather modestly: ‘During the first years of quantum mechanics Göttingen remained a centre for theoretical physics, where numerous excellent students from many countries gathered’ (Born, 1978, p. 234). In fact, the cream of the young theoretical physicists now considered

<sup>44</sup> Ehrenfest was evidently quite interested in Born’s work on extending the validity of his ‘adiabatic principle’ to the new quantum mechanics. In a paper submitted in September 1927, he also studied the use of the (classically defined) force in wave mechanics, demonstrating the analogy between the behaviour of a wave packet and a particle. For a solution of the one-dimensional wave equation

$$ - \frac{h^2}{8\pi^2 m}\frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial x^2} + V(x)\psi - i \frac{h}{2\pi} \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial t} = 0 $$

and for the solution $\psi^*(x)$ of the conjugate equation, he derived the equation:

$$ m \frac{d^2}{dt^2} \int \psi^* \psi dx = \int \psi^* \left( - \frac{dV}{dx} \right) \psi dx $$

or, briefly,

$$ m\ddot{x} = -\frac{dV}{dx}. $$

Thus, Newton’s second law holds for the mean values of position and force (Ehrenfest, 1927c). Ehrenfest based his analysis on the probability interpretation of the wave packet $\psi\psi^*$ (Ehrenfest, *loc. cit.*, p. 456).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0087 -->

I.4 Pascual Jordan’s ‘New Foundation’ of Quantum Mechanics 55

his institute as *the* proper place to learn and make progress in quantum mechanics, well comparable, or even preferable, to Copenhagen and Munich. As we have already noted, Oppenheimer and Dirac<sup>45</sup> arrived in 1926; Walter Heitler (from Zurich) and Léon Rosenfeld (from Paris) followed in 1927, and both of them became Born’s assistants. Many Russians—besides Vladimir Fock, Igor Tamm, and Yuri (George) Borisovich Rumer—turned up; the most gifted Hungarians—Eugen (Eugene) Wigner, Johannes (John) von Neumann, and Edward Teller (all coming via Berlin)—the first two being officially associated with the mathematician David Hilbert, also found themselves in Göttingen. Several excellent students took their doctoral degrees under Born: J. Robert Oppenheimer (in 1927), Max Delbrück (in 1930), and Maria Goeppert and Viktor Weisskopf (in 1931).

Although Born’s statistical interpretation also became quickly accepted in the mathematical circle around Hilbert—to which the physicist Lothar Nordheim belonged—it strangely encountered some resistance from his colleague James Franck, whose collision experiments had provided its basic foundation. As Pascual Jordan recalled: ‘For him [Franck] the idea of causality was so important that he did not like to give it up.’ (Jordan, AHQP Interview, Session IV, p. 25) Still, Franck believed in the great progress achieved by quantum mechanics, which described his own experiments so well, and he participated in achieving the high point of Göttingen science until 1933, when atomic physics flourished at the University of Göttingen through the close and lively interaction of theoretical and experimental physics and mathematics, at whose centre were the seminal ideas of Max Born.

## I.4 Pascual Jordan’s ‘New Foundation’ of Quantum Mechanics

On 29 July 1926, Pascual Jordan addressed a very personal letter to Niels Bohr. He wrote:

<sup>45</sup> Dirac submitted two papers for publication from Göttingen. The first one, on ‘The Quantum Theory of Dispersion’ (Dirac, 1927c), treated a problem, which in the work of Heisenberg and Kramers (1925), had helped to pave the way for quantum mechanics. In matrix theory, this problem had been dealt with in close analogy with the classical theory. Dirac felt that the quantum theory was now so well established that one could leave behind the bridge provided by the correspondence principle and use the theory of interaction between atoms and radiation, which he had just developed (Dirac, 1927b). The difficulty in the calculation of effects concerning absorption, emission, and scattering of radiation had been the choice of the electric field for the atom. Dirac concluded that the dipole field model he had used for the atom would give consistent results for the dispersion and resonance radiation in the first approximation; however, if one tried to calculate the width of a spectral line on the basis of this model, one would meet with a divergent result (Dirac, 1927c).

Dirac’s second paper from Göttingen was ‘Über die Quantenmechanik der Stoßvorgänge’ (‘On the Quantum Mechanics of Collision Processes,’ Dirac, 1927d). Born had discussed this subject in wave mechanics, and it had led him to the statistical interpretation of the wave function. Dirac also used the wave equation, which he had derived ‘honestly’ from quantum mechanics in his previous paper (Dirac, 1927a), but he now formulated it in momentum space. He applied his method to the absorption of radiation by atoms, thus treating an old problem of his own rather in the spirit of Born.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0088 -->

56 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

Highly esteemed Professor Bohr: Professor Franck informed me that you were so kind as to provide a sum of money to enable me to have a treatment for removing my speech impediment. I hasten to express my most cordial thanks to you for your great friendliness.

I expect to use the now starting vacation months fully for restoring my health. On the advice of my doctor, I shall go first to Bad Pyrmont for several weeks. Further, I intend to consult a neurologist, A. Adler in Vienna, whom Professor Lenz in Hamburg recently recommended to me strongly; the latter has been cured there of his nervous gastropathy.

At the beginning of the winter semester I plan to return to Göttingen and expect, if the treatment has led to the desired success, to obtain [my] *Habilitation* there.

Please allow me once more to express my sincerest thanks to you for your great kindness. I remain, with my most obliging greetings and highest respects, yours truly,

Pascual Jordan.

Upon obtaining his doctorate in fall 1924, Pascual Jordan, then Born’s personal assistant, had accomplished a lot of work within a couple of years. Especially, with Born, he had embarked upon two programmes: in the first half of 1925, they explored the consequences of the discrete, prequantum-mechanical approach to aperiodic systems (Born and Jordan, 1925a; Jordan, 1925b); then, they worked on the matrix formulation of Heisenberg’s pioneering ideas in summer 1925 (Born and Jordan, 1925b) and, joined by Heisenberg in fall, developed the complete matrix mechanics of multiply periodic systems (Born *et al.*, 1926). The Göttingen quantum mechanics, although conceptually very satisfactory (because it took care explicitly of the essential discreteness observed in all phenomena of quantum physics), had turned out to be rather cumbersome in handling practical problems; still, Heisenberg and Jordan, early in 1926, had succeeded in solving—by a clever extension of the matrix methods—one of the most complex problems of atomic theory: the anomalous Zeeman effects of many-electron atoms (Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926).<sup>46</sup>

Besides participating in these main quantum-theoretical efforts of the Göttingen team, Jordan had followed two further lines of investigation. One emerged from the problem for his doctoral dissertation, in which he had tried to bridge the gap between Einstein’s light-quanta and the Bohr–Kramers–Slater radiation theory (Jordan, 1924). His result had elicited a critical reply from Albert Einstein himself, but afterward a fruitful scientific exchange between the two scientists continued for many years. In that context, Jordan was very proud of a particular success that he had obtained by treating blackbody radiation with matrix-mechanical methods: namely, a formula that seemed to agree with Einstein’s famous energy-fluctuation formula (for radiation of frequency $\nu$ in a volume $V$),

$$ \bar{\Delta}_\nu^2 = (\overline{E_\nu^2} - \bar{E}_\nu^2) = h\nu \bar{E}_\nu + \frac{\bar{E}_\nu^2}{z_\nu V}, \qquad (53) $$

<sup>46</sup> See our discussion in Volume 3, Section V.5.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0089 -->

I.4 Pascual Jordan’s ‘New Foundation’ of Quantum Mechanics 57

where the first term described the corpuscular aspects and the second (with $z_\nu = 8\pi \nu^2 d\nu/c^3$, $c$ being the velocity of light *in vacuo*) the undulatory aspects of blackbody radiation.<sup>47</sup> Upon learning about this calculation, Einstein raised several objections.<sup>48</sup> Thus, for instance, he claimed that an important consequence of the light-quantum hypothesis did not follow (Einstein to Jordan, 6 March 1926); Jordan agreed that the formula for the probability of large fluctuations,

$$ W = \left( \frac{V}{V_0} \right)^{E/h\nu}, \qquad (54) $$

with $V$ denoting a small fraction of the total volume $V_0$, could not yet be obtained from matrix mechanics; however, he promised to continue his efforts on the problem.<sup>49</sup> For the time being, he considered another aspect of the light-quantum and matter-wave problem: In a paper, submitted in April 1926 to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, he demonstrated how earlier discussions (by William Duane, Arthur Compton, and others) about the interference of radiation from crystals ‘inevitably led to the conclusion that a material particle possesses certain physical properties, which obtain a visualizable (*anschauliche*) interpretation by the wave assigned to it by de Broglie’ (Jordan, 1926a, p. 376).

The second of Jordan’s research pursuits also went back to the year 1924, when—right after the completion of his dissertation—he had been drawn into a time-consuming project: ‘[James] Franck engaged me to help him with the preparation of the book *Anregung von Quantensprüngen durch Stöße*’ (Jordan, AHQP Interview, Session III, p. 7). This collaboration not only forced him to follow in detail the published literature, but also led to his own investigations on the structure of complex spectra (Jordan, 1925a, c). After much investment of time and effort—Jordan confided to Einstein in December 1925 that he hoped to have finished all of this work by the end of the following month—he and Franck finally signed the preface to the book in June 1926; it stated the outcome as:

> The numerous individual results of many investigations combine to provide a secure proof for the basic concepts of Bohr’s theory, in which they simultaneously find their general interpretation. The simple and profound idea of finite energy steps between

<sup>47</sup> See Volume 3, Section IV.2.

<sup>48</sup> Jordan communicated his result prior to publication to Einstein in a letter in fall 1925. Einstein then attacked the role played by zero-point energy (which, he thought, did not really exist in nature), to which Jordan replied: ‘My opinion about zero-point energy is roughly this: it is just a quantity of the calculation having no direct physical meaning. One can define physically only the thermal energy in the case of [temperature] $T = 0$; the fluctuations, which formally come out as fluctuations of the thermal and zero-point energy, are of course *identical with the fluctuations of the thermal energy*’ (Jordan to Einstein, 15 December 1925). Perhaps, he argued further, the calculation of the radiation pressure on the walls of the cavity might show a zero-point energy, but this could only be an improper (‘ungeschickte’) interpretation that had to be removed by a later, consistent matrix theory of the electromagnetic field.

<sup>49</sup> Letter from Jordan to Einstein, undated (spring 1926); see also the later review (Jordan, 1928), which we shall discuss in Chapter II.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0090 -->

58 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

discrete states of atoms and molecules in connection with energy conservation and the $h\nu$-relation succeeds in an amazing manner to account for all observations on the elementary processes caused by atomic collisions. Concerning the important question for the probabilities of quantum transitions, only poor material is available; but, as far as it can be seen up to now, Bohr’s correspondence principle also acts as a safe guide. (Franck and Jordan, 1926a, p. v)

The book of Franck and Jordan received a warm welcome, as several reviews revealed. Thus, the spectroscopist Walter Grotrian emphasized that the authors had not avoided problematic aspects of the collision phenomena and were rather critical of both experimental and theoretical methods found in the existing literature:

> It so happens that some of the older papers are not mentioned at all, and the results of other investigations are interpreted differently from what the authors did themselves. Hence the book, especially in those parts which deal with the interpretation of experiments, presents itself so-to-say as an actual panoramic view of the present ideas on atomic collisions. Because of the reputation of the authors, who constitute a fortunate combination of experimentalist and theoretician, it is evident that this view has been taken with a camera lens of the highest quality and particular depth and sharpness of focus [*Tiefenschärfe*], and therefore reveals many peculiarities which could not be recognized on any partial photograph (i.e., original paper). This fact renders the reading of the book specially thrilling. (Grotrian, 1927, p. 18)

The young theoretician Pascual Jordan, thus highly praised as a specialist on atomic collision processes, had much reason in summer 1926 to be quite exhausted. The hard work on the above-mentioned book added to the strenuous search for extending the Heisenberg–Born–Jordan scheme of matrix mechanics. At the same time, the successful Göttingen theoretical crew received a blow from the first publications on a rival scheme of atomic theory, the wave mechanics of Erwin Schrödinger. Jordan recalled this event:

> Well, I heard about it through a physicist in Göttingen, who was Austrian and somehow knew Schrödinger personally; he had become acquainted with the topic from the author, and he then reported to us in Göttingen. But at that time we did not yet know what to do with it. Then when Schrödinger’s paper became available, we were of course strongly impressed and convinced that it contained something which was correct. (Jordan, AHQP Interview, Session III, p. 12)

Soon after Schrödinger’s first communication appeared, Jordan received a letter from his friend Wolfgang Pauli, who called the paper ‘one of the most important ones written recently,’ and then explained the connection of the wave-mechanical results with those of the Göttingen matrix mechanics (Pauli to Jordan, 12 April 1926).$^{50}$ Pauli’s letter and Schrödinger’s communication on the equivalence of the two theories that appeared several weeks later convinced Jordan: ‘Then the mean-

$^{50}$ We have discussed Pauli’s letter to Jordan in detail in Volume 5, Part 2, Section IV.3.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0091 -->

I.4 Pascual Jordan’s ‘New Foundation’ of Quantum Mechanics 59

ing of the thing seemed to us completely clear, in the sense that the conceptual-physical content was not changed *vis-a-vis* our point of view, but now a new mathematical method was available to solve the equations of motion of quantum mechanics’ (Jordan, *loc. cit.*). As Born’s collaborator in treating aperiodic processes, he knew about the difficulty, if not impossibility, of applying the matrix scheme to such problems, and he welcomed and immediately approved Born’s new wave-mechanical collision theory of June and July 1926. However, unlike before, he did not assist Born in this task, and it is easy to conclude from the above-mentioned preoccupations that Jordan simply did not have the time to do so (or was too exhausted) to embark upon a new investigation.

As he had written to Bohr at the end of the summer semester, he spent the following months of summer and early fall first in Bad Pyrmont, to recover from the stress of previous work, and then in Vienna seeking to cure his speech impediment with the help of Dr. Adler. In Vienna, he heard exciting news about wave mechanics and its interpretation. He recalled:

> For a while Schrödinger entertained the hope of abolishing quantum mechanics completely. I was then in Vienna and listened to a lecture by Schrödinger, in which he explained his ideas and said, for example, that the emission [of radiation] from an excited state to the ground state can only happen when both eigenfunctions are excited, then interfere and give rise to a beat frequency. (Jordan, *loc. cit.*)

Evidently, this point of view contradicted decisively the Göttingen concepts of quantum mechanics and the physical interpretation derived from them, and Jordan recalled having criticized Schrödinger right after the lecture. He repeated the same criticism a year later when he reviewed the collection of Schrödinger’s communications, *Abhandlungen zur Wellenmechanik*:

> Admittedly, these papers of Schrödinger should not be placed in the hands of a beginner without emphasizing the grave differences between the quantum-theoretical concepts adopted by the majority of physicists and the views which Schrödinger has used as guiding ideas for his mathematical investigations. The origin of these differences lies, in short, in the fact that Schrödinger does *not* really wish to consider his results as a continuation of the ideas of Planck, Einstein and Bohr. These investigators had introduced *discontinuities*, *quantum jumps*, etc., into the theory—that is, concepts which can be explained in no way by models within the context of ideas of classical mechanics . . . Now Schrödinger has . . . (with reference to de Broglie) discovered the possibility to deduce from some wave system, which can be constructed easily, the physical properties of a quantum-mechanical system. While the majority of the physicists shares the opinion that this representation of the physical properties of the system has the same symbolic meaning as the matrix-theoretical representation . . . —and that it, like the other, can only assist in quantitatively describing the possible quantum jumps of the system and the probabilities in the case of different types of external actions—Schrödinger has attempted on his part not to use his results for quantitative sharpening but for *overcoming* Bohr’s theory: he has ascribed to the wave system associated with a moving quantum-mechanical particle a genuine reality

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0092 -->

60 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

in the sense of the classical theory; replacing the corpuscular view by a wave view should suffice to render the assumption of “quantum jumps” completely superfluous; the wave system should provide a complete model of the atom, operating in a totally classical and causal manner. (Jordan, 1927e, p. 413)

Jordan concluded that Schrödinger’s interpretation implied consequences that differed, for instance, in the case of the radiating atom, crucially from those of Bohr’s theory and the Göttingen quantum mechanics, and that the ‘causal model’ especially contradicted Einstein’s 1916 derivation of Planck’s radiation law.

After his return to Göttingen later in the fall of 1926—evidently with an improvement of his health and speech impediment—Jordan immediately concerned himself with demonstrating the essential correctness of the Göttingen view of quantum mechanics. Soon, toward the end of November, he submitted a note ‘Über quantenmechanische Darstellung von Quantensprüngen’ (‘On the Quantum-Mechanical Representation of Quantum Jumps,’ Jordan, 1927a), the intentions and results of which he summarized in the abstract as:

> According to the elementary views of quantum theory the interaction of atoms in collisions, with radiation, etc., can be described by assuming discontinuous quantum jumps. In contrast to this, the exact quantum mechanics must consider these interactions as being connected with a continuous energy exchange formally represented by slow beats. In the case of a simple but characteristic example a detailed proof is presented for the fact that both types of description yield, in spite of very different methods, the same results for all conclusions that are capable of being tested empirically. (Jordan, 1927a, p. 661)

Evidently, Jordan had convinced himself that the interactions between atoms and electrons or radiation had to be described by quantum-mechanical or wave-mechanical methods, which formally accounted for the processes by slow, *continuous* beats; the laws of quantum mechanics, however, also made sure that in ‘all experimentally decidable (*entscheidbaren*) problems the same answers were obtained (in first approximation) as followed from the elementary, discontinuous description of the processes.’ (Jordan, *loc. cit.*)

To prove his assertion, Jordan selected a system of two different atoms, such that, in the case of no coupling, the energy of the quantum states $n_1 = 0, n_2 = 1$ is the same as the energy of the quantum states $n_1 = 1, n_2 = 0$ (i.e., the system is degenerate with the exchange of the atoms 1 and 2). In order to obtain the exchange of two atoms in matrix mechanics, he switched on the interaction term $\lambda \mathbf{H}^1$ and calculated the transformation matrix $\mathbf{T}$, which allowed him to diagnoilize the full Hamiltonian. Jordan then found: if the matrix elements of $\mathbf{T}$ for the vanishing parameter $\lambda$ denoted the probabilities for atoms to be finally in the states 0 and 1, respectively, then the (infinitesimally) slow, continuous quantum-mechanical process, establishing that the exchange of the quantum states of the two atoms yielded identical results, as had been derived from the assumption of elementary, discontinuous jumps in a suitable interval of time. The task remained

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0093 -->

I.4 Pascual Jordan’s ‘New Foundation’ of Quantum Mechanics 61

also to establish the identity of the matrix elements with the corresponding observed probabilities; this could be accomplished by means of three experimental methods:

(1) One creates certain quantum jumps of one of the atoms and concludes, from the energy transitions involved and the probabilities of these jumps, the previous state of the atom.
(2) One measures the average value of a quantity, which is a constant for an isolated atom, the average value of its square, etc., directly.
(3) One accelerates the atom by an external force, which acts differently on the states $n_1 = 0$ and $n_1 = 1$ of an isolated atom.

Jordan calculated only the (theoretical) results for the situation (1), and added in a footnote: ‘A detailed discussion of “method B” [(2)] can be found in a manuscript, which I got to see after completing this note’ (Jordan, *loc. cit.*, p. 666).$^{51}$

The November note constituted just a small exercise in the quantum-mechanical formalism, as compared with the next work, which Jordan completed less than a month later and submitted for publication under the self-confident title ‘Über eine neue Begründung der Quantenmechanik’ (‘On a New Foundation of Quantum Mechanics,’ Jordan, 1927b). The abstract indicates what Jordan, at that time, Born’s sole assistant—because both Heisenberg and Friedrich Hund stayed for the winter semester 1926–1927 in Copenhagen—accomplished, namely:

> The four hitherto developed schemes of quantum mechanics—matrix theory, the theory of Born and Wiener, wave mechanics, and [Dirac’s] theory of $q$-numbers—are contained as special cases in a more general formal theory. Following an idea of Pauli, this theory can be based on some simple fundamental postulates of a statistical nature. (Jordan, *loc. cit.*, p. 809)

The new paper established, as Jordan explained further, ‘a close connection’ between these fundamental schemes, of which the three latter (i.e., of Dirac, Born and Wiener, and Schrödinger) ‘stood there without any relation between each other,’ because: ‘The general proof was missing that they led to equivalent results, even where they went beyond the matrix theory’ (Jordan, 1927b, p. 810). The method he selected for providing the proof consisted in applying *canonical transformations* to the fundamental equation, which in the case of wave mechanics took the form of Schrödinger’s equation; in particular, he pioneered what later came to be called the ‘statistical transformation theory’ of quantum mechanics.

Already in 1926 Jordan had investigated the form and use of canonical transformations in quantum mechanics. First, he had shown in the paper on the interference scattering of radiation by lattices (mentioned earlier) how a canonical transformation can serve in the Born–Wiener or Dirac scheme to obtain the solu-

$^{51}$ Jordan referred to a paper of his colleague Werner Heisenberg (who was then in Copenhagen), entitled ‘Mehrkörperprobleme und Resonanz in der Quantenmechanik. II’ (‘Many-Body Problems and Resonance in Quantum Mechanics. II’, Heisenberg, 1927a), which we shall discuss later.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0094 -->

62
Chapter I
The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

tion of the problem—a canonical transformation being defined by the property that it preserves the Heisenberg–Born–Jordan commutation relations of momentum and position variables, $p_k$ and $q_k$ (Jordan, 1926a). In his second solo paper of 1926, entitled ‘*Über kanonische Transformationen in der Quantenmechanik*’ (‘On the Canonical Transformations in Quantum Mechanics’) and received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* only five days later, Jordan provided—as we have discussed already in Section I.2—the proof that the most general canonical transformation $\mathbf{S}$ can be written in the matrix form: $\mathbf{P}_k = \mathbf{S}p_k\mathbf{S}^{-1}$ and $\mathbf{Q}_k = \mathbf{S}q_k\mathbf{S}^{-1}$ (Jordan, 1926b). More than two months after that—in between, the author must have been occupied with the completion of the Franck–Jordan book—he would submit a second note on the same subject (Jordan, 1926c).

The July paper started from the Hamilton–Jacobi formalism of classical mechanics, with $S$ denoting the characteristic function. Jordan now proposed to describe ‘point’ or canonical transformations by the *Ansatz*,

$$S(\alpha, q) = \sum_n f_n(\alpha)g_n(q), \tag{55}$$

with $f_n$ and $g_n$ representing functions of the arguments $\alpha(= \alpha_k)$ and $q(= q_k)$, respectively, and he took the known transformation equations, i.e.,

$$p_k = \frac{\partial S(\alpha, q)}{\partial q_k} \quad \text{and} \quad \beta_k = \frac{\partial S(\alpha, q)}{\partial \alpha_k}. \tag{56}$$

Evidently, the $p_k$, $q_k$ and $\alpha_k$, $\beta_k$ were two sets of canonically conjugate pairs of momentum and position variables. The classical transformation ‘matrix’ $T(\alpha, \beta)$—with $p_k = T\alpha T^{-1}$ and $q_k = T\beta T^{-1}$—could then be written as

$$T(\alpha, \beta) = \exp\left[\frac{2\pi i}{h} \sum \phi_n(\alpha)\psi_n(\beta)\right], \tag{57}$$

and its logarithm was related to the characteristic function $S$ (for a system of $f$ degrees of freedom) by the equation

$$\ln T = \sum_{k=1}^f \alpha_k q_k - S(\alpha, q). \tag{58}$$

This formalism, Jordan argued, might be easily taken over into the quantum-mechanical theory: one had just to observe that the variables represented ‘$q$-numbers.’ He did not proceed further, and we also notice that, by the middle of 1926, Jordan did not refer specifically to any of the quantum-mechanical theories that had meanwhile become available—probably because of lack of time.
Jordan had proceeded thus far when he interrupted his scientific work for

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0095 -->

I.4 Pascual Jordan’s ‘New Foundation’ of Quantum Mechanics
63

several months. When he returned to the problem in November 1926, a serious competition had arisen. Fritz London had employed himself with canonical transformations connected with action-angle variables in quantum mechanics since spring 1926; he had found in May—as we have discussed in Section I.2—that the Born–Heisenberg–Jordan unitary matrix $\mathbf{S}$, which transforms the variables of a multiply periodic atomic system to action and angle variables, should play a crucial role in the quantum-theoretical analogue of the classical Hamilton–Jacobi formalism (London, 1926b). He continued his interest in this topic later on, when he switched from the Göttingen–Cambridge algebraic schemes to discussing ‘*Winkelvariable und kanonische Transformationen in der Undulationsmechanik*’ (‘The Angle Variables and Canonical Transformations in Undulatory Mechanics’)—which was the title of a paper he completed early in September (London, 1926d). That is, London now attempted to create the analogue of the successful classical action-angle formalism also in Schrödinger’s wave mechanics. Such a method had not yet been developed, he claimed, because the previous evaluations of problems connected with periodic atomic systems by Schrödinger and others had so far employed only ‘point transformations’ $Q = f(q)$ of the position variables. Thus, in the introduction of his paper, London stated:

> The description of the undulatory processes to which Schrödinger reduced quantum-theoretical events, made use exclusively of the “$q$-spaces” as manifolds of the mathematical formalisms. It is known [on the other hand] what an extraordinary symmetry classical mechanics displays if—instead of the coordinates and their time derivatives—one introduces coordinates and momenta as “canonical” variables, and thus opens the possibility of reducing the solution of a mechanical problem to searching for the transformation to uniformizing variables. (London, *loc. cit.*, p. 193)

Consequently, he proposed to generalize the ‘point transformation’ of wave mechanics appropriately, and—in analogy to canonical transformations—gave them the form

$$Q = F\left(q, \frac{\partial}{\partial q}\right) \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{\partial}{\partial Q} = G\left(q, \frac{\partial}{\partial q}\right). \tag{59}$$

The functions $F$ and $G$ cannot be chosen arbitrarily, of course, but only such that, given the operator $F$, $G$ must be defined as a ‘differential operation which really means the differentiation with respect to the operator $Q$ as defined by $F$’ (London, *loc. cit.*, p. 194). Further, the transformation (59) had to leave the ‘commutation relation’

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial q}q - q\frac{\partial}{\partial q} = 1 \tag{60}$$

invariant.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0096 -->

64
Chapter I
The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

London interpreted the condition (60) as characterizing the product rule of differentiation; he further noticed that the sum rule for the differentiation can be satisfied for arbitrary operators $G$. With all of these relations, however, $G$ was defined only up to an additive function $f(Q)$—but this term would not cause difficulties in practical applications. Then, he constructed the canonical transformations by ‘simply taking over the representation in matrix mechanics (not the one in classical mechanics) and replacing everywhere $p$ by $(h/2\pi i)\partial/\partial q$’ (London, *loc. cit.*, p. 195). In order to establish the full analogy with the Hamilton–Jacobi method, London proposed the following *Ansatz* for the operator $Q$:

$$Q = \frac{\partial S[q, (h/2\pi i)(\partial/\partial Q)]}{\partial P}$$

and

$$\frac{h}{2\pi i}\frac{\partial}{\partial q} = \frac{\partial S[q, (h/2\pi i)(\partial/\partial Q)]}{\partial q}, \tag{61}$$

with $S = S(q, P)$ an arbitrary function of the variables $q$ and $P$, denoting the original position coordinate $q$ and the transformed momentum variable $P$ (as in the classical case). Evidently, Eqs. (61) defined a canonical transformation in quantum mechanics, with $\partial/\partial P$ and $\partial/\partial q$ representing suitable differential operations.$^{52}$ London referred to Jordan’s earlier paper (Jordan, 1926c) and then demonstrated that the eigenvalues $E^*$ of the transformed Schrödinger equation,

$$\left[H\left(Q, \frac{\partial}{\partial Q}\right) T\left(q, \frac{\partial}{\partial Q}\right), \psi^*(Q)\right] = E^* \left[T\left(Q, \frac{\partial}{\partial Q}\right), \psi^*(Q)\right], \tag{62}$$

were identical with the eigenvalues $E$ of the original equation,

$$\left[H\left(q, \frac{\partial}{\partial q}\right), \psi(q)\right] = E\psi(q), \tag{62a}$$

provided the operator of transformation $T$—with $q = T^{-1}QT$ and $\frac{\partial}{\partial q} = T^{-1}\frac{\partial}{\partial Q}T$—satisfied the equation

$$\left[T\left(Q, \frac{\partial}{\partial Q}\right), \psi^*(Q)\right] = \psi(Q). \tag{63}$$

$^{52}$ In general, $S$ has to be properly symmetrized in the products of the operators.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0097 -->

I.4 Pascual Jordan’s ‘New Foundation’ of Quantum Mechanics
65

London now proposed to interpret the formalism, expressed in Eqs. (62), (62a), and (63) in the following language—as he said, an ‘interpretation which has been guessed already in matrix mechanics but not yet fully realized’—namely:

> The canonical transformations are rotations in [an infinite dimensional] Hilbert space. . . .
> The canonical transformations of the matrices then are transformations induced by the rotation of arbitrary linear transformations of the simultaneous system [of eigenfunctions] $\psi_k$. . . .
> The intensities [i.e., matrix elements] are therefore invariants of the rotations, the eigenvalues on the other hand [are] affine invariants in the Hilbert space. (London, 1926d, pp. 197–200)

With the new formalism, which London found largely to coincide with older mathematical schemes,$^{53}$ he demonstrated that the solution of the Schrödinger equation corresponded to a ‘Hermitean eigenvalue problem’ (London, *loc. cit.*, pp. 200–201), and that angle variables in wave mechanics may be introduced with the help of the Jacobi function $S$,

$$S(q, J) = \sum_\nu f_\nu(q)g_\nu(J), \tag{64}$$

yielding the following orthogonal system of eigenfunctions$^{54}$

$$\psi_n(q) = \psi(J, q) = \exp\left[\frac{2\pi i}{h} S(q, J)\right], \quad \text{with } J = nh/2\pi, \quad n = 0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots \tag{65}$$

After deriving several known results with the help of the new transformation-theoretical scheme (London, *loc. cit.*, pp. 202–205), London concluded his paper by discussing the concept of angle variables in matrix mechanics (pp. 205–209).
When Jordan returned to the problem of canonical transformations in quantum mechanics, London’s detailed investigation on this topic had not yet appeared in print.$^{55}$ Hence, it could not and did not influence Jordan in dealing again with the quantum-mechanical transformation theory during the last months of 1926.

$^{53}$ London wrote in a footnote: ‘Only after finishing the paper I have noticed the close connection of the results of this section with quite general, abstract work especially of Italian mathematicians on *distributive functional operators*. So S. Pincherle (*Math. Ann.* 49, 325, (1897)) proves that our differential operations are essentially identical with the distributive operations [i.e., $[T, (\phi + \psi)] = [T, \phi] + [T, \psi]$; further, T. Cazzaniga (*Torino Rend.* 34, 510, (1899)] showed that to these there correspond the affine representations’ (London, 1926d, footnote 2, p. 199).
$^{54}$ London mentioned that this result agreed with the earlier observations of Léon Brillouin (1926a) and Gregor Wentzel (1926d).
$^{55}$ In a footnote of his memoir, Jordan mentioned: ‘The formal results of the following paper have been obtained partially also by F. London and presented in a paper [London, 1926d], which was published after the completion of my manuscript, in a very clear and intelligible manner’ (Jordan, 1927b, p. 809).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0098 -->

66 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

Rather different motives revived Jordan’s interest, in particular, the acquaintance with undulatory mechanics, Born’s statistical interpretation of the wave function, and Schrödinger’s alternative causal interpretation. Although he agreed fully with Born’s views, he recalled how he rejected Schrödinger’s from the very beginning and tried to defend the Göttingen interpretation:

> I am not entirely certain, but I wanted to demonstrate exactly with respect to Schrödinger’s interpretation—which I rejected—that the [Göttingen] quantum-mechanical interpretation is completely self-contained, and is therefore in a position—in principle —to deal consistently with collision processes and the like. (Jordan, AHQP Interview, Session III, p. 14)⁵⁶

In other words, after Born had proposed his statistical interpretation and applied it to collision processes, ‘there arose the necessity to provide a generalized physical interpretation, ... the physical idea was a generalization, one might say, of the statistical interpretation of the Schrödinger function,’ not really a formal extension of Jordan’s previous results on the quantum-mechanical transformation theory (which London had provided) (Jordan, *loc. cit.*).
Upon Jordan’s procedure, however, another physicist—Wolfgang Pauli— exerted a crucial influence. He would be acknowledged both in Jordan’s publication and later recollections: ‘At that time we often conducted many discussions. We were together in vacations in Neuwerk, and we met each other in Göttingen or Hamburg, or else partly in Copenhagen. Of course, we discussed then quite a lot, which I cannot reproduce now in detail.’ (Jordan, AHQP Interview, *loc. cit.*, p. 15) In his paper, Jordan then referred explicitly to an idea ‘stemming from Pauli, by which the real (*eigentliche*) meaning of the quantum-mechanical laws was put into a new light (‘*in ein neues Licht gerückt wird*,’ Jordan, 1927b, p. 810), and this was:⁵⁷

> Pauli, in connection with Born’s considerations, has proposed the following physical interpretation of Schrödinger’s eigenfunctions: If $\phi_n(q)$ is normalized, then $|\phi_n(q)|^2 dq$ denotes the probability for the situation that the coordinate $q$ assumes a value in the interval between $q$ and $q + dq$, provided the system is in the state $n$.

And further:

> Pauli has thought of the following generalization: Let $q, \beta$ be two Hermitean quantum-mechanical variables, which we here, for the sake of convenience, consider both to be continuously changing; then there will always exist a function $\phi(q,\beta)$, such

⁵⁶ Jordan stressed upon the fact that in Göttingen all theoreticians shared the opinion against Schrödinger’s interpretation and recalled the following episode: ‘Once, on a walk Born—with Dirac, Oppenheimer, myself and perhaps one or two others—I read a letter of Schrödinger. Later Oppenheimer told me jokingly that Born had summoned his troops like a general and explained to them how wrong were the ideas that Schrödinger had expressed in his letter.’ (Jordan, *loc. cit.*)
⁵⁷ Pauli also mentioned the substance of these remarks in a letter to Heisenberg, dated 19 October 1926. (See Pauli, 1979, pp. 340–349.)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0099 -->

I.4 Pascual Jordan’s ‘New Foundation’ of Quantum Mechanics 67

that $|\phi(q_0,\beta_0)|^2 dq$ determines the (relative) probability that, for a fixed numerical value $\beta_0$ of $\beta$, the variable $q$ assumes a numerical value in the interval between $q_0$ and $q_0 + dq_0$. Pauli calls the function $\phi(q,\beta)$ a *probability amplitude*. (Jordan, *loc. cit.*, p. 811)

This idea of Pauli’s brought Jordan to ask: ‘How can one formulate the problem, which has been answered by introducing the Schrödinger eigenfunction, in a totally general manner?’ (Jordan, *loc. cit.*) Indeed, it would appear to be quite unnatural to assume that a statistical relation should only exist between energy and position variables, but not similar ones in more general cases.
Jordan split his long memoir ‘*Über eine neue Begründung der Quantenmechanik*’ (‘On a New Foundation of Quantum Mechanics’), which he completed in the middle of December 1926, into two (not quite equal) parts: the shorter Part I contained the physical motivation and the outline of the theory, and in Part II, Jordan developed the mathematical details and methods, which he concluded with a generalization of the idea (so cherished in Göttingen) of quantum jumps. Before embarking upon the analysis of this weighty paper, let us mention that, simultaneously with Jordan’s investigation, the distinguished old mathematician David Hilbert gave (in the winter semester of 1926–1927) a course at the University of Göttingen on the mathematical foundations of quantum mechanics. Hilbert’s lectures, prepared with the assistance of Lothar Nordheim—and later worked out and published together with Johannes (John) von Neumann (1928)—showed certain points of contact with the investigations of Jordan, who might have obtained some stimulus from them.⁵⁸
In spite of certain influences from the outside, whether from Pauli or Hilbert, Jordan followed his own line of interest in his investigations. He had an ambitious goal in mind, namely, to establish the equivalence of all of the different schemes of quantum mechanics, including problems dealing with aperiodic phenomena (where the previous formal proofs of Schrödinger, Pauli, and others did not work). He noticed, in particular, that the envisaged task might be accomplished by answering the following question (see Jordan, 1927b, pp. 809–810):

Given the Schrödinger equation with the Hamiltonian (operator) $H(p, q)$,
$$
\left\{ H \left( \frac{h}{2\pi i} \frac{\partial}{\partial y} \right) - W \right\} \phi(y) = 0, \quad [(66)]
$$
and a canonical transformation of the original variables, $p \left( = \frac{h}{2\pi i} \frac{\partial}{\partial y} \right)$ and $y$, to new variables, $P, Q$ (or $\frac{h}{2\pi i} \frac{\partial}{\partial x}$ and $x$), then the transformed Schrödinger equation with

⁵⁸ Note also the citation of Jordan’s work in the publication of Hilbert, von Neumann, and Nordheim (1928). It can be safely assumed that Jordan attended Hilbert’s lectures.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0100 -->

68 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

the Hamiltonian $\bar{H}(P, Q)$,
$$
\left\{ \bar{H} \left( \frac{h}{2\pi i} \frac{\partial}{\partial x}, x \right) - W \right\} \psi(x) = 0 \quad [(67)]
$$
is obtained with the new wave function $\psi(x)$. What is the relation of $\psi(x)$ to the wave function of the original Schrödinger equation [(66)]?

When asked whether the above question, by which Jordan opened his paper, also represented an ‘autobiographical’ introduction—i.e., it stood at the beginning of the work—he replied:

> I believe that is the way in which I started the problem ... As far as the formal, mathematical side is concerned: just as I tried to write down the most general forms of canonical transformations, I also tried to interpret the Schrödinger equation as a completely special case of the relations, which quite generally may be established between [quantum-mechanical] variables, that have some well-determined mutual relation with one another. (Jordan, AHQP Interview, Session III, p. 16)

Actually, the approach emerged directly from adapting the previous Göttingen programme of quantum mechanics to the recent advance of the wave-mechanical scheme. Thus, Jordan explained:

> The main stimulus and the main goal was, I think, to generalize the Schrödinger eigenfunctions and their statistical meaning. [I] attempted not to restrict [myself] to the knowledge of this one special relation—namely, for a given energy of an atom there exists a definite probability for the position of an electron—but rather to consider this to be a special case of a quite general problem.
> One can also say this: in establishing the matrix theory, we started from the basic idea only to consider observable quantities. All quantities which cannot be observed should be abolished from the theory. We had at first only recognized as observable quantities the energy of the atoms [i.e., of atomic states] and the transition amplitudes. Now with Schrödinger’s ideas, in the changed form which we had given to them, the possibility emerged to determine the *position*..., at least one talked about the probability that an electron possesses a definite position.... At any rate, now the possibility was suggested that one could also talk about other observable quantities, not just transition probabilities and energies. Hence the problem arose in a quite general sense: Which quantities must now be acknowledged somehow as observable? This was then the [guiding] idea: in the general situation any function of coordinates and momenta, considered as *q*-numbers [in the definition of Dirac] should be an observable quantity. Consequently, as in the case of Schrödinger’s eigenfunctions, one had to write down the corresponding statistical relations. (Jordan, AHQP Interview, Session IV, p. 11)

Further, because one could connect different pairs of canonical variables (functions of coordinates and momenta) by canonical transformations (with suitable characteristic functions $S$), it must be possible to establish as well a relation be-

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0101 -->

I.4 Pascual Jordan’s ‘New Foundation’ of Quantum Mechanics 69

tween the various quantum-mechanical schemes, each of which was evidently characterized by a particular choice of the pair of canonical variables and a particular characteristic function [see Eqs. (66) and (67)].
The Göttingen quantum mechanics rested upon a discrete formulation, being the natural consequence of commutation relations involving pairs of canonically conjugate variables. Because Schrödinger had attacked this fundamental procedure and confronted it by his continuous formulation, Jordan sought to provide a ‘new foundation of quantum mechanics’ without renouncing the advantages of the discrete view. This view seemed to be assured by the probability interpretation. Hence, he remarked later:

> According to the outline of the paper, I wished indeed to start with the probability relations.... Therefore, if one states that $p$ and $q$ are two variables, with an *a priori* probability relation existing between them, one might conclude the following: if the multiplication is defined, then the commutation rules emerge. It was my desire not to begin with the commutation relations but rather to derive them as a consequence of something else. (Jordan, AHQP Interview, Session III, pp. 16–17)

As ‘something else,’ the basic concept to start with, he chose what Pauli called ‘the probability amplitude’ $\phi(q,\beta)$, which should satisfy two postulates:

*Postulate I:* The function $\phi(q,\beta)$ does not depend on the mechanical nature (i.e., the Hamiltonian) of the system, but is only determined by the kinematic relation between $q$ and $\beta$.
*Postulate II:* If $\psi(Q_0, q_0)$ is the probability amplitude for the numerical value $Q_0$ of [the variable] $Q$, when $q$ assumes a fixed value $q_0$, then the amplitude $\Phi(Q_0, \beta_0)$ for a certain $Q_0$, when $\beta$ assumes a fixed value $\beta_0$, turns out to be
$$
\Phi(Q_0, \beta_0) = \int \psi(Q_0, q) \phi(q, \beta_0) dq, \quad [(68)]
$$
and the integration must be extended to the whole range of values of $q$. (Jordan, 1927b, p. 811)

Jordan emphasized the difference between his probability amplitude scheme and the previous probability schemes in physics: ‘The fact that not the probabilities themselves, but the amplitudes obey the usual combination law of probability calculus, may be called “the interference of probabilities”’ (Jordan, *loc. cit.*, p. 812).
Jordan’s paper was not easy reading, primarily because it attempted to present the theory in a rigorous mathematical language on the basis of proper postulates (axioms) and definitions. Jordan later recalled a discussion with Paul Ehrenfest, who was very interested in his approach, though he also remarked jokingly: ‘Since you have formulated the problem in an axiomatic manner, this only means that one must read the paper backwards’ (Jordan, AHQP Interview, Session III, p. 17). In any case, the axiomatic formulation implied lots of notation, often very cum-

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0102 -->

70 **Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory**

bersome. ‘I quite laboriously stirred around the formulae,’ Jordan admitted (Jordan, *loc. cit.*). With all of these facts in mind, the basic content of Section 2 of Part I could be summarized as follows (here, the ‘statistical foundations of quantum mechanics’ are sketched without proofs and mathematical details).

Jordan began by defining a quantum-mechanical variable $q$ as a quantity that varies on a certain set of points in the complex plane; the set, he said, may consist of segments of curves and discrete points. Although the multiplication of the values of quantum-mechanical variables obeys the rules of and multiplication of (real) numbers, those of the variables themselves were different and determined by the commutation rules. As noted above, however, Jordan did not consider the combination rules of variables among the ‘primary postulates of the theory,’ but preferred to use as such the statistical connections between two quantum-mechanical variables, $q$ and $\beta$, which had a definite kinematical relation. Then, he argued, two (complex-valued) functions $\phi(x, y)$ and $\psi(x, y)$ existed—Jordan called them ‘amplitude’ and ‘supplementary (*Ergänzungs-*) amplitude’ of probability—whose product $\phi(x, y)\psi^*(x, y) dx$ ($\psi^*$ being the complex conjugate of $\psi$) determines the probability $w$ that, for a fixed value of the variable $\beta$, $q$ assumes values between $x$ and $x + dx$ (*Postulate A*). With the help of *Postulate B*, Jordan defined the amplitude for the commuted pair $\beta, q$—i.e., $\bar{\phi}(x, y) = \psi^*(y, x)$ and $\bar{\psi}(x, y) = \phi^*(y, x)$—and derived the symmetry property for the probability, namely: ‘The probability $w(x, y) = \phi(x, y)\psi^*(x, y)$ for a value $xdq$, if $q$ assumes the value $y$, is the same as the probability for the value $y$ of $\beta$, if $q$ assumes the value $x$’ (Jordan, 1927b, p. 813). *Postulate C* then demands that the probabilities combine to yield characteristic interference effects.

From *Postulates B* and *C*, the orthogonality relations immediately followed,

$$ \int \phi(x, \beta'') \psi^*(x, \beta') dx = \int \phi(\beta'', x) \psi^*(\beta', x) dx = \delta_{\beta', \beta''}. \quad (69) $$

On defining the variable $p$ to be ‘canonically conjugate’ to the variable $q$, Jordan proposed—something that he knew already from the special case of momentum and position variables—the probability amplitude to have the form

$$ \rho(x, y) = \exp\left(-\frac{2\pi i}{h} xy\right) \quad (70) $$

for any value $x$ of $p$, if $q$ assumes the value $y$.$^{59}$ This definition evidently led to the conclusion: ‘For a given value of $q$ all possible values of $p$ have equal probability’ (Jordan, 1927b, p. 814). Finally, *Postulate D* was added, namely: ‘For any variable $q$ there exists a conjugate momentum $p$.’ (Jordan, *loc. cit.*)

---
$^{59}$ When asked how he came upon Eq. (70), Jordan answered: ‘It seemed to me interesting to take it as definition, because this definition remained applicable also to such cases as the spinning electron, where we have only finite matrices’ (Jordan, AHQP Interview, Session III, p. 16).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0103 -->

**I.4 Pascual Jordan’s ‘New Foundation’ of Quantum Mechanics 71**

Now, the amplitude $\rho(x, y)$ for canonically conjugate variables—$\rho(x, y)$ can be shown to be identical with the corresponding ‘supplementary amplitude’—satisfies the set of differential equations:

$$ \left\{ x + \frac{h}{2\pi i} \frac{\partial}{\partial y} \right\} \rho(x, y) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \left\{ - \frac{h}{2\pi i} \frac{\partial}{\partial x} - y \right\} \rho(x, y) = 0. \quad (71) $$

Also, amplitude $\phi(x, y)$, obtained from $\rho(x, y)$ by the action of a linear transformation $T$ (e.g., $T = \int dz \Phi(y, z) \dots$), then obeys the set of functional equations:

$$ \left\{ -TxT^{-1} + \frac{h}{2\pi i} \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \right\} \phi(x, y) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \left\{ T \frac{h}{2\pi i} \frac{\partial}{\partial x} T^{-1} - y \right\} \phi(x, y) = 0. \quad (72) $$

With the help of these equations, Jordan *derived* the commutation rule for any pair of canonical variables, $x$ and $\frac{h}{2\pi i} \frac{\partial}{\partial y}$, or

$$ pq - qp = \frac{h}{2\pi i}. \quad (73) $$

Jordan further argued: ‘The linear operators, which can be constructed from $\frac{h}{2\pi i} \frac{\partial}{\partial y}$ and $x$ by finitely or infinitely many multiplications and additions, are so general that one can be convinced that any linear operator might be formally written in this way. This means, from our statements and conclusions, that every mechanical variable can be constructed by symbolic multiplications and additions from $p$ and $q$. Simultaneously, the functional equations [(72)] can be rewritten as differential equations—in general, of infinitely high order.’ (Jordan, *loc. cit.*, pp. 815–816)

In Part II of the paper (§3 and §4), Jordan proved—by a mathematical discussion of the corresponding differential equations—that the *Postulates A* to *D* did not contradict each other. For that purpose, he introduced several formal steps and definitions, such as ‘adjoint quantities’ (obtained by inverting the order of factors in products of quantities and replacing all numbers by their complex-conjugate values) and ‘transposed quantities,’ and then showed the mathematical consistency of his theory. In doing so, he established the validity of the following well-known results:

(1) the Schrödinger equation, together with its boundary conditions (yielding quantized energy states);
(2) Dirac’s *q*-number scheme, including its application to the Compton effect and the evaluation of Heisenberg’s matrix elements;
(3) the Born–Wiener operator method, plus the construction of generalized Heisenberg matrices.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0104 -->

# Chapter I  The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

Finally, Jordan demonstrated that the general scheme of quantum mechanics thus proposed allowed one to extend the concept of quantum jumps to cases other than the usually considered discontinuous changes of states in the course of time. Indeed, the method of probability amplitudes displayed here seemed to provide a ‘new foundation of quantum mechanics’ covering at least all of the substantiated results of all previous schemes. A few weeks after the submission of the paper, Jordan presented his *Habilitation* lecture on ‘*Kausalität und Statistik in der modernen Physik*’ (‘Causality and Statistics in Modern Physics,’ published in English under the title ‘Philosophical Foundations of Quantum Theory,’ Jordan, 1927c). Of course, it dealt with the latest applications of ‘probability amplitudes’ and mentioned at the end ‘the pertinent considerations carried through in Copenhagen and here in Göttingen’ (Jordan, *loc. cit.*, English translation, p. 569).

## I.5  The Transformation Theory of Paul Dirac

Werner Heisenberg, then in Copenhagen, replying to his friend Pascual Jordan in Göttingen, wrote:

> Your second remark on canonical transformations is very good. I look forward to studying your paper when I receive it. I hope that your paper does not contain exactly the same results as a paper which Dirac has composed here. Dirac’s basic idea is the following: the physical interpretation of the [elements of the transformation matrix] $S_{\alpha, \beta}$ in my note on fluctuations can be generalized quite a bit; even to the extent that all physical applications of quantum mechanics, which are available up to now and will—as Dirac says—ever be obtained, may be covered. $S$ turns out to be the solution of a principal-axis transformation problem, hence also of a differential equation *à la* Schrödinger, however, not at all always in $q$-space [i.e., coordinate space]. It is possible to introduce matrices of a very general type, for example, $S(q, E)$ with indices $q$ and [energy value] $E$. The $S(q, E)$ which solves Born’s principal-axis problem in Quantum Mechanics II [Born, Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926], Chapter 3, Eq. (13), is the [eigenfunction] $S(q, E) = \psi E(q)$ of Schrödinger. The more general case can be called a simple application of [Cornelius] Lanczos’ ‘field equation.’ (The same may be true also for your $\phi(y) = \int K(x, y) \psi(x) dx$ ??) In fact, I have always claimed that Lanczos [i.e., his paper] was not so bad. (Heisenberg to Jordan, 24 November 1926)

Exactly one month later, Heisenberg’s fear turned out to be substantiated, when Paul Dirac wrote to Jordan: ‘Dr. Heisenberg has shown me the work you sent him, and as far as I can see it is equivalent to my own work in all essential points. The way of obtaining the results may be rather different though’ (Dirac to Jordan, 24 December 1926).

In this section, we shall analyze the origin and development of the ideas leading to Dirac’s transformation theory, together with the main contents of the final paper, to which Dirac ambitiously gave the title: ‘The Physical Interpretation of

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0105 -->

Quantum Mechanics.’⁶⁰ We shall especially describe the external background, the stimulating Copenhagen atmosphere in which the investigation was completed, the influence of other visitors at Bohr’s Institute, as well as colleagues outside—notably, of Wolfgang Pauli in Hamburg. All of these external aspects of the story combined with and strengthened the internal line of arguments of Paul Dirac, the English theoretician, who, in his first stay abroad, demonstrated his extraordinary qualities as one of the most original contributors to quantum mechanics, a genuine peer of the young geniuses in Copenhagen, Göttingen, and Hamburg.

Dirac, who, during the summer of the previous year, had appeared like a comet in the firmament of quantum mechanics by casting Heisenberg’s pioneering ideas into his own elegant algebraic formalism of $q$-numbers (Dirac, 1925d), had already published in 1926 five important papers in scientific journals promoting the new theory.⁶¹

> (1) ‘Quantum Mechanics and a Preliminary Investigation of the Hydrogen Atom’ (Dirac, 1926a; received 22 January and published in May), dealing with an application of $q$-numbers to the problem of the hydrogen atom;
>
> (2) ‘The Elimination of Nodes in Quantum Mechanics’ (Dirac, 1926b; received 27 March and published in May), extending the action-angle formalism to many-electron atoms;
>
> (3) ‘Relativity Quantum Mechanics with an Application to Compton Scattering’ (Dirac, 1926c; received 29 April, published in June);
>
> (4) ‘On Quantum Algebra’ (Dirac, 1926e, received in July), explaining and refining the mathematical details of the $q$-number calculus);
>
> (5) ‘On the Theory of Quantum Mechanics’ (Dirac, 1926f; received 26 August and published in October), using Schrödinger’s wave mechanics to obtain some fundamental consequences, especially the two types of statistics (i.e., Bose and Fermi statistics) of identical particles in quantum mechanics.

In addition, Paul Dirac had composed a dissertation on ‘Quantum Mechanics,’ in which he summarized in more than 130 pages (in 22 sections) the results of his unique approach to the theory to obtain his Ph.D. at Cambridge University (Dirac, 1926d).⁶²

Without a doubt, in England, Dirac had to be considered as the foremost expert on the new atomic theory; consequently, his professor, Ralph Fowler, assigned to
