The laws of the ordinary quantum theory can then be deduced.’ (Kragh, 1990, footnote 49, p. 320)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0106 -->

74 *Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory*

him the task of giving lectures on quantum mechanics for the (few) Cambridge students of theoretical physics.$^{63}$ Most of these students became renowned quantum physicists later on, notably, Douglas R. Hartree, John A. Gaunt, Nevill F. Mott, and the American visitor J. Robert Oppenheimer. Bertha Swirls, the only female student, reported about it:

Dirac gave us what he himself had recently done, some of it already published, some, I think, not. We did not, it is true, form a very sociable group, but for anyone who was there it is impossible to forget the sense of excitement at the new work. I stood in some awe of Dirac, but if I did pluck up courage to ask him a question I always got a direct and helpful answer, with no beating about the bush if I was getting things wrong. (Bertha Swirls Jeffreys in Eden and Polkinghorne, 1972, p. 21)

In the following years, Dirac would present further courses on the topic, out of which finally grew his celebrated book, *The Principles of Quantum Mechanics* (Dirac, 1930d).

The completion of his Ph.D. thesis evidently marked the stage when the new Cambridge graduate, who became 24 years old in the following August, thought of going abroad, primarily to spend some time at the great European centres of atomic theory. Göttingen, where quantum mechanics had been discovered, seemed to him to be the first choice; he had also become acquainted with Heisenberg already in summer 1925 and had carried on some correspondence with the admired German physicist of his own age concerning the developing subject of quantum mechanics since then.$^{64}$ On the other hand, Fowler insisted that Dirac first go to Copenhagen, and wrote to Niels Bohr about it on 9 April 1926. Bohr answered at once quite encouragingly: 'He shall certainly be welcome to work here next term. We are full of admiration of his work. Dirac's coming will also be a great pleasure to Heisenberg. ... Already last summer he suggested a visit of Dirac as most desirable.' (Bohr to Fowler, 14 April 1926) That Heisenberg had taken over since May 1926 the position of lecturer in theoretical physics in Copenhagen (previously occupied by Hendrik Kramers), persuaded Dirac to follow Fowler's advice; with Max Born, who visited Cambridge (and attended the Oxford meeting of the *British Association*) in August 1926, he agreed to spend the second part of his leave of absence, from February to June 1927, in Göttingen.

Dirac arrived in Copenhagen shortly after Erwin Schrödinger's visit there.$^{65}$ That visit had been quite exciting, as Bohr, Heisenberg, and others had had vigorous arguments with the visitor about the appropriate interpretation of the wave-mechanical scheme; notably, they had tried to persuade Schrödinger to accept the

$^{63}$ The lecture course was entitled 'Quantum Theory (recent developments).' For this, and other details of Dirac's biography, see Helge Kragh (1990), Chapter 2, and our Volume 4.

$^{64}$ See, e.g., Volume 4, pp. 757–759.

$^{65}$ See the discussion of Schrödinger's visit in Volume 5, Part 2, pp. 820–828. Schrödinger had arrived in Copenhagen on 1 October 1926, presented a lecture on wave mechanics at the Danish Physical Society, and left soon afterward.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0107 -->

*I.5 The Transformation Theory of Paul Dirac* 75

existence of quantum jumps. Of course, the outcome of the debate greatly interested Dirac, who had dealt with Schrödinger's theory in his recent Cambridge paper and derived several interesting results, especially the statistics of many-particle systems on its basis (Dirac, 1926f). In the continuing discussions on the interpretation of the quantum-mechanical theory, which were going on in Copenhagen at that time, he hoped to play his own (as usual) independent part. First, however, he had to acquaint himself with the new surroundings.$^{66}$

Life in Copenhagen was quite different from the one in Cambridge. Dirac did most of his work at the Institute instead of the library or his rooms. Also, he met the various people who were at the Institute more often than he had done in Cambridge. In Copenhagen, for example, he regularly saw Heisenberg, Friedrich Hund, and Oskar Klein, and occasionally Paul Ehrenfest and Wolfgang Pauli (when they came for a visit). Moreover, the Copenhagen style of doing physics deviated greatly from that in Cambridge (even from that in most other places): the permanent members of the Institute and the visitors gathered to discuss frequently and openly their ideas and work. At the centre of this lively exchange and activity stood Niels Bohr, a personality very different from other senior professors. As Dirac recalled later: 'Without Bohr I think there would have been nothing; I was very much impressed by hearing Bohr talk.' At that time, Bohr had practically stopped contributing to the active technical development of theoretical physics, but 'he seemed to be the deepest thinker I ever met' (Dirac, *Conversations with J. Mehra*).$^{67}$ Dirac was far less impressed by the manner in which Bohr composed his papers by dictating them to his assistants or visitors to the Institute, especially by his custom of constantly making changes and corrections in the text. On one such occasion, when Dirac was taking the dictation, he remarked to Bohr during a pause: 'Professor Bohr, when I was at school, my teacher taught me not to begin a sentence until I knew how to finish it.' Afterward, Dirac never served as the person to whom Bohr dictated a full paper. (See Mehra, 1972, footnote 29, p. 54.)

In Copenhagen, Dirac lived in 'Pension Scheck,' which was near the town hall in the centre of the city. As a rule, he used to walk from the pension to the Institute, which took about 20 minutes along the lakes. On Sundays, he would go on a long hike or excursion out in the country, often alone, but sometimes with Bohr and others with a larger group. During working days, he came to the Institute at about 9:30 a.m.; he would go back to take his meals at the pension and then return to work. He would often think about his research problems as he walked back and forth, as well as in the evenings. Still, of course, he talked to people, especially Heisenberg and Klein, though he often felt that the interaction just went one way; i.e., he 'mostly listened to others.' At any rate, his own work progressed very well.

$^{66}$ One of the reasons why Dirac had preferred to go first to Göttingen was that he knew German, and he hesitated to go to a country (Denmark) where he did not speak the language (Dirac, *Conversations with J. Mehra*).

$^{67}$ Interviews and conversations with J. Mehra (Mehra, 1972) and Dirac, 1977. As Dirac further recalled, Bohr often discussed problems not (only) concerned with physics, but also having to do with the psychology of gunmen and stock-exchange people.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0108 -->

76 *Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory*

Dirac published the first outcome of the Copenhagen period within a month of his arrival: on 8 November 1926, the Cambridge Philosophical Society received a paper on 'The Compton Effect in Wave Mechanics' (Dirac, 1926g). Evidently, the Compton effect played an important role in the discussions around Bohr because of the apparent involvement of the light-quantum, and Dirac had already treated the problem in Cambridge on the basis of his *q*-number theory and the light-quantum concept (Dirac, 1926c). Now, he referred to his earlier procedure as 'a rather artificial method' and claimed: 'A more natural and more easily understood method of obtaining the matrices is provided by Schrödinger's wave mechanics.' (Dirac, *loc. cit.*, p. 500) In Dirac's new treatment, especially the previous difficulty of finding the correct Hamiltonian operator (or *q*-number) could be avoided, as the matrix elements for the component of the polarization of radiation were obtained directly with the help of Schrödinger's eigenfunctions. At the same time, Dirac showed how the light-quantum effect arose from the undulatory scheme. In a footnote, added in proof, he compared the method chosen with that of another recently published paper: 'Gordon's [1926] method makes use of an expression for the electric density for determining the field produced by the scattering electron, and differs from the present paper, in which the wave equation is used merely as a mathematical help for the calculation of matrix elements, which are then interpreted in accordance with the assumptions of matrix mechanics' (Dirac, 1926g, p. 507). Clearly, Dirac wished to remain on the side of the Göttingen–Copenhagen point of view while interpreting the quantum-mechanical formalism. With the same intention in mind, he started to work on the following paper, which Ralph Fowler would communicate less than a month later to the *Proceedings of the Royal Society*.

Niels Bohr vividly recalled the initial phase of that investigation about thirty-five years later as follows:

In this context I recall that Heisenberg, in a colloquium at the Institute, drew attention to the fact that matrix mechanics not only allowed the determination of the expectation value of a physical quantity, but also the expectation value of every power of the quantity, and here Dirac said in the ensuing discussion that this remark would provide the key to general transformations [in quantum mechanics]. (Bohr, 1961, p. XI)

Bohr's recollection is confirmed by a remark in the introduction of Dirac's paper, stating:

Recently Heisenberg has obtained another point of contact between the theory and experiment of a somewhat different nature. If one considers the problem of two atomic systems in resonance, i.e., with energy pulsating from one to the other, one can find the time mean of the energy of one of them, by assuming this time mean to be given by a diagonal element of the matrix that represents the energy of that system. Similarly one can find the time mean of the square of its energy, and of the cube of its energy, and so on. Heisenberg has shown that these calculated time means are

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0109 -->

*I.5 The Transformation Theory of Paul Dirac* 77

just what one would expect from the assumption that the energy changes discontinuously from one quantized value to another. The theory can thus be considered to show that the energy actually does change discontinuously from one quantized value to another, and it enables one to calculate the fraction of the total time during which the energy has any particular value, but it can give no information about the times of the transition. (Dirac, 1927a, p. 622)

Dirac obtained this information, as he stated in a footnote, from Heisenberg prior to the latter's publication, entitled 'Schwankungserscheinungen und Quantenmechanik' ('Fluctuation Phenomena and Quantum Mechanics,' Heisenberg, 1926e). That study confirmed the claim of Bohr, Born, Heisenberg, Jordan, and their close associates that—in contrast to Schrödinger's assertion—quantum mechanics cannot do without quantum jumps. Heisenberg proved the anti-Schrödinger opinion by applying matrix methods: he showed that the typical wave-mechanical beat phenomena resulted, and insisted at the same time that 'quantum mechanics always agrees with the fluctuation formulae, as required on the discontinuum theory' (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*, p. 501).$^{68}$ He submitted the paper in early November to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (it was received on 6 November), but he had already sketched the contents in a letter to Wolfgang Pauli, informing him simultaneously about the new considerations of Dirac on the interpretation of quantum-theoretical variables:

In order to clarify Schrödinger's density, Dirac has reflected upon it in a very funny way. Question: 'What is the quantum-mechanical matrix of the external density?' Definition of density: I. It is zero everywhere where there is no electron, or in equations,

$$
\left.\begin{aligned}
\rho(x_0, y_0, z_0, t)(x_0 - x(t)) &= 0, \\
\rho(x_0, y_0, z_0, t)(y_0 - y(t)) &= 0, \\
\rho(x_0, y_0, z_0, t)(z_0 - z(t)) &= 0.
\end{aligned}\right\} \quad [(74)]
$$

Furthermore [II.], the total charge is $e$,

$$
\int \rho(x_0, y_0, z_0, t) \, dx_0 \, dy_0 \, dz_0 = e. \quad [(75)]
$$

The solution (as can be easily proved) is

$$
\rho_{nm}(x_0, y_0, z_0, t) = e \psi_n \psi_m^*(x_0, y_0, z_0, t), \quad [(76)]
$$

where $\psi_n$ and $\psi_m$ are Schrödinger's normalized functions. This formulation really seems quite attractive to me; in particular, this matrix formulation yields again (as far

$^{68}$ Heisenberg did not actually calculate the higher powers of quantum-mechanical variables explicitly; he just indicated that the higher-order fluctuations can be worked out easily and yield the desired result.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0110 -->

78 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

as I can see) the correct fluctuation expression for the fluctuation of the electric charge in a small volume element (hence the charge fluctuations which correspond to the motion of point charges). (Heisenberg to Pauli, 28 October 1926, in Pauli, 1979, p. 351)

The above letter illustrates the direct interaction with Dirac, who seems to have been drawn into the close exchange of ideas on the interpretation of the quantum-mechanical formalism that went on at that time between Heisenberg and Pauli. We must assume that in this way Dirac also became acquainted with Pauli's generalization of Born's statistical interpretation of the Schrödinger function (see our discussion in the previous section). Finally, Heisenberg reported again to Pauli on 23 November: 'Here we have also thought about the physical meaning of the transformation function $S$, and Dirac has accomplished an extraordinarily far-reaching (*großzügige*) generalization of this assumption from my note on fluctuation [phenomena].' He then outlined the essence of this generalization, in a manner similar to what he had written in his letter to Jordan, dated 24 November, quoted earlier. He concluded his letter to Pauli by saying:

The above-mentioned physical interpretation of the function $S$, however, contains also all the physical statements that could have been made up to now: e.g., Born's collision processes, Jordan's transformations, etc. Dirac's investigations have many points in common with your and my work. Moreover, they are very general, since they apply, e.g., as easily and safely for continuous changes as for those in periodic systems. I consider that Dirac's paper represents an extraordinary progress. (Heisenberg to Pauli, 23 November 1926, in Pauli, 1979, p. 358)

Having embedded Dirac's work on the transformation theory into the scientific background of his close colleagues at that time, attention should be directed to the internal development of the author's ideas. First, the question arises concerning how the consideration of higher order fluctuations led him to consider general transformations in quantum mechanics. The introduction of Dirac's paper perhaps provides the necessary hint as, after the passage dealing with the time means, it continued: 'This result is capable of wide extensions. It can be applied to any dynamical system, not necessarily one composed of two parts in resonance with one another, and to any dynamical variable, not necessarily one that can take only quantized values.' (Dirac, 1927a, p. 622) Having calculated the time mean of a dynamical variable $g$, of its square and cube, one obtains information about $g$ as a function of time, notably, 'the fraction of the total time during which $g$ lies between any two specified numerical values, $g'$ and $g''$ say,' but: 'One can say nothing about the intervals of time during which this condition is satisfied except the fraction they form of the whole time.' (Dirac, *loc. cit.*) This conclusion stimulated Dirac to investigate those types of questions that one can take over from the classical theory and ask in quantum mechanics. One such question evidently was: for what fraction of the total time will a specified condition hold? Still, this question received a definite answer only for nondegenerate atomic systems. On the

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0111 -->

I.5 The Transformation Theory of Paul Dirac 79

other hand, the most general question of classical mechanics seemed to be the following: 'What is the value of any constant of integration [of motion] $g$ of a given dynamical system for any given initial conditions, specified by the numerical values $q_{ro}', p_{ro}'$, say, for the initial coordinates and momenta $q_{ro}, p_{ro}$.' (Dirac, *loc. cit.*, p. 623) The Hamilton-Jacobi theory provides the definite answer, expressing $g$ as a function of $q_{ro}$ and $p_{ro}$; however, in quantum mechanics, the answer turns out to be ambiguous due to the noncommutativity of the coordinate and momentum variables. Yet, in case that $g$ depends only on coordinates *or* momenta, the answer would become definite.

Dirac thus arrived at directing his attention to the transformation theory in quantum mechanics, which he had encountered already rather early in his *q*-number theory. What was the role of the transformation

$$y = bxb^{-1} \tag{77}$$

of a variable $x$ with the help of a nonsingular *q*-number $b$? In his paper 'On Quantum Algebra' (1926e), which outlined the general mathematical structure of the scheme in some detail, Dirac had detected certain restrictions of the method that did not seem to follow from physics, but had to be introduced—for the time being—as an extra (mathematical) assumption or axiom; only with these restrictions satisfied, would the integration of the equation of motion by possible and give the desired results.$^{69}$ The problem now emerged, whether the restrictions threw any light on the physical conditions in quantum systems. The new considerations clarified the situation in the following way:

One cannot answer any question on the quantum theory which refers to the numerical values for both $q_{ro}$ and $p_{ro}$. One would expect, however, to be able to answer questions in which only the $q_{ro}$ or only the $p_{ro}$ are given numerical values, or, more generally, when any set of constants of integration $\xi_r$ that commute with each other are given numerical values. . . . Questions of this type appear to be the only ones to which the quantum theory can give a definite answer, and they are probably the only ones to which the physicist requires an answer. (Dirac, 1927a, p. 623)

To obtain the numerical values for $\xi_r$, Dirac continued, one needs a scheme 'of matrices to represent the dynamical variables, whose rows and columns refer to the numerical values of the $\xi_r$.' For most atomic problems—namely, the multiply periodic ones—the action variables $J$ might yield the right result; however, in the case of problems 'for which the electrons are not initially in definite orbits' (e.g., as in the case of $\beta$-particles emitted from radioactive nuclei), 'we should require a matrix representation of the dynamical variables whose rows and columns refer to other constants of integration of the system than the action variables.' That is, in the case of $\beta$-decay,

$^{69}$ See our discussion in Volume 4, Section V.1.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0112 -->

80 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

it would be probably convenient to have the matrix rows and columns referring to the coordinates of the $\beta$-particle at the time of emission, $t = t_0$, say. We should be interested only in those rows and columns of the matrices that refer to the $\beta$-particle being in the nucleus at the time $t = t_0$, and could calculate the range in which its initial momentum must lie in order that any special kind of interaction, specified by numerical values of certain constants of integration, must take place. We should thus obtain the probability of that kind of interaction, on the assumption that all directions of emission are equally possible. (Dirac, *loc. cit.*, p. 624)

Evidently, Dirac required 'a theory of more general schemes of matrix representation, in which the rows and columns refer to any set of constants of integration that commute, and to the laws of transformation from one scheme to another.' This new theory, he claimed, 'must be regarded as a development of Lanczos's field theory, the field representation in Lanczos's theory being really the same as a matrix representation with matrices that have a continuous range of rows and columns instead of the usual discrete sets' (Dirac, *loc. cit.*).

In his paper 'Über eine feldmäßige Darstellung der neuen Quantenmechanik' ('On a Field-Like Representation of the New Quantum Mechanics,' Lanczos, 1926a), Cornelius Lanczos had reformulated the original Göttingen matrix mechanics in terms of integral equations with kernel functions, thus obtaining an essentially continuous representation. He had, however, avoided to step forward, as Dirac would do now, namely to introduce a singular function, called the 'delta function.' Dirac indeed wondered 'why people did not introduce it earlier,' because 'it is just a question of notation'; perhaps the fact that the function was ill-behaved worried the mathematicians (and would continue to worry them for a while). On the other hand, the physicists could understand it immediately to denote a function that is narrower than any distance one is ever concerned with.$^{70}$

Dirac had approached the use of this singular delta function gradually since August 1926. In his paper 'On the Theory of Quantum Mechanics,' he considered the general solution of the Schrödinger equation, i.e.,

$$\psi = \sum c_n \psi_n, \tag{78}$$

with $\psi_n$ a set of eigenfunctions and $c_n$ arbitrary constants, and noticed that 'there may be continuous sets $\psi(\alpha)$, depending on a parameter $\alpha$, and satisfying the differential equation for all values of $\alpha$ in a certain range, in which case the sum in [(78)] must be replaced by an integral $\int c_n \psi(\alpha) d\alpha$, or both a discrete set and a continuous set may occur together' (Dirac, 1926f, p. 664). He further added in a footnote: 'The general solution may contain quantities, such as $\psi_{\alpha}$ and $\partial \psi_{\alpha} / \partial \alpha$, which satisfy the differential equation [of Schrödinger], but which cannot strictly be put in the form $\int c_{\alpha} \psi_{\alpha} d\alpha$, although they may be regarded as limits of a series of

$^{70}$ Dirac, in interviews and conversations with J. Mehra; see Mehra, 1972.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0113 -->

I.5 The Transformation Theory of Paul Dirac 81

quantities which are of this form' (Dirac, *loc. cit.*). In the next published paper, the study of the Compton effect in wave mechanics, he considered $\psi_{\alpha}$, the solution of the relativistic Schrödinger equation, such that the constant of motion could be expressed as

$$\frac{\partial S_a}{\partial \alpha_r} = -\frac{ih}{2\pi} \iint c(\alpha', \alpha) \psi_{\alpha'} d\alpha_2' d\alpha_3' d\alpha_4', \tag{79}$$

'where $c(\alpha', \alpha)$ is a certain very discontinuous "function" of the $\alpha_2' \alpha_3' \alpha_4'$, which is equal to zero except when $|\alpha_2 - \alpha_2'|$, $|\alpha_3 - \alpha_3'|$, and $|\alpha_4 - \alpha_4'|$ are very small, and very large and positive when $\alpha_r'$ is a little greater than $\alpha_r$, and very large and negative when $\alpha_r'$ is a little less than $\alpha_r$' (Dirac, 1926g, p. 503).$^{71}$ Thus, Dirac increasingly felt the need for the explicit use of the new type of function in physics.$^{72}$ Now, in the general transformation theory, the explicit use of the $\delta$-symbol or $\delta$-function could not be avoided.

An elementary—the mathematicians would say, naive—introduction of the delta function presented no deep problem, as Dirac showed in Section 2 of his paper (Dirac, 1927a, pp. 624–627). Starting from the matrix $g$ in matrix mechanics, where for a system of $u$ degrees of freedom the rows and columns can be labelled by specific—i.e., $\alpha_1', \alpha_2' \dots \alpha_u'$ for the constants of motion $\alpha_1, \alpha_2 \dots \alpha_u$—such that

$$g = g(\alpha_1', \alpha_2' \dots \alpha_u'; \alpha_1'', \alpha_2'' \dots \alpha_u'') = g(\alpha', \alpha''), \tag{80}$$

he wrote, in the case in which the labelling parameters $\alpha', \alpha''$ assume continuous values, the multiplication law is

$$ab(\alpha'\alpha'') = \int a(\alpha'\alpha''') d\alpha''' b(\alpha'''\alpha''); \tag{81}$$

here, $d\alpha'''$ denotes $d\alpha_1''' d\alpha_2''' \dots d\alpha_u'''$, and the range of integrations extends over all values of the $\alpha'''$ that label rows and columns of the matrices. Dirac then continued:

One cannot go far in the development of the theory of matrices with continuous ranges of rows and columns without needing a notation for the function of a *c*-number $x$ that is equal to zero except when $x$ is very small, and whose integral through a range that contains the point $x = 0$ is equal to unity. We shall use the

$^{71}$ Evidently, $c(\alpha, \alpha')$ is what Dirac would soon call the $\delta'$-function.
$^{72}$ As Dirac said later: 'I noticed the need for it very much in a certain place of Eddington's book on *The Mathematical Theory of Relativity* [i.e., in a footnote on p. 190 of the 1923 edition]' (Dirac, Conversations with Mehra). We shall discuss the mathematical prehistory and justification of the delta function later in Chapter III. (See, however, the following footnote 74.)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0114 -->

symbol $\delta(x)$ to denote this function, i.e., $\delta(x)$ is defined by

$$\delta(x) = 0 \quad \text{when } x \neq 0,$$ [(82a)]

$$\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} dx \delta(x) = 1.$$ [(82b)]

Strictly, of course $\delta(x)$ is not a proper function of $x$, but can be regarded only as a limit of a certain sequence of functions. All the same one can use $\delta(x)$ as though it were a proper function for practically all the purposes of quantum mechanics without getting incorrect results. One can also use the differential coefficients $\delta(x)$, namely $\delta'(x), \delta''(x) \ldots$, which are even more discontinuous and less “proper” than $\delta(x)$ itself. (Dirac, *loc. cit.*, p. 625)

Indeed, the elementary properties of the delta function and its derivative followed immediately as:

$$\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f(x) \delta(a - x) \, dx = f(a)$$ (83)

and

$$\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f(x) \delta'(a - x) = f'(a).$$ (84)

Finally, Dirac expressed the unit matrix for continuous ranges of row and column labels in the form

$$1(\alpha' \alpha'') = \delta(\alpha_1' - \alpha_1'') \delta(\alpha_2' - \alpha_2'') \ldots \delta(\alpha_u' - \alpha_u'').$$ (85)

With these notations, he proceeded to develop his general transformation theory for quantum-mechanical systems.

It is interesting to speculate what could have happened if Born, Heisenberg, and Jordan in fall 1925 (while developing matrix mechanics) had already made use of the simple trick of Dirac’s delta function. Would they have been in the situation to apply their scheme also to continuous energy states of the atoms and molecules? Would they have then hit upon the Schrödinger equation? But they had not done so, and several reasons may have prevented them. The first was that Born, who formally proceeded to the largest extent in the direction of treating very general atomic systems, restricted himself to the mathematics developed earlier by Hilbert (who had not used the improper delta function). Born’s collaborators, on the other hand, were happy enough to restrict themselves to periodic problems and to show that matrix mechanics worked in these cases. Later on, when Born and Wiener turned to the operator formalism, they did not develop it far enough to also

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0115 -->

consider delta functions—although Norbert Wiener worked at that time toward a generalization of harmonic analysis, which provided one of the foundations of what later became the mathematical theory of generalized functions or distributions (of which Dirac’s $\delta$-function is a special example).

In any case, the new ‘notations’ allowed Dirac to proceed quickly with his general transformation theory, which assumed a very compact and elegant shape, such that when he first presented it in a seminar at Copenhagen, his colleagues found it difficult to grasp. As Oskar Klein recalled:

> It took us some time to understand the thing. Because he gave some lectures, and he wrote all the figures on the blackboard very nicely, and he said a few words [about] them, but they were very hard to get—so I cannot remember quite when I understood it. . . . But I know that Heisenberg followed his [Dirac’s] work closely . . . so I think he got it earlier. . . . Then he told me a little about Dirac’s and Jordan’s work on transformation theory, with great admiration of both. (O. Klein, AHQP Interview, Session V, pp. 14–15)

Jordan, who would have grasped Dirac’s work quickly, was not present in Copenhagen, but learned about Dirac’s theory only through Heisenberg’s letters until the author gave him an extended report. As this report might resemble the above-mentioned presentation in the Copenhagen seminar, we shall reproduce it here together with some additional comments from the published paper. Dirac wrote to Jordan on 24 December 1926, as follows:

> In my paper I approach the general contact transformation by considering the equation
>
> $$G = b g b^{-1}$$ [(86)]
>
> which transforms $g$ to $G$. Written in terms of matrix elements, this gives ($\alpha$ means $\alpha_1 \alpha_2 \alpha_3 \ldots$, the first integrals of the equations of motion; $d\alpha = d\alpha_1 \, d\alpha_2 \ldots$)
>
> $$G(\alpha' \alpha'') = \iint b(\alpha' \alpha''') \, d\alpha''' \, g(\alpha''' \alpha'''') \, d\alpha^{(4)} \, b^{-1}(\alpha^{(4)} \alpha'')$$ [(87)]
>
> if one takes for definiteness the case when the $\alpha$’s can take continuous ranges of values. When one makes a contact transformation one can at the same time make any interchange of rows and columns of the new matrices $G$, and there is no one-to-one correspondence between the rows and columns of the new matrices $G$ and those of the original matrix $g$. This is brought out more clearly if we use different symbols ($\xi_r$, say) to denote the rows and columns of the new matrices $G$, so that we write the transformation equation
>
> $$G(\xi' \xi'') = \iint b(\xi' \alpha') \, d\alpha' \cdot g(\alpha' \alpha'') \, d\alpha'' \cdot b^{-1}(\alpha'' \xi'').$$ [(87')]

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0116 -->

84 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

A better but equivalent notation is,

$$g(\xi'\xi'') = \iint (\xi'|\alpha') d\alpha' \cdot g(\alpha'\alpha'') d\alpha''(\alpha'|\xi''). \qquad [(88)]$$

Here, one may pause for a moment and recall what Dirac intended to do. He started from the scheme of matrix mechanics, which consists of finding a set of matrices representing dynamical variables and satisfying the conditions:$^{73}$

(i) The quantum condition, $q_r p_r - p_r q_r = ih$, etc.
(ii) The equations of motion, $gH - Hg = ih\dot{g}$, or if $g$ involves the time explicitly

$$gH - Hg + ih\frac{\partial g}{\partial t} = ih\dot{g}.$$

(iii) The matrix representing the Hamiltonian must be a diagonal matrix.
(iv) The matrices representing real variables must be Hermitean. (Dirac, 1927a, p. 627)

In matrix mechanics, all nonsingular transformation matrices, which do not depend on time, but satisfy the extra condition that $b(\alpha'\alpha'')$ and $b^{-1}(\alpha''\alpha')$ are conjugate imaginaries, yield a Hermitean $G$ (if $g$ is Hermitean) and lead to new variables, in agreement with the conditions (i) to (iv). Dirac now wanted to proceed beyond the original Göttingen approach, for he announced: 'We shall work out also the theory of the more general kind of transformation scheme of matrices that need satisfy only the conditions (i) and (ii), which means that $b$ and $b^{-1}$ satisfy only the condition that their matrix elements do not involve the time $t'$ (Dirac, *loc. cit.*, p. 628). For this general quantum dynamics, the formulation (87') seemed preferable to (87), especially because 'the $\xi'$'s may take quite different ranges of values from the $\alpha'$'s, or one could even have the $\xi'$'s taking on only discrete sets of values while the $\alpha'$'s can take on continuous ranges of values, or *vice versa*' (Dirac, *loc. cit.*). To simplify the notation further, Dirac wrote for the transformation functions $b(\xi'\alpha')$ and $b^{-1}(\xi')$ the abbreviation $(\xi'|\alpha')$ and $(\alpha'|\xi')$; then, immediately, besides the transformation equation (88), equivalent ones could be formulated, such as

$$\iint (\alpha'|\xi') d\xi' \cdot g(\xi'\xi'') d\xi''(\xi''|\alpha'') = g(\alpha'\alpha'') \qquad (88')$$

or

$$\iint g(\xi'\xi'') d\xi''(\xi''|\alpha') = \iint (\xi'|\alpha'') d\alpha'' \cdot g(\alpha''\alpha') = g(\xi'\alpha'). \qquad (88'')$$

---

$^{73}$ Dirac's constant $h$ is given by Planck's constant divided by $2\pi$. We shall follow this notation here for brevity in the interest of historical accuracy. Later on, Dirac would write $\hbar = \frac{h}{2\pi}$, where $h$ is the usual Planck constant.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0117 -->

I.5 The Transformation Theory of Paul Dirac 85

(These equations replace the matrix equations $b^{-1}Gb = g$ and $Gb = bg$, respectively.)
Because the matrices $b$ and $b^{-1}$ satisfy the relations $bb^{-1} = b^{-1}b = 1$, two equations can be derived involving the $\delta$-symbol, i.e.,

$$\int b(\xi'\alpha') d\alpha' b^{-1}(\alpha'\xi'') = \int (\xi'|\alpha') d\alpha'(\alpha'|\xi'') = \delta(\xi' - \xi''), \qquad (89a)$$

and

$$\int b^{-1}(\alpha'\xi') d\xi' b(\xi'\alpha'') = \int (\xi'|\alpha') d\alpha'(\xi'|\alpha'') = \delta(\alpha' - \alpha''), \qquad (89b)$$

or: 'The $(\xi'|\alpha')$ and $(\alpha'|\xi')$ are mutually orthogonal and normalized systems of functions.' This observation refers to the elements of the generalized transformation matrices. On the other hand, Dirac wrote about the transformed variables:

> The $g(\alpha'\alpha'')$ and $g(\xi'\xi'')$ are two matrices that represent the same variable $g$ in two different schemes of matrix representation of $q$-numbers, the first of the schemes making the $\alpha'$'s diagonal matrices, and the second making in the same way certain variables $\xi_1, \xi_2 \dots$ diagonal matrices. Any set of variables that commute with one another may be made diagonal matrices by such a transformation. (Dirac to Jordan, 24 December 1926)

Expressed in terms of formulae, the commuting variables $\xi_r, r = 1, 2 \dots u$ (for a system of $u$ degrees of freedom) possess the matrix elements

$$\xi_r(\xi'\xi'') = \xi'_r \delta(\xi'_1 - \xi''_1) \delta(\xi'_2 - \xi''_2) \dots \delta(\xi'_u - \xi''_u). \qquad (90)$$

Turning to the specific dynamics of quantum-mechanical systems, Dirac went on to state:

If we put

$$g(\xi'\alpha') = \int g(\xi'\xi'') d\xi''(\xi''|\alpha') = \int (\xi'|\alpha'') d\alpha''g(\alpha''\alpha'), \qquad [(91)]$$

then we can regard $g(\xi'\alpha')$ as a matrix representing $g$ according to a new scheme in which the rows and columns refer to different dynamical variables. The matrix elements of the $\xi'$s in the new scheme are easily verified to be

$$\xi_r(\xi'\alpha') = \xi'_r(\xi'|\alpha') \qquad [(92)]$$

and if $\eta_r$ are the variables canonically conjugate to the $\xi'$s [we obtain]

$$\eta_r(\xi'\alpha') = -ih\frac{\partial}{\partial \xi'_r}(\xi'|\alpha'). \qquad [(93)]$$

(Dirac to Jordan, *loc. cit.*)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0118 -->

86 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

Clearly, Eq. [(93)] followed from the reformulated 'quantum condition,'

$$(\xi\eta - \eta\xi)(\xi'\xi'') = ih(\xi' - \xi''), \qquad (94)$$

and from the special representations, Eq. (90) for $\xi_r$ and

$$\eta_r = -ih\delta(\xi'_1 - \xi''_1) \dots \frac{\partial}{\partial \xi'_r} \delta(\xi'_r - \xi''_r) \dots \delta(\xi'_u - \xi''_u) \qquad (95)$$

for $\eta_r$. From Eqs. (92) and (93), Dirac immediately derived the main results:

> More generally, if $f(\xi_r, \eta_r)$ is any function of the $\xi$'s and $\eta$'s, its matrix elements in this scheme are easily verified to be
>
> $$f(\xi_r, \eta_r)(\xi'\alpha') = f\left( \xi'_r - ih \frac{\partial}{\partial \xi'_r} \right) (\xi'|\alpha'). \qquad [(96)]$$
>
> If $f(\xi_r, \eta_r)$ is a diagonal matrix in the $(\alpha)$ scheme, we should have in a similar way
>
> $$f(\xi_r, \eta_r)(\xi'\alpha') = f(\alpha')(\xi'|\alpha'). \qquad [(97)]$$
>
> where $f(\alpha')$ are its diagonal elements. A comparison of the two expressions gives just the Schrödinger equation in the case when $f(\xi_r, \eta_r)$ is the Hamiltonian, expressed as a function of the $\xi$'s and $\eta$'s. The quantities $(\xi'|\alpha')$ of the transformation theory are thus the eigenfunctions of Schrödinger's theory. (Dirac to Jordan, *loc. cit.*)

Although Dirac's letter to Jordan contained all essential details of the new transformation theory, even the mathematically gifted Jordan might have encountered some difficulty in grasping the short-hand description of his colleague. However, Dirac's published paper of January 1927, which contained more details, finally brought full understanding. The most important message was contained in Section 5, entitled 'Transformation Theory' (Dirac, 1927a, pp. 633-637). In it, Dirac first derived Eq. [(97)], from which there followed indeed an equation that could be expressed in a suitable notation as

$$H\left( q, -ih\frac{\partial}{\partial q} \right) \psi_E(q) = E\psi_E(q), \qquad (98)$$

i.e., the fundamental differential equation of wave mechanics (with $H$ denoting the Hamiltonian function and $E$ the diagonal elements of the generalized matrix). Secondly, Dirac went on to obtain from his general transformation scheme also the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, namely,

$$H\left( q_r, -ih\frac{\partial}{\partial q_r} \right) (q'|\alpha') = ih\frac{\partial}{\partial t} (q'|\alpha'), \qquad (99)$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0119 -->

I.5 The Transformation Theory of Paul Dirac 87

with $(q'|\alpha')$ the corresponding time-dependent transformation functions. Thirdly, he showed how the general Hamilton-Jacobi theory—sketched earlier by Jordan (1926b) only in the classical case—could actually be formulated in his new scheme. One had just to use the *Ansatz* for the action function $S$,

$$S = \sum_r f(\xi_r)g(\alpha_r), \qquad (100)$$

and then to identify the transformation function $(\xi'|\alpha')$ with the expression

$$(\xi'|\alpha') = \exp\{iS/h\}. \qquad (101)$$

In his letter to Jordan, Dirac described the contents of the next Section 6, entitled 'Physical Interpretation of Matrices' (Dirac, 1927a, pp. 637-641), by the following statement: 'The last part of my paper is a development of Heisenberg's fluctuation theory, which was also obtained independently by you.' He illustrated this statement with a quite abstract presentation of his fluctuation theory, namely:

> If $(g)$ denotes another scheme of matrix representation, in which $g_1, g_2 \dots$ are diagonal matrices, then
>
> $$\int_{g'}^{g''} (\xi'|g') dg' \cdot (g'|\xi''),$$
>
> considered as a matrix with elements defined by $(\xi', \xi'')$, may be shown to be the matrix that represents the function of the dynamical variables which is equal to unity when each $g_r$ satisfied $g'_r < g_r < g''_r$ and zero when these conditions are not fulfilled. Its diagonal elements determine the average value of this function over the whole $\eta$-space, which is the same as the fraction of the whole of $\eta$-space for which $g'_r < g_r < g''_r$. If all points in $\eta$-space are equally probable (*and only when* this is so) these diagonal elements determine the probability of each $g_r$ lying in the range $g'_r - g''_r$ for given values $(\xi'_r)$ of $\xi_r$'s. (Dirac to Jordan, 24 December 1926)

At the end of his published paper, Dirac emphasized the *full agreement* of his results 'with the assumption formerly used that the square of the amplitude of the wave function in certain cases determines a probability' (Dirac, 1927a, p. 639). Although the proof in the case of the standard atomic systems (even with time-dependent perturbations) was straightforward, Born's scattering problem required some consideration until the assertion was demonstrated. Dirac concluded by saying that the general transformation theory 'suggests a point of view for regarding quantum phenomena rather different from the usual [classical] ones,' namely:

One can suppose that the initial state of a system determines definitely the state of the system at any subsequent time. If, however, one describes the state of the system at an arbitrary time by giving numerical values to the coordinates and momenta, then one cannot set up a one-one correspondence between the values of these coordinates and

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0120 -->

# 88 Chapter I The Probability Interpretation and the Statistical Transformation Theory

momenta initially and their values at a subsequent time. All the same one can obtain a good deal of information (of the nature of averages) about the values at the subse- quent time considered as functions of the initial values. The notion of probabilities does not enter into the ultimate description of mechanical processes; only when one is given some information that involves a probability (e.g., that all points in $\eta$-space are equally probable for representing the system) can one deduce results that involve probabilities. (Dirac, *loc. cit.*, p. 641)

This conclusion implied what Dirac considered to be the crucial aspect of *his* personal 'physical interpretation of the quantum dynamics,' his final word in the later epistemological debate on that topic. We shall discuss this interpretation in its proper context along with those of the other quantum physicists.

Dirac's profound and elegant treatment of the general transformation theory with its powerful consequences won the respect of the physicists involved, who often had greater problems with the mathematical formulation of the equivalent theory of Pascual Jordan.$^{73\text{a}}$ Jordan later added an extension to the formalism that took care of certain discrete quantized variables, such as electron spin, which the papers of Jordan and Dirac of December 1926 had not covered (Jordan, 1927g). Finally, Hilbert, von Neumann, and others would improve the mathematical foundations of the statistical transformation theory of the physicists, notably, they would deal with the necessary generalization of the results from the theory of bounded operators to that of unbounded ones. All of these developments will be discussed in Chapter III.

More than four and a half decades after the publication of his paper on 'The Physical Interpretation of the Quantum Dynamics,' Dirac would still remember that:

> This work gave me more pleasure in carrying it through than any of the other papers which I have written on quantum mechanics either before or after ... Many of my papers were consequences of an idea that had come to me rather accidentally. The early work on Poisson brackets, for instance, and my later work on the relativistic wave equation were very definitely of this nature. They were consequences of an idea which had just come out of the blue. I could not very well say how it occurred to me. And I felt that work of this kind was a rather undeserved success. On the other hand, my work on the physical interpretation of quantum mechanics was a deserved suc- cess. There I was tracking a problem which was not too diﬃcult to be solved by a direct approach. There were various stages in this problem which had to be disposed of one by one.

---

$^{73\text{a}}$ In his transformation theory, Dirac's principal step had been to introduce the $\delta$-function as a mathematical tool. Although the $\delta$-function is connected with Dirac's name, it had been introduced in physics much earlier. It was indicated by G. Kirchhoﬀ (1882, especially, p. 644) and suggested by O. Heaviside (1893a, b); also, P. Hertz (1916, p. 503). Dirac gave the $\delta$-function a sharper meaning, when he remarked: 'Strictly, of course, $\delta(x)$ is not a proper function of $x$, but can be regarded only as a limit, of a certain sequence of functions' (Dirac, 1927a, p. 625). The mathematical foundation of the $\delta$-type functions was thus initiated by Dirac's intuitive use; from the work of Hadamard, Schwartz, Gel'fand, and his school, a theory of generalized functions emerged that cannot be regarded as closed even today. (See Mehra, 1972, p. 39, and footnote 50 on p. 56; L. Schwartz, 1950, and see especially later in Chapter III.)

# I.5 The Transformation Theory of Paul Dirac 89

During the course of the work I was continually faced with the question of getting a suitable notation for writing down the equations that I was then dealing with. There was a frequent modification of notation. Everything proceeded step by step in a rather logical way, and led to a piece of work which laid the foundation of the general transformation theory of quantum mechanics, and also provided the essential fea- tures of a suitable notation.

With regard to this notation, I had to face the problem of writing down symbols which would contain an explicit reference to those factors which it was important to mention explicitly, and which left understood those quantities which it was safe to leave understood, to keep at the back of one's mind and not to write down explicitly. Well, this led to the notation which, with some slight modifications, has become the standard notation for use in quantum mechanics at the present time [Dirac's 'bra' and 'ket' notation].

I had a very successful time in Copenhagen, because I developed this general physical interpretation [transformation theory] which gave me so much pleasure.... (Dirac, 1977a, pp. 137–138)

And further: "I think that is the piece of work which has most pleased me of all the works that I've done in my life ... The transformation theory (became) my darling.... I just couldn't face giving up the transformation theory [for any- thing]." (Dirac, Report KFKI-1997-62, *Hung. Acad. Sci.*)

We may end this discussion dealing with the development of the transformation theory of quantum mechanics with a story related by Oskar Klein:

> I remember that Heisenberg told me on some occasion that Bohr joked a little bit about some British physicists who had a competition over who was the greatest [theoretician], Darwin or Fowler. Then Heisenberg said that he thought Dirac was really it ... It must have been in the winter of '27 or rather in the fall of '26. (O. Klein, AHQP Interview, Session V, pp. 14–15)

In any case, after the two papers of Dirac and Jordan had appeared and 'when one came to know them,' Klein continued, 'they were regarded as the end of the fight between matrix and wave mechanics, because they covered the whole thing and showed that they [i.e., matrix and wave mechanics] were just different points of view' (O. Klein, *loc. cit.*, p. 15).

# Chapter II
## Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

# Introduction 90

In the previous volumes of *The Historical Development of Quantum Theory*, the questions of the conceptual and mathematical formulation of the new atomic theory and its immediate applicability to old and new phenomena observed in atomic physics constituted the contents of the story. The present chapter assumes a quite different character, as for the first time the physical interpretation of the new theory occupies an almost exclusive place in it. In particular, the fundamental steps of providing the epistemological analysis of the theory were undertaken between spring 1926 and fall 1927 by two leading quantum physicists. At that time, Werner Heisenberg and Niels Bohr attempted and, in the eyes of most physicists of their time and later, accomplished nothing less than the resolution of paradoxes and riddles encountered in the description of atomic phenomena—such as quantum jumps, paths of atomic particles, electron spin, etc.—by introducing certain new concepts that allowed a consistent intellectual interpretation, comparable to the one that had been achieved in the classical theories of the previous centuries. Al- though both of them worked at the same place—the University Institute for The- oretical Physics in Copenhagen—and regularly discussed the detailed problems and their general goals during the whole period, Heisenberg and Bohr approached their tasks from basically different premises. Each proceeding separately in ana- lyzing the facts and situations occurring in quantum theory, they united their re- spective conclusions only at the end of the whole endeavour to fashion what has later been quite properly called the 'Copenhagen interpretation.'$^{74}$

In the course of roughly eighteen months, Bohr and Heisenberg also talked and corresponded with friends and colleagues, who assisted them in their efforts by agreeing with or criticizing the conclusions reached. At the same time, many other leading pioneers in the development of atomic theory presented their own attempts at a physical interpretation of quantum mechanics; in doing so, they often entered into surprising coalitions as far as the preferred methods or epistemological con- sequences derived from them were concerned. Thus, although Erwin Schrödinger —with his 'intuitive' or 'visualizable' (*anschauliche*) view of wave mechanics— occupied one extreme of the interpretation spectrum, Max Born and Pascual

---

$^{74}$ A vast amount of literature exists on the origin and development of the Copenhagen interpreta- tion. We refer especially to the books of Meyer-Abich (1965) and Jammer (1974), and several historical articles will be referred to later in their proper context.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0123 -->

# Introduction 91

Jordan—who had collaborated in developing matrix mechanics—also seemed, at least for a while, to turn entirely to the undulatory scheme: like Schrödinger, they now claimed that it provided the *sole* description of *all* atomic phenomena. In contrast to them, Heisenberg and Pauli made use of Schrödinger's methods eﬀec- tively to solve particular problems, but regarded them merely as a practical *tool for computation* rather than as the bearer of further physical insights. Bohr fol- lowed a systematically odd pattern, for he took during the period under con- sideration what appeared—to both outsiders and insiders—to be a zigzag course between the principal mathematical schemes and their physical interpretation. As in previous years, he concerned himself only little with details of the theoretical– technical description of the phenomena, but pondered about the seemingly oppo- site concepts used, such as particles and waves or quantum jumps and continuous processes. A more consistent course was followed by Wolfgang Pauli; though from the first moment, when it appeared in print, he had emphasized the profound sig- nificance of Schrödinger's undulatory theory, he never expressed any doubt about the necessity of interpreting the formalism in a *nonclassical* and *discontinuous* manner. Ever since 1923, he had battled against any visualization of quantum- theoretical concepts like stationary states and spin of the electron; after the advent of quantum and wave mechanics, he even refused to participate in achieving great success in solving certain problems, if the procedures employed implied the aban- donment of his rigid principles for interpreting them.$^{75}$ Perhaps he still saw his foremost occupation, as he had done since fall 1922, in acting as the main discus- sion partner for Bohr, often sharply criticizing the latter's first ideas about the physical interpretation of particular situations; only after Bohr's efforts had assumed a clearer and more definite shape in the formulation of the comple- mentarity principle would he pursue other things.$^{76}$ Another essential partner in developing the Copenhagen views was Paul Dirac. Though far less, if at all, interested in philosophical questions, he served Bohr and Heisenberg's enterprise during his stay in Copenhagen from fall 1926 to early 1927; with his mathematical techniques, he provided Heisenberg with the tools necessary for deriving his most important result: the uncertainty relations. Bohr, on the other hand, also regarded Dirac's later relativistic electron theory as being completely consistent with the complementarity principle, a principle that Dirac never quite appreciated.

In his 'Erinnerungen an die Zeit der Entwicklung der Quantenmechanik' ('Re- collections of the Period of the Development of Quantum Mechanics,' Heisenberg, 1960), dedicated to the memory of his old friend, Heisenberg had described the important role played by Pauli for the final success of the efforts made in Co-

---

$^{75}$ Thus, apart from composing review articles (still devoted to the prequantum-mechanical status of the theory, e.g., Pauli, 1926b), Pauli wrote very few papers in the years 1926 and 1927. Some of his important results (e.g., on the equivalence of matrix and wave mechanics or the intensities of spectral lines in wave mechanics) were published by colleagues, while to others, he just alluded in passing when he finally submitted a major piece of work (e.g., Pauli, 1927a, b).

$^{76}$ For a specific discussion of Pauli's role in the creation of quantum mechanics and the significance of the Bohr–Pauli dialogue in developing the Copenhagen interpretation, see Hendry (1984).

92 &emsp; Chapter II &emsp; Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

penhagen to achieve the physical interpretation of quantum mechanics, and we shall give here an extended excerpt from it. Heisenberg wrote:

The discussions of Schrödinger’s theory occupied Pauli and me quite a lot. While we immediately recognized the great mathematical progress [it had made], we remained sceptical regarding its physical interpretation [by Schrödinger]. I was deeply stirred by the attempt to establish a wave interpretation as the physical basis of the theory. Letters of summer 1926 contain statements like this: “The more I ponder about the physical part of Schrödinger’s theory, the more ugly do I find it. Schrödinger indeed throws everything quantum-theoretical simply overboard: the photoelectric effect, Franck[-Hertz] collision phenomena, the Stern-Gerlach effect, etc.; then it is easy to establish a theory, but it does not agree with experiments. The big success of Schrödinger’s theory consists in calculating matrix elements.”

Thus our own interest turned to the still not understood interpretation of the mathematical formalism of quantum and wave mechanics. In 1926 Born, in his theory of collision processes, developed and interpreted the wave in configuration space—pursuing an earlier idea of Bohr, Kramers and Slater—correctly as a probability wave. Pauli then explained to me in a letter that Born’s interpretation was just the special case of a much more general prescription. Thus, e.g., one might interpret $|\psi(p)|^2 dp$ to denote the probability of a particle to assume a momentum between $p$ and $p + dp$. This result agreed well with considerations which I had obtained when discussing the fluctuation phenomena. In fall 1926 Dirac worked out his transformation theory, in which the absolute square of matrix elements of the unitary transformation matrix was interpreted as probability.

...

At the same time, in fall 1926, already the uncertainty relations gradually took on shape in the exchange of correspondence between Pauli and myself. In a letter of 28 October there occurs the statement: “The relation $pq - qp = -i\hbar$ therefore corresponds in the wave picture always to the fact that it makes no sense to speak about a monochromatic wave at a given instant of time (or in a very short interval of time).” Pauli remarked in the margin [of this letter of Heisenberg]: “In a time interval which is short with respect to the period [of the wave] it also does not make sense to talk about the state (energy value [of an atom]).” Further my letter says: “Analogously it makes no sense to talk about the position of a corpuscle with a definite velocity. However, if one does not take velocity and position too accurately, it does make sense.” In his response, Pauli tried to divide the phase space into definite cells of size $h$, and to argue that one could not say of a particle whether [or not] it is in a given cell. But I raised the objection: “If you can fix the walls of the cell sharply and can still determine how many particles are in each cell, shouldn’t one then be able to find the number of atoms in arbitrarily small cells by selecting [new] cell walls very close to the original ones? I mean, does it make sense to choose particular cell walls? Perhaps the real situation is that one can, e.g., only determine the relation between two cell walls, not the position of a definite one.”

Closely as these considerations touched upon the correct interpretation, still another three months passed until the formulation arrived at was clear enough that Pauli and I could dare to talk about a final understanding of quantum mechanics. Bohr tried to place the dualism between the wave picture and the particle picture at the starting point of the physical interpretation, while I attempted to complete my goal, which seemed to be fixed already, by using quantum mechanics and Dirac’s

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0125 -->

Introduction &emsp; 93

transformation theory without borrowing [anything] from wave mechanics. These intense discussions, repeated all over again in the case of physical examples, not only succeeded in slowly building a bridge between the two, originally so different, points of departure, but they also helped in providing the accumulation of new material which could be worked out profitably according to both views [of quantum and wave mechanics]. In spite of all efforts, however, we did not succeed in establishing real clarity in quantum theory. The new connections were so unusual, so different from what had been considered in physics to be the safe transmitted treasure of knowledge, hence we were not able to feel familiar with them. On 23 November [1926], following an extended discussion of Dirac’s transformation theory, I wrote to Pauli: “I often ponder about the real meaning of all these formal connections, but it’s horribly (*schauderhaft*) difficult to make something out of them.”

The Christmas vacation [1926] interrupted the discussions on the interpretation only for a short time. It was probably a sign of exhaustion, caused in all of us by the continuous discussions, that Bohr went on a vacation in Norway in the middle of February [1927]. Certainly he wished to use the time, besides skiing, for thinking quietly and undisturbed about the foundations of quantum theory. It also became easier for me to assemble my thoughts; hence, on 23 February, I wrote a letter of 14 pages to Pauli, the content of which coincided essentially with that of the later paper on the uncertainty relations. Pauli’s reply sounded much more positive than I had expected: ‘Day is dawning in quantum theory [*Es wird Tag in der Quantentheorie*],’ so approximately sounded his answer, which encouraged me to formulate the contents of my considerations in a detailed paper. I sent this paper to Pauli a few days afterwards asking for his criticism, so that I could show the already refereed paper to Bohr upon his return [to Copenhagen]. Bohr then was not satisfied with several points of the paper, quite correctly, hence it could be submitted for publication only sometime later with important improvements. Meanwhile Bohr had also developed his concept of complementarity to the extent that the physical content of quantum theory could be surveyed clearly in the same way from [our] different points of departure. Insofar as there still remained conceptual differences, they just referred to the different starting points or to the different ways of expressing things but no longer to a different physical interpretation of the theory. This interpretation had now been clarified completely, and Pauli was the first one outside the Copenhagen circle who agreed without reservation with the new interpretation, to which he had himself contributed so much.

The external conclusion of the whole development then occurred at the Solvay Conference in fall 1927 at Brussels, where Einstein and Lorentz were our most important discussion partners in the interpretation of quantum theory. The disputes between Bohr and Einstein dominated the conference. Though we did not succeed in persuading Einstein that the new interpretation of quantum mechanics was satisfactory in every respect, he had to admit ultimately that it was complete in itself and free of contradictions. Pauli, of course, contributed decisively to the result of the conference, where he often raised his voice. (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*, pp. 43–47)

Besides emphasizing the vital participation of Pauli in achieving the final formulation of the ‘Copenhagen interpretation,’ this extended quotation from Heisenberg’s recollections sets up the framework of the present chapter. As before, we shall not take the later statements of an individual participant in the development as representing the *entire* historical truth. Rather, every detail of them has to be

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0126 -->

94 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

checked against the original documents of the period, i.e., the published papers,
manuscripts, letters, etc. However, one aspect of the story may already be taken
as certain: the main issues of the interpretation problem had been raised, treated,
and resolved by a handful of eminent physicists, whom we have already encoun-
tered as the pioneers of quantum mechanics. Notably, Heisenberg and Bohr were
assisted by a few friends and colleagues, and were challenged by one or two great
opponents, notably, Einstein and, to a lesser extent, Schrödinger. Indeed, the fact
that Einstein assumed the principal role of an *advocatus diaboli* emerges already
from Heisenberg's recollections. The old revolutionary of quantum theory, now in
fall 1927, argued against almost every result achieved in the interpretation of the
new atomic mechanics and forced the partisans of the Copenhagen view to prove
it in many detailed *Gedanken* experiments.

Let us recall at this point that Einstein had been the first person to start the
whole business of a nonclassical interpretation of quantum phenomena, when he
proposed in 1905 the light-quantum hypothesis, a concept that violently contra-
dicted the then well-established undulatory picture of radiation. Eight years later,
Bohr had formulated his atomic model on the basis of the quantum-theoretical
ideas of Planck and Einstein; especially, he had used the nonclassical frequency
condition. In his attempts to refine the model during the following decade, how-
ever, Bohr had occasionally deviated from Einstein's views, notably, in his views
on the nature of radiation, in which he stuck to the undulatory theory. When we
now discuss the roots of the Copenhagen interpretation, we have to depart from
this earlier 'Bohr–Einstein dialogue,' which had begun in the years after 1913.$^{77}$
Hence, we shall begin Section II.1 of the present chapter with a summary of the
main aspects of the Bohr–Einstein exchange on atomic structure and spectral
lines. Then follow brief accounts of several dialogues concerning atomic theory,
involving Einstein and several of his colleagues: they deal with fundamental ideas
on the concept of matter (the Einstein–Weyl–Pauli–Eddington dialogue, 1918–
1923), the nature of identical particles (the Planck–Ehrenfest–Schrödinger dia-
logue, 1919–1925), and the foundations of the Bohr–Sommerfeld atomic theory
and the quantum-theoretical description of radiation (the Bohr–Pauli–Einstein
dialogue, 1922–1926). Covering the entire decade from 1916 to 1926, these dia-
logues, disputes, or debates reveal the essential elements of all serious, early at-
tempts to arrive at a physical interpretation of the quantum phenomena, and their
results also influenced the debates that occurred between 1926 and 1930 on the
interpretation of the new quantum and wave mechanics. Even more, the scientific
style of these earlier debates became refined and intensified in the new ones, which
reached perhaps the highest level of intellectual exchange in the history of science.

More than previously, when he worked on the decisive steps toward formulat-
ing quantum mechanics, Heisenberg—in 1926—began to search specifically for a
physical interpretation of the mathematically completed theory. Still, in his char-

77 For the early discussion on the interpretation of quantum theory, the one between Planck and
Einstein on the significance of the quantum of action, see Volume 1, Part 1, Chapter I.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0127 -->

95 Introduction

acteristic way of proceeding, he would not restrict himself to merely philosophical
deliberations; he rather made use of a unique combination of boldly original
physical ideas and more or less consistent mathematical methods, listening care-
fully at the same time to certain stimulating key hints provided by his usually
severe critic and advisor on epistemological questions, Wolfgang Pauli. The par-
ticular stimulating atmosphere that existed in Copenhagen during the second
half of 1926 and early 1927 provided the background for Heisenberg's creative
work. With Bohr as the towering personality and head of the Institute for Theo-
retical Physics and Heisenberg as his chief assistant, those who were scientifically
active included—besides students and a few senior collaborators—quite a large
number of guests and visitors from abroad, who eagerly applied the various
schemes of modern atomic theory using matrix- or wave-mechanical methods:
e.g., David Dennison from the United States and Friedrich Hund from Germany.
Thus, the Swede Oskar Klein extended Schrödinger's undulatory theory to a five-
dimensional wave mechanics, and the English physicist Paul Dirac produced a
very effective symbolic mathematical formalism, which allowed him to demon-
strate the complete equivalence of all existing (and other imaginable) quantum-
mechanical schemes. This unique local setup, a genuinely bubbling (with ideas to
solve fundamental problems) Copenhagen kitchen, will be described in Section
II.2.

While Bohr at first kept himself a bit in the background, or even annoyed
Heisenberg by leaning toward completely contrary views concerning what con-
cepts might play a role in the interpretation of quantum mechanics, Pauli, in dis-
tant Hamburg, supported his friend's endeavours wholeheartedly, assisting him
substantially in carrying out an ambitious programme: to approach the daunting
task of interpretation directly by analyzing, in terms of Dirac's new and most
general quantum-mechanical transformation formalism, the most precise relations
between the fundamental variables, such as the position and momentum of atomic
particles. This enterprise led Heisenberg to obtain the so-called uncertainty rela-
tions, which implied a characteristic restriction of the classical use of these con-
cepts (Section II.3).

After this fundamental result had been achieved, Bohr stepped into the fore-
ground. He soon clarified and further developed the earlier vague ideas of his own
and others on the wave and particle pictures used for the description of atomic
phenomena into a new epistemological principle, which he would eventually call
the 'principle of complementarity.' As had become his custom for some time, Bohr
avoided to call upon any detailed and complicated computations or to refer con-
sistently to any of the particular mathematical schemes; he rather employed simple
terminology and elementary equations to describe the essential content of this very
central piece of the 'Copenhagen interpretation' (Section II.4).

So far, the story of the physical interpretation of quantum mechanics developed
along a straight path, and one could round it up by reporting the successful pre-
sentation of the uncertainty relations and the complementarity principle at the
fifth Solvay Conference in Brussels in 1927, as well as the lively debate that de-

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0128 -->

96 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

veloped there and continued afterward between the two giants of physical thought:
Bohr and Einstein. However, as it so often happens, the actual history does not
proceed in a linear fashion; side stories interrupt the straight-line development, by
either supporting or delaying the acceptance of later results. Such a side story is
provided by the emergence of a new topic—the quantum theory of fields—which
is usually discussed as a special application or extension of the quantum- or
wave-mechanical schemes, but it must be treated here as an essential vehicle for
promoting Bohr's interpretation efforts. Quantum field theory, though initiated
already in matrix mechanics by Pascual Jordan (in fall 1925), assumed real life
early in 1927 when Dirac treated the problems of radiation theory by writing a
quantum-mechanical formalism for the emission and absorption of light by atoms.
Jordan and Klein, on the one hand, and Jordan and Eugen (Eugene) Wigner, on
the other, used this formalism to develop a systematic approach to treat quantized
nonrelativistic fields obeying Bose and Fermi statistics, respectively. Five years
later, Pauli somewhat derogatorily wrote about their theory in his *Handbuch*
article on wave mechanics:

Here a peculiarly mathematical method must be described which stems from Jordan
and Klein (in the case of symmetrical states) and Jordan and Wigner [for the anti-
symmetrical states] and which may be called a repeated quantization [which had
already been termed "second quantization" ("*zweite Quantelung*")] by Jordan in fall
1927, and first employed in the titles of papers by Jordan (1932a) and Fock (1932);
the basic concept of second quantization, without naming it so had, however, been
first introduced by Dirac, 1927b, of waves in the usual three-dimensional space. This
method grew out of considering the analogy between material particles with sym-
metrical states, on the one hand, and light-quanta of radiation, on the other hand. It
is doubtful whether one deals here with a real physical analogy, and it has been
proven in addition that all results of wave mechanics can be obtained also without
applying this method. (Pauli, 1933c, p. 198)

Back in 1927, the situation appeared quite differently. Bohr especially felt that the
method of 'repeated' or 'second' quantization, and the thus developed scheme of
quantum fields in three dimensions, did supply a most adequate picture of micro-
scopic quantum particles, because it permitted one to describe them properly in a
wave language. We shall therefore discuss this pioneering work on quantum fields
in Section II.5.

Section II.6 then discusses the public presentation of quantum and wave me-
chanics, together with its interpretations by the leading quantum physicists at the
Solvay Conference in October 1927. In particular, we shall reconstruct the reac-
tions of selected participants to the Copenhagen interpretation and the legendary
debate on the consistency of quantum mechanics between Niels Bohr and Albert
Einstein, as well as the later continuation of this debate at the sixth Solvay Confer-
ence in 1930. Although Einstein and Schrödinger in Berlin remained active in mount-
ing attacks on the validity of the uncertainty relations, Bohr proceeded to expand
the application of his complementarity principle beyond the realm of physics.

97 II.1 Dialogues on the Concepts of Atomic and Quantum Theory (1913–1926)

Again, these developments do not exhaust the efforts concerning the physical
interpretation of quantum mechanics in the years between 1927 and 1930. Very
fundamental problems remained to be considered regarding the nature of matter
or its smallest constituents. It seemed that so far a good understanding of the
nature of radiation and of spinless material particles had been achieved. On the
other hand, the elementary particles of matter known at that time, the electrons
and protons, possessed a spin of $1/2 \frac{h}{2\pi}$. Could this elementary unit of intrinsic
angular momentum be derived from a deeper principle? Wolfgang Pauli and
Charles Galton Darwin wrote down the first description of this property in quan-
tum mechanics and derived consistent rules for atomic phenomena. They were
overtaken by Paul Dirac's relativistic electron equation; based on the new mathe-
matics of spinors, it permitted—so to say—a natural explanation of half-integral
spin and all observed properties of the electron, notably, the fine structure of
spectral lines (in agreement with Arnold Sommerfeld's formula of 1915). These
enormous successes were contrasted by serious problems or paradoxes, reminding
the physicists of the situation before the quantum-mechanical revolution took
place. Did a new crisis occur here requiring a deeper push toward the formulation
of a consistent future relativistic quantum field theory? The answer remained open,
because Heisenberg, Pauli, and Jordan succeeded in extending quantum field
theory into a Lorentz covariant scheme: a genuinely relativistic quantum electro-
dynamics, taking into account the interaction between light-quanta, electrons and
protons appeared to be within reach, but for certain difficulties occurring in the
calculation of the inner structure of these 'elementary particles,' and (of course)
with the relativistic Dirac particles. However, this relativistic quantum field
theory obeyed the suitably generalized quantum-mechanical rules and could be
interpreted according to the Heisenberg–Bohr principles. Thus, in March 1929,
Heisenberg eulogized 'that "*Kopenhagener Geist der Quantentheorie*" which has
directed the entire development of atomic physics' (Heisenberg, 1930a, p. x).$^{78}$

## II.1 Dialogues on the Concepts of Atomic and Quantum Theory (1913–1926)

In 1949, Niels Bohr wrote:

When invited by the editor of the series, "*Living Philosophers*," to write an article for
this volume in which contemporary scientists are honouring the epoch-making con-
tributions of Albert Einstein to the progress of natural philosophy and are acknow-
ledging the indebtedness of our whole generation to the guidance his genius has given
us, I thought much of the best way of explaining how much I owe to him for inspi-

78 See Heisenberg's preface to his 1929 Chicago lectures on '*The Physical Principles of the Quantum Theory*' (Heisenberg, 1930a). (The foreword to the book is dated March 1930.)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0130 -->

98 &emsp; Chapter II &emsp; Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

ration. In this connection, the many occasions through the years on which I had the privilege to discuss with Einstein epistemological problems raised by the modern development of atomic physics have come back vividly to my mind and I have felt that I could hardly attempt anything better than to give an account of these discussions which, even if no complete concord has so far been obtained, have been of greatest value and stimulus to me.

With these words, Niels Bohr opened his article, ‘Discussions with Einstein on Epistemological Problems in Atomic Physics,’ which was published in Paul Arthur Schilpp’s book *Albert Einstein: Philosopher-Scientist* (Bohr, 1949, p. 200). Bohr’s detailed recollections of the debates constituted the first example of an old literary genre connected with the history of modern atomic theory.$^{79}$ Perhaps the most extensive item in this kind of literature is Werner Heisenberg’s *Der Teil und das Ganze* with the subtitle ‘*Gespräche im Umkreis der Atomphysik*’ (‘Conversations in the Environs of Atomic Physics,’ Heisenberg, 1969). As Heisenberg himself explained the particular choice of style in the preface to the English translation of his book:

Science rests on experiments; its results are obtained through talks among those who work on it and who consult one another about their interpretations of their experiments. Through them the author hopes to demonstrate that science is rooted in conversations. (Heisenberg, 1971, p. xvii)

Although the literal reconstruction of the actual conversations may be impossible after so many years have passed, the outcome should serve the purpose of bringing up ‘time and again, philosophical and political problems,’ demonstrating especially ‘that science is quite inseparable from these more general questions’ (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*).

The personal accounts of Bohr and Heisenberg, the two principal actors in the drama of the interpretation of quantum mechanics, stimulated some historians of science to investigate the role of dialogues in the development of the theory.$^{80}$ According to the definition in a renowned reference work, ‘Dialogue, in its widest

In this article, entitled ‘*Massträgheit und Kosmos. Ein Dialog*’ (‘Inertia of Mass and Cosmos. A Dialogue’), Weyl formulated his profound ideas and analysis of the problem in the form of a witty dialogue between St. Peter and St. Paul; St. Peter appeared as a staunch defender of Mach’s assumption or principle that the inertia of bodies is caused by the action and cooperation of all masses in the universe, especially the distant ones; St. Paul, on the other hand, attacked the principle, basing his arguments on general relativity theory and its extensions. Weyl’s dialogue illuminated the most elementary and fundamental question to be asked in relativity theory, that is: in how far does the physical situation, described by the theory, really depend on relative motion, as Mach had demanded since 1883, and not on some absolute motion?
