II.1 &emsp; Dialogues on the Concepts of Atomic and Quantum Theory (1913–1926) &emsp; 99

sense, is the recorded conversation of two or more persons,’ and, ‘As a literary form it is a carefully organized exposition, by means of invented conversation, of contrasting philosophical positions or intellectual attitudes.’$^{81}$ In ancient Greece, the literary technique of the dialogue was especially perfected by Plato in his Socratic *Dialogues*; having successors in the Roman Antiquity and the Christian Medieval Ages, the technique of the dialogue was revived at the turn of the Renaissance by politicians (like Johann von Tepl in his *Der Ackermann aus Böhmen*, 1400), poets, and scientists (notably, Galileo Galilei in his *Discorsi e Dimonstrazioni Matematiche interno a due nuove scienze* (‘Dialogue on Two New Sciences,’ 1638), retaining much of the style of medieval university disputes. Modern philosophy has created another concept of ‘*dialogical* thinking’ that emphasizes, in spite of subjective differences, the possibility of protagonists getting together at a higher plane of discussion. One may ask as to how far the discussions between physicists on the content and interpretation of quantum theory fit into these philosophical forms of dialogues, but certainly one fact should be registered: the ‘conversations’ or ‘debates’ between the leading experts, who put forward their characteristic positions, illustrate important aspects of the historical development. The quantum theoreticians indeed carried out dialogues, by directly talking to each other when assembled at institutes, conferences, vacation resorts, etc., by discussing specific problems in letters, or by publishing papers emphasizing sharply different points of view in interpreting the results of their calculations. All of these types of dialogue took place in the dozen years following the appearance of Niels Bohr’s fundamental work on quantum theory. Although Bohr did not meet Albert Einstein personally until April 1920, their publications on the stationary states and the nature of radiation in quantum theory developed into the first such dialogue between them. The next dialogue, which we shall outline, took place entirely through the medium of correspondence between Albert Einstein, Wolfgang Pauli, Hermann Weyl, and Arthur Stanley Eddington. Another lengthy debate concerning the individuality of atomic particles, involving Paul Ehrenfest, Max Planck, and later Erwin Schrödinger, again occurred mostly through published papers. When he spent a year from fall 1922 to fall 1923 in Copenhagen, Pauli discussed with Bohr the validity of semiclassical atomic models; later, he participated by the exchange of letters in the second Bohr–Einstein dialogue on the nature of atomic radiation (1924–1925), and, more or less in the same way, he conducted with Bohr a debate on the concept of electron spin from December 1925 to March 1926 (see Volume 1, Part 2, Section VI.4).

**(a) Stationary States, Emission and Absorption of Atomic Radiation, and the Light-Quantum (1913–1922)**

Bohr’s exchange with Einstein on quantum-theoretical concepts began immediately after he wrote the rules for his atomic models. These rules included, in par-

100  Chapter II  Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

ticular, the existence of stationary states and the frequency condition (for the emitted and absorbed spectral lines) ‘given by Planck’s theory’ in accordance with Einstein’s equation for the photoelectric effect (Bohr, 1913b, p. 7). Einstein, who first learned about Bohr’s theory at the Vienna *Naturforscherversammlung* in September 1913, reacted very positively, as George de Hevesy wrote to Bohr: ‘He told me, it [i.e., the theory] is a very interesting one, important one if it is right.’ Einstein especially liked that, according to Bohr’s assumption, ‘the frequency of [the emitted and absorbed] light does not depend at all on the frequency of the electron [as followed from the classical theory],’ and he called this ‘an *enormous achiewement* [*sic*]’ (de Hevesy to Bohr, 23 September 1913). Three years later, Einstein based his new derivation of Planck’s blackbody radiation law explicitly on atoms (emitting and absorbing radiation) to exist in stationary states (Einstein, 1916d). He further assumed, in the same paper, that the transitions from atomic states of higher energy to those of lower energy obeyed statistical laws similar to those of radioactive decay processes; finally, he introduced, besides the ‘spontaneous radiation,’ what he called ‘induced radiation,’ which is connected with the transition to a lower energy state under the influence of an external radiation field having a characteristic transition frequency. Bohr immediately accepted these new assumptions of Einstein in his extensive memoir submitted in November 1917 (Bohr, 1918a). Thus, the views of Bohr and Einstein on the quantum problem seemed to agree essentially, as far as the fundamental postulates were concerned.

Still, one fundamental difference of opinion could be detected with respect to the light-quantum concept. Although Einstein, in the years between 1912 and 1916, had tried to abandon his light-quantum hypothesis of 1905, he expounded in the second, more detailed paper on the radiation theory of 1916 a quite clear return to his old concept. In particular, he wrote:

    If a bundle of radiation acts such that a molecule hit by it absorbs or emits (by irradiation) the energy quantum $h\nu$ as radiation in an elementary process, then the momentum $h\nu/c$ is always transferred to the molecule, notably in the direction of the bundle’s propagation if the energy is absorbed and in the opposite direction if the energy is emitted.

    If a molecule suffers without an external excitation an energy loss of the amount $h\nu$ by giving away this energy in the form of radiation (by emission), then also this process is a *directed* one. Emission in the form of spherical waves does not exist. The molecule suffers in an elementary process a recoil of the amount $h\nu/c$ in a direction that is, according to the present state of the theory, only determined by “accident.” (Einstein, 1917a, p. 127)

This extended light-quantum concept certainly met with the approval of some quantum physicists, like Arnold Sommerfeld, who even suggested a ‘reconciliation of quantum and wave theory’ in the following way:

    The wave process occurs alone in the aether which satisfies Maxwell’s equations and acts quantum-theoretically like a linear oscillator of undetermined frequency $\nu$. The atom only supplies a certain amount of *energy* and *angular momentum* as the ingre-

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0133 -->

II.1  Dialogues on the Concepts of Atomic and Quantum Theory (1913–1926)  101

dients of the wave process; but it has nothing to do directly with the (wave-) oscillation itself. From the energy the aether takes—according to your $h\nu$-law—its frequency, and from the angular momentum its polarization. (Sommerfeld to Bohr, 18 May 1918)

In support of his proposal, Sommerfeld cited his assistant Adalbert Rubinowicz’s selection rules for atomic radiation (Rubinowicz, 1918a), but Bohr adamantly disagreed both with the light-quantum hypothesis and with Sommerfeld’s conclusions.

In the comprehensive memoir on atomic spectra cited above, Bohr had derived the selection rules not from any angular momentum conservation laws applied to atoms and individual radiation-quanta, but rather from his correspondence principle (Bohr, 1918a, pp. 34–35). When, three years later, Rubinowicz (1921) reiterated the light-quantum aspects to explain the polarization of atomic spectral lines further, Bohr attacked the result and rather insisted: ‘We do not know the laws which apply to the coupling of partial systems of the total system consisting of atoms and radiation’ (Bohr, 1921b, p. 5).$^{82}$ Bohr repeated this point even more sharply in a report on ‘Atoms and Electrons’ prepared for the third Solvay Conference on Physics in April 1921; there, he stated that the light-quantum hypothesis, although it ‘seems to offer the only possibility of accounting for the photoelectric effect, if we adhere to the unrestricted applicability of the ideas of energy and momentum conservation,’ still ‘presents apparently insurmountable difficulties from the point of view of the phenomena of optical interference’ (Bohr, 1923e, pp. 241–242). Or, as Paul Ehrenfest—who had assisted Bohr in working out his report to the 1921 Solvay Conference—remarked to Einstein: ‘He [i.e., Bohr] is much more willing to renounce energy and momentum theorems (in their classical form) for elementary atomic processes, and to maintain them only statistically, than to “lay blame on the aether”’ (Ehrenfest to Einstein, 17 January 1922).$^{83}$

That Einstein did not share at all such a statistical interpretation (as the consequence following from his radiation paper of 1916) may be seen from the interest that he took in 1921 in an experiment that should prove the ‘elementary process of light-emission’ (Einstein, 1921b). Shortly after the experiment was performed (in Berlin by Hans Geiger and Walther Bothe), Einstein noted: ‘One may conclude that the emission field [of radiation] does not have a component having simultaneously the two properties of being (a) undulatory and (b) uniform (*allseitig*)’ (Einstein to Ehrenfest, 11 January 1922). That confirmed, in his view, the light-quantum hypothesis, but Ehrenfest criticized Einstein’s arguments as being fallacious, and the latter finally agreed ‘that deeper conclusions cannot be derived from the experiment concerning the nature of the emission process’ (Einstein, 1922b, p. 22).$^{84}$ Thus, the question remained open through most of 1922, until Arthur

Holly Compton demonstrated with his experiments on the scattering of X-rays by light-atoms the existence of a new effect, which he proposed to take as a second clear evidence—even more definite than the ‘complicated’ photoelectric effect—for the existence of Einstein’s light-quantum (A. H. Compton, 1923a, b). The detailed discussion of this effect initiated a new, second, Bohr–Einstein dialogue.

**(b) The Weyl–Eddington and Pauli–Weyl–Eddington Dialogues on the Unified Theory of Matter (1918–1923)**

In the year he published his new derivation of Planck’s radiation law (involving the statistical decay law and the assumption of stimulated emission), Einstein completed his General Relativity Theory, a theory of matter and gravitation (Einstein, 1915g, 1916c). Simultaneously with Einstein (and based on previous exchanges with the latter), David Hilbert in Göttingen presented a paper to the Göttingen Academy, entitled ‘*Die Grundlagen der Physik*’ (‘The Foundations of Physics’), in which he combined the earlier ideas of Gustav Mie’s ‘*Grundlagen einer Theorie der Materie*’ (‘The Foundations of a Theory of Matter’: Mie, 1912a, b, c) with Einstein’s new assumption of general covariance to develop an even more general theory of matter and electricity (Hilbert, 1915).<sup>85</sup> Einstein did not like Hilbert’s approach at all. ‘It is needlessly specialized and, as far as matter is concerned, unnecessarily complicated. It is not honest (Gaussian) in design, [and reflects] the pretension of a superman by a camouflage of techniques,’ he declared to Ehrenfest (letter quoted in Seelig, 1954, p. 199). To Rudolph Humm, a Göttingen student of Hilbert’s circle, he expressed himself more politely. As Humm recalled: ‘He [i.e., Einstein] himself never thought so formally. . . He does not rush immediately to generalize as we do in Göttingen.’ And, further:

> I [Humm] suggested to him that he had taken recourse to quantum theory in order to modify the theory of gravitation, while Hilbert on the other hand wanted to derive the quantum theory from the theory of gravitation. At this he made a roguish grin. This would not do, he said, even though the theory of gravitation was more general. But the ideas of relativity could not yield anything more than gravitation. (Quoted in Seelig, 1954, p. 188)

Evidently, as we shall see below, this was not Einstein’s last word.
With Einstein staying away from generalizing General Relativity further—instead he sought to draw cosmological consequences from the new field equations of gravitation—Hilbert’s former disciple Hermann Weyl jumped into the fray. He first extended the geometrical foundations of the theory, arguing:

> In Riemannian geometry [as used by Einstein] a last [remaining] element of a geometry at-a-distance has been retained—without any real (*sachlich*) reason, as far as I

<sup>85</sup> For details, see Mehra, 1973.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0135 -->

II.1 Dialogues on the Concepts of Atomic and Quantum Theory (1913–1926) 103

can see. The quadratic form $\left[ ds^2 = \sum_{i,k} g_{ik} dx_i dx_k \right]$ indeed allows one not only to compare (with respect to their lengths) two vectors at the same point but also at two distant [space] points. The genuinely infinitesimally-close geometry, however, should *recognize only one principle of transferring a length from one point to an infinitesimally adjacent one*, and then it can be assumed that the problem of length transfer from one point to another at a finite distance is integrable, just as sparingly as in the problem of transfer of directions. By removing this in consequence, a geometry is obtained which, when applied to the [real] world, surprisingly *does not only explain the phenomena of gravitation but also of electricity*. In this theory, *all physical quantities have a meaning in the world geometry: the action variable, in particular, occurs in it as a real number. It leads to a world law which is essentially uniquely defined; it even permits us to understand, in a way, why the world is four-dimensional*. (Weyl, 1918c, pp. 466–467)

After pronouncing these words that carried great importance, Weyl went on to construct a formal expression for the action variable, and ‘in order to pass from geometry to physics,’ he turned more or less (as Hilbert had done) to Gustav Mie’s ideas. Thus, his unified theory of gravitation and electricity also satisfied a new ‘*Maßstab–Invarianz*’ (later called ‘gauge invariance’) under the transformation (derived from the transfer-of-length principle),

$$g'_{\mu\nu} = \lambda g_{\mu\nu} \quad \text{and} \quad \phi'_\mu = \phi_\mu - \frac{1}{\lambda} \frac{\partial \lambda}{\partial x^\mu} \qquad (102)$$

for the gravitational tensor $g_{\mu\nu}$ and the electromagnetic vector potential $\phi_\mu$.
Weyl’s grand scheme (*Entwurf*) of a unified theory, which Einstein submitted on his behalf to the Prussian Academy, did not meet the approval of the Berlin physicists, especially that of Max Planck and Walther Nernst, who asked Einstein to add his criticism to Weyl’s paper. In contrast to the Berlin physicists, Arnold Sommerfeld in Munich and Arthur Eddington in Cambridge found Weyl’s theory ‘truly wonderful’ and a ‘master symphony.’<sup>86</sup> Einstein liked the beauty of the proposal, but declared it to be impossible ‘that the theory corresponded with Nature’ (Einstein to Weyl, 15 April 1918).<sup>87</sup> Hence he rather defended his choice of introducing fixed measures and wrote in the addendum:

> Such a definition of the elementary distance $ds$ would only be illusory if the concepts of ‘unit-rod’ and ‘unit-clock’ rest on a fundamentally wrong assumption; this would be the case if the length of a unit-rod (or the gear-velocity of a unit-clock) depended on the prehistory. If this were really so in Nature, then no chemical element with spectral lines of definite frequency could exist; but the relative frequency of two (spatially neighbouring) atoms of the same chemical element would be different in general. Since this is not the case, I am sorry to say: the fundamental hypothesis of the theory appears to me to be unacceptable, though every reader must admire the depth and boldness of the theory. (Einstein in Weyl, 1918c, p. 478).

<sup>86</sup> For details of the reception of Weyl’s theory and the following disputes, see Hendry, 1984, Chapters 2–4.
<sup>87</sup> The translation of this sentence in Hendry, 1984, p. 11, is misleading.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0136 -->

104 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

Upon this, Weyl answered that the situation outlined by Einstein might occur only in strong fields (either gravitational or electromagnetic); further, neither Einstein’s theory nor his own allowed one to predict the period of a clock, or explicitly: ‘One has to observe that the mathematical-ideal process of vector transfer, which underlies the mathematical construction of geometry, has nothing to do with the real phenomena of the motion of a clock, whose course is determined by natural laws.’ (Weyl, *loc. cit.*, p. 480)

At this point, one may ask: what does this dispute concerning a classical unified field theory have to do with the fundamental problems of quantum theory? Several answers may be given. First, both Einstein and Weyl were deeply interested in the two revolutionary theories of the period—relativity and quantum theory—the common overlap between and the separation of which had not yet been fully clarified. Second, Einstein and Weyl would continue to participate in later dialogues dealing with particular mathematical and epistemological problems of quantum theory. Third, by entering into a dialogue with Weyl and Eddington on the unified field theory, Wolfgang Pauli made his debut as an important philosophical thinker on fundamental questions in physics; he would contribute to this interest by his profound interventions in the quantum-theoretical debates.
Einstein thought seriously of avoiding the features that he found repugnant in Weyl’s theory, hoping at the same time to get rid of the cosmological constant, the auxiliary construct that he had introduced in seeking to apply General Relativity to the problem of the Universe. He hinted at the solution of both tasks in a paper, communicated on 10 April 1919, to the Prussian Academy under the title ‘*Spielen Gravitationsfelder im Aufbau der materiellen Elementarteilchen eine wesentliche Rolle?*’ (‘Do Gravitational Fields Play an Essential Role in the Structure of Elementary Particles?’, Einstein, 1919). Einstein first admitted that the original field equations of gravitation

$$R_{ik} - \frac{1}{2} g_{ik} R = -\gamma T_{ik} \qquad (103)$$

(with $R_{ik}$ and $R$ denoting the Riemannian curvature tensor and scalar, respectively, $g_{ik}$ denoting the metric tensor, and $\gamma$ denoting Newton’s constant of gravitation) necessarily lead to Mie’s theory if the mass tensor $T_{ik}$ originates from the antisymmetric electromagnetic field tensor $\phi_{\alpha\beta}$ alone, i.e.,

$$T_{ik} = \frac{1}{4} g_{ik} \phi_{\alpha\beta} \phi^{\alpha\beta} - \phi_{i\alpha} \phi_{k\beta} g^{\alpha\beta}. \qquad (104)$$

Upon replacing the factor 1/2 in front of the $R$-term in Eq. (103) by 1/4, however, he obtained a different result: ‘The curvature scalar now plays the role of a negative pressure which assumes a constant value $R_0$ outside the electrical corpuscle. Within each corpuscle there exists a negative pressure ($R - R_0$), whose descent establishes a balance against the electrodynamical force’ (Einstein, 1919, p. 352).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0137 -->

II.1  Dialogues on the Concepts of Atomic and Quantum Theory (1913–1926)  105

As a consequence, he derived the stability of a static, closed universe without having to introduce an extra cosmological constant plus the stability of any spherically symmetric distribution of electricity. Einstein found only one defect in his new theory, namely: ‘The problem of the constitution of elementary quanta [i.e., of light-quanta in particular] cannot be solved on the basis of the given field equations’ (Einstein, *loc. cit.*, p. 356).

The young Wolfgang Pauli, then 18 years old, reacted differently. Having become familiar with the work of Einstein and Weyl (Pauli, 1919a), he began to derive consequences from Weyl’s theory on the advance of the perihelion of Mercury and the deflection of light rays by the Sun (Pauli, 1919b, c). He obtained agreement of the results with those from Einstein’s original equation of General Relativity, provided the ‘world function’ (i.e., the action function in Weyl’s theory) was chosen suitably (see Weyl, 1919). Although the theory so modified allowed Pauli to remove certain obstacles to propel it toward its recognition, other difficulties—some of them more serious—remained. As Pauli emphasized:

> The main difficulty—besides Einstein’s objection which has not really been adequately refuted—is that the theory does not explain satisfactorily the asymmetry of both types of electricity [i.e., the difference in masses of positively charged hydrogen nuclei (protons) and negatively charged electrons]. That won’t be easy to remove. I also do not want to forget about a physical-conceptual objection. In Weyl’s theory one operates constantly with the field strength in the interior of the electron. For the physicist, however, this quantity [field strength] is defined only as a force acting on a test-body; and, since there exist no smaller test-bodies than the electron itself, the concept of an electric field strength in a mathematical point appears to be an empty, meaningless fiction. In physics, one would prefer to stick to introducing only those quantities which can, in principle, be observed. Might we not altogether be on the wrong track in considering *continuum-field theories* for the field in the interior of the electron? (Pauli, 1919 c, pp. 749–750)

We have pursued the discussion of the last objection (which was intended to constitute the basic principle for establishing any physical theory)—Pauli may have inherited it from his godfather Ernst Mach—when it became operative in a special quantum-theoretical situation, namely, in the story of Heisenberg’s taking his first step in the discovery of quantum of quantum mechanics; there it became his guiding principle, and little more need be said here.$^{88}$ In 1919, Weyl took this argument seriously, while Einstein did not agree. Thus, he stated in a letter: ‘I myself do not believe that the solution to the quanta [which, for him, also included charged particles] has to be found by giving up the continuum’ (Einstein to Born, 27 January 1920). Later, at the Bad Nauheim *Naturforscherversammlung*, Einstein openly replied to Pauli: ‘With the increasing refinement of the system of scientific concepts, the manner and procedure of associating the concepts with experiences becomes increasingly more complicated.’ In the case of new experiences, he argued,

$^{88}$ See Volume 2, Section V.2.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0138 -->

106 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

one rather has ‘to replace the system of associating concepts [with experiences] by a more complicated one’ (Einstein, in the discussion of Weyl, 1920, p. 651). Six years later, he would express himself even more definitely in a conversation with Werner Heisenberg in Berlin: ‘It is the theory which decides what we can observe.’⁸⁹ Arthur Stanley Eddington, finally, would take Pauli’s ‘operationalist’ criticism—that is, a physical theory should be expressed exclusively in terms of observable quantities—to heart. In 1921, Eddington wrote a series of papers, in which he considered the shape and size of an electron as being indeterminable by observation, but hoped to get a handle on these properties by turning to a generalized version of Weyl’s theory depending on further parameters (see, especially, Eddington, 1921a). Two years later, he published a book on *The Mathematical Theory of Relativity*, in which he provided a full access to his ideas on this subject. The section entitled ‘Natural Geometry and World Geometry’ contained his credo, namely:

to give all our variables . . . a suitable graphical representation in some new conceptual space—not actual space. With sufficient ingenuity it ought to be possible to accomplish this, for no hypothesis is implied as to the nature of quantities so represented. This generalized graphical scheme may not be helpful to the progress of our knowledge; we attempt it in the hope that it will render the interconnection of electromagnetic and graphical phenomena more intelligible. I think it will be found that this hope is not disappointed. (Eddington, 1923b, p. 197)

Pauli, to whom Eddington had sent a copy of the new book, thanked him, but disagreed with Eddington’s distinction between mathematical and real geometry. In contrast, he stressed again the ‘unprovable viewpoint’ that every physical theory must start with a definition of its variables, which includes a statement of how to measure it. Then, he continued:

We now know both from experimental results and from quantum-theoretical considerations . . . that even an electron in a light wave does not in fact move at all as specified [by the classical theory]. The field as a light source is therefore at present undefined. But the path of an electron . . . is just as little so. Indeed one can only define this through the action of an electron on other elementary particles, and in a non-static field this again fails to satisfy the classical laws. Some physicists have fallen upon the idea . . . of completely abandoning the concept of the field of a light wave and of only describing the notion of the electron. This we wholly reject; for on the one hand it scarcely helps us overcome the difficulty, and on the other hand it renders a connection with the classical theory, which has proved itself so brilliant for large-scale phenomena, quite impossible. We can proceed only through a modification, not through an abandonment of the field concept. (Pauli to Eddington, 20 September 1923, in Pauli, 1979, pp. 116–117).⁹⁰

II.1 Dialogues on the Concepts of Atomic and Quantum Theory (1913–1926) 107

Such was the opinion that Pauli expressed in fall 1923, after some negative experiences in not being able to derive the behaviour of the electrons of many-electron atoms in magnetic fields. Soon, he would advocate more radical changes, but these occurred in another dialogue that he got into with Niels Bohr during the next few years.

**(c) The Planck–Ehrenfest–Schrödinger–Einstein Dialogue on Identical Particles in Quantum Theory (1919–1925)**

This dialogue has been outlined in some detail in connection with the Schrödinger story.⁹¹ It deals with the problem of finding the correct quantum-theoretical behaviour of systems consisting of identical atomic particles, i.e., quantum statistics. Max Planck had initiated the topic by assuming the indistinguishability of identical objects (oscillators) in his radiation theory of 1900 and extended the assumption later to atomic particles and molecules (Planck, 1900f, 1916b). In 1920, Paul Ehrenfest raised objections against this procedure (Ehrenfest and Trkal, 1920). The key to the solution was provided by Einstein (1925a) before the new quantum mechanics became available, in the sense of Planck, based on Stayendra Nath Bose’s counting method for light-quanta and Louis de Broglie’s hypothesis of matter waves.

**(d) The Bohr–Pauli–Einstein Dialogue on the Fundamental Problems of Atomic Structure and Radiation Theory (1922–1926)**

In June 1922, Wolfgang Pauli heard Niels Bohr for the first time when the latter delivered a set of seven lectures on atomic theory in Göttingen; these lectures summarized the then current status of the quantum theory of atomic structure, a triumphant presentation of the principles and applications obtained since 1913. On the same occasion, Bohr invited Pauli to join him in Copenhagen for a year and help him in formulating some of his papers.⁹² This stay, from September 1922 to October 1923, not only fostered Pauli’s career immensely, it also involved him in a constant dialogue with his host Niels Bohr on the principles of atomic and radiation theory, which lasted for several decades. Here, only the early phase of this dialogue will be summarized.⁹³

Besides helping Bohr in formulating his ideas, Pauli displayed during the first few months of his stay in Copenhagen an interest in the difficult helium problem, on which Bohr and Kramers had been working for years and which occupied

⁹¹ We refer to Volume 5, Part 2, pp. 361–366 and pp. 385–402.
⁹² Pauli’s assistance was acknowledged in Bohr’s memoir on fundamental postulates of the quantum theory (Bohr, 1923a) and in a paper on line spectra (Bohr, 1923c); furthermore, Pauli translated Bohr’s Nobel lecture into German (Bohr, 1923b).

108 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

Heisenberg in Munich and Göttingen independently at the same time. All of these efforts, however, did not yield the desired success; ultimately, an investigation by Max Born and Heisenberg dealing with the excited states of the helium atom, rather, demonstrated a failure beyond any doubt.⁹⁴ Early in 1923, Bohr and Pauli attacked another of the major unsolved problems, the anomalous Zeeman effects, on which Heisenberg, Alfred Landé, and Arnold Sommerfeld had published several pioneering papers.⁹⁵ In contrast to their predecessors, Bohr and Pauli in Copenhagen did not wish to employ arbitrary assumptions to achieve a fit with the available data. Proceeding in their own way, they submitted in February 1923 a note to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, but did not have it published because, as Bohr wrote in a letter: ‘It was an attempt of despair (*Verzweiflungsversuch*) to stick to integral quantum numbers, hoping to obtain from the paradoxical situation a hint about how to proceed towards a solution of the anomalous Zeeman effects.’ (Bohr to Landé, 3 March 1923) Later that spring, Pauli also attempted to make use of the Heisenberg–Landé half-integral quantum numbers without arriving at a description of the anomalous Zeeman effects that (otherwise) satisfied the principles of the existing atomic theory. Thus, he described the failure of the whole scheme in a letter to his former teacher Sommerfeld:

I have now got to know Bohr’s theory of the periodic system quite well, its strengths as well as its defects. . . . The defect of the theory is that it does not yield an explanation of the values 2, 8, 18, 32, . . . for the length of periods, since one cannot draw any safe conclusions at which point [atomic numbers] the periods are closed. Moreover, in particular, it does not provide at all—because of the additional failure of classical mechanics ‘to account for the stationary states themselves in case of systems having more than one electron—sufficient foundation for the quantitative evaluation of the spectra of such systems. (Pauli to Sommerfeld, 6 June 1923, in Pauli, 1979, p. 95)

As Pauli reported further, Bohr admitted ‘the necessity of formally introducing half-integral quantum numbers,’ but interpreted it as ‘pointing an aspect of the phenomena that means something completely foreign and new to the theory of conditionally periodic systems [i.e., the standard quantum theory of atomic structure]’ (Pauli, *loc. cit.*, p. 96).

Thus far, Pauli worked on the problems of atomic structure and largely agreed with Bohr in all respects. However, he would soon abandon the latter’s somewhat compromising line of the interpretation of quantum phenomena and demand more radical changes, especially after Bohr’s departure in September 1923 for a visit to the United States. Pauli’s scientific output during the year he spent in

II.1  Dialogues on the Concepts of Atomic and Quantum Theory (1913–1926)  109

Copenhagen seemed to be quite a meagre one: two papers on the anomalous Zeeman effects, one submitted in April (Pauli, 1923a) and another in October (Pauli, 1924a). He described the poor result as: ‘At the moment, as far as the theory of the anomalous Zeeman effects and atoms having more than one electron as a whole is concerned, it is a great misery’ (Pauli to Sommerfeld, 19 July 1923, in Pauli, 1979, p. 106). He also felt miserable during the months after his return to Hamburg; not being able to work successfully on the desperately difficult problems of atomic theory himself, he severely criticized instead Heisenberg’s further attempts to do so. ‘When I think about his ideas, they appear terrible to me and I grumble about them to myself,’ he confessed to Bohr in February 1924, adding: ‘The reason is that he is very *unphilosophical* [our emphasis], and he does not care about the clear formulation of the basic assumptions and their connection with the established theories.’ (Pauli to Bohr, 11 February 1924, *loc. cit.*, p. 143) He wished to return soon to Copenhagen to discuss the status of various problems. Bohr replied that he would be happy to welcome Pauli in April and sent him a copy of his most recent memoir that he had just submitted to the *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Bohr et al., 1924), requesting some ‘proposals for an improvement in the language of the presentation’ (Bohr to Pauli, 16 February 1924, *loc. cit.*, p. 146). Pauli did so and accepted Bohr’s invitation to visit Copenhagen in spring; in Copenhagen, Bohr and Kramers succeeded in winning Pauli’s support for their new radiation theory, but after a few months, he resolutely turned against it and became its severest critic.

As we have outlined above, Bohr had initially paid little attention to the problems of radiation theory; he more or less hoped that the undulatory approach might suffice if one would just add some correspondence-like arguments, as had been the case for obtaining Rubinowicz’s selection rules. Still, he remembered quite well the problems posed by light-quantum effects, and he had reflected for some time on the ways out of these problems; for instance, in an unpublished manuscript, entitled ‘Principles of Quantum Theory’ (of 1917–1918, quoted in Bohr, 1984, p. 15), he had written: ‘It would seem that any theory capable of an explanation of the photoelectric effect as well as the interference phenomena must involve a departure from the ordinary theorem of conservation of energy as regards the interaction between radiation and matter.’$^{96}$ Bohr continued to stick to this opinion in the following years; then, in December 1922, the situation changed drastically, because Arthur Holly Compton of St. Louis, Missouri, discovered the new effect that would be named after him (Compton, 1923a, b). Compton explained perfectly the change in wavelength observed in the scattering of X-rays by light-atoms by applying Einstein’s light-quantum hypothesis and strict energy and

$^{96}$ The same point was raised by Charles Galton Darwin of Cambridge in a letter to Bohr, dated 20 July 1919. In his prepared reply, which he did not send, Bohr emphasized that the interaction between the electromagnetic forces (of radiation) and matter ‘conservation of energy seems to be quite out of question’ (Bohr, 1984, p. 16).

Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

momentum conservation. Although the Compton effect was vigorously debated in America and Europe,⁹⁷ Bohr did not react to it in public.⁹⁸ On the other hand, Pauli—his personal assistant in those days—wrote in summer 1923 (while visiting Hamburg for vacation) a paper dealing with the thermal equilibrium between radiation and free electrons, in which he made use of the Compton effect, including energy and momentum conservation (Pauli, 1923b). When that paper appeared in print (October 1923), Bohr was visiting America, and there he could be persuaded to take the effect seriously. Finally, he got alarmed; evidently, his keen old idea concerning the statistical conservation of energy and momentum—devised to rescue the undulatory radiation theory also for light-quantum type of effects—was at stake. Thus, Edwin Kemble of Harvard University, who attended a meeting of the American Physical Society in Cincinnati, where Compton’s genuine light-quantum interpretation scored a victory, wrote to Bohr: ‘It seems to me hopeless to try to hold on to the wave theory.’ (Kemble to Bohr, 4 January 1924) He quickly added, however, ‘Slater’s recent scheme for a combination of wave theory and corpuscular theory may solve your difficulties.’ John Clarke Slater, actually a student of Kemble’s, had meanwhile arrived in Copenhagen, and Bohr and Kramers joined forces with him to develop a suitable version of ‘The Quantum Theory of Radiation,’ which allowed them to unite Slater’s proposals with Bohr’s statistical approach to the conservation of energy and momentum (Bohr *et al.*, 1924). The new theory rested on two key assumptions:

(1) The atoms in a given state are immersed in a ‘virtual’ radiation field containing all frequencies of transition from this state to another allowed one (Slater).
(2) The causal connection between the transitions in distant atoms is abandoned, especially a direct application of the principle of energy and momentum conservation—the latter quantities are only conserved on the statistical average (Bohr, Kramers).

Apparently, the Bohr–Kramers–Slater radiation theory offered great prospects for obtaining immediate successes; in particular, Hendrik Kramers used it to derive a formula for the dispersion of light by atoms (Kramers, 1924a, b).⁹⁹ Several prominent physicists, including Max Born, Erwin Schrödinger, Rudolf Ladenburg, and Richard Becker, applauded the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory of radiation. Some of them (such as Schrödinger) liked the statistical aspects of the theory, and others admitted the success obtained in treating dispersion-like atomic problems. Strenuous objections arose also: thus, Sommerfeld called it a ‘lousy’

compromise (‘fauler’ *Kompromiß*), and to Edmund Stoner it appeared to be simply ‘unnatural.’¹⁰⁰ The sharpest rejection, however, came immediately from Einstein, who was followed—with some delay—by Pauli. The exchange of correspondence and the public dispute developed into a veritable Bohr–Einstein–Pauli dialogue, and this time, the opinions clashed quite sharply.¹⁰¹
On 24 April 1924, Einstein wrote to Born: ‘Bohr’s opinion about radiation theory is of great interest to me. But I should not want to be forced into giving up strict causality without defending it more strongly than I have done so far.’¹⁰² A month later, he spoke about the paper of Bohr, Kramers, and Slater in the Berlin Colloquium, and on 31 May, he finally summarized his objections in a letter to Ehrenfest:¹⁰³

(1) Nature seems to adhere strictly to the conservation laws (Franck-Hertz, Stokes’ rule). Why should actions-at-a-distance be expected?
(2) A mirror box with internal radiation, placed in a radiation-free empty space, would execute continually increasing Brownian motion.
(3) The definite renunciation of strict causality is difficult to tolerate.
(4) One would almost be inclined also to demand an acoustic (elastic) *virtual* radiation field in solid bodies for it is not easy to believe that quantum *mechanics* needs to be based on an electric theory of matter.
(5) The process of ordinary scattering (not at the proper frequency of the molecule), which is above all decisive for the optical behaviour of bodies, fits partly into the scheme—for virtual radiation is not supposed to result directly in other virtual radiation, but only probabilities [exist] for the transition between molecular states. Of course, this is only an “architectural” objection.

Einstein also repeated these criticisms in Göttingen (as Heisenberg reported to Pauli on 8 June 1924). There, he raised another objection: in the Bohr–Kramers–Slater (BKS) theory, an emission line might become wider than an absorption line, and this would contradict the fundamental law of spectroscopy established by Gustav Kirchhoff.

Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

Pauli met Einstein at the *Naturforscherversammlung* at Innsbruck in September 1924, where the latter discussed the topic with Sommerfeld, Pauli, and other participants. Pauli soon reported to Bohr about it; he wrote further:¹⁰⁴

> The points raised by Einstein are not so much what disturbs me about your interpretation of radiation theory. And if you should ask me what I believe about statistical independence of quantum processes in spatially distant atoms, I would honestly have to answer: I don’t know. Geiger’s experiment, which I hear is already being started, will presumably soon settle this question experimentally. To me it makes no difference if it comes out one way or the other. (Pauli to Bohr, 2 October 1924, in Pauli, 1979, p. 165)

However, what particularly bothered Pauli was the possible existence of two different types of resonance radiation (according to the BKS theory), one emerging from excited atoms, the other from nonexcited atoms. ‘I am really convinced that this distinction does not at all occur in reality, and there exists no experiment in principle that makes it possible to determine separately the respective contributions of excited and non-excited atoms to the scattered radiation,’ he insisted (Pauli, *loc. cit.*).
The Bohr–Pauli dialogue proceeded vividly and vigorously—in contrast to the Bohr–Einstein dialogue—during the following months. Thus, Bohr wrote to Pauli on 11 December 1924: ‘I must confess that I am nevertheless convinced that the swindle of mixing the classical theory and the quantum theory will still prove fruitful in many ways in tracking down the secrets of Nature.’ (Pauli, 1979, p. 185) That ‘swindle’ (‘*Schwindel*’) included, of course, the BKS theory as a basic element. On the other hand, Pauli wrote to Heisenberg in February 1925 that he would ‘*not* discuss the radiation phenomena from the Copenhagen standpoint’ in his comprehensive article ‘for the Springer *Handbuch*’ (Pauli to Heisenberg, 28 February 1925, *loc. cit.*, p. 211). A renewed stay in Copenhagen (in April 1925), where he especially discussed his resonance-radiation argument with Bohr and others, did not alter his verdict: ‘I would always much rather say that I have so far no complete picture of radiation phenomena than even temporarily put up with a hideousness (*Scheußlichkeit*) of this kind which hurts my physical sensibility. This is my last word in this matter.’ (Pauli to Kronig, 21 May 1925, *loc. cit.*, p. 216)¹⁰⁵ By that time, the experiment of Walther Bothe and Hans Geiger had settled the case against the BKS theory and in favour of Einstein’s light-quantum hypothesis and energy-momentum conservation in individual atomic processes (Bothe and Geiger, 1925a, b). Hence, Pauli wrote categorically to Kramers later in July: ‘I consider it to be enormously lucky that the view of Bohr, Kramers and Slater has been refuted so quickly by the beautiful experiments of Geiger and Bothe as well as the recently published [results] of Compton.’ (Pauli to Kramers, 27 July 1925, *loc. cit.*, p. 234) With a heavy heart, Bohr gave in.

II.1 Dialogues on the Concepts of Atomic and Quantum Theory (1913–1926)
113

The radiation problem did not remain the only point of disagreement between Bohr and Pauli during those years. Pauli took the failure of the old quantum theory to yield the correct energy states of helium and other more complex atoms very seriously. He began to ponder (independently of and more radically than Bohr) about the reasons for this failure; already in his letter of February 1924, he had expressed doubts whether ‘one can still talk at all about definite orbits of electrons in stationary states,’ and added: ‘Heisenberg has hit this point, in my opinion, exactly right by questioning the possibility of talking about definite orbits. Previously, Kramers has never admitted to me that doubts of that sort are reasonable. Nevertheless, I must insist on this, because the matter seems to me to be too important.’ (Pauli to Bohr, 21 February 1924, *loc. cit.*, p. 148) In December of that year, Pauli sent Bohr the manuscript of the paper in which he introduced the fourth quantum number of the electron and the exclusion principle (Pauli, 1925b), accompanied by a letter (Pauli to Bohr, 12 December 1924). In this letter, he again stressed the necessity of modifying radically the classical concepts that still existed in the quantum theory, and especially to abolish electron orbits and motions. Although his new proposal solved the problem of the lengths of periods in the periodic system consistently, Pauli insisted that the fourth quantum number of the electron should not be interpreted visually, though George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit would suggest so in October 1925 (Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, 1925).¹⁰⁶ Pauli then raised any number of objections against the ‘electron spin,’ including relativistic arguments, and accused Bohr—who, at that time, obtained Einstein’s support in favour of the idea of the spin of the electron—of inconsistency, until he finally succumbed to the (likewise) relativistic argument of Llewellyn Hilleth Thomas, establishing the missing factor 2 in the gyromagnetic ratio (Thomas, 1926). We have reported on this second Bohr–Pauli dialogue earlier and need not report the story here in detail (see Volume 3, Section V.5).
The epistemological dialogues on quantum theory conducted between 1913 and 1926 involved several personalities—Bohr, Einstein, Pauli, and Weyl, and, to a lesser extent, Eddington, Ehrenfest, Planck, and Schrödinger. The principal discussion partners assumed and defended their characteristic epistemological positions, which would come up again in the following dialogue on the physical interpretation of quantum mechanics. Einstein, in spite of his boldness in proposing new, nonclassical concepts (such as the light-quantum), hesitated to give up complete causality; he hoped to account for the nonclassical features of atomic physics by using partial differential equations containing field variables, which are ‘overdetermined’ and thus bring in the quanta into the theory (Einstein, 1923d). He further advocated the point of view that physical theories must be based on imagination and ingenuity, and Nature then chooses the proper scheme. Weyl, on the other hand, emphasized the role of beauty and perfection of mathematical theories, from which the physical phenomena could only be derived by suitable

¹⁰⁶ For details of the story of electron spin, see Van der Waerden, 1960; also Volume 1, Part 2, Section VI.4, and Volume 3, Section V.5.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0146 -->

114 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

interpretation: thus, he was not worried too much by such ‘discrepancies’ between theory and experiment as existed in the masses of particles with positive (hydrogen nucleus, the proton) and negative charge (electron). In contrast to Weyl, Pauli strongly insisted upon the identity of theoretical (including mathematical) description and experimental confirmation; hence, nonobservable quantities had to be excluded from physical theories. Finally, Bohr was aware of the discord between the formal (theoretical) description of atomic phenomena (e.g., by means of the light-quantum hypothesis, the old quantum theory of atomic structure, etc.) and their physical nature. The four different philosophical positions toward atomic phenomena and their theoretical description could not be associated in detail with any standard philosophical scheme, like realism, positivism, and others, which may seem to be obvious in some cases.¹⁰⁷ Rather, the scheme of physical theory—called quantum mechanics—which accounted so successfully for the detailed behaviour of atomic systems, first determined the philosophical consequences—that is, the physical interpretation of the formalism—by itself; notably, internal self-consistency—both physical and mathematical (with reference to the experimental facts)—played an essential role in this procedure (Step 1). Only then could one attempt, with greater or smaller success, to fit the results into a standard philosophical scheme (Step 2). In the development of the physical interpretation up to 1930, we shall restrict ourselves to Step 1, and shift the discussion of Step 2 to Chapter IV, Sections 1 and 2.

## II.2 The Copenhagen Atmosphere (1926)

In his condensed description of how the *Universitetets Institut for teoretisk Fysik* (the University Institute for Theoretical Physics in Copenhagen) originated, J. Rud Nielsen wrote in his introduction to Volume 3 of *Niels Bohr: Collected Works*:

> When Bohr began his professorship at the University of Copenhagen in September 1916, he had only a single room next to the Physics Library of the old Technical University (*Den Polytekniske Laereanstalt*). He got a secretary only at the beginning of 1920.
> Bohr soon felt the need of a laboratory where his theories could be tested, and he proposed the establishment of such an institute. The realization of this plan was greatly furthered by the donation of a considerable sum by a small group of private individuals led by Aage Berlème, an old schoolmate and friend of Bohr’s. This sum was used to acquire a suitable plot belonging to the Municipality of Copenhagen. The State twice appropriated funds, and the Carlsberg foundation made contributions. The erection of the first building took place during 1919 and 1920, and the planning and equipping of it took much of Bohr’s time and energy, and undoubtedly con-

tributed to his frequent complaints of overwork during this period. A great handicap with regard to the equipping of the building was the growing inflation sweeping over Europe.
In a letter to Ehrenfest of January 20, 1921, Bohr wrote that he and Kramers had then just moved papers and books to the new building. The library and offices were finished by then, but not the laboratories.
The Institute for Theoretical Physics (*Universitetets Institut for teoretisk Fysik*) was formally dedicated on March 3, 1921. Official representatives from the Government and University and several interested citizens were present, in addition to most of Danish and a few foreign physicists and chemists. (Nielsen, in Bohr, 1976, p. 24)

The completion of the building and equipment had been recommended eagerly by Ernest Rutherford and Arnold Sommerfeld, both experts on the importance of Bohr’s work in atomic physics. During his visit to Berlin in April 1920, Bohr had become acquainted not only with Max Planck, Albert Einstein, and other celebrated scientists, but also with members of the brilliant younger generation, such as James Franck and Lise Meitner. Franck had then assisted, together with the Danish experimental spectroscopist Hans Marius Hansen, in devising the apparatus. Now, he came to participate in the inauguration ceremony of the new Institute. The Copenhagen newspaper *Politiken* of 20 March 1921, published a photograph of Bohr encircled by his close collaborators: Franck, the Hungarian chemist George de Hevesy, a friend since the Manchester period, who had arrived in Copenhagen already in 1920, and Hansen, as well as the Dutch theoretician Hendrik Kramers (a student and close collaborator of Bohr since 1916).¹⁰⁸ More than a hundred guests had been invited to the ceremony: the Danish Prime Minister as well as the Minister of Education showed up, and the Rector of the University, the philologist Otto Jesperson, addressed Bohr with the words: ‘You have known to gather around you both native and foreign researchers and have thus in the most beautiful way resumed international work which was severed during the World War. With a sense of joy and expectation, I declare this Institute to be open.’¹⁰⁹

Work at the Institute on Blegdamsvej 17, an address that would become famous in the entire scientific world, was not confined to theory, as Bohr announced right away in his opening speech. Besides studies on spectroscopy and atomic collisions, the experimental programme should include, in particular, research on radioactive phenomena under de Hevesy (who had specialized in this field in Manchester and at the Vienna *Institut für Radiumforschung*). Further, Bohr emphasized a ‘matter of greatest interest as the portent of successful growth,’ namely:

> This Institute is not intended solely for scientific research but is also to be homestead for the teaching of physicists and others with special interest in physics. . . . In fact, it is the nature of scientific researches that no one dares give definite promises for the future; we must be prepared for the possibility that, on the road that at this moment

116 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

is believed to lie open and smooth before us, obstacles pile up which essentially bar the road, or to the overcoming of which entirely new ideas are required. It is therefore of the greatest significance not just to depend on the abilities and powers of a limited circle of researchers; but the task of having to introduce a constantly renewed number of younger people into the results and methods of science contributes in the highest degree to continually taking up questions for discussion from new sides; and, not least through the contributions of young people themselves, new blood and new ideas are constantly introduced into the work. (Bohr, 1976, pp. 25–26)

Both in research and in acquainting younger, new people with the problems of quantum physics, the Copenhagen Institute for Theoretical Physics served its declared purpose very well. To begin with, in 1921, Bohr developed an extension of his atomic theory that offered the hope of explaining the entire periodic system of chemical elements, and de Hevesy and the Dutch visitor Dirk Coster provided a definite, as it seemed, proof of this scheme when they discovered the new element ‘Hafnium’ in December 1922 at the right place in the periodic table of elements. At the same time, Bohr received the highest scientific honour, the Nobel Prize in physics, for ‘his services in the investigation of the structure of atoms, and of the radiation emanating from them.’ (*Nobel Foundation*, ed., 1965, p. 1)

In the following years, Bohr experienced a hard time in his research. Already, when he submitted, toward the end of 1922, his article ‘*Über die Anwendung der Quantentheorie auf den Atombau. I. Die Grundpostulate der Quantentheorie*’ (‘On Application of the Quantum Theory to Atomic Structure, I. The Fundamental Principles’) to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, he mentioned in the third chapter (entitled ‘The Formal Nature of the Quantum Theory’) several ‘fundamental difficulties which stand in the way of the efforts to reconcile the appearance of discontinuities in atomic processes with the application of the conceptions of classical electrodynamics,’ namely:

(1) The hypothesis of light-quanta.
(2) The coupling principle (i.e., ‘the possibility of the transference of energy between two [atomic] systems which are to a first approximation independent’).
(3) The phenomena of reflection and dispersion.
(4) The conservation of energy and momentum in quantum theory. (Bohr, 1923a; English translation, pp. 34–42)

The other problems he hoped to deal with in Part II of the series opened with the above-mentioned paper, but only the manuscript of 1923 (originally unpublished, but available in the Niels Bohr Archives in Copenhagen) survives; it ended with a reference to another unsolved problem, the anomalous Zeeman effects.¹¹⁰ Later attempts did not get very far either; for instance, a short draft in Danish of summer 1924, entitled ‘Problems of Atomic Theory,’ stopped after eight handwritten pages (containing essentially an enumeration of the well-known ‘fundamental assumptions of the atomic theory’).

II.2 The Copenhagen Atmosphere (1926) 117

We would like to quote the introduction of the draft, because it states clearly the points of view that guided Bohr’s thinking on the whole for years to come. Bohr wrote:

> The present state of development of the atomic theory is distinguished by the problem of accounting for the characteristic physical and chemical properties of the elements on the basis of a general knowledge of the building stones of atoms obtained by the study of phenomena not directly contingent upon these properties. The most prominent feature of the attempts to solve this problem is the conviction that no progress can be made without an essential departure from the viewpoints by which we heretofore, with so great success, have attempted to account for the phenomena which are immediately accessible to observation by our senses, and which depend on the collective action of huge number of atoms. However, the searching character, which efforts to uncover the laws governing the behaviour of single atoms must necessarily have, can hardly be emphasized more strongly than by the recognition that not only it is the description of the properties of the elements based on observations interpreted in terms of the concepts of classical physics but even our knowledge of the building stones of atoms is, in the nature of the matter, contingent upon the use of laws of classical physics. (Bohr, 1976, p. 569)

With respect to investigating the concrete details of Bohr’s programme, mostly younger visitors to the Institute played an important role. The earliest visitors included the Norwegian physicist Svein Rosseland and the young Swedish student Oskar Klein; the former stayed in Copenhagen from 1920 to 1924, and the latter came in 1918 and stayed until 1922.¹¹¹ Klein accompanied Bohr to Göttingen in June 1922, where the latter presented his famous lecture series on the theory of atomic structure and the periodic system of elements. In Göttingen, they became acquainted with two very promising younger physicists, Wolfgang Pauli and Werner Heisenberg, both of whom would spend long periods of stay at Bohr’s Institute in the following years. The first visits of Pauli and Heisenberg coincided with the failure of two decisive aspects of the old quantum theory of atomic structure. Thus, Pauli helped in 1923 in demolishing the theory of many-electron atoms, and Heisenberg witnessed in 1924 and 1925 the rise and fall of the radiation theory, which Bohr and Kramers had developed on the basis of the idea of ‘virtual oscillators’ proposed by another brilliant young visitor, John Clarke Slater from Harvard University. As a consequence of these disasters, Bohr looked forward to many years of strenuous labour until the situation in atomic theory would improve substantially—but history would decide differently.

Around the mid-1920s, the Copenhagen Institute for Theoretical Physics became the busiest place in the whole world, for everyone interested in the problems of atomic physics wanted to spend some time there. Major groups of visitors turned up, especially from England—where Bohr maintained the closest relations

---

118 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

with Cambridge; there (his mentor and friend Ernest Rutherford had become, in 1919, the Cavendish Professor of Experimental Physics, and Ralph Fowler, Rutherford’s son-in-law, had begun to establish a school of theoretical physics devoted to the study of atomic and quantum problems)—in Germany and the United States. Many students and research scholars obtained for their stay at Bohr’s Institute through one of the invaluable American grants and fellowships awarded by the International Education Board or the Rockefeller Foundation.$^{112}$ Werner Kuhn of Zurich arrived in 1924 on such a fellowship, and Slater’s stay at Copenhagen was financed by the Sheldon Traveling Fellowship from Harvard University; the visit of the senior Japanese experimentalist Yoshio Nishina was supported by his home institution as well. During the great period of change, when *the* decisive steps to the new, long-awaited atomic mechanics were actually occurring in Göttingen, Cambridge, and Zurich, Bohr counted among the guests at his Institute (for shorter or longer periods): Fowler, Samuel Goudsmit from Leyden, Heisenberg, the young American Ph.D. Ralph Kronig from Columbia University, Pauli, the Cambridge research student (of Fowler) Llewellyn Hilleth Thomas, and the experienced researcher Gregor Wentzel from Munich.$^{113}$ All of these visitors, except perhaps Slater,$^{114}$ enjoyed their stay. ‘You can hardly imagine,’ Heisenberg wrote to Bohr after his first visit during Easter vacation 1924, ‘how much these days in Copenhagen meant for me scientifically, but not only scientifically.’ (Heisenberg to Bohr, 6 April 1924) Similarly, other visitors expressed their unreserved gratitude in letters to Bohr. To have been with Bohr for some time in Copenhagen was considered by everyone working on atomic physics as a kind of joining the band of knights at ‘King Niels’s Round Table,’ which carried lifelong prestige.

The two most outstanding students of Bohr during the early 1920s, Werner Heisenberg and Wolfgang Pauli, took away very different feelings from Copenhagen: Heisenberg, upon his return to Göttingen in April 1925, after a most satisfactory and successful stay of six months in Copenhagen, opened his first letter to Bohr with the remarks:

Rockefeller, Jr., in January 1923 for ‘the promotion and advance of education throughout the world.’ Wickliffe Rose, who in 1922 had become president of the General Education Board, proposed the idea and became the first president of IEB. Originally, he had thought of concentrating on the fields of physics, chemistry, and biology and to select ‘inspiring, productive men in each of these fields . . . willing to train students from other countries.’ Bohr, who went to the United States later in 1923, and Ernest Rutherford became the first beneficiaries of the Board. In May 1924, the University of Copenhagen received a sum (not exceeding $40,000) for guests and visitors. For more details, see Pais, 1991, pp. 258–260. In contrast to the International Education Board, the Rockefeller Foundation had previously given (and still continued to give afterward) fellowships to Americans for study abroad.

II.2 The Copenhagen Atmosphere (1926) 119

Highly esteemed, dear Professor: Before I write any details about my paper, the typescript of which I found yesterday upon my arrival here, I want to thank you again cordially for the wonderful recent time, during which I had the privilege to learn and work at your Institute, and for all the kindness which you and your wife have shown to me in this period. With respect to science the past half year was for me the most beautiful of my entire life as a student. I am almost sad about the fact that [scientifically] I must carry on wretchedly alone by myself in the future. (Heisenberg to Bohr, 21 April 1925)

A year and a half earlier, Pauli had returned from Copenhagen to Hamburg far less happy, because all of his efforts to deal with the problem of the anomalous Zeeman effects ended in complete failure. Another half a year later, his mood had recovered, and in a letter to Bohr on 11 February 1924, he expressed his ‘extraordinary joy’ if he could return to Copenhagen even for a short period. In the course of the year 1924, then, he began to criticize seriously the BKS radiation theory, and he developed his own approach toward understanding atomic structure (based on his exclusion principle). Pauli remained critical of the Copenhagen physics also in 1925 and beyond, especially with regard to the concept of electron spin—which Bohr accepted in December 1925, whereas Pauli fought against it until March 1926. When, after wrong argumentation, Pauli called the note of Llewellyn Hilleth Thomas (1926a) erroneous and then asked whether Bohr would still welcome him in Copenhagen. The latter replied: ‘I need not tell you how grateful I am to you for your assistance and criticism in this matter.... I long very much for talking to you about all that and hope that you can come here for a visit during your vacations’ (Bohr to Pauli, 9 March 1926). Thus, both aspects of serious cooperation on physical problems, i.e., devoted assistance in carrying out the ideas of Niels Bohr, on the one hand, and honest, sharp criticism of his dearly held concepts (or prejudices), on the other, were equally well accepted gratefully in Copenhagen. The hypercritical Pauli and the optimistic, cooperative Heisenberg assumed obvious, crucial roles in Bohr’s research programme in the transition period from 1924 to 1926.

Whenever Bohr could free himself from his exhausting administrative duties—he had to attend to the construction of an extension to the buildings of the Institute (completed in 1926a) as well as to an extensive, far-flung correspondence (with colleagues, visitors, etc.)—he tried to think about the problems of atomic theory. Heisenberg often recalled in conversations that Bohr seemed to be the only person ‘who personally suffered from these problems.’ Two aspects dominated the period from summer 1924 to spring 1926: the new development of the dispersion theory and the old question of the constitution of atoms in connection with an explanation of the periodic system of elements.

In connection with the ‘fundamental principles’ of November 1922, Bohr had mentioned several problems of quantum theory, which we have quoted earlier (Bohr 1923a). In early 1924, the possibility seemed to arise to solve points 1 to 4 in one fell swoop: by means of the BKS theory of radiation. By renouncing strict

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0152 -->

120 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

energy and momentum conservation in interactions (couplings) between radiation and atomic states, apparently a quantum theory of dispersion followed (formulated in Kramers, 1924a, b, and Kramers and Heisenberg, 1925), which explained all observed phenomena (as well as some others that had yet to be observed). While the new dispersion theory stimulated Heisenberg to achieve his major breakthrough—the formulation of the first consistent quantum-mechanical scheme—it hindered Bohr from proceeding further, for he insisted upon what he thought to be its basic assumption: namely, the BKS theory. In a paper, which he submitted in March 1925 to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, he developed a general theory of atomic collisions, differentiating between ‘reciprocal’ and ‘nonreciprocal’ collisions—of these, the reciprocal ones satisfied energy and momentum conservation, and the irreciprocal ones were reactions of systems that ‘can be only connected by means of probability laws,’ and ‘the conservation laws, in the first instance, appear as statistical laws’ (Bohr, 1925a, p. 150). Then, the next catastrophe occurred: the Bothe–Geiger experiment demonstrated that also in nonreciprocal interactions between radiation and atoms the conservation laws held (Bothe and Geiger, 1925a, b).

Bohr immediately admitted defeat, and in an addendum to the collision paper, dated July 1925, he drew clear consequences, namely:

>In this state of affairs one must be prepared to find that the generalization of the classical electrodynamic theory that we are striving for will require a fundamental revolution of the concepts on which the description of nature has been based up to now.
> . . . we must not only, as for reciprocal collisions, expect behaviour [*Wirkungen*] that is incompatible with the properties of mechanical models, but we must in fact even be prepared to find behaviour that is alien to the application of ordinary space-time pictures as the coupling of individual processes in distant atoms is to a wave description of optical phenomena. (Bohr, 1925a, pp. 155–156)

And he continued further: ‘The renunciation of space-time pictures is characteristic of the formal treatment of problems of the radiation theory and of the mechanical theory of heat attempted in the recent papers of de Broglie and Einstein’ (Bohr, *loc. cit.*). In other words, the failure of his own cherished goals appeared to him to point in the same direction as the new matter-wave concept of Louis de Broglie (1924e) and Albert Einstein’s application of Satyendra Nath Bose’s (1924a) statistical treatment of light-quanta to the atoms of ideal gases (Einstein, 1924c, 1925a). Giving up the last attempt to rescue the classical electrodynamic radiation theory—and this, Bohr felt, was his BKS theory—could mean physically only one thing: one had to abandon the ordinary space-time pictures in atomic theory. The Göttingen quantum mechanics, which was soon developed by Heisenberg, Born, and Jordan, evidently confirmed this conclusion; thus, Bohr remarked in the publication of a lecture on ‘Atomic Theory and Mechanics,’ which appeared in the issue of *Nature* dated 5 December 1925:

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0153 -->

II.2 The Copenhagen Atmosphere (1926) 121

Quite recently, Heisenberg . . . has taken a step probably of fundamental importance by formulating the problem of the quantum theory in a novel way but in which the difficulties attached to the use of mechanical pictures may, it is hoped, be avoided. In this theory the attempt is made to transcribe every use of mechanical concepts in a way suited to the nature of the quantum theory, and such that at every stage of the computation only directly observable quantities enter. In contrast to ordinary mechanics, the new quantum mechanics does not deal with a space-time description of the motion of atomic particles. (Bohr, 1925b, p. 852)

Although this development led away from the conventional mechanical pictures, the other problem in which Bohr got involved signalled a partial return to the classical description. In 1924, two British scientists, the chemist J. D. Main Smith and the physicist Edmund Clifton Stoner, proposed—on the basis of chemical and (rather recent) spectroscopic evidence—a reorganization of the electronic (quantum) states in the atom, which deviated crucially from the previously so successful Copenhagen scheme of the periodic system of elements of 1921 and 1922. After some hesitation, Bohr accepted the new scheme, especially when two further steps had been taken in 1925: (1) in January, Pauli submitted the paper on ‘the completion of electron groups in the atom,’ where he associated four quantum numbers with each electron and expounded the exclusion principle (Pauli, 1925b); (2) in October, George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit enunciated the hypothesis of electron spin as the physical interpretation of Pauli’s fourth quantum number (Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, 1925). Although Pauli warned Bohr not to accept the spin hypothesis, the latter became ‘a prophet of the magnetic electron gospel’ in the period that followed.<sup>115</sup> The transformation occurred in Leyden, at the celebration of the fiftieth anniversary of Hendrik Antoon Lorentz’s doctorate, in December 1925, where many celebrities—including Albert Einstein —had assembled. As Bohr described in a letter to Ralph Kronig:

>When I came to Leyden to the Lorentz festivals, Einstein asked the very first moment I saw him what I believed about the spinning electron. Upon my question about the cause of the necessity of the mutual coupling between spin axis and the orbital motion, he explained that this coupling was an immediate consequence of the theory of relativity. This remark acted as a complete revelation to me, and I have never since faltered in my conviction that we at last were at the end of our sorrows. (Bohr to Kronig, 26 March 1926)

After his conversion at Leyden, Bohr became actively involved in the spin story. On Christmas Eve 1925, Paul Ehrenfest asked his disciples Goudsmit and Uhlenbeck to send the draft of a letter to *Nature* on the ‘Spinning Electron and the Structure of Spectra’ (Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, 1926) to Bohr. Ehrenfest also requested Bohr that Goudsmit be allowed to spend some time at his Institute in

<sup>115</sup> For details of the electron-spin story, see Van der Waerden (1960); the introduction by Erik Rüdinger and K. Stolzenburg in *Niels Bohr: Collected Works*, Volume 5 (1984), pp. 219–232; and our presentation in Volume 1, Part 2, Section VI.4.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0154 -->

122 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

Copenhagen. Bohr reacted positively to the latter request, but he wished to make a few changes in the text of Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit’s letter, to which he added a postscript saying:

>Having had the opportunity of reading this interesting letter by Mr. Goudsmit and Mr. Uhlenbeck, I am glad to add a few words which may be regarded as an addition to my article on atomic theory and mechanics, which was published as a supplement to *Nature* of December 5, 1925. As stated there, the attempts which have been made to account for the properties of the elements by applying the quantum theory to the nuclear atom have met with serious difficulties in the fine structure of spectra and the related problems. In my article expression was given to the view that these difficulties were inherently connected with the limited possibility of representing the stationary states of the atom by a mechanical model. The situation seems, however, to be somewhat altered by the introduction of the hypothesis of the spinning electron which, in spite of the incompleteness of the conclusions that can be derived from models, promises to be a very welcome supplement to our ideas of atomic structure. In fact, as Mr. Goudsmit and Mr. Uhlenbeck have described in their letter, this hypothesis throws new light on many of the difficulties which have puzzled the workers in this field during the last few years. Indeed, it opens up a very hopeful prospect of our being able to account more extensively for the properties of elements by means of mechanical models, at least in the qualitative way characteristic of applications of the correspondence principle. This possibility must be the more welcomed at the present time, when the prospect is held out of a quantitative treatment of atomic problems by the new quantum mechanics initiated by the work of Heisenberg, which aims at a precise formulation of the correspondence between classical mechanics and the quantum theory. (Bohr, 1926a, p. 265)

Very clearly, Bohr wavered between the description of atomic phenomena by models, which allowed one to establish the relation to classical pictures (in space-time), and the sole use of abstract formalism, which avoided completely the reference to classical pictures. As much as he praised the new progress achieved by Heisenberg and his colleagues, he also defended the ‘spin gospel’ against the attacks of Wolfgang Pauli, its severest critic, and he was happy when he finally won the argument in March 1926.

At about the same time, a substantial change, even a break, occurred at Bohr’s Institute. Hendrik Kramers, Bohr’s close associate since 1916, and later his research assistant and lecturer at the University of Copenhagen (where he shouldered Bohr’s lecturing responsibilities) since 1919 and 1922, respectively, returned to Holland, where he accepted a professorship in Utrecht.<sup>116</sup> Thus, he had served, for a full decade, as the closest collaborator—so to say, as ‘his master’s voice’—and executed most loyally Bohr’s thoughts and ideas in good times and bad, sharing triumphs and failures. In his biography of Hendrik Kramers, Max Dresden speculated about the psychological reasons for this return to his native country:

<sup>116</sup> Kramers succeeded Willem Henri Julius in this position; Julius had died in early 1925. See Dresden, 1987, Chapter 15.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0155 -->

II.2 The Copenhagen Atmosphere (1926) 123

It is hard to escape the impression that, after the BKS debacle and Heisenberg’s spectacular successes, Kramers was anxious, maybe even desperate, to find a new basis and start anew on his own, away from Copenhagen and Bohr. The move to Utrecht presented a wonderful opportunity to do just that. Even though this enabled him to be geographically separate from Copenhagen, the scientific and intellectual ties to Copenhagen remained strong. Kramers made many attempts to go his own way in physics; his further intellectual evolution can be viewed as a gradual but never complete emancipation from the Copenhagen influence. (Dresden, 1987, p. 314)

This might hint at a strong, abrupt, breaking away from Copenhagen, but it certainly did not happen very rapidly, as far as it can be seen from his publications. On the one hand, Kramers had grown accustomed to not publishing frequently, and he retained this habit in the following years: thus, in the two years between fall 1925 and fall 1927, he submitted only two research papers, one on matrix mechanics to the Dutch journal *Physica* (Kramers, 1925c) and the other on wave mechanics to the *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Kramers, 1926).<sup>117</sup> On the other hand, in spite of great formal ability and a quick grasp of all kinds of theoretical and physical problems, his careful mind took time in developing a programme of his own, focusing on the mathematical structure and special problems of non-relativistic quantum mechanics, paramagnetism and magnetic behaviour at low temperatures, spin problems, radiation, and field theory. Of all of these new studies, only the papers on the Kramers–Kronig dispersion relations (Kramers, 1927; Kronig, 1926e) may be connected with his earlier Copenhagen interests.

Heisenberg, the new man, to whom Bohr offered Kramers’s dual assignment—as his closest collaborator and institute assistant as well as lecturer (‘*Lektor*’) at the University of Copenhagen—in November 1925, was certainly the most brilliant star of the new atomic theory: quantum mechanics.<sup>118</sup> He had been known in Copenhagen already for two years as a pleasant and productive man, highly interactive and brimming with physical intuition.<sup>119</sup> He had also collaborated successfully with his predecessor Hendrik Kramers, whose personal qualities he respected and admired.<sup>120</sup> However, despite Bohr’s attractive offer, which made Heisenberg very happy,<sup>121</sup> some resistance soon arose. First, Max Born, Heisenberg’s director at the Institute for Theoretical Physics in Göttingen, then on leave of absence in the United States, had to be asked, and Bohr wrote to him immediately emphasizing

that 'no one in Germany need fear that [Heisenberg] will stay here [in Copenhagen]
very long' (Bohr to Born, 25 October 1925). A few months later, however, Bohr's
