mission of the University of Leipzig—led by the two physics professors Otto
Wiener and Theodor Des Coudres—debated the succession of George Cecil Jaffé,
extraordinary (i.e., associate) professor 'for applied mechanics and thermody-
namics,' and suggested three candidates in the following order: Werner Heisen-
berg, Wolfgang Pauli, and Gregor Wentzel.122
    When Heisenberg received the offer from the Saxon Ministry of Culture, he was
quite disturbed by it and called it 'a wicked thing (*eine schlimme Geschichte*)'
(Heisenberg to Bohr, 5 April 1926), because he was just then preparing for his
move to Copenhagen. Still, he hesitated to turn down the Leipzig call, the first
offer he had received of a professorship in Germany, especially because his father,
August Heisenberg, a well-established professor in Munich, had warned him not
do so. On the other hand, the people in Göttingen and Berlin—Born was still
absent—argued differently. In particular, the influential mathematician Richard
Courant, in full agreement with James Franck and the Göttingen faculty, reported
to Bohr: 'I urged him [Heisenberg] to go *under all circumstances* and not to sacri-
fice the scientific and human advantages of his stay in Copenhagen to the super-
ficial advantages of the call from Leipzig.' (Courant to Bohr, 24 April 1926).
Heisenberg—so Courant thought—'can calmly forgo this first opportunity in
Germany,' and the Berlin authorities Einstein and Planck, whom Heisenberg met
on 28 April, shared the same opinion. In order to compete financially with the
Leipzig offer,. Bohr had Heisenberg's Copenhagen salary raised from 2800 to 3600
Kroner.123 Before that happened, Heisenberg passed through Leipzig on 25 April,
met his prospective colleagues Wiener and Des Coudres, then went on to Dresden,
where he received a telegram from Bohr requesting him 'to make no final decision
before you have talked to us in Copenhagen' (Bohr's telegram to Heisenberg, April
1926). Accordingly, Heisenberg dealt with the Saxon Culture Ministry on 26 April
and proceeded to Berlin. From there, he wrote a letter to his parents announcing that
he was ready to decline the first call to a German professorship. 'If I continue to
produce good papers, I will always receive another call; otherwise I don't deserve
it,' he argued (Heisenberg to his parents, 29 April 1926). He arrived in Copenha-
gen the following day and settled there for the next one and a half years.
    Several months after these events took place, his father August Heisenberg took
the opportunity of contacting Niels Bohr. He congratulated Bohr on his election
as foreign member of the Bavarian Academy of Sciences, and then thanked him for
the cordial treatment his son Werner had received in Copenhagen. Bohr answered
promptly:

Dear Colleague: Your letter pleased me immensely. Especially, it went to my heart
what you wrote about your son. I need not tell you how highly I estimate his scientific
gifts and accomplishments. In spite of his youth he has succeeded in realizing hopes,
of which one hardly dared to dream earlier. For a scientist there exists surely no
higher future than to witness the flourishing of these gifts and to support them as
much as one can. In addition, the fresh and harmonious personality of your son
makes it a daily pleasure to be together with him and to work for a common goal.
(Bohr to A. Heisenberg, 4 August 1926)

Bohr's words were not just flattering; they expressed fully his personal convictions.
Although the collaboration between the great teacher and his highly gifted student
would go through some stormy times of disagreement on scientific matters, during
this period, they always joined together their best efforts to achieve the important
goal of clarifying the physical interpretation of quantum mechanics.
    The transition from Kramers as Bohr's deputy to Heisenberg in the same posi-
tion went on quite smoothly. Kramers, as the new professor of theoretical physics,
delivered his inaugural lecture at Utrecht on 15 February 1926; he then returned
to Copenhagen and stayed there until May, when Heisenberg took over.124
Kramers and Heisenberg's advisory duties overlapped during this period, as may
be seen in the case of several foreign visitors. For example, the American David
M. Dennison, a postdoctoral research scholar from the University of Michigan (he
had completed his Ph.D. with O. Klein and W. F. Colby in 1925), began to work
in summer 1925 on the analysis of molecular spectra, assisted by 'Professor N.
Bohr and Dr. H. Kramers through their constant interest and through their many
valuable suggestions' (Dennison, 1926, p. 333). On 27 April 1926, he submitted
another paper on molecular theory from Copenhagen; although he now employed
in it the methods of matrix mechanics, he again received the help of Kramers
(because Heisenberg had not yet arrived).125 He then stayed on in Copenhagen,
apparently without needing detailed advice from Kramers's successor for his work
(Dennison, 1926).126 For two other American visitors, namely, Jane M. Dewey
from Columbia University and the more senior physicist John Stuart Foster from
McGill University in Montreal, the situation changed.127 In 1926, Miss Dewey
became acquainted with the recent data obtained in Copenhagen by Toshio

Takamine¹²⁸ and Sven Werner on the intensities of the so-called combination lines occurring in the spectra of helium atoms under the influence of strong electric fields, the ‘quadratic Stark effect’ (Takamine and Werner, 1926); in particular, she applied to it the dispersion formulae of Kramers and Heisenberg (1925), which had been substantiated in the new quantum mechanics by Born, Heisenberg, and Jordan (1926). At the end of her paper, which she submitted in August 1926 to the *Physical Review*, she properly thanked both of her advisors in Copenhagen, ‘Professor Kramers and Dr. Heisenberg for valuable assistance in handling the theory’ (Dewey, 1926, p. 1124).

Foster, on the other hand, had already worked by himself experimentally on the Stark effect of helium lines at Yale University and later at McGill, so he could be considered as an expert of long-standing when he arrived at Bohr’s Institute in 1926. Effectively assisted by Heisenberg, the theoretical expert on the helium atom, Foster finally presented in summer 1927 a detailed paper on the ‘Application of Quantum Mechanics to the Stark Effect in Helium,’ so to say, the final theoretical analysis of the data to obtaining which he had contributed so much (Foster, 1927c). Regarding the final editing procedure of this substantial work, Heisenberg wrote to Bohr:

In Foster’s paper I have changed what seemed to me necessary to improve [it]. I also was not very happy about the introduction; I would have written it quite differently, but I could not change so much. I have therefore added on p. 2 and on p. 4 [of the manuscript] certain pieces which seem to clarify the connections. Also, on p. 1, I have altered the beginning, but I do not know whether this constitutes an improvement; indeed, I am not yet content with it. Perhaps you may return to the original version, or correct it somehow differently. At any rate, Foster and I shall welcome, of course, any improvement by you. Otherwise, most of the paper seems alright to me.... I, therefore, hope that Foster’s work will not take anymore much of your time and effort. (Heisenberg to Bohr, 23 July 1927)

Still, in August 1927, Bohr communicated Foster’s paper to the *Proceedings of the Royal Society of London*; it contained proper thanks to him and Heisenberg by the author.

Besides assisting visitors in their research and giving lecture courses in Danish at the University of Copenhagen,¹²⁹ Heisenberg did not remain idle in looking for problems for his own research: the Copenhagen atmosphere in 1926 also proved to be quite stimulating, and he solved a number of important problems of atomic theory ‘producing good papers’—as he had promised in the letter of 29 April to his parents. The first problem he attacked was quite an old acquaintance from the

days of his studies in Munich and Göttingen: to determine the energy states of
the helium atom. Now, after the advent of the new quantum mechanics and the
incorporation of the concept of electron spin into it (e.g., in the Göttingen paper
on the anomalous Zeeman effects: Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926), the solution of
the helium problem indeed appeared to be overdue. Pauli had also mentioned it in
two letters of March 1926 to Copenhagen, where at that time Samuel Goudsmit,
one of the creators of electron spin hypothesis, stayed for several weeks. In the
first, he had written quite impatiently:

> I am not pleased to hear from Goudsmit that he had not obtained any progress in the
> two most important problems still unsolved, namely the calculation of the separation
> between singlet and triplet terms [e.g., in the case of ortho- and parhelium] and the
> physical basis of the formal exclusion rules for equivalent orbits. (Pauli to Kramers, 8
> March 1926, in Pauli, 1979, p. 307)

Four days later, he then addressed Bohr personally: 'I hope that your zeal (*Eifer*)
is stimulated so far that you will also [after substantiating the spin hypothesis
through the visitor L. H. Thomas] soon have solved the other point of the pro-
gramme,' adding in parenthesis: 'the helium spectrum, separation [of] singlet-
triplet systems, equivalent orbits' (Pauli to Bohr, 12 March 1926, *loc. cit.*, p. 311).
Still nothing had happened with this programme until Heisenberg arrived in Co-
penhagen and got involved in it. Already, a few days after his arrival, he reported
good news to Hamburg, namely:

> We have found a rather decisive argument that your exclusion of equivalent orbits is
> connected with the singlet-triplet spacing. Consider the energy written as a function
> of the transition probabilities. Then a large difference results if one—at the energy of
> H-atoms—has transitions to 1s, or if, according to your ban [exclusion principle], one
> puts them equal to zero. That is, par- and ortho-[helium] do have different energies,
> independently of the interaction between the magnets [associated with the electron
> spin]. (Heisenberg to Pauli, 5 May 1926, in Pauli, 1979, p. 321)

In the following weeks, this initial idea resulted in a solid quantum-mechanical
description of the energy states of two-electron atoms.130 Heisenberg first ex-
plained what happened in a simplified model consisting of two rotating electrons
(not necessarily of the same frequency). There, the energy of the total system ex-
hibited degeneracy with respect to the exchange of the electron, a situation that
would always occur in any quantum-mechanical system built from two subsystems
of identical atomic objects coupled by an interaction term (however small it might
be). In the helium atom, the subsystems are the 'orbiting' electrons, and the inter-
action term is given by the Coulomb repulsion between the electrons. Heisenberg
immediately derived two consequences:

$^{130}$ The individual steps leading to Heisenberg's final solution of the helium problem have been
treated in Volume 3, Section V.6. Here, we just summarize the results to illustrate Heisenberg's success
in scientific research upon arrival in Copenhagen.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0160 -->

128        Chapter II  Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

(1) The interaction energy determines the singlet–triplet spacing in helium and
helium-like atoms or ions.
(2) The energy terms of the two-electron atoms split into two sets of 'equivalent
states' that do not mix by transitions, unless additional interactions (such as the
small couplings of the two electron-spin magnets) are considered, in which case, a
more complicated situation would arise.

    The paper containing the theoretical key to the helium problem was submitted
in June 1926 to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Heisenberg, 1926b). For the sake of his-
torical accuracy, it should be emphasized that Heisenberg formulated his ideas
entirely in the matrix language. About six weeks later, the same journal received a
further paper, in which the author reformulated the two-electron problem in the
language of undulatory mechanics (Heisenberg, 1926c). This language appeared
to be more appropriate for calculating the energy states of the real two-electron
system in the Coulomb field of the helium nucleus—at least with the 'steam roller
(*Dampfwalze*),' as Heisenberg mentioned to Pauli in a letter on 8 June 1926. After
all—as Schrödinger and Pauli (in his letter to Jordan, sent from Copenhagen on
12 April 1926) had shown—a one-to-one relationship existed among the crucial
elements of the interaction–Hamiltonian matrix and the corresponding integrals
of the Schrödinger method, which could be obtained in some approximation by
taking the overlap of two one-electron wave functions, the so-called 'exchange
integral.' Although the results—including also the magnetic electron–spin inter-
action, which again introduced two separated term systems—came out indeed
quite crudely, 'there followed a satisfactory description of the most essential
properties of these spectra' (Heisenberg, 1926c, p. 499). The helium problem that
had haunted the theoreticians since 1913 and had contributed primarily in 1923 to
the recognition of the failure of the old quantum theory had finally been resolved
—and Heisenberg announced it proudly among the major successes of quantum
mechanics to a large (German) audience in September 1926 at the 89th *Versamm-
lung deutscher Naturforscher und Ärzte* (Assembly of German Natural Scientists
and Physicians), a meeting of great tradition in Middle Europe, in Düsseldorf
(Heisenberg, 1926d, especially, p. 993).
    The solution of the helium problem added to the fame of Copenhagen, in gen-
eral, and to the personal reputation of Heisenberg, Bohr's new chief associate, in
particular. However, Heisenberg still considered his triumph far from being a
complete one. The blame lay less with the approximation used or just the partial
understanding of electron statistics that he had achieved; rather, he became both-
ered by the existence of the second, apparently quite successful new atomic
theory—wave mechanics—in several respects. First, it deprived his own invention,
quantum mechanics, of the monopoly of representing the only valid approach to
atomic problems; of course, this might have mattered less, as one could declare
that wave mechanics constituted just an alternate garb of the same theory (which
might be used occasionally more conveniently than the somewhat clumsy matrix-

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0161 -->

129

II.2 The Copenhagen Atmosphere (1926)

or quantum-algebraical scheme). However, since summer 1926, Erwin Schrödinger and others also raised the additional claim that wave mechanics was indeed the superior, in fact, more correct, answer to atomic problems: in particular, it seemed to reestablish a causal, 'visualizable (*anschauliche*)' interpretation. The pioneers of the Göttingen–Cambridge quantum mechanics were quite alarmed by the 'presumption' of the now opposite camp; they responded to it vigorously and in detail, as we have shown in the case of Born, Jordan, and Dirac in Chapter I.¹³¹ Heisenberg took a very strong stand, for he felt that the very foundation of his work was at stake. In the next paper, after the solution of the helium problem (with the methods of wave mechanics), submitted early in November 1926, he avoided the use of Schrödinger’s theory altogether when discussing a problem that seemed to be particularly suited for it: the fluctuation phenomena of radiation (Heisenberg, 1926e).¹³² Later, in December, he completed his extended memoir on the quantum-mechanical many-body problem, so to say, the extension and completion (in the mathematical sense and the physical interpretation) of his previous work on the two-electron atoms (Heisenberg, 1927a). Although the wave-mechanical language might have been most suitable in formulating the rather complicated fundamental equations, Heisenberg again avoided in his Section I on 'General Principles' all references to the 'hostile' scheme, using only matrix and operator (*à la* Born–Wiener) expressions. Just for practical purposes—in Section II: 'Atomic Systems with Two Electrons,' and Section III: 'Resonance Effect in the Theory of Band Spectra'—did he permit himself to speak about wave functions (properly interpreted in the 'anti-Schrödinger' sense of Max Born).¹³³

Heisenberg’s message in the second half of 1926 was clear: wave mechanics may serve as a powerful slave, as a practical instrument for calculating the details of atomic problems, but for the discussion of physical principles it had to be excluded. In this context, it may be mentioned that Friedrich Hund, Heisenberg’s friend and colleague from Göttingen, who spent a few months in winter 1925/26 in Copenhagen investigating molecular spectra, did make full use of wave-mechanical methods. He showed no particular interest, however, in questions of principles or interpretation. Finally, another representative of Schrödinger’s theory, Erwin Fues of Stuttgart, also stayed and worked at Bohr’s Institute in Copenhagen from January to April 1927; in the paper on 'Lebensdauern aus Resonanzerscheinungen' ('Lifetimes from Resonance Phenomena'), emerging from this visit, however, he fully accepted the Göttingen and Copenhagen probability interpretation, and he derived from a wave-mechanical description of the Auger effect a result in agreement with Heisenberg’s uncertainty relations (Fues, 1927a).

¹³¹ For details of Schrödinger’s claim and its discussion in Munich and Copenhagen, see Volume 5, Part 2, Section IV.5.
¹³² We shall deal with the contents of this paper in the next section.
¹³³ This paper will also be discussed later. Because of the pioneering applications of group-theoretical methods and the fruitful applications of Heisenberg’s idea and methods, the contents of Heisenberg’s paper (1927a) will play a role in Chapter III.

130 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

He thanked Heisenberg and Bohr for advice in carrying out his investigation (Fues, *loc. cit.*, footnote, p. 727).<sup>134</sup>

The description of the Copenhagen Institute for Theoretical Physics in the period around 1926 cannot be complete without talking about another 'senior' theoretician among the young quantum physicists: Oskar Klein. He had returned in summer 1925 from his assistant professorship at the University of Michigan to Europe and Copenhagen; having fallen ill in the autumn of the same year, he assumed in 1926 the position of a lecturer ('*Lektor*') at the University of Copenhagen. He spent the summer of 1926 as Lorentz Fellow and Lecturer at the University of Leyden, then became an active participant in the great debates between Bohr and Heisenberg that followed in winter 1926/27 and continued until full agreement was reached in fall 1927, resulting in nothing less than what one would later call the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics.

## II.3 Mechanical Concepts, Observation, and Restriction: The Origin of the Uncertainty Relations

### (a) Heisenberg's Embarking Upon Philosophical Questions

On 19 February 1916, in the middle of World War I, the Austrian physicist, philosopher of science and pacifist, Ernst Mach, died in the home of his son Ludwig in Haar near Munich. Albert Einstein wrote his obituary in the 1 April issue of *Physikalische Zeitschrift*, in which he especially praised the epistemological concerns of his colleague. He emphasized:

> The significance of minds, such as Mach, does not lie in the fact that they satisfy certain philosophical needs of their time, which the incarnate specialist may call luxury. Concepts, which have turned out to be useful in organizing things, easily obtain such an authority over us that we forget about their earthly origin and take them to be irrevocable facts. They then are stamped to be "necessities of thought," or given "*a priori,*" etc. The path of scientific progress is often blocked off by such misjudgments. Therefore it is not an idle pastime at all, if we are trained in analyzing the concepts to which we are accustomed since long, and in pointing out the conditions on which their validity and usefulness depend, how they emerged from the facts of experience. By this procedure their too high authority is broken. They will be removed, if they cannot be legitimized suitably; they will be corrected, if their association with real things was too loose; and they will be replaced by others, if a new system [of concepts] can be established which we prefer for some reason. (Einstein, 1916a, p. 102)

<sup>134</sup> In 1926, Walter Heitler from Munich also resided in Copenhagen, but he was sent by Arnold Sommerfeld on a Rockefeller Foundation Fellowship not to Bohr but to Niels Bjerrum to continue his investigations on a physicochemical problem. Only later, when he went to Zurich and met Fritz London, did he turn to wave-mechanical problems and then developed the theory of covalent chemical bond on the basis of Heisenberg's exchange integral.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0163 -->

II.3 Mechanical Concepts, Observation, and Restriction 131

Ten years later, on 28 April 1926, the young Werner Heisenberg presented a talk on his new quantum mechanics at the famous Berlin colloquium organized by the Nobel laureate Max von Laue. Among the celebrities assembled there, besides the organizer, were Walther Nernst, Rudolf Ladenburg, Lise Meitner, and, in particular, Albert Einstein. After the lecture, Einstein invited Heisenberg to accompany him on the half-hour walk from the Physical Institute of the University of Berlin to his apartment in the *Haberlandstraße*, where they became involved in a discussion of the situation in atomic theory. Forty years later, Heisenberg reconstructed the details of their conversation.<sup>135</sup> According to his account in *Physics and Beyond*, it started this way:

> As soon as we were indoors, he [i.e., Einstein] opened the conversation with a question that bore on the philosophical background of my recent work. "What you have told us sounds extremely strange. You assume the existence of electrons inside the atom, and you are probably quite right to do so. But you refuse to consider their orbits, even though we can observe electron tracks in a cloud chamber. I should very much like to hear more about your reasons for making such strange assumptions."
>
> "We cannot observe electron orbits inside the atom," I must have replied, "but the radiation which an atom emits during the discharge enables us to deduce the frequencies and corresponding amplitudes of its electrons. After all, even in the older physics wave numbers and amplitudes could be considered substitutes for electron orbits. Now, since a good theory must be based on directly observable magnitudes, I thought it more fitting to restrict myself to these, treating them, as it were, as representatives of the electron orbits."
>
> "But you don't seriously believe," Einstein protested, "that none but observable magnitudes must go into a physical theory?"
>
> "Isn't that precisely what you have done with relativity?" I asked in some surprise. "After all, you did stress the fact that it is impermissible to speak of absolute time, simply because absolute time cannot be observed; that only clock readings, be it in the moving reference or the system at rest, are relevant to the determination of time."
>
> "Probably I did use this kind of reasoning," Einstein admitted, "but it is nonsense all the same. Perhaps I could put it more diplomatically by saying that it may be heuristically useful to keep in mind to what one has actually observed. But, on principle, it is wrong to try founding a theory on observable magnitudes alone. In reality the opposite happens. *It is the theory which decides what we can observe* [our italics]." (Heisenberg, 1971, pp. 62–63)

Einstein then argued that 'observation is a very complicated process' consisting of events stimulated by the phenomena in the measuring apparatus; additional processes in the apparatus and our sense impressions would happen by which 'we fix the effects in our consciousness.' All of these effects, he insisted, however, depend on our theories, and: 'Your claim that you are introducing none but observable magnitudes is therefore an assumption about a property of theory that you are trying to formulate.' (Einstein in Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*, pp. 63–64)

<sup>135</sup> Heisenberg reported about the invitation to Einstein's home in the letter to his parents, dated 29 April 1926, but he did not give any hint about the content of their conversation. David Cassidy, in his biography of Heisenberg, has given a slightly different reconstruction (Cassidy, 1992a, pp. 237–239).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0164 -->

132 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

Heisenberg was completely puzzled by Einstein's new arguments, and he referred to the previous procedure in special relativity theory, where Einstein had followed Mach's suggestions regarding adherence to observables and sense impressions (sensations). Einstein, however, simply replied that he did not believe anymore in that, because:

> Mach rather neglects the fact that the world really exists, that our sense impressions are based on something objective. . . . He pretends that we know perfectly what the word "observe" means and thinks this exempts him from having to discriminate between "objective" and "subjective" phenomena. (Einstein in Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*, p. 65)

Having rejected the epistemological position that had influenced him in his youth, Einstein turned to criticize certain details of Heisenberg's quantum mechanics, notably, the claim that no electron paths should exist in atoms. Heisenberg replied that he believed the quantum-mechanical formalism to be correct, but the proper understanding of the theory, especially in the traditional language, had not yet been obtained. Then, Einstein wanted to know what role the light-quantum played in the new theory, and Heisenberg admitted frankly that the Göttingen and Copenhagen physicists were really puzzled by the radiation phenomena: in particular, situations in atomic physics existed in which one could not speak about a definite behaviour, e.g., in the time-dependent transition process between stationary states. Referring to the beauty and reliability of his new atomic theory, Heisenberg concluded: 'In the present [situation] the simplicity of the mathematical scheme has the further consequence that it ought to be possible to think up many experiments whose results can be predicted by the theory. And if the actual experiments should bear out the predictions, there is little doubt that the theory reflects nature accurately in this particular realm.' (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*, p. 69)

We do not have documentary evidence, independent of these recollections, about what Einstein and Heisenberg spoke to each other in their historic encounter on 28 April 1926.<sup>136</sup> We do know from first-hand sources, however, the scientific and epistemological positions of the two protagonists, and this knowledge supports the above reconstruction of their discussion.

After a quite positive initial reaction—'*Heisenberg hat ein grosses Quantenei gelegt*,' Einstein to Ehrenfest, 20 September 1925—Einstein soon began to object to the Göttingen matrix mechanics; e.g., he claimed that the treatment of radiation in the three-man paper yielded the wrong result and could not reproduce the actual

<sup>136</sup> See also Footnote 135. On other occasions, e.g., in the AHQP Interviews, Heisenberg gave a similar description of the contents. Perhaps we can argue in favour of the reliability of the account in the following way: Heisenberg met Einstein only a few times; besides Berlin in April 1926, they saw each other in October 1927 at the fifth Solvay Conference on Physics in Brussels and then again three years later at the sixth Solvay Conference, and finally in fall 1954 at Princeton (see Heisenberg, 1977). Heisenberg always cherished highly the memories of these rare exchanges, and carefully preserved the few letters that he received from Einstein until they were stolen (or removed) by the ALSOS Mission in May 1945 from his home in Urfeld. Hence, one should conclude that he tried very carefully to reconstruct the contents of the Berlin encounter in April 1926.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0165 -->

II.3 Mechanical Concepts, Observation, and Restriction 133

fluctuations (Einstein to Jordan, 6 March 1926). Moreover, when he learned about Schrödinger's alternative theory, he praised the undulatory approach; in particular, two days before his meeting with Heisenberg occurred in Berlin, he had written to Schrödinger:

> I am convinced that you have obtained decisive progress with your formulation of the quantum conditions, as much as I am convinced that the Heisenberg-Born path leads astray. ("*Ich bin überzeugt, daß Sie mit Ihrer Formulierung der Quantenbedingung einen entscheidenden Fortschritt gefunden haben, ebenso wie ich überzeugt bin, daß der Heisenberg-Bornsche Weg abwegig ist.*") (Einstein to Schrödinger, 26 April 1926).

Heisenberg, on the other hand, was convinced of the correctness of the 'physical foundations and the mathematical formulation of the kinematical and mechanical equations' of his theory, the essence of which he had presented earlier at David Hilbert's mathematical seminar in Göttingen (and summarized in an article submitted in December 1925 to the *Mathematische Annalen*: Heisenberg, 1926a). If one adheres to using only observable quantities, he had argued, a close analogy to the undulatory description of radiation (as stated in the Bohr-Kramers-Slater theory of 1924) and the simultaneous validity of energy and momentum conservation (as demanded by the light-quantum hypothesis) might indeed be combined consistently in quantum mechanics. He had admitted, though, that the new theory still denied complete understanding, notably:

> The real geometrical or kinematic meaning of the fundamental assumption [i.e., the matrix representation of the position variable] has not yet been clarified totally. In particular, a grave difficulty lies in the following: time plays a different role in the theory and is treated differently from the spatial coordinates. The formal character of the time coordinate becomes especially evident from the fact that so far in the theory the question as to the time sequence of an event makes no immediate sense and that the concepts "before" and "after" can hardly be defined exactly. (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*, p. 705)

Apparently, it was the lack of the representation of a time sequence in matrix mechanics that prevented a detailed consideration of absorption and emission processes of light in the usual (classical) sense.

The discussion between Einstein and Heisenberg took place when Schrödinger's first communication on wave mechanics had just appeared but hardly been fully appreciated by Heisenberg. The Göttingen matrix scheme, the Cambridge *q*-number theory, and their slight modifications (e.g., Born and Wiener, 1926a, b; Wentzel, 1926a) were, however, available, and the main efforts of the young quantum physicists concentrated on using these methods to investigate further atomic problems: for example, Heisenberg and Jordan just succeeded in obtaining the first complete theoretical description of the complex spectra and their anomalous Zeeman effects (Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926). Most of the old puzzles of atomic physics were thus solved, and these results overwhelmingly spoke in favour

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0166 -->

134 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

of quantum mechanics. Also epistemologically, the Göttingen–Cambridge theory seemed to be based on clear and sound physical assumptions: (1) the elimination of electron orbits in atoms (first enunciated by Heisenberg and Pauli, 1924–1925); (2) the existence of discontinuities, as, for instance, in collision processes and radiative transitions (reemphasized by Born Heisenberg and Pauli from 1923 to 1925); (3) the ‘analogy’ of the laws of atomic mechanics to classical mechanics (Born, between 1924 and 1925). The last assumption evidently included the fact that the creators of quantum mechanics also retained the basis of particle mechanics—which underlay the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory of atomic structure—in their new approach.<sup>137</sup> Of course, they were also aware of its essential defects. Thus, for instance, Heisenberg had confessed in October 1925: ‘I have not arrived at a clear picture about the transition [of quantum mechanics] into the classical theory’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, 23 October 1925). A little later, he had thanked Pauli very cordially for a ‘philosophical letter,’ in which the latter had brought up the problem of time sequence in atomic processes.<sup>138</sup> He had gone on to say:

Unfortunately my own private philosophy is by far not so clear, but a muddle of all possible moral and aesthetic rules of computation, through which I often do not find a path myself. . . .
Your problem of the time sequence plays, of course, a fundamental role, and I had figured out for my own private use (*Hausgebrauch*) something about it. First I believe that one can distinguish between “a coarse and a finer” time sequence. If a point in space does not assume in the new theory a definite role or can be formulated only symbolically, then the same is true for an instant of time of an event. But there always will exist a coarse time sequence, like a coarse position in space—that is, *within* our geometric visualization one will be able to carry out a *coarse* description. I think it might be possible that this *coarse* description is perhaps the only thing that can be demanded from the formalism [of quantum mechanics]. (Heisenberg to Pauli, 24 November 1925, in Pauli, 1979, pp. 262–263)

In his letter to Pauli, Heisenberg had gone on to say that for purely periodic motions even such a coarse description in position and time sequence could not

<sup>137</sup> Mara Beller, in a study of the philosophy of ‘Matrix Mechanics before Schrödinger,’ has argued that the Göttingen theory was *not* a theory of *corpuscles* before Born’s probabilistic interpretation (Beller, 1983). Although, viewed from the later solution of the problem of interpretation this may appear to be a natural conclusion—so to say, it is correct from the standpoint of a global science theory—historically this was not felt to be so by the pioneers. We refer for this fact, e.g., to Born’s introduction in his published MIT Lectures of winter 1925/26 on *Problems in Atomic Dynamics* (Born, 1926d, p. 1) and to various quotations given below. **Because of evident historical reasons, we also cannot agree with Beller’s conclusion that the quantum mechanics of Heisenberg, Dirac, Born, and Jordan was not recognized in general as a breakthrough in 1926 (in contrast to Schrödinger’s new undulatory scheme): see, especially, our detailed analysis of the situation in Volume 4, Part 2, and Volume 5, Part 2, Chapter IV (which cannot be rejected on the basis of Beller’s less detailed investigations; indeed, our claim is based strictly on the evaluation of the response of the community of quantum physicists in 1925 and 1926).**
<sup>138</sup> Pauli had discussed this point not only in a (lost) letter to Heisenberg, but also in a (preserved) letter to Bohr, dated 17 November 1925. He had stated there that the time plays essentially no role in quantum mechanics, and: ‘The fact is that the concepts of “time period” or “time sequence” of an event have become only formal ones. The ‘formal character of the frequency condition’ is due to the formal character of time and not due to the formal character of energy’ (Pauli to Bohr, in Pauli, 1979, p. 260).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0167 -->

135 II.3 Mechanical Concepts, Observation, and Restriction

be defined, because one only knows, say, that the electron must stay close to an atomic nucleus. However:

if one considers an aperiodic orbit, i.e., a Fourier integral [in quantum mechanics] then the—let’s say—infrared part of the spectrum agrees with the classical theory; for this the usual rules of computation [i.e., not the matrix or *q*-number rules!] are valid in good approximation (the better so the larger the wavelengths), and exactly this infrared part represents the coarse time sequence. (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*, p. 263)

These considerations on the time sequence and the coarse description, arising in the context of pondering about the way in which the transition from quantum to classical mechanics might occur,<sup>139</sup> constituted perhaps the real start of Heisenberg’s involvement in ‘philosophical’ questions arising in the interpretation of the quantum-mechanical formalism.<sup>140</sup> The philosophical considerations, however, would not continue to preoccupy him; he soon became ‘diverted’ again into ‘practical’ problems, notably, the discussion and incorporation of the hypothesis of electron spin into matrix mechanics or a suitable extension of the formalism. Even after the memorable discussion with Einstein in April 1926, Heisenberg did not change this habit, for he soon treated the unsolved helium–atom problem, even taking recourse—for practical reasons—to Schrödinger’s wave-mechanical methods.<sup>141</sup>

**(b) Wave Mechanics: A Mathematical Tool or Superior Physical Theory? (June–October 1926)**

The reception of Schrödinger’s wave mechanics by the Göttingen theoreticians appears to have been a very mixed one. Thus, Max Born recalled a year later in a letter to Schrödinger:

You know that after the publication of your first paper I immediately expressed my enthusiasm for your ideas very strongly in a paper of my own. Heisenberg did not share, from the beginning, my opinion that your wave mechanics had a greater physical significance than our quantum mechanics; the simple possibility of treating with it aperiodic processes (collisions) made me first believe that your conception was superior. (Born to Schrödinger, 16 May 1927)

<sup>139</sup> As an example for discussing this situation, Heisenberg referred in his letter to Pauli (of 24 November 1925) to the passage of an alpha particle through matter, close to an atomic nucleus (an example frequently discussed in Bohr’s circle).
<sup>140</sup> Evidently, the passages on the role of time in quantum mechanics appearing in Heisenberg’s lectures at Hilbert’s seminar were triggered by his correspondence with Pauli on this topic.
<sup>141</sup> However, one must not conclude from the programme, which Heisenberg embarked upon in Copenhagen in May 1926, that he forgot entirely about the discussion with Einstein; he certainly reported its details faithfully to Bohr, and was guided by it later in dealing with the problem of the interpretation of quantum mechanics.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0168 -->

136 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

Heisenberg indeed did not share Born’s enthusiasm about the physical superiority of wave mechanics; later, Born recalled in his recollections:<sup>142</sup>

Heisenberg was at first not happy about my using Schrödinger’s wave mechanics. I got a letter from him in which he reproached me for deserting matrix mechanics which he, like Jordan, regarded as more fundamental than wave mechanics. (Born, 1978, p. 233)

Especially, in summer 1926, an event occurred that stirred Heisenberg’s resistance against Schrödinger’s theory and brought him to devote greater attention again to the ‘philosophical problems’: he heard, toward the end of July 1926 (while he was on vacation with his parents), lectures at the University of Munich in which Schrödinger himself presented his new continuum interpretation of atomic theory and at the same time criticized the treatment of these questions in the rival quantum mechanics.<sup>143</sup>
Just a few weeks earlier, Schrödinger had submitted two papers for publication that (in his opinion) changed the situation completely. The first, a note on ‘*Die stetige Übergang von der Mikro- zur Makromechanik*’ (‘The Continuous Transition from Micro- to Macro-Mechanics,’ which appeared in the issue of 9 July 1926 of *Naturwissenschaften*), demonstrated in the simple case of the linear oscillator how the wave-mechanical solutions cooperated to produce, in the case of large quantum numbers, the classical behaviour of the system (Schrödinger, 1926g).<sup>144</sup> The second paper, his (larger and more important) fourth communication on wave mechanics (Schrödinger, 1926h), had been sent by Schrödinger to Willy Wien, editor of the *Annalen der Physik*, together with a letter dated 18 June 1926. He had mentioned how grateful he was that Wien, like Max Planck, eagerly supported his approach and then written: ‘It seems that at present not all people are convinced that a turn away from the fundamental discontinuities should be welcomed *if* it works. But I have always hoped arduously that this will be possible.’ After giving an outline of the paper on the time-dependent wave equation and its application to atomic problems, he had finally concluded:

<sup>142</sup> Though we do not have available Heisenberg’s letter that Born referred to; in addition, Born’s recollections mixed up certain events that occurred in 1926 and 1927. Still, it is certain that Heisenberg regarded Born’s first paper on collision phenomena with some suspicion (see Heisenberg’s letter to Pauli, 28 July 1926: ‘By the way, what do you think about Born’s last note in the *Zeitschrift* [für *Physik*]? One sentence [in it] reminded me vividly of a chapter from the Christian Confession: “An electron *is* a plane wave.”’ In a conversation in March 1955, Born recalled that when he used wave mechanics in treating atomic collision phenomena, Heisenberg accused him ‘of going over to the enemy camp’ (Born, Conversations with Mehra, March 1955, p. 59).
<sup>143</sup> Schrödinger had been invited by Sommerfeld to give a talk in his Seminar. He also gave a talk in the *Munich Colloquium* on 23 July 1926, which was entitled: ‘*Grundgedanken einer auf Wellenlehre begründeten Atomphysik*’ (‘Basic Ideas of an Atomic Physics Founded on Wave Theory’). See our account in Volume 5, Part 2, Section IV.5, especially, pp. 796–804.
<sup>144</sup> For a less trivial example, see the papers of Gregor Wentzel, Hendrik Kramers, and Léon Brillouin, treated in Section I.3.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0169 -->

137 II.3 Mechanical Concepts, Observation, and Restriction

One feels oneself again fully confirmed in the conviction that we face here [in the examples treated] completely real processes in space and time and that all philosophy about “non-observability in principle” only conceals our inability to guess the right pictures. (Schrödinger to Wien, 18 June 1926)

Wien, in his reply, had expressed his great pleasure at this news and expressed the expectation that Schrödinger would soon present his ideas in the *Munich Colloquium*. At the same time, he had stressed how much he disliked the work of ‘the younger physicists’ in theory, ‘the swamp of whole and half-quanta, discontinuities, and arbitrary use of the classical theory’ (Wien to Schrödinger, 23 June 1926). Evidently, when speaking about ‘younger physicists,’ he had in mind the former Munich student Werner Heisenberg; Schrödinger should teach him the right lesson.
Even eighteen years after the incident in Munich, Heisenberg vividly remembered ‘the hot July days in the small colloquium room of Sommerfeld’s institute,’ where:

Experimental and theoretical physicists were fully assembled, in spite of the wonderful weather, and listened with rapt attention to the lecture which unfolded a new picture of atomic physics before our eyes. After Schrödinger had presented the charge distribution [of, say, an electron] composed of eigenvibrations which now could act as a source of radiation [Wilhelm] Wien spontaneously rose and spoke enthusiastically about the fact that now obviously the assumption of quantum jumps had been replaced by something reasonable, and that one might finally succeed in clarifying atomic physics with similar visualizability (*Anschaulichkeit*) as one was used to in classical physics. Even the theoreticians, full of amazement, recognized that here existed for the first time an *audacious* picture of the radiating atom leading to the correct frequency of the emitted light. In spite of this, however, Sommerfeld and [I] had to contradict the optimism expounded by Wien. [We] explained the great difficulties opposing every interpretation without quantum jumps; a quite excited debate followed in which Wien almost felt insulted that one was not eager to return with full sails into the land of classical physics. (Heisenberg, 1946, pp. 4–5)

In another recollection, Heisenberg stressed that Wien nearly threw him out of the room upon having dared to doubt the validity of Schrödinger’s interpretation (e.g., Heisenberg, 1971, p. 73).<sup>145</sup> In a letter to Pauli, written immediately after the event, Heisenberg first mentioned that reading Pauli’s recent *Handbuch* article on quantum theory (Pauli, 1926b) ‘meant a real recovery (*Erholung*) after Schrödinger’s lecture here in Munich’ and continued:

<sup>145</sup> It is not clear where the reported clash between Heisenberg and Wien occurred, whether in the *Colloquium* talk or in Sommerfeld’s *Seminar*; Heisenberg’s account in *Physics and Beyond* implies that it was in the latter, and that he ‘returned home very sad,’ apparently having been left alone in his position. On the other hand, Sommerfeld at least took his side in a letter to Pauli: ‘My general impression is that though “wave mechanics” is an admirable micro-mechanics, it does not solve the fundamental quantum riddles at all (*im Entferntesten*)’ (Sommerfeld to Pauli, 26 July 1926).

Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

Just as nice as Schrödinger is personally, as strange do I find his physics; when one listens to him, one feels 26 years behind times [i.e., back to the year 1900 before Planck introduced the quantum hypothesis]. Schrödinger throws overboard everything "quantum theoretical": namely the photoelectric effect, Franck [-Hertz] collisions, the Stern-Gerlach effect, etc. It is then not difficult to establish a theory [of the kind that Schrödinger has in mind]. But it just does not agree with experience. (Heisenberg to Pauli, 28 July 1926, in Pauli, 1979, pp. 337–338)

In the same letter to Pauli, Heisenberg also reported a point of detail from the discussion, dealing with an interpretation of Wien’s experiments concerning the damping of atomic radiation. 'According to Schrödinger, these experiments *cannot* be easily explained by the [quantum-mechanical transition amplitudes] $A_n^m$,' he wrote and commented: 'In my opinion (and certainly also yours) they really can' (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*).¹⁴⁶ Then, he took a vacation from physics, while his antagonist Wien proceeded, in the beginning of August 1926, from Munich to England and participated in the Oxford meeting of the *British Association*. There, he discussed, as he informed Schrödinger later, 'one of the most serious difficulties of wave mechanics in detail (*eingehend*) with Bohr and Born' obtaining—what, for him, were unpleasant answers. He wrote:

> Both are convinced that the photoelectric effect is not compatible with wave mechanics. [Bohr] believes that the representation in space and time is impossible, while [Born] wants to renounce the causal law. I am not able to follow both of them on these paths, since they have not yet shown that abandoning these foundations [of the classical physics] can result in a satisfactory system [of a new physical theory]. How the photoelectric effect should be explained is not clear to me. (Wien to Schrödinger, 20 August 1926)

Wien was so disturbed by the situation that he invited Schrödinger to his mountain retreat near Mittenwald to discuss the problems of emission of light and the photoelectric effect in wave mechanics. Schrödinger promised to come, and he did so later in September (after his planned vacation in South Tyrol). Regarding the opinions expressed by Born and Bohr to Wien, Schrödinger wrote as follows:

> I do not want today anymore to assume with Born that such a single event (*ein solches einzelnes Ereignis*) [in atomic physics] is "absolutely arbitrary," i.e., [it] is completely undetermined. I do not believe anymore that one can gain much with this assumption (which I advocated four years ago very energetically)... I believe that Born overlooks [when he interprets the wave function as probability for the real motion of light-quanta] that it still remains up to the observer *what* he wants to consider as *real*, the particle or the guiding field. A philosophical criterion for reality does not exist, if one does not wish to say: the only real thing is the complex sensations, the rest is nothing but particles.

¹⁴⁶ This point would play a role in the further discussions between Wien and Schrödinger (as well as in Heisenberg’s thinking), as we shall see below.

II.3 Mechanical Concepts, Observation, and Restriction

> Bohr’s point of view I reject *a limine*. Physics does not consist only of atomic research, science not only of physics, and life not only of science. The purpose of atomic research is to fit our *experiences* about it into the rest of our thinking. This entire rest of thinking is acting, as far as the external world is concerned, in space and time. If the process of fitting does not succeed, the total purpose has been missed, and one does not know *which* purpose should then be served at all. (Schrödinger to Wien, 25 August 1926)

At about the time when Schrödinger and Wien met at Mittenwald to discuss these questions, Heisenberg presented (on 26 September 1926) at the Düsseldorf *Naturforscherversammlung* a grand report on 'Quantum Mechanics,' dealing with the Göttingen–Cambridge and the Schrödinger schemes (Heisenberg, 1926d). At this meeting, he declared that the success of wave mechanics 'consists mainly in the fact that it allows a simple determination of transition probabilities which, in general, is very difficult by other methods' (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*, p. 991). However, he condemned the physical interpretation of Schrödinger’s scheme in the following strong words:

> In recent times the suggestion has occasionally been made (Schrödinger, Flamm) that on the basis of Schrödinger’s differential equation a purely continuous description of the quantum-theoretical experiences becomes feasible, say, in the sense of the classical theory; that, therefore, quantum theory in its previous form is illusory. If one carries out this point of view strictly, however, one leaves the basis of de Broglie’s theory, hence of quantum mechanics and all quantum theory altogether, and one runs, in my opinion, into a complete contradiction with experience (law of blackbody radiation, dispersion theory). Therefore, this path cannot be followed. The genuine reality of de Broglie waves lies rather in the interference phenomena, which ridicule every interpretation on the basis of classical concepts. The exceptional physical importance of Schrödinger’s results is connected with the observation that a visualizable interpretation of the quantum-mechanical equations involves both the typical features of a corpuscular and the typical features of wave theory. (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*, p. 992)

The last sentence reflected to a large extent the point of view assumed by Bohr in those days (and afterward), and Heisenberg may have inserted it indeed only in the proofs of the paper published in the 5 November issue of *Naturwissenschaften*. In the meantime, the Copenhageners had had the opportunity of debating the issues with Schrödinger himself, who had come for a visit in the first week of October 1926.¹⁴⁷ Besides presenting a lecture on 'Grundlagen der undulatorischen Mechanik' ('Foundations of the Undulatory Mechanics') on 4 October, Schrödinger became involved in thorough discussions 'centering gradually on the problem of the physical reality of the postulates of the atomic theory' (Bohr to R.

¹⁴⁷ Details of Schrödinger’s visit have been reported in Volume 5, Part 2, pp. 820–828. Also, see Stolzenburg, 1977, and Jørgen Kalckar’s introduction in Volume 6 of *Niels Bohr Collected Works* (Kalckar, 1985, especially, pp. 7–16); also Beller, 1992b, for a shorter account.

Fowler, 26 October 1926).¹⁴⁸ Similar to the situation in Munich in July, Schrödinger was now confronted by Bohr and Heisenberg expressing the stern opinion that no genuine quantum-theoretical effect could be explained unless one assumed the existence of quantum jumps. In his recollections, Heisenberg emphasized how mercilessly Bohr insisted on this point, while Schrödinger felt that he had been treated quite nicely in Copenhagen and rather excused himself for 'the stubbornness, with which in our dialogues I continued to adhere to my "wishes" for a physics of the future [without quantum jumps]' (Schrödinger to Bohr, 23 October 1926).¹⁴⁹ But, in spite of all efforts, Bohr could not persuade Schrödinger about his views; thus, Bohr’s letter to Fowler indicated only a minimum agreement:¹⁵⁰

> We agreed that a continuity theory in the form indicated in his last paper at a number of points leads to expectations fundamentally different from those of the usual discontinuity theory. Schrödinger himself continued in his hope that the idea of stationary states and transitions was altogether avoidable, but I think that we succeeded at least in convincing him that for the fulfillment of his hope he must be prepared to pay a cost, as regards reformulation of fundamental concepts, formidable in comparison with that hitherto contemplated by the supporters of the idea of a continuity theory of atomic phenomena. (Bohr to R. Fowler, 26 October 1926)

Schrödinger’s visit left the Copenhagen quantum theorists back in a very busy state, in spite of the fact that they believed to have won their case—or, at least, repelled the opponent’s attack. Heisenberg, in particular, described the situation in the following words:

> From then on the discussions between Bohr and his coworkers in Copenhagen became more and more concentrated on the central problem in quantum theory: how the mathematical formulation was to be applied to each individual problem, and thus how the frequently discussed paradoxes, such as, e.g., the apparent contradiction between the wave and particle models could be cleared up. Ever new imaginary experiments were thought up, each displaying the paradoxes in a more clear-cut way than its predecessors, and we tried to guess what answer nature would probably give to each experiment. In the course of those efforts Bohr and I went off in somewhat different directions.... Bohr felt correctly that the apparent dualism [between the particle and wave models of radiation] was so central a phenomenon that he thought

Bohr gave no written report, except in one letter to Fowler (cited above) and another to Schrödinger (on 2 December 1926). II.3 Mechanical Concepts, Observation, and Restriction
141

that it should be the natural starting point for any interpretation. I myself put my trust in the newly developed mathematical formalism. In as much as the interpretation of certain quantities was already determined by the fundamental assumptions of quantum mechanics, I believed that a simple consequent development of these assumptions would result in the obvious general interpretation and that one should not increase one's debt to illustrative models. Thanks to this difference of views these difficult problems were illuminated and investigated from all sides, though the paradoxes were not easy to eliminate. (Heisenberg, 1967, p. 104)

This later recollection, like the memory of any participant in an important and complex story, naturally reflects the development from a very personal point of view, also one biased by the final outcome. On the other hand, Heisenberg was the first of the two Copenhagen spokesmen who took over the initiative, and one has to admit that the available documents, incomplete as they are at times, essentially support his narrative and provide many details illuminating and fixing his procedure between July 1926 and February or March 1927. The intricate development indicated by these documents may be organized in the following six steps, which will be discussed subsequently in some detail:

(1) Immediately after Schrödinger's talks in Munich, Heisenberg returned systematically and demonstratively to the matrix formalism; i.e., from then on, he tried to treat all fundamental problems of atomic physics without employing undulatory methods, even when the latter offered an easier access to the solution.
(2) In Copenhagen, Heisenberg became somewhat isolated, because nobody—neither Bohr, Klein, nor a visitor from Göttingen, Friedrich Hund—followed his strict refusal to employ wave-mechanical methods.¹⁵¹
(3) In contrast to the Copenhagen theoreticians, Wolfgang Pauli showed sympathy toward the programme and goals of his friend; he participated through letters in a deepened conceptual analysis of collision phenomena and related problems that eventually set Heisenberg on the route to his uncertainty relations.
(4) The other important input was provided by Paul Dirac. Heisenberg interacted quite closely with the reserved and independent Dirac: while the latter was stimulated by his physical suggestions on the path to transformation theory, Heisenberg in turn happily profited from Dirac's elegant mathematical calculus involving the delta-function, because it allowed one to replace Schrödinger's wave formalism by an equivalent quantum-mechanical one.
(5) The intense debates between Bohr and Heisenberg, which went on from October 1926 to February 1927, focused on constructing (often artificial) situations in atomic physics that particularly highlighted the paradoxes in the physical interpretation.
(6) In February 1927, the study of the fundamental problem of simultaneous measurement of position and momentum led Heisenberg to consider a new, decisive *Gedankenexperiment*, the γ-ray microscope; the theoretical and mathematical analysis (via the Dirac–Jordan transformation theory) and physical analysis (via the Compton effect) resulted in establishing the uncertainty relations.

¹⁵¹ Similarly, Born and Jordan in Göttingen continued to use Schrödinger's theory and methods in analyzing quantum-mechanical phenomena. (See Chapter I for details.)

142 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields  

**(c) The Quantum Phenomena in Matrix Formulation**  
(July–November 1926)  

In the discussion of his lectures in Munich, Schrödinger claimed that experiments measuring the decay times of excited states of atomic hydrogen would not be explained by the matrix methods. In his and Wilhelm Wien’s eyes—Wien was the expert experimentalist in this question—this provided an important argument in favour of wave mechanics and its classical interpretation. Heisenberg, on the other hand, insisted—as he wrote in his letter to Pauli on 28 July—on the fact that Einstein’s description of the transition amplitudes \( A^m_n \) of 1916, which had been fully incorporated into his quantum mechanics of 1925, did yield the correct theory (and a quantitative evaluation would agree with Wien’s data).<sup>152</sup> The ‘damping problem’ played a prominent role in the correspondence between Schrödinger and Wien during the following months. Thus, Schrödinger, after his visit to Copenhagen, reported to Wien (in his letter of 21 October 1926) the result of Heisenberg’s calculations of the damping constant of the Balmer lines ‘in a manner that seems to be correct to me’: the value for the first line was consistent with Wien’s observation, though of the further lines disagreed, as shorter lifetimes were predicted. ‘With the unshakable trust of a theoretician,’—so Schrödinger wrote to Wien—Heisenberg had assumed that light-stimulating collisions might be responsible for (Wien’s) false experimental values, but Wien promptly replied: ‘Heisenberg belongs among those young theoreticians who totally and exclusively adhere to theory, and do not have the slightest idea about experiment.’ (Wien to Schrödinger, 23 October 1926) The analysis of the experimental situation rather seemed to contradict Heisenberg’s particular assumptions, but Schrödinger pointed out possible loopholes in Wien’s arguments, which raised further questions (Schrödinger to Wien, 23 November 1926). Although Wien worked eagerly to clarify the situation, he had to admit a year after Schrödinger’s talks in Munich: ‘The theory of damping is still in its infancy, in spite of the contrary opinion of the younger theoreticians. If this is not so, the worse for reality.’ (Wien to Schrödinger, 7 August 1927)  

For Heisenberg, on the other hand, the theoretical situation was rather definite. In his view, quantum mechanics demanded that excited atoms emit spontaneous radiation, whereas from Schrödinger’s interpretation, the following conclusion followed: If an atom exists only in the first excited state, then it would not emit any radiation, because it then represents a constant charge density; only if it is partly in the lower (ground) state and partly in the upper (first excited) state, i.e., when interference between the charge distribution becomes possible, radiation may be emitted. Evidently, the latter assumption contradicted Einstein’s radiation theory of 1916 leading to Planck’s blackbody radiation law; hence, Schrödinger’s interpretation could not be consistent even with the very first quantum-theoretical  

<sup>152</sup> In this context, Heisenberg referred ‘to the accurate presentation of the physical connections’ in Pauli’s Handbuch article (Pauli, 1926b, p. 71).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0175 -->

143 II.3 Mechanical Concepts, Observation, and Restriction  

law. Heisenberg also put his trust into another of Einstein’s previous results, the fluctuation formula of 1909 for radiation—which, by the way, was also a consequence of Planck’s law. ‘I have thought recently occasionally about fluctuations—everything seems to be in order,’ he informed Pauli on 28 October 1926. A little later, he announced the publication of a note on the subject that ‘for you and all reasonable physicists contains nothing new,’ as he confessed to his dear friend, but: ‘The reason why I have written it, is purely pedagogical via-a-vis the gentlemen of continuum theory.’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, 4 November 1926)  

In this note on ‘Schwankungserscheinungen und Quantenmechanik’ (‘Fluctuation Phenomena in Quantum Mechanics’: Heisenberg, 1926e), Heisenberg wished to close the gap between the treatment of radiation in the three-man paper and the light-quantum approach of Einstein.<sup>153</sup> ‘The following note therefore provides a generalization and renders more precise the considerations which have been made by Born, Jordan and the author previously in connection with the general development of quantum mechanics,’ Heisenberg noted in the abstract of his paper (Heisenberg, loc. cit., p. 501). Einstein had suspected that the correspondence-theoretical use of the classical radiation theory could not give rise to the large fluctuations obtained with Bose’s light-quanta, but Heisenberg now simply referred to his matrix formulation of the helium problem to prove the opposite.  

In his paper of June 1926, he had treated, in particular, a system of two harmonic oscillators coupled by a weak interaction term. He had said then that it could be described either by the light-quantum picture (of Einstein) or by referring to the correspondence analogy with the classical coupling of two oscillators (Heisenberg, 1926b); and, in the course of further evaluation, he had replaced the matrix treatment by a wave-mechanical one (Heisenberg, 1926c). Now, however, in October 1926, he changed his attitude and stressed the fundamental difference between the two schemes. For instance, a difference arose in the interpretation of the quantum-theoretical result when compared with the classical picture involved: Although in a classical theory the energy of the atomic system (represented in his model by the two oscillators) entered as a function of the time, in quantum mechanics only time averages of a time-dependent variable made ‘physical sense,’ Heisenberg argued. Certainly, ‘the energy of an atom can be formally expressed by a matrix which is a harmonic function of time,’ but the ‘harmonic terms in this matrix are associated each with two states of the total system’ (Heisenberg, 1926e, p. 502). The two theoretical descriptions—i.e., the quantum-mechanical and the undulatory ones—would yield identical results only for quantities that are ‘observable in principle.’ The simple model calculation allowed for a generalization to problems involving different atoms; here, the transformation matrix describing the transitions just assumed a more complex shape. In all examples, the square of the transition elements had to be identified with the transition probabilities, i.e., the probability that a system originally in the state α passes over into a state of β after  

<sup>153</sup> Einstein had criticized the older matrix-mechanical treatment, both in letters to Pascual Jordan and in his discussion with Heisenberg in April 1926.

the interaction (e.g., after the interaction potential had faded off or the collision process ended). However, all energy states occurring in the quantum mechanics of stationary systems have to be considered as ‘discrete’ ones. As a consequence, Heisenberg concluded: ‘One can foresee without actually performing it, that the calculation of the average-square fluctuation and the higher fluctuation averages will yield the same result in quantum mechanics as is obtained on the Bose-Einstein light-quantum statistics.’ (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*, p. 506)

**(d) The Bohr–Klein Attitude Toward Wave Mechanics (Fall 1926)**

In contrast to Heisenberg, Niels Bohr pursued the analysis of the quantum-theoretical concepts by not relying exclusively on matrix methods; rather, he invoked undulatory concepts explicitly. Writing to Ralph Fowler on 26 October 1926, he pointed to a much more positive attitude toward Schrödinger’s formalism; he even spoke about an agreement between the opposite camps with respect to the ‘continuity theory.’ He explained in detail:¹⁵⁴

> I understood that Schrödinger had been working under the impression that the essential characteristic of the matrix mechanics was the final recognition of the impossibility of ascribing a physical reality to a single stationary state, but I think this is a confounding of the means and aims of Heisenberg’s theory. Just in the wave mechanics we possess now the means of picturing a single stationary state which suits all purposes consistent with the postulates of quantum theory. In fact, this is the very reason for the advantage which the wave mechanics in certain respects exhibits when compared with the matrix method which in other respects is so wonderfully suited to bring out the true correspondence between the quantum theory and the classical ideas. (Bohr to R. Fowler, 26 October 1926)

Bohr certainly did not wish to stick to Heisenberg’s puritanical use of the quantum-mechanical scheme. For him, mathematical formalism figured as a secondary device, just purely a tool, but not the essence of physics. Oskar Klein, who had worked earlier on the relativistic wave-mechanical theory,¹⁵⁵ supported Bohr actively: in December 1926, he submitted a paper, entitled ‘*Elektrodynamik und Wellenmechanik vom Standpunkt des Korrespondenzprinzips*’ (‘Electrodynamics and Wave Mechanics from the Point of View of the Correspondence Principle’), to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (O. Klein, 1927a), which Bohr in turn announced to Schrödinger as ‘exploiting wave mechanics for the understanding of atomic processes involving discontinuities’ and leading to the conclusion: ‘Actually it is possible, on the basis of wave mechanics, to build a correspondence theory as closed as matrix mechanics, which, on the other hand, may be regarded as a correspondence theory

¹⁵⁴ Bohr’s letter to Fowler is reproduced in Kalckar, 1985, pp. 14–15.
¹⁵⁵ See the relativistic extensions of the Schrödinger equation, reported in Volume 5, Part 2, Section IV. 5.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0177 -->
