145

based on the corpuscular mechanics’ (Bohr to Schrödinger, 2 December 1926).¹⁵⁶ Such a statement, which deprived matrix mechanics of the privilege that it alone expressed *the* correspondence to the classical theory, could only irritate Heisenberg; at any rate, it did not fit at all into his personal programme; hence, he had to look for support elsewhere.

**(e) The Heisenberg–Pauli Exchange on Collision and Related Problems (October–November 1926)**

The Pauli correspondence contains four letters exchanged between him and Heisenberg in the period from 19 October to 15 November 1926; this exchange provided the crucial stimulus which put Heisenberg straight on the route to the uncertainty relations.¹⁵⁷ In the first letter of 19 October, Pauli treated two problems at length: Fermi statistics and its application to material particles (notably electrons) and the collision theory.¹⁵⁸ ‘Now I shall come to the other chapter, the collision problem,’ he began the longer second part, adding that it appeared to him ‘an undigested dumpling’ in the ‘embryonal status of considerations,’ and that he might not have written about it without having been encouraged to do so by Heisenberg. Then, he sketched the main idea in the one-dimensional example of a mass point running across an obstacle characterized by a potential $V(x)$ that falls off sharply and whose maximum is lower than the energy of the mass point. According to Born’s scattering theory, a probability of reflection exists given by the square of the amplitude $\psi_1(x)$ for $x \ll x_0$ (the coordinate of the potential maximum),

$$ \psi_1(x) = \frac{1}{2ik} \exp (-ikx) \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \exp (ik\xi) V(\xi) d\xi \tag{105} $$

(with $k$ denoting the wavenumber, the one-dimensional wave vector). In the next, specific example, Pauli treated a rotator disturbed by an angle-dependent potential $V(\vartheta)$, the evaluation could be carried out by matrix-mechanical methods: the problem exhibited degeneracy, because the object could rotate either in the positive or in the negative sense around the potential with equal frequency. Pauli then commented:¹⁵⁹

¹⁵⁶ The translation of Bohr’s letter to Schrödinger, from German into English, is given in Kalckar, 1985, p. 14.
¹⁵⁷ One letter from each partner in the exchange has been lost. Pauli answered on 19 October an earlier letter of Heisenberg, and so did Heisenberg on 15 November referring to one previously written by Pauli.
¹⁵⁸ Both of these problems might have been raised by Heisenberg because they bothered him at that time. He and Pauli would also soon publish papers on the question of statistics (Heisenberg, 1927a; Pauli, 1927a).
¹⁵⁹ Pauli, 1979, p. 344. The translation is contained essentially in Hendry, 1984, p. 98. Hendry discusses this and other letters in some detail.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0178 -->

146 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

And now comes the beauty: The integral, which according to Born’s formula [(105)] gives the probability of reflection, is none other than the matrix element $V_{+n, -n}$ [with $n$ the rotational quantum number] when one goes to the limit of infinitely great radius of the rotator. $|V_{+n, -n}|^2$ is (up to a factor $1/k$) proportional to the probability, while $2|V_{+n, -n}|^2$ determines the energy splitting of the secular perturbation. (Pauli to Heisenberg, 19 October 1926, in Pauli, 1979, p. 345)

The calculation—which must have sounded very familiar to Heisenberg—admitted an extension to three-dimensional examples, both with Cartesian canonical variables or action-angle pairs. Especially, the straight-line motion could thus be treated by Pauli; however, ‘the $q$’s cannot be defined uniquely, because the system is degenerate.’ Thus followed what Pauli called the ‘dark spot’ of the result, namely:

The $p$’s must be taken as *controlled*, the $q$’s as *uncontrolled*. That is, one can always calculate just the probabilities of definite changes for the $p$’s for their given initial values, *averaged over all possible values of the $q$’s*. (Pauli, 1979, p. 345)

This conclusion now created two problems of interpretation, as Pauli continued:

The first question is, why may only the $p$’s, and in any case not both the $p$’s and $q$’s be described with arbitrary accuracy. This is the old problem…: because of diffracting any weak radiation there do not exist arbitrarily narrow rays in the wave optics of the $\psi$-field, and one is not allowed to associate simultaneously with both “$p$-numbers” and “$q$-numbers” ordinary “$c$-numbers.” One can see the world with the $p$-eye, and one can see it with the $q$-eye, but if one opens both eyes together, then ones goes astray. (Pauli, *loc. cit.*, pp. 346–347)

The second problem arose with the interpretation of the matrix elements, which ‘must be connected in principle with observable (perhaps statistical) data of the particles considered to be in stationary states’ (Pauli, *loc. cit.*, 347). How do they determine the probabilities of the collision process? Pauli now suggested: the probability, that for a given stationary state of a system with particle coordinates ($k = 1, \ldots, f$) lies between $q_k$ and $q_k + dq_k$, can be obtained from the *Ansatz*,

$$W_q = |\psi(q_1 \ldots q_f)|^2 dq_1 \ldots dq_f, \tag{106}$$

where $\psi$ denotes the Schrödinger function. Similarly, one might determine a probability in momentum space as

$$W_p = |\phi(p_1 \ldots p_f)|^2 dp_1 \ldots dp_f. \tag{107}$$

The matrix elements of any function of the position and momentum variables should then follow from multiplying these functions with the probabilities, $W_q$ and

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0179 -->

II.3 Mechanical Concepts, Observation, and Restriction 147

$W_p$, and integrating over the variables ($q_1 \ldots q_f$ or $p_1 \ldots p_f$, respectively). At any rate, Pauli finally concluded his letter of twelve pages at 2:30 a.m.: ‘One always strikes the point that one cannot ask simultaneously for $p$ and $q$.’ (Pauli, *loc. cit.*, p. 348)

In his response, given nine days later, Heisenberg first reported that everybody in Copenhagen—Bohr, Dirac, and Hund—had eagerly studied Pauli’s letter; he also mentioned that the examples given in it showed some similarities with those treated by Friedrich Hund in connection with molecular problems, or by himself for studying the resonance problem (see Heisenberg, 1927a). Then, he turned to ‘the most interesting in your remarks, of course the “dark spot,”’ and commented:

I tend to believe that your $p$-waves possess as much physical reality as the $q$-waves, though perhaps less practical importance. The equation $pq - qp = \frac{h}{2\pi i}$ therefore always corresponds in wave interpretation to the fact that it does not make sense to talk about a monochromatic wave at a definite instant of time (or a very small interval of time). If, however, one does not have too sharp a line and too small a time interval, then it does make sense. Analogously, it does not make sense to talk about the position of a corpuscle of definite velocity. However, if one does not consider too accurate velocity and position, it does make sense. (Heisenberg to Pauli, 28 October 1926, *loc. cit.*, p. 350)

Evidently, Heisenberg went on, such a conclusion would allow one to define in macroscopic physics position and velocity to a good approximation, but in atomic physics, it might turn out that ‘space and time are only statistical concepts, like temperature, pressure, etc., in a gas,’ and continued:

I mean that space and time concepts of a [single microscopic] particle do not make sense but become more meaningful the more particles are present. I often try to go in this direction, but so far I have not yet succeeded. Your calculations have encouraged me very much, because they demonstrate that Born’s dogmatic point of view about probability waves is only one of many possible schemes. (Heisenberg to Pauli, *loc. cit.*)

Pauli’s letter of 19 October stimulated Heisenberg further, and a week later he again wrote to Hamburg. In particular, he concluded that letter by saying:

One should therefore state in general: each scheme which satisfies [the commutation rule] $pq - qp = \frac{h}{2\pi i}$ is a “correct” one and can be used in physics. One is perfectly free in choosing how to satisfy this relation, whether with matrices, operators, or otherwise. By the way, your wave function $\phi$ in $p$-space seems to me to be the Laplace transform of the Schrödinger function $\psi$ in $q$-space, $\phi(p) = \int \exp(ipq)\psi(q) dq$, and vice versa. But your functions in other spaces, e.g., $J$ and $w$, are something else. The problem of canonical transformations in the wave picture thus appears to be solved. (Heisenberg to Pauli, 4 November 1926, *loc. cit.*, p. 352)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0180 -->

148 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

Heisenberg then requested Pauli to comment on his consideration, and Pauli must have provided them (in a lost letter), because on 15 November, Heisenberg thanked him for new suggestions. In particular, he was ‘fully in agreement in every respect with the direction’ of Pauli’s attempts, though he ‘did not know whether the way in which you [i.e., Pauli] carry out this approach is careful enough.’ Pauli had evidently referred to the well-known division of the phase space (in statistical mechanics) into cells of finite size $h$.${}^{160}$ However, Heisenberg raised serious doubts that this procedure would suffice to describe the quantum case correctly and stated:

If you define the walls of the cells sharply and can still determine how many particles are there in a cell, isn’t one then able to find the number of atoms in arbitrarily small cells? I mean: does the choice of *definite* cell boundaries make sense in physics? Perhaps one can give, say, the ratio of relative position of the two cell walls but not the position of a single one. The same objection applies to the $E, t$ partition. (Heisenberg to Pauli, 15 November 1926, *loc. cit.*, p. 354)

Although he criticized particular points of Pauli’s suggestions, Heisenberg shared his ‘opinion that the “dark spot” will ultimately become a “bright spot,”’ and he opened new vistas by the following comments:

If space [and] time are somehow discontinuous, then it is very satisfying that it does not make sense to talk, say, about a velocity $\dot{x}$ in a definite position $x$. Because one needs, in order to *define* a velocity, always two points which certainly will *not* be infinitely close in a discontinuous world. If we talk about position or velocity, we use words which obviously are not defined properly in a discontinuous world. (Heisenberg to Pauli, 15 November 1926, *loc. cit.*, pp. 354–355)

These remarks indicated that Heisenberg had now begun to focus on the very central question of defining the concepts of position and momentum in the quantum world.

**(f) Heisenberg’s Exchange with Dirac on the Transformation Theory (October–December 1926)**

Since late October 1926, Heisenberg’s letters to Pauli also provide information about his most fruitful discussions with the English visitor Paul Dirac.${}^{161}$ Heisenberg seems to have talked regularly with Dirac and knew most about his research. Thus, he reported to Pauli on 28 October that ‘Dirac has made a very funny con-

${}^{160}$ Since 1906, Max Planck had used such a procedure to explain the quantum effects in blackbody radiation and gases. (See Volume 1, Parts 1 and 2.)

${}^{161}$ Dirac had arrived in Copenhagen shortly after Schrödinger’s visit there, and he became involved in the discussions that were going on. See Section I.5 for details.

sideration to illustrate Schrödinger’s electric [charge] density’; this ‘funny’ consideration was simply to introduce the delta-function—see Section I.5, Eqs. (74)—which he found ‘really agreeable’ for two reasons. First, it allowed one to associate matrix elements with point-like objects; notably, it provided the ‘quantum-mechanical matrix of the electrical density,’ i.e.,

$$\rho_{nm}(x_0, y_0, z_0, t_0) = e\psi_n\psi_m^*(x_0, y_0, z_0, t_0), \tag{108}$$

with $\psi_n$ and $\psi_m$ denoting normalized Schrödinger functions. Second, ‘this matrix formulation reproduces the right square fluctuation for the fluctuation of the electric charge in a small volume element, hence the large fluctuations corresponding to a motion of point charges,’ as he noted further (Heisenberg, in Pauli, 1979, p. 351). Consequently, it was the Dirac formalism that completed Heisenberg’s demonstration that matrix mechanics led to the fluctuation phenomena for light-quanta and atoms demanded by Einstein.

Heisenberg’s next letter to Pauli, dated 4 November 1926, again referred to a consideration of Dirac, this time dealing with the symmetric treatment of space and time coordinates in the relativistic Klein–Gordon equation. Then, in a letter dated 23 November, Heisenberg outlined in some detail the contents of a new investigation of Dirac. He began by revealing the motivation of the whole enterprise: ‘Here we have often thought further about the physical meaning of the transformation function $S$, and Dirac has accomplished an extraordinarily remarkable generalization of the assumption [made in] my fluctuation note.’ (Heisenberg, in Pauli, 1979, p. 357) The assumption in question stated that the elements of the transformation matrix $S_{nm}$ in the energy-eigenvalue problem determined, if squared, the transition probabilities for the interaction processes considered. Heisenberg then went on to outline the decisive aspects and steps in Dirac’s paper on the quantum-mechanical transformation theory.${}^{162}$ In particular, he emphasized Dirac’s fundamental question and the answer given by him: Dirac, he wrote, had asked what quantum mechanics says about a function $f(p, q)$ of the canonical variables and answered that, in contrast to the case of classical mechanics, one cannot determine $f$ as a continuous function; however, it should be possible to determine ‘how large is the domain (interval) of $p$ for which $f$ assumes values between two $c$-numbers $f$ and $f + df$. (*loc. cit.*, p. 358)

Heisenberg liked this answer because it immediately implied—on choosing for the canonical $(p, q)$ pair the variables $E$ and $t$ and for $f$ the interaction energy—the result of his note on fluctuations (Heisenberg, 1926e). Now, if one selected again $E$ and $t$ as the canonically conjugate pair, identified the function $f$ with the position variable $q$, and asked for the fraction of time in which $q$ lies between $q$ and $q + dq$, one would obtain Schrödinger’s square expression $\psi(q)\psi^*(q)$. Finally, he announced the main result of the investigation:

${}^{162}$ For details, see the previous chapter, Section I.5.

150 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

Dirac has succeeded in also solving the general problem mathematically. The matrix S, whose indices for the general problem $(f, p, q)$ are $S_{f,q}$, serves as a probability function. As always, the $S_{f,q}$ are solutions of a principal-axis transformation of a Hermitean matrix. The principal-axis transformation can be reduced to a differential equation *à la* Schrödinger. (Heisenberg to Pauli, 23 November 1926, in Pauli, 1979, p. 358)

That is, Dirac’s formulation provided the general tool for determining the transformation matrix $S$; in particular, for the set $(E, t, q)$, Schrödinger’s eigenfunction $\psi_E(q)$,

$$S_{q,E} = \psi_E(q), \quad (109)$$

results. ‘Hence Schrödinger’s function is identical with $S$ of Born’s principal-axis problem for determining the energy values $W$,’ Heisenberg commented on this very important conclusion of Dirac’s work.
The new ‘physical interpretation of $S$’ applied to all previously obtained results, be it in the three-man paper, Born’s collision theory, or Jordan’s transformation theory.$^{163}$ It works for both discontinuous and continuous changes, that is, in periodic and aperiodic quantum systems. Although he praised Dirac’s work as ‘an extraordinary progress,’ Heisenberg still had ‘horrible difficulties to understand the real meaning of the whole formal connections,’ and he closed his letter with the following remarks:
> That the world should be continuous, I consider more than ever before to be totally out of question. But as soon as it is discontinuous, there appear in all our words which we use to describe a situation [in atomic physics] too many *c*-numbers. One does not know anymore what the word “wave” or “corpuscle” means. (Heisenberg to Pauli, *loc. cit.*, p. 359)

At that time, toward the end of November 1926, Heisenberg was himself a bit uncertain how to proceed with the problem of interpretation. As usual, when he could not proceed further with one problem, he turned to another. In December, therefore, Heisenberg ‘relaxed’ by dealing with a more practical question, the quantum statistics of several identical particles. Dirac had earlier treated this problem on the basis of wave mechanics (Dirac, 1926f); now, it became a matter of principle for Heisenberg to examine it again from the point of view of matrix mechanics, and he did so in a paper entitled ‘*Mehrkörperprobleme und Resonanz in der Quantenmechanik. II*’ (‘Many-Body Problems and Resonance in Quantum Mechanics. II’), which he submitted for publication shortly before Christmas (Heisenberg, 1927a). He started from his preliminary paper on helium (Heisenberg, 1926b) and sought to generalize the matrix procedure given there to many-

$^{163}$ Heisenberg did not refer to Jordan’s later transformation theory of December 1926 (Jordan, 1927b), but only to the earlier papers of Jordan (1926b, c).

electron atoms. As in the previous investigation, he formulated the ‘general foundations’ entirely in the matrix language—now given in the extended version of Dirac.$^{164}$ Thus, he demonstrated in another, quite complex, case again the perfect ability of the Göttingen–Cambridge quantum mechanics to deal with atomic problems.$^{165}$

**(g) The Bohr–Heisenberg Discussions in Winter 1926/27**

Although Bohr, Heisenberg, and Klein later remembered quite vividly the debates and discussions they conducted since fall 1926 on the interpretation of quantum mechanics, hardly any trace has survived of their conversations in the documents of that time. For example, in the letters that Heisenberg wrote to Pauli between October 1926 and March 1927, Bohr’s name appears only in those of 28 October and 2 March, respectively, i.e., just at the beginning and end of the crucial period during which the uncertainty principle took shape.$^{166}$ Perhaps the recollections of Oskar Klein provide a reason for the absence of Bohr’s name in the central Heisenberg–Pauli exchange; as he recalled:
> Bohr had been talking the whole winter about something which had, in some way, to do with complementarity. I don’t think it was clear to him and certainly not to anybody else. But I think it just contained the beginning. He talked much with Heisenberg also.... I think he had found some difficulty already at that time in his discussions with Heisenberg. Heisenberg, of course, always made a point in stating his view rather sharply. But Bohr’s views were then working towards clarity.... So I think there was some difficulty and some friction at that time. (O. Klein, AHQP Interview, 1963)

In similar cautious terms, Heisenberg confirmed what Klein said when he roughly spoke of ‘that time’:
> At that time I lived in the attic of the Institute on Blegdamsvej, and Bohr often came up to my room late at night to talk with me of the difficulties in quantum theory which tortured both of us. On the one hand, we felt that the solution was just around the corner, insofar as we possessed a mathematical description which was evidently free of contradiction, while on the other hand we did not know how this mathematics should be used to describe even the most simple experimental situations such as, e.g., the track of an electron in a cloud chamber. In quantum mechanics one had started out on the assumption that such electron tracks just do not exist, and, from the

viewpoint of wave mechanics, it was difficult to understand how a localized wave phenomenon, something like a wave packet, did not disperse again after a short time. (Heisenberg, 1967, p. 104)

The essential aspect confirmed by these recollections was that the *respective programmes of Niels Bohr and his chief assistant, Werner Heisenberg, then ran into quite different directions* and could not be brought easily into harmony. As often before (when he was sure), Heisenberg trusted mathematical equations and tried to exploit or derive their physical implications; Bohr, however, did not care for any formalism before he had fully grasped the physical content of the ideas. As Heisenberg recalled:
> The difficulty in the discussion between Bohr and myself was that I wanted to start entirely from the mathematical scheme of quantum mechanics and use the Schrödinger theory perhaps as a mathematical tool sometimes, but never enter into Schrödinger’s interpretation, which I could not believe. Bohr, however, wanted to take the interpretation [of Schrödinger] in some way very seriously and play with both schemes. (Heisenberg, AHQP Interview, 25 February 1963)

Evidently, such an attitude ran counter to Heisenberg’s refusal to make use of the undulatory theory since summer 1926.
Besides this difference toward theories, still another explanation existed for the absence of detailed documentary information on the Bohr–Heisenberg dialogue from contemporary sources. Due to other preoccupations—Bohr, at the time, was concerned mainly with Klein’s relativistic wave-field approach, and Heisenberg with the work of Dirac, Jordan, Pauli, and others—the actual times available for overlap and discussions were restricted.$^{167}$ Heisenberg, for his part, seems to have interrupted thinking intensely about the interpretation problem toward the end of November 1926, and he would not resume it until a couple of months had passed. In the meantime, he worked out his paper on the many-body problem, which he submitted for publication after 20 December (Heisenberg, 1927a), then went on Christmas vacation, from which he did not return to Copenhagen until the first days of January 1927. About a month later, on 5 February, he sent the first letter to Pauli in which he commented on four items: (1) perturbation theory for the relativistic Schrödinger equation; (2) Charles Galton Darwin’s representation of electron spin with the help of polarized de Broglie waves; (3) Paul Ehrenfest’s idea of ‘impenetrable particles’ satisfying Pauli’s exclusion principle; (4) the recent paper of Ehrenfest and George Uhlenbeck on the wave-mechanical interpretation of Boltzmann’s statistics.$^{168}$ Then, he concluded his letter by announcing his intention to mount a fresh attack on the interpretation problem, remarking in particular:

II.3 Mechanical Concepts, Observation, and Restriction 153

For private pleasure, I have returned once again to deal with the logical foundations of the whole (nonrelativistic) $pq - qp$ swindle and I am gradually obtaining some clarity with respect to certain connections. I found Jordan’s essay in *Naturwissenschaften* [Jordan, 1927c] quite nice—though not very accurate at times. What does he mean, e.g., [by] “the probability that the electron occupies a certain point,” if the concept “position of the electron” is not defined decently? But otherwise I consider it a great pleasure to read such non-mathematical formulations. Jordan’s big paper in the *Zeitschrift für Physik* [Jordan, 1927a], however, I could not understand. The “postulates” are so little to grasp and ill-defined that I cannot make anything out of it. But enough for today and many greetings to all physicists. (Heisenberg to Pauli, 5 February 1927, in Pauli, 1979, pp. 374–375)

Heisenberg signed the letter ‘in youthful sloppiness about all the continuity swindle’ and began to devote himself again wholeheartedly to his old problem. He wished to complete, after a careful study of the mathematical papers of Dirac and Jordan, the interpretation of nonrelativistic quantum mechanics, leaving the relativistic adventures to his colleagues.$^{169}$ A new idea would soon promote this programme: the discussion of the ‘$p, q$ swindle’ with the help of the $\gamma$-ray microscope.

**(h) The $\gamma$-ray Microscope: The Breakthrough to the Uncertainty Relations (February 1927)**

In February 1927, the nightly discussions with Bohr on the paradoxes in quantum theory assumed great intensity. Heisenberg described them with a special simile when he remarked:
> Like a chemist who tried to concentrate his poison more and more from some kind of solution, we tried to concentrate the poison of the paradox, and the final concentration was on such experiments like the two electrons with [i.e., going through] the two holes [in the screen] and so on. They were just the quintessence of what was the trouble. (Heisenberg, AHQP Interview, 1963)

The tension between the two men—their personal disagreements mentioned above, as well as the fact that Heisenberg impatiently drove to a solution of the interpretation problem—became extremely, almost unbearably, high. ‘Bohr wisely decided to go on a skiing trip to Norway,’ Jørgen Kalckar described the situation, and added: ‘That he stayed away no less than four weeks testifies to his need for relaxation and clarification of his mind.’ (Kalckar, 1985, p. 16) Bohr indeed left Heisenberg and Copenhagen around the middle of February and returned only after the middle of March.$^{170}$

$^{169}$ At that time, Klein, Darwin, and Pauli had started to concern themselves with the relativistic extensions of quantum mechanics, as we shall discuss in the sections to follow.
$^{170}$ These dates can be derived from letters of O. Klein to M. N. Saha, 18 February (after Bohr had left), and Bohr to Kronig, 18 March (upon his return). See also Heisenberg to Pauli, 14 March 1927: ‘Bohr should return tonight.’ (Heisenberg, in Pauli, 1979, p. 388)

154 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

In Bohr’s absence, the strain fell from Heisenberg; he now pushed forward much more freely and soon achieved important progress in the following way:

I now concentrated all my efforts on the mathematical representation of the electron path in the cloud chamber, and when I realized fairly soon that the obstacles before me were quite insurmountable, I began to wonder whether we might not have been asking the wrong sort of question all along. . . .
It must have been one evening after midnight when I suddenly remembered my conversation with Einstein and particularly his statement, “It is the theory which decides what we can observe.” I was immediately convinced that the key to the gate that had been closed for so long must be sought right here. I decided to go on a nocturnal walk through Faelled Park and to think about the matter. (Heisenberg, 1971, pp. 77–78)

The walk though the park, so Heisenberg claimed, stimulated in him, as he had hoped, the right ideas: that an electron path in the cloud chamber actually consists only of a series of ill-defined spots; that one rather had to ask the question, ‘Can quantum mechanics represent the fact that an electron finds itself approximately in a given place and that it moves approximately with a given velocity?’ Further, ‘Can we make these approximations so close that they do not cause experimental difficulties?’ After his return to the Institute from the walk in the park, Heisenberg calculated the approximate situation and arrived at the decisive result: ‘The product of the uncertainties in the measured values of position and momentum cannot be smaller than Planck’s constant’ (Heisenberg, 1971, p. 78).
Of course, this recollection—taken literally—does dramatize the situation quite a bit. We know, for instance, that Heisenberg had followed Einstein’s advice (to let the theory, i.e., quantum mechanics, decide what one can observe) essentially since summer 1926. However, by mid-February 1927, a new stage in the game had been achieved, because Heisenberg had available and understood well by then the quantum-mechanical formalism in the form of that generalization which he absolutely needed to attack the task in full. Only now was he prepared to pass from loose preliminary statements—such as, ‘if the position is determined, the momentum is completely undetermined’—to derive an exact estimate of how much position and momentum of an electron will be approached maximally by observation. Now, he was ready to use effectively the mathematical transformation theory of Dirac and Jordan, which he had learned in all the necessary detail during the past few months.
Still, he had to take another important step before he could seriously follow Einstein’s advice in calculating the accuracy of position and momentum measurement, and here Heisenberg was again helped by recalling an earlier conversation, not with a senior scientist, but with Burkhardt Drude, a fellow student in Göttingen.<sup>171</sup> He remembered:

<sup>171</sup> In his AHQP Interview of 1963, Heisenberg placed the event in winter of either 1923/24 or 1924/25. The circumstances speak in favour of the first date, because Heisenberg was in Göttingen then, and doubted for the first time the existence of electron orbits in atoms.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0187 -->

II.3 Mechanical Concepts, Observation, and Restriction 155

When discussing the difficulties involved in the concept of electron orbits, he [Drude] had said that it ought to be possible, in principle, to construct a microscope of extraordinarily high resolving power in which one could see or photograph the electron’s path inside the atom. Such a microscope would not, of course, work with ordinary light but perhaps with gamma rays. (Heisenberg, 1971, pp. 78–79)

We do not know why Heisenberg had not, in that context, thought of the Compton effect,<sup>172</sup> but now in February 1927, he definitely did so and demonstrated how it served to establish an easily ‘visualizable’ result concerning how accurate the measurement of position and momentum might be, and ‘After a few more calculations of this kind, I sat down and summarized my results in a long letter to Wolfgang Pauli’ (Heisenberg, loc. cit., p. 79).
The long letter to Pauli does indeed exist and was written on 23 February, i.e., about a week after Bohr had left for his vacation. ‘Today I want to write to you about a part of my considerations on the visualizable meaning (*anschaulichen Sinn*) of the nonrelativistic quantum mechanics which really has been completed by the work of Dirac and Jordan; thus I hope to obtain clarity myself,’ he began the letter to Pauli, in which he summarized his considerations in eight sections (Heisenberg to Pauli, 23 February 1927, in Pauli, 1979, pp. 376–381). The contents of the letter may be condensed as follows:

(1) The concept ‘position of an electron’ has to be replaced by the prescription ‘how the position of an electron can be determined.’ For that purpose, ‘one takes a microscope of sufficiently high resolving power and observes the electron.’ Evidently, the accuracy of the observation depends on the frequency of light used; it increases for shorter wavelengths, but the electron—defined this way as a corpuscle—is disturbed in its mechanical behaviour on account of the Compton effect (or an equivalent collision with a fast particle), in agreement with the position-momentum commutation rule.
(2) The ‘trajectory’ of a corpuscle will be determined by observing the positions at different instants of time; in the case of planets orbiting the sun, the observation disturbs the motion of the planets negligibly.
(3) In the case of the 1*S*-electron orbits in the hydrogen atom, any single observation of position more accurate than 10<sup>−8</sup> cm will destroy the orbit. ‘However, a repeated observation of many 1*S*-hydrogen atoms yields an exactly defined probability for the electron positions, namely $\psi_{1S}(q)\psi_{1S}^*(q)$, corresponding to the average value of the classical orbit over all *phases*.’ That is, the knowledge of the energy terms destroys the knowledge of phases, in agreement with the commutation relation for the action-angle variables.
(4) Similarly, the definition of the concept ‘velocity of the electron’ has to be replaced by prescribing the following experimental observation: ‘At a given instant of time all forces on the electron are reduced to zero; then the velocity of the rectilinear motion can be determined, say, by the Doppler effect of light as red as possible.’ Clearly, the scattering process then requires a long force-free motion of the elec-

<sup>172</sup> In 1923/24, the Compton scattering was already known, but its interpretation was still being hotly debated. See Volume 1, Part 2, Chapter V.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0188 -->

156 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

tron; hence, its position becomes quite undetermined; in particular, a (continuous) function $p(t)$ cannot exist in the case of a 1*S*-orbit of the hydrogen atom.
(5) On repeating similar considerations for arbitrary pairs of canonical variables, one may conclude for all conceivable experiments that: ‘If a quantity *p* can be determined up to an accuracy characterized by the average error *p*₁, then the canonically conjugate coordinate *q* can be defined only to an accuracy characterized by the average error $q_1 \approx \frac{h}{2\pi p_1}$.’<sup>173</sup> Hence, Heisenberg concluded:

The commutation relations play the same role in quantum mechanics as the relativity of simultaneity in relativity theory. If ever an experiment exists that allows one to determine *p* and *q* accurately at the same time, then quantum mechanics must of necessity be wrong. It is impossible to associate with quantum-mechanical variables or matrices a definite [*c*]-number, one can only give numbers with a definite uncertainty. For these numbers, the classical Hamiltonian equations, within the given accuracy, remain valid. (*loc. cit.*, p. 378)

(6) The most important point that Heisenberg noticed was how micromechanics passes over into macromechanics. Schrödinger’s idea of just adding together the eigenfunctions of electrons in an atom would not work (except in the case of the harmonic oscillator: Schrödinger, 1926g). One must rather follow the prescription: ‘The orbit is built up just by the fact that we observe it.’ For large quantum numbers (very peripheral orbits), then, light of large wavelengths might be used in the observation yielding the corresponding smeared-out wave packet. That is, according to the uncertainty of the position measurement, after some time, only a statistical knowledge of the position can be registered. By a further observation, however, ‘a definite solution will be selected from the wealth of solutions provided by the smeared-out wave packet; this [solution] may again be replaced by a wave packet, due to the uncertainty associated with it, which again diverges [in the course of time], etc.’ The essential linearity of the transformation equations and the wave equations led to an important consequence, as Heisenberg emphasized: For the result of an observation of the position at time *t*₂, it does matter indeed whether one has observed the particle already earlier at time *t*₁; if it had not been observed at *t*₁, all that one knows about it is contained in a full, large wave packet. Each experimental result represents a particular selection from the solutions of the matrix equations yielding a given state, and the initial conditions contain a *necessary* uncertainty.
(7) and (8) To illustrate the general result [Heisenberg treated two examples]: the transition from an excited state to the ground state in an atom, and the case of resonance fluorescence. The latter example yields the special situation that the phase of the radiation gets to be accurately determined, while the energy (or action variable) remains completely unknown; the application of a magnetic field then changes the mechanical system such that the energy becomes determined and the knowledge of the phase disappears.<sup>174</sup>

<sup>173</sup> Mathematically, this conclusion followed from Jordan’s *Ansatz* for the probability amplitude. Although Heisenberg stated in his letter to Pauli that he had not yet worked through all of the details of Jordan’s paper (1927b), this assumption seemed to be evident to him.
<sup>174</sup> Heisenberg had referred to this example as ‘Bohr’s *Gedankenexperiment*’ already in a letter to Pauli, dated 16 November 1925, and they had discussed it again at the Düsseldorf *Naturforscherversammlung* in September 1926 (of which he reminded Pauli now).

II.3 Mechanical Concepts, Observation, and Restriction 157

‘With these examples one can continue *ad infinitum*,’ Heisenberg concluded his weighty letter, and added:

If one believes, as I do, that physical laws can be understood in a visualizable manner, if one can tell immediately in every case the result intuitively, then considerations such as the above help a little bit. . . . But I do recognize quite well that one might argue this to be, first, “old snow,” second, vague speculation without real further background, and third, quite unclear in many aspects. (Heisenberg to Pauli, *loc. cit.*, p. 381)

The last objection just stimulated him to write the letter, he said, and he expected Pauli’s ‘merciless criticism’ very eagerly. However, from Hamburg, Pauli sent an unusually ‘mild criticism’ (as Heisenberg noted in his reply of 9 March to the lost letter); apparently Pauli only raised questions concerning the Stern–Gerlach effect, and he warned his friend not to believe that he could derive from the given relation,

$$p_1q_1 \sim \frac{h}{2\pi},$$ (110)

the entire quantum-mechanical theory.<sup>175</sup> To this remark, Heisenberg responded by saying that he was far from such thoughts; the situation, he said, should rather be compared with that in relativity theory, where the constant velocity of light *in vacuo* provided an important hint to develop the relativistic scheme without exhausting its content. Otherwise, Pauli’s reactions had ‘inspired’ him ‘to new deeds,’ and he announced on 9 March 1927: ‘I have finished today a preliminary manuscript which I enclose herewith, with the request that you return it in a few days (by registered mail, since I do not have another copy). It contains essentially the same [material] as the letter [of 23 February].’

**(i) The Uncertainty Relations and the ‘Intuitive Content’ of Quantum Mechanics (March 1927)**

Less than two weeks after completing the manuscript—Pauli had meanwhile returned it with a letter ‘which pleased me very much’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, 14 March 1927)—Heisenberg submitted the paper bearing the title ‘*Über den anschaulichen Inhalt der quantentheoretischen Kinematik und Mechanik*’ (‘On the Intuitive Content of the Quantum-Theoretical Kinematics and Mechanics’) to *Zeitschrift für Physik*. In a footnote at the end of the introduction, he expressed his indebtedness to Bohr, Einstein, and especially Pauli, with the following words:<sup>176</sup>

The present paper has emerged from efforts and desires to which other investigators have already given clear expression before the devlopment of quantum mechanics. I draw attention here especially to Bohr’s papers on the basic postulates of quantum theory (e.g., Bohr, 1923a) and Einstein’s discussions on the connection between wave fields and light-quanta. In recent times the problems dealt with here have been discussed most clearly, and they have been partly answered by W. Pauli (1926b); quantum mechanics has changed only slightly the formulation of these problems as given by Pauli. It is also a special pleasure to thank *Herrn* Pauli at this time for the repeated stimulus I have received from our oral and written discussions which have contributed decisively to the present work. (Heisenberg, 1927b, pp. 173–174)

In a two-page introduction, Heisenberg outlined his starting positions: the contradictions arising in quantum theory with the use of the conventional ‘intuitive space-time concepts’; the ability of the new quantum-mechanical scheme to account for the observed phenomena, but the necessity to revise the kinematical and mechanical concepts (as a consequence of the fundamental commutation relation). However, Heisenberg went on to argue that one need not abandon the usual space-time geometry, ‘because on choosing sufficiently heavy masses [of the objects involved] we can approximate the quantum-mechanical laws by the classical ones, even when arbitrarily small spaces and times are involved’ (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*, pp. 172–173).<sup>177</sup> He then presented new ‘more precise analysis’ of the basic concepts in four sections:

(1) Concepts: position, path, velocity, energy.
(2) The Dirac–Jordan Theory.
(3) The transition from micro- to macromechanics.
(4) Discussion of a few special *Gedanken*-experiments.

A short apology concluded the paper, addressing directly Schrödinger’s criticism of quantum mechanics. Let us now turn to the contents of the paper in more detail.<sup>178</sup>
In Section 1, Heisenberg repeated essentially the arguments presented in the letter of 23 February to Pauli concerning the kinematic and mechanical concepts: that the position of a microscopic particle can be determined either by scattering ($\gamma$-)radiation from it or by a collision process, and that the orbit of an atomic electron does not make sense; that rather a probability function (due to Born and Jordan) might be ascribed to the position of the electron in an atom. Heisenberg also took over another statement from his letter to Pauli, namely, the probability to consider the ‘statistical interpretation’ of the theory perhaps as a secondary effect, and pointed out: ‘If one wishes, one can say with Dirac that the statistics is introduced by our experiments.’ (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*, p. 177) He added a treat-

---

ment of the Stern–Gerlach effect as another example of properly defining energy states in quantum mechanics.<sup>179</sup> Heisenberg showed that, indeed, the shorter the time period $t_1$, during which the magnetic field acts on the atom, the less accurate the energy measurement ($E_1$). The detailed study resulted in the relation for the energy-time ‘uncertainties,’

$$E_1t_1 \sim h, \tag{111}$$

where $E_1$ and $t_1$ evidently denote the accuracies of the corresponding observations. These results contributed to the fundamental conclusion:

*All concepts which can be used in classical theory for the description of a mechanical system can also be defined exactly for atomic processes in analogy to the classical concepts. The experiments which provide such definitions themselves suffer from an indeterminacy introduced purely by the observational procedures that we use when we ask of them the simultaneous determination of two canonically-conjugate quantities. The magnitude of this indeterminacy is given by the relation [(110)]—generalized to any canonically conjugate quantities whatsoever.* (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*, p. 179)

The uncertainty contained in Eq. (110) ‘just creates room for the validity of the relations that find their accurate expression in the quantum-mechanical equations

$$pq - qp = \frac{h}{2\pi i}; \tag{112}$$

it [i.e., Eq. (110)] allows for this expression [(112)] without requiring a change in the physical meaning of the quantities $p$ and $q$’ (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*, p. 180). Perhaps, Heisenberg continued, it might even assist in discovering the quantum-theoretical formulation of further phenomena, notably, those of (relativistic) electrodynamics.<sup>180</sup>
In Section 2, Heisenberg derived the ‘uncertainty relations’ from the existing quantum-mechanical scheme, especially the new Dirac–Jordan transformation theory. According to Jordan, the probability amplitude $S(\eta, q)$,

$$S(\eta, q) \sim \exp\left\{ - \frac{(q - q')^2}{2q_1^2} - \frac{2\pi i}{h} p'(q - q') \right\}, \tag{113}$$

expresses, for a given value of some parameter $\eta$, the possibility to obtain the position $q$ of an electron at the value $q'$ with the accuracy $q_1$; that is, its absolute

---

<sup>179</sup> Pauli had asked Heisenberg to discuss it upon receiving his letter of 23 February.
<sup>180</sup> Dirac, Pauli, and Klein were dealing at that time with the extension of quantum mechanics to electromagnetic phenomena.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0192 -->

160 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

square, or

$$S \bar{S} \sim \exp\left\{ - \frac{(q - q')^2}{q_1^2} \right\}, \tag{114}$$

denotes the probability. Similarly, the probability amplitude for the momentum variable may be obtained by starting from the relation

$$S(\eta, p) = \int S(\eta, q) S(q, p) dq. \tag{115}$$

Now, on the basis of Jordan’s *Ansatz*

$$S(p, q) = \exp\left\{ \frac{2\pi i p q}{h} \right\}, \tag{116}$$

it can be concluded that $S(\eta, p)$ deviates appreciably from zero only for $2\pi(p - p')/h \le 1$. Then, Heisenberg derived immediately,

$$S(\eta, p) \sim \int \left\{ \frac{2\pi i (p - p') q}{h} - \frac{(q - q')^2}{2q^2} \right\} dq$$
$$= \exp\left\{ - \frac{(p - p')^2}{2p_1^2} + \frac{2\pi i}{h} q'(p - p') \right\}, \tag{117}$$

and for the probability

$$S(\eta, p) \bar{S}(\eta, p) \sim \exp\left\{ - \frac{(p - p')^2}{2p_1^2} \right\}, \tag{118}$$

where $p_1$ satisfies the condition

$$p_1q_1 = \frac{h}{2\pi}. \tag{119}$$

He noted: ‘The assumption [(113)] for $S(\eta, q)$ therefore corresponds to the experimental fact that the value $p'$ is measured for $p$, and the value $q'$ for $q$ with the accuracy [(119)]’ (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*, p. 181).
From this result, Heisenberg proceeded to derive a physical interpretation of the Dirac–Jordan scheme, which offered the opportunity to obtain from relations between the (matrix) variables $p$, $q$, and $E$ the corresponding equations for all

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0193 -->

II.3 Mechanical Concepts, Observation, and Restriction 161

possible quantum-mechanical variables.<sup>181</sup> In particular, he could provide the strict mathematical definition of the observed quantitites and their statistical errors as:

*Associated with every quantum-theoretical variable is a number [i.e., a c-number] which gives its “value” with a certain definite statistical error. The statistical error depends on the coordinate system. For every quantum-theoretical variable there exists a coordinate system in which the statistical error for this quantity is zero. Therefore, a definite experiment can never give exact information on all quantum-theoretical variables. Rather it divides the physical quantities into “known” and “unknown” (or more and less accurately determined quantities). The results of two experiments can be derived exactly from one another only when the two experiments divide the physical quantities in the same way into “known” and “unknown” ones. . . . When the experiments use different division. . . , then their results can be related only statistically.* (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*, pp. 181–182)

After discussing in detail the specific examples of Stern–Gerlach effect and certain repetitions of it, Heisenberg expressed the relations between subsequent experiments in the following clear physical and mathematical way:

*We can deduce from one experiment the possible results of another by definite statistical rules. The other experiment selects out of the wealth of possibilities [for the quantum-mechanical results] a quite definite one and thereby limits the possibilities for all later experiments. Such an interpretation of the equation for the transformation matrix or the Schrödinger wave equation is only possible because the sum of solutions is again a solution. In this circumstance we recognize the deep significance of the linearity of Schrödinger’s equations; hence they can be understood only as equations for waves in phase space; and consequently we may consider as hopeless every attempt to replace these equations, say in the relativistic case (of several electrons), by nonlinear equations.* (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*, p. 184)

The ideas from point 6 of his letter to Pauli (on 23 February) went, in a slightly extended and clarified version, into Section 3 of the paper. Heisenberg stressed that the equations of motion exhibited the same structure in microscopic and macroscopic dynamics, but the statistical laws in the two cases were quite different. This section also contained the mathematical analysis of two examples: (1) the case of the force-free, straight-line motion of a mass point [which yielded the result, known from Schrödinger’s (1926g) treatment that the wave packet or probability packet would diverge in the course of time, the more it was concentrated originally]; and (2) the reflection of an electron current from a lattice (the quite different microscopic behaviour would nevertheless pass over, under proper conditions, into the classical behaviour).

---

<sup>181</sup> With great satisfaction, Heisenberg noticed that Dirac’s *q*-number theory, the offspring of the Göttingen theory, could express the most general situation, in contrast to Schrödinger’s wave mechanics.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0194 -->

162 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

In Section 4, Heisenberg finally involved several *Gedanken*-experiments to determine from atomic transitions the ‘instant of quantum jumps’; the calculations yielded in all cases the energy-time uncertainty relation (111). In particular, he analyzed Bohr’s *Gedanken*-experiment mentioned in the letter to Pauli and finally resolved several paradoxes (uncovered mainly by Paul Ehrenfest and his collaborators) in the early 1920’s.

The new physical interpretation indeed seemed to work in all microscopic situations that had been figured out so far, yielding for the first time consistent answers. Heisenberg therefore confidently summarized the important conclusions:

(1) Quantum-theoretical kinematics and mechanics deviate considerably from their classical counterparts. Although classical intuition cannot be applied to situations in atomic physics, one may still obtain with the help of Eq. (110) qualitatively the correct results of all experiments. Therefore, quantum mechanics should be regarded as less ‘visualizable’ than classical mechanics.

(2) Further consequences from Eq. (110), e.g., the derivation of the quantitative laws of quantum mechanics, cannot be accomplished: ‘We rather believe that quantum-mechanical laws can be understood from the visualizable [intuitive] foundations only on the basis of the principle of greatest simplicity’ (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*).<sup>182</sup>

(3) Quantum-mechanical statements must be taken to be as ‘real’ as those of classical mechanics, in particular:

> ‘The statement that, say, the velocity in the *x*-direction is “in reality” not a number but the diagonal term of a matrix, is perhaps not more abstract and not more unvisualizable than the statement that the electric field strengths are “in reality” the time-part of an anti-symmetric tensor in the space-time world. The phrase “in reality” is as much or as little justified as it is in any mathematical description of natural processes. As soon as one accepts the fact that all quantum-theoretical variables are “in reality” matrices, the quantitative laws hold without difficulty.’ (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*)

The above sentences should be regarded as a strong reply to Erwin Schrödinger’s one-year-old attack on matrix mechanics, which Heisenberg stressed even more in a footnote saying:

> Schrödinger calls quantum mechanics a formal theory of frightening, indeed repulsive, univisualizability and abstractness. Certainly one cannot overestimate the value of the mathematical (and in that sense also visualizable) mastery of the quantum-mechanical laws as achieved by Schrödinger. However, as regards questions of physical principle, the popular visualizability [intuitiveness] of wave mechanics has, in my opinion, led away from the straight path which has been marked by the papers of Einstein and de Broglie, on the one hand, and by the work of Bohr and quantum mechanics, on the other. (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*, p. 196)

---

<sup>182</sup> In this context, Heisenberg criticized such a far-reaching proposal as the one of Pascual Jordan, which started from the probability amplitude relation of the type of Eq. (115) as a proper basis for developing the known quantum-mechanical scheme.

II.4 Complementarity 163

Thus spoke the young prophet of quantum mechanics, and this he considered to be his last word on the question of its interpretation. Immediately after the manuscript was completed, Bohr returned from his vacation in Norway. He not only pointed out a conceptual flaw in Heisenberg’s discussion of the $\gamma$-ray microscope, but also showed that the whole question could be looked at in an equally correct, and perhaps even more general way, from a different point of view: the Principle of Complementarity.

### II.4 Complementarity

#### (a) Introduction to the Background of Complementarity

On 17 April 1925, Hans Geiger informed Niels Bohr that ‘the results of our measurement strongly favour the old view of Compton and Debye’; i.e., the just completed investigations of Geiger and Walther Bothe disproved the radiation theory developed by Bohr, Hendrik Kramers, and John Slater (the BKS theory) in the previous year. Bohr reacted promptly: he immediately informed Heisenberg, then in Göttingen, that he and Kramers would have to withdraw some recent manuscripts based on the BKS theory from publication.<sup>183</sup> He continued:

> In spite of all obscurity, at the moment things are probably still relatively better with the secrets of atoms than with the general description of space-time occurrence of quantum processes. Stimulated especially by conversations with Pauli, I am forcing myself these days with all my strength to familiarize myself with the mysticism of nature and am attempting to prepare myself for all eventualities, indeed even for the assumption of a coupling of quantum processes in separated atoms. However, the costs of this assumption are so great that they cannot be estimated within the ordinary space-time description. (Bohr to Heisenberg, 18 April 1925, in Bohr, 1984, pp. 79–80)

Heisenberg, who had been kept informed further about the matter by Ralph Kronig, commented: ‘To judge from your letter, a terrible confusion about the radiation theory must reign in Copenhagen. If I were there, I would, as in the case of Zeeman effects, plead for a *dualistic theory: everything must be described both in terms of the wave theory and in terms of the light-quanta*’ (Heisenberg to Kronig, 8 May 1925, our italics).

What Heisenberg proposed in his perceptive and prophetic remark, it would take Bohr more than two years to develop this dualistic theory. The first written account of a new general principle in atomic theory, which would replace the formerly dominant correspondence principle, was published by Bohr both in English

---

<sup>183</sup> For details of the Bothe–Geiger experiment and the conclusions from it, see, e.g., Volume 1, Part 2, pp. 609–613, and K. Stolzenburg’s introduction to Part I of Bohr, 1984, pp. 3–96, especially, pp. 69–93.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0196 -->

164 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

and in German, and a French translation appeared in the proceedings of the fifth Solvay Conference on Physics (Bohr, 1928e, d, f). The editors of the ‘Special Supplement’ issue of *Nature* added an introduction, giving the following introduction:<sup>184</sup>

> The strange conflict which has waged between the wave theory of light and the light-quantum hypothesis has resulted in a remarkable dilemma. Now we have a parallel dilemma, for a material particle manifests some of the attributes of wave motion. Can these apparently contradictory views be reconciled? According to Bohr, the pictures ought to be regarded not as contradictory but as complementary. Radiation in free space is not open to observation, and is a mere abstraction. An isolated material particle likewise can never be observed and is always an abstraction. It is only through their interaction with other systems that the properties of these abstractions can be defined and observed. (*Nature*, Editorial, 14 April 1928, p. 579)

The unprepared reader must indeed have been puzzled by Bohr’s new essay on the quantum problem containing ‘the idea of complementarity’ (Bohr, 1928e, p. 590); after that, however, this idea received—and still continues to receive—an enormous attention by scholars in diverse fields: physicists, other scientists, philosophers, linguists, and even theologians.<sup>185</sup> In this section, we are primarily concerned with the prehistory of this concept and the essential steps that were taken to create it, which Max Jammer—in his pioneering book on *The Conceptual Development of Quantum Mechanics*—summarized by saying:

> The often repeated statement that Bohr derived the notion of complementarity from Heisenberg’s uncertainty relations is erroneous both from the historical and conceptual point of view. Heisenberg’s uncertainty relations were for Bohr rather a confirmation of conceptions he had been groping for long before Heisenberg derived his principle from the Dirac-Jordan transformation theory. True, Heisenberg’s work prompted Bohr to give his thoughts on complementarity a consistent and final formulation, but these thoughts . . . can be traced back at least to July 1925. (Jammer, 1966, p. 345)

Perhaps in light of our discussion of the development of the uncertainty relations and Heisenberg’s ‘duality theory’ (Section II.3), one should not play down too much the role of outside influences on Bohr’s conception of complementarity. In any case, the detailed investigation of the events that led Bohr from the middle of 1925 onward to the final formulation of complementarity in late 1927 or early 1928 reveals a very complex interrelationship of ideas and results brought together by the principal actors in the drama, notably, Bohr and Heisenberg, and their chief supporters, Oskar Klein and Pauli, respectively.

II.4 Complementarity 165

the subject, proposed the following sequence in ‘the emergence of the complementarity argument’ (Kalckar, 1985b, pp. 7–51):

(1) The Copenhagen discussions prior to the establishment of the uncertainty relations (August 1925–February 1927).

(2) The uncertainty relations and the $\gamma$-ray microscope (March–June 1927).

(3) Bohr’s preparation for his lecture at Como (June–September 1927).

(4) The Como Conference and continued work on the manuscript (September–October 1927).

(5) The fifth Solvay Conference on Physics (October 1927).

(6) The final touches (November 1927–April 1928).

A more detailed presentation of the historical facts and the interactions between the participants requires a two-part treatment of point (1). We shall postpone the discussion of points (5) and (6) to Section II.6, which follows the treatment—in Section II.5—of another important development that contributed directly to Bohr’s final formulation of the complementarity argument: quantum field theory. Hence, we arrive at an organization of the present section in five points:

(1') The need for a new general principle (summer 1925–October 1926), starting from the breakdown of the BKS theory (and, to a certain extent, of the correspondence principle) and reviewing new aspects of atomic theory (matrix mechanics, electron spin, wave mechanics) and their consequences for the interpretation of quantum phenomena (e.g., the existence of quantum jumps).

(2') The merits of the wave theory (October 1926–spring 1927), also reporting Bohr’s collaboration with Oskar Klein on this topic and heated arguments with Heisenberg.

(3') The $\gamma$-ray microscope and the uncertainty relations of Heisenberg (March–June 1927), dealing with Bohr’s initial positive reactions and later criticism, including the intervention of Klein and Pauli in the Bohr–Heisenberg debate.

(4') Toward the preparation of the complementarity argument for presentation at the Como Conference, reporting about Bohr’s various attempts to draft—with the help of Klein—the first manuscript.

(5') The formulation of the decisive talk (October 1927), which Bohr gave at the fifth Solvay Conference.

When he outlined ‘Niels Bohr’s Contribution to Epistemology’ at the ‘special commemorative session’ of the American Physical Society, held on 23 April 1963, Bohr’s long-time collaborator Léon Rosenfeld tried to give a more precise meaning to the concept and content of complementarity. He concluded by simply stating:

> Complementarity is no system, no doctrine with ready-made concepts. There is no *via regia* to it; no formal definition of it can ever be found in Bohr’s writings, and this worries many people. The French are shocked by this breach of the Cartesian rules; they blame Bohr for indulging in “clair-obscur” and shrouding himself in “les brumes du Nord.” The Germans in their thoroughness have been at work distinguishing several forms of complementarity and studying, in hundreds of pages, their relations to Kant. Pragmatic Americans have dissected complementarity with the scalpel of symbolic logic and undertaken to define this gentle art of the correct use of words

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0198 -->

166  
Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields  

without using any word at all. Bohr was content to teach by example. He often evoked the thinkers of the past who had intuitively recognized dialectical aspects of existence and endeavoured to give them poetical and philosophical expression; our only advantage over these great men, he would observe, is that in physics we have been presented with such a simple and clear case of complementarity that we are able to study it in all detail and thus arrive at a precise formulation of a logical relationship of universal scope. The nature of this relation he regarded as sufficiently illustrated by his analysis of the limits of validity of classical physical concepts. (Rosenfeld, 1963, p. 52)  

No doubt, complementarity served as a kind of philosophical principle; it not only replaced the correspondence principle, which had served earlier as an epistemological principle in Bohr’s consideration of nature, but it also fitted nicely into his ‘older philosophical ideas,’ which Heisenberg illustrated by relating an episode that occurred in those days (probably in 1928) ‘on a sailing trip from Copenhagen to Svendborg on the island [of] Fyn’:  

At that time Bohr and a colleague and friend owned a sailing boat, the captain of which was the brilliant and extremely charming chemist [Niels] Bjerrum. The distinguished surgeon [Ole] Chievitz kept high spirits even in stormy weather, and the other friends contributed each in his way to this happy and untroubled existence. Bohr was full of the new interpretation of quantum theory, and as the boat took us full sail southward in sunshine, there was plenty of time to tell of this scientific event and to reflect philosophically on the nature of atomic theory. Bohr began by talking of the difficulties of language, of the limitations of all our means of expressing ourselves, which one had to take into account from the very beginning if one wants to practise science, and he explained how satisfying it was that this limitation had already been expressed in the foundations of atomic theory in a mathematically lucid way. Finally, one of the friends remarked drily, “But Niels, this is not really new, you said exactly the same ten years ago!” (Heisenberg, 1967, pp. 106–107)  

Before turning to the rise of the complementarity principle, let us therefore first consider briefly the philosophical background of Bohr’s shaping of his philosophical attitudes prior to the crucial years from 1925 to 1927.  

**(b)  The Philosophical Influences on Niels Bohr**  

‘The philosophers, whom I heard Bohr mention most often, were Socrates and William James,’ recalled Carl Friedrich von Weizsäcker, adding: ‘Finally a deep congeniality with his fellow-countryman Kierkegaard cannot be denied.’ (Weizsäcker, 1985, p. 314) In discussing the philosophical influences on the physicist Bohr, many authors have mentioned the same names.186 The closer associates and students of Bohr, however, did not detect any direct descendence of his thoughts  

186 Thus, Klaus Meyer-Abich (1965) and Max Jammer (1966, especially, pp. 359–360) drew attention to the connections of the complementarity idea and the statements contained in the American philosopher William James’s work on psychology. Jammer also considered a direct influence of the Danish philosopher Søren Kierkegaard.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0199 -->

167  

from either James or Kierkegaard. Thus, Léon Rosenfeld said that only ‘much later, sometime in the thirties, his old friend the psychologist [Edgar] Rubin called his attention to William James’ Principles [of Psychology].’ (Rosenfeld, 1963, p. 52) Finally, David Favrholdt found in a careful analysis no evidence of a direct influence of Kierkegaard (Favrholdt, 1978).187 Jørgen Kalckar, in a section entitled ‘Glimpse of the Young Niels Bohr and His World of Thought’ (contained in the introduction to Bohr, Collected Works, Volume 6), has tried to provide a balanced view (Kalckar, 1985a), which we adopt by and large.  

Evidently, the first to impress the young Niels Bohr was his father, a physiologist and lover of science. Christian Bohr (1855–1911) had also formed a close circle of friends, consisting of the physicist Christian Christiansen, the philologist Vilhelm Thomsen, and the philosopher Harald Høffding.188 ‘From the time that we were old enough to benefit from listening to the conversations and until the gatherings were interrupted on our part by the early death of my father we brothers [Niels and Harald] were allowed to be present when the meetings were held in our home, and from there we have some of our earliest and deepest impressions,’ recalled Bohr in his memorial lecture on Høffding.189 When they became students, the brothers Niels and Harald Bohr attended various lecture courses of Høffding, e.g., on formal logic and on the history of philosophy. According to Rosenfeld:  

Høffding’s lectures on the history of philosophy had, at any rate, the merit of not enforcing any system on his audience. He was more concerned to present the problems than the solutions proposed by the various systems; for, he said, the systems come and go, but the problems remain. It was not, however, in Bohr’s nature to be attracted by anything so vague as the classical problems of philosophy; his interest could only be awakened by some concrete, sharply defined situation which could grip his imagination. He liked Spinoza’s conception of the psychological parallelism, in which he was later tempted to see an endeavour to express the complementarity relations in the realm of psychological phenomena.... He read Kierkegaard, but admired the virtuosity of his style more than his deeply strung meditations. (Rosenfeld, 1963, p. 48)190

In this context, it is not surprising to recall that Bohr derived his knowledge of the Hegelian philosophy mainly from a literary book of Poul Martin Møller, the Adventures of a Danish Student. As Rosenfeld explained:191  

Here at least, in the character of the soul-searching licentiate desperately struggling to keep his ideas together, he could see a vivid picture of the dramatic situation which might confront the unwary ponderer on the intricacies of human thinking: ‘... and then I came to think of my thinking about it, again I think that I think of my thinking about it, and divide myself into an indefinitely retracting succession of egos observing each other. I don’t know which ego is the real one to stop at, for as soon as I stop at any one of them, it is another ego again that stops it. My head gets all in a whirl with dizziness, as if I were peering down a bottomless chasm, and the end of my thinking is a horrible headache.’ Habeant sua fata libelli! Poul Møller had little imagined that his light-handed banter would one day start a train of thought leading to the elucidation of the most fundamental aspects of atomic theory and the renovation of the philosophy of science. Yet it is hardly an exaggeration to say that the perplexities of this licentiate, especially his struggle with many egos, were the only lesson in dialectical thinking that Bohr ever received, and the only link between his highly original reflection and philosophical tradition. (Rosenfeld, 1963, p. 48)  

Although Bohr developed a clear dislike of philosophical systems (perfectly consistent with the beliefs of his philosophy teacher Høffding), he was also, as Kalckar recalled:  

deeply attracted by the true “philosophers of life” like Confucius, Lao-Tse, Socrates or Spinoza, whom he ranked as poets or religious thinkers like Buddha or the old Jewish prophets, in their common endeavour to interpret the condition of human life. Often in conversations he would measure one with the other and would often incline to credit the poet with the deeper understanding. (Kalckar, 1985a, p. xx)  

However, it must be remembered that Bohr became deeply familiar with his favourite thinkers only after he had applied their characteristic conceptions to his own.192 At any rate, one fact remains certain: during his university studies, Bohr concerned himself deeply with philosophical problems and even planned to write (and publish!) a book about his epistemological views. Some aspects to be discussed might have been the following:

192 In this context, Kalckar refers to the fact that ‘as the beautiful simile about our being actors as well as spectators in the drama of existence, which Bohr later used to associate with ancient oriental thinkers, already appears in the lecture to the Scandinavian scientists from 1929,’ and that Bohr possibly derived it from an episode in Poul Møller’s Adventures (Kalckar, 1985a, p. xxii).

II.4  Complementarity  
169  

As far as we know, Bohr’s youthful philosophical ideas revolved around the problem raised by the movability of the partition between subject and object—a theme which was to recur in full orchestration in his mature writings on epistemology. In these early days Bohr did not look to physics but to mathematics for logical analogies, and he found them in Riemann’s theory of multi-valued complex functions. He pictured the singular role of the subject in the description as an analogy to a branch point in the complex plane. Just as the uniqueness of the function depends on a specification of the sheet of the Riemannian surface under consideration, the unambiguous communication of experience drawn from introspection demands the fixation of the position between subject and object. (Kalckar, loc. cit., pp. xxiv–xxv; see also Rosenfeld, 1963, p. 49)193  

However difficult it might be to trace the influence of philosophers and their thoughts on the later physicist Bohr,194 it is certain that he profited from participating in the philosophical lectures in still another aspect: some students in Høffding’s introductory course founded a private discussion group (‘Ekliptika’) to debate philosophical and scientific problems. Vilhelm Slomann, a member of this group, recalled fifty years later:  

When the discussions were beginning to tail off, it often happened that one of them [i.e., Niels or Harald Bohr] said a few generous words about the lecture and continued in a low voice, at a furious pace and with vigorous intensity, but was often interrupted by his brother. Their way of thinking seemed to be coordinated; one improved on the other’s or his own expressions, or defended in a heated, yet at the same time good-humoured manner his choice of words. Ideas changed their tone and became polished; it was not a defence of preconceived opinions, but something new which came into being. This way of thinking a deux was so deeply ingrained in the brothers that nobody could join in. The chairman used to put his pencil down quietly and let them carry on; but when everybody moved in closer to them [one] might say ineffectively, ‘Louder, Niels.’ (Kalckar, loc. cit., p. xxiv)  

Perhaps it was this ‘thinking a deux’ that Bohr hoped to continue with Heisenberg on the deeper meaning of quantum mechanics; this was the style he had already learned to apply to epistemological problems when he was young.  

**(c)  The Need for a New Principle in Quantum Theory (Summer 1925–October 1926)**  

In his paper, ‘Bohr and the Philosophy of Science,’ Aage Petersen described Bohr’s first major contribution to the subject as follows:
