170 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

The idea of correspondence concerns the logical relation between classical and quantum theory. At first, the idea was expressed as a requirement that predictions yielded by the two theories should coincide in the limit of large quantum numbers. Later the core of the idea became the formal analogy or structural similarity between the two theories that began to emerge in the theory of line spectra. In the context of that theory the analogy appeared as a "correspondence" between the classical Fourier components of the motion of an atomic electron and the quantum transition between its stationary states. The discovery of quantum mechanics made it clear that the formal analogy had been a sign that the quantum formalism was to be a mathematical generalization of the classical formalism.
In Bohr’s view, the significance of the correspondence idea goes beyond the mathematical requirement of maximum standard similarity. His work on the interpretation of the general quantum formalism may be described as an attempt to clarify the epistemological consequences of the fact that quantum mechanics is a generalization of classical mechanics. This work has produced the outlines of a new view of the foundations of physics. (Petersen, 1968, pp. 282–283)

As a young physicist, Bohr had already introduced the notion of such a correspondence in his pioneering work on atomic constitution (Bohr, 1913b): the ‘analogy’ as he called it then, between the results of the classical and the quantum description determined an important constant in his final result, the formula for the spectrum of the hydrogen atom.¹⁹⁵ It had then become the guiding principle in Bohr’s programme to explain the line spectra of atoms and the band spectra of molecules, to arrive at a theory of the periodic system of chemical elements, and to determine the influences of external forces on atomic radiation or even a new radiation theory.‘After about a dozen years of successful application of the correspondence principle, the situation seemed to have developed into a dramatic paradox: on the one hand, the just discovered quantum mechanics of Heisenberg, Born, Jordan, and Dirac provided the final triumph of the correspondence principle; on the other, it suffered a complete defeat, and this defeat seemed to affect the very roots of this so successful philosophical principle: the connection to the ‘old electrodynamics.’¹⁹⁶
Prior to April 1925, Bohr could feel perfectly safe in assuming that, whatever followed from quantum theory regarding the frequencies and intensities of atomic radiation, the nature of this radiation remained identical with the one that followed from the classical electromagnetic theory; hence, he could easily dismiss Albert Einstein’s light-quantum hypothesis. Now, however, the experimental proof for the existence of nonclassical radiation quanta had been provided by Walther Bothe and Hans Geiger’s detailed experimental investigation of the Compton effect, soon to be confirmed by another experiment of Arthur Compton and Alfred Simon (1925c) in America. Hence, the good news emerging from the

¹⁹⁵ See Volume 1, Part 1, pp. 247–257; also Rosenfeld and Rüdinger, 1967.
¹⁹⁶ On 6 March 1913, at the start of his theory of atomic structure, Bohr had written to Rutherford that he had just discovered ‘the most beautiful analogy between the old electrodynamics and the considerations in my papers.’

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0203 -->

II.4 Complementarity &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; 171

quantum-mechanical confirmation of the correspondence principle was soon rendered obsolete: the only available philosophical principle, which had held together the often contradictory assembly of conceptual puzzles during several previous years, had evidently to be given up. In contrast to the other quantum theoreticians who threw themselves into the new quantum mechanics and worked out its applications, Bohr fell into a deep depression that paralyzed him for many months. Thus, in August 1925, addressing the *Sixth Scandinavian Mathematical Congress* on atomic theory, he lamented:

> From these results it seems to follow that, in the general problem of the quantum theory, one is faced not with a modification of the mechanical and electrodynamical theories describable in terms of the usual concepts, but with an essential failure of the pictures in space and time on which the description of natural phenomena has hitherto been based. This failure appears also in a closer consideration of impact phenomena. In particular, for impacts in which the collision is short compared to the natural periods of the atom and for which very simple results are to be expected according to the usual [classical]-mechanical ideas, the postulate of stationary states would seem to be irreconcilable with any description of the collision in space and time based on the accepted ideas of atomic structure. (Bohr, 1925b, p. 848)

The last remark derived from a rather defensive addendum of July 1925, which Bohr had supplied to his paper on atomic collisions (written and sent to *Zeitschrift für Physik* just before he learned about the Bothe–Geiger result: Bohr, 1925a). Pauli, on receiving a copy of the manuscript of Bohr’s Copenhagen talk, sympathized with the author. On the other hand, he felt quite optimistic about Heisenberg’s new quantum-mechanical theory, though he admitted certain temporary limitations:

> The theory, for the moment, is only adapted to those cases where all particles remain confined to finite regions of space; thus, for instance, in its present formulation, it is not suitable for describing collision phenomena and the problem of understanding simultaneously both the coupling and interference [of radiation]. In particular, we do not have any logically unified theory which includes, in the case of large [quantum] numbers, *all* the applications of classical theory. (Pauli to Bohr, 17 November 1925, in Pauli, 1979, p. 260)

The main obstacle for obtaining such a unified theory, Pauli continued, lies in the definition of the time-instant of transition processes, because: ‘The actual situation now is that the concept of “time-sequence” of a process, and especially the concept of “time period” or “frequency” have become totally formal quantities.’ In other words, the ‘formal character of the frequency condition’—emphasized in Bohr’s lecture—‘arises from the formal character of the time and not from the formal character of the energy.’ Pauli then suggested that one should proceed from the result of ‘coupling experiments’ (such as the Bothe–Geiger experiment) in the following manner:

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0204 -->

172 &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; Chapter II &nbsp; Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

> I vaguely imagine something like an attempt to *define* time just somehow only through the energy via the quantum of action *h* which has the dimension of erg.sec. For measuring the time one needs of course periodic processes, and these satisfy quantum laws. (Pauli, *loc. cit.*)

The agreement between Bohr and Pauli’s opinions, however, did not last, but was soon interrupted by disagreement on the question of spin. In this case, unlike the case of coupling of radiation, Bohr won, and soon felt optimistic again, for he reported to his former mentor Ernest Rutherford:

> It looks now that at any rate in the qualitative way characteristic for the correspondence principle we shall be able by means of such [mechanical] pictures supplemented with the new [spin] idea to account comprehensively for building up of atoms and for their properties; of course insofar as they are independent of the structure of the nucleus. At any rate I am at present just as optimistic as regards this problem as I was when I gave my first lectures in Cambridge 5 years ago [on the periodic system]. (Bohr to Rutherford, 27 January 1926, in Bohr, 1985, p. 458)

Still, the absolute primacy of the correspondence principle could not be reestablished, as Bohr perfectly recognized, and new advances in atomic theory supported this conclusion.

Already in the addendum to the collision paper, Bohr had observed toward the end: ‘The renunciation of space-time pictures characterizes the formal treatment of radiation-theory problems and of the mechanical theory of heat attempted by de Broglie [1924e] and Einstein [1924d, 1925a]’ (Bohr, 1925a, p. 152). Shortly after the middle of March 1926, Erwin Schrödinger’s first communication on wave mechanics appeared in print (Schrödinger, 1926c), and Bohr had the opportunity to discuss its contents with Pauli who visited Bohr’s Institute in Copenhagen in early April. Bohr immediately reported to Fowler in England:

> It looks indeed that we are on the high road to advance now.... Pauli ... has just in these days [in Copenhagen] succeeded in proving that the beautiful method of determining energy values for stationary states proposed by Schrödinger in the last issue of *Annalen der Physik* will always lead to results identical with those derived by the method of Heisenberg, Born and Dirac. It looks even that Schrödinger’s method may offer a simplification in the calculations especially as regards the determination of the transition probabilities. (Bohr to Ralph Fowler, 14 April 1926, in Bohr, 1985, p. 9)

Bohr evidently rejoiced, as did Heisenberg and Pauli, about the ability of wave mechanics to provide a suitable method of calculation.$^{197}$ It would soon enable Heisenberg to evaluate the energy states of the helium atom and thus solve one of the toughest problems of atomic structure. In Göttingen, Max Born applied the wave-mechanical method to establish the first quantum-mechanical collision

$^{197}$ We do not see, however, that Bohr was initially more sympathetic to wave mechanics than the Göttingen quantum theorists (see, e.g., Kalckar, 1985b, p. 9).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0205 -->

II.4 Complementarity &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; 173

theory. Contradicting earlier statements—e.g., that of Pauli to Bohr (in the letter of 17 November 1925): ‘I definitely believe that in the fundamental laws of a satisfactory theory the concept [of] “probability” should not appear’—the new quantum-mechanical collision theory contained an essential element of probability in the interpretation of the wave function. Although Schrödinger developed an alternative, more classical, interpretation of his waves, Bohr and Heisenberg, in a serious debate lasting several days in early October 1926, sought to convince him that any causal and continuous interpretation would fail to explain even the most elementary quantum-theoretical features, such as Planck’s radiation law.

However, Schrödinger’s visit also made a decisive impression on Bohr, who wrote about it a few weeks later:

> Just in the wave mechanics we possess now the means of picturing a single stationary state which suits all purposes consistent with the postulates of the quantum theory. In fact, this is the very reason for the advantage which the wave mechanics in certain respects exhibits when compared with the matrix method which in other respects is so wonderfully suited to bring out the true correspondence between the quantum theory and the classical idea. (Bohr to Ralph Fowler, 26 October 1926, in Bohr, 1985, p. 15)

Having emphasized this point—the existence of stationary states belonged, after all, to the fundamental postulates of Bohr’s quantum theory of atomic structure—he concluded: ‘After the discussion with Schrödinger it is very much in my mind to complete a paper dealing with the general principles of quantum theory such as I spoke of already during your visit.’ (Bohr, *loc. cit.*)

Bohr had not published anything in 1926 since submitting in January a short note to *Nature*, in which he endorsed the concept of electron spin (Bohr, 1926a). For the first time, we learn from the above lines to Ralph Fowler that he had planned since September 1926 to compose ‘a new paper’ dealing with the general principles of quantum theory—i.e., a paper going essentially beyond the one published in the less fortunate previous year (Bohr, 1925b).$^{198}$ What were the topics he wished to treat, the problems he wished to discuss? Because no manuscript, draft, or further letter exists, one can only make a guess. Perhaps Erwin Schrödinger provided some starting points in the letter, which he wrote to Bohr after his Copenhagen visit and in which he tried to define more clearly their conflicting views. He had stated:

> You, as it seems to me, have found a certain preliminary position in the view that all the apparently visualizable pictures can really be regarded only symbolically, above all—as pointed out by Dirac in his most recent publication and also advocated by Born—that the *c*’s, the amplitudes of or coefficients of the individual proper vibrations, merely convey statistical statements on the behaviour of single systems. Here I am quite unable to set my mind at rest with this preliminary solution. It appears to me *in general* just as inapplicable as my own. When a light wave strikes a large

$^{198}$ Fowler had visited Copenhagen in September 1926 (see Bohr to Fowler, 14 April 1926).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0206 -->

174  
Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields  

number of atoms (like in a gas), then every single atom must after all emit a weak secondary wave, otherwise one cannot understand the attenuation and dispersion of the light wave. On the other hand, if the light wave has just the resonance frequency, *then* only a few single atoms may in fact suffer a *considerable* change (“being raised to the higher state”).  
Apparently there is a contradiction here, and you say: here the words and concepts used no longer suffice. I do not feel satisfied with this ascertainment, and from it I cannot deduce that I am justified in continuing to operate with contradictory statements. One may weaken the statements by saying, e.g., that the collection of atoms “in certain respects behaves as if …” and “in certain respects so as if …,” but this is so-to-speak merely a juridical expedient that cannot be converted into a clear reasoning.  
...  
Even if a hundred attempts have failed, one ought not to give up hope of arriving at the goal, I don’t say through classical pictures, but through logically consistent conceptions of the true structure of the space-time events. It is extremely likely that this is possible. (Schrödinger to Bohr, 23 October 1926, English translation in Kalckar, 1985, pp. 12–13)  

In any case, after several weeks, Bohr had the first results available, and he reported them to Schrödinger in a letter dated 2 December 1926, acknowledging the assistance of Oskar Klein in particular.  

**(d) Oskar Klein and the Advantages of the Undulatory Theory (April 1926–February 1927)**  

Toward the end of April 1926, shortly before Heisenberg arrived in Copenhagen, Oskar Klein submitted from there a paper entitled ‘*Quantentheorie und fünfdimensionale Relativitätstheorie*’ (‘Quantum Theory and Five-Dimensional Relativity Theory,’ O. Klein, 1926a).¹⁹⁹ Klein not only obtained a relativistic Schrödinger equation, but also proposed to connect the quantum-theoretical aspects with the fifth dimension, arguing:  

> Although the introduction of the fifth dimension into our physical considerations might appear, at first sight, quite odd, a radical modification of the geometry underlying the field equations suggests itself again in a quite different way on the quantum theory. Because it has become less and less probable that the quantum phenomena admit a unified space-time description; on the other hand, the possibility to represent these phenomena by a system of five-dimensional field equations should not be excluded from the very beginning. (O. Klein, *loc. cit.*, pp. 905–906)  

Klein added a footnote (on p. 906) that ‘Professor Bohr made on several occasions remarks in this direction’; still, when he discussed the five-dimensional approach a little later with Bohr and Heisenberg, he remembered that ‘they listened with kind skepticism’ (O. Klein, 1968, p. 65).  

¹⁹⁹ See our discussion of Klein’s paper in Volume 5, Part 2, Section IV.5.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0207 -->

175  
II.4 Complementarity  

Klein’s work received, however, a very positive reception by an outside authority, as he recalled vividly:  

> Not long after having sent the paper to *Zeitschrift für Physik* I got to my great surprise and pleasure a letter from H. A. Lorentz—for whom I had a special veneration. … He extended a most kind invitation to spend some weeks in Leyden in June that year and tell about my attempts regarding five-dimensional relativity. … The stay in Leyden was most animated and refreshing after a rather hard year. Lorentz came to my lectures, taking part in the discussions in his quiet and lucid way. Among the physicists I met, in first place, Ehrenfest and his wife, I shall mention Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, which led to much pleasant discussion. (O. Klein, *loc. cit.*)  

Lorentz soon confirmed Klein’s impression in a letter sent to Copenhagen. ‘Dr. Klein gave us a very good account, as clear and easy to understand as it could be, of his work,’ he wrote, and added: ‘I made his acquaintance with great pleasure and was very favourably impressed both by the keenness of his insight and his modesty.’ (Lorentz to Bohr, 7 June 1926)  
Lorentz, in the same letter, pursued another purpose, i.e., he invited Bohr to ‘another “Conseil de Physique” to be held in Brussels during 5 or 6 days in October 1927.’ In the name of the ‘Administrative Commission’ and the ‘Scientific Council’ of the *Institut International de Physique Solvay*, he outlined the programme of the planned conference:  

> Our subject will be the conflict between the classical theories and the quantum theory (“La théorie des quanta et les théories classiques du rayonnement”) and with you the following gentlemen are invited: Born, W. L. Bragg (Manchester), L. Brillouin, L. de Broglie, A. H. Compton, Debye, Deslandres, Ehrenfest, Fowler (Cambridge), Heisenberg, Kramers, Planck, Schrödinger and C. T. R. Wilson. The meeting will be attended by the members of the Scientific Council, namely Madame Curie, van Aubel, W. H. Bragg (London), Einstein, C. E. Guye, Knudsen, Langevin and myself and the physicists of the University of Brussels (de Donder, Henriot, Piccard) will also be invited. (Lorentz to Bohr, *loc. cit.*)  

‘I personally shall be very glad if you came this time,’ Lorentz continued and requested a ‘reply at your earliest convenience.’ Already on 24 June, Bohr accepted by letter Lorentz’s invitation to attend the meeting; in preparing his report, which was to be called eventually ‘Le Postulat des Quanta et le Nouveau Développement de l’Atomistique,’ Klein became his principal assistant.  
Before Klein returned to Copenhagen from Leyden, he entered upon a new investigation. As he recalled:  

> One day, Ehrenfest brought us a new paper by Dirac containing a quantum-dynamical theory of the Compton effect [i.e., Dirac, 1926c, published in May 1926] which we tried to read, but without success [in understanding its contents]. It occurred to me that it [the problem of the Compton effect] could be treated the Schrödinger way in analogy with the transition from one stationary state to another, the states being

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0208 -->

176  
Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields  

those of an electron in a box under the influence of a radiation field. Uhlenbeck and I began to calculate but, although it looked all right qualitatively, we never reached the quantitative result in the short time at my disposal. (O. Klein, 1968, pp. 65–66)  

In Copenhagen, Klein continued to work on the Compton problem, again not making decisive progress. One obstacle seemed to be the inability of Schrödinger’s wave mechanics to provide the derivation of the dispersion formulae of Kramers and Heisenberg. Only much later that year—meanwhile Schrödinger’s visit had occurred and stimulated greater efforts in Copenhagen to understand his theory—Bohr could announce that ‘Klein is in the process of finishing a paper on the possibilities of exploiting wave mechanics for the understanding of atomic processes involving discontinuities.’ He further reported about the detailed contents of Klein’s work:  

> For you this paper is hardly going to bring anything new, but I think that you will enjoy seeing how well wave mechanics is suited to exhibit the correspondence between classical electrodynamics and quantum theory. Actually it is possible, on the basis of wave mechanics, to build up a correspondence theory just as closed as matrix mechanics, which may on the other hand be regarded as a correspondence theory based on the corpuscular mechanics. In this connection it is interesting to see how the concept of wave or corpuscle presents itself as the more suitable concept, according to the point in the description where the assumption of discontinuities actually appears. In my opinion this is easily understood, since the definition of every concept or rather every word presupposes the continuity of the phenomena and hence becomes ambiguous as soon as the presupposition cannot be upheld. (Bohr to Schrödinger, 2 December 1926, translation in Kalckar, 1985b, p. 14)  

Evidently, Bohr’s new views were hardly acceptable to Schrödinger, but they showed how Bohr was stimulated on his path toward the complementarity interpretation by Klein’s results.  
The paper advocated here so strongly by Bohr bore the title ‘*Elektrodynamik und Wellenmechanik vom Standpunkt des Korrespondenzprinzips*’ (‘Electrodynamics and Wave Mechanics from the Point of View of the Correspondence Principle’) and was submitted to *Zeitschrift für Physik* in fact on 4 December 1926 (O. Klein, 1927a). Starting from his (and others’) relativistic equation for a ‘one-electron’ problem with spin, Klein first derived wave-mechanical expressions for the electric charge density $\rho$ and the electric current vector $\mathbf{J}$, notably,  

$$
\rho = -\frac{\varepsilon}{2\mu c^2} \left\{ -\frac{h}{2\pi i} \left( \psi \frac{\partial\psi^*}{\partial t} - \psi^* \frac{\partial\psi}{\partial t} \right) + 2\varepsilon V\psi^*\psi \right\} \tag{120}
$$  

and  

$$
\mathbf{J} = -\frac{\varepsilon}{2\mu} \left\{ \frac{h}{2\pi i} (\psi \operatorname{grad}\psi^* - \psi^* \operatorname{grad}\psi) + 2\frac{\varepsilon}{c}\mathbf{A}\psi^*\psi \right\}, \tag{121}
$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0209 -->

177  
II.4 Complementarity  

with $\varepsilon$ and $\mu$ denoting the charge and mass of the electron (described by the complex fields $\psi$ and $\psi^*$), and $V$ and $\mathbf{A}$ denoting the given scalar and vector potentials, respectively. Eqs. (120) and (121) became, in the suitably chosen limit $h \rightarrow 0$, identical with the classical relativistic expressions,  

$$
\rho = -\frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{1 - \mathbf{v}^2c^2}} \tag{120a}
$$  

and  

$$
\mathbf{J} = -\frac{\varepsilon \mathbf{v}}{\sqrt{1 - \mathbf{v}^2/c^2}}, \tag{121a}
$$  

with $\mathbf{v}$ having the components of the electron’s velocity ($c$ being the velocity of light *in vacuo*).²⁰⁰ Klein, however, emphasized ‘that the limit procedure used here must be regarded to be a purely formal one, and it cannot answer the deeper question of how—starting from the properties of the wave-mechanical electron model—one arrives continuously at the results of classical electron theory’ (O. Klein, 1927a, p. 415). Schrödinger’s interpretation of a particle as a wave packet would not really solve the problem, because this wave packet does not hold together for all times; hence, one should rather ‘consider the existence of the particles as a quantum problem,’ as he had suggested already earlier (O. Klein, 1926b).²⁰¹  
In the central Section 3, dealing with the ‘correspondence-like use of wave mechanics for the case of a static field of force,’ Klein provided proper expressions for charge and current densities in terms of the eigenfunction $\Psi_n$ of the relativistic wave equation. Any arbitrary function $\psi$ could be written as  

$$
\psi = \sum_n \Psi_n \exp(-2\pi i T_n t), \tag{122}
$$  

with $T_n$ denoting the term values related to the energy eigenvalues $E_n$ by the equation  

$$
E_n = -h T_n. \tag{123}
$$  

This result of wave mechanics, Klein warned again, should not be taken ‘as supporting the programme of a purely wave-mechanical theory in which the postu-  

²⁰⁰ To obtain Eqs. (120a) and (121a), Klein made the *Ansatz* for the wave function $\psi = \exp\left(-\frac{2\pi i}{h}S\right)$, with $S$ denoting the characteristic function whose derivatives provide the components of the ‘ray velocity’ $\mathbf{v}$.  
²⁰¹ This remark illustrated the Copenhagen answer to the efforts at obtaining an ‘anschauliche’ interpretation of wave packets [e.g., Erwin Madelung (1926a, b), as discussed in Volume 5, Part 2, Section IV.5].

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0210 -->

178 &emsp; Chapter II &emsp; Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

lates of quantum theory do not occur explicitly anymore,' because 'Wave mechanics has not helped us in overcoming the fundamental difficulty showing up in the existence of spectra which have found their expression in the postulates' (O. Klein, 1927a, p. 417). On the other hand, his own formulae for $\rho$ and $\mathbf{J}$, namely,

$$ \rho = \sum_n \sum_m \rho_{nm}, $$

with

$$ \rho_{nm} = - \frac{\varepsilon}{\mu c^2} \left[ - \frac{h(T_n + T_m)}{2} + \varepsilon V \right] \cdot \Psi^* \Psi \exp[2\pi i(T_n - T_m)t], \quad (124) $$

and

$$ \mathbf{J} = \sum_n \sum_m \mathbf{J}_{nm}, $$

with

$$ \mathbf{J}_{nm} = - \frac{\varepsilon}{2\mu} \left[ \frac{h}{2\pi i} (\Psi_m \text{grad } \Psi^*_n - \Psi^*_n \text{grad } \Psi_m) + 2 \frac{\varepsilon}{c} \Psi^*_n \Psi_m \right] \exp[2\pi i(T_n - T_m)t], \quad (125) $$

permitted a consistent quantitative description of the quantum phenomena observed with electrons bound in atoms, a description also fulfilling the requirement that in the correspondence-principle limit $\rho$ and $\mathbf{J}$ pass over into the expressions of classical electrodynamics. The same result remained true in the case of radiation fields or other external fields acting on the atom under consideration. Thus, Klein obtained not only the well-known quantum-mechanical (or wave-mechanical) results in the case of atomic spectra, but he also supplied the basis for obtaining the dispersion-theoretical formulae of Kramers and Heisenberg properly from the wave-mechanical scheme. Further, he sketched how the Compton effect might be treated according to his scheme.$^{202}$

In the final section, Klein returned to his favourite topic of a 'five-dimensional relativity and wave mechanics.' The solution of the corresponding wave equation, in the limit of geometrical optics, assumed the form

$$ U = \psi^* \exp\left( - \frac{2\pi i \varepsilon}{h c} x_0 \right) + \psi \exp\left( - \frac{2\pi i \varepsilon}{h c} x_0 \right); \quad (126) $$

---

$^{202}$ In an addendum in proofs, Klein mentioned that Walter Gordon had meanwhile provided a complete derivation of the Compton effect along these lines (Gordon, 1926). Schrödinger had also submitted similar results (Schrödinger, 1927a); however, both authors had 'not made statements about the general questions' (O. Klein, 1927a, p. 442).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0211 -->

II.4 &emsp; Complementarity &emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp; 179

i.e., the fifth coordinate $x_0$ enters just as a periodic factor. He triumphantly argued:

The periodicity of [Eq. (126)] in $x_0$, by which Planck's constant enters into the wave equation, allows a simple geometrical interpretation on the assumption that the five-dimensional space is closed in the direction of $x_0$. It suggests itself to connect the absence of the fifth coordinate in our usual physical equations with this interpretation, and to consider these equations as average values of more general equations containing the fifth coordinate. (O. Klein, *loc. cit.*, p. 441)

He finally concluded:

We see how the "observable" quantities entering into the usual physical description contain just the products of conjugate wave functions, by which the characteristic duality of quantum phenomena finds its expression. By assuming such a closedness in the fifth dimension, there follows not only the possibility of introducing Planck's constant into the theory, which is naturally connected with the world view of relativity theory, but it also leads to the four-dimensional correspondence-like representation of the one-electron problem based on wave mechanics. (O. Klein, *loc. cit.*, p. 442)

Klein's plea in favour of a five-dimensional relativistic scheme for incorporating the quantum of action in a 'natural manner' was supported by Fritz London in Stuttgart, though he connected it with different ideas following from Hermann Weyl's unified field theory of gravitation and electromagnetism (London, 1927a, b, c).$^{203}$ While London's work prepared the way to the recognition of a new fundamental symmetry, soon to be called 'gauge symmetry,' Klein pursued his particular goal of assigning to the fifth dimension a crucial role in the foundations of quantum mechanics. He recalled later:

Hence, after the paper was finally [sent] off to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, I began to look more closely into this matter. First, I convinced myself that Schrödinger's emission theory leads to the Rayleigh formula and not to that of Planck, in agreement with what Bohr and Heisenberg have maintained. Then I tried to see whether anything like the quantal treatment of the many-particle problem might come out of the five-dimensional theory. But the result was discouraging. (O. Klein, 1968, p. 66)

In spite of the initial failure of his attempts to solve the many-particle problem, this programme eventually brought success: it led to the development of a new subject, quantum field theory, which explained many quantum phenomena in nonrelativistic and relativistic physics and especially helped in preparing the way to what became the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics.$^{204}$

---

$^{203}$ We recall that Weyl's theory had stimulated Schrödinger in 1922 to obtain a relation between it and the quantum theory (Schrödinger, 1922c). See Volume 5, Part 1, pp. 312–318.
$^{204}$ Though much of the pioneering research work on quantum field theory was performed before Bohr completed the formulation of the idea of complementarity treated here, we shall postpone its presentation to the following section.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0212 -->

180 &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; Chapter II &nbsp; Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

Before joining the new programme on quantum field theory, Klein served as Bohr’s devoted collaborator and sounding board in helping him to formulate his ideas. Bohr appreciated the fact that Klein, unlike Heisenberg, was *not* biased against the wave theory.$^{205}$ Besides, he found Klein’s electrodynamical considerations to be ‘a very satisfactory compromise,’ as he confided in a letter to Charles Galton Darwin:

> In this way the wave mechanics may indeed be considered as a self-consistent theory, just as Heisenberg’s matrix mechanics, and it is very interesting to see how the notion of a corpuscle or a wave presents itself as the more convenient quite according to the place in the construction where the feature of discontinuity involved in the postulates is explicitly introduced. Indeed this is only what might be expected since every notion, or rather every word, we use is based on the idea of continuity, and becomes ambiguous as soon as that idea fails. (Bohr to Darwin, 24 November 1926)$^{206}$

Bohr now called wave mechanics ‘a wonderful discovery’ (Bohr to de Hevesy, 28 January 1927), and he made ample use of it in discussing the paradoxes of atomic physics—‘which are deeply rooted in nature and at present unavoidable in the description of empirical facts’—on the basis of the wave-particle dualism, discovered in 1909 by Einstein for radiation and extended to material particles by Louis de Broglie and Schrödinger in the 1920s. ‘It is very interesting to see,’ he wrote to Bidhu Bhushan Ray on 22 January 1927, ‘how the notion of a corpuscle or a wave presents itself the way in which the theory is formulated, i.e., at what place the discontinuous element is explicitly introduced.’ ‘Bohr and I had many discussions, we were talking [a great deal] about the wave theory,’ recalled Klein who stressed that Bohr ‘knew much about the classical wave theory, but he didn’t know this quantum wave theory.’ Thus, Bohr and Klein complemented each other perfectly; they met quite often to talk about how to apply the wave theory to describe quantum phenomena, and the results then entered into Bohr’s debates with Heisenberg in February 1927. Because Heisenberg did not really like to accept wave-theoretical arguments, he had trouble agreeing with Bohr. In particular, he recalled: ‘Whenever Bohr could give an example, in which I could not find an answer [on quantum-mechanical arguments], then it was clear that we had not understood what the actual situation was. . . . In some way we couldn’t agree and so we were a bit angry about it’ (Heisenberg, AHQP Interview, 25 February 1963). As we know, Bohr interrupted the unpleasant encounters by taking a long vacation in Norway in the middle of February, and after that the situation changed.

$^{205}$ In addition, Klein pursued—in the crucial months from October 1926 to February 1927—relativistic considerations that had provided the key to the electron spin problem earlier in 1926. Bohr, like Klein, felt that relativity theory might have much to do with the quantum theory, while Heisenberg insisted at that time upon first restricting the problem of interpretation to the nonrelativistic case.

$^{206}$ In considering the role of continuity in describing the motion of objects, we notice a general agreement between Bohr and Heisenberg. (See the previous section.)

## II.4 Complementarity

181

### (e) Bohr's Response to the Uncertainty Relations and the Subsequent Debate with Heisenberg (March–June 1927)

On 10 March 1927, Heisenberg wrote a letter from Copenhagen to the still vacationing Bohr informing him about the latest situation concerning visitors at the Institute and the progress of their scientific work. He also briefly indicated the advance in his own efforts in dealing with the problem of interpretation of quantum mechanics and his exchange with Pauli on that subject. Five days later, Bohr would return to Copenhagen and see Heisenberg's completed manuscript. Kalckar has argued that 'the paper must have been sent off from Copenhagen at a time when Bohr's return was imminent,' and further: 'One may venture to guess that after the many months of preceding discussions, and knowing as he did Bohr's thorough method of working, Heisenberg was eager to get the manuscript off before every paragraph of it would be overhauled by Bohr. But things were not to work out that way' (Kalckar, 1985a, p. 16). Though such an assumption may seem to be understandable on psychological grounds, it does not really conform to facts. According to Heisenberg's information (given in his letter to Pauli, dated 14 March 1927), Bohr arrived in Copenhagen on 15 March (and was back in his office certainly on 18 March, when he sent a letter to Kronig). On the other hand, the *Zeitschrift für Physik* received Heisenberg's paper on the uncertainty relations only on 23 March, leaving Bohr sufficient time to examine the manuscript before submission. Hence, we rather assume that he did so and approved of its contents in general. In agreement with this assumption, one may read what Bohr wrote to Einstein on 13 April, when he sent the latter a copy of the proofs of Heisenberg's paper with remarks of approval, without revealing the slightest unhappiness about its contents.$^{207}$ However, if one examines the following correspondence closely, one also recognizes that slowly discussions about Heisenberg's paper on uncertainty relations began to become more intense in Copenhagen.$^{208}$

In a letter to Pauli, dated 4 April 1927, Heisenberg referred first to some discussions with Bohr on the subject.$^{209}$ After mentioning his agreement with the

---

$^{207}$ Also, the letter from Bohr to Pauli, dated 25 March 1927, which David Cassidy has called 'a cry for help' (Cassidy, 1992a, p. 241), does not sound dramatic or indicate any major conflict yet with Heisenberg. Bohr rather invited Pauli to come to Copenhagen, not to assist him in his arguments with Heisenberg, but to meet Charles Galton Darwin, Samuel Goudsmit, and Ivar Waller, in whose work he might be interested.

$^{208}$ In any case, it is reasonable to assume that Bohr, after his extended vacation in Norway, only slowly got back to serious scientific work—having first to take decisions about more pressing administrative matters.

conclusion that the paradox of Ehrenfest and Breit did not really exist,²¹⁰ he continued:

> I quarrel with Bohr on the extent to which the relation $p_1 q_1 \sim h$ originates from the wave side or the discontinuum side of quantum mechanics. Bohr emphasizes that, e.g., for the $\gamma$-ray microscope the diffraction of waves is essential, while I stress the fact that the light-quantum theory and even the Geiger-Bothe experiment are essential. By exaggerating one side or the other, one can discuss a lot without saying anything new. (Heisenberg to Pauli, 4 April 1927, in Pauli, 1979, p. 391)

Still, Heisenberg indicated only a continuation of the debate that he had carried on with Bohr since fall 1926 rather than any dramatic conflict.²¹¹ On the whole, the Copenhagen atmosphere still appeared to be quite undisturbed even during the following days, as can be discerned from Heisenberg's report to Ralph Kronig: 'In the last few months I have worked out a paper on the visualizable content of the (of course discontinuous) quantum mechanics, which in my view, finally constitutes a closed system answering also the question: light-quanta or waves.' (Heisenberg to Kronig, 8 April 1927)

Heisenberg then left Copenhagen to take (a long deserved) Easter vacation in Munich and the Bavarian mountains. After his return, he wrote a letter to Paul Dirac, dated 27 April.²¹² Evidently, Dirac had raised (in a lost letter) certain questions about the uncertainty results, to which Heisenberg now gave an answer. In particular, he treated the example of the $\gamma$-ray microscope for the first time in two ways:

(i) If one knows the velocity of an electron, one can measure its position with the help of a $\gamma$-ray microscope. Now according to Bohr, "The point is that one cannot calculate the velocity afterwards, because the direction of the scattered light-quantum after the collision [of the electron with the $\gamma$-ray] is *not* known. If you think of an ordinary type of real microscope, you want an angle of aperture $\phi$ as large as possible, in order to get the accuracy $\lambda$ [for the position measurement]. If $\phi$ is small, your accuracy will not be $\lambda$ but $\lambda/\phi$, the uncertainty in the direction of the light-quantum will be $\phi$ and $p_1 = \frac{h\nu}{c} \phi$, $q_1 = \frac{\lambda}{\phi}$, $p_1 q_1 \sim h$."

---

²¹⁰ In 1922, Ehrenfest and Breit discussed a rotator (imagined as a toothed wheel having a mechanism that inverts the direction of rotation after *f* rotations, with *f* a large number). The period $T(=4ft)$ of the system is large compared with the period $t$ of the rotator; hence, one has very closely spaced energy states. Because, from the point of view of a consistent quantum theory, the authors argued, all stationary states have equal statistical weight, for *T* large enough, all energy states will occur with the same frequency, in contrast to rotational quantum states. As Heisenberg showed in his later publication (1927b, pp. 194–195), this paradox of the old quantum theory can be resolved by studying in detail the mechanism of inverting the direction of rotation as a coupling mechanism: even a small coupling will change the energy values of the free rotator drastically.

²¹¹ One may read Heisenberg's last remark in his letter to Pauli in the same sense: 'It is a great pity that you are not coming! Darwin would like to know about your calculation' (Heisenberg to Pauli, 4 April 1927, in Pauli, 1979, p. 391). Darwin, not Bohr and Heisenberg, needed Pauli's presence more in Copenhagen.

# II.4 Complementarity

183

(ii) According to Heisenberg, on the other hand, the incident light of wavelength $\lambda$ passes through holes of width $d > \lambda$ giving rise to a diffraction pattern of the order $\lambda/d$. Hence: "The accuracy of the [position], however, will be $d = q_1$, if the electron is not too far from the screen. The direction of the light-quantum is again uncertain by the amount $\lambda/d$ and $p_1 = \frac{\lambda}{d} \frac{h\nu}{c}$. [Thus it follows that] $p_1 q_1 \sim h$." (Heisenberg to Dirac, 27 April 1927, reproduced in Kalckar, 1985b, pp. 17–18)

Heisenberg also demonstrated how in the case of an observation of the velocity of microscopic objects with the help of the Doppler effect (obviously Dirac's second question), the uncertainty relation was satisfied. He concluded, still in a very calm manner: 'Professor Bohr says, that in all these examples, one sees the very important role the *wave*-theory plays in my theory and, of course, he is right' (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*).

In a similar nondramatic tone, Heisenberg wrote to Pauli more than two weeks later:²¹³

> Since my return from the Easter vacation—this time particularly pleasant—we have discussed quantum theory at length. Bohr plans to write a general treatise on the "conceptual organization (*begriffliche Aufbau*)" of quantum theory from the point of view: "There exist waves or corpuscles"—if one starts right away from this [conception], one can of course make everything consistent. In respect to this work, Bohr has drawn my attention to the fact that in my paper yet another essential point has been overlooked (Dirac also asked me about it later): With the $\gamma$-ray microscope one might first imagine that one determines the direction of the incident light-quantum as well as the reflected light-quantum. Then *after* the Compton effect both the position and the velocity are known very accurately (more accurately than $p_1 q_1 \sim h$). However, this cannot really be done, because of the diffraction of the light (wave theory!). To achieve an accuracy $\lambda$, the microscope must have an aperture of the order of 1. Thus the relation $p_1 q_1 \sim h$ is of course obtained, but not quite in the manner I thought. Furthermore, certain points could be better expressed and discussed in every detail, if only one begins a quantitative discussion directly with the waves. (Heisenberg to Pauli, 16 May 1927, in Pauli, 1979, pp. 394–395)

The last sentences indicate certain changes in Heisenberg's previous views: he now admits—in contrast to his discussions with Bohr in February—that wave-theoretical considerations may possess some virtue in the discussion of quantum mechanics. Still, he continued:

> Nevertheless, my opinion is of course just as beforehand that in the quantum theory only the discontinuities are interesting and that one can never emphasize them enough. For this reason I am also now, as previously, very happy with my latest paper—in spite of the error mentioned. All results of the paper are correct after all, and I am also in agreement with Bohr concerning these. Otherwise, there is a considerable difference of taste between Bohr and me regarding the word "visualizable." (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*)

# Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

184

So far, the letter to Pauli still documents essential harmony in the Copenhagen circle. However, the next sentences reveal, for the first time, a greater conflict of opinions, as Heisenberg wrote:

> Unfortunately, recent discussions have led to serious personal misunderstandings between Bohr-Klein and me, for which I am partly responsible. I do not of course want to write about it, but I want to ask you to send me the letter (if you still have it) which I wrote to you *before* 31 January 1927 and in which I reported on Klein's work. Klein indeed believes that I have put down his and Bohr's work before you, Hund and others. It would be nice if you would soon write to Klein yourself. (Heisenberg to Pauli, *loc. cit.*, p. 395)

Evidently, Klein's coalition with Bohr on the use of the wave picture created personal misgivings between him and Heisenberg.²¹⁴ Two weeks later, again in a letter to Pauli, Heisenberg became rather explicit by telling him 'what moved me in the past weeks more than anything else in a long time,' namely:

> As you know, I held the Dirac-Jordan [transformation] theory to be superior to wave mechanics (even in the discontinuous correspondence-like formulation [of Klein]), because the Dirac-Jordan theory is less visualizable and more general and allows one to include the discontinuities in an easier way. Therefore I became involved into a struggle for matrices and against waves. In the passion of this struggle I often criticized Bohr's objections against my paper without knowing or intending to hurt him personally. I can well understand that Bohr was unhappy (*ungehalten*) about it [i.e., Heisenberg's criticism]. Into these personal differences, for which I am guilty, there entered Klein, and his intervention seemed to make matters worse. I therefore thought that this might be connected with your letter—since I had unintentionally offended Klein by not showing him your letter, while Waller did see it accidentally.²¹⁵ Meanwhile I came to the conclusion that Klein only wanted to assist Bohr and has assumed this position only because of his friendship with Bohr. Your letter, on the other hand, has not much to do at all with the whole situation. Thank God, we all understand each other better now, and we all try to forget as much as possible what has happened earlier. (Heisenberg to Pauli, 31 May 1927, *loc. cit.*, pp. 396–397)

The days of intense arguments and struggle were over indeed: on 3 June, Heisenberg sent off another letter to Pauli, happy to be able to 'write again purely about physics and forget about all other things.' Then, Pauli came personally to Copenhagen and straightened out the last remaining ruffles. 'You hardly know what pleasure and refreshment your visit has given to all of us,' Bohr confessed afterward. (Bohr to Pauli, 15 July 1927) Life in Copenhagen had returned to normality, as Bohr reported to Fowler:

# II.4 Complementarity

185

In the Institute we have a little lively time lately with quite a number of visitors. For the present Jordan, who is very much in the style of Dirac, is here on an International Education Board stipend, and we are just in these days having a visit of Pauli and Wentzel. (Bohr to Ralph Fowler, 10 June 1927)

The very dramatic events of May 1927 have been reconstructed in the foregoing mainly from the documents of one of the participants, namely, Heisenberg. However, they find an echo also in the (much later) recollections of another participant, Oskar Klein, who first described the situation preceding Heisenberg's uncertainty relations paper from the point of view of the other side (i.e., Bohr's and his own):

> I hadn't read anything of [Schrödinger's papers] carefully, and I don't think that Bohr had either, because he was beginning also to learn more then from the wave side. Probably Heisenberg had told us, and especially Bohr, about these things; but one never understands quite things which one isn't working with. . . . I don't remember how it is in Jordan's paper and Dirac's paper, as I read it very carefully then . . . So I think it was really the achievement of Heisenberg to get such more concrete points definitely out of that. . . . I don't think that either Bohr or Heisenberg had any clear idea about this [i.e., the uncertainty relations] until Heisenberg began. (O. Klein, AHQP Interview, 16 July 1963)

However, after Heisenberg's work had been completed, a new situation arose, as Klein confirmed:

> I must say that Heisenberg made a very important contribution to this, which was a very great inspiration to Bohr, and that by a little "phase difference" there came some tension. . . . That there was a tension between their points of view could have done much to bring out the complementarity point of view. (O. Klein, *loc. cit.*)

That is, Bohr, though being very impressed by Heisenberg's result, became increasingly unhappy by the latter's refusal to adopt his wave arguments. Klein continued: 'The tension that came had a little to do with these things happening so fast. He [Bohr] had almost unbounded admiration for Heisenberg, and that was an extra shock when Heisenberg did not see through these things. . . . That made him upset there.' (O. Klein, *loc. cit.*)

The shock lasted, as reported above, for two or three weeks—the heated discussions once even drove Heisenberg 'to break out in tears' (Cassidy, 1992a, p. 242)—until he accepted Bohr's arguments and wrote toward the end of May 1927 a 'postscript in proofs' to his paper.²¹⁶ It read:

> After conclusion of the present work, recent investigations by Bohr have led to points of view that permit an essential deepening and refinement of the analysis of quantum-mechanical relationships attempted in this paper. In this connection Bohr has drawn

my attention [to the fact] that in some of the discussion contained I have overlooked essential points. First and foremost, the uncertainty in the observation does not exclusively rest upon the occurrence of discontinuities but is directly related to the requirement of doing justice at the same time to the different experiences, which find their expression in the corpuscular theory, on the one hand, and the wave theory, on the other. E.g., one must, when using an imaginary $\gamma$-ray microscope, take into consideration the necessary divergence of the beam of radiation; only this has the consequence that in observing the position of the electron in the direction of the Compton recoil is just known with an uncertainty which eventually leads to the [uncertainty] relation. Furthermore, it has not been sufficiently emphasized that the simple theory of the Compton effect can be applied strictly only to free electrons. The caution which is accordingly necessary in applying the uncertainty relation is, as Professor Bohr has clarified, among other things essential for a general discussion of the transition from micro- to macrophysics. Finally, the considerations on resonance fluorescence are not quite correct, because the connection between the phase of light and that of electron's motion is not so simple as assumed there. (Heisenberg, 1927b, pp. 197–198)

Heisenberg concluded by expressing his 'sincerest gratitutde to Professor Bohr' for his becoming 'acquainted with and discussing the aforementioned recent investigations of Bohr, which will soon appear in a paper on the conceptual structure of quantum theory' (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.* p. 198). In a letter sent to Bohr at about the same time, Heisenberg emphasized the agreement between their opinions that had been reestablished by saying: 'I was very happy about Pauli's visit. Now I have understood much better that it really matters very much to put the concepts in that order of precedence which you want and not how I put it in my paper; and I also see very well' that in this way it has certainly become much more beautiful.' (Heisenberg to Bohr, 18 June 1927)

**(f) Bohr's Preparation for the First Presentation of the Complementarity Principle at the Como Conference (April–September 1927)**

In his memorial article on 'Glimpses of Bohr as Scientist and Thinker,' Oskar Klein wrote:

> In spring of 1927 Bohr received the impetus for his definitive clarification of this side [i.e., the physical interpretation] of quantum theory through a very important paper of Heisenberg, in which the so-called indeterminacy principle was formulated. . . . While Bohr was deeply impressed by the general formulation of such relations, on second thought he could not help but feel critical about Heisenberg's discussion of ideal experiments. However, both the results and the failures of Heisenberg's work became a source of inspiration to him, and from then on he worked almost day and night on these questions. The problem was also in perfect harmony with Bohr's natural bent, where his powerful grasp and fine feeling for the limits of visualizability and his philosophical-critical sense were added to his thoroughgoing knowledge of the properties of wave motion derived from his early studies of Rayleigh's work. Still he was up against difficulties, which were comparable with those he met in his early work [on atomic structure]. (O. Klein, 1967, pp. 88)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0219 -->

II.4 Complementarity 187

These remarks describe the situation very adequately regarding the moment when Bohr finally really entered into the formulation of his ideas on complementarity. Although the composition of such a paper had been stimulated nearly a year previously, i.e., in June 1926, by Hendrik Lorentz's invitation to the fifth Solvay Conference on Physics, Bohr had not yet written a line before April 1927. His letter of 13 April to Albert Einstein, in which he reported Heisenberg's 'very important contribution to the discussion of the general problems of quantum theory' and presented his own analysis of the $\gamma$-ray microscope experiment based on the wave-theoretical approach to the formation of images by optical instruments, must be taken as the first document connected with Bohr's future paper.²¹⁷ In the same letter, Bohr also analyzed an experiment on the interference properties of canal rays that had been proposed the previous year by Einstein: the measurement in question was the spectral resolution of the light emitted by a moving atom and observed through a slit perpendicular to the direction of the motion (Einstein, 1926a, b). With the method of using both the wave theory and an energy-balance consideration (representative of the particle picture), Bohr arrived at a resolution of Einstein's paradox. He concluded with a praise of Heisenberg:

> Heisenberg shows in an exceedingly brilliant manner how his uncertainty relations may be utilized not only in the actual development of quantum theory, but also for the judgment of its visualizable content. Insofar as this relation is a direct consequence of the quantum-mechanical formalism, the whole constitutes a very closed system, at least when one limits oneself to mechanical phenomena. (Bohr to Einstein, 13 April 1927, English translation in Kalckar, 1985b, p. 25)

From hereon emerged Bohr's own programme of dealing with the interference problem, which he outlined to Einstein as follows:

> As regards such a pedagogically coloured concept as visualizability, however, it seems to me instructive to keep always in mind how indispensable are the concepts of the continuous field theory in the present stage of science. As long as we only talk about particles and quantum jumps, it is difficult to find a simple presentation of the theory, which is based on referring to the limitation in the possibilities of observation. This is because the uncertainty mentioned is not only connected with the presence of discontinuities but also to the very impossibility of a detailed description in harmony with those properties of the material particles and light that find their expression in the wave theory. The representation of an electron by a group of de Broglie waves is of course closely analogous to the representation of a light-quantum by a group of electromagnetic waves. . . . Now it follows directly from the uncertainty in the group velocity, corresponding to the uncertainty in the electron momentum, that the group in the course of time spreads out also in the direction of propagation, all this exactly as Heisenberg has worked it out on the basis of quantum mechanics in association with Dirac's matrix transformation theory. (Bohr to Einstein, *loc. cit.*)

²¹⁷ The main points of Bohr's analysis were reported by Heisenberg to Dirac in his letter dated 27 April 1927 (see the above discussion).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0220 -->

188 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

This letter, of course, opened up a new Bohr–Einstein dialogue that would reach its first climax at the Solvay Conference in the following October. For the moment, in April 1927, it encouraged Bohr to embark upon assembling further his thoughts for a detailed manuscript. Oskar Klein, for some time his closest confidant, became involved in helping Bohr to formulate the paper until September 1927, when the first presentation of complementarity eventually took place at the Como Confrence.²¹⁸ He recalled Bohr's procedure as follows:

> As usual, he started writing very soon, i.e., dictating, and at the same time new ideas and doubts would come to him, so that what was written one day was rejected the next. In this way we spent what remained of the spring and the whole summer, when the work was done at Bohr's summer resort in Tisvilde. (O. Klein, 1967, p. 89)

The most important problem which Bohr attacked first was, of course, the proper analysis of the $\gamma$-ray experiment. Klein wrote:

> Heisenberg had now noted that the Compton effect in the scattering of light would produce a change of the momentum of the electron, its value after the measurement being different from what it was before. He regarded it as the feature corresponding to the lack of definition of the momentum, which, according to the indeterminacy principle, was associated with accurate definition of the position. However, Bohr showed that the lack of definition of the momentum is not directly related to its being changed by the Compton effect but is connected with the necessary uncertainty in the knowledge of the Compton effect in an arrangmenet that can be used for an accurate measurement of position. (O. Klein, *loc. cit.*)

Yet, after carrying out the detailed investigation, Bohr arrived at the same result as Heisenberg had.

As Bohr had pointed out to Einstein earlier, the consistent description of the atomic situation was a matter of a careful definition of the concepts rather than—as Heisenberg believed—being a matter of observable quantities. The words 'particle' and 'wave' had a special meaning in the microscopic world. Thus, as Klein remembered:

> 'He was very much against an idea which [Arthur] Eddington wrote a little later when he wanted to call them "wavicles" or something like that, a combination of waves and particles, because he [Bohr] stressed very strongly that neither the word 'wave' nor the word 'particle' can be taken literally, but [both] are just short expressions for the experience of having this feature of indivisibility, or individuality, and at the same time you had the other feature, which is symbolized by waves. (O. Klein, AHQP Interview, 16 July 1963)

²¹⁸ In connection with an exhibition memorializing the centenary of the death of Alessandro Volta at Como (where he was born and died), a *Congresso Internazionale dei Fisici* (International Congress of Physicists) was announced to be held (see *Physikalische Zeitschrift* **28**, p. 492, issue of 1 July 1927). It seems that this announcement came out only *after* Bohr had decided to write the paper, but then he wanted to discuss the subject at this congress—see also the following.

II.4 Complementarity 189

Indeed, Bohr criticized the fact that Heisenberg, in his uncertainty paper, did not take the dual nature of atomic objects seriously, but tried to get along with a rather refined particle picture.²¹⁹ It appeared certain to him that without using the wave properties of quantum objects, in whatever sense they were defined, one would never succeed in understanding the measurement of canonically conjugate variables, and the only way of expressing the situation in a proper language was to apply the *classical wave theory*. Later, after the clarification of the complementarity view, Bohr would formulate the whole situation more accurately in his theory of the measurement process, which was a theory of concepts in contrast to the mathematical theory of John von Neumann and his followers.

So far, Heisenberg had provided the point of departure for Bohr's thoughts. The next step in Bohr's procedure was triggered by a letter from the older British physicist Norman Campbell in the *Nature* issue of 28 May 1927 (Campbell, 1927). The writer, referring to an article on 'Philosophical Foundations of Quantum Theory' printed in a previous issue of 16 April (Jordan, 1927c),²²⁰ had criticized Pascual Jordan's statements on measuring the time instant of a quantum jump. Such a concept of time, Campbell had argued, made no sense at all; in that situation, one must rather use 'the concept of a statistical time,' which he had himself proposed for years (Campbell, 1921, 1926). In order to explain the meaning of the 'statistical time,' he had suggested an analogy:

> If all "regular clocks" were abolished from our laboratories, and we were forced to use radium clocks, in which the defining events are the disintegrations of individual atoms, it would be very difficult to demonstrate some of the experiments on which our conceptions of "continuous processes" and "causal relations" are based. That difficulty, I think, is precisely the difficulty which we encounter when we proceed from the world of atomic aggregates to that of individual atoms. (Campbell, 1927, p. 779)

In the same issue of *Nature*, Jordan had replied by calling attention to Heisenberg's recently discovered uncertainty relations and the consequences derived therefrom for the time measurement. 'Undoubtedly this discussion is too short and too accurate to elucidate the point completely,' he had concluded and referred 'Dr. Campbell to Heisenberg's paper [1927b], in which these questions are treated in detail' (Jordan, 1927f, p. 779).

²¹⁹ Mara Beller, in her account of Bohr's complementarity, has tried to analyze the antagonism between Bohr and Heisenberg (Beller, 1992a). We have difficulty in following some of her conclusions in the light of the following facts: (1) Heisenberg did not avoid the use of the correspondence principle in 1925 when he invented quantum mechanics; (2) the pioneers of quantum mechanics (Heisenberg, Born, Jordan, and Dirac) did use the particle description. Heisenberg's particle picture in the uncertainty relation just arose from his particle formalism; hence, Bohr knew exactly what Heisenberg implied and even found the latter's use of the formalism perfectly correct, but he just did not approve of how Heisenberg analyzed the measurement situation.
²²⁰ Actually, this article was the English translation of Jordan's *Habilitation* lecture in Göttingen [entitled 'Kausalität und Statistik in der modernen Physik,' published before in *Naturwissenschaften* (Jordan, 1927c)], which had also been carefully studied in Copenhagen (see Heisenberg to Pauli, 5 February 1927) and our earlier reference to it.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0222 -->

190

## Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

Here, Bohr entered into the discussion, for he believed that he had in hand a superior treatment of the question; in any case, a statistical time (or space) concept did not fit into his thinking.$^{221}$ So, he finally began the process of writing by comparing several drafts of an answer to Campbell's letter.$^{222}$ To complicate matters for the historian, he simultaneously worked on a longer manuscript, which he announced in a letter to Ralph Fowler with the words: 'At present I am busy myself preparing a paper on the more philosophical aspect of quantum theory, which as you know I have planned so long, but for which I think I now have collected the material.' (Bohr to R. Fowler, 10 June 1927) As he had become accustomed, Bohr dictated the paper to Oskar Klein, and the latter knew that this would turn into a lengthy and at times frustrating job:

> The worst I had was in the summer of 1927 working on complementarity. We were not in the country then, and I came every day to him, and he began to dictate. The next day, that which he had dictated, was not used, and we began over [again]. I think ... he tried to write a little too early. Partly he was tired, and partly the ideas were still not at the stage to be written. (O. Klein, AHQP Interview, 1963)

However, during those days, the pressure of time on Bohr increased, for he had agreed to attend, besides the fifth Solvay Conference on Physics in October, also the *Congresso Internazionale dei Fisici* in Como. Thus, many pages of manuscripts were written by Bohr and Klein.$^{223}$

Only very slowly did Bohr's ideas take shape. On 2 July 1927, he started with a study of the space-time description in quantum and wave mechanics and emphasized in a manuscript dated 8 July 'the peculiar dualistic character which the description [of atomic phenomena] possesses at present'; the manuscript of 10 July contains the first mention of the concept of 'complementarity,' and it opens, in English translation, with the statements:

> All information about atoms expressed in classical concepts.
> All classical concepts defined through space-time pictures.
> Therefore beginning of quantum [theory] piecewise use of space-time-pictures formally connected by relations containing Planck's constant. And on conservation of energy and momentum.

---

Klaus Stolzenburg provided in his doctoral dissertation a more detailed discussion of the contents of these manuscripts (Stolzenburg, 1977).

The connections of essentially discontinuous and statistical kind. The endeavours of connecting the statistical laws with the properties of pictures thus implied that they appeared as generalization of classical theory, and in particular converge to the demands of this theory in the limit [where] in statistical applications one may disregard the discontinuous element. Led to the recognition of a far-reaching correspondence between the quantum theory and the classical theory and of the programme of developing a [consistent?] quantitative description [by] looking for analogous features in the classical theory. However, it proved impossible to express this quantitatively by space-time pictures. [Indeed?], the theory exhibited a duality when one considered on the one hand the superposition principle and on the other hand the conservation of energy and momentum.
Complementary aspects of experience that cannot be united into a space-time picture based on classical theories. (Bohr in Kalckar, 1985b, p. 61)

Bohr then continued to sketch cases of 'strong conflict with the classical space-time description' (light waves and matter waves), mentioned the fact that 'measurement of energy and momentum with given accuracy implies ... impossibility of interferences and superposition,' and turned to the 'statistical use of classical concepts' as 'first attempted by connecting space-time pictures with conservation of energy and momentum.' He finally concluded:

> Modern development provides the means. The means symbolic. And treatment fundamentally statistical. Heisenberg's investigation of the relationship between statistics and the conditions of measurements. Gives an essential contribution to the understanding of the *consistency* of the theory and at the same time to its *proper* application. Close relations to the space-time problem. (Bohr, *loc. cit.*, p. 62)

Klein added to Bohr's handwritten manuscript the topics: 'Impossibility of consistency and the principles for the application of the theory' and 'The problem of visualizability.'

As already mentioned, the writing of the note to *Nature* and of the long paper went on hand in hand. On 19 August 1927, Bohr informed Pauli that he now 'wanted to apply full force to obtain a somewhat clarified form' for his Como lecture and therefore shifted the completion of the *Nature* note. A week later, he confirmed the work on the lecture in a letter to Heisenberg and remarked about its contents:

> These are essentially the points we have discussed so often; but I constantly find new insights (*Belehrung*) by stressing how in particular the non-observability or, more correctly, the impossibility to define phases provides the possibility of unifying the demand for the individuality of the single processes with the principle of superposition. (Bohr to Heisenberg, 24 August 1927)

Finally, he just stated: 'I hope in Como to be able to give a reasonably clear account of my views.' (Bohr to Darwin, 29 August 1927)

The last few days before departing for Como became very hectic, and Klein recalled:

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0224 -->

> Bohr was trying to finish [his lecture]. Then he suddenly said: "Now everything is ready except the 'letter to the editor.'" We were a little astonished, but he meant a special [covering] letter accompanying the "letter to the editor," and he wrote "Niels Bohr." Then he got very upset because he should have written "N. Bohr." So his brother said: "But your name *is* Niels." They were going to take a taxi to the station; their train was going a little after 12:00. I left for home, I think, a little before that. The next morning, when I came, I heard immediately that they had just left in the morning, and that was because in the last minute they couldn't find their passports.
> I heard also that the paper was not sent away, but that he had taken it with him.
> (O. Klein, AHQP Interview, 1963)

These remarks imply that the letter to *Nature* had been finished eventually, but not the Como lecture.$^{224}$

### (g) The Como Lecture and Its Publication (September–October 1927)

The Italian physicists invited their colleagues to the large international Volta Congress to be held in Como from 11 to 20 September. In the *Istituto Carducci*, a nearly complete assembly of the leading atomic physicists from all over the world came together: Niels Bohr, Max Born, Louis de Broglie, Léon Brillouin, Arthur H. Compton, Peter Debye, William Duane, Enrico Fermi, James Franck, Jacob Frenkel, Walther Gerlach, Edwin H. Hall, Werner Heisenberg, Hendrik Kramers, Max von Laue, Hendrik Lorentz, Robert A. Millikan, Friedrich Paschen, Wolfgang Pauli, Max Planck, Léon Rosenfeld, Megh Nad Saha, Adolf Smekal, Arnold Sommerfeld, Otto Stern, Richard C. Tolman, Eugene Wigner, Pieter Zeeman, and the very interested and able mathematician John von Neumann.$^{225}$ Bohr's lecture on 16 September—by then partly written—could not reach a more distinguished audience.

The contents of the lecture may be reconstructed from the eight-page manuscript prepared at the last minute—i.e., on 13 September 1927—which became rather sketchy toward the end.$^{226}$ After a brief introduction pointing out the fun-

---

$^{224}$ Among the 'Como Lecture II' files in the Niels Bohr Archive, a practically finished manuscript of the intended letter to *Nature* exists, for which Kalckar (1985b, p. 28) assumed a later date, 'perhaps even shortly before Bohr's departure.' On the other hand, in the same file another manuscript of eight handwritten pages exists, entitled 'Fundamental Problems of the Quantum Theory' and dated 13 September 1927—hence, it must have been written in Como, just three days before the lecture and represents a draft for it. In a letter to Yoshio Nishina, dated 6 September 1927, Bohr wrote: 'I am leaving for Como tomorrow and will be away for some weeks,' which would imply that he left Copenhagen either on 7 or 8 September.

$^{225}$ Those most conspicuous by their absence were Albert Einstein, who was invited but could not attend, just as Paul Dirac and Erwin Schrödinger could not; Satyendra Nath Bose had been invited, but the invitation to him was addressed simply as Professor Bose, Physics Department, Calcutta University, Calcutta, India. The invitation was clearly intended for S. N. Bose, who, at that time was at Dacca University; the only Bose present in the Physics Department at Calcutta University was 'Debendra M.' Bose, who received the invitation addressed to 'Bose' at Calcutta and attended the congress at Como (S. N. Bose, *Conversations*, quoted in Mehra, 1975b).

$^{226}$ See Footnote 224; the facsimile of the English manuscript and a transcription have been reproduced in Bohr, 1985, pp. 75–88.
