II.4 Complementarity 193

damental limitations of the concepts of classical physics when applied to atomic phenomena, especially the breakdown of the standard procedure of measurement—'we cannot speak of independent tools of measurement'—Bohr displayed the new methods of observation based on the properties of light and material particles (according to de Broglie) and thus derived the general commutation relations,

$$ \Delta x \cdot \Delta p_x \sim \Delta y \cdot \Delta p_y \sim \Delta z \cdot \Delta p_z \sim \Delta t \cdot \Delta E \sim h, \quad (127) $$

limiting the position $(x)$, momentum $(p)$, time $(t)$, and energy $(E)$ measurements. Then, he sketched out a particular experiment in some detail:

> Let a light beam or beam of electrons pass out of a hole. Let us assume that a plane wave falls on a hole, in order that we may know where they are and let us assume that we close the hole in order to know what time they come out. We see at once that if we open the hole a time $t$, the frequency is only defined by $\Delta \nu = \frac{1}{t}$, and the energy of the light-quantum and the electron is therefore only known by an accuracy $\Delta t \Delta E \approx h$. Let us in order to know the energy not care about the time and the hole be left open, what is then the accuracy with which we know the momentum? If the diameter of the hole is $l$, the outpassing wave will be diffracted over an angle of magnitude $\alpha = \lambda/l$. Now the absolute value of the momentum is $h/\lambda = p$. The component parallel to the hole however will be underdetermined to the amount
>
> $$ \Delta p = \alpha p, \quad [\text{hence}] \text{ also } \Delta p \cdot \Delta l \sim h. \quad [(128)] $$

Of course these illustrations give nothing new, everything is contained in the above general formula [(127)]; it shows however clearly how impossible it is in experimental arrangements to go beyond the limitations discussed. (Bohr, 1985, p. 79)

The following items (of the lecture) were just sketched briefly, either in complete sentences or (finally) in phrases, such as:

> The complementary features of the apparent contrary claims of individuality and superposition [find their] explanation thereby that such agencies as free material particles and radiation in empty space are abstractions according to quantum theory. They can only be observed through their interactions.
> In order to discuss the possibilities of observation let us consider the simplest case, that of Compton effect ... (General Compton effect).
> General interpretation problem.
> ...
> Symbolic method. Observability $\cong$ Unobservability.
> ...
> Quantum paradoxes. (Bohr, *loc. cit.*, pp. 79–80)

It must be assumed that Bohr went in his lecture beyond what he had written in the above manuscript, which thus gives only an indication of what he presented in

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0226 -->

194  Chapter II  Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

more detail before his audience. On the other hand, the Como lecture also deviated from the paper published in the conference proceedings, which was formulated afterward. Probably what Bohr said might be properly described by his own words in introducing the published paper:

> I shall try by making use of simple considerations and without going into any details of technical-mathematical character to describe to you a certain general point of view which I believe is suited to give an impression of the general trend of the development of the theory from its very beginning and which I hope will be helpful in order to harmonize the apparently conflicting views taken by different scientists. (Bohr, 1928a, p. 565)

The printed discussions of the lecture throw further light on the lecture itself. One first notices that only well-known experts of the subject of quantum mechanics and—besides Enrico Fermi—only those close to Bohr participated. Thus, Max Born started by praising the ‘pertinent manner’ of Bohr’s presentation, then added a few remarks on the indeterminism in the theory, as he had shown himself in the case of collision problems, and finally drew attention to the recent mathematical work of von Neumann on the operators in quantum mechanics and their distribution law. Kramers, in an extended remark dealing with the Compton effect, concluded that:

> the main point in the modern explanation is, that the conservation laws in these experiments only have a meaning to a certain approximation due to the fact that on the wave mechanics the occurrence of a Compton effect in a definite region in space, and within a definite region of time, can only be described by means of light waves and matter waves, which are not exactly monochromatic waves with a definite direction of propagation in space, but which form beams limited in time and space. (Kramers, in Bohr, 1928a, p. 592)

Heisenberg first compared the situations in relativity and quantum theory, respectively, before he stressed a major feature of the process of observation in atomic physics:

> In quantum mechanics, as Professor Bohr has displayed, observation plays a quite peculiar role. One may treat the whole world as *one* mechanical system, but then only a mathematical problem remains while the access to observation is closed off. To get an observation, one must therefore cut out a partial system somewhere from the world, and one must make “statements” or “observations” just about this partial system. Therefore one destroys the fine connections of phenomena, and the very point where we place the cut between the observed system, on the one hand, and the observer and his apparatus, on the other hand, we have to expect difficulties for our conception (*Anschauung*). (Heisenberg, in Bohr, 1928a, p. 593)

After discussing the force-free motion of an electron, Heisenberg emphasized the importance of ‘the discontinuous change of the wave picture of observation’;

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0227 -->

II.4  Complementarity  195

hence, ‘One must therefore take seriously the concept of “probability waves.” These waves do not have the immediate reality which we earlier associated with the waves of Maxwell’s theory. One must interpret them as probability waves, and therefore expect sudden changes with each new observation’ (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*, p. 594). The further discussion remarks of Fermi, Heisenberg, and Pauli concerned various aspects of statistics and radiation theory.

Unlike these experts, other participants were not terribly impressed, and Bohr often referred to a remark of Eugene Wigner summarizing the prevailing feeling as: ‘This lecture will not induce any of us to change his own opinion about quantum mechanics.’<sup>227</sup> Notably, Rosenfeld stated about Bohr’s lecture: ‘This complementarity business was just a way of putting [into] words the situation that everybody knew. I suppose if you look at it now, the Como lecture did not clinch the argument; all this question about defining the concepts came later.’ (Rosenfeld, AHQP Interview) Perhaps Klein, though not present at the meeting, hit the mark when he assigned the major fault to the fact that Bohr had not yet well organized his ideas in the manuscript he used because ‘this was so short that nobody could have understood it really.’ However:

> After Como Pauli went with him to a place at Lake Como … I think they stayed [there] for a week or a fortnight even. Then Pauli got him to write it down in a very extended way, and that was the main manuscript …, I think, written in German. But then came proofs and proofs and proofs, and finally after many proofs he [Bohr] wrote a new manuscript because there were so many corrections during the winter. (O. Klein, AHQP Interview, 1963)

The correspondence of that period confirms Klein’s story. Thus, e.g., Bohr reported to Darwin on 16 October 1927: ‘On the way back [from Como] we spent a very nice week in Azzano on the lake.’ On 11 October, he sent the result of the joint endeavour with Pauli, slightly enlarged by additions, to *Naturwissenschaften*, and a copy to Pauli inviting criticism.<sup>228</sup> Although the wording differs from the one in the later published paper in the proceedings of the Volta Congress, the first four sections of the latter can be found in the October manuscript; only the fifth section of the Como publication containing a discussion of the Stern–Gerlach effect and other examples provide material beyond the manuscript.<sup>229</sup> Thus, the

> In fact, my own view of the Como lecture when I read it was that Bohr was just putting in a rather heavy form things which had been expressed much more simply by Born and which were current in Göttingen at that time. I did not see, did not feel any of the subtlety that was in it, and I suppose that this was the general feeling in Göttingen. (Rosenfeld, AHQP Interview)

<sup>228</sup> A copy of this manuscript does not exist in the Niels Bohr Archive; however, a fairly complete English translation, dated 12–13 October, was sent to Darwin with the letter on 16 October, evidently intended for publication in *Nature* (see Bohr, 1985, pp. 91–98).

196  Chapter II  Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

English manuscript and the published paper (also in English: Bohr, 1928a) do provide a fair impression of what Bohr actually presented at Como (although not verbatim and in full detail, of course).

The first item (of the manuscript, which corresponded also to Section 1 of the paper) deals with the general conditions for observation and description in atomic physics. It starts with two guiding sentences: ‘The quantum theory is characterized by the acknowledgement of a fundamental limitation in the classical physical ideas when applied to atomic phenomena. The situation thus created is of a peculiar nature, since our interpretation of the experimental material rests exclusively upon the classical ideas.’ Yet, an atomic theory exists whose essence can be expressed by the quantum postulate, ‘which to any atomic process open to direct observation attributes an essential discontinuity or rather individuality, completely foreign to classical theories.’ This quantum postulate also implies ‘that no observation of atomic phenomena is possible without an essential disturbance’; hence, ‘the idea of means of observation independent of phenomena (and vice versa) cannot be maintained.’ The consequences include, notably, the statistical character of the description of microscopic systems; therefore, one must ‘regard the space-time coordination and the claim of causality, the union of which characterizes the classical theories, as complementary features of the description of experience, symbolizing the idealization of observation and definition respectively’ (Bohr, 1985, p. 91).

Indeed, Bohr proposed a dualistic description of the quantum phenomena—i.e., by particle and wave pictures—united by the idea of complementarity.<sup>230</sup> From this point of view, he rejected a new proposal of Louis de Broglie to join ‘the two apparently contradictory sides of the phenomena by regarding the individual particles or light-quanta as singularities in the wave field’ as ‘resting upon the concepts of classical physics,’ hence, ‘not suited to help us over the fundamental difficulties’ (Bohr, 1985, p. 92).<sup>231</sup> Bohr’s dualistic description rested on Einstein’s relativistic equations

$$E = h\nu \quad \text{and} \quad P = h\sigma \qquad (129)$$

<sup>229</sup> The manuscript, however, states toward the end that ‘a number of simple applications were recently given at the Volta Congress at Como’ (Bohr, 1985, p. 98).

<sup>230</sup> Bohr explained this dual description in some detail in a lecture, entitled ‘The Quantum Postulate and the Recent Development of Atomic Theory’ and presented on 18 November 1927, before the *Royal Danish Academy of Sciences* (see Bohr, 1985, p. 108, and the abstract, Bohr, 1928b). Neither in his Como lecture nor the latter one did Bohr explicitly define complementarity. Perhaps Pauli was the first to give a precise definition of this notion. In his article for the *Handbuch der Physik*, Pauli called two classical concepts—and not two modes of description—complementary ‘if the applicability of the one (e.g., position coordinate) stands in the relation of exclusion to that of the other (e.g., momentum)’ in the sense that any experimental setup for measuring the one interferes destructively with any experimental setup for measuring the other (Pauli, 1933c, p. 89). In contrast to Bohr, Pauli ascribed complementarity to two notions that belong to the same classical mode of description (e.g., the particle picture) and not to two mutually exclusive descriptions. In Pauli’s view, it was this notion of complementarity that was *the* characteristic feature of quantum mechanics, which he therefore proposed to call the ‘theory of complementarity’ (*Komplementaritätstheorie*) in analogy to the ‘theory of relativity.’ (See Jammer, 1966, p. 355; see also our discussion in Chapter IV.)

<sup>231</sup> For the theory of the ‘double solution,’ see L. de Broglie (1927d, e) and his Solvay report (L. de Broglie, 1928) and our discussion in Section II.6 below.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0229 -->

II.4  Complementarity  197

for energy $E$ and momentum $P$ of the light-quantum, with $\nu$ and $\sigma$ denoting the frequency and the wave number, respectively, or similar formulae of de Broglie for matter waves. Within the classical wave description—i.e., the theory of optical instruments—the relations

$$\Delta t \Delta \nu \sim 1 \quad \text{and} \quad \Delta x \Delta \sigma_x \sim 1 \qquad (130)$$

followed, where $\Delta t$ and $\Delta x$ denote the extension of the wave field in time and a given space direction ($x$), and $\Delta \nu$ and $\Delta \sigma_x$ give the order of magnitude of the corresponding variation of the frequency and the wavenumber of the wave groups. Turning to the particle picture, ‘the greatest attainable accuracy with which the energy and momentum can be defined’ is

$$\Delta t \Delta E \sim \Delta x \Delta P_x \sim h. \qquad (131)$$

These relations represent the ‘uncertainty relations’ of Heisenberg (1927b), but in contrast to the latter’s opinion Bohr now concluded: ‘It must be remembered that the uncertainty in question is not a simple consequence of a discontinuous change of energy and momentum … the question is rather that of the impossibility of defining rigorously such a change, when the space-time coordination of the individuals is also contained’ (Bohr, 1985, p. 93).

Bohr then turned to the formulation of the laws of interaction. He claimed that, after the preliminary correspondence-limit results of Hendrik Kramers in 1924, the quantum mechanics of Heisenberg, Born, Jordan, and Dirac as well as the extension of this scheme to radiation (Dirac, 1927b) had provided a proper description.<sup>232</sup> On the other hand, this successful theory still exhibited limitations, as Bohr stated:

> It must not be forgotten, however, that it has not yet been possible in the formulation of the matrix problems to do justice to the claims of relativity theory. This is intuitively connected with … the simplification of the atomic problem appearing in the resignation as to time relations.
>
> Although the matrix theory directly takes cognizance of the individual processes thus placing the question of the possibilities of observation into the foreground, still the inner consistency of the theory is achieved only at the expense of any immediate interpretation of the results of calculation. (Bohr, 1985, p. 95)

In contrast to such deficiencies of the matrix formulation, which, in Bohr’s opinion, could not be resolved even in the generalized transformation theory of Dirac and Jordan, ‘a simple description of the situation involving the complementary ideas of individuality and superposition provided by the method of wave mechanics developed by Schrödinger on the basis of the ideas of de Broglie’ existed (Bohr, *loc. cit.*, p. 96).

<sup>232</sup> These parts of the manuscript (Bohr, 1985, pp. 95–97) were later extended into Section 3 of the published paper (Bohr, 1928a).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0230 -->

198 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

On the other hand, the continuum interpretation of atomic phenomena by classical resonance phenomena also fails because the wave picture needs a reinterpretation ‘by the explicit use of the quantum postulate and the concept of material particles’—as occurred in Klein’s discussion of the radiation problem.²³³ The interference of waves naturally leads to washing out the phases of a wave group describing individual objects, whether light-quanta or electrons. Uncertainty relations, however, which take care of this fact, do not exhaust the statistical character of the description of a general quantum problem. ‘On the whole it appears that only by taking the possibilities of definition and of observation simultaneously into account it is possible to obtain an adequate representation of the correspondence between the quantum theory and the classical theory as well as their fundamental difference,’ Bohr concluded (Bohr, loc. cit., p. 98).

In the manuscript, Bohr finally pointed out that Schrödinger’s formulation ‘depends essentially on the artifice of a multidimensional space … which prevents a direct comparison with the space-time description of the classical theory.’ Bohr claimed, however:

In interpreting observation it is always possible to reduce the considerations to three of the spatial coordinates only. This is connected with the fact that in all direct experiences about atomic properties we are concerned with the behaviour of atoms in interaction with radiation or free particles. We must even admit that the definition of all concepts entering in the description of observational results presupposes these abstractions. (Bohr, loc. cit.)

The latter statement did not receive the blessing of Pauli, to whom Bohr sent the original German manuscript and requested his critical comments. On 17 October, Pauli wrote back:

This I hold not to be correct, and I should raise objections to it, because it is a point which is especially dear to my heart. If we have a system consisting of several particles, then the eigenfunctions ψ(q₁ … q_N) in the multidimensional configuration space can, as far as I can see, in principle be empirically ascertained by statistical utilization of results of observation. And this applies to the function itself, not only to a mean value integrated over all except three coordinates. … Now one can in principle reduce the ascertainment of this function to the observation of free particles if one performs collision experiments, in which the system under investigation is struck simultaneously by several particles … It is true that after all we have here to do with free particles, however with several of them, and it seems to me quite misleading to say that one may here restrict oneself to a total of three (space- or momentum-like) coordinates. (Pauli to Bohr, 17 October 1927, in Pauli, 1979, p. 412; English translation in Kalckar, 1985b, p. 34)

Pauli also clarified several other points, but finally admitted: ‘By and large I am very pleased with your paper, and I believe that the passages mentioned above can

II.5 The Origin of Quantum Field Theory 199

still be easily improved.’ (Pauli to Bohr, 17 October 1927) However, what Bohr had in mind with considerations in ‘three space coordinates only’ must be derived from the simultaneous development of a new discipline: quantum field theory.

## II.5 The Origin of Quantum Field Theory

### (a) Introduction

In (the published version of) his Como lecture, Niels Bohr included the following statement on the radiation theory:

> The treatment of the radiation problem by the new quantum-theoretical methods meant to begin with just a quantitative formulation of this correspondence situation [i.e., drawing conclusions from the use of classical electrodynamics in a certain quantum-theoretical reformulation]. In the more rigorous form of theory developed by Dirac (1927b) the radiation field itself is included in a closed system under consideration. Thus it becomes possible in a rational way to take account of the atomistic character of radiation demanded by the quantum theory. The renunciation regarding space-time pictures characterizing this treatment may be regarded as a striking illustration of the complementary character of quantum theory. (Bohr, 1928e, p. 585)

In the Solvay report, which he wrote later, Bohr mentioned not only Paul Dirac’s work of early 1927, but also a more recent investigation of Pascual Jordan and Oskar Klein (1927). In particular, he said that these authors:

> have recently arrived at the formulation of the problem of interaction expressed by the Schrödinger wave equation [for particles] taking as starting point the wave representation of individual particles and applying a symbolic method closely related to the deepgoing treatment of the radiation problem developed by Dirac from the point of view of the matrix theory. (Bohr, 1928e, p. 587)

The topics referred to here implied the creation of a new method, quantum field theory, which immediately permitted an extension of quantum mechanics into the relativistic domain. This method might appear to be an obvious consequence, because a proper treatment of the most original relativistic system, namely, electromagnetic radiation, served as the initial model for handling arbitrary assemblies of material particles with either low (i.e., nonrelativistic) or high (i.e., relativistic) velocities. In one respect, the new method pioneered by Dirac, Jordan, and Klein, and subsequently extended by Jordan and Wigner (1928) and Jordan and Pauli (1928), opened new applications of the quantum-mechanical formalism. In another respect, and this is the essential one in the present context, quantum field theory assumed a unique role in providing a perfect scheme for unifying the basic wave and particle duality of atomic phenomena. The contents of the present section can best be summarized in the words of Jordan and Wigner, who, in February 1928, wrote:

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0232 -->

200 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

Already the first investigations on a systematic formulation of the matrix scheme of quantum mechanics yielded hints to the fact that the known difficulties of radiation theory may be overcome by applying the quantum-mechanical method not only to material atoms but also to the radiation field (Born, Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926). In this respect, progress has been achieved recently on the quantum-mechanical description of the electromagnetic field, on the one hand, and on formulating the quantum mechanics of particles, on the other, which avoids the wave representation in the abstract [multidimensional] coordinate space in favour of a representation by quantum waves in the usual three-dimensional space and attempts to explain the existence of material particles in a way similar to the existence of light-quanta (or of any physical phenomenon that can be accounted for by the assumption of light-quanta) by the quantization of electromagnetic waves. (Jordan and Wigner, 1928, p. 631)

Consistent with this first-hand report, the historical events connected with the creation of quantum field theory$^{234}$ proceeded in three approaches, each motivated slightly differently:

(1) the quantum-theoretical reformulation of classical fields—so to say, a continuation of the original Heisenberg programme of 1925—by Jordan and Dirac in early 1927;
(2) the quantization of the de Broglie waves—a programme initiated by Born and Bohr in 1926 and explored in particular by Jordan and Klein in the middle of 1927;
(3) the systematic quantization of Bose and Fermi fields—a programme of Jordan, Klein, and Wigner in the second half of 1927 and early 1928.

Simultaneously with the topics (2) and (3), Jordan and Pauli laboured on a genuinely relativistic quantum electrodynamics along the same lines.

**(b) The Quantum-Theoretical Reformulation of the Radiation Field (September 1925-November 1926)**

The first paper on matrix mechanics ended 'with an attempt to incorporate electromagnetic field laws in the new theory' (Born and Jordan, 1925b, p. 858). Although the authors conceded the 'provisional character' of their considerations, they gave a clear description of how to treat a system of free electromagnetic waves, namely, as a system of harmonic oscillators. Because of the linearity property of Maxwell's equations, Born and Jordan saw no problem in reformulating them as matrix equations and doing the same for a Hertzian dipole. Subsequently, they derived a quantum-mechanical expression for the radiative energy loss, that is

$$ -\frac{dW}{dt} = \frac{64\pi^4 e^4}{3c^2} \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left[ \sum_{k<n} \nu(n,k)^4 |q(n,k)|^2 \right], \quad (132) $$

$^{234}$ For a sketchy historical review of the origin of quantum field theory, see Darrigol, 1986; also, for a more personal story, see Dirac, 1983.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0233 -->

II.5 The Origin of Quantum Field Theory 201

with $q(n, k)$ denoting the matrix components of the position vector.$^{235}$ A few months later, in the three-man paper submitted in November 1925, Jordan introduced the next attempt at a quantum-theoretical reformulation of the radiation problem. By treating the statistical behaviour of eigenvibrations in matrix mechanics, he derived 'for the interference fluctuations the right result, i.e., both the classical and the Einstein [light-quantum] terms,' and he succeeded in doing so without involving explicitly 'a mixture of theoretical wave and light-quantum considerations.'$^{236}$ Jordan would later consider his contribution always as the starting point of quantum field theory, though the result—originally called 'particularly encouraging'—soon fell into oblivion or was played down even by his collaborators.$^{237}$ Also, other experts in quantum theory, especially Einstein, disagreed; hence, Jordan abandoned his pursuit of this topic for the next two years. In his place, another young quantum physicist, Paul Dirac, proceeded to deal with the radiation problem in the new theory.

Dirac, who had embarked upon his work on quantum mechanics—following Heisenberg's key discovery—and developed his own generalized $q$-number theory, began to occupy himself with radiation problems in the new theory in a paper that was received on 27 March 1926, by the *Proceedings of the Royal Society of London* (Dirac, 1926c).$^{238}$ In particular, he applied a relativistic $q$-number scheme to treat the Compton effect, i.e., the scattering of X-rays by electrons, obtaining satisfactory expressions for the scattered intensities.$^{239}$ A couple of weeks after completing this investigation, he received a letter from Copenhagen, in which Heisenberg drew his attention to Schrödinger's wave mechanics—'which should be closely related to quantum mechanics'—and asked the question: 'Have you considered how the Schrödinger treatment of the hydrogen atom is connected with the quantum-mechanical one? The mathematical problem interests me especially, because I believe that one can win from it a great deal for the physical significance of the theory.' (Heisenberg to Dirac, 9 April 1926)$^{240}$ Dirac, still preoccupied with his own problem, reacted a little unhappily,$^{241}$ and recalled:

> Well, my answer was that I had not considered Schrödinger's theory. I felt at first a bit hostile to it. The reason was that I felt that we had already a perfectly good quantum mechanics, which I believed could be developed for handling all the prob-

$^{235}$ For details, see Volume 3, Section III.5.
$^{236}$ The quotations are from the letter of Heisenberg to Pauli, 23 October 1925, and Born, Heisenberg, and Jordan, respectively. See also our discussion of the problem in Volume 3, Section IV.2.
$^{237}$ Thus, Jordan recalled that 'Heisenberg later explicitly doubted whether this application, which I had made of quantum mechanics to the case of a system of *infinitely many degrees of freedom*, was correct' (Jordan to Van der Waerden, 10 April 1926).
$^{238}$ See Volume 4, Section V.4.
$^{239}$ Dirac was quite proud of his result, and he immediately informed Arnold Sommerfeld, who visited Cambridge in spring 1926, about it (see Dirac, 1977, p. 132).
$^{240}$ The letter was written in German; for the translation, see Brown and Rechenberg, 1987, especially, p. 122.
$^{241}$ Dirac's reply to Heisenberg has been lost.

202 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Chapter II &nbsp;&nbsp;Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

lems of atomic theory. Why should one go back to the pre-Heisenberg stage when we did not have a quantum mechanics and try to build it up anew? (Dirac, 1977, p. 131)

Indeed, Dirac, initially, rather 'resented' wave mechanics and showed 'a hostility which persisted for a while'—at least until some time after he had completed the paper on Compton radiation.²⁴² Heisenberg, however, upon the receipt of Dirac's negative answer, did not give up, for in his next letter, he wrote: 'I quite agree with your criticism of Schrödinger's paper with regard to the wave theory of matter. This theory must be inconsistent just like the wave theory of light.' Still, he ventured to continue in a more positive vein:

I see the real progress made by Schrödinger's theory in this: that the same mathematical equation can be interpreted as point-mechanics in a non-classical kinematics and as a wave theory according to Schrödinger. I had always hoped that the solution to the paradoxes of quantum theory could later on be found in this way. (Heisenberg to Dirac, 26 May 1926)

In the same letter, Heisenberg gave 'a detailed exposition of the connection between the Schrödinger theory and matrix mechanics,' which Dirac later found 'very helpful.' Nevertheless, he did not concern himself with wave mechanics before several more months had passed.²⁴³ Then, gradually, his attitude changed, and ultimately he took up the study of wave mechanics 'with enthusiasm,' learning everything about it, because it employed a 'new technique [of eigenvalues and eigenvectors] very little known in Cambridge' (Dirac, 1977, p. 133). In summer 1926, Dirac applied what he had learned to a new problem: atomic systems containing many particles. He obtained the important result that assemblies of identical particles obeying Bose or Fermi statistics were described by symmetrical and antisymmetrical wave functions, respectively (Dirac, 1926f).²⁴⁴
This paper, completed before Dirac left Cambridge for extended periods of stay in Copenhagen and Göttingen, exhibited several peculiar features characterizing Dirac's opinions and intentions. To begin with, he considered Schrödinger's equation as a representation of the very principles of (the Göttingen–Cambridge) quantum mechanics, notably, the characteristic and fundamental commutation relations. Although the familiar methods of differential calculus easily permitted the generalization of the wave-mechanical scheme—e.g., to deal with relativistic problems in which space and time coordinates appear on the same footing—and to calculate the matrix elements of quantum-mechanical problems, Dirac expected the 'very satisfactory characteristic of Heisenberg's matrix mechanics'—i.e., the

²⁴² The fact that Schrödinger's communication on the hydrogen atom came out in March, shortly after Dirac had published his own paper on the subject (Dirac, 1926a), and the arrival of a rival scheme dealing successfully with the same problem must have annoyed him considerably.
²⁴³ In the meantime, i.e., in May and June 1926, Dirac wrote his Ph.D. thesis, in which he made no reference to Schrödinger's theory.
²⁴⁴ The paper 'On the Theory of Quantum Mechanics' was submitted toward the end of August 1926. For details, see Volume 5, Part 2, pp. 757–768.

II.5 &nbsp;&nbsp;The Origin of Quantum Field Theory &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;203

fact that 'it enables one to calculate just the quantities that are of physical importance'—'to persist in all future developments of the theory.'²⁴⁵ Hence, in particular, the main result of the symmetrical or antisymmetrical wave equation follows from the 'physical indistinguishability' of systems, in which identical atoms or electrons exchange their roles. Further, in applying the wave-mechanical methods to systems involving arbitrary perturbations, Dirac used the standard (Göttingen–Cambridge) prescription, namely, to identify the particle number with absolute squares of quantum-mechanical amplitudes. That is, in his opinion, it was quantum mechanics that determined the physical content, and Schrödinger's theory merely provided an elegant mathematical method for treating practical problems.
As an example of this procedure, he treated a perturbed atomic system, depending on the variables $p$ (momentum), $q$ (position), and $t$ (time), described by the Schrödinger equations,

$$
(H_0 - W + V)\psi = 0, \tag{133}
$$

with $H_0$ denoting the Hamiltonian operator of the unperturbed system, $V$ a real perturbation potential (Dirac used the symbol $A$), and $W$ the eigenvalues of the perturbed system. Then, the *Ansatz*,

$$
\psi = \sum_m a_m \psi_m, \tag{134}
$$

evidently solved this equation of motion, provided the coefficients $a_m$ of the eigenfunctions $\psi_m$ (describing the discrete states $m$) depend on time and their absolute square determines the momentary number of atoms in the $m$-th state,

$$
N_m(t) = a_m(t) \cdot a_m^*(t). \tag{135}
$$

From Eq. (133), an equation of motion for $N_m$ followed, i.e.,

$$
\frac{ih}{2\pi} \dot{N}_m = \frac{ih}{2\pi} (\dot{a}_m a_m^* + \dot{a}_m^* a_m) = \sum_n (a_n V_{mn} a_m^* - a_m^* V_{nm} a_m), \tag{136}
$$

where $V_{mn} ( = V_{mn}^*)$ denote the time-dependent matrix elements of the perturbing potential $\left( V\psi_m = \sum_m V_{mn} \psi_m \right)$. Now, in the special case of $V$ describing the perturbation of the atom by the incident radiation polarized in $y$-direction (with

²⁴⁵ See Dirac, 1926f, p. 667. Joan Bromberg, in a perceptive historical analysis that received the assent of Dirac himself, has put Dirac's paper at the beginning of the path leading to quantum electrodynamics (Bromberg, 1977). Our discussion that follows generally agrees with her conclusions; however, we also discuss the possible influence of the Copenhagen environment (and the presence there of Bohr, Heisenberg, and Klein) on Dirac's further contributions and vice versa.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0236 -->

204 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Chapter II &nbsp;&nbsp;Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

$\eta_{mn}$ the polarization matrix, $\kappa$ the strength of the potential, and $c$ the velocity of light *in vacuo*), Dirac wrote,

$$
V_{mn} = \frac{\kappa}{c} \dot{\eta}_{mn} \exp\left[ \frac{2\pi i}{h} (W_m - W_n)t \right], \tag{137}
$$

and expanded the solution $a_m$ as a power series in the parameter $\left( \frac{2\pi}{ihc} \right) \kappa$. He thus calculated the expressions for the intensities of the scattered radiation, and ultimately obtained for the Einstein coefficients of equilibrium blackbody radiation (i.e., unpolarized radiation interacting with atoms in a cavity),

$$
B_{n \to m} = B_{m \to n} = \frac{8\pi^3}{3h^2c} |P_{nm}|^2 \tag{138}
$$

(with $|P_{nm}|^2$ the sum of the squares of the matrix elements associated with the three polarizations). Hence, he almost arrived at a nearly quantum-mechanical derivation of the blackbody law along Einstein's path of 1916 without invoking light-quanta, except that 'one cannot take spontaneous emission into account without a more elaborate theory involving the position of the various atoms and the interference of their individual emissions'—so Dirac concluded in August 1926 (Dirac, 1926f, p. 677).
The same attitude of using 'the wave equation merely as a mathematical help for the calculation of the matrix elements which are then interpreted in accordance with assumptions of matrix elements' persisted in the next paper on 'The Compton Effect in Wave Mechanics,' which Dirac submitted from Copenhagen in November (Dirac, 1926g).²⁴⁶ Evidently, the discussion with Niels Bohr and Oskar Klein, who stressed at that time the value of the wave theory as an approach independent of matrix mechanics, had not made much impact on Dirac. Again, a month later, in the introduction to his paper on transformation theory, he considered what he called 'Schrödinger's wave representation of quantum mechanics' just to provide 'new ways of obtaining physical results from the theory based on the assumption that the square of the amplitude of the wave function can in certain cases be interpreted as a probability' (Dirac, 1927a, p. 621). That is, he unabashedly stuck to the Göttingen–Cambridge programme, except that he would not follow the latest move of Born and Jordan, who assumed the 'notion of probability' to constitute a necessary element entering 'into the ultimate description of mechanical processes' (Dirac, loc. cit., p. 641). Rather, he joined Heisenberg in the view—not at all shared by Bohr!—that the generalized (matrix) formulation of quantum mechanics alone would decide the interpretation of all microscopic phenomena without requiring any extra wave-theoretical elements.

²⁴⁶ The above quote is from the 'Note added in proof' of Dirac, 1926g, p. 507. In this paper, Dirac did not use his Copenhagen address; he submitted it as being from St. John's College, Cambridge.

II.5 &nbsp;&nbsp;The Origin of Quantum Field Theory &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;205

**(c) Dirac's Quantum Theory of Emission and Absorption of Radiation (December 1926–April 1927)**

In the last two months of his Copenhagen stay, Dirac composed a third publication, at the end of which he expressed his thanks to Bohr 'for his interest in this work and much friendly discussion about it.' Still, the contents of the paper, as described in the summary, did not reveal much persuasion to the wave-theoretical point of view as a result of these friendly discussions. In particular, Dirac wrote:

The problem is treated of an assembly of similar systems satisfying the Einstein-Bose statistical mechanics, which interacts with another different system, a Hamiltonian function being obtained to describe the motion. The theory is applied to the interaction of an assembly of light-quanta with an ordinary atom, and it is shown that it gives Einstein's laws for the emission and the absorption of radiation.
The interaction of an atom with electromagnetic waves is then considered and it is shown that if one takes the energies and phases of the waves to be $q$-numbers satisfying the proper quantum conditions instead of $c$-numbers, the Hamiltonian function takes the same form as in the light-quantum treatment. The theory leads to the correct expressions for Einstein's $A$'s and $B$'s. (Dirac, 1927b, p. 265)

It is quite evident that the new investigation on 'The Quantum Theory of Emission and Absorption of Radiation,' although it addressed one of the fundamental problems that had bothered Bohr for more than a dozen years, pursued the familiar path of quantum mechanics and followed Dirac's peculiar intentions, including his standard wish to obtain a fully relativistic theory. Still, he failed to achieve the latter goal, as he admitted:

It appears to be possible to build up a fairly satisfactory theory of the emission of radiation and the reaction of the radiation field on the emitting atom on the basis of a kinematics and dynamics which are not strictly relativistic.... The theory is non-relativistic only on account of the time being counted throughout as a $c$-number, instead of being treated symmetrically with the space-coordinates. The relativistic variation of mass with velocity is taken into account without difficulty. (Dirac, loc. cit., p. 244)

Otherwise, he proceeded from 'very simple ideas' that essentially agreed with those employed by the Göttingen matrix theoreticians, notably, Jordan, more than a year previously.
The radiation field is described as an assembly of linear oscillators, i.e., as being composed of Fourier components belonging to an energy $E_r$ and a canonically conjugate 'phase' $\theta_r$ (denoting rather the time in which the wave was in a given phase). Both variables had to be described by $q$-numbers satisfying the standard commutation relations,

$$
\theta_r E_r - E_r \theta_r = \frac{ih}{2\pi}. \tag{139}
$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0238 -->

‘[Eq. (139)] immediately gives light-quantum properties to the radiation,’ Dirac argued, referring to the paper of Born, Heisenberg, and Jordan (1926).²⁴⁷ Dirac then applied his recent general transformation theory involving delta-function expressions to represent the matrix elements of continuous variables, $\xi_k$ and $\eta_k$,
$$\xi_k(\xi', \xi'') = \xi_k' \delta(\xi_1' - \xi_1'') \delta(\xi_2' - \xi_2'') \cdots \delta(\xi_k' - \xi_k'') \delta(\xi_{k+1}' - \xi_{k+1}''),$$
$$\eta_k(\xi', \xi'') = -\frac{ih}{2\pi} \delta(\xi_1' - \xi_1'') \delta(\xi_2' - \xi_2'') \cdots \delta'(\xi_k' - \xi_k'') \delta(\xi_{k+1}' - \xi_{k+1}''), \quad (140)$$
where $\delta'$ is the derivative of $\delta$. Based on these ideas and special tools, Dirac indeed managed to finish successfully the questions in radiation theory that had been left open in August 1926.

As was his custom, Dirac formulated the problem in the most general form as a system consisting of an ensemble of Bose objects (whether oscillators of a radiation field or Einstein atoms) interacting with (or being perturbed by) an atom or another perturbing force $V$.²⁴⁸ To solve the corresponding time-dependent Schrödinger equation (133)—in which the $W\psi$-term corresponds to a time-derivative $\frac{ih}{2\pi} \frac{\partial}{\partial t}$ of the wave function—for the many-body system considered, Dirac proceeded in the following steps, which consisted essentially of a sequence of canonical transformations according to his generalized scheme of December 1926:

**Step 1:** The coefficients $a_r$ of the expansion (134) and their complex conjugates $a_r^*$ (multiplied by $\frac{ih}{2\pi}$) are regarded as a canonical pair of dynamical variables associated with the ‘Hamiltonian function’ $F_1$,
$$F_1 = \sum_{rs} a_r^* V_{rs} a_s, \quad (141)$$
where $V_{rs}$ denote the matrix elements of the perturbing potential.

**Step 2:** A canonical (or contact) transformation
$$a_r = N_r^{1/2} \exp\left(-\frac{2\pi i}{h} \phi_r\right), \quad a_r^* = N_r^{1/2} \exp\left(\frac{2\pi i}{h} \phi_r\right) \quad (142)$$

---

²⁴⁸ Note that now the perturbing potential is due to the atoms, and the unperturbed system consists of the assembly of radiating oscillators. At the end, however, when the equilibrium radiation is considered, it does not matter whether one considers the oscillators of the radiation field or of the atoms (whose frequencies are associated with the term differences).

207

introduces new real variables $N_r = (a_r a_r^*)$ and $\phi_r$, describing the probable number of microscopic objects in the state $r$ and the corresponding phases (up to a factor $\frac{h}{2\pi}$), respectively.

**Step 3:** If appropriate time factors (connected with the energy of the unperturbed ensemble members) are split off, one can go over to the new variables
$$b_r = a_r \exp\left(-\frac{2\pi i}{h} \theta_r\right), \quad b_r^* = a_r^* \exp\left(\frac{2\pi i}{h} \theta_r\right). \quad (143)$$
The equation of motion for the perturbed system then involves the Hamiltonian $F$—expressed in terms of the particle numbers and phases, Eqs. (142) and (143)—
$$F = \sum_{rs} b_r^* H_{rs} b_s = \sum_r W_r N_r + \sum_{rs} v_{rs} N_r^{1/2} N_s^{1/2} \exp\left[\frac{2\pi i}{h}(\theta_r - \theta_s)\right], \quad (144)$$
with the matrix elements of the constant (in time) perturbation.
$$v_{rs} = V_{rs} \left[\frac{2\pi i}{h} (W_r - W_s)t\right]. \quad (145)$$
The expression (144) permits a straightforward ‘visualization’ as: ‘The first term $\sum_r W_r N_r$ is the total proper energy of the [unperturbed] assembly, and the second may be regarded as the addition energy due to the perturbation’ (Dirac, *loc. cit.*, p. 250).

When applied to an assembly of quantum-mechanical objects (‘particles’) obeying Bose statistics, the canonical variables $b_r$ and $b_r^*$ satisfied the commutation relations
$$b_r b_s^* - b_s^* b_r = \delta_{rs} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{for } r = s, \\ 0 & \text{for } r \neq s, \end{cases}$$
$$b_r b_s - b_s b_r = b_r^* b_s^* - b_s^* b_r^* = 0. \quad (146)$$
The transformed canonical variables $N_r$ (particle number) and $\theta_r$ (phase) were obtained via the equations
$$b_r = (N_r + 1)^{1/2} \exp\left(-\frac{2\pi i}{h} \theta_r\right) = \exp\left(-\frac{2\pi i}{h} \theta_r\right) N_r^{1/2},$$
$$b_r^* = N_r^{1/2} \exp\left(-\frac{2\pi i}{h} \theta_r\right) = \exp\left(-\frac{2\pi i}{h} \theta_r\right) (N_r + 1)^{1/2}. \quad (147)$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0240 -->

‘The equations show that the $N_r$ have only integral characteristic values not less than zero, which provides us with a justification for the assumption that the variables are $q$-numbers in the way we have chosen,’ Dirac commented, and added: ‘The numbers of systems in the different states are now ordinary quantum numbers.’ (Dirac, *loc. cit.*, p. 251) With the new variables, the Hamiltonian of the perturbed Bose system obtained the simple form
$$F = \sum_r W_r N_r + \sum_{rs} v_{rs} N_r^{1/2} (N_s + 1 - \delta_{rs})^{1/2} \exp\left[\frac{2\pi i}{h}(\theta_r - \theta_s)\right], \quad (148)$$
and the equation of motion derived from the Schrödinger equation became, accordingly,
$$\frac{ih}{2\pi} \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \psi(N_1', N_2', N_3', \ldots)$$
$$= \sum_{rs} H_{rs} N_r^{1/2} (N_s' + 1 - \delta_{rs}) \psi(N_1', N_2', \ldots N_r' - 1, \ldots N_s' + 1, \ldots), \quad (149)$$
where the squared wave function $|\psi(N_1', N_2', \ldots)|^2$ ‘will be the probability of that distribution in which $N_1'$ systems are in the state 1, $N_2'$ in the state 2, $\ldots$ at any time’ (Dirac, *loc. cit.*, p. 252).

The central point of Dirac’s paper may be seen in the demonstration that the symmetrical wave function $b(r_1 r_2 \ldots)$ of a Bose system satisfying the usual many-body, time-independent Schrödinger equation (Dirac, 1926f); i.e.,
$$\frac{ih}{2\pi} \dot{b}(r_1 r_2 \ldots) = \sum_{s_1 s_2} H_A(r_1 r_2 \ldots; s_1 s_2 \ldots) b(s_1 s_2 \ldots)$$
$$= \sum_m \sum_{s_m \neq r_m} H_{r_m s_m} (r_1 r_2 \ldots r_{m-1} s_m r_{m+1} \ldots) + \sum_n H_{r_n r_n} b(r_1 r_2 \ldots) \quad (150)$$
[with $H_A = H(n)$, where $H(n)$ is the Hamiltonian for the $n$-th system] can be related to the above function $\psi(N_1', N_2, N_3', \ldots)$ of Eq. (149)—which, also dropping the primes, is simply written $b(N_1, N_2, N_3 \ldots)$—through the equation
$$b(N_1 N_2 \ldots) = (N! / N_1! N_2! \ldots)^{1/2} b(r_1 r_2 \ldots). \quad (151)$$
This equation establishes the proper normalization of the Schrödinger–Dirac wave functions, which then become genuine probability amplitudes. Now, the ‘theory may be readily extended to the case when the perturbation consists of interaction with a perturbing dynamical system, the reaction of the perturbed system on the perturbing system being taken into account’ (Dirac, 1927b, p. 255). In Section 4 of his paper, Dirac worked out the case in which he had to add an extra term $H_P(J)$

209

to the Hamiltonian to take into account the proper energy of the perturbing system explicitly; he then derived the results of Born’s scattering theory.²⁴⁹

The last two sections, entitled ‘Application to Light-Quanta’ and ‘The Probability Coefficients for Emission and Absorption,’ respectively, presented the important conclusions on the new quantum theory of radiation. Thus, Dirac derived *all* of the results of Einstein’s light-quantum approach of 1916 (Einstein, 1916d, 1917a); that is, he obtained the light-quantum features from his $q$-number radiation theory. Finally, he discussed ‘the interaction of an atom and radiation from the wave point of view’ by starting from a Hamiltonian involving a classical field. By applying the formal scheme developed in Eqs. (141) to (149), he showed that ‘thus the wave point of view is consistent with the light-quantum point of view and gives values for the unknown interaction coefficients $v_{rs}$ in the light-quantum theory’ (Dirac, 1927b, p. 263). Indeed, a systematic calculation from the wave point of view now yielded the desired expressions for Einstein’s $A$ and $B$ coefficients.

For Bohr, the last results must have been very welcome, as he insisted at that time increasingly on the importance of the wave point of view. He also must have agreed with the contents of the following paper dealing with ‘The Quantum Theory of Dispersion,’ which Dirac submitted in early April 1927 from Göttingen. Dirac opened the introduction by summarizing the results of his previous work at Copenhagen as follows:

> It appears that one can treat a field of radiation as a dynamical system, whose interaction with an ordinary atomic system may be described by a Hamiltonian function. The dynamical variables specifying the field are the energies and the phases of its various harmonic components, each of which is effectively a simple harmonic oscillator. One must, of course, in the quantum theory take these variables to be $q$-numbers satisfying the proper quantum conditions. One finds then that the Hamiltonian for the interaction of the field with an atom is of the same form as for the interaction of an assembly of light-quanta with the atom. There is thus a complete formal reconciliation between the wave and the light-quantum points of view. (Dirac, 1927c, pp. 710–711)

Of course, these conclusions were received favourably in Göttingen by Max Born and Pascual Jordan, who took his new results on dispersion theory as completing their own efforts on the matrix theory. In calculating the scattering of radiation by an atom, Dirac also removed a difficulty that had appeared in the dispersion formulae of Kramers and Heisenberg (1925): there, the expressions became infinite for the frequency of the incident radiation coinciding with that of a spectral line of the atom; in the $q$-number theory of radiation, this infinity disappeared.²⁵⁰

In spite of the fact that Dirac’s $q$-number theory allowed him to approach the description of electromagnetic radiation and matter waves, so to say, on a unified

level, Dirac stressed the difference between the classical wave concept and the quantum-theoretical de Broglie wave quite clearly. In particular, he noted:

> Firstly, the light-wave is always real, while the de Broglie wave associated with a light-quantum moving in a definite direction must be taken to involve an imaginary exponential. A more important difference is that their intensities are to be interpreted in different ways. The number of light-quanta per unit volume associated with a monochromatic light-wave equals the energy per unit volume of the wave divided by the energy $h\nu$ of a single light-quantum. On the other hand, a monochromatic de Broglie wave of amplitude $a$ (multiplied into the imaginary exponential factor) must be interpreted as representing $a^2$ light-quanta per unit volume for all frequencies. (Dirac, 1927b, p. 247)

### (d) The Quantization of de Broglie Waves (February–August 1927)

With respect to the probability interpretation of the Schrödinger wave function, Dirac agreed fully with the Göttingen theorists, notably, Born and Jordan, who had invented this interpretation and made it (since summer 1926) the centrepiece of their investigations.$^{251}$ Still there arose differences between Göttingen and Cambridge in judging the role played by the probability argument in quantum mechanics. This fact may be illustrated by comparing the standpoints of Jordan and Heisenberg—who stood close to Dirac—in early 1927:$^{252}$

#### Jordan’s Standpoint

   (1) Experimental situations exist that cannot be described by the quantum-mechanical scheme, i.e., either matrix mechanics or its extensions (by Dirac, Born, Wiener, etc.).
   (2) Quantum theory is an essentially statistical theory.
   (3) The question of determinism is one of both the completeness of knowledge of the initial conditions and the special character of the physical law.
   (4) So far, one cannot give a conclusive answer to the questions of determinism in the quantum domain.

#### Heisenberg’s Standpoint

   (1′) Quantum mechanics, notably, in its extended (by the general transformation theory of Dirac and Jordan) version, allows for a description of *all* situations occurring in atomic physics.

$^{251}$ For details, see Chapter I, Sections I.3 and I.4.

$^{252}$ See Beller, 1985, pp. 346–347. In contrast to the analysis presented there, however, we cannot recognize a ‘strong influence’ of Jordan on Heisenberg during the period in question (i.e., when Heisenberg worked on the uncertainty relations). For example, Heisenberg emphasized the important point by starting from the quantum-mechanical commutation relations already in October–November 1926 in his exchange with Pauli, i.e., before he could read Jordan’s paper on transformation theory (of December 1926). He further said that he had enjoyed reading Jordan’s philosophical article (Jordan, 1927b, i.e., his *Habilitation* lecture) but also found it ‘not very accurate at places’ (see Heisenberg to Pauli, 5 February 1927).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0243 -->

211 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;II.5 The Origin of Quantum Field Theory

(2′) The statistical interpretation is a consequence of the transformation theory; the statistical hypothesis does not enter into the theory as an *a priori* condition (or fundamental postulate).

(3′) The question of determinism can be reduced to the question of whether the initial conditions of a quantum-theoretical system are complete; because the uncertainty relations admit only incomplete knowledge, the answer is quite obvious.

(4′) Quantum mechanics does not admit a deterministic interpretation.

One should not, however, overrate these differences, as the Göttingen and Copenhagen physicists shared many convictions about how the quantum-theoretical laws had to be interpreted. For instance, Jordan stated such points of agreement in a popular article that he wrote in Göttingen but published during his stay in Copenhagen in summer 1927. In it he concluded:

> All interpretations of physical laws by “visualizable” (“*anschauliche*”) pictures provide nothing else but illustrations of these laws by means of analogies from the domain of visualizable, tangible (*greifbare*) objects. But the laws of microphysics are of such a special and peculiar nature that it is impossible to obtain for them complete analogies in macrophysics. One has to be satisfied if at least the laws of logical and mathematical reasons are general enough to embrace the laws of quantum physics and to reproduce them theoretically (*sie gedanklich nachbilden*). Though this theoretical description of the fundamental physical laws demands, as the development proceeds, an increasingly higher ability for abstraction from the physicist, and the domain of tangible visualizability must be left behind further and further, we receive compensation in the wealth of knowledge we have gained for our new and final possession. (Jordan, 1927h, p. 648)

In those days, Dirac assumed a position close to Heisenberg’s. Especially, he shared the latter’s enormous confidence in the Göttingen–Cambridge quantum-mechanical theory, and he made use of it unreservedly to derive physical consequences. Jordan also relied faithfully on the mathematical formalism, but, in contrast to Dirac, he let himself be guided by very general ideas concerning the *philosophical and mathematical foundations* of the theory. Thus, he devoted the first two research papers submitted in 1927 to work out the details of his transformation theory (Jordan, 1927d, g). In other publications, he spoke quite openly about his personal philosophy regarding the general development of quantum theory. Thus, for instance, in his review of Schrödinger’s *Abhandlungen zur Wellenmechanik*, he sharply criticized the author’s ‘guiding principles’ as being opposed to those ‘of the majority of physicists,’ outlining them in detail:

> Schrödinger has tried to make use of his results not to obtain a quantitative sharpening of Bohr’s theory but in overcoming it; he has attributed to the wave system associated with a quantum-mechanical particle motion a genuine reality in the classical sense; [in his view] the replacement of the corpuscular concept by the wave concept should suffice in rendering the assumption of “quantum jumps” totally dispensable, and the wave system should provide a complete model of an atom functioning totally on classical and causal principles. (Jordan, 1927e, p. 413)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0244 -->

212 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

Erwin Schrödinger complained about such critical remarks in a letter to Göttingen, and Born replied promptly. Although Born 'essentially (*sachlich*) shared Jordan's opinions,' he did not agree with the manner of attack, which he excused on psychological grounds, and wrote: 'Among my younger collaborators there prevails an eagerness to fight, because the overwhelming success of wave mechanics does not seem to us to be justified by the actual situation; it may be ascribed to the fact that it [wave mechanics] meets the desire of most [physicists] to return to the classical form of physics.' (Born to Schrödinger, 16 May 1927)$^{253}$ Jordan himself also wrote to Schrödinger:$^{253}$

> It seemed to me that I only reproduced your own views by stating that your interpretation stands in harsh contrast to the fundamental assumptions of Bohr. Now it is correct that all quantum-mechanical theoreticians—Bohr, Born, Heisenberg, Pauli, Dirac, Wentzel, Oppenheimer, Gordon, von Neumann—are convinced that the fundamental assumptions of Bohr must be upheld without exception. Therefore, I do not believe that I exaggerated when I stated that the majority of physicists take a standpoint different from yours. (Jordan to Schrödinger, 16 May 1927)

Still, he apologized for the seemingly 'unfriendly tone' of the book review, and Schrödinger calmed down. In summer 1927, he wrote to Jordan a 'friendly' letter in which he expressed interest in the contents of a new paper of Jordan's dealing with the wave description of particles obeying Fermi statistics (Jordan, 1927j). Jordan replied:$^{254}$

> The ideas that I set out in the last paragraph of my work on the Fermi gas have, as I claimed, an earlier origin; but my earlier conceptions were contained essentially in private communications to Born, Heisenberg and Pauli. At that time I had given a lot of thought to Einstein's gas theory and had specified the representation in a way similar to your investigation [on Einstein's gas theory] in the *Physikalische Zeitschrift* (Schrödinger, 1926b): the number of atoms in a cell corresponds to the quantum number of a cavity-mode oscillator (we also briefly made this point in the 'three-man paper') ... The need to represent the light field as a quantum-mechanically operating field was obvious to me after obtaining the result of analyzing the fluctuation properties of quantized waves (in the 'three-man paper'). (Jordan to Schrödinger, summer 1927)

The main reason why he 'gradually began to doubt the whole representation,' Jordan wrote further, was provided by the new statistics (due to the Pauli principle) that had to be applied to material particles; hence, 'Pauli and Heisenberg did not wish to hear about it, while Born—though initially very favourably disposed —later withdrew his support completely' (Jordan to Schrödinger, *loc. cit.*).
When Jordan wrote this letter, he had finally shown up in Copenhagen for his

II.5 The Origin of Quantum Field Theory 213

long-planned visit supported by the International Education Board. He immedi-
ately got exposed to the Copenhagen atmosphere and (unlike Heisenberg and
Dirac) joined fully the spirit of Niels Bohr's programme, which we have described
in the previous section, notably, the emphasis on the *dual* roots for interpreting
atomic phenomena by employing *simultaneously* Schrödinger's undulatory and the
(Göttingen–Cambridge) quantum-mechanical descriptions. As a first exercise, he
reformulated the problem of describing the polarization of a single light-quantum
in wave theory (Jordan, 1927i).<sup>255</sup> This study fitted into the game played in those
days at Bohr's Institute, which Heisenberg had criticized earlier: 'I am always
annoyed when people still continue writing for any matrix study a corresponding
wave-mechanical one; I think people should rather learn both schemes.'

Heisenberg referred, in particular, to the efforts of a new visitor, Charles Galton
Darwin, to Copenhagen, who at that time 'translated the older formulae of Jordan
and myself (Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926) into the wave language or, rather, has
obtained them also from waves' (Darwin, 1927b), adding triumphantly: 'The cal-
culations are for anybody who knows matrix theory several orders of magnitude
more complicated than the older ones—so at least it seems to me.' (Heisenberg to
Pauli, 16 May 1927, in Pauli, 1979, p. 395)<sup>256</sup> Pauli then—this time with the
consent of Heisenberg—entered into the game himself and wrote a paper in which
he duplicated Darwin's earlier work on electron spin by treating it on the basis of a
simpler quantum-mechanical formalism involving spin matrices (Pauli, 1927b).<sup>257</sup>
His description entered into Jordan's next paper, entitled 'Zur Quantenmechanik
der Gasentartung' ('On the Quantum Mechanics of Gas Degeneracy,' 1927j), and
summarized in the abstract as:

> Dirac (1927b) has recently shown how Einstein's idea of representing the ideal
material gas, in analogy to the light-quantum gas, by *quantized waves in the conven-
tional three-dimensional space* can be carried out exactly [i.e., in a mathematically
consistent quantum-mechanical scheme] and brought into relation to an earlier rep-
resentation (Dirac, 1926f), which is connected with Schrödinger's method (represen-
tation by eigenfunctions in an abstract space of numerous dimensions). In this paper
the corresponding theory will be developed for the Fermi gas replacing the Einstein
gas. (Jordan, *loc. cit.*, p. 473)

In his first paper on the quantum-mechanical radiation theory, Dirac had
claimed that the new method he had proposed would fail to work in the case of
atomic particles obeying Fermi's statistics instead of Bose's (Dirac, 1927b, p. 247).
Jordan now contradicted that statement as based on wrong conclusions from the

---
