214 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

commutation relations. Indeed, from his own recent generalization of the transfor-
mation theory (Jordan, 1927g), he derived the following result: if the canonically
conjugate variables $q_r$ and $p_r$ of a quantum system describe discrete properties,
say, the electron spin, then the usual commutation relation

$$
p_r q_r - q_r p_r = \frac{h}{2\pi i} \tag{152}
$$

need not necessarily hold. Hence, Jordan could generalize Dirac's *Ansatz* relating
his canonical variables $b_r$ and $b_r^*$ to the observables $q_r$ and $p_r$ as

$$
q_r = \frac{1}{2}(b_r + b_r^*) \quad \text{and} \quad p_r = \frac{\omega h}{2\pi i}(b_r - b_r^*), \tag{153}
$$

where $\omega$ assumes a constant value still to be determined. A 'far-reaching freedom
in choosing the eigenvalues $\theta_r$ and $N_r$' thus arose, of which Jordan selected two
special cases (Jordan, 1927j, pp. 473–474, 478):

(1) The eigenvalues are

$$
N_r' = 0, 1, 2, \ldots; \quad 0 < \theta_r' < h, \tag{154a}
$$

yielding Dirac's case of Bose–Einstein statistics and $\omega = 1$.
(2) The eigenvalues are

$$
N_r' = 0, 1; \quad \theta_r' = \pm \frac{h}{4}, \tag{154b}
$$

yielding the case of Fermi statistics and $\omega = \pi$.

In the latter case (2), Eq. (147) must be replaced by

$$
\left.
\begin{aligned}
b_r &= (1 - N_r)^{1/2} \exp\left( -\frac{2\pi i}{h} \theta_r \right) = \exp\left( -\frac{2\pi i}{h} \theta_r \right) N_r \\
b_r^* &= N_r^{1/2} \exp\left( \frac{2\pi i}{h} \theta_r \right) = \exp\left( \frac{2\pi i}{h} \theta_r \right) (1 - N_r)^{1/2}.
\end{aligned}
\right\} \tag{147'}
$$

As in the Bose case (1), the microscopic objects obeying Fermi statistics satisfied a
matrix equation of the Schrödinger type, namely,

$$
\left( F + \frac{h}{2\pi i} \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \right) \psi(N_1', N_2', \ldots) = 0, \tag{155}
$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0247 -->

II.5 The Origin of Quantum Field Theory 215

with the Hamiltonian function given explicitly by

$$
F = \frac{16}{h^2} \sum_{r,s} H_{rs} N_r \theta_r \theta_s N_s
$$

$$
= \sum_{r,s} H_{rs} \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}_r \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}_r \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}_s \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}_s. \tag{156}
$$

The quantum field equation (155) was shown again to be equivalent to a
Schrödinger equation in the multi-dimensional coordinate space for systems com-
posed of many Fermi particles, as considered by Dirac and Heisenberg in 1926.
Hence, Jordan concluded:

> The results obtained hardly admit any doubt that—in spite of the validity of Pauli's
[i.e., Fermi's] statistics instead of Bose's for electrons—a quantum-mechanical theory
of matter can be constructed, in which the electrons can be described by waves in
the conventional three-dimensional space, and that the natural formulation of the
*quantum-theoretical electron theory* can be obtained in such a way that light and
matter are considered simultaneously as interacting waves in the three-dimensional
space. (Jordan *loc. cit.*, 480)

He noticed further:

> The fundamental fact of electron theory, the *existence of discrete electric particles*,
turns out here to constitute a characteristic quantum phenomenon, namely to be
equivalent to the fact that matter waves appear only in *discrete quantum states*. The
Schrödinger eigenfunctions of material particles constructed by Dirac and Heisenberg
play within this picture a role which does not allow one to consider them as the an-
alogue of electromagnetic waves. They rather turn out to be the special case of the
general probability amplitudes which have to be used as a mathematical tool to de-
scribe the statistical behaviour of quantized light and matter undulations. (Jordan,
*loc. cit.*)

The hypothesis that the discrete electric charge of the electron must be a con-
sequence of the quantum theory had already been anticipated by Oskar Klein
during the summer of 1926 on the basis of his five-dimensional extension of the
relativistic Schrödinger equation (O. Klein, 1926b). As mentioned in the previous
section, Klein had then pushed the five-dimensional formulation further in con-
nection with a correspondence-like approach to electrodynamics (O. Klein,
1927a). Especially, he tried in early 1927 'to see whether anything like a quantal
treatment of the many-body problem might come out,' but, as he recalled later,
'the result was discouraging':

> Then there came a new paper by Dirac containing an application of the quantization
procedure to the radiation field considered in the Rayleigh manner as a system of

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0248 -->

216 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

uncoupled oscillators corresponding to its resolution into standing waves. This made
me try to use the same procedure on a Schrödinger field coupled electrostatically to
itself by means of a scalar potential derived in the usual way from a density. I pre-
ferred this approach, starting from a space-time formulation, to that based on a
quantum theory translation of general Hamiltonian mechanics of a system of par-
ticles. Apart from a [perturbing] term, where the non-commuting factors had the
wrong order, the result of my calculation agreed with Schrödinger's equation in
configuration space. This was in March 1927. . . . From then on I was convinced that
a generalized field theory, whether four or five-dimensional, ought to be a quantum
field theory and not a theory of the classical type. (O. Klein, 1968, pp. 66–67)

Still, the quantal treatment of the many-body problem did not work, as Klein
wrote to Dirac after considering the nonrelativistic Coulomb interaction between
charged particles:

> I got a formula corresponding to your formula (12) [i.e., Eq. (150), the quantized
Schrödinger equation for the variable $b$], where the general term agreed with the
general term in the corresponding formula for the symmetrical eigenfunctions of a
multitude of electrons acting on one another with electrostatic forces. But those terms
where several indices were alike (i.e., the self-energy terms) did not agree and the
formula I got did not lead back to the ordinary equation for $N = 1$. So this only
stresses the difference between light and material particles. (O. Klein to Dirac, 24
March 1927)

Nevertheless Klein remained hopeful that a quantized theory of waves would
ultimately succeed in obtaining discrete electric charges and that a five-dimen-
sional formulation was the first candidate for such a theory. In the introduction to
a new paper dealing only with the classical objects, he wrote:

> The fact that a free electric particle always has a definite charge however leads, ac-
cording to the opinion expressed here, to the non-observability in principle of the
new [fifth] dimension. This is a simple consequence of the Dirac-Jordan statistical
formulation of quantum theory. . . . This non-observability of the new dimension—
agreeing with the fact that our experiences, apart from the limitation derived from the
quantum postulate, can be organized with the help of space-time concepts—should
not be counted as proof that the concept of the fifth dimension is superfluous. As a
characteristic example of the usefulness of a non-observable quantity in quantum
mechanics, we may mention the eigenfunction of the electron which is classically de-
scribed with the help of an angle that cannot be observed in principle on quantum
theory. (O. Klein, 1927b, p. 190)

Even before sending this investigation for publication in *Zeitschrift für Physik* in
October 1927, Klein submitted another paper on the nonrelativistic many-body
problem in quantum mechanics that he had composed together with Jordan. They
summarized the contents of this paper in the sentence: 'In leaning towards Dirac,

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0249 -->

II.5 The Origin of Quantum Field Theory 217

the symmetric solution of the wave equation in coordinate space for several electric particles—including their mutual interaction—is represented as a "quantization" of the de Broglie waves in the three-dimensional space' (Jordan and O. Klein, 1927, p. 751). This result clearly went beyond Dirac's treatment of the radiation theory because it involved the self-interaction of the assembly of Bose particles.

About the start of his collaboration with Jordan, Klein recalled: 'In the autumn [of 1927] Jordan, who independently had started the same approach, came to Copenhagen. He showed me that my troubles had to do with the electrostatic self-energy which in this particular case was cancelled by an interchange of the non-commuting factors, and we wrote a joint paper.' (O. Klein, 1968, p. 67) That Klein and Jordan only combined their efforts in fall 1927 may be quite surprising. In fact, Jordan had been in Copenhagen already for several months without getting into scientific exchange with Klein (who, of course, had been heavily involved in the task of assisting Bohr in formulating his ideas on complementarity during that period). Rather, he had worked on his investigation on the Fermi gas (Jordan, 1927j), apparently without any exchange with Bohr and Klein. Thus, Bohr had written about this to Pauli in July: 'I enclose a paper of Jordan who asked me before leaving Copenhagen to pass it on after I had read it. As you will note, Jordan shows how the statistics of an ideal gas can be treated fully in parallel with Dirac's Ansatz for the radiation theory.... In this context he announces a treatment of the general problem which does not make use of many-dimensional coordinate systems.' Bohr also added that Klein had recently concerned himself with the same problem in a relativistic approach, but: 'None of us has talked to Jordan shortly before he left, and therefore we do not know in detail how he intends to overcome the decisive difficulties by the new methods' (Bohr to Pauli, 15 July 1927, in Pauli 1979, pp. 401–402).

Pauli, who was thus called in as a referee, replied to Bohr that he agreed with the main part of Jordan's paper. From a phenomenological point of view, he wrote, all microscopic material particles (i.e., electrons and atoms alike) correspond to de Broglie waves, independent of whether they obey Bose or Fermi statistics. This particular question Jordan had solved. He added, however:

> There is [so far] no electromagnetic field involved in the game. Now at the end of Jordan's paper suddenly problems are addressed in a quite decisive tone that are not at all connected with the main part of his work. (This is typical Göttingen *Unart*, i.e., bad manners.) In fact one is dealing there with the task of establishing a somewhat organic—as you would say a natural (*ungezwungenes*)—relation between the de Broglie field and the electromagnetic field; in this context one must turn to the second point of view for which the property of electric charge of the elementary particle and its structure (spin!) are essential. (Only from this point of view can one hope to find the internal reason why electrons and protons obey Fermi statistics.) For this task, however, we still lack the proper methods. (Pauli to Bohr, 6 August 1927, *loc. cit.*, p. 403)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0250 -->

218 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

Pauli firmly believed that a satisfactory treatment between matter (represented by quantized de Broglie waves) and the electromagnetic field required necessarily a deeper look into the structure (especially the spin structure) of the elementary particles—electrons and protons—a belief shared fully by Dirac.$^{258}$ Then, a couple of months later, Pauli received the manuscript of a further paper from Copenhagen, written by Jordan and Klein, which he called ‘really beautiful’ (Pauli to Bohr, 22 October 1927), despite the fact that it did not address the task he had mentioned earlier.

**(e) Intermezzo on the Charge-Free Relativistic Quantum Electrodynamics (March–December 1927)**

Already, toward the end of the year 1926, Wolfgang Pauli was thinking about the problem of formulating a relativistic quantum electrodynamics, and he communicated his first considerations about this topic in a letter to Erwin Schrödinger dated 12 December 1926. These considerations included:

(1) The differential equation for the de Broglie (scalar) field $\psi$ does not involve the absolute values of the electromagnetic four-potential $\Phi_k$, because the substitution

$$ \Phi_k = \Phi_k + \frac{\partial \lambda}{\partial x_k} \quad \text{with } \lambda = \lambda(x_i) \tag{157} $$

leaves all observable quantities—e.g., current density and $\psi\bar{\psi}$, electromagnetic field strengths ($F_{ik} = \partial\Phi_k/\partial x_i - \partial\Phi_i/\partial x_k$), etc.—invariant and just multiples $\psi$ by the factor $\exp(i\lambda)$.$^{259}$

(2) Besides the conservation laws for electric charge and current (discussed in Schrödinger, 1926h), a further conservation law for the energy-momentum part of the relativistic matter tensor $T_{\mu\nu}$ exists, namely,

$$ \text{Div } T_{i4} + \frac{\partial}{\partial t} T_{44} = 0, \tag{158} $$

where $T_{i4}$ and $T_{44}$ denote the energy current (the product of momentum density and $c^2$) and the energy density, respectively, which can be written in terms of the differential expressions of first order and second degree in the $\psi$-function and the electromagnetic potentials.

(3) For closed systems, further ‘centre-of-mass theorems’ can be derived.

Pauli concluded: ‘You will take the above considerations as more grist for your continuum mill. But I am convinced, now as before, that the quantum phenomena cannot be grasped with the conceptual means of continuum physics alone.’ (Pauli to Schrödinger, 12 December 1926, in Pauli, 1979, p. 366)

$^{258}$ For more discussion of this aspect, see Section II.7.
$^{259}$ This transformation, multiplying the wave field $\psi$ by the space-dependent factor $\exp(i\lambda)$, became known later under the name ‘gauge transformation.’

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0251 -->

II.5 The Origin of Quantum Field Theory 219

Upon receipt of this letter, Schrödinger replied:

> Your opinion that the conservation theorem means more grist for my continuum mill is not correct. Nearly the opposite is true. The "closed system of equations" [combining the energy-momentum tensor for the electromagnetic quantities] does not apply. (Schrödinger to Pauli, 15 December 1926, *loc. cit.*, p. 367)

In reality, say, in the case of the hydrogen atom—so Schrödinger explained in detail in a paper entitled '*Der Energieimpulssatz der Materiewellen*' ('The Energy-Momentum Theorem for Matter Waves'), which he had just submitted for publication—the evaluation of the action of electromagnetic potentials from the 'combined equation' yielded higher-order effects, 'which, if the procedure converges at all, certainly does *not* lead to the correct hydrogen terms' (Schrödinger, 1927b, p. 271). To obtain the correct terms, one has to insert for the electromagnetic potentials $\Phi_{\alpha}$ just the given Coulomb potential of the nucleus plus eventually the potential of the electromagnetic field.$^{260}$

In the following months, Pauli concerned himself mainly with the electron-spin formalism, until he returned to the problem of quantum electrodynamics in March 1927. 'The classical part of the problem I shall soon be able to write down to some extent,' he informed Jordan, adding: 'The Hamilton-Jacobi theory of the Maxwell equations I now believe to have understood essentially . . . We shall see whether I'll succeed in establishing quantum electrodynamics. At the moment I am in good spirits.' (Pauli to Jordan, 12 March 1927, in Pauli, 1979, p. 386) A couple of weeks later, he wrote to Bohr in Copenhagen:

> At the moment I am very occupied with quantum electrodynamics. I am actually in good spirits and judge the present situation in physics to be a rather favourable one. It almost seems that the solution of the quantum riddle is not very far away. About my point of view concerning quantum electrodynamics I have recently written to Heisenberg, and I would like to hear his opinion about it. . . I do not agree with the physical interpretation which Klein has presented in the *Zeitschrift für Physik* about the dispersion theory and the Compton-effect. (Pauli to Bohr, 29 March 1927, in Pauli, 1979, p. 389)

Less than a week later, Heisenberg's expected answer arrived in Hamburg; he agreed with the main points of Pauli's proposed programme, especially with the electromagnetic fields **E** and **H** assumed as being described by *q*-numbers that lead to some sort of commutation relation; still, he doubted the occurrence of an inverse volume factor in the result: 'I quite see how it enters but I find it very unappealing. The fundamental quantum-theoretical relations between **E** and **H** ought not to depend on such an arbitrary concept as the volume of a cavity' (Heisenberg to Pauli, 4 April 1927, *loc. cit.*, pp. 390–391).

In May and June 1927, further letters were exchanged between Hamburg and

---

220 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

Copenhagen, which give some idea about the status of the programme. In particular, Pauli then introduced a relativistically extended delta-function into the theory. In a letter of 3 June, Heisenberg mentioned another collaborator, when he referred to 'your [i.e., Pauli's] and Jordan's preliminary studies' or even 'your and Jordan's theory' (In Pauli, 1979, pp. 397–398). Jordan had indeed become a partner in the enterprise in the spring of that year, probably during Pauli's visit to Göttingen in April.$^{261}$ Four months later, Pauli reported 'briefly about our quantum-electrodynamical considerations without giving the associated mathematical formalism'; he mentioned, in particular:

> So far we are only dealing with the electrodynamics of radiation in the absence of charged particles. To take into account the energy fluctuations of radiation and the light-quantum concept, one has to introduce here additional quantum conditions of some kind. We now refer to Dirac's method and write this quantum condition in the form of commutation relations, similar to those of the material oscillator; these relations can then always be expressed just as well with the help of $\psi$-functions which depend on the entire electromagnetic field.
>
> Jordan and I have succeeded in formulating these conditions in such a way that *the spatial coordinates are no longer, as in Dirac's paper, singled out with respect to time but rather all conditions of relativistic invariance are satisfied*. The interpretation finally obtained consists in this: though Maxwell's equations for the charge-free space will be retained explicitly in quantum electrodynamics, because of the additional quantum conditions a description of the radiation by sharply defined solutions of these equations ceases to make sense, and one can only work with *probability amplitudes of different continuously distributed solutions of Maxwell's equations* which have to satisfy given mathematical conditions. These conditions may be regarded as postulates which the actual measurements (*Messungsmöglichkeiten*) of electromagnetic field strengths must fulfil. (Pauli to Bohr, 6 August 1927, *loc. cit.*, pp. 403–404)

Pauli, of course, was aware that an electrodynamics of the charge-free space would not allow one to carry out a real measurement process for the field strengths; however, he hoped to be able to treat the relativistic many-body problem, but failed to obtain substantial progress. Thus, Jordan and Pauli just submitted a paper in early December 1927 on '*Zur Quantenelektrodynamik ladungfreier Felder*' ('The Quantum Electrodynamics of Charge-Free Fields'), whose contents they summarized as follows:

> Upon extending Dirac's theory [of radiation] by regarding the electrodynamical field quantities as non-commuting numbers (*q*-numbers), we establish here commutation relations having a *relativistically invariant* form, at least in the special case of absence of charged particles (pure radiation field). It will be shown that these relations can also be formulated without using the Fourier decomposition of the field. Further, a general mathematical method is presented that allows one to re-interpret relations between *q*-numbers, which depend on space-time coordinates in a continuous way

---

$^{261}$ Pauli wrote to Bohr on 29 March 1927, that he had arranged with Born and Jordan at a meeting in early April (see Pauli, 1979, p. 389).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0253 -->

**(q-functions), as relations between suitably chosen operators that can be applied to generalized $\psi$-functions depending on the whole development of the field (functionals). (Jordan and Pauli, 1928, p. 151)**

In detail, Jordan and Pauli opened Part I of their paper (entitled ‘The Method of $q$-Functions and $q$-Numbers’) by decomposing the spatial components of the electromagnetic fields $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ connected with free radiation in terms of eigenvibrations of a cavity having volume $L^3$, i.e., writing

$$ \mathbf{E} = \sum_s \mathbf{E}_s \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbf{H} = \sum_s \mathbf{H}_s. \tag{159} $$

Then, they expressed the components of $\mathbf{E}_s$ and $\mathbf{H}_s$ by harmonic vibrations having wave vectors $\mathbf{k}_s \left( \mathbf{k}_s^2 = \frac{\nu_s^2}{c^2} \right)$ besides the polarizations vectors ($\mathbf{e}_\xi^{(s)}$ and $\mathbf{e}_\eta^{(s)}$, say), the corresponding Dirac amplitudes $a_s^{(1)}, a_s^{(2)}$ and $b_s^{(1)}, b_s^{(2)}$, satisfying the commutation relations

$$ a_s^{(1)}, b_s^{(1)} - b_s^{(1)}a_s^{(1)} = a_s^{(2)}b_s^{(2)} - b_s^{(2)}a_s^{(2)} = ih, \tag{160} $$

where the superscripts (1) and (2) denote two possibilities of linear polarization of electromagnetic waves.$^{262}$ Jordan and Pauli then replaced the discrete sum in Eq. (159) by integrals over continuous values of $s$ and thus generalized the commutation relations (160) as

$$ A(\mathbf{k})B(\mathbf{k}') - B(\mathbf{k}')A(\mathbf{k}) = ih\delta(\mathbf{k} - \mathbf{k}'). \tag{161} $$

In spite of the manifestly noncovariant form of Eqs. (160) and (161), the commutation relations were shown to be invariant under Lorentz transformations.
In a second step, Jordan and Pauli renounced the standard Fourier decomposition that had so far characterized the approach to radiation in quantum mechanics; instead, they introduced what they called ‘$q$-functions,’ i.e., a *continuum of $q$-numbers*. For the purpose of writing commutation relations in this case, they had then to define a relativistic generalization of Dirac’s delta-function, which they proposed to obtain by the following limiting procedures:

$$ \Delta(x, y, z, ct) = \lim_{N \to \infty} \Delta_N(x, y, z, ct), \tag{162} $$

where (with $|\mathbf{k}| = k_x^2 + k_y^2 + k_z^2$) they defined the function $\Delta_N$ by$^{263}$

$$ \Delta_N(x, y, z, ct) = \iiint_{\substack{\text{sphere} \\ |\mathbf{k}|<N}} \frac{dk_x \, dk_y \, dk_z}{|\mathbf{k}|/2} \cdot \sin[2\pi(k_x x + k_y y + k_z z - |\mathbf{k}|ct)]. \tag{162a} $$

$^{262}$ Evidently, the other pairs of variables $a_s^{(1,2)}$ and $b_s^{(1,2)}$ commute, and the energy $E_s$ assumes the values $\frac{1}{2} \nu_s (a_s^2 + b_s^2)$; that is, $\frac{1}{2}(a_s^2 + b_s^2)$ must have the values $N_s = 0, 1, 2, \dots$.
$^{263}$ The *Ansatz* (162a) was motivated by the fact that the original delta-function could be obtained from a limiting sequence $\delta_N(x) = 2 \int_0^N \cos(2\pi kx) \, dk$.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0254 -->

222 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

Eq. (162) allowed for a ‘visualizable’ interpretation, namely, as ‘a spatially isotropic spherical-shell wave concentrated in the limit to an infinitely thin shell $r = ct$, which first contracts with light-velocity to hit the origin $r = 0$ at time $t = 0$ and then expands again with light-velocity’ (Jordan and Pauli, *loc. cit.*, p. 161). In addition, the new relativistic delta-function satisfied the relation

$$\Delta(-x, -y, -z, -ct) = -\Delta(x, y, z, ct),$$ (163)

and the four-dimensional continuity equation

$$\sum_{\alpha=1}^4 \frac{\partial^2\Delta}{\partial x_\alpha^2} = 0.$$ (164)

Finally, the commutation relations for the individual components of the electric and magnetic fields—now treated as ‘$q$-functions’ in the four-dimensional space of points $P$ and $P'$—assumed the special form

$$\mathbf{E}_i(P)\mathbf{E}_k(P') - \mathbf{E}_k(P')\mathbf{E}_k(P) = [\mathbf{E}_i(P), \mathbf{E}_k(P')]$$
$$= [\mathbf{H}_i(P), \mathbf{H}_k(P')] = \frac{ihc}{8\pi^2} \left( \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_i \partial x_k} - \delta_{ik} \frac{\partial^2}{c^2 \partial t^2} \right) \Delta(P' - P),$$ (165a)

and

$$[\mathbf{E}_i(P), \mathbf{H}_k(P')] = [\mathbf{H}_i(P), \mathbf{E}_k(P')] = \frac{ihc}{8\pi^2} \frac{\partial^2}{c^2 \partial t^2} \Delta(P' - P),$$ (165b)

where Eq. (165a) holds for $i,k,l = 1, 2, 3$, and the (all different) $i,k,l$ in Eq. (165b) must constitute an even permutation of the sequence 1, 2, 3. Similar commutation relations followed for the components of the antisymmetric $F_{ik}$-tensor originating from the electric and magnetic field components.
Jordan and Pauli devoted Part II of their paper (entitled ‘Method of Functionals and Functional Operators’) to an application of ‘Volterra’s functional mathematics,’ to deal even better with the problem of having continuously many quantum-mechanical position variables $q(x)$, which characterizes quantum field theory. The method works with the functionals $\Psi\{q(x)\}$, whose differential quotient in a point $x_0 = P$ is given by the definition

$$\Psi_{q(x); P} = \lim \frac{\Psi\{q(x) + \bar{q}(x)\} - \Psi\{q(x)\}}{\int \bar{q}(x) dx},$$ (166)

with $\bar{q}(x)$, a small variation of $q(x)$, being finite only in a small interval contracting to $x_0$ in the limit taken. In the case of a relativistic problem involving a scalar

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0255 -->

II.5 The Origin of Quantum Field Theory 223

variable $g(x_i)$, the functional differentiation was given by the expression

$$\Psi_{g(x_i); P} = \lim_{\alpha \to 0} \frac{1}{\alpha} \Psi\{g(x_i) + \alpha \bar{g}(x_i)\} - \Psi\{g(x_i)\},$$ (167)

where the prime should indicate the limit of the variation function $\bar{g}(x_i)$ approaching $\Delta(P - P')$. With these and other definitions from Volterra’s functional mathematics, Jordan and Pauli expected to formulate all of the problems of relativistic quantum field theory and, at the end of their paper, they declared:

The equations given in the last section of this Part II, for which there exists so far, by the way, no direct method of integration, must be considered as preliminary in a still higher degree than the considerations developed on the $q$-functions in Part I. However, we hold the introduction of functionals in a systematic quantum-theoretical reformulation of the classical field physics in general to be an adequate tool, despite many unsolved problems in carrying out specific steps. (Jordan and Pauli, *loc. cit.*, p. 173)

Surely, it does not make sense to speculate too much, at this point, about what hopes Jordan and Pauli cherished in 1927 in connection with the application of Volterra’s mathematics. It would also play a role in the further considerations on quantum electrodynamics; hence, we shall return to the method in Section II.7. On the other hand, one notices that Jordan and Pauli had not proceeded far with the programme announced at the beginning of that year. The main advance through their efforts may be seen, apart from the discussion of the proper formulation of the problems, in presenting a relativistic generalization of Dirac’s delta-function by the definition given in Eq. (162). In his letter to Schrödinger of 12 December 1926, Pauli had declared the problem of finding the form of the fundamental commutation relations for the electromagnetic fields to be the ‘main task (*Hauptfrage*).’ He had accomplished this main task, together with Jordan, at least for the free fields. Both of them also shared considerable optimism about succeeding soon in solving the problem also in the case of interacting quantum electrodynamics, encouraged by the success obtained in the nonrelativistic quantum field theory of Bose particles, which Jordan had achieved a couple of months earlier in an investigation carried out jointly with Oskar Klein.

**(f) The Quantization of (Nonrelativistic) Bose and Fermi Fields with Interaction (September 1927–January 1928)**

Proving quantum-mechanically the existence of the electron and treating properly its interaction with radiation constituted a very ambitious programme of a group of theoretical physicists in 1927. They hoped to reach this goal by a quantization of the de Broglie wave field $\psi(x)$ in the (at least) four-dimensional physical world. Toward the end of the year, they realized that only a minor part of that programme had been achieved: the nonrelativistic theory involving action-at-a-distance forces.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0256 -->

224 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

Jordan, perhaps the most versatile member of the quantum field theory group, would summarize the results (obtained up to early 1929) in his talk on ‘*Der gegenwärtige Stand der Quantenelektrodynamik*’ (‘The Current Status of Quantum Electrodynamics’) at the Kharkov Conference on ‘*Fragen der neuen Einsteinschen Feldtheorie und Quantenmechanik*’ (‘Problems of the New Einsteinian Field Theory and Quantum Mechanics’) in May 1929. He explained in particular:

The transition from a theory in coordinate space [as represented by the Schrödinger equation] to the matrix-wave theory (‘*Matrixwellentheorie*,’ i.e., the theory of Dirac, Klein and Jordan), and *vice versa*, is based on a quite extended mathematical theory which has been developed in several steps:
1. The first question was: Consider an ideal gas obeying Bose-Einstein statistics represented by a quantized de Broglie field; what then do the symmetrical eigenfunctions used in the coordinate-space theory mean? The question was solved by Dirac in his well-known paper on the emission and absorption of light by atoms.
2. Second, one had to ask: how one could extend the theory of the ideal gas consisting of non-interacting particles to a theory of the gas including the interaction of the particles (in the form of action-at-a-distance forces independent of time (*zeitlose Fernwirkungskraft*)? Upon solving this question, the theory of Bose-Einstein gases (say, of a gas of $\alpha$-particles) has been settled to a certain extent.
3. Now, however, the electron gas—whose treatment we wish to approach by a quantized de-Broglie field—is not governed by Bose statistics but by Pauli’s exclusion principle; hence the practicality of our programme depends on whether in this case a theory analogous to the Bose case can be established. Indeed, one does succeed—though mathematically not quite as easily as in the case of the Bose-Einstein gas—eventually with convincing transparency. (Jordan, 1929b, p. 706)

Besides Dirac’s radiation theory of February 1927, Jordan referred for the steps 2 and 3 to his own work performed between September 1927 and January 1928 in collaboration with Oskar Klein in Copenhagen and Eugen (Eugene) Wigner in Göttingen, respectively.
Jordan and Klein, although displaying a strong common interest in the problem of relativistic quantum field theory, had not joined forces during the first few months (from May to July 1927) that Jordan spent in Copenhagen.$^{264}$ When the latter returned to Bohr’s Institute, however, after spending his summer vacation in Germany, they combined their efforts to work out the theory of describing a nonrelativistic system of several Bose particles having (nonrelativistic) electromagnetic interactions. In their final paper, entitled ‘*Zum Mehrkörperproblem der Quantentheorie*’ (‘On the Many-Body Problem of Quantum Theory’) and received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 4 October 1927, they gave the reason for the preliminary restriction of the more ambitious programme (Jordan and Klein, 1927): first, only a nonrelativistic Schrödinger equation was available so far for treating many-body systems, because in the case that electromagnetic fields had a finite velocity

---
$^{264}$ The main reason was that, as we explained before (see also the previous section), Bohr kept Klein absorbed in assisting him with the formulation of his ideas on complementarity.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0257 -->

II.5 The Origin of Quantum Field Theory 225

of propagation no Hamiltonian seemed to exist. Second, they assumed nevertheless that the new field-theoretical treatment might open a path to a relativistic generalization. Third, they expected to be able to remove in their procedure the difficulties observed by Schrödinger in his unified classical theory of light and matter waves (Schrödinger, 1927b).
According to the treatment of Olivier Darrigol, who has condensed the Jordan–Klein paper, the following can be reported about it:

Together in Copenhagen, Klein and Jordan could reconsider the problem [of interacting Bose particles] and they found that the self-energy difficulty was easily circumvented by choosing the right order (now called normal-ordering) of products of quantized waves $\psi(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_\alpha b_\alpha(\mathbf{r}|\alpha)$. Specifically, one has to use the following expressions for the $F$-operator generating Dirac’s $F$-Hamiltonian [see Eq. (144)]

$$F = \int d^3\mathbf{r}\psi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}) \left( -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \right) \Delta\psi(\mathbf{r}) + \frac{e^2}{8\pi} \int d^3r'\psi^\dagger(\mathbf{r})\psi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}')|\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}'|^{-1}\psi(\mathbf{r})\psi(\mathbf{r}'), \quad [(168)]$$

with all [creation operators] $\psi^\dagger$ on the left side [and $\hbar = h/2\pi$].
The Schrödinger [time] evolution given by $F$ was equivalent, as desired, to the Schrödinger evolution in configuration space given by the Hamiltonian

$$\sum_i \left( -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \Delta_i + \sum_{i<j} (e^2/4\pi)|\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_i|^{-1} \right). \quad [(169)]$$

Normal-ordering eliminated the extra infinite self-energy terms $(e^2/4\pi)|\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_j|^{-1}$.
(Darrigol, 1986, pp. 234–235).

In the original paper, the procedure leading to these essential results—as has been noted earlier, it was indeed the self-energy problem that had halted Klein’s investigation in spring, and it was Jordan who now showed how to overcome the difficulty by a proper ordering of the field operators and their complex conjugate partners—was contained in four long and quite technical sections entitled:

(1) Quantization of de Broglie waves in the case of electric interaction.
(2) Comparison with the wave equation in coordinate space.
(3) On the question of the sequence of factors in the energy expression.
(4) Treatment of the general interaction between the particles.

A more detailed analysis reveals the aims of the authors and how they achieved their goals.
Jordan and Klein considered a system of de Broglie waves describing spinless particles (‘electrons’) of charge $-\varepsilon$ and mass $\mu$, acted upon by an electrostatic potential $V$—consisting of an external part $V_0$ and the Coulomb interaction of the particles (in principle, also including their self-interaction). For the charge density, they took Schrödinger’s classical expression, but neglected relativistic effects and

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0258 -->

226 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

magnetic contributions; further, they avoided any convergence problems by enclosing the system within finite boundaries. The complex wave functions, $\phi(\mathbf{r}, t)$ and $\phi^*(\mathbf{r}, t)$, obeyed the (classical) equations of motion

$$-\frac{h^2}{8\pi^2\mu}\Delta\phi + \frac{h}{2\pi i}\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial t} - \varepsilon V\phi = 0 \tag{170a}$$

and

$$-\frac{h^2}{8\pi^2\mu}\Delta\phi^* - \frac{h}{2\pi i}\frac{\partial\phi^*}{\partial t} - \varepsilon V\phi^* = 0. \tag{170b}$$

The electrostatic potential, on the other hand, satisfied the (likewise classical) Laplace equation

$$\Delta V = 4\pi\varepsilon\phi^*\phi, \tag{171}$$

whose solution might be written as

$$V(\mathbf{r}) = V_0(\mathbf{r}) - \varepsilon \int d^3\mathbf{r} G(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}') \phi^*(\mathbf{r}')\phi(\mathbf{r}'), \tag{172}$$

with the Green's function

$$G(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}') = \frac{1}{|\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}'|}. \tag{173}$$

Note that Eqs. (170a, b) were derived from a Hamiltonian principle involving the Hamilton function

$$E = \int d^3\mathbf{r} \left\{ \frac{h^2}{8\pi^2\mu}(\text{grad } \phi^* \cdot \text{grad } \phi) - \varepsilon V_0\phi^*\phi + \frac{1}{8\pi}[\text{grad}(V - V_0)]^2 \right\}. \tag{174}$$

As a next step, the authors expanded the (classical) de Broglie fields in terms of $u_s(\mathbf{r})$, the normalized eigenfunctions of the time-independent Schrödinger equation,

$$\frac{h^2}{8\pi^2\mu}\Delta u + (E + \varepsilon V_0)u = 0, \tag{175}$$

that is, as

$$\phi(\mathbf{r}, t) = \sum_s b_s(t)u_s(\mathbf{r}) \quad \text{and} \quad \phi^*(\mathbf{r}, t) = \sum_s b_s^*(t)u_s(\mathbf{r}). \tag{176}$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0259 -->

227 II.5 The Origin of Quantum Field Theory

The time-dependent coefficients $b_s$ and $b_s^*$—or, more accurately, $\frac{h}{2\pi i}b_s$ and $b_s^*$—may be taken as sets of canonical-variable pairs of the dynamical problem given by the Hamiltonian (174), which assumes the new form (where $E_s$ is the eigenvalue of $u_s$):

$$E = \sum_s b_s^*b_s E_s + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} \sum_{\mu\nu rs} A(\mu\nu|rs)b_\mu^*b_\nu^*b_rs$$
$$A(\mu\nu|rs) = \int d\mathbf{r}' d\mathbf{r}'' G(\mathbf{r}', \mathbf{r}'') u_\mu(\mathbf{r}'')u_\nu(\mathbf{r}')u_r(\mathbf{r}')u_s(\mathbf{r}''). \tag{177}$$

Equations (170) to (177) represented the 'classical level of description' of the system considered. Jordan and Klein then introduced what they called 'quantized de Broglie waves' by leaving Schrödinger's ideas and turning to Dirac's (in Dirac, 1927b). They now worked with 'adjoint' pairs $b_s$ and $b_s^\dagger$, where $b_s^\dagger$ is obtained from $b_s$ by replacing all factors $i$ by $-i$ (which yields $b_s^*$) and then inverting the order of all $q$-number factors in $b_s$. The $b$'s and $b_s^\dagger$'s have to satisfy the quantum-mechanical commutation rules

$$b_\mu b_\nu^\dagger - b_\nu^\dagger b_\mu = \delta_{\mu\nu}, \tag{178a}$$
$$b_\mu b_\nu - b_\nu b_\mu = b_\mu^\dagger b_\nu^\dagger - b_\nu^\dagger b_\mu^\dagger = 0. \tag{178b}$$

Again, following Dirac, new canonical variables $N_s$ and $\theta_s$ (to be identified with the $q$-numbers describing particle numbers and phases, respectively) were defined by

$$b_s = \exp\left(-\frac{2\pi i}{h}\theta_s\right)N_s^{1/2} \quad \text{and} \quad b_s^\dagger = N_s^{1/2}\exp\left(\frac{2\pi i}{h}\theta_s\right), \tag{179}$$

in which the Hamiltonian (174) assumed the form

$$E = \sum_s N_s E_s + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} \sum_{\mu\nu rs} A(\mu\nu|rs)N_r^{1/2} \exp\left(\frac{2\pi i}{h}\theta_r\right) \times$$
$$N_s^{1/2} \exp\left[\frac{2\pi i}{h}(\theta_s - \theta_\mu)\right] N_\mu^{1/2} \exp\left(-\frac{2\pi i}{h}\theta_\nu\right) N_\nu^{1/2}. \tag{180}$$

Simultaneously, the canonical commutation relations, i.e.,

$$N_\mu \exp\left(\frac{2\pi i}{h}\theta_\mu\right) - \exp\left(\frac{2\pi i}{h}\theta_\mu\right) N_\mu = \exp\left(\frac{2\pi i}{h}\theta_\mu\right), \tag{181}$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0260 -->

228 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

stated: the application of the $q$-number $\exp\left(\frac{2\pi i}{h}\theta_\mu\right)$ on a function of the particle numbers (represented by a $q$-number or matrix) would replace the eigenvalues $N'_\mu$ by $N'_\mu - 1$.

With the above canonical transformations *à la* Dirac, the solution of the quantum-mechanical problem, including the resolution of the self-energy difficulty, followed immediately. The function $\phi(N'_1, N'_2, \dots)$, whose absolute square determines the probability for the values $N'$ in the case of no mutual interaction between the 'electrons,' satisfies a Schrödinger-type equation [see Eq. (149)],

$$\frac{ih}{2\pi}\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\phi(N'_1, N'_2, \dots) = E\phi(N'_1, N'_2, \dots), \tag{182}$$

with the Hamiltonian (180). Due to the operator property of the phases, $E$ can be rewritten finally in the quite transparent form

$$E = \sum_s N_s E_s + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} \sum_{\mu\nu rs} A(\mu\nu|rs)N_s^{1/2}(N'_r - \delta_{rs})^{1/2}(N'_\nu + 1 - \delta_{\nu s} - \delta_{\nu r})^{1/2}$$
$$(N'_\mu + 1 + \delta_{\mu\nu} - \delta_{\mu s} - \delta_{\mu r})^{1/2} \exp\left[\frac{2\pi i}{h}(\theta_r + \theta_s - \theta_\mu - \theta_\nu)\right]. \tag{183}$$

Hence, Jordan and Klein arrived at the following conclusions:

(1) The eigenvalues $N'_s$ are indeed integer numbers.
(2) The quantity $N$,

$$N = \sum_s N_s = \sum_s b_s^\dagger b_s, \tag{184}$$

can be shown to be a constant of motion and identified with the total number of particles in the ($N$-body) system.
(3) For the special case of a one-particle system, i.e., $N'_s = \delta_{s\sigma}$, the interaction becomes zero, because in Eq. (183) the sum over $\mu, \nu, r$, and $s$ contains only the terms $s = \sigma$, which are multiplied by $N'_r - \delta_{s\sigma} = 0$ (because either $N'_r = 1$ and $r = \sigma$ or $N'_r = 0$ and $r \neq \sigma$). That is, no self-interaction of the electrically charged Bose particle exists in that case, a result that also applies to the general situation of many particles.

As a second major point of the programme, Jordan and Klein established in Section 2 the equivalence of Eq. (182) and the $N$-particle, time-dependent Schrödinger equation in coordinate space [with $G(\mathbf{r}_k, \mathbf{r}_\ell)$ denoting Green's functions],

$$\sum_{k=1}^N \left[ -\frac{h}{8\pi^2\mu}\Delta_k\psi - \varepsilon V_0(\mathbf{r}_k)\psi \right] + \varepsilon^2 \sum_{k<\ell} G(\mathbf{r}_k, \mathbf{r}_\ell)\psi + \frac{h}{2\pi i}\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial t} = 0, \tag{185}$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0261 -->

229 II.5 The Origin of Quantum Field Theory

which is solved by the symmetrized eigenfunction

$$\psi = \sum_{n_1, n_2, \dots} b(n_1, n_2, \dots) u_{n_1}(\mathbf{r}_1)u_{n_2}(\mathbf{r}_2) \dots, \tag{186}$$

where $|b|^2$ determines the probability of the state. Upon introducing the properly normalized wave function

$$b(N'_1, N'_2, \dots) = \left( \frac{N'!}{N'_1! N'_2! \dots} \right) b(n_1, n_2, \dots) \tag{187}$$

—with $N' = \sum_k N'_r$ ($N'_r$ being the number of those $n_k$ that assume the value $r$) and $n_k$ denoting one of the value systems of numbers $n_k$ belonging to given numbers $N'_1, N'_2 \dots$ —into Eq. (185), a straightforward evaluation yields the result,

$$b(N'_1, N'_2, \dots) = \phi(N'_1, N'_2, \dots), \tag{188}$$

with $\phi(N'_1, N'_2, \dots)$ indeed satisfying Eq. (182), as asserted.

In the next Section 3, Jordan and Klein considered a crucial question arising in quantum mechanics, namely, the order of factors in the Hamiltonian $E$. In the classical theory, the pure interaction term of the wave fields—on account of 'visualizability' (i.e., multiplying two particle densities)—would be written as

$$I_{\text{cl}} = \frac{\varepsilon^2}{2} \iint G(\mathbf{r}', \mathbf{r}'') \phi^*(\mathbf{r}')\phi(\mathbf{r}') \phi^*(\mathbf{r}'') \cdot \phi(\mathbf{r}'') d^3\mathbf{r}' d^3\mathbf{r}''. \tag{189}$$

Of course, the field variables $\frac{h}{2\pi i}\phi(\mathbf{r})$ and $\phi^*(\mathbf{r})$ constitute a canonical pair of variables for the dynamics of an infinite system (field) defined at all points of the three-dimensional space. The corresponding commutation relations involving Dirac's delta-function,

$$\phi(\mathbf{r}')\phi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}'') - \phi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}'')\phi(\mathbf{r}') = \delta(\mathbf{r}' - \mathbf{r}''), \tag{190}$$

must be satisfied in the general case. However, in rewriting the classical interaction function (189) in terms of $q$-numbers, the authors evidently chose in Eq. (177) a different sequence of factors or, expressed by the fields,

$$I_{\text{q.t.}} = \frac{\varepsilon^2}{2} \iint G(\mathbf{r}', \mathbf{r}'') \phi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}')\phi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}'') \phi(\mathbf{r}')\phi(\mathbf{r}'') d^3\mathbf{r}' d^3\mathbf{r}''. \tag{191}$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0262 -->

230 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

By taking the particle-number variable, i.e.,

$$N(\mathbf{r}) = \phi^\dagger(\mathbf{r})\phi(\mathbf{r}), \tag{192}$$

the interaction term can finally be split into two terms, i.e.,

$$I_{q.t.} = \frac{\varepsilon^2}{2} \iint G(\mathbf{r}', \mathbf{r}'')N(\mathbf{r}')N(\mathbf{r}'') \, d^3\mathbf{r}' \, d^3\mathbf{r}'' - \frac{\varepsilon^2}{2} \int G(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r})N(\mathbf{r}) \, d\mathbf{r}, \tag{193}$$

upon which Jordan and Klein commented as follows:${}^{265}$

> The expression for the interaction energy used above is exactly the one which must be expected for the correspondence analogue of the classical theory. The non-commutative multiplication of quantum mechanics enables one in a remarkable way to reduce the difference between a double and a single volume integral in [Eq. (191)] to a double volume integral; thus the fact that the "eigenfield" of an electron does not exert the same force on the electron itself as the "external" field can be expressed analytically in a simple way. (Jordan and Klein, 1927, p. 762)

In the last Section 5 of their paper, Jordan and Klein went beyond their minimum programme by showing how the magnetic interaction between the electrons (up to second order in $v/c$), as well as retardation effects of electric forces (in the same approximation to relativistic motion) might be treated. They found that a slight generalization involving the Hamiltonian

$$H = \int d^3\mathbf{r} \phi^\dagger(\mathbf{r})H_1(p', q')\phi(\mathbf{r}) + \frac{1}{2} \iint d^3\mathbf{r}' d^3\mathbf{r}'' \phi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}')\phi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}'')H_2(p', q'; p'', q'')\phi(\mathbf{r}')\phi(\mathbf{r}'') \tag{194}$$

would do $(p' = \frac{h}{2\pi i} \frac{\partial}{\partial q'})$ and $q'$ denote momentum and position operators associated with the space-point $\mathbf{r}'$, etc.).${}^{266}$ These results admittedly did not lead very far into the relativistic theory. In addition, Jordan found in a second paper (written

${}^{265}$ If applied to the interaction of mass points, the result (193) states simply:

$$\frac{\varepsilon^2}{2} \sum_{k,l} G(\mathbf{r}_k, \mathbf{r}_l) - \frac{\varepsilon^2}{2} \sum_k G(\mathbf{r}_k, \mathbf{r}_l).$$

${}^{266}$ For the magnetic interaction of the electrons, the interaction term $H_{kl} = -\frac{\varepsilon^2}{4c^2\mu^2} \left( \mathbf{p}_k \frac{1}{r} \mathbf{p}_l + \mathbf{p}_l \frac{1}{r} \mathbf{p}_k \right)$ is obtained. Similarly, the retardation effects of order $v^2/c^2$ can be calculated for the magnetic interactions, as Charles Galton Darwin had already figured out in a prequantum-mechanical investigation (Darwin, 1920).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0263 -->

II.5 The Origin of Quantum Field Theory 231

by himself alone) that Eq. (194) cannot describe the situation in which charged polarized particles act upon each other (Jordan, 1927k). For this purpose, he proposed to add a further term, namely,

$$\frac{1}{3!} \iiint d^3\mathbf{r}' \, d^3\mathbf{r}'' \, d^3\mathbf{r}''' \phi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}')\phi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}'')\phi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}''')H_3(p', q'; p'', q''; p''', q''')\phi(\mathbf{r}')\phi(\mathbf{r}'')\phi(\mathbf{r}'''), \tag{195}$$

to the Hamiltonian (195). The same paper, "Über Wellen und Korpuskeln in der Quantenmechanik" ("On Waves, and Particles in Quantum Mechanics," Jordan, 1927k), contained several other formal and mathematical generalizations, but its main practical value is that, in the newly established theory of the "quantized wave field," the fluctuations in the Bose case now satisfied all requirements following from Einstein's light-quantum treatment of 1924 and 1925.${}^{267}$

The success with the interacting Bose fields, at any rate, stimulated Jordan to cast the theory of quantized Fermi fields into the same language. Back in Göttingen, he gained the collaboration of Eugene Wigner in carrying out the mathematical details. The two of them worked out the appropriate scheme by writing expressions for the Fermi fields in close analogy to those of the Jordan–Klein paper in the Bose case; thus, e.g., the commutation relations took on the form (cf., Eq. 190)

$$\psi(\mathbf{r}')\psi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}'') + \psi^\dagger(\mathbf{r}'')\psi(\mathbf{r}') = \delta(\mathbf{r}' - \mathbf{r}''). \tag{196}$$

We shall not go into the details of the very elaborate technical presentation of Jordan and Wigner, which was mostly carried out in the discrete version. We shall instead give a comparative summary in a table (taken from Jordan and Wigner, 1928, p. 640).${}^{268}$

| Bose–Einstein Case | Pauli [i.e., Fermi–Dirac] Case |
| --- | --- |
| $b_\alpha(\beta')b_\alpha(\beta'') - b_\alpha(\beta'')b_\alpha(\beta') = 0$ | $a_\alpha(\beta')a_\alpha(\beta'') + a_\alpha(\beta'')a_\alpha(\beta') = 0$ |
| $b_\alpha^\dagger(\beta')b_\alpha(\beta'') - b_\alpha(\beta'')b_\alpha^\dagger(\beta') = \delta(\beta' - \beta'')$ | $a_\alpha^\dagger(\beta')a_\alpha(\beta'') + a_\alpha(\beta'')a_\alpha^\dagger(\beta') = \delta(\beta - \beta'')$ |
| $b_\alpha^\dagger(\beta')b_\alpha(\beta') = N_\alpha(\beta')$ | $a_\alpha^\dagger(\beta')a_\alpha(\beta') = N_\alpha(\beta')$ |
| $b_\alpha(\beta') = \sum_{q'} \Phi_{\alpha p}(\beta', q')b_p(q')$ | $a_\alpha(\beta') = \sum_{q'} \Phi_{\alpha p}(\beta', q')a_p(q')$ |

In the Fermi case, the multiplication rules for $a$ and $a^\dagger$ turn out to be especially powerful: they not only determine the eigenvalues for $N(\beta') - N'(\beta') = 0$ or $1$,

${}^{267}$ See also Jordan's review article "Die Lichtquantenhypothese" ("The Light Quantum Hypothesis," Jordan, 1928).

${}^{268}$ Evidently, the equations in the Bose case (Jordan and O. Klein, 1927) correspond to Eqs. (178), (179), etc. In the Fermi case, $N_\alpha(\beta')$ assumes the values 0 or 1 in the discrete case, while $N(\beta')$ would satisfy $N(\beta')[\delta(\beta' - \beta'') - N(\beta'')] = N(\beta')N(\beta'')$ for $\beta' \neq \beta''$ and 0 for $\beta' = \beta''$ in the continuous case.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0264 -->

232 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

but also the matrices themselves up to canonical transformation. Similar to what Jordan and Klein had done in the Bose case, Jordan and Wigner now established the equivalence of the quantum-field scheme—described by the quantized wave function in the three-dimensional space—and Schrödinger's undulatory scheme—with the antisymmetrical wave function in the multidimensional coordinate space. "Finally we would like to emphasize that the multiplication laws for the amplitudes can be generalized easily for relativistic fields, in analogy with the relativistically invariant multiplication laws of the charge-free electromagnetic field," Jordan and Wigner concluded in an optimistic tone; that is, also in the case of Fermi fields, "a quantization of de Broglie waves in a relativistic form can be achieved" (Jordan and Wigner, loc. cit., p. 650). Shortly after they wrote these words, an investigation by Dirac provided a new relativistic equation for the electron, having a quite different structure from those considered before (Dirac, 1928a). Although the Dirac equation opened new vistas and created new problems and puzzles, the quantum-field theoretical description could still be applied in that case, and the results obtained by Jordan and Wigner remained valid.

## II.6 The Solvay Conferences of 1927 and 1930 and the Consistency Debate

### (a) Introduction

In early 1927, Wolfgang Pauli received a letter from Hendrik Antoon Lorentz inviting him "in the name of the Scientific Committee of the Institut International de Physique Solvay to the conference scheduled from 24 to 29 October at Brussels." Lorentz added:

> This conference will be devoted to the new quantum mechanics and to questions connected with it, and we shall have, in order to introduce the discussions, reports of Born and Heisenberg, W. L. Bragg, L. de Broglie, Compton and Schrödinger.

The sessions would be attended by "the members of the Scientific Committee: Madame Curie and Messieurs [E.] Van Aubel, [A.] Einstein, [C. E.] Guye, [P.] Langevin, [H. A.] Lorentz, [M.] Knudsen, and [O. W.] Richardson" as well as by the invited participants "[M.] Planck, [M.] Born, [N.] Bohr, [W. L.] Bragg, [R.] Fowler, [P. A. M.] Dirac, C. T. R. Wilson, [A. H.] Compton, L. de Broglie, [H.] Deslandres, L. Brillouin, [E.] Schrödinger, [P.] Debye, [H.] Kramers, [P.] Ehrenfest, and the professors of the University of Brussels [T.] de Donder, [E.] Henriot, [A.] Piccard and [E.] Verschaffelt as secretary.${}^{269}$

Pauli accepted the coveted invitation and went to attend the fifth Solvay Conference on Physics, dealing officially with the topic "Éléctrons and Photons," to listen to and discuss the following reports:

${}^{269}$ See Wolfgang Pauli's Scientific Correspondence, 1979, pp. 408–409.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0265 -->

II.6 The Solvay Conferences of 1927 and 1930 and the Consistency Debate 233

The Intensity of the Reflection of X-rays, by William Lawrence Bragg;
Disagreement between Experience and the Electromagnetic Theory of Radiation, by Arthur H. Compton;
The New Dynamics of Quanta, by Louis de Broglie;
The Mechanics of Quanta, by Max Born and Werner Heisenberg;
The Mechanics of Waves, by Erwin Schrödinger;
The Quantum Postulate and the New Development of Atomistics, by Niels Bohr.
(Électrons et Photons, Institut International de Physique Solvay, 1928)

One might say that nearly all of the principal architects of the old and the new quantum theory were assembled at the 1927 Solvay Conference, with the exception of two very important personalities: notably, Arnold Sommerfeld from the older generation and Pascual Jordan from the younger generation.${}^{270}$ Sommerfeld, however, would return (after his participation in the first two conferences in 1911 and 1913, respectively) to Brussels for the sixth Solvay Conference on Physics, held from 20 to 25 October 1930, and having the general theme "Magnetism," or more specifically, "The Magnetic Properties of Matter." At this conference also, the debate on the consistency of quantum mechanics, especially the uncertainty and complementarity aspects, between Niels Bohr and Albert Einstein was continued, which had begun already at the 1927 conference.

The present section is concerned with the discussion of the completed complementarity arguments by Bohr. The fifth Solvay Conference served him as the first opportunity for doing so, especially the animated discussions with Einstein on the central questions. The proceedings of the conference, though, carry very little information about these discussions. Although Born, de Broglie, Heisenberg, and Schrödinger expressed their respective views in carefully prepared reports and discussions, and Bohr also gave an account (modified as compared with the Como lecture, which has been analyzed in Section II.4), the Rapports et Discussions du Cinquième Conseil de Physique (published in 1928) would not include much of what Bohr and Einstein exchanged on the consistency problem. Hence, our account in the following will be based on the recollections of the participants and, especially, on a lively account given by Paul Ehrenfest in a letter written to his Leyden collaborators shortly after the close of the 1927 conference. We then turn our attention to the development that Bohr's ideas on complementarity underwent in the following years, and then focus on the counter-arguments advanced by his main opponents, Einstein and Schrödinger, before concluding with some remarks on the Bohr–Einstein debate in 1930.

### (b) Light-Quanta, Wave Fields, and Particles: Einstein's Preparation for the Fifth Solvay Conference (Spring 1926–Fall 1927)

The three and a half years since the fourth Solvay Conference on Physics—which had been held in April 1924 on the topic of "Electrical Conductivity of Metals

${}^{270}$ In a letter to Born, dated 14 June 1927, Planck regretted in particular that Sommerfeld was not invited and that he, therefore, hesitated to accept the invitation to Brussels.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0266 -->

# Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

and Related Problems'—were marked by enormous progress in quantum physics. Partly based on discoveries and ideas that had been available already before 1924—such as the Compton effect and matter waves—the new atomic theory had arisen, which did more than throw new light on the difficulties discussed at the 1924 conference: quantum or wave mechanics went right to the heart of the problems posed by atomic phenomena. The two subjects put programmatically into the title of the fifth Solvay Conference—electrons and photons—designated the crucial points of interest, because 'electrons' also stood for the smallest, massive constituents of matter, and they now became associated with waves, and 'photons' (a name given only recently, in October 1926 by the physical chemist Gilbert N. Lewis, to Einstein’s light-quanta) characterized the quantum-theoretical aspect of electromagnetic radiation. It was the declared intention of the Scientific Committee of the *Institut International de Physique Solvay* to contribute by scientific reports and discussions about them to the clarification of the scientific concepts in the physics of the day. In retrospect, one may indeed attribute an important success to the 1927 Solvay Conference in marking the completion of the ideas that had first been discussed in the international physics community sixteen years previously at the first Solvay Conference of 1911.

From amongst the members of the Scientific Committee, two had already played a leading role in 1911: the Chairman Hendrik Lorentz and Albert Einstein; the latter had presented then the most revolutionary report. In spring 1926, in the early stage of preparing for the new conference, Lorentz again requested Einstein to write a report. The latter answered promptly: ‘If you wish that I take over the report on quantum statistics, I shall do so with pleasure; because, without being in great difficulty, I shall never say “no” to you.’ (Einstein to Lorentz, 1 May 1926) Because Lorentz had also asked him to propose further topics and the names of other rapporteurs, Einstein wrote further:

> Schrödinger’s version of the quantum rule impresses me greatly; it seems to me to be a part of the truth, though the meaning of waves in \(n\)-dimensional \(q\)-space remains quite dark. The choice between the people from the whole group of Heisenberg, Franck, Born, Pauli, certainly is not an easy one. If I had to decide regardless of personalities only on account of originality and the expected enrichment which the [conference] will obtain, I probably would select Heisenberg and Franck, as the two others [i.e., Born and Pauli] do not have inventions of such importance to display. If one wishes to restrict oneself to theoreticians, I’d choose Heisenberg and Born since it would be unfair to prefer Pauli over Born. Still such a choice always involves something brutal, but one cannot change this.

Though Einstein’s main efforts had shifted over the decade to the task of extending his theory of general relativity, especially to obtain a fundamental field theory of matter by unifying gravitation and electromagnetism, he had not entirely given up working on certain quantum aspects of atomic phenomena; thus, he had con-

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0267 -->

# II.6 The Solvay Conferences of 1927 and 1930 and the Consistency Debate

centrated notably on explaining the statistical behaviour of microscopic objects and the nature of radiation.²⁷¹

Indeed, in 1926, Einstein also devoted considerable attention to the development of the new quantum theory by his colleagues in Göttingen and Zurich. He corresponded about and discussed the details with Werner Heisenberg and Erwin Schrödinger, the originators of quantum and wave mechanics, respectively, keeping a sharp and critical eye on, and a certain distance from, both schemes—as he confided especially to his friends Hendrik Lorentz and Paul Ehrenfest in Holland. To Ehrenfest, he wrote:

> I am standing vis-à-vis quantum mechanics with a mixture of admiration and distrust. I do not at all understand the particularities of Dirac (Compton effect).… Schrödinger is initially captivating. But waves in \(n\)-dimensional coordinate space are too heavy to digest, similarly the absence of any understanding for the frequency of the emitted light. I have written to you that the canal ray experiments have totally turned out to confirm the undulatory theory. On the one hand waves, on the other quanta! The reality of both is firm as a rock. But the devil makes a verse out of this (which *really* rhymes) [Aber der Teufel macht einen Vers darauf (der sich wirklich reimt)]. (Einstein to Ehrenfest, 28 August 1926)

Actually, Berlin was a good place to keep such a distance from all this hubbub, because at that time none of the physicists there participated actively in any of the rival schemes of quantum and wave mechanics. On the other hand, the Berlin physicists were interested enough to criticize the new developments and even try to put their results to test. Even after Hans Geiger had left to accept a professorship at the University of Kiel, Walther Bothe—who, with Geiger, had performed the crucial experiment establishing the physical reality of light-quanta and now succeeded him in his position at the *Physikalisch-Technische Reichsanstalt*—devised further experiments to understand the nature of light (Bothe, 1926a, b). Also, Einstein, the originator and continuous advocate of the concept of the light-quantum, joined the party by his ‘Vorschlag zu einem die Natur des elementaren Strahlungs-Emissionsprozesses betreffenden Experiment’ (‘Proposal for an Experiment Concerning the Nature of the Elementary Process of Emission of Radiation,’ Einstein, 1926a). In particular, he devised a method for observing the interference of light, emitted by canal rays, at a wire lattice; if interference existed, he argued, this should confirm the undulatory theory—if not, it would disprove the latter; he claimed further that the experimental technique developed by Emil Rupp in his

---

For more specific details of Einstein’s contributions to quantum theory until 1925, see our Volume 1, Parts 1 and 2, especially Chapter V, and Howard (1990). We agree with the view expressed by Howard that Einstein definitely thought that generalizing the field theories of gravitation and electromagnetism would bring one closer to the solution of the deep quantum riddles; this aspect of Einstein’s thinking is also discussed in Mehra (1973).

# Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

Heidelberg *Habilitation* thesis allowed one to obtain the answer (Rupp, 1926a).²⁷² On 8 July 1926, Einstein presented a paper entitled ‘Über die Interferenzeigenschaften des durch Kanalstrahlen emittierten Lichtes’ (‘On the Interference Properties of the Light Emitted by Canal Rays’) to the Prussian Academy of Sciences (Einstein, 1926b). He now arrived at the conclusion that ‘a failure of the classical undulatory theory envisaged on this topic can almost be excluded’ (Einstein, *loc. cit.*, p. 334): an evident consideration—the assumption that shifting an extended light source parallel in space would not alter the outcome—resulted in the fact that ‘the interference phenomena observed with homogeneous canal rays must emerge from the classical theory of light emission, i.e., as if the canal-ray particles were moving Hertzian oscillators’; hence, ‘an influence of the [still possible] quantum structure of radiation cannot be expected.’ Einstein concluded by announcing that his earlier note of ‘May 1926 guided Mr. Rupp in performing experiments . . . [which] fully confirmed the theory’ (Einstein, *loc. cit.* p. 340).

Einstein finally presented the results of Rupp, who had meanwhile moved to Göttingen, at a later Academy meeting (of 21 October 1926): Rupp had used two setups—one containing a grating, the other a rotating mirror—and checked the observed interference pattern against Einstein’s theory. ‘The results of both experiments follow from the undulatory theory, speaking in favour of a finite (interference) emission time of the atom, which emits according to the experimental arrangement at different times and different positions waves that can interfere,’ Rupp summarized his results, and stated further: ‘No influence of the instantaneous quantum processes of emission on the interference phenomena can be noticed in our experiments.’ (Rupp, 1926b, p. 351)

While these considerations and their experimental test seemed to display fully the undulatory features of radiation, others performed by Bothe strongly exhibited the light-quantum aspects. At the *Physikalisch-Technische Reichsanstalt*, Walther Bothe used the successful coincidence method and Geiger counters, as had been done before in the famous experiment of 1925. Now, he mounted two counters on opposite sides of a metallic foil (consisting of material containing copper or iron), in which fluorescence radiation is stimulated by the incident \(K_{\alpha}\)-radiation from molybdenum (Bothe, 1926a). By carefully subtracting the coincidences caused by radioactive alpha and beta particles (from the counter), Bothe was left with no coincidences, which had to be present, however, if the Bohr–Kramers–Slater radiation theory were valid. Because ‘another type of statistical coupling, different from this [theory] cannot be imagined without very arbitrary changes of the classical [radiation] theory,’ he concluded further:

> Hence one does not go beyond the allowed consequences, if one derives from the experiments here repeated . . . that each single act of emission results in exactly one act

---

of absorption. This connection can be described simply by the picture of Einstein’s light-quanta; one has just to denote the direction in which the light-quantum is emitted in this language [of light-quanta] as “accidental.” (Bothe, *loc. cit.*, p. 562)

Already, three years earlier, in a discussion of the photoelectric effect, Bothe had elaborated an interpretation that agreed with these conclusions as follows:

> Perhaps the [following] assumption opens up some possibilities [of explaining the riddle of the nature of radiation]: classical electrodynamics must only be revised concerning the *Ansatz* for the energy density, say, to the extent that the wave field contains only a vanishing fraction of the total energy emitted, and it essentially just acts as a “Führungsfeld” (“guiding” or “pilot” field) for the main part concentrated in the light-quanta. (Bothe, 1923c, p. 151)

Now, in April 1926, he rephrased the concept of the ‘pilot’ field as follows:

> Though there exists a wave field propagating according to classical laws, the energy is nevertheless not continuously distributed as classical electrodynamics requires but is concentrated in light-quanta; the function of the wave field consists in steering the light-quanta in such a way that on the average the classical energy distribution results. (Bothe, 1926a, p. 562)

Bothe was aware of the difficulties resulting from the assumption of pilot waves, especially if one goes beyond the case of plane waves—because only in the latter case does the ratio of energy to momentum density assume the value \(c\) (the velocity of light *in vacuo*) in classical theory. So far, only energy conservation had been verified beyond doubt; however, further experiments had to demonstrate whether the ‘energy transport’ occurred through localized radiation. Bothe himself proposed one such experiment in fall 1926: X-rays are scattered by two symmetrically placed paraffin prisms, and the scattered rays having equal intensity interfere thereby creating the intensity flux equal to zero (Bothe, 1926b). The ‘Compton effect’ of the radiation scattered from the third prism should then decide whether the light-quantum represented (1) an entire wave field, or (2) a plane partial wave, as Bothe now preferred to believe. In case (1), the light-quantum would move with a velocity smaller than that of light and suffer a smaller Compton effect (red shift), and in case (2), the normal Compton effect had to occur. Because the measurements did not exhibit any deviation from the Compton–Debye formula, the light-quanta had to be associated with plane partial waves, or at least with an ‘elementary bundle’ having a small frequency band, a large coherence length, and a small angle of aperture. Still, this picture lacked, as Bothe recognized, a certain visualizability, because ‘one cannot talk at all about a continuous “motion” of the quanta’; in a way, ‘one may say that the light-quantum jumps’ (Bothe, *loc. cit.*, p. 1281).

In a longer paper, published in *Zeitschrift für Physik*, Bothe presented a detailed explanation of all radiative processes based upon his ideas: emission, scattering,

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0270 -->

238 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

interference, and absorption in the language of light-quanta (Bothe, 1927a).<sup>273</sup> At the same time, he hinted at the connection of his interpretation of the phenomena with that obtained on the basis of wave mechanics for material particles, adopting here the 'probability field' interpretation of Max Born: 'However, in this case one must again abandon the idea of describing the motion of a material particle in detail ... Just in this one may see an indication that light-quanta need not possess less reality than electrons.' (Bothe, 1927a, p. 344)

Previously, in the *Naturwissenschaften* (Bothe, 1926b, p. 1281), Bothe had claimed that his results contradicted an earlier assumption presented by Louis de Broglie (in a recent letter to *Nature*) according to which light-quanta moved with variable velocity perpendicular to the planes of equal phases of the wave field (L. de Broglie, 1926c). During the years 1926 and 1927, de Broglie, the inventor of the conception of matter waves, attempted to develop—in a series of notes and papers (which we shall describe below in this section)—a wave-mechanical formulation that would mediate between the particle and the wave nature of microscopic objects. Although de Broglie's efforts, especially to describe the 'real' particles by singularities of differential equations, showed some similarity to Einstein's programme of a (classical) field theory at that time, Einstein did not refer to them in his papers.

Indeed in early 1927, Einstein proceeded along his own lines. As he reported to Paul Ehrenfest:

> The problem of motion has turned out nicely, even if a small hooklet has remained ... At any rate, it is interesting that equations of motion can determine the motion. I even believe that this will once determine the development of quantum theory, but the path toward that cannot yet be foreseen. My heart does not get warm with the Schrödinger stuff (*Schrödingerei*)—the latter is acausal and too primitive in any case. Masses *do* exist; this you cannot take away from me. I do not believe that kinematics has to be given up. (Einstein to Ehrenfest, 11 January 1927)

Einstein's own research in 1927 concentrated on a new approach to the problem of the motion of particles in a general field theory. Already on 6 January, he had spoken in the Berlin Academy about '*Allgemeine Relativitätstheorie und Bewegungsgesetz*' ('General Relativity Theory and the Law of Motion'). The report, which he had composed with Jakob Grommer, showed that 'in the case of a pure gravitational field the mechanical behaviour of singularities can be derived,' a result that in Einstein's opinion 'opened the possibility to obtain, on the basis of the field equations, a theory of matter characterized as discontinuities in space.'<sup>274</sup>

<sup>273</sup> In a further paper dealing with the statistics of cavity radiation, Bothe derived the Bose statistics for light-quanta and the correct fluctuation behaviour of Einstein's earlier result (Bothe, 1927b). See also Einstein, 1927c, for a positive reaction to Bothe's ideas.

<sup>274</sup> See the summary in *Sitzungsberichte der Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften*, 1927, p. 1, under the announcement of Einstein's talk.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0271 -->

II.6 The Solvay Conferences of 1927 and 1930 and the Consistency Debate 239

After Einstein had tried for years to obtain a theory of material particles in a generalized field theory by describing these objects with the help of continuous functions, Einstein and Grommer now proposed 'to consider elementary particles as singular points or singular world lines, respectively,' motivated by the observation 'that both the equations of the pure gravitational field and the equations augmented by Maxwell's electromagnetic field possess simple spherically-symmetric solutions which contain a singularity' (Einstein and Grommer, 1927, p. 4). Finally, they arrived at the result: in the approximation of the gravitational field obtained by solving linearized equations, the equation of motion for a singularity is completely determined—at least in the case of equilibrium—and corresponds to the law of a geodetic line.

Because at the time no electrically neutral elementary particles were known, Einstein—in two further communications—studied an extension of the general relativistic situation to include the electromagnetic field (Einstein, 1927a, b). 'It can be shown that the unification of gravitation and Maxwell's theories may be achieved in a completely satisfactory manner by the five-dimensional theory of Kaluza, Klein and Fock,' he wrote to Lorentz on 16 February 1927, summarizing the results of these investigations. In a further paper on the law of motion in a pure gravitational theory (presented in November of the same year), Einstein removed some of the restrictions imposed in the earlier work with Grommer (Einstein, 1927d). He characterized the attempts of 1927 again in a letter to Ehrenfest as:<sup>275</sup>

> That the derivation of the laws of motion in relativity theory has finally been accomplished, I believe to have shown to you. However, the result is only the classical one. I think Kaluza-Klein have indicated the direction to proceed further. (Einstein to Ehrenfest, 21 January 1928)

Whatever positive result came out of his efforts, at the end of 1927, Einstein was not prepared at all to abandon the long-cherished hope to obtain quantum phenomena directly from a general field theory. The standard attempts in quantum mechanics, including those of Bothe, did not appear to him to be very convincing. Thus, he had already made some remarks at the University of Berlin on '*Theoretisches und Experimentelles zur Frage der Lichtentstehung*' ('Theoretical and Experimental Remarks on the Question of the Creation of Light,' Einstein, 1927c); in referring to Bothe's new experiments on radiation (Bothe, 1927a), he claimed there that 'the geometrical characteristics and the interference phenomena cannot be explained by the quantum conception' and stated: 'What nature demands from us is not a quantum or a wave theory; rather, nature demands from us a synthesis of

<sup>275</sup> Einstein had shown an interest in Oskar Klein's work on the five-dimensional theory of Theodor Kaluza already in 1926. See Pais, 1982a, pp. 333–334.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0272 -->

240 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

both conceptions, which, to be sure, until now still exceeds the power of thinking of the physicists.'<sup>276</sup>

In trying to improve on the situation in 1927, Einstein did suffer a defeat, as may be seen from the following story. Late in April or early May, he wrote a short note to Born, indicating that one can 'associate with Schrödinger's wave mechanics quite definite motions [of microscopic particles] without employing any statistical interpretation.'<sup>277</sup> Then, on 5 May 1927, he read a paper to the Prussian Academy, entitled '*Bestimmt Schrödingers Wellenmechanik die Bewegung eines Systems vollständig oder nur im Sinne der Statistik?*' ('Does Schrödinger's Wave Mechanics Determine the Motion of a [Microscopic] System Completely or only in the Statistical Sense?').<sup>278</sup> Of course, the rumour of a nonstatistical interpretation by Einstein excited the extreme curiosity of people in Göttingen and Copenhagen. Heisenberg, in particular, wrote directly to Einstein in Berlin for a clarification:<sup>279</sup>

> If I understood correctly your point of view, then you would gladly sacrifice the simplicity [of quantum mechanics] to the principle of [classical] causality. Perhaps we should comfort ourselves: the dear Lord could go beyond [quantum mechanics] and maintain causality. I do not really find it beautiful, however, to demand more than a physical description of the connection between experiments. (Heisenberg to Einstein, 10 June 1927)

Unlike Heisenberg, however, Einstein did demand more from a physical theory. He rather assumed the following point of view:

> About quantum mechanics I think that it contains as much truth about ponderable matter as the theory of light without quanta. It might be a correct statistical theory but [it] constitutes an insufficient conception [*Auffassung*] of the individual elementary process. (Einstein to Sommerfeld, November 1929, in Einstein and Sommerfeld, 1968, p. 112)

It was this stand that he would defend at the fifth Solvay Conference, where he attacked vigorously the foundations of the interpretation developed by the Göttingen–Cambridge–Copenhagen pioneers of quantum mechanics, notably, Heisenberg's uncertainty relations.
