II.6 The Solvay Conferences of 1927 and 1930 and the Consistency Debate 241

**(c) The 1927 Solvay Reports and Their Preparation (Summer 1927)<sup>280</sup>**

On 17 June 1927, Einstein wrote to Lorentz:<sup>281</sup>

> I recall having committed myself to you to give a report on quantum statistics at the Solvay [Conference]. After much reflection back and forth, I came to the conclusion that I am not competent for giving such a report in a way which really corresponds to the state of the thing. The reason is that I have not been able to participate as intensively in the modern development of quantum theory as would be necessary for that purpose. This is in part because I have on the whole too little receptive talent for fully following the stormy developments, in part also because I do not approve of the purely statistical way of thinking on which the new theory is founded. ... Up until now, I kept hoping to be able to contribute something of value in Brussels; I have now given up that hope. I beg you not to be angry with me because of that; I did not take this lightly but tried with all my strength.

As a substitute speaker for the topic assigned to him, he proposed either Enrico Fermi from Italy or Paul Langevin from France. Ultimately, however, neither of them gave the report on Einstein's subject. Instead, Niels Bohr agreed to contribute a report on a different topic: namely, on his latest considerations on the problem of the interpretation of quantum mechanics.

The rapporteurs at the fifth Solvay Conference fell into three groups: the experimentalists Bragg and Compton; the theoreticians advocating the Göttingen–Cambridge–Copenhagen versions of quantum mechanics—Bohr, Born, and Heisenberg; and those of the wave-mechanical camp—de Broglie and Schrödinger.

The selection of Arthur Holly Compton seemed to be most appropriate, because the Compton effect—discovered in late 1922—had been one of the crucial results triggering the entire development (which ended with the new atomic theory) by providing Einstein's light-quantum hypothesis of 1905 a firm experimental foundation. Since its discovery, and even more so after the refutation of the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory of radiation—the last attempt to rescue a purely wave theory of radiation—in April 1925 by the Bothe–Geiger (and later that year by the Compton–Simon) experiment, Einstein's fundamental light-quantum conception, which Gilbert N. Lewis had christened the 'photon' in October 1926 (Lewis, 1926), became a physical reality. Compton's report dwelt on the conceptual consequences rather than on experimental details (Compton, 1928). In particular, he addressed the questions of the aether and of electromagnetic waves, on the one hand, and the phenomena contradicting the (classical) wave concepts, on the other: such as the photoelectric effect, X-ray diffraction, certain electron-recoil effects (observed by C. T. R. Wilson and W. Bothe in 1923), and the individual interaction between radiation-quanta and electrons (i.e., the Compton effect).

<sup>280</sup> A detailed account of the reports and discussions at the fifth Solvay Conference of Physics is given in Mehra, 1975a, Chapter 6.

<sup>281</sup> See Pais, 1982b, pp. 431–432, for the translation.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0274 -->

242 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

Compton showed also in some detail how the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory failed to account for these observations.

The report of William Lawrence Bragg, a regular participant in the Solvay Conferences since 1913, appeared to address, on first inspection, less central points (Bragg, 1928). However, from his presentation of the material on reflection of X-rays, one easily recognizes the strategy of the Scientific Committee of the Conference: Bragg had to take over the task of stressing those radiation phenomena that could be described by the wave theory, namely, the diffraction of X-rays by crystal lattices. Consequently, he gave the story from Laue’s discovery in 1912, over the subsequent work of his father William Henry Bragg and himself, to the later investigations of Paul Ewald, William Duane, and others. Bragg demonstrated in detail how the old and the new wave theories worked to describe the phenomena of diffraction and refraction of X-rays. In the discussion of Bragg’s report, Hendrik Kramers presented at some length the recent development of the dispersion theory by himself and Ralph Kronig.<sup>282</sup>

Both experimental reports served as a firm basis for the discussion of the theoretical concepts, which provided the central theme of the conference. This significance was shown by the discussions immediately following them. Compton’s talk especially gave rise to a lively exchange of ideas and arguments, in which, besides the experimentalists (e.g., Bragg, Madame Curie, O. W. Richardson, and C. T. R. Wilson), almost all of the theoretical experts present participated—i.e., Bohr, Born, Debye, Dirac, Ehrenfest, Lorentz, Pauli, and Schrödinger—with one important exception: according to the published proceedings of the fifth Solvay Conference (*Électrons et Photons*, Institut International de Physique Solvay, 1928), Einstein *remained silent* after the presentations of Compton and Bragg.

Moving on to the theoretical rapporteurs, one should stress from the outset that the experts on quantum mechanics did not by any means constitute a monolithic faction, at least before they went to Brussels (as we have outlined in the previous sections). Max Born, for instance, was not, and never really became, a complete partisan of the Copenhagen camp. One reason for this may have been his status as a senior professor, his slightly stiff character, and his emphasis on the formal, mathematical learning (*Gelehrsamkeit*). On the other hand, he interacted directly with James Franck, his experimental colleague and friend in Göttingen. As he recalled later: ‘I was witnessing the fertility of the particle concept every day in Franck’s brilliant experiments on atomic and molecular collisions and was convinced that particles could not simply be abolished.’ (Born, 1968, p. 55) Hence, he mainly searched for a way to ‘reconcile’ the fundamental concept of particles with the wave properties emerging from quantum mechanics. An adequate tool enabling such a reconciliation seemed to him to be the ‘ghost field’ (‘*Gespensterfeld*’) of his friend Einstein. As he wrote to the latter in fall 1926:

<sup>282</sup> Their actual publications were Kramers, 1927, and Kronig, 1926c, yielding the later famous Kramers–Kronig dispersion relations.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0275 -->

II.6 The Solvay Conferences of 1927 and 1930 and the Consistency Debate 243

About me it can be said that physics-wise I am entirely satisfied since my idea to look upon Schrödinger’s wave field as a “*Gespensterfeld*” in your case proves better all the time. Pauli and Jordan have just made beautiful advances in this direction. The probability field does of course not move in ordinary space but in phase- (or rather configuration-) space … Schrödinger’s achievement reduces itself to something purely mathematical; his physics is quite pitiful (*recht kümmerlich*). (Born to Einstein, 30 November 1926)<sup>283</sup>

Upon which Einstein replied:

Quantum mechanics is very impressive. But an inner voice tells me that it is not yet the real thing. The theory produces a good deal, but it does not bring us any closer to the secret of the “Old One.” I am at all events convinced that *He* does not play dice. (Einstein to Born, 4 December 1926, in Einstein *et al.*, 1969, p. 130)

Born, however, was exactly convinced that the ‘Old One’ did play dice, or in other words: ‘The fundamental idea of probability wave will persist in one form or another’ (Born, 1927a, p. 357). Much as he admired Einstein for his understanding of Nature, this time he disagreed fundamentally, and retained his point of view during the rest of his life.

In the course of the year 1927, the Copenhagen physicists, Heisenberg among them, clarified their ideas on the interpretation of atomic phenomena. Although they admitted the existence (and persistence) of statistical relations in quantum mechanics, they searched for—and succeeded in—formulating principles that, in their opinion, at least, provided the deeper reason for these statistical features: the uncertainty relations and the complementarity principle. In spite of this difference in attitude toward what they regarded as truly fundamental and actually derived, Heisenberg felt no difficulty in preparing a joint Solvay report together with his former teacher Max Born.<sup>284</sup> Their report provided a review of the work performed in Göttingen and Cambridge in establishing quantum mechanics, with chapters on matrix mechanics and its transformation into wave mechanics (I), the physical interpretation of the theory (II), and the uncertainty principle (III). The balance in representing the main interests of the two authors was achieved insofar as Section II dealt with Born’s statistical interpretation and Section III with Heisenberg’s limitation on measurements in quantum mechanics. Moreover, the Born–Heisenberg report also signalled the agreement reached by Heisenberg and Niels Bohr during the summer of 1927.

The reports on the wave-mechanical formulation at the fifth Solvay Conference were presented by Louis de Broglie and Erwin Schrödinger, respectively. De Broglie had at first been surprised when, early in 1926, Schrödinger came out with wave mechanics. He later recalled his reactions in some detail, which consisted at first in

<sup>283</sup> See Pais, 1982b, p. 1197.
<sup>284</sup> Heisenberg would not leave the writing to Born alone, but did his share in contributing to it (Heisenberg to Bohr, 23 July 1927).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0276 -->

244 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

seeking (independently of Oskar Klein, Walter Gordon, and others) a relativistic generalization of the wave equation (L. de Broglie, 1926a) and then turning to a new task:

When the first ideas of wave mechanics began to take shape for me, I did not doubt for a moment that now a new synthetic theory had to be found, which would leave aside the conventional aspects of the concepts of wave and corpuscle.... But how to carry out this programme?... In a series of papers published between 1925 and 1927 the progress of my ideas on that topic can be followed. I arrived at a rather subtle explanation, which I called “the theory of the double solution” and of which I gave a detailed presentation in an article for *Journal de physique* (L. de Broglie, 1927d)....

To understand the nature of my efforts, one should note that one of the first principles in order to understand the physical meaning of wave mechanics was exactly the following: “The square of the Ψ-wave amplitude, which associated with a corpuscle, determines at every position and each instant of time the probability of the corpuscle to exist at this space-time point and moment.” This principle, (the interference principle) constituted from the very beginning one of the most evident and established principles of the physical interpretations of the new formalism. If one now assumes the shape of the wave associated with a corpuscle as known, then one may assume that the intensity of this wave determines at every point of space and each instant of time (given by |Ψ|²) as defined by the density of the fictive fluid body moving in space in the course of time; the amount of this fluid body contained in a volume element, then, will provide the probability of the corpuscle to be present in that volume element. (L. de Broglie, 1953a, pp. 464–466)

A ‘hydrodynamical interpretation,’ as mentioned above, had been published already by Erwin Madelung in Germany (see Madelung, 1926a, b), but de Broglie now proceeded further, because he wanted to ‘*incorporate* the corpuscle into the wave, in order to obtain a clear picture, generally consistent with the classical conceptions, one of the wave-particle dualism in space and time.’ This goal appeared within reach, if he assumed ‘the corpuscles to constitute in reality a kind of permanent singularity in the interior of the propagating wave.’ However, he also knew that wave mechanics (of Schrödinger) had so far worked perfectly without any discontinuities, simply with continuous waves whose intensity at each point yielded (according to Born) the probability for the corpuscle to be present. ‘How could one bring together both conceptions—the corpuscles associated with the waves—into harmony?’ de Broglie asked, and answered:

For that purpose I tried to develop the idea that the equations of “wave mechanics” always admit two mutually coupled solutions: the first, implying a singularity, should really represent the corpuscle incorporated into the wave phenomenon; the second, having a continuously varying amplitude, should only express the statistical transport of the corpuscular cloud. Hence I presented the wave-corpuscle duality in a way suited to the old physics, while I still continued to justify the use of the propagating [continuous] Ψ-wave and connected it with the essential property expressed by the [statistical] interference principle. In this way I again arrived at the hydrodynamical interpretation of Madelung, which had been turned into a double solution with the

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0277 -->

II.6 The Solvay Conferences of 1927 and 1930 and the Consistency Debate 245

help of the structural picture of a wave with a corpuscular singularity. (L. de Broglie, 1953a, pp. 466–467)

However, before he put these ideas (which he had developed in L. de Broglie, 1927d, and extended to the case of a gravitational field in L. de Broglie, 1927e, f) into the Solvay report, he recognized ‘clearly all the difficulties’ that showed up when he tried to prove the mathematical existence and consistency of the double solution. Hence, de Broglie decided to adopt in his paper a ‘more moderate point of view,’ which he described later with the words:

By assuming the existence of corpuscles and the validity of the equations of wave mechanics as being given *a priori*, I transferred, briefly and to the point, the corpuscle into the interior of the propagating wave and suggested that it will be carried along.... According to this hypothesis, the Ψ-wave, so to say, “guides” the motion of the corpuscle; hence I called the less rigid formulation of my ideas up to that point “the theory of the pilot wave.” This gentler formulation abandoned [the ideas of] incorporating the corpuscle into the wave and restricted itself to stating the wave-corpuscle dualism without attempting to explain it. In my eyes it [i.e., the pilot-wave theory] still had the advantage of retaining the visualizable concept of a point-like corpuscle, which could be exactly localized in space, and of not abandoning strict determinism with respect to the [corpuscle’s] motion. (L. de Broglie, 1953a, pp. 467–468)

Louis de Broglie’s ideas of resolving the corpuscle-wave duality with the help of the double-solution did not escape the attention of his colleagues.<sup>285</sup> Wolfgang Pauli called the proposal ‘an interesting and inspiring attempt,’ but at the same time criticized the fact that de Broglie had failed to provide a mathematical proof that the two solutions were connected. Altogether, he found the whole theory ‘highly uncongenial and suspicious’ because, in his opinion, it turned back the wheel of history: first, it somehow reintroduced the previously abandoned definite electron orbits in atoms; second, it did not seem to describe the well-established Franck–Hertz collision phenomena. In spite of these fundamental objections, Pauli thought that de Broglie’s paper treated the wave-particle problem on a ‘much higher level than the childish papers of Schrödinger, who still today believes that he can escape the statistical interpretation of his [wave] function and abolish material points’ (Pauli to Bohr, 6 August 1927).

The presentation of the theoretical reports at the Solvay Conference proceeded by following the historical order in which the ideas had been published between 1923 and 1926: thus, de Broglie’s talk came first, then Born and Heisenberg’s, followed by Schrödinger’s, and finally Bohr’s. Louis de Broglie entitled his report ‘The New Dynamics of Quanta’ (1928); he covered the story from his first ideas on matter waves (in 1923–1924) to the advent of Schrödinger’s equation (in 1926) and

<sup>285</sup> In the first half of 1927, de Broglie published a note in *Comptes rendus* (on the connection between electrodynamics and wave mechanics: L. de Broglie, 1927a) and two papers in *Journal de physique* (one on the five-dimensional theory: 1927c, and the other on the double solution: 1927d).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0278 -->

246 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

on to the new pilot-wave theory (in 1927). He further applied the pilot-wave theory to the problem of the hydrogen atom and claimed that the treatment yielded an easier understanding of the actual situation; finally, he spoke about the experimental verification of matter waves obtained recently in the experiments of Clinton Joseph Davisson and Lester Halbert Germer (1927a) and George Paget Thomson and Alexander Reid (1927). Born and Heisenberg (1928) summarized mainly the Göttingen path of quantum mechanics, applications and the statistical interpretation of wave mechanics, and completion of the equivalence demonstration of both schemes by Dirac, Heisenberg, and Jordan. Erwin Schrödinger (1928), on the other hand, concentrated on the mathematical aspects of his wave-mechanical scheme, the time-independent as well as the time-dependent equations, the formal equivalence of wave mechanics to the Born–Heisenberg–Jordan matrix scheme, and the relativistic wave equation. At the end of the conference, Niels Bohr presented a modified version of his Como lecture under the title ‘The Quantum Postulate and the New Development of Atomic Theory’ (1928f).

**(d) The Official (Published) Discussions of Reports (October 1927)**

The participants of the conference later recalled lively discussions on the fundamental concepts of quantum mechanics and its interpretation. Thus, for instance, Louis de Broglie related:

> In a fine opening speech Lorentz presented and sharpened the point of view of classical physics. Born, Heisenberg and Bohr assured us how necessary were the somehow revolutionary conceptions which their pure probability interpretation of the new mechanics implied. Schrödinger stuck to a rather classical point of view and tried to identify corpuscles and wave trains, a hypothesis which did not appear satisfactory to me. Einstein, who was hostile towards the pure probability interpretation from the depth of his heart, contradicted with troublesome objections which Bohr rejected with sharply-formulated considerations. (L. de Broglie, 1953a, p. 468)

Similarly, Heisenberg and other participants remembered the Solvay discussions (see, e.g., Heisenberg, 1971, pp. 71–81). Still, very little of what they said came through in the official published discussions.
Although the Born–Heisenberg and Schrödinger reports provoked only technical questions, that of de Broglie and especially the one of Bohr stimulated some conceptual discussion. Thus, Lorentz asked de Broglie how the old Sommerfeld quantum conditions could be obtained from the new matter-wave ideas, and Pauli provided an appropriate calculation using the conservation law for the relativistic electric current; also, Léon Brillouin illustrated some ‘optical’ applications of matter waves. Finally, Bohr’s report at the end provided the proper start for a very excited ‘General Discussion of the New Ideas Put Forward.’<sup>286</sup>

<sup>286</sup> See the title of the general discussion in the published proceedings of the conference: *Éléctrons et Photons: Institut International de Physique Solvay*, 1928, pp. 248–289.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0279 -->

II.6 The Solvay Conferences of 1927 and 1930 and the Consistency Debate 247

Upon an opening reflection of Hendrik Lorentz—who expressed some reservation with respect to the new pictures of electrons in quantum and wave-mechanics—and a technical illustration of Max Born for dealing with many-electron systems in the probability scheme, Einstein addressed an elementary problem in the physical interpretation of the theory. He suggested, in particular, to consider an electron passing through a slit in a screen and to discuss the diffraction phenomena obtained. He claimed that ‘with respect to [quantum mechanics] one can take two standpoints regarding its validity,’ namely:

*Interpretation I*: The de Broglie-Schrödinger waves do not correspond to a single electron, but to an electron cloud, extended in space. The theory does not give [then] any information about an ensemble of an infinity of elementary processes.
*Interpretation II*: The theory claims to be a complete theory of individual processes. Each particle which moves towards the screen, as far as one can determine from its position and velocity, is described by a de Broglie-Schrödinger wave packet of small length and small aperture. This wave packet is diffracted and, after diffraction, arrives partly at the film *P* [where it is registered in a resolved state]. (Einstein, in *Électrons et Photons*, Institut International de Physique Solvay, 1928, pp. 254–255)

Evidently, *Interpretation II* went beyond *I* and even included the latter; it also implied that the conservation laws (especially for momentum) were valid for individual atomic processes, thus explaining the Bothe–Geiger experiment as well as other experiments. Still, Einstein also objected to this interpretation, because: ‘If $|\Psi|^2$ were simply considered as the probability for a particle to be at a place at the definite instant, it might happen that *one and the same* elementary process would cause an action at *two or more* places on the screen,’ which would imply an action-at-a-distance, hence, a violation of the relativity postulate. The only way out of this difficulty had to be sought with de Broglie in further attempts to localize the microscopic particle (with the help of the double solution of the pilot wave). Einstein claimed further that the multidimensional phase space assumed for many-particle systems in quantum or wave mechanics and the corresponding permutation properties contradicted the new statistical results.
Although Lorentz tried to illuminate the statistical argument further, Wolfgang Pauli contradicted Einstein by referring to the recent work of Paul Dirac, Pascual Jordan, and Oskar Klein on field quantization. He also refuted another argument of Einstein’s, that the range of forces in quantum mechanics might create problems, by pointing to the work of Walter Heitler and Fritz London on molecular binding. Dirac, at first, supported Pauli’s plea; then, he stated his ‘opinion about determinism and the significance of numbers which occur in the calculus of quantum theory,’ notably:

> In the classical theory one starts from certain numbers which completely specify the initial state of the system, and one deduces certain numbers which specify the final state. This determination applies only to an isolated system. (Dirac, in *Électrons et Photons*, Institut International de Physique Solvay, 1928, p. 261)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0280 -->

248 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

Now, according to Bohr, isolated systems are by definition unobservable, because any observation must disturb the system; as a result, already ‘the classical deterministic theory cannot be defended.’ Furthermore:

> In the quantum theory, one starts from certain numbers from which one deduces certain [other] numbers. . . . The perturbations, which an observer inflicts on a system in order to observe it, are directly subject to his control and are acts of his free will. *It is exclusively the numbers, which describe these acts of free choice, that can be taken as initial numbers for a calculation in the quantum theory*. Other numbers specifying the initial state of the system are fundamentally unobservable and do not appear in the quantum-theoretical treatment. (Dirac, *loc. cit.*)

The result of an experiment, or the final number, Dirac continued, must be a ‘permanent registration.’ It describes the final state that enters into the further development of the system, which is what one observes in a Wilson cloud chamber registering the path of an electron, hence, that observation ‘agrees perfectly with the new quantum theory,’ because:

> it describes the state of the world at any instant by a wave function $\psi$, which normally develops according to a causal law so that its initial value determines its value at any later instant. It may happen, however, that at a given instant, $t_1$, $\psi$ can be expended in a series of the form $\psi = \sum_n c_n \psi_n$, where the $\psi_n$ are wave functions of such a nature that they cannot interfere with each other at any instant later than $t_1$. If this is the case, the state of the world at instants later than $t_1$ will be described not by $\psi$, but one of the $\psi_n$. One may say that nature chooses whatever $\psi_n$ it pleases, since the only information which the theory provides is that the probability of choosing any $\psi_n$ is $|c_n|^2$. Once the choice is made, it is irrevocable and affects any future state of the world. The value of $n$ chosen by nature can be determined by an experiment, and *the result of all experiments* are numbers describing similar choices by nature. (Dirac, *loc. cit.*, p. 262)

After Dirac had illustrated his interpretation of the quantum-mechanical process and its observation in the case of a sample collision experiment, Heisenberg remarked that he did ‘not agree’ with Dirac, saying ‘that in the experiment described nature makes a choice,’ because:

> Even if you place yourself very far from your scattering material, and if you measure after a very long time, you can obtain interference by taking two mirrors. If nature were to make a choice, it would be difficult to imagine how the interference can be produced. Evidently, we can say that nature’s choice can never be known until the decisive experiment has been done; for this reason we cannot make any real objection to this choice, because the expression “nature makes a choice” does not have any physical consequences. I would say, as I have done in my latest paper {Heisenberg, 1927b], that the *observer himself* makes the choice, because it is not until the moment when the observation is made that the “choice” becomes a physical reality and that the phase relation in the waves, i.e., the ability to interfere, is destroyed. (Heisenberg, in *Éléctrons et Photons*, Institut International de Physique Solvay, 1928, pp. 264–265)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0281 -->

II.6 The Solvay Conferences of 1927 and 1930 and the Consistency Debate 249

So far, this lively exchange of ideas on the question of interpretation can be derived from the recorded and published discussions at the fifth Solvay Conference.<sup>287</sup> Bohr, who did not participate in this ‘official exchange,’ wrote privately in a note stating that the whole problem of the interpretation of experiments might be put more simply into his own language:

> Just the distinction between derivation and definition allows to let the quantum mechanics appear as generalization [of the classical theory]. What does [it] mean: get records which do not allow to work backwards. Even if we took all molecules in [a] photographic plate, one would have [a] closed system. If we tell [i.e., speak] of a record, we give up [the] definition of a plate. [The] whole point lies in that by observation we introduce something which does not allow us to go on. (Bohr, 1985, p. 105)

The differences in interpretation among the main pioneers of quantum mechanics that showed in this exchange, notably, between Bohr (and Heisenberg) and Dirac, would become more pronounced in the future (see, in particular, the following section).
Bohr’s private notes further contain an answer to Einstein’s discussion remark. At first, he wrote:

> I [find] myself in a very difficult position because I don’t understand what precisely is the point which Einstein wants to [make]. No doubt it is my fault.
> . . .
> As regards [the] general problem I feel its difficulties. I would put [the] problem in [an]other way. I do not know what quantum mechanics is. I think we are dealing with some mathematical tools which are adequate for [the] description of our experiments. Using a rigorous wave theory, we are claiming something which the theory possibly cannot give. [We must realize] that we are away from the state where we could hope to describe things on classical theories. [I] understand [the] same view is held by Born and Heisenberg. I think that we are actually just trying to meet, as in other theories, some requirements of nature, but [the] difficulty is that we must use words which remind [us] of older theories. The whole foundation for [a] causal space-time description is taken away by quantum theory, for it is based on [the] assumption of observations without interference [between the object of observation and the subject of observer]; excluding interference means exclusion of experiments and the whole meaning of space and time observation . . . because we [have] interaction [between object and measuring apparatus], and thereby we put [ourselves] on a quite different standpoint than we thought we could take in classical theories. If we speak of observations, we play with a statistical problem. . . . The saying that space-time is an abstraction might seem a philosophical triviality, but nature reminds us that we are dealing with something of practical interest. (Bohr, *loc. cit.*, p. 103)

The scribbled notes reproduced here contain, of course, a part of Niels Bohr’s programme of dealing with the process of measurement in quantum theory, which

<sup>287</sup> In the foregoing quotations from Dirac and Heisenberg, we have made use of the English translation of their remarks given in Bohr, 1985, pp. 101–105.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0282 -->

250 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

he worked out in further detail in the following years (both before and after 1930). In our opinion, they are not intimately connected with the conceptual discussion that was taking place between him and Einstein, to which we shall turn next.²⁸⁸

After the Einstein–Pauli–Dirac–Heisenberg exchange, the general discussion turned to more technical problems connected with the description of photons and electrons in quantum mechanics, as well as with the details of de Broglie’s recent ideas. Though these points possess some intrinsic interest, they do not throw much light on the interpretation debate, which is of primary concern to us in this chapter.

**(e) The Bohr–Einstein Debate in October 1927— Earlier and Later Recollections**

As we have already mentioned, in the recollections of some participants of the fifth Solvay Conference, the exchange between Bohr and Einstein on fundamental questions concerning the interpretation of quantum mechanics stands out vividly. Thus, Bohr, after more than twenty years, wrote a detailed account of his ‘Discussions with Einstein on Epistemological Problems in Atomic Theory,’ where he introduced the important part dealing with the 1927 exchange by saying:

> At the general discussions in Como, we all missed the presence of Einstein, but soon after, in October 1927, I had the opportunity to meet him in Brussels at the Fifth Physical Conference of the Solvay Institute . . . At the Solvay meetings, Einstein had from their beginning been a most prominent figure, and several of us came to the Conference with great anticipations to learn his reaction to the latest stage of the development which, to our view, went far in clarifying the problems which he had himself from the outset elicited so ingeniously. During the discussions, where the whole subject was reviewed by contributions from many sides. . . , Einstein expressed, however, a deep concern over the extent to which causal account in space and time was abandoned in quantum mechanics. (Bohr, 1949, pp. 211–212)

The official discussions referred to above throw light on some of the exchanges on the questions that did interest Einstein, although Bohr’s participation in them does not seem to have been so active. For example, no answer from Bohr to Einstein’s analysis of the electron’s passage through a slit or screen was recorded. As we have reported, Bohr just made some notes, which are to be found in his files, and, as Louis de Broglie recalled: ‘[Also] Einstein said hardly anything beyond presenting a very simple objection to the probability interpretation. Then he fell silent’ (L. de Broglie, 1962, p. 150). However, Heisenberg took away quite a different impression from the conference, and decades later, he wrote enthusiastically:

²⁸⁸ These notes were written during the general discussion at the end of the conference as an *aide mémoire*, while the Bohr–Einstein debate on the consistency of quantum mechanics extended over the whole meeting.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0283 -->

II.6 The Solvay Conferences of 1927 and 1930 and the Consistency Debate 251

The discussions were soon focused upon a duel between Einstein and Bohr on the question as to what extent atomic theory in its present form could be considered to be the final solution of the difficulties which had been discussed for several decades. We generally met already at breakfast in the hotel, and Einstein began to describe an ideal [*Gedanken*] experiment in which he thought the inner contradictions of the Copenhagen interpretation were especially clearly visible. Einstein, Bohr and I walked together from the hotel to the conference building, and I listened to the lively discussion between those two people whose philosophical attitudes were so different, and from time to time I added a remark on the structure of the mathematical formalism. During the meeting and particularly in the pauses we younger people, mostly Pauli and I, tried to analyze Einstein’s experiment, and at lunch time the discussions continued between Bohr and the others from Copenhagen. Bohr had usually finished the complete analysis of the ideal experiment by late afternoon and would show it to Einstein at the supper table. Einstein had no good objection to this analysis, but in his heart he was not convinced. Bohr’s friend Ehrenfest, who was also a close friend of Einstein, said to him, “I am ashamed of you, Einstein! You put yourself here just in the same position as your opponents in their futile attempts to refute your relativity theory.” (Heisenberg, 1967, p. 107)

Otto Stern related a similar story in a discussion with Res Jost on 2 December 1961:

> Einstein came down to breakfast and expressed his misgivings about the new quantum theory, every time [he] had invented some beautiful experiment from which one saw that [the theory] did not work. . . . Pauli and Heisenberg, who were there, did not pay much attention, “*ach was, das stimmt schon, das stimmt schon*” [ah, well, it will be alright, it will be alright]. Bohr, on the other hand, reflected on it with care, and in the evening, at dinner, we were all together and he cleared the matter in detail. (See Pais, 1991, p. 318)

We should note, however, that this recollection could not refer to the 1927 conference, in which Stern did not take part, but to the sixth Solvay Conference in 1930, where the Bohr–Einstein debate was continued (and then Heisenberg and Pauli were not so interested in Einstein’s objections anymore!).

In light of the little evidence of the Bohr–Einstein debate in the official conference documents, one may be a little concerned as to whether perhaps Bohr and Heisenberg’s recollections also referred to the later 1930 meeting, but we do have a first-hand witness, namely, Paul Ehrenfest, who reported about them shortly after the conference. On 3 November 1927, he wrote to his students and associates Samuel Goudsmit, George Uhlenbeck, and Gerhard Diecke, giving them a full account, which we quote in full:

> Brussels was fine! Lorentz, Planck, Einstein, Bohr, Heisenberg, Kramers, Pauli, Dirac, Fowler, Brillouin, Bragg, Compton, Langmuir, Schrödinger, de Broglie, Curie, Wilson, Richardson, Knudsen, Debye and I. Bohr towering completely over everybody. At first not understood at all (Born was also there), then step by step defeating everybody.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0284 -->

> Naturally once again the awful Bohr incantation terminology. (Poor Lorentz as interpreter between the British and the French who were absolutely unable to understand each other. Summarizing Bohr. And Bohr responding with polite despair.) (Every night at 1 a.m. Bohr came into my room just to say ONE SINGLE WORD to me, until 3 a.m.) It was delightful for me to be present during the conversations between Bohr and Einstein. Like a game of chess. Einstein all the time with new examples. In a certain sense a sort of Perpetuum Mobile of the second kind to break the UNCERTAINTY RELATION. Bohr from out of philosophical smoke clouds constantly searching for the tools to crush one example after the other. Einstein like a jack-in-the-box, jumping out fresh every morning. Oh, that was priceless. But I am almost without reservation pro Bohr and contra Einstein. His attitude to Bohr is now exactly like the attitude of the defenders of absolute simultaneity towards him.

Something like this: Consider first solely the questions of LIGHT. Then immediately from pure WAVE KINEMATICS the following uncertainties (for example) $\Delta t \Delta \nu \sim 1$. The shorter the time duration at a wave signal, the greater the uncertainty in the definition of its frequency (analogously the wave number and the inverse wavelength). Further, from this result, on account of the Planck-Einstein relation $\varepsilon = h\nu, p = \frac{h}{\lambda}$ (momentum), the ‘reciprocal uncertainty relations’
>
> $$\delta t \cdot \delta \varepsilon \sim h, \quad \delta x \cdot \delta p \sim h.$$
>
> Thus, the reciprocal uncertainty of the space-time data as opposed to the dynamical data emerge in general FIRST OF ALL IN THE DOMAIN OF LIGHT
>
> $$x\ y\ z\ t \quad \text{contra} \quad p\ q\ r\ \varepsilon.$$
>
> (In the exponent of the wave function they appear just in the combination
>
> $$\frac{2\pi i}{h}(x_1 p_1 + x_2 p_2 + x_3 p_3 + x_4 p_4).$$

Now, however, such effects like the Compton effect in particular prove that the CONSERVATION LAW for the energy-momentum vector is valid in the interaction between light and movable matter. THUS, it follows for every such interaction that thanks to the conservation laws (!!!!!!!!!!) the above reciprocal uncertainty relations are transferred from light to matter (!!!!!!! BRAVO BOHR !!!!!!!). This might cause you complete despair (witness indeed the desperate attempt of Slater-Kramers-Bohr) if it with non-permutative matrix calculus were also “coming up with uncertainties” just from the matter aspect. And not even somehow with an uncertainty of a different width than the optical, but wonder upon wonder again of width $h$. Thus Bohr: Downright undeserved harmony!!!! And by means of the conservation laws you can now with full confidence let the uncertainty relation propagate

II.6 The Solvay Conferences of 1927 and 1930 and the Consistency Debate 253

> itself into an arbitrary corner of physics. For instance to an entire microscope! Thus consider simply the collision between an electron and the moon. The conservation laws see to it that the uncertainty in the dynamical quantities is transferred from the electron to the moon. It is so easy to overlook the fact that the $h$-uncertainty of $x$ contra $p$ also applies to the larger bodies. Because indeed $x$ and the VELOCITY can be so accurately determined at the same time. However, the uncertainty in the velocity should of course be multiplied by the large mass to yield the uncertainty in the momentum.
>
> In private discussions with Einstein, Bohr has developed other very nice points. The following, e.g.: Large, massive, rigid reference systems with imperturbable [“unverstörbaren”] clocks are particularly suited for the fixation of $x\ y\ z\ t$. But at the same time unable to indicate momentum or energy transfer. This is the way the uncertainty relation shows up in classical mechanics (difficult to notice, but quite unmistakable).
>
> By faintly illuminating a small, freely moving body, one may determine its position rather nicely every hour and evaluate the intermediate velocity and momentum with enormous accuracy. Thereby the uncertainty relation APPEARS to be violated. This is, however, merely a misunderstanding. One has here only EVALUATED the momentum for the intermediate time, but not actually measured it. Furthermore, one also notices that these position measurements at 0 1 2 3 o’clock do NOT allow an exact evaluation of the momentum BEFORE 0 o’clock and AFTER 3 o’clock, but only within the uncertainty associated with Compton recoil. Altogether the notion of a “conceptual tracking of the particle between the moments of observation” should be rejected just as the notion of a “tracking of light-corpuscle through the wave field between emission and absorption” (I hope that with this formulation I do not offend against Bohr’s view.)
>
> In the forthcoming article in *Naturwissenschaften* you will see how Bohr constantly emphasizes the “complementary description” of all experience. On the one hand, the mathematically unambiguous MULTIDIMENSIONAL or matrix computation machinery establishing the carefully close stomach (*sorgfältig abgeschlossen bleibende Bauch*) [i.e., description] of an isolated system (defined uniquely sharply but beyond all observation and $x, y, z, t$ description). On the other hand, the terribly crude (namely, at least $h$-strong intrusion by each observation into this idyll) “establishment of a particle in $x, y, z, t$” but connected with the uncertainty relation.
>
> Bohr says: For the time being we have at our disposal only those words and concepts that yield such a complementary mode of description. But at least we see already the famous INTERNAL CONTRADICTION of quantum theory to arise only because we operate with this language, which has not been revised satisfactorily (I know for sure that my last statement would drive Bohr to COMPLETE DESPAIR). Now read it for yourselves! (For the original German text and English translation, see Bohr, 1985, pp. 415–481 and pp. 37–41, respectively)

Ehrenfest’s letter to his disciples in Leyden signalled a complete agreement in principle with the quantum-theoretical standpoint of Bohr. Not much can be read in it that expresses any sympathy with the classical argument of Einstein, which reminds one of the exchange of notes between Ehrenfest and Einstein during one of the lectures at the 1927 conference: Ehrenfest passed on a note to Einstein, saying ‘Don’t laugh! There is a special section in purgatory for professors of quantum theory, where they will be obliged to listen to lectures on classical physics

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0286 -->

254 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

ten hours every day'; to which, Einstein replied, 'I laugh only at their naïveté; who
knows who would have the laugh in a few years?'²⁸⁹

In spite of the fact that Ehrenfest’s letter to his Leyden collaborators does not
contain details of Einstein’s objections or examples challenging the uncertainty–
complementarity interpretation advocated by Bohr, it does provide an intimate in-
sight into the atmosphere of the 'private' exchange between Bohr and Einstein, both
of whom Ehrenfest venerated as gigantic opponents in the conceptual debate.²⁹⁰ It
was Bohr himself who put Einstein’s problem and his own reply to it into his paper
of 1949, where he stated: 'Einstein’s attitude gave rise to ardent discussions within
a small circle, in which Ehrenfest, who through the years had been a close friend of
us both, took part in a most active and helpful way.' Further:

Surely, we all recognized that in the above example [of the single slit given by
Einstein, which we have mentioned earlier], the situation presents no analogue to the
application of statistics in dealing with complicated mechanical systems [in classical
dynamics], but rather recalled the background of Einstein’s own early conclusions
about the unidirection of individual radiation effects, which contrasts so strongly with
a simple wave picture. The discussions, however, centered on the question of whether
the quantum-mechanical description exhausted the possibilities of accounting for
observable phenomena or, as Einstein maintained, the analysis could be carried fur-
ther and, especially, [of] whether a fuller description could be obtained by bringing
into consideration the detailed balance of energy and momentum in individual pro-
cesses. (Bohr, 1949, p. 213)

Bohr then illustrated the course of his debate with Einstein by referring to two
examples: (1) the case of a particle penetrating through a hole in a screen or dia-
phragm, with a shutter present or absent; (2) the case of adding to this arrange-
ment a second diaphragm having a double slit. Now, in case (1), the shutter would
not help, Bohr argued, to reduce the uncertainty below Heisenberg’s limiting value,

$$\Delta p \Delta q \approx h \quad \text{or} \quad \Delta E \Delta t \approx h,$$
(197)

because the motion of the shutter, which keeps the hole open during the time $\Delta t$,
involves an energy exchange with the particle of the size

$$v \Delta p \approx \frac{\Delta q \cdot \Delta p}{\Delta t} \approx \frac{h}{\Delta t}.$$
(198)

²⁸⁹The note exchanged between Ehrenfest and Einstein at the 1927 Solvay Conference during the
second part of Compton’s lecture said originally:

Ehrenfest: [Dienstag (Compton II) "Lache nicht, es gibt eine spezielle Abteilung im Fegefeuer
für ‘Professoren der Quantentheorie,’ dort werden ihnen 10 Stunden pro Tag Vorlesungen über
Klassiche Physik gehalten." Einstein: "Ich lache nur über die Naivität. Wer weiss, wer in einigen
Jahren lacht." (Miss Helen Dukas gave me a photocopy of this note in January 1971, J. Mehra.)

²⁹⁰It appears that Ehrenfest perhaps played down a bit the active participation of, say, Heisenberg,
Kramers, and Pauli in the debate, and rather concentrated on his heroes.

II.6 The Solvay Conferences of 1927 and 1930 and the Consistency Debate 255

'The problem raised by Einstein was now to what extent a control of the momen-
tum and energy transfer, involved in a location of the particle in space and time,
can be used for a further specification of the state of the particle after passing
through the hole,' Bohr noted. It was exactly to decide this question that case (2)
had been considered in 1927, and: 'Einstein suggested that a control of the mo-
mentum transfer would permit a closer analysis of the phenomenon, and, in par-
ticular, make it possible to decide through which of the two slits [of the second
diaphragm] the electron had passed before arriving at the plate.' Bohr concluded:

A closer examination showed, however that the suggested control of the momentum
transfer would involve a latitude in the knowledge of the position of the diaphragm
which would exclude the appearance of the interference phenomena in question. In
fact, if $\omega$ is the small angle between the conjectured paths of a particle passing
through the upper or the lower slit, the difference of momentum transfer in these two
cases will, according [to the fundamental equations $E = h\nu$ and $p = h\sigma$], be equal to
$h\sigma\omega$, and any control of the momentum of the diaphragm with an accuracy sufﬁcient
to measure this difference will, due to the indeterminacy relation, involve a minimum
latitude of the position of the diaphragm, comparable with $1/\sigma\omega$. (Bohr, *loc. cit.*,
p. 217)

As a consequence, Bohr could show indeed that the interference effect on the plate
disappeared if the resulting wave phenomena were properly discussed.

We are left with 'a choice of *either* tracing the path of a particle *or* observing
interference effects,' which allows us, however, 'to escape from the paradoxical
necessity of concluding that the behaviour of an electron or a photon should de-
pend on the presence of a slit in the diaphragm through which it could be proved
not to pass'; hence, Bohr concluded his reminiscence of the 1927 debate with the
words:

We have here to do with a typical example of how the complementary phenomena
appear under mutually exclusive experimental arrangements and are just faced with
the impossibility, in the analysis of quantum effects, of drawing any sharp separation
between an independent behaviour of atomic objects and their interaction with the
measuring instruments which serve to define the conditions under which the phe-
nomena occur. (Bohr, *loc. cit.*, p. 218)

In spite of the serious divergence of approach and opinions, 'a most humorous
spirit animated the discussions,' Bohr remembered. 'On his side, Einstein mock-
ingly asked us whether we could really believe that the providential authorities
took recourse to dice-playing ('*ob der liebe Gott würfelt*'), to which I replied by
pointing to the great caution, already called for by ancient thinkers, in ascribing
attributes to Providence in everyday language' (Bohr, 1949, p. 218).²⁹¹
Thus, by piecing together the contemporary documents (of 1927) with the later

²⁹¹See also the letter of Bohr to Oseen, 5 November 1928, confirming this episode, quoted in

recollections of the participants, a fairly consistent historical picture of the great
epistemological debate between Bohr and Einstein has arisen. The fifth Solvay
Conference would not end this debate, however. Both participants returned to the
problems involved again and again, especially at the sixth Solvay Conference in
1930 and, a few years later, in 1935. Still, quantum mechanics had already scored
the main points in its favour. 'The most important success of the Brussels meeting
was that we could see that against any objections, against any attempts to disprove
the theory, we could get along with it,' Heisenberg summarized the result in an
interview in 1963, and added: 'At that time [in 1927] it was practically Bohr, Pauli
and myself, perhaps just the three of us. That very soon spread out' (Heisenberg,
AHQP Interview, 27 February 1963).

### (f) The Formulation Given to the Complementarity Principle (1928)

In 1928, a paper of Niels Bohr appeared in three languages: in German as *'Das
Quantenpostulat und die Entwicklung der Atomistik'* (published in the *Naturwissen-
schaften*, issue of 13 April 1928), in English as 'The Quantum Postulate and the Re-
cent Development of Atomic Theory' (in the Supplement to *Nature*, issue of 14 April
1928), and, finally, in French as *'Le Postulat des Quanta et le Nouveau Développement
de l’Atomistique,'* which came out in the proceedings of the 1927 Solvay Conference
(Bohr, 1928d, e, f, respectively). The three versions agreed, apart from linguistic
subtleties, completely. In the German and English versions, a footnote stated:

The content of this paper is essentially the same as that of a lecture on the present
state of the quantum theory delivered on September 16, 1927, at the Volta celebra-
tions in Como. For a summary of the theory just previous to the development of
the new methods the reader is referred to a lecture of the author, 'Atomic Theory
and Mechanics,' published in this periodical (Bohr, 1925b). The rapid development
which has taken place since has given rise to a considerable number of publications.
The present paper is confined to a few references to recent articles which have a spe-
cial bearing on the subject now under discussion (Bohr, 1928e, p. 580).

Among the 'recent articles' referred to, Bohr mentioned in particular the papers of
Pascual Jordan and Oskar Klein (1927) and Paul Dirac (1928a), which came out
*after* the Como and Solvay Conferences of 1927. Indeed, Bohr’s account of 1928
reproduced in detail neither the Como nor the Brussels lecture, but rather an
advanced status of his considerations on the same theme: a summary of his efforts
to formulate the complementarity ideas.²⁹²
On 18 November 1927, Bohr gave a lecture before the Danish Academy, an
abstract of which appeared both in Danish and English, stating:

The quantum postulate and the recent development of atomic theory. The dualism
which characterizes the formulation of the quantum theory has received much illu-

²⁹²We have reported earlier in this section on Bohr’s efforts to formulate the Como lecture and to
prepare the Brussels report.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0289 -->

II.6 The Solvay Conferences of 1927 and 1930 and the Consistency Debate 257

mination through the recent great progress in atomic theory. In the present state of
science, this dualism would seem unavoidable and may be regarded as direct expres-
sion of the fundamental limitation of the ordinary principles of classical physics
postulated by the quantum theory. (Bohr, 1928b, p. 78)

This further lecture on the subject, however, did not—like the previous efforts of
Pauli before the Solvay Conference²⁹³—promote greatly the final redaction of the
promised paper. Still, more than two months after the Brussels meeting, Bohr
reopened the correspondence with Pauli in Hamburg, stating:

You must certainly have often wondered why my article in *Naturwissenschaften* has
not yet appeared, in spite of your assistance with the corrections. But you certainly
have heard through Nishina that I sent, after doing much work on it, an entirely new
manuscript to [Arnold] Berliner [the editor of *Naturwissenschaften*]! I believe that it
has become much better and clearer, and after you have once unburdened your heart
by scolding me sufficiently (which is well deserved), I believe you will think the same
(Bohr to Pauli, 8 January 1928, in Pauli, 1979, pp. 420–421).

At the same time, he announced his visit to Hamburg on the return from his
'wonderful vacation' in the Swiss mountains in Arosa. Pauli, in a most cheerful
mood, replied that he and the other physicists in Hamburg—namely, Wilhelm
Lenz, Otto Stern, and Peter Paul Koch—would be happy to see Bohr, and he
further remarked:²⁹⁴

The paper-scissors and glue pots of the Institute are being prepared for you in the best
manner. I am really quite happy that you have altered the manuscript. Indeed, after
some time I did not particularly like the old one, especially as it seemed to me that
'the complementarity of causal and space-time description' requires still further
elucidation, and the statistical interpretation of the results of theoretical computation
seemed to me to be introduced too abruptly. In any case I already look forward to
seeing the new manuscript, and I have the best intentions of exhibiting as critical an
attitude towards it as at all possible (the result of this will be that you are going to
prolong your sentences still further). (Pauli to Bohr, 13 January 1928, *loc. cit.*, p. 425)

Bohr was equally happy, and he wrote back at once that he would show up
in Hamburg on 22 January, and that he looked forward to Pauli’s critical remarks:
'I am very grateful for the offer of paper-scissors and glue pot, and if it is possible
I should like to send off the proofs from Hamburg, since after all the whole thing
must come to an end sometime.' (Bohr to Pauli, 15 January 1928) Still, as late as
10 March, Pauli inquired from Bohr 'whether the last proofs have now really been
sent off, so that you have nothing more to do with it,' upon which Bohr (having just

²⁹³See Section II.4 and the letter of Pauli to Bohr dated 17 October 1927: 'If you were to be in
Hamburg already on Friday, it would be fine! Then I could also help you with the corrections, and we
could send off the proofs [to *Naturwissenschaften*] eventually from here.'

²⁹⁴For the English translation of these and further passages from the Bohr–Pauli correspondence
and the story of the completion of Bohr’s paper, see Kalckar, 1985b, pp. 41–46.

258        Chapter II  Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

returned from a visit to Ehrenfest in Leyden) answered that he was ‘just expecting
to get a last copy any day [from the publisher] to see whether all corrections have
been properly introduced’ (Bohr to Pauli, 13 March 1928). Ultimately, the paper
was really finished a few days later, and it appeared both in German and in English
on 13 and 14 April 1928, respectively.
    Just as Pauli had assisted with the German version, Paul Dirac had supervised
the English one. ‘I am very thankful for your kind help with the proofs of my
article,’ Bohr wrote to Dirac, and added:

    From our discussions in Cambridge and from what Klein told me, I do not know,
however, whether you are quite in sympathy with the point of view from which I have
tried to represent the paradoxes of the quantum theory. Although of course I realize
the tentative character of the formulation, I still believe that the point of view of
complementarity is suited to describe the situation. I think, we cannot too strongly
emphasize the inadequacy of our ordinary perception when dealing with quantum
problems. (Bohr to Dirac, 24 March 1928, in Bohr, 1985, p. 48)

Bohr, in his letter to Dirac, went on to say: ‘Of course I quite appreciate your
remarks that in dealing with observations we always witness through some permanent
effects a choice of nature between different possibilities.’ He considered,
however, yet the ‘permanency of the observational results . . . the very essence of
the ordinary causal space-time description’; and in order to ‘represent the statistical
quantum-theoretical description as a natural generalization of the ordinary
causal description [in classical theory],’ he had placed emphasis on the subjective
character of the idea of observation: ‘Indeed I believe that the contrast between
this idea and the classical idea of isolated objects is decisive for the limitation
which characterizes the use of all classical concepts in the quantum theory’ (Bohr,
loc. cit.).
    At the end of his letter to Dirac, Bohr addressed another point that he wanted
to pursue, namely, ‘the question of the uni-direction of time.’ He wrote:

    For an isolated system this question has of course no sense. In considering observations,
however, it is essential that the light travels towards our eye or the photographic
plate. I believe that a close analysis offers the proper answer to such paradoxes
regarding the nature of light as brought forward especially by [G. N.] Lewis. I
have been considering to send a short note to Nature concerning these paradoxes, and
in this connection I should like also to discuss some of the remarks brought forward
at the Solvay Conference by Einstein and by yourself. Before a publication of course
I should wish to discuss these questions in detail with you, but I hope your [forthcoming]
visit here will offer a good opportunity also in this respect. (Bohr, loc. cit.)

Before Bohr entered into these extensions, however, some years would pass.$^{295}$
    In April 1928, Bohr was satisfied to have completed the very cumbersome task

of a first complete formulation of complementarity, which contained several central
points—as he emphasized in a letter to Erwin Schrödinger—namely:

    The apparent contrast between the superposition principle and the individuality postulate
has revealed the complementary nature of the space-time coordinates and the
conservation laws . . . We are here concerned with a philosophically consistent and
hence satisfactory extensions of the foundations of our description of nature . . . There
is also no question of a more or less arbitrary limitation in the applicability of the
classical concepts, but we have to do with the recognition of an inescapable feature of
complementarity that emerges in an analysis of the concept of observation and which
in many respects recalls the recognition of the general [feature of] relativity. (Bohr to
Schrödinger, 23 May 1928, in Bohr, 1985, p. 48)

Bohr, in his letter to Schrödinger, made the optimistic remark: ‘I believe that . . .
quantum theory is approaching a certain temporary completion. Indeed, I believe
that it is already possible to say that any application of classical concepts that
permits an unambiguous definition, may also be ascribed a physical interpretation’
(Bohr, loc. cit.). In this sense, he also considered his article of 1928 on the quantum
postulate as exhibiting a ‘temporary completion.’$^{296}$
    For the occasion of the 450th anniversary of the University of Copenhagen in
November 1929, Niels Bohr was asked to contribute to a ‘Festschrift.’$^{297}$ Instead
of following the usual procedure (and also due to lack of time for producing a new
text), he collected three of his earlier lectures and publications under the title
‘Atomic Theory and Description of Nature,’ in particular, the elaborated text of a
talk given before the Scandinavian Mathematical Congress in August 1925 (Bohr,
1925b), the Como lecture of September 1927 (Bohr, 1928a), and a more recent
paper dedicated to Max Planck on the latter’s golden jubilee of his doctorate
(Bohr, 1929b). Bohr added a detailed ‘Introductory Survey’ (Bohr, 1929d) to the
collected articles.$^{298}$ In it, he remarked:

    When I was requested to write a paper for the Year Book 1929 of the University of
Copenhagen, I first intended to give, in the simplest possible form, an account of the
new points of view brought about by the quantum theory, starting from an analysis
of the elementary concepts on which our description of nature is founded. However,

my occupation with other duties did not leave me sufficient time to complete such an
account, the difficulty of which arose, not least, from continuous development of the
points of view in question. Sensing this difficulty, I gave up the idea of preparing a
new exposition and was led to consider using instead a translation in Danish, made
for this occasion, of some articles which, during recent years, I have published in
foreign journals as contributions to the discussion of the problem of quantum theory.
(Bohr, 1929d, English translation, pp. 5–6; reprinted in Bohr, 1985, pp. 282–284)

These articles, Bohr continued in the introduction, ‘attempted to give a coherent
survey of the state of atomic theory’ at the various instants, in 1925, 1927, and
1929, respectively. About his contribution on the occasion marking Planck’s doctoral
jubilee, he wrote in particular:

    In the third article . . . I have discussed in more detail the general philosophical aspects
of the quantum theory. Partly in view of the regret, so widely expressed, with
regard to the renunciation of a strictly causal mode of description for atomic phenomena,
[I attempt] to show that the difficulties concerning our forms of perception,
which arise in the atomic theory because of the indivisibility of the quantum of action,
may be considered as an instructive reminder of the general conditions underlying the
creation of man’s concepts. The impossibility of distinguishing in our customary way
between physical phenomena and their observation places us, indeed, in a position
quite similar to that which is so familiar in psychology where we are continually
reminded of the difficulty of distinguishing between subject and object. (Bohr, loc. cit.,
p. 15; reprinted in Bohr, 1985, p. 293)

Clearly, this article and the lecture of August 1929 before the Scandinavian
Meeting of Natural Scientists—where Bohr ‘emphasized that the development of
the atomic theory has . . . first of all given us a recognition of laws which cannot be
included within the frame formed by our accustomed modes of perception; the
lessons we have learned by the discovery of the quantum of action open up to us
new prospects which may perhaps be of decisive importance, particularly in the
discussion of the position of living organisms in our picture of the world’ (Bohr,
loc. cit., p. 22 or p. 300)—constituted an extension of the original complementarity
views, expressed so vigorously in the lectures at Como and Brussels and written in
the big article of 1928.

(g)  Bohr’s New Philosophical, Physical, and Biological Insights
       (1928–1929)

To the origin of the extension of Bohr’s original ideas on the complementarity
principle, many influences—especially several of his friends—contributed.$^{299}$ To
begin chronologically, we should mention an exchange with the Danish philosopher

$^{299}$For more information, see J. Kalckar’s introduction to ‘Part II: Further Elucidation of the
Complementarity Argument,’ in Bohr, 1985 (i.e., Kalckar, 1985b), and especially Stolzenburg, 1977,

Harald Høffding, the old colleague and friend of Bohr’s father and the
former teacher of the Bohr brothers, Niels and Harald (see Section II.4). For
Høffding’s eighty-fifth birthday, Bohr now contributed a newspaper article, in
which he emphasized the close connection between philosophy and science, and
praised the philosophers:$^{300}$

    Without having been endangered by external circumstances, the philosophers, being
carried along by pure desire for harmony in sense and thought, have deepened our
recognition and created a general attitude towards the difficulties which have arisen
and a quite common understanding of relativity and complementarity in all human
concepts. (Bohr, in Kalckar, 1985a, p. xx)

In the correspondence with Høffding that followed the article, Bohr again stated
the general agreement between the philosopher’s ideas and his own, though he admitted
that the latter’s were still ‘preliminary’ (‘unabgeschliffen’). He continued:$^{301}$

    In the recent time I have tried to work a bit on the more accurate analysis of the
concept of observation as used in shaping the physical forms of perception, and I
hope to represent the problem concerning the foundation of the description of nature
somewhat more clearly than in my paper [Bohr, 1928d, e, f], even though I do feel
my lack of philosophical knowledge also in this connection more and more strongly.
As regards the psychological problems treated in your presentation, I feel this lack
even more strongly if this is possible; however, I am strongly impressed by the possible
range of general considerations with which you close your presentation. At times
it appeared in my mind that perhaps there exists the possibility of proving a similar
complementarity relation between the sense-determined and the will-determined
aspect and the associated aspect of the description of individual psychological processes
as has been revealed by the quantum theory in connection with physical elementary
processes—between momentum and energy conservation, on the one hand,
and the space-time description, on the other. The difficulty of pursuing such an
analogy in detail does certainly lie in the impossibility of establishing in the domain
of psychology—at least in the present stage of the development of this field—a definition
of an elementary process which possesses a simplicity and uniqueness comparable
to that which can be achieved in the physical domain of the quantum postulate.
(Bohr to Høffding, 1 August 1928)

While in this exchange with Høffding one may recognize Bohr’s first move
toward extending the concept of physical complementarity to the psychological
domain, different topics were addressed in another exchange that developed in
summer 1928 between Bohr and his student Christian Møller, who spent a semester
with Erwin Schrödinger in Berlin and tried to propagate the Copenhagen
complementarity ideas there. In a letter, dated 10 June 1928, Møller dealt with
