262 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

the use of matter waves, claiming that ‘the description of motion of a particle by the de Broglie wave is more symbolic [than the description by the usual classical methods], *because* nothing corresponds in nature directly to a single wave $A \cos 2\pi(t\nu - x\sigma_x - y\sigma_y - z\sigma_z + \delta)$.’ In particular, he pointed out: ‘The quantities $x, y, z, t$, entering this expression are not the usual coordinates of an observable event, because these one could then view as a signal which, in contrast to the relativity principle, [moves with a velocity] greater than the velocity of light.’ Only when one obtains a wave packet with the help of the superposition principle can a connection with reality be established, because a wave packet—according to the quantum postulate—possesses the properties of an individual particle. Bohr replied to Møller that he essentially agreed with the latter’s argumentation; he further emphasized the great care that one had to apply in using the conventional concepts of visualizability also in quantum theory, and added:

> One does not run so easily into this difficulty when working with the matrix formulation, in which the rules of calculation deviating from the conventional algebra [of numbers] always maintain the peculiar nature of quantum theory before our eyes. . . . If one thinks of the wave theory, it is just its “intuitiveness” (“perceptibility”) which is simultaneously its strength and fallaciousness, and here I have tried to point out the great difference with the classical theory by emphasizing the symbolic character of the treatment. (Bohr to Møller, 14 June 1928)

Later, in fall 1928, Bohr corresponded with another physicist, his Swedish friend Carl Wilhelm Oseen, on the meaning of complementarity. Besides pointing out the philosophical consequences and illustrating the application of the uncertainty relations to certain *Gedanken* experiments involving rigid bodies and impenetrable clocks or diaphragms with holes and shutters, respectively, he raised another aspect of the concepts involved. He wrote in particular:

> I guess Waller has told you that a new particularly instructive example has recently been brought to light by [O.] Klein, who is extremely familiar with the symbolic methods that at the present form the basis of work in these areas. It appears as if the difficulties, with which we are confronted here, are very deep-rooted and demand an even greater renunciation as regards visualizability than the one to which we have already had to accustom ourselves. (Bohr to Oseen, 5 November 1928, in Kalckar, 1985b, p. 191)

By the instructive example, Bohr meant the so-called ‘Klein’s paradox,’ which occurs when one considers a relativistic electron passing through a barrier in Dirac’s theory—as we shall discuss in the following section (O. Klein, 1928).$^{302}$

$^{302}$ Bohr enlarged on this example in a talk, entitled ‘Quantum Theory and Relativity’ and presented to the Danish Academy of Sciences on 19 October 1928. The abstract reads: ‘An examination of the difficulties brought to light by the attempts of a reconciliation of the quantum postulate with the idea of relativity seems to require a further revision of our physical concepts as regards their application to atomic phenomena’ (Bohr, 1929a, p. 424).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0295 -->

II.6 &nbsp;&nbsp;The Solvay Conferences of 1927 and 1930 and the Consistency Debate &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 263

Instead of enlarging upon any ‘greater renunciation of visualizability,’ Bohr passed over in early 1929 to clarifying the epistemological concepts of existing atomic theory. Stimulated by two recent articles in *Naturwissenschaften* on the problem of chance and causality in physics—i.e., Erwin Schrödinger’s belatedly published 1922 inaugural address at the University of Zurich, arguing that perhaps all natural laws are statistical (Schrödinger, 1929a), and Joseph Petzold’s paper advocating the necessity of a causal explanation of physical processes (Petzold, 1929)—he took the opportunity of summarizing in plain words the contents and consequences of his complementarity interpretation of atomic theory. He started from the historical step in 1900 of the introduction of the quantum of action into the classical framework of the principle of least action—for, after all, the article was prepared for the special issue of *Naturwissenschaften* of 28 June 1929, devoted to the celebration of the golden jubilee of Planck’s doctorate—and pointed out:

> This principle symbolizes, as it were, the peculiar reciprocal symmetry relation between the space-time description and the laws of the conservation of energy and momentum, the great fruitfulness of which, already in classical physics, depends upon the fact that one may extensively apply them without following the course of phenomena in space and time. It is this very reciprocity which has been made use of in a most pregnant way in the quantum-mechanical formalism. (English translation of Bohr, 1929b, p. 94)

The nature of the physical observation implies, Bohr continued, ‘that all experience must ultimately be expressed in terms of classical concepts neglecting the quantum of action’; hence, the known ‘limited applicability of the classical concepts’ leads to an ‘inherent limitation’ of ‘the results attainable by any measurement of atomic phenomena,’ as Heisenberg had revealed in his discovery of the uncertainty relations. The limitations can be placed on the influence of radiation, whose interaction with atoms allows for the observation (of the latter); the dual ‘aspects of radiation’ then lead to the ‘complementarity principle,’ which Bohr now wished to generalize and replace by the ‘reciprocal symmetry’ because it ‘occurs already in classical mechanics’ (Bohr, *loc. cit.*, p. 95).
In the second part of his paper, Bohr turned to the following epistemological problem:

> For describing our mental activity, we require, on one hand, an objectively given content to be placed in opposition to a perceiving subject, while, on the other hand, as is already implied in such an assertion, no sharp separation between object and subject can be maintained, since the perceiving subject also belongs to our mental content. (Bohr, *loc. cit.*, p. 96)

In other words, ‘the conscious analysis of any concept stands in a relation of exclusion to its immediate application’ (Bohr, *loc. cit.*). Bohr then traced the ‘complementary or reciprocal mode of description’ back to ‘familiar psychological problems.’ As in the case of atomic physics, where the causal chain of events con-

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0296 -->

264 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

tradicts the essential (and conserved) exchange of momentum and energy between the individual entities, ‘the analysis of our sense impressions discloses a remarkable independence of the psychological foundations of the concepts of space and time, on the one hand, and the conceptions of energy and momentum, based upon actions of force, on the other hand,’ he argued and concluded:

> When considering the contrast between the feeling of free will, which governs the psychic life, and the apparently uninterrupted causal chain of the accompanying psychological processes, the thought has, indeed, not eluded philosophers that we may be concerned here with an unvisualizable relation of complementarity. (Bohr, *loc. cit.*, pp. 99–100)

Max Planck, in a letter dated 14 July 1929, thanked Bohr warmly for his article and expressed the hope for having ‘a longer discussion’ with him to be able to pursue the details. Wolfgang Pauli also wrote, stating in particular that he was ‘very satisfied’ with the presentation of Bohr’s ideas omitting all physical details, ‘for once this was something new, original and exciting’ (Pauli to Bohr, 17 July 1929, in Pauli, 1979, p. 513). At the same time, Pauli announced that he would like to see Bohr in August at the latter’s summer resort.$^{303}$ Bohr replied that Pauli would indeed be welcome, and that he hoped to debate with him the use of ‘artificial words’ like ‘complementarity’ and ‘reciprocity’: he now felt ‘afraid that the change of name was a blunder’ (Bohr to Pauli, 31 July 1929, *loc. cit.*, p. 517).
Shortly after his meeting and discussions with Pauli, Bohr—on 26 August 1929—delivered a lecture at the 18. *Skandinaviske Naturforskermøde* (18th Meeting of Scandinavian Scientists), which provided another opportunity to improve upon the formation of the general problem of interpretation in atomic physics and its philosophical consequences, notably, an extension to other fields.$^{304}$ He opened the lecture at the meeting of the Scandinavian scientists in Copenhagen by sketching some details from the history of quantum and atomic theory since 1900 (and a little before): the recognition of atomic structure from the discovery of the electron to Rutherford’s nuclear atom, Planck’s quantum of action and its role in the description of atomic spectra, the successes and difficulties of the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory of atomic structure, the discovery of quantum mechanics, and finally the decisive concepts for understanding the new atomic theory, notably, Heisenberg’s uncertainty relations and de Broglie’s matter waves. Concerning the latter, he remarked:

$^{303}$ Pauli planned to take a vacation in Sweden with the mathematician Erich Hecke and to arrive in Tisvilde around the middle of August.

$^{304}$ From a letter to Hendrik Kramers, dated 7 December 1929, we learn that Bohr gave yet another talk on the same topic to a Copenhagen association, ‘which calls itself the Society for Philosophy and Psychology.’ Bohr remarked: ‘I learned a great deal from the ensuing discussion. In particular, I now know better which points non-physicists resent, and I also believe that for this very reason I found on this occasion better words than previously to answer the objections.’ Apart from an announcement kept in the Niels Bohr Archive, no notes, manuscript, or publication concerning this lecture can be found; the lecture was given on 11 November 1929. (See Kalckar, 1985b, p. 196.)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0297 -->

II.6 &nbsp;&nbsp;The Solvay Conferences of 1927 and 1930 and the Consistency Debate &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 265

However, we must bear in mind that the application of matter waves is limited to those phenomena, in the description of which it is essential that the quantum of action be taken into account and which, therefore, lie outside the domain where it is possible to carry out a causal description corresponding to our customary forms of perception and where we can ascribe to words like “the nature of matter” and “the nature of light” meanings in the ordinary sense. (Bohr, 1929c; English translation, p. 111)

Bohr emphasized the ‘extensive range of experience’ that quantum mechanics makes it possible to master, such as the details of the physical and chemical properties of atoms and even the interpretation of the radioactive transformation (alpha decay); he then mentioned the still unresolved difficulties with the relativistic extension of quantum mechanics, and finally turned to the new description of atomic phenomena: the essentially statistical concepts entering into observation based on the fundamental indeterminacy (uncertainty relations).
After referring to the epistemological consequences of the quantum postulate and drawing attention to the ‘peculiar parallelism between the renewed discussion of the validity of the principle of causality and the discussion of a free will’—‘the feeling of volition and the demand of causality are equally indispensable elements in the relation between subject and object which forms the core of the problem of knowledge’—Bohr touched ‘upon the question as to what light can be thrown upon the problems regarding living organisms by the latest development of our knowledge of atomic phenomena’ (Bohr, *loc. cit.*, p. 117). To enter into this new field of experience, he referred to the known physiological fact that sense impressions often depend on physical and chemical processes that involve the action of only a few atoms and light-quanta. This fact implies ‘that the needs of the organism for independence and sensibility are here satisfied to the utmost limit permitted by the laws of nature, and we must be prepared to come upon similar conditions also at other points of decisive significance for the formulation of biological problems’ (Bohr, *loc. cit.*). Hence, one would expect, Bohr continued, to also approach in biology ‘the limit for an unambiguous description with the help of our ordinary visualizable conceptions,’ or:

> With regard to the more profound biological problems, . . . we must expect to find that the recognition of relationships of wider scope will require that the same conditions be taken into consideration which determine the limitation of the causal mode of description in the case of atomic phenomena. Besides, the fact that consciousness, as we know it, is inseparably connected with life ought to prepare us for finding that the very problem of the distinction between the living and the dead escapes comprehension in the ordinary sense of the word. (Bohr, *loc. cit.*, pp. 118–119)

Clearly, in August 1929, Bohr pushed the door open to a very universal application of his principle of complementarity, to which he would return again and again in later decades.

Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields  

**(h) Opposition from Berlin and the Sixth Solvay Conference (1928–1930)**  

When the reprint of Bohr’s *Naturwissenschaften* article of 14 April 1928 (Bohr, 1928d), became available, he immediately dispatched a copy of it to Erwin Schrödinger in Berlin. The latter soon acknowledged its receipt and commented on two points:  

It seems that there is a very strange relation between Heisenberg’s uncertainty relation and the claim of discrete quantum states. On account of the former the latter can really not be experimentally tested. This is best seen for the action and angle variables. For these  

\[
\Delta J \Delta w = h. \qquad [(199)]
\]  

If you now let $\Delta w$ have the magnitude 1, i.e., if you renounce all knowledge whatsoever of the angle variables (since of course everything is periodic in $w$ with period 1), then you have $\Delta J = h$, i.e., just equal to the difference in $J$-values of neighbouring quantum states. (Schrödinger to Bohr, 5 May 1928; English translation in Kalckar, 1985b, p. 47)  

Secondly, ‘if you want to describe a system, e.g., a mass point by specifying its [momentum] $p$ and [position] $q$, then you find that this description is only possible with a limited degree of accuracy,’ Schrödinger argued; hence, it seemed to him ‘imperative to demand the introduction of *new* concepts, with respect to which this limitation *no longer* applies.’ For, he believed: ‘What is in principle not observable should not at all be contained in our conceptual scheme; it should not be possible to represent it in the latter.’ Schrödinger closed his letter to Bohr by saying: ‘However, it will no doubt be *very* difficult to invent this conceptual scheme, since—as you emphasize so impressively—the new-fashioning required touches upon the deepest levels of our experience: space, time and causality.’ (Schrödinger, *loc. cit.*, pp. 47–48)  

In his reply, Bohr first thanked Schrödinger for his ‘not altogether unsympathetic attitude towards considerations of the tendency’ contained in the presentation of his ideas on complementarity. Still, he did not join Schrödinger’s call for ‘new concepts’ in atomic theory because of the following reasons:  

We have not only, as far as I can see, no basis for such a new-fashioning so far, but the “old” empirical concepts appear to me inseparably linked to the foundations of the human means of visualization. . . . In my opinion there is also no question of a more or less arbitrary limitation in the applicability of the classical concepts, but we have to do with the recognition of an inescapable feature of complementarity that emerges in an analysis of the concept of observation and which in many respects recalls the recognition of the general [feature of] relativity. (Bohr to Schrödinger, 23 May 1928; *loc. cit.*, p. 48)  

On the difficulty of having a large phase-angle uncertainty $\Delta w$, mentioned by Schrödinger, Bohr answered that the phase did not play any role in solving the wave equation for atomic systems, because:

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0299 -->

II.6 The Solvay Conferences of 1927 and 1930 and the Consistency Debate  
267  

In the interpretation of experiments by means of the concept of stationary states, we are indeed always dealing with such properties of an atomic system as depend on the phase relations over a large number of consecutive periods. (Bohr, *loc. cit.*, p. 49)  

Similarly, the uncertainty relation involving the momentum and position of a particle would not imply any ambiguity, but rather ‘provide a particularly striking example of the general complementary nature of the description.’ Bohr ended with the remark that, ‘after many years of struggling in the dark,’ he now felt ‘especially strongly the fulfilment of the old hopes’ that the ‘new discoveries’ of Schrödinger and others had initiated. He suggested that Schrödinger might perhaps discuss the content of his letter with Planck and Einstein in Berlin.  

Bohr’s arguments did not convince Schrödinger. He passed on the letter to Einstein, with his comment about applying the uncertainty relations to an ideal gas: namely, one ‘could not achieve an accuracy in momentum that allows me to distinguish between neighbouring quantum values,’ which he found distasteful (Schrödinger to Einstein, 30 May 1928, in Schrödinger, *et al.*, 1963, p. 28). Einstein replied to him the next day signalling full agreement:  

I think you have hit the nail on the head. The subterfuge with the arbitrarily large domain for cyclic variables in order to narrow down $\Delta p$ is very clever to be sure. But an uncertainty relation interpreted in this manner appears hardly enlightening. The thing is contrived for free particles and suits only this case in a natural way. Your demand that the concepts $p$, $q$ should be abandoned, since they can only claim such a “wavering sense” (“*Wackelbedeutung*”), seems to me quite justified. The Heisenberg-Bohr soothing-philosophy—or religion?—is so cleverly concocted that for the present it offers the believers a soft pillow of repose from which they are not so easily chased away. Let us therefore let them rest. (Einstein to Schrödinger, 31 May 1928, in Przibram, 1963, p. 29)  

Einstein maintained that, in spite of all arguments of Bohr in favour of $E$ *and* $v$, there could be only the decision ‘$E$ *or* $v$.’ However, he added: ‘I cannot devise a mathematical verse from this [idea]. My brain is also already too stale (“*abgeleiert*”).’ (Einstein, *loc. cit.*)  

Unlike Einstein, who devoted his attention entirely to problems of his general field theory during the next couple of years, Schrödinger did continue to deal with the problem of the physical interpretation of quantum mechanics, both in popular and scientific writings (see, especially, Schrödinger, 1929b, c, 1930). In a communication to the Prussian Academy in Berlin on 5 June 1930, entitled ‘*Zum Heisenbergschen Unschärfeprinzip*’ (‘On Heisenberg’s Uncertainty Principle’), he derived a generalized relation that—in the case of a microscopic particle of mass $m$—yielded the following result for the uncertainty in position:  

\[
\Delta q = \sqrt{\frac{ht}{2\pi m}} \qquad (200)
\]

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0300 -->

268  
Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields  

(Schrödinger, 1930, p. 302). Schrödinger noticed that this *nonrelativistic* result agreed with the fluctuation behaviour of classical theory and exhibited a ‘peculiarly absolute character,’ as the accuracy of position did not depend on the magnitude (and uncertainty) of the initial momentum, but only on the elapsed time $t$. Still, he found a position uncertainty for a free electron of a macroscopic magnitude, i.e., about 1 cm. However, for large particle velocities $v$, Eq. (200) had to be generalized relativistically to  

\[
\Delta q = \sqrt{1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}} \sqrt{\frac{ht}{2\pi m}}. \qquad (201)
\]  

That is, the position uncertainty of a relativistic particle becomes smaller than the value given by Eq. (200) and even zero for $v$ assuming the value $c$, the velocity of light *in vacuo*. He concluded:  

This result is quite satisfactory. Because the limiting process described above is exactly the one by means of which one always hopes to derive a correct result for light-quanta. Now for light-quanta, since Maxwell’s waves do not show any dispersion, the initially obtained accuracy of position remains the same for infinitely long times; it can be increased without limit, since the strong momentum dispersion connected with it does not have damaging influence. (Schrödinger, *loc. cit.*, p. 303)  

At the same time, serious controversies went on about the relativistic extension of the uncertainty relations; hence, Schrödinger’s work did not receive an immediate response from the camp of Copenhagen and Göttingen quantum theorists; moreover, it did not leave a deep impression on those who read the paper. On the other hand, later in 1930, Einstein’s attempt at disproving the uncertainty relation was gloriously defeated by Niels Bohr on the basis of a consideration from general relativity theory. Indeed, a new Einstein–Bohr debate again took place in Brussels, as Bohr recalled nearly twenty years later:  

At the next meeting with Einstein at the [sixth] Solvay Conference in 1930, our discussions took quite a dramatic turn. As an objection to the view that a control of the interchange of momentum and energy between the objects and the measuring instruments was excluded if these instruments should serve their purpose of defining the space-time frame of the phenomena, Einstein brought forward the argument that each control should be possible when the exigencies of relativity theory were taken into consideration. In particular, the general relationship between energy and mass, expressed in Einstein’s famous formula  

\[
E = mc^2 \qquad [(202)]
\]  

should allow, by means of simple weighing, to measure the total energy of any system and thus, in principle to control the energy transferred to it when it interacts with an atomic object. (Bohr, 1949, pp. 224–225)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0301 -->

II.6 The Solvay Conferences of 1927 and 1930 and the Consistency Debate  
269  

To demonstrate his point, Einstein imagined a box having a hole in one side and a shutter attached to it; the latter could be moved by means of a clockwork within the box, which could open or close the hole. Now, the box is filled initially with radiation of a certain amount; then, at a given time, the shutter opens such that a single photon leaves the box at an instant known with great accuracy. Weighing the box before and after this event should allow one to determine the photon’s energy with arbitrary accuracy; hence, the uncertainty relation involving time and energy might be violated. Léon Rosenfeld, a participant in the sixth Solvay Conference, remembered vividly how Einstein raised the problem in the *Club de la Foundation Universitaire*, and further:  

It was quite a shock for Bohr to be faced with that problem; he did not see the solution at once. During the whole evening he was extremely unhappy, going from one to the other and trying to persuade them that it couldn’t be true, that it would be the end of physics if Einstein were right; but he could not produce any refutation. I shall never forget the vision of the two antagonists leaving the club: Einstein, a tall majestic figure, walking quietly, with a somewhat ironical smile, and Bohr trotting near him, very excited, inefficiently pleading that if Einstein’s device would work, it would mean the end of physics. The next morning came Bohr’s triumph and the salvation of physics. (Rosenfeld, 1968, p. 232)  

Perhaps Bohr and Rosenfeld have exaggerated the dramatic aspects of the situation in retrospect. This type of puzzle, of which Einstein’s new one was an example, was already known to Bohr from the discussions at the previous Solvay Conference in 1927: the use of movable diaphragms and the opening and closing of shutters had been applied then in some detail to examples demonstrating or rejecting the uncertainty relations. For example, Bohr had described then the following arrangement that allowed one to establish a time coordination: ‘a shutter rigidly connected with a robust clock resting on a support which carries a diaphragm and on which further parts of similar character, regulated by the same clockwork or by other clocks standardized relatively to it, are also to be fixed,’ and he had argued: ‘In securing the opening of the hole at a definite moment, an apparatus of this type might, for instance, be used for an accurate measurement of the time an electron or a photon takes to come from the diaphragm to some other place.’ If one is interested, on the other hand, in drawing conclusions on the energy of the particle, and especially to test the energy-time uncertainty relation—so Bohr concluded—‘we must use an arrangement where the shutter devices can no longer serve as accurate clocks, but where the knowledge of the moment when the hole in the diaphragm is open involves a latitude connected with the accuracy of the energy measurement’ (Bohr, 1949, pp. 220–221). So, everything with the quantum-mechanical relation had seemed to be fine in 1927.  

In the years between 1929 and 1930, Bohr had continued to study in detail thought experiments involving diaphragms and shutters, rigid bodies, and accurate clocks; moreover, he had familiarized himself, especially in cooperation with Oskar Klein, with relativistic situations. However, he had never come across the

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0302 -->

270 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

problem posed to him by Einstein in October 1930. Thus, the seemingly simple situation must have really bothered him and, together with Einstein, he ‘found it necessary to look closer into the consequences of the identification of inertial and gravitational mass implied by the relation [(202)]’: ‘Especially, it was essential to take into account the relationship between the rate of a clock and its position in a gravitational field—well known from the red-shift of the lines in the sun’s spectrum—following from Einstein’s principle of equivalence between gravity effects and the phenomena observed in accelerated reference frames’ (Bohr, *loc. cit.*, p. 226). In that endeavour, by means of which Bohr wanted to rescue physics from ignominious demise, ‘Einstein himself contributed very effectively’ (Bohr, *loc. cit.*).

What came out finally as a physically correct *Gedanken-experiment* to decide upon the problem posed by Einstein was to suspend the box ‘in a spring balance furnished with a pointer to read its position on a scale fixed to the balance support.’ Consequently: ‘The weighing of the box may thus be performed with an accuracy $\Delta m$ by adjusting the balance to its zero position by means of suitable loads.’ However, now comes the crucial point: ‘Any determination of this [zero] position with a given accuracy $\Delta q$ will involve a minimum latitude $\Delta p$ in the control of the momentum of the box connected with $\Delta q$ by the [uncertainty] relation.’ Hence, with the help of this mechanism and general-relativity arguments, it followed that:

(i) This latitude [of momentum, $\Delta p$] must be smaller than the total impulse which, during the whole [time] interval $T$ of the balancing procedure, can be given by the gravitational field to a body with a mass $\Delta m$, or

$$ \Delta p \approx \frac{h}{\Delta q} < T \cdot g \cdot \Delta m \quad \text{[(203)]} $$

where $g$ is the gravity constant. The greater the accuracy of the reading $q$ of the pointer, the larger must, consequently, be the balancing interval $T$, if a given accuracy $\Delta m$ of the weighing of the box with its [radiation] content shall be obtained.

(ii) According to general relativity, a clock, when displaced in the direction of the gravitational force by an amount of $\Delta q$, will change its rate in such a way that its reading in the course of a time interval $T$ will differ by an amount $\Delta T$ given by the relation

$$ \frac{\Delta T}{T} = \frac{1}{c^2} g \Delta q. \quad \text{[(204)]} $$

(Bohr, *loc. cit.*, pp. 226–227)

From the two Eqs. (203) and (204) thus derived, it finally followed that after the weighing procedure the latitude of the adjustment of the clock, $\Delta T$, became

$$ \Delta T > \frac{h}{c^2 \Delta m}, \quad \text{(205)} $$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0303 -->

II.7 Relativistic Electrons and Quantum Fields 271

or, with Eq. (202), the uncertainty relation followed,

$$ \Delta T \cdot \Delta E > h, \quad \text{(206)} $$

in agreement with what Heisenberg and Bohr had always assumed. ‘Consequently, a use of the apparatus as a means of accurately measuring the energy of the photon will prevent us from controlling the moment of escape,’ Bohr concluded triumphantly this new round on the problem of interpretation.

Was Einstein defeated by the power of arguments deduced from his own cherished theory of gravitation in the domain of atomic phenomena? One would assume so, but Bohr rather recalled:

> Notwithstanding the most suggestive confirmation of the soundness and wide scope of the quantum-mechanical way of description, Einstein nevertheless, in a following conversation with me, expressed a feeling of disquietude as regards the apparent lack of firmly laid down principles for the explanation of nature, in which all could agree. From my viewpoint, however, I could only answer that, in dealing with the task of bringing order into an entirely new field of experience, we could hardly trust in any accustomed principles, however broad, apart from the demand of avoiding logical inconsistencies and, in this respect, the mathematical formalism of quantum mechanics should surely meet all requirements. (Bohr, *loc. cit.*, p. 228)

Whatever may have been the misgivings of Einstein and a few other outspoken opponents about the ‘soft pillow’ of the Bohr–Heisenberg philosophy, the first great and serious battle over the consistency of quantum mechanics had been gloriously won. Although most physicists adopted the ‘Copenhagen view’ or ‘Copenhagen interpretation’ of quantum mechanics in the 1930s and afterward, Einstein would not give in and, after several years, open publicly a new front, now calling into question the ‘completeness’ of the quantum-mechanical description. Only a few other major physicists, including Max von Laue, Max Planck, and Erwin Schrödinger, took his side, although in their various talks and publications they criticized different aspects of the new quantum mechanics. We shall treat this renewed discussion in the 1930s and beyond in Chapter IV.

## II.7 Relativistic Electrons and Quantum Fields

### (a) Introduction

To characterize this section, we select two aspects, a personal one and another stressing the topical contents. The personal aspect may be found in the growing enthusiasm of Werner Heisenberg toward the complementarity programme of Niels Bohr. Starting from a rather hostile attitude in early 1927, he defended it two years later as *the* physical verity and made it the basis of the lectures that he presented in spring 1929 at the University of Chicago and published under the title:

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0304 -->

272 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

*The Physical Principles of the Quantum Theory* (Heisenberg, 1930a). Thus, he wrote in the preface:

> On the whole the book contains nothing that is not to be found in previous publications, particularly the investigations of Bohr. The purpose of the book seems to me to be fulfilled if it contributes somewhat to the diffusion of the “*Kopenhagener Geist der Quantentheorie*” (“Copenhagen Spirit of Quantum Theory”), if I may so express myself, which has directed the entire development of modern atomic physics. (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*, p. x)

In an interesting psychological study, David Cassidy has attempted to provide a motivation for Heisenberg’s initial opposition to the complementarity ideas (Cassidy, 1992b). He explained Heisenberg’s ‘stubborn defense of his position in a battle’ with Bohr as being due to the ambition of the young assistant to achieve a complete scientific revolution of his own, which would then lead to his most coveted goal, namely, a university chair in Germany. This ambition, Cassidy has pointed out, suffered a serious blow when Bohr reminded Heisenberg of a conceptual mistake in the $\gamma$-ray microscope example (Cassidy, *loc. cit.*, especially, pp. 69–70). In light of a more detailed study of the development, given in the previous sections (especially, Section II.4), this interpretation appears to be somewhat superficial. It is certainly true that in spring and summer 1927 Heisenberg expected and did receive calls to German chairs.$^{305}$ Still, the debate between Bohr and Heisenberg on questions of the interpretation of quantum mechanics should rather be connected with internal scientific arguments, which (including Heisenberg’s erroneous $\gamma$-ray microscope discussion) emerged from the very different points of departure of the two protagonists. Admittedly, in light of the eventual outcome, Bohr’s standpoint proved to be the superior one; however, it was based on Heisenberg’s prior result, obtained independently of his debatable microscope discussion, whose incorrectness moreover followed only if one applied Bohr’s interpretation.

The topics treated below are summarized in the important report submitted by Wolfgang Pauli at the sixth Solvay Conference of October 1930 in Brussels.$^{306}$ Pauli treated there, in some detail, besides the ‘Theory of the Magnetic Properties of Solid Bodies,’ especially, ‘The Relativistic Quantum Mechanics of the Electron,’

---

Later that year, in August, he received the offer for the Leipzig chair, which he ultimately accepted (Heisenberg to Bohr, 21 August 1927). dealing with the spin of free electrons, Dirac’s relativistic wave equation, the possi-
bility of obtaining polarized electron waves, negative energy states, and the diffi-
culties of Dirac’s theory. A rich and lively discussion followed Pauli’s program-
matic talk, with most of the invited participants (notably, Bohr, Dirac, Heisenberg,
and others, who had similarly contributed importantly to these topics) commenting.
    In the years between 1925 and 1927, the new quantum mechanics had been
worked out for massive particles described by a scalar wave function and the
electromagnetic radiation described by a vector field, i.e., microscopic objects
associated with spin 0 and 1, respectively. However, it had also become evident
that the fundamental constituents of matter known then, the electrons and pro-
tons, possessed spin 1/2 (in units of h/2π). For electrons, this property had been
demonstrated beyond doubt when George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit
introduced the proper angular momentum as the ‘mechanical interpretation’ of
Pauli’s fourth quantum number.^{307} For the proton, the spin-1/2 property arose much
less dramatically; it rather sneaked in as a side remark in Heisenberg’s second
investigation on ‘Mehrkörperprobleme und Resonanz in der Quantenmechanik. II’
(‘Many-Body Problems and Resonance in Quantum Mechanics. II’), when he
discussed the spectra of molecules consisting of two identical atoms, e.g., H₂ or
N₂. With respect to these molecules, he assumed ‘that both nuclei of the molecules
under consideration possess a proper rotation, say, like that of electrons, of the
size s = 1/2[h/2π]’ and continued:

    Then the term scheme [of the diatomic molecule] given above is completely analogous
    to the term scheme of the helium atom. Both systems A and B (the ortho- and para-
    system) will occur, and they exhibit very feeble intercombination transitions. In the
    one case (A), the nuclear magnets are in antiparallel, in the other (B) in parallel
    positions. All terms of the system (B) therefore possess the [statistical] weight 3, those
    of the system (A) the weight 1. (Heisenberg, 1927a, p. 264)

Now, the realization of either case can be derived from the existing diatomic
spectra, the band lines: in case (B), those associated with transitions ... 5 → 5,
3 → 3, 1 → 1 should be three times stronger than the lines associated with the
transitions ... 4 → 4, 2 → 2, 0 → 0. Heisenberg concluded that ‘such cases of
change in intensity seem to occur empirically in the case of N₂, perhaps also in the
case of H₂’ (Heisenberg, loc. cit., p. 265).

# Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

lating quantum-mechanically the specific heat of hydrogen with spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ nuclei (Dennison, 1927). This success was rated so highly that it played a role in the citation for Heisenberg's 1932 Nobel Prize.$^{309}$

The observation of the spin property of elementary particles required new theoretical investigations into the nature of and the consequences from Fermi statistics and the description of these objects by suitable wave functions. Concerning the first question, Pauli obtained very encouraging success when he explained the paramagnetic properties of metals, and Paul Ehrenfest with his young collaborator George Uhlenbeck tried to interpret the exclusion principle visually as the impenetrability of Fermi particles. In the second question, Charles Galton Darwin proposed the first step when he represented the electron by a vector wave instead of a scalar wave; then, Pauli entered into the arena and developed his two-dimensional spin matrices, claiming that they would avoid the danger of visualization of electron spin. Finally, Dirac approached the question with the help of a new (at least for the physicists) algebraic scheme, the four-dimensional gamma matrices; they allowed him to formulate a fully relativistic electron equation, which immediately scored a great triumph, namely, the explanation of Sommerfeld's fine structure, but also raised new problems of a very peculiar character: negative energy states. On the one hand, these could not be understood at all; on the other, they were needed to establish a quantum-mechanical description of dispersion phenomena. The problems of the Dirac equation persisted in the relativistic generalization of quantum field theory achieved by Heisenberg and Pauli in 1929, which completed the efforts of Jordan, Klein, and Wigner of 1927. By 1930, the principal actors—Bohr, Dirac, Heisenberg, and Pauli—had presented their authoritative accounts on the physical interpretation of quantum mechanics. In spite of the difference in emphasis on certain aspects, they provided a consistent picture for all practitioners of quantum theory.

## (b) Are Elementary Particles Impenetrable? (September 1926–January 1927)

When Pauli learned about the electron-spin hypothesis, he reacted quite negatively toward the proposal of George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit.$^{310}$ In particular, he did not believe that the mechanical picture of a rotating electron provided an adequate, *allowed* description of his fourth quantum number, because such an eigenrotation would imply unacceptable consequences for the structure of the electron. Even after another crucial objection, the difficulty about the factor 2 in the gyromagnetic ratio of the electron, had been removed by a relativistic calculation (Thomas, 1926a), Pauli raised further complaints, some of which dis-

# II.7 Relativistic Electrons and Quantum Fields 275

appeared during the year 1926: notably, Heisenberg explained the origin of the large singlet–triplet term separation in two-electron atoms (Heisenberg, 1926c), and Dirac (1926f) found a connection between the permutation symmetry property of many-particle wave functions and the two observed types of quantum statistics. Both statistics, the one proposed by Satyendra Nath Bose (1924a) and the other by Fermi (1926b), exhibited strange features that especially irritated Paul Ehrenfest of Leyden, who began a closer study of systems consisting of free Bose or Fermi particles to understand the deviation of their behaviour from that of free particles obeying the classical Boltzmann statistics.

In September 1926, Albert Einstein received the typescript of a paper, entitled 'Führt die Bose-Einstein-Statistik bei idealen Gasen zu einer Entartungs-Condensation'' ('Does Bose-Einstein Statistics Imply a Degeneracy Condensation?'). The authors, Ehrenfest and his doctoral student Uhlenbeck, jocularly indicated that they intended to submit this note to 'Zeitschrift für mieße Physik'—i.e., 'Journal for Miserable Physics'—and asked Einstein for critical comments on their conclusions. In particular, they claimed to have shown that the condensation effect, which Einstein had derived in his ideal (Bose) gas theory for high density and low temperature (Einstein, 1925a), did not exist in reality, but resulted from doubtful mathematical manipulations, especially the replacement of a quantum-theoretical sum by an integral. 'We want to ask *Herrn Geheimrat Einstein* very humbly, whether he seriously believes that his integral approximation is still valid in the domain considered, and how he accomplishes the purely mathematical wonder that the quantity $\left[ n = \sum_{s=0}^{\infty} (\alpha^{\beta\varepsilon_s} - 1)^{-1} \right]$ can still be kept finite for $\alpha$ equaling $e^{-\beta\varepsilon_0}$,' the Leyden physicists concluded.$^{311}$ 'Your jokes are good but your arguments are bad,' Einstein replied and pointed out that even without applying his attacked integral transformation—which he still considered to be fully justified—a proper treatment of the sum $[n]$ would give rise to a real condensation (Einstein to Ehrenfest, 24 September 1926).

Ehrenfest and Uhlenbeck, though not convinced by Einstein's counterarguments, did not publish their note and turned to a different aspect of the quantum-statistical problem. In a short paper submitted to *Zeitschrift für Physik* in the middle of December 1926, they investigated the question whether wave mechanics admitted only the counting methods known as Bose and Fermi statistics, as their colleagues generally assumed at that time (see, in particular, the papers of Heisenberg and Dirac quoted above); they arrived at the conclusion that the general solution of the Schrödinger equation for identical particles (demonstrated explicitly in the case of a one-dimensional quantum gas) 'does not force us to give up the

Indeed, the $N$-particle solution admitted not just two counting solutions, but rather $(N!/n_1!n_2!\ldots)$ solutions, with $n_1, n_2, \ldots$ denoting the number of molecules occupying the quantum states of energy $\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2, \ldots$ If one wanted to obtain Bose or Fermi statistics, the authors claimed, one needed extra assumptions, particularly the selection of the purely symmetric or the purely antisymmetric solution. The old (classical) Boltzmann statistics, on the other hand, just corresponded to admitting *all* possible solutions of the Schrödinger equation.

In January 1927, Ehrenfest returned to the exchange with Einstein on the degeneracy question. He wrote that he would stick to the following two opinions:

> I. That the (over-proportional) occupation of the lowest quantum state cannot be called a "condensation" because nothing at all happens that would somehow correspond to a transition from a pure one-phase system to a two-phase system, when a certain number of molecules is surpassed.
> II. That your approximation by integrals really and absolutely ceases to be permitted as soon as one has, by increasing the number of molecules, arrived at that situation where the occupations of the first, second and third quantum state already differ strongly, that is where you triumphantly (but incorrectly) expound: "Look how the condensation into the lowest state happens." (Ehrenfest to Einstein, 8 January 1927)

Even without referring to the mathematical subtlety of argument II, Ehrenfest insisted on the one-phase nature of the Bose gas of high density and low temperature and mentioned that: 'Pauli has agreed with us, when I wrote to him about it.'$^{312}$ Einstein replied: 'I don't care whether you consider the molecules in the lowest state to constitute a peculiar phase or not; the only essential point is that with the hypothesis assumed [namely, Bose's counting method] there follows an increasing number of zero-energy molecules once a certain density has been reached' (Einstein to Ehrenfest, 11 January 1927). This argument could not convince Ehrenfest, who protested:

> There does not exist at all such a singular density, where something new begins, because there exists already for small densities a super-normal occupation of the lower quantum states as compared to the Boltzmann distribution which becomes worse with increasing density. However, in this connection, no particular density can be distinguished at which something new begins; *hence* I deny any analogy to a two-phase system in which something really new comes about at a definite density. (Ehrenfest to Einstein, 13 January 1927)

The detailed evaluation of this impenetrability argument was displayed by Ehrenfest in letters, which he submitted to *Naturwissenschaften* and *Nature* (Ehrenfest, 1927a), respectively, whose contents were identical and which he opened by stating:

> When collisions between the molecules of an ideal gas are taken into consideration, then the motion of the gas does not appear to be multiply periodic. It is therefore impossible to quantize this motion by means of the "classical" quantum theory. Moreover, in the treatment of the ideal gas by means of the new "undulatory mechanics," hitherto only the impenetrability of the walls of the vessel has been taken into account, and not the reciprocal impenetrability of the molecules (Schrödinger, 1926b). I propose to show that, in the case of impenetrable moving *mass-points*, wave mechanics gives an exact and very elementary solution. Simultaneously, we arrive at the relation mentioned in the title [i.e., between reciprocal impenetrability of matter and the exclusion principle]. (Ehrenfest, *loc. cit.*, p. 196)

Ehrenfest went on to prove this result in a one-dimensional model consisting of $N$ molecules. The solutions of the Schrödinger equation between impenetrable walls can then be written as

$$ \psi = \sum C(p_1, \ldots p_N) \cos(a_1 x_{p_1}) \cos(a_2 x_{p_2}) \ldots \cos(a_N x_{p_N}), \qquad (207) $$

where $p_1, \ldots, p_N$ denotes one permutation of the numbers $1, \ldots, N$, and the sum must be taken over *all* permutations. The reciprocal impenetrability of the molecules might be taken into account 'by means of the additional "diagonal restriction," which in wave mechanics corresponds to the impossibility of two molecules occupying the same point in space at the same,' ' Ehrenfest argued, or: 'Of all the solutions of the form [(207)], only those are admitted which are *also* equal to zero at all points of the $N(N - 1)/2$ flat 'diagonal space' of $N - 1$ dimensions which are represented by the equations $x_h = x_k$ ($h, k = 1, \ldots, N$)' (Ehrenfest, *loc. cit.*, p. 196). This mathematical condition now imposed a restriction on the constants $C(p_1, \ldots, p_N)$, namely, that they all 'must have values equal to each other or opposite in sign, according as the arguments $p_1, \ldots, p_N$ are derived from the numbers $1, \ldots, N$ by an even or an odd number of simple permutations.' ### (c) The Electron Wave Equation in Quantum Mechanics: Vector or Spinor? (December 1926–May 1927)

Besides Ehrenfest and Einstein, a third quantum theoretician, already mentioned, became quite involved in the statistical properties of matter at the same time: Wolfgang Pauli. He had also followed the pioneering investigations of Heisenberg and Dirac, notably, the conclusion expounded clearly by Dirac ‘that for a material gas Fermi’s statistics, not the one of Einstein and Bose, must be applied.’ This conclusion provided the starting point of Pauli’s paper on gas degeneracy and paramagnetism, which he submitted in the middle of December 1926 to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Pauli, 1927a).³¹⁸ Being aware that Dirac’s assumption ‘destroys the analogy postulated by Einstein between the statistical behaviour of the material gas and of the light-quantum gas,’ a fact that might ‘seem to be a grave argument against Fermi’s statistics,’ Pauli hastened to assemble several arguments in its favour. Firstly, ‘material systems (e.g., a crystal lattice) are distinguished from radiation generally because of the existence of zero-point energy, and exactly in this respect the Fermi statistics leads to more satisfactory results than the one of Bose-Einstein’; secondly, the existence of a universal velocity *c* for all light-quanta in contrast to the variable phase velocity *c²/v* for material particles resulted in the consequence ‘that for several moving particles a representation of the de Broglie field can also be described with many light-quanta being present in the conventional three-dimensional space.’ The (Einstein and) de Broglie analogy between light-quanta and material particles, and the considerations of the correspondence limit relating these objects in the case of vanishing mass of material particles, would not weaken these arguments, Pauli insisted, because the limiting procedure implied that one knew ‘how to formulate in the quantum mechanics of many identical bodies the finite propagation property of force actions (i.e., the retardation of the [electromagnetic] potentials)’ (Pauli, *loc. cit.*, p. 84).
Having thus formulated the basic ideas, Pauli proceeded further in 1927. He first recalled the formal description of electron spin, given earlier by Heisenberg

$$

Before he arrived at a proper wave-mechanical reformulation, another attempt to incorporate the electron spin into the undulatory theory appeared in the literature.
Charles Galton Darwin from Edinburgh submitted early in 1927 an article to *Nature*, which was entitled ‘The Electron as a Vector Wave’ and was published in the issue of 17 February 1927 (Darwin, 1927a). He also knew about the defects of the previous treatment of electron spin in quantum mechanics, and wrote:

> When what is required is to double the number of states of the electron, it is at least generous to introduce extra three degrees of freedom and then make an arbitrary (though not unnatural) assumption which cuts down the triple infinity to two.... Now we regard the electron as the most primitive thing in Nature, and it would therefore be much more satisfactory if the duality could be obtained without such great elaboration. (Darwin, *loc. cit.*, p. 282)

It was the superfluous degree of freedom, Darwin claimed, that had hindered previously obtaining a rigorous Hamiltonian including the electron spin (see Thomas, 1926a; Frenkel, 1926). ‘Wave mechanics definitely excludes half-quantum numbers for the spin, and so would lead to triplets instead of doublets—$1, 0, -1$ instead of $\frac{1}{2}$, or $-\frac{1}{2}$,’ he continued and argued ‘that quantum mechanics is largely guided by the principle that nothing unobservable is to be explained, so that a theory is to be regarded as suspect, which introduces a large number of higher quantum states of rotation, only to bar them later’ (Darwin, *loc cit.*).

that one might understand the nature of spin within three months (starting from the
beginning of December [1926]). (Heisenberg to Pauli, 5 February 1927, in Pauli,
1979, pp. 373–374)

Although Heisenberg had not yet seen the details of Darwin’s paper, he disliked
the very tendency of its approach; when he finally read it, he found it ‘abominable’
(‘abscheulich,’ Heisenberg to Pauli, 9 March 1927), in contrast to the new ideas
that Pauli had written to him, which he found to be ‘nice’ and informed Pascual
Jordan in Göttingen instantly about them.
    Apparently, Jordan showed great interest and wrote a postcard to Pauli in
Hamburg, upon which he received more information from there. ‘Meanwhile I
have supplemented my calculation on the magnetic electron in the following two
points,’ wrote Pauli to Jordan on 12 March 1927, explaining:

    Firstly, I look for the most general linear substitution

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sigma_x(\psi_\alpha) &= C_{11}^{(x)} \psi_\alpha + C_{12}^{(x)} \psi_\beta, \quad \text{etc. for } y \text{ and } z, \\
\sigma_x(\psi_\beta) &= C_{21}^{(x)} \psi_\alpha + C_{22}^{(x)} \psi_\beta, \quad \text{etc. for } y \text{ and } z,
\end{aligned}
\Bigg\} \tag{[(213)]}$$

with Hermitean matrices C and σ_x^2 + σ_y^2 + σ_z^2 a diagonal matrix which, when inserted
as operators for σ_x^2 + σ_y^2 + σ_z^2, satisfy the relation

$$\sigma_x \sigma_y - \sigma_y \sigma_x = 2i \sigma_z. \tag{[(214)]}$$

These most general C^{(x)}, C^{(y)}, C^{(z)}, which may occur in physics, are evidently ob-
tained from the special ones σ^0 given by me through the application of the substitu-
tion σ = Sσ^0S^{−1}, with S orthogonal. Secondly, I found that my equations of motion
can also be obtained from a variational principle, where

$$\psi_\alpha \overline{\psi}_\alpha - \psi_\beta \overline{\psi}_\beta, \quad \psi_\beta \overline{\psi}_\alpha + \psi_\alpha \overline{\psi}_\beta, \quad \text{and} \quad i(\psi_\beta \overline{\psi}_\alpha - \psi_\alpha \overline{\psi}_\beta)$$

(the bar denoting the complex conjugate) serve formally as for volume densities of
the x, y, z components of the spin momentum. Now, your comment that besides the
already mentioned relations further ones,

$$\sigma_x \sigma_y = -\sigma_y \sigma_x = i \sigma_z, \dots \text{etc.}, \quad \text{and} \quad \sigma_x^2 = \sigma_y^2 = \sigma_z^2 = 1 \tag{[(215)]}$$

are valid, is very welcome. Indeed I see that these relations exactly characterize the
fact that spin can assume only two positions in a [magnetic] field. (Pauli to Jordan, 12
March 1927, in Pauli, 1927, pp. 385–386)

Pauli further expected that ‘one might deduce from [(215)] that m_s can only
assume the values ±1/2, while it is known that the usual equations [(214)] can be

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0317 -->

satisfied with arbitrary integral or half-integral values for the spin,’ and that ‘per-
haps now already the problem of a relativistic generalization (higher approxima-
tion) may be solved’ (Pauli, loc. cit., p. 386). To achieve this goal, he proposed to
replace the ‘nonrelativistic’ vector σ<sub>x</sub>, σ<sub>y</sub>, σ<sub>z</sub> by a relativistic six-vector σ<sub>ik</sub> and
to interpret quantum mechanically the equations σ<sub>ik</sub>P<sub>k</sub> = 0 (with P<sub>k</sub> the four-
dimensional energy-momentum vector), but he did not proceed further along such
a programme.<sup>320</sup> At the beginning of the summer semester, he finally submitted a
paper, entitled ‘Zur Quantenmechanik des magnetischen Elektrons’ (‘On the
Quantum Mechanics of the Magnetic Electron’), to Zeitschrift für Physik, where it
was published two months later (Pauli, 1927b).

In the introduction to his new investigation, Pauli stressed (as Darwin had done
earlier) that, in contrast to the situation in matrix mechanics, the introduction of
the electron spin into matrix mechanics met with formal difficulties arising from
the double-valuedness of the eigenfunctions. Instead of choosing the path of
Darwin—Pauli found that this involved insurmountable difficulties—he rather
proposed a simpler method, namely, ‘to add to the position variables of the centre-
of-mass of the electron the components of the spin of each electron in a fixed
direction (instead of the rotating angle conjugate to the spin variable)’ (Pauli, loc.
cit., p. 603). Consequently, the eigenfunction of the electron consisted in each
quantum state (of energy E) of two functions, ψ<sub>α,E</sub>(q<sub>k</sub>) and ψ<sub>β,E</sub>(q<sub>k</sub>), whose
absolute square if multiplied by the differentials dq<sub>k</sub>—i.e., |ψ<sub>α,E</sub>(q<sub>k</sub>)|<sup>2</sup> dq<sub>1</sub> dq<sub>2</sub> dq<sub>3</sub>
and |ψ<sub>β,E</sub>(q<sub>k</sub>)|<sup>2</sup> dq<sub>1</sub> dq<sub>2</sub> dq<sub>3</sub>, respectively—yielded the probabilities that the spin
component either assumed the value +½ h/2π or −½ h/2π. Evidently, the ψ<sub>α</sub> and ψ<sub>β</sub>
satisfied the orthogonality relations

$$
\int (\psi_{\alpha,n}\psi_{\alpha,m}^* + \psi_{\beta,n}\psi_{\beta,m}^*) dq_1 dq_2 dq_3 = \delta_{nm} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{for } n = m, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \tag{216}
$$

The Hamiltonian in the Schrödinger equation for the magnetic electron then had
to involve the ‘spin matrices’ s<sub>x</sub>, s<sub>y</sub>, s<sub>z</sub>, which composed a matrix vector satisfying
the relations (with [,] denoting the ‘vector product’)

$$
[\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{s}] = -\frac{h}{2\pi i} \mathbf{s}, \quad \mathbf{s}^2 \left(\frac{h}{2\pi}\right)^2 s(s+1), \quad \text{with } s = \frac{1}{2}, \tag{217}
$$

and Jordan’s Eqs. (215)—provided one replaced **s** by ½ h/2π σ (what we shall also do
in the following).<sup>321</sup> Finally, Pauli wrote the ‘most simple Ansatz’ for his spin

<sup>320</sup>Pauli wrote to Jordan that he had instead become involved again in developing relativistic
quantum field theory (see also Pauli to Bohr, 29 March 1927).
<sup>321</sup>Pauli thanked Jordan in a footnote on pp. 607–608 (of his paper, Pauli, 1927b) for advice:
Jordan had also told Pauli about the relation of the matrices σ<sub>k</sub> to the mathematical quaternions. By
the way, Pauli kept the same notation s<sub>k</sub> for both s<sub>k</sub> and σ<sub>k</sub>.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0318 -->

matrices, namely,

$$
\sigma_x(\psi) = \begin{pmatrix} 0, & 1 \\ 1, & 0 \end{pmatrix}\psi, \quad \sigma_y(\psi) = \begin{pmatrix} 0, & -i \\ +i, & 0 \end{pmatrix}\psi, \quad \sigma_z(\psi) = \begin{pmatrix} 1, & 0 \\ 0, & -1 \end{pmatrix}\psi, \tag{218}
$$

where ψ represents the two-component wave function $\begin{pmatrix} \psi_\alpha \\ \psi_\beta \end{pmatrix}$. The time-
independent, nonrelativistic Schrödinger equation of the magnetic electron then
consisted of a pair of equations,

$$
\begin{aligned}
H\left(\frac{h}{2\pi i}\frac{\partial}{\partial q}, q_k, \sigma_x, \sigma_y, \sigma_z\right)\psi_{E,\alpha} &= E\psi_{\alpha}, \\
H\left(\frac{h}{2\pi i}\frac{\partial}{\partial q}, q_k, \sigma_x, \sigma_y, \sigma_z\right)\psi_{E,\beta} &= E\psi_{\beta}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{219}
$$

In Section 3 of his paper, Pauli showed how the rotations of the functions ψ<sub>α</sub>
and ψ<sub>β</sub> could be achieved with the help of Cayley–Klein parameters, as defined in
the well-known book of his teacher Sommerfeld (Klein and Sommerfeld, 1897,
§2–§4). He noted explicitly that ψ<sub>α</sub> and ψ<sub>β</sub> could not be determined by giving the
direction of the z-axis alone (a phase remaining arbitrary); ‘hence it seems hardly
possible to associate with the magnetic electron directed (vectorial) eigenfunctions
à la Darwin’ (Pauli, loc. cit., p. 614). Pauli then found the behaviour of the chosen
eigenfunctions in magnetic and Coulomb fields of an atom to coincide with those
determined by Heisenberg and Jordan in matrix mechanics (Section 4). Also, it was
easy to generalize the spin-function for systems containing several (N) electrons
(§5). For that purpose, Pauli introduced 3N spin matrices σ<sub>1x</sub>, σ<sub>1y</sub>, σ<sub>1z</sub>, ...
σ<sub>Nx</sub>σ<sub>Ny</sub>σ<sub>Nz</sub> in the wave function and stated: ‘The skew-symmetric solution is also
in the most general case of electrons the one which satisfies the “equivalence rule”
and shows up alone in nature,’ adding in a footnote: ‘I want to stress that the sole
occurrence of the skew-symmetric solution can be demanded for electrons with
spin so far only from experience.... The probability of other types of statistics
[than Fermi statistics] for different material gases still remains open.’ (Pauli, loc.
cit., p. 623)

In spite of the criticism of his ‘light-like description’ of magnetic electrons by
polarized vectors, Darwin published an extended version of it after a visit to
Copenhagen. Encouraged by discussions with Niels Bohr and Oskar Klein,
Darwin now complained that Pauli ‘is more disposed to regard the wave theory
[of Schrödinger] as a mathematical convenience and less as a physical reality’ and
‘stops short of the point which was the guiding principle to me, and refuses to
interpret the two functions that we both obtain as formed from a vector’ (Darwin,
1927c, p. 227).<sup>322</sup> However, in detail, Darwin did not display more than the

<sup>322</sup>For different opinions regarding Darwin’s work, see Schrödinger to Darwin, 4 October 1927,
and Born to Darwin, 7 April 1927, quoted in Kragh, 1981a, footnote 69, p. 47.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0319 -->

already published results; further, he worked out the connection to the quatern-
ion calculus and noted that it hinted at ‘an interesting unity between the electric
charge and the magnetic moment’ (Darwin, loc. cit., p. 243). In comparing his
vector scheme with Pauli’s spin matrix formalism, Darwin ‘emphasized that there
is absolutely no difference in mathematical result between them, but only a ques-
tion of interpretation’ (Darwin, loc. cit.), and he pointed to ‘the greater elegance of
the formulae’ and ‘the real advantage of the vector conception that it should more
readily suggest extensions of applications’ (Darwin, loc. cit., p. 245). However, he
also admitted: ‘In the most important such extension, the relativistic transforma-
tion, the simplest form of generalization gives a wrong result,’ but, so he claimed,
Pauli could do even less. Indeed, the latter had stated in his paper that he had not
succeeded ‘in obtaining a relativistically invariant formulation of the quantum-
mechanical magnetic electron which can be viewed as sufficiently natural and
necessary’; already, the classical model demanded extra forces (so-called ‘Zwangs-
kräfte’); hence, ‘a more detailed model of the electron beyond the simple repre-
sentation by an infinitely tiny magnetic dipole might be required’ (Pauli, 1927b,
p. 619). It would soon be shown that nothing of the sort was really necessary;
rather, as Paul Dirac showed, a much simpler equation existed than Pauli or
Darwin had anticipated for the relativistic magnetic electron.

**(d) Dirac’s Magnetic Electron Equation (January 1927–January 1928)**

In December 1925, at the golden jubilee celebration of Hendrik Lorentz’s doctor-
ate in Leyden, Niels Bohr and Albert Einstein were both present. ‘Einstein asked
the very first moment I saw him what I believed about the spinning electron,’ Bohr
recalled in a letter to Ralph Kronig, and continued:

Upon my question about the cause of the necessity of the mutual coupling between
spin axis and the orbital motion, he explained that this coupling was an immediate
consequence of the theory of relativity. This remark acted as a complete revelation to
me, and I have never faltered in my conviction that we at last were at the end of our
sorrows. (Bohr to Kronig, 26 March 1926)

Still, after the first introduction of the electron spin, it took a little while until
the leading quantum physicists acknowledged the idea; especially, a visitor from
Cambridge at Bohr’s Institute in Copenhagen, Llewellyn Hilleth Thomas, had to
remove in February 1926 the difficulty about the factor 2 in the gyromagnetic ratio
for the electron with the help of a general relativistic calculation of the orbital
motion (Thomas, 1926a). Then, however, the path seemed to be open to under-
stand electron spin with the help of accepted theories. Thus, Arnold Sommerfeld
wrote to Einstein on 5 August 1926: ‘Surely you are already trying to incorporate
the spinning electron (which is indispensable!) into general relativity theory? That
would be the greatest triumph of relativity theory.’ (‘Sie versuchen wohl schon, das

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0320 -->

spinnende Elektron (das unentbehrlich ist!) in die allgemeine Relativitätstheorie
einzuordnen? Das wäre der größte Triumph der Relativitätstheorie,’ Einstein and
Sommerfeld, 1968, p. 107.) To which Einstein replied: ‘I freely admit that one
cannot doubt the spinning electron. But for the moment there exists little hope of
comprehending its necessity within the scheme.’ (‘Ich gebe Ihnen gerne zu, dass an
dem spinnenden Elektron nicht zu zweifeln ist. Aber einstweilen ist wenig Hoffnung
seine Notwendigkeit von innen heraus zu begreifen,’ loc. cit., pp. 107–108.) The task
had to wait for more than a year until Dirac discovered the solution.
In his contribution to the Pauli memorial volume, Ralph Kronig reported
about the crucial steps toward a proper relativistic quantum-mechanical descrip-
tion of the magnetic electron:

In the formulation of quantum mechanics reported so far, the material particles are
considered as characterized by position coordinates only. It now became an urgent
task to incorporate the phenomenon indicated by the term “spin” into the new
scheme of things. The initial step was taken by Pauli himself [1927b], who proposed
that the wave function of an electron, besides being determined by continuously
variable position coordinates, should be considered as also depending on a spin
variable, capable of two values only.... Thereby Pauli paved the way for the rela-
tivistic theory of the electron and of hydrogen-like atoms which we owe to Dirac
(1928a). (Kronig, 1960, p. 32)

Dealing with the same topic, Bartel Van der Waerden stressed: ‘Pauli’s matrices
s<sub>k</sub> were used by Dirac to form a relativistic first-order equation.... Dirac’s
wave equation contains matrices and is similar to Pauli’s, but not to the old rela-
tivistic [Klein-Gordon] equation. The step from one to two components is large,
whereas the step from two to four components is small’ (Van der Waerden, 1960,
p. 223).
Thus spoke two contemporaries of Dirac, who knew him personally, one a
theoretical spectroscopist and the other a mathematician, but the originator of the
final result, the relativistic electron equation, would seriously disagree.<sup>323</sup> Dirac
remembered the first step connected with the genesis of his equation:

It was towards the end of my stay in Copenhagen, probably in January 1927, that
Pauli visited Copenhagen. I explained to him my work on the physical interpretation
and the transformation theory of quantum mechanics. We discussed how these ideas
would apply to the spin of the electron. We were led to the introduction of the three
σ-variables to describe the three components of spin. I believe I got these variables
independently of Pauli, and possibly also Pauli got them independently of me. (Dirac,
1977, p. 138)

<sup>323</sup>Dirac has presented his story of the path leading him to the electron theory at several places,
e.g., in Dirac, 1977, and Dirac, 1979; see also his interview with J. Mehra, 28 March 1969, quoted in
Mehra, 1972.

**II.7 Relativistic Electrons and Quantum Fields** 289

The very last statement is certainly correct, because Pauli had reported about his work on electron spin already in November 1926 to Heisenberg.$^{324}$ On the other hand, we have no evidence that Pauli visited Copenhagen toward the end of Dirac's first stay there; rather, on his way to his next station, Göttingen, Dirac stopped at the University of Hamburg—where Pauli was—in early February 1927, and there he attended the joint meeting of the *Gauverein Niedersachsen* of the German Physical Society, held on 5 and 6 February.$^{325}$ There, he surely also met Pauli and discussed with him the spin problem.

During his following stay in Göttingen, Dirac directed his interest to working out the consequences of his new quantum-theoretical approach to radiation theory (Dirac, 1927b), dealing in particular with the dispersion problem (Dirac, 1927c). There, he attended lectures, e.g., those of Hermann Weyl on group theory, and met and made friends with J. Robert Oppenheimer and others.$^{326}$ Before returning to Cambridge by the end of June 1927, he stopped (with Oppenheimer) in Leyden to see the old Hendrik Lorentz and to discuss physics with Paul Ehrenfest there, and with Hendrik Kramers in Utrecht.$^{327}$ Finally, he arrived at home to take some vacation—hence, Oppenheimer asked him later: 'Did you keep your promise to stop quantum mechanics over the summer?' (Oppenheimer to Dirac, 28 November 1927)—and then started to prepare himself for work during the new term at St. John's College.

In late October 1927, Dirac then attended the fifth Solvay Conference on Physics in Brussels, participating actively in the discussions of quantum mechanics and its interpretation, as we have reported in Section II.6. He further recalled the following incident:

> During the period before the lecture started on one occasion, Bohr came up to me and asked me: "What are you working on now?" I said: "I'm trying to get a relativistic theory of the electron." Then Bohr said: "But Klein has already solved this problem." I was a bit taken aback by this. I began to explain that Klein's solution of the problem, based on the Klein-Gordon equation, was not satisfactory because it could not be fitted in with my general physical interpretation of quantum mechanics. However, I was not able to explain very much to Bohr before the start of the lecture interrupted our conversation, and I had to leave the question rather in the air. (Dirac, 1977, p. 141)

Continuing with his efforts in Cambridge, Dirac finally found how to arrive at a relativistic equation by generalizing Pauli's (and his own!) two-dimensional spin

$^{325}$ See *Verhandlungen der Deutschen Physikalischen Gesellschaft 1927*, p. 9; Dirac's recollection of the meeting recalled the presentations there as 'largely concerned with a discussion of exponential results about spectra' (Dirac, 1977, p. 139).

matrices. However, confronted later with Sommerfeld's statement—'The discovery of the Pauli equation was an important step leading to the recognition of the true nature of the electron, i.e., the Dirac equation' (Sommerfeld, 1929, p. 226)—he would insist:

> This statement is not true, so far as I am concerned. I was not interested in bringing the spin of the electron into the wave equation, did not consider the question at all and did not make any use of Pauli's work. The reason for this is that my dominating interest was to get a relativistic theory agreeing with my general physical interpretation and transformation theory. I thought that this problem should first be solved in the simplest possible case, which was presumably the spinless particle, and only after that should one go to consider how to bring in spin. It was a great surprise to me when I later on discovered that the simplest possible case did not involve the spin. (Dirac, 1977, p. 139)

These recollections given in 1972—i.e., forty-five years after the events—seem to be quite definite and consistent, but they must be checked against historical evidence and documents.$^{328}$ One of the crucial items in the above story concerns Dirac's claim that he arrived at a similar description of the electron spin by matrices as Pauli in the first month of the year 1927, and that he discussed this problem with Pauli in early February. We can indeed trace clear evidence for this claim in the 'Lectures on Modern Quantum Mechanics,' which the future Fellow of St. John's College, Cambridge, prepared during summer 1927.$^{329}$ The title of lectures 13 to 16 is 'The Magnetic Electron,' and the topic begins with the remark: 'The quantum theory applied to electrons considered as point charges does not give results in agreement with experiment.' Dirac then discussed the 'more complicated kind of electron,' which had been introduced to explain electron statistics, anomalous Zeeman effects, and the fine structure of the hydrogen atom, notably, the proposals of Darwin and Pauli.$^{330}$ Two aspects of Dirac's presentation are noteworthy: firstly, Dirac stressed the difficulties in associating a

$^{328}$ We owe the most thorough study of the 'genesis of Dirac's relativistic theory of electrons' to Helge Kragh (1981a). He scanned carefully through the background of earlier attempts at relativistic quantum mechanics until 1927, the role of spin in quantum mechanics in the years between 1925 and 1927, in sum, all of the events and incidents that led Dirac to the path to his equation. An abbreviated account may be found in Kragh's biography of Dirac (1990), Chapter 3. In contrast to Kragh, we would not overemphasize the nonreliability of Dirac's own account; most of the incorrect statements—e.g., with respect to the places where the events occurred—can be easily resolved, and we can even assemble some arguments in favour of Dirac's reconstruction later in life. Most details, as given by him, are quite reliable as far as facts are concerned, but perhaps not so sound regarding individual dates and places.

$^{329}$ Dirac's handwritten notes for these lectures have been preserved (see AHQP, file M/f No. 36, Section 11); the comments state 'probably October 1927' and: 'The lecture course evidently continued for two terms. The numbers in the margins indicate the material covered in each lecture.'

$^{330}$ Interestingly, in the main text, Dirac just treats Darwin's paper of February in *Nature* (Darwin, 1927a) and a later one published on the anomalous Zeeman effects (Darwin, 1927b), but refers to the further extended presentation of the vector-wave theory in the *Proceedings of the Royal Society* (issue of September 1927) only in the margin of the manuscript. Hence, one should conclude that he prepared the lecture notes before Darwin's paper (1927c) appeared in print.
