II.7 Relativistic Electrons and Quantum Fields 321

Because they wanted to take the spin property of elementary particles into account, Heisenberg and Pauli used the Dirac equation to represent the fundamental one-particle matter-wave equation. Then, the Lagrangian function became

$$
L = -\sum_\mu \sum_\sigma \sum_\rho \left[ \gamma_{\rho\sigma}^\mu \psi_\rho^\dagger \left( \frac{hc}{2\pi i} \frac{\partial}{\partial x_\mu} + e\Phi_\mu \right) \psi_\sigma - imc^2 \psi_\rho^\dagger \psi_\rho \right], \tag{279}
$$

with $\Phi_\mu$ denoting the electromagnetic potentials ($\mu = 1, \ldots, 4$) and $\psi_\rho, \psi_\rho^\dagger$ (defined by $\psi_\sigma^* = \sum_\rho \gamma_{\rho\sigma}^4 \psi_\rho^\dagger$, with $\psi_\sigma^*$ the complex conjugate) the charged matter fields, whose four-dimensional electric current $s_\mu$,

$$
s_\mu = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \Phi_\mu} = (-e) \sum_{\rho, \sigma} \gamma_{\rho\sigma}^\mu \psi_\rho^\dagger \psi_\sigma, \tag{280}
$$

can be shown to be a conserved quantity. The Hamiltonian formalism of relativistic quantum fields involves the canonically conjugate momentum $P_{\sigma 4}$, defined as,

$$
P_{\sigma 4} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \frac{\partial \psi_\sigma}{\partial x_4}} = - \frac{hc}{2\pi} \psi_\sigma^*, \tag{281}
$$

and the canonical commutation relations (at equal times) are given by

$$
\left. \begin{aligned} [\psi_\rho, \psi_\sigma']_+ &= [\psi_\rho^*, \psi_\sigma^{*'}]_+ = [\psi_\rho^\dagger, \psi_\sigma^{\dagger'}]_+ = 0, \\ [\psi_\rho, \psi_\sigma^{*'}]_+ &= \frac{1}{i} \sum_\tau \gamma_{\tau\sigma}^4 [\psi_\rho, \psi_\tau^{\dagger'}]_+ = \delta_{\rho\sigma} \delta(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}'). \end{aligned} \right\} \tag{282}
$$

The plus sign as subscript in the bracket means that for the Fermi particles the usual 'commutator' expression must be replaced by the 'plus-commutator' or the sum:$^{367}$

$$
[\psi, \psi^{*'}]_+ = \psi \psi^{*'} + \psi^{*'} \psi. \tag{283}
$$

Having established this relativistically invariant quantum-mechanical many-body scheme, the authors concluded that, in contrast to Jordan's earlier claim (Jordan, 1928, p. 206), 'both types of solutions, namely those obeying Bose-Einstein statis-

322 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

tics on the one hand, and those following the exclusion principle on the other hand, seem to have completely equal rights, hence a satisfactory explanation for favouring the second possibility in nature cannot be obtained' (Heisenberg and Pauli, 1929, pp. 29–30). Further, they claimed that *both protons and electrons must be described by the 'same' Dirac equation*, except for the different masses: protons with matter field $\psi^\dagger$ and positive elementary charge follow in fact the 'adjoint' equation$^{368}$

$$
\sum_\mu \sum_\sigma \gamma_{\sigma\rho}^\mu \left( \frac{h}{2\pi i} \frac{\partial}{\partial x_\mu} - \frac{e}{c} \Phi_\mu \right) \psi_\sigma^\dagger + imc\psi_\rho^\dagger = 0. \tag{284}
$$

To formulate the interaction of the matter-wave fields with the electromagnetic field—the only interaction between elementary particles (besides the gravitational) known then—Heisenberg and Pauli turned to the already mentioned trick (*Kunstgriff*) of adding a term $L'$, Eq. (268), to the Lagrangian, Eq. (279). This trick modified the Maxwell's equations slightly, but provided a finite canonically conjugate momentum $P_{44}$ to the scalar potential $\Phi_4$, namely,

$$
P_{44} = \varepsilon \sum_{\alpha=1}^4 \frac{\partial \Phi_\alpha}{\partial x_\alpha}, \tag{285}
$$

and thus a proper canonical commutation relation arose, i.e.,

$$
[P_{44}, \phi_4'] = \frac{hc}{2\pi} \delta(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}'). \tag{286}
$$

With these additions, the full Hamiltonian scheme for the combined electromagnetic and matter fields as well as the commutation relation for all fields were established, and the authors especially pointed out the commutability of all electromagnetic quantities with all matter quantities, which made it possible to simplify the formalism of relativistic quantum field theory considerably as compared with the one developed earlier for the nonrelativistic case.

In the following Section 5 of their paper, Heisenberg and Pauli related the new quantum electrodynamics to the previous theory that Jordan and Pauli had worked out in late 1927 (see our Section II.5 above for the charge-free case). In the latter, use had been made of a consistent four-dimensional formalism even more symmetrically, including the singular function $\Delta(x_1, x_2, x_3, t)$ for expressing the

Although the older charge-free scheme manifestly exhibited relativistic invariance, which had to be established in the new formalism, Heisenberg and Pauli dismissed this advantage, claiming that their 'three-dimensional point of view' would simplify the practical calculation, and concluded: 'For all physical applications only three-dimensional integrals for $t = constant$ have to be considered, hence the three-dimensional viewpoint possesses a closer connection to the physical content of the theory than the four-dimensional one.' The last section of Part II (§6) provided the conservation laws of energy and momentum for the entire system consisting of electromagnetic fields and matter waves, but for a physical defect, that is:

> It must be emphasized, however, that in the given expression for the electromagnetic part of energy and momentum there is contained a zero-point energy of radiation, as well as a self-energy of the electron, which does not correspond to the real situation. (Heisenberg and Pauli, *loc. cit.*, p. 39)

Although Jordan and Klein had been able to remove the self-energy term in the nonrelativistic theory by reordering factors in the energy expression (which was equivalent to adding certain bracket symbols $[\phi, \psi]$), this trick did not work in the relativistic theory, where the $\Phi_\mu$ and $\psi$ always commute. Still, Heisenberg and Pauli were not bothered for the moment, because in all calculations of physical problems presented in Sections 7 and 8 of their paper the above-mentioned difficulty did not occur.

For the physical applications, the authors passed over the standard definition of the electromagnetic potentials ($\Phi_\mu \rightarrow \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}} \Phi_\mu$, $\mu = 1, 2, 3$, and $\Phi_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi i}} \Phi_4$) and the current ($s_\mu \rightarrow \sqrt{4\pi} s_\mu$). Then, the Hamiltonian for the electromagnetic radiation assumed the form (with $\delta$ a small parameter and $\Pi_k$, $\Pi_0$ the momenta con-

By inserting periodic *Ansätze* for the potentials $\Phi_k$ and $\Phi_0$ and the conjugate momenta $\Pi_k$ and $\Pi_0$ in a finite cubic cavity of length $l$—describing the harmonic modes and their amplitudes—the well-known solutions for $H_0^{(s)}$ were obtained: they yielded in the limit $\delta \rightarrow 0$ an aperiodicity in the potential; it made sure that $\Phi_0$ connected with $\Phi_k$, but disappeared in the derived expressions for the field strengths (§7). When one passes over to quantum mechanics, the classical Fourier coefficients $p_i^{\pm}$ and $q_i^r$ (for the momenta and potentials, respectively) have to be replaced by the operators $P_i^r$ and $Q_i^r$, which satisfy the momentum-defining relations (for each mode $r$)

$$
P_i^r = \frac{1}{2\pi \nu_{r, i}} \dot{Q}_i^r, \quad P_0^4 = - \frac{1}{2\pi \nu_{r, 0}} \dot{Q}_0^r, \tag{289}
$$

and the usual (minus) commutation relations ($i, k = 1, 2, 3, 0$),

$$
\left. \begin{aligned} [P_i^r, P_i^s] &= [Q_i^r, Q_k^s] = 0, \\ [P_i^r, Q_k^s] &= \delta_{ik} \delta_{rs} \frac{h}{2\pi i}. \end{aligned} \right\} \tag{290}
$$

Now, the authors introduced the phase factors $\left( \exp \frac{2\pi i}{h} \chi_r \right)$ and the photon numbers $M_{r, \lambda}$ of Dirac's radiation theory (Dirac, 1927b) to rewrite the radiation Hamiltonian (288) in the diagonalized form (with frequencies $\nu_{r, \lambda}$) as

$$
E_0^{(s)} = \sum_{r, \lambda} \left( M_{r, \lambda} + \frac{1}{2} \right) h \nu_{r, \lambda}. \tag{291}
$$

The last term in the bracket denotes the zero-point energy (which is infinite, but can usually be dropped). The interaction-free matter waves would add to the radiation terms $E_0^{(s)}$ in the Hamiltonian, the term $\sum_s E_s N_s$ with $N_s$ the number of (massive) particles having the energy $E_s$. Finally, the interaction of matter waves with the radiation field ($\Phi_k^0$ and $\Phi_0^0$ external and $\Phi_k$, $\Phi_0$ internal potentials),

In Section 8, Heisenberg and Pauli progressed to a perturbation scheme in their relativistic quantum field theory; that is, they calculated corrections to the eigenvalue expressions following from the free Hamiltonian (of photons and massive particles) under the assumption that the interaction terms could be expanded in a series of small perturbations, say, $\phi = \phi_0 + \phi_1 \dots$. Thus, they were able to obtain a first-order solution, $\phi_1$, for the probability amplitudes of Bose or Fermi systems, respectively, which turned out to be basically identical with the second-order solution of a many-body Schrödinger equation (in configuration space), if only Coulomb forces between the charged particles were taken into consideration. The Heisenberg–Pauli solution, however, also contained divergent terms of the form $1/r_{PP}$ (the subscript $P$ referring to the position of the particle), which corresponded to the self-interaction of the charged particle, say, the electron. This additive infinite term occurring in the energy of the total system may simply be neglected (subtracted), so long as the number of electrons does not change. The magnetic terms, on the other hand, yield contributions having the order of magnitude $(v/c)^2$, with $v$ denoting the velocity of the particles, and the effects of retardation of the potentials can be neglected as being very small. To conclude §8, Heisenberg and Pauli mentioned three tasks that had to be investigated further: (1) the contribution of higher order perturbations, which might compete with the one considered; (2) a different scheme, in which the interactions between electrons are not considered as being small perturbations, but rather an expansion in powers of $(v/c)$ is attempted; and (3) the role of the self-energy of electrons in the order $(v/c)^2$.

Finally, the authors applied their theory to situations in atomic and nuclear physics, in which the electrons pass through a potential barrier emitting light. For the relative probability of these emission processes (as compared with the usual spontaneous transitions), and they calculated expressions of the order $(e/hc)(v/c)^2$ and, in particular, they concluded: 'If one applies this result to the Gamow-Gurney-Condon theory of the radioactive decay of nuclei, one would derive that the $\beta$-spectra can never consist of sharp lines, since all radiation effects of electrons in nuclei have the order of 1.' (Heisenberg and Pauli, 1929, pp. 60–61) In spite of this result, which was very welcome at that time, because it accounted for the continuous electron–energy spectra observed then, they warned against taking it too seriously because no continuous $\gamma$-ray spectra were observed in connection

Perhaps one might argue that the pioneering paper of Heisenberg and Pauli on relativistic quantum field theory produced just a straightforward general formalism and a few, even debatable, applications. This sentiment was not felt by the expert quantum theorists, who considered it as an essential step forward in extending the limits of the modern atomic theory, in which an increasing number of physicists had faith in being able to solve all problems of atomic, and even subatomic, physics.

**(g) The 'Copenhagen Spirit' and Its Interpretation (1928–1930)**

In the story of relativistic quantum field theory related above, one misses, to a large extent, the name of Pascual Jordan, although he belonged—through his collaboration with Wolfgang Pauli in 1927—among the founding fathers of the subject (Jordan and Pauli, 1928). We have noted that he was kept informed by his friends from Hamburg (Pauli) and Leipzig (Heisenberg), yet it seems that after 1928 he more or less retired from the pursuit of the programme he had helped to initiate. $^{371}$ This retirement must have had external reasons (not yet mentioned), and, indeed, one may refer to the new aspects connected with his personal career: between 1927 and 1929, Jordan moved from Göttingen to Hamburg and finally to Rostock. $^{372}$ These moves reduced his zeal for producing papers considerably: from 1928 to 1930 he published, besides the paper with Pauli, only the review article on the light-quantum in *Ergebnisse der exakten Naturwissenschaften* (Jordan, 1928) and the review papers on quantum theory and quantum electrodynamics (Jordan, 1929a, b); besides, he worked, together with his former teacher Max Born, on the book *Elementare Quantenmechanik*, dealing in detail with the matrix formulation of quantum mechanics (Born and Jordan, 1930).

In the long, fifty-page article of 1928, Jordan reviewed the development of the light-quantum concept from Einstein's 1905 hypothesis, over Einstein's 1916 paper (on his $A$ and $B$ coefficients and the derivation of Planck's radiation formula), to

He asked Pauli to read carefully through the manuscript and return it with his comments to Japan if he did not agree with its contents. On the other hand, if Pauli agreed, he should combine the note with the Pauli–Oppenheimer considerations in a three-man paper, or publish it separately.

Pauli was very happy about Heisenberg's new ideas and chose the second proposal, namely, to publish it in a second two-man paper with Heisenberg. $^{376}$ While visiting Copenhagen at the end of August 1929, Pauli composed this work, and wrote about it to Hermann Weyl:

In the new paper of Heisenberg and myself it will be shown that exactly with the help of gauge invariance these $\varepsilon$-terms [of Eq. (268)] can be avoided. As gauge invariance I consider a substitution [of the matter fields $\psi$ and $\bar{\psi}$ and the electromagnetic potentials $\Phi_\mu$]

$$\psi' = e^{i\lambda} \psi, \quad \bar{\psi}' = e^{-i\lambda} \bar{\psi}; \quad \Phi'_\mu = \Phi_\mu - \frac{\partial \lambda}{\partial x_\mu}, \quad [(293)]$$

where $\lambda$ may even be a $q$-number but one connecting with $\psi$ and $\bar{\psi}$ on every space-like section $t = \text{const.} \dots$ This limitation for $\lambda$ guarantees the gauge invariance of the commutation relation

$$[\psi_\rho^{(P)}, \bar{\psi}_\sigma^{(P')}]_{\pm} = \delta(p - p') \cdot \delta_{\rho\sigma}. \quad [(294)]$$

Now it turns out that the gauge-invariant quantities are already completely determined, if besides the given commutation relations only others are assumed among the gauge-invariant quantities themselves. And the latter are consistent with the frightful equation $\text{div } \mathbf{E} = \sum_\rho \psi_\rho^* \psi_\rho$. On the other hand, commutation relations between the $\psi$ and the [electromagnetic] field strengths are therefore superfluous. Hence one can dispense with the $\varepsilon$-terms. (Pauli to Weyl, 26 August 1929, *loc. cit.*, pp. 519–520)

The new investigation (much shorter than the first) '*Zur Quantentheorie der Wellenfelder. II*' ('On the Quantum Theory of Wave Fields. II,' Heisenberg and Pauli, 1930) then dealt with the following topics in twenty-three printed pages:

(1) General methods and momentum theorems.
(2) Conservation of charge.

It reflected, to a large extent, ‘the essential progress’ obtained by work on the invariance properties of the quantum-mechanical Hamiltonian, which Weyl had published in his book *Gruppentheorie und Quantenmechanik* (Weyl, 1928b). In 1929, Pauli exchanged ideas with Hermann Weyl, his colleague in Zurich, who was spending a leave of absence at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, through a lively correspondence, and he generalized the elegant group-theoretical methods of Weyl to the case of wave fields; these efforts helped him decisively to cast the Heisenberg–Pauli scheme into a much simpler, nearly elegant shape.

The main advances over the first paper concern the Section 3 on gauge invariance. Heisenberg and Pauli rewrote the gauge transformation (293) now in the form

$$ \Phi_{\nu} \rightarrow \Phi_{\nu} + \frac{\partial \chi}{\partial x_{\nu}}, \quad \psi_{\rho} \rightarrow \psi_{\rho} \exp \left( -\frac{2\pi i e}{h c} \chi \right) \psi_{\rho}^{*} \rightarrow \psi_{\rho}^{*} \exp \left( \frac{2\pi i e}{h c} \chi \right), \qquad (295) $$

by a suitable redefinition of the gauge parameter $\chi$. They considered the scalar potential $\Phi_0$, as in the classical theory, to be an arbitrary function that commutes with all variables and can be put equal to zero. Then, the variation concerns only the space components $\Phi_1, \Phi_2, \Phi_3$, and the equation $\text{div } \mathbf{E} = \rho$ might not follow, only a more general one, i.e.,

$$ \text{div } \mathbf{E} + e \sum \psi_{\rho}^{*} \psi_{\rho} = C. \qquad (296) $$

Still, the authors demonstrated that the constant $C$ in Eq. (296) was allowed to vanish, adding the remark:

> [Eq. (296)], read as a $q$-number equation, is only satisfied for gauge-invariant $q$-numbers, while other quantities—e.g., $\psi$ and $\Phi_\mu$—cannot be connected with it. However, since $C$ commutes with the energy operator, [Eq. (296)] may be used as a subsidiary condition for Schrödinger functionals. (Heisenberg and Pauli, 1930, p. 178)

Evidently, such a procedure did not appear to be Lorentz invariant, but Heisenberg and Pauli proved ‘that all statements about gauge invariant quantities satisfy the condition of relativistic invariance, if [Eq. (296)] is added’ (Heisenberg and Pauli, *loc. cit.*). The scheme can therefore be freed totally from Heisenberg’s artificial $\varepsilon$-trick, Eq. (268); the authors showed in detail in Section 6 how it could be accomplished. There, they also evaluated the electrostatic interaction, obtaining

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0362 -->

330 Chapter II Uncertainty, Complementarity, and Quantum Fields

the same result (including the infinite self-interaction of electrons) as in the first paper.$^{377}$ In Section 7, they turned to consider the situation in configuration space, where they obtained—in the nonrelativistic limit—the earlier results of Dirac, Jordan, and Klein, and Jordan and Wigner. For the relativistic evaluation, Heisenberg and Pauli cited a ‘soon to be published work of R. Oppenheimer’ (Oppenheimer, 1930a), whose assistance they acknowledged in their paper.$^{378}$

While Pauli continued to work on the relativistic quantum field theory in Europe, Heisenberg tried to do the same in the United States, where he arrived in March 1929 to lecture on ‘The Physical Principles of the Quantum Theory’ at the University of Chicago. The lecture course provided the first up-to-date overview of the complementarity interpretation of atomic phenomena and the quantum-mechanical theory, including the latest developments in relativistic quantum fields. Heisenberg devoted special attention to the following topics:

(1) Critique of the physical concepts of the corpuscular theory (with a discussion of the uncertainty relations and their application in determining position, momentum, and energy of free and bound electrons).
(2) Critique of the physical concepts of the wave theory (with a discussion of the measurement of the electromagnetic field strengths).
(3) The statistical interpretation of the quantum theory (dealing with the interference of Born’s probability amplitudes and Bohr’s complementarity principle).
(4) Discussion of important experiments (i.e., the observations in Wilson chambers, diffraction and dispersion experiments, the Compton effect, and fluctuation of radiation) and relativistic quantum theory.

(See the list of contents of the published lectures in Heisenberg 1930a.)

Heisenberg claimed that he presented, in his lectures, ‘nothing that is not to be found in previous publications, especially in the investigations of Bohr,’ and felt that his mission ‘seems to be fulfilled if it contributes somewhat to the diffusion of that “Kopenhagener Geist der Quantentheorie” ... which has directed the entire development of modern atomic physics’ (Heisenberg, *loc. cit.*, p. X). In the U.S., he also met Paul Dirac, the other emissary of modern European atomic theory, whose latest electron theory had been incorporated by Heisenberg and Pauli into the scheme of relativistic quantum field theory, another outgrowth of ‘that Copenhagen spirit.’ From the U.S., Heisenberg and Dirac (who had given lecture courses at Madison, Wisconsin) continued their travel to Japan, where they further propagated the latest results.$^{379}$

One may argue that the treatment of the subject and the style of presentation of the material allowed Dirac to avoid the concept and any judgment about it; he equally avoided any negative statement about it in his book, although he expressed it later in interviews. On the other hand, Heisenberg, Pauli, and the other supporters of Bohr’s views made complementarity *the* guideline for discussing the *same* topics that Dirac treated in his book, and *they did include also the relativistic equation for the electron into the general Copenhagen interpretation*.$^{382}$

In a letter to Bohr, dated 25 April 1929, Pauli mentioned: ‘Schrödinger, who is also here [in Zurich] for a visit, now thinks much more mildly (*denkt jetzt viel milder*) about the statistical interpretation of wave-mechanics.’ (Pauli to Bohr, in Pauli, 1979, p. 496) Schrödinger—the creator of wave-mechanics—had expressed himself accordingly in a public talk in November 1928 in Berlin, where he said:

> The new principle of the theory of cognition states: what is localizable in detail in space and time and what is observable are not, as one previously thought, identical things. The wave conception is the symbol or the representative of what is localizable in detail, the outcome of our efforts pointing in this direction. The corpuscle (electron, light-quantum, etc.,) is the symbol of small, though always finite, acts of observation. The waves cannot be observed directly, the corpuscle cannot be localized in detail. (*Das neue erkenntnistheoretische Prinzip besagt: das räumlich-zeitlich im Detail Lokalisierbare und das Beobachtbare sind nicht, wie man früher dachte, ein und dasselbe. Die Wellenvorstellung ist das Symbol oder der Niedeschlag unserer in dieser Richtung zielenden Bestrebungen. Die Korpuskel (Elektron, Lichtquant usw.) ist das Symbol der kleinen aber stets endlichen Beobachtungsakte. Die Wellen sind nicht direkt beobachtbar, die Korpuskel nicht im Detail lokalisierbar.*) (Schrödinger, 1929c, p. 16)

One can hardly express the situation more in the style of Bohr than Schrödinger did at that time. He did not stick to this ‘mild’ view, however, as later statements would reveal.

1929, the first of a series of great ‘Copenhagen Conferences’ began that would be held annually through the 1930s at Bohr’s Institute.$^{383}$ Léon Rosenfeld recalled about the host’s introductory talk:

> He had begun with a few general considerations, calculated, no doubt, to convey to the audience that peculiar situation of having the ground suddenly removed from under their feet, which is so effective in providing receptiveness for complementary thinking. This preliminary result being readily achieved, he had eagerly hastened to his main subject and stunned all (except Pauli) with the non-observability of the electron spin. I spent the afternoon with Heitler pondering on the scanty fragments of the hidden wisdom which we had been able to get down in our notebooks. (Rosenfeld, in Bohr, 1985, p. 305)

That the electron spin created difficulties with respect to its visual realization has been debated by physicists ever since Pauli introduced his fourth quantum number.$^{384}$ Even after the spin hypothesis of Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit had been widely accepted, Ralph Kronig hinted at serious problems that were connected with the ‘dimensions’ of an electron, especially when it was considered as a constituent of atomic nuclei (as was the custom then: Kronig, 1926a, b). Early in 1927, Léon Brillouin asked a further question, namely: can one measure the magnetic moment of an electron? In all known situations, he concluded, the magnetic moment could not be experimentally perceived; therefore, he proposed a new method to determine this quantity in an inhomogeneous magnetic field (Brillouin, 1927). In fall 1928, Niels Bohr turned to discuss the electron-spin concept more closely: he argued with Oskar Klein in Copenhagen and by letters with Abraham Joffé that this purely quantal concept, vanishing in the classical limit, could not possibly be brought into direct relation with classical concepts like angular momentum or magnetic moment. When Klein objected by citing the Stern–Gerlach effect, Bohr showed that no Stern–Gerlach experiment carried out with a free electron would work, because the effect of the Lorentz force would inevitably destroy any observable splitting.

At the 1929 spring meeting in Copenhagen, Nevill Mott from Cambridge discussed the problem of obtaining polarized electrons from double-scattering experiments. He then quickly wrote a paper on this problem, in the appendix to which he discussed also the measurability of the free electron’s magnetic moment (Mott, 1929a). On 1 July, Bohr then sent a short note of himself to Pauli on his (i.e., Bohr’s) own problem, upon which the latter replied:

> I liked the note on the magnetic electron so much that I deeply regretted that it has not been completed and sent off for printing. If I may give you a piece of advice, then it would be to send off the note *before anything else and do so as soon as possible*. (Pauli to Bohr, 17 July 1929, in Pauli, 1979, p. 512)

II.7 Relativistic Electrons and Quantum Fields 333

Still, Bohr did not proceed according to this emphatic advice of Pauli; hence, Pauli included the arguments a year later in his own report to the sixth Solvay Conference on Physics.
The occasion for this weighty report on ‘*Les théories quantiques du magnétisme: L’électron magnétique*’ (‘The Quantum Theories of Magnetism: The Magnetic Electron’) was used by Pauli as a general platform not only to assemble all of the results obtained by a quantum-mechanical treatment of the topics involved, but also for presenting the results in light of the correspondence principle as he, Pauli, understood it (Pauli, 1932).385
Pauli divided his report into two chapters, the first being devoted to the quantitative description of the magnetic properties of solid bodies, and the second being devoted to the relativistic quantum mechanics of the electron. Following a short introduction, he first turned to describe his own work on the Fermi statistics of free electrons (Pauli, 1927a).386 Then, he added a section on diamagnetism, presenting essentially the not yet published work of Lev Landau, one of the guests at his institute in Zurich, and a general approach to describe the mutual interaction of atoms by a perturbation scheme, making use of the methods of Paul Dirac and John Slater; in the following section, he displayed Heisenberg’s theory of ferromagnetism, and finally, he discussed the studies of Jean Becquerel and Johannes Wander de Haas on the paramagnetic rotation of the plane of polarization in crystals.387
In Section 1 of Part II, Pauli discussed in detail ‘the experimental arrangements to determine the spin momentum of free electrons,’ i.e., Bohr’s crucial question of 1928. He claimed, in particular, that the size of the magnetic moment, $\mu = \frac{eh}{4\pi m_0 c}$, just established the following fact: ‘The condition for the situation, in which the action of the [magnetic] forces on the spin momentum is not masked by the Lorentz force, has exactly the consequence that the first effect cannot be observed because of the existence of diffraction phenomena’ (Pauli, 1932, pp. 544–545). As the first example, Pauli discussed (following Bohr’s earlier consideration) the proposal of Brillouin: that is, the deceleration of electrons having a given spin orientation. By considering the detailed situation, he showed that the condition $mv_z \cdot \Delta x \ll h$ must be satisfied to detect an effect on the decelerating field; however,

Van Vleck (‘The Susceptibility of Samarium and Europium Ions’), B. this condition would contradict the wave nature of the electron. The Stern–Gerlach experiment with a field of homogeneity $\partial H_z / \partial z$ of the magnetic field in $z$-direction, on the other hand, implied a Lorentz force in $z$-direction of size
$$
F_L = \frac{e}{c} v_y \frac{\partial H_z}{\partial z} \Delta x. \qquad (297)
$$
In order to observe an effect on the magnetic moment, the expression on the right-hand side must be smaller than $\mu_0 \frac{\partial H_z}{\partial z}$, which implies $\Delta x \ll \lambda$, or the (classical) mechanical laws cannot be applied. (One reaches a similar conclusion in the case of an electron moving in $x$-direction.) The third example concerned the action of an electric field on the magnetic moment of the electron to compensate for the Lorentz force.388 Here, Pauli demonstrated that the angle of deflection due to the action of the electric field remains unobservable, because it is much smaller than the angle of diffraction. As the last example, he calculated the magnetic field created by a moving electron, which exceeds by far the one created by electron spin (hence, again, it cannot be observed directly).389
In the discussion, Niels Bohr summarized the main result of Pauli’s presentation by saying that ‘one can see in a very general way that it is impossible to detect experimentally the intrinsic magnetic moment of the electron,’ and continued:

Any attempt in this direction would actually be based on an application of the classical concepts, in particular that of the trajectory of an electron, which essentially amounts to ignoring the elementary quantum of action. Now, in Dirac’s theory, *all* effects due to the intrinsic magnetic moment of the electron automatically disappear if Planck’s constant is put equal to zero. This theory is actually based on an expression for the Hamiltonian derived from the classical theory of electrons in which, apart from the velocity of light, only the mass and the charge of the electron enter. It follows that these quantities are the only ones which can be determined from considerations based on analysis of the classical concept of trajectory. (Bohr, in discussion of Pauli, *loc. cit.*, pp. 603–604; English translation in Bohr, 1985, pp. 347–348)

Paul Dirac, who next spoke in the discussion, said on that occasion he would ‘agree with Bohr in a general way’ (Dirac, in Pauli, *loc. cit.*).
So far, it appears that by 1930 the quantum theorists did agree on *one* theory and its interpretation; thus, a paradigm in the sense of Thomas Kuhn had been established. Looking at the situation more closely, however, it is very difficult to

II.7 Relativistic Electrons and Quantum Fields 335

fix this paradigm. A closed theory, called quantum-mechanics, did not exist, which accounted for *all* phenomena in the atomic and subatomic world, although most active researchers had cherished the hope that it might be accomplished, at least by the end of 1930. Especially, in the realm of relativistic phenomena, new and serious difficulties had been detected already and, as we have tried to show and to argue that, on account of the historical development between 1926 and 1930, *nonrelativistic and relativistic quantum mechanics cannot be really separated*. Niels Bohr, in his Faraday Lecture, delivered on 8 May 1930, before the fellows of the Chemical Society of London, not only summarized the results of the successful atomic theory, but also emphasized its current limitation:390

The fertility of quantum mechanics as applied to the problem of atomic stability lies just in the fact that the linear dimensions of the regions ascribed to even the firmest electron-bindings outside the nucleus are still very large as compared with the classical electron diameter. (Bohr, 1932a, pp. 377–378)

Because Dirac’s relativistic electron theory exhibited the particular negative-energy problem, it indicated difficulties in smaller regions, or:

Such considerations . . . would seem to trespass the limit of applicability of the correspondence argument, and the difficulties inherent in any symbolism resting on the idealization of the electron as a charged material point appear also most instructively in the recent attempt of Heisenberg and Pauli to build up a theory of electromagnetic fields on the lines of quantum mechanics. Their formalism leads, in fact, to consequences inconsistent with the finite mass of the electron and the small coupling between atoms and electromagnetic radiation fields, on which rests the interpretation of the empirical evidence regarding spectra, based on the idea of stationary states. Under these circumstances, we are strongly reminded that the whole attack on atomic problems leaning on the correspondence argument is an *essentially approximate procedure*, made possible only by the smallness of the ratio between the square of the elementary unit of electric charge and the product of the velocity of light and the quantum of action which allow us to a large extent to avoid the difficulties of relativistic quantum mechanics in considering the behaviour of extra-nuclear electrons. (Bohr, *loc. cit.*, p. 378)

Bohr argued, indeed, that the determination of the ratio mentioned, normally called Sommerfeld’s fine-structure constant, should be expected as forming an integral part of a general consistent theory ‘in which the existence of elementary particles and the existence of the quantum of action are both naturally incorporated,’ though he admitted that ‘these problems would appear to be out of the

Similarly out of reach appeared to be an explanation of the nuclear constitution, in which according to common knowledge, protons and electrons were involved, especially the mass defects and the statistical behaviour of nuclei (due to the observed hyperfine structure of spectral lines). The puzzle of the continuous electron spectra emerging from $\beta$-decay even indicated nonconservation of energy. Bohr somehow sympathized with that idea, because he had in 1924 applied it to the radiation theory with Hendrik Kramers and John Slater (Bohr *et al.*, 1924).391 Then, the new quantum mechanics of Heisenberg and others had overthrown any energy and momentum conservation violation, but in summer 1929 Bohr sent two notes to Pauli, the first dealing with the magnetic electron as mentioned earlier, and, as he wrote:392

The other is a little piece about the $\beta$-spectra, which I had in mind for a long time, and which has been typed in the last few days, but I have not yet made up my mind to send it off, since it yields so few positive results and has been written so sketchily. (Bohr to Pauli, 1 July 1929, in Pauli, 1979, p. 509)

Pauli replied that the note on $\beta$-rays gave him ‘little satisfaction’ (Pauli to Bohr, 17 July 1929), and he would continue to battle with Bohr for the next four years about the validity of energy and momentum conservation, which he certainly was not prepared to give up at all. The resolution of this question in Pauli’s favour occurred in late 1933, and then it led to another crucial confirmation of standard quantum mechanics, though at the expense of introducing a new elementary particle, the neutrino.393 Before entering into these new fields of applications, we must interrupt the story here to focus on two other aspects: the overwhelming experimental confirmations, which the theory received in the late 1920s and early 1930s, on the one hand, and the deepened mathematical foundations added to it during the same period. Both of these important developments form the contents of the next chapter.

# Chapter III  
## The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics  

### Introduction  

In introducing Werner Heisenberg for his evening lecture ‘From a Life of Physics’ in June 1968 at Trieste, Italy, Paul Dirac stressed Heisenberg’s discovery of quantum mechanics and added: ‘In doing so he started the golden age of theoretical physics, and for a few years after that it was easy for any second rate student to do first rate work.’ (Dirac, in Heisenberg, 1968, p. 32) Dirac described an obviously new situation in the development of quantum theory, which, by the way, did not begin immediately after Heisenberg’s pioneering paper appeared in print in summer 1925, but rather a couple of years later. Then, however, many newcomers in theoretical physics entered the field of modern atomic theory—which had in the meantime become quite an advanced scheme mathematically and conceptually, in the more discrete, algebraic, or continuous wave formulation—and applied it to solve an increasing number of old and new problems, thereby obtaining ‘final’ and satisfactory explanations of atomic, molecular, and solid-state phenomena as well as problems in other fields. The difference from the situation in the early period—following the discovery of quantum mechanics—was that the first successful tests of the new scheme between 1925 and 1927 involved as a rule theoreticians who had gathered experience in dealing with quantum problems already in the years prior to the great breakthrough, while now a new generation of young researchers and students, who had not gone through the agony and failures of the old (*ältere*) quantum theory, entered into the field. Where, one may ask, did these freshmen come from, and where did they publish the results of their endeavours?  

In looking at the bulk of publications in the years between 1927 and 1932, we do not notice much change in the titles of the journals carrying them: still, the German *Zeitschrift für Physik* and, to a less but steadily growing extent, the British *Proceedings of the Royal Society of London* and *Nature*, and the American *Physical Review* contained the majority of papers, with the well-established *Annalen der Physik, Physikalische Zeitschrift*, and *Philosophical Magazine* falling back a little. On the other hand, new authors began to show up from an increasing number of nations. Besides scientists from Middle European and Scandinavian countries, who had been associated with the pioneers of quantum theory before 1926, two large groups assumed a prominent role: they came from the United States and the Soviet Union.  

In the U.S., support for postdoctoral research in quantum physics came pri-

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0370 -->

marily from one side, the Rockefeller Foundation, which ‘served as a crucial source of funds for physics during the 1920s’ and supplied ‘most of the money granted through the National Research Council, the International Education Board and the General Education Board, three agencies that pioneered large-scale subsidization of basic research in physics’ (Coben, 1971, p. 447). In further detail:  

The National Research Council (NRC), chartered by the Federal Government but controlled by the scientific associations through the American Association for the Advancement of Science, launched a programme of postdoctoral fellowships in 1919 with a gift of $500,000 from the Rockefeller Foundation. Rockefeller officials had been considering the establishment of a research institute for the physical sciences analogous to the Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research. When presented with a choice, however, they decided to postpone implementation of this idea in favour of supporting fellows chosen by the NRC. Physicists obtained over one hundred of these fellowships during the 1920s; seventeen of them were for study solely in aspects of quantum theory, others for related work that was partly experimental . . . Although these funds were supposed to be used in American universities only, the NRC permitted most of the young quantum physicists it supported to study in Europe. (Coben, *loc cit.*, pp. 447–448)

later political developments in Germany, many of the recipients of these grants eventually went to the United States and helped to establish their research there and even founded, together with their American colleagues, schools of atomic and nuclear physics.$^{397}$  

The young Soviet Union followed a policy similar to that of the United States in supporting their young physicists to learn quantum theory. The Communist regime, which had taken over Russia in 1917, only gradually overcame the hardships of a lost international war and the following internal civil strife. Still, a new generation of most talented and dedicated physics research students emerged, who were especially interested in the modern quantum and relativity theories. Paul Ehrenfest, who had spent five years from 1906 to 1911 in St. Petersburg (where he had married his Russian wife Tatyana) before returning to the West and succeeding Hendrik Antoon Lorentz in the chair of theoretical physics at the University of Leyden in Holland, strongly supported after World War I the exchange with Soviet physicists, recommending them to fellowships of the Rockefeller and the Tyler Foundations: among these, were Jakov Frenkel, Vladimir A. Fock, Igor E. Tamm, Lev D. Landau, and George A. Gamow. They learned the new atomic theory firsthand at the European centres in Berlin, Copenhagen, Göttingen, Hamburg, and Leipzig, and took their knowledge back to Leningrad, Kharkov, and Moscow. The high point of the travels of young Russian scholars extended from 1926 to 1932. During this period, several international physics conferences were also held in the Soviet Union, attended by Western teachers and experts in quantum theory, especially Niels Bohr, Max Born, Paul Dirac, Pascual Jordan, and Wolfgang Pauli. The exchange of scientific ideas was promoted by a new journal with the German title *Physikalische Zeitschrift der Sowjetunion*, which published papers in German and English. Soon after 1932, the open and liberal period of scientific exchange came to an end, although after political changes in Germany several physicists from there (like Herbert Fröhlich, Fritz Houtermans, Nicholas Kemmer, and Viktor Weisskopf) initially found shelter for one or more years at Soviet institutes.$^{398}$  

As a consequence of the establishment of quantum and wave mechanics and the influx of a steadily increasing number of research students and some senior research workers, a specialization occurred in quantum physics, especially with respect to the topics of applications. At various places, in conjunction with the interests of the local scientific community or tasks assigned to the physicists from outside (by their colleagues or by industry), schools were formed dealing with subfields, say, atomic, molecular, solid-state, or nuclear physics. For instance, in Leningrad (the renamed former Russian capital of St. Petersburg), Abram Joffé

**Introduction** 341

enabled physicists at many places, even different from the active centres of research on quantum theory, to apply the new scheme to certain topics for which (experimentally motivated) local interest was available—say, in spectroscopy, chemistry, or solid-state physics.⁴⁰¹

A very characteristic point of view must be noticed in the history of applying quantum mechanics, as will be told in the present chapter. Here, we have to concentrate upon telling the story of specific topics and the advances made in them within a period of about seven years, in contrast to the more concentrated developments we have described so far. As a consequence, the individual sections will focus on more or less specific ‘success’ stories in linear progression. Of course, this fact lies in the very nature of the material; moreover, one must add that, in these years, most problems of atomic, molecular, and solid-state physics that were attacked were also successfully treated, leaving open only a few details or difficulties to be solved later (which we will address in Chapter IV and the Epilogue). On the other hand, in the field of nuclear, and of what came to be called high-energy, physics, difficulties arose immediately that seemed to inaugurate new revolutions lying beyond the domain of quantum mechanics. Hence, the empirical foundations presented here exhibit a mixed picture: although characteristic quantum-mechanical concepts and features received full experimental verification and entire physical topics served to substantiate them, new topics with many unsolved puzzles appeared as well.

Quite a different story is told in the other part of this chapter, which deals with the mathematical foundations of quantum mechanics. In fact, the community of mathematicians and theoretical physicists that participated in this enterprise initially remained very limited in size, comprising essentially of a small circle around the great pioneer David Hilbert in Göttingen: it consisted essentially of physicists like Eugene Wigner and Lothar Nordheim and a few mathematicians like Hilbert’s former disciple Hermann Weyl, John von Neumann, Bartel Leendert van der Waerden in Berlin and Göttingen, and Aurel Wintner in Leipzig. By having a very intense and fruitful interaction, they created the improved mathematical methods to deal with quantum-mechanical problems, though many problems—both of principle and detail—remained unresolved and had to be solved in the following decades with the help of more powerful mathematical methods employing greater rigour.

In spite of the diverging character of the two parts, the two developments—empirical and mathematical—which occurred at the same time, also exhibit certain relationships and thus form, to some extent, a unit in the development of quantum mechanics. We have organized the material in seven, largely self-contained sections that loosely follow a certain (albeit not too strict) time sequence. Section III.1, after dealing with a synopsis of the principal prior experiments supporting the emergence of quantum theory between 1900 and 1926, focuses on the confirmation

N. Hinshelwood, in which the physicists Max Born, Peter Debye, Ralph Fowler, Werner Heisenberg, and others participated (Hartley *et al.*, 1932).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0374 -->

342 **Chapter III** *The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics*

of the basic quantum-mechanical concepts by new empirical findings, notably, those obtained on dispersion phenomena and the wave nature of atomic particles. The next three sections deal with mathematical topics: chiefly, the extension of the known Hilbert space methods to provide a consistent foundation of the operator and matrix methods applied in nonrelativistic quantum mechanics (Section III.2), the mathematical description of the measurement process (Section III.3), and the group-theoretical methods that assisted the physicists effectively in obtaining the energy of atoms, molecules, and solids (Section III.4). Then, we turn, in Sections III.5 and III.6, to the fundamental applications of quantum mechanics to molecular (which form the basis of quantum chemistry) and solid-state problems (enabling one to understand and evaluate for the first time the properties of compact matter). In contrast to these very successful applications on nonrelativistic quantum mechanics to atoms, molecules, and solids, those to nuclear phenomena in the interior of atoms seemed to fail largely with a few exceptions (Section III.7): here, the leading quantum physicists expected that nuclear problems might be closely connected with the grave difficulties that had been noticed in the relativistic quantum field theory and argued that both *could be solved only after a drastic change in the formalism had occurred*, comparable with the quantum-mechanical revolution of 1925/26. Therefore, the situation in the early 1930s exhibited two facets: on the one hand, quantum mechanics appeared to be quite a satisfactory theory in the microscopic domain; on the other hand, new ideas and concepts lying beyond the existing theory were deemed necessary to proceed further. After many brilliant successes, a triumph had been achieved, but it was not at all considered to be a complete one.

### III.1 The Empirical Verification of Quantum Concepts

In 1900, when the canon of physical theories seemed to approach final completion, and for some scientists, only a few ‘dark clouds’ remained that obscured the horizon of physics, an experimentally and technically quite complex phenomenon—blackbody radiation—appeared that eventually dashed the hopes of the ‘classical’ physicists. Initially, Max Planck’s ingenious hypothesis of finite energy quanta had hardly been noticed until Albert Einstein proposed a second, even bolder, hypothesis: that of considering light as corpuscles governed by the constant $h$ of Planck’s law. After ten years of active experimental and theoretical investigations—which started essentially upon the completion of the classical theories in 1905 (having brought statistical mechanics and the relativistic kinematics of the electron into a satisfactory shape)—the experts arrived at the conclusion, fixed notably to the first (1911) Solvay Conference in Brussels (and shortly thereafter), that the tiny, though finite, quantum of action $h$ violated the validity of the classical laws in the domain of atomic phenomena. Again and again, $h$ appeared to govern the physical behaviour in this region, whether it concerned the specific heats of gases or solids, the size of atoms and molecules, or the spectra emitted by them. A fundamental

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0375 -->

III.1 *The Empirical Verification of Quantum Concepts* 343

breakthrough in the latter question occurred in 1913, when Niels Bohr introduced the quantum hypothesis in the most recent model of the atom, the ‘nuclear atom’ of Ernest Rutherford. From that moment onward, details of the constitution of atoms could be derived from ingenious experiments and their interpretation, these results not only added a new field to atomic physics—nuclear physics (which had to be connected with the already known phenomena of radioactivity)—but also opened the path to explaining the empirical phenomena of a different science: chemistry. Thus, Planck’s energy-quantum hypothesis received full support from the observations in atomic physics and chemistry. The confirmation of Einstein’s light-quantum hypothesis took a longer time: the opposition to it (showed by most quantum physicists, including Max Planck) faded away slowly only after Arthur Compton’s discovery, in late 1922, of a subtle effect observed in the scattering of X-rays by the atoms of light elements resulting in the increase of the wavelength of the incident radiation.

Although these and other effects and phenomena confirmed the basic concepts of quantum theory, the new nonclassical branch of physical theory that received an ever-increasing number of applications during the first twenty-five years of its existence, these concepts did not fit into a mathematically and logically consistent scheme (as known from the previous classical theories). In fact, the more one studied the details of the quantum phenomena and their description, the clearer the discrepancies emerged. Although certain parts fitted perfectly and confirmed notably the detailed atomic models devised by Bohr and Arnold Sommerfeld, others contradicted the explanations based upon them. Finally, after 1922, the entire structure of the so-called ‘old quantum theory’ suffered a complete breakdown. During the same period, when the absolute failure of the conceptual foundations of the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory became increasingly evident, new foundations were laid that in 1925/26 helped to found a new quantum theory based on entirely different concepts.

To some extent, these new foundations were motivated by subtle experimental findings. As a particular example, we may cite here the puzzling data obtained from the analysis of spectra of complex atoms and their anomalous Zeeman effects, which ultimately led Wolfgang Pauli to enunciate his exclusion principle early in 1925 and George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit to propose the concept of electron spin later that year. Another example is provided by the effect, observed in 1922 by Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach, which implied an instantaneous orientation of angular momenta in atoms (space quantization) contradicting classical dynamics. Further new hypotheses followed from systematic theoretical considerations of the properties of atoms and their constituents, notably, Louis de Broglie’s proposal of matter waves in 1923 or the introduction of negative dispersion terms by Hendrik Kramers in 1924. Both of these hypothetical considerations (as well as the detailed dispersion theory of Kramers and Werner Heisenberg) lacked empirical support, though Walter Elsasser connected in July 1925 the idea of matter waves with some anomalies observed earlier by Carl Ramsauer (in the scattering of slow electrons by the atoms of noble gases) and by Clinton Joseph

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0376 -->

344 **Chapter III** *The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics*

Davisson and Charles Henry Kunsman (in the reflection of electrons from metallic surfaces). It is the empirical foundation of these concepts, which characterize the new quantum and wave mechanics, that we want to present in this section. We must note, however, that this foundation was provided only after the quantum-mechanical description had been firmly established and was believed to be the adequate theory by most physicists. The observation of one particular effect in the scattering of light by atoms, normally connected with the name of Pierre Auger, but noticed earlier by Lise Meitner, provides an exception to this rule.

#### (a) The Discrete Energy States and the Auger–Meitner Effect (1923–1925)

Niels Bohr expounded the hypothesis of stationary states in the atom in April 1913 as one of the basic assumptions underlying his quantum theory of atomic constitution (Bohr, 1913b). A year later, James Franck and Gustav Hertz’s observation of inelastic collisions between electrons and mercury atoms at fixed energy values, which resulted in the emission of quantum-theoretical frequencies (Franck and Hertz, 1914a, b) provided an immediate proof for the existence of these states, as Bohr emphasized in the following year (Bohr, 1915b). Since that time, a number of experts employed the collision method, which won Franck and Hertz the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1925, to determine the energy levels in atoms and molecules (see, e.g., the review of Compton and Mohler, 1924). In June 1926, James Franck and Pascual Jordan signed the preface to their monograph *Anregung von Quantensprüngen durch Stöße* (‘Excitation of Quantum Jumps by Collisions’), where they remarked:⁴⁰²

> The simple and deep idea of finite energy steps existing between discrete states of atoms and molecules, in connection with the energy conservation law and the $h\nu$-relation, succeeds in a remarkable way to describe all observations on the elementary processes created by collisions with atoms. . . . Also the excitation of quantum jumps in molecules is governed by this large set of rules. However, here exactly so many processes occur, hence we should not wonder about the fact that a secure knowledge of the elementary processes can be obtained only in rare cases. (Franck and Jordan, 1926a, p. v)

A refinement of the original method enabled Franck and his student E. Einsporn even to obtain metastable states of the mercury atom, which cannot be excited by other means (Franck and Einsporn, 1920).

In 1921, Oskar Klein and Svein Rosseland postulated the existence of the reverse effect, which was called ‘collision of the second kind,’ namely, the case that, in an electron–atom collision, a discrete amount of energy was transferred from

⁴⁰² In Volume 23 of *Handbuch der Physik*, certain chapters were reprinted (Franck and Jordan, 1926b).

the atom to the electron, leaving the atom in a (stationary) state of lower energy without the emission of radiation (Klein and Rosseland, 1921). Two years later, Rosseland predicted a peculiar type of this second kind of collision, namely, the transfer of excitation energy of an atom to another electron (than the one involved in the original excitation) of the same atom (Rosseland, 1923). ‘Such an effect . . . has recently been shown with great certainty by Auger, who used the Wilson method to visualize the path of corpuscular radiation,’ Franck and Jordan noted, and explained:

    An atom which has been deprived of a *K*-electron may close this defect by the transition of electrons from outer shells, emitting then in the familiar manner (first discussed by Kossel) characteristic X-rays; instead of radiation, however, a[nother] loosely bound [outer] electron can be emitted, which obtains a kinetic energy calculated from the energy of the radiation quantum *hν* that is replaced according to the photoelectric equation of Einstein *E*<sub>kin</sub> = *hν* − *P* (where *P* denotes the ionization energy of the electron in question). (Franck and Jordan, 1926a, p. 216)

The French physicist Pierre Auger of Paris mentioned here studied in late 1924, with a cloud chamber, ‘the phenomena presented by secondary *β*-rays produced by X-rays in an atmosphere of hydrogen containing a small admixture of a heavier gas’ (Auger, 1925a, p. 65).<sup>403</sup> Especially, in the case of krypton, the secondary electron leaving the *K*-shell results in a tertiary electron (observed on photographic plates) and assuming a kinetic energy that depends on the shell (*L*, *M*, *N*, etc.) from where it is emitted by the *K*-radiation. Auger described the phenomenon in detail in his note in the *Comptes rendus* of 5 January 1925, cited above, and in a later paper submitted in May of that year to *Journal de physique* (Auger, 1925b). He also published further studies on this effect (e.g., Auger, 1926). More than sixty years later, Richard Sietmann talked about a ‘false attribution’ when he wrote:

When the war was over, Auger became Director of Higher Education in France (1945–1948); then, he initiated with Frédéric Joliot the Atomic Energy Commission in 1948. From 1948 to 1960, he headed the Department of Exact Sciences of UNESCO; at a UNESCO meeting in 1952, he helped to establish the ‘*Conseil Européen pour la Recherche Nucléaire*,’ the organization leading to the establishment of the high-energy physics laboratory CERN in Geneva. Later in the 1950s, he moved on to foster space research and served first as president of the French Space Commission (1960–1962) and from 1964–1967 as Director-General of the European Research Organization.     Becoming an expert on cosmic ray research since 1928 (e.g., discovering the large cosmic-ray showers in 1938), Auger also carried out pioneering studies of neutron production from beryllium bombarded by alpha particles. He received many honours for his scientific and administrative work, including the International Feltrinelli Prize of the Lincei Academy (Rome) in 1961 and the title of a Commander of the French *Légion d’Honneur*.

**(b) The Experimental Proof of Negative Dispersion (1926–1931)**

Rudolf Ladenburg of the *Kaiser Wilhelm Institut für Physikalische Chemie* in Berlin, a pioneer in the field of optical dispersion, published in the second half of the 1920s a two-part article on the quantum-theoretical dispersion formula and its experimental verification, the first part in December 1926 and the second part two and a half years later, in May 1929 (Ladenburg, 1926, 1929). The interaction of light and matter that leaves essentially no changes in the scattering matter has been called dispersion; it results primarily in a dependence of the propagation velocity of the radiation, or the refractive index *n* of the medium, on the wavelength or frequency *ν* of the incident radiation. Moreover, the dispersion phenomena have been extended beyond the ‘normal’ to the ‘anomalous’ ones—the latter occurring at frequencies close to the absorption or eigenfrequencies *ν*<sub>s</sub> of the material under consideration, leading even to refractive indices *n* < 1, in accordance with the classical formula

$$n^2 - 1 = \frac{e^2}{\pi m} \sum_{s} \frac{N \cdot f_s}{\nu_s^2 - \nu^2}, \tag{298}$$

where *e* and *m* denote the charge and mass of the oscillating electron, *N* denotes the number of atoms per unit volume of the medium, and *f*<sub>s</sub> denotes the number of ‘dispersion’ electrons per atom. In the quantum theory, Hendrik Kramers had replaced Eq. (298) by the corresponding, slightly more complicated formula

$$n^2 - 1 = \frac{e^2}{\pi m} \sum_{j} N_j \left[ \sum_{k} A_{kj} \frac{g_k}{g_j} \frac{\tau_{kj}}{3} \frac{1}{\nu_{kj}^2 - \nu^2} - \sum_{i} A_{ji} \frac{\tau_{ji}}{3} \frac{1}{\nu_{ji}^2 - \nu^2} \right] \tag{299}$$

(Kramers, 1924a, b). In Eq. (299), the classical frequencies are replaced by the quantum-theoretical (discrete) transition frequencies (connected with the quantum jumps *j* → *k* and *j* → *i*). Further, the classical ‘oscillator strength’ *f*<sub>s</sub> obtains a quantum-theoretical reinterpretation involving the coefficients of the transition probability *A*<sub>kj</sub> and *A*<sub>ji</sub>, which Einstein had introduced in his fundamental paper of 1916 (Einstein, 1916d); the associated ‘damping times’ are *τ*<sub>kj</sub> and *τ*<sub>ji</sub>, and the statistical weights of the stationary states *k* and *j* are, respectively, *g*<sub>k</sub> and *g*<sub>j</sub>.<sup>407</sup>

<sup>407</sup> We have discussed Kramers’s dispersion formula (299) and its origin in detail in Volume 1, Part 2, Section VI.1. A very detailed historical account of Kramers’s theory and the parallel investigations of John H. Van Vleck (1924a, b), and the relation to Einstein’s old paper, has been given by Hiroyuki Konno (1993).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0381 -->

III.1 The Empirical Verification of Quantum Concepts 349

The conspicuous difference between Eq. (299), which remained valid in quantum and wave-mechanics of 1925 to 1926, and Eq. (298) must be seen in the existence of the second sum of ‘negative dispersion terms’ occurring in Kramers’s formula. Though negative terms do not occur in many actual situations—namely, for atoms in the ground state or in metastable states—they assume a crucial significance for the validity of the quantum-theoretical dispersion formula.$^{408}$ Still, as late as December 1926, Ladenburg—himself a pioneering expert in and contributor to the quantum-theoretical dispersion theory—had to take note of the lack of empirical evidence, when he wrote:

> Even for strong excitation, in general the number of atoms in higher quantum states ($j$ and $k$, respectively) is smaller by several orders of magnitude than that of the lower quantum states ($i$ and $j$, respectively). Hence an influence of the negative dispersion terms cannot be expected in general. Perhaps one can think of particular setups to prove this influence. (Ladenburg, 1926, p. 1210)

Actually, the proof of the quantum-theoretical dispersion formula consisted of two parts: first, the connection between dispersion and the transition probabilities had to be checked; second, the existence of the negative dispersion had to be established. Ladenburg, who had concerned himself with the dispersion problem since he came to the University of Breslau in 1907, and continued to do so after he went to Berlin in 1924, completed the first part of this programme essentially before the advent of the quantum-mechanical schemes, especially with the assistance of Rudolf Minkowski, who later continued to work on the problem in Göttingen and Hamburg.$^{409}$ Ladenburg also opened the era of dispersion theory after quantum mechanics with his review of 1926 (referred to already). A year later, he inaugurated new detailed experiments on anomalous dispersion, whose publication would extend over six years, by noting the ‘following investigations and tasks’ whose theoretical foundations had to be accomplished.$^{410}$

In order to estimate the influence of negative dispersion, Ladenburg (1928, pp. 17–18) rewrote Eq. (299) by explicitly collecting the terms with equal denominators $v_{kj}^2 - v^2$, i.e.,

$$(n^2 - 1) \frac{\pi m}{e^2} = \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \sum_{k=j+1}^{\infty} \frac{A_{kj}}{3} \frac{\tau_{kj}}{(v_{kj}^2 - v^2)} \left[ \frac{g_k}{g_j} N_j - N_k \right]. \qquad (300)$$

In the vicinity of an isolated spectral line of frequency $v_{kj} = \frac{c}{\lambda_s}$ (with $\lambda_s$ denoting

---

the corresponding wavelength) of a dilute gas of atoms, he then obtained the quasi-classical expression

$$n - 1 = \frac{e^2}{4 \pi c^2 m} \frac{\lambda_s}{\lambda - \lambda_s} N_s, \qquad (301)$$

where $N_s$ is the number of dispersion electrons (in the classical theory), i.e.,

$$N_s = N_j f_{kj} \left( 1 - \frac{N_k}{N_j} \frac{g_j}{g_k} \right), \qquad (301a)$$

with $f_{kj} (= f_s)$—called the ‘oscillator strength’ in classical theory—$^{411}$

$$f_s = f_{kj} = A_{kj} \frac{g_k}{g_j} \frac{m c^3}{8 \pi^2 e^2 \nu_{kj}^2} = A_{kj} \frac{g_k}{g_j} \frac{\tau_{kj}}{3}. \qquad (301b)$$

Kramers’s terms for negative dispersion are then contained in the factor $1 - \frac{N_k}{N_j} \frac{g_j}{g_k}$. As has been mentioned earlier, in the case of gases in the ground state or just moderately excited to a higher state, $\frac{N_k}{N_j}$ can be regarded as a small correction.

The experimental programme of Ladenburg and his associates consisted of detailed tests of Eq. (301) taken for excited states (even the lower state $j$ had to be an excited one); hence, ‘exact measurements of [anomalous] dispersion for electrically excited gases in the vicinity of their spectral lines under strictly controlled conditions’ had to be made (Ladenburg, *loc. cit.*, p. 28). The Berlin group first checked, in particular, whether the applied excitation current and the density of the gas under investigation exerted an influence on the transition probabilities and arrived at the answer ‘no.’$^{412}$ In the first investigation of the new programme, Ladenburg was assisted by Hans Kopfermann (Kopfermann and Ladenburg, 1928a, b).

Shortly after Ladenburg joined Fritz Haber’s Institute in Berlin, Kopfermann (who had just graduated from the University of Göttingen) arrived and became his

They found, in particular, that ‘with rising excitation current the anomalous dispersion increases rapidly—i.e., the number of $N_{s_i}$-atoms in the states $s_5$, $s_4$, and $s_3$ grow more or less—but soon approaches a saturation value, which is reached approximately for 50 mA’ (Kopfermann and Ladenburg, 1928a, p. 26). They were able to explain theoretically the increase of the number of $s_5$, $s_4$, and $s_3$ atoms, as well as the dependence on the pressure of the neon gas in the discharge tube.$^{414}$ In their second paper—actually, the third paper of the series—subtitled *‘Übergangswahrscheinlichkeit und Dichte angeregter Atome im Neon; statistisches Gleichgewicht in der positiven Säule’* (‘Transition Probability and Density of Excited Atoms in Neon; Statistical Equilibrium in the Positive Column’), Kopfermann and Ladenburg determined in particular the relative oscillator strengths $f_{kj}$ and the transition probabilities $A_{kj}$ of the spectral lines (Kopfermann and Ladenburg, 1928b).$^{415}$

A couple of weeks later, a female student of Ladenburg’s, Agathe Carst, entered the scene by submitting, together with the professor, the fourth paper in the series,

$^{413}$ Hans Kopfermann was born on 26 April 1895, in Breckenheim near Wiesbaden. He began his studies of mathematics and physics in Erlangen and Berlin. After his service in World War I, he continued his studies in Göttingen and obtained his doctorate in 1924 under James Franck. In 1932, Kopfermann became a *Privatdozent* at the University of Berlin, and then spent a year in Copenhagen at Bohr’s Institute. From 1933 to 1937, he served as a *Dozent* at the *Technische Hochschule* in Berlin and worked as a senior assistant to Gustav Hertz; in 1937, he was invited to a full professorship at the University of Kiel, but in 1942 he moved to the University of Göttingen and in 1953 finally to Heidelberg as head of the First Physical Institute there (succeeding Walther Bothe). He died on 28 January 1963.

Kopfermann devoted his scientific career entirely to spectroscopic investigations: following the fundamental work with Ladenburg on dispersion, he began in 1931 studies of the hyperfine structure of spectral lines, thus becoming one of the pioneers in measuring nuclear spins (see his book *Kernmomente*, 1940); later, he moved on to investigate quadrupole moments of nuclei. In Göttingen, he built a 6-MeV betatron; he studied the biological effects of radiation, atomic beams, and resonance; he developed methods of optical interferometry and supervised the education of many talented students. During the Heidelberg period, Kopfermann also served on many national and international commissions, e.g., in the council of CERN. The academies of Göttingen, Heidelberg, and Copenhagen elected him to memberships.

dealing with ‘Anomalous Dispersion of Hydrogen; The True Intensity Ratio of the Hydrogen $H_\alpha$ and $H_\beta$ Lines’ (‘*Anomale Dispersion des Wasserstoffs; wahres Intensitätsverhältnis der Wasserstofflinien $H_\alpha$ und $H_\beta$*,’ Carst and Ladenburg, 1928). Again, the authors applied the dc-current method, which had already been used before by the American spectroscopist Robert W. Wood in 1921 and 1922, and more recently by their Berlin colleague Karl Friedrich Bonhoeffer in 1924 and 1925 for observing hydrogen lines. With a setup that they had described earlier,$^{416}$ Carst and Ladenburg now measured the anomalous dispersion curve in the region of $H_\alpha$ and $H_\beta$ lines observing stable conditions. Thus, they derived the number of dispersion electrons $N_s$ per unit volume and, upon inserting this in Eq. (301a), they obtained the oscillator strength $f_{kj}$. Evidently, the ratio $f_{H\alpha}/f_{H\beta}$ satisfies the equation

$$\frac{f_{H\alpha}}{f_{H\beta}} = \frac{N_\alpha}{N_\beta} \frac{1 - \frac{N_4 g_2}{N_2 g_4}}{1 - \frac{N_3 g_2}{N_2 g_3}}, \qquad (302)$$

with $N_1, \dots, N_4$ giving the occupation numbers of the hydrogen levels having the main quantum numbers $1, \dots, 4$, respectively (which can be estimated for small negative dispersion). By substituting the results of their observations into Eqs. (301) and (302), Carst and Ladenburg concluded that ‘taking into account the negative dispersion has in any case the effect that the value for $f_\alpha/f_\beta$ calculated from the observed ratio $N_\alpha/N_\beta$ is increased and approaches the theoretical one’ (Carst and Ladenburg, 1928, p. 203).

In 1928, Ladenburg reported at the 6th Congress of the Russian Physicists in Moscow about the ‘experimental proof of “negative” dispersion’ (Kopfermann and Ladenburg, 1928c). He and Kopfermann had studied again the neon gas, their favourite substance, observing the anomalous dispersion in the region of yellow–red lines. The crucial points of the proof could be summarized as follows:

> For increasing current density in the positive column of a neon discharge up to 0.1 ampere per cm$^2$, one finds an increase of the anomalous dispersion of the yellow-red $s-p$ lines ($p$ is the higher, more energetic state, $s$ the lower, less energetic one). This means a similar increase of the number of excited atoms in the $s$-states. However, if one further enlarges the current density, a gradual decrease of the amount of the anomalous dispersion (i.e., the $N$-values) for the various $s_5 - p_k$ ($k = 10, 9, 8, 6, 4, 2$) with increasing current, is observed, exactly as can be expected from the quantum-theoretical dispersion formula on account of the influence of “negative” dispersion, namely because of the larger degree of excitation of the atoms in the $p_k$-states. Cross-check experiments exclude different interpretations of the result, especially because of the systematically different decrease of the $N$-values of the $s_5$-lines combining with

---

$^{416}$ See Ladenburg *et al.*, 1926. The interference patterns obtained from a Jamin refractometer was analyzed by two different gratings borrowed from Friedrich Paschen of the *Physikalisch-Technische Reichsanstalt* and James Franck of the University of Göttingen, respectively.

III.1 The Empirical Verification of Quantum Concepts 353

different $p_k$-levels: The lower is the corresponding $p$-level and the more strongly it is excited, the larger turns out to be the decrease of the corresponding anomalous dispersion. (Kopfermann and Ladenburg, *loc. cit.*, p. 375)

In spite of the fact that Kopfermann and Ladenburg were not able to find the change of sign in the anomalous dispersion, as predicted by the quantum-theoretical formula (301), they confidently stated: ‘The decrease of our curves [for $\mathcal{N}_s$] in the case of higher currents and the different amount of decrease in the energy of the upper state doubtlessly demonstrates the effect of “negative” dispersion’ (Kopfermann and Ladenburg, *loc. cit.*, p. 385). Two years later, Ladenburg and collaborators published two further papers on the anomalous dispersion in neon close to the absorption lines and confirmed the decisive results of 1928, thus establishing the existence of Kramers’s negative term (Kopfermann and Ladenburg, 1930; Ladenburg and Levy, 1930).$^{417}$ Finally, in December 1933, Ladenburg submitted the last results on his anomalous dispersion programme at the *Kaiser Wilhelm Institut* to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Ladenburg and Levy, 1934a, b). In the first paper, entitled ‘Anomale Dispersion an den Bandenlinien des $\text{Li}_2$-Moleküls’ (‘Anomalous Dispersion at the Band Lines of the $\text{Li}_2$ Molecule’), the authors discussed the rather complex (and at that time not entirely resolved) situation with lithium molecules.$^{418}$ The second publication, subtitled ‘Die Übergangswahrscheinlichkeit der rot-gelben Neonlinien ($s$-$p$) und die Lebensdauer der $p$-Zustände’ (‘The Transition Probabilities of the Red-Yellow Neon Lines (s-p) and the Lifetime of the p-States,’ Ladenburg and Levy, 1934b), formed the last publication, No. VIII, of the whole series. Though the actual experimental investigations had been carried out already two years earlier, owing to Ladenburg’s absence—who, in 1931, had been appointed successor to the professorship held by Karl T. Compton at Princeton University—the finished paper was received only on 23 December 1933. Also, the coauthor, S. Levy, had meanwhile left Berlin and gone to Moscow. Fritz Haber, the director of the institute where all of this fundamental work had been done over so many years, lived as a refugee away from Germany; by the time the paper appeared (in April 1934), he had died and could not personally appreciate the ‘sincere’ thanks of Ladenburg and Levy (Ladenburg and Levy, *loc. cit.*, p. 468).

**(c) The Discovery of the Raman Effect (February–March 1928)**

354 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

Adolf Smekal described ‘a new type of quantum transitions’ obtained when scattering monochromatic radiation from atoms, which he called ‘translational quantum transitions’ (‘Translationsquantenübergänge,’ Smekal, 1923c, especially, p. 874). To discuss the origin of these transitions, Smekal avoided all reference to the classical undulatory radiation theory and made use only of two assumptions: first, a certain probability, $C_{m,\nu}^{n,\nu'}$, per unit time existed that the atom struck by the radiation frequency $\nu$ passed over from the $m$-th to the $n$-th quantum state and changed its velocity of translation $v$ (against the incoming radiation) to $v'$, and simultaneously, the incident radiation altered its frequency $\nu$ into the scattered frequency $\nu'$; second, energy and momentum were conserved in the process. In the case of small relativistic corrections of the atomic motion, the energy relation

$$ \frac{M v^2}{2} + E_m + h \nu = \frac{M v'^2}{2} + E_n + h \nu' \quad (303) $$

was applicable, where $M$ denotes the mass of the atom or molecule. ‘Because of the *change in direction* of the radiation effected by them [i.e., by the translational quantum transitions], we shall speak in the case $m = n$ about *normal* dispersion, and in the case $m \neq n$ about *anomalous* dispersion,’ Smekal stated in his paper (Smekal, *loc. cit.*, p. 874).

Smekal’s treatment contradicted the opinion then held by most experts in the field of atomic structure, in particular by Niels Bohr, who insisted on the wave nature of radiation.$^{419}$ However, a good year later, Hendrik Kramers and Werner Heisenberg succeeded with their new dispersion approach—which, from the Copenhagen point of view, seemed to allow a compromise with the undulatory radiation theory—to obtain Smekal’s ‘anomalous dispersion’ or what they called ‘non-coherent scattering of radiation’ (Kramers and Heisenberg, 1925, especially, §4).$^{420}$ The later dispersion theory—developed on quantum-mechanical (Heisenberg, 1925c), wave-mechanical (Schrödinger, 1926h), or quantum field-theoretical considerations (Dirac, 1927c)—also allowed one to derive Smekal’s formula; it even took the ‘anomalous dispersion’ as a granted fact, though at least Schrödinger admitted that:

> The existence of this remarkable kind of secondary radiation … has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The *present* theory also shows distinctly that the occurrence of this scattered radiation is dependent on special conditions, which demand researches expressly arranged for that purpose. Firstly, two eigenvibrations $u_k$ and $u_l$ must be strongly excited, so that all experiments made on atoms in their normal state … are to be rejected. Secondly, at least *one* third state of equilibrium must exist (i.e., be possible—it need to be *excited*), which leads to powerful spontaneous emission, when combined with $u_k$ as well as with $u_l$. For the extraordinary scattered ra-

$^{419}$ For details of the situation in radiation theory around 1923 in the context of the old quantum theory, see our discussion in Volume 1, Part 2, Sections V.1 and V.2.
$^{420}$ For details, see Volume 2, Section III.5.
