III.1 The Empirical Verification of Quantum Concepts 355

diation, which is to be discussed, is proportional to the product of the spontaneous emission coefficients in question ($a_{kn}b_{ln}$ and $a_{ln}b_{kn}$). (Schrödinger, 1926h, pp. 121–122; English translation, p. 111)

Five years after Schrödinger had emphasized these problems concerning the observation of Smekal’s predicted effect, the first non-Western (or non-Russian) scientist, the Indian physicist Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman from Calcutta, was awarded ‘the Nobel Prize in Physics of 1930 for his work on the scattering of light and for the discovery of the effect named after him.’ Professor H. Pleijel, Chairman of the Nobel Committee for the Prize, traced in his presentation speech the origin of the ‘Raman effect’ back to a suggestion of Lord Rayleigh on a detailed feature of the well-known Tyndall effect—that is, the observation that blue light is scattered in a medium more appreciably than that of longer wavelengths—especially:

> The divergence from what was to be expected [on the classical theory] was made the starting point of a searching study of the nature of scattered light, in which Raman thought to find an explanation of the anomalies in asymmetry observed in the molecules. During these studies of his in the phenomena of scattering, Raman made, in 1928, the unexpected and highly surprising discovery that the scattered light showed not only the radiation that derived from the primary light but also a radiation that contained wavelengths, which were foreign to the primary light. (Pleijel, in Nobel Foundation, 1965, p. 264)

Indeed, the path to detect the ‘extraordinary scattered radiation’ of Smekal, or Kramers and Heisenberg, turned out to be quite tricky; it started even before Adolf Smekal predicted the ‘new type of quantum transitions’ and led away from the European centres of atomic physics.

The biographical sketch appended to the (later) publication of Raman’s Nobel lecture noted:

> Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman was born in Trichnopoly in Southern India on November 7th, 1888. His father was a lecturer in mathematics and physics so that from the first he was immersed in an academic atmosphere. He entered Presidency College, Madras, in 1902 and in 1904 passed his B.A. examination winning the first place and the gold medal in physics; in 1907 he gained his M.A. degree, obtaining the highest distinctions. (Pleijel, in Nobel Foundation, *loc. cit.*, p. 276)$^{421}$

One may perhaps add that from his father Raman gained, besides an early interest in science, a lifelong love for music and musical instruments, while his mother, Parvati Amal (who belonged to a family known for Sanskrit scholarship), endowed him with a sense of self-reliance and a strong personality. When after graduation with his M.A. degree ill health prevented Raman to pursue higher studies at one

$^{421}$ For details on the life and work of C. V. Raman, see Bhagwantam, 1971, Mehra, 1975b, and Keswani, 1980.

356 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

of the great British universities, and India offered him no possibility of a further career in science, he entered the Indian Audit and Accounts Service in Calcutta and worked for ten years in the finance department, simultaneously performing research, particularly on vibrations, sound, and the theory of musical instruments, such as violin and Indian drums, mostly in the laboratory of the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science in Calcutta.$^{422}$ In 1917, Raman’s research and scientific publications won him the newly established Palit Professorship of Physics at the University of Calcutta. There, Satyendra Nath Bose and Megh Nad Saha became for a while his junior colleagues, and Calcutta was on the way to becoming a centre of scientific research in India.$^{423}$

The path to the great discovery began for Raman with a visit to the British Empire Universities Congress, held at Oxford in summer 1921, where he represented the University of Calcutta. On the return voyage, he was struck by the deep opalescent blue of the sea, which had been explained before by Lord Rayleigh as a reflection of the blue sky. By applying the Einstein–Smoluchowski theory of fluctuations, Raman found that the scattering of light by the molecules of water created the ocean’s colour. It was, however, his work on acoustics (he had lectured on stringed instruments in London in 1921), which won him election to the Fellowship of the Royal Society (1924) and got him invited to write the article on musical instruments for the prestigious German *Handbuch der Physik* (Raman, 1927). Travels to Toronto (to attend the meeting of the *British Association for the Advancement of Science* in 1924), Philadelphia (Franklin Institute celebrations in 1924) and Pasadena (five months at Caltech in 1924/25 at the invitation of Robert A. Millikan) in the U.S.A., to the Soviet Union, Germany, and Switzerland promoted Raman’s scientific reputation further.

His biographical sketch in *Nobel Lectures* noted: ‘In 1922 he published his work on the “Molecular Diffraction of Light” (Raman, 1922), the first of a series of investigations with his collaborators which ultimately led to his discovery, on the 28th February, 1928, of the radiation effect which bears his name’ (Nobel Foundation, 1965, pp. 276–277). With his associates, Raman studied in particular the scattering of light with the available frequencies by a number of substances, notably, fluids.$^{424}$ In his Nobel lecture of December 1930, the new laureate spoke about the first results of this research programme as follows:

$^{422}$ Raman’s wife, Loka Sundari Ammal, a highly talented woman whom he married before entering public service, shared his interest in musical instruments. They had two sons, born in 1921 and 1929, respectively.
$^{423}$ Unfortunately, both Bose (in 1921) and Saha (in 1923) soon left Calcutta, but Raman began to assemble a growing number of excellent students, including K. R. Ramanathan, K. Seshagiri, V. Venkateswaran, and, especially, K. S. Krishnan.
$^{424}$ While K. R. Ramanathan, Kameswara Rao, and L. A. Ramdas investigated various scattering phenomena in fluids, K. S. Krishnan, Ramakrishna Rao, and Ramachandra Rao concerned themselves with the phenomena caused by optical anisotropy of molecules in liquids and gases. Finally, Raman himself derived, together with Ramanathan and Krishnan, ‘a revised opalescence formula which differed from that of Einstein and yielded results in better agreement with observation’ (Raman, 1965, p. 269).

III.1 The Empirical Verification of Quantum Concepts 357

While our experiments in the main appeared to support the electromagnetic theory of light, evidence came to hand at a very early stage of the investigations of the existence of a phenomenon which seemed to stand outside the classical scheme of thought. The scattering of light in transparent fluids is extremely feeble, much weaker in fact than the Tyndall effect usually observed in turbid media. It was experimentally discovered that associated with the Rayleigh-Einstein type of molecular scattering, was another and still feebler type of secondary radiation, the intensity of which was the order of magnitude of a few hundredth of the classical scattering, and differed from it in not having the same wavelength as the primary or incident radiation. The first observation of this phenomenon was made in Calcutta in April 1923 by Ramanathan who ... found that after exhaustive chemical purification and repeated distillation of the liquid in vacuum, the new radiation persisted undiminished in intensity, showing that it was a characteristic property of the substance studied and not due to any fluorescent impurity. Krishnan observed a similar effect in many other liquids in 1924, and a somewhat more conspicuous phenomenon was observed by me in ice and in optical glasses. (Raman, 1965, pp. 269–270)

Then came a series of cumbersome studies of 'this puzzling phenomenon' until, later in 1927, Venkateswaran found 'the highly interesting result that the colour of sunlight scattered in a highly purified sample of glycerine was brilliant green instead of the usual blue' (Raman, *loc. cit.*, p. 270): that is, the new type of scattered light, which was registered also with different substances, was clearly displaced toward the red and appeared to be strongly polarized. By improving the observational techniques—in particular, by applying suitable filters to the sunlight used, and ultimately replacing it by a mercury arc (for providing highly monochromatic primary radiation) in combination with a condenser of large aperture and a cobalt-glass filter, finally came the actual breakthrough that revealed the discovery:

> With these arrangements the spectrum of the scattered light from a variety of liquids and solids was visually examined, and the startling observation was made that the spectrum generally included a number of sharp lines or bands on a diffuse background which were not present in the light of the mercury arc. (Raman, *loc. cit.*, p. 272)

Raman and Krishnan announced the discovery in three letters, sent to the British journal *Nature* on 16 February, 8 March, and 22 March 1928, respectively. The first note, properly entitled ‘A New Type of Secondary Radiation’ and published in the issue of 31 March, described the ‘modified scattered radiation’ obtained from substances (still) illuminated by powerful filtered sunlight radiation. It stated in particular: ‘That the effect is a true scattering and not a fluorescence is indicated firstly by its feebleness in comparison with ordinary scattering and secondly by its polarization, which is in many cases quite strong and comparable to the polarization of ordinary scatter’ (Raman and Krishnan, 1928a, p. 501). In the second note, signed by Raman alone and entitled ‘A Change of Wavelength in Light Scattering,’ he spoke first about the use of the mercury arc as a source of incident radiation; on cutting out all radiation of wavelength larger than 4358 Å

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0390 -->

by a filter and examining the scattered radiation by a spectroscope, the author noticed ‘some bright lines additional to those present in the incident light, the wavelength being larger than 4358 Å,’ and concluded: ‘The preliminary visual observations appear to indicate that the position of the principal modified lines is the same for all substances, though their intensity and that of the continuous spectrum do vary with their chemical nature’ (Raman, 1928a, p. 619).
The last note of this set, again jointly authored by Raman and Krishnan, bore the title ‘The Optical Analogue of the Compton Effect’ and presented a series of secondary spectra, together with a ‘tentative explanation of the new spectral lines,’ namely:

> It may be assumed that an incident quantum of radiation may be scattered by the molecules of a fluid either as a whole or in part, in the former case giving the original wavelength, and in the latter case an increased wavelength. This explanation is supported by the fact that the diminution in the frequency is of the same order of magnitude as the frequency of the molecular infrared absorption line. Further, it is found that the shift of wavelength is not quite the same for different molecules, and thus supporting the explanation suggested. (Raman and Krishnan, 1928b, p. 711)

From this cautious description, one should not conclude that the authors had only vague ideas about what they were observing. Indeed, Krishnan wrote in his diary already on 5 February 1928, quite clearly:

> After the meals at night, Venkateswaran and myself were chatting together in our room when Professor [Raman] came to the house (at about 9 p.m.) and called for me. When we went down he was very much excited and came to tell me that what we had observed this morning must be the Kramers-Heisenberg effect, we had been looking for all these days. We therefore agreed to call the effect "modified scattering."425

Evidently, it was Krishnan who served as Raman's most important collaborator.426 He coauthored most of the notes and papers published on the new effect,

including the first detailed account dealing with it in the *Indian Journal of Physics* (Raman and Krishnan, 1928c).427 Krishnan's diary also reveals clearly the last decisive steps taken by Raman and himself in the discovery:

*7th February (1928) Tuesday*
Tried to verify the polarization of fluorescence exhibited by some of the aromatic liquids in the near ultraviolet region. Incidentally discovered that all pure liquids show a fairly intense fluorescence also in the visible region, and what is much more interesting all of them strongly polarized. . . .
When I told Raman about the results, he would not believe that all liquids can show polarized fluorescence and that in the visible region. When he came in up to the room, I had a bulb of pentene in the tank, and a blue-violet filter in the path of the incident light, and when he observed the track with a combination of green and yellow filters, he remarked: “You do not want to suggest, Krishnan, that all of this is fluorescence.” However, when he transferred the green-yellow combination also in the path of the incident light, he could not detect a trace of the track. He was very much excited and repeated several times that it was an amazing result. One after another, the whole series of liquids were examined and each one of them showed the phenomenon without exception. He wondered that we missed discovering all that five years ago. (Diary quoted in Ref. 425, p. 170)

In the evening of that day, then, Raman associated the finding with the ‘Kramers–Heisenberg effect.’
The systematic study of the effect began, when three weeks later, Krishnan's diary again carried an important message: he, Krishnan, came to the laboratory ‘only in the afternoon,’ proceeding there with Raman ‘to examine the influence of the wavelength of the incident light on the phenomenon’; they ‘used the usual blue–violet filter coupled with a uranium glass, the range of wavelengths transmitted by the combination being much narrower than that transmitted by the blue–violet filter alone’ finally: ‘On examining the track with a direct vision spectroscope we found to our great surprise the modified scattering was separated

on the magnetic properties of crystals; in 1933, he returned to the Indian Association in Calcutta as Mahendra Lal Sircar Professor of Physics, investigating further the magnetic and electric properties of complex crystalline structures and explaining the diamagnetism of graphite (paper with Ganguli in 1941). Invitations to Cambridge (by Ernest Rutherford) and to the Royal Institution of London by (William Henry Bragg) in 1937, as well as the award of the University of Liège medal, honoured his scientific accomplishments. In 1942, he became Professor of Physics at the University of Allahabad. When, after India gained independence in 1947, the National Physical Laboratory was established in New Delhi, Krishnan was chosen as its first director. His later work included theoretical investigations of the conductivity of metals and alloys, the analysis of the dispersion formulae of Drude and Lorentz, and the development of a new method to determine the saturation pressure of electrons in metals. Krishnan received many honours (e.g., in 1940, the Fellowship of the Royal Society of London; in 1946, the knighthood), and he served as chairman or president of many national and international scientific bodies. He died on 13 June 1961, of a heart attack in New Delhi.

‘This encouraged us to see [the] monochromatic incident light.’428 On the same day, Raman went public and announced the results of the discovery to the press; the news, distributed by the Associated Press of India under the title ‘Professor Raman's Discovery,’ appeared on 29 February 1928, and read:

> Professor Raman, F.R.S., of the Calcutta University, has made a discovery which promises to be of fundamental significance in physics. It will be remembered that Prof. A. H. Compton of the Chicago University was recently awarded the Nobel Prize for his discovery of the remarkable transformation which X-rays undergo when they are scattered by atoms. Shortly after Prof. Compton's discovery, the other experimenters sought to find out whether a similar transformation occurs also when ordinary light is scattered by matter and reported definitely negative results. Professor Raman with his research associates took up this question afresh, and his experiments have disclosed a new kind of radiation from atoms excited by light.
> The new radiation exhibits features even more startling than those discovered by Professor Compton with X-rays. The principal feature observed is that when matter is excited by light of one colour, the atoms contained in it emit light of two colours, one of which is different from the exciting colour and is lower down the spectrum. The astonishing thing is that the altered colour is quite [this “quite” was later crossed out and replaced in the margin by “approximately”] independent of the nature of the substance used. It changes, however, with the colour of the exciting radiation, and if the latter gives a sharp line in the spectrum, the second colour also appears as a second sharp line. There is in addition a diffuse radiation spread over a considerable range of the spectrum. (Keswani, 1988, p. 609)

The report closed by stating that “He [Raman] will deliver a lecture demonstrating these phenomena first at Bangalore on the 16th March.”

Raman went on to give the details of the effect in the second letter to *Nature*, which he signed alone on 8 March 1928, and which presented ‘further observations by Mr. Krishnan and myself,’ especially obtained with the help of the improved technique of observation, namely, ‘to use a mercury arc as a source of light, [with] all radiations of longer wavelength than 4358 Å being cut out by a filter,’ then:

> The scattered radiation when examined with a spectroscope showed some sharp bright lines additional to those present in the incident light, their wavelength being longer than 4358 Å; at least two such lines were prominent and appeared to be accompanied by some fainter lines, and in addition a continuous spectrum. (Raman, 1928a, p. 619)

> It may be assumed that an incident quantum of radiation may be scattered by the molecules of a fluid either as a whole or in part, in the former case giving the original wavelength, and in the latter case an increased wavelength. This explanation is supported by the fact that the diminution in frequency is of the same order of magnitude as the frequency of the molecular infrared absorption line. Further, it is found that the shift of wavelength is not quite the same for different molecules, and this supports the explanation suggested. (Raman and Krishnan, 1928b, p. 711)

More than the Indian press report of 29 February 1929, referred to above, the three notes in *Nature* published between 31 March and 5 May, and the reprint of the Bangalore lecture—which Raman worked out immediately upon his return to Calcutta as an article for the *Indian Journal of Physics*, entitled ‘The New Radiation’—propagated the fame of the discovery to the scientific world.⁴³⁰ The aged Robert Williams Wood (1868–1955) of Johns Hopkins University, for decades a world expert in the study of resonance radiation, cabled to *Nature* from Loomis Laboratory, New York:

> Professor Raman’s brilliant and surprising discovery that transparent substances illuminated by very intense monochromatic light scatter radiation of modified wavelength, and that frequency difference between emitted radiation and an exciting medium is identical with frequency of infrared absorption bands, opens up wholly new field in study of molecular structure. I have verified this discovery . . . It appears to me that this very beautiful discovery, which resulted from Raman’s long and patient study of phenomena of light scattering, is one of the most convincing proofs [of the] quantum theory of light which we have at present time. (Wood, 1928a, p. 349)

Wood included in his cable, printed in the issue of *Nature* dated 8 September 1928, several of his own results that he would soon publish in detail in several papers on what he (and others) immediately called the ‘Raman effect’ (Wood, 1928b, c; 1929). The international interest in the discovery of Raman and his associates resulted in a flood of articles and notes on the Raman effect, which became one of the most discussed issues of quantum theory in 1928.⁴³¹

**(d) The Exploration of the Raman Effect and the Independent Russian Discovery (1928–1930)**

Robert W. Wood’s cable of early September 1928 indicated that the American spectroscopist had already verified the discovery himself, ‘using improved apparatus which makes it possible to photograph [the] strongest lines in a few minutes.’ He especially announced the following results:

> Anti-Stokes’ terms of intensity nearly equal that of lines of wavelength greater than [the] exciting line obtained [in] chloroform, carbon tetrachloride, [the] latter giving [a] triplet [on] each side [of the] 4046, 4358, 5461 lines [of the] mercury arc. Raman reported no trace [of] modified lines excited [by the] latter line, but [the excitations] are strong with carbon tetrachloride. Triplet short wavelength sides exciting lines appear mirror images [of] those lone wavelength side, considering exciting line [as the] mirror. Crystalline quartz gives strong line identified as 20 µ absorption band, and fainter line very close [to the] exciting line corresponds infrared absorption [at] about 75 µ. (Wood, 1928a, p. 349)

‘Raman’s discovery thus makes possible investigation [in the] remote infrared regions [that are] hitherto little explored owing [to] experimental difficulties,’ Wood continued and announced his own ‘very efficient method of illumination employed’ allowed him to resolve the structure of Raman lines (Wood, *loc. cit.*). The details of Wood’s cable appeared in a paper signed by him on 8 September 1928, and submitted from Loomis Laboratory in Tuxedo, New York (Wood, 1928b).⁴³² The main experimental improvement introduced by Wood consisted

Then, he obtained a position at the University of Wisconsin (1897–1900) and eventually became a professor at Johns Hopkins University in 1900. After retiring in 1938, he stayed on as a research professor; he died on 11 August 1955, at Amityville on Long Island, New York.

in using an extended glass pipe, which contained the scattering substance and provided much more intense scattering radiation. Moreover, his spectrograph was specially mounted and had a higher resolution. In December 1928, Wood published—again in the British journal *Philosophical Magazine*—a short note, reporting on details of the Raman spectra of benzol and carbon tetrachloride ‘photographed with a 6-inch plane grating combined with a lens of 3-metre focus’ (Wood, 1928c, p. 1283). S. Bureau of Standards and the senior Canadian spectroscopist John Cunningham McLennan. Meanwhile, however, the European physicists also jumped on the bandwagon of Raman spectroscopy. In France, Jean Cabannes of Montpellier opened the field and reported observations made with his associate Pierre Daure on various organic fluids, which they submitted to the meeting of 4 June 1928, of the Paris Academy (Cabannes and Daure, 1928).⁴³⁴ Both Cabannes and Daure continued to contribute to the application and understanding of the Raman effect (Cabannes, 1928; Daure, 1928a, b). In Germany, Peter Pringsheim of Berlin, so far an expert on fluorescence, changed his research to Raman scattering, soon to be followed by other spectroscopists (e.g., Walther Gerlach in Tübingen and Clemens Schaefer in Breslau). Nissi in Tokyo), considerable interest arose. The number of papers on the subject increased steadily, and within a year, the Raman effect had made its way into the *Handbuch der Experimentalphysik* (Joos, 1929).

The early research on the new effect yielded important results, deepening the ones obtained by the discoverers. Thus, Pringsheim and his collaborator B. Rosen found that the additional detailed purification methods, which Raman and associates had applied in their pioneering investigations, were not actually necessary; the usual ‘purest substances’ (‘*reinste Substanzen*’) that could be purchased in chemical shops sufficed to obtain good secondary spectra (Pringsheim and Rosen,

### III.1 The Empirical Verification of Quantum Concepts 365

Raman has already shown that the same shifted lines or bands occur in water and crystalline ice. Hence it seemed evident to carry out analogous investigations with different crystals. When this problem was about to be studied [in Berlin], we got to know by correspondence that Landsberg and Mandelstam in Moscow have observed already, independently of Raman, shifted lines in the case of quartz and other crystals (Landsberg and Mandelstam, 1928a). (Pringsheim, 1928, p. 605)

In fact, in a letter to *Naturwissenschaften*, dated 6 May 1928, the Russian authors did announce ‘A New Phenomenon in the Dispersion of Light by Crystals’ (‘*Eine neue Erscheinung bei der Lichtzerstreuung in Kristallen*’), which they described as follows:

While studying molecular scattering in solids, with the goal of clarifying the question whether a change of wavelength is involved as suspected from Debye’s theory of specific heats, we have discovered a new phenomenon which—it appears to us—invites considerable (*bedeutendes*) interest.
  This phenomenon consists of a change in wavelength which, however, is of another order of magnitude than expected by us [on the basis of Debye’s theory] and which has quite a different origin. (Landsberg and Mandelstam, 1928a, p. 557)

The Moscow experiment, as described by Landsberg and Mandelstam in their letter, was the following: intense radiation from a mercury arc lamp was sent through a quartz crystal and the light scattered perpendicular to the primary beam was analyzed by a quartz spectrograph (and photographed with an exposure time of 2 to 14 hours). The authors then registered ‘one clearly defined satellite’ connected with each mercury line and, in addition, further weak satellite liens, all having a longer wavelength than the primary line. ‘We consider it to be premature to give already now a definite interpretation of the phenomenon described,’ Landsberg and Mandelstam noted, but they also dared to propose ‘a possible theoretical interpretation,’ namely:

In the scattering process of light certain frequencies of quartz may be excited at the expense of the dispersed light, and thus the energy of the scattered quanta, and consequently their frequency, would be diminished by the size of the corresponding infrared quanta. If one assumes the [quanta] frequency corresponding to the wavelength $\lambda = 20.7$ µ, then a good agreement is obtained between the calculated and observed values. (Landsberg and Mandelstam, *loc. cit.*, pp. 557–558)

They then concluded with the statement: ‘Whether and how much the phenomenon observed by us is connected with the one just recently described by Raman and Krishnan [they referred to Raman and Krishnan, 1928a, and Raman, 1928a], we cannot judge at the moment, as the description given [there] is too gross (*zu summarisch*)’ (Landsberg and Mandelstam, *loc. cit.*, p. 558).
  Grigory Landsberg and Leonid Mandelstam had collaborated since 1925 at the University of Moscow, and had at first worked on the Rayleigh scattering in

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0398 -->

366 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

crystals.<sup>437</sup> These investigations soon concentrated on the influence of internal defects in crystals, and Landsberg succeeded in separating molecular scattering from other effects by making use of the temperature dependence of the former (Landsberg, 1927a, b). Then, both Landsberg and Mandelstam turned to study the frequency composition of light scattered by a quartz crystal, obtaining in fall 1927 the first indications of changes in the wavelength of the incident radiation, as mentioned in their letter of 6 May to *Naturwissenschaften* (Landsberg and Mandelstam, 1928a). This letter also contained, as said above, the definite results of ‘the new phenomenon,’ observed when scattering mercury light from quartz. In a paper, dated 9 July 1928, and submitted to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, the authors then described details of their observations, in particular:

Each original line (*Grundlinie*) of the incident light (from a mercury lamp) is accompanied by several satellites. One finds both satellites shifted towards the red and those lying symmetrically to them shifted towards the *violet*. In each system the difference $\Delta \nu_i$ of the satellite frequencies and the corresponding original line is constant for all original lines. (Landsberg and Mandelstam, 1928b, p. 769)

Having presented the experimental setup and the results, Landsberg and Mandelstam discussed carefully the theoretical explanation on the basis of Adolf Smekal’s prediction of 1923 and Kramers and Heisenberg’s dispersion theory of 1925.

### III.1 The Empirical Verification of Quantum Concepts 367

Though they generally found agreement with respect to the predicted frequencies, they noted a difference in the intensity of the red and violet satellites; hence, they made further investigations of the problem.<sup>438</sup> Finally, they spoke about the relation of their work to the initial discovery:

We observed the occurrence of satellites in the dispersion of light through quartz already before the publications of Raman and Krishnan (Raman and Krishnan, 1928a; Raman, 1928b), which described a change in wavelength of the light scattered by some vapours and fluids, appeared. It is highly probable, especially according to the recently reported observations of Cabannes and Daure (1928), that in both cases one is dealing in principle with the same phenomenon. (Landsberg and Mandelstam, *loc. cit.*, p. 777)

In spite of the fact that the Russians had priority in uncovering the effect in crystals, especially quartz, as Pringsheim observed in his review paper (see above), further investigations would be carried out in Berlin. Thus, Pringsheim and Rosen reported in detail in their paper of July 1928 ‘the Raman spectrum of crystalline quartz in the region of longer wavelengths (between 3650 and 5461 [Å]), finding a much larger number of shifted lines’; notably, they detected, besides the Raman lines that could be associated with the known infrared absorption bands of the same substance, ‘two further values . . . at 38 µ and 80 µ . . . which fall into a special region of the infrared spectrum, where until now quartz was supposed to have no absorption bands’ (Pringsheim and Rosen, 1928, pp. 753–754). Finally, they tried to clarify a point, which Raman had suggested for the interpretation of his effect: he had argued especially ‘that the radiations of the altered wavelengths from neighbouring molecules are coherent with each other,’ because the heating of liquid carbon dioxide showed an increased intensity of the effect (Raman, 1928a, p. 619). Now, Pringsheim and Rosen found in molten quartz ‘not the faintest indication of somehow shifted lines’; hence, they concluded, contrary to Raman’s expectations, that amorphous quartz cannot transfer energy quanta to or from incident radiation (Pringsheim and Rosen *loc. cit.*, p. 755). Pringsheim, rather, suggested that the effect might be ‘connected with a phase shift of an undetermined size,’ similar to Compton effect, and argued:

If the same were valid for the Ramsauer effect, then its increase when the critical state [of the scattering substance] is approached would be due to an erroneous observation. Hence the Raman effect, in contrast to the Tyndall effect, cannot be identified with a fluctuation effect at all, and its intensity will be determined only by the number of molecules and the probability of the transitions that can be excited in the molecules. (Pringsheim, 1928, p. 605)

Later studies of the polarization of Raman lines in the case of benzene and toluene revealed a more complex situation: different Raman lines showed indeed a different polarization (Carelli, *et al.*, 1928; Raman and Krishnan, 1928e).

368 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

Besides Pringsheim, another German author took early notice of the Russian work: H. Kornfeld of Dortmund; in a letter to *Naturwissenschaften*, dated 27 July 1928, he discussed the preliminary results of Landsberg and Mandelstam (1928a) on quartz and calcium carbonate (Kornfeld, 1928). He also pointed out that the shifted wavelength in the latter example (which the Russian authors had presented in an addendum to their letter of 6 May) corresponded to an optical line, which had been derived earlier by Clemens Schaefer and collaborators from combination frequencies (Schaefer *et al.*, 1926). Pringsheim and associates confirmed this conclusion a little later (see Carelli *et al.*, 1928, pp. 515–516). Their investigation, dealing with the relation between Raman spectra of dissolved molecules and the same molecules bound in (ionic) crystals, went far beyond that result; the authors showed rather generally that it was certain molecular groups that gave rise to Raman spectra, like NO$_3$, NO$_2$, NH$_3$, etc., while nothing could be observed in aquatic solutions of rocksalt or hydrochloric acid, because there only single ions like Na$^+$, H$^+$, and Cl$^-$ occured:

Hence it seems to us very possible that the same applies to crystals, i.e., that one will recover there only those infrared frequencies in Raman spectra, which are derived from definite molecular groups, but not from those belonging to the whole ionic lattice. . . . Even if this question cannot be answered definitely at the moment, at least only until now only such Raman spectra have been exclusively observed whose $\Delta \nu$-values can be derived from frequencies of inner groups. (Carelli *et al.*, *loc. cit.*, pp. 516–517)

The immediate and great attention, which the new effects discovered by Raman and collaborators and Landsberg and Mandelstam received, had two reasons. First, a phenomenon had been revealed that, by applying simple (and, so to say, inexpensive) and well-known instrumentation allowed one to ‘open a great, totally new field of spectroscopy’ (Pringsheim, 1928, p. 605). Second, the crucial importance of the experimental discovery was instantly recognized for substantiating the underlying quantum-mechanical process. Two letters published in *Naturwissenschaften* addressed the second aspect: In a note, dated 26 June (and published in the issue of 3 August 1928), Adolf Smekal emphasized that the Raman effect confirmed his prediction of 1923 (Smekal, 1928). He also drew attention to an earlier interpretation of the Compton effect as a limiting special case of his theoretical effect (Smekal, 1926b, footnotes 495 and 575, p. 1080 and pp. 1107–1108, respectively). Indeed, the interpretation of the Raman effect on a quantum-theoretical basis would supply ‘a new confirmation for the far-reaching analogy between electron and light-quantum, which has assumed such a crucial importance in the latest development of the quantum doctrine,’ Smekal now concluded, and added:

Thus one would demonstrate *that the change of energy state of an atomic system may be obtained by collisions of first or second kind with light-quanta of arbitrary initial frequency as well as by electron collisions of first or second kind with the electrons having arbitrary initial velocities*. (Smekal, 1928, p. 613)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0401 -->

III.1 The Empirical Verification of Quantum Concepts 369

In the other letter, dated 2 August and published in the issue of 28 August 1928, Max Born commented on a statement of Pringsheim, namely: ‘The requirements of Kramers’ dispersion theory agree perfectly with ... statements on the relative intensities of the single [Raman] lines .... The new Schrödinger wave mechanics, however, seems to contradict them’ (Pringsheim, 1928, pp. 604–605). According to Schrödinger, a Raman line of frequency \( \nu_0 \pm \nu_k^l \) will arise only if both the upper and the lower energy levels (whose distance determines the atomic transition frequency \( \nu_k^l \)) are occupied, ‘hence the intensity of the single Raman line ... should quickly decrease ... with increasing distance from the primary line’; also, ‘for any given \( \nu_k^l \) the Stokes and anti-Stokes line should possess the same intensity.’ Because both consequences do not follow from observation, they ‘just present a particularly noticeable and clear example of the difficulty, which the wave-mechanical interpretation also exhibits in other fields of optics as well’ (Pringsheim, *loc. cit.*, p. 605). Born now considered this judgment to be completely justified, ‘provided one interprets with Pringsheim the equations of the quantum-mechanical dispersion theory, as Mr. Schrödinger has proposed’ (Born, 1928, p. 673). However, he added that Schrödinger’s conception had already been ruled out by ‘other difficulties and must be replaced by the statistical interpretation of quantum mechanics,’ hence:

Then the observations of Raman and Krishnan fit completely into theoretical considerations, as they have already been won before from the matrix formulation of quantum mechanics. ... Raman’s discovery had been fully predicted by quantum mechanics and can be claimed to be a justification of the latter. (Born, *loc. cit.*)

The complete importance of the Indian discovery having thus been revealed, we may finally turn to a concluding point, namely, why the effect quickly became known as the ‘Raman effect.’ As we have noticed already, Pringsheim and Wood immediately gave the phenomenon this name.439 Only a few people, such as Fritz K. W. Kohlrausch, who spoke about the ‘Smekal-Raman effect,’ recalled the man who had first thought of the phenomenon (Kohlrausch, 1931).440 As regards the experimental contribution of Landsberg and Mandelstam, on the other hand, the priority is quite clear: Raman and Krishnan submitted their first note in February, while the Russian scientists followed only in May 1928. A still different question has been debated concerning the importance of the role of Raman’s collaborators, especially K. S. Krishnan, in the discovery. Most of the early publications were signed by Raman and Krishnan together; also, in the first sole contribution, Raman spoke about ‘further observations by Mr. Krishnan and myself on the new kind of light-scattering discovered by us’ (Raman, 1928a, p. 619). In his presi-

dential address at the 16th Indian Science Congress, held in Madras on 2 January 1929, Raman again praised the ‘conspicuous originality’ and ‘personal contribution’ of his associates K. R. Ramanathan and K. S. Krishnan, but one may detect here already some reservation of Raman toward the latter, whose ‘seeing eye made the discovery in Raman’s laboratory’ (Keswani, 1988, p. 611).441 Several reasons may be given to explain why the physicists eventually associated the discovery with Raman’s name alone: first, ‘it was Raman’s experience, imagination, inspiration and status which made it possible for the discovery to be known and immediately acknowledged’ (Keswani, *loc. cit.*); even more, Raman alone had been known for years in the scientific world, mainly through his researches on the physics of musical instruments and the scattering of light (which won him already in 1924 the Fellowship of the Royal Society of London) and his travels abroad (to Europe and to the U.S.A.). Second, Wood, Pringsheim, and many British colleagues acknowledged him as an important, independent personality, who had developed a school at his institute in Calcutta. Thus, Raman was not only knighted by the British government in 1929, but also received the prestigious Hughes Medal of the Royal Society later on; on the latter occasion, Ernest Rutherford, then President of the Society, remarked (in *Nature* **126**, 898, 1930):

Sir Venkata Raman is one of the leading authorities in optics, in particular on the phenomenology of scattering of light. In this connection about three years ago he discovered that the light’s colour could be changed by scattering.... The “Raman effect” must rank among the best three or four discoveries in experimental physics of the last decade.

Evidently, the Nobel Committee for Physics in 1930 could do no less than follow the British example and honour Raman by the award of the Nobel Prize ‘for the discovery of the effect named after him.’442 Independently of the arguments for or against including Krishnan officially in the discovery, one should note that the Nobel Prize to Raman constituted the first such award given to a scientist not from Europe or the United States. Hence, his prize was greatly celebrated in India, and Raman became one of the best known physicists of his time all over the world.443

III.1 The Empirical Verification of Quantum Concepts 371

**(e) The Discovery of Matter Waves (1927–1931)**

In his detailed report on the Raman effect, Pringsheim gave the reasons why this phenomenon—though predicted already in 1923—had not been detected earlier. He wrote:

That one did not succeed until Raman’s discovery is certainly connected with the fact that, in order to have as simple conditions as possible, the observations could have been made preferably with monatomic gases or vapours, hence \( \nu_a \) [i.e., the shift of the incident frequency \( \nu_0 \)] would coincide with an absorption line (lying in the visible or ultraviolet region), most probably a resonance line. If this absorption line possessed a wavelength of 5000 Å (the shorter the wavelength, the less acceptable were the conditions), one would have to select—as a primary [incident] line—one lying in the ultraviolet region, say at 2500 Å, in order to find the [Raman] line \( \nu_0 - \nu_a \) in the part of the spectrum which can be photographed comfortably. However, if one wanted to obtain an observable intensity of the Raman effect, a considerably still greater Tyndall effect must be produced (since only some percentage of the total scattering energy goes into the altered wavelength); that is, one has to work with vapour pressures of at least one atmosphere or higher. It is well known that all metallic vapours (other gases with resonance lines in the visible or near ultraviolet regions do not exist) exhibit for such pressure so intense absorption spectra in the entire short-wavelength region that a primary line from this region would not at all be scattered but rather be quantitatively absorbed. (Pringsheim, 1928, p. 604)

Now, Raman had rather accidentally used infrared lines of polyatomic molecules; hence, the primary incident lines (of sunlight or the mercury arc) were only shifted a little and remained in the region of small absorption of the substances investigated. Only then could Smekal’s prediction be actually verified, though, in general, quantum physicists firmly believed in its reality before. The situation was quite different in the case of another predicted effect of the year 1923: Louis de Broglie’s matter waves. They might have been confirmed already immediately, had the experts been able to analyze and understand properly two anomalies firmly established at that time.

The first phenomenon was detected by Carl Ramsauer of Heidelberg as early as 1920.444 Ramsauer first reported on his findings at the Bad Nauheim *Naturforscherversammlung* of September 1920 (Ramsauer, 1920, 1921a) and again, having studied the effect in more detail with noble gases, at the *Deutsche Physikertag* in Jena in September 1921 (Ramsauer, 1921b). In Jena, the results aroused great interest, and Max Born soon wrote to Albert Einstein about ‘Ramsauer’s nearly crazy assertion that the mean free path of electrons in argon becomes infinite as their velocity vanishes (slow electrons freely penetrate through atoms),’ and added: ‘We would be happy to [be able] to refute it.’ In order to explain the anomalous

Åkeson: in his 1916 dissertation at Lund, Åkeson referred to strange maxima and minima in the absorbing power of gases, such as methane, propylene, and nitrogen, for slow electrons (Åkeson, 1916).

372 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

behaviour, Born thought, one had to change the usual description of the collision of electrons and atoms, that is, to consider the collision effects (contrary to previous ideas) as small against the effects caused by the ‘distribution of the space charge’ (‘*Raumladungsverteilung*’). Because that idea seemed to work very well for Ramsauer’s anomaly, he concluded: ‘Minkowski will start experiments, together with Miss Sponer; these will certainly be very tricky.’ (Born to Einstein, 29 November 1921, in Einstein *et al.*, 1969, pp. 93–94)

About a year later, Rudolph Minkowski and Hertha Sponer published results confirming the ‘crazy’ Ramsauer effect (Minkowski and Sponer, 1923). Independently of their work, others concluded the same. Thus, James Franck wrote to Niels Bohr on 21 February 1922, that his friend Gustav Hertz had apparently made the same ‘inexplicable observations on the mean free path in argon’ as Ramsauer. Consequently, Franck proposed some ideas of his own to account for the phenomena, as Friedrich Hund recalled later.445 Namely, ‘that an electron would [suddenly in its path] turn around an angle of 2π and then proceed in the old direction, perhaps due to a special field of force.’ This idea then provided in summer 1922 the starting point for Hund’s Göttingen doctoral dissertation.446 Several experimentalists continued to study the problem, and Ramsauer (who had meanwhile moved to Danzig, having accepted a professorship at the *Technische Hochschule* there), concluded in 1923: ‘Unlike gases in general, *all* noble gases exhibit the common feature that the effective cross section reaches a maximum and then falls off as the velocity of the electron decreases.’ (Ramsauer, 1923, p. 351) In their review article, ‘Über den Durchgang von Elektronen durch Atome’ (‘On the Passage of Electrons Through Atoms’) published in 1924 in *Ergebnisse der exakten Naturwissenschaften*, Minkowski (Hamburg) and Sponer (Göttingen) connected the Ramsauer effect with another peculiar observation, presented sometime earlier by the Americans Clinton Joseph Davisson and Henry Kunsman of Western Electric Company in New York City.447 However, it seemed to the reviewers that in the latter case an explanation of the maxima and minima could be given on the basis of the standard Bohr–Sommerfeld atomic model involving several electron shells. That model would break down definitely for the Ramsauer effect, i.e., the passage of extremely slow electrons through atoms of noble gases (Minkowski and Sponer, 1924, especially, p. 84). Still, it would be the Davisson–Kunsman effect rather than Ramsauer’s, which eventually led to demonstrate the breakdown of the classical concepts in atomic theory.

In a series of investigations, about which Davisson and Kunsman reported first in fall 1921 (both in the journal *Science*: Davisson and Kunsman, 1921, and at an APS Meeting in Chicago, 25–26 October 1921: Davisson and Kunsman, 1922a), the Western Electric physicists observed the scattering of electrons by nickel. They contained the following result:

III.1  The Empirical Verification of Quantum Concepts 373

A study of the number of these high speed electrons emitted [from the nickel target when bombarded by electrons] per unit solid angle in various directions in a plane through the incident beam shows that the distribution for bombarding potentials at least to 500 volts is characterized by two maxima. One of these lies in a direction opposite to that of the motion of the incident electrons, and the other in a direction making an angle with this that depends for its value on the bombarding potential. The maximum in the direction of the beam is not directly observed but is inferred from the form of the distribution curves in the angular range from the lateral maximum to a direction 25 degrees from the incident beam. The angle between the principal and the lateral maxima is about 70 degrees for a bombarding potential of 200 volts and is greater for both higher and lower potentials. (Davisson and Kunsman, 1929a, p. 254)

The authors tried to explain their observation on the basis of the existing atomic model. On first inspection, it seemed that the standard assumptions of Niels Bohr (consistent with chemical data) had to be given up, as the electrons of the nickel atom had to be arranged in two (instead of three or four) shells, but Davisson and Kunsman quickly added that ‘minor details due to other shells may be found when the distribution curves are studied with greater resolving power, and other features may appear in as yet unexplored ranges of bombardment potential’ (Davisson and Kunsman, loc. cit., p. 255).$^{448}$

The work in New York proceeded systematically, and new materials (platinum and magnesium) in particular were bombarded with low-speed electrons. In April 1923, Davisson and Kunsman submitted a very detailed article on the subject to *Physical Review*, in which they also carefully compared their results with those of other authors (Davisson and Kunsman, 1923). They now concluded that their observed angular intensity pattern of reflected electrons (for different initial electron energies) could indeed be described by the standard Bohr model of those days, though ‘admittedly ... in the most hazy manner’ (Davisson and Kunsman, loc. cit., p. 257). Two years later, in 1925, the intensity curves obtained by Davisson and Kunsman excited the interest of the theoreticians in Göttingen, who had meanwhile become very doubtful about the old atomic models. When Walter Elsasser, a student at Franck’s institute, came up with the idea of connecting both the Ramsauer effect and the Davisson–Kunsman maxima and minima in the intensity patterns of scattered electrons with Louis de Broglie’s matter-wave hypothesis, Max Born wrote to Albert Einstein:

>The considerations of our Mr. Elsasser are not yet O.K. for the moment, it seemed that he was sadly mistaken—but I believe that the essential [part] of his idea can be saved, in particular concerning the reflection of electrons. I also speculate a bit about de Broglie’s waves. It appears to me that a connection (of a quite general nature) exists between these and that mystical explanation of reflection, diffraction and interference by “spatial” quantization, which has been proposed by Compton and Duane, and further investigated by Epstein and Ehrenfest. (Born to Einstein, 15 July 1925, in Einstein *et al.*, 1969, p. 120)

$^{448}$ Davisson and Kunsman found similar results in the scattering of electrons from an aluminum target (1922b).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0406 -->

374  Chapter III  The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

At any rate, on 18 July, Elsasser sent off his letter to *Naturwissenschaften*, containing ‘*Bemerkungen zur Quantenmechanik freier Elektronen*’ (‘Remarks on the Quantum Mechanics of Free Electrons’), in which he claimed that no peculiar nonmechanical force was responsible for the anomalies, *but rather the wave nature of the electrons* (Elsasser, 1925).$^{449}$

The young Elsasser tried to confirm his speculation by his own experiments, but left to his own devices he did not get very far. Then, in early 1926, came Schrödinger’s wave mechanics, which built a new atomic dynamics entirely on the basis of de Broglie’s matter waves. In June 1926, Born (after his return from an extended visit to the U.S.A.) proposed the wave-mechanical treatment of electrons colliding with atoms (Born, 1926a, b). In particular, he concluded that ‘the normal cross section of atoms is very much smaller for slow electrons than for fast electrons’ and noticed that this fact ‘corresponds to a diffraction phenomenon,’ as suggested first by Elsasser (Born, 1926b, p. 825).$^{450}$ In August 1926, Born attended the Oxford meeting of the *British Association for the Advancement of Science*, where he presented a paper on the ‘Physical Aspects of Quantum Mechanics’ (Born, 1927a). There, he met Clinton J. Davisson, who later recalled in his Nobel lecture: ‘The New York experiment was not, at its inception, a test of the wave theory. Only in summer of 1926, after I had discussed the investigation in England with Richardson, Born, Franck and others, did it take on this character’ (Davisson, 1938, p. 478).

Davisson had obtained his Ph.D. in 1911 from Princeton under the British physicist Owen Willans Richardson, with a thesis on ‘Positive Thermions from Salts of Alkaline Earths.’$^{451}$ Research on emission of thermionic electrons from oxide-coated cathodes had become his first programme at Western Electric Company after World War I, leading also to the particular results published with Kunsman from 1921 to 1923. When Kunsman dropped out, Davisson obtained the assistance of another collaborator, Lester Halbert Germer, who had joined the New York laboratory at the same time as Davisson and started to work with him from 1922 (see, e.g., Davisson and Germer, 1922).$^{452}$ Davisson and Germer

Upon graduating from Cornell University in 1917, he joined Western Electric, but then served as a fighter pilot in World War I. On his return to New York, he became a member of the staff of the Western Electric Laboratory; in 1930, he was promoted to the position of a Research Physicist at the Bell Telephone Laboratories (the renamed Western Electric Research Laboratories); and in 1962, he moved as Professor of Physics to Cornell University (where he had obtained his doctorate in 1927). While rock climbing on the Shawangank Cliffs near Gardiner, New York, he died on 3 October 1971. After discovering electron diffraction with Davisson, Germer devoted his scientific work to numerous applications of the phenomenon to crystal studies, to the perfection of a low-energy diffraction display apparatus, and to research on surface structure with this device.

described the last phase of experiments leading to the final discovery of matter waves as follows:

During the course of this work a liquid air bottle exploded at a time when the target was at a high temperature: the experimental tube [containing the metal] was broken, and the target heavily oxidized by the inrushing air. The oxide was eventually reduced and a layer of the target removed by vaporization, but only after prolonged heating at various high temperatures in hydrogen and in vacuum.
>When the experiments were continued it was found that the distribution-in-angle of the scattered electrons had completely changed. . . . This marked alteration in the scattering pattern was traced to a recrystallization of the target that occurred during the prolonged heating. Before the accident and in previous experiments we had been bombarding many small crystals, but in the tests subsequent to the accident we were bombarding only a few large ones. In particular, the authors observed: ‘The most characteristic of these beams [reflected from the crystal] is a one-to-one correspondence ... which the strongest of them bear to Laue beams that would be found issuing from the same crystal if the incident beam were a beam of X-rays.’ (Davisson and Germer, loc. cit., p. 707)

As Davisson stressed in his Nobel lecture ten years later (cited earlier), however, though the lucky accident occurred already in 1925, i.e., after Louis de Broglie’s doctoral thesis had appeared in print (L. de Broglie, 1925), neither it nor Elsasser’s *Naturwissenschaften* letter (Elsasser, 1925) had any influence on the experimental work in New York. It was not before the discussions of summer 1926 in England with Born and Franck drew Davisson’s attention to Elsasser’s note that his outlook changed completely, for as he himself recalled:

>The search for diffraction beams was begun in autumn of 1926, but not until early in the following year were any found—first one and then twenty others in rapid succession. Nineteen of these could be used to check the relationship between wavelength and momentum and in every case the correctness of the de Broglie formula, $\lambda = h/p$, was verified to within a limit of accuracy of the measurement. (Davisson, 1938, p. 478)

The new findings also threw light on the validity of Elsasser’s previous conclusions, as Davisson and Germer stated in their detailed paper of 1927:

We would like to agree with Elsasser in his interpretation of these curves, but are unable to do so. The maxima in the scattering curves are of the type of single maximum in the curves for nickel [of Davisson and

Kunsman, 1923] and are, we believe, unrelated to crystal structure. (Davisson and Kunsman, 1927b, p. 707)

The very careful and experienced Bell Lab physicists had indeed only now, in 1927, detected real electron diffraction from crystals; they possessed the proper special apparatus, consisting of an ‘electron gun’ and a field-free vessel containing the nickel target, including a double Faraday-box collector that was allowed to rotate so as to collect the reflected beams in different directions. Of this reliable and perfect setup, Elsasser, being alone at Franck’s institute in Göttingen, could only dream.$^{453}$

Immediately after their discovery, the authors submitted the results on single crystals of nickel in a letter, dated 3 March 1927, to the British journal *Nature*, which was published in the issue of 16 April (Davisson and Germer, 1927a). In the longer paper, sent in late August to *Physical Review*, they gave a complete account of the details.$^{454}$ The careful and controlled preparation of the nickel crystals, the time-consuming observation of the intensity patterns using electron beams of different velocity and nickel crystals in different orientation, and finally the thorough theoretical discussion of the data followed by a comparison with the known X-ray data could hardly be surpassed. Still, the authors must be congratulated for having presented a short announcement of the discovery that was quickly published in *Nature*, because already two and a half months later another couple of researchers sent to the same journal a letter on ‘Diffraction of Cathode Rays by a Thin Film,’ in which they reported the observation of a ring-like electron diffraction pattern obtained from scattering electron beams by celluloid films. The British authors, George Paget Thomson and Alexander Reid, explained their results as a Debye–Scherrer-like scattering of de Broglie waves (Thomson and Reid, 1927).

G. P. Thomson, son of Joseph John Thomson, the discoverer of the electron, was born on 3 May 1892, in Cambridge and attended school and university there. Following a brilliant undergraduate career, he entered in 1913 the Cavendish Laboratory directed by his father, elected to a fellowship, and appointed to a teaching position of his college (Corpus Christi). When the war broke out, he enlisted immediately and served at the front in France; in summer 1918, he returned to England to work on aircraft stability at the Royal Aircraft Factory, Farnborough, together with Francis W. Aston and Frederick A. Lindemann. In 1919, he returned to the Cavendish, where he investigated the isotopic constitution of alkali metal atoms. Thus, for example, in early 1926, he studied ‘the free path of slow protons in helium,’ i.e., the Ramsauer effect (G. P. Thomson, 1926). Then, he entered into research with his student Alexander Reid, stimulated by the matter-wave idea of Louis de Broglie.⁴⁵⁵ The letter to *Nature*, dated 24 May 1927, contained the first experimental proof given by the British scientists. It opened with the words:

> If a fine beam of homogeneous cathode rays is sent nearly normally through a thin celluloid film (of the order of $3 \times 10^{-6}$ cm thick) and then received by a photographic plate 10 cm away and parallel to the film, we find that the central spot formed by the undeflected rays is surrounded by rings, recalling in appearance the halos formed by mist round the sun. (Thomson and Reid, 1927, p. 890)

Upon evaluating this ring pattern with a photometer device, the authors were able to detect details not visible to the naked eye, which they described:

> With rays of about 13,000 volts two rings have been found inside the obvious one. Traces have been found of a fourth ring in other photographs, but not more than three have been found in any exposure. This is probably due to the limited range of intensity within which photometric measurements are feasible. (Thomson and Reid, *loc. cit.*)

Varying the energy of the cathode rays from 3,900 volts to 16,500 volts led to decreasing diameter of the observed rings with increasing energy, the radius of every given ring being inversely proportional to the velocity.

Thomson and Reid related the new phenomenon to another one reported by Edmund Gilbert Dymond of Princeton University about a year earlier: Dymond had directed an electron beam of homogeneous energy into helium gas of 0.03-mm pressure and observed the intensity-in-angle patterns of the electrons, especially of the electrons losing energy by inelastic collisions; he had thus found figures resembling the ones of Davisson and Kunsman (Dymond, 1926).⁴⁵⁶ Thomson and Reid now used Louis de Broglie’s formula,

$$\lambda = h/mv, \tag{304}$$

to obtain a wavelength $\lambda = 1.0 \times 10^{-9}$ cm for electrons of mass $m$ and velocity $v$. Although this wavelength did not contradict the size of their rings (e.g., 3.5 and 6.7 mm for 13,800-volt electrons), they cautioned:

The Aberdeen team indeed carried out the promised further investigations in the course of the following year, with Reid concentrating on diffraction by celluloid foils and Thomson turning to metal foils, all having a thickness of $10^{-6}$ cm. > The purpose of the said experiments was to verify the theory of de Broglie, and to this end was utilized the knowledge of the arrangement of the atoms in a crystal, this knowledge having been previously acquired as a result of investigations by means of X-rays. Now that the law of de Broglie has become known and acknowledged, the

**(f) The Theory of the Ramsauer Effect and Further Quantum Phenomena**

While the diffraction of electrons, atoms, and molecules from crystal and other lattices supported, at least since 1927, the matter wave hypothesis fully, the situation with the Ramsauer effect remained unclear as far as its theoretical explanation was concerned. Notably, in 1928, a debate issued whether it followed from wave mechanics that a plane de Broglie–Schrödinger wave, if scattered by an atom, did suffer any diffraction. Then, Paul Ehrenfest and his student A. J. Rutgers in Leyden claimed, referring to an investigation of Lucie Mensing on the scattering of light waves by an inhomogeneity (Mensing, 1927), in particular:

> The usual hint of an analogy with the Rayleigh phenomenon—dispersion of light by a small optical inhomogeneity occurs proportional to $\lambda^{-4}$—is insufficient.... The perturbation created by the atomic field on the primary electron wave corresponds mathematically to an optical inhomogeneity, whose diffraction number is ... exactly proportional to $\lambda^4$, hence it compensates the other factor.... Without further assumptions the Rayleigh analogue leads, even for arbitrarily small velocities of the primary electron, to elastic collisions. (Ehrenfest and Rutgers, 1928, p. 184)

Ehrenfest and Rutgers then tried to figure out the extra conditions required to arrive at the observed vanishing of elastic scattering. With reference to a model calculation of a mass point colliding with a rotator (Fermi, 1926c), they argued that a certain symmetry condition, if imposed upon the forces acting between the scattering atom and the scattered electrons, might indeed lead to the Ramsauer effect. Their letter to *Naturwissenschaften*, dated 22 February 1928, and published in the issue of 16 March, soon received an answer from Copenhagen.

Johan Peter Holtsmark, a Norwegian visitor at Bohr’s Institute, submitted on 3 July 1928, also a letter to *Naturwissenschaften*, in which he discussed the Ramsauer effect in quantum mechanics from the Copenhagen point of view

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0413 -->

III.1 The Empirical Verification of Quantum Concepts 381

(Holtsmark, 1928b).⁴⁶⁰ He had treated the topic already in the previous year, also in Copenhagen, where he collaborated then with Hilding Faxén from Stockholm (Faxén and Holtsmark, 1927).⁴⁶¹

Faxén and Holtsmark had started from the observation that the diffraction index for waves in a nuclear atom assumes a singularity in the vicinity of the nucleus on account of the increasing atomic field inside; hence, the wavelength of radiation remains finite within the atom even when it becomes infinite outside. This theoretical result would provide, Holtsmark now argued, an explanation of the Ramsauer effect, because: ‘The essential feature of the effect, in obvious agreement with the experimental results, does not consist in the absence of scattering for infinitely large wavelengths but in the vanishing [of scattering] for a wavelength depending upon the atomic field under consideration.’ (Holtsmark, 1928b, p. 615). And he demonstrated in his *Naturwissenschaften* letter how this conclusion could be interpreted as the quantum-mechanical analogue of Rayleigh’s classical scattering theorem. Indeed, from the equations derived in the paper with Faxén, a dependence of large-wavelength scattering followed proportional to $\lambda^{-4n}$, with $n$ denoting the order of scattering. Hence, Holtsmark concluded:

> Rayleigh’s $\lambda^4$-law therefore applies to scattering of first order, similar to the situation in [classical] optics and acoustics; the scattering of zeroth order, on the other hand, approaches a constant value. This constant, however, can assume the value zero for a suitable atomic field, and then the scattering of zeroth order vanishes. (Holtsmark, *loc. cit.*)

The latter situation can actually occur, Holtsmark stated, arguing: the eigenfunction of the electron of zeroth order in the atomic field is given by the expression

$$
\psi_0 = \frac{R(r)}{r} \sin \left( \frac{2\pi r}{\lambda} + \phi(r) \right), \tag{305}
$$

where $R$ and $\phi$ denote functions of the distance $r$ of the incident electron inside the atom and constants outside. Now, if $\sin \phi(\infty)$ is zero, then the scattering of zeroth order does indeed vanish. In other words, the Ramsauer effect just expresses that

P. J. Holtsmark was born in Oslo on 13 February 1894, and studied physics at the university of his native city from 1911. After obtaining his doctorate in 1918, he went abroad in 1919 to continue his studies at the universities of Würzburg, Leipzig, Göttingen, and London. In 1920, he became a lecturer in physics at the Technical University in Trondheim, where he served as professor from 1923 to 1942. In 1943, he returned to the University of Oslo to occupy a chair of physics. He retired in 1964.

In 1927, he was called to the Technical University of Stockholm as an associate professor, and moved in 1930 to the University of Göteborg as full professor. From 1935 to 1958, he occupied a chair of physics again at the Technical University of Stockholm.

As Holtsmark remarked: ‘By the way, one has to expect that the assumption of a fixed atomic field yields results that are the more reliable, the higher is the atomic number involved,’ and finally added:

> From the theory [thus displayed] one can see, in particular, why for elements of low atomic number the conditions of the Ramsauer effect are not satisfied or only incompletely satisfied, since the scattering can disappear only if at least half a wavelength is contained in the atomic diameter (i.e., if the wave suffers [on its path] until the centre of the atom at least a phase shift of $\pi$). The calculation of the scattering by argon and neon atoms seems to confirm our conclusion (Holtsmark, 1928a). One obtains for argon nearly the exact experimental scattering values, while the agreement is worse for neon. (Holtsmark, *loc. cit.*)

Immediately, Wolfgang Pauli wrote to Niels Bohr: ‘Just now I read with interest Holtsmark’s note in *Naturwissenschaften*, dealing with one of your hobby-horses.’ Without doubting the correctness of the conclusion, however, Pauli criticized the pedagogical presentation, because it did not give the conditions for which the formula employed was valid. Further, he remarked: ‘By the way, I consider the introduction to be an unsuccessful attempt to create the impression on the reader that he (and, respectively, his students) are polite towards Ehrenfest. ... The approximation method used by Ehrenfest (and Fermi) goes back to Born and cannot be compared with the one used by Holtsmark; in reality, it is completely unsuitable when applied in the case of small electron velocities’ (Pauli to Bohr, 10 August 1928, in Pauli, 1979, p. 471).

The debate on the validity of the different approaches taken in Leyden and Copenhagen, respectively, continued during the following years, and Gregor Wentzel and J. Robert Oppenheimer also became involved (Wentzel, 1928; Oppenheimer, 1928b) besides Holtsmark and others. While Wentzel raised doubts about Faxén and Holtsmark’s method of treating the situation as a one-body problem (see also Holtsmark, 1928a), Oppenheimer refined Born’s method (criticized by Pauli as being not applicable to the Raman effect) by taking into account the possibility of electron exchange: because Pauli’s exclusion principle applied to electrons, he derived an additional ‘exchange term.’ Based on this refinement, Harrie Stewart, Wilson Massey, and C. O. B. Mohr indeed calculated electron-scattering curves that allowed one to describe the low-velocity scattering by atoms at least in principle (Massey and Mohr, 1931). Carl Ramsauer then summarized the status of the theoretical description of his effect in an authoritative review, written together with Rudolf Kollath, for the *Handbuch der Physik*:

> The fundamental phenomena of electron-wave diffraction by atoms can be visualized according to [Nevill F.] Mott as follows:
>
> 1. The atom is given by a field of force having a definite potential distribution. ... (Faxén and Holtsmark, 1927; Allis and Morse, 1931).

We have dealt with the Ramsauer effect in such detail because it played the role it did in establishing the fundamental matter-wave concept. Its actual theoretical explanation turned out to be a rather complex one; yet, eventually the phenomenon was understood in wave mechanics, at least in principle. Many other empirical observations allowed a much more direct check of the quantum-mechanical theory. In the *Naturwissenschaften* issue of 28 June 1929, celebrating the golden jubilee of Max Planck’s doctorate, Pascual Jordan summarized ‘the empirical foundations of quantum theory’ (‘Die Erfahrungsgrundlagen der Quantentheorie,’ Jordan, 1929a). He began his extended review by confronting the general situation with empirical evidence in classical and quantum theory, respectively. Although he noticed that the classical theories of Newton, Maxwell, and Einstein (i.e., the two relativity theories) were actually based on very few fundamental empirical facts, he found that:

> In contrast to this, in the field of quantum theory such an immense abundance of experiences, facts and rules are available that one has problems in recognizing where and how the different fundamental postulates are based on empirical evidence. Everything which we know about the infinite multitude of atomic and molecular spectra, all that testifies in every detail to the validity of the profound (*gedankentiefen*) theory of quanta, as it has developed since 1900, initially in a groping and searching way, then increasingly rapidly and successfully, until it reached its full splendour (*volle Entfaltung*) in the past years. Old experiences, never quite understood, such as those concerning electric conduction, have now been explained on the quantum theory. Some new and flourishing fields of research, as for example modern astrophysics, cannot be imagined without the guidance of quantum theory. Quantum theory has even encroached upon the neighbouring science of chemistry—one may recall such topics as photochemistry, the investigation of reaction rates, and today’s knowledge of the nature of molecules and chemical binding. (Jordan, *loc. cit.*, pp. 498–499)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0416 -->

384 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

In spite of that overwhelming wealth of empirical facts relating to the foundation of quantum theory, Jordan singled out a set of experiments and experiences, through which (in his opinion) the fundamental postulates of quantum theory obtain their ‘immediate test and justification’ (‘unmittelbare Prüfung und Rechtfertigung,’ Jordan, *loc. cit.*, p. 499). He then put them together in five sections, entitled: I. Planck’s [Radiation] Law; Statistical Effects of Discrete Energy States (‘Energiestufen’); II. Light-Quanta; III. Discrete Energy States of Atoms; IV. Transition Probabilities (of Atomic and Nuclear Processes); V. Matter Waves. That is, he included all of the topics we have mentioned in this section, and a few more that have been reported as the empirical foundation of the old quantum theory and quantum and wave mechanics in previous volumes. On the other hand, one must count further the topics, referred to by Jordan as the ‘new flourishing fields of research,’ to provide a similar empirical justification for the fundamental concepts and laws of quantum mechanics. We shall report about these new fields in some detail below, in Sections 5 to 7, after dealing with the important progress obtained in the mathematical formulation of quantum mechanics in the years between 1926 and 1932.

### III.2 The Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

In spite of the fact that Henri Poincaré had already raised in 1911 (at the first Solvay Conference) the question of whether the existence of quantum phenomena would not change drastically the classical concept of a natural law, especially the formulation by means of differential equations, quantum physicists did not immediately abandon their conventional mathematical methods; rather, they waited for another dozen years until the breakdown of the old quantum theory forced them to take proper action. The new quantum mechanics, discovered in 1925 by Werner Heisenberg, demanded a genuinely different mathematical description, which Max Born and Pascual Jordan, as well as Paul Dirac, subsequently worked out in discrete algebraic terms. On the other hand, the wave mechanics, discovered by Erwin Schrödinger half a year later, seemed to achieve the same goal by describing the quantum-mechanical phenomena with the usual differential equation methods. Soon, the physicists learned (or reminded themselves) that earlier in the century David Hilbert and his students had obtained a mathematical theory, which accounted both for algebraic and differential equation structures and even allowed one to demonstrate a certain equivalence of both. However, the physicists and the mathematicians quickly recognized that the previously known Hilbert-space methods had to be extended to meet squarely the tasks of the quantum theory. This section deals with the necessary steps toward that goal, in which Hilbert again took the first initiative. He was soon replaced by Janos or Johannes (John) von Neumann, a young Hungarian mathematical genius. He showed that, in contrast to the opinion of most physicists, one did not need Paul Dirac’s ‘improper’ delta-function as a new mathematical tool, whose mathematical foun-

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0417 -->

III.2 The Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics 385

dation appeared to be very shaky; one, rather, could, by a proper extension of the rigorous methods of linear integral equations and Hilbert space, arrive at a satisfactory mathematical description of the so-called 'unbounded operators' and their eigenvalue spectrum. Independently, an enterprise with the same goal started in Leipzig, where Aurel Wintner rather focused on the tool of infinite matrices. The physicists, though they scarcely referred to the publications of their mathematical colleagues, were nevertheless quite happy and satisfied, when the latter proved and demonstrated with unquestionable rigour the results that they themselves had obtained by more intuitive evaluation.

**(a) The Mathematics of the Pioneers of Quantum Mechanics**

Heisenberg formulated his pioneering quantum-mechanical ideas by inventing a new version of Fourier series, in which the (observed) quantum frequencies $v(n, m)$ and the corresponding transition amplitudes $a(n, m)$ replaced the classical harmonics; as a crucial consequence, he noticed that the dynamical variables thus represented did not commute with one another, as they did in classical mechanics (Heisenberg, 1925c).$^{462}$ What he introduced, so-to-say, as provisional rules of the game, Max Born and Pascual Jordan turned into 'a systematic theory of quantum mechanics,' using the well-known 'matrix calculus as a mathematical tool' (Born and Jordan, 1925b, p. 858).$^{463}$ However, they instantly realized, essentially from the noncommutativity or 'quantum condition' for momentum and position variables $p$ and $q$,

$$ \sum_k [p(n,k)q(k,n) - q(n,k)p(k,n)] = \frac{h}{2\pi i} \cdot \mathbf{1}, \tag{306} $$

that the matrices $p(n, m)$ and $q(n, m)$ involved had to be infinite matrices (because otherwise the trace of the commutator on the left-hand side would disappear while the trace on the right right-hand side remained finite) and further: 'Also they do not belong to the class of "bounded" infinite matrices so far considered nearly exclusively by the mathematicians' (Born and Jordan, *loc. cit.*, p. 870, footnote 1). Then, in fall 1925, Born tried to make use in the three-man paper (Born *et al.*, 1926, Chapter III) of the existing mathematical theory of quadratic Hermitean forms of infinitely many variables, which went back to his Göttingen teacher David Hilbert (1904a, b; 1905; 1906a, b; 1910) and Ernst Hellinger (1909), another student of Hilbert's. He adapted, in particular, the latter's mathematical method for obtaining the eigenfrequency spectrum of Hermitean forms to the problem of calculating the energy states of quantum-mechanical systems, emphasizing that the method allowed in principle to reduce arbitrary Hermitean forms by an orthogonal transformation to the sum of squares, denoted by an index $n$. Born added:
