For infinite matrices ... it can however occur that the index $n$ on the right-hand side runs not only through a set of discrete numbers but also through a continuous range of values. . . .
The quantities $W_n$ are termed "eigenvalues"; their ensemble is the "mathematical spectrum" of the form, made up of "point" and "continuous" spectra. As we shall see, this is identical with the "term spectrum" in physics. (Born *et al.*, 1926, pp. 583–584, English translation, pp. 350–351)

Born knew that Hilbert and Hellinger's theory had dealt mostly with 'bounded' or even 'completely continuous' Hermitean forms, while the quantum-mechanical problems demanded 'unbounded' forms; still, he expected that the mathematical results obtained earlier remained valid also for the problems of atomic theory.
Independently of and simultaneous with the theoreticians in Göttingen, Paul Dirac in Cambridge translated Heisenberg's quantum-mechanical Fourier rules into the different algebraical language of what he termed '$q$-numbers' (Dirac, 1925d; 1926a, b, e). Although he did not explicitly refer, for a mathematical justification, to Hilbert and his followers, Dirac drew inspiration from his former professor in geometry, Henry Baker, who relied on the same traditions as Hilbert. Dirac, the young Cambridge research student, formerly educated in Bristol as an electrical engineer, handled the available mathematical methods quite freely, inventing his own rules and concepts whenever he needed them to account for the physical phenomena.$^{464}$ Thus, he succeeded in solving the problem of many-electron systems, which the standard matrix scheme of Born, Heisenberg, and Jordan could not do: the action-angle method of $q$-numbers described in a natural way also the steadily growing, i.e., nonlibrating, coordinates.$^{465}$
Dirac further evaluated the first scattering problem in quantum mechanics, the Compton scattering of radiation by electrons (bound in atoms), with his relativistically extended $q$-number theory, to which matrix mechanics had no access either (Dirac, 1926c). Indeed, Born had declared before that the formal matrix expressions (i.e., the integrals) occurring in the treatment of all problems with continuous energy spectrum are 'improper or altogether divergent,' arguing:

This is related to the fact that aperiodic motions approach uniform rectilinear motion asymptotically in the limit of infinite distance. This motion has evidently no period and represents a case of greatest singularity. It is not amenable to matrix representation, even if continuous matrices are mustered for that purpose. (Born, 1926d, p. 124)

To describe the aperiodic motion quantum mechanically, Born enlisted the assistance of the American mathematician Norbert Wiener. The latter referred him to operators as the generalization of matrices, which he—Wiener—had explored previously in an attempt to provide the old operator calculus of the British telegraph employee, Oliver Heaviside, a mathematical basis; with Born, he then de-

III.2 The Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics 387

veloped, at the turn of 1925 to 1926, an operator formulation of quantum mechanics (Born and Wiener, 1926a, b).$^{466}$ They replaced the matrices $(q(m, n))$ of the Born–Heisenberg–Jordan scheme first by functions $q(t, s)$, i.e.,

$$ q(t, s) = \sum_{m,n} \exp \left[ \frac{2\pi i}{h} (W_m t - W_n s) \right] \tag{307} $$

(with $W_m$ and $W_n$ denoting discrete energy terms, $t$ and $s$ time variables), and then defined the operator $q = q(t)$ by the integral relation

$$ q = \lim_{\tau \to \infty} \frac{1}{2\tau} \int_{-\tau}^{+\tau} q(t, s) ds. \tag{308} $$

They immediately realized, however, that, even in the case of the discrete harmonic oscillator, the representation of $q$ by a trigonometric series (307) did diverge. Still, the authors argued, it made sense to use the linear operator $q$, and they derived with it the quantity (corresponding to the sum of row-elements in a matrix) $q(t, W)$, namely,

$$ q(t, W) = \exp \left( - \frac{2\pi i}{h} Wt \right) q \exp \left( \frac{2\pi i}{h} Wt \right). \tag{309} $$

Born and Wiener then continued:

The function of $q(t, W)$ may exist in cases where the "matrix" $q(V, W)$ does not exist in the proper sense. In these cases, $q(t, W)$ does not admit of a harmonic analysis in the proper sense. We may nevertheless employ the methods of generalized harmonic analysis to isolate the elementary harmonic components. We may say in the same sense as above that $q(t, W)$ represents the "motion with energy $W$." (Born and Wiener, 1926a, p. 87)

As a particular linear operator for their purpose, they finally selected the linear differential operator $D = d/dt$, which had played a central role also in Heaviside's operator calculus, and solved with its help the problem of the one-dimensional uniform motion of a massive particle in quantum mechanics.
Though the work of Wiener and others had provided the Heaviside formalism already some mathematical respectability, it did not win the favour of physicists (with a few exceptions); rather, they turned to other type of operator methods, brought into play by Cornelius Lanczos and Erwin Schrödinger. The Hungarian Lanczos first (in December 1925) reminded one that the theory of quadratic forms, addressed by Born, Heisenberg, and Jordan, had grown out of Hilbert's treatment

that all results of the theory may also be expressed in the form of integral equations; thus they obtain a formulation which may appear most natural to the physicist—who is used to analytical methods—than the matrix formulation. (Lanczos, 1926a, pp. 812–813)

While a one-to-one relation existed between the continuum-like, integral equation formulation and the discontinuous matrix formulation, 'for the fundamental interpretation of the theory, the integral formulation has the advantage that it is in immediate harmony with the field-like conceptions of physics,' Lanczos suggested (Lanczos, *loc. cit.*, p. 812).$^{467}$ This advantage counted even more in favour of the other field-like scheme of quantum mechanics, the undulatory or wave mechanics, which worked with the conventional partial differential equations (plus suitable boundary conditions). The author, Schrödinger, even claimed additional advantages for his scheme: first, it seemed to provide a more 'usual picture' of atomic phenomena, though one could establish a complete equivalence of the wave- and matrix-mechanical expressions for atomic quantities; second, it proved to be a more powerful tool to apply, e.g., to both periodic and aperiodic atomic problems (Schrödinger, 1926c, d, e, f, g, h; Eckart, 1926a, b).$^{468}$ Schrödinger and Lanczos acknowledged, as the mathematical basis of their theoretical schemes, the pioneering investigations of Hilbert and his disciples before 1910; however, they did not go beyond in attempting at the necessary extensions.
For example, several theoreticians (including, besides Schrödinger and the American Carl Eckart, also Wolfgang Pauli) established the relation between the Göttingen infinite matrices and the expressions in undulatory mechanics, but the opposite direction was not immediately attacked until Dirac and Jordan worked out their mathematical transformation theories (Dirac, 1927a; Jordan, 1927b), which established one-to-one relations between all quantum-mechanical schemes. We have discussed both proposals and their successful application to deal with the interpretation problem in Chapters I and II, respectively. Here, we want to focus on the mathematical problem, which the physicists raised in their treatment and did not—at least in the opinion of rigorous mathematicians—solve. Jordan's probability-amplitude approach, on the one hand, rather, sketched a programme for a mathematical theory that had to be, and actually would be, carried out in detail by the mathematicians (as we shall see below). On the other hand, Dirac, in

his ‘Physical Interpretation of the Quantum Dynamics,’ actually proposed a complete, evidently consistently operating mathematical scheme, but it was based on a new mathematical concept of the delta-function, which he introduced—and we shall quote here his remark in full:

> One cannot go far in the development of the theory of matrices with continuous ranges of rows and columns without needing a notation of that function of a *c*-number $x$ that is equal to 0, except when $x$ is very small, and whose integral through a range that contains the point $x = 0$ is equal to unity. We shall use the symbol $\delta(x)$ to denote this function, i.e., $\delta(x)$ is defined by
> $$\delta(x) = 0 \quad \text{when } x \neq 0, \quad [(310)]$$
> and
> $$\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} x \delta(x) = 1. \quad [(311)]$$

Strictly, of course, $\delta(x)$ is not a proper function of $x$, but can be regarded only as a limit of a certain sequence of functions. All the same one can use $\delta(x)$ as though it were a proper function for practically all purposes of quantum mechanics without getting incorrect results. One can also use the differential coefficients $\delta(x)$, namely $\delta'(x)$, $\delta''(x)$, $\dots$, which are even more discontinuous and less “proper” than $\delta(x)$ itself. (Dirac, 1927a, p. 625)

With the help of his ‘improper function,’ Dirac then gave a completely satisfactory proof of the one-to-one relation between all of the different formulations or representations of quantum mechanics introduced so far, and no further problems seemed to occur with the foundations of quantum mechanics.

As we have mentioned already in Section I.5, Dirac approached the $\delta$-function in systematic steps when dealing with the application of wave mechanics (i.e., in Dirac, 1926f and 1926g). In interviews, he pointed out that he had ‘noticed the need for it very much’ early in his Cambridge studies, namely, ‘at a certain place in Eddington’s book on *The Mathematical Theory of Relativity*.’$^{469}$ He also always emphasized: ‘The delta-function came in just for picturing the infinities as something approximating to them.’ This personal approach to the object was confirmed in his standard treatise of 1930, *The Principles of Quantum Mechanics*, when he introduced the ‘improper’ delta-function by the words:

When these operations are permissible, the $\delta$-function may be used freely by dealing with the representatives of the abstract symbols, as though it were a continuous function, without leading to incorrect results. A serious question may be asked at this point. Why did Dirac not refer to previous uses of what he called the $\delta$-function? One can mention, in particular, two precursors of $\delta$-function-like objects in the physical and technical literature.$^{470}$ One arose in connection with applying Green’s theorem (Green, 1828): when Gustav Kirchhoff treated the optical wave equation, he specified the auxiliary function $v(\bar{x}, t)$ as
$$v = \frac{F(|\bar{x} - \bar{x}'| + at)}{|\bar{x} - \bar{x}'|}. \quad (312)$$

Now, $F$ is a function:

> which for, every finite, positive or negative, value of its argument vanishes and satisfies the condition
> $$\int F(\zeta) d\zeta = 1 \quad [(313)]$$
> if the integration is extended from a finite negative to a finite positive value of $\zeta$. (Kirchhoff, 1882, §2; 1891, p. 24)

III.2 The Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics 391

While Kirchhoff’s function was only occasionally introduced in the physical literature (see, e.g., Hertz, 1916), the operator calculus of Oliver Heaviside constituted a rather standard topic in the education of an electrical engineer, which Dirac received before coming to Cambridge in 1923. In Heaviside’s formalism, the step function of time $t$,
$$H(t) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{for } t < 0, \\ 1 & \text{for } t > 0, \end{cases} \quad (314)$$
played a central role, and Dirac’s $\delta$-function coincides essentially with the time derivative of $H(t)$. Of course, the mathematicians doubted the rigour of the methods for some time; only recently they had obtained a justification on the basis of an extension of Laplace transforms (Carson, 1925), on the one hand, and a generalization of the harmonic analysis (Wiener, 1926a), on the other.$^{471}$ Heaviside had not cared much about the criticism of mathematicians. ‘Shall I refuse my dinner because I do not fully understand the process of digestion?’ he had argued (quoted in Kármán and Biot, 1940). Dirac now might have repeated such a statement.

As in previous cases—for example, in the case of Kirchhoff’s function $F$ in optical problems (see Lützen, 1982, p. 101)—rigorous mathematicians did not justify directly the intuitive approach of physicists, but chose a path around the difficulty. Thus, John von Neumann, in the preface of his book *Mathematische Grundlagen der Quantenmechanik*, stated:

> The method of Dirac, mentioned above, (and this is overlooked today in a great part of quantum-mechanical literature, because of the clarity and the elegance of the theory), in no way satisfies the requirements of mathematical rigour—not even if these are reduced in a natural and proper fashion to the extent common elsewhere in theoretical physics. For example, the method adheres to the fiction that each self-adjoint operator can be put in diagonal form. In the case of those operators for which this is not actually the case, this requires the introduction of “improper” functions with contradictory properties. The insertion of such a mathematical “fiction” is frequently necessary in Dirac’s approach, even though the problem is merely one of calculating numerically the results of a clearly defined experiment. There would be no objection here if these concepts, which cannot be incorporated into the present day framework of analysis, were intrinsically necessary for the physical theory. Thus, as Newtonian mechanics first brought about the development of the infinitesimal calculus, which, in its original form, was undoubtedly not self-consistent, so quantum mechanics might suggest a new structure for our “analysis of infinitely many variables”—i.e., the mathematical technique would have to be changed, and not the physical theory. But this is by no means the case. It should rather be pointed out that the quantum-mechanical “transformation theory” can be established in a manner

> which is just as clear and unified, but which is also without mathematical objections. It should be emphasized that the correct structure need not consist in a mathematical refinement and explanation of the Dirac method, but rather that it requires a procedure differing from the very beginning, namely, the reliance on the Hilbert theory of operators. (von Neumann, 1932; English translation, pp. viii–ix)

That is, von Neumann not only criticized Dirac’s methods for not having mathematical rigour, but he also claimed that the whole statistical transformation theory and the very description of experimental facts in quantum mechanics required a very different formulation. It was this formulation that he, as a mathematician, wished to provide on the basis of a generalization of the secure methods of Hilbert.

### (b) David Hilbert’s Axiomatic Foundations of Physics

On 8 August 1900, at the International Congress of Mathematicians, connected with the Centennial Exhibition (World’s Fair) in Paris, David Hilbert presented a prophetic talk on ‘Mathematical Problems,’ dealing with 23 items that still had to be—and he hoped that they would be—solved in the future.$^{472}$ Problem No. 6 read:

> *Mathematical treatment of the axioms of physics.* The investigations on the foundations of geometry suggest the problem: *To treat in the same manner, by means of axioms, those physical sciences in which mathematics plays an important part; in the first rank are the theory of probabilities and mechanics.* (Hilbert, 1900, English translation, p. 454)

To study the physical theories in a manner similar to those of geometry implied, to ‘try first by a small number of axioms to include as large a class as possible of physical phenomena, and then by adjoining new axioms to arrive gradually at the more special theories.’ That is, the mathematician would not only organize the known physical theories perhaps in a way different than what the physicists had done so far, but he ‘will have also to account not only for those theories coming near to reality, but also, as in geometry, of all logically possible theorems,’ because: ‘He must always be alert to obtain a complete survey of all conclusions derivable from the system of axioms assumed’ (Hilbert, *loc. cit.*).

As a particular task for the mathematician, in deriving what he later would call ‘the foundations of physics,’ Hilbert emphasized:$^{473}$

$^{472}$ Actually, in Paris, Hilbert did not talk about all of them. It may be added that in due course most of these problems were actually solved, some by Hilbert himself.

$^{473}$ Actually, Hilbert gave the title already in 1900 by referring to a statement of the famous Berlin mathematician Karl Weierstrass: ‘The final object always to be kept in mind is to arrive at a correct understanding of the *foundations of science*.’ (Hilbert, 1900; English translation, p. 455; our italics)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0425 -->

III.2 The Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics 393

Further, the mathematician has the duty to test exactly in each instance whether the new axioms are compatible with the previous ones. The physicist, as his theories develop, often finds himself forced by the results of his experiments to make new hypotheses, while he depends, with respect to the compatibility of the new hypotheses with the old axioms, solely upon the experiments or upon a certain physical intuition, a practice which in the rigorously logical building up of a theory is not admissible. The desired proof of the compatibility of all assumptions seems to me also of importance, because the effort to obtain such proof always forces us most effectively to an exact formulation of the axioms. (Hilbert, *loc. cit.*, p. 455)

Hilbert's active concern with physics began a decade later, after the death of his mathematical colleague in Göttingen, Hermann Minkowski, with whom (and also partly together with Felix Klein) he had conducted regularly seminars on problems of theoretical physics.$^{474}$ Since Minkowski's successor, Edmund Landau, being a pure mathematician, showed no interest in such topics, Hilbert felt obliged to replace his friend, both in holding lecture courses regularly and contributing original papers on topics of current research in physical theories. First, he dealt with kinetic gas theory (Hilbert, 1912a), and then he turned in three papers to what he called the 'foundations of elementary radiation theory' (Hilbert, 1912b, 1913, 1914).$^{475}$ In these contributions, Hilbert did not invent new physical theories; rather, he intended to provide a logical and rigorous formulation, based on just a few axioms or theorems that did not contradict each other. Thus, Hilbert developed the kinetic gas theory from what he considered to be its two fundamental assumptions: (1) the molecules are mutually identical and completely spherical; (2) the change of their velocity distribution is determined by Boltzmann's collision equation. Besides these assumptions (which he used as the 'axioms' of the theory), he just relied on the entirely self-evident and precisely formulated continuity and boundary conditions for the velocity distribution. The latter was then expanded in powers of a parameter: the first approximation of the relations for the velocity distributions yielded the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, the second yielded the propagation of the average velocities (determining heat conduction) in space and time. Now, every approximation could be expressed as a linear integral equation with an asymmetrical kernel and therefore be solved according to the mathematical theory developed earlier by Ivar Fredholm (1903) and Hilbert himself (1904a, b; 1905; 1906a, b; 1910).$^{476}$

As a second physical application of his mathematical theory, Hilbert selected:

394 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

another field of physics, the principles of which have not yet been studied from the mathematical point of view and for the foundations of which the tool of integral equations is necessary ... the elementary radiation theory, i.e., that phenomenological part of radiation theory which is based directly on the concepts of emission and absorption, culminating in Kirchhoff's relations between emission and absorption. (Hilbert, 1912b, reprint, p. 1057)$^{477}$

In further papers on the subject, Hilbert sharpened the fundamental assumptions on which he had derived the line integral equation of the Fredholm type for the emission coefficient (whose unique eigenfunction solution guaranteed the proportionality between emission and absorption in each case: Hilbert, 1913, 1914). Eventually, he put forward the following 'axioms of radiation theory':

*Axiom A (Axiom of the Balance of Total Energy).* The radiation of every optical system can assume an equilibrium state. In this state the total energy for all colours emitted from a volume element equals the total energy absorbed by it.
*Axiom B (Axiom of the Energy Balance for Each Colour).* For every optical system a state of radiation equilibrium can be achieved. ... The equilibrium exists *per se* for radiation of each frequency.
*Axiom C (Axiom of the Physical Nature of Radiation Density).* In the equilibrium state the radiation density for each wavelength depends on the physical constitution of matter.
*Axiom D (Axiom of the Existence of Different Substances).* ... (Hilbert, 1914, pp. 879–880)

Hilbert was particularly satisfied to demonstrate:

that all statements in our axioms ... constitute a closed system of theorems, which are logically connected and do not contradict one another, and are further consistent with the laws of elementary optics. (Hilbert, *loc. cit.*, p. 888)

Hilbert's efforts to provide an axiomatic foundation for radiation theory did not always meet the approval of the physicists. Especially, Ernst Pringsheim, the blackbody radiation expert from Breslau, was very critical: he had earlier tried to formulate the physical principles of the theory in some detail himself, and he now pointed out that Hilbert's first proposal in Münster was incomplete and did not add at all to the understanding of Kirchhoff's law (Pringsheim, 1913a). On Hilbert's reply (Hilbert, 1913) he polemically added 'that neither the attempt of an axiomatic presentation of the theory nor the two attempts at a rigorous derivation

---

Marian von Smoluchowski and Arnold Sommerfeld as well as other physicists participated actively in the discussion. For example, when Sommerfeld asked Hilbert whether he might be able to derive also the shape of Kirchhoff's function, i.e., the law of blackbody radiation, from his foundations, the latter answered decisively: 'No, no!' (*loc. cit.*, p. 1064)

III.2 The Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics 395

of Kirchhoff's law have given an acceptable result' (Pringsheim, 1913b, p. 849). Hilbert remained unconvinced by Pringsheim's claims, as 'none of the factual objections of Mr. Pringsheim appear to me to hit upon the [basic] point' (Hilbert, 1914, reprint, p. 878). Evidently, the dispute between the mathematician and the physicist rested less on a few disagreements about the validity of particular theoretical derivations or proofs than primarily on a different interpretation of respective goals. Pringsheim placed the main emphasis on formulating the empirical facts of radiation theory as completely as possible, while Hilbert's interest was focused on the mathematico-logical structure of the theory, the consistency of its axioms and consequences. Once the axioms had been fixed in agreement with the physical facts, he argued, the rest was a 'purely mathematical task'—in his opinion the physicists rather often relied on 'the big computer nature (*die große Rechenmachine Natur*).' (See Blumenthal, 1935, p. 417.)

The same disparity between the goals of the physicist and the mathematician may be recognized in the following engagement of Hilbert's, when he participated in the creation of a new physical theory: the theory of general relativity.$^{478}$ On 20 November 1915, Hilbert spoke at the Göttingen Academy on 'The Foundations of Physics,' dealing in detail with 'a new system of fundamental equations of physics, which are of an ideal beauty and which combine the solution of the problems' of Gustav Mie's electrodynamical field theory of matter and of Albert Einstein's general relativity theory of gravitation (Hilbert, 1915, p. 395). In particular, the new foundations rested on two axioms:

*Axiom I (Mie's Axiom of a World Function).* The law of physical processes ("*Geschehnisse*") is defined by a world function $H$ containing the following elements: (1) $g_{\mu\nu}, g_{\mu\nu l} = \partial g_{\mu\nu}/\partial x_l, g_{\mu\nu lk} = \partial^2 g_{\mu\nu}/\partial w_l \partial w_k$; (2) $q_s, q_{sl} = \partial q_s \partial x_l (s, l = 1, 2, 3, 4)$, such that the variation of the integral $\int H \sqrt{g} \, d\omega$ (with $g = det|g_{\mu\nu}|$), $d\omega = dw_1 dw_2 dw_3 dw_4$ vanishes for each of the 14 potentials $g_{\mu\nu}, q_s$.
*Axiom II (Axiom of General Invariance).* The world function $H$ is an invariant with respect to an arbitrary transformation of the world parameters $w_s$. (*loc. cit.*, p. 396)

Hilbert then derived equations for the gravitational field $g_{\mu\nu}$ and the electromagnetic field $q_s$, which coincided, as he concluded happily, with those obtained 'in the grand theory of general relativity expounded by Einstein in his later publications [Einstein, 1915g, 1916c],' on the one hand, and in Mie's electrodynamics (Mie, 1912a, b, c), on the other hand.

Evidently, the axiomatic method involving the variational principle (which Hilbert handled with great virtuosity) allowed him to derive the general relativistic law of gravitation, which Einstein first wrote (after previous less complete attempts: Einstein, 1915d, e, f) on 25 November 1915, i.e., five days after Hilbert's Göttingen lecture. Earlier, on 14 November, Hilbert announced in a letter to Einstein his

---

396 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

'axiomatic solution of your great problem.'$^{479}$ At Einstein's request, he sent a copy of his manuscript for the Göttingen lecture to Berlin. Einstein replied on 18 November: 'The system [of equations] given by you agrees—as far as I can see—exactly with what I found in recent weeks and submitted to the Berlin Academy.'$^{480}$ At the same time, he damped Hilbert's enthusiasm with the axiomatic procedure by continuing:

> The difficulty was not to find generally covariant equations for the $g_{\mu\nu}$; this is easy with the help of the Riemann tensor. What was difficult indeed was to recognize that these equations form a generalization, and, that is, a simple and natural generalization of Newton's law. (Einstein to Hilbert, 18 November 1915)

That is, independently of the fact as to who had arrived at the solution earlier, in Einstein's opinion, it was the physical arguments that counted in the derivation of the equations of gravitation.

From the publications (i.e., Hilbert, 1915, and Einstein, 1915g), it might be derived that Hilbert preceded Einstein in writing for the first time the final field equations of gravitation,

$$K_{\mu\nu} - \frac{1}{2}g_{\mu\nu}K = T_{\mu\nu}, \qquad (315)$$

where $K_{\mu\nu}$ and $T_{\mu\nu}$ denote (the latter apart from a constant factor) the curvature and matter tensors and $K$ denotes the trace of the curvature tensor (Hilbert, 1915, p. 404). In a recent historical study, it was disclosed that Hilbert's original draft of the Göttingen lecture of 20 November 1915, did not contain Eq. (315), and that the author stopped short of it; hence, it was concluded that: (1) Einstein could not have copied the equation from Hilbert; (2) 'Hilbert did not anticipate Einstein.' (Corry *et al.*, 1997, p. 1270) It was further claimed that Hilbert's scheme lacked general covariance, because he had added in his manuscript a third axiom stating the equations of energy and momentum conservation; these had, in Einstein's previous investigations, destroyed general covariance (Einstein and Grossmann, 1913; Einstein, 1914c). Can one derive from these observations the conclusion that Hilbert's role began only *after* the physical theory of gravitation was completed?

The answer is certainly more complex than an investigation of the documents on the assumption of a physicist–mathematician competition can reveal. One should rather keep in mind that Einstein in fall 1915 analyzed the possible formalism of general relativity from the point of view of physical arguments (the

One should add that Hilbert's original manuscript did not contain the detailed equations of gravitation; hence, Einstein could not notice that the equations following from Hilbert's variational principle did *not* exactly agree with his own: namely, they revealed an extra trace-term, which Einstein introduced only in his report presented to the Berlin Academy on 25 November 1915 (Einstein, 1915g). III.2 The Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics 397

Newtonian limit of the equations of gravitation, the perihelion motion of Mercury, etc.). Hilbert aimed with his mathematical approach, built upon previous ideas of Gustav Mie and Albert Einstein, at a consistent scheme that would unify all phenomena of field theory, especially the electromagnetic and gravitational ones. He proceeded initially quite independently of Einstein and just added, beginning in the summer of 1915, more of the latter's considerations on the field theory of gravitation. His driving idea was a general invariance principle, from which the fundamental equations for both sets of phenomena followed. Einstein rejected, *after* 18 November 1915, all direct connections between gravitation and electricity, and it may well be that the knowledge of Hilbert's manuscript provided the motive: in contrast to Hilbert, he found Mie's theory confusing and having no physical value at all.$^{481}$ The final big paper on the foundations of general relativity theory in *Annalen der Physik* then confirmed the important conclusion: from general relativity theory one cannot conclude anything about the structure of the electromagnetic field (Einstein, 1916c, p. 815). On the Göttingen publication of the unified scheme (Hilbert, 1915), he remarked in a letter: 'I don't like Hilbert's presentation ... unnecessarily specialized ... needlessly complicated ... not honest in design (vision of the superman, 'Übermensch') by a camouflage of techniques.' (Einstein to Ehrenfest, 24 May 1916)

Hilbert stuck to his programme: the axiomatic scheme not only led to the correct field equations of gravitation, but also provided the link to the electrodynamical theory of matter.$^{482}$ In a second contribution on 'The Foundations of Physics,' he continued to build upon the proposed unified scheme; in particular, a 'space-time axiom' was added that allowed him to formulate a causality principle for the whole theory (Hilbert, 1917). Hilbert also gave several lecture courses at the University of Göttingen in the following years, notably: in the winter semester 1917/18 on 'The Theory of the Electron'; in winter 1918/19 on 'Space and Time'; in the summer semester 1920 on 'The Basic Ideas of Relativity Theory'; and in the winter semester 1923/24 on 'Our Conceptions of Gravitation and Electricity.' In these lectures, some highly technical and others that addressed a wider audience, Hilbert combined elements of his own axiomatic approach with the latest conceptions of the physicists. In 1924, Hilbert reprinted a slightly shortened and somewhat rearranged version of his two papers on 'The Foundations of Physics' (Hilbert, 1924). Meanwhile, Einstein and others also searched for a unification of gravitation and electromagnetism, and Hilbert was 'quite convinced that [his own work on the unified theory] ... contains an enduring core,' though he doubted 'whether in fact the ideal of a pure field-theoretical unity is a definite one' (Hilbert, 1924, p. 2). At that time, he had abandoned a further keen hope, which he had

(395).

398 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

cherished later in the 1910s, namely, that the field-theoretic approach might also solve the quantum problem.$^{483}$

In the 1920s, Göttingen advanced to become a centre of atomic and quantum theory, especially with the arrival of the theoretician Max Born and the experimentalist James Franck. More than ever before, Hilbert had the opportunity to get first-hand information about the latest developments and to discuss the outstanding problems and difficulties with people most directly in the know. As had become his custom, he also gave his own lecture courses on what he considered as the foundations of the theory, notably, two in the winter semesters 1922/23 and 1926/27, respectively. The first was entitled 'Mathematische Grundlagen der Quantentheorie' ('Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Theory'), and it coincided in time with the crucial period when Born and his associates became involved in thorough calculations of atomic systems according to the rules of the (old) Bohr–Sommerfeld quantum theory.$^{484}$ In his lectures, Hilbert displayed in great detail the classical 'Hamilton-Jacobi theory of higher dynamics,' the theoretical scheme that not only was the basis of celestial mechanics, but also of the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory. 'It is the ABC of quantum theory, and its detailed knowledge is essential for understanding the latter,' he opened his course (Lecture Notes 1922/23, p.1). This implied, as far as the mathematical method was concerned, the use of the variational calculus, the 'only method which permits a complete insight into the nature of the problem.'$^{485}$ According to his lecture notes, he covered the entire mathematical apparatus (including the discussion of the Hamilton–Jacobi equation, canonical transformations, action-angle variables, and Hamilton's principle) and its application to atomic theory (including perturbation methods for non-degenerate and degenerate systems).$^{486}$ In their research papers, Born and his collaborators (notably, Werner Heisenberg and Wolfgang Pauli) then proved, on the basis of these semiclassical methods, the final insufficiency of the old quantum theory. On the other hand, they very much influenced the presentation of 'Atomic Mechanics,' the lectures given by Max Born in the following winter semester 1923/24 and published later as a book (Born, 1925). Inasmuch as this book contained the methods advocated by Hilbert, and the extent to which these methods determined the path of Heisenberg, Born, and Jordan to the discovery of quantum mechanics, Hilbert's spirit and his selection of mathematical tools guided the physicists in Göttingen.

$^{483}$ For example, Hilbert expressed such a hope in his 1917/18 lectures on electron theory: a 'pure continuum-theory' may give rise to the quantum-theoretical orbits of electrons in atoms. When Einstein learned about these ideas in 1917 via a student coming from Göttingen, he commented: 'It is too great an audacity to draw already now a picture of the world, since there are still so many things which we cannot remotely anticipate.' (Einstein, quoted in Seelig, 1960, p. 261) A couple of years later, Einstein himself became the primary advocate of this 'audacity,' and remained one until the end of his days.
$^{484}$ See Volume 1, Chapters III and IV, and Volume 2, Chapter II.
$^{485}$ Hilbert, himself a master of the calculus of variations, used to treat dynamical problems with these methods in his lectures.
$^{486}$ Hilbert's lecture notes of 1922/23 were worked out by Lothar Nordheim and Gustav Heckmann (and are preserved in the *Niedersächsische Staats- und Universitätsbibliothek*, Göttingen).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0431 -->

III.2 The Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics 399

Hilbert announced the second lecture course on 'Mathematische Methoden der Quantentheorie' ('Mathematical Methods of Quantum Theory') to be held in fall 1926, a moment chosen quite suitably: quantum and wave mechanics existed already as physical theories describing an increasing wealth of atomic phenomena; still, the internal connection between the two schemes had not yet been established, as far as mathematical rigour was concerned. In addition, the true physical content, even the basic ingredients finally to be used, had not been clarified. Here, Hilbert could hope that his axiomatic method might be able to contribute to a final breakthrough.$^{487}$ In Göttingen, which besides Copenhagen, constituted one of the two central places of progress in quantum mechanics, he had a large number of experts available for consultation concerning specific questions: besides the theoreticians Born and Pascual Jordan (and occasionally their guests, such as Paul Dirac and Robert Oppenheimer), Hilbert's assistant Lothar Nordheim played the main role as mediator of new ideas and attentive reader of recent literature. In addition, the Mathematical Institute had the privilege to house a guest, who became deeply and most effectively involved in the task of what Hilbert considered the 'mathematical foundations of quantum mechanics': John von Neumann.

Again, the lecture notes on 'Mathematical Methods' shows that the now sixty-four-year-old Hilbert really tried to cover most completely the existing quantum-mechanical theories, which he declared to be 'in an evident state of *immaturity* (*in einem offensichtlichen Zustand der Unfertigkeit*).'$^{488}$ However, as he continued:

> For the young striving student this state possesses a peculiar charm; we believe so firmly in the unity of science that we cannot assume a permanence of this state of affairs. Perhaps only a short period will elapse until it will be dissolved. It is the goal of my lecture course to lead you to the frontiers of our knowledge and to prepare you for a most open reception of the new discoveries which have to be expected. (Hilbert, lecture notes on *Mathematische Methoden*, 1926/27, p. 2)

In his lecture course, Hilbert covered the following topics:

Part I. The Old Quantum Theory: On variational calculus; The Hamilton-Jacobi theory; Foundations of the old quantum theory; System with several degrees of freedom; The correspondence principle.

Part II. The New Quantum Mechanics: Matrix mechanics; The general theory of matrix equations; Theory of infinitely many variables and integral equations; Schrödinger's differential equation; Further development of the theory; Application of quantum mechanics to statistical mechanics; The statistical interpretation of quantum mechanics.

$^{487}$ It should be noted that the physical interpretation by means of the transformation theories of Dirac and Jordan, the uncertainty relations of Heisenberg and Bohr's principle of complementarity, had yet to be formulated.
$^{488}$ See 'Mathematische Methoden der Quantentheorie. Vorlesungen gehalten im *W*[inter] *S*[emester] 1926/27 von Geheimrat Prof. Hilbert,' elaborated by L. Nordheim (deposited in the *Niedersächsisches Staats- und Universitätsbibliothek*, Göttingen).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0432 -->

400 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

These topics, and especially the contents of the lectures, make the lecture notes of 1926/27 the most complete review of the entirety of theoretical ideas that were known until then under the name of quantum theory. Of course, Hilbert emphasized with particular care the mathematical aspects (and foundations) of the physical theory, but he also discussed the examples of all characteristic phenomena. His profound knowledge of physical details astounded the auditors, and the later reader must wonder how much of the systematic presentation of quantum mechanics by Hilbert would exist also in the books of the contemporary pioneering quantum physicists, like those of Max Born, Pascual Jordan, Werner Heisenberg, or even Arnold Sommerfeld. For example, Hilbert built the old quantum theory upon the two postulates: (1) The restriction of (classical) mechanics by the (Bohr–Sommerfeld) quantum conditions; (2) The Planck–Einstein frequency condition for atomic radiation. Then followed the Hamilton–Jacobi formalism applied to systems of electrons and atomic nuclei (cf., Hilbert's earlier lecture course of 1922/23). With similar expertise, he developed the topics of the new quantum mechanics, starting with Heisenberg's historic breakthrough and the systematic formulation of his 'quantum-theoretical' Fourier series as 'matrix mechanics' by Born and Jordan.$^{489}$

Hilbert then turned to the 'general integration theory,' i.e., the methods dealing with the eigenvalue problem in quantum mechanics. Starting from the situation in matrix mechanics (see Born, Heisenberg, and Jordan, 1926, Chapter III), he stressed:

> The spectra of infinite forms have been studied under definite convergence conditions. It has been shown that, for quite general assumptions (i.e., for bounded forms) the spectrum consists of two parts, a normal discrete point spectrum and a residue integral—the *Strecken* spectrum; hence, in general, it follows:
> $$\sum H_{nm} x_n \bar{x}_n = \sum W_n y_n \bar{y}_n + \int W(s) y(s) \bar{y}(s) ds \qquad [(316)]$$
> [with $H_{nm}$ denoting the elements of the Hamiltonian matrix having the diagonal terms $W_n$, the diagonalization being achieved by the orthogonal linear transformation $x_n \to y_n$; $\bar{x}_n$ denoting the complex conjugate of $x_n$, etc.].

This result evidently conformed to the real physical situation, since according to experience the discrete term spectrum of [atomic] series is followed in general by a continuous manifold of possible states, i.e., a continuous spectrum. However, one will not succeed in treating these states by the matrix mechanics discussed so far, but must pass over to more general mathematical quantities. (Hilbert, *Mathematische Methoden*, p. 127)

$^{489}$ In these passages, Hilbert followed rather closely Heisenberg's pioneering papers and his review lecture ('Über quantenmechanische Kinematik und Mechanik'), given in December 1925 in the Göttingen mathematical seminar (Heisenberg, 1926a).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0433 -->

**III.2 The Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics** $\qquad$ **401**

These quantities, Hilbert continued, were provided by the mathematical theory of linear integral equations, which formally allowed to pass over from matrix mechanics to Erwin Schrödinger’s wave mechanics; he then discussed its foundations and principal applications (including the statistical behaviour of identical atomic particles) in some detail.

Hilbert opened the last part of his lecture course (entitled ‘*Die statistische Bedeutung der Quantentheorie*’—‘The Statistical Significance of Quantum Theory’) with a discussion of the time-dependent Schrödinger equation and continued with the presentation of Born’s statistical interpretation of the wave amplitudes of scattered atomic particles, i.e., the introduction of the notion of ‘probability amplitudes’ (pp. 204–213). With that, he outlined a final goal, still to be attained, namely:

> Regarding the high importance of quantum mechanics, it appears natural that one attempts to formulate its principles as clearly and generally as possible. Now Jordan has figured out for the foundation [of quantum mechanics] an axiomatics which embraces also a further interpretation, given by Pauli and Dirac to Schrödinger’s equation. These considerations and conceptions of ideas (*Gedankenbildungen*) do indeed require the establishment of an axiomatics according to the principles and points of view that I applied a generation ago to the foundations of geometry. I also believe that in this way certain aspects can be expressed more easily and precisely, and that one does not need for the understanding of these ideas a physical divination (*Hellsehertum*) but just pure logic. (Hilbert, *loc. cit.*, p. 204)

The first half of the section by and large followed §2 of Pascual Jordan’s paper on the transformation theory (Jordan, 1927b). That is, Hilbert’s axioms 1 to 4 developed here corresponded largely to Jordan’s postulates A to D, apart from slight modifications. After this, Hilbert turned to discuss in general a scheme of operators, by which he gave the Schrödinger equation a more secure mathematical basis. We shall return to this part in the following when treating the joint publication of Hilbert with Nordheim and von Neumann (1928).

**(c) John von Neumann and the Elaboration of Hilbert’s Lectures (1927)**

Early in 1926, Hilbert asked the International Education Board to grant a fellowship to the twenty-two-year-old Hungarian Janos von Neumann. When the Secretary of the Board, Augustus Trowbridge, replied that the candidate might not fall into ‘the class of man well advanced in his career, who had already published a sufficient amount so that one can form a judgment of his technical ability,’ Richard Courant wrote back on behalf of Hilbert. He stressed two important facts: first, ‘Mr. von Neumann, in spite of his youth ... is a completely exceptional personality who has already done very productive work’; second, Hilbert would need the candidate especially ‘for investigations in the foundations of mathematics and a programme on completely epoch-making lines initiated by Hilbert ... which

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0434 -->

**402** **Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics**

Mr. von Neumann has already pursued independently.’ With this insistence, the young von Neumann got the stipend and came to Göttingen in fall 1926.$^{490}$

Janos Neumann von Margitta (or John von Neumann, as he called himself later) was born on 28 December 1903, in Budapest, the son of the banker Max von Neumann. In 1914, he entered the Lutheran Gymnasium for males, passing his ‘matura’ in 1921.$^{491}$ According to a classmate, Janos’s mathematical abilities were soon discovered, and he received special attention in this field, notably, from Michael Fekete, an assistant at the University of Budapest. It was also with him that von Neumann published his first scientific paper (Fekete and von Neumann, 1922). Immediately after graduation, he went for higher studies abroad, beginning with mathematics at the University of Berlin (1921–1923) and then concentrating on chemical engineering at the ETH in Zurich, where he received in 1926 the master’s degree in chemistry (‘*Diplomingenieur in Chemie*’). Simultaneously, von Neumann registered at the University of Budapest and passed all of the necessary examinations in course work; thus, he received, also in 1926, his doctorate in mathematics in Hungary with a thesis on axiomatic set theory.

We should add here that not only in Berlin (mainly under the guidance of Erhard Schmidt), but also in Zurich he devoted himself—apart from his engineering studies—in the first place to mathematics: he kept close contacts with George Polya and Hermann Weyl; once, when Weyl had left Zurich for a short period, von Neumann took over his course. Already in the following year, he applied for *Habilitation* at the University of Berlin and submitted a thesis on ‘*Der axiomatische Aufbau der Mengenlehre*’ (‘The Axiomatic Construction of Set Theory’). Supported actively by Schmidt, and having Isaai Schur and Richard von Mises as further referees, the twenty-four-year-old von Neumann passed the colloquium examination on 9 December 1927; he obtained the official degree on 13 December.$^{492}$ However, he would not become a very regular lecturer at the University of Berlin, where he gave his first course in the winter semester 1928/29.$^{493}$

von Neumann opened his paper on set theory for the renowned German *Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik* with the words: ‘The aim of the present work is to give a logically unobjectionable axiomatic treatment of set theory’ (von Neumann, 1925, p. 219). Abraham Fraenkel, an expert on set theory, later recalled about the origin of this paper as follows:

Though he announced a course in Berlin for the summer semester of 1933, it did not materialize because of the policies of the new Nazi government; hence, he gave up his *venia legendi* in Berlin and went to the U.S.A. for good.

**III.2 The Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics** $\qquad$ **403**

Around 1922–23, being a professor at Marburg University, I received from Professor Erhard Schmidt, Berlin (on behalf of the *Redaktion* of the *Mathematische Zeitschrift*), a long manuscript by an author unknown to me, Johann von Neumann, with the title *Die Axiomatisierung der Mengenlehre*, this being his eventual doctoral dissertation which appeared in the *Zeitschrift* only in 1928 (Vol. **27**). I was asked to express my view since it seemed to be incomprehensible. I don’t maintain that I understood everything, but enough to see that it was an outstanding work and to recognize *ex ungue leonem*. While answering in this sense, I invited the young scholar to visit me (in Marburg) and discussed with him, strongly advising him to prepare the ground for the understanding of so technical an essay by a more informal essay which should stress the new access to the problem and its fundamental consequences. He wrote such an essay under the title *Eine Axiomatisierung der Mengenlehre*, and I published it in 1925 in the *Journal für Mathematik* (Vol. **154**) of which I was the Associate Editor. (Ulam, 1958, footnote, p. 10)

von Neumann began his informal paper by mentioning the objections raised at the turn of the century against the ‘naive’ set theory of Georg Cantor, notably, the antinomies of Bertrand Russell and others. To remove those objections, he said, two approaches had been taken: Russell, Luizen, E. J. Brouwer, Hermann Weyl, and their followers argued that the logical foundations of exact sciences had to be restricted to prevent the appearance of antinomies, while Ernst Zermelo, Fraenkel, and others advocated a less radical point of view. von Neumann joined the latter group, because he refused to give up what was considered by Hilbert and many of his colleagues as the major part of mathematics. He therefore outlined in the informal essay an appropriate system of axioms establishing the complete set theory, which he then presented more technically and in a somewhat sharpened form in the publication for *Mathematische Zeitschrift* (von Neumann, 1928b).$^{494}$

von Neumann’s work and general attitude, as expressed already clearly in the earlier publication of 1925, obviously supported the central endeavours of David Hilbert on the axiomatization of mathematics. In a programmatic lecture, given in spring 1922 at Copenhagen and in summer of the same year at the University of Hamburg (and published afterward), Hilbert had proposed a ‘new foundation of mathematics,’ turning simultaneously against the ‘wrong path’ taken by the ‘renowned and highly respected mathematicians Weyl and Brouwer’ (Hilbert, 1922, especially, p. 157).$^{495}$ By operating with a *finite* number of symbols and formulae, he had built a complete set of axioms, which allowed him to derive all known theorems of arithmetic and demonstrated its consistency, i.e., that it was free of contradictions. In these efforts, he had implied as a lemma that every mathematical program can be decided in principle; and, finally, he gave the solution

$^{495}$ See also his lecture presented in September 1922 at the Leipzig *Naturvorscherversammlung* (Hilbert, 1923).

of the toughest problem, that of the continuum.$^{496}$ What von Neumann promised to accomplish in axiomatizing set theory also seemed ‘to realize Hilbert’s goal of treating mathematics as a finite game’ (Ulam, 1958, pp. 11–12); hence, great interest arose to get the young man quickly to Göttingen. We might mention right away that he fully justified the hopes of Hilbert and Courant in supporting the whole ‘new foundations’ programme. In the essay *Zur Hilbertschen Beweistheorie* (‘On Hilbert’s Theory of Proofs’), published in 1927, he reached many of Hilbert’s goals. ‘His great paper (von Neumann, 1927d) is devoted to the problem of the freedom from contradictions of mathematics,’ and his biographer Stanislaw Ulam summarized its contents as follows:

> This classical study contains an exposition of the primitive ideas underlying mathematical formalisms in general. It stressed that the whole complex of problems, originated and developed by Hilbert and also treated by [P.] Bernays and [W.] Ackermann, have not been satisfactorily solved. In particular, it is pointed out that Ackermann’s proof of freedom from contradiction cannot be carried through in classical analysis. It is replaced by a rigorous finitary proof for a certain subsystem. In fact von Neumann’s proof shows (though this is not stated explicitly) that finitely iterated application of quantifiers and propositional convectives to any finitary (i.e., decidable) relations is consistent. This is not far from the limit of what can be obtained on the basis of Hilbert’s original programme, i.e., with strictly finite methods. (Ulam, 1958, p. 13)

von Neumann would also contribute materially to the fifth of Hilbert’s Paris problems in a paper on the analytical properties of groups of linear transformations (von Neumann, 1929d).$^{497}$

After von Neumann had arrived in Göttingen, Hilbert began his lecture course on the mathematical methods of quantum theory. Lothar Nordheim, Hilbert’s assistant for physics, recalled:

Hilbert was quite ill in these years, and not the same man he was before he had pernicious anemia. And he was just saved in time by the development of the liver treat-

Lubben (who did the same for the spherical geometry in a plane); others succeeded in some three-dimensional geometries. ment.... I had to teach him quantum mechanics and wave mechanics.... It was also the duty of his assistant to prepare his lectures which was sometimes rather strenuous. You had to make clear outlines of the number of sessions and so on. (Nordheim, AHQP Interview, p. 10)

Hilbert had not only witnessed the rise of the new quantum mechanics, but also showed immediate interest in it from the outset. Already, in November 1925, he invited Werner Heisenberg to talk about his discovery and the ensuing work of Max Born, Pascual Jordan, Paul Dirac, and himself in the Göttingen mathematical seminar (Heisenberg, 1926a). The rapid growth of the new atomic theory in 1926—including Schrödinger’s wave mechanics—demanded, however, great attention by an outsider like Hilbert, and Nordheim had a tough time in assisting him to understand the details that formed the content of Part II of the lectures given by him (Hilbert) in the winter semester 1926/27. ‘At that time the first papers on what we call now the transformation theory in quantum mechanics appeared by Dirac, and in a very tortuous form by Jordan,’ Nordheim recalled, and in particular:

In one of the courses of Hilbert I tried to prepare this for him, and then at that time von Neumann came to Göttingen, and he helped a little bit in the elaboration of it. This paper (Hilbert, von Neumann and Nordheim, 1928) I think is quite elegant, but it is absolutely unacceptable mathematically. Such integral operations over improper functions and all these things occur, but they stimulated von Neumann to develop his theory. He really brought the proper mathematical tools to bear on the mathematics of the transformation theory: the Hilbert operators and so on. (Nordheim, AHQP Interview, p. 13)

From the lecture notes of ‘*Mathematische Methoden der Quantentheorie*,’ referred to earlier, however, not much influence of Dirac’s ‘improper’ methods can be recognized, except at one place in connection with the kernel of unit integral operator (of Axiom 3 on p. 117), where Hilbert introduced a function about which he mentioned: ‘Such a function does not really exist but one can consider it as a limit of a sequence of continuous functions . . . and then use it in calculations as if it were a real function.’ (Hilbert, *Mathematische Methoden*, p. 117)⁴⁹⁸ As Nordheim recalled later, he translated, after the lecture course and for the paper, just Dirac’s ideas into Hilbert’s mathematical language involving the operators, ‘and then von Neumann helped very much polishing it up and bringing it into final form’ (Nordheim, AHQP Interview, p. 13).
The thirty-page paper that emerged from these joint efforts therefore developed from Hilbert’s lectures, but did not reproduce at all its contents; it was received by *Mathematische Annalen* on 6 April 1927. The introduction stated properly about the origin:

406 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

The present memoir has emerged from a lecture course given by Hilbert in the winter semester 1926/27 on the more recent development of quantum mechanics, in which L. Nordheim assisted materially. Important parts of the mathematical elaboration were contributed by J. von Neumann. The final version has been prepared by L. Nordheim. We believe that the formulation of the ideas by Jordan and Dirac, at which we have arrived here, has become much simpler and therefore more transparent and more easy to understand. (Hilbert *et al.*, 1928, p. 1)

The physical content of quantum mechanics, so the authors recognized, consisted in replacing the strict functional relations of the classical mechanics by probability relations, such that between two quantum-mechanical quantities a probability relation always exists. To obtain the mathematical scheme for this task, Hilbert and associates proceeded in the following way:

One imposes certain physical conditions on the probabilities which are suggested by our present knowledge. . . . Then one seeks, in a second step, a simple analytic apparatus containing quantities that satisfy the same relations [between the probabilities]. This analytic apparatus, and therefore the quantities involved, now obtain on the basis of the physical requirements a physical interpretation. The goal is to formulate the physical requirements so completely that they fix the mathematical apparatus entirely. (Hilbert *et al.*, *loc. cit.*, p. 2)

Evidently, the whole procedure led to an axiomatization of quantum mechanics, similar to the one given before by Hilbert in geometry. The objects entering the relations of geometry—namely, points, straight lines, and planes—can be described by the analytical apparatus of linear equations; in quantum mechanics, the real facts—i.e., the measurable values of physical quantities—follow from relations between operators describing dynamical variables, and these operators constitute the analytical (mathematical) apparatus.
When physicists establish a new theory, they normally proceed along a different path: they guess the analytical apparatus well before having recognized all physical requirements, that is, the complete system of axioms; the fundamental physical relations are then obtained by the interpretation of the chosen mathematical formalism. ‘It is very difficult to understand such a theory if one does not distinguish clearly both aspects, the formalism and its physical interpretation,’ Hilbert and associates reproached this procedure; rather, they promised to carry through the necessary separation ‘as clearly as possible,’ even ‘though we do not and cannot yet formulate, due to the present state of the theory, a complete axiomatics,’ adding:

What is so far fixed uniquely is the mathematical apparatus which—from the purely mathematical point of view—cannot be changed. What may be changed, however, and also will be changed, is the physical interpretation, for which there exists a certain freedom and arbitrariness. (Hilbert *et al.*, *loc. cit.*, p. 3)

And finally they claimed: ‘By the axiomatization the previously somewhat vague concepts, such as probability, etc., lose their mystical nature, because they are then

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0439 -->

III.2 The Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics 407

defined implicitly by axioms.’ Though Hilbert himself ‘did almost none of the work, the spirit was quite definitely his’ (Reid, 1970, p. 183).
In establishing the system of axioms for quantum mechanics, the authors (in §2 of their paper) followed more closely (than Hilbert had done in his lectures) in the footsteps of Pascual Jordan (in the paper on the transformation theory, 1927b), but they extended the four postulates of Jordan into six axioms; in addition, they did not mix physical conditions with relations for the analytic apparatus (as Jordan had done). Thus, Axiom I of Hilbert and associates defined the probability amplitude $\phi(x, y; F_1, F_2)$ in the case of two dynamical quantities $F_1$ and $F_2$, namely, that for a given value $y$ of $F_2$ the value of $F_1$ assumes a value between $x$ and $x + dx$. Axiom III demanded that in the relation of a quantity $F$ to itself a sharp determination is possible—that is, with each dynamical quantity a definite numerical value can be associated. Axiom IV established the addition and multiplication theorems for probability amplitudes, and Axiom VI required that the probabilities do not depend on the choice of the coordinate system.
Section 3 outlined the analytic formalism chosen by the authors, namely, a system of what they called ‘complete (*vollständige*)’ operators $T_{(y)}^{(x)}$ defined by their action on functions as

$$T_{(y)}^{(x)}(f(y)) = (Tf)(x). \qquad (317)$$

These particular operators can then be represented by integral operators, i.e.,

$$T_{\phi (y)}^{(x)}(f(y)) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \phi(x, y)f(y) dy, \qquad (318)$$

with the kernels $\phi(x, y)$. Next, Hilbert and associates introduced Dirac’s function $\delta(x - y)$ as a special kernel, namely, to define the unit operator $I_{(y)}^{(x)}$ in their system,

$$I_{(y)}^{(x)}(f(x)) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \delta(x - y)f(y) dy = f(x). \qquad (319)$$

Now, they claimed: ‘With the help of such kernels one can in general represent each operator as an integral operator.’ (Hilbert *et al.*, *loc. cit.*, p. 8) The system thus generalized satisfied the usual relations for linear operators, including the composition rule

$$\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \phi(x, u)\phi^{-1}(u, y) du = \delta(x - y). \qquad (320)$$

The new formalism allowed, in particular, to define the two special operators $F$ and $G$,

$$F_{(x)}^{(x)} = T_{\phi (x)}^{(x)} x T_{\phi (x)}^{(x)} \quad \text{and} \quad G_{(x)}^{(x)} = T_{\phi (x)}^{(x)} \left( \varepsilon \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \right) T_{\phi (x)}^{-1(x)} \qquad (321)$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0440 -->

408 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

(with $\varepsilon = h/2\pi i$), which satisfy the functional equations

$$(F_{(x)}^{(x)} - y)\phi(x, y) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \left(G_{(x)}^{(x)} + \varepsilon \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\right)\phi(x, y) = 0. \qquad (322)$$

Eqs. (322) played a fundamental role when Hilbert and associates formulated the canonical version of their operator scheme in §4 of their paper. For this purpose, they introduced the fundamental operators $q$ and $p$ through the defining equations

$$qf(x) = xf(x) \quad \text{and} \quad pf(x) = \varepsilon \frac{\partial f(x)}{\partial x}. \qquad (323)$$

Then, $F$ and $G$ simply represent the result of a canonical transformation of the operators $p$ and $q$, which (also) satisfy the quantum-mechanical commutation relations

$$GF - FG = \varepsilon 1. \qquad (324)$$

Further, every $F$ can be obtained from $q$ by a canonical transformation; and the same holds for $G$ and $p$.
For a physical interpretation of their mathematical formalism, the authors had to provide the physical relations for the probability amplitudes, which they did by following Erwin Schrödinger’s procedure (in §5). Schrödinger had obtained operators $F(p, q)$ from the corresponding classical variables (as functions of their arguments, the momentum and position coordinates) by inserting quantum-mechanical operators $p \left(= \varepsilon \frac{\partial}{\partial q} \right)$ and $q$, up to the well-known ambiguity of the sequence of operator factors $p$ and $q$ in operator products. The central interpretation rule was thus formulated by Hilbert and associates as:

The probability amplitude $\phi(x, y; q, F)$ connecting the coordinate $q$ and an arbitrary mechanical variable $F(p, q)$—i.e., for the situation that, for a given value $y$ of $F$ the coordinate $q$ assumes values between $x$ and $x + dx$—is given by the kernel of the integral operator, which transforms the operator $q$ into the operator associated with the mechanical quantity. (Hilbert, *et al.*, *loc. cit.*, p. 14)

When this situation is generalized to the case of two dynamical variables $F_1(p, q)$ and $F_2(p, q)$, the corresponding probability amplitude $\phi(x, y; F_1, F_2)$ will be determined by the kernel of the operator product $T_1^{-1}T_2$, where $T_1$ and $T_2$ are the operators that transform $q$ into the operators $F_1$ and $F_2$, respectively. Both definitions were then shown to satisfy all axioms or postulates of §2.
According to the fundamental Axiom I, the probability density $w(x, y; F_1, F_2)$—i.e., the relative probability density for the situation that, for a given value $y$ of

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0441 -->

III.2 The Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics 409

$F_2$, the value of $F_1$ lies between $x$ and $x + dx$—is determined by the absolute square of the complex amplitude $\phi(x, y; F_1, F_2)$, i.e.,

$$ w(x, y; F_1, F_2) = \phi(x, y; F_1, F_2) \bar{\phi}(x, y; F_1, F_2), \quad (325) $$

where the bar denotes the complex conjugate. In physics, these probability densities must come out both real and positive (§6). Then, the amplitude $\phi(x, y; F_1, F_2)$ must satisfy the equation

$$ \phi^{-1}(y, x; F_2, F_1) = \bar{\phi}(x, y; F_1, F_2). \quad (326) $$

For the operator system used by Hilbert and associates, this implied that quantum-mechanical operators must be Hermitean, or symbolically,

$$ A = A^\dagger, \quad (327) $$

because $A$ and the adjoint operator $A^\dagger$ satisfy the integral relation

$$ \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} [g(u) A^{(u)} f(u) - f(u) \bar{A}^{\dagger (u)} g(u)] du = 0 \quad (328) $$

identical in arbitrary functions $f(u)$ and $g(u)$. Evidently, the kernel of the adjoint operator $A^\dagger$ will be $\bar{\phi}(y, x)$, if $\phi(x, y)$ is the kernel of $A$.
The Hermiticity of the quantum-mechanical operators leads to practical consequences, which the authors summarized in §7 of their paper, notably: (1) for an arbitrary composite operator $A(p, q)$, one obtains the adjoint by inverting the order of factors in the products of $p$ and $q$ and replacing all constants $c$ (except $\varepsilon$) by the complex-conjugate $\bar{c}$. (2) To every Hermitean operator $F$, a 'canonically conjugate' operator $G$ (in the sense of §4) corresponds that is also Hermitean. (3) Canonical transformations must be expressed by operators $T$ that are 'Hermitean orthogonal' or satisfy the condition

$$ T^\dagger T = 1. \quad (329) $$

The physical implication of these 'reality requirements' appeared so obvious that the authors simply stated: 'We shall assume that only Hermitean operators may be connected with physical quantities' (Hilbert *et al.*, *loc. cit.*, p. 23). In particular, the Hermiticity requirement fixed the order of operators in operator products in the quantum-mechanical Hamiltonian by symmetrization (§8).
In Sections 9 and 10, the authors proceeded to derive some important conclusions from their formalism in quantum mechanics. First, they obtained for the special amplitude $\phi(x, y; q, p)$, up to an unimportant factor, the expression

$$ \phi(x, y; q, p) = \exp(xy/\varepsilon), \quad (330) $$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0442 -->

410 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

yielding the fundamental result: For a given value $x$ of the position coordinate $q$, all values $y$ of $p$ are equally probable. The same followed in the case that the canonically conjugate pair is replaced by any other such pair $F$ and $G$. Second, if $F$ is identified with the Hamiltonian $H$ of a quantum-mechanical problem, then from the first Eq. (322)—with the Schrödinger amplitude $\phi(x, W; q, H)$ replacing $\phi(x, y)$—time-independent Schrödinger equation resulted in

$$\left\{ H \left( \varepsilon \frac{\partial}{\partial x}, x \right) - W \right\} \phi(x, W; q, H) = 0, \qquad (331)$$

where $W$ denotes the energy values. On the other hand, the time-dependent Schrödinger equation arose from the second Eq. (322) with the identification $G = H$ and the canonically conjugate $t(p, q)$ replacing $F(p, q)$,

$$\left\{ H \left( \varepsilon \frac{\partial}{\partial x}, x \right) + \varepsilon \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \right\} \phi(x, y; q, t). \qquad (332)$$

The general solution of Eq. (331) was written by Hilbert, von Neumann, and Nordheim in the form

$$\phi(x, y; q, H) = \sum_{n} c_n \psi_n(x) \delta(W - W_n) + \psi(x, W) c(W). \qquad (333)$$

That is, the energy spectrum of the system described by the Hamiltonian $H$ contains a discrete (the sum) and a continuous term [in which the normalization constants $c_n$ and $c(W)$ denoted the statistical *a priori* probabilities of the single discrete quantum states and the intervals of the continuous spectrum]. 'Formally one can, by a suitable application of the improper function, write the [operator] calculus as a kind of matrix calculus and thus express clearly the genuinely discrete nature of quantum mechanics, as Dirac has essentially done,' the authors commented and added:

> From the mathematical point of view the method of calculation used this way must be considered unsatisfactory, since one never knows to what extent the operations occurring can be really performed. Therefore we shall not enter further into the elaboration of these ideas. (Hilbert *et al.*, *loc. cit.*, p. 30)

In a footnote, they announced a paper of von Neumann to appear very soon in the Göttingen *Nachrichten*. Indeed, von Neumann found the manipulations with improper functions particularly unsatisfactory and eagerly searched for their replacement by more rigorous methods of calculation.
In spite of such reservations, Hilbert and his collaborators concluded optimistically:

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0443 -->

III.2 The Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 411

The general theory certainly receives in our presentation such a transparent and formally simple shape that we have carried it through here in the mathematically still imperfect version, since a completely rigorous presentation might turn out to be much more laborious and intricate. (Hilbert *et al.*, *loc. cit.*)

In the following subsection, we shall see how von Neumann succeeded in obtaining what was considered to be the completely rigorous presentation, i.e., *the mathematical foundation of quantum mechanics*.

**(d) von Neumann’s Mathematical Foundation of Quantum Mechanics**

The paper of Hilbert, von Neumann, and Nordheim attempted the mathematical formulation of quantum-mechanical problems in terms of operators describing physical (mechanical or dynamical) variables and kernel functions describing probability amplitudes. About six weeks after the completion of this work, von Neumann submitted a different approach to the *Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften* in Göttingen in a paper, entitled simply ‘*Mathematische Begründung der Quantenmechanik*’ (‘Mathematical Foundation of Quantum Mechanics,’ von Neumann, 1927a). In the introduction, he explained the motivation of this new study: The two theoretical schemes proposed by the physicists did not really allow one to obtain the eigenvalue spectrum of the quantum-mechanical Hamiltonians. Thus, matrix mechanics exhibited insurmountable diagonalization difficulties unless the energy spectrum of the problem under consideration was discrete; also, Dirac’s proposal of ‘continuous matrices’ could not be justified with mathematical rigour, because ‘one must introduce with it concepts like infinitely large matrix elements or infinitely close diagonals’ (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 2). Schrödinger’s wave-equation method, on the other hand, had to be complemented by the probability considerations derived from matrix mechanics; however, ‘the complete procedure, as developed by Jordan (1927b) into a closed system is subject to grave objections as well,’ von Neumann complained (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 3). In addition, he argued, both matrix and wave mechanics worked with quantities that were unobservable and therefore made no physical sense: undetermined phases of eigenfunctions and undetermined orthogonal transformation matrices in degenerate problems. Though the final results of the calculations in both schemes of the physicists turn out to be free of such unsatisfactory features, ‘the detour via unobservable and non-invariant elements’ should not be admitted. ‘In the present paper we try to give a method which remedies these abuses and summarizes, so we believe, in a unified and systematic way, the statistical point of view in quantum mechanics.’ (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 3)<sup>499</sup>

<sup>499</sup> It must be mentioned that von Neumann was not yet aware of the development of the physical interpretation of quantum mechanics, which occurred at the same time in Copenhagen. Indeed, he would not refer at all, in the work we are about to discuss, to the uncertainty relations and the complementarity considerations. He would, rather, adopt a point of view closer to Dirac’s, namely, that these Copenhagen considerations should follow from the mathematical formalism.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0444 -->

412 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

Von Neumann organized the long fifty-seven-page memoir into six parts, to which he added a summary and several appendices. As a central task, he addressed the following: instead of proposing, like the physicists (notably, Dirac, 1927a), a new calculus of ‘improper functions,’ he exploited all available methods of the mathematicians, especially, the largely developed theory of Hilbert spaces.$^{500}$ von Neumann derived the idea for the new approach to a ‘mathematical foundation’ from the following criticism of the quantum-mechanical transformation theory developed by the physicists, as he recalled later:

> The method [of the physicists] . . . resulted in an analogy between the “discrete” space of index values $Z(= 1, 2, \dots)$ and the continuous state space $\Omega$ of the mechanical system ($\Omega$ is $k$-dimensional, where $k$ is the number of classical-mechanical degrees of freedom). That this cannot be achieved without some violence to the formalism and to mathematics is not surprising. The spaces $Z$ and $\Omega$ are in reality very different, and every attempt to relate the two must run into great difficulties.
>
> What we do have, however, is not a relation of $Z$ to $\Omega$, i.e., between the sequences $X_1, X_2, \dots$ which are the functions in $Z$, and the wave functions $\phi(q_1, \dots, q_k)$ which are functions in $\Omega$. These functions, furthermore, are the entities which enter most essentially into the problems of quantum mechanics. (von Neumann, 1932a, pp. 15–16; English translation, p. 28)

What could one do to establish a better relation between the two different spaces?
In the first (and longest) part of his memoir, entitled ‘*Der Hilbertsche Raum* (The Hilbert Space),’ von Neumann identified $Z$ with a ‘complex Hilbert space’ $\mathcal{H}_0$ of denumerably many dimensions, and $\Omega$ with another Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ of square-integrable Schrödinger functions. Because both spaces exhibit many properties that formally agree—as was confirmed by the equivalence proofs of the physicists—von Neumann found: ‘It is suggestive to characterize all these spaces by their common properties, and to call a space which possesses all given characteristics the “abstract Hilbert space.”’ (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 15) He denoted this abstract Hilbert space by $\overline{\mathcal{H}}$ and defined it through the following axioms:

A. $\overline{\mathcal{H}}$ is a linear space.
B. $\overline{\mathcal{H}}$ is a metrical space, the metric arising from a Hermitean-symmetric bilinear form $Q(f, g)$.
C. $\overline{\mathcal{H}}$ possesses infinitely many dimensions.
D. There exists a sequence that is everywhere dense in $\overline{\mathcal{H}}$.
E. In $\overline{\mathcal{H}}$ the convergence condition of Cauchy applies.
(von Neumann, 1927a, pp. 15–17)

Von Neumann later on called the Hilbert space satisfying the property D as the ‘separable Hilbert space’ (von Neumann, 1932a, p. 26). From these axioms, he

***

# III.2  The Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

413

immediately derived consequences, in particular, the existence of completely normalized orthogonal systems.

In the second part (on ‘Operatorkalkül’ or the ‘Operator Calculus’), von Neumann presented a calculus of linear operators that did not depend on their specific realization (either in \( Z \) or \( \Omega \)): these operators are functions defined in the abstract \( \mathcal{H} \)-space (or parts of it), having as values the points (elements) of \( \mathcal{H} \). Besides the elementary operators \( O \) (the zero operator) and \( I \) (the unit operator), he introduced what he now called ‘Einzeloperatoren’ \( E \)—later renamed ‘Projektionsoperatoren’ (‘Projection Operators’). They satisfy the relation

\[ E^2 = E \tag{334} \]

and exhibit many convenient properties, especially the fact that they all commute with each other.⁵⁰¹

In the following part, ‘Das Eigenwertproblem’ (‘The Eigenvalue Problem’), von Neumann followed Hilbert’s 1906 procedure closely in the new language of operators; thus, he expressed, instead of a symmetrical bilinear form, a symmetrical operator in the ‘eigenvalue representation’

\[ T = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} l \, dE(l), \tag{335} \]

where \( l \) denotes the eigenvalue parameter.⁵⁰² He remarked: ‘In this memoir Hilbert has essentially solved the eigenvalue problem of bounded bilinear forms. However, we omit here always the separation of point and continuous spectrum.’ (von Neumann, 1927a, footnote 26, p. 33) He immediately added, however:

> At the moment it is not self-evident whether each symmetrical operator admits an eigenvalue representation, and whether this is uniquely defined. For bounded operators, according to Hilbert’s theorem [quoted in Footnote (501)], always one and only one such representation [having a discrete and a continuous eigenvalue spectrum in general] exists; for unbounded operators at least the uniqueness is certain. (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 34)

In a footnote added to the last sentence, he referred to a further investigation soon to be published in the *Mathematische Annalen*, in which he could indeed show
