⁵⁰² He called \( E(l) \) ‘the decomposition of unity (Zerlegung der Einheit)’ connected with the operator \( T \) (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 33). The operator \( E(l) \) is a projection operator; hence, it satisfies Eq. (334). It is constant everywhere, except at the eigenvalues, where it makes a discontinuous jump such that \( E(l) \) increases monotonically. The representation (335) makes sense only for functions \( f \) giving rise to a finite integral \( \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} l^2 \, dQ(E(l)f) \), with \( Q(E(l)f) \) denoting the norm of the Hilbert-space ‘vector’ \( E(l)f \).

414  Chapter III  The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

that, for real symmetrical operators, a unique solution always followed, Eq. (335), and the same might be ‘guessed’ for Hermitean operators. Before we treat this publication, which actually appeared only some time later (von Neumann, 1929a), let us complete the discussion of the 1927 investigation.

Having defined the notion of ‘the absolute value of an operator’ and given its properties in the fourth part of the paper, von Neumann turned—in the fifth part, entitled ‘Der statistische Ansatz der Quantenmechanik (The Statistical Formulation of Quantum Mechanics)’—to what he proclaimed to be ‘our mathematically rigorous unification of statistical quantum mechanics’ (von Neumann, 1927a, p. 42). In particular, he succeeded in generalizing, within his operator formalism, the probability Ansatz of Pauli and Dirac—who had claimed that the probability for a quantum-mechanical system in the \( n \)-th discrete state (with wave function \( \phi_n \)) to lie in a fixed region \( K \) of the coordinate space is given by \( \left| \int_K |\phi_n(q)|^2 dq \right| \)—in the following way:

> If the values of the quantities \( R_1, R_2 \ldots, R_i \) lie in the intervals \( I_1, I_2 \ldots, I_i \), and those of the quantities \( S_1, S_2 \ldots, S_j \) in the intervals \( J_1, J_2 \ldots, J_j \), the product \( E_1(I_1) \cdot \ldots \cdot E_i(I_i) \cdot F_1(J_1) \cdot \ldots \cdot F_j(J_j) \) must be formed (in this general way such that the multiplication law of probabilities is valid!). Its absolute value
>
> \[ \left[ E_1(I_1) \cdot \ldots \cdot E_i(I_i) \cdot F_1(J_1) \cdot \ldots \cdot F_j(J_j) \right] \]
>
> \[ = \left[ E_1(I_1) \cdot \ldots \cdot E_i(I_i), F_1(J_1) \cdot \ldots \cdot F_j(J_j) \right] \tag{336} \]
>
> then determines the relative probability of their coexistence. (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 50)

The square brackets denote the ‘scalar product’ of the Hilbert-space vectors involved.⁵⁰³ From his Eq. [(336)], von Neumann arrived at important physical conclusions, namely:

One should notice that in this scheme a separation of cause and effect need not exist at all *a priori*; it will rather be created automatically *a posteriori* by the commutation relations: if all \( E_\mu(I_\mu) \), on the one hand, and all \( F_\nu(J_\nu) \), on the other hand, commute mutually, then the product automatically splits into two groups. Within one group the sequence of factors does not matter, just as the sequences of both groups as a whole—that is, it does not matter what is called “cause” and what “effect”.

---

⁵⁰³ In Eq. [(336)], the \( E \)’s and \( F \)’s are the projection operators representing the eigenvalue spectrum, according to Eq. (335), of the operators associated with the quantities \( R \) and \( S \), respectively. Evidently, Eq. [(336)] is the generalization of the Pauli–Dirac definition, because in the case of \( R \) and \( S \) being represented by the Hamiltonian operator and the position operator, respectively, one can write

\[ \sum_{l_n \text{ in } I} \int_J |\phi_n(q)|^2 dq = \sum_{l_n \text{ in } I} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} |F(q)\phi_n(q)|^2 dq \]

\[ = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \int_\Omega |F(q)E(l', l'')\phi_n(q)|^2 dq = [E(I), F(J)], \]

where \( l_n \) are the discrete energy states and \( \phi_n(q) \) is the Schrödinger function.

# III.2  The Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

415

However, [the commutation relations] exclude certain distributions [of operators in groups \( E \) or \( F \), respectively]: it is not possible to enforce the usually existing absolutely sharp causal connection among commuting quantities in all cases [i.e., for all quantities] by observing (as in classical mechanics) all coordinates and all conjugate momenta, and put them all together into the group of causes, say of \( R_\mu \)’s … The reason is that the operators of a position coordinate \( q_\mu \) and its conjugate momentum \( \left( \frac{h}{2\pi i} \right) \partial / \partial q_\mu \) do not commute; they will always automatically separate [into two groups]: one must be the cause, the other the effect (that is, be the observed and the predicted, respectively). (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, pp. 50–51)

Four months after submitting the above weighty memoir, in September 1927, von Neumann spoke at the fourth *Deutsche Mathematikertag* in Bad Kissingen on the (already mentioned) continuation of his programme. In a talk entitled ‘Eigenwertprobleme symmetrischer Funktionaloperatoren’ (‘Eigenvalue Problems of Symmetrical Functional Operators’), he sketched ‘the extension of Hilbert’s theory to *all* symmetrical operators,’ which he had already promised in May (von Neumann, 1928a, p. 13). Again, he relied on the procedure involving the ‘Einzel operators’; the difficulties that might arise in the case of unbounded operators were removed by reducing the range of the operators, i.e., an unbounded symmetrical operator is defined *only in a dense part of the Hilbert space* (and cannot be extended beyond without losing its symmetry property). For these so-called ‘maximal operators,’ a unique eigenvalue-spectrum representation could always be proven. von Neumann wrote the details in another long memoir with the title ‘Allgemeine Eigenwerttheorie Hermitescher Funktionaloperatoren’ (‘General Eigenvalue Theory of Hermitean Functional Operators’) and used it for his *Habilitation* thesis in December 1927. The actual publication in *Annalen der Mathematik* appeared more than a year afterward (von Neumann, 1929a). Again, the results were described in a more than eighty-page memoir with proper mathematical rigour and care in a systematic order with the following subsections:

(1) The abstract Hilbert space \( \mathcal{H} \);  
(2) Operators in \( \mathcal{H} \);  
(3) Linear manifolds and projection operators;  
(4) Reducibility of operators;  
(5) The Cayley transformation;  
(6) Elements of generalization;  
(7) The defect indices;  
(8) The process of continuation;  
(9) The hypermaximal operators and the eigenvalue representation;  
(10) Maximal but not hypermaximal operators;  
(11) Semi-boundedness;  
(12) Pathology of unbounded operators.

von Neumann also added four appendices, on ‘functional spaces,’ ‘the eigenvalue problem of unitary operators,’ ‘operators and matrices,’ and ‘the operator \( R \),’ respectively.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0448 -->

416  Chapter III  The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

From the formal outline of the paper, one can guess the mathematical erudition displayed by von Neumann to deal with his task. One of the main outcomes of the effort was the following: in order to get a unique eigenvalue spectrum of unbounded operators, the author had to restrict their range of validity further beyond what he had called ‘maximal’ in September 1927 to what he now called ‘hypermaximal.’⁵⁰⁴ He also showed that every semibounded linear Hilbert space operator can be continued to become a hypermaximal operator (Theorem 43 of Section XI).⁵⁰⁵ We may recognize in this result an overlap with the conclusions by another mathematician, who also extended Hilbert’s eigenvalue theory of unbounded bilinear forms: Aurel Wintner (see the following subsection).

By and large, the Herculean work of the young Hungarian mathematician—John von Neumann—in 1927, to which he added several further investigations later, established the hopes and guesses of the theoretical physicists on a solid basis, which did satisfy the requirements of rigour demanded by his professional colleagues. Still, he emphasized that ‘the general theory of Hilbert operators does not reproduce everywhere the behaviour generally suspected and assumed [by the physicists] in the “transformation theory” on the basis of the analogy with bounded or even finite-dimensional operators’ (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 62). In his second paper of 1929, ‘Zur Theorie der unbeschränkten Matrizen’ (‘On the Theory of Unbounded Matrices’), von Neumann stressed another difficulty: in order to obtain the eigenvalues of an unbounded Hermitean matrix, one needed another restriction, namely, the matrices had to be ‘quadrebar (squarable)’—or the sum of the absolute squares of row elements must assume a finite value (von Neumann, 1929b).⁵⁰⁶

In Chapter III of his later book ‘Mathematische Grundlagen der Quantenmechanik’ (‘Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics’), von Neumann provided a systematic, more pedagogical, account of his results obtained between 1927 and 1929 on the rigorous formulation of the quantum-mechanical transformation theory (von Neumann, 1932a). From this book, the mathematicians, and especially the physicists, could learn the mathematical apparatus of modern atomic theory: the necessary definitions and axioms of the abstract separable Hilbert space and the theorems that could be proved for those Hermitean operators, which then had to be identified with the quantum-mechanical variables. As an example, we refer to the careful treatment of the fundamental position and momentum operators in Section 8 of Chapter III. The *Mathematische Grundlagen*, of which the English translation appeared only as late as 1955, has been used by students and professionals alike and given rise to many further investigations,

III.2 The Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics 417

extensions, and refinements, as well as to some criticism in matters of detail. ‘Apart from the great didactic value of this work which presented the ideas of the new quantum theory in a form congenial and technically interesting to mathematicians,’ judged Stanislaw Ulam, a colleague and occasional collaborator of von Neumann’s:

> it is a contribution of absolutely first importance, considered as an attempt to make a rational presentation of a physical theory which, as originally conceived by physicists, was based on non-universally communicable intuitions. While it cannot be asserted that it introduced ideas of novel physical impact . . . von Neumann’s treatment allows at least *one* logically and mathematically clear basis for a rigorous treatment. (Ulam, 1958, pp. 22–23)

One must emphasize, at this point, that the *Mathematische Grundlagen* remained the standard account for decades after this judgment.$^{507}$ On the other hand, the book contained much material on the mathematical foundation of quantum mechanics beyond what has been discussed above, notably, precise and definite ideas on the role of statistical mechanics and the problem of measurement, which he first addressed in a third fundamental contribution of the year 1927; we shall discuss its ingenious contents in the next section (III.3).

**(e) Aurel Wintner and The Spectral Theory of Infinite Matrices (1925–1929)**

The Leipzig mathematician, Leon Lichtenstein, when introducing a new work of a ‘young, highly gifted author’ also from Leipzig, Aurel Wintner—who that spring had completed his book entitled ‘*Spektraltheorie der unendlichen Matrizen* (*The Spectral Theory of Infinite Matrices*, Wintner, 1929)’—made the following general statements:

> Through the latest development of quantum theory connected with Werner Heisenberg, the theory of infinite matrices founded by Hilbert and continued by Hellinger and Toeplitz has obtained a renewed actuality. While, as far as applications are concerned, up to now in first place the theory of continuous (*vollstetig*) forms played a role, now in particular the deep-lying Hilbert-Hellinger spectral theory of bounded forms obtains prominence. The Hermitean forms of matrix mechanics are, by the way, not even bounded . A complete, mathematically consistent, theory of quantum-mechanical matrices is so far absolutely lacking. Both analysis and theoretical physics, therefore, take an interest in the further development of the theory. (Lichtenstein, in Wintner, 1929, pp. vii and viii)

$^{507}$ What George Mackey, a specialist in the field, remarked in his review article on ‘Quantum Mechanics and Hilbert Space’—namely, that ‘the formulation given here is based essentially on what can be found in von Neumann’s classic book’ (Mackey, 1957, p. 57)—had to be repeated many times in later decades.

418 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

Lichtenstein, a senior mathematics professor at the University of Leipzig, showed great interest in problems of theoretical physics.$^{508}$ He worked in particular on problems of hydrodynamics, but also on the mathematical treatment of astronomical and other physical topics; thus, he founded a mathematical school in Leipzig whose members, including his students Ernst Hölder and Herbert Beckert, continued the programme of mathematical physics even beyond 1933.$^{509}$ In the summer semester 1927, Aurel Wintner, a senior student from Hungary, joined Lichtenstein’s circle.$^{510}$ Wintner had studied from 1920 to 1924 at the University of Budapest and worked from 1922 to 1927 as an employee of a bank; he interrupted this employment twice to study theoretical astronomy in Vienna and finally continued his academic education in early 1927 at the University of Göttingen. In Leipzig, he passed his doctoral examination already in summer 1928. Lichtenstein, who had given him the position of a private assistant, served, together with the astronomer Julius Bauschinger, as supervisor of the thesis, entitled ‘Über die Konvergenzfragen der Mondtheorie (On the Convergence Problems of Lunar Theory).’ Werner Heisenberg pronounced Wintner’s thesis to be ‘excellent’ and stated after the oral examination: ‘Extended knowledge of physics, and in some special fields the candidate is excellently informed.’$^{511}$ A fine career seemed to open up for the fresh Ph.D., who, besides working in Lichtenstein’s Institute, also served as editorial assistant (*Redaktionsassistent*) for the *Mathematische Zeitschrift* and the *Jahrbuch über die Fortschritte der Mathematik*.

Heisenberg’s attestation of Wintner’s extended, even excellent, knowledge in certain fields of physics, can be easily gleaned from the previous work of the young Hungarian scholar, who had introduced himself already for some years to the community of physicists through a number of publications submitted to *Zeitschrift für Physik* and *Annalen der Physik*. In the first paper, ‘Störungstheorie und Perihelformel’ (‘Perturbation Theory and the Perihelion Formula’), he pointed out that ‘one cannot, on the basis of the usual argumentation, consider it to be proven that from Einstein’s theory [of general relativity] the perihelion formula of Einstein

$^{508}$ Leon Lichtenstein, born on 16 May 1878, in Warsaw, Poland, had studied in Berlin, both engineering (mechanical and electrical) at the *Technische Hochschule* and mathematics (with Hermann Amandus Schwarz, Leo Frobenius, and Edmund Landau) at the Friedrich Wilhelm University. In 1902, he joined the Siemens & Halske Company as an electrical engineer. Simultaneously, he started an academic career, obtaining first doctoral degrees from both Berlin universities in 1907 and 1909, respectively; in 1910, he became *Privatdozent* at the *Technische Hochschule* in Berlin, and in 1918, he was promoted there to an associate professorship. In 1920, he obtained a mathematics chair at the University of Münster, and in April 1922, he eventually joined the University of Leipzig. (For details of Lichtenstein’s life and work, see Beyer, 1996, pp. 343–345.)

$^{509}$ See Beyer, 1996, for further information. When the Nazis came to power, Lichtenstein was forced to leave Germany. He died soon afterward on 21 August 1933, in Zakopane, Poland.

$^{510}$ Aurel Friedrich Wintner was born in Budapest on 8 April 1903, the son of the merchant Thomas Eduard Wintner from Rotterdam who became a Hungarian citizen during World War I. Aurel attended school in Rotterdam, Vienna, and finally graduated from the *Königliche Gymnasium* in Budapest. (This and further information on Wintner’s life is available from his handwritten ‘*Lebenslauf*,’ an autobiographical sketch, dated 12 June 1931, and kept in the Leipzig *Universitätsarchiv*.)

III.2 The Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics 419

follows’ (Wintner, 1925, p. 635).$^{512}$ The next two papers, also in *Zeitschrift für Physik*, dealt with an application of Hilbert’s theory of continuous and bounded forms to free oscillations in denumerable infinite systems (Wintner, 1926a, b). As special examples, Wintner examined the conditions that allowed one to prove mathematically rigorously the well-known physical lattice theory of crystals of Max Born and his followers. What bothered him in particular was how the physicists dealt with the continuous eigenvalue spectrum with the mathematical theory of Hilbert, Hellinger, Toeplitz, and others. Therefore, he devoted a series of four papers, submitted in the second half of 1926 to *Annalen der Physik*, to a more careful mathematical discussion of this important physical topic (Wintner, 1926c, d, e; 1927a, b). He summarized the conclusion of the first paper of the series by noting:

> I have started this investigation with the expectation that it will be possible to master the description of small free oscillations of cyclic lattices. One contents oneself [here he cited the papers of the physicists Paul Ewald and Max Born] that one can sum up certain potential expressions . . . in the Poisson sense for $t = 0$ without asking the question whether a motion can develop for $t \neq 0$ and, if so, what is the solution. The opinion prevails that the algebraic theory of Hilbert, Hellinger and Toeplitz can be considered to be the analytic foundation of the theory for the infinite systems of differential equations. Had the matrices occurring in lattice theory been bounded matrices, we could apply our results immediately. A brief look reveals that they are, at least in the most simple cases, unbounded. (Wintner, 1926c, p. 584)

Wintner expressed the hope that he might be able to extend the known mathematical theory to unbounded matrices and thus obtain a solid basis for the physical lattice theory of crystals, notably, the method of approximating the matrices of the latter by unbounded ones. He demonstrated the proof for this suggestion in the following papers on the subject (Wintner, 1926d; 1927a, b). For the physical application, the following result was derived: if the coefficients of the oscillation equations satisfied certain, quite general conditions, the existence of eigenvibrations followed for all real values $t \geq 0$. In a later paper of March 1928, Wintner returned to the lattice problem with new rigour and more refined methods; he proudly announced his results in the abstract as follows:

> A direct theory of lattice vibrations is sketched which—since it possesses mathematically a wider range of application than the usual methods of treatment—is suitable to throw new light on the physical aspects of lattice dynamics (optical and acoustical spectrum, group motion of plane waves, resonance points, etc.). The algebraic considerations of the method introduced by Born and von Kármán and extended by Born may, as will be shown, be immediately and *explicitly* derived from the more transcendental results thus obtained, while a practical application, say, of the Born-Kármán distribution law fails due to the lack of explicit procedures of calculation. By

$^{512}$ Wintner had published this conclusion already before in the *Astronomische Nachrichten* (see Wintner, 1925, footnote 1, p. 635).

420 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

the following, however, one seems to have gained an exact foundation of the lattice-like theory of specific heats. (Wintner, 1928b, p. 495)

Wintner thus hoped to have solved the task envisaged two years earlier and announced a more detailed display of his new foundations of the crystal-lattice theory in the *Mathematische Zeitschrift*. His optimism though was thwarted: in a note correcting the previous paper, he admitted that Born had informed him about several failures of the proposed approach; in particular, ‘the differential system determining the vibrations of a three-dimensional lattice does not belong to the class of differential systems’ considered, hence ‘a consistent mathematical application [of the theory of infinite matrices] to lattice dynamics is still lacking’ (Wintner, 1928e, p. 296).

In dealing with the lattice problem, Wintner based his approach—besides the theory of infinite matrices of Hilbert and associates—also, on the mathematical investigations of the Hungarian Frédéric Riesz, the Swede T. Carleman, and the Dane Harald Bohr. He used the same methods again for the next programme, which he would pursue in Leipzig, namely, to provide a mathematical basis for the matrix formalism used by the quantum physicists. This programme must be considered as being quite opportune at this moment, because in October 1927 Werner Heisenberg, the inventor of the quantum-mechanical matrix formalism, also arrived at the University of Leipzig. About a month later, on 7 November, Leon Lichtenstein communicated to the Saxon Academy of Sciences a memoir of his talented assistant, entitled ‘Theorie der quantenmechanischen Matrizen von wasserstoffähnlichem Spektrum’ (‘Theory of the Quantum-Mechanical Matrices Having a Hydrogen-like Spectrum,’ Wintner, 1927b). Wintner opened it by pointing out the known fact that the quantum-mechanical matrices did not belong to the class of bounded matrices; hence, the available mathematical theory would ‘not suffice to treat even the simplest quantum-mechanical problems,’ and continued:

> In the following, we shall demonstrate, however, that the mathematical *Ansätze* of Hilbert, Hellinger and Carleman, when extended suitably, allow one to establish a mathematically rigorous theory of hydrogen-like spectra. (Wintner, *loc. cit.*, p. 145)

Wintner based his approach on the concept of a ‘$Q$-matrix,’ i.e., a real symmetric—or, more generally, a Hermitean—infinite matrix $\|a_{ik}\|$ that consists of elements such that the sum of the squares of elements of an arbitrary row converges absolutely, i.e.,$^{513}$

$$K_i = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} |a_{ik}|^2 < +\infty. \tag{337}$$

Two classes of $Q$-matrices exist: Class I embraces those whose spectral matrix

$^{513}$ Such $Q$-matrices had been considered earlier by Hilbert and his disciples, and by Carleman.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0453 -->

III.2 The Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics 421

$\|\sigma_{ik}(\mu)\|$ is uniquely defined, and Class II embraces the others that possess more than one spectral matrix. Although so far ‘no practically applicable criteria’ had been proposed, which allowed one to characterize those mathematical problems of quantum mechanics whose matrices belonged to Class I, Wintner now promised to close this gap:

> I shall prove, among others, that the $Q$-matrices for which Heisenberg’s energy levels are contained in a semi-straight line (*Halbgeraden*) certainly are contained in Class I. The Hermitean matrix, whose spectrum has this form, I shall call (for obvious reasons) “semi-bounded.” It will become evident that for these semi-bounded (hydrogen-like) matrices everything essential [i.e., everything needed to solve the eigenvalue problem and prove the uniqueness of the spectrum] is contained already implicitly in the work of Hilbert and Toeplitz on bounded matrices. (Wintner, *loc. cit.*, p. 146)

In his investigation, Wintner analyzed in detail and quite pedantically the mathematical conditions fixing the eigenvalue spectrum of symmetric (or Hermitean) matrices that, according to Hilbert’s fundamental theorem,$^{514}$ consists of a point spectrum $\mathscr{P}$ (discrete eigenvalues $\lambda_n = 1, 2, \dots$), its cumulative points $\mathscr{H}$, and a continuous spectrum (*Streckenspektrum*) $\mathscr{S}$ (continuous eigenvalues $\lambda' \leq \lambda \leq \lambda''$). By making use of various theorems of Hilbert, Toeplitz, and Carleman, in a slightly extended form if necessary, Wintner proceeded to his uniqueness theorem for semibounded symmetric matrices, i.e., those whose spectrum is given by

$$0 \leq \lambda_n, \quad \lambda < \infty, \qquad (338)$$

which he formulated and proved in four detailed theorems (Wintner, *loc. cit.*, pp. 154–155). In the final section, he also demonstrated how the principal-axis problem would be solved in this case (Wintner, *loc. cit.*, p. 156). He added the speculative hope that this conclusion might even hold for matrices that do not satisfy the $Q$-condition (338), but emphasized:

> Due to its very nature, the task cannot be completed in our general case with the above rather primitive tools as completely as for bounded matrices in Hellinger’s theory of orthogonal invariants (Hellinger, 1907), and for the moment it may be questionable whether a complete solution is possible at all. Yet, for securing the physical results, our conclusions as concerns the Hellinger-Carleman theory are sufficient. (Wintner, *loc. cit.*, p. 157)

With this preparation, Wintner appeared to be perfectly qualified to present a lecture course on infinite matrices ‘before a smaller circle of members of the mathematical seminar, trying to satisfy the justified demands of physicists and mathematicians’ (Lichtenstein, in Wintner, 1929, p. vii), and he did so in the

$^{514}$ See Hilbert, 1906a, Theorem I, p. 175.

422 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

winter semester 1927/28 at the University of Leipzig. The lectures satisfied the audience, and Lichtenstein persuaded Wintner to write the material in the book *Spektraltheorie der unendlichen Matrizen*, with the subtitle ‘*Einführung in den analytischen Apparat der Quantenmechanik*’ (‘Introduction to the Analytic Methods of Quantum Mechanics’). Lichtenstein characterised the contents and the presentation in the following words:

> The task is not solved quite easily and hardly without compromises and sacrifices. Thus the first chapter devoted to the algebraic foundations provides only methodologically new insights to the mathematician: the author deals here with finite matrices giving mostly proofs which can, at least partially, be immediately transferred to infinite matrices. The second chapter treats some fundamental concepts less known to the physicists, namely those of real analysis, functions of limited fluctuation, Stieltjes’s integrals, convergent sequences, and the like. Also here the mathematician will still not recover his investment, notably because in respect of the space available certain proofs have only been indicated. Lebesgue’s integral content will not be used in the book … In spite of all these compromises the mathematically less experienced physicist will occasionally find that the spectral theory of infinite matrices does not always constitute an easy reading. To this one should answer that the book of nature is just formulated in mathematics. The author has done whatever he could to make this language understandable—he has done so with great ability, knowledge and elegance (*mit viel Geschick, Sachkenntnis und Eleganz*).
>
> The developments dealt with in the third and the following chapters lead from a peculiarly formulated theory of bounded operators to that of certain unbounded and non-Hermitean matrices. In some rather remarkable recent publications the author has succeeded in obtaining for what he called “semi-bounded” and “almost periodic” matrices surprisingly elegant and definite results. One has gained, in the theory of semi-bounded matrices, a mathematically satisfactory theory of quantum-mechanical matrices exhibiting a hydrogen-like spectrum; on the other hand, the almost periodic matrices permit one to rewrite classical mechanics in the language of infinite matrices. The treatment of nearly periodic matrices is followed by considerations connected with certain problems and results of Lagrange and Levi-Civita in perturbation theory. The mathematician will have tremendous joy (*seine helle Freude haben*) in these topics …, the same joy which I felt when I read the first book of the young, highly talented author. (Lichtenstein, *loc. cit.*, pp. vii–viii)

In 1928, Wintner continued to publish further original contributions on the mathematical foundation of quantum-mechanical formalism in *Zeitschrift für Physik*.$^{515}$ In the first, received on 11 March, he used Otto Toeplitz’s theory of Laurent matrices or $L$-matrices (1911) to justify Heisenberg’s *Ansatz* about the quantum-theoretical Fourier series (Wintner, 1928a).$^{516}$ Heisenberg had introduced three years previously a real-valued function $f(t)$ to describe a quantum-

III.2 The Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics 423

theoretical state (Heisenberg, 1925c),

$$f(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{+\infty} a_n \exp(i\nu_n t), \qquad (339)$$

with the frequency $\nu_n$ that was not periodic.$^{517}$ The question now had to be asked how the spectrum of the Hamiltonian matrix associated with the transition amplitudes $a_n$ (in which the frequencies $\nu_n$ enter only indirectly) can be related to $\nu_n$. By generalizing the theory of $L$-matrices with the help of Harald Bohr’s theory of almost-periodic functions, Wintner found:

> that under quite general assumptions, which are surely satisfied in the applications—e.g., if the function is almost-periodic in Bohr’s sense—*the set of values of the Hermitean form coincides with the set of values of the function $f(t)$ for $-\infty < r \leq +\infty$.* For the special case of periodic functions, this result goes over into the central theorem of Teoplitz’s theory of Laurent matrices. (Wintner, 1928a, p. 149)

This study of Heisenberg’s *Ansatz* (339) involved diophantine and group-theoretical methods, which the author employed again in the second fundamental paper entitled ‘Über den analytischen Apparat der Quantenmechanik’ (‘On the Analytic Methods of Quantum Mechanics,’ Wintner, 1928d).$^{518}$

Wintner argued there that the claim that ‘certain presentations of [Niels] Bohr’s frequency condition with Heisenberg’s theory [i.e., quantum mechanics] may suggest that the energy theorem is to be obtained as a necessary consequence of the commutation relations’ is not really justified ‘because the introduction of the discrete terms (usually denoted by $W_n$) postulates from the very beginning that the Hamiltonian matrix can be considered to be a diagonal matrix’ (Wintner, 1928d, p. 684). He added: ‘However, the fact is rather that the energy theorem is compatible with the commutation relations only if the Hamiltonian matrix contains no continuous spectrum.’ For example, the quantum-mechanical hydrogen problem certainly possesses a continuous spectrum; there, the logical difficulty arises that the commutation relations are not defined without adding the energy theorem, and they are determined when this is done. The task therefore arose to demonstrate in matrix language the validity of the commutation relations not only for the discrete states, but also for the continuum states—this seemed to follow indeed from Schrödinger’s translation prescription of matrices as wave-mechanical expressions.

Wintner approached the task by analyzing the matrix-mechanical transformation theory of Born, Heisenberg, and Jordan within the formalism of Ernst Hellinger’s theory of quadratic forms (Hellinger, 1907). A general Hermitean form

$^{518}$ Besides the work on the lattice theory mentioned above (Wintner, 1928b, e), the author wrote a further small note on ‘the pseudo-spectrum of the energy matrix’ (Wintner, 1928c)—a small addendum to the great memoir presented to the Saxon Academy (Wintner, 1927b).

can always be brought in by a unitary substitution of the variables $x_i$ into the so-called normal form, which is the sum of two special Hermitean forms $\mathscr{A}$ and $\mathscr{B}$, i.e.,

$$\alpha(x_1, x_2, \dots) = \mathscr{A}(\xi_1, \xi_2 \dots) + \mathscr{B}(\eta_1, \eta_2 \dots), \qquad (340)$$

where $\mathscr{A}$ contains no continuous spectrum and $\mathscr{B}$ no point spectrum (and no $\xi$ coincides with any $\eta$). Practically, the transformation $\alpha$ to yield the principal-axes form $\mathscr{A}$ may be achieved by a finite, or at least a denumerable, number of steps; hence, e.g., the discrete values of the hydrogen spectrum do follow already without the knowledge of an additional continuous spectrum—as Wolfgang Pauli showed in his matrix calculation. (Pauli, 1926a). On the other hand, it can be assumed that the continuous spectrum $\mathscr{B}(\eta_1, \eta_2, \dots)$, if it exists at all, possesses *a priori* the normal form.$^{519}$

In the remaining sections of his paper, Wintner proved several results on Hermitean, notably, semibounded matrices—both for point and continuous spectra, and in classical and quantum-theoretical applications, respectively—illustrating especially ‘the real purpose of the paper,’ namely:

> to point out the fact that in the mathematical literature there exist rich and detailed methods concerning those matrices, which play a role in quantum mechanics; so far they have only been recovered partly or not yet been exploited by the physicists. (Wintner, 1928d, p. 693)

Thus, he also stressed that the proper mathematical treatment of the quantum-mechanical problems on the basis of the ‘Hellinger forms’ and their transformation properties ‘serves from the very beginning the purpose to formulate mathematical Dirac’s delta-foldings—like Stieltjes’s integral concept renders superfluous all the considerations of delta-functions’ (Wintner, *loc. cit.*, p. 679).

After 1928, Wintner left—apart from writing his book *Spektraltheorie*, which he completed in June 1929—the subject of quantum mechanics and returned to deal with the problems of classical physics, especially the motion of astronomical bodies.$^{520}$ This change of interest may have been strengthened by his official employment on astronomical problems in the summer semester 1929. When he obtained a fellowship of the Rockefeller Foundation in October 1929 to travel abroad, he selected the University of Rome (to work with the mathematician Tullio Levi-Civita) and the University Observatory in Copenhagen (to work with Bengt Strömgren). The following year he was invited as a research associate to Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland; there, he became a staff

## (f) The First Response of the Physicists and Later of the Mathematicians

The meticulous efforts of John von Neumann and Aurel Wintner on the mathematical foundations of the quantum-mechanical scheme received only little attention in the publications of the physicists. One finds most references in Wolfgang Pauli's *Handbuch* article on the principles of wave mechanics (Pauli, 1933c). Especially, in the sections on "Stationery States as Eigenvalue Problem" (6. *Stationäre Zustände als Eigenwertproblem*), "General Transformations of Operators and Matrices" (7. *Allgemeine Transformationen von Operatoren und Matrizen*), and "The General Formulation of the Laws of Motion" (8. *Die allgemeine Form des Bewegungsgesetzes*), Pauli cites at several places the papers of von Neumann (1927a, b; 1929a, b) and Wintner (1929). Among the eminent physicists, Pauli always excelled in paying detailed attention to such mathematical questions as defining integrals over discontinuous functions (see Pauli, 1933c, p. 122–123) or evaluating correctly the eigenvalue spectrum of Hermitean operators (Pauli, *loc. cit.*, pp. 142–143). The other physicist who steadily demonstrated interest in the investigations of the mathematicians, Pascual Jordan, wrote a sensible review of Wintner's book. After mentioning Wintner's matrix treatment of the problems of classical physics (notably, oscillating continua), he continued:

> Especially timely are today the relations of the mathematical theory . . . to quantum theory. . . . The situation here is that the mathematical theory which the quantum theorist needs does not exist in a complete and rigorous state. While in the former [pre-quantum-mechanical] applications primarily the (comparatively simple) theory of so-called "continuous" quadratic forms sufficed, now even the already much deeper-going Hilbert-Hellinger theory of "bounded" forms cannot be considered satisfactory. The first successful advances in the field of the [mathematical] problems connected with [quantum mechanics] we owe to the author [Wintner], on the one hand, and to J. von Neumann, on the other. Wintner's book provides the physicist for the first time the possibility of penetrating more deeply into the matter. (Jordan, 1930, p. 571)

---
⁵²¹ The paper submitted by Wintner as his Habilitation thesis had already been published. In 1933, Wintner then was dismissed from the University of Leipzig because of racial reasons. He stayed on at the Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, where he received a long delayed appointment to a full professorship only in 1946. Before that, he spent the year 1937/38 as a member of the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton—during that year, he also collaborated with G. D. Birkhoff at Harvard University—and in 1941, he held a Guggenheim Foundation Fellowship, which he partly spent in Cambridge, Massachusetts, with the idea of writing a book together with Norbert Wiener; this plan did not materialize, because Wiener soon became involved in war-related work.
In the U.S.A., Wintner continued to work on problems of celestial mechanics (see his book: *Analytical Foundations of Celestial Mechanics*, Princeton University Press, Princeton, 1941), but the work on almost-periodic functions (whose connection with the problems of quantum mechanics and celestial mechanics he had shown earlier) occupied most of his time until 1945, besides studying aspects of analytic number theory and some other topics—partly in collaboration with other, often younger, mathematicians (e.g., F. D. Murnaghan, D. C. Lewis, B. Jessen, P. Erdös, and M. Kac), and his students (including E. K. Haviland, R. B. Kerschner, and P. Hartman). He had a close friendship and fruitful collaboration with E. R. van Kampen on convolution theory. After the war, during which he wrote three monographs (on *Eratosthenian Averages*, 1943; *Theory of Measure in Arithmetical Semi-Groups*, 1944; and *Arithmetical Approach to Ordinary Fourier Series*, 1945), he returned to the field of his first interest, the theory of ordinary differential equations and differential geometry. From 1936 until his death, Wintner devoted much time and energy to the *American Journal of Mathematics*, serving as associate editor from 1936 to 1944 and editor from 1944 to 1958. A learned man, proud of his classical education, and exhibiting a great interest in the history of mathematics, celestial mechanics, and other fields, he disliked the trends of modern mathematics toward abstraction and generalization. Aurel Wintner died on 15 January 1958, in Baltimore. (For details of his bibliography, see Hartman, 1962.)

# 426  Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

Of course, Jordan admitted that the physicist in general shows less interest in the "epsilontics" of the mathematician and might "notice not without a certain shiver (*gewissen Schauder*) which formalities are necessary to prove in a mathematically decadent manner what he is convinced of (because of physical reasons) anyway." He concluded: "However, these questions will become increasingly urgent as more and more complex applications of quantum mechanics to practical problems arise," and he added:

> Their successful treatment will demand the cooperation and mutual understanding of mathematicians and physicists. In this endeavour the present book might become an indispensable tool. (Jordan, *loc. cit.*)

One might wonder, on the other hand, why Heisenberg never responded publicly to the work of Wintner in Leipzig. After all, he must have been quite happy with the detailed interest with which his mathematical colleagues analyzed his own daring steps taken in 1925 and showed how they could be fitted into a rigorous scheme. As Jordan did not fail to mention in the above-mentioned review, however, the physicist's attention was directed toward "other things" (*weil er seine Aufmerksamkeit in erster Linie auf andere Dinge richten muß,* Jordan, *loc. cit.*), and these involved for Heisenberg (between 1927 and 1929) especially the extension of the quantum-mechanical formalism to relativistic problems—a topic in which mathematical subtleties did not play any role. Certainly, however, Heisenberg also followed the efforts of the mathematicians from some distance and agreed, e.g., to what his student and assistant Felix Bloch wrote in the review of von Neumann's *Mathematische Grundlagen der Quantenmechanik*:

> Quantum mechanics has received a certain completion by the transformation theory; with it the formal apparatus was created which in general yields information about all possible observations within a system, whose properties are somehow known by previous measurements. In the elegant expression given to it by Dirac, however, there occur improper functions having the character of the well-known δ-function. Even though the physicist has since long become acquainted with its application and is thus hardly led to wrong consequences, one will still welcome the fact that this book shows how they can be replaced by a mathematically more rigorous formulation. (Bloch, 1933b, p. 183)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0459 -->

# 427  III.2 The Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

In contrast to quantum physicists, the prime inventor of the "ill-famed" (among the pure mathematicians) δ-function would not worry about the complaints of the mathematicians at all. "In quantum theory whenever an improper function appears it will be something which is to be used finally only in integrands," he wrote in *The Principles of Quantum Mechanics* (Dirac, 1935, p. 74). He considered the δ-function from the very beginning to be a part of his "symbolic method" that "enables one to express the physical laws in a neat and concise way, and will probably be increasingly used in the future as it becomes better understood and its proper mathematics gets developed" (Dirac, 1930d, preface, p. vi). Twenty-two years after its introduction, in August 1949, Dirac met at the Canadian Mathematical Congress in Vancouver a French mathematician who had available the proper mathematics for the improper δ-function: Laurent Schwartz of Nancy, at that time, was about to complete his *Théorie des distributions* (*Theory of Distributions*), which evolved from Dirac's improper function. Schwartz introduced his pioneering book on the new mathematical topic with the following historical remarks:

> More than fifty years ago the engineer Heaviside (1893a, b) introduced his rules of a symbolic calculus in an audacious memoir where a powerful, though little justified, mathematical calculus was used for the solution of physical problems. . . . Since the introduction of the famous δ-function by Dirac (1927a) . . . the formulae of the symbolic calculus have become even less acceptable for the rigour of the mathematicians. . . . How can one explain the success of these methods? When such a contradictory situation arises, it rarely happens that there does not arise a mathematical theory which justifies, in a modified way, the language of the physicists; it will even be an important source of progress in mathematics and physics. (Schwartz, 1950, pp. 5–6)

Several rigorous mathematical methods had been proposed since 1927 that, though being acceptable to mathematicians, did not satisfy the physicists, because they implied a modification of the physical problems, Schwartz continued.⁵²² Instead, taking seriously the demands of the physicists, he now reported:

> We have generalized the notion of a function, first by that of a measure, then by that of a distribution. δ will be a measure and not a function. δ' [its derivative] will be a distribution and not a measure. (Schwartz, *loc. cit.*, p. 6)

Schwartz was perfectly aware that he had predecessors among his colleagues, and he cited papers and books, notably, by J. Leray, D. Hilbert and R. Courant, and S. Bôchner, who had studied problems of potential theory. In addition, he referred to the work of S. L. Soboleff, K. O. Friedrichs, and V. I. Kryloff in the 1930s and early 1940s, who had introduced generalized derivatives of generalized functions in the special case that these derivatives are also functions.⁵²³ Still, much older and more involved paths led to the theory of distributions that have been outlined in some detail in an extended historical account by Jesper Lützen (1982).⁵²⁴ We shall not enter into this prehistory, but rather return to the story of Laurent Schwartz.

# 428  Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

In his contribution to *Aspects of Quantum Theory*, Paul Dirac's seventieth birthday *Festschrift*, Schwartz wrote:

> It was in 1935 that I heard talk about the δ-function for the first time. I was a student, and a colleague went to attend a conference on theoretical physics and [afterwards] told me about this as follows: "These people there introduced a so-called δ-function, which is zero everywhere except at the origin, where it is infinity such that $\int \delta(x) dx = +1$. In view of the methods of these people one cannot collaborate with them." We pondered a little bit together on this subject and then dropped it; I did not think about it [again] until 1945. At that moment the situation was quite different, because I had defined the distribution. I was tormented by the "generalized solution" of partial differential equations. If we consider the equation of a vibrating string,
>
> $$\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} - \frac{1}{v^2} \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} = 0, \tag{(341)}$$
>
> and write down its general solution in the form $u(x, t) = f(x+vt) + g(x-vt)$, where $f$ and $g$ are twice differentiable; now if they were only continuous and once differentiable functions, one would surely have the impression that the $u$ so defined is still, in some sense, a solution of the equation of the vibrating string. (Schwartz, 1972, p. 179)

Schwartz then defined $u$ to be a "generalized solution" "if all its "regularizations" $u * \phi$, where $\phi$ is a sufficiently often differentiable function such that $u * \phi$ possesses derivatives of arbitrary order, are solutions of the equation." While other mathematicians before had introduced such generalized solutions, he now stressed the unsatisfactory features that neither the term $\partial^2 u/dx^2$ nor $(1/v^2)(\partial^2 u/\partial t^2)$ individually made sense. To improve the situation, he created the concept of "distributions," which eventually provided the key to understanding these and other mathematically ill-defined objects then used by the physicists.

Schwartz entered the stage with his pioneering paper, entitled "*Généralisation de fonction, de dérivation, de transformation de Fourier, et applications mathématiques et physiques*" ("Generalization of the Notion of Function, Derivative, Fourier Transformation and Mathematical and Physical Applications," Schwartz, 1945), which he expanded in the following five years into the two-volume book quoted earlier.

Generalized Differentiation and Generalized Solution of Differential Equations; 3. Generalized Fourier Transforms; 4. Early Generalized Functions; and 5. De Rham Currents.

above.⁵²⁵ This book emerged from the observation that the $\delta$-function might be interpreted in two ways. First, Dirac had introduced it to represent the kernel of an integral equation,

$$
\phi(x) = \int \delta(x - y)\phi(y) dy. \tag{342}
$$

Thus, $\delta(x - y)$ acted as a distribution in two variables, $K_{x,y}$, and if $\phi$ was an infinitely often differentiable function with compact support, one can associate with it a distribution $T$, written as $K \cdot \phi$, or, explicitly,

$$
T_x = \int K_{x,y}\phi(y) dy. \tag{342'}
$$

$T$ then defines a linear transformation of $\mathcal{D}_y$ (the vector space of complex functions of the variables $y$, infinitely often differentiable and having a compact support) into the vector space $\mathcal{D}_x'$. 'The kernel theorem states precisely that all linear continuous transformations of $\mathcal{D}_y$ into $\mathcal{D}_x'$ can be written in a unique way, starting from a kernel distribution,' Schwartz remarked and later added: 'This theorem, which I derived in 1950, was directly inspired by reading Dirac' (Schwartz, 1972, p. 180). At the same time, he identified the $\delta$-function as the 'measure of Dirac,' i.e., 'the measure formed by a mass $+1$ at the origin of $x = 0$ of [the $n$-dimensional vector space] $R^n$,' and concluded:

> It follows ... that $\delta$ is the simplest example of a measure which is not a function. If the physicists stick in calling it the *Dirac function*, this is for being able to carry out with it certain operations which are not defined except for functions and not for measures (for example, the derivation). But we carry out all these operations on measures whether they are functions or not. (Schwartz, 1950, p. 19)

Besides having outlined the principal ideas that led Schwartz to the theory of distributions and the recognition of the true mathematical nature of Dirac's improper $\delta$-function, we shall not proceed further along these lines. The theory of generalized functions can be considered as one of many topics in mathematics that have originated from the ideas of physicists. In spite of the specialization of the

L. Schwartz was born on 5 March 1915, in Strassbourg and graduated in 1935 from the École Normale Supérieure in Paris. Following military service, he began to do research in 1940 in his hometown, but fled to Clermont-Ferrand during German occupation; there, he received his doctorate in 1943. Schwartz entered his academic career in 1944 as an assistant at the University of Grenoble and was promoted to a professorship the following year in the faculty of sciences at Nancy; in 1953, he was called to Paris, where he occupied after 1959 a chair of mathematics at the École Polytechnique. From the beginning, he joined the team writing N. Bourbaki's *Éléments de Mathématique*. In 1950, he received the prestigious Field's Medal for his theory of distributions. Having left-wing opinions, he participated in many political activities.

sciences, this episode documents again the intimate connection between physics and mathematics, which has dominated these branches of human civilization for millennia. Indeed, in the twentieth century, Laurent Schwartz continued brilliantly the line of his predecessors David Hilbert, Hermann Weyl, John von Neumann, and Aurel Wintner, who contributed materially to the mathematical foundations of the physical theory of quantum mechanics. In the following two sections, we shall discuss further the very fruitful interplay of mathematicians and physicists to complete, between 1927 and 1932, the foundations of quantum mechanics and to provide at the same time powerful methods for solving conceptual and practical problems of microphysics.

## III.3 Quantum-Mechanical Statistics and the Theory of Measurement

Leon Van Hove summarized the essential outcome of the mathematical programme, which John von Neumann had begun in 1927 and completed in 1929 in the papers described in the previous section, as follows:

> In the course of his formulation of quantum mechanics in terms of vectors and operators in Hilbert space von Neumann also gave in complete generality the basic statistical rule of interpretation of the theory. This rule concerns the result of the measurement of a given physical quantity on a system in a given quantum state and expresses its probability distribution by means of a simple and now completely familiar formula involving the vector representing the state and the spectral resolution of the operator which represents the physical quantity. (Van Hove, 1958, p. 97)

The present section addresses a connected, but different, aspect of the mathematical foundations of quantum mechanics. It deals with the formulation and consequences of the statistical hypothesis introduced by Max Born (1926a, b), which 'was for von Neumann the starting point of a mathematical analysis of quantum mechanics in entirely probabilistic terms,' Van Hove emphasized and further stated:

> The analysis carried out in a paper of 1927 [i.e., von Neumann, 1927c] introduced the concept of an ensemble of systems which are not necessarily all in the same quantum state. The statistical matrix (now called $\rho$-matrix although von Neumann's notation was $U$) has become one of the magic tools of quantum physics, and it is through this contribution that von Neumann's name became familiar to even the least mathematically minded physicist. (Van Hove, *loc. cit.*)

In the same paper, John von Neumann entered into the theoretical formulation of the quantum-mechanical process of measurement, and he used the results to lay the foundation of a consistent quantum-theoretical thermodynamics (von Neumann, 1927c). He continued this enterprise further in a spectacular way in a paper pub-

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0463 -->

lished later, in which he presented a proof of the ergodic hypothesis in quantum mechanics (von Neumann, 1929c).

Still, these contributions did not exhaust von Neumann's work on the mathematical foundations of the new atomic theory. Apart from systematic group-theoretical investigations carried out in collaboration with Eugene Wigner—which we shall discuss in the next section—the author got involved (when composing his pioneering book on *Mathematische Grundlagen der Quantenmechanik*, von Neumann, 1932a) 'into a point which had not been discussed in the 1927 papers and which was later the subject of much controversy,' as Van Hove remarked:

> It is the question of the possible existence of "hidden variables," the consideration of which would eliminate the noncausal element involved in the measuring process. Von Neumann could show that hidden parameters with these properties cannot exist if the basic structure of quantum theory is retained. Although he mentioned the latter restriction explicitly, his result was often quoted without due reference to it, a fact which sometimes gave rise to unjustified criticism devoted through the years to the possibility of an entirely deterministic reformulation of quantum theory. (Van Hove, 1958, p. 98)

The developments briefly summarized above all found their proper place in von Neumann's classic book of 1932, e.g., the quantum-statistical and thermodynamical considerations in Chapters III and IV, entitled 'Die quantenmechanische Statistik' ('The Quantum-Mechanical Statistics') and 'Deduktiver Aufbau der Theorie' ('The Deductive Development of the Theory'). The problems connected with the measurement process, on which von Neumann continued to work for several years after 1927, were displayed in Chapters V and VI, entitled 'Allgemeine Betrachtungen' ('General Considerations') and 'Der Meßprozeß' ('The Measurement Process'). For the historical analysis, the later book—admittedly more systematically and pedagogically written—cannot be used alone to reconstruct the development of von Neumann's programme properly; one must rather undertake a detailed study of the original, quite technical papers and their relation to contemporary work of the physicists. In spite of the fact that von Neumann acted as the decisive driving personality in the whole saga of the mathematical foundations of quantum mechanics, these colleagues initiated crucial steps or suggested similar ideas. In addition, especially the mathematician Hermann Weyl must be mentioned, besides, notably, the physicists Niels Bohr, Lev Landau, Wolfgang Pauli, Leo Szilard, and Eugene Wigner. Their interaction completed and illuminated the brilliant work of the principal hero in the game: John von Neumann.

### (a) The Probability-Theoretical Formulation of Quantum Mechanics (1927–1928)

On 11 November 1927, John von Neumann's paper on 'Wahrscheinlichkeitstheoretischer Aufbau der Quantenmechanik' ('Probability-Theoretical Formulation of Quantum Mechanics') was presented to the Göttingen Academy (von Neu-

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0464 -->

mann, 1927b). In introducing this paper, the author began with a criticism of the existing formulation of the physical theory:

> The method used thus far in statistical quantum mechanics was essentially a deductive one: the absolute square of certain expansion coefficients of the wave function, or also of the wave function itself, was rather dogmatically identified with the probability—and the agreement with experiment was verified *a posteriori*. However, a systematic derivation of quantum mechanics from the facts of experience, or probability-theoretical fundamental assumptions, i.e., an inductive foundation has not been given so far. In addition, the relation [of the theory] to the conventional probability calculus has been clarified only insufficiently: in particular, the validity of the fundamental laws [of the latter], such as the laws of addition and multiplication, has not been discussed satisfactorily. (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 245)

Here, von Neumann referred to some contradictory statements in the papers of Pascual Jordan (1927b) and Werner Heisenberg (1927b), who had applied the mathematical laws mentioned either to probability amplitudes or their squares. To remove such discrepancies and to provide the proper systematic treatment, he proposed the following programme:

> In the present paper such an inductive [probability-theoretical] formulation will be attempted. In this, we shall assume the unrestricted validity of the usual probability calculus. The result is that this is not only compatible with quantum mechanics but also suffices—connected with hardly far-reaching and formal assumptions—to derive its laws in a unique manner. Indeed, we shall succeed on this basis to succeed on this basis in establishing the whole time-independent quantum mechanics. (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 246)

In order to formulate the probability theoretical basis of quantum mechanics, atomic systems had to be considered as members of an ensemble ($\mathscr{S}_1, \mathscr{S}_2, \mathscr{S}_3 \ldots$). Each such system possesses physical quantities $a, b, \ldots$, and 'to establish a statistics of the quantity $a$ means to submit every system $\mathscr{S}_1, \mathscr{S}_2, \ldots$ to the experimental "measurement of $a$" and to register the value distribution thus resulting' (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 247). Two such extreme value distributions can be singled out: in a 'sharp (*scharfe*) statistics' the same value is observed in all systems of the ensemble, i.e., the whole value distribution consisted of a single number; on the other hand, in an 'elementary disordered ensemble,' the possible states of all systems occur with equal probability, i.e., no knowledge of any system exists. Having 'knowledge (*Kenntnis*)' of a system $\mathscr{S}'$ of an ensemble ($\mathscr{S}_1', \mathscr{S}_2', \ldots$), therefore, means that an expectation value $E(\alpha)$ can be given every property of $\alpha$ of $\mathscr{S}'$.⁵²⁶ With these definitions, von Neumann went on to formulate the fundamental assumptions or postulates of his scheme; they consisted of two sets, the first of which concerned properties of the expectation values, notably:

⁵²⁶ Here, von Neumann not only assumed that $E(\alpha)$ is given, but also that all average values of the momenta of the distribution under investigation are given .

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0465 -->

III.3 Quantum-Mechanical Statistics and the Theory of Measurement &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 433

A. The expectation values [for the quantities $a$, $b$, and $c$] obey the linearity relation (for finitely or infinitely many terms)

$$ E(\alpha a + \beta b + \gamma c + \cdots) = \alpha E(a) + \beta E(b) + \gamma E(c) + \cdots, \qquad [(343)] $$

with $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ denoting real numbers.
B. For quantities $a$, having exclusively non-negative values, it also follows that

$$ E(a) \ge 0. \qquad [(344)] $$

(von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, pp. 249-250)

As regards the physical quantities, the author took over the results of his former paper (von Neumann, 1927a), namely, that they are to be represented by linear Hermitean operators with a soluble eigenvalue problem (he called them 'normal operators'), and they obeyed the postulates:

C. Let $S$, $T$, $\ldots$ be normal operators (finite or infinite in number) and so are $\alpha S + \beta T + \cdots$. Then, if $S$, $T$, $\ldots$ are associated with the quantities $a$, $b$, $\ldots$, so are $\alpha S + \beta T + \cdots$ with the quantities $\alpha a + \beta b + \cdots$.
D. Let $S$ be a normal operator associated with the quantity $a$, and $f(x)$ a function (defined for real $x$ and assuming real values), then the quantity $f(a)$ is associated with $f(S)$.
(von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 252)

Before making use of the above fundamental assumptions, von Neumann introduced for describing the 'knowledge' of a system $\mathscr{S}'$, or even ensembles of systems, a linear 'symmetric' (more accurately, Hermitean) operator $U$. ('Knowledge' evidently meant describing the expectation values of operators $S$, etc., which he represented in the following, for the sake of simplicity, by matrices $\{s_{\mu\nu}\}$.)$^{527}$ He composed the operator $U$ from the unit matrix $A_\mu$ (with diagonal matrix elements 1), the symmetric matrix $B_{\mu\nu}$ (having elements $b_{\mu\nu} = b_{\nu\mu} = 1$ for $\mu < \nu$, and zero otherwise), and the antisymmetric matrix $C_{\mu\nu}$ (with elements $c_{\mu\nu} = -c_{\nu\mu} = i$ for $\mu < \nu$, and zero otherwise), defining

$$ U = \begin{cases} u_{\mu\mu} = E(A_\mu), \\ u_{\mu\nu} = \frac{1}{2} E(B_{\mu\nu}) + i \frac{1}{2} E(C_{\mu\nu}), \\ u_{\nu\mu} = \frac{1}{2} E(B_{\mu\nu}) - i \frac{1}{2} E(C_{\mu\nu}), \end{cases} \quad \mu < \nu. \qquad (345) $$

$^{527}$ Since von Neumann had shown in his earlier investigation how to generalize the matrices to those having continuous indices, the generalization is straightforward.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0466 -->

434 &nbsp;&nbsp; Chapter III &nbsp;&nbsp; The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

The expectation value $E(S)$ could then be written as

$$ E(S) = \sum_{\mu\nu} s_{\mu\nu} \bar{u}_{\mu\nu}, \qquad (346) $$

where $\bar{u}_{\mu\nu}$ denotes the complex conjugate of $u_{\mu\nu}$, and von Neumann proved the important result:

> All possible 'knowledge' of a system $\mathscr{S}'$, i.e., of all possible statistical ensembles $\{\mathscr{S}'_1, \mathscr{S}'_2, \ldots\}$, corresponds uniquely in a one-to-one relation to the definite linear operators $U$. This correspondence is described by the expectation-value formula [(346)], where $S$ and $U$ are represented by the matrices $\{s_{\mu\nu}\}$ and $\{u_{\mu\nu}\}$, respectively.
> (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 255)

Finally, he defined a special ensemble, the so-called 'pure (*reines*)' or 'uniform (*einheitliches*)' ensemble, as the one for which all systems are in the same state. Although in classical theory every variable in pure ensembles assumes a sharp distribution, in quantum mechanics this would not follow in general. Therefore, von Neumann required that a pure ensemble is defined by the property that its 'statistical operator' $U$ cannot be written as a linear combination of two operators $U^*$ and $U^{**}$ characterizing different ensembles, i.e., as

$$ U = \eta U^* + \theta U^{**}, \qquad (347) $$

unless $U^* = \text{const. } U^{**}$. Then, he proved that $U$ for a pure ensemble becomes identical with the projection operator $P_\phi$ for the pure state $\phi$, and the expectation value formula (346) was simplified to

$$ E(S) = Q(\phi, S\phi) \qquad (348) $$

(with $Q$ denoting the square root of the scalar product of the two Hilbert space vectors $\phi$ and $S\phi$). Hence, he obtained the specific conclusion:

> In order that the value distribution of the quantity $a$ (represented by the operator $S$) be sharp, it is necessary and sufficient that $\phi$ constitute an eigenfunction of $S$; the value of $a$ then becomes equal to the eigenvalue associated with $\phi$. (von Neumann, 1927b, p. 249)

With these basic assumptions, definitions, and results, von Neumann was finally in a position to achieve his primary goal, namely, to formulate in a concise mathematical language the concept of measurement and the statistical connection between different measurements in quantum mechanics. In particular, he determined in some detail what were the measurements in 'pure' systems, in 'mixed' systems, and in 'elementary disordered' systems, respectively, and he proved the fundamental result, Eq. (336), of the previous paper (von Neumann, 1927a), providing the probability distribution for sets of physical variables.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0467 -->

III.3 Quantum-Mechanical Statistics and the Theory of Measurement &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 435

In the summary of his paper, von Neumann claimed to have demonstrated 'that quantum mechanics is not only compatible with the usual probability calculus—but with a few plausible factual assumptions added—, it is even the only possible [theoretical] solution' (von Neumann, 1927b, p. 271). 'These basic assumptions were,' he continued:

1. Every measurement changes the observed object, and two measurements always disturb each other—if they cannot be replaced by a single one.
2. However, the change created by a measurement is of such a nature that this measurement always remains valid, that is, when it is repeated *immediately* afterwards, the same result will be obtained.

Further a formal assumption:
3. The physical quantities have to be described by functional operators satisfying some simple formal rules.

These principles already automatically lead to quantum mechanics and its statistics.
(von Neumann, *loc. cit.*)

The result, the author concluded finally, agrees with the consequences obtained by Heisenberg earlier in 1927, notably, that 'the statistical "acausal" nature of quantum mechanics is determined alone by the deficiency (in principle) of the measurement process, because a system left to itself (and not disturbed by measurements) develops completely causally in time' (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*). 'However,' he continued:

> in connection with experiments the statistical character cannot be avoided: though for every experiment there exists a state fitted to it, in which the result comes out uniquely (the experiment just creates such states, if they had not been there before); but to every state there exist "non-fitting" experiments, whose performance will destroy it—and then create, according to the laws of chance, fitting states. (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 272)

One must indeed admire the keen insight of the young mathematician, who in a single stroke sketched and completed the probability-theoretical formulation of quantum mechanics. He moved rapidly with great assurance on a path in which only a few intuitive ideas had been suggested before. In this context, we can only mention two contemporary papers that independently developed some of von Neumann's concepts. First, the similarly young Russian physicist, Lev Davidovich Landau of Leningrad, when dealing with the problem of radiation damping in quantum mechanics, introduced in the case of two coupled systems a new method of description (Landau, 1927). In particular, he obtained for the average $\bar{f}$ of a function $f$, depending on the coordinates and the momenta of the first system, the expression

$$ \bar{f} = \int f \Psi \Psi^* d\tau d\tau' = \sum_{n} \alpha_{nm} f_{nm}, \qquad (349) $$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0468 -->

436 &nbsp;&nbsp; Chapter III &nbsp;&nbsp; The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

with $\Psi$ denoting the wave function of the total system (formed by the product $\psi = \sum_{n} a_n \psi_n$ and $\psi' = \sum_{r} b_r \psi_r'$ of the wave functions of the two systems), i.e.,

$$ \Psi = \psi \psi' = \sum_{n} \sum_{r} a_n b_r \psi_n \psi_r = \sum_{n,r} c_{nr} \psi_n \psi_r, \qquad (349\text{a}) $$

and

$$ \left. \begin{aligned} \alpha_{nm} &= \sum_{r} c_{nr}^* c_{mr}, \\ f_{nm} &= \int f \psi_n^* \psi_m d\tau. \end{aligned} \right\} \qquad (349\text{b}) $$

Then, he claimed:

> Now the "state" of the system can *be characterized by the quantities* $\alpha_{nm}$. For a system $[\psi]$ given by the quantities $a_n$ one has, as is well known,
>
> $$ \bar{f} = \int f \psi \psi^* d\tau = \sum_{n} \sum_{m} a_n^* a_m f_{nm}. \qquad [(350)] $$
>
> In this special case, therefore, $a_{nm}$ is identical with $a_n^* a_m$; in general, such a representation cannot be achieved, and $a_{nm}$ must then be considered to be a certain average of this quantity. (Landau, *loc. cit.*, p. 431)

Later on, the physicists identified Landau's 'average' matrix $a_{nm}$ with von Neumann's $U$-matrix; hence, his proposal even preceded that of von Neumann's as far as the date of publication was concerned.$^{528}$ However, Landau just used his matrix $\{a_{nm}\}$ for the special example considered, while von Neumann made the density operator $U$ the central point of his most general discussion of statistical quantum mechanics. Moreover, von Neumann evidently developed his concept independently of Landau.$^{529}$

The other publication having some overlap with von Neumann's 'probability-theoretical formulation' was Hermann Weyl's on '*Quantenmechanik und Gruppentheorie*' ('Quantum Mechanics and Group Theory'), received by *Zeitschrift für*

$^{528}$ For illustration, Landau's formula (24) on p. 434 should be compared with Pauli's expression for von Neumann's density matrix, Eq. (206) on p. 149 of Pauli, 1933c.

$^{529}$ In spite of the hypothetical possibility that von Neumann could have seen Landau's paper (which appeared in print later in 1927) *before* finishing his paper (1927c, which was presented on 11 November 1927), we have not been able to find any trace of a direct influence of Landau's publication, in contrast to what Max Jammer stated: 'Following a suggestion of Landau, von Neumann introduced ... the statistical operator' (Jammer, 1966, p. 308). Probably, von Neumann—who had two papers presented (1927b and 1927c) to the Göttingen Academy on 11 November—had finished the manuscript of the first one before he noticed Landau's paper.

III.3 Quantum-Mechanical Statistics and the Theory of Measurement 437

*Physik* on 13 October 1927. Weyl began his paper with a reference to von Neumann’s previous work on the mathematical foundation of quantum mechanics (von Neumann, 1927a), which he praised as providing a ‘clear and far-reaching answer’ to the fundamental question on the physical interpretation of Hermitean forms in quantum mechanics. ‘But it does not state everything which can be said about it, does not embrace all the *Ansätze* which have already been used successfully in the literature,’ he continued and added:

> I believe that I have completed the problem in this direction to a certain extent by establishing the concept of the “pure case (*reiner Fall*).” A pure case of atoms is given if the atomic beam considered possesses the highest degree of homogeneity that can be realized. The monochromatic beam of light is another example from a different field. The pure case is represented by the *variables* of Hermitean form; the form itself provides information about the values which the quantity represented by it can assume, and with *which probability or frequency these values occur in the pure case under consideration*. On this theory of the pure case, then, the statistics of *mixed cases* can be based; von Neumann’s *Ansatz* [in 1927a] only referred to a special question in this field. (Weyl, 1927, pp. 1–2)

In a footnote, added in proof, the author then remarked: ‘As Mr. von Neumann has told [me] in a private communication, he has meanwhile also arrived at this concept.’ (Weyl, *loc. cit.*, second footnote, p. 1)
Weyl defined the concept of a pure state in greater detail in the example of an electron beam used in the Stern–Gerlach experiment (Weyl, *loc. cit.*, §2, pp. 7–9). There, he also gave an explanation for the notation, namely:

> The difference between a pure case and a mixture, which I establish here, is analogous to the biological concepts of the “pure lineage” (within the pure lineage Mendel’s laws of heredity are valid) and the “population” (to which the laws of Galton apply). Here [in quantum mechanics] as there [in biology] the art of experiment has the important task to isolate the pure lineage. The discrimination—theory of the pure cases, on the one hand, and statistics of the mixture, on the other—seems to me to be fundamental for the correct understanding of the meaning of quantum mechanics. (Weyl, *loc. cit.*, p. 8)

We shall postpone the discussion of the details of Weyl’s ideas to the following section (III.4), because they are quite embedded in group-theoretical arguments. Perhaps we should just draw attention here to the fact that Hermann Weyl watched quite carefully the work of John von Neumann, his former Zurich pupil, and approved of his results.
In any case, Weyl would very soon take over the essence of von Neumann’s probability-theoretical formulation of quantum mechanics—especially, the aspects connected with the statistical matrix $U$ (which he named $A$)—into his book *Gruppentheorie und Quantenmechanik* (Weyl, 1928b). After showing how Eq. (348) followed for the pure case, he generalized it to a ‘statistical aggregate

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0470 -->

438 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

(ensemble),’

$$\langle Q \rangle = \text{Trace}(AQ), \tag{351}$$

where $\langle Q \rangle$ denotes the expectation value of the quantity $Q$—called $E(Q)$ by von Neumann—and then stated:$^{530}$

> As J. von Neumann has remarked, this formula can be derived from the simple axioms (von Neumann, 1927b):
> 1. If $P$, $Q$ are physical quantities and $\lambda$ a real number, then $\langle \lambda P \rangle = \lambda \langle P \rangle$, $\langle P + Q \rangle = \langle P \rangle + \langle Q \rangle$.
> 2. If the quantity $Q$ is capable of assuming only positive values (i.e., if the form $Q$ is positive definite), then $\langle Q \rangle \geq 0$.
> 3. If $Q$ is a pure number, i.e., if it is independent of all physical conditions, then $\langle Q \rangle = Q$.

Assuming not only that any physical quantity $Q$ is represented by an Hermitean form, but also conversely that any Hermitean form represents some quantity associated with the system, then it follows that

$$\langle Q \rangle = \sum_{i,k} a_{ki} q_{ik}, \tag{[(352)]}$$

where the coefficients $a_{ki}$ are independent of $Q$. The matrix $A = \|a_{ik}\|$ must be Hermitean since $\langle Q \rangle$ is always real....
The probability that in the statistical aggregate $A$ the quantity $Q$ assumes the value $\kappa$ is

$$w = \text{Trace}(A E_{\kappa}), \tag{[(353)]}$$

where $E_{\kappa}$ is the idempotent form [*Eigenform*] associated with the characteristic number [eigenvalue] $\kappa$.
We can also distinguish “pure states” among general statistical aggregates, “mixed states,” by the fact that they cannot be obtained by mixing two or more different statistical aggregates. This corresponds to the theorem that an Hermitean matrix $A$ [of the form $a_{ik} = a_i \bar{a}_k$, with $\bar{a}_k$ complex conjugate to $\bar{a}_k$] is not expressible as the sum $B + C$ of two positive Hermitean forms which are not merely multiples of $A$. (Weyl, *loc. cit.*, pp. 68–69)

Hermann Weyl closed this passage by singling out two special statistical ensembles, namely: ‘The simplest statistical ensemble is the one characterized by the unit Hermitean form with unit matrix $\mathbf{1}$; it represents *total ignorance*. In thermodynamics the important role is played by the canonical aggregate $A = e^{-H/k\theta}$; $H$ is here the Hermitean form which represents the energy, $k$ the Boltzmann constant
