III.3 Quantum-Mechanical Statistics and the Theory of Measurement 439

and the number $\theta$ the temperature’ (Weyl, 1928b, English translation, pp. 79–80). At that point, he referred to another paper of von Neumann that dealt with the thermodynamics of quantum-mechanical ensembles (von Neumann, 1927c). We shall deal with this work immediately below.$^{531}$

### (b) The Thermodynamics of Quantum-Statistical Ensembles

John von Neumann outlined the programme of his second paper presented [as the foregoing, von Neumann (1927b) on 11 November 1927] to the Göttingen Academy as follows:

> The “elementary disordered” ensemble studied earlier [in von Neumann, 1927b: these are defined by $U = 1$, or all states $\phi$ having the same *a priori* probability!] represents an absolute equilibrium state; that is, it corresponds in the language of thermodynamics—if this can be applied—to infinite temperature.... In the present paper, ensembles of finite temperature shall be investigated, i.e., a proper thermodynamics of these shall be established. (von Neumann, 1927c, p. 275)

In order to achieve the expounded goal, he had evidently to introduce the characteristic thermodynamical concepts of temperature $\mathbf{T}$ and entropy $\mathbf{S}$ into quantum mechanics; further, the total energy $\mathbf{E}$ will assume an important role as a factor determining the thermodynamical systems; in particular, $\mathbf{E}$ is not available in unlimited amounts.
Now, in quantum mechanics, a peculiar thermodynamical aspect arises when physical quantities are measured, which do not assume sharp values for a given state $\phi$. In a perturbation-theoretical treatment (implying suitable, small potentials), then, the mixed state obtained may be expanded into infinitely many pure states, but this mathematical procedure implies an irreversible physical process with proper entropy increase. How can this be calculated? In classical thermodynamics, the entropy difference between two ensembles $\mathscr{G}_1$ and $\mathscr{G}_2$, each consisting of an identical number $N$ of systems $\mathscr{S}$, is obtained by performing a reversible change of the first into the second ensemble—with an infinite heat reservoir of temperature $\mathbf{T}$ taking over an amount of energy from system $\mathscr{S}_1$, which is compensated by a negative heat $\mathbf{Q}$. Then, the entropy gain of $\mathscr{G}_2$ over $\mathscr{G}_1$ becomes

$$\mathbf{S} = -\frac{\mathbf{Q}}{\mathbf{T}}. \tag{354}$$

In order to obtain a proper method of evaluating Eq. (354) in quantum mechanics, von Neumann referred to a consideration of Albert Einstein.
In a paper of July 1914, Einstein had suggested to derive two quantum-

---
$^{531}$ We should point out that Weyl’s presentation of von Neumann’s results quoted above perfectly overlapped with the synopsis given by von Neumann himself in the introduction of this new paper (i.e., von Neumann, 1927c, pp. 274–275).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0472 -->

440 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

theoretical results—namely, Planck’s radiation law and Nernst’s heat theorem—from purely thermodynamic reasoning (Einstein, 1914b). In particular, he had outlined the following procedure for dealing thermodynamically with a system of quantum-theoretical resonators:

> We consider a chemically uniform gas, each molecule of which carries a resonator. The energy of this resonator should not adopt any arbitrary value but only discrete ones, $\varepsilon_{\sigma}$. I shall now take the liberty to consider two molecules as chemically different, i.e., they may be separated by semi-permeable walls if their resonator energies $\varepsilon_{\sigma}$ and $\varepsilon_{\tau}$ differ. Then I am allowed to view the gas, considered originally as chemically uniform, also as a mixture of chemically different gases whose parts are characterized by a certain $\varepsilon_{\sigma}$. By establishing the condition that this mixture exists in a thermodynamical equilibrium with respect to all changes of the $\varepsilon$-values of the molecules, I shall obtain a statistical law describing the distribution of the resonator energy among the molecules. Then, on treating the resonator energy again as a “thermal energy,” I shall obtain that part of the specific heat of the gas which emerges from the resonators connected with the molecules. (Einstein, *loc. cit.*, pp. 820–821)

Assuming, in addition, that the entropy constants for all resonators are identical, Einstein had been led to Planck’s blackbody radiation law. Also, a special expression of Walther Nernst’s heat theorem followed from a generalization of Einstein’s procedure, which he had given in his paper:

> We consider a physical system playing the role of the “molecule.” For that purpose it is necessary that we consider this system not as an isolated one but connected with an infinitely large heat reservoir. The state of the system is then thought to be characterized thermodynamically by the temperature and one (or several) parameter $\lambda$ (e.g., the volume). The possible states of the system will depend then, like the realizable energy values $\varepsilon_{\sigma}^*$, on the values of the parameter $\lambda$. (Einstein, *loc. cit.*, p. 825)

As the first result from this treatment, Einstein had derived the Planck–Boltzmann formula for the entropy $S$, expressed in terms of the temperature-dependent average energy of the system $\bar{\varepsilon}^*$ and the ‘sum over states,’ i.e.,

$$S = \frac{\bar{\varepsilon}^*}{T} + k \log \sum_{\sigma} \exp\left(-\frac{\varepsilon_{\sigma}^*}{kT}\right), \tag{355}$$

with $k$ denoting Boltzmann’s constant.$^{532}$ He had then generalized Eq. (355) to systems with variable parameters $\lambda$ by using Paul Ehrenfest’s adiabatic hypothesis and obtained the conclusion: ‘The entropy of a system possesses for all (thermodynamically defined) states of the system the same value, which can be realized in the sense of quantum theory by the same number of possibilities.’ (Einstein, *loc. cit.*, p. 827)

---
$^{532}$ Einstein wrote $R/N$ for $k$.

### III.3 Quantum-Mechanical Statistics and the Theory of Measurement 441

von Neumann knew from his friend Leo Szilard that Einstein’s procedure of 1914 ‘allows in a superior way to obtain a foundation of statistical thermodynamics in the non-quantum case.’$^{533}$ More important for his own work of 1927 was that it could be used for creating a quantum-mechanical thermodynamics. Thus, he first defined thermodynamical ensembles $\mathscr{G}$ on the lines proposed by Einstein, notably:

> We take every element of $\mathscr{G}$ (i.e., the systems $\mathscr{S}$) as a single element, isolated from the environment, and enclose it in a box. To each box we attach a weight whose mass is much superior to that of the system (such that changes of $\mathscr{S}$ hardly alter the mass of the whole object, hence they cannot be noticed directly), and we call the object thus obtained a “molecule.” We enclose all these molecules in a very large box (their volume can be neglected compared to volume of the box), and we let this box have contact with an infinite heat reservoir of temperature $\mathbf{T}$. The whole thing we then call the gas (of temperature $\mathbf{T}$) associated by $\mathscr{G}$. If the weights connected with the molecules and the volume of the big box are large enough (depending on $\mathbf{T}$), we may speak of an ideal gas. (von Neumann, 1927c, pp. 276–277)

In the ensembles so defined, a reversible process may be carried out changing the state of a gas from an ensemble $\mathscr{G}_1$ into another ensemble $\mathscr{G}_2$, and the entropy may be calculated properly.
Applying the procedure just mentioned, von Neumann wanted to prove the following results in quantum mechanics:$^{534}$

(1) The entropy of molecules in ‘pure ensembles’ is identical and can be put equal to zero.
(2) The entropy of a mixture (with $N$ molecules) having the statistical operator $U$ is given by the equation
$$\mathbf{S} = -Nk \text{ Trace}(U \log U). \tag{356}$$
(3) The state of equilibrium will be obtained by searching, for a given average energy $\mathbf{E}$, the ensemble that possesses the maximum entropy $\mathbf{S}$, according to Eq. (356), under the subsidiary conditions
$$\text{Trace } U = 1 \tag{357a}$$
and
$$\mathbf{E} = \text{Trace}(UH), \tag{357b}$$
where $H$ is the energy operator. This evaluation yields
$$U_{\text{equilibrium}} = \alpha \exp(\beta H), \tag{357c}$$

$^{533}$ See von Neumann, 1927c, p. 275, footnote 1. We shall return to Szilard’s work (1925) in connection with the quantum-mechanical theory of measurement below.
$^{534}$ See von Neumann, 1927c, pp. 277–280.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0474 -->

442 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

with the ‘constants’ $\beta$ and $\alpha$ defined as$^{535}$
$$\beta = -\frac{1}{k\mathbf{T}}, \quad \text{and} \quad \alpha = \frac{1}{\text{Trace } \exp(\beta H)}. \tag{358}$$
That is, the equilibrium ensemble is characterized by the expressions
$$U = \frac{1}{\text{Trace}\left(\exp\left(-\frac{H}{k\mathbf{T}}\right)\right)} \exp\left(-\frac{H}{k\mathbf{T}}\right), \tag{359a}$$
$$\mathbf{E} = \frac{\text{Trace}\left(H \exp\left(-\frac{H}{k\mathbf{T}}\right)\right)}{\text{Trace}\left(\exp\left(-\frac{H}{k\mathbf{T}}\right)\right)}, \tag{359b}$$
and
$$\mathbf{S} = \frac{N}{k\mathbf{T}} \frac{\text{Trace}\left(H \exp\left(-\frac{H}{k\mathbf{T}}\right)\right)}{\text{Trace}\left(\exp\left(-\frac{H}{k\mathbf{T}}\right)\right)} + Nk \log \text{Trace}\left(\exp\left(-\frac{H}{k\mathbf{T}}\right)\right) \tag{359c}$$
for the statistical operator, the average energy, and the entropy.

Evidently, the last expression, Eq. (359c), corresponds perfectly to the entropy formula (355) obtained by Einstein in 1914.
In order to prove Eqs. (359a–c), which was the essence of his paper, von Neumann had to translate the standard concepts of classical thermodynamics into quantum mechanics, notably, that of a ‘semi-permeable wall’ and of a reversible change of a system. In general, walls with holes and shutters, which reflect or let particles or other microscopic objects pass through, make no sense in quantum mechanics. Still, one can distinguish microscopic objects by the measurement of a quantity $a$, i.e., according to whether they are in an eigenstate of $a$, because if they are not, the measurement would change their state. Further, von Neumann argued, it is possible to distinguish by measurement between particles having different eigenstates; of course, this measurement also exerts an influence on a semi-permeable wall functioning with particles of different energies, but this influence can be compensated. A reversible change between two pure ensembles $\mathscr{G}_1$ (with projection operator $P_\phi$) and $\mathscr{G}_2$ (with projection operator $P_\psi$) is possible and yields an appropriate result (depending on the energy differences of the states $\phi$ and $\psi$).

$^{535}$ $\beta$ follows from the thermodynamical definition of the temperature, $\mathbf{T} = Nd\mathbf{E}/d\mathbf{S}$, and Eq. (357a).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0475 -->

### III.3 Quantum-Mechanical Statistics and the Theory of Measurement 443

However, it would not follow from a measurement of a quantity in $\mathscr{G}_1$ having $\psi$ (of $\mathscr{G}_2$) as an eigenfunction, because the $\phi$ and $\psi$ are orthogonal eigenfunctions. The correct procedure to calculate the entropy difference of the two ensembles involves a third state $\chi$, orthogonal to both $\phi$ and $\psi$: one changes $\phi$ in very many (perhaps even infinitely many) fine steps into $\chi$ and then similarly into $\psi$; consequently, the projection operator $P_\phi$ passes over—with only negligible compensation effects (as von Neumann demonstrated by a detailed evaluation)—into $U_p$ (the statistical operator of the $p$-th step in the procedure), and in the limit of $p$ very large or infinity $U_p$ passes over $P_\psi$. As a result, it is also possible to define a semipermeable wall in quantum mechanics that works, however, only properly on states having orthogonal eigenfunctions $\phi$ and $\psi$.$^{536}$
After these preparations, von Neumann turned to calculate the entropy increase in the following process: a pure ensemble $\mathscr{G}_1$, whose systems have the eigenstate $\phi$, is transformed into the mixture $\mathscr{G}_2$ of pure ensembles of states $\psi_1, \psi_2, \dots$, with the weights $w_1 \ge 0, w_2 \ge 0, \dots$, such that $w_1 + w_2 + \dots = 1$. For this purpose, he proposed the following procedure:

> We insert into the gas of $\mathscr{G}_1$ [consisting of $N$ “molecules”] a series of partitions such that they cut out volumes $w_1V, w_2V, \dots$ from the total volume $V$. Each of these partial volumes contains only molecules in the state $\phi$; these will be transformed in a reversible manner according to [the method given above] into the states $\psi_1, \psi_2, \dots$, respectively. We then expand the portions of gases of the pure ensembles of states $\psi_1, \psi_2, \dots$ (with particle numbers $w_1N, w_2N, \dots$) by an isothermal, reversible process (from their volumes $w_1V, w_2V, \dots$) into the [full] volume $V$. Then we enclose the first [portion of the] gas in a box surrounded by semi-permeable walls, which let [the molecules with eigenfunctions] $\psi_2, \psi_3, \dots$ pass undisturbed while they reflect [those with] $\psi_1$; the second [portion of the] gas in a box surrounded by semi-permeable walls, which let pass completely $\psi_1, \psi_3, \dots$ and reflect the $\psi_2$ molecules, etc., etc. We now put all these boxes into one another and thus obtain the desired mixture $\mathscr{G}_2$ (within the unchanged volume $V$). (von Neumann, 1927c, pp. 286–287)

Only one process of the entire procedure turns out to be an irreversible one, namely, the ‘isothermal reversible expansions’ of the gases with states $\psi_1, \text{ and } \psi_2, \dots, \text{because they require energy exchange with the heat reservoir.}$ Hence, the entropy of the final mixture $\mathscr{G}_2$ increases by the positive amount
$$\mathbf{S} = -Nk \sum_\mu w_\mu \log w_\mu. \tag{360}$$
Because the ensemble $\mathscr{G}_2$ is described by the statistical operator $U$ defined as
$$U = \sum_\mu w_\mu P_{\psi_\mu}, \tag{361}$$

$^{536}$ von Neumann proved the last statement by assuming Eq. (354) and constructing a proper statistical operator that allowed the semipermeable wall to perform the operation properly (von Neumann, 1927c, pp. 285–286).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0476 -->

444 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

its entropy can be expressed simply as
$$\mathbf{S} = -Nk \text{ Trace}(U \log U). \tag{362}$$
This result agrees perfectly with Eq. (356), because the pure ensemble $\mathscr{G}_1$ just possesses the entropy zero.
Now, the condition for equilibrium leads to an ensemble having the maximum entropy or a minimum value for Trace $(U \log U)$. von Neumann, therefore, had to solve the variational problem
$$\frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \text{ Trace}\{(U + \varepsilon V) \log(U + \varepsilon V)\}_{\varepsilon=0} = 0 \tag{363}$$
(with $V$ denoting any Hermitean operator and $\varepsilon$ a parameter) under the subsidiary conditions
$$\text{Trace } V = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \text{Trace}(VH) = 0. \tag{364}$$
He obtained the result
$$\log U + 1 = \alpha' 1 + \beta H, \tag{365}$$
which confirmed Eqs. (359a) and (359b), provided $\alpha' = 1 + \log \alpha$, except for the relation between $\beta$ and the temperature $\mathbf{T}$—which can be obtained in the usual way known from classical thermodynamics.
von Neumann concluded his paper by a remark concerning the validity of his results. Evidently, all formulae thus obtained made sense only as long as the series for the ‘sum over states ($Zustandssumme$)’ $Z$,
$$Z(\beta) = \text{Trace}\{\exp(\beta H)\} \quad \left(\text{with } \beta = -\frac{1}{k\mathbf{T}}\right), \tag{366}$$
and its derivative $Z' = dZ/d\beta$ converged.$^{537}$ These mathematical restrictions implied a condition on the energy operator $H$ of the physical system, for which the new thermodynamical approach was valid. In particular, von Neumann noted:

> In any case, $H$ should not have a continuous spectrum, and its eigenvalues $\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2, \dots$ have to converge towards $+\infty$. This is evidently the formal consequence of the fact that the system $\mathscr{S}$ can be enclosed in a box. It is even more characteristic that the above series [for $Z$ and $Z'$] diverge for temperatures surpassing a certain $\mathbf{T}$; this means that, though it is possible to enclose a system $\mathscr{S}$ for a sufficiently small tem-

$^{537}$ Because the energy operator $H$ has the eigenvalue $\varepsilon_\mu$, the sum over states (366) reduces to the well-known expression of Planck, $\sum_\mu \exp(-\varepsilon_\mu / k\mathbf{T})$. Evidently, $U, \mathbf{E}$, and $\mathbf{S}$ in Eqs. (359a–c) can also be written in terms of $Z$ and $Z'$ (see von Neumann, 1927c, pp. 290–291).

III.3 Quantum-Mechanical Statistics and the Theory of Measurement 445

perature in a box, there exists a certain temperature \( \mathbf{T} \) for which an “explosion” occurs. (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 291)

Perhaps we should add here that von Neumann denoted, in his original paper, both eigenvalues of the statistical operator \( U \) and of the energy operator \( H \) by the same letter \( w_\mu \), which might puzzle the reader. Actually, a simple relation between the probabilities \( w_\mu \), of a given quantum state and its energy \( \varepsilon_\mu \), exists i.e.,

$$
w_\mu = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{kT}\varepsilon_\mu\right) / \sum_{\mu} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{kT}\varepsilon_\mu\right). \tag{367}
$$

Then, the average energy \( \mathbf{E} \) assumes the well-known expression

$$
\mathbf{E} = \frac{\sum_{\mu} \varepsilon_\mu \exp\left(-\frac{1}{kT}\right)}{\sum_{\mu} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{kT}\right)}, \tag{368}
$$

and so does the expression for the entropy \( \mathbf{S} \).<sup>538</sup>

### (c) The Ergodic Hypothesis and the H-Theorem in Quantum Mechanics (1927–1929)

With his fundamental essay of November 1927, von Neumann was not the first pioneer to investigate the connection between thermodynamics and quantum mechanics. Rather, it was Erwin Schrödinger who initiated the field in a paper, entitled ‘*Energieaustausch nach der Wellenmechanik*’ (‘Energy Exchange According to Wave Mechanics’), which he submitted to *Annalen der Physik* in June 1927 (Schrödinger, 1927c). This work continued his long-term programme of demonstrating the superiority of the undulatory approach in understanding in a visualizable manner the physical behaviour of atomic systems (see, e.g., Schrödinger, 1927b). In particular, he discussed the wave-mechanical energy exchange, i.e., how Heisenberg’s resonance or exchange phenomena occurring in coupled degenerate systems should be interpreted in his undulatory language. Quite happily, he noticed that:

> without assuming any discrete energy levels and quantum-like exchange, even without having to employ a different meaning of eigenvalues than as *frequencies*, we can still give a simple explanation. . . . Without referring to quantum postulates, we arrive at such a behaviour, *as if* the quantum postulates were rightly valid (*zu Recht bestehen*). . . . I cannot resist feeling that to admit the quantum postulates besides the resonance phenomena would mean accepting *two* explanations for the same fact. (Schrödinger, 1927c, pp. 961–963)

<sup>538</sup> For details of the demonstration, see von Neumann’s book (1932c, Section V.3).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0478 -->

446 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

While this feeling confirmed Schrödinger’s prejudices against the energy-quantum concept, another fact also stressed the apparent similarity of wave-mechanical and classical systems: the description of atomic systems in quantum mechanics needed a ‘statistical hypothesis,’ just as in classical statistical mechanics, in order to account for their thermodynamical behavior. This hypothesis then made it possible to fix the ‘quantum weights’ and confirmed the results of the previous semiclassical quantum statistics.<sup>539</sup> On the other hand, Schrödinger arrived at the firm conclusion: ‘As far as I can see, one is never able to obtain a unidirectional (irreversible) process without adding a hypothesis concerning the relative probability of the different possible initial distributions of the probability amplitudes.’ (Schrödinger, *loc. cit.*, p. 968) This result strengthened his reservation toward Max Born’s probability interpretation of the wave function, especially:

> because one should demand of a theory, which postulates an absolute primary probability as a natural law, that it liberate us for this price at least from the old “ergodic problem” and allow us to understand the unidirectional development of natural processes without further assumptions. (Schrödinger, *loc. cit.*)

The following quantum-mechanical treatments of irreversible processes by Lothar Nordheim and Wolfgang Pauli also did not work without extra assumptions. Thus, Nordheim, then on a Rockefeller grant with Ralph Fowler in Cambridge, made use of a quantum-theoretical reformulation of Boltzmann’s collision equation (containing collision terms involving products of the collision function \( f \)) to describe the time-development of Bose and Fermi gases (Nordheim, 1928b). By this procedure, he not only derived the well-known Einstein or Fermi distributions for ideal quantum gases at equilibrium, but also a quantum-mechanical \( \mathcal{H} \)-theorem of the Boltzmann type,

$$
\frac{d\mathcal{H}}{dt} \leq 0, \tag{369}
$$

with \( \mathcal{H} \) denoting the negative logarithm of the ‘complexion number’ and defined by the phase-space (\( \Omega \)) integral<sup>540</sup>

$$
\mathcal{H} = \int [f \log f \mp (A \pm f) \log (A \pm f)] d\Omega. \tag{370}
$$

‘It seems clear that the entire theory of gases can be developed in a completely analogous way as in classical physics,’ Nordheim concluded and added:

<sup>539</sup> Schrödinger demonstrated how to derive the quantum weights in a simplified model system having few eigenstates and being placed in a ‘heat bath,’ i.e., a large system exhibiting a very dense eigenvalue spectrum (Schrödinger, 1927c, pp. 965–967).

<sup>540</sup> In Eq. (370), \( A \) is a constant and the alternative signs apply to the different quantum statistics.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0479 -->

It would perhaps not be too difficult to carry those calculations further, for instance to compute the viscosity and heat conduction at least in the case of nearly complete degeneracy. But, since at the present time a possibility of observation hardly seems to exist, we shall not go into further detail. (Nordheim, 1928b, p. 696)

Instead, he went on to treat an important problem in the electron theory of conductivity by his scheme, the collision of electrons with ions in a metal, finding that these collisions have no influence on the equilibrium distribution of electrons.<sup>541</sup>

At about the same time as Nordheim, Wolfgang Pauli approached the \( \mathcal{H} \)-theorem problem at some greater length, as he reported to Niels Bohr:

> Stimulated by our conversations during my last visit to Copenhagen [in March 1928] on the problem of the uni-direction of the arrow of time, I have recently thought somewhat about the question: under what condition and in which generality may an “\( \mathcal{H} \)-theorem” about increasing entropy be derived from the new quantum mechanics? . . . Now I believe that I am able to give the following answer to the problem of the \( \mathcal{H} \)-theorem:
> 1. One can demonstrate the increase of entropy quite generally, that is, not only for special systems (such as the ideal gas) but independent of their specific composition.
> 2. However, one *still cannot* dispense with the particular assumption concerning “disordering”—in contrast to my original hope. This assumption, corresponding to the *Stoßzahlansatz* in classical mechanics, can be formulated in wave mechanics always in such a way that the *phases* of certain groups of eigenvibrations are independent of each other. I shall try in the next days to write up the thing and shall then send you a copy of it. (Pauli to Bohr, 16 June 1928, in Pauli, 1979, p. 462)

Pauli, who had discussed this topic already before with Heisenberg (who, in a letter to Pauli dated 13 June, commented on the uncertainty entering into the quantum-mechanical measurement process by the act of observation), completed the paper and sent a copy to Bohr on 14 July (Pauli, 1928). Simultaneously, he submitted it to Peter Debye, the editor of the *Festschrift*, honouring their common teacher Arnold Sommerfeld on his sixtieth birthday.<sup>542</sup> Pauli outlined to Bohr the essential points as follows:

<sup>541</sup> These results and others obtained by Nordheim on the electron theory of metals will be discussed in Section III.6.

<sup>542</sup> In a letter dated 23 April 1928, Debye had asked thirty-four former students of Sommerfeld for contributions to the *Festschrift*: the selection began with the electrical engineer Walter Rogowski of Aachen and the mathematician Otto Blumenthal, and ended with the ‘young’ quantum theoreticians Pauli, Heisenberg, and Fritz London (see the letter of Debye, reprinted in Pauli, 1985, pp. 708–710). Apparently, Pauli received the invitation many weeks later, in June 1928, for he wrote back: ‘I shall answer your letter of the 27th immediately. I intend to send you for the *Sommerfeld-Festschrift* an essay on the \( \mathcal{H} \)-theorem concerning “the increase of entropy from the point of view of the new quantum mechanics.” Does it matter if its length surpasses a bit 10 pages of print? The larger part of the paper I have written up already, and I am certain to have the whole thing ready in two weeks’ (Pauli to Debye, 30 June 1928, *loc. cit.*, p. 710). By the way, Heisenberg also contributed to the *Festschrift* a paper connected with the statistical mechanics of ferromagnetism (Heisenberg, 1928b).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0480 -->

448 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

You may, in the first reading, pass over §1 of Chapter I, where special cases are dealt with. §2 of Chapter I gives the essential result. I consider the most important result of Chapter II to be the fact that even in wave mechanics a special assumption of “disorder” has still to be made. . . . I hope you will agree with this point. (Pauli to Bohr, 14 July 1928, in Pauli, 1979, p. 462)

Let us now turn to the contents of the paper in more detail.

Pauli devoted Chapter I to the ‘description of processes in statistical ensembles by transition processes between stationary states [of atomic systems]’—one may call this a ‘phenomenological treatment’ of the quantum-theoretical \( \mathcal{H} \)-problem. With the characterization as ‘phenomenological,’ we address the fact that Pauli developed models of atomic processes, which allowed him to imitate to some extent the classical procedure of Boltzmann and others. Thus, in §1, he dealt with collision processes between force-free Bose or Fermi particles, whose frequency was determined by the law

$$
Z_{\kappa\lambda, \mu\nu} = A_{\kappa\lambda, \mu\nu} n_\kappa n_\lambda (g_\mu + \alpha n_\mu)(g_\nu + \alpha n_\nu), \tag{371}
$$

with the transition coefficient \( A_{\kappa\lambda, \mu\nu} \) symmetric in each of the pairs of indices, and \( n_\mu \), \( n_\nu \) denoting the numbers of the corresponding molecules, \( g_\mu \) and \( g_\nu \) denoting the statistical weights of the final states, and \( \alpha = +1 \) for Bose and \( -1 \) for Fermi particles. From Eq. (371), the total change of the number of molecules, \( dn_\kappa/dt \), and the entropy can be computed, yielding an increase of entropy in the collision process. Furthermore, Pauli obtained in the equilibrium case the Einstein or the Fermi distribution (as Nordheim had done in the more sketchy study discussed earlier).<sup>543</sup>

In §2, Pauli replaced the consideration of the individual system of molecules and light-quanta by a consideration of ensembles of such particles. Let \( \mathscr{G}_n \) be the number of stationary states of the total system, then \( \log \mathscr{G}_n \) can be identified essentially with the entropy \( S \), i.e.,

$$
\log \mathscr{G}_n = \frac{1}{k} S = \sum_k \left[ \frac{1}{\alpha}(g_\kappa + \alpha n_\kappa) \log (g_\kappa + \alpha n_\kappa) - n_\kappa \log n_\kappa - \alpha g_\kappa \log g_\kappa \right], \tag{372}
$$

where \( k \) denotes Boltzmann’s constant. Since the whole system may not be fully determined by a single \( \mathscr{G}_n \), but rather by a mixture of them, with probabilities \( W_n \) (with \( \sum_n W_n = 1 \)), its entropy assumes the value

$$
S = k \sum_n W_n (\log \mathscr{G}_n - \log W_n). \tag{373}
$$

<sup>543</sup> Pauli also evaluated explicitly the case of the interaction between an ideal gas (of molecules having both statistics) and light-quanta. Again, he found an increase of entropy in this process and, in the case of equilibrium, Planck’s blackbody distribution for the light-quanta.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0481 -->

### III.3 Quantum-Mechanical Statistics and the Theory of Measurement  
449  

Also, in this case, the frequencies (per unit time) of transition processes can be defined by an *Ansatz* similar to Eq. (371), notably,  
$$ Z_{nm} = A_{nm} \mathcal{G}_m W_n, \tag{374} $$  

with \( A_{nm} \) the corresponding transition probabilities (which are symmetric in \( n \) and \( m \), due to Liouville’s theorem). Hence, the \( W_n \) obey a decay rule analogous to that of a ‘radioactive’ process, i.e.,  
$$ \frac{dW_n}{dt} = -\sum_m A_{nm} \mathcal{G}_m W_n + \sum_m A_{mn} \mathcal{G}_n W_m. \tag{375} $$  

Upon inserting Eq. (375) into Eq. (373), Pauli then derived the second law of thermodynamics, or  
$$ \frac{dS}{dt} \geq 0, \tag{376} $$  

where the equilibrium condition \( \left( \frac{dS}{dt} \geq 0 \right) \) requires a symmetric \( Z_{nm} = Z_{mn} \) (in the equilibrium state). He concluded that:  

> statistical laws for the frequency of transitions between stationary states of the type of radioactive laws ... already guarantee such a degree of irregularity for the microscopic processes as is required for the proof of the second heat theorem. (Pauli, 1928b, p. 39)  

So far, the demonstration had concentrated on a translation and adoption of the procedures known from classical statistical mechanics to the quantum statistical case. The question then arose whether the quantum-mechanical formalism and its statistical interpretation, as completed by Heisenberg’s uncertainty relations and Bohr’s complementarity principle, did not permit the treatment of the problem directly with fewer assumptions [that is, without the *Ansatz* (371) or (374)]. Now, the results of Heisenberg and Bohr revealed two nonclassical elements connected with the process of observation, which might provide the key to the proof of a quantum-mechanical \( \mathcal{H} \)-theorem: first, every measurement of, say, energy \( E \) is restricted in accuracy by its time duration \( t \),  
$$ \Delta E \sim h/t; \tag{377} $$  

second, the discontinuous element is introduced into the description of atomic systems essentially by the act of observation—otherwise, the wave-mechanical equations determine a completely continuous evolution of the systems.  

To investigate the effect of observation on an atomic system, Pauli considered a

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0482 -->

450 | Chapter III: The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics  

model: an ‘isolated system,’ given by the idealized limiting case of a system that is left alone for a sufficiently long period of time. This system can be described by the harmonic wave function  
$$ \psi(q, t) = u(q) \exp \left( \frac{2\pi i}{h} Et \right), \tag{378} $$  

and possesses a completely (sharp) energy \( E.544 \) The observation of the time dependence of the isolated system would then change the latter into an ‘open system,’ described by a linear combination of all eigensolutions \( u_n(q) \)—with energies \( E_n \)—of the time-independent Hamiltonian \( H_0 \). The time-dependent probabilities \( a_n(t) \) multiplying each \( u_n(q) \) followed from a solution of the perturbed Hamiltonian \( H = H_0 + V \), according to Dirac’s method of variation of constants,  
$$ \frac{h}{2\pi i} \frac{da_m}{dt} = \sum_n V_{mn} \exp \left\{ \frac{2\pi i}{h} (E_n - E_m)t \right\} a_n, \tag{379} $$  

with constant matrix elements \( V_{mn} = \int u_m^* V u_n \) of the Hermitian matrix associated with the perturbation operator \( V.545 \) Here, Pauli assumed the additional potential \( V \) to act only during the time interval between 0 and \( t \), and the state of the system to be known before the instant 0 and after the instant \( t \), respectively; it is then given as \( u_n(q) \) with the probabilities \( |a_n(0)|^2 \) and \( |a_n(t)|^2 \), respectively. Or, if one is only interested in finding the system in a definite ‘elementary region’ of states, the corresponding probability assumes the value \( \sum_n |a_n|^2 \), with the sum extending over all states in the region. Such a result does not yet represent the actual situations in thermodynamics, however, where one would rather like not to turn off the action of a potential, Pauli continued. Also, this procedure is possible, provided the time \( \tau \) of measurement is made so short that the action of \( V \) on the system can be neglected, but ‘then the elementary regions of stationary states have to be chosen such that the energy with \( \Delta E \) covered by each of them satisfies the relation  
$$ \Delta E \gg \frac{h}{\tau}, \tag{380} $$

> The concept of “stationary state” is, in my opinion, essentially connected with observation and not with isolated systems, since the word “stationary” makes no sense as long as one does not observe. Here you argue just like von Neumann, whose paper you have criticized so harshly. (Heisenberg to Pauli, 31 July 1928, in Pauli, 1979, p. 466)

### III.3 Quantum-Mechanical Statistics and the Theory of Measurement  
451  

(Pauli, 1928, p. 41). In the special case that \( \tau \ll T_n \) (with \( T_n \) the inverse of the sum of the ‘transition probabilities’ of the spontaneous processes that can be started from a state \( n \)), it is even possible to use a single quantum state as an elementary region (for the probability considerations).  

Paul Dirac, in his papers on the emission and absorption of radiation (referred to in footnote 545), had already derived statistical laws of the type of Eq. (371). Pauli now demonstrated explicitly that the decay formula (375), which allows one to prove the quantum-mechanical \( \mathcal{H} \)-theorem, would indeed follow from Eq. (379) and by a suitable application of the time-dependent procedure of Dirac. In the case that the elementary regions consisted only of single states, he required no extra conditions—but in practice this case hardly occurs. Still, for the general case, the \( \mathcal{H} \)-theorem can also be proved for all initial conditions [including \( W_n(0) = 0 \) and \( W_m(0) = 1 \), which describe an absorption process], if the initial Dirac coefficients \( a_\alpha(0) \) satisfy what Pauli called the ‘wave-mechanical form of the hypothesis of “elementary disorder,”’ that is:  

> ‘The phases of the single \( a_\alpha(0) \) are independent of each other, the absolute values of the different \( a_\alpha(0) \) are equal’ (Pauli, *loc. cit.*, p. 44).  

Thus, he finally stated as the ‘essential result’ of his considerations that  

> in all cases, when elementary regions containing several states possess a non-vanishing initial probability, one must introduce, for establishing the validity of the \( \mathcal{H} \)-theorem, an assumption of an elementary disorder, analogous to the *Stoßzahlansatz* in classical mechanics. This states that the phases of the eigenvibrations belonging to the elementary region under investigation must be assumed as being disordered. (Pauli, *loc. cit.*, p. 45)  

He then added the remark:  

> Although in general the observations themselves will favour such a disorder, cases like those in classical physics cannot be excluded, for which the conditions guaranteeing the validity of the \( \mathcal{H} \)-theorem are not justified automatically [i.e., without introducing the above condition of “molecular disorder”]. (Pauli, *loc. cit.*)  

Less than a year later, John von Neumann attacked Pauli’s conclusion in a mathematically detailed memoir, boldly entitled *‘Beweis des Ergodensatzes und des \( \mathcal{H} \)-Theorems in der neuen Mechanik’* (‘Proof of the Ergodic Theorem and the \( \mathcal{H} \)-theorem in the New Mechanics’), submitted in May and published in August 1929. He summarized the contents in the short abstract simply as:  

> It is shown how the apparent contradiction between the microscopic concept of the phase-space and the validity of the uncertainty relations can be resolved. Then the central concepts of statistical mechanics are reformulated in quantum mechanics, and the ergodic theorem and the \( \mathcal{H} \)-theorem are stated and proved without the “assumptions of disorder.” There follows a discussion of the physical meaning of the mathematical conditions fixing the range of validity [of the two theorems]. (von Neumann, 1929c, p. 30)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0484 -->

452 | Chapter III: The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics  

How did von Neumann confirm this bold announcement? Evidently, he selected a different path from those of his predecessors, Schrödinger, Nordheim, and Pauli, appealing to a wider range of concepts than the quantum physicists.  

We know from classical statistical mechanics that two approaches explained the occurrence of irreversibility. Besides Boltzmann’s method of the *Stoßzahlansatz* or ‘hypothesis of molecular disorder’—which had been taken over into quantum mechanics by Nordheim and Pauli—the canonical ensemble treatment existed. Josiah Willard Gibbs used, especially in connection with the latter, the so-called ‘quasi-ergodic theorem.’ Although its proof has presented in classical theory ‘a mathematically absolutely invincible problem’ (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 31), the new quantum mechanics possessing a much simpler structure than classical mechanics offered new perspectives. In any case, von Neumann wanted to follow the Gibbsian path, and he immediately began by searching for a reformulation of its central concept, the phase-space of position and momentum variables. In quantum mechanics, no accurate determination of any canonically conjugate pair \( Q_k \) and \( P_k \) of position and momentum variables was possible; consequently, neither a continuous phase-space nor the division of the latter into discrete phase cells made sense in the new theory. Still, von Neumann claimed that one might avoid this principal difficulty by means of the following idea: one associates with the measurement procedure, which is a *macroscopic* process, variables \( Q' \) and \( P' \) deviating from the quantum-mechanical, microscopic variables \( Q \) and \( P \): the ‘macroscopic variables’ \( Q' \) and \( P' \) always commute and approximate \( P \) and \( Q \) only as far as the uncertainty relations allow, i.e., the product of the corresponding deviations \( \varepsilon \) and \( \eta \) is given by  
$$ \varepsilon \cdot \eta = C \frac{h}{4\pi} \tag{381} $$  

with \( C \) a constant \( \geq 1.546 \) The association with the simultaneous commutable quantities \( Q' \) and \( P' \), then, ‘determined the nature of the macroscopic measurement’ in quantum mechanics (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 34).  

Turning now to the formulation of the ‘ergodic theorem’ in quantum mechanics, von Neumann observed that it seemed on first inspection quite easy to do so: an ‘energy surface’ might be constructed simply by the following equation: \( 547 \)  
$$ \sum_n |a_n|^2 \varepsilon_n = \text{const.} \tag{382} $$  

Then, the ergodic theorem was satisfied if the quantum frequencies did not exhibit  


---

⁵⁴⁶ The macroscopic variables may also be associated with a complete orthogonal set of eigenfunctions \( \phi_n, n = 1, 2, \ldots \) and the corresponding eigenvalues.  

⁵⁴⁷ To avoid confusion with notation of this section, we replace the energy eigenvalues \( W_n \) of von Neumann by \( \varepsilon_n \).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0485 -->

too many resonances; in fact, even a weaker condition would suffice to prove ergodicity, namely, if no degenerate energy states exist in the system under consideration. However, von Neumann was not satisfied with such cheap results, because they did not make use of the macroscopic aspects of the problem; therefore, he argued:

So far we only operated with the completely known [microscopic] system, in which for example the energy surface is given by the exact specification of all $|a_n|^2$. To approach the insufficiently known systems occurring in statistical mechanics we must further change the formulation of the problem. (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 38)

For this purpose, the energy surface had to be rather defined in terms of macroscopic variables. A microcanonical ensemble then, also in the new atomic theory, consists of a set of states, whose energy statistics (distribution) cannot be distinguished macroscopically from a given one. Consequently, the procedure known from classical statistical mechanics can be copied: first, to show that for every quantity the statistics in time coincides with the statistics of the microcanonical ensemble; second, that for the above defined macroscopic quantities the microcanonical average exhibits only small fluctuations. In quantum mechanics, where energy states and eigenvalues are exactly (microscopically) given, one must define the energy surfaces and their division into phase cells with the help of macroscopic measurements. Then, the quantum states not only have to be nondegenerate, but their number in every phase cell must also be very large, even with respect to the number of phase cells on the energy surface. With these preliminary assumptions, von Neumann formulated what he considered to be ‘the essential statement of the $\mathcal{H}$-theorem,’ namely:

The time-average of the entropy of $\psi_t$ [denoting the solution of the time-dependent Schrödinger equation] deviates only little from the entropy of the microcanonical ensemble—and since the latter is the upper limit of the former, this implies that the latter is surpassed by the entropy of $\psi_t$ only rarely at all by more than little. (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 41)

We shall explain the exact meaning of the definitions in this formulation in the course of presenting von Neumann's proof in the following account.
The proof required the proper definitions of the concepts of macroscopic operators, the phase cells, the energy surface, and the statistical operator for the microscopic ensemble, which von Neumann provided in Part I of his paper under the heading ‘*Quantenmechanische Formulierungen und Begriffsbildungen der Gibbsschen statistischen Mechanik*’ (‘Quantum-Mechanical Formulation of the Conceptions of Gibbs's Statistical Mechanics’, von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, pp. 42–48). Macroscopic operators assume the same values for sets of microscopic states with wave functions $\omega_{1_p}, \dots \omega_{s_p p}$, $p = 1, 2, \dots$. The statistical ensemble connected with each

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0486 -->

value of $p$ possesses the statistical operator

$$
\frac{1}{s_p} \mathbf{E}_p = \frac{1}{s_p} \sum_{\lambda=1}^{s_p} \mathbf{P}_{\omega_{i,p}} \qquad (383)
$$

(with $\mathbf{P}_{\omega_{i,p}}$ denoting the corresponding projection operator). $\frac{1}{s_p} \mathbf{E}_p$ then becomes the equivalent of the phase cell in Gibbs's statistical mechanics, and $s_p$ denotes the number of microscopic states in the phase cell. The (microscopic) energy eigenvalues may be organized into groups $\epsilon_{p,a} (\rho = 1, \dots, S_a)$ of closely neighbouring ones representing the macroscopically measurable energy. The quantity $\Delta_a$, defined as

$$
\Delta_a = \sum_{\rho=1}^{S_a} \mathbf{P}_{\phi_{\rho, a}} = \sum_{\nu=1}^{N_a} \mathbf{E}_{\nu, a}, \qquad (384)
$$

then determines the equivalent of the energy surface, or as von Neumann explained in more detail:

$\frac{1}{S_a} \Delta_a$ corresponds to the energy surface, i.e., to the microcanonical ensemble; $N_a$ denotes the number of phase cells $\mathbf{E}_{\nu, a}$ on the energy surface, and $S_a = \text{Trace } \Delta_a$ gives the number of real states, i.e., of the quantum states, on it. (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 45)

Evidently, the macroscopic energy measurements decompose the ensemble of possible states into the energy surfaces $\Delta_a$, $a = 1, 2, \dots$; other energy-measurements (which dissolve $\Delta_a$ into the states $\phi_{\rho, a}$, $\rho = 1, \dots, S_a$) do not exist. However, further macroscopic measurements exist, which do not commute with the (microscopic) energy operator $\mathbf{H}$, and these decompose $\Delta_a$ into the phase cells $\mathbf{E}_{\nu, a}$, $\nu = 1, \dots N_a$. Again, a decomposition of the phase cells into the states $\omega_{\lambda, \nu, a}$, $\lambda = 1, \dots s_{\nu, a}$, cannot be achieved by any macroscopic measurement. Hence, the magnitude of the number $N_a$ determines the effect of the uncertainty relation on the accuracy of the macroscopic energy measurement, the magnitude of $s_{\nu, a}$ (i.e., the size of the phase cells $\mathbf{E}_{\nu, a}$) determines the inaccuracy of the macroscopic methods, and $S_a = \sum_{\nu=1}^{N_a} s_{\nu, a}$ gives the total inaccuracy of the energy measurement.
With these preparations, von Neumann formulated the main equations of his paper. For an arbitrary state $\psi$, he wrote the following expressions:

(1) the probability of finding $\psi$ via macroscopic measurements in the phase cell $\mathbf{E}_{\nu, a}$,

$$
(\mathbf{E}_{\nu, a} \psi, \psi) = \sum_{\lambda=1}^{s_{\nu, a}} |(\psi, \omega_{\lambda, \nu, a})|^2; \qquad (385)
$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0487 -->

(2) the occupation number of the energy surface $\Delta_a$,

$$
(\Delta_a \psi, \psi) = \sum_{\rho=1}^{S_a} |(\psi, \psi_{\rho, a})|^2 = \sum_{\nu=1}^{N_a} (\mathbf{E}_{\nu, a} \psi, \psi); \qquad (386)
$$

(3) the statistical operator for the microcanonical ensemble connected with the state $\psi$, i.e.,

$$
\mathbf{U}_{\psi} = \sum_{a=1}^{\infty} \frac{(\Delta_a \psi, \psi)}{S_a} \Delta_a; \qquad (387)
$$

(4) the entropy for the state $\psi$, i.e.,

$$
S(\psi) = - \sum_{a=1}^{\infty} \sum_{\nu=1}^{N_a} (\mathbf{E}_{\nu, a} \psi, \psi) \log \frac{(\mathbf{E}_{\nu, a} \psi, \psi)}{s_{\nu, a}}; \qquad (388)
$$

(5) the entropy for the microcanonical ensemble, to which $\psi$ belongs, i.e.,

$$
S(\mathbf{U}_{\psi}) = - \sum_{a=1}^{\infty} (\Delta_a \psi, \psi) \log \frac{(\Delta_a \psi, \psi)}{S_a}. \qquad (389)
$$

(See von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, pp. 46–48.)

von Neumann mentioned about the entropy expressions (388) and (389) that ‘they are obtained from the point of view of an observer, who can carry out all measurements that are possible in principle,’ and he commented:

If one takes into account that the observer can only perform a macroscopic measurement, then one finds other entropies—larger ones, because the observer is then less capable and can obtain only less mechanical energy from the system. (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, pp. 47–48)

A theory describing the latter situation had been established already by von Neumann's friend and fellow countryman, with whom he had discussed the whole problem in detail, and ‘Mr. E. Wigner communicated his results on this topic orally to the author’ (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 48). Still, von Neumann did not make use of this extension, but rather worked with Eqs. (388) and (389) expressing minimum entropy.
In Part II of his paper (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, pp. 48–70), von Neumann finally developed the proof of the ergodic theorem. First, he calculated the time-dependent entropy $S(\psi_t)$, with $\psi_t$ being a solution of the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, obtaining

$$
S(\psi_t) = - \sum_{a=1}^{\infty} \sum_{\nu=1}^{N_a} x_{\nu, a} \log \frac{x_{\nu, a}}{s_{\nu, a}}, \qquad (390)
$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0488 -->

with

$$
x_{\nu, a} = (\mathbf{E}_{\nu, a} \psi_t, \psi_t). \qquad (390\mathrm{a})
$$

For the corresponding ensemble entropy, there followed

$$
S(\mathbf{U}_{\psi_t}) = - \sum_{a=1}^{\infty} u_a \log \frac{u_a}{S_a}, \qquad (391)
$$

with

$$
u_a = (\Delta_a \psi_t, \psi_t). \qquad (391\mathrm{a})
$$

Since $u_a = \sum_{\nu=1}^{N_a} (x_{\nu, a})$ does not depend on $t$ at all, $S(\mathbf{U}_{\psi_t})$ coincided with $S(\mathbf{U}_{\psi})$, Eq. (389). Also, all entropy expressions assumed positive or zero values. Then, the ergodic theorem would hold, provided the entropy for the ensemble does not deviate appreciably from that of the time-dependent $\psi_t$. On evaluating this difference carefully, von Neumann found the result

$$
S(\mathbf{U}_{\psi}) - S(\psi_t) \leq \sum_{\nu=1}^{N_a} \frac{S_a}{s_{\nu, a}} (\mathbf{M}_{\nu, a} + \mathbf{N}_{\nu, a}), \qquad (392)
$$

where $\mathbf{M}_{\nu, a}$ and $\mathbf{N}_{\nu, a}$ were independent of $\psi_t$ and $t$. The right-hand side indeed turned out to be small for the ‘overwhelming majority’ of states, provided the system satisfied the condition

$$
\sum_{\nu=1}^{N_a} \frac{1}{s_{\nu, a}} \ll \frac{1}{\log \bar{s}_a}, \quad \text{with } \bar{s}_a = \frac{S_a}{N_a}, \qquad (393)
$$

held, or, expressed in physical terms, ‘if the phase cells $\mathbf{E}_{\nu, a}$ are large in relation to their number on the energy surface $\Delta_a$’ (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 48). This statement concluded von Neumann's ergodicity proof for quantum-mechanical systems.

**(d) The Reception of von Neumann's Work on Quantum Statistical Mechanics (1929)**

When working on the $\mathcal{H}$-theorem and the ergodic hypothesis, von Neumann competed with the physicists Schrödinger, Nordheim, and Pauli. Because he mentioned their efforts only in passing, and claimed superiority of his own results, one may expect that the physicists also commented on the assertions of their competi-

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0489 -->

### III.3 Quantum-Mechanical Statistics and the Theory of Measurement 457

tor.$^{548}$ Indeed, their answer came in due course, though Schrödinger and Pauli stated it rather privately. Before dealing with it, we report about some reactions on von Neumann's other ideas, which had occurred in his statistical formulation of quantum mechanics. In sum, the comments may be organized into four categories: first, Max Born and Pascual Jordan popularized the statistical concepts (of von Neumann, 1927b, c) by presenting them in a simpler algebraic form; second, Paul Dirac employed the density-matrix approach in several problems of nonrelativistic and relativistic quantum mechanics; third, Erwin Schrödinger applauded von Neumann's discussion of the $\mathcal{H}$-theorem (von Neumann, 1929c); and fourth, Wolfgang Pauli remained rather reserved.

In Chapter 6 of their book *Elementare Quantenmechanik*, Born and Jordan (1930) translated von Neumann's operator formulation of the statistical content of quantum mechanics into the language of vectors and tensors, which was more familiar to physicists (at least in Göttingen). In particular, they rewrote the *Einzel* operators as Hermitean *Einzel* tensors, which allowed them to express the quantum-theoretical probabilities independently of the coordinate system chosen. In particular, if $A$ and $B$ are two physical quantities represented by diagonal matrices in the coordinate systems $\Sigma^{(1)}$ and $\Sigma^{(2)}$ of the quantum-mechanical Hilbert space, the probability that the quantity $A$ assumes eigenvalues $a_n$ and simultaneously the quantity $B$ the eigenvalues $b_k$, respectively, becomes (Born and Jordan, *loc. cit.*, p. 297)

$$w_{nk} = \text{Trace}(F^{(n)} \cdot G^{(k)}), \tag{394}$$

where $F^{(n)}$ and $G^{(k)}$ denote the corresponding *Einzel* tensors (or *Einzel* matrices). Further, Born and Jordan defined what they called the 'probability vector (*Wahrscheinlichkeitsvektor*)' $\boldsymbol{c}$, i.e., the normalized Hilbert-space vector associated with the eigenvalue $a_n$ of A; it possesses only one component in $\Sigma^{(1)}$ and the components $c_k$ in the coordinate system $\Sigma^{(2)}$, or

$$w_{nk} = |c_k|^2 = (G^{(k)}\boldsymbol{c}, \boldsymbol{c}), \tag{395}$$

where the round brackets denote the scalar product of two vectors $(\boldsymbol{G}^{(k)}\boldsymbol{c})$ and $\boldsymbol{c}$ (Born and Jordan, *loc. cit.*, p. 301). The *Einzel* tensor $F^{(n)}$ may be written as the tensor product of $\boldsymbol{c}$ with itself, i.e.,

$$\boldsymbol{F}^{(n)} = \boldsymbol{c} \times \boldsymbol{c}. \tag{396}$$

Now, one can easily obtain the probability $w_k$ for the eigenvalue $b_k$ of the quantity $B(= \sum b_k G^{(k)})$, if we have the 'pure case' for the quantity A, i.e., the system is in

---

Pauli [1928], describe the macroscopic situation by the assumptions of disorder, and therefore follow a different direction.' (von Neumann, 1929c, p. 41)

### 458 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

a given eigenvalue $a_n$ of A, then it is simply$^{549}$

$$w_{nk} = (\boldsymbol{G}^{(k)}\boldsymbol{c}, \boldsymbol{c}). \tag{397}$$

For the statistical average (expectation) value $\bar{B}$ of the quantity $B$ in the pure case described above—this is again represented by vector $\boldsymbol{c}$—there follows the expression

$$\bar{\boldsymbol{B}} = (\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{c}, \boldsymbol{c}), \tag{398}$$

and one easily derives the result that the average of the sum of two quantities $B_1$ and $B_2$ is equal to the sum of two averages (Born and Jordan, *loc. cit.*, p. 302).
With this preparation, Born and Jordan were able to discuss the main problems of statistical quantum mechanics (see Sections 57-59, entitled 'Statistics of Quantum-Mechanical Mixtures,' 'The Pure Case as a Special Mixture,' and 'The General Mixture as a Composition of Pure Cases': Born and Jordan, *loc. cit.*, pp. 305-322). They introduced the necessity of dealing with 'mixtures' as follows:

> For a number of identical atoms the non-degenerate quantity $A$ may be measured to assume partly the value $a_1$, partly the value of $a_2$, partly the value $a_3$, etc. We now single out an arbitrary atom of this set without knowing its eigenvalue with respect to $A$ and try to make predictions about the behaviour of this atom when new experiments are made: to the uncertainty arising from the statistical nature of quantum-mechanical laws then the uncertainty connected with the *incompleteness of our knowledge* will be added, if we want to predict the future reaction of the system considered. (Born and Jordan, *loc. cit.*, p. 305)

The situation described can be handled properly, Born and Jordan continued, by the statistical ensembles of von Neumann (1927b) involving the notion of the statistical operator, which they rewrote as the Hermitean tensor $\Phi$. Thus, the expectation value of a quantity $A$ for the ensemble will be written in the form

$$\bar{A} = \text{Trace}(\Phi A), \tag{399}$$

and the tensor $\Phi$ satisfies the equation

$$(\Phi x, x) \ge 0; \tag{400}$$

i.e., it is positive definite. While from a pure ensemble, $\Phi$ might be identified with an *Einzel* tensor $F^{(n)}$, for a mixture it had to be written obviously as

$$\Phi = \sum w_r F^{(r)}. \tag{401}$$

### III.3 Quantum-Mechanical Statistics and the Theory of Measurement 459

Thus, von Neumann's formalism assumed a comparatively simple shape in the Göttingen matrix formalism, which was easy to understand and handle by the physicists.
Paul Dirac, whose $\delta$-function von Neumann had banned from his rigorous formulation of quantum mechanics, did not revenge by neglecting von Neumann's results. In fall 1928, he rather used his critic's concepts in a paper on 'The Basis of Statistical Quantum Mechanics' (Dirac, 1929a). In his introduction, he declared:

> The basis of the quantum treatment of [Gibbs's ensembles] has been given by [von] Neumann (1927b). The description obtained by [von] Neumann of an ensemble on the quantum theory *is not more complicated than the corresponding classical description*. Thus the quantum theory, which appears to such a disadvantage on the scope of complication when applied to individual systems, recovers its own when applied to an ensemble. (Dirac, *loc. cit.*, p. 62)

What Dirac wished to demonstrate in his note was the particular simplicity of the quantum-mechanical description of Gibbs's ensembles, besides stressing simultaneously the analogy between the quantum and the classical treatment.
In classical theory, 'an ensemble of systems [e.g., point particles] can be represented by a dust of points in this space [i.e., the phase space], which dust will be describable by a density function $\rho(p_r, q_r)$ giving the number of points per unit 2n-dimensional volume in the neighbourhood of the place $(p_r, q_r)$,' wrote Dirac (Dirac, *loc. cit.*, pp. 62-63). He added that $\rho$ had to satisfy 'the hydrodynamical equation of continuity,' namely,

$$\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \sum_{m} \left\{ \frac{\partial}{\partial q_r} (\rho \dot{q}_r) + \frac{\partial}{\partial p_r} (\rho \dot{p}_r) \right\} = 0, \tag{402}$$

which he cast with the help of the well-known Poisson bracket (involving $\rho$ and the Hamiltonian $H$) into the elegant form$^{550}$

$$\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} = -[\rho, H]. \tag{403}$$

In quantum mechanics, Dirac replaced $\rho$ by a Hermitean matrix, whose matrix elements he wrote as

$$\rho_{nm} = \frac{1}{u} \sum_{s=1}^{u} c_m c_n \tag{404}$$

in the case of an ensemble consisting of $u$ systems (here, the $c_m$ denoted the prob-

where the square bracket now represented the commutator $\rho$ with the Hamiltonian matrix $H$.
Although in the paper of October 1928 Dirac just reformulated von Neumann's scheme in his own elegant language, he later applied the density matrix effectively in the problems of relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum mechanics. In March and May 1930, he submitted two papers to the Cambridge Philosophical Society. The first, 'On the Annihilation of Electrons and Protons' (Dirac, 1930b), dealt with a particular question arising in Dirac's new interpretation of the negative energy states in the relativistic electron theory as protons (Dirac, 1930a). It appeared to Dirac that the usual method of solving the complicated problem involving the electrons carrying spin and having interactions with the electromagnetic fields can be quite adequately replaced by considering an ensemble rather than a single relativistic system in quantum mechanics. He thus obtained a result for the probability of annihilation of an electron–'proton' pair, which turned out to be 'much too large to agree with the known stability of electrons and protons' (Dirac, 1930b, p. 375). The second 'Note on Exchange Phenomena in the Thomas Atom' made use of the density matrix to calculate the behaviour of a system of nonrelativistic electrons in an atom, providing a theoretical foundation for the so-called Thomas model of the atom (Dirac, 1930c).$^{551}$
Erwin Schrödinger addressed von Neumann's proof of the $\mathcal{H}$-theorem directly in a letter to the author, dated 25 December 1929, which he opened by stating:

> Your statistical paper did interest me quite a lot. I am quite happy about it, especially about the wonderful clarity and accuracy of the conceptions and the careful presentation (*Evidenzhaltung*) of what has been achieved in all points. (Schrödinger to von Neumann, 25 December 1929)

Schrödinger recognized as the central issue (*Kernpunkt*) of von Neumann's considerations the introduction of the concepts 'operator of a macroscopically measurable quantity' and the 'orthogonal system of the macroscopic observation (*Orthogonalsystem der Makrobeobachtung*)': 'This is an extraordinarily happy move (*ein außerordentlich glücklicher Griff*), and I believe that it will obtain a significance far beyond the present problems.' Because he had always found the idea disagreeable to associate the peculiar operators of quantum mechanics with the measurement process, Schrödinger remarked in his letter of 25 December that

he now welcomed a detailed use of von Neumann’s concepts as ‘an adequate representation of real number measurements within the scheme of quantum mechanics (*eine wirkliche Abbildung der wirklichen Messungen auf das Schema der Quantenmechanik*).’552

The difference between his own earlier treatment of the irreversibility problem (Schrödinger, 1927c), in which he had introduced an extra statistical hypothesis for the initial quantum-theoretical values, and the new treatment he saw in the following aspects: von Neumann needed the time-averaging only ‘for the squares of amplitudes which occur when one expands the wave functions in terms of products of the two decoupled parts of the system,’ which, in contrast to the quantum-mechanical amplitudes, are not constant in time; further, he did not assume a high degree of degeneracy in the total system, but rather the excitation of many closely neighbouring microscopic eigenfunctions. With these assumptions, the time-average theorem indeed followed for the second decoupled coordinate system, which is rotated against the first one. ‘You are able to demonstrate that, *provided these rotations are strong enough*, the theorem is sufficiently valid,’ Schrödinger summarized admiringly von Neumann’s proof, and he added:

> You are further able to show that the overwhelming majority of the *conceivable* rotations *is* strong enough. . . . In the case of *such* a rotation, the theorem is valid for every *ψ*, even if originally only *one* proper eigenfunction [of the microscopic system] was excited; the rotation of the coordinate system already makes sure that this *one* amplitude square is distributed evenly in the time-average (about the same as a solid body, in which only a high Debye vibration is excited, has still the same temperature everywhere). (Schrödinger to von Neumann, 25 December 1929)

Though the ergodic theorem had been proved quite satisfactorily in this way for most cases, Schrödinger—in his letter—pointed out a difficulty in von Neumann’s argumentation, which could give rise to exceptions. ‘One can, of course, also think of couplings, for which the energy of a subsystem does not follow Boltzmann’s law, say by oscillating periodically,’ he wrote, and added:

> It is not the strength of the coupling which decides but rather the fact that it is *complicated enough*. Also there exist methods of observation, which we can interpret as violations of the entropy law, namely Brownian motion. (Schrödinger to von Neumann, *loc. cit.*)

In all cases, in which the extra assumption of ‘complication’ must be made, some hypothesis of ‘elementary disorder’ would sneak in again. ‘In any case, you have helped very much to understand the bundle of problems—and not only this—

In the case of Wolfgang Pauli, we do not have available any direct and immediate statement in letters or elsewhere concerning, in particular, von Neumann’s proof of the ergodic theorem in quantum mechanics. He also avoided mentioning this topic in his *Handbuch* article on ‘Die allgemeinen Prinzipien der Wellenmechanik’ (Pauli, 1933c).553 On the other hand, he reported in an insert in Section 9 (entitled ‘Determination of the Stationary State of a System by Measurement’ (*‘Bestimmung des stationären Zustandes eines Systems durch Messung’*) in quite some detail about the ‘density matrix *P*, defined first by J. von Neumann, which allows in a convenient manner to compute the expectation values of any quantity in a given state’ (Pauli, *loc. cit.*, p. 148). Thus, at the end of the insert, he discussed the quantum-mechanical definition of the entropy and a definition of the canonical ensemble through the equation

$$P = \exp[(F - H/\theta)], \tag{406}$$

with *F* denoting the free energy, as given by the equation

$$\exp\left(-\frac{F}{\theta}\right) = \text{Trace}\left(-\frac{H}{\theta}\right), \quad \text{with } \theta = \text{kT}. \tag{407}$$

As we said, Pauli did not react in those years publicly to von Neumann’s ergodicity proof in quantum mechanics, or even to the later proof of the same author in classical mechanics (von Neumann, 1932b, c). Perhaps Pauli’s true opinion about these mathematical proofs must be noted from the answer that he gave on a later occasion in a conversation: ‘Ja, *Herr von Neumann, wenn Beweisen Physik wäre, wären Sie ein großer Physiker!*’ (‘Ah, Mr. von Neumann, if physics consisted of giving proofs, you would be a great physicist!’)554

### (e) The Mathematical Foundations and the Theory of Measurement in Quantum Mechanics (1929–1932)

In 1932, the *Verlag von Julius Springer* in Berlin published two important books by mathematicians dealing with the foundations of quantum mechanics and a characteristic method, John von Neumann’s *Mathematische Grundlagen der Quantenmechanik* (von Neumann, 1932a) and Bartel Leendert Van der Waerden’s *Die gruppentheoretische Methode in der Quantenmechanik* (Van der Waerden,

### III.3 Quantum-Mechanical Statistics and the Theory of Measurement

463

1932). We shall discuss Van der Waerden’s book in the following section. In his book, von Neumann condensed and extended the contents of his impressive investigations since 1927 on the theory of infinite Hermitean operators and their eigenvalues and the statistical methods in quantum mechanics. Apart from going into some details of a systematic presentation of the results of his original papers, which we discussed earlier, and providing special examples of application—e.g., to the radiation theory of Dirac—von Neumann achieved in his book decisive progress in two important questions: on the one hand, he demonstrated that the statistical theory of quantum mechanics excluded the existence of ‘hidden variables,’ which might allow one to return to a causal description of atomic phenomena; on the other hand, he developed in the last chapter of his book a complete theory of the quantum-mechanical process of measurement.

By ‘hidden variables’ (‘*verborgene Parameter*’), von Neumann referred to the well-known analysis of the situation in the classical kinetic theory of gases: although the usual thermodynamical description (including the second heat theorem) works only with a few measurable parameters, such as temperature, volume, pressure, and entropy, these can be connected in some complicated way with the causal mechanical behaviour of a very large number of gas molecules. In quantum mechanics, which is characterized by the intrinsically probabilistic relation between the Schrödinger function *ϕ* and the values of the physical quantities, one may perhaps adopt the following interpretation:

> In reality, *ϕ* does not determine the state exactly. In order to know this state absolutely, additional numerical data are necessary. That is, the system has other characteristics or coordinates in addition to *ϕ*. If we were to know all these, then we could give the values of all physical quantities exactly and with certainty. On the other hand, the use of *ϕ* alone, just as in classical mechanics when only some of the $q_1, \ldots, q_k$, $p_1, \ldots, p_k$ are known, only statistical pronouncements are possible. Of course, this concept is only hypothetical. It is an attempt whose value depends on whether or not one actually succeeds in finding the additional coordinates contributing to *ϕ*, and in building, with their help, a causal theory which is in agreement with measurement, and which gives the statistical assertions of quantum mechanics when only *ϕ* is given. (von Neumann, 1932a, p. 108; English translation, p. 209)

Some ‘prominent members’ of the physics community, so von Neumann noted, supported the idea that, by invoking enough of those ‘hidden parameters,’ the statistical relations of quantum mechanics might be reduced to a perfectly causal behaviour of *all* parameters of atomic theory.555 ‘It would brand the present form

---

555 von Neumann did not mention the names of these prominent physicists, so we can only guess that he referred to well-established members of the Berlin scientific community, such as Einstein, Planck, and von Laue. We shall return to the topic of hidden variables in some detail in Chapter IV and the Epilogue. Here, we just mention that it was Max Born—in his paper expounding the statistical interpretation of the wave function—who drew attention to the fact that it might perhaps be avoided by ‘additional parameters not yet introduced into the theory that determine the individual event’ (Born, 1926b, p. 825); he also reported that the Russian theoretician Jakov Frenkel had informed him ‘that this may still be feasible.’
