of the theory as provisional, since then the description of the states [by quantum mechanics] would be essentially incomplete,’ he commented, but also immediately added: ‘We shall show later that an introduction of hidden parameters is certainly not possible without a basic change in the present theory’ (von Neumann, 1932a, English translation, pp. 209–210).

In Section IV.2 of his book, von Neumann indeed provided the proof of the impossibility of ‘hidden parameters,’ which would exclude a fully causal behaviour of atomic processes. He based his proof on the two fundamental laws obeyed by quantum-mechanical operators—I. if the operator of a quantity ℛ is given by *R*, then the quantity *f*(ℛ) possesses the operator *f*(*R*); II. the sum of the quantities ℛ + 𝒮 + · · · is associated with the sum of the operators, *R* + *S* + · · ·—and the definition of the expectation value (346). That is, he asked specifically ‘the question as to whether the dispersions of the homogeneous ensembles characterized by the wave function *ϕ* (i.e., by [Eq. (346)]) are not due to the fact that these are not the real states, but only mixtures of several states—while for the knowledge of the actual state additional data, besides the data of the wave function *ϕ*, would be necessary (these would be the “hidden parameters,”) which together would determine everything causally, i.e., lead to dispersion-free ensembles’ (von Neumann, 1932c, pp. 170–171; English translation, pp. 323–324). And he immediately gave the answer in the negative:

> But this is impossible for two reasons: First, because then the homogeneous ensemble could be represented by a mixture of two different ensembles, contrary to its definition. Second, because the dispersion-free ensembles, which would have to correspond to “actual” states (i.e., which consist only of systems in their own “actual states”), do not exist. It should be noticed that we need not go any further into the mechanism of the “hidden parameters,” since we now know that the established results in quantum mechanics can never be rederived with their help. In fact, we have even ascertained that it is impossible that the same physical quantities exist with the same connections (i.e., that I., II., hold), if other variables (i.e., “hidden parameters”) should exist in addition to the wave function. (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 171; English translation, p. 324)

Even the discovery of new physical quantities would not help in this question, von Neumann continued; hence, he concluded: ‘It is therefore not at all, as is often assumed, a question of reinterpretation of quantum mechanics—rather the present system of quantum mechanics would have to be objectively false, in order that another description of the elementary processes [in atomic physics] than the statistical one be possible.’ (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*; English translation, p. 325)

The second essential addition in the book (over the previous original papers) concerned a detailed theory of the measurement process in quantum mechanics. This problem had been addressed already earlier by other authors. Thus, Born and Jordan analyzed in *Elementare Quantenmechanik* an important aspect of the problem, namely, the influence of a measurement on the observed atomic system (Born and Jordan, 1930, pp. 322–326). While in classical mechanics one might

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0497 -->

III.3 Quantum-Mechanical Statistics and the Theory of Measurement

465

assume in principle that ideal observations of a closed system at an initial instant of time allow one to predict its behaviour at any later time, in quantum mechanics, this prerequisite of a causal theory cannot be satisfied, as Heisenberg had shown in his paper on the uncertainty relations (Heisenberg, 1927b). Indeed, an atomic system 'experiences through carrying out a *measurement process* necessarily a decisive *influence*,' which Born and Jordan demonstrated with the help of the following consideration.
Let $A$, $B$, and $A'$ be arbitrary, in general, noncommuting, quantities, and $\Sigma^{(1)}$, $\Sigma^{(2)}$, and $\Sigma'$ be the corresponding principal-axis coordinate systems connected by the unitary transformations $U' : \Sigma^{(1)} \to \Sigma'$ and $U'' : \Sigma' \to \Sigma^{(2)}$. Then, in a system of atoms, for which the value of $A$ has been found to be $a_n$, the measurement of $B$ yields the value $b_k$ with the probability

$$w_{nk} = \left| \sum_m U'_{nm} U''_{mk} \right|^2 . \tag{408}$$

However, if before observing the value $B$ a measurement of the quantity $A'$ is actually performed on each atom of $\mathcal{S}$, the originally pure system (i.e., all values of $A$ are identical $a_n$) changes into a mixture (now consisting of the fractions $w'_{nm} = |U'_{nm}|^2$ of atoms having the value $a'_m$). When the quantity $B$ is measured for that mixture, the value $b_k$ will be obtained rather with the probability

$$\bar{w}_{nk} = \sum_m | U'_{nm} U''_{mk} |^2 . \tag{409}$$

'This probability $\bar{w}_{nk}$ is quite different from the above $w_{nk}$, [Eq. (408)],' the authors emphasized; hence, 'the measurement process $A'$ has changed the system drastically'—and they concluded:

> One sees here quite clearly that the process of measurement has quite a different meaning in quantum mechanics than in macroscopic physics: We are not dealing anymore with the simple *registration* of a fact, which existed already before the measurement independently of the latter, but with the *creation* of a new fact by a physical *operation* (*Eingriff*) on the system. If before the value $a_n$ of a quantity $A$ has been measured for an atom, belonging to the (un-decomposable) *Einzel* tensor $F^{(n)}$, and now the quantity $B$ is observed which does not commute with $F^{(n)}$, *then a definite value $b_k$ of $B$ is created only by the process of measurement*. It is the measurement which forces the atom to decide itself for an eigenvalue of $B$; on the other hand, $A$ then loses its previously defined value. One therefore notices that the analysis of the laws of microphysics, as discovered by quantum mechanics, leads necessarily to radical consequences: not only the classical-macroscopic conceptions of space, time and causality turn out to be insufficient in the range of atomic reactions, even the conventional concepts of subject, object and reality lose their usual meaning. (Born and Jordan, 1930, pp. 324–325)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0498 -->

466

Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

The main difference between the classical theory and the quantum theory lies, of course, in the occurrence of probability amplitudes within the latter, which involves the 'interference of probabilities,' Born and Jordan noted; this situation can be visualized in the classical example of the interference of light amplitudes, which are to be interpreted 'in a certain sense as probabilities of the discontinuous impingement of a corpuscular light-quantum.' Indeed, 'The formula [(408)] for the *pure case* is related to formula [(409)] for the *mixture* as the intensity formula for *coherence* is to the intensity formula of non-coherence,' because:

> In [Eq. (408)] the amplitudes $U'_{nm} U''_{mk}$ are first summed up (over $m$) and then squared; in [Eq. (409)], on the other hand, they are first squared and then summed up. Hence one might also talk about a *coherent statistics* of the pure case, in contrast to an *incoherent statistics* of a mixture. (Born and Jordan, *loc. cit.*, p. 325)

This analogy, Born and Jordan stressed finally, would provide 'not just a superficial similarity,' because one actually has 'to include the interference of light into the general quantum-mechanical statistics' (Born and Jordan, *loc. cit.*, p. 326).
A couple of years later, von Neumann published a full, physically, and mathematically quite detailed theory of 'the measuring process' in Chapter VI of his *Mathematische Grundlagen*. It was based on a fundamental consequence following from the quantum-mechanical formalism.$^{556}$ On one hand, a state $\phi$ changes under the influence of the energy operator $H$ according to the time-dependent Schrödinger equation,

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial t} \phi_\tau = - \frac{2\pi i}{h} H \phi_\tau, \tag{410}$$

in the interval $0 \leq \tau \leq t$ from $\phi_0 = \phi$ into $\phi'$, given by the expression (or time-evolution)

$$\phi' = \exp \left( - \frac{2\pi i}{h} t H \right) \phi. \tag{411}$$

And this time-evolution represents a *completely causal change*, which would result into a likewise causal change of the density operator for a mixture,

$$U' = \exp \left( - \frac{2\pi i}{h} t H \right) U \exp \left( \frac{2\pi i}{h} t H \right). \tag{412}$$

On the other hand, the state $\phi$ undergoes an *acausal change* in a measurement, because the measurement creates from the pure state $\phi$ a mixture of states

$^{556}$ See von Neumann, 1932c, p. 222. It was the same consequence that had already played a crucial role in the proof of the ergodic theorem (von Neumann, 1929c, p. 48 ff.).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0499 -->

III.3 Quantum-Mechanical Statistics and the Theory of Measurement

467

$\phi_1, \phi_2, \dots$, with probabilities $|(\phi, \phi_1)|^2, |(\phi, \phi_2)|^2, \dots$. Hence, $U'_{meas.}$ gets determined not simply by the projection operator $P_{[\phi]}$—as in Eq. (411)—but by a combination of $P_{[\phi_n]}$, or

$$U'_{meas.} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty |(\phi, \phi_n)|^2 P_{[\phi_n]} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty (U\phi_n, \phi_n) \cdot P_{[\phi_n]}. \tag{413}$$

von Neumann emphasized that 'the difference between these two processes, $U \to U'$ and $U \to U'_{meas.}$, is a very fundamental one: aside from different behaviours in regard to the principle of causality, they are also different in that the former is (thermodynamically) reversible, while the latter is not' (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, pp. 222–223; English translation, p. 418).
This particular result followed from extending the earlier discussion of thermodynamical processes in quantum mechanics in Chapter V of the book. There, the author demonstrated, by a purely thermodynamical consideration, that all (pure) distributions $U = P_{[\phi_n]}$, for arbitrary states $\phi_n$, do have the entropy zero (see also von Neumann, 1927c), but the $U'_{meas.}$ obtained from a measurement would not represent a pure state, unless all $|(\phi, \phi_n)|^2$ are zero except one: 'Therefore, each measurement on a state is irreversible, unless the eigenvalue of the measured quantity (i.e., this quantity in the given state) has a sharp value, in which case the measurement does not change the state at all' (von Neumann, 1932c, p. 202; English translation, p. 380). Evidently, the above conclusion generalized the observation of Born and Jordan, reported earlier, and in doing so, von Neumann was inspired by the epistemological ideas of two physicists (who may indeed have been responsible for the fact that von Neumann went ahead to complete the mathematical formulation of the quantum-mechanical measurement theory).
The first was Niels Bohr, who, in his article for the *Planck-Festschrift*, expressed the idea that specific measurement processes in physics should have some relation to the psychological processes determining human decisions in general. In particular, Bohr wrote:

> When considering the contrast between the feeling of free will, which governs the psychic life, and the apparently uninterrupted causal chain accompanying physiological processes, the thought has, indeed, not eluded philosophers that we may be concerned here with an unvisualizable relation of complementarity. . . . We can hardly escape the conviction that in the facts which are revealed to us by the quantum theory and lie outside the domain of our ordinary forms of perception we have acquired a means of elucidating general philosophical problems. (Bohr, 1929b; English translation, pp. 100–101)

With the facts 'revealed to us by the quantum theory,' Bohr meant the special conclusion, confirmed again and again, 'that a detailed tracing of atomic processes is impossible and that any attempt to acquire a knowledge of such processes involves a fundamentally uncontrollable interference with their cause' (Bohr, *loc. cit.*, p. 100).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0500 -->

468

Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

von Neumann cited Bohr's paper as 'the first to point out that the dual description which is necessitated by the form of the quantum-mechanical description of nature [e.g., by Eqs. (412) and (413)] is fully justified by the physical nature of things that it may be connected with the principle of psycho-physical parallelism' (von Neumann, 1932, footnote 207, p. 262; English translation, p. 420). It inspired him to take the following view of the measurement process:

> Measurement or the related process of subjective perception is a new entity relative to the physical environment and not reducible to the latter. Indeed, subjective perception leads us into the intellectual inner life of the individual, which is extra-observational by its very nature (since it must be taken for granted by any conceivable observation or experiment). . . . Nevertheless, it is a fundamental requirement of the scientific viewpoint—the so-called principle of the psycho-physical parallelism—that it must be possible so to describe the extra-physical process of the subjective perception as if it were in reality in the physical world—i.e., to assign to its parts equivalent physical processes in the objective environment, in ordinary space. . . . That is, we must always divide the world into two parts, the one being the observed system, the other the observer. In the former we can follow up all physical processes (in principle at least) arbitrarily precisely. In the latter this is meaningless. The boundary between the two is arbitrary to a large extent. . . . That this boundary can be pushed arbitrarily deeply into the interior of the body of the actual observer is the content of the psycho-physical parallelism—but this does not change the fact that in each method of description the boundary must be put somewhere, if the method is not to proceed vacuously, i.e., if a comparison with experiment is to be possible. (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, pp. 223–224, English translation, pp. 420–421)

Thus, von Neumann formulated the essence of the general process of measurement in science in a rational scheme by separating clearly between the parts 'observed system' and 'observer,' respectively. He pointed out that there must be defined in all cases a sharp 'boundary (*Grenze*)'—it would later be called von Neumann's 'cut (*Schnitt*)'—which may, however, be shifted to some extent without changing the result of the observation.
Although the psychophysical parallelism applies, in principle, to all processes of measurement, von Neumann turned immediately to the special case of quantum mechanics. He wrote:

> Quantum mechanics describes the events which occur in the observed portions of the world, so long as they do not interact with the observing portion, with the aid of the process [(412)], but as soon as such an interaction occurs, i.e., a measurement [takes place], it requires the application of the process [(413)]. The dual form is therefore justified. However, the danger lies in the fact that the principle of psycho-physical parallelism is violated, so long as it is not shown that the boundary between the observed system and the observer can be displaced arbitrarily in the sense given above. (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 221; English translation, pp. 420–421)

To prove the desired parallelism and to establish the proper measurement theory based on it, von Neumann proposed to divide the world into three portions, I, II,

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0501 -->

**III.3 Quantum-Mechanical Statistics and the Theory of Measurement** 469

and III: I denotes the observed system, II denotes the measuring instrument, and III denotes the actual observer. 'It is to be shown,' he argued, 'that the boundary can just as well be drawn between I and II + III as between I + II and III' (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 244; English translation, p. 421).

Although carrying out the detailed considerations, von Neumann referred to the fact that he owed 'essential elements to conversations with L. Szilard' (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, footnote 208, p. 262, or p. 421, respectively). Since the time of their common studies in Berlin, he had interacted with his senior Hungarian fellow-countryman.$^{557}$ Not a very prolific writer himself, Szilard published in the 1920s two papers on thermodynamics that influenced von Neumann. The first, entitled '*Über die Ausdehnung der phänomenologischen Thermodynamik auf die Schwankungserscheinungen*' ('On the Extension of the Phenomenological Thermodynamics to Fluctuation Phenomena,' Szilard, 1925), arose from his doctoral dissertation with Max von Laue; it was largely stimulated by Einstein's paper (1914b), which played a role in von Neumann's (already discussed) application of quantum mechanics to thermodynamical problems (von Neumann, 1927c; see footnote 11, p. 276 of this paper). In the second, '*Über die Entropieverminderung in einem thermodynamischen System bei Eingriffen intelligenter Wesen*' ('On the Entropy Decrease in a Thermodynamical System upon Intervention by Intelligent Beings,' Szilard, 1929), the author showed that a kind of *perpetuum mobile of the second kind* can be constructed, and:$^{558}$

> that already a kind of memory which distinguishes a system, in which measurements are made, may lead to a permanent decrease of entropy and thus to a violation of the second law of thermodynamics, if the measurements were not themselves connected necessarily with entropy production.... Then with the help of an inanimate apparatus, which allows one to carry out measurements (constantly producing entropy), the entropy arising is calculated and found to be just as large as is necessary for a full compensation [of the entropy decrease created by intelligence]. (Szilard, 1929, p. 840)

This paper contained 'several of the ideas which form the basis of the [later] information theory' (Wigner, 1969, p. 338)—but in 1930, it provided von Neumann

$^{557}$ Leo Szilard was born on 11 February 1898, in Budapest, where he completed his high school education and began to study at the Institute of Technology; his studies were interrupted by World War I, when he served as an officer in the Austro-Hungarian Army. After the war, he went to Berlin to obtain an engineering degree at the *Technische Hochschule*, but he soon changed to physics. According to Wigner's obituary notice, Szilard then:

> introduced himself with characteristic directness, to Albert Einstein. I believe it was largely Szilard's doing that Einstein gave a seminar on statistical mechanics at which, in addition to Szilard himself, several of his friends, including D. Gabor and the present writer, participated.... The seminar also inspired, I believe, Szilard's doctoral dissertation (1922). (Wigner, 1969, p. 338)

$^{558}$ Szilard attributed the idea of an entropy decrease by the action of an intelligent being to Marian von Smoluchowski (von Smoluchowski, 1914a, p. 89).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0502 -->

470 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

the necessary epistemological basis, on which he could proceed to the mathematical formulation of the quantum-mechanical measurement theory.$^{559}$

To obtain the computational tools for this purpose, von Neumann considered in Section VI.2 of *Mathematische Grundlagen* the rules for composing two quantum-mechanical systems I and II to the unified system I + II, and for the inverse process of decomposing I + II into the separate systems I and II, respectively. He found that, provided certain conditions were satisfied, the procedures led to unique results, e.g., for the statistical operator $U$ of the system I + II in terms of the corresponding statistical operators of I and II or for the relations between quantities $A$ and $B$ in the systems I and II when determined by the Hilbert space vector $\Phi$ in the combined system I + II. In particular, he derived the results:

> If I is in the state $\phi(q)$ and II in the state $\xi(r)$, then I + II is in the state $\Phi(q,r) = \phi(q)\xi(r)$. If, on the other hand, I + II is in the state $\Phi(q,r)$ which is not a product of $\phi(q)\xi(r)$, then I and II are mixtures and not [pure] states, but $\Phi$ establishes a one-to-one correspondence between the possible values of certain quantities. (von Neumann, 1932c, p. 232. English translation, pp. 436–437)

With these results, von Neumann immediately demonstrated that 'the non-causal process [(413)] is not produced by the incomplete knowledge of the state of the observer,' which he therefore assumed to be always completely known (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 233, or p. 439).

Now, von Neumann attacked his central problem of showing that the 'boundary' in a quantum-mechanical measurement can be shifted between the systems I, II, and III, as described above, by a direct calculation of measurements in the two cases:

(1) I is the 'observed system' in the state $\phi$, and $A$ is a quantity having eigenfunctions $\phi_n$; II + III (i.e., the 'measuring instrument' and the 'actual observer') form the system 'observer.' Evidently, in this case, the measurement of $A$ must satisfy the irreversible Eq. (413) and yield for the values $a_n (n=1, 2, \dots)$ the probabilities

$$w_n|(\phi, \phi_n)|^2, \quad \text{for } n=1, 2, \dots \tag{414}$$

(2) I + II is taken to be the 'observed system' and III is the registering 'observer.' Then, II is a measuring device that obtains the value of $A$ (in I); the position of the pointer on its scale is a physical quantity (in II), which is actually registered by III.$^{560}$ That is, one has to consider besides the values $a_1, a_2, \dots$ of $A$ in I also

He went to the United States in 1938 (naturalized in 1943); he first worked at Columbia University (1938–1942), then at the Metallurgical Laboratory of the University of Chicago (the Manhattan Project), basically on nuclear chain reactions. He participated actively in writing the famous 'Franck Report' (against the use of nuclear weapons) of June 1945 to the U. S. Secretary of War, and changed his interests to molecular biology in 1949 (occupying since 1946 a professorship at the University of Chicago). He died on 30 May 1964, in La Jolla, California.

$^{560}$ If II is a part of the observing body, then we have to replace the pointer and scale by the corresponding physiological concepts, as Bohr had discussed earlier (Bohr, 1929b).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0503 -->

**III.3 Quantum-Mechanical Statistics and the Theory of Measurement** 471

those of the physical quantity $B$ (namely, $b_1, b_2, \dots$) denoting the position of the pointer on the scale in system II. The process of measurement then consists of three steps:

(a) System I is in the (unknown) state $\phi(q)$, system II in the (known) state $\xi(r)$; hence, the combined system (I + II) possesses the state $\Phi(q,r) = \phi(q)\xi(r)$.

(b) The measurement performed in time $t$ by II on I follows the reversible Eq. (411) and transforms $\Phi$ into $\Phi'$

$$\Phi'(q,r) = \exp\left(-\frac{2\pi i}{h} t H\right)\Phi(q,r). \tag{415}$$

(c) The measurement process performed by III on (I + II) then yields the actual information, namely, the pair $(a_n, b_n)$ of values for $A$ and $B$—they are so closely related that any pair $(a_n, b_m)$ with $m \neq n$ occurs with probability zero. It suffices that III looks on II and registers the position of the pointer, $b_n$, with the probability $w_n$, given by Eq. (414).

'If this [result] is established, then the measuring process so far as it occurs in II, is "explained" theoretically, i.e., the division of I/(II + III) is shifted to (I + II)/III,' von Neumann stated the crucial problem of his theory of measurement (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 234; English translation, p. 440).

He then outlined the proof along two different paths. First, he constructed explicitly a unitary 'abstract' operator $\Delta$ as the representative of the operator $\exp\left(-\frac{2\pi i}{h} t H\right)$ in Eq. (415), which transforms the initial state of the system I + II, i.e., $\Phi(q,r) = \phi(q)\xi(r)$, into the final state, $\Phi'(q,r)$; the latter consists of a sum of product terms $\phi_n \cdot \xi_n$ (with $\phi_n$ and $\xi_n$ denoting eigenstates in I and II), and each product is multiplied indeed with the required probability. That is, von Neumann obtained the result$^{561}$

$$\Phi'(q,r) = \Delta\Phi(q,r) = \sum_n (\phi, \phi_n) \phi_n(q) \xi_n(q). \tag{416}$$

Second, he made use of the time-dependent Schrödinger equation,

$$\frac{h}{2\pi i} \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \psi_t(q,r) = -\frac{h}{2\pi i} q \frac{\partial}{\partial r} \psi_t(q,r), \tag{417}$$

to calculate the final state $\Phi'(q,r) = \psi_\tau(q,r)$ after the time interval $\tau$ in the system (I + II), and arrived at the result

$$\psi_\tau(q,r) = \Phi(q, r - \tau q) = \phi(q)\xi(r - \tau q), \tag{418}$$

$^{561}$ von Neumann even found that the probability amplitudes coincided in both equivalent measurement procedures. (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 235)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0504 -->

472 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

when at the time zero $\psi_0(q,r) = \Phi(q,r) = \phi(q)\xi(r)$. As a special example, he treated the measurement of the position $q$ in I by the system II. In case the coordinate of the measuring apparatus was very well known—or $\xi(r)$ could be concentrated in a small space element [i.e., $\xi(r)$ is different from zero only in a narrow interval $r_0 - \delta' < r < r_0 + \delta'$ and properly normalized, $\int |\xi(r)|^2 dr = 1$]—he found for the probability that $q$ lies in a very small interval $q_0 - \delta < q < q_0 + \delta$ the expression

$$\int_{q_0-\delta}^{q_0+\delta} \int_{r_0-\delta'}^{r_0+\delta'} |\Phi'(q,r)|^2 dq dr = \int_{q_0-\delta}^{q_0+\delta} |\phi(q)|^2 dq. \tag{419}$$

He remarked that '$q, r$ are tied to each other with arbitrary closeness, and the probability density has the value furnished (*gefordert*) by quantum mechanics'; hence, 'The relations of the measurement ... are realized.' (von Neumann, *loc. cit.*, p. 237; English translation, p. 445) With this demonstration and the suggestion that 'the discussion of more complicated examples ... is left to the reader,' von Neumann completed his task and simultaneously finished the book.

### III.4 Group Theory and Quantum Mechanics

For introducing the story dealing with the influence of the mathematical theory of groups on the development of quantum mechanics, especially in the period between 1927 and 1931, let us quote two excerpts from the scientific correspondence of Wolfgang Pauli. On 10 February 1928, Pauli wrote to Ralph Kronig:

> Now I wish to add something concerning your paper on band spectra which appeared today in *Zeitschrift für Physik* [Kronig, 1928a]. I believe that the subject will become much more transparent if one goes back to the group-theoretical methods discussed by [Eugene] Wigner [1927b, c]. The invariance of the differential equation [for the atoms] with respect to rotations and reflections of the coordinate system (in the absence of external fields) leads, according to Wigner, immediately to Laporte's rule as a consequence. For molecules an analogous invariance exists, if one simultaneously carries out the reflections of the coordinates of both the electron and the molecule (in a coordinate system fixed in space). (Pauli, 1979, pp. 433–434)

Upon being appointed professor of theoretical physics at the ETH in Zurich in April 1928, Pauli soon 'learned from [Hermann] Weyl so much erudite (*gelehrte*) group theory that [he] could really understand the papers of [Eugene] Wigner and [Walter] Heitler' (Pauli to Bohr, 16 June 1928; *loc. cit.*, p. 463).$^{562}$ Thus, he was addressed as an expert in this field by colleagues, e.g., by Paul Ehrenfest, who wrote to him concerning his forthcoming visit to Leyden:

$^{562}$ Pauli had already been interested in the mathematical methods of group theory in Hamburg—see von Meyenn, 1987.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0505 -->

III.4 Group Theory and Quantum Mechanics 473

On the other hand, I shall have to present to you a thick bundle of questions on the terribly many new "papers on the group-pestilence (*Gruppenpest-Arbeiten*)," of which I cannot read a single one beyond the first page, hence I struggle very hard with them. I do hope that, if I just show you where in all the places I get stuck (unfortunately, I have also got stuck helplessly in the papers of Heisenberg on helium and lithium and in the papers of [Friedrich] Hund on symmetries), then you will certainly be able to put my head straight (*mein Gehirn einrencken*). Perhaps I was just stopped nearly everywhere by misunderstanding some of the concepts or statements. (Ehrenfest to Pauli, 22 September 1928; *loc. cit.*, p. 474)

The situation was certainly not as simple as Ehrenfest imagined. Actually, a new favourite method had sprung up in the papers of some of the younger theoreticians, which proved to be a very useful, even quite powerful, tool in solving old and new problems in atomic and molecular physics. Notably, the mathematical methods of group theory provided the proper means of dealing with the questions of symmetries and conservation laws not only in classical but also in quantum mechanics. Before we turn to the developments in the five years between 1926 and 1931, the origin of group theory and its relation to symmetry problems in classical physics will be sketched briefly.

**(a) Symmetries, Group Theory, and Classical Physics**

The observation of symmetries in nature dates back to the origin of Western (and probably even of pre-Western) science. Thus, the Milesian natural philosopher Anaxaminder, who lived up to 545 B.C., discussed the symmetrical shapes of the Earth (disc) and of Heaven (sphere) and drew some physical consequences from their regularity. Then, symmetries played a powerful role in the harmonics of Pythagoras and his school, and they pervaded the world views of Plato and Aristotle. They occurred again and again in the sciences of the Medieval times, and were resumed forcefully afterward by Nicolaus Copernicus and Johannes Kepler —note, especially, the analysis of spherical harmonies in the Heavens and symmetries of the snow flakes on Earth. Later on, the concept of symmetry entered into the dynamics of Isaac Newton and finally the electrodynamics of James Clerk Maxwell.⁵⁶³ In the nineteenth century, the description of symmetric regularities got established in two different branches of science—crystallography and mathematics —and both fields soon developed a fruitful interaction, and thereby, a symbiosis evolved that established a new description transcending the previous rather static one.

In a lecture on ‘Symmetry Principles in Old and New Physics,’ presented to the American Mathematical Society in January 1968, Eugene Wigner, a pioneer of symmetry methods in physics, drew attention to the twin birth in 1830 of the mathematical group theory and the analysis of symmetries in crystal lattices (Wigner, 1968), connected with the names of Evariste Galois and Johann Chri-

⁵⁶³ For a review of symmetries in the older times, see Roche, 1987.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0506 -->

474 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

stian Hessel. In that year, the German crystallographer Hessel of Marburg wrote a detailed review on ‘Krystallo metrie, Krystallo nomie und Krystallo graphie’ in a dictionary of physics (Hessel, 1830).⁵⁶⁴ As the main result of his own investigations and those of others, he divided the crystalline forms occurring in nature into thirty-two ‘crystal classes’ according to the existence of certain symmetry axes and their ‘measure (*Maass*).’ Hessel’s followers translated his results into the language of group theory, in which the crystal classes corresponded to representations of groups of rotation (plus reflections) in space, all the elements of which are of the order 2, 3, 4, and 6. As Wigner said:

> When the total symmetries of crystal lattices, that is symmetries including spatial displacements, were investigated just before the turn of the century by [Evgeni Stepanovic] Federov and Arthur Schoenflies, Hessel’s groups appeared as the 32 different factor groups of all possible space groups [rotations plus displacements], the displacements forming the normal subgroups. The space groups are the discrete subgroups of the Euclidean group which contain three noncoplanar translations. There are 230 of them, as determined by Schoenflies and Federov—by means of group-theoretical methods which became, by the time familiar at least to some crystallographers. . . . The consequences of the symmetry properties of crystals in terms of macroscopic properties yielded a fascinating amount of information—information that was derived principally by [Paul] Groth with full understanding of the group property of symmetry operations though, as a rule, not in the language of group theory. (Wigner, 1968, p. 797)

The origin of group theory, whose role in crystallography he stressed above, Wigner associated with the name of the French mathematician Evariste Galois.⁵⁶⁵ The most famous of Galois’s mathematical contributions constitutes his classification of the solutions of algebraic equations in the theory named after him: The young mathematician attacked the long-standing problem of solving an equation of the *n*-th degree, $F(x) = 0$, by the method of resolvents by introducing a function $V(x_j)$ of the roots $x_j$ (of the original equation), having values that are different if one permutes the $x_j$—hence, all $x_j$ can be expressed in a rational way by $V(x_j)$. Galois then introduced the concept of a ‘group T’ for a set of permutations of the roots $x_j$, and he also spoke about ‘normal divisors’ of a group and a classification of groups into ‘simple’ and ‘composite’ groups. Finally, he defined the

⁵⁶⁴ Hessel was born on 27 April 1796, in Nuremberg, the son of a merchant, and studied medicine at the Universities of Erlangen and Würzburg, obtaining his *Dr. med* in 1817. Then, he continued his studies in Munich and Heidelberg, where he learned crystallography, mathematics, and chemistry (doctorate and *Habilitation* in 1821). In fall 1821, he was appointed to an extraordinary (associate) professorship at the University of Marburg; promoted to full professor in 1825, he stayed in Marburg until his death on 3 June 1872.
⁵⁶⁵ Galois was born on 25 October 1811, in Bourg-la-Reine near Paris. Already, during the high school years, he started to publish on mathematical problems. After failing twice in 1829, the entrance examination to the prestigious *École Polytechnique*, he went to study at the *École Normale Supérieure*, but was dismissed in 1830. He then became involved in political activities against the French government and spent several months in prison. He died on 31 March 1832, in Paris, in a duel arising from a love affair. For a brief characterization of Galois’s mathematical work, see F. Klein, 1926, pp. 88–93.

III.4 Group Theory and Quantum Mechanics &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 475

concepts of ‘cyclic’ and ‘metacyclic’ groups, obtaining the result: the necessary
and sufficient condition of an irreducible equation of prime number degree to be
soluble is the existence of at least one metacyclic group.
Galois’s group theory has often been considered to provide the explosive prog-
ress in algebra during the nineteenth century.<sup>566</sup> These developments are con-
nected both with considerations of formal structures (e.g., in George Boole’s logic)
and with particular mathematical objects or ‘hyper-complex systems’ (such as
William Rowan Hamilton’s quaternions, Arthur Cayley’s matrices, and Hermann
Graßmann’s ‘*Stufen*’). As one of the prominent results of ‘abstract’ group theory,
we quote ‘Cayley’s theorem’: every finite group is isomorphic to a ‘permutation’
group, a subgroup of the ‘symmetric’ group. The end of the first epoch was
marked by Camille Jordan’s *Traité des substitution et des équations algébriques*;
Jordan summarized there the important results following from extending Galois’s
work on the permutation group and many other related topics (Jordan, 1870).<sup>567</sup>
He also performed pioneering investigations on finite groups of linear substitutions
(depending on several variables) that helped to prepare the next important theme
in group theory, the infinitesimal groups of Sophus Lie. Felix Klein described the
starting point of Lie’s and his own interest in group theory, which occurred when
both of them spent some months in Paris, as follows:<sup>568</sup>

When Lie and I undertook [in 1870, after the publication of Jordan’s book] to work
out the importance of group theory for different fields of mathematics, we said:
“group” is the epitome (*Inbegriff*) of unique *operations* $A, B, C, \ldots$ such that any two
operations $A, B$ combined also yield an operation of the epitome:

$$A \cdot B = C. \tag{420}$$

In his further considerations on infinite groups, Lie was then forced to require
explicitly that, besides $A$, also the inverse $A^{-1}$ should be an element of the group.
(F. Klein, 1926, p. 335)

There, Lie discovered contact transformations and Klein conceived the first ideas

Returning to Norway (after some adventures in Paris), Lie became an assistant at the University of

of his ‘Erlangen programme.’⁵⁶⁹ Back in Norway, Lie founded his theory of transformation groups, i.e., a general theory of continuous groups of substitutions depending on finitely many parameters, and of the associated Lie algebras (connected with the corresponding infinitesimal substitutions).⁵⁷⁰

The ideas of Felix Klein and Sophus Lie—one may even speak of a joint programme, though each of them went in a different direction—had a deep background in earlier investigations. In particular, Cayley had proposed in 1845 a theory of linear transformations and initiated in it the concept of invariants, which his friend James Joseph Sylvester developed into a powerful theory; Sylvester also first used in 1852 the concept of an ‘infinitesimal transformation.’ Then, Camille Jordan considered the continuous and discrete subgroups of the Euclidean space and especially Hermann von Helmholtz published his paper ‘Ueber die Thatsachen, welcher der Geometrie zum Grunde liegen’ (‘On the Facts which Lie at the Basis of Geometry,’ Helmholtz, 1868). In Helmholtz’s work, the real geometry of (Euclidean) space was derived from four physical postulates:

(1) the continuity and the dimension of space;
(2) the existence of a freely moving rigid body;
(3) the free (translational) motion of the body;
(4) the connection between rotation and identity of the body.

Expressed in more modern terms, Helmholtz assumed the continuity and homogeneity of space, the translational and the rotational invariance of the dynamics. A few years later, Lie succeeded in formulating these ideas in his theory of continuous contact transformations (Lie, 1875), and Klein created his ‘Erlangen programme’ (F. Klein, 1872).

The essence of Klein’s programme consisted in the central idea to use the invariants of the group of transformations for the characterization of the geometry associated with them, or as he said himself:

Given a manifold and in it a group of transformations; one should investigate the forms (*Gebilde*) in this manifold with respect to properties that are not changed by the transformations of the group. One should [then] develop the theory of invariants related to the group. (F. Klein, 1927, p. 28)

Thus, the theory of invariants (of Cayley and Sylvester), the group theory of substitutions (of Jordan and Lie), and the geometry of spaces associated with groups (Helmholtz, Klein) merged together into a kind of unity, which later on led to such important physical consequences as the four-dimensional space-time theories of special and general relativity. The interpretation of symmetry-invariants as physical quantities, on the other hand, resulted in Emmy Noether’s theorem

# III.4 Group Theory and Quantum Mechanics
477

(1918), which demonstrated the intimate relation between the symmetry properties of the dynamical equations (i.e., their invariance under infinitesimal Lie transformations) and the conservation laws recognized to be valid in the given dynamics.⁵⁷¹
Returning to the development of the mathematical theory of groups, we should mention the investigations of Felix Klein and others on finite ‘polyhedron groups’ in the late nineteenth century and to those of Georg Ferdinand Frobenius and Issai Schur on the representation of groups in the early twentieth century. The mathematical work split into two major parts: first, studies of the nature of (abstract) groups, and second, studies of their representations. The abstract groups shared only a few postulates, namely:

(1) The associative law of operations,

$C(BA) = (CB)A;$ (421)

(2) the existence of a unit element 1, such that

$1A = A1 = A;$ (422)

(3) the existence of an inverse element

$A^{-1}$ to a given $A$, such that $AA^{-1} = A^{-1}A = 1.$ (423)

They were further characterized by additional specific relations (so as to give rise to the different geometries in Klein’s ‘Erlangen programme’). On the other hand, their representation by transformations required the assumption of a given field (of points), in which to every element $A$ of the group a transformation $T(A)$ is associated, satisfying the relations corresponding to the above postulates,

$T(BA) = T(B)T(A),$ (424)

$T(A1) = T(1)T(A) = T(A),$ (425)

and

$T(A)T(A^{-1}) = T(1),$ (426)

where

$T(A^{-1}) = T^{-1}(A).$ (427)

⁵⁷¹ For a review of the historical development of the relations between invariants of symmetry transformations and physical conservation laws, see Kastrup, 1987.

# 478 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

Hence, it follows that,

$T(1) = I,$ (428)

where $I$ denotes the identical representation.
Evidently, the study of the different possible representations of a given group and their properties constituted an extensive topic of its own in the mathematical literature, and it was especially this part of group theory that attracted the physicists in the twentieth century, notably when they worked on the new schemes of relativity and quantum theories. Group theory, one of the main pillars of algebra since 1830, provided a wonderful mathematical language that possessed a rich and elegant vocabulary and a wealth of powerful theorems waiting to be applied to physical problems—but this language remained unfamiliar to many, if not most, physicists during their professional education. Fortunately, when an urgent need arose to use these powerful and elegant mathematical methods, an extremely competent interpreter became available in the person of Hermann Weyl, a professional mathematician of the first rank, who not only contributed himself very importantly to group theory in the 1920s, but also paved the path to its entrance in modern physics.

**(b) Hermann Weyl: Group Theory and Natural Philosophy (1922–1928)**

In the preface to his new book *Gruppentheorie und Quantenmechanik*, Hermann Weyl wrote in August 1928:

There exists, in my opinion, a plainly discernible parallelism between the more recent developments of mathematics and physics. Occidental mathematics has in the past centuries broken away from the Greek view and followed a course which seems to have originated in India and which has been transmitted, with additions, to us by the Arabs; in it the concept of number appears as logically prior to the concept of geometry. The result of this has been that we have applied this systematically developed number concept to all branches, irrespective of whether it is most appropriate for these particular applications. But the present trend in mathematics is clearly in the direction of a return to the Greek standpoint. . . . The newer mathematics, including the modern theory of groups and ‘abstract algebra,’ is clearly motivated by a spirit different from that of ‘classical mechanics,’ which found its highest expression in the theory of functions of a complex variable. The continuum of real numbers has retained its ancient prerogative in physics for the expression of physical measurements, but it can justly be maintained that the essence of the new Heisenberg-Schrödinger-Dirac quantum mechanics is to be found in the fact that there is associated with each physical system a set of quantities, consisting of a non-commutative algebra in the technical mathematical sense, the elements of which are the physical quantities themselves. (Weyl, 1928b, p. VI; the English translation is from Weyl, 1931, p. viii)

Hermann Weyl had already previously shown from time to time an interest in

# III.4 Group Theory and Quantum Mechanics
479

problems of quantum theory,⁵⁷² but now he turned his full attention to a very general question, namely, ‘the importance of the standpoint afforded by the theory of groups for the discovery of the general laws of quantum theory’ (Weyl, *loc. cit.*, p. V). At that moment, this question seemed to be quite obvious to Weyl (who, in the previous years, had been deeply involved in the theory of representation of continuous groups), as the results could be applied readily to solve several problems in the new atomic theory. Let us briefly sketch in the following how Weyl came to work on quantum theory, and how he then combined his mathematical results with a broad interest in fundamental physical theories.
Following his doctoral dissertation on singular integral equations (Weyl, 1908), Hermann Weyl—a student of David Hilbert in Göttingen—extended during the following years until 1915 Hilbert’s theory of linear integral equations and treated a series of mathematical and physical problems; notably, he studied the asymptotic distribution of natural frequencies for oscillating continua.⁵⁷³ In 1913, the *Idee der Riemannschen Fläche* (The Idea of the Riemann Surface), which emerged from lectures that he gave as a *Privatdozent* at the University of Göttingen, opened the distinguished list of Weyl’s numerous publications in book form. At the same time, he obtained his first chair at the ETH in Zurich and began to investigate a variety of mathematical topics, especially those dealing with the theory of numbers. Then, after 1916, the physical theory of general relativity absorbed his interest for years: he plunged into its mathematical, physical, and philosophical contents, which led him not only to write his great classic *Raum-Zeit-Materie* (*Space-Time-Matter*, first published as 1918b, with five editions by 1923), but also to propose a unified field theory of gravitation and electricity (1918c, 1919, 1920). The study of the mathematical problems in this theory, such as the affine structure of *n*-differentiable manifolds and the question of the metric in the spaces considered forced Weyl to delve deeply into the mathematical and philosophical problem of space.⁵⁷⁴ The lecture series on ‘*Mathematische Analyse des Raumproblems*’ (‘The Mathematical Analysis of the Problem of Space’), delivered in spring 1922 on a tour of Spain (Madrid and Barcelona) and published as a book (Weyl, 1923a), presented a renewed analysis of the question first treated by Helmholtz in 1868, namely, to characterize space by the groups of movements (i.e., the mobility of bodies in space): Weyl now approached the problem of extending Sophus Lie’s proof of Helmholtz’s assertion in the language of his infinitesimal geometry. ‘This he did by analyzing the meaning of the assumption that the metric, i.e., the group of movements, uniquely determines the affine connection, and he showed that this

# 480 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

assumption and the conservation of volume suffice to characterize the group of infinitesimal rotations at a point as the set of linear transformations that leave a non-degenerate quadratic differential form invariant’ (Newman, 1957, p. 316).⁵⁷⁵ Thus, Weyl was driven to tackle a new big mathematical topic, the theory of groups—in particular, of Lie groups.
‘Another push into Lie groups came, in a way, again from the tensor calculus [in Weyl, 1921], but for a completely different reason,’ wrote the Zurich mathematician Armand Borel in his analysis of ‘Hermann Weyl and Lie Groups’ and explained:

In 1923 E[duard] Study, a well known expert in Invariant Theory for over thirty years, published a book on Invariant Theory (Study, 1923). In a long foreword, he complained that Invariant Theory, in particular the so-called symbolic method to generate invariants, had been all but forgotten and that several mathematicians did less by other methods than would be possible [by] using it. Among those was H. Weyl, identified by a quote, criticized for his treatment of tensors. Apparently H. Weyl was stung by this. This can already be seen by the rather sharply worded footnote in his answer to Study . . . but it was also remembered about 25 years later by one of his colleagues here at that time, M. Plancherel, who mentioned it to me as an example of the extraordinary ability of H. Weyl had, shared only by J. von Neumann among the mathematicians he had known, to get into a new subject and bring an important contribution to it within a few months. In fact, H. Weyl published two papers on Invariant Theory in 1924 (Weyl 1924d, e), which brings me back to the achievements already alluded before [namely, the Lie groups]. (Borel, 1986, pp. 54–55)

Weyl’s sharp answer to Study’s criticism appeared in the general essay ‘*Randbemerkungen zu Hauptproblemen der Mathematik*’ (‘Marginal Remarks on the Fundamental Problems of Mathematics,’ Weyl, 1924c, p. 131—not in Weyl, 1923a, as Borel noted in the above quote). There, he admitted that he possessed ‘little knowledge of the literature and little experience in invariant theory, but even if I were able to compete in this with Mr. Study, I would not have applied the symbolic method in *Raum-Zeit-Materie*, and would not have mentioned a single word at all (*ein Sterbenswörtschen*) about the algebraic completeness theorems of the invariant theory’ (Weyl, *loc. cit.*). In the same year 1924, when he wrote the two papers on the invariant theory, he also stepped into the depths of group theory, being stimulated especially by the work of the French mathematician Élie Cartan. ‘Since I got to know the theory of general relativity, nothing has touched me so much and filled me with enthusiasm as the study of your papers on continuous groups,’ he wrote to Cartan in early 1925 (Weyl to Cartan, 22 March 1925, quoted in the original German by Borel, 1986, p. 54).

However, there he had proven the assumption only for $n = 2$ and 3 dimensions of space; later, he generalized it to arbitrarily many dimensions (Weyl, 1922).

III.4 Group Theory and Quantum Mechanics 481

Élie Cartan, an expert on the theory of groups for decades, had read the fourth edition of Weyl’s *Raum-Zeit-Materie* (1921) in the French translation of 1922 and supplied a proof of the generalized Helmholtz–Lie theorem (mentioned above) within the framework of his own methods of determining the irreducible representations of simple Lie groups (Cartan, 1923). Excited by Cartan’s interest, Weyl now acquainted himself with the work of his French colleague on group transformations and, in addition, with the recent results of Issai Schur from Berlin (Schur, 1924a, b, c) dealing with the representations of the orthogonal group and its invariants.$^{576}$ Weyl, who had been concerned with the continuous group of orthogonal transformations already before (see his paper, Weyl, 1923b) and was informed by Schur in advance of the 1924 results, immediately wrote back to Berlin:

> I have succeeded, by a modification of your method, in solving the problem of representation for all simple (and semi-simple) groups including the calculation of characteristics. Of particular importance of course are the group $\mathcal{G}$ of all homogeneous linear transformations with determinant 1, and the groups $\mathcal{C}$ and $\mathcal{D}$ of those among them which leave a non-degenerate skew-symmetric and symmetric bilinear form—[xx'] or (xx')—invariant. If one goes back, with Lie, to the infinitesimal groups $\mathfrak{g}$, $\mathfrak{c}$, and $\mathfrak{d}$, then one needs for the "integral" problem certain conditions of differentiability. The integral method replaces, according to the skillful method (*Kunstgriff*) of [Adolph] Hurwitz, the complex groups $\mathcal{G}$, $\mathcal{C}$, and $\mathcal{D}$ first by their subgroups $\mathcal{G}_u$, $\mathcal{C}_u$, and $\mathcal{D}_u$ of unitary transformations. ... Then one gets along, as you have demonstrated in the case of the real rotation group $\mathcal{D}_u$, with the condition of continuity alone. Each of the irreducible representations of $\mathcal{G}_u$, $\mathcal{C}_u$, and $\mathcal{D}_u$ immediately provides one for [the entire groups] $\mathcal{G}$, $\mathcal{C}$, and $\mathcal{D}$. (Weyl to Schur, in Weyl, 1924f, p. 338)

Thus, Hermann Weyl outlined his programme to establish his goals; he added the remark that, for showing the completeness of the representations and their decomposition into irreducible parts, still the condition of differentiability must be made, but once this has been done everything would follow by referring to the situation with infinitesimal groups. In the letter to Schur, Weyl then sketched some details of the procedure for simple examples; and Schur, who admired the progress obtained, presented the latter to the Berlin Academy in its meeting of 11 December 1924, and encouraged Weyl to write his results in detail and publish them in the *Mathematische Zeitschrift*, where his paper (Weyl, 1925–1926) appeared in three parts and one addendum.

We shall not enter into a discussion of the proofs and arguments in that big memoir on representation theory for continuous semisimple groups, which Weyl

$^{576}$ Schur, on his side, had extended the theory of characteristics and the orthogonality relations previously developed by Frobenius and himself for finite groups: The ‘characteristics’ $\chi_{\pi}$ are associated with an irreducible representation $\pi$ of a group; they form a basis of the field $C$ of the group. If the representation is orthogonal (and the orthogonality relations can be applied), the average of the characteristics $\chi_{\pi}$ over the group $\mathcal{G}$ gives the dimension of the space of fixed vectors. Weyl renamed the characteristics later as ‘characters.’ In matrix theory, the name ‘character’ is used to denote the sum of all characteristic roots (i.e., the eigenvalues), hence, the trace of a matrix.

482 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

‘considered to be his greatest single contribution to mathematics’ (Newman, 1957, p. 317).$^{577}$ They are technically quite involved and make full use of the advanced erudition (*Gelehrsamkeit*) of the researches performed during the previous decade by outstanding experts in group theory and related topics, notably, Cartan, Frobenius, Hurwitz, and Schur. As Weyl’s biographer, Newman, summarized, the three notes of the memoir:

> are concerned with the representations of a semi-simple Lie group **a** by linear transformations of a finite dimensional vector space $V$ over the complex field. ... For a finite group, this had been attained in principle by the work of Frobenius, Burnside and Schur in the period 1895–1905. Weyl’s results, completed in an essential point by the famous Peter-Weyl theorem, go a long way towards solving the corresponding problem for semi-simple groups, and effectively the whole way for compact Lie groups. He obtained explicit formulae for the characters and the degrees of the irreducible representations by a powerful combination of the infinitesimal methods of E. Cartan, the method of invariant integration over the group-manifold of a compact Lie group (first used in a special case by Hurwitz and later by Schur) and topological considerations. (Newman, *loc. cit.*, 317)

The Peter–Weyl theorem mentioned above served to prove the completeness of the system of orthogonal functions formed by the coefficients of the inequivalent irreducible representations—i.e., the completeness of what the authors (Weyl and his student F. Peter) called the ‘primitive representations of a closed continuous group’ in the title of their paper (Peter and Weyl, 1927, p. 737). In two further publications, Weyl drew certain consequences arising from the application of his methods to the complex group $\mathcal{C}$ and the rotation group $\mathcal{D}$; notably, he discussed the ‘counting of invariants’ and the composition of certain reducible representations of the group (Weyl, 1926a) and derived several elementary theorems (Weyl, 1926b). Having completed this Herculean task, Weyl returned to physics and applied the new group-theoretical tools especially to derive important results for the detailed structure of quantum-mechanical systems.

As the theoretical physicist Chen-Ning Yang wrote in his memorial article on ‘Hermann Weyl’s Contributions to Physics’ in 1985: ‘In the midst of Weyl’s profound research on Lie groups there occurred a great revolution in physics, namely the development of quantum mechanics,’ and he immediately added: ‘We shall perhaps never know Weyl’s initial reaction to this development, but he soon got into the act and studied the mathematical structure of the new mechanics. There resulted a paper and later a book.’ (Yang, 1986, p. 9) Actually, we have mentioned in previous volumes Weyl’s early reactions to both matrix mechanics (in 1925) and wave mechanics (in early 1926), and they were very enthusiastic. Therefore, we have to assume quite firmly that it was only his deep involvement with the last stages of his work on the theory of semisimple continuous groups that prevented Weyl ‘to get into the act’ immediately. Now, by fall 1927, he was again free, and

III.4 Group Theory and Quantum Mechanics 483

already in October of that year, he submitted a paper with the programmatic title ‘*Quantenmechanik und Gruppentheorie*’ (‘Quantum Mechanics and the Theory of Groups,’ Weyl, 1927). Like ten years earlier in the case of general relativity, the new paper signalled Weyl’s deep involvement in the problems of atomic physics, which lasted for several years and bore many fruits.

In particular, Weyl addressed two questions in the new physical theory: ‘1. How do I arrive at the matrix, i.e., the Hermitean form which represents a given quantity of a physical system whose constitution is known? 2. Once the Hermitean form has been obtained, what is its physical interpretation and which physical consequences can be derived from it.’ (Weyl, 1927, p. 1) We have already presented the discussion of the second question in Section III.3 in connection with the statistical interpretation of John von Neumann and others, to which Weyl contributed in particular the concept and description of the ‘pure case’ (Weyl, 1927, Part I, pp. 3–15). ‘Part II deals with the more fundamental (*tiefer liegende*) question 1, which is connected with the question concerning the nature and the correct interpretation of canonical variables,’ Weyl noted in the introduction. So far, he said, only one ‘attempt in this direction containing a serious gap’ had been made, and this was Pascual Jordan’s (Jordan, 1927b). The ‘serious gap’ consisted in the fact that neither Jordan nor any other physicist had provided a rigorous method for obtaining the matrix representation $f(Q)$ for a function of a variable $f(q)$ from the matrix representation of the variable $q$ itself, and, in addition, shown how functions of canonically conjugate variables $p$ and $q$ should be represented properly. ‘Here I believe that [I have] arrived at a deeper insight into the real facts with the help of *group theory*,’ Weyl claimed and argued, in particular:$^{578}$

> The principal inner reason for the canonical pairing [of the variables] shows up clearly in the situation occurring in the case that the fundamental group [of the dynamics] is a continuous one; still the *Ansatz* embraces the discrete cases as well, e.g., the magnetic electron (a group of four elements), where one cannot speak sensibly about canonical pairing. In the continuous region, I emphasize the *integral standpoint* against the differential one by replacing the infinitesimal group—to which one has stuck up to now when formulating the problem—by the full continuous group. Then the transition [from the equations of matrix mechanics] to Schrödinger’s wave equation can be performed with every necessary rigour. (Weyl, 1927, p. 2)

The group-theoretical analysis of the quantum-mechanical formalism then allowed one to solve the outstanding problem mentioned by Weyl, namely, to establish the correct functional expression for the Hamiltonian operator $H$ by the variables $p$ and $q$ (and give, especially, the correct order of factors in their product).

In Part II, which he entitled ‘Kinematics as a Group,’ Weyl first acquainted the physicists with the concepts and methods of the theory of groups, their representa-

$^{578}$ In a footnote on the same p. 2, Weyl pointed out that his group-theoretical approach to quantum mechanics pursued a rather different goal from that of Eugene Wigner (which we shall discuss below); the latter tried to determine, with the help of group-theoretical methods, just ‘the structure of the spectra from the qualitative point of view.’

484 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

tion by unitary transformations, and the ‘algebras of quantities’ (‘*Größenalgebra*’) connected with the group. In particular, he defined a ‘quantity’ (‘*Größe*’) $X$ in a group by associating with each group element $s$ a number $\xi(s)$ and taking
$$
X = \sum_s \xi(s) U(s), \tag{429}
$$
where $U(s)$ denotes a unitary representation of $s.$$^{579}$ The multiplication law of quantities then read
$$
Z = XY = \sum_{t,t'} U(t) U(t') \xi(t) \eta(t') = \sum_s U(s) \zeta(s), \tag{430}
$$
with
$$
U(s) = U(t) U(t') = U(t, t') \quad \text{and} \quad \zeta(s) = \sum_{t,t'} \xi(t) \eta(t'). \tag{431}
$$

Evidently, the quantities form an algebra, as they ‘can be *added, multiplied by numbers* and multiplied with each other, such that the most important axioms of algebra are satisfied ... but for the commutative law of multiplication and the axiom which excludes zero divisors’ (Weyl, *loc. cit.*, p. 17). Finally, Weyl discussed the special case of Abelian groups, in which the composition of elements is commutative; then, all unitary representations $U(s)$ can be transformed simultaneously to principal axes, or all irreducible representations of Abelian groups are one-dimensional.

Armed with the group-theoretical tools mentioned above, Weyl addressed a specific representation problem of quantum mechanics that does not occur in the classical theory, namely: ‘In quantum mechanics it is not the vectors which have a physical meaning but only the rays which characterize the different pure cases’ (Weyl, *loc. cit.*, p. 18). Consequently, the system space of a quantum-mechanical symmetry group is the ‘field of rays’ (not the field of vectors), and a unitary matrix $U(s)$ representing an element $s$ coincides with the matrix $\varepsilon U(s)$, with the ‘gauge factor’ $\varepsilon$. The multiplication rule for representations (431) must be replaced by
$$
U(s) = U(t) U(t') \simeq U(t, t'), \tag{432}
$$
where
$$
U(t) U(t') = \delta(t, t') U(t, t'), \tag{433}
$$

$^{579}$ $X$ possesses as many components $\xi(s)$ as group elements and may be regarded as a vector in the space given by the group.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0517 -->

III.4 Group Theory and Quantum Mechanics 485

with $\delta(t, t')$ being a numerical factor of absolute value 1 whose phase depends on $t$ and $t'$. $^{580}$

Now, for ray-fields, the one-dimensional representations are trivial, because they simply correspond to the identity transformations. Hence, even the irreducible representations of quantum-mechanical Abelian groups become multidimensional.$^{581}$ Thus, for example, the 'group of four elements (*Vierergruppe*)' $1, a, b, c$, with

$$a^2 = b^2 = c^2 = 1 \quad \text{and} \quad bc = cb = a, \quad ca = ac = b, \quad ab = ba = c, \tag{434}$$

constitutes the simplest noncyclical Abelian group, which is found to be isomorphic to the rotation group represented by the two-dimensional Pauli spin matrices,

$$U(1) = \begin{Vmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{Vmatrix}, \quad U(a) = \begin{Vmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{Vmatrix},$$

$$U(b) = \begin{Vmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{Vmatrix}, \quad U(c) = \begin{Vmatrix} 0 & i \\ -i & 0 \end{Vmatrix}, \tag{435}$$

normalized by $U(a)^2 = U(a)U(a^{-1}) = U(1)$. The associated algebra turns out to be the *non-Abelian algebra* of quaternions having the 'real' quantities$^{582}$

$$X = \rho 1 + \xi a + \eta b + \zeta c \tag{436}$$

(with $\rho, \xi, \eta$ and $\zeta$ denoting real numbers), which can be represented by the two-dimensional matrices

$$X = \begin{Vmatrix} \rho + \xi, & \eta + i\zeta \\ \eta - i\zeta, & \rho - \xi \end{Vmatrix}. \tag{437}$$

That is, to the commutative groups, in quantum mechanics, correspond non-commutative algebras, in contrast to the situation in classical mechanics.

Having displayed further properties of Abelian rotation groups in the ray representation, Weyl went on to discuss continuous groups and their infinitesimal unitary-transformation representations (Lie's scheme) and presented his new integral point of view (developed in mathematical papers between 1924 and 1926).

486 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

In classical mechanics, the rotation groups are Abelian groups (in the normal vector space) and can be described by infinitesimal matrices $C_i$, having a zero commutator$^{583}$

$$C_iC_k - C_kC_i = 0. \tag{438}$$

In the quantum-mechanical ray-space, however, Eq. (438) must be replaced by

$$C_\mu C_\nu - C_\nu C_\mu = ic_{\mu\nu}\mathbf{1}, \tag{439}$$

with $c_{\mu\nu}$ denoting a skew-symmetric system of real numbers and $\mathbf{1}$ the unit matrix. From Eq. (439), Weyl derived important consequences: first, he found for the composition of two $f$-parametric rotations $U(\sigma)(= U(\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_f))$ and $U(\tau) (= U(\tau_1, \dots, \tau_f))$ the formula

$$U(\sigma + \tau) = \exp\{\frac{1}{2} h(\sigma, \tau)\} U(\tau)U(\sigma) = \exp\{-\frac{1}{2} h(\sigma, \tau)\} U(\sigma)U(\tau), \tag{440}$$

with the ‘commutator form’ $h(\sigma, \tau)$ defined as

$$h(\sigma, \tau) = \sum_{\mu, \nu} c_{\mu\nu}\sigma_\mu \tau_\nu. \tag{441}$$

Second, on assuming irreducible representations of the rotation group, the number of quantum variables must be even, say, $2f$, and the coefficient matrix $c_{\mu\nu}$ decays into two-row matrices $\left\| \begin{matrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{matrix} \right\|$ along the main diagonal. Third, by rewriting the $2f$ variables $C_1, \dots, C_{2f}$ in the form of a ‘canonical basis’,

$$iP_\nu = C_\nu, \quad \nu = 1, \dots, f,$$
$$iQ_\nu = C_\nu, \quad \nu = f + 1, \dots, 2f, \tag{442}$$

the ‘commutation relations’ followed:

$$i(P_\nu Q_\nu - Q_\nu P_\nu) = \mathbf{1}, \quad i(P_\mu Q_\nu - Q_\nu P_\mu) = 0 \text{ for } \mu \neq \nu$$

and

$$(P_\mu P_\nu - P_\nu P_\mu) = 0, \quad (Q_\mu Q_\nu - Q_\nu Q_\mu) = 0 \text{ for all } \mu, \nu. \tag{443}$$

The scheme, described by Eqs. (439)–(443), now allowed one to formulate the

III.4 Group Theory and Quantum Mechanics 487

most general system of real (quantum) variables, namely, as the Hermitean forms

$$F = \int \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} d\sigma d\tau \exp\{P\sigma + Q\tau\} \quad (444)$$

in the case of one canonical pair of variables $P, Q$, and the expression (444) automatically established the correct order in the product terms of $P$ and $Q$, when $F$ is written as a power series in $P$ and $Q$; hence, the difficulty in defining product terms in quantum mechanics completely disappeared. Weyl happily concluded this demonstration by saying:

> The kinematical character of a [quantum-mechanical] physical system obtains its [mathematical] expression in an irreducible Abelian rotation group, whose substrate is the ray field of “pure cases.” The real quantities of this group region (*Gruppengebiet*) are the physical quantities; the Hermitean matrices, as which they appear via the representation of the abstract group by rotations, are the representatives of the physical quantities. (Weyl, 1927, p. 29)

He further showed by explicit construction that a two-parameter continuous Abelian group allows only for *one* irreducible ray representation (except the identical one), namely, the one that leads to the Schrödinger equation (Weyl, *loc. cit.*, pp. 30–34).

An attempt to discuss also the quantum-mechanical *dynamics* on the basis of group theory, i.e., to include the time variable in the scheme, did not yield results of similar importance (Weyl, *loc. cit.*, Part III, pp. 34–44). Weyl, therefore, did not mention them in his lecture course in Zurich in the winter semester 1926/27 or in his *Gruppentheorie und Quantenmechanik*. Otherwise, he included all topics of the 1927 paper in the new book, whose preface (signed in August 1928) opened with the remarks:

> It is the second time that I dare to enter the stage with a book which belongs only half to my professional field of mathematics, the other half to physics. The external reason is not very different from that which led some time ago to the origin of the book *Raum-Zeit-Materie*. In the winter term [1927/28] Zurich was deprived, by the simultaneous [departures] of Debye and Schrödinger, of all theoretical physics. I tried to fill the gap by changing an already announced lecture course on group theory into one on group theory and quantum mechanics.
> ...
> Since I have for some years been deeply concerned with the theory of the representation of continuous groups, it has seemed to me appropriate to give an account of the knowledge won by mathematicians working in this field in a form suitable for the requirements of quantum physics. (Weyl, 1928b, p. VI)

Weyl then pointed out that, ‘from the purely mathematical standpoint it is no longer justifiable to draw such sharp distinctions between finite and continuous

groups in discussing the theory of their representations'--a fact that would agree fully with the standpoint of quantum mechanics.

Weyl's book emerged from notes taken by a student named F. Bohnenblust. In his lectures, Weyl tried to formulate the mathematical results in the simplest technical language possible, though he still retained the spirit of his own group-theoretical investigations; of these considerable parts, for example, the extension of Schur's representation methods to closed continuous groups, entered into the presentation for the physicists, as did most of the contents of his 1927 paper, particularly those concerning the rotations of the ray-field and their application to the problems of quantum kinematics. In addition, Weyl displayed in some detail the formalism of the rotation groups in the three-dimensional space as well as that of the permutation group (in particular, in connection with the Pauli principle); finally, he included some results on the quantization of wave equations from the paper of Jordan and Wigner (1928) from the point of view of group theory.⁵⁸⁴ Weyl devoted a special section to the group of Lorentz transformations and its applications. As he stated in the foreword:

> The course of events is so cogent (*zwingend*) that nearly everything new contained in the lectures has since been published by others, namely in papers by Messrs. C. G. Darwin, F. London, J. von Neumann and E. Wigner. ... The case is different with Dirac's wave equation of the electron, by which an essentially new idea has been introduced into the [physical] theory at the time the book was written. (Weyl, 1928b, p. VI)

**(c) Werner Heisenberg and Eugene Wigner: The Pioneers of Group Theory in Quantum Mechanics (1926-1928)**

The Dutch mathematician, Bartel Leendert Van der Waerden, himself an expert on group theory and its application to quantum mechanics, noted:

> Wigner's paper [1927] seems to be the first in which group theory was applied to [quantum] physics. In this paper, some rules of term zoology were deduced, but the spin was still left out of account. In the papers of von Neumann and Wigner [1928a, b, c], the whole apparatus of group characters and representations was put into action and the complete system of term zoology, including selection rules, intensity formulae, [and] Stark effect was developed. (Van der Waerden, 1960, p. 228)

However, this statement is slightly oversimplified, as far as the origin of the idea and its exact time are concerned.

In the preface of his *Atombau und Spektrallinien*, Arnold Sommerfeld had written: 'What we nowadays extract from the language of spectra is real celestial music of the atom, an accord of integral-number relations, a growing order and

harmony in spite of all plurality.' (Sommerfeld, 1919, p. viii) Evidently, the rather successful organization of spectroscopic lines and their patterns since 1913 strongly suggested the impression of an underlying symmetry: one certainly was convinced that the spectroscopic rules reflected underlying symmetries, but this feeling did not find expression in any detailed considerations with properly developed mathematical formalisms for that purpose. The advent of quantum mechanics and the formulation of its laws in terms of matrices and operators was also deemed to provide new insight into the symmetrical content of the new atomic mechanics, though it took the theoreticians a while before they approached this problem. It began with Heisenberg's paper of June 1926 on the many-body problem and resonance, in which he studied the eigenfunctions of two resonating atomic systems; he then registered the existence of two classes of solutions, one symmetric and the other antisymmetric with respect to the exchange of the individual systems (Heisenberg, 1926b). In the following paper, submitted on 24 July 1926, he explicitly addressed the symmetry and antisymmetry property of the solutions, notably, in the case of the energy terms of the two-electron atoms of helium (Heisenberg, 1926c). Later, in December 1926, he continued the investigation of many-electron systems in a detailed second article on '*Mehrkörperprobleme und Resonanz in der Quantenmechanik.II*' ('Many-Body Problems and Resonance in Quantum Mechanics II'), and there he introduced a special method to define different, noncombining term classes or term systems, with the following passage:

> Let $u$ and $v$ be the eigenfunctions of two *different* systems, then the integral $\int u^* v f\,d\xi$ should vanish, if $f$ is a symmetric function of the electrons [with $\xi$ denoting the coordinates].
>
> We now try to construct such systems and start from the eigenfunction
>
> $$u = l_1m_2 \ldots p_n. \tag{445}$$
>
> All eigenfunctions $l,m,\ldots p$ [the index in (445) refers to the subsystems $1,2,\ldots n$] should be different. In the unperturbed system there exist $n!$ terms having equal energy; the associated eigenfunctions arise from Eq. [(445)] if the indices denoting the number of the electrons are permuted in any possible way. Let us call a substitution in the number of electrons $S$, and let us write $S$, as is usually done in group theory [our italics], as
>
> $$S =
> \begin{pmatrix}
> 1 & 2 & \cdots & n\\
> a_1 & a_2 & \cdots & a_n
> \end{pmatrix}. \tag{446}$$
>
> We further denote with $Su$ the eigenfunction
>
> $$Su = l_{a_1}m_{a_2}\ldots p_{a_n}. \tag{447}$$
>
> The multiple application of the same substitution is called the power of a substitution, with $S^0 = 1$ being the "identical" substitution. There always exists a smallest power $S^\nu$ yielding (for $\nu > 0$)
>
> $$S^\nu = 1, \tag{448}$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0522 -->

and this $\nu$ is called the degree of the substitution. The problem of non-combining term-systems now has a very close connection to the theory of permutation groups. (Heisenberg, 1927a, pp. 245-246)

Heisenberg, who referred for details of the method to an old book on higher algebra of the French mathematician Joseph Serret (1879), wrote the $\nu$ eigenfunctions of the system (which is invariant under the group of $\nu$ permutations $1,S,S^2,\ldots S^{\nu-1}$) as

$$
U_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\nu}}\{u + Su + S^2u + \cdots + S^{\nu-1}u\},
$$

$$
U_\omega = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\nu}}\{u + \omega Su + \omega^2 S^2u + \cdots + \omega^{\nu-1}S^{\nu-1}u\},
$$

$$
U_{\omega^{\nu-1}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\nu}}\{u + \omega^{\nu-1}Su + \omega^{2(\nu-1)}S^2u + \cdots + \omega^{(\nu-1)^2}S^{\nu-1}u\}, \tag{449}
$$

where $\omega$ is a root of the equation $\omega^\nu = 1$. Now, the functions $U_1,\ldots U_{\omega^{\nu-1}}$ might not exhaust all $n!$ possibilities, because in general $\nu$ is a divisor of $n!$ [and in order to obtain the rest, one would have to apply other permutations than those contained the group $1,S,\ldots S^{\nu-1}$, which then yield functions different from those given by Eqs. (449)], but Heisenberg assumed that the groups given above should just determine different term systems $\Gamma_1,\Gamma_\omega,\ldots \Gamma_{\omega^{\nu-1}}$ of the quantum-mechanical $n$-particle object. Even in the situation that some, or all, of these term systems can split (under the action of a perturbing force) into subsystems--this occurs if a substitution $T$ is given that commutes with $S$, or

$$T^{-1}ST = S \tag{450}$$

--the treatment with the permutation groups provided a proper tool to obtain the eigenfunctions, Heisenberg concluded. As an example, he considered the lithium atom with three electrons and obtained three term systems, $\Gamma_1$, $\Gamma_\varepsilon$, and $\Gamma_{\varepsilon^2}$, where $\Gamma_1$ can split further into a symmetric and an antisymmetric system.⁵⁸⁵ He further brought the electron spin into the lithium problem, and finally suggested that the new group-theoretical method might be applied also to the problem of molecular spectra.

In a footnote added in proof, Heisenberg mentioned: 'In a paper published in the meanwhile, E. Wigner has arrived independently at results for the three-electron problem, which are equivalent to those given here.' (Heisenberg, 1927a,

⁵⁸⁵ Heisenberg could not answer the general question: In how many noncombining term systems do the energy states of an $n$-electron atom split? Practically, the substitution of highest degree, namely, the cyclic substitution, provides the largest number of term systems; this leads for the lithium atom to the term system given above.
