p. 249) This remark referred to the first note of a young colleague from Berlin, entitled '*Über nicht kombinierende Terme in der neueren Quantentheorie*' ('On Non-Combining Terms in the Recent Quantum Theory'), which was received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 12 November 1926, and published in an issue of that journal the following month (Wigner, 1926). Eugene Wigner started from Heisenberg's paper of June 1926, in which Heisenberg had proposed the existence of $n!$ groups of terms in an $n$-electron system, of which one might satisfy Pauli's exclusion principle (and possibly Bose-Einstein statistics), and from Dirac's paper on wave mechanics, which established the relation between systems described by symmetric or antisymmetric wave functions, on the one hand, and Bose and Fermi statistics, on the other. As the main result, he announced 'that the terms [of many-electron system] really split into several groups' and further that:

> The groups cannot intercombine with each other, and there exist among them two groups which have the following properties: both contain about the $(1/n!)$th part of the total system; one system satisfies Pauli's exclusion principle, and the weight distribution of the other is given by the Bose-Einstein statistics. All the other systems are degenerate; the degeneracy is of such a nature that it cannot be removed by any perturbation which is symmetric in the single, identical particles. (Wigner, *loc. cit.*, p. 492)

Wigner proved these statements by explicit evaluations of the Schrödinger wave functions for two- and three-electron problems, both for the unperturbed case and for the case of an interaction symmetrical in the three space coordinates. He concluded: 'In a second communication I hope to solve the problem for more than three electrons.' (Wigner, *loc. cit.*, p. 500) Two weeks later, on 26 November 1926, he submitted his second paper on noncombining terms, the results of which he mentioned in a few introductory remarks: emphasizing the complications of the previous calculations, namely, that 'the elementary methods can hardly be used for four electrons as the computational difficulties increase too much,' he announced that:

> there exists a well developed mathematical theory which can be applied: the theory of transformation groups which are isomorphic to the symmetry group (the group of permutation); this theory was founded towards the end of last century by [Ferdinand] Frobenius and later completed by [William] Burnside and [Issai] Schur. Mr. J. v. Neumann has kindly mentioned to me their papers; he also predicted, when I told him the result of the calculation for $n = 3$, the general result. (Wigner, 1927a, p. 883)

At this time, Eugen (or Eugene, as he would call himself later after first visiting the United States) Paul Wigner was still a fairly unknown young physicist in Berlin. He had been born in Budapest on 17 November 1902, where his father Antal [Anthony] Wigner, of Austrian Jewish descent, worked in a flourishing leather-tanning factory (later as director).⁵⁸⁶ He attended the prestigious private Lutheran

⁵⁸⁶ Eugene Wigner had two sisters: the older Bertha, called Biri, and the younger Margit, called Manci. In 1934, Manci married Paul Dirac.

Gymnasium of his hometown, where he received an excellent education, especially from his mathematics teacher László Ratz, who also greatly influenced John von Neumann, one year his junior at school.⁵⁸⁷ Also, the physics teacher Sándor Mikola went quite far in his teaching, and introduced the talented boys to Maxwell's electromagnetic theory. Eugene Wigner was a very good student in every subject except singing; he graduated from high school in 1920 and began to study chemical engineering, first at the Technical University of Budapest (1920–1921), and then in Berlin at the *Technische Hochschule* in Berlin-Charlottenburg.⁵⁸⁸ For his *Diplomarbeit* (master's thesis with the physical chemist Hermann Mark), completed in 1924, Wigner studied the crystal-lattice structure of rhombic sulphur.

Wigner's main attraction was not for engineering, but rather for pure science, especially theoretical physics, which in those days was represented in Berlin by the great stars Albert Einstein, Max Planck, Walther Nernst, and Max von Laue at the neighbouring *Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universität*. Wigner regularly attended the famous Berlin physics colloquium. In 1925, he obtained his *Dr. phil.* with Michael Polanyi, a fellow countryman working at Fritz Haber's *Kaiser-Wilhelm-Institut für physikalische und Elektrochemie*. The title of his thesis was 'Statistische Mechanik und Reaktionsgeschwindigkeit' ('Statistical Mechanics and Reaction Rate'), and the young chemical engineer dealt in it with reaction rates and the mechanism of the creation and decay of molecules.⁵⁸⁹ In the publication arising from this thesis, a rather interesting conclusion was obtained: namely, the quantum-theoretical formula for the so-called velocity constant of an elementary two-atomic reaction implied the relation

$$\Delta\varepsilon \cdot \tau = h,$$ (451)

where $\Delta\varepsilon$ denoted the energy uncertainty and $\tau$ denoted the lifetime of the molecule (Polanyi and Wigner, 1925, p. 432)—‘a very feeble expression of the [later] uncertainty relation,’ as Wigner would remark later.

After completing his doctorate, Wigner returned to Budapest and worked for a while in his father's leather-tanning factory. However, Polanyi recommended him to Richard Becker, professor of theoretical physics at the *Technische Hochschule*, and Wigner accepted (in spite of the low salary) and returned to Berlin as a scientist. He studied the recent physics literature and soon found a problem to work on:

III.4 Group Theory and Quantum Mechanics 493

There was an article by Heisenberg on the symmetry of atoms during the exchange of electrons. This was a magnificent article, but like a number of other papers by Heisenberg, it was not fully correct mathematically. So I studied that paper, and worked on the problem of symmetry in the case of three electrons. I showed it to Professor Becker, and he said: “You should publish it. It’s very interesting and quite different from how I would conceive this problem.” So I published it and showed that the problem was much more complicated in the case of four, five, or six electrons. I consulted my close friend von Neumann, and he said: “Read the articles of Frobenius and Schur.” (Wigner, in Mehra, 2000, p. 7)

Armed with the knowledge obtained from the mathematical literature, Wigner then composed his second article on noncombining terms (Wigner, 1927a), in which he first made a consistent use of a much more advanced status of group theory than had Heisenberg. This is the true reason why he is usually mentioned as having introduced group-theoretical methods into quantum mechanics.
The basic physical results that Wigner achieved beyond Heisenberg were the following. First, he provided a formula for the degeneracy of the term system characterized by the decomposition $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \cdots + \lambda_i$ of $n$ electrons, namely,

$$N_{\lambda_1, \lambda_2 \dots \lambda_i} = \frac{n!}{\lambda_1! (\lambda_2 + 1)! \dots (\lambda_i + i - 1)!} \prod_{j < l} (\lambda_l - \lambda_j + l - j). \quad (452)$$

Second, he considered the perturbed wave function

$$\Psi_k = \sum_{R=E}^{H_{h-1}} b_R^k \phi_R, \quad (453)$$

where $\phi_R$ is the product wave function obtained from the permutation $R$,

$$\phi_R(\mathbf{r}_1, \mathbf{r}_2, \dots \mathbf{r}_n) = \psi_1(\mathbf{r}_{\alpha_1}) \psi_2(\mathbf{r}_{\alpha_2}) \dots \psi_n(\mathbf{r}_{\alpha_n}), \quad (454)$$

where the permutation $R$ (denoted by $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \dots \alpha_n$) runs from the unit element $E$ (or the identical permutation, which we have written as 1 earlier) to $H_1, H_2, \dots H_{h-1}$ (with $h = n!$), i.e., through all elements of the symmetry group. Then, the equation for the energy perturbation $\Delta\varepsilon$ is given by the determinant equation involving a symmetrical matrix of degree $h$. Now, Wigner turned to the representation theory of the symmetric group, which allows the reduction of the degree of the determinant equation from the larger number $h$ to $k$, the dimensionality of the irreducible representation. In a $k$-dimensional irreducible representation of the symmetry group, the perturbation energy $\Delta\varepsilon$ then satisfies an equation of degree $k$; each of the $k$ solutions of this equation can be shown to be a $k$-fold solution of the original equation of degree $n!$ for the perturbation energy. Thus, by calculating *all solutions of the different irreducible representations* of the symmetric group, one finally arrives at *all possible solutions* for the energy terms of the perturbed system.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0526 -->

494 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

In this way, Wigner succeeded in constructing, with the help of the representations of the symmetric or permutation group, the different term systems given earlier by Heisenberg, especially for the case of three-electron systems. He concluded his paper with the remarks:

> From a physical point of view it may seem at first that this investigation of term-systems is not necessary, since according to Dirac [1926f] only the one, nondegenerate, term-system must be taken [corresponding to the antisymmetric wave function]. However, one notices that because of the proper rotation (spin) of the electron also the other groups [in space] obtain a meaning, as Heisenberg has shown explicitly for helium. (Wigner, *loc. cit.*, p. 892)

Encouraged by his obvious success, Wigner proceeded further. In the next paper, submitted in early May 1927 again to *Zeitschrift für Physik* and entitled ‘Einige Folgerungen der Schrödingerschen Theorie für die Termstrukturen’ (‘Some Consequences from Schrödinger’s Theory for the Term Structures’), he provided an ambitious, systematic outline of how to use the group theoretical methods in atomic theory (Wigner, 1927b). In the ‘General Part’ (pp. 625–635), he summarized briefly the concepts, representations, and theorems needed for the ‘substitution groups’ of a differential equation, especially the permutation and the rotation groups. In particular, he described the representations by Hermitean matrices (with discrete and continuous indices) and the corresponding orthogonal normalized eigenfunctions of the (Schrödinger) differential equation, the concepts of irreducible and reducible representations, and the degeneracy of eigenvalues—including the ‘normal degeneracy’ in a given irreducible representation and the ‘accidental degeneracy’ of terms belonging to different irreducible representations. Further, he considered the case of a perturbation introduced into the original differential equation, obtaining the results: (1) if the perturbation function satisfies the original symmetries, then a normal degeneracy will not be removed at all, while accidentally degenerate terms may split or not split; (2) if the perturbation function is not invariant under the full original group—the substitution group of the new equation can still be a subgroup of substitutions applicable to the unperturbed equation—then the normal degeneracy might be removed. The representations of the various subgroups thus obtained (besides the groups mentioned already, Wigner considered certain reflection groups) obeyed the physically important theorem (which Wigner called ‘trivial’):

> If the substitution group of a differential equation consists of a direct product of several substitution groups (say, one group being the mutual exchange of electrons, the other the exchange of the hydrogen nuclei [in a molecule]), i.e., if the differential equation admits two different commuting substitution groups, then *each* pair of irreducible representations of the two groups defines an irreducible representation of the whole group. This representation, as well as the terms connected with these representations, one denotes, for practical reasons, by giving the symbols of both representations. (Wigner, 1927b, p. 635)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0527 -->

III.4 Group Theory and Quantum Mechanics 495

In the ‘Special Part’ of his programmatic paper (corresponding, so to say, to Weyl, 1927), Wigner addressed in some detail the question of substitution groups for the Schrödinger equation (pp. 635–652), namely:

(1) The permutation of the coordinates of all electrons.
(2) The permutation of the coordinates of other identical particles.
(3a) In the case of no external field, when the space is isotropic, the three-dimensional rotation–reflection group (having $(2l + 1)$-dimensional representations and a pure reflection at the origin (for which two different representations, a ‘normal’ and a ‘reflected’ one exist).
(3b) In the case of magnetic and other external fields, when the space-isotropy is disturbed and the coordinate system can only be rotated around the axis of the fields (two-dimensional rotation–reflection group) and be reflected in a plane, either parallel to the electric field or perpendicular to the axis of the magnetic field, the whole group is a direct product of a two-dimensional rotation group [with irreducible representation by matrices (1), $(\exp(i\alpha))$, $\exp(-i\alpha)$, $(\exp(2i\alpha))$, $(\exp(-2i\alpha))$, $\dots !$) and a reflection (represented by matrices (1) and $(-1)$!].

Wigner then viewed in particular the situation of crossed electric and magnetic fields and the situation of no external fields at all, working out the proper representations in both cases and obtaining agreement with data—occasionally, he had to add further assumptions to exclude nonexisting terms in nature (the reason for this being that he had not included electron spin in the treatment). Further, he derived the known selection rules for azimuthal quantum numbers, as well as the term structure and selection rules when electric or magnetic fields were acting. Finally, he treated with the new group-theoretical methods the successive capture of electrons by a given ion to come to grips with the building-up principle (*Aufbauprinzip*) of atoms. As a particularly impressive result, he derived Otto Laporte’s famous rule in the following way:

> Since the eigenfunctions of an electron are always normal [to each other], the eigenfunction of the $i$-th electron passes over by reflection at the origin into $(-1)^{l_i}$ times the eigenfunction, and therefore the total eigenfunction of the atom into the $(-1)^{l_1 + l_2 + \dots + l_n}$-fold value. Thus, if $l$ is the azimuthal eigenvalue of the atom, the associated term is “normal” or “reflected” according to whether $(-1)^{l_1 + l_2 + \dots + l_n - l}$ is $+1$ or $-1$. Now transitions do occur only between normal or between reflected terms, hence $l_1 + l_2 + \dots l_n - l$ can only be $+1$ or $-1$, also $l_1 + l_2 + \dots l_n$ can only change by an even number. (Wigner, *loc. cit.*, p. 651)

Wigner stressed ‘how little this interpretation [of Laporte’s rule] can be understood visually (*anschaulich*).’ Nevertheless, he certainly had achieved the main goal he had envisaged, namely, ‘to demonstrate that one can, by rather simple symmetry considerations with the Schrödinger equation, already explain an essential part of the purely qualitative spectroscopic experience’ (Wigner, *loc. cit.*, p. 652).
Wigner perfected the group-theoretical ‘explanation of certain properties of spectra’ in three later communications by taking care of the specific ‘quantum

mechanics of the spinning electron,’ which he signed together with his friend John von Neumann and submitted in December 1927, February 1928, and June 1928, respectively (von Neumann and Wigner, 1928a, b, c). At that time, Wigner was in Göttingen, having accepted Hilbert’s invitation to be his assistant for physics. ‘The salary they offered was miserable, but this did not really matter,’ he reminisced later: ‘Hilbert was a very great man, the greatest mathematician in the world living at that time.’ (Conversations with Mehra, in Mehra, 2000, p. 11) Though the great mathematician was very sick at the time of Wigner’s assistantship—he suffered from pernicious anemia and hardly interacted with people—Wigner found his year in Göttingen to be extremely exciting; he came to know and interacted intensely, besides with Max Born, in particular, with a number of younger quantum theorists, such as Pascual Jordan and Walter Heitler.$^{590}$ von Neumann frequently came from Berlin to discuss matters with Wigner, who recalled:

> These articles were written principally by me, but I felt that I had to express my gratitude to von Neumann for having introduced me to the work of Frobenius and Schur; therefore I proposed to him that we should publish them together. He was a marvellous mathematician, and I never encountered another mathematician who was quicker and more knowledgeable. (Wigner, in conversations with Mehra, *loc. cit.*)

Still, the work with von Neumann, and another with the American visitor Enos E. Witmer in Göttingen (which will be discussed in the next section on molecular physics and quantum chemistry), established Wigner’s reputation as an active and productive quantum theoretician. After his return to Berlin, he settled down as a *Privatdozent* at the *Technische Hochschule*, where he was promoted in 1930 to ‘*nichtbeamteter außerordentlicher Professor*’ (‘honorary associate professor’). We shall now return to the contents of the three von Neumann–Wigner papers.
The authors began their first paper with the remark that ‘the purpose of the present note is to use Pauli’s description of the rotating electron [Pauli, 1927b] for an explanation of certain spectroscopic rules—by a method which has already been applied by one of the authors to derive a part of the spectroscopic experiences from quantum mechanics (without the rotating electron!)’ (von Neumann and Wigner, 1928a, p. 203), and announced the following programme of Part I: (1) to obtain the kinematics of the electron from Pauli’s idea; (2) to apply the theory to derive those spectroscopic laws that are strictly valid if the magnetic interactions of the spinning electron are included; and (3) to consider the rules for the situation in which these interactions can be neglected. That is, von Neumann and Wigner wished—by exploiting the elementary symmetry properties of atomic systems (notably, the identity of all electrons and the equality of all space direc-

Evidently, the combined operation \( Q_{\gamma} = P_{\gamma}^{-1} O_{\gamma} \) accomplishes the permutation of the spin-coordinates alone, due to  

\[ Q_{\gamma} \phi(\boldsymbol{r}_1, \dots \boldsymbol{r}_n; s_{\alpha_1}, \dots s_{\alpha_n}) = \phi(\boldsymbol{r}_1, \dots \boldsymbol{r}_n; s_1, \dots s_n). \]  
(460)  

Like the previously considered rotation operator \( O_{\mathcal{R}} \), the permutation operator \( O_{\gamma} \) could be taken to be an orthogonal operator that leaves the ‘inner product’ of two hyperfunctions invariant (with \( \tilde{\psi} \) Hermitean conjugate of \( \psi \)), i.e.,  

\[ \int O_{\gamma} \phi \cdot \widetilde{O_{\gamma} \psi} = \int \phi \tilde{\psi}, \]  
(461)  

where the integration extends over the entire space of all coordinates and is summed over all \( 2^n \) values of \( s_1, \dots s_n \).  

Armed with these tools, the authors went on to treat the *Aufbauprinzip* in quantum mechanics. They considered the full Hamiltonian of an atom to consist of two parts,  

\[ H = H_1 + H_2, \]  
(462)  

such that \( H_1 \) describes the centre-of-mass motion of the electrons plus the electromagnetic interaction with this motion, and \( H_2 \) accounts for the rest, involving in particular the magnetic moments of the electrons. The Hamiltonian \( H_1 \) admits invariance with respect to the permutation operators \( O_{\gamma} \) and \( P_{\gamma} \) (and \( Q_{\gamma} = P_{\gamma}^{-1} O_{\gamma} \)); hence, switching on \( H_2 \) would in general cause a splitting of the terms from \( H_1 \). Further, the Pauli principle requires the restriction to ‘antisymmetric’ hyperfunctions, or more accurately,  

\[ O_{\gamma} \phi = \pm \phi, \]  
(463)  

where the plus sign applies for even and the minus sign for odd permutations. The proper execution of the symmetry operations with the known *Ansätze* for the Hamiltonian (462) indeed allowed von Neumann and Wigner to derive the observed term structure of the atoms in the periodic system of elements, including their multiplet structure and the intensity and selection rules for the spectral lines emitted and absorbed; especially, they proved Laporte’s rule and other empirical regularities, e.g., for the Stark effect (von Neumann and Wigner, *loc. cit.*, §2–§13, pp. 75–93).  

In Part III, the ambitious programme of the Hungarian duo was completed (von Neumann and Wigner, 1928c). There, the authors derived the prequantum-mechanical rules for small splittings of the different lines in a multiplet—such as

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0531 -->

III.4 Group Theory and Quantum Mechanics

499

the famous $g$-formula of Landé and parts of the Burger–Dorgelo sum rules, as well as the so-called interval rules.$^{592}$

All of the results of Wigner (and his collaborator von Neumann) were cited and presented in *Gruppentheorie und Quantenmechanik* (Weyl, 1928b, footnote 1, p. 278). As we have mentioned, Weyl claimed that he had arrived independently at the same conclusions. For example, Landé’s formula for the gyromagnetic factor $g$ in a complex multiplet (see Volume 1, Part 2, p. 483),

$$
g = 1 + \frac{j(j+1) - l(l+1) + s(s+1)}{2j(j+1)} \qquad (464)
$$

followed immediately from the group-theoretical multiplication formula

$$
\mathfrak{D}_s \times \mathfrak{D}_l = \sum_{j=|l-s|}^{l+s} \mathfrak{D}_j, \qquad (465)
$$

with $\mathfrak{D}_s$, $\mathfrak{D}_l$, and $\mathfrak{D}_j$ denoting the rotation groups associated with spin, orbital, and total angular momenta, and $s$, $l$, and $j$ the degrees of their representation (Weyl, *loc. cit.*, pp. 161–170, especially, p. 167). No doubt, the group-theoretical method had achieved a great triumph in explaining, at least qualitatively and without any calculation of the specific dynamics of the problem, the structure of atomic energy states and the spectra arising from them. It even provided practical hints to simplify the actual term evaluations by the appropriate perturbation schemes. Therefore, it is not surprising that the quantum physicists expected many further fruitful applications, in the first place, to the so far underdeveloped theory of molecules: one hoped, in particular, to derive qualitatively their term structure and maybe come to grips with a problem that was still not solved in principle: the nature of the chemical bond.

**(d) Group Theory for Molecules and John Slater’s Battle Against the ‘*Gruppenpest*’ (1927–1929)**

On 27 May 1927, Friedrich Hund of Göttingen submitted a manuscript, entitled ‘*Symmetriecharaktere von Termen bei Systemen mit gleichen Partikeln in der Quantenmechanik*’ (‘Symmetry Characters of Terms in Quantum-Mechanical Systems Consisting of Identical Particles’), to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Hund, 1927d). He had become involved in the topic when he investigated the wave-mechanical theory of molecular spectra during his visit to Copenhagen. ‘The symmetry possi-

---

Now, these rules were obtained without such additional assumptions, by starting from the $n$-electron problem of an atom.

bilities for few particles are the same as for a tetrahedron (intersection of the four-dimensional coordinate system with the [plane] $x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + x_4 = const.$),' he wrote in his scientific diary on 12 February 1927, and added: 'They can be represented by 1; $(x_1 - x_2)$; $(x_1 - x_2)(x_3 - x_4)$; $(x_1 - x_2)(x_2 - x_3)(x_3 - x_1)$ and $\prod(x_\alpha - x_\beta)$.'<sup>593</sup> Hund was familiar with the previous symmetry considerations of Heisenberg (1927a) and Wigner (1927a), which made use of the standard techniques of the mathematical group theory, but he proposed a different approach, namely, 'to connect the non-combining [term]-systems directly, *without the assumption of group-theoretical laws*, with the *symmetry of the eigenfunctions* [in the coordinates] *of the identical particles* and to take into account *arbitrary couplings between the particles*' (Hund, 1927d, pp. 788–789). To achieve his goal, he represented the noncombining term system by what he called 'symmetry character' and spoke about antisymmetric characters $A$ and symmetric characters $B$.<sup>594</sup> He introduced, in particular, 'normal forms' of a given character $A$ or $B$, because every arbitrary wave function can be obtained from a normal form by a permutation of the particles involved.<sup>595</sup> Now in the important physical situation determined by Pauli's exclusion principle, Hund observed that 'the antisymmetric normal forms of symmetry characters admit in simple cases an intuitive (*anschauliche*) interpretation,' notably:

> In the case of three particles, the eigenfunctions $\Psi$ are spatial functions in the three-dimensional space; the coordinates of the three particles [for each particle only one position variable is taken] we consider as coordinates $(x_1\ x_2\ x_3)$ of a Cartesian space. Then the symmetry properties of the function $\Psi$ can be characterized by the position of the planes $\Psi = 0$, i.e., by the nodes of the associated oscillation. $\Psi(\{1,2,3\})$ has at least three nodal planes, namely the planes $x_1 = x_2$, $x_2 = x_3$ and $x_3 = x_1$; $\Psi(\{1,2\},3)$ has at least one nodal plane $x_1 = x_3$, while $\Psi(\overline{1,2},3)$ needs to have no such plane. [Here the curly brackets denote antisymmetry with respect to permutation of the numbers in the bracket, and the bar denotes symmetry.] (Hund, 1927d, p. 792)

The intuitive content of the different characters could be shown by a regular triangle, in which the characteristic nodes are represented by inner lines and shaded sections. Similarly, Hund succeeded in visualizing the antisymmetric characters in the case of four identical particles with the help of regular cubes. (Hund, *loc. cit.*, p. 793)
Hund now indicated how his symmetry characters should be applied to obtain the structure of terms of atomic and molecular systems. In doing so, he proved the main theorem (of empirical spectroscopy): 'Two terms with different symmetry

III.4 Group Theory and Quantum Mechanics 501

characters do not combine.' (Hund, *loc. cit.*, p. 796) Altogether, he succeeded in reproducing the results derived earlier by Wigner with the standard methods of group theory. However, he also went beyond Wigner by applying his peculiar symmetry scheme to a new, physically important situation, when he noted:

> Frequently the eigenfunctions of quantum-mechanical systems can be written, in an approximation, as products (or linear combinations of those) eigenfunctions of simplified problems having a definite symmetry character. Thus the eigenfunctions of a molecule may be expressed in the first approximation as products of eigenfunctions of a multiple-centre problem of electrons, of an oscillating system of nuclei, and of a rigid body (gyroscope). Similarly, the eigenfunctions of an atom, or of the electron-part of a molecule, can be written as the products of the eigenfunctions of the centre-of-mass motion of the electrons and eigenfunctions of the interaction of their magnetic momenta. (Hund, *loc. cit.*, pp. 798–799)

Though the products of eigenfunctions in general—because of possible degeneracy not arising from the identity of particles (the 'accidental degeneracy' of Wigner)—do not exhibit a definite symmetry character, they can be represented by a function or a linear combination of functions having a definite character and 'the eigenfunctions derived from higher approximations are continuously connected with these functions of a definite character' (Hund, *loc. cit.*, p. 799). Hund finally obtained an important theorem that was applicable when an eigenfunction $\Psi$ of a given character was multiplied by a factor having a likewise definite character, especially:

> (i) If an eigenfunction $\Psi$ becomes symmetric by adding an eigenfunction $\psi$ as a factor and [taking] a linear combination, then $\Psi$ and $\psi$ possess the same symmetry character.
> (ii) If an eigenfunction $\Psi$ becomes antisymmetric by adding an eigenfunction $\psi$ as a factor and [taking] a linear combination, $\Psi$ and $\psi$ possess reciprocal symmetrical characters. (Hund, *loc. cit.*)

Hund completed his paper on symmetry with a discussion of the term system of atoms (obtaining an explanation of the periodic system of elements). In the following paper, actually, the third communication of the series on 'the interpretation of molecular spectra,' he applied the scheme to determine the symmetry characters of oscillation—and rotation terms of many-atom molecules; he was thus able to account for several recent experimental findings with these complex systems (Hund, 1927e).<sup>596</sup>

In 1927, Hund (in Copenhagen and Göttingen) was not alone in pioneering the quantum-mechanical theory of molecules. In particular, he received competition from Zurich, where Walter Heitler and Fritz London began to investigate the problem of forces acting between two neutral atoms and, by making use of Heisenberg's exchange integral, provided an explanation of the 'homopolar (*homö*-'

---

The 'similar lines' would not, however, include the special method that he pursued in his next paper (Heitler, 1927), because it 'initiates the group-theoretical approach to quantum chemistry,' but:

> London did not join me in that; he thought it was too complicated. Wigner's paper had appeared by that time, and I saw immediately that it could be useful for further development of the theory of chemical bonds, but London wanted to go on in his more intuitive way. . . .
> So I started to study group theory. I first read the book of [Andreas] Speiser (1923), a very nice classical book on group theory, and especially on the permutation group. Later on, I read papers by Schur and other people. The very nice thing about this was that the mathematicians had prepared group theory so well for the use of the physicists without knowing it that sometimes I could just copy, word for word, pages from a group-theory paper and use them for my purposes. (Heitler, AHQP Interview, p. 19)

Heitler's paper, which he submitted in October 1927 still from Zurich, dealt with the question of the 'perturbation energy and exchange in a many-body system'—as the title read in English translation. That is, Heitler wished to answer in it the quite general question concerning the value of the exchange energy in atomic systems.<sup>598</sup>

In Part I, Heitler recapitulated the necessary results of the theory of permutation groups; then he added a section summarizing several theorems about the character of a group element that helped in determining the energy of the atomic systems. For example, he presented the following theorem: if an eigenfunction of an *n*-electron system is invariant with respect to all permutations of a given class (to a class of permutation group belong all elements commuting with a definite element $S$), then the matrix $(b_{ik}^{P})$ of the irreducible representation of $P$ must be the unit matrix (Heitler, 1927, p. 56). Heitler then immediately derived the result that the centre-of-mass value of the energy $E^{\sigma}$ of the term system (associated with the *n*-electron system) can be obtained from the simple equation

$$E^{\sigma} = \sum_{s} \chi^{\sigma}_{P} J_{P}, \tag{466}$$

with $\chi^{\sigma}_{P}$ denoting group characters [i.e., the trace of the transformation matrix

$$J_{P} = \int H \psi_{E} \psi_{P} d\tau. \tag{467}$$

In Eq. (467), $\psi_E$ indicates the 'primitive' product eigenfunction $\alpha(1)\beta(2) \dots \zeta(n)$, and $\psi_P$ indicates the one obtained from it by the permutation $P$. Now, to derive the values for the characters of a given term system, Heitler made use of Hund's 'symmetry characters': these then easily allowed him to fix the permutation classes and the degree of degeneracy.

In Part II of the paper, Heitler discussed a number of physical consequences (Heitler, *loc. cit.*, §6–§9, pp. 63–72). For instance, he found that the perturbation created by the integral (467) may lead to a reduction of the number of terms in a given term system (Heitler, *loc. cit.*, p. 66; he called it 'Ausartung').<sup>599</sup> The most important result for spectroscopy—and chemistry—could be formulated in the sentence: '*By the interaction* [of a system $A$] *with the closed shells* [of a system $B$] *no new splitting of the terms occurs*.' This conclusion is 'solely responsible for the existence of a periodic system with *homologous sequences*, in which the elements exhibit *homologous spectroscopic* and *chemical* properties' (Heitler *loc. cit.*, p. 70). The interaction with closed shells just created a negative shift of the terms (Heitler, *loc. cit.*, p. 72).

Heitler continued to investigate the 'group theory of the covalent bond' in a second paper that he completed on 25 January of the following year (Heitler, 1928), and he managed to impart his enthusiasm even to the initially hesitant Fritz London.<sup>600</sup> Three years later, Heitler wrote a final paper on this topic together with Yurii Borisovich (George) Rumer, in which the authors suppressed most of the group-theoretical formalism in favour of a different method, that of Slater's determinants (Heitler and Rumer, 1931). When looking back, Heitler remarked:

> This subject [i.e., group theory] had a great fascination for me. What was unfortunate [was] that it became rather complicated, and I did not see the simplification which was really possible. This simplification was brought out by a paper of Slater. (Heitler, AHQP Interview, 18 March 1963, p. 19)

504 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

> The theory of complex spectra is treated in this paper by the method of wave mechanics. The results of the calculation may be divided into two parts: first, the classification of terms into multiplets; second, the energy values of these multiplets. The first part contains no new results of physical interest, for it leads precisely to Hund's scheme of classification, and uses almost the identical steps that Hund [1927b] uses. Its value lies in the fact that this well-known scheme is shown in an elementary way to follow directly from wave mechanics. The second part, however, is almost entirely new, and leads to definite formulas for the intervals between the different multiplets which could previously be considered only very roughly from an empirical rule of Hund, which proves to have no general significance. These calculations, of course, give the intervals in terms of certain integrals, which we do not calculate but merely estimate well enough to permit some comparison with experiment. The agreement is in general fairly good. A third part would also be included, dealing with the intervals within multiplets, produced by the magnetic interaction, were it not that Goudsmit (1928) had already answered the question by a method closely analogous to that used here. (Slater, 1929b, pp. 1292–1293)

The above declaration by Slater, then an associate professor at Harvard, sounded quite ambitious: he promised to provide a more or less complete wave-mechanical description of many-electron systems, for which the previous work of Heisenberg, Wigner, and Hund had just given the first steps. Moreover, Slater announced right from the beginning that he had no part in the main trend followed at that time by so many quantum theoreticians, when he emphasized:

> It will be noted that the objects of the present paper resemble closely those aimed by Heisenberg, Wigner, Hund, Weyl and others [here he cited in particular Heisenberg, 1927a; Wigner, 1927a and b; Hund, 1927d; Heitler, 1928; and Weyl, 1928b], who employ the methods of group theory. That method is not used at all in the present calculation, and, in contrast, no mathematics other than the simplest is required, until one actually comes to the computation of integrals. (Slater, *loc. cit.*, p. 1294)

Apparently, Slater was perfectly acquainted with the competing European enterprises, but found a clever device to avoid becoming involved in group theory.

After his return from Europe in 1924 (where he had spent a year on a Harvard Traveling Fellowship at Cambridge and Copenhagen), Slater had joined the faculty of Harvard University, first as an instructor and, from 1926 onward, as an associate professor.<sup>601</sup> His scientific investigations in those years dealt initially with the application of a prequantum-mechanical dispersion approach to explain optical phenomena and spectra; later, he showed considerable interest in the use of electron spin in atomic theory. Then, the year 1926 had brought 'Schrödinger's monumental papers,' and he recalled:

> [Edwin] Kemble and I and the students in our seminar had been barely able to keep up with the progress of that year. It is rarely that a subject that seemed almost completely mysterious at the beginning of a year is all cleared up by the end. Hund went

---

<sup>601</sup> For an account of Slater's European stay, see Volume 1, Part 2, pp. 541–553.

on to write a book on line spectra of the elements, which did not appear until 1927, after Schrödinger’s work, but which represented work done almost entirely before wave mechanics. I wrote a very prosaic paper on the dynamics of the coupling of the electrons in the atom, the sort of thing I had been using in lecture notes for the students in the seminar. But I was glad, later in 1929, that I had studied complex spectra as soon and as thoroughly as I had, for it was in 1929 that I worked on the determinantal method for incorporating these results into wave mechanics. . . I found much of my work already done for me in my seminar notes of 1925 [or 1926]. (Slater, 1975, p. 30)

Slater indeed published a paper on ‘A Dynamical Model for Complex Atoms’ in 1926; it was based on the ideas of Hund and others and involved the electron-spin hypothesis, but the dynamical model adopted was basically a classical one (Slater, 1926). Only slowly did he adapt himself to the new quantum mechanics and began to work with it; thus, he submitted in May 1928 the results of an investigation on the structure of atoms (Slater, 1928a), in which he made use of an approximation method due to Douglas Rayner Hartree from Cambridge, the method of the ‘self-consistent field’ (Hartree, 1927a).<sup>602</sup> The self-consistent field approximation consisted of the following procedure: (1) a separate wave function $\psi$ is taken for each electron of an atom; (2) the individual electron of charge distribution proportional to $\psi\psi^*$, averaged over different directions, yields a spherical distribution of density; (3) these distributions from all electrons, but one, are added to obtain the electric potential (‘mean field’) for the wave function of the remaining electron; and (4) the energy term of the electron considered is finally obtained by solving the corresponding Schrödinger equation.<sup>603</sup> Slater was now especially concerned about the accuracy of Hartree’s solution; thus, he first took the entire wave function of the $n$-particle system to be given by the product of Hartree’s functions for the individual electrons and declared this to be ‘a good approximation to the real solution,’ because the nondiagonal terms in the energy matrix could be shown to be small in general. To a lesser accuracy than the wave function of a neutral atom, he obtained that of an ion by leaving one electron function out of the product, and then he derived by a proper perturbation method the ionization potential in reasonable agreement with several observations.<sup>604</sup>

In view of the later development, it may perhaps be surprising that Slater referred in 1928a (p. 344) also to ‘the group theory developed by Wigner, Heitler

<sup>603</sup> Hartree achieved the consistency of his method by applying an iterative method: he started from an initial field, then he corrected it for each core electron; as a third step, he solved the wave equation for core electrons and obtained the new charge distribution, which yielded the final field. The self- consistency then required the initial field to be the same as the final field (Hartree, 1927b).

and others,’ and even made some use of it when completing his calculations of the perturbation energy (arising from the exchange of two electrons). By June 1929, he had changed his originally favourable opinion of group theory completely, as he recalled later:

    It was at this point [i.e., the consideration of the situation of two electrons] that Wigner, Hund and Weyl entered the picture with their ‘‘Gruppenpest’’: the pest of the group theory, as certain disgruntled individuals who had never studied group theory in school described it. The mathematicians have made a great study of what is called the symmetric group, or the permutation group. . . . The authors of the ‘‘Gruppenpest’’ wrote papers which were incomprehensible to those like me who had not studied group theory, in which they applied these theoretical results to the study of the many-electron problem. The practical consequences appeared to be negligible but everyone felt that to be in the mainstream of quantum mechanics, one had to learn about it. . . . It was a frustrating experience, worthy of the name of a pest. (Slater, 1975, p. 60)

Because Slater developed ‘a feeling of outrage at the turn which the subject had taken,’ he thought about a way out, as he recalled in his reminiscences:

    The simple process by which Heisenberg and Dirac had replaced the exclusion principle by the statement that the wave function had to be antisymmetric in the coordinates of the electron was an obvious step in the right direction, and Heisenberg had shown that it led to an understanding of Hund’s rule. Its only lack was that it dealt with only three of the four quantum numbers of an electron, namely $n$, $l$, and $m_l$ [i.e., principal, orbital, and projection of the orbital quantum numbers] but disregarded the fourth [namely, the projection of the electron spin]. Was it not possible, I asked, to generalize this antisymmetry to a case in which the fourth quantum number $m_s$ was included as well, and to get the complete statement of the exclusion principle in this simple form? When I started work in December 1928, to try to answer this question, the first thing I did was to find how to incorporate the spin and its quantum number into the wave function. (Slater, *loc. cit.*, p. 61)

That is, the main innovation in which Slater deviated from earlier treatments (especially those of Dirac and Heisenberg) consisted in taking into account the spin function in the determinantal expression that represented the totally antisymmetric wave function of the $N$-particle system

$$
u = \det \begin{vmatrix}
u_1(1) & u_1(2) & \cdots & u_1(N) \\
u_2(1) & u_2(2) & \cdots & u_2(N) \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
u_N(1) & u_N(2) & \cdots & u_N(N)
\end{vmatrix},
\tag{468}
$$

where $u(i)$ denotes the wave function of the $i$-th electron, i.e.,

$$
u(i) = u(n_i|x_i),
\tag{469}
$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0539 -->

having the spatial coordinates $x_i$ and the quantum number quadruple $n_i$ (actually the set of four quantum numbers $n_i, l_i, m_{l_i}$, and $m_{s_i}$). Slater then noted ‘that this is the only antisymmetric combination of these [individual electron] functions,’ and ‘it leads at once to the familiar interpretation of the exclusion principle . . . thus there is no solution corresponding to the case where two electrons have the same set of quantum numbers’ (Slater, 1929b, p. 1300).<sup>605</sup>

The wave function $u$, Eq. (468), with the $u(n_i|x_i)$ taken as Hartree’s one-electron solution, constitutes an approximate solution of the Schrödinger equation for the $n$-electron atom (with the Hamiltonian $H_0$). The next step was to introduce the interaction between the various angular momenta of the different electrons as a perturbation (interaction term $H_1$) and to calculate a perturbed wave function without destroying the property of antisymmetry. The energy matrix $H_0 + H_1$ yields after diagonalization a good approximation for the energy values of the problem, the remaining errors having the order of square of the ratio of the non-diagonal to diagonal terms. Finally, the full energy operator must be used—which involves the electric interactions between electrons and the nucleus, and between electrons and electrons, respectively (replacing the interaction between electrons and the fictitious central field)—yielding matrix elements with the previously obtained wave functions (from the Hamiltonian $H_0 + H_1$). The diagonalization of the new matrix then leads to the actual energy values in fair agreement with the empirical term values (provided a criterion for the accuracy of the solution is satisfied, which is the case if a number of coinciding terms do not exist). ‘Thus the problem of degeneracy is the essential part of the calculation for complex spectra,’ Slater concluded (*loc. cit.*, p. 1301). He also discovered, however, ‘a feature which greatly simplifies the calculation,’ that is, that the energy matrix possesses—in the approximation in which the magnetic energy can be neglected—no components for which the sums $\Sigma m_l$ and $\Sigma m_s$ change. Thus, he stated his procedure in the following sentences:

    First we show, by fundamental methods, that the total angular momentum matrix can have components only between states of the same energy. Since we can show that the angular momentum matrix is diagonal, this proves that there must be at least several states of each energy, in order that the angular momentum can have components between them. This breaks up the terms associated with a given set of *n*’s and *l*’s into sets each of the same energy. Next we show that each of these sets is just the sort we need for a multiplet. We do this by detailed consideration of the angular momentum matrix; the essential point being that the entire matrix can be determined uniquely from certain commutation relations between the $x$, $y$, $z$ components of the angular momentum vector, and that these relations are just the same for the whole atom as for a singular momentum vector, so that we must have just the same matrix. We then have the complete proof that the wave functions of the atom really break up into sets each having all the properties of a multiplet; the $M_L - M_S$ diagram of such a

<sup>605</sup> For the detailed calculation of the spin-independent Hamiltonian, Slater introduced the particular wave function $u(nlm_l|xyz)u(m_s|m_s) = u(nlm_l|xyz)\delta(m_s|m_s)$.

multiplet is just as we assumed in the first section [of the paper]; and the result is that the same method of finding what multiplets arise from any configuration of electrons, is precisely the method of Hund. (Slater, *loc. cit.*, pp. 1303–1304)

From detailed theoretical computations of the energy in Part 2 of his paper, Slater derived a great number of results, among them: (1) ‘As far as multiplet separations are concerned, closed shells exert no influences at all; they affect only the position of the whole set of multiplet terms’ (Slater, *loc. cit.*, p. 1315)—this result agreed with what Heitler had obtained nearly two years earlier from group-theoretical methods. (2) Exceptions to Hund’s rule exist in determining the order of terms (Slater, *loc. cit.*, p. 1319).

Even more deeply than by the practical results in determining the energy states of complex many-electron atoms, Slater impressed his colleagues by the method of his new approach. He recalled proudly the reactions 46 years later:

    As soon as this paper became known, it was obvious that a great many other physicists were disgusted as I had been with the group-theoretical approach to the problem. As I heard later, there were remarks made such as ‘‘Slater has slain the ‘Gruppenpest.’’’ I believe that no other piece of work I had done was so universally popular. (Slater, 1975, p. 62)

Already, the first person who heard about it (namely, Friedrich Hund when lecturing early in 1929 at Harvard) ‘was much pleased about it,’ Slater claimed, and so were Douglas Hartree, whom he met on his following European trip (on a Guggenheim Fellowship in summer 1929) in Zurich, or Felix Bloch in Leipzig, where he stayed for a longer period in fall. Again he recalled:

    When I arrived in Leipzig at the end of September 1929, Heisenberg as well as Hund proved to be much interested in the new methods, which in a very real sense were extensions of the work they had done several years earlier. I worked on applications of the method there . . . Late in November [on a visit of the Leipzig group to Berlin] I had my first chance to meet Wigner. . . . I found that he had been studying my paper with much interest, that he was entirely in sympathy with it, and that in fact he had thought of doing the same thing himself, but not got around to it. (Slater, *loc. cit.*, pp. 62–63)

Only Pauli, who came to attend a seminar in Leipzig, which Slater presented shortly before leaving, ‘lived up to his usual reputation, and broke in with remarks to the effect that ‘‘he couldn’t understand a word of it,’’’—so Slater remembered, but also: ‘Heisenberg came to my aid and helped explain things, and before we were through everyone was satisfied with the state of the theory.’ (Slater, *loc. cit.*, p. 63)<sup>606</sup> Happy with this success, Slater returned home, where he soon received Karl Compton’s invitation to head the physics department at MIT.

<sup>606</sup> According to Slater’s recollection, besides the people already mentioned, Fritz London, Rudolf Peierls, and Edward Teller were also assembled in Leipzig.

# III.4 Group Theory and Quantum Mechanics
**509**

**(e) The Group Theorists Fight Back: Further Applications and Extensions**

The prestigious (Geiger–Scheel) *Handbuch der Physik*, in its Volume 3 on 'Mathematische Hilfsmittel der Physik' ('Mathematical Aids for Physics'), contained a short section on group theory, which provided the principal definitions and concepts of the subject and referred mainly to the special cases of the permutation groups and groups of transformations in space (Duschek, 1928, pp. 69–80). This treatment illustrated the restricted use of the mathematical theory of groups in physics *before* the developments in modern atomic physics, described above, occurred. Indeed, quantum mechanics changed its outlook completely, as Eugene Wigner sketched in a programmatic essay, entitled 'Über die Erhaltungssätze in der Quantenmechanik' ('On the Conservation Laws in Quantum Mechanics'), which Max Born presented to the Göttingen Academy on 10 February 1928 (Wigner, 1928). In this paper, Wigner described the relation between the unitary operators $O$, which commute with the energy operator $H$, and the conservation laws for physical quantities. The operators $O$, having the property that $O\psi$ is an eigenfunction with the same eigenvalue $\varepsilon$ as $\psi$, or

$$H(O\psi) = \varepsilon\psi \quad \text{if} \quad H\psi = \varepsilon\psi, \tag{470}$$

allow in special cases the following visualizable (*anschauliche*) interpretation:

(1) The orthogonal space-translation operator is connected with the centre-of-mass theorem (or momentum conservation).
(2) The orthogonal rotation operation is connected with angular-momentum conservation.

Only the space-reflection operator (connected with the concept of parity), which can also be introduced here, does not seem to play a role in classical physics and therefore lacks proper visualization. In general, however, the theory of group representations can be closely tied to the known conservation laws, and they are 'obtained from unitary transformations leaving the energy operator invariant' (Wigner, 1928, p. 381).

The treatment of the spectral terms of atoms and molecules by Wigner, von Neumann, Weyl, Heitler, and Hund, as described above, revealed an overwhelming wealth of information that could be derived from very few conservation laws. The antigroup-theoretical movement, started by Slater in 1929, would not really affect the effectiveness of the mathematical theory. Of course, even in Middle Europe, where the use of group theory in quantum mechanics had begun, 'a great reluctance among physicists toward accepting group-theoretical arguments and the group-theoretical point of view' existed, recalled Wigner almost a quarter century later.$^{607}$ At the same time, he remembered also a noteworthy exception:

$^{607}$ See the preface to the English translation of his book on the subject (Wigner, 1959, p. v).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0542 -->

# Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics
**510**

Of the older generation it was probably Max von Laue who first recognized the significance of group theory as the natural tool with which to obtain a first orientation in problems of quantum mechanics. Von Laue’s encouragement of both publisher and author contributed significantly to bringing this book into existence. I like to recall his question as to which results of the present book I considered most important. My answer was that the explanation of Laporte’s rule ([by] the concept of parity) and the quantum theory of the vector addition model appeared to me most significant. Since that time, I have come to agree with his answer that the recognition that almost all rules of spectroscopy follow from the symmetry of the problem is the most remarkable result. (Wigner, 1959, p. V)

In the United States, Carl Eckart ‘dared’ to oppose John Slater and published a very detailed article on ‘The Application of the Group Theory to the Quantum Dynamics of Monatomic Systems’ in one of the first issues of the new *Physical Review Supplement* or *Reviews of Modern Physics* (Eckart, 1930). ‘This report is intended to furnish an account of so much of the theory of groups as has been found useful in the solution of the dynamical problems,’ Eckart stated cautiously in the short introduction (Eckart, *loc. cit.*, p. 306). In particular, he avoided all more mathematical details, except for what could be applied specifically to the quantum-mechanical problems, such as ‘[Issai] Schur’s lemma,’ and he restricted himself to demonstrating the usefulness of the group-theoretical method in the theory of complex spectra. Thus, he included the essential results of Hermann Weyl, Eugene Wigner, and John von Neumann, but not those of the molecular theory pioneers Friedrich Hund and Walter Heitler. It is of interest to note that, in dealing with the $n$-electron problem, Eckart did not refer to Slater’s antigroup theory paper, but rather quoted Paul Dirac’s note on the ‘Quantum Mechanics of Many-Electron Systems’ (Dirac, 1929b), which constituted a precursor of the determinant method as it demanded (as Slater pointed out himself) that the wave function $\psi$ ‘be antisymmetrical in the $x$’s and $\sigma$’s [denoting the space and spin coordinates] together’ (Dirac, 1929b, p. 723). After all, Dirac had confirmed that ‘group theory should form a part of quantum mechanics,’ and stated further:

> It should therefore be possible to translate the methods and results of group theory into the language of quantum mechanics and so obtain a treatment of the exchange phenomena which does not presuppose any knowledge of groups on the part of the reader. . . . The treatment of groups on the lines of quantum mechanics has the advantage that it often gives a simple physical meaning to an abstract theorem in the theory of groups, enabling one to remember the theorem more easily and perhaps suggesting a simpler way of proving it. A further advantage of the treatment of the exchange phenomena on these lines is that one can avoid doing more work in the theory of groups than is strictly necessary for the physical applications, which results in a considerable shortening in the method. (Dirac, *loc. cit.*, p. 716)

In his review article, Eckart more or less followed Dirac’s arguments. Thus, he established, as a proper example for a result of group theory in quantum

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0543 -->

# III.4 Group Theory and Quantum Mechanics
**511**

mechanics, the so-called Wigner–Eckart theorem.$^{608}$ We know from Eq. (470) that, if $O$ is an element of the group $\mathcal{G}_H$ of the Hamiltonian operator $H$ (of an atomic system) and $u$ is an eigenvector of $H$, then also $Ou$ must be an eigenvector; as a necessary consequence, all eigenvectors of $\mathcal{G}_H$ have the same eigenvalue $\varepsilon$ and the term energy becomes degenerate. Applied to the theory of normal atomic multiplets, to each energy level of the spin-free equation there will be associated $(2l + 1)(2s + 1)$ eigenfunctions forming a single energy level; only when spin-interactions are turned on, would these levels split. This is the content of the Wigner–Eckart theorem.

The ‘further advantage’ mentioned by Dirac, namely, to ‘avoid more work in group theory than is strictly necessary,’ was exactly followed in Slater’s determinantal method. Even a fervent advocate of the group-theoretical formalism, such as Eugene Wigner, appreciated the shortcut in work provided by it and described it in some detail in Chapter XXIV of his *Gruppentheorie und ihre Anwendung auf die Quantenmechanik der Atomspektren* (1931):

> The significant feature of the Slater method is that it *makes it possible to avoid entirely the consideration of symmetry of the Schrödinger equation under permutation of the Cartesian coordinates alone*, by considering instead the invariance and rotations $\mathbf{Q}_R$ of the spin coordinates. . . . Although there must exist situations in which more extensive conclusions can be obtained by considering the permutation $\mathbf{P}_P$ of the Cartesian coordinates than by means of $\mathbf{Q}_R$ alone, it is surprising to what extent the group of $\mathbf{Q}_R$ can be used to derive the results which follow, more directly from the invariance under the group $\mathbf{P}_P$. (Wigner, 1931, p. 316; English translation, 1959, p. 317)

Similarly, however, he clearly addressed the limitations of the shortcut, when he continued:

> An essential requirement for the applicability of Slater’s method is that the internal coordinates of the particle considered can assume only two values. If one were dealing with particles which had three possible orientations. . . , the conclusions which one could derive in such a theory from the rotational invariance (invariance with respect to $\mathbf{Q}_R$) would be more restricted than the consequences of the invariance with respect to $\mathbf{P}_P$. In fact, in this case several levels of the Schrödinger equation coincide, and this coincidence could not be explained by consideration of the $\mathbf{Q}_R$ alone. It would then be necessary either to introduce further operators, thereby losing the simplicity of the theory, or to use the symmetry under the operator $\mathbf{P}_P$. (Wigner, *loc. cit.*, English translation, pp. 317–318)

In sum, Wigner rather explicitly defended the general usefulness of the group-theoretical method, which he presented in all necessary detail to ‘a wider public’ (than the specialized mathematicians) in his book, in the preface to which, he wrote:

$^{608}$ Eckart sharpened (1930, pp. 368–369) a result of Wigner (1928).

# Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics
**512**

One has often raised the objection against the group-theoretical treatment of the Schrödinger equation that it is “not physical.” However, it seems to me that the conscious use of elementary symmetry properties must correspond to the physical situation more than the more computational treatment. The objection mentioned may be reduced to the fact that group theory possesses an essentially different character from those parts of mathematics with which the physicist is mainly familiar, hence it requires certainly some time before one gets on friendly terms with it. The theory notably consists of a great number of tiny conclusions, of which each single one may be trivial, but their totality cannot be easily overseen. (Wigner, *loc. cit.*, p. V)

Wigner’s book did not present ‘the physically especially important investigations of Hund, London and Heitler on molecules,’ because he rather preferred ‘to treat one topic [of physics, namely the theory of atoms] as completely as possible than to yield to the appealing idea of listing the most beautiful results of all topics’ (Wigner, *loc. cit.*, p. VI). He could also not include the results from the work of another physicist, Hendrik B. G. Casimir of Leyden, because of two reasons: first, it was connected with the theory of molecules, and second, it was contained in a doctoral thesis published only in November 1931.

Hendrik Casimir, a very talented student of Paul Ehrenfest, became involved very early in studying group theory, learning it especially from Weyl’s book (1928b).$^{609}$ After Samuel Goudsmit and George Uhlenbeck left Leyden for the University of Michigan at Ann Arbor, Casimir advanced to become the closest collaborator of Ehrenfest, who recommended him early in 1929 to Niels Bohr.$^{610}$

$^{609}$ As a student, Casimir spent two months in summer 1928 in Göttingen to brush up on his German and met there Eugene Wigner, Bartel Van der Waerden, and Walter Heitler (Casimir, 1982, p. 699). For more details of his life, see Casimir, 1983, and von Meyenn, 1989; also, Casimir to Rechenberg, 18 February 1998. (We are grateful to Professor Casimir for numerous private communications.)
Casimir was born on 15 July 1909, at The Hague, the son of a secondary school teacher (who, in 1918, became an extraordinary professor at the University of Leyden). In 1926, he enrolled at the University of Leyden to study physics. He obtained the award of a fellowship to work with Niels Bohr in Copenhagen from 1929 to 1931, but in summer 1930, he accompanied Ehrenfest to go to the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor. In November 1931, he completed his doctoral dissertation at Leyden, entitled ‘Rotation of a Rigid Body in Quantum Mechanics’; then he became Ehrenfest’s assistant, but already in summer 1932 (from June to August) he stayed for a couple of months with Lise Meitner in Berlin to replace her absent theoretical assistant, Max Dellbrück, at the *Kaiser Wilhelm Institut für Chemie*, and then he accepted Wolfgang Pauli’s offer to become his assistant at the ETH in Zurich. In September 1933, he was called back to Leyden, but he arrived too late—only after the death of Ehrenfest, who had committed suicide. Casimir then became assistant to Ehrenfest’s successor Hendrik Kramers (who came to Leyden from Utrecht in fall 1934). After he had become interested in low-temperature physics, Casimir was hired in 1936 as senior assistant at the Kamerlingh Onnes Laboratory in Leyden. In 1939, he was promoted to an extraordinary (i.e., associate) professorship (succeeding Gill Holst) at the university, but in 1942, he left Leyden to join the Philips Company in Eindhoven as scientific director.
$^{610}$ Ehrenfest personally introduced Casimir to Bohr in Copenhagen at the April 1929 meeting at Bohr’s Institute on relativistic quantum mechanics and nuclear physics, where he left a very favourable impression (see von Meyenn, 1989, pp. 101–103). Goudsmit, who came for a visit to Europe in 1929, wrote to America: ‘At Leyden we have a very young, clever boy, 19 years [old]; he knows all about quantum mechanics.’ (Goudsmit to Harrison Randall, 12 May 1929; in von Meyenn, 1989, pp. 103–104)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0545 -->

# III.4 Group Theory and Quantum Mechanics
## 513

From 1929 to 1931, Casimir spent several periods of stay in Copenhagen (especially from September to December 1929, from February to April and September to December 1930 and in March 1931), and there he hit upon the problem that became the subject of his doctoral dissertation. In a paper submitted in October 1929, Oskar Klein ‘reduced the problem of quantizing the asymmetric top to the simple algebra of momentum components developed by Dirac [1926b] as well as by Born, Heisenberg and Jordan [1926]’; that is, he solved the quantum-mechanical equations for the angular momentum components $M_x, M_y$, and $M_z$ having the usual commutation relations

$$i \frac{h}{2\pi} M_x = M_z M_y - M_y M_z \quad (471)$$

(*O.* Klein, 1929b). Now, Casimir worked out the intensity problem for both the symmetric and asymmetric spinning top by taking over the formulae given in Weyl’s book (1928b, pp. 159–160) for the representation of the angular momentum components in a paper dated November 1929 (Casimir, 1930).

More than a year later, Casimir selected the topic for his doctoral dissertation, and on 1 May 1931, he wrote from The Hague a long letter to Hermann Weyl dealing with an important mathematical conclusion:

> While studying the quantum-mechanical properties of the asymmetrical rotator ... I arrived at some “results” (?) concerning the representation of continuous groups. ... The matter is as follows:
> The matrix elements of the irreducible representations of the three-dimensional rotation group are eigenfunctions of the Schrödinger equation of the spherical rotator. This equation has the form

$$\left(\sum_i Q_i^2\right) \psi = \lambda \psi, \quad [(472)]$$

> in which $Q_i$, applied to some function of the Eulerian angles, indicates the change undergone by this function at an infinitesimal rotation about the $i$-axis. ... I tried to transfer this result to general groups. We have, for an arbitrary function of the parameter $f(t)$, which is subject to the $i$-th infinitesimal transformation,

$$f(t') f(t) = L_i f(t) = d_i^\nu(t) \partial_\nu f(t). \quad [(473)]$$

> For the representation we now have

$$L_i M_{nm}(t) = \sum_p (L_i)_{np} M_{pm}(t), \quad [(474)]$$

> in which [the matrix] $\|(L_i)_{np}\|$ denotes the representation of the $i$-th infinitesimal transformation. Now assume that a differential operator $\mathfrak{G}$ is given, which commutes with all $L_i$ and which has the form

$$h^{ik} L_i L_k \text{ (with } h^{ik} \text{ constant)}, \quad [(475)]$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0546 -->

## 514
# Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

then this would lead to a matrix, which commutes with all $\|L_i\|$ and which consequently would be proportional to the unit matrix. The matrix elements would therefore be eigenfunctions of this operator. Now $h^{ik} L_i L_k$ only commutes with all $L_i$, when $h^{ik}$ is connected in an invariant way with [coefficients] $c_{ik}^l$ [occurring in the momentum commutator $M_i M_k - M_k M_i = c_{ik}^l M_l$. For the case of semi-simple groups one may choose

$$\mathfrak{G} = g^{ik} L_i L_k, \quad [(476)]$$

in which $g_{ik}$ is the reversed form

$$g_{ik} = c_{im}^l c_{lk}^m. \quad [(477)]$$

Casimir then showed in his letter that every eigenfunction is a linear combination of the matrix elements, or

$$\psi_n(g^*) = \sum_l M_{nl}(g') \psi_l(g), \quad (478)$$

where $g, g'$, and $g^*(= g' \cdot g)$ denote elements of the group $\mathfrak{G}$. Then, he concluded:

> It now seems to me that these facts could perhaps be used to obtain a new proof for the completeness theorem (*Vollständigkeitstheorem*). However, I must confess that I do not know whether the completeness theorem for partial differential equations has been proved in its full generality. In the three-dimensional case the problem is facilitated by the fact that the equation can be separated in the Eulerian angles. It seems plausible to me to assume that the separation can be performed in general cases as well. (Casimir to Weyl, in von Meyenn, 1989, pp. 112–113, quoted here with some corrections)

Evidently, Weyl replied to Casimir’s question ‘whether the case is worth considering’ in the affirmative; hence, Casimir submitted his arguments quickly in a paper to the *Proceedings of the Amsterdam Academy* (Casimir, 1931a) and included them in Chapter IV of his doctoral thesis (Casimir, 1931b, Theorem III, p. 93). The main theorem thus proved stated: the operator $\mathfrak{G}$, Eq. ([476])—later called the ‘Casimir operator’ and denoted by $\mathfrak{C}$—is a multiple of the unit operator; it possesses a fixed value for each irreducible representation; in other words, its value can be used to characterize the irreducible representations of a given continuous group. At this point, we should add that some years later Casimir reworked his proof and thus removed the objections of algebra-minded mathematicians against Weyl’s treatment of group theory (Casimir and Van der Waerden, 1936). Wolfgang Pauli, who stimulated this return, recalled the reasons in a letter to Hermann Weyl (dated 1955) that he had attended the lectures of Emil Artin in Hamburg in the winter semester 1927/28 and:

> At the beginning of the lecture Artin said that he could not discuss the continuous groups, because no algebraic proof existed for the theorem of the complete re-

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0547 -->

# III.4 Group Theory and Quantum Mechanics
## 515

ducibility of the representations of semi-simple continuous groups. The only known proof, that of Weyl, unfortunately used integrals concerning the group of multiplicity. With these words Artin threw his well-known angry glances around his audience. (Pauli to Weyl, 1955, in von Meyenn, 1989, p. 114)

Although Pauli ‘was impressed by the fact that Artin, a representative of the algebraic school ... preferred the ascetic omission of an entire field of applications rather than include a method which he considered to be inadequate from his point of view,’ while he himself ‘did not think it was so bad with the difficulties raised here by the algebraic ladies and gentlemen’ (among whom he also counted Emmy Noether and Bartel Van der Waerden). In any case, when Casimir was his assistant in Zurich (in 1932/33), he [Pauli] ‘drew his attention to this problem, for the case of the three-dimensional rotation group’ and: ‘He [Casimir] quickly gave a simple, purely algebraic proof of the theorem’ and ‘sent it to Van der Waerden in Leipzig who could easily generalize it to arbitrary semi-simple groups’ (Pauli to Weyl, *loc. cit.*).

Thus, the work of the physicist Hendrik Casimir received a secure place in the rigorous mathematical literature on group theory. His collaborator Van der Waerden, on the other hand, had succeeded in entering the physical literature already earlier with a likewise strong contribution to relativistic quantum mechanics. Upon arrival in Göttingen in 1926, he had witnessed a good portion of the development of quantum mechanics even though he was under the influence of rigorous mathematicians, especially Emmy Noether’s; after obtaining his *Habilitation* in Göttingen (1927), he was called already in 1928 to a full professorship at the University of Groningen.$^{611}$ In July 1929, Richard Courant presented a paper of Van der Waerden to the Göttingen Academy; it was entitled ‘*Spinoranalyse*’ (‘Spinor Analysis’), and the author began his introduction with the following words:

> Let us call the new quantities, which occurred in the quantum mechanics of the spinning electron, besides vectors and tensors and which are transformed quite differently from tensors with respect to [transformations of] the Lorentz group, in short “spinors.” “Does there exist a spinor analysis that can be learned by physicists, as there is a tensor analysis, with the help of which one can first form all spinors and second all invariant equations containing spinors?” Mr. Ehrenfest asked me this question, and I shall give the following answer. (Van der Waerden, 1929, p. 100)

$^{611}$ Bartel Leendert Van der Waerden was born in Amsterdam on 2 February 1903, and pursued his education, including attending the university, in his hometown (doctorate in 1926). From 1927 on, he served as *Privatdozent* at Göttingen, but in 1928 he received two offers of chairs: first to the University of Rostock, and then on 6 May 1928, to the University of Groningen, which he accepted. He published a large number of important papers dealing with investigations in the fields of algebra, algebraic geometry, number theory, and topology. In particular, he contributed to the field of ‘*abzählende Geometrie*’ (‘enumerable geometry’), the development of which David Hilbert had demanded in Problem 15 of his Paris lecture of 1900. (See the letter of the *Philosophische Fakultät der Universität Leipzig* to the *Ministerium für Volksbildung zu Dresden*, dated 17 May 1930; *Universitätsarchiv Leipzig*.) In 1931, Van der Waerden went to Leipzig and stayed there until 1945; later on, he held professorships in Baltimore (1947), Amsterdam (1948–1951), and Zurich (after 1951). He died in Zurich on 16 November 1995.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0548 -->

## 516
# Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

Van der Waerden was indeed perfectly prepared to provide the spinor formalism requested by Ehrenfest, for he knew that such a formalism had actually already been furnished by the mathematical work of Eduard Study and his student E. Weiss (1924). They had investigated, in particular, the forms of binary variables, and their work stimulated Van der Waerden, when he took up the subject in 1929.$^{612}$ As his point of departure, he considered the possibility to rewrite the equation of the light cone in the four-dimensional space,

$$x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - c^2 t^2 = 0, \quad (479)$$

as

$$x^1 x^2 - x^3 x^4 = 0, \quad (480)$$

where the components with upper indices were given by

$$x^1 = x + iy, \quad x^2 = x - iy, \quad x^3 = (ct + z), \quad x^4 = (ct - z). \quad (480a)$$

If the coordinates $x^1, \dots x^4$ were interpreted to be homogeneous coordinates in a projective three-dimensional space, Eq. (480a) would describe a surface (‘quadric’) in this space. Linear transformations that leave this surface invariant, especially the Lorentz transformations, might be formulated, and the problem might be posed whether alternative types of vectors, tensors, and so on, exist in the geometry determined by the Lorentz group. Now, Van der Waerden discovered that, to each world vector $(x, y, z, t)$ of the conventional type, a quantity characterized by two indices, $a_{\dot{\alpha}\beta}$, corresponded, of which one has to be dotted—because it possesses a different transformation property.$^{613}$ These quantities, with components given by

$$a_{\dot{2}1} = x + iy, \quad a_{\dot{1}2} = x - iy,$$
$$a_{\dot{1}1} = ct + z, \quad a_{\dot{2}2} = ct - z, \quad (481)$$

constitute the simplest representatives of what Ehrenfest called ‘spinors.’ Similarly, the spinor with four indices, $b_{\dot{\alpha}\beta, \dot{\gamma}\delta}$, replaced a four-dimensional tensor $t_{\kappa, \lambda}$.

In the first published paper on spinor analysis, Van der Waerden did not speak about the above-detailed motivation. He rather briefly addressed Ehrenfest’s question by remarking:

$^{612}$ For details we refer to Van der Waerden, 1960, pp. 236–240. In this account, the author recalled that Ehrenfest had asked him the question for the spinor analysis in summer 1929 in Göttingen, where they spent some time together.

$^{613}$ If one requires that real points on the surface always be transformed into real points, then to those parts of a quantity associated with the dotted indices the complex-conjugate transformations must be applied.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0549 -->

III.4 Group Theory and Quantum Mechanics                                                                    517

> One can answer the question asked without any new tools. In order to find all possible spinors, one only needs to write down all representations of the Lorentz group which are known [here he referred to Weyl, 1928b]. Further, to obtain a theory of invariants for the spinors, one just has to exploit the known two-step isomorphy between the Lorentz group and the binary unimodular group in a manner known as well in order to establish a "translation principle (*Übertragungsprinzip*)" for the covariants of both groups [here he referred to Weiss, 1924]; and one has to use a known theorem of the theory of invariants in order to recognize that really all possible invariant equations can be written as binary tensor equations. (Van der Waerden, 1929, p. 100)

After these indications, he turned immediately to deal with the binary groups, i.e., the groups of a field given by a pair of two complex variables $\xi_1$ and $\xi_2$ and its complex conjugate $\bar{\xi}_1$ and $\bar{\xi}_2$. They transformed under a linear transformation (with complex coefficients $\alpha_{ik}$), respectively,

$$
\left.\begin{aligned}
\xi'_1 = \alpha_{11}\xi_1 + \alpha_{12}\xi_2, \quad \xi'_2 = \alpha_{21}\xi_1 + \alpha_{22}\xi_2, \\
\bar{\xi}'_1 = \bar{\alpha}_{11}\bar{\xi}_1 + \bar{\alpha}_{12}\bar{\xi}_2, \quad \bar{\xi}'_2 = \bar{\alpha}_{21}\bar{\xi}_1 + \bar{\alpha}_{22}\bar{\xi}_2.
\end{aligned}\right\} \tag{482}
$$

Then, the light-cone expression on the left-hand side of Eq. (479) assumed, after inserting Eq. (481), the following binary form:

$$
x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - c^2t^2 = -\frac{1}{2} a^{\dot{\alpha}\dot{\beta}} a_{\alpha\beta} \tag{483}
$$

in terms of the new spinor variables.

Van der Waerden thus arrived at the result that 'every real Lorentz transformation can be obtained in this way' (Van der Waerden, *loc. cit.*, p. 102), i.e., by a transformation of the form given in Eq. (482) with the determinant of the coefficient matrix $||\alpha_{ik}||$ assuming the value 1. Because Eq. (483) remained invariant also when the signs of all $\alpha_{ik}$ were changed, the linear transformations (482) provided a two-valued (*zweideutige*) representation of the Lorentz group.$^{614}$ Van der Waerden therefore happily concluded §1 of his paper by stating:

> The "quantities" associated with the Lorentz group are exactly these binary tensor representations of the Lorentz group. We call them, viewed as "quantities of the Lorentz group," *spin-tensors* or *spinors*, that is, spin tensors of first, second, . . . rank depending on the number of indices. Especially, the quantities with just a single index (assuming the values 1, 2) are called *spin-vectors*. (Van der Waerden, *loc. cit.*, p. 103)

Next, Van der Waerden defined world vectors, world tensors, and their derivatives (in §2)—with such symbols as $\partial_{\dot{1}1}, \dots \partial_{\dot{2}2}$—and he developed the theory
