of spinor invariants with the help of the antisymmetric symbol $\varepsilon^{\alpha\beta}$ whose components were given by $\varepsilon^{12} = -\varepsilon^{21} = 1, \varepsilon^{11} = \varepsilon^{22} = 0$ (in §3). In §4, he rewrote the Dirac equation for an electron in a four-potential $(\Phi_0, \Phi_r)$ as

$$\frac{1}{c} \left( \frac{h/2\pi}{i} + \Phi_0 \right) \psi = \sum_{r=1}^{3} \gamma_r \left( \frac{h/2\pi}{i} \frac{\partial}{\partial x_r} + \Phi_r \right) \psi - mc\gamma_0 = 0, \qquad (484)$$

where the $(4 \times 4)$-component $\gamma$ matrices are given by (with $\sigma_r$ and $I$ denoting the four spin matrices of Pauli)

$$\gamma_r = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_r & 0 \\ 0 & -\sigma_r \end{pmatrix} \quad \text{and} \quad \gamma_0 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & I \\ I & 0 \end{pmatrix},$$

in the new spinor language as the *two* equations

$$\left. \begin{aligned} -\left( \frac{h}{2\pi i} \dot{\partial}^\lambda_\mu + \dot{\Phi}^\lambda_\mu \right) \psi_{\dot{\lambda}} + mc\chi_\mu &= 0, \\ \left( \frac{h}{2\pi i} \partial^\lambda_{\dot{\mu}} + \Phi^\lambda_{\dot{\mu}} \right) \chi_\lambda + mc\psi_{\dot{\mu}} &= 0, \end{aligned} \right\} \qquad (485)$$

respectively, for the first two ($\psi_1$ and $\psi_2$) and the last two components ($\chi^1, \chi^2$) of the ‘Dirac spinor’ $\psi$.^615 By a second differentiation, he then obtained second-order wave equation, e.g.,

$$\partial^{\dot{\lambda}\mu} \partial_{\dot{\lambda}\mu} \chi_\nu = \frac{2m^2 c^2 i^2}{(h/2\pi)^2} \chi_\nu, \qquad (486)$$

and a similar equation for $\psi_{\dot{\mu}}$, in the case of zero four-potential. These results led to the following important physical consequences: if a linear wave equation of first order was required for the two-component spinor vectors $\psi_{\dot{\mu}}$ or $\chi_\nu$, the particles described had to possess zero mass; only a second-order wave equation admitted finite mass for particles described by the two-component spinors.
    Though these consequences were recognized only much later to play a crucial role in elementary particle physics, they were not connected primarily with Van der Waerden’s spinor formalism of 1929, but rather with a slightly earlier discussion of Hermann Weyl. Weyl had also considered (in two papers published since April 1929) the splitting of Dirac’s four-component wave function into two pairs (which he denoted by $\psi_1^+$ and $\psi_2^+$ and $\psi_1^-$ and $\psi_2^-$, respectively), and pointed to the fact that one can associate mass zero with each pair only if one considers the

$^{615}$ Van der Waerden noticed that the upper and the lower components of the four-spinor $\psi$ transform in a way as complex conjugate and contragradient to each other.

III.4	Group Theory and Quantum Mechanics	519

gravitational field (Weyl, 1929a, b).⁶¹⁶ At that time, i.e., during the academic year 1928/29, Weyl held a guest professorship in mathematical physics at Princeton University. ‘The lectures which I gave there and in other American institutions afforded me a much desired opportunity to present anew, and from a more pedagogical standpoint, the connection between groups and quanta. The experience thus obtained found its expression in a new edition, in which the subject was treated from a more thoroughly elementary standpoint,’ he mentioned in the preface to the second edition of his *Gruppentheorie und Quantenmechanik* (Weyl, 1931b; English translation, p. ix). The more pedagogical standpoint also governed his third paper of 1929, which the author submitted to the *Rice Institute Pamphlet* (Weyl, 1929c). Besides dealing with a two-component theory of the electron, all of these publications contained another great contribution to quantum physics, again based on group theory, namely, a renewed application of what he had earlier called ‘gauge invariance’—now used to introduce an essential equality of positive and negative electric charge, a forerunner of the later concept of charge invariance.⁶¹⁷

Weyl started out by analyzing Dirac's relativistic electron theory.⁶¹⁸ Because the equations for the electrons in an electromagnetic field $\Phi_\alpha$ exhibited the characteristic term $\frac{\partial}{\partial x_\alpha} + \frac{ie}{h/2\pi}\Phi_\alpha$, he argued:

> They differ strictly from those of classical physics in that *they contain the fundamental atomic constants* $e, h, m \ldots$. By this new situation, which introduces an atomic radius [i.e., $h/2\pi mc$] into the field equations themselves ... my principle of *gauge invariance*, which I had hoped [earlier] to relate gravitation and electricity [see Weyl, 1918c], is robbed of its support. But it is now very agreeable to see that this principle has an equivalent in the quantum-theoretical field equations which is exactly like it in formal respects; the laws are invariant under the simultaneous replacement of $\psi$ by $e^{i\lambda}\psi$, $\Phi_\alpha$ by $\Phi_\alpha - \frac{\partial \lambda}{\partial x_\alpha}$, where $\lambda$ is an arbitrary real function of position and time [and $\psi$ is the original four-component Dirac spinor]. Also the relation of this property of invariance to the law of conservation of electricity remains exactly as before. (Weyl, 1929c, pp. 284–285)

> ⁶¹⁶ Note that Weyl did not write equations of the form (485) explicitly, but obtained the conclusion concerning mass in a more complex way, e.g., as: ‘In a satisfactory theory it must therefore be impossible to introduce a non-vanishing mass without the gravitational field as it is to introduce charge without the electromagnetic field.’ (Weyl, 1929a, p. 323) Much more clearly, he wrote in the introduction to the next paper:
>
> > The theory of Dirac, in which the wave field of the electron is described by a potential with four components and provides twice the amount of energy levels; hence one should be able to return, without renouncing relativistic invariance, to Pauli's two-component theory. One is prevented from doing this by the term in Dirac's equation containing the mass as a factor. (Weyl, 1929b, pp. 330–331)
>
> The paper, Weyl (1929a), appeared in the issue of April 1929 of the *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the USA*; the second paper, Weyl (1929b), was submitted early in May to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, where it appeared in an issue of July 1929.
>

520	Chapter III	The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

Weyl further concluded that ‘the principle of gauge invariance has the character of general relativity since it contains an arbitrary function $\lambda$, and can certainly only be understood in terms of it’ (Weyl, *loc. cit.*, p. 285). Encouraged by this observation, he entered upon a detailed investigation of Dirac's equation in the framework of general relativity, with the ultimate goal of finding a method to resolve the mass problem. By the problem of mass, he not only addressed the difficulty of introducing a mass into a two-component version (as has been mentioned above), but also the question that the relativistic electron theory seemed to describe both of the charged elementary particles known at that time, i.e., the negatively charged electron and the positively charged, but much more massive, proton.

In his most detailed publication of 1929, Weyl first worked on a ‘two-component theory’—to a large extent based on ideas exhibiting a close similarity with those of Van der Waerden; he also derived, by referring to some geometrical considerations, the action function and the ‘energy tensor’ of the electron (Weyl, 1929b). Because all of these considerations followed essentially from group-theoretical and tensor-representation arguments, Weyl even expressed the remarkable opinion: ‘The fundamental *Ansätze* of quantum theory have therefore a less fundamental (*prinzipieller*) character than may have been assumed originally. They are [rather] connected with the special [form of the] action function.’ (Weyl, *loc. cit.*, p. 345) He claimed that in this situation it was general relativity that had to play a decisive role, and worked out the gravitational equations involving the description of an electron by a two-component spinor. Finally, he investigated the effect of an (additional) electromagnetic field and thereby rediscovered gauge invariance (see our discussion of Weyl, 1929c, given above), which led him to the following conclusions:

(1) ‘For an action quantity like the term in Dirac's theory carrying mass as a factor, there is no place in the two-component theory.’ (Weyl, 1929b, p. 351)

(2) ‘Electricity is a phenomenon accompanying the material wave field, not a phenomenon arising from gravitation.’ (Weyl, *loc. cit.*, p. 352)

The second statement expressed the impossibility to connect the field theories of gravitation and electricity in such a way that both a mass term is created and the fundamental gauge invariance is established. By whatever mechanism the mass of Dirac particles would eventually emerge, Weyl was convinced that ‘the theory in its present form contains only the *electron*’ and ‘there can be no doubt that the *proton* must be introduced into the field equations before they are quantized’; hence, ‘In place of one law of conservation of electricity we should have two.’ (Weyl, 1929c, p. 292)

Weyl took over these fundamentally important results from his 1929 papers into the second edition of his book on group theory and quantum mechanics (Weyl, 1931b, §12, especially, p. 264; see also Weyl, 1931a), but his views had only little impact on the thinking of the physicists in the next decades. One of them noted after more than fifty years:

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0553 -->

III.5 From Molecular Theory to Quantum Chemistry &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 521

His book was very famous and was recognized as profound. Almost every physicist born before 1935 had a copy of it on his bookshelves. But very few read it. Most are not accustomed to Weyl’s concentration on the structural aspects of physics and feel uncomfortable with his emphasis on concepts. The book was just too abstract for most physicists. (Yang, 1986, p. 10)

One cannot really say that the other mathematician involved in establishing the spinor formalism, Van der Waerden, immediately had greater success with his book *Die gruppentheoretische Methode in der Quantenmechanik* (1932). Admit-tedly, Van der Waerden chose a form more suitable for the physicists; further-more, he included (thus, going beyond Wigner’s earlier book on the same topic) a chapter on molecular spectra, which were discussed very eagerly at that time by many physicists and chemists. Still, the results from group-theoretical studies only partially entered into the investigations of the physicists (and even less those of the chemists), but in the late 1920s and during the 1930s they were repeatedly used in the discussions of problems in atomic, molecular, solid-state, nuclear, and ele-mentary particle physics.

**III.5 From Molecular Theory to Quantum Chemistry**

For Volume XXIV, Part One, of the Geiger–Scheel *Handbuch der Physik*, Frie-drich Hund wrote an extensive article of 134 pages on ‘*Allgemeine Quanten-mechanik des Atom- und Molekelbaues*’ (‘The General Quantum Mechanics of Atomic and Molecular Structure,’ Hund, 1933). In the introduction, he wrote: ‘The theory of the atom and the molecule is not only one of the principal fields of application of quantum mechanics, but it constitutes in particular a field with which the essential part of the development of the theory has been connected.’ He added:

After the creation of the new quantum mechanics and the following conceptual clar-ification of the theory by Born, Jordan, Dirac, Bohr and Heisenberg, the path was open for an application to molecules and solids, to collision and scattering phenom-ena. One has not yet fully succeeded in obtaining a generalization in a quantum theory of atomic nuclei and a quantum theory of the electromagnetic field. One found the reason in [the fact] that quantum theory sufficed only for situations in which no velocity comparable to the velocity of light was involved and for dimensions much larger than the size of the electron. (Hund, 1933, p. 561)

In the next two sections (**III.6** and **III.7**), we shall deal with the application of quantum mechanics to solids, where—according to Hund—it sufficed, and to nu-clear and high-energy phenomena, where it did not do so. In the present section, on the other hand, we discuss the creation of the molecular theory to the extent that Hund summarized in his *Handbuch* article, in particular, the crucial steps that he included in the following topics: ‘The Theoretical Clarification of the Molecular

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0554 -->

522 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

Spectra (Mulliken, Hund and others, 1926 to 1930), the Theory of Molecules (Born–Oppenheimer, [R.] de L. Kronig, 1927 to 1928), and the Interpretation of the Chemical Bonds (Heitler–London, Slater and others, 1927 to 1931).’ (Hund, 1933, p. 562) Before discussing these topics in detail, however, we shall give a brief synopsis of the prehistory, that is, the prequantum-mechanical theory of mole-cules, beginning with the recognition of the physical and chemical properties of molecules in the nineteenth century leading to a great puzzle in the early decades of the twentieth century, namely, the existence of two apparently contradictory concepts of the electron, an elementary constituent of atoms and molecules.

**(a) The Chemical and the Physical Electron (1800–1925)**

The modern story of the structure of matter began right away in 1800 with the dis-covery of the phenomenon of electrolysis (by Johann Wilhelm Ritter and William Cruikshank, respectively), that is, the decomposition of chemical substances, such as water and solutions of salts, by electric currents. John Dalton then figured out the first symbolic notation of chemical elements and their compounds in his book *A New System of Chemical Philosophy* (Dalton, 1808), which Jöns Jacob Berzelius replaced in 1814 by what became the modern notation in letters (denoting the elements) and numbers (denoting their relative amounts in a compound). Berzelius also expounded in 1811 the hypothesis that chemical bonds are created by electric forces: he assumed that compounds consist of electrically oppositely charged con-stituents. Michael Faraday, when continuing the earlier investigations of Berzelius and Humphrey Davy, established in 1833 and 1834 the three fundamental laws of electrolysis, namely: (1) the masses of different chemical substances obtained by electrolysis are related as their equivalent weights; (2) the precipitation of one gram-equivalent of a substance needs a fixed amount of electricity; and (3) this constant is called Faraday’s constant $F$. The rapid progress of chemistry in the nineteenth century revealed an increasing wealth of chemical compounds whose structure was carefully analyzed in symbolic forms, which expressed chemical bonds from about 1860 by dashes or double dashes (note Adolf Kékulé’s famous ring formula of 1872 for the model of benzene)—double dashes were supposed to represent particularly strong chemical bonds.

The physical explanation of the chemical constitution of substances again began from electrolysis. In his Faraday lecture of 1881, Hermann Helmholtz drew consequences from the experimental observations as follows:

> The same definite quantity of either positive or negative electricity always moves with each univalent ion, or with any unit of affinity of a multivalent ion, and accompanies it during all its motions through the interior of the electrolytic fluid. This quantity we may call the electric charge of an atom. . . . If we accept the hypothesis that the ele-mentary substances are composed of atoms, we cannot avoid concluding that elec-tricity also, positive as well as negative, is divided into definite elementary portions, which behave like atoms of electricity. (Helmholtz, 1881, reprint p. 69)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0555 -->

III.5 From Molecular Theory to Quantum Chemistry &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 523

And he further stated: ‘I think the facts leave no doubt that the very mightiest among the chemical forces are of electric origin. The atoms cling to their electric charges, and opposite electric charges cling to each other; but I do not suppose that other molecular forces are excluded, working directly from atom to atom.’ (Helmholtz, *loc. cit.*, pp. 85–86)

These words must be considered as being truly prophetic. Still, they fitted well into the British climate of that time. Thus, Joseph John Thomson discussed two years later the chemical forces with the help of a special model of the atom, the then fashionable vortex-ring atom: compounds of chemical elements can be viewed as consisting of pairs of such vortex rings (Thomson, 1883). The same Thomson laid, sixteen years after Helmholtz’s Faraday lecture, the foundation of a more realistic model of the atom by discovering what Helmholtz had called the ‘atom of electricity,’ namely, the corpuscular ‘electron’ as a constituent of the atom (Thomson, 1897a). Then, in 1904, he published several papers proposing the so-called plum-pudding model of the atom, in which the electrons were arranged in coplanar, circular orbits inside a positively charged sphere (see, e.g., Thomson, 1904c). This model seemed to explain, as Thomson emphasized, the periodic table or system of elements (*PSE*), especially the chemical properties of the elements quite well on the basis of an electron exchange, i.e., the formation of attracting oppositely charged ions—hence, it predicted the sole existence of polar chemical forces (Thomson, 1907c). Again, seven years later, however, Thomson also ad-mitted nonpolar forces, which he viewed as a tube of force formed between an electron of the first atom and the nucleus of the second atom, and another tube between an electron of the second atom and the nucleus of the first atom (Thom-son, 1914).<sup>619</sup>

Thomson’s fresh approach made use of a new atomic model, the ‘nuclear atom’ of Ernest Rutherford, which consisted of a very concentrated, massive, positively charged nucleus surrounded by electrons circulating in rings (Rutherford, 1911a). The nuclear atom not only explained the phenomena of the radioactive transitions but, if supplemented by the quantum hypothesis, it also served to account for the classical line-spectra of chemical elements (Bohr, 1913b; Sommerfeld, 1915b, c). In 1916, Walter Kossel analyzed whether the Rutherford–Bohr model could provide an explanation of the chemical facts: he noticed certain difficulties emerging from the structure of many-electron atoms, especially in the process of the formation of molecules; hence, he proposed to derive, from (empirical) chemical observation rather than from physical dynamics, what the electron configurations in atoms and molecules should be like (Kossel, 1916a). Three years later, he published an article on the physical nature of valence forces, which he concluded with the following remarks:

> Hence one cannot doubt, in spite of the fact that a strict evaluation is still missing —this will only be possible if the complete structure of any single atom has been

<sup>619</sup> For details of the story of electrons in chemistry, see Arabatzis and Gavroglu, 1997.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0556 -->

fixed—that the well-known physical forces do determine the valence properties (*Valenzbetätigungen*) of atoms. One will have to introduce, in the final, complete representation, all electromagnetic forces, i.e., one must not restrict oneself to the electrostatic part but also consider the electrodynamical (magnetic) forces. Further, the electromagnetic processes within the atom reveal themselves to be dominated by peculiar additional conditions, which are characterized by the quantum of action, and it may be that these conditions play a more direct role for the detailed knowl-edge, say, of the stability of the atomic bonds than hitherto assumed. Today, it has become extremely improbable that we should have to guess still new, so far unknown, natural forces behind the valence properties. (Kossel, 1919, p. 366)

Since the 1880s the chemists had followed with critical interest the endeavours of the physicists to provide a physical basis for the foundation of chemical forces.<sup>620</sup> To some extent, the strange atomic models that had been proposed rather amused the more pragmatic scientists of the neighbouring field: the chemists in general imagined their atoms to be represented by solid balls with certain hooks and eyes to denote the chemical forces. Still, after the physicists discovered the electron, the chemists also recognized its value and connected its action in the atom with the chemical bond, as was done by Richard Abegg in his systematic review of valence and the *PSE* (Abegg, 1904). He stated, in particular, that the ‘normal’ valence of an atom amounted to the definite number of electrons which the atom would give (positive valance) or take (negative valence) upon its com-bination with another atom to form a molecular compound—Abegg called this valence type ‘heteropolar.’ Another type of valence may also exist, the ‘homopolar valence’ (‘*homöopolare*’), which does not rest on the extreme polarity of the atom: atoms of a compound formed by the homopolar bond rather appear ‘equal valued’ (‘*gleichwertig*’).<sup>621</sup> In 1916, Gilbert N. Lewis of Berkeley composed a program-matic article, entitled ‘The Atom and the Molecule,’ for the *Journal of the Ameri-can Chemical Society*; his goal was to determine the detailed nature of ‘polar’ and ‘non-polar’ types of compounds (Lewis, 1916). For that purpose, he referred to two ideas: first, the concept of ‘the cubic atom’ that he had developed already in an unpublished memorandum of March 1902 (see Lewis, *loc. cit.*, p. 767), and, second, the assumption published in ‘an extremely interesting paper by Mr. A. L. Parson . . . that the electron is not merely an electric charge but is also a small magnet, or, in his terminology, a magneton [Parson, 1915]’ (Lewis, *loc. cit.*, p. 773).

Lewis viewed the atom as a cube, whose corners could be occupied by up to eight electrons, because eight was the maximum chemical valence observed.<sup>622</sup>

<sup>620</sup> See Arabatzis and Gavroglu, 1997, pp. 150–153.
<sup>621</sup> Abegg’s homopolar valence showed up essentially in what Thomson called in 1914 ‘class-I compounds,’ defined as compounds of neutral atoms, while the heteropolar valence acts in ‘class-II compounds’ consisting of oppositely charged ions.
<sup>622</sup> We have mentioned G. N. Lewis’s cubic model previously in connection with atomic models around 1920, especially those proposed by Alfred Landé. See Volume 1, Part 1, p. 317 (also for Lewis’s biographical sketch).

525 III.5 From Molecular Theory to Quantum Chemistry

These cubic shapes somehow presented a model of the outer shells of Bohr’s atoms and followed a number of postulates—for example, ‘an atom tends to hold an even number of electrons in a shell’ (postulate 3), ‘two atomic shells are mutually impenetrable’ (postulate 4), or ‘electrons may ordinarily pass from one position in the outer shell to another’ (postulate 5)—which determined especially the composition of atoms in compounds. Further, Lewis noticed that ‘electric forces between particles which are very close together do not obey the law of inverse squares which holds for grater distances’ (Lewis, *loc. cit.*, p. 768). The latter observation also agreed with Parson’s assumption of a ‘magneton’ or magnetic moment of the electron. Whatever the details of his chemically motivated atomic model, Lewis believed that the main assumption of Bohr’s atomic theory of 1913, ‘that an electron can move freely in any one of the series of orbits in which the velocities differ by steps … and that radiation occurs when the electron passes from an orbital velocity to the next,’ did not describe the real situation, but:

> It seems to me far simpler to assume that an electron may be held in the atom in stable equilibrium in a series of different positions, each of which having definite constraints, corresponds to a definite frequency of the electron, the intervals between the constraints in successive positions being simply expressible in terms of ultimate rational units. (Lewis, *loc. cit.*, p. 773)

Now, according to Parson, polar bonds were formed by the transfer of magnetons, whereas nonpolar bonds consisted of pairs of magnetons that were created by the strong magnetic attraction of two neighboring magnetic electrons (overcoming the electrostatic repulsion of the electrons). Lewis essentially took over the idea that electrostatic and magnetostatic forces together established his cubic atom and that pairs of closest electrons yielded the chemical bonds of both types.

The static atom that thus arose was accepted by Irving Langmuir of Schenectady, though he relaxed the assumption of completely fixed electrons to approach Bohr’s otherwise successful dynamical model: the electrons now could either be stationary or rotate, revolve, or oscillate about definite positions in the atom (Langmuir, 1919a, b). Hence, his model attracted quite some interest, both in the academic circles of physicists and chemists as well as among industrial chemists, because it seemed to unite the advantages of Lewis’s model in explaining the observed chemical bonds and of Bohr’s model in explaining the spectra. However, when in the early 1920’s Bohr’s theory ran into insurmountable difficulties, Lewis argued quite candidly that even the famous hydrogen atom model of 1913 was not ‘something more than a mere working hypothesis’ (Lewis, 1923, p. 50). Still, at the Cambridge meeting of the Faraday Society on ‘Electron Theory of Valency’ in July 1923, he expressed little doubt that sooner or later quantum theory would explain the central issue of the chemical bonds, which was electron pairing; and this opinion was not only shared by the physicist Ralph Fowler (who spoke on ‘Bohr’s Atom in Relation to the Problem of Valency,’ Fowler, 1923c), but also by the organic chemist Robert Robertson, then President of the Faraday

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0558 -->

526 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

Society. Robertson, in particular, pointed out ‘that the applications of present day conceptions to the mechanism of chemical reactions is clearly in a transition stage’ (quoted by Arabatzis and Gavroglu, 1997, p. 156). The year 1923 indeed marked a low point in the validity of the old quantum theory of atomic structure of Bohr and his followers; even the results that were considered secure, such as the calculation of the excited-helium energy terms, led to wrong results, and only additional hypotheses incompatible with the spirit of the theory occasionally yielded agreement with the data (e.g., the Sommerfeld–Landé vector model for the anomalous Zeeman effects). A similar situation occurred in Bohr’s 1921 theory of the periodic system of elements (for example, in the case of hafnium in 1922), which did not solve the problem of describing the chemical properties of atoms. Again, only the use of additional hypotheses—like the ones following from the so-called ‘octet theory’—ensured some success in explaining complex molecular structures.$^{623}$

Then, the theory of atomic structure underwent fundamental changes. First, in early 1925 a new property of the electron, the ‘fourth quantum number,’ of Pauli was discovered, soon to be interpreted (by Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit) as the intrinsic angular momentum or ‘spin’ of the electron, which led to a specific magnetic moment of the electron.$^{624}$ Second, Heisenberg (in summer 1925) and Schrödinger (around 1925/26) created a new atomic theory: quantum mechanics or the equivalent wave mechanics. This theory especially removed the previous discrepancy with the observed spectra of many-electron atoms and promised to throw light on chemical problems as well. Thus, the renowned British chemist Nevil Vincent Sidgwick wrote in the preface to his book on *The Electronic Theory of Valency* quite confidently:

> In developing a theory of valency there are two courses open to the chemist. He may use symbols with no definite physical connotation to express the reactivity of the atoms in a molecule, and may leave it to the subsequent progress of science to discover what realities these symbols represent; or he may adopt the concepts of atomic physics—electrons, nuclei, and orbits—and try to explain the chemical facts in terms of these. But if he takes the latter course, as is done in this book, he must accept the physical conclusions in full, and must not assign to these entities properties which the

III.5 From Molecular Theory to Quantum Chemistry 527

physicists have found them not to possess: he must not use the terminology of physics unless he is prepared to recognize its laws. I have endeavoured to conform to the principle, and not to lay myself open to the reproach of an eminent physicist, that “when chemists talk about electrons they use a different language from the physicists.” I have been careful to avoid as far as possible the introduction of any physical hypotheses which are not already sanctioned by those who are best qualified to judge them. (Sidgwick, 1927, p. ii)

Sidgwick himself could not yet employ the full quantum-mechanical theory of molecules and their chemical bonds. This theory was just about to be created by several theoretical physicists who pioneered the field between 1926 and 1928, first Friedrich Hund in Göttingen and Copenhagen, then Walter Heitler and Fritz London in Zurich, Göttingen, and Berlin; soon, the chemist Robert Mulliken from Chicago and the physicist Eugene Wigner from Berlin joined the pursuit, and finally the physicists Gerhard Herzberg in Göttingen and John Slater in Cambridge (Mass.) and the physicochemist Linus Pauling from California developed a consistent quantum chemistry, in which indeed the fundamental physical concepts and methods involved had no other meaning than the one given to them by the physicists.

**(b) Friedrich Hund and the Quantum Theory of Molecules (1925–1927)**

In Göttingen, the discussion of molecular phenomena with the help of quantum theory had acquired some tradition since Max Born and James Franck joined the university as professors in 1921. Thus, Born entered into the theory of atomic systems with a letter to *Naturwissenschaften*, dated 27 June 1922, dealing with a model of the hydrogen molecule in the then current Bohr–Sommerfeld scheme and its relation to possible models of the helium atom (Born, 1922). In the following years, Born returned repeatedly, partly together with his collaborators, to treat the problems of molecular theory. In their paper, entitled ‘Zur Quantentheorie der Moleküle’ (‘On the Quantum Theory of Molecules’) and submitted toward the end of the year 1923, Born and Heisenberg developed a systematic perturbation scheme for the dynamics of molecules revealing five different levels of the problem: (1) the rigid rotator; (2) the rotator with nuclear rotations; (3) the interaction of rotations with oscillations; (4) the influence of the angular momentum of the electrons; and (5) the full molecular problem of nuclei and electrons (Born and Heisenberg, 1924a, pp. 1–2). They showed, still in the framework of the old semiclassical quantum theory, the detailed relation between the orders of perturbation, on the one hand, and the different levels of the physical description of the dynamics of the molecules, on the other.

Friedrich Hund also belonged among Born’s favourite collaborators; in fact, after completing his doctorate in 1922, he was appointed senior assistant at the Institute of Theoretical Physics, where he helped Born especially with the editing of the *Vorlesungen über Atommechanik* (i.e., the lecture course on ‘atomic mechanics,’ presented by Born in the winter semester 1923/24), which dealt with the application of the Hamilton–Jacobi theory to atomic and molecular systems

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0560 -->

528 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

(Born, 1925). In 1925, Hund first worked on certain ideas concerning the shape of polar molecules and the types of crystal lattices they were composed of (Hund, 1925a, b), and then he analyzed with the greatest success the spectra of complex atoms by employing Pauli’s exclusion principle and Heisenberg’s prequantum-mechanical correspondence considerations (Hund, 1925c, d, e).$^{625}$ From October 1925 to 29 September 1926, Hund essentially wrote his first book, *Linienspektrum und periodisches System der Elemente* (Line Spectrum and the Periodic System of Elements, Hund, 1927b).$^{626}$ It contained a detailed discussion of the data and theoretical description of atomic line spectra, based on models in which the quantum theory was corrected by the recent results of electron and quantum mechanics; in particular, Hund presented his own investigations on complex spectra. The book confirmed Hund’s stature as ‘one of the best connoisseurs of the spectral laws,’ as Born wrote to Niels Bohr on 10 October 1925.$^{627}$ Already during this period of most strenuous work, however,—besides writing his book on the line spectra and the periodic system of elements, the fresh *Privatdozent* Hund delivered his first lecture course in the winter semester 1925/26 and assisted David Hilbert and James Franck in conducting seminars at the University of Göttingen (while Max Born was on leave of absence in the U.S.A.)—he began a new research programme of his own on the theoretical investigation of molecular spectra.

Thus, on 22 November 1925, Hund noted in his *Tagebuch*:$^{628}$ ‘For molecular zoology the two-centre problem serves as a model. $\text{H}_2^+$-term [can be obtained] from relativistic Stark effect and atom with split nucleus [Hund imagines that the atomic nucleus of an atom splits into two nuclei to form a molecule].’ But soon he became a little disappointed, because ‘the empirical bands do not agree with my conception’ (Hund, 27 November 1925). Still, he continued the study of molecular spectra in the following months and submitted in early March 1926 his first paper on the subject to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Hund, 1926).$^{629}$ Based on recent data of the

$^{625}$ The results obtained in late spring and early summer 1925 included, for instance, ‘Hund’s rule,’ namely, the observation that among the energy terms associated with a given electron configuration that one is lowest that has (a) the greatest sum of spins and, (b) for terms having the same of spins, the one having the largest sum of orbital angular momenta. The rule allows for exceptions in the case of higher terms.

$^{626}$ For details of Hund’s life and early work, see Volume 1, Part 2, p. 622, and Rechenberg, 1996.

$^{627}$ In his letter to Bohr, Born recommended Hund for a fellowship to be spent in Copenhagen, to which Bohr immediately agreed (Niels Bohr Archive, Copenhagen).

$^{629}$ In a later interview, he said:

> I studied much of the *Zahlenmaterial* [i.e., the data on molecular spectra]. I also remember that I drew a many-line spectrum on millimetre paper and I gazed at it intently. I further remember a figure in one of the earlier editions of Sommerfeld [i.e., *Atombau und Spektrallinien*] certain accumulations [of lines] for which something like a Rydberg formula applied—which is also correct because it corresponds to the capture of an electron. (Hund, AHQP Interview, 26 June 1963, p. 13)

III.5 From Molecular Theory to Quantum Chemistry  
529  

experimentalists Reinhard Mecke, Robert Mulliken and Raymond Birge, who had analyzed the ‘fine structure bands’ and found certain ‘relations to atomic spectra’ —in addition to some older observations of Torsten Heurlinger and Adolf Kratzer —Hund noticed that the problem levels listed earlier by Born and Heisenberg under (1), (2), and (3) had already been properly treated by the new quantum mechanics.⁶³⁰ Therefore, he now turned ‘to contribute to the basic clarification of problems involving the connection of the electronic motion with the band spectra, using the conceptions and rules discovered in the investigation of atomic spectra that enabled one to obtain a qualitative interpretation even of very complex spectra’ (Hund, 1926, p. 657). He succeeded in doing so by looking at the situation in a classical model of molecules consisting of electrons and nuclei, considering this to be the correspondence limit of the quantum theory; then, he assumed that in a two-atomic molecule the two nuclei influence the electronic states similar to a quadratic Stark effect in an atom. He concluded: ‘Among other results, there follows an understanding of the occasionally noticed similarity of the fine structures in molecules and atoms having the same number of outer (valence) electrons.’ (Hund, *loc. cit.*)  

In spring 1926, after the completion of the above paper, Hund began to learn the new quantum mechanics more systematically, though he did not proceed much beyond the matrix treatment of the rotator. Then, the strenuous work of completing the book on line spectra absorbed him until October, when he finally arrived in Copenhagen on an International Education Board Fellowship. After settling in the new surroundings, he embarked with great zeal upon the quantum-mechanical theory of molecules. He noted in his *Tagebuch*:  

> Coarse structure of the two-centre problem (fixed centre), fine structure with interactions, watch the resonance of identical nuclei. Two-centre problem: symmetrical and non-symmetrical orbits [do] not [exist] with the same quantum numbers. . . Transitions between both still possible.—Relation, symmetric to nonsymmetric, when the centres are removed from each other adiabatically: [Quantum numbers] *l* stay, *n* change in general. Suspicion: no term will be lost. Count orbits around each centre separately.—Start from the investigation of [the Hamiltonian] \( H = p^2\lambda(9 \mp 1) \), due to Schrödinger. (Hund, entry in *Tagebuch*, 20/21 October 1926)  

These key phrases reveal some details of how Hund worked in those days. First, let us remember that in Copenhagen he again met Werner Heisenberg, his friend and colleague from Göttingen, and had the opportunity to discuss with him his interpretation on the helium atom and other many-particle systems (Heisenberg, 1926c, 1927a); thus, he became acquainted with the symmetry considerations of Heisenberg and Paul Dirac, who arrived in Copenhagen at about the same time as Hund. Second, he became fully familiar with the Schrödinger wave equation  


⁶³⁰ Hund referred to the initial discussions in Heisenberg (1925c) and Born, Heisenberg, and Jordan (1926). For the empirical data and their description, he quoted the extensive review of Adolf Kratzer (1925) and the original papers of Mecke and Mulliken (see below).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0562 -->

530 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics  

and how to work with it.⁶³¹ In fact, he recalled that he first tried to pursue symmetry considerations in molecular theory with the help of matrices, and:  

> I remember that [I] filled large sheets of paper to cope with the symmetries, and then I got a bit furious; then I turned of course to the Schrödinger equation and realized that this works much better. (Hund, AHQP Interview, 26 June 1936, p. 22)  

While Heisenberg at that time showed himself to be reluctant to use wave-mechanics, Hund found people in Copenhagen who were disposed toward this method in a most friendly manner. Hund thus characterized his own procedure: ‘Since I always liked to think *anschaulich*, I tried to make myself familiar with the Schrödinger equation in the case of one-dimensional models by using the graphical method.’ (Hund, *loc. cit.*, p. 21) Indeed, he quickly advanced in his investigations; thus, already on 23 October 1926, he understood the ‘nature of the polar molecules,’ for on 29 October he presented the results in a colloquium at Copenhagen, and on 18 November he sent the paper ‘*Zur Deutung der Molekelspektren. I*’ (‘On the Interpretation of Molecular Spectra I’), having obtained the full approval of his host Niels Bohr, to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Hund, 1927a).  

The classical model for the diatomic molecules had been described by Max Born in his Göttingen lectures on atomic mechanics in 1923/24: the electrons move in the electric field of two nuclei, and their orbits can be obtained in elliptical coordinates (Born, 1925, pp. 276–281). Hund now translated the previous formalism point by point into the language of wave mechanics, and he derived the result that qualitatively a term spectrum for electronic states should be obtained ranging between the types given by a quadratic Stark effect (for the case of large distances between the nuclei) and a linear Stark effect (for narrow distances between the nuclei), respectively. In more detail, he showed, again by qualitative argumentation, how the term values of the two-centre system change by an adiabatic separation of the centres due to the potentials acting on the electrons. In particular, he found that the number of terms remains conserved; thus, every term from the lowest one onward is transformed into a corresponding term of the transformed molecule. A similar conclusion must also be derived from a discussion of polyatomic molecules. Hund thus summarized the situation as follows:  

> The possibility exists of relating the stationary states of such a system to those of partial systems which are created by an infinite removal of the minima [of potential energy] from each other by an infinitely growing potential between them. Consequently, there exists, in contrast to the classical theory, an adiabatic connection between the states of two separated atoms or ions, the states of two-atomic molecules,  


⁶³¹ Of course, Schrödinger’s wave-mechanical papers had appeared already in spring 1926 and had been noticed immediately also in Göttingen, but apparently Hund was too deeply absorbed in his own research programme and teaching duties to work through them; in summer 1926, he taught the official course on classical mechanics with problem sessions for Max Born, which left him no time to pursue other things.

III.5 From Molecular Theory to Quantum Chemistry  
531  

and the state of an atom that can be figured as emerging from a fusion of the nuclei. This connection allows one to establish a qualitatively valid term scheme for the molecule, and to interpret the concepts of a “polar molecule” and an “ionic lattice.” (Hund, 1927a, p. 742)  

Especially, ‘a molecule is called polar if it passes over into two oppositely charged ions when the nuclei are separated’ (Hund, *loc. cit.*, p. 762), and an ionic lattice is given ‘when its ground state passes over adiabatically into the states of the ions’ (Hund, *loc. cit.*, p. 764).  

With this preparation, Hund attacked the next task, namely, to explain ‘the empirically detected [term] systematics of Mulliken and Birge’ (Hund, 1927c, p. 93). In a paper, submitted in July 1925 to *The Physical Review*, Robert S. Mulliken had introduced two types of multiplicity in the band spectra of diatomic molecules (Mulliken, 1925c). As Raymond T. Birge emphasized later in a letter to *Nature*:  

> One type is essentially a function of the rotation of the two nuclei about their common center of gravity and has no counterpart in atomic spectra. . . The other type is essentially independent of rotation and vibration, and, as Mulliken has pointed out, leads to multiple electronic levels in the molecule which may be correlated with the multiple levels of atoms. (Birge, 1926, p. 300)  

The senior molecular specialist Birge, after some comparison of the data of Mulliken and other investigators (notably, Erik Hulthén, Hertha Sponer, Alfred Fowler, and Reinhard Mecke), concluded: ‘*The energy levels associated with the valence electrons of the molecules agree in all essential aspects with those associated with the valence electrons of atoms.*’ (Birge, *loc. cit.*, p. 301) Evidently, this observation perfectly agreed with Hund’s theory, as the latter stated in his second paper on the interpretation of molecular spectra, submitted in early February 1927 (Hund, 1927c).  

As Hund had shown previously, the molecular spectra possessed a coarse structure (*Grobstruktur*) depending on the rotations and oscillations of the nuclei, and a fine structure (*Feinstruktur*) described by two quantum numbers \( i_l \), i.e., the total angular momentum of the electrons about the axis joining the nuclei and \( s \) (the total spin of the electrons). When drawing the rotational energy as a function of the rotational quantum number \( p \), the \( i_l = 0 \) curves consisted of a single parabola for \( s = 0 \), which for higher values of \( s \) split for increasing \( p \)-values starting from a single point on the energy axis; the \( i_l > 0 \) curves consisted (except for the values \( s = 0 \)) of several distinct parabolas starting from different term values (see Hund, 1927c, pp. 94–95 and p. 96 for the magnitude of the splittings). The empirical classification, given by Birge and Mulliken with terms denoted by \( ^1S, ^1P, ^1D, . . ., ^2S, ^2P, ^2D, . . ., \) coincided with Hund’s terms, because the \( S \)-terms of the experimentalists corresponded to \( i_l = 0 \) terms of Hund, the \( P \)-terms to the \( i_l = 1 \) terms, and so on, and the upper left index just coincided with Hund’s \( 2s + 1 \) (see Mulliken, 1926a, b). Thus, all observed terms of molecules with different nuclei

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0564 -->

532 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics  

and molecules with identical nuclei could be described by the theory. In the latter case, just an ‘exchange symmetry’ must be taken into account, and the term system splits into symmetric and antisymmetric states (as designated by the permutation property of the corresponding eigenfunctions—for those symmetry considerations, however, the rotational and the electronic motions must be viewed together).⁶³²  

A study of the intensity of the band lines in the same paper led Hund to a remarkable interpretation of the empirically observed intensity changes. ‘*The intensity change means that both the symmetric and the antisymmetric system in the nuclei occur [in nature] but with a different weight*,’ he argued (Hund, 1927c, p. 113), and continued:  

> Of course, one can try to reduce the occurrence of both symmetry systems to that of a single one by admitting the hypothesis that the *atomic nuclei* do not constitute simple point charges, or are spherically symmetric, but in addition *possess still another property* enabling them to assume different positions. Then the eigenfunction existing for a state with point charge are multiplied by a factor arising from the position of nuclei. . . Exactly as in the helium situation, also in the case of the molecules weak intercombinations should occur between symmetric and antisymmetric terms, if one assumes a new property of the nuclei [i.e., nuclear spin]. (Hund, *loc. cit.*, p. 114)  

As Hund concluded, however, these intercombination lines might turn out to be very weak and hardly observable. On the other hand, intensity changes seemed to exist in the hydrogen-molecule bands that confirmed what was then called the ‘nuclear spin hypothesis.’  

In later recollections, Hund stated that he had discussed the above question in some detail with Heisenberg, and the latter had suggested to him to relate intensity changes of band lines with symmetry considerations, but Heisenberg had claimed that arbitrary statistical weights should be assumed. At this, Hund had replied: ‘One obtains a [weight] ratio of 3:1 if one attributes to the nucleus a new property which allows it to assume a position analogous to the electron.’ (Hund, AHQP Interview, 26 June 1963, p. 18) This discussion also left a mark in Heisenberg’s second paper on a many-body system submitted in December 1926; there, Heisenberg discussed the possibility of an ‘eigenrotation \( s = \frac{1}{2}h/2\pi \)’ of each of the two nuclei of a diatomic gas and then obtained a term situation similar to that of the helium atom, upon which he added the footnote: ‘The hint for this I owe to Mr. Hund.’ (Heisenberg, 1927a, p. 264) Hence, one has to conclude that the idea of nuclear (and proton) spin arose in the discussions between Hund and Heisenberg in December 1926 [nobody at that time recalled that Pauli had proposed the existence of nuclear spin in connection with hyperfine structure already in 1924].  

Finally, Hund—still in the same paper—studied in some detail the case of the hydrogen molecule, both for nuclei with and without the extra spin property. An analysis of the available data on band spectra—Hund cited the observations of G. H. Diecke and J. J. Hopfield and the preliminary results of T. Hori—did not

III.5 From Molecular Theory to Quantum Chemistry 533

yet allow a clear decision for or against the nuclear spin hypothesis. Hund then turned to a discussion of the rotational heat of hydrogen, whose temperature dependence had not been explained since Arnold Eucken’s measurements of 1912.$^{633}$ He followed essentially the treatment of Erwin Schrödinger (1924f)—see Volume 5, Part 1, pp. 354–357—and found a reasonable description of the specific-heat curve for the values $\beta \approx 2$ and the moment of inertia $I = 1.54 \times 10^{-41} \text{ g.cm}^2$ (Hund, 1927c, p. 120). Here, $\beta$ denotes a ratio of weights for the symmetric and antisymmetric terms: it assumes the value 3 if the proton were a spin-zero and 1/3 if it were a spin $\frac{1}{2}h/2\pi$ particle.$^{634}$ About two months after the publication of Hund’s paper, in early June 1927, Ralph Fowler in Cambridge received a note from David M. Dennison on the specific heat of the hydrogen molecule, which he communicated to the *Proceedings of the Royal Society of London* (Dennison, 1927). Dennison, from the University of Michigan, a former Rockefeller Foundation Fellow in Europe, pointed out that Hund’s derivation of the specific heat did not really fit the data. Referring to the recent observations of Takeo Hori, which established different parameters for the hydrogen molecule than obtained previously (notably, $I = 4.67 \times 10^{-41} \text{ g.cm}^2$), he proposed an alternative approach to the problem: the hydrogen gas should consist of two types of molecular states, which are symmetric and antisymmetric in the nuclear eigenrotations; these states do not combine during a long time. Furthermore, in an addendum of 16 June, Dennison pointed out that ‘the ratio 3 to 1 of the antisymmetrical and symmetrical modifications of the hydrogen is just what is to be expected from a consideration of the equilibrium at ordinary temperatures if the spin is taken equal to that of the electron, and only the complete antisymmetrical solution of the wave equation allowed.’ (Dennison, *loc. cit.*, p. 486)$^{635}$

Thus, it was Dennison whose analysis ultimately decided in favour of the proton spin, which emerged in the discussions of Hund and Heisenberg. Hund commented simply on the conclusion of the story:

> At that time I was very interested in the analysis of Hori. . . . I remember when Hori was ready I knew something was wrong [in my paper]. Then, however, already Dennison came, otherwise I might have analyzed the Hori results somewhat more accurately, but then Dennison put it right. (Hund, AHQP Interview, 26 June 1963, p. 19)

Now, Dennison wrote in his paper that he was greatly indebted ‘to Hori for allowing him to see the manuscript of his work’ (Dennison, 1927b, p. 484). Indeed,

534 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

Takeo Hori, a graduate of Kyoto University and later professor at Lu Shun Institute of Technology at Port Arthur, Manchuria, had just spent a research fellowship at Copenhagen since 1926, together with Hund.$^{636}$ ‘Bohr suggested to Hori that he study the band spectrum of $\text{H}_2$’, his student and brother-in-law Sinitiro Tomonaga said later, and:

> Hori therefore performed a very elaborate experiment and a laborious analysis on the band spectrum of the hydrogen molecule which had been discovered by [Sven] Werner only in the previous year 1926. As a result he discovered the intensity alternation in the hydrogen rotational spectrum. He found that the intensities of spectral lines are weaker for transitions between levels with even [angular momentum] $J$ and stronger for transitions between levels with odd $J$. He did not state the intensity ratio, but . . . when a scholar by the name of D. M. Dennison asked him about the intensity ratio, Hori answered that it was approximately 1:3. (Tomonaga, 1997, p. 73)

Hori’s paper was signed April 1927, though received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* only on 19 July and finally published in a September issue (Hori, 1927). By that time, Hund had turned his attention to different aspects of molecular theory.

Upon returning to Göttingen in early April 1927, Hund first prepared for his duties as a *Privatdozent* at the university—he lectured on ‘*Molekülbau*’ (‘Molecular Structure’)—then, later in May, he submitted two papers that he had essentially worked out in Copenhagen, the paper on ‘symmetry characters’ (Hund, 1927d), which we have already reviewed in the previous section, and the other entitled ‘*Zur Deutung der Molekelspektren. III.*’ (‘On the Interpretation of Molecular Spectra,’ Hund 1927e).$^{637}$ The main purpose of *Molekelspektren. III* was to extend the wave-mechanical treatment to molecules built of more than two atoms. Unlike the case of diatomic molecules, experimentalists had so far provided only meagre data on electronic spectra; hence, Hund restricted himself to discussing the peculiarities of the vibrational and rotational spectra, making ample use of his symmetry scheme to explain the details in the case of molecules containing two or more equal nuclei.

In order to deal with the oscillations of polyatomic molecules, Hund wrote the Schrödinger equation for the energy $W$ of $n$ point-like atoms having different masses $m_i (i = 1, \dots m)$ and Cartesian position coordinates $q_i$,

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{2m_i} \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial q_i^2} + \frac{4\pi^2}{h^2} \left( W - \sum_{i,k=1}^n \alpha_{ik} q_i q_k \right) u = 0, \tag{487}
$$

---

$^{636}$ Takeo Hori was born on 7 December 1899, in Toyama Prefecture. After graduating in 1922 from Kyoto University, he obtained a position at Tokyo University (1923–1925); in 1925/26, he returned to Kyoto as a lecturer in a secondary school, and then he continued his studies in Europe and the U.S. (1926–1928), receiving his doctorate at Kyoto University, after which he took over the professorship in Port Arthur. From 1935 on, he occupied a chair in physics at the Hokkaido University in Sapporo. He died in 1994.

$^{637}$ For both papers, we find the corresponding entries in Hund’s *Tagebuch*, dated February and March 1927.
