III.5 From Molecular Theory to Quantum Chemistry 535

where $\alpha_{ik}$ denote constants. By a change of the scale and orthogonal linear transformations, Eq. (487) could be brought into the form of a separable wave equations,

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial \xi_i^2} + \frac{4\pi}{h^2} \left( 2W - \sum_{i=1}^n \omega_i \xi_i^2 \right) u = 0, \tag{488}
$$

whose solutions $u$ turned out to be the products of functions $u_i$, each solving one of the $n$ equations

$$
\frac{\partial^2 u_i}{\partial \xi_i^2} + \frac{4\pi}{h^2} (2W_i - \omega_i^2 \xi_i^2) u_i = 0. \tag{489}
$$

Now, for more than three nuclei, Hund noticed that the relative distances do not suffice to fix the relative positions of the individual nuclei: in particular, for every system having fixed distances of the nuclei from each other, two mirror-symmetric (left and right) systems exist. By a clever introduction of new coordinates, the members of the mirror-symmetric pair might differ only by a change of sign in *one* coordinate. As a function of this coordinate, then, the potential $V$ of the molecule is totally symmetric and possesses two minima, the equilibrium positions; the eigenfunctions of the two mirror-symmetric systems correspond to the symmetric case (in the given coordinate) and the antisymmetric case, respectively. Depending on the shape of the potential between the minima, a beat frequency $|\nu_1 - \nu_2|$ can be defined that describes the change of the state from a symmetric to an antisymmetric eigenfunction.

Hund claimed that this situation characterized a new phenomenon in molecular physics. Using Born’s statistical interpretation of the wave function, he said that ‘the beat frequency determines the average lifetime of the left and right state,’ that ‘stationary states are composed of right and left states,’ and further that for excited states the lifetime is of the order of magnitude of the oscillation period, while for the lower states it may become very large (Hund, *loc. cit.*, p. 810). Evidently, the large stability of right- and left-symmetric modifications of complex molecules in nature did follow easily from a one-dimensional model calculation: with reasonable assumptions on the form of the potential, Hund obtained beat periods up to millions of years, especially when the ratio of the value of the potential at position zero, $V$, to the oscillation quantum, $Q$, was a large number (about 60 to 70—see the table, Hund, *loc. cit.*, p. 814). Hence, he concluded: ‘The transition from a [given] constitution into the mirror-reflected constitution corresponds to a frequency [beat frequency]. This fact does not contradict the existence of optical isomers.’ (Hund, *loc. cit.*, p. 805) He got more than the desired explanation, however, as would become evident soon from other applications of the new phenomenon, which was properly baptized the ‘tunnel effect.’ In Hund’s own concise and well-balanced narrative, the story reads as follows:

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0568 -->

536 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

The consequences of the overlap of the wave functions for atomic nuclei were shown by Hund in May 1927, especially that in this way beat periods between atomic and cosmic frequencies can result. In August 1927 Oppenheimer treated generally in a calculation the overlap between two wells and applied the results to [the problem of] a hydrogen atom in an electric field. The influence of a surface layer, idealized as a [potential] barrier, in the thermal emission [of electrons] from metals was demonstrated by Nordheim in December 1927, and Nordheim and Fowler then showed the role of the overlap for electron emission in strong electric fields. The most impressive consideration of this kind was certainly the explanation of alpha decay of radioactive nuclei by the penetration of a potential barrier between a field of force keeping alpha particles in the interior of the nucleus and the external region, simultaneously proposed by Gurney and Condon (in July 1928) and Gamow (in August 1928). (Hund, 1984, p. 199)

We shall deal with these powerful applications of the Hund phenomenon in the following sections on solid-state (III.6) and nuclear physics (III.7).

Finally, still in the paper on *Molekelspektren. III*, Hund worked out the consequences for the oscillatory wave functions of molecules having equal numbers of nuclear constituents with the help of his characters: his method indeed allowed him to write immediately the formal structure of terms, in principle, for all polyatomic molecules. He then applied similar considerations in the discussion of the terms in rotational spectra. The May 1927 paper concluded the first series of molecular investigations of Friedrich Hund. In summer semester 1927, he lectured, as mentioned above, on ‘*Molekülbau*’ (‘Molecular Structure’), which provided him the opportunity to acquaint himself more deeply with the literature on this topic. He also received the prestigious invitation to review the ‘progress of all systematics and theory of molecular spectra’ at the September meeting of the German Physical Society in Bad Kissingen: see his talk, entitled ‘*Fortschritte der Systematik und Theorie der Molekelspektren*’ (Hund, 1927f).

The empirical knowledge of molecular data had advanced considerably during the previous years, say, beyond the report Adolf Kratzer had presented on the ‘properties of molecules and band spectra’ at the 1924 Innsbruck *Naturforscherversammlung* (Kratzer, 1924). Notably, a new star had risen in this field in Germany, Reinhard Mecke of Bonn.$^{638}$ Beginning in 1923, he entered into the analysis of band spectra on the basis of the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory (e.g., Mecke and P. Lindau, 1924). In a paper on the intensity anomalies observed in certain examples, Mecke derived a ‘theorem of changing multiplicities,’ the molecular

---

$^{638}$ Reinhard Mecke was born in Stettin on 14 July 1895, and studied physics at Marburg, where he obtained his doctorate in 1919. Then, he went to Bonn, where he joined the institute of the well-known spectroscopist Heinrich Konen. In 1923, he was promoted to *Privatdozent*, and in 1927, to an *Extraordinarius*. In 1930, Mecke moved to the University of Heidelberg, and he eventually advanced to a full professorship of theoretical physics at the University of Freiburg; from 1942 to 1963, he served there as professor of physical chemistry. He died in Freiburg on 30 July 1967. Mecke’s scientific work was devoted almost exclusively to the investigation of molecular structure, which he established by explaining data on the basis of physical laws. One of his great pastimes was the determination of the structure of water.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0569 -->

analogue of the ‘*Wechselsatz*’ (‘alteration rule’) in atomic spectra (Mecke, 1924), and in a later note, he demonstrated that the magnitude of the doublet-splitting found in the sequence of molecules, MgF, MgCl, …, BaBr, BaJ, …, differed only little from the splitting of the lowest *p*-term in the neighbouring alkaline atoms, thus obtaining a kind of Landé’s doublet formula for molecules (Mecke, 1925b). These important studies, and the later finding of Raymond Birge, Robert Mulliken, and again Mecke (for the former, see the papers mentioned earlier; for the latter, see Mecke, 1926) led to ‘the conjecture that molecular multiplets, whose splittings remain finite for vanishing rotation, have a similar origin as atomic multiplets’ (Hund, 1927f, p. 780). Mecke also contributed two highly competent and exhaustive reviews on band spectra (Mecke, 1925a; Mecke and Guillery, 1927), to which Hund referred in his talk at Bad Kissingen.

The other main contributor to molecular spectra whom Hund met in those days in spring 1927, as he recalled, was Robert S. Mulliken:

> When I came back [from Copenhagen] to Göttingen, Göttingen was flooded with American visitors. There I got to know Robert Mulliken. He was, of course, interested in my approach to molecular constitution—since he was a specialist in molecular investigations—and I learned many details from him. Our researches ran parallel for a while. (Hund, in Rechenberg, 1994, p. 102)

After the appearance of Hund’s first paper on molecules in April 1926, Mulliken referred to the theoretical work of his German colleague quite regularly.<sup>639</sup>

Hund opened his lecture at Bad Kissingen with the remarks:

> Now two years have passed since our knowledge about the systematics of atomic spectra quite suddenly could be brought into a—with respect to the great wealth of phenomena—surprisingly lucid and simple form. Hence the question could emerge whether the time has come to organize in a similarly lucid way the empirical material on molecular spectra—a task which looks even more complicated—and to give, since the new quantum mechanics provides the possibility of exact calculation, perhaps an exact [i.e., quantitative] theory of molecules. Of the goals [now] appearing, namely *lucid systematics* and *qualitative description of molecular spectra* and, further, a *quantitative calculation of terms*, meanwhile even the former has not been accomplished. But there are *Ansätze*, and I wish to report about them here. (Hund, 1927f, p. 779)

Hund organized the steps of the ‘rapid development’ of the theory of molecular spectra (at least, a far as the analogy to the theory of atomic spectra is concerned) in the following three steps: (1) A systematics of molecular electronic terms in

<sup>639</sup> See the reference in Mulliken’s paper (1926c, note added in proof):
> In a recent important paper, Hund has discussed the importance of the phenomena of electronic multiplicity and fine structure in band spectra. Hund’s theoretical deductions have also a close relation to the more empirical results of the present series of papers. The subject will probably be further treated later. (Mulliken, *loc. cit.*, p. 506)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0570 -->

analogy with atomic spectra is established. (2) By taking over the successful model concepts describing atoms, a systematics of molecular fine structures is obtained. (3) Quantum mechanics also supplies the proper systematics of the coarse structure of molecular spectra and yields more exact results on rotational and oscillational terms.

Evidently, step (1) had been completed by the work of the spectrascopists Birge, Mecke, and Mulliken; in particular, the latter had found the similarity between the spectra of the molecules BO, CN, CO<sup>+</sup>, N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>, and that of the sodium atom (Mulliken, 1925b). Step (2) the systematics of fine structures, had been taken by Mulliken (1926a) and Hund himself (1926) in his first paper, the results of which confirmed the term notation of Birge and Mulliken, as discussed above. With respect to the quantum mechanics of the coarse structure [step (3)], Hund referred to the rotator calculations of Lucy Mensing (1926a) and David Dennison (1926) with matrix methods and Erwin Fues (1926a, b) with wave-mechanical methods; besides, he mentioned some numerical calculations of simple molecules, like H<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> or H<sub>2</sub> (Burrau, 1927). Finally, he summarized his own studies on the motion of electrons in many-centre molecules (Hund, 1927e) and the molecules with equal nuclei giving rise to the prediction of nuclear spin (Hund, 1927c). He concluded in a quite optimistic tone:

> *We have got the principles for a systematics of the coarse structure and the fine structure of the electronic terms*, which enable one to derive qualitatively a term-system for every single molecule. *We know exactly the contribution of the nuclear motion to the terms, we can calculate* in simple cases the electronic terms, and we have obtained a new *Ansatz* to investigate [the properties of] nuclei. (Hund, 1927f, p. 784)

Hund would not return after the Bad Kissingen meeting to Göttingen, but he moved to the University of Rostock, where he had accepted the offer of an extraordinary (associate) professorship a few weeks earlier.

In Göttingen, however, research on molecular theory would not be abandoned. Rather, Max Born and his American student J. Robert Oppenheimer had become involved in the topic and completed in August 1927 a paper entitled ‘*On the Quantum Theory of Molecules*’ (‘On the Quantum Theory of Molecules’), which may be considered as the quantum-mechanical reformulation of the Born–Heisenberg paper of 1924 (Born and Oppenheimer, 1927). Having completed the formalism of the new atomic theory at hand, the authors now wrote a systematic molecular theory based on a quantum-mechanical perturbation scheme in powers of the parameter $\sqrt[4]{m/M}$, where $m$ and $M$ denoted the masses of the electron and the average nucleus, respectively, involved in the constitution of the molecules considered. The abstract summarized the results of their quite formal presentation as:

> The oscillations of the nuclei correspond to the terms of the second order [in $\sqrt[4]{m/M}$], the rotations to those of fourth order in the energy expansion, while the terms of the first and third order vanish. The non-existence of first-order terms stems from the “equilibrium position” of the nuclei, for which the energy of electrons assumes a

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0571 -->

minimum for nuclei at rest. The fourth-order terms for the rotational energy generalize the known *Ansatz* of Kramers and Pauli (Kramers, 1923b; Kramers and Pauli, 1923), who have described the behaviour of molecules by that of a spinning top with a built-in fly wheel. To determine the eigenfunctions, and thus also the transition probabilities, even in zeroth order, one has to pursue the energy calculation up to terms in fourth order (i.e., rotations). One obtains for the probabilities of simultaneous jumps of electronic, oscillational and rotational quantum-number expressions, by which the conceptions developed by Franck and extended formally in detail by Condon received a precise formulation. (Born and Oppenheimer, 1927, p. 458)

With the last remark, Born and Oppenheimer referred to the so-called ‘Franck-Condon principle,’ which Franck had suggested in 1925 in a talk before the Faraday Society in London and Condon had worked out in the following year (Franck, 1925; Condon, 1926). The latter described Franck’s idea in the following words:

> In a “cold” gas the molecules are not vibrating and are in the lowest electronic level so that the unclear motions are governed by [a potential $V_1(r)$]. If now a light-quantum is absorbed which is of sufficient energy to bring the molecule into an excited state, it is natural to suppose that in thus changing the electronic energy of the molecule no other specific action is exerted by the light on the molecule. The absorption of light merely substitutes a new law of interaction, say $V_2(r)$ for the old one $V_1(r)$. But since this new one has a different equilibrium position, the atoms, at the instant after the absorption, will be away from equilibrium and so start to vibrate. Should it happen that
> 
> $$V_2(r_{01}) > V_{2_{\text{max}}} \tag{490}$$
> 
> where $V_{2_{\text{max}}}$ is the maximum value of $V_2(r)$ in the range $r_{01} < r < \infty$ then the molecule will tend to execute oscillations of infinite amplitude. Thus Franck contemplates the photo-chemical dissociation of a molecule by a simple absorption of light. (Condon, 1926, p. 1185)

Condon used Franck’s idea in particular to obtain relative intensities of various bands in a system of electronic bands of molecules; thus, he found, for example, that ‘the theory predicts the existence of two especially favoured values of the change in the vibrational numbers, in accord with the empirical facts as discussed by Birge’ (Condon, *loc. cit.*, p. 1183).<sup>640</sup> Born and Oppenheimer now derived the Franck–Condon principle directly by analyzing their expression for the electric moment of the molecule (Born and Oppenheimer, 1927, p. 476).

The August 1927 paper of Born and Oppenheimer just indicated the beginning of a longer renewed involvement of Max Born and his collaborators in molecular theory. Soon afterward, Walter Heitler and Eugene Wigner would arrive in Göt-

<sup>640</sup> For the origin of Condon’s interest in Franck’s principle, see his report describing how Franck had sent the proofsheets of his 1925 paper to his student Hertha Sponer (then staying in Berkeley), who then showed it to Condon (Condon, 1947, especially, p. 366).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0572 -->

tingen, who would work on the topic. Indeed, Göttingen became one of the centres of modern molecular physics, to which the close cooperation between the institutes of Max Born and James Franck contributed vitally.

**(c) The Heitler–London Theory of the Covalent Bond (1927–1928)**

Just before Friedrich Hund left Copenhagen to return to Göttingen, he delivered a talk on his symmetry investigations with applications to atomic spectra (see Hund, 1927d). He recalled the presence of a visitor in his audience:

> I talked about the thing in Copenhagen, and Heitler was there. He had also not really understood Wigner [i.e., the group theory of Wigner] and this was hard for him. In particular, then I made—and this Wigner had not yet done—the application to multiplet systems, and Heitler was interested in it because he had thought about spectra and the like, and this pleased him. (Hund, AHQP Interview, 26 June 1963, p. 25)

Like Hund, Walter Heitler hailed from Karlsruhe, where he was born on 2 January 1904, as the son of a professor of engineering at the *Technische Hochschule*, of Jewish origin.<sup>641</sup> Although his gymnasium education concentrated on Latin and Greek, Heitler’s interests in science went far beyond the curriculum. In 1922, he began to study at the *Technische Hochschule* in Karlsruhe; a year later, he went to Berlin and attended the lectures of Max Planck on physics and of Richard von Mises on mathematics. He also regularly attended the famous Berlin colloquium with Einstein, Planck, Nernst, and von Laue present. Because Heitler felt that, due to his restricted previous education, he had no chance of completing a doctorate in Berlin—‘The attitude of the professors was more or less: “All right, if you have an idea, work it out and write a thesis; we will either accept it, or we’ll refuse it.” But you could get no help from the professors’ (Heitler, AHQP Interview, 18 March 1963, p. 4)—hence, he went to Munich. ‘My chief line of interest was statistics and thermodynamics, a sort of borderline between physics and chemistry, so it was quite natural that for the Ph.D. thesis I attached myself to [Karl] Herzfeld rather than to Sommerfeld, but I was in Sommerfeld’s department and accepted as a research student.’ (Heitler, *loc. cit.*, p. 5)<sup>642</sup> The subject of Heitler’s thesis concerned the theory of solutions, and he did pass the examinations with Sommerfeld and Willy Wien in 1926. Immediately afterward, Sommerfeld secured for him an International Educational Board fellowship, and recommended him to Niels Bjerrum at the University of Copenhagen.<sup>643</sup> In Copenhagen, Heitler also had

<sup>641</sup> For Heitler’s life and work, see Mott’s biographical memoir of him (Mott, 1982).

<sup>642</sup> Through Herzfeld, Heitler certainly became acquainted with the problem of chemical valence, because this was one of Herzfeld’s favourite topics.

<sup>643</sup> At that time, Heitler published only on the subject of his thesis, although he did write a paper on Einstein’s derivation of Planck’s law (Heitler, 1926) and another, unfortunately wrong one, on the intensity of spectra—‘hence Sommerfeld thought it would be better if I stuck to the subject of my thesis, which was somewhat between physics and chemistry’ (Heitler, *loc. cit.*, p. 3).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0573 -->

III.5 From Molecular Theory to Quantum Chemistry 541

contacts with Niels Bohr’s Institute and with some of the people there, including Werner Heisenberg and Oskar Klein, which strengthened his desire to change to real theoretical physics, especially quantum physics. ‘Well, then I wrote to Schrödinger and asked him if he would accept me for the second half of the Rockefeller [fellowship] time, and he reluctantly did agree, and I went to Zurich to work with Schrödinger. In Zurich, of course, I met [Fritz] London, which was to be the decisive turning point in my career.’ (Heitler, *loc. cit.*, p. 12)<sup>644</sup>

Heitler acquainted himself thoroughly with wave mechanics, but could not develop a collaboration with his professor, Erwin Schrödinger. Fortunately, he soon got to know Fritz London, and the two visitors at once joined efforts to work together on a common task. Heitler recalled about how they got into the particular problem of determining the forces between two atoms:

> We thought just as a small “by the way” problem, to consider the question of van der Waals forces, and we thought that this would be answered by calculating just the interaction of the charges of two atoms. So we set out to calculate the interaction of two hydrogen atoms and their charge densities without thinking even of the exchange. Well, the result was not very encouraging; we got what we later on called the “Coulomb integral,” which was much too big for the van der Waals forces, although it gave some attraction. So we were really stuck, and stuck for quite a while; we didn’t know what it meant and didn’t know what to do with it. (Heitler, *loc. cit.*, pp. 15–16)

Of course, Heisenberg’s papers on the many-body problem and the quantum-mechanical exchange had appeared already (Heisenberg, 1926b, c, e; 1927a), but Heitler and London did not see the connection between the cases treated in those papers with their own problem, because for Heisenberg ‘somehow the exchange was mixed up with resonance—with the resonance of two electrons in the same atom, one excited, one in the ground state,’ and since ‘Heisenberg himself represented it in such a way that the two things seemed inseparable, so that we did not think that the exchange played a role.’ (Heitler, AHQP Interview, 18 March 1963, p. 15) The standstill lasted a few weeks, during which Heitler and London discussed matters frequently before the breakthrough occurred. ‘One day there was a very disagreeable day in Zurich,’ Heitler recalled. *Föhn*, a very hot south wind blew in, disturbing people, some becoming quite cross, others just sleepy. Heitler continued:

> I slept till very late in the morning, found [that] I couldn’t do work at all, had a quick lunch, went to sleep again in the afternoon and slept until five o’clock. When I woke up . . . I had clearly . . . the picture before me of the two wave functions of two hydrogen molecules joined together with a plus and minus and with the exchange in it. So I was very excited, and I got up and thought it out. As soon as I was clear that the exchange did play a role, I called London up, and he came to me as quickly as

---
<sup>644</sup> Heitler left no great impression in Copenhagen; he remembered only that Klein showed a little interest in one of his papers on thermodynamics and statistics of quantum processes (Heitler, 1926a)—but, as he recalled, this paper ‘received a great deal of interest in Göttingen’ (Heitler, *loc. cit.*, p. 12).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0574 -->

542 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

possible. Meanwhile I had already started developing a sort of perturbation theory. We worked together then until rather late at night, and then by that time most of the paper was clear. . . . Well, . . . at least it was not later than the following day that we had the formation of the hydrogen molecule in our hands, and we also knew that there was a second mode of interaction which meant repulsion between two hydrogen atoms—also new at the time—new to the chemists, too. (Heitler, *loc. cit.*, p. 16)

Thus, the idea of the Heitler–London paper on ‘*Wechselwirkung neutraler Atome und homöopolare Bindung nach der Quantenmechanik*’ (‘The Interaction of Neutral Atoms and Homopolar Bond According to Quantum Mechanics’) dramatically saw the light of day—a paper that Linus Pauling would call ‘the greatest single contribution to the clarification of the chemist’s conception which has been made since G. N. Lewis’s suggestion in 1916 that the chemical bond between two atoms consists of a pair of electrons held jointly by the two atoms’ (Pauling and Wilson, 1935, p. 340).

In June 1927, Schrödinger’s young associates completed their manuscript, the results of which they described in the abstract as:

> The interplay of forces between two neutral atoms exhibits a characteristic quantum-mechanical ambiguity . . . suitable to embrace the different behaviours given by experience: for hydrogen, for instance, the possibility of homopolar bond and elastic reflection, respectively, for noble gases *only* the latter—and this already as effects having about the right order of magnitude in the first-order of approximation. In selecting and discussing the different behaviours, the Pauli principle stands the test when applied to systems of *several* [identical] atoms. (Heitler and London, 1927, p. 455) .

Expressed in mathematical language, the crucial idea figured out by Heitler on that *Föhn* day in Zurich for the hydrogen atom consisted in solving the Schrödinger equation for the wave function $\chi$ of the hydrogen molecule ($\Delta_{12}$ being the d’Alembertian operator in position variables)

$$L(\chi) = \Delta_{12}\chi + \frac{8\pi^{2}m}{h^{2}} \left\{ E - \left( \frac{e^{2}}{R} + \frac{e^{2}}{r_{12}} - \frac{e^{2}}{r_{a_{1}}} - \frac{e^{2}}{r_{a_{2}}} - \frac{e^{2}}{r_{b_{1}}} - \frac{e^{2}}{r_{b_{2}}} \right) \right\} = 0 \qquad (491)$$

—with $R$, $r_{12}$, $r_{a_{1}}$, $r_{a_{2}}$, $r_{b_{1}}$, and $r_{b_{2}}$ denoting the distances between the two nuclei $a$ and $b$, the two electrons 1 and 2, and between the electrons and the nuclei, respectively—by perturbative methods starting from the zeroth-order wave functions $\alpha$ and $\beta$, i.e.,

$$\alpha = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 + 2S}} (\psi_{1}\phi_{2} + \psi_{2}\phi_{1}) \qquad (492\text{a})$$

and

$$\beta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 - 2S}} (\psi_{1}\phi_{2} - \psi_{2}\phi_{1}). \qquad (492\text{b})$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0575 -->

III.5 From Molecular Theory to Quantum Chemistry 543

In Eqs. (492), the $\psi$’s and $\phi$’s are given by the well-known eigenfunctions for the hydrogen atom of the electrons 1 and 2; that is, they solve the Schrödinger equation with potentials $e^{2}/r_{a_{i}}$ or $e^{2}/r_{b_{i}}$ providing the ground state energy $E_{0}(= -13.5 \text{ eV})$ for the lowest state of the nuclei $a$ and $b$,

$$\psi_{i} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \left( \frac{1}{a_{0}} \right)^{3/2} \exp \left( - \frac{r_{a_{i}}}{a_{0}} \right) \qquad (493\text{a})$$

and

$$\phi_{i} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \left( \frac{1}{a_{0}} \right)^{3/2} \exp \left( - \frac{r_{b_{i}}}{a_{0}} \right) \qquad (493\text{b})$$

(where $a_{0}$ gives the radius of the first Bohr orbit). Further, $S$ represented the double volume integral over the hydrogen functions, i.e.,

$$S = \int \psi_{1}\phi_{1}\psi_{2}\phi_{2} d\tau_{1} d\tau_{2}. \qquad (494)$$

Now, the perturbed eigenfunctions of the hydrogen molecule were written as

$$\chi_{\alpha} = \alpha + v_{\alpha} \qquad (495\text{a})$$

and

$$\chi_{\beta} = \alpha + v_{\beta}. \qquad (495\text{b})$$

The perturbation terms then satisfied the inhomogeneous differential equations

$$\sqrt{2 + 2S} L(v_{\alpha}) + \left( E_{1} - \frac{e^{2}}{r_{12}} - \frac{e^{2}}{R} \right) \alpha + \left( \frac{e^{2}}{r_{a_{1}}} + \frac{e^{2}}{r_{b_{2}}} \right) \psi_{2}\phi_{1} + \left( \frac{e^{2}}{r_{b_{1}}} + \frac{e^{2}}{r_{a_{2}}} \right) \psi_{1}\phi_{2} = 0 \qquad (496\text{a})$$

and

$$\sqrt{2 - 2S} L(v_{\beta}) + \left( E_{1} - \frac{e^{2}}{r_{12}} - \frac{e^{2}}{R} \right) \beta + \left( \frac{e^{2}}{r_{a_{1}}} + \frac{e^{2}}{r_{b_{2}}} \right) \psi_{2}\phi_{1} - \left( \frac{e^{2}}{r_{b_{1}}} + \frac{e^{2}}{r_{a_{2}}} \right) \psi_{1}\phi_{2} = 0, \qquad (496\text{b})$$

with the perturbation energy $E_{1}$ defined obviously as

$$E_{1} = E - 2E_{0}. \qquad (497)$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0576 -->

544 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

Evidently, the solution of Eqs. (496) for an eigenvalue $E_{1}$ compatible with the solution of the homogeneous Eq. (491)—and the eigenvalue $E$, due to Eq. (497)—demands ‘that the inhomogeneities [i.e., the terms in $\alpha$, $\psi_{2} \phi_{1}$ and $\psi_{1} \phi_{2}$ in Eqs. (496a) and (496b)] are orthogonal on all eigenfunctions of the homogeneous equations, notably, on $\chi_{a}$ and $\chi_{\beta}$ belonging to the same eigenvalue’ (Heitler and London, 1927, p. 459). The definitions of $\alpha$ and $\beta$, Eqs. (492), already fulfilled a part of the requirement [the inhomogeneity of Eq. (496a) is orthogonal to $\beta$ and the inhomogeneity of Eq. (496b) is orthogonal to $\alpha$]; the other part of the requirement [namely, the inhomogeneity of Eq. (496a) is orthogonal to $\alpha$, and that of Eq. (496b) is orthogonal to $\beta$] yielded the perturbed eigenvalues

$$E_{\alpha} = E_{11} - \frac{E_{11}S - E_{12}}{1 + S} \qquad (498\text{a})$$

and

$$E_{\beta} = E_{11} - \frac{E_{11}S - E_{12}}{1 - S}, \qquad (498\text{b})$$

where $E_{11}$ and $E_{12}$ were given by the expressions

$$E_{11} = \int d\tau_{1} d\tau_{2} \left\{ \left( \frac{e^{2}}{r_{12}} + \frac{e^{2}}{R} \right) \frac{\psi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2} + \psi_{2}^{2}\phi_{1}^{2}}{2} - \left( \frac{e^{2}}{r_{a_{1}}} + \frac{e^{2}}{r_{b_{2}}} \right) \frac{\psi_{2}^{2}\phi_{1}^{2}}{2} - \left( \frac{e^{2}}{r_{a_{2}}} + \frac{e^{2}}{r_{b_{1}}} \right) \frac{\psi_{1}^{2}\phi_{2}^{2}}{2} \right\} \qquad (499\text{a})$$

and

$$E_{12} = \int d\tau_{1} d\tau_{2} \left\{ \left( \frac{2e^{2}}{r_{12}} + \frac{2e^{2}}{R} - \frac{e^{2}}{r_{a_{1}}} - \frac{e^{2}}{r_{a_{2}}} - \frac{e^{2}}{r_{b_{1}}} - \frac{e^{2}}{r_{b_{2}}} \right) \frac{\psi_{1}\phi_{1}\psi_{2}\phi_{2}}{2} \right\}. \qquad (499\text{b})$$

The results contained in Eqs. (498) meant, as Heitler and London explained, ‘that two neutral atoms can interact with each other *in two different ways*,’ and:

> We are still quite far from understanding this fact. But it is desirable to obtain at least a clear idea how this strange ambiguity arises. The essential point is obviously that the problem exhibits a double degeneracy corresponding to the two possibilities of distributing the electrons among the neutral atoms. The removal of the degeneracy is connected [in first-order perturbation], as one sees from [Eqs. (498)], with a non-vanishing eigenfunction of the atom $a$ at the position of the atom $b$ and *vice versa* (otherwise $\psi\phi_{1} = 0$, hence $E_{12} = 0$ and $S = 0$); this means that there must exist a finite probability for the electron of atom $a$ to belong to the atom $b$. The exponential behaviour of $\psi$ and $\phi$ [see Eqs. (493)] indeed satisfies this condition. One will interpret the quantity $\frac{1}{h}(E_{\beta} - E_{\alpha})$ as the average frequency for an *exchange* of the two elec-

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0577 -->

545 III.5 From Molecular Theory to Quantum Chemistry

electrons. For large distances, this difference decreases as $\frac{e^{2}}{a_{0}} \exp \left(-\frac{2}{a_{0}} R\right)$, hence distant atoms do have only rare exchanges [thus for gas-kinetic distances of $3.3 \times 10^{-7}$ cm the period assumes a value of the order of $10^{33}$ years, while for crystal distances of $3 \times 10^{-8}$ cm the value is about $10^{-11}$ sec]. (Heitler and London, *loc. cit.*, pp. 460-461)

The observed phenomenon, which had no analogue in classical physics, had clearly to do with an exchange of particles in atoms and molecules; hence, Heitler and London found it to be 'closely related to the quantum-mechanical resonance phenomenon treated by Heisenberg [1926b],' but they also claimed that it was *not identical* with the latter, because of the following reasons:

> While for the resonance phenomenon electrons, having *different* orbital motions *in one and the same sequence of eigenfunctions* [e.g., in the helium atom considered by Heisenberg in 1926b and c], exchange their energy, we have *here* electrons *of the same excited state* (i.e., of the same energy), but *different* systems of eigenfunctions ($\psi$ and $\phi$) exchanging their *positions*. There [i.e., in the situations considered by Heisenberg] the two-fold occurrence of the same *transition frequency* is characteristic (resonance phenomenon); however, *here* one should not talk about *resonance*. (Heitler and London, *loc. cit.*, p. 461)

After this conceptual remark—it seems that Heitler and London had overstated the case and stuck too closely to the helium-atom example of Heisenberg instead of taking into account the generality of the whole resonance approach (see, especially, Heisenberg, 1926e, 1927a)<sup>645</sup>—the authors turned to a qualitative discussion of the interaction energies in Eqs. (498). They first concluded from the general property of the eigenvalue problem—explicitly from the 'Sturm-Liouville eigenvalue problem with homogeneous boundary conditions'—that

$$E_{\beta} > E_{\alpha} \qquad (500)$$

(because the antisymmetric solution has a node that the symmetrical one lacks) and interpreted the expression $E_{11}$ intuitively (*anschaulich*) as the Coulomb interaction of the charge distribution in question, notably,

$$E_{11} = \frac{e^{2}}{a_{0}} \exp \left(-\frac{2}{a_{0}} R\right)\left(\frac{a_{0}}{R}+\frac{5}{8}-\frac{3}{4} \frac{R}{a_{0}}-\frac{1}{6} \frac{R^{2}}{a_{0}^{2}}\right). \qquad (501)$$

---
<sup>645</sup> It would be Linus Pauling, who would later emphasize the 'resonance' aspect in the Heitler-London exchange-integral approach (as we shall discuss). Therefore, we cannot agree with this overstatement of a difference between the Heisenberg and the Heitler-London use of the exchange-integral, as is occasionally stressed in the historical literature (see, e.g., Carson, 1996). Of course, this does not take away from the fact that Heitler and London initiated by their hydrogen-molecule investigation a new and fundamentally important application of Heisenberg's concept of quantum-mechanical resonance.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0578 -->

546 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

For the integral $S$, they wrote

$$S = \left(1 + \frac{R}{a_{0}} + \frac{R^{2}}{3 a_{0}^{2}}\right)^{2} \exp \left(-\frac{2 R}{a_{0}}\right), \qquad (502)$$

and for $E_{12}$, they only derived an upper limit

$$E_{12} < -\frac{2 e^{2}}{a_{0}}\left(\frac{11}{16} + \frac{27}{16} \frac{R}{a_{0}} + \frac{27}{24} \frac{R^{2}}{a_{0}^{2}} + \frac{R^{3}}{3 a_{0}^{3}}\right) + \frac{e^{2}}{R} S. \qquad (503)$$

Consequently, the solution $E_{\beta}$ always represented repulsion, and $E_{\alpha}$ always exhibits attraction for large distances, a minimum distance at $R = \frac{3}{2} a_{0}$, and repulsion for smaller distances. 'The non-polar attraction found here shows up as a characteristic quantum-mechanical effect,' Heitler and London emphasized and added that it emerged already without considering the perturbations caused by the polarization effect. On the other hand, also, the repulsion obtained in the solution $E_{\beta}$ 'goes back to this quantum-mechanical effect, not to the Coulomb interaction' (Heitler and London, 1927, p. 462). Altogether, 'the antisymmetrical solution with the interaction energy $E_{\beta}$ corresponds to the *van der Waals repulsion* (i.e., the elastic reflection) of the two hydrogen atoms,' while the symmetrical solution $E_{\alpha}$ corresponds to the situation that 'the two hydrogen atoms combine to [form] a *homo-polar* molecule, with the minimum of $E_{\alpha}$ representing the level [of energy]' (Heitler and London, *loc. cit.*, pp. 462-463). They finally noticed that the solution given yielded approximately the properties of the hydrogen molecule: the diameter, the dissociation energy, and the moment of inertia.

Another remarkable result of the Heitler-London paper consisted in the authors' demonstration that in the case of two *non-excited* noble gas atoms no attractive solution $E_{\alpha}$ exists. In particular, the unperturbed eigenfunctions, $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$, and $\delta$, would then form four noncombining term systems; then, the Pauli principle would immediately exclude the attractive $E_{\alpha}$-solution, and the remaining $E_{\beta}$-solution would exhibit no binding effect.<sup>646</sup> The same conclusion applied to all molecules built from atoms or ions having closed electron shells.

Heitler and London completed their detailed and thorough investigation by discussing the situation of the hydrogen-molecule ions. They demonstrated especially that 'the polar molecule formation [for H<sup>−</sup> and H<sup>+</sup> combining to form a hydrogen molecule] does not represent a stable configuration of the two hydrogen atoms in a molecule' (Heitler and London, *loc. cit.*, p. 471). Ultimately, they concluded their paper with the optimistic statement: 'We tend to believe that the

---
<sup>646</sup> The eigenfunctions considered by Heitler and London had the following property: they changed or retained their sign when two electrons were exchanged having the same or different spin. For the hydrogen molecule, the solution $E_{\alpha}$ (corresponding to $1^1S$-state of the helium atom) exhibited strong attraction, and the solution $\beta$ (for electrons with the same spin) had to be excluded. Heitler and London did not yet consider the spin of the hydrogen nuclei.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0579 -->

547 III.5 From Molecular Theory to Quantum Chemistry

types of degeneracies and symmetry relations obtained here are characteristic of a large domain of facts which are connected with the mutual interactions of atomic systems, especially with the discontinuities in their chemical behaviour.' Moreover, further applications, such as in the collision of electrons with atoms or of alpha particles with atomic nuclei seemed feasible (footnote 3, pp. 471-472).

As Heitler recalled, the paper on the hydrogen molecule came about by 'rather quick and easy work': the authors 'had a little trouble with the evaluation of one integral [i.e., the one appearing in the expression for $E_{12}$]' because they 'were not very good mathematicians'; and they 'had to struggle with the proper formulation of the Pauli principle' (Heitler, AHQP Interview, 26 June 1963, p. 16). The latter difficulty indeed gave the scheme developed some provisional character, but Heitler and London would improve on this very soon, after they went to places where they learned how to handle the problem properly by group-theoretical methods—namely, Heitler to Göttingen and London to Berlin. Before these moves took place, Heitler presented some of their results in a local meeting of the German Physical Society at Freiburg on 12 June 1927, where the chemists in particular (like George de Hevesy) received them favourably.<sup>647</sup> The authors also sent copies of their manuscript to Göttingen and Munich. 'Born showed it to Franck and he replied immediately very enthusiastically,' recalled Heitler, and further that it took Sommerfeld somewhat longer; then, he accepted their solution and recommended Heitler, whose Rockefeller fellowship ended in fall 1927, to a vacant assistantship in Cologne. On his way to Cologne, Heitler made a detour via Göttingen; there, Born offered him 'the just vacant position of his assistant' (Heitler, *loc. cit.*, p. 18); Heitler accepted and succeeded Lothar Nordheim, who had gone on a fellowship of the International Education Board to Cambridge, England.

Fritz London left Zurich at about the same time as Walter Heitler; in October 1927, Erwin Schrödinger succeeded Max Planck in the chair of theoretical physics at the University of Berlin, and he invited Fritz London to accompany him as his assistant. We have mentioned London's name several times at earlier places, notably, in connection with Schrödinger's work (in Volume, Part 2, pp. 312-313) and here in Chapter I, where quantum-mechanical transformation theory was discussed. London was four years senior to Heitler; he had studied philosophy at the University of Munich from 1918 to 1921 and obtained his doctorate in 1921.<sup>648</sup>

While he planned to become a gymnasium teacher (examinations in 1922 and 1924), his interest shifted to physics (see his paper on similitude: London, 1922), but only in 1925 did he start his new career at Sommerfeld's institute in Munich.<sup>649</sup> In Munich (April to October 1925), he was drawn into a collaboration on band spectra with Helmut Hönl (Hönl and London, 1925), and Sommerfeld recommended the former young philosopher to his old student Paul Ewald as an assistant at the *Technische Hochschule* in Stuttgart (October 1925 to April 1927); from there, London went on a Rockefeller Foundation fellowship to Zurich.<sup>650</sup> 'London was very, very fond of Greek,' recalled Heitler, and 'He was very much interested in philosophy, and he took physics ... as a tool to a more philosophical outlook on the world.' Also, 'his interest in theoretical physics was much broader than mine. ... London always urged me to study the more general aspects of quantum mechanics.' (Heitler, *loc. cit.*, p. 17) Initially, it seemed that London showed less interest in formal mathematical aspects, for as Heitler recalled: 'Wigner's papers had appeared by that time, and I saw immediately that they would be useful for further development of this theory of chemical bonds, but London wanted to get on in his more intuitive way.' (Heitler, *loc. cit.*) So Heitler turned in summer 1927 to a study of group theory; already, in October, he submitted, still from Zurich, the next paper on the exchange of electrons and the chemical bonds (Heitler, 1927). About a month later, London finished his next investigation dealing with a similar topic, but working only with a few symmetry considerations, taken from Hund's paper on symmetry characters (London, 1928a).

Heitler opened his new contribution with a general introduction on the 'quantum-mechanical exchange phenomenon,' which 'creates in helium the spectroscopic separation of singlet and triplet terms and provides the possibility that two neutral atoms either repel each other or join in a homopolar bond' (Heitler, 1927, p. 47). That is, by now he had obviously come to the conclusion, different from what he and London had stated earlier, that Heisenberg's 'resonance phenomenon' and the Heitler-London 'exchange phenomenon' were the same quantum-mechanical phenomena, caused in a two-electron problem by the (exchange) integral $J$, where

$$J = \pm \int H\psi(1)\psi(2)\phi(1)\phi(2) d\tau, \qquad (504)$$

with $H$ the perturbation function (of the Hamiltonian) and $\psi$ and $\phi$ denoting

Although this statement underlined the nonvisual character of the quantum-mechanical exchange phenomenon, Heitler now hoped to be able to use the perturbation theory of the previous paper with London to establish a relation between the many-dimensional $q$-space and the usual three-dimensional coordinate space.$^{653}$ ‘If the perturbation energy consisted always of a sum of *exchange* terms,’ he argued, ‘then one might be tempted to think of replacing the $q$-space description by a description in terms of exchanges’ (Heitler, *loc. cit.*).$^{654}$ In obtaining the perturbation scheme for quantum-mechanical problems involving more than three particles, the group-theoretical methods of Heisenberg, Wigner, and Hund—Heitler explicitly cited the publications: Heisenberg, 1927a; Wigner, 1927a and b; and Hund, 1927a—now seemed to be adequate. Although these authors had already obtained general information about the classification of eigenfunctions, a systematic knowledge of the corresponding energy values was still lacking, a task that Heitler now attacked ‘following closely the procedure of Wigner and Hund’ (Heitler *loc. cit.*, p. 49).

In §1–§3 of his paper, Heitler recapitulated the main results from the mathematical theory of permutation groups and their representations, including the theorems of group characters. Then, he presented (in §4) the theorem on the centre-of-mass energy expressed in terms of group characters.$^{655}$ Finally, he introduced Hund’s symmetry characters and showed how they might be used to calculate the group characters $\chi_{\lambda}^{\sigma}$ in Eq. (466). By applying these methods to many-body systems, Heitler showed that ‘each system is distinguished by a characteristic term frequency $\nu_{\sigma}$, which is the *sum* (or *difference*, respectively) *of simple exchange frequencies $\nu_P$*’ (Heitler, *loc. cit.*, p. 63), and further:

550 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

In *classical mechanics* the number of principal oscillations [modes] is equal to the number of degrees of freedom. In *quantum mechanics* the number of term-systems is determined by the multiplicity of the permutation group. The newly arising perturbation frequencies thus appear as *exchange* frequencies. (Heitler, *loc. cit.*)

We have already discussed the other results of Heitler’s investigation in Section III.4 above, and shall proceed to talk about three further papers, all dealing with the quantum theory of the homopolar bond. In the first, Fritz London timidly approached symmetry methods, but he was less concerned with the practical calculations of energy terms (as Heitler was) than he wished ‘to discover the conceptual essentials (*begriffliche Wesenheiten*), which have been substantiated in chemistry even in complicated cases as guide through a variety of possible compounds, also in their quantum-mechanical description, and to view them in the context of the structure of atoms’:

> One would, in particular, attempt to provide the valence-numbers of the homopolar compounds a suitable interpretation based on the conceptions of wave mechanics, in a way corresponding to how the *polar* valence-numbers found a fruitful, though not in all details satisfactory, interpretation through the ideas of Kossel and Lewis. (London, 1928a, p. 455)

London claimed that the points of view worked out by Heitler and himself previously to characterize the quantum-mechanical behaviour of hydrogen and helium atoms toward molecular bonds might be generalized, such that the so-called homopolar bonds in chemistry could be explained as a special case of a much larger group of nonpolar bonds (in which probably the different metallic, carbonic, and noble-gas-like bonds have to be included).

The analysis of the quantum-mechanical $n$-electron problem had, since the pioneering studies of Heisenberg in June 1926, yielded a certain multivaluedness of the interaction energy of such systems as a function of the atomic distance, restricted by Pauli’s principle. The electron spin, together with the Pauli principle, was found to give rise to the homopolar attraction in the case of hydrogen. London now worked out the case of combining an $n$-electron system with an $m$-electron system. By introducing eigenfunctions separated in the spin and the space coordinates, i.e., $\psi(1,2,\dots n)u(1,2,\dots n)$ and $\phi(1,2,\dots m)v(1,2,\dots m)$, he obtained term systems according to Wigner’s procedure (1927a), arriving at the result:

> *If two atomic systems, whose states are given, are brought into interaction, then besides the original symmetric connections* [in the spatial functions] *only those occur as new, which combine disconnected electrons from different atoms. . . .*
>
> *If the eigenfunctions of atoms contain only arguments connected symmetrically in pairs (e.g., in the case of noble gases), then the addition of a new atom cannot create a new symmetric connection.* (London, 1928a, p. 463)

These considerations might be extended when a third atom is included into the system, though one must then take into account in which sequence they will then be brought together into interaction.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0583 -->

**III.5** From Molecular Theory to Quantum Chemistry 551

The conclusions obtained so far allowed London to interpret directly the concept of valence in terms of quantum mechanics according to the following rules (see London, *loc. cit.*, §4, pp. 465–467):

(1) If a combination of two originally separate atomic systems increases the number of symmetrically combined parts of electron position coordinates, then one homopolar valence becomes saturated.
(2) A once-saturated valence cannot become effective again (this follows from the theorem that a pair of symmetrically bound electrons can form with a third one only a symmetrical aggregate that is excluded by Pauli’s principle).
(3) The free valence of a group of atoms denotes a property of a peculiar atom; hence, the use of ‘valence dashes’ in chemistry can be founded in quantum mechanics.
(4) The valence electrons of an atom have antisymmetrically combined centre-of-mass coordinates; the valuedness of an atom is smaller by one unit than the multiplicity of the term considered and equals the resulting electron spin in a weak magnetic field (in units of $h/4\pi$).
(5) The saturation of a valence is accompanied by the reduction of the resulting spin by one unit; a double-bond is connected with a reduction of two units.

In §5, London demonstrated how these rules would apply in practical cases, and in §6, he distinguished clearly between the concepts of homopolar and ionic bonds: basically, if the distance between atoms $R_s$ is larger than the extension of the electron clouds, the bond is ionic; smaller $R_s$, on the other hand, leads to a homopolar bond.$^{656}$

In two further papers of 1928, which originated apparently without knowledge of each other’s work, Heitler and London tried to calculate the interaction energies of homopolar bonds assisted by group-theoretical methods (Heitler, 1928; London, 1928b).$^{657}$ Heitler gave a summary of his work ‘*Zur Gruppentheorie der homöopolaren chemischen Bindung*’ (‘On the Group Theory of Homopolar Chemical Bond’), dealing with the perturbation energy of two atoms $A$ and $B$ having $n$ valence electrons each, in the sentence: ‘If both atoms are in the highest state of multiplicity (namely $(n+1)$-fold), there exists among the various interaction energies one—sometimes several—which describes an *attraction* between $A$ and $B$, thus implying the formation of a molecule’ (Heitler, 1928, p. 835). In Heitler’s opinion, this conclusion explained the most important homopolar molecules, notably, the $\text{N}_2$- and $\text{CH}_4$-molecules. London, on the other hand, criticized aspects of the perturbation treatment of his former collaborator. He wrote in particular: ‘It seems to me that this formalism [as in Heitler, 1928] does not correspond to the interaction of *exactly* given atoms and cannot lead to a clear answer to the ques-

$^{656}$ The density distributions of homopolar-bound hydrogen molecules overlap; i.e., the lines of equal density enclose both nuclei; in the case of two helium atoms (which allow only elastic reflections), the lines of equal densities in the electron clouds enclose mostly only one nucleus (see London, 1928a, Figures 2 and 3, p. 1476).

$^{657}$ Even the initially hesitant London now made use of the refined mathematical results of Frobenius and Schur (see the references in London, 1928b, pp. 29, 32, 33).

552 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

tion dealt with here, since by neglecting all interactions of the external electrons we *cannot define sufficiently* the state of the actually reacting atoms’ (London, 1928b, footnote, pp. 26–27).

We shall not enter into the details of the quite elaborate arguments of Heitler and London, but just register the fact that they continued further their ambitious programme of obtaining a basis for the chemical bonds in quantum physics. Instead, we shall conclude this subsection with a few remarks on a different paper written by Eugene Wigner and E. E. Witmer (who spent some time in Göttingen on an American research fellowship). In their lengthy memoir, entitled ‘*Über die Struktur der zweiatomigen Molekelspektren nach der Quantenmechanik*’ (‘On the Structure of Diatomic Molecular Spectra due to Quantum Mechanics’) and submitted in July 1928, the authors systematically studied molecular spectra with Wigner’s previously developed group-theoretical methods for atoms (Wigner and Witmer, 1928).

The theoretical basis of the new work of Wigner and Witmer was provided by the general scheme of Born and Oppenheimer (1927), the experimental input and its analysis was provided by the papers of Ralph Kronig and Isidor Rabi (1927) and Robert S. Mulliken (1926c, d; 1927a, b, c, d). Finally, the authors occasionally referred to the theory of Heitler and London (1927) and Heitler’s (1928) and London’s (1928b) recent papers. The results of this perhaps strictest group-theoretical discussion of molecular spectra agreed essentially with those obtained by Hund (1926; 1927a, c, d).$^{658}$ At the end of their paper, Wigner and Witmer talked about a new, as yet unpublished work of Hund that seemed to open new vistas in molecular theory, especially:

> Hund has the advantage of becoming largely independent of the knowledge of atomic terms. The method used by us [and by Hund earlier] has the advantage that the removal of nuclei corresponds to a process that can be recognized directly in the way the bands converge, hence the association of the molecular terms to the terms of the separated atom is given uniquely by the spectra themselves. To the decoupling of the electron’s interaction [i.e., Hund’s new method] there does not correspond a similar process, hence the association of terms to the “unperturbed terms” may often occur in an arbitrary way. (Wigner and Witmer, 1928, p. 886)

Nevertheless, the building up (*Aufbau*) scheme of molecules addressed here would become a serious competitor of the Heitler–London theory in explaining the homopolar chemical bond.

**(d) The Foundation of Quantum Chemistry (1928–1932)**

Since 1927, a substantial change had occurred in the knowledge of forces that created chemical compounds, as Hans Grimm and H. Wolf explained in their

$^{658}$ Just in a matter of detail, Wigner and Witmer deviated from Hund’s earlier analysis, which they ascribed to an incomplete consideration of all of the symmetry properties in the latter.

### III.5  From Molecular Theory to Quantum Chemistry <span style="float:right;">553</span>

article on ‘*Atombau und Chemie*’ (‘Atomic Structure and Chemistry’) in the second edition of Geiger–Scheel’s *Handbuch der Physik*. They wrote:

    The classification of the chemical forces will be introduced according to the type of their bonds, and in particular we distinguish between the following four types of bonds: 1. Ionic bonds; 2. Atomic bonds; Metallic bonds; Bonds due to van der Waals forces. . . .
    The compounds, in which one discovers no sign of a constitution of ions will be called—apart from the metallic ones—atomic bonds or *homopolar* bonds (due to James Franck). The latter notation, which has also been applied recently by London and others, stems from Abegg and Kossel. Dumas and Nernst have called it *unitary* (*unitarisch*) besides talking about valence bonds or genuine *chemical bonds* (Grimm and Wolf, 1933, p. 949 and p. 968)

Before that time, only two types of chemical bonds were mentioned, the ‘polar’ and the ‘nonpolar’ ones (Grimm and Wolf, *loc. cit.*, footnote 2, p. 968).<sup>659</sup> It was the physicists who contributed most to the clarification of the nature of the chemical bond, and it may be suitable to begin the story with an invited talk that Friedrich Hund gave in May 1928 before the *Bunsen-Gesellschaft* (German Association for Physical Chemistry) in Munich, entitled ‘*Quantenmechanik und chemische Bindung*’ (‘Quantum Mechanics and the Chemical Bond’) (Hund, 1928a).
After arriving in Rostock in October 1927, Hund would not stop working on molecular theory. He soon thought—as the entry in his *Tagebuch* on 7 November indicated—about the symmetry of the rotation of the CH₄ molecule, which later led to a paper on that subject (Hund, 1928b) and about the selection rules for molecular spectra.<sup>660</sup> Toward the end of the first semester as professor in Rostock, Hund received a prestigious invitation to give a talk at the Munich meeting of the German physicochemists in May, and he prepared his manuscript between 16 March and 3 April 1928. He began his lecture by saying that:

    since the new quantum mechanics of Heisenberg and Schrödinger permits, according to the opinion of the theoretical physicists, to calculate in principle all the properties of the molecules, it must be possible also to formulate the hitherto empirical concepts (ionic molecules, atomic molecules, and valence) either rigorously or approximately or prove them to be unsuitable. (Hund, 1928a, p. 437)

What Hund strived for was ‘to gain a theoretical interpretation of the empirical [i.e., chemical] concepts,’ notably, ‘to derive simple facts known for a long time from the laws of quantum mechanics.’ He employed a method that the physicists had learned long before the advent of the new atomic theory, namely, the adiabatic change of couplings between the constituents of atoms and molecules, such

<sub>659</sub> In their *Handbuch* article, Grimm and Wolf wished to avoid talking simply about polar and nonpolar bonds, because the appellation ‘polar’ was also used for substances bound by homopolar forces having a permanent dipole moment, such as HCl or H₂O.
<sub>660</sub> On 3 January 1928, he wrote in his *Tagebuch*: ‘The ‘Laporte’ selection rule, $\Delta\Sigma n$ = odd, applies also to molecules.’

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0586 -->

### 554  Chapter III  The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

that, for instance, a continuous transition occurs between two atoms, a two-centre molecule and a more complex atom; then, the terms pertaining to the molecule can be related to those of the complex atom, in a manner shown in his previous papers of 1926 and 1927 discussed earlier. Moreover, Hund pointed out, a certain relation can be established between the spectra of atoms and molecules: in particular, an ‘ionic molecule’ (i.e., a molecule bound by ionic or polar forces) is often shown to possess the ground state of an ion, while that of an ‘atomic molecule’ (i.e., one bound by homopolar forces) possesses the ground state of an atom. ‘Unfortunately, this distinction is only apparently a rigorous one,’ he emphasized, because:

    If, for instance, in a continuous change of a property of the mechanical system [i.e., in the adiabatic transition described above], once two terms coincide and then separate again by further change, then the association of the terms before and after the coincidence cannot always be made unambiguously. It might even happen that terms, which cross over in an approximate calculation, do not coincide in the rigorous evaluation. (Hund, *loc. cit.*, p. 439)

Obtaining the systematics of terms (i.e., the term scheme) for a diatomic molecule would not automatically decide the problem of the lowest energy state, Hund stated in his talk in Munich. Indeed, only a few cases had been evaluated with some rigour so far, as for instance the hydrogen molecule ion (Sugiura, 1927). Even the method advocated by Heitler and London (1927) for the hydrogen molecule and its generalization by London (1928a)—i.e., that strongly bound molecules arise only from increasing the number of equivalent electron pairs—would not do the job. Hund criticized this method, because ‘one has to assume that such a qualitative argument does not allow sufficient insight into the detailed energetic situation, similarly the observation that the concept of valence does not always give the chemist an entirely secure answer about the compounds existing in reality’ (Hund, *loc. cit.*, pp. 440–441).
Indeed, Hund had already earlier raised objections against certain details of the Heitler–London theory of molecular bonds, e.g., against the role that these authors had given in it to the Pauli principle.<sup>661</sup> Now, in May 1928, he stressed that Heitler’s calculation of the energy states (in Heitler, 1928) ‘was valid only for particularly simple cases’ (Hund, 1928a, p. 441), and he argued that whether the formalization of an electron pair did produce a chemical bond must also depend on the energetic behaviour of the rest of the molecule, because sometimes the energy gain by pairing happens to be very small.<sup>662</sup> After the meeting, Friedrich Hund exchanged letters with Fritz London, who did not agree with some of the formulations of the Munich talk. Hund recalled that they really advocated different interpretations of the chemical-bond problem:

<sub>661</sub> Thus, Hund noted in his *Tagebuch* on 2 September 1927: ‘Heitler and London’s interpretation of the role of Pauli’s principle in the formation of molecules, I consider to be wrong (*schief*).’
<sub>662</sub> Hund remarked more sharply in his *Tagebuch* on 21 June 1928: ‘London’s valence interpretation leads to difficulties. The symmetric combination of electrons does not always lead to the lowest state.’

### III.5  From Molecular Theory to Quantum Chemistry <span style="float:right;">555</span>

London insisted on a representation of the chemical conception of valence in the language of quantum mechanics, while I considered this to be a formal representation; however, I did not understand the real [question] of the bond. London relied on the fact that an exchange integral will provide the right sign—he could not actually evaluate it, while for me the lowering of the molecular state was the important thing. Starting with the separated atoms, one must obtain a lowering of the ground state, and this lowering I just recognized in the overlap of the eigenfunctions, in the absence of a node in between. Though Herzberg later formulated this idea much better and more correctly in chemistry—I still regret that I did not do it as well, even a year later—, for me the lowering of the ground state of the atom was always important.
(Hund, AHQP Interview, 26 June 1963, p. 26)

To sum up, in May 1928, Hund stated clearly that the task of applying quantum mechanics to chemistry actually consisted of three problems: first, what was the position that the *concept of valence* assumed in quantum mechanics; second, which molecules existed for given atoms or atomic compounds *and how strongly were they bound*; third, what did the *term scheme and the spectrum of molecules look like*? Only the first question (by London) and the third question (by Hund) had thus far received a preliminary treatment and answer.
To answer the second question, which had essentially to do with determining the exact position of the lowest state of a molecule, Hund introduced a building-up principle (*Aufbauprinzip*, similar to the one known in atomic physics) for molecules in the next programmatic talk, which he gave on 21 September 1928, at the *Naturforscherversammlung* in Hamburg (Hund, 1928c). He formulated it as follows: one takes a system of two nuclear centres at an arbitrary distance and then lets the nuclei approach each other to assume an equilibrium position; in the course of this procedure, two electrons may couple to a $\sigma$-electron pair (having zero angular momentum about the axis connecting the two nuclei); thus, *closed shells of molecules are obtained in a process starting from electrons in atomic shells* (Hund, 1928c, p. 851). For details of the new principle, Hund referred to a recent paper published in the August issue of the *Physical Review* (Mulliken, 1928a).<sup>663</sup>
Its author, the American physical chemist Robert Sanderson Mulliken, was of the same age as Friedrich Hund and was at that time an assistant professor of chemistry at New York University; he had already contributed to molecular spectroscopy for years.<sup>664</sup> His research on the isotope effect in band spectra (Mulliken, 1925a, b, c) had already received considerable interest in Europe (see Volume 2, p. 270). In 1925, he also visited several European centres of atomic and molecular

<sub>664</sub> Robert S. Mulliken was born on 7 June 1896, in Newburyport, Massachusetts, and studied from 1913 to 1917 at MIT. In 1917, he joined the U. S. Bureau of Mines (as a junior chemical engineer, and later a chemist); in 1919, he continued his studies at the University of Chicago, where he received his Ph.D. in 1921. From 1921 to 1925, he held a National Research Council Fellowship, working first at the University of Chicago and later (from 1923) at Harvard University; in 1926, he joined New York University.

spectroscopy, including London (Alfred Fowler) and Bonn (Reinhard Mecke); two years later, he went to Copenhagen and Göttingen, where he spent some time at Max Born’s Institute.
Mulliken recalled that quite early in the 1920s he was deeply impressed by the *Aufbau* principle in atomic theory:

    I have a sort of feeling that it was after getting to Harvard that I was really looking at it intensively. . . . I thought it was very exciting but then perhaps there was an interval and I got the *Aufbau* idea. (Mulliken, AHQP Interview, 1 February 1964, p. 14)

By the ‘*Aufbau* idea’ Mulliken meant the concept of translating the orbitals in atoms into corresponding orbitals in molecules. Earlier indications of molecular orbits may perhaps be traced to a remark in the paper of Hendrik Kramers and Wolfgang Pauli (1923, p. 364), where they interpreted the complex structure of band spectra as being due to electron configurations. Afterward, several authors wrote about electron orbits in molecules, notably, Reinhard Mecke (1924) and John William Nicholson (1925). In his notes to the *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences* of March 1926, Mulliken—referring to the analogy between molecular and atomic spectra noticed by Raymond Birge and Reinhard Mecke—explicitly constructed $S$-, $P$-, and $D$-orbits of molecules (Mulliken, 1926a, b), and in the paper submitted in June of the same year to *Physical Review*, he expressed the band spectra of diatomic molecules in terms of such electron orbits (Mulliken, 1926c). In 1927, he extended these investigations to include also a discussion of the intensity relations from the point of view of the correspondence principle (Mulliken, 1927a, b). At the same time, he began to establish the connections with Hund’s quantum-mechanical theory of molecules (Hund, 1926). In particular, he stated in the abstract of the second paper:

    After a brief review of Hund’s theory of molecular electronic states and band spectra, and a discussion of the intensity relations and selection principles in terms of the correspondence principle, it is shown that practically all the available evidence, as embodied in previous papers of this series and elsewhere, is in agreement with the theory. (Mulliken, 1927b, p. 637)

Then, in April 1928—after an intense meeting with Hund in Göttingen the previous summer<sup>665</sup>—Mulliken finally submitted the first of a new series of papers, entitled ‘The Assignment of Quantum Numbers for Electrons in Molecules,’

Hund and I were talking very closely together about that; I was presenting all these things organized from a rather empirical viewpoint, and he translated properly and explained them in the right way. In 1928, just after that I got out a paper on the electronic states rather in terms of what he had been doing. (Mulliken, AHQP Interview, 1 February 1964, p. 15)

III.5 From Molecular Theory to Quantum Chemistry

557

and—as he wrote explicitly in the abstract—“the methods used involve the application and extension of Hund’s theoretical work on the electronic states of molecules” (Mulliken, 1928a, p. 186).

In comparison with Hund’s earlier work (until 1927), Mulliken especially wanted to go further in assigning individual quantum numbers to the states of the molecule. To achieve his goal, he explicitly introduced two assumptions: the first claimed that the solutions for a given molecule must somehow be an interpolation between two limiting cases, (1) two separate atoms and (2) the united atom.<sup>666</sup> Mulliken described the second assumption as follows:

> Bohr’s method of determining electron configurations in atoms by imagining all electrons removed, and then returning them one by one, each to the available orbit of lowest energy, is less applicable to molecules on account of the difficulties in predicting binding energies for various orbit-types. But once a body of information in regard to binding energies has been built up on the basis of spectroscopic and other facts, this method should be helpful. (Mulliken, loc. cit., p. 190)

This second assumption, of course, represented what Mulliken (and Hund) called the *Aufbau* (building-up) principle in molecular physics. Mulliken further emphasized that, due to Hund (1927a), the Pauli principle sometimes forces electrons in the molecule to assume a higher quantum number than in the separated atoms (from which the molecule emerges); hence, they become what he called ‘promoted’ electrons (Mulliken, 1928a, p. 194). Altogether, he classified the electrons in a molecule ‘according to their *bonding power*, positive, zero, or negative,’ i.e.:

> Electrons whose presence tends to hold a molecule together, as judged by the fact that their removal from a stable molecule, causes a decrease in the energy of dissociation *D* or an increase in the equilibrium internuclear separation *r*<sub>0</sub>, may be said to have *positive bonding* power, and are identified, or defined as *bonding electrons*. The definitions of bonding power in terms of changes of *D*, and the changes of *r*<sub>0</sub>, are unfortunately not in general equivalent, and we must accordingly distinguish “energy-bonding power” and “distance-bonding power.” On the whole, promoted electrons tend to show a negative energy-bonding power, unpromoted electrons positive energy-bonding power, but much should depend on “orbit dimensions.” (Mulliken, loc. cit., p. 186)

With these and further rules, Mulliken evaluated the quantum numbers for diatomic molecules, such as BO, CO<sup>+</sup>, CN, N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>, CO, N<sub>2</sub>, NO, O<sub>2</sub>, etc. He found especially that BO, CO<sup>+</sup>, and CN have a low-lying <sup>2</sup>P-state (as compared with the <sup>2</sup>P-state of the analogous Na atom), and that the N<sub>2</sub> molecule must have metastable levels (due to the nonexistence of certain band lines). Finally, let us mention that Mulliken did cite the pioneering papers of Heitler and London (1927), Heitler

<sup>666</sup> Hund had used this assumption in his molecular theory from the very beginning, as we have discussed earlier.

Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

(1927, 1928), and London (1928a) but, like Hund, he expressed some criticism with respect to the validity of some of their conclusions.<sup>667</sup>

Mulliken’s new paper, of which Hund received an advance copy—for he noted it in his *Tagebuch* already on 12 and 13 July—pleased the latter very much, though he was working on a long paper of his own, the fourth and final one in the series ‘Zur Deutung der Molekelspektren’ (‘On the Interpretation of Molecular Spectra’) published since the previous year. He worked on the manuscript of that paper before the end of the summer semester and finished the first draft on 24 July, completing a revised version on 9 October 1928.<sup>668</sup> He devoted the main part of the new investigation to diatomic molecules (Hund, 1928d, pp. 762–791); only in the last few pages did Hund add a few remarks on multi-atomic molecules. As Mulliken had done, he used the *Aufbau* principle to construct the lowest energy states of a molecule (Hund, *loc cit.*, pp. 765–770) and considered the various couplings of the electrons qualitatively in some detail, thus obtaining a variety of possible term schemes. As particular examples, Hund selected molecules containing a hydrogen atom (hydrites) whose spectra allowed a relatively clear interpretation. In the case of multi-atomic molecules, the Heitler–London interpretation of the chemical bond seemed to him less doubtful than in the diatomic case, because in the former molecules each quantum orbit contains not more than two electrons; he wrote:

> The fertility of the concept of the binding electron pair (Lewis, London) apparently rests on the fact that in the molecule the number of electrons per closed shell is often only 2, in some cases 4. When such a four-[electron] shell contains only two electrons, by a small change of the coupling relations a situation can be obtained in which all the electrons are in closed shells. For complex molecules, we have reason to assume only the existence of two-[electron] shells. (Hund, *loc cit.*, p. 794)

As Hund emphasized, however, the simple Heitler–London concept of binding electron pairs deviated from chemical reality, as the C-atom would possess only two instead of four valences; further, in London’s theory, occasionally unsaturated valences can occur in existing molecules.

<sup>667</sup> Mulliken got to know the ideas of Heitler and London already in summer 1927. As he recalled:

> At the end of the summer Hund invited me to go with him … on a memorable hiking trip in Schwarzwald (the Black Forest). After that I visited Zurich, where I went to call on Erwin Schrödinger. He told me that two men were working at his Institute who had some results which he thought would interest me; he then introduced me to W. Heitler and F. London, whose important paper on the chemical bond in the hydrogen molecule (H<sub>2</sub>) was published not long after. This paper was the first of many using the “valence bond method.” This method explained the structure of molecules in terms of atoms linked together by quantum-mechanical “exchange” forces. Chemists had long talked about valence bonds between atoms in molecules, but could not explain the forces involved … Being human, I was not especially enthusiastic about the Heitler-London or valence-bond method since Hund and I had a rival and perhaps broader method for dealing with the structure of molecules. (Mulliken, 1989, pp. 60–61)

<sup>668</sup> On 12 July, Hund wrote in his *Tagebuch* that Mulliken’s work did not render his own ‘superfluous.’

III.5 From Molecular Theory to Quantum Chemistry

559

Hund continued, perhaps at a slightly slower pace, the work on molecular spectra during the following winter semester. He concerned himself with the so-called “Thomas-Fermi method” (see his *Tagebuch* for 18–19 November 1928) and submitted a note on the association of multiplet lines in atoms and molecules with the series limits (Hund, 1928e).<sup>669</sup> On 4 January 1929, Friedrich Hund received a call (*Berufung*) to take a professorship of mathematical physics at the University of Leipzig, which he accepted a month later, for it meant becoming part of a new active centre of atomic physics and joining Peter Debye (experimental physics) and Werner Heisenberg (theoretical physics) as his colleagues.<sup>670</sup> Before that, however, on 6 December 1928, he noted in his *Tagebuch*: ‘Official Invitation to [Visit] America, Unofficial One to Japan.’

The invitation to America included, in particular, the request to deliver a course of lectures in his special field, ‘molecular structure,’ at Harvard University, and other invitations to visit the General Electric Company (Schenectady)—where Irving Langmuir worked—the Universities of Toronto and Chicago, and MIT followed. Thus, Hund started from Rostock later in February 1929 and undertook until mid-May an enormous programme of lectures and talks, with headquarters in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and spending long weekends at other places.<sup>671</sup> When he travelled to Chicago in April, he met his friend Mulliken and succeeded in clarifying an important question, as he recalled many years later (in a videotape cassette at a dinner following the first annual Mulliken Memorial Lecture at the University of Chicago on 9 May 1988):<sup>672</sup>

> At that time it became urgent to establish a unitary nomenclature of molecules: the symbols α, π, δ for orbitals, capital Σ, Π, Δ for terms, *g*, *u* for symmetry, etc. Mulliken and I discussed the possibilities in the long train trip between Chicago and New York; then other colleagues agreed. A picture I took during a meeting of the American Physical Society in Washington shows [P.] Morse, [H. F.] Crawford, Mulliken, and [D. M.] Dennison, and has a note: “*Einigung über die Bezeichnung der Molekelzustände* (agreement on the notation for molecular states).”

The APS meeting in Washington, which took place from 18 to 20 April 1929, brought them all together, in particular, with Philip Morse and the Swiss theoretical physicist Ernst C. G. Stueckelberg, whose calculations (1929) showed ‘that for H<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> the Stark effect essentially determines the term structure’ (Hund, *Tagebuch*, 19 March 1929).

<sup>669</sup> In winter semester 1928/29, Hund gave two lecture courses at Rostock, one on ‘Maxwell’s Theory’ and the other on ‘The Structure of Crystal Lattices.’

<sup>670</sup> Already in June 1928 the University of Halle had offered Hund a full professorship, which he declined when he was promoted to the same status at Rostock.

<sup>671</sup> The plan to visit Japan apparently did not materialize, probably because of a lack of time; Hund had to be present in Leipzig for summer semester 1929, to take over Heisenberg’s lecture courses, while Heisenberg went on leave of absence to visit the U.S.A. and Japan.

<sup>672</sup> In 1929, Mulliken was appointed associate professor of chemistry at the University of Chicago. In 1966, he would receive the Nobel Prize in chemistry.
