Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

Hund had proposed earlier, in his talk at Hamburg, a nomenclature for the terms of diatomic molecules, namely:

> The states of the two-centre system can be described by symbols of the sort 1sσ<sup>2</sup>, 2sσ<sup>2</sup>, 2pσ<sup>2</sup>, 2pπ<sup>4</sup>, 3sσ<sup>2</sup>, etc. The symbol given means that when the coupling between the electrons weakens, two electrons become σ-electrons (with angular momentum 0 about the axis connecting the nuclei), and finally 1s-electrons if the nuclei coincide, also that two electrons become σ-electrons on decoupling and 2s-electrons when the nuclei coincide. For close centres, the energetic sequence is the same as in the atoms; a simple consideration shows that σ comes [in energy] before π if all other quantum numbers are identical. … For more distant centres some σ-orbits are preferred over the π-orbits; for a certain distance the sequence might be, say, 1sσ<sup>2</sup>, 2pσ<sup>2</sup>, 3sσ<sup>2</sup>, 3pσ<sup>2</sup>, 2pπ<sup>4</sup>, … From the energy-sequence of the orbits the *lowest state* immediately follows. Closed shells yield <sup>1</sup>Σ-terms (singlet-terms with resulting momentum 0 about the nuclear connection-axis); when a two-electron group (σ<sup>2</sup>) is built up, we obtain the terms <sup>2</sup>Σ. <sup>1</sup>Σ; when a four-π group is built up we get <sup>2</sup>Π (angular momentum 1 about the nuclear connection), <sup>3</sup>Σ, <sup>2</sup>Π, <sup>1</sup>Σ. … (Hund, 1928c, p. 851)

Now, in the review article arising from his American lectures and published in *Ergebnisse der exakten Naturwissenschaften*, Hund stated simply: ‘R. S. Mulliken and the reviewer have agreed on the given quantum numbers as follows: *IJK*, *i*, *λ* (in harmony with the notation of Wigner and Witmer [1928]; and the term symbols: … 1sσ, 2sσ, 2pπ …’ (Hund, 1929, p. 154). Besides reporting this agreement on the formal notation of the terms, Hund commented on the most recent literature—the work of many colleagues, including the investigation of Hendrik Kramers (1929) on O<sub>2</sub>, and of Heitler and Herzberg on the connection between molecular spectra and the Heitler–London theory of chemical valence (Heitler and Herzberg, 1929a).

Gerhard Herzberg, at that time a visitor at Max Born’s Institute in Göttingen, then submitted in July 1929 a weighty theoretical study of his own, entitled ‘Zum Aufbau der zweiatomigen Moleküle’ (‘On the Constitution of the Diatomic Molecules’), to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, which he summarized as follows:<sup>673</sup>

> The number of molecular terms following, due to Wigner and Witmer, group-theoretically from the terms of separated atoms is extraordinarily large. The investigations of Heitler and London, on the one hand, and of Mulliken and Hund, on the other, have dealt with the question of how many of them correspond to stable

<sup>673</sup> Gerhard Herzberg was born on 25 February 1904, in Hamburg; he obtained a *Dr. Ing.* degree at the *Technische Hochschule* in Darmstadt. From 1928 to 1930, he spent two years on a grant from the *Studienstiftung des Deutschen Volkes* in Göttingen (1928–1929) and Bristol (1929–1930). In 1930, he obtained his *Habilitation* in Darmstadt, but after 1933 he emigrated to Canada, where he worked at the University of Saskatchewan (1935–1945), and from 1945 to 1948, he was associated with the Yerkes Observatory of the University of Chicago in Williams Bay, Wisconsin; then, he became a staff member of the National Research Council in Ottawa; in 1955 he became Director of the Division of Pure Physics. In 1971, he received the Nobel Prize in chemistry.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0593 -->

molecular states. The stable states of molecules and their association with the separated atoms on the basis of these theories do not agree with experience in a series of important cases. The present paper pursues the goal of explaining these contradictions. This is possible by extending the Hund-Mulliken method of an *Aufbau* principle for the molecules. To obtain the experimental associations, we assume that the molecular quantum numbers of each single electron-shell would remain fixed when the transition from the situation of far distant nuclei to the molecule is performed. In the transition only the energetic sequence of the different electron-shells is changed. From the way in which it is changed, one can derive consequences on the stability of molecular terms without using, as Hund and Mulliken have done, the relation to the [final] united atom, which often leads to wrong results. The concept of binding-electron pairs of Heitler, London and Lewis, which had no place in the Mulliken-Hund theory, can be kept, with certain additions, in the new method [proposed here]. The new conception will be discussed in the light of the existing empirical material; especially the dissociation processes in a series of molecules will be studied in detail. (Herzberg, 1929, p. 601)

Herzberg indeed observed that Hund’s adiabatic procedure to obtain the final united atom could run into trouble, especially because the terms of CN and CO spectra do cross empirically, in contrast to the theoretical assumptions of the Hund–Mulliken scheme.⁶⁷⁴ Therefore, he proposed ‘the much farther-reaching assumption that in the transitions from the separated atoms to the molecules not only the number of σ–, π–, . . . electrons is conserved but also all molecular quantum numbers’; thus, ‘when the oscillation-quanta of the molecules are increased in a given state, it is not the quantum numbers of the individual electrons that change but just their energetic order, hence *the terms having the same electronic configuration must be associated with each other*’ (Herzberg, *loc. cit.*, p. 608). This Herzberg rule then indeed accounted for all deviations of the experimental facts from the Hund–Mulliken theory and further established the desired connection between their *Aufbau* principle and the Heitler–London theory of valence. Moreover, it had the advantage that, while the transition between the molecule and the complex atom arising from the final unification of the separated centres of the molecule, which played a crucial role in Hund’s theory, did not correspond to any process that could be observed in principle, the new rule was consistent with such a process as constructed by Herzberg and confirmed by the experimentalist James Frank (Herzberg, *loc. cit.*, pp. 608–610). Finally, it occasionally led to a considerable rise in the energy level of an electron shell, in contrast to the conclusion of the Hund–Mulliken scheme. This rise in the energy level then accounted for the Heitler–London repulsion due to the exchange-degeneracy (Herzberg, *loc. cit.*, p. 615). In view of these improvements of his theory, Hund admitted in 1988:

⁶⁷⁴ Even Mulliken’s restriction of Hund’s association rule—assuming the constancy of the number of σ–, π–, . . . electrons in the transition from the separated atoms to the molecule and admitting occasionally crossover terms of similar type (Mulliken, 1928b)—would not explain all of the experimental observations.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0594 -->

We [i.e., Mulliken and Hund] had not invented Quantum Chemistry. Heitler and London began this discipline in 1927. Both Mulliken and I had some difficulty in understanding them within the framework of molecular orbitals. It was Gerhard Herzberg who explained chemical binding in a simple and convincing manner with bonding- and anti-bonding electrons, where an anti-bonding electron could counter-balance a bonding electron. Of course, Mulliken’s early concept of promoted electrons came near to the idea. (Hund, *loc. cit.*)

Hund fully acknowledged Herzberg’s work, though he hinted in his last, fifth, paper on the series on the interpretation of molecular spectra, submitted in June 1930, at a few empirical deviations (Hund, 1930, p. 726). In this investigation, which treated in particular the excited electron terms of molecules consisting of identical nuclei (H₂, He₂, Li₂, N₂⁺, N₂, . . .), he also gave a clear definition of the chemical bond:

Generalizing the considerations of Mulliken, Heitler, London, Lennard-Jones [and he should have added Herzberg here] we talk about a genuine chemical bond or a *valence bond*, if the energy gained from approaching the two-atoms [forming the molecule] stems from a *reorganization in the energetic sequence of the electron orbits*. We shall say: an electron . . . relaxes a bond favoured by the other electron, because the corresponding term is raised above other terms when the nuclei approach each other. . . . If we speak in this sense about *binding* (*bindende*)- *and relaxing* (*lockende*)-*electrons*, then the strength of the bond depends roughly on the number of binding-minus the number of relaxing-electrons (Hund, *loc. cit.*, p. 731)

He added: ‘This formulation makes sense for the moment only for molecules consisting of identical atoms. It can be generalized; but we do not claim that then the concept of a valence bond is fully described.’ (Hund, *loc. cit.*, p. 732)

Not only did Herzberg, Hund, and Mulliken develop the concept of a valence bond in quantum mechanics further, but so did Heitler and London between 1928 and 1931.⁶⁷⁵ In particular, Heitler tried to explain the O₂-bond by an extra degeneracy in the magnetic quantum numbers of the molecule and spoke about ‘a *second type of valence, the l-valence* of atoms having *l* > 0’ (Heitler, 1929, p. 547). In a later paper, composed with the Russian visitor Yurii Borisovich (George) Rumer in Göttingen, he tried to extend the exchange-integral method to multi-atom molecules (1931), making use of John Slater’s antisymmetric matrices described in Section III.4 (Slater, 1929b). It should also be mentioned that in Berlin, F. London and R. Eisenschitz succeeded in providing the quantum-mechanical explanation of the van der Waals forces toward the end of 1929, a problem that had started in spring 1927 the exchange-integral approach of Heitler and London in Zurich. For that purpose, they considered the most general interaction between two neutral molecules in a systematic perturbation theory; in the second-order approximation, they obtained an attractive force having the long-range behaviour

⁶⁷⁵ See the papers of London, 1928c, 1929, 1930a, b; Heitler, 1929, 1930; and Heitler and Rumer, 1931.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0595 -->

r⁻⁶, which they identified with the weak attraction observed in nature at comparatively large distances (Eisenschitz and London, 1929, especially, p. 515).⁶⁷⁶ Substantial progress in promoting the Heitler–London theory then came in 1931 from the United States, contributed by the physicochemist Linus Pauling and the theoretical physicist John Slater.

**(e) Slater and Pauling’s Generalization of the Heitler–London Method and Mulliken’s Final Formulation of Molecular Orbitals**

Early in 1929, John Slater had listened carefully to Friedrich Hund’s lectures on molecular structure at Harvard University, and had then developed his own approach to the spectra of complex atoms involving the determinant method to describe the overall antisymmetric behaviour of many-electron wave functions (Slater, 1929b). Later in the same year, Slater visited Europe, especially Pauli’s Institute in Zurich and Heisenberg’s in Leipzig, where Felix Bloch got interested in his idea.⁶⁷⁷ Then, he ‘felt that the Heitler-London approach was one that should be pushed further,’ because ‘it was a nice illustration of the same methods that I used on atomic structure’ (Slater, AHQP Interview II, p. 23).⁶⁷⁸ Before he could publish anything particular on molecules, however, Max Born noticed the possibility of using Slater’s method for that purpose. In a note ‘*Zur Quantentheorie der chemischen Kräfte*’ (‘On the Quantum Theory of Chemical Forces’), he showed how it might serve ‘quite succinctly and in an elementary way to derive some further results of the quantum theory of the chemical bond, which have been derived by Heitler and London with considerable effort from group theory’ (Born, 1930, p. 729).

Max Born, who followed with great interest the flourishing work on molecular structure and the chemical implications being pursued in his Institute and elsewhere, also prepared an extended review for *Ergebnisse der exakten Naturwissenschaften*, where he presented of course in detail the results of Heitler and collaborators (Born, 1931). With this task in mind, he also attempted to popularize among the still hesitant theoreticians the principal theorems of the mathematical group theory and the invariant theory for treating molecular problems. Thus, he especially summarized the conclusions obtained since 1927 to explain the concepts of ‘polar’ and ‘nonpolar’ valences; in particular, he established in some detail the connection between the physical concept of electron spin and the chemical concept of valence (e.g., in his Section 3 on ‘Combinatorics of Valences and Spin Sums,’ pp. 398–402), and then outlined the application of the Slater determinant method to atomic and molecular theory (in Sections 4 and 5, pp. 402–410). In Section 6 on

spin rotations, he explained Hermann Weyl’s recent interpretation of valence with the help of spin invariants (Weyl, 1930, 1931b and c)⁶⁷⁹ in a simplified way:

If one associates with the atoms as many of the signs *x, y, z, . . .* as they have valences, then one can attribute to each action of the valence (*Valenzbetätigung*) instead of a valence dash *x* – *y* the sign [*x, y*], and with the free valence the sign [*x, l*]. Then there corresponds to a given chemical formula exactly one symbol [written, e.g., as a product [*x, l*][*y, l*]². [*x, y*] . . . ] and *vice versa*. This symbol, which is a spin invariant, now possesses a real physical meaning, hence Weyl proposes to call a state of a system which is associated with a spin invariant a *pure valence state* [see Weyl, 1931b, §15 of Chapter V]. The stationary states of the molecule, i.e., those having definite energy values then are different from these valence states, because they are obtained as solutions of the [Schrödinger-type] equations for the bonds, that is, they are linear combinations of pure valence states. (Born, 1931, pp. 420–421)

Equations for the bonds could indeed be formulated for the hydrogen molecule of Heitler and London (1927) and the more general cases considered later. At the end of his review, Born discussed the recent approach of Heitler, emphasizing the new bond-type emerging from a ‘degeneracy in direction’ (i.e., the *l*-valence, see Heitler, 1929, 1930) and referred to two more investigations of Linus Pauling (1931a) and John Slater (1931a).

Stimulated, perhaps even alarmed, by the competitive work in Germany, Slater finally formulated his own ideas on molecular structures and valence himself in two papers submitted in January and August 1931, respectively (Slater, 1931a, b).⁶⁸⁰ In his first paper, entitled ‘Directed Valence in Polyatomic Molecules,’ Slater stated: ‘It has already been noticed by Born [1930] that the method applied by the writer to the problem of complex spectra is equally adaptable to molecular structure,’ and further:

When applied to molecular problems in general, however, it yields not only the familiar results on diatomic molecules, but also information regarding valence in polyatomic molecules, particularly in the matter of directional properties, which seem to be new and which is capable of correlating a good deal of experimental material. (Slater, *loc. cit.*, p. 481)

To ensure his own priority, Slater mentioned that ‘the general ideas described in the paper were outlined [by me] in an informal talk at the Washington meeting of the American Physical Society last April [i.e., in 1930]’ (Slater, *loc. cit.*).
Slater described the essence of his new approach as follows:

Two atoms containing all their electrons in closed shells repel each other. But if each atom has one wave function containing only one electron, rather than two of oppo-

III.5 From Molecular Theory to Quantum Chemistry 565

site spin, attraction is possible. This actually occurs if the spins of the electrons in question in the two atoms are oppositely directed. The attraction pulls the atoms together until the wave functions from which the electrons are missing overlap as much as possible, when equilibrium occurs. In consequence of resonance, the charge concentrates at the place where the functions are overlapping, and in an approximate way we may consider that the two electrons, of opposite spin, spending their time in this region, form a closed shell. This is a homopolar valence bond, and two electrons forming such a bond are inactive in forming further bonds, just as if they were in closed shells within a single atom. (Slater, *loc. cit.*)

Slater then discussed how the conception proposed would apply qualitatively in actual situations, starting with the $\text{H}_2$-molecule (where two $1s$-electrons of the individual atoms overlap) and the $\text{I}_2$-molecule (where each I-atom lacks one $p$-electron in the outer shell), and progressed finally to explain the structure of the benzene molecule.

In the second, very extensive paper, entitled 'Molecular Levels and Valence Bonds,' Slater presented a detailed formalism on the basis of these ideas (Slater, 1931b).$^{681}$ The main task consisted in establishing—as in the cases of complex atoms (considered in Section III.4)—a suitable perturbation theory for an $n$-electron molecular system that involved two types of degeneracy, 'spin degeneracy' and 'orbital degeneracy.' As Heitler and London had done in their pioneering paper, Slater selected for the orbital functions a combination of products of the solutions of (an electron in) a central field problem. For a many-atom (or many-centre) molecule, the choice of a proper *Ansatz*, however, was much more difficult to obtain than in the simple diatomic hydrogen molecule, because many axes existed connecting the different centres; the best choice—and one most practical for the evaluation—for the orbital wave functions in those cases turned out to be that 'they must be [selected] such as to give as much overlapping as possible with the other electrons to which they are held by valence bonds, and as little as possible with electrons to which they are not held,' that is, 'they must be *concentrated bond functions*' (Slater, *loc. cit.*, p. 1114, our italics). More explicitly, Slater started from the most general energy operator $H$ for a molecule with fixed nuclei (denoted by $\alpha$ and $\beta$) and $n$ electrons (denoted by $i$ and $j$),

$$H = -\frac{h^2}{8\pi^2 m} \sum_i \nabla_i^2 - \sum_{i,\alpha} \frac{Z_\alpha e^2}{r_{i\alpha}} + \sum_{\alpha,\beta} \frac{Z_\alpha Z_\beta e^2}{r_{\alpha\beta}} + \sum_{i,j} \frac{e^2}{r_{ij}} , \quad (505)$$

where the $Z$'s (multiplied by the absolute value of the electron's charge $e$) represent the nuclear charges and the $r$'s represent the distances between the particles indicated by the suffixes.

$^{681}$ Slater emphasized that his calculations went beyond the more specialized, already published treatments of Heitler and Rumer (1931) and Hermann Weyl (1930, 1931c), as these authors 'assume the energy involved in molecular binding is small compared with that involved in the atomic multiplet structure in the atoms which compose the molecule, so that one can neglect all but the lowest atomic levels in discussing the molecular formation,' an assumption that 'is hardly justified in actual cases' (Slater, 1931b, p. 1109).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0598 -->

566 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

indicated by the suffixes. This operator then acted on the product wave function $a(1)\dots a(n)$ of the electrons, or

$$Ha(1)\dots a(n) = \left[ \sum_\alpha (V_\alpha - E_\alpha) - \sum_{i,\alpha} \frac{Z_\alpha e^2}{r_{i\alpha}} + \sum_{\alpha,\beta} \frac{Z_\alpha Z_\beta e^2}{r_{\alpha\beta}} + \sum_{i,j} \frac{e^2}{r_{ij}} \right] a(1)\dots a(n), \quad (506)$$

where the second-order derivative $\sum_i \nabla_i^2$ has been replaced by the one-electron Schrödinger-equation solution $\sum_\alpha (V_\alpha - E_\alpha)$ for each individual electron. Now, all terms but the last one were either constants or functions of single electrons; hence, they contributed to quantities $f$, in which only single electrons were involved, and the last sum over electron-pairs played a role in quantities $g$ characterized by electron-pairs.

The solution of the secular equation for the Hamiltonian (505) turned out to be more difficult than in the case of atoms, where the quantization of the (total) angular momentum $M_L$ and the spin angular momentum $M_S$ about a fixed axis permitted a factoring of the full determinant equation into smaller parts. However, in the molecular problem, Slater argued:

> The orbital angular momentum is no longer quantized, and the only special fact which we have left is that the levels are separated into groups with different values of $M_S$, resulting in a factoring of the equation into subequations, and the occurrence of all the roots of one equation in the next lower equation. The net result is that we can break up the terms into groups, each containing all the terms of the same multiplicity. Thus if there is just one term of a given multiplicity, its energy will be given linearly in terms of the various integrals; if there are two the energies will be given as roots of a quadratic, and so on. In other words, for practical purposes we are limited, as far as exact solutions are concerned, to cases where no more than two terms of the same multiplicity occur. (Slater, *loc. cit.*, p. 1118)

Explicitly, in a case in which all electrons have different orbital wave functions, only a spin degeneracy occurs, and then two electrons form a singlet and a triplet and three electrons a quartet and two doublets—with the quartet energy being a linear function of the integrals, and the doublet energies arising as the two roots of a quadratic. The situation obviously soon became rather complicated unless additional symmetries entered into the problem, as was the case for diatomic molecules.

In the longest section (5) of his paper, Slater gave several examples for the application of his method (Slater, 1931b, pp. 1113–1142). Thus, in the case of two atoms forming the molecule with one (external) electron, the term formulae,

$$W_{triplet} = \frac{(ab|H|ab) - (ab|H|ba)}{1 - (ab|1|ba)} \quad (507a)$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0599 -->

III.5 From Molecular Theory to Quantum Chemistry 567

and

$$W_{singlet} = \frac{(ab|H|ab) + (ab|H|ba)}{1 + (ab|1|ba)} , \quad (507b)$$

resulted, with $(ab|H|ab)$ and $(ab|H|ba)$ denoting the matrix elements for the Hamiltonian and $(ab|1|ba)$ the overlap of the wave functions associated with the different atoms. The quartet energy of a molecule, in which three electrons having only spin degeneracy play a role, came out as

$$W = \{(abc|H|abc) - (abc|H|bac) - (abc|H|acb)$$
$$- (abc|H|cba) + (abc|H|bca) + (abc|H|cab)\}$$
$$\cdot \{1 - (abc|1|bac) - (abc|1|acb) - (abc|1|cba)$$
$$+ (abc|1|bca) + (abc|1|cab)\}^{-1}, \quad (508)$$

of which the last two terms of the numerator and the denominator were small (because the orbital wave functions $a, b, c$ are nearly orthogonal). All of the terms could be interpreted physically; e.g., for four-electron molecules, the term $(abcd|H|abcd)$ denotes the Coulomb interaction, and the terms $(abcd|H|dbca)$, $(abcd|H|acbd)$, can be identified with possible resonance interchanges of pairs of electrons that produce the valence bonds or the repelling pair. As the most complicated example, Slater discussed a molecule consisting of five atoms, one having four $s$- and $p$-electrons, the other one $s$-electron (Slater, *loc. cit.*, pp. 1140–1142). 'By the use of these methods it is believed that approximate solutions for the lowest states of most molecules might be obtained, accurately enough for rough discussion of the chemical problems and the band spectra,' he concluded finally (Slater, *loc. cit.*, p. 1142), and further suggested the use of different methods in treating the problems of spin and orbital degeneracy in molecular theory: in the former case, an approximate solution should be obtained from a perturbation-theoretical approach, and in the latter, the variational method is to be preferred.

At several places in his paper, Slater quoted the results obtained by a California scientist, Linus Pauling. The latter published between February 1931 and May 1932 a series of investigations in the *American Journal of Chemistry*, to which he gave the title 'The Nature of the Chemical Bond' (Pauling, 1931, 1932a and b). The first, two-part paper, opened with a reference to Heitler and London having justified the rules for the electron-pair bond of G. N. Lewis, and continued:

> In the following paper it will be shown that many more results of chemical significance can be obtained from the quantum-mechanical equations, permitting the formulation of an extensive and powerful set of rules for the electron-pair bond supplementing those of Lewis. These rules provide information regarding the relative

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0600 -->

568 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

strengths of bonds formed by different atoms, the angles between bonds, free rotation or lack of free rotation about bond axes, the relation between the quantum numbers of bonding electrons and the number and spatial arrangement of bonds, etc. A complete theory of the magnetic moments is also developed, and it is shown that for many compounds involving elements of the transition groups this theory together with the rules for electron-pair bonds leads to a unique assignment of electron structures as well as a definite determination of the types of bonds involved. (Pauling, 1931, p. 1367)

Linus Pauling, the physicochemist from the California Institute of Technology, had become acquainted with this topic already many years ago when he spent the period 1926/27 on a Guggenheim Fellowship in Munich, Zurich, and Copenhagen.$^{682}$ When he arrived in Munich in 1926, wave mechanics was just appearing on the scene, and Sommerfeld and his associates began applying the new theory to various problems. As Pauling remarked in 1984 in an interview:

> There was a physicist named Gregor Wentzel in Munich, ... the *Privatdozent* or assistant with Sommerfeld. He published a paper on the properties, certain properties, of atoms containing any number of electrons from 1 to 92. I read Wentzel's paper in *Zeitschrift für Physik* when it came out ... I worked through it, going from one equation to the next equation. Wentzel had entitled his paper "Eine Schwierigkeit mit der Theorie des Kreiselektrons" [Wentzel, 1926c]. ... Well, my equations soon turned out to be different from Wentzel's ... [they] gave theoretical results in agreement with experimental results. ... The important part was that Wentzel had proposed a way of making theoretical calculations for atoms that may contain many electrons, and that was the sort of problem that interested me. (Pauling, interview with Hans Kuhn, quoted in Latzel, 1994, p. 112)

With the help of Sommerfeld, Pauling published a paper on his Munich work in *Proceedings of the Royal Society of London* (1927a). The next important event was that he met Walter Heitler, who, with Fritz London, developed in the following year the simple theory of the chemical bond for the hydrogen molecule (Heitler and London, 1927). 'I think they published their theory just before I arrived in Zurich,' Pauling recalled:$^{683}$

> They were working then on the extension of the theory to many-electron atoms and their group-theory discussion of chemical bondings, but they didn't invite me to participate in the work. In fact, I spent most of my time in Zurich attempting to treat the situation of the two helium atoms. ... I was trying to evaluate these integrals rigorously, and this was before Sugiura [1927] had evaluated them. ... Here, I think, I had

569

the feeling that if I worked in this field I would probably make some discovery … Of course, it led to hybridization and all this stuff.… I put a lot of things in the 1931 paper … The concentration of electrons along the band axis, you might say, would mean the contribution of $d$- and $f$-functions in the methane molecule, say to the bond orbitals of carbon; it means that they are not just $s$-, $p$-hybrids but share $d$- and $f$-contributions, too. (Pauling, AHQP Interview, 27 March 1964, p. 17)

Until this happened nearly four years later, Pauling was first offered an assistant professorship at Caltech by Arthur A. Noyes, followed by a promotion to associate professor in 1929 (and in 1931 to a full professor). ‘Then something very interesting occurred in 1931, or perhaps December 1930,’ he recalled:

> One day, late in the day, towards evening, I think, I had an idea. It was the basic idea of hybrid orbitals. I was trying to understand why the carbon atom is tetrahedral, forms bonds directed towards the 4 corners of tetrahedron. Even as early as 1924 I had made a model of methane, in which I said the 4 outer electrons of the carbon are in orbits directed towards the corners of a tetrahedron.… When quantum mechanics came along, a result was confirmed that had been accepted earlier, that the four outer electrons in the carbon are of two different kinds [a symmetrical, $2s$, three $2p$, arranged along the $x$, $y$, $z$ axes].… I thought the basic principles of quantum mechanics permit us to combine these functions from the Schrödinger equation in another way. And I said to myself: “Let’s suppose that I look just at the distribution in various directions, and not worry about the difference in the radial distribution for those.”
> That permitted rather simple calculations to be made in a straightforward manner. The first result I got was that the best bonds that the carbon atom can form are directed towards the 4 corners of a tetrahedron. So, in 1931, I had a simple theory of the tetrahedral carbon atom and explanation of a great bit of organic chemistry.
> (Pauling, Interview, 1984, in Latzel, 1994, p. 114)

In Part I of his paper, Pauling (1931) wrote six rules for the electron-pair bond that he derived from the observation of diatomic molecules. Three of them had been stated already earlier by others: (1) the formation of the electron-pair bond by unpaired electrons; (2) the electron pair does not contribute to the paramagnetic susceptibility; and (3) the electrons of a pair cannot take part in forming additional pairs. The others were:

4. *The main resonance terms for a single electron-pair bond are those involving only one eigenfunction from each atom.*
5. *Of two eigenfunctions with the same dependence on $r$, the one with the larger value in the bond direction will give rise to the stronger bond, and for a given eigenfunction the bond will tend to be formed in the direction with the largest value of the eigenfunction.*
6. *Of two eigenfunctions with the same dependence on $\theta$ and $\phi$, the one with the smaller mean value of $r$, that is, the one corresponding to the lower energy level for the atom will, give rise to the stronger bond.*
[Here $r$, $\theta$ and $\phi$ denote spherical coordinates.] (Pauling, 1931, p. 1368)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0602 -->

570
Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

Pauling then outlined the proof of these rules on the basis of quantum-mechanical calculations. The main point was that the term values of a ‘diatomic’ molecule ($AB$) had the form
$$E = W_A + W_B + J_E + J_X - \sum_{Y} J_Y - 2\sum_{Z} J_Z, \tag{509}$$
where $W_A$ and $W_B$ denoted the energy of the groups $A$ (i.e., the first atom considered plus all atoms to which it might be bound, except to the second atom considered) and $B$ (i.e., the second atom plus all other atoms in the molecule, except for the first one considered above), and $J_E$ the Coulomb energy. The $J_X$, $J_Y$, and $J_Z$ expressed ‘resonance integrals’; i.e., they corresponded to the three possible types of exchanges ($X$ between two single electrons, $Y$ between an electron and a pair-electron, $Z$ between an electron of a pair and an electron of another pair). He then noticed:

> The resonance integrals $J_X$, $J_Y$ and $J_Z$ have been found to have negative signs in the case of single molecules for which calculations have been made, and it is probable that these signs obtain in most cases. The resonance integrals depend qualitatively on what may be called the *overlapping* of the single-electron eigenfunctions involved; if $\psi_A$ and $\psi_B$ are single-electron eigenfunctions, the product $\psi_A(1)\psi_B(2)\psi_A^*(2)\psi_B^*(1)$ occurs in the resonance integral corresponding to the permutation involving electrons 1 and 2, and the value of the integral increases as the magnitude of the product in the region between the two nuclei increases.
> (Pauling, *loc. cit.*, p. 1370)

Further, Pauling pointed out that the integral $J_X$ dominated the others by far in what he called ‘concentration of the bond eigenfunctions.’
Still, in Part I of the same paper, Pauling studied the various eigenfunctions of atoms and their contributions to molecules; thus, he demonstrated, e.g., the result of which he had dreamt for years, namely, that ‘the four bonds formed by a carbon atom are equivalent and are directed towards the tetrahedron corners’ (Pauling, *loc. cit.*, p. 1374). Then, he proceeded to even more complex cases with bonds involving $d$-functions. Finally, he devoted Part II to the discussion of the magnetic moments of molecules and complex ions proving, in particular, the result: ‘The magnetic moment of a molecule or complex ion is determined entirely by the number of unpaired electrons, being equal to
$$\mu_s = 2\sqrt{S(S+1)}, \tag{510}$$
*in which $S$ is one-half that number.*’ (Pauling, *loc. cit.*, p. 1393)
In the following papers (Pauling, 1932a, b), Pauling extended his approach and showed convincingly that the theoretical scheme was perfectly confirmed by the ‘experimental values of heats of formation and combustion of gaseous molecules, with the use of the assumption that the energy of formation from separated atoms to which a single Lewis electronic structure can be assigned is the sum of constant

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0603 -->

III.5 From Molecular Theory to Quantum Chemistry
571

terms representing the various bonds’ (Pauling, 1932b, p. 3582). His approach using the quantum-mechanical formalism but written for chemists convinced them. As Friedrich Hund remarked later: ‘*Die Chemiker lesen Pauling*’ (‘The chemists read Pauling’)! (Hund, AHQP Interview, 26 June 1963, p. 30) Yet, back in 1931, he had pleaded that his own and Mulliken’s conceptions sufficed to answer the question of the chemical bond (Hund, 1931, 1932a, c), though he admitted at the same time the heuristic advantage brought about by the new treatment and extension of the Heitler–London conceptions by Slater and Pauling. And Mulliken strongly supported this view: in a new series of two papers, entitled ‘Electronic Structure of Polyatomic Molecules and Valence,’ submitted in February and April 1932, he stated in particular: ‘The electronic structures of polyatomic molecules can probably best be understood by expressing them in terms of one-electron wave functions. The forms of these are conditioned by the symmetry of the molecule, which is given by the arrangement of nuclei’ (Mulliken, 1932a, p. 55). The one-electron wave functions used by Hund and himself seemed ‘at first sight not closely related to that given by Pauling and Slater’ (Mulliken, *loc. cit.*, p. 56), and they could be properly expressed by the following concept:

> A molecule here is regarded as a set of nuclei, around each of which is grouped an electron configuration closely similar to that of a free atom in an external field, except that the parts of the electron configuration surrounding each nucleus usually belong, in part, jointly to two or more nuclei. The electron configuration can be described to a good approximation *with reference to that nucleus* in terms of its own set of electronic quantum numbers or one-electron wave functions. In the case of shared electrons, the same wave functions may be given quite different approximate formulations or descriptions from the point of view of different nuclei.
> (Mulliken, *loc. cit.*, pp. 57–58)

Altogether, Mulliken claimed that the above procedure ‘is useful for a qualitative understanding of many features of chemical valence, especially combustion ratios and valence saturation’ (Mulliken, *loc. cit.*), and he argued in a note added in proof: ‘The present method also goes beyond that of Pauling and Slater in its ability to deal with spectroscopic terms and ionization potentials.’ (Mulliken, *loc. cit.*, p. 61)
The method of description in terms of what he called ‘atomic and molecular orbitals’ or ‘one-electron orbital wave functions’ Mulliken explained further in the next paper, primarily in two programmatic points:

> Unshared electrons are considered as occupying atomic orbitals associated with the various nuclei to which the electrons are described from several points of view, whose simultaneous consideration should give a better understanding of their condition and functions in the molecule.
> (Mulliken, 1932b, p. 49)

Like Hund, Mulliken was convinced of the advantage of their ‘molecular-orbital method’ over the Heitler–London–Pauling–Slater quantum-mechanical electron-pair bond concept’; the latter, he claimed, ‘differs markedly from Lewis’s, also that

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0604 -->

572
Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

it is of more restricted application to chemical data’ (Mulliken, *loc. cit.*). Let us give Friedrich Hund—as the originator of the whole quantum-mechanical development—the last word here.⁶⁸⁴ In his review article, ‘*Allgemeine Quantenmechanik des Atom- und Molekelbaues*’ (‘General Quantum Mechanics of the Structure of Atoms and Molecules,’ for the Geiger–Scheel *Handbuch der Physik*, Hund described three different theoretical explanations of the chemical bond as follows:

(a) One approximates the (electronic) state of the molecules by a state of the separated atoms, where each atom possesses a term denoted by $S$ and $L$. This concept has been carried out only under restricted conditions. …
(b) One approximates the state of the molecule also by a state of the separated atoms, but describes this by states of the single electrons. The essential splittings for the chemical bond occur in the same approximation as the splittings in the atomic terms which belong to the same state of the single electron. The applicability of this concept reaches farther than the concept (a); it reveals also more features of the chemical valence. The method of calculation is a generalization of the calculation of the atomic terms in case of normal coupling with eigenfunctions of the single electrons due to Slater. …
(c) One approximates the state of molecules by the state of the single electrons of the many-centre system. The interaction of the electrons is considered first only as a screening effect; the chemical bond, therefore, is considered to be a coarse effect, comparable to the splitting of an atomic or a molecular state with given quantum numbers of the single electrons in terms having different $S$ and $L$ or $\Sigma$ and $\Lambda$. Concerning the eigenfunctions of the single electrons, we can easily introduce qualitative assumptions. For large distances of the centres the perturbation method of Heitler and London may be applied.
(Hund, 1933, pp. 676–677)

Obviously, Heitler and London suggested the concept (a), Slater and Pauling the concept (b), and Hund and Mulliken the concept (c). All three concepts provided a firm basis for the developing field of quantum chemistry.

#### (a) Introduction: The Prequantum-Mechanical Theory

The discovery of the negatively charged subatomic corpuscle, the electron, by Joseph John Thomson, Emil Wiechert, Walther Kaufmann, and Willy Wien in 1897 immediately led Eduard Riecke in Göttingen to argue that it played a

III.6  The Metal Electrons and Solid State Theory

573

central role in the electrical conductivity of metals (Riecke, 1898a, b, c).⁶⁸⁵ In two memoirs, submitted in February and September 1900 to *Annalen der Physik*, Paul Drude of Leipzig established what he called ‘the electron theory of metals’ (Drude, 1900a, b). Although he avoided taking into account the specific properties of the electron, i.e., its definite charge $-e$ and mass $m_e$—he rather spoke of ‘positive’ and ‘negative’ nuclei (*Kerne*) having charges $\pm e, \pm 2e, \dots$ and kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2} m_1 u_1^2, \frac{1}{2} m_2 u_2^2, \dots$, or masses $m_1, m_2, \dots$ (and velocities $u_1, u_2, \dots$) representing either the ‘ponderable’ or ‘apparent’ (*scheinbare*) masses (the latter being created by the ‘self induction’ of the moving nuclei)—he succeeded in describing many properties of metals: the electrical conductivity, the thermal conductivity, the Thomson effect, the galvanomagnetic and thermomagnetic effects. Drude’s theory was based on the assumption that his ‘electrons’ formed a gas satisfying the known kinetic theory (of gases) and obeying Boltzmann’s equation

$$\frac{1}{2} m u^2 = \alpha T, \qquad (511)$$

with a constant $\alpha$ having roughly the value

$$\alpha = 5.6 \times 10^{-17} \text{ c.g.s. units.} \qquad (511a)$$

In particular, he obtained for the ratio of thermal ($\sigma_{th}$) to the electrical conductivity ($\sigma_{el}$) the relation

$$\frac{\sigma_{th}}{\sigma_{el}} = \frac{4}{3} \left( \frac{\alpha}{e} \right)^2 T = 3 \left( \frac{k}{e} \right)^2 T. \qquad (512)$$

The expression (512) followed from Max Planck’s identification of the ‘Boltzmann-Drude constant’ $\alpha$ with $k$, the Boltzmann constant (Planck, 1900f). Equation (512) perfectly agreed with the empirical ‘Wiedemann-Franz law,’ which had been known for a while. However, when Hendrik Antoon Lorentz repeated Drude’s calculation with proper (Maxwell–Boltzmann) statistics, he derived a somewhat different law, namely,

$$\frac{\sigma_{th}}{\sigma_{el}} = 2 \left( \frac{k}{e} \right)^2 T, \qquad (513)$$

upon which he commented as follows:

> What is the meaning of this deviation is difficult to say. Perhaps, and this would be most pleasing, my calculation contains an error, or a still more accurate consideration ... leads to a result less different from Drude’s. However, it also may be possi-

ble that the facts are really not so simple as we have assumed and that, notably for the heat conduction, different processes than the position of the completely free electrons play a role. (Lorentz, 1905; reprint, p. 109)

Two decades later, at the fourth Solvay Conference in April 1924 at Brussels, Lorentz again presented a report on the topic ‘Application of the Electron Theory to the Properties of Metals,’ in which he emphasized again exactly the same defect (Lorentz, 1927). He mentioned that Niels Bohr and Owen Willians Richardson had suggested extending the simple kinetic gas model used by assuming that the atoms in a metal do not behave like elastic spheres when colliding with the electrons, but exert a repulsive force on them proportional to some power of the distance. Like other participants at the conference, Lorentz listed a series of defaults of the existing classical theory, principally: (1) it did not account for the phenomenon of superconductivity observed at very low temperatures in several metals; (2) it offered no explanation for the negligible contribution of the electrons to the specific heat of metals. Percy W. Bridgman of Cambridge, Massachusetts, claimed that many problems disappeared if one just assumed that in solids only *very few free electrons* existed compared to the number of atoms, while Owen W. Richardson thought of avoiding problems if the electron orbits in solids were just quantized (he even approached superconductivity with this idea). Finally, Edwin H. Hall of Harvard University suggested the following possibility to account for the observed variety of effects caused by the action of magnetic fields on the electrical conductivity of metals: the electrons had to be divided into two classes, the free electrons and the ‘associated electrons,’ i.e., those bound to the ions.⁶⁸⁶

Obviously, 1924—when the old quantum theory was undergoing a deep crisis and only vague ideas emerged on the horizon for overcoming the fundamental difficulties—was not a suitable time to expect a breakthrough in the problems of the ‘Electrical Conductivity of Metals’; the reports and discussions at the Solvay Conference could only reveal the extent of the debacle existing in the understanding of the complex properties of metals. Fortunately, the breakthrough in the underlying, more fundamental problem of atomic theory was soon about to occur; following the discoveries between summer 1925 and spring 1926, the theoreticians began to apply the new quantum mechanics already in 1926 and 1927 to molecules, and a more realistic hope sprang up of being able to also describe properly the behaviour of electrons in solids and thus of resolving the difficulties that had been addressed so vigorously in 1924. Besides having the new quantum- or wave-mechanical theory in hand, which governed the dynamics of the microscopic constituents of matter, the physicists endowed the electrons with an entirely new type of statistics (deviating strongly from the classical Maxwell–Boltzmann statistics)—the Fermi statistics (Fermi, 1926b)—and an additional property, the electron spin (Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, 1925). These essentially different features encouraged some pioneers to turn, beginning in late 1926, to the old problems of

metal electrons. The breakthrough occurred so suddenly that two contemporary reviews of the subject (published in 1927 and 1928 by well-known experts) could hardly take notice of this development.⁶⁸⁷

The present section deals with the successes of the quantum-mechanical theory of metal electrons and the establishment of the modern microscopic theory of solids in the years between 1926 and 1933. In contrast to the topics treated in the previous sections of this chapter, already several quite detailed historical studies of this development exist. Indeed, it already attracted great interest of the physics community in the early days and gave rise to a host of review articles published since 1931: we just mention here the two books of Léon Brillouin (1931) and Herbert Fröhlich (1936), both in the famous Springer Series on ‘*Struktur der Materie*,’ and the articles of Rudolf Peierls (1932b), Felix Bloch (1933a), Arnold Sommerfeld and Hans Bethe (1933), Lothar Nordheim (1934), and John Slater (1934c) in various handbooks and other publications. The theory of metals became, so to say, the first field of application of quantum mechanics, whose results were universally acknowledged by scientists, engineers, and industrial people alike.⁶⁸⁸ A more recent ‘International Project on the History of Solid State Physics,’ based at the Center for History of Physics of the American Institute of Physics, the University of Aston, Birmingham, and the *Deutsches Museum*, Munich, investigated in the 1980s with great effort the event in the crucial period of the development of solid-state physics, publishing reports and books (Hoddeson et al., 1987; Hoddeson et al., 1992). The preparation for this project occurred in a meeting on ‘The beginnings of Solid State Physics,’ organized by Sir Nevill Mott at the Royal Society of London and held from 30 April to 2 May 1979, which assembled as speakers many of the still surviving pioneers of the field, thus providing most valuable, first-hand reminiscences.⁶⁸⁹ In this symposium, Lillian

576  Chapter III  The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

Hoddeson and Gordon Baym delivered an account of ‘The Development of the Quantum-Mechanical Electron Theory of Metals: 1900–1928’ (Hoddeson and Baym, 1980), which provided the introduction to their later extended article with Michael Eckert in *Reviews of Modern Physics*, entitled ‘The Development of the Quantum-Mechanical Electron Theory of Metals: 1928–1933’ (Hoddeson et al., 1987). Notably, these two articles, together with the personal reminiscences of the pioneers at the symposium organized by Mott and the interviews of Bethe, Bloch, Peierls, and others for the Project on *Sources for the History of Quantum Physics* (directed by Thomas Kuhn for the American Physical Society and the American Philosophical Society), must be consulted by anyone who wants to learn about the historical events connected with the emergency of modern solid-state physics.

While it may not be necessary to exceed the condensed analysis given in the literature cited above, we shall present in the following a slightly varied story, by placing greater emphasis on the historical sequence of events rather than following strictly topical connections. Thus, the two central aspects of metal electrons—ferromagnetism and electron propagation in periodic crystals—pioneered in Leipzig by Werner Heisenberg and Felix Bloch, respectively, will be grouped together; also, later, the problems of electrical conductivity and magnetism cannot be clearly separated, when the progress of solid-state theory is considered in Zurich and other places after 1929. Further, we shall also not follow the previous historians of science in calling the free-electron gas approach of Pauli, Sommerfeld, and others a ‘semi-classical theory,’ because this particular approach, though operating with elementary mathematical formalism and without detailed wave-mechanical methods, has been perfectly justified within the quantum-mechanical theory. It can be called semiclassical only insofar as Sommerfeld used the model of the classical electron theory of metals of Riecke, Drude, and Lorentz, namely, the free-electron gas, but he also translated it into the new quantum theory and not into the old semiclassical quantum theory.

As we have indicated above, it was the discovery of the Fermi statistics and its incorporation into the wave-mechanical formalism by Dirac (and Heisenberg) that opened the path to modern solid-state theory. Thus, Pauli recalled in 1956:

> Dirac was in Copenhagen in the autumn of 1926 and I wrote to him there, whether he knew how the spin of the atom (or electrons) would modify the results [of Dirac’s paper, 1926f]. I also mentioned Fermi’s paper. He answered me that he never considered this question and that Fermi’s paper was entirely new to him. Immediately after that I started to work on the question myself (autumn 1926) and I found very quickly all the answers. (Pauli’s letter to F. Rasetti, quoted by Hoddeson and Baym, 1980, pp. 12–13)

Still, he was not the first to come out with the results on the quantum-mechanical Fermi gas. Already, in the December issue of the British journal *Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society*, Ralph Fowler of Cambridge published a note, in which he treated the dense matter in a star with Fermi statistics (Fowler, 1926). In particular, he showed that the electrons are in a degenerate state and possess

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0609 -->

III.6 The Metal Electrons and Solid State Theory 577

zero-point energy (which has important consequences for the law of pressures). Pauli’s simultaneous work on the electron gas (Pauli, 1927a), on the other hand, directly initiated Sommerfeld’s theory of metal electrons: Sommerfeld worked it out, partly together with a group of students and visiting physicists, between early 1927 and summer 1928, with only a few details added after this exciting period. This work, the last great contribution to atomic theory from Sommerfeld’s Institute, will be discussed in the next subsection. In the following, the stage shifts to Leipzig, where Heisenberg and his doctoral student Felix Bloch laid two cornerstones of the foundation of solid-state theory: the quantum-mechanical theories of ferromagnetism and of electrical conductivity. Both of these theories employed a more realistic model of solids than had Pauli and Sommerfeld, considering the electrons in a periodic crystal. The following subsections deal with the extension of the foundations laid in Leipzig. The contributions now came, besides from Heisenberg’s Institute, from various other places, where the initial ideas had spread out: notably, from Pauli’s Institute in Zurich, but also from Cambridge, Utrecht, Paris, Leningrad, and the United States. There, the basis was given for a nearly complete understanding of conductors, insulators, and semiconductors, as well as the fruitful concept of spin waves was introduced to describe the dynamical processes in ferromagnetic crystals.

### (b) The Metal Electrons as a Free Fermi Gas (1926–1928)

On the occasion of the centenary of Alessandro Volta’s death, an International Congress of Physicists (*Congresso Internazionale dei Fisici*), which assembled a large number of scientific celebrities from all over the world—including Francis Aston, Niels Bohr, Arthur Compton, Arthur Eddington, Hendrik Lorentz, Robert Millikan, and Robert Wood—was held in Como, Volta’s birthplace, from 11 to 17 October 1927. The unusually large contingent of participants from Germany was led by the Nobel Prize winners James Franck, Max von Laue, and Max Planck, and included Arnold Sommerfeld.$^{690}$ In the special issue of ‘*Voltiana*,’ published by the organizing committee of the conference, Sommerfeld figured as the first famous participant with his photograph and the following description:

> Professor of Theoretical Physics at the University of Munich in Bavaria. Physicist and mathematician of great power, he has contributed to the solution of fundamental problems in the field of electricity and hydrodynamics, optics, and relativity. His investigations in atomic physics have exerted a most spectacular (*spiccatissima*) influence on the method of investigation by physicists throughout the world in the past two decades. (‘*Voltiana*,’ 1927, p. 5)

The entry did not mention that Sommerfeld’s lecture at the conference, announced under the title ‘*Elektronentheorie der Metalle und des Volta-Effektes*

$^{690}$ The *Congresso* moved on 17 October to Pavia and on 18 October to Rome.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0610 -->

578 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

*nach der Fermischen Statistik*’ (‘Electron Theory of Metals and of the Volta Effect According to Fermi Statistics’, 1928a), not only constituted a most suitable contribution to the centenary, but also emphasized—besides the great Italian physicist of the past—a young countryman, Enrico Fermi, a veritable successor of Volta in the twentieth century. Actually, Sommerfeld surprised his colleagues with another demonstration of his creativity, as he presented a brand new quantum-mechanical theory that resolved the difficulties of the classical theory of metals with the help of what he called Fermi’s ‘new approach to the statistical problem.’ After reporting the results on electrical and thermal conductivity, the Thomson, Peltier, thermoelectric, and Hall effects, and the Richardson and the Volta effects, Sommerfeld concluded his talk by saying:

> We have dealt only with a small part of the immense field of metallic conduction properties. The general impression, which enforces itself, is undoubtedly [the fact] that with the help of the new statistics the contradictions of the old theory are removed, and the empirical facts are represented in part quantitatively, in other parts qualitatively in the correct manner.
> The present considerations are characterized by the lack of any special hypothesis concerning the interaction between the electrons and the metal ions. We have just taken over the primitive concepts of the old theory and improved on it by the compulsorily prescribed procedure of the Fermi statistics. Through the agreement [of the results] with the data on metallic conduction this statistics obtains a firm empirical basis. (Sommerfeld, 1928a, p. 469)

Since early 1926, Arnold Sommerfeld, the great pioneer of the old quantum theory, had begun to participate actively in the new quantum mechanics, especially after he had gained insight into Schrödinger’s wave-mechanical approach. Hans Bethe, who had just arrived from Frankfurt in the spring of that year and registered duly for Sommerfeld’s course on the differential equations of mathematical physics (the last in Sommerfeld’s series of six lecture courses), recalled further:

> I went to call on him and he said, “Well, from what [Karl Wilhelm] Meissner [the spectroscopist in Frankfurt] wrote me, I will admit you to my seminar.” ... So I went to this seminar, and this seemed quite different at first, but very soon ... the seminar was about Schrödinger’s papers. ...
> Sommerfeld got the galley proofs of the papers that were going to appear, and he just distributed them among the members of the seminar. Each of us had to give a talk about something. The first seminar was given by Unsöld and was about the introduction of the Hamilton-Jacobi equations. ... Then came the Schrödinger equation ..., and once you had the Schrödinger equation you could do things with it. (Bethe, AHQP Interview, 17 January 1964, p. 7)

Besides Albrecht Unsöld, who would write a paper with Sommerfeld on the spectrum of hydrogen, which referred to Schrödinger’s publications (Sommerfeld and Unsöld, 1926b), the senior student Karl Bechert participated in the seminar—he ‘had the job of coaching the students before they gave a talk’ (Bethe, *loc. cit.*,

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0611 -->

III.6 The Metal Electrons and Solid State Theory 579

p. 8)—then Heinrich Ott and, later that year, Linus Pauling, a Guggenheim fellow from California, all took part.$^{691}$ For a semester, Gregor Wentzel still stayed on in Munich, who hurriedly picked up Schrödinger’s method as well.$^{692}$ According to Bethe, ‘he really knew things, ... probably he knew more than Sommerfeld’ (Bethe, *loc. cit.*). At any rate, Sommerfeld found wave mechanics ‘tremendously appealing’ and affected his students and associates with his enthusiasm.$^{693}$ During the year 1926, Sommerfeld’s Seminar again filled up with a number of very talented students and visitors, comparable with the earlier times in the 1910s and early 1920s: thus, in 1927, the American postdocs Carl Eckart and William V. Houston arrived, as did the senior Professor Edwin Kemble, as Guggenheim fellows; Edward U. Condon from California and Isidor Rabi from Columbia University came on International Education Board fellowships, and finally the young student Rudolf Peierls arrived from Berlin. The central issue in Munich soon became the metal electrons, which had been imported from Hamburg, where it had been initiated by Wolfgang Pauli, Sommerfeld’s former student.
On 19 October 1926 (in reply to a letter evidently lost),$^{694}$ Pauli wrote to Werner Heisenberg in Copenhagen about the problem of gas degeneracy, which, since 1924 (and Einstein’s proposal), he had always criticized:

> I now think much more mildly abut the Fermi-Dirac statistics, and now several arguments seem to speak in its favour. There exists already a difference between a crystal lattice and radiation, namely as far as the zero-point energy $\frac{h\nu}{2}$ is concerned.
> Now it is reasonable *a priori* also to assume that the ideal gas possesses zero-point energy. This can be implanted only artificially on the Einstein-Bose theory, and this speaks from the outset against this theory and in favour of Fermi-Dirac. To visualize the situation for myself, I have repeated the fluctuation consideration of Einstein [1925a] now from the point of view of the Fermi-Dirac theory. (Pauli, 1979, p. 340)

The expression for the fluctuation term $\overline{\Delta_s^2}$ in the Fermi case derived by Pauli,

$$\overline{\Delta_s^2} = N_s - \frac{N_s^2}{Z_s}, \quad (514)$$

$^{691}$ Probably also Hans Grimm, a *Privatdozent* and occasional collaborator of Sommerfeld, attended, as did Walter Heitler, before he went to Copenhagen.
$^{692}$ See Volume 5, Section IV.4, pp. 687–689 and 714–719. In fall 1926, Wentzel left to become an extraordinary professor of theoretical physics at the University of Leipzig, after Heisenberg and Pauli had declined the offer.
$^{693}$ Sommerfeld soon acquainted himself so thoroughly with wave mechanics that he could write the *Wellenmechanischer Ergänzungsband*, an addition to *Atombau und Spektrallinien* (Sommerfeld, 1929).
$^{694}$ It is the same letter in which Pauli suggested the generalization of Born’s interpretation of the collision-wave function and thus stimulated both Jordan and Dirac to develop the mathematical transformation theory (see Section I) and Heisenberg to formulate his uncertainty relations (see Section II).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0612 -->

580 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

(with $N_s$ and $Z_s$ denoting the number of particles and phase cells, respectively), contained a minus sign in contrast to the Bose–Einstein case; hence, Pauli argued:

> If one believes, however, in zero-point energy, it seems reasonable that $\overline{\Delta_s^2}$ must be smaller than the classical case, since it must then assume the value zero at absolute zero, in spite of the non-vanishing $N_s$. (Pauli, *loc. cit.*, p. 341)

He further noted that ‘the application of Dirac’s theory to atomic gases with angular momentum has the consequence that a monatomic vapour, which is normally paramagnetic at high temperatures, ceases to be paramagnetic as soon as the degeneracy sets in for decreasing temperature’ (Pauli, *loc. cit.*). Perhaps this result would explain the (small) magnetism of solid and fluid alkali atoms (which must be degenerate Fermi gases), Pauli concluded the discussion in his letter to Heisenberg. About two months later, he submitted his paper ‘Über Gasentartung und Paramagnetismus’ (‘On Gas Degeneracy and Paramagnetism’) to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Pauli, 1927a).
Pauli had been acquainted with the problem since he had discussed it seven years earlier the ‘Quantum Theory and the Magneton’ (Pauli, 1920c). At that time, he had realized that empirically monatomic substances do not exhibit any paramagnetism. Now, in the case of a gas of Fermi particles, the explanation appeared obvious, because:

> In the limiting case of high temperatures or low density, respectively, where the classical equation of state is satisfied, ... the usual behaviour of the gas in a magnetic field (Curie’s law) would not be changed essentially. In the other limiting case of a strongly degenerate gas (for simplicity, one may think of absolute zero temperature), on the other hand, all cells corresponding to a small kinetic energy of the atoms will often be completely filled. According to our assumption , however, a full occupation of a cell is only possible if each orientation of the atom exists just once, hence the resulting magnetic moment of all atoms in the cell vanishes. A magnetization shall only be possible if a part of the atoms is removed from the cells under consideration (i.e., are “excited”), which must in general lead to an increase of the kinetic energy of the gas. (Pauli, 1927a, pp. 85–86)

Evidently, Pauli took as a model for a metal an assembly of atoms whose electrons have a spin $\frac{1}{2} h/2 \pi$ and fall into quantum cells.
In order to prove the above guess, Pauli considered the Fermi gas of electrons according to the model of eigenvibrations used by Erwin Schrödinger (1926b) in the fall of 1925 to reevaluate Einstein’s gas theory with de Broglie’s matter-wave hypothesis.$^{695}$ Thus, he made sure that the results obtained would be consistent with wave mechanics. Moreover, he considered for the derivation of the statistical behaviour a canonical ensemble both in energy *and* particle number, hence he

$^{695}$ We have discussed this model in Volume 5, pp. 434–442.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0613 -->

III.6 The Metal Electrons and Solid State Theory 581

worked with the parameters $\beta$ and $\alpha$, defined as

$$ \beta = \frac{1}{kT} \quad \text{and} \quad \alpha = - \frac{\Psi + pV}{NkT}, \quad (515) $$

where $\Psi$ is the free energy and $p$, $V$, and $T$ denote pressure, volume, and temperature of the gas, respectively ($k$ being Boltzmann's constant). Then, the energy $E$ and particle number $N$ were given by the expressions

$$ N = V \left( \frac{2\pi m_e k T}{h^3} \right)^{3/2} F(\alpha) \quad (516a) $$

and

$$ E = \frac{3}{2} V \left( \frac{2\pi m_e}{h^3} \right)^{3/2} (kT)^{5/2} G(\alpha), \quad (516b) $$

with $F(\alpha)$ and $G(\alpha)$ representing Debye-like functions for electrons of mass $m_e$, i.e.,

$$ F(\alpha) = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_0^\infty \frac{x^{1/2} dx}{\exp(\alpha + x) + 1} \quad (517a) $$

and

$$ G(\alpha) = \frac{4}{3\sqrt{\pi}} \int_0^\infty \frac{x^{3/2}}{\exp(\alpha + x) + 1}. \quad (517b) $$

Equations (516a, b) described the behaviour of a free Fermi gas perfectly: for large positive values of $\alpha$, the high-temperature and low-density situation (i.e., the limiting classical case) followed, whereas, for very large negative values of $\alpha$, 'degeneracy' was obtained, associated with the zero-point energy per atom $\varepsilon_0$ [Fermi, 1926b, Eq. (36), p. 911], where

$$ \varepsilon_0 = \frac{E_0}{N} = \frac{3}{40} \left( \frac{6}{\pi} \right)^{2/3} \frac{h^2}{m_e} \left( \frac{N}{V} \right)^{2/3} \quad (518) $$

Further, Pauli derived the fluctuation formula (514) of his letter to Heisenberg.

This treatment could be immediately generalized to the case of a magnetic field $H$, in which the electrons assumed the discrete magnetic energy $\varepsilon_m$,

$$ \varepsilon_m = -mg\mu_0 H \quad (519) $$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0614 -->

582 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

[with $m$, the magnetic quantum number, $g$, the Landé factor, $\mu_0 \left( = \frac{eh}{4\pi m_e c} \right)$, the Bohr magneton, and $H$, the magnetic field]. Thus, $\varepsilon_m$ (through the parameter $\alpha$) and the $m$-sum entered into the expressions for $N$ and $E$, Eqs. (516), and Pauli calculated for the total magnetization the straightforward result

$$ MH = -\sum_{m=-j}^{+j} N_m \varepsilon_m = -V \left( \frac{2\pi m_e k T}{h^2} \right)^{3/2} \sum_{m=-j}^{+j} \varepsilon_m F\left( \alpha + \frac{\varepsilon_m}{kT} \right), \quad (520) $$

which he approximated for low fields (up to terms of order $H^2$) as (with $F'(\alpha) = \frac{dF(\alpha)}{d\alpha}$ )

$$ MH = -V \left( \frac{2\pi m_e k T}{h^2} \right)^{3/2} \frac{1}{kT} F'(\alpha) \sum_{m=-j}^{+j} \varepsilon_m. \quad (520') $$

In the high-temperature approximation ($\alpha \gg 1$), this turned into Curie's $T^{-1}$-law for paramagnetic susceptibility, $\chi (= M/V)$, whereas in the low-temperature case ($\alpha \ll 0$), $\chi$ approached the finite zero-point value $\chi_0$, i.e.,

$$ \chi_0 = \frac{3}{10} \frac{N \mu^2}{V \varepsilon_0} \quad (521) $$

(with $\mu = \sqrt{j(j+1)} \, g\mu_0$). Pauli concluded:

> As mentioned [above], we want to treat the electrons in a metal, which we identify with the valence electrons, provisionally as an ideal gas. This can be considered, as may be easily checked for the actually existing density of electrons, always as being degenerate, hence Eq. [(521)] is valid. The atomic core, consisting of the remaining electrons plus the positive nucleus, will not contribute any paramagnetism, provided it constitutes a closed shell. On the other hand, one must deduct from $\chi_0$, Eq. [(521)], always the diamagnetic effect created by the atomic core and the conduction electrons through induction. (Pauli, 1927a, p. 101)

A closer look at some empirical data of the alkaline metals confirmed these conclusions, both in the order of magnitude of the effect ($\chi_0 = 10^{-7}$) as in the dependence on the atomic number (the diamagnetic contribution should increase for heavier elements).

Pauli reported his results to Gregor Wentzel when he had nearly completed the paper, in a letter dated 5 December 1926; in the same letter, he told Wentzel about a local meeting of the German Physical Society to be held in Hamburg early next

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0615 -->

III.6 The Metal Electrons and Solid State Theory 583

February, and that Sommerfeld would attend it (Pauli, 1979, p. 362).$^{696}$ According to Pauli's later recollections, Sommerfeld then looked at the galley-proofs of his paper on paramagnetism, and:

> The next day he said to me that he was very much impressed by it and that one should make further applications to other parts of metal theory like the Wiedemann-Franz law, thermo-electric effects, etc. As I was not eager to do that, he made then this further application himself. (From a letter of Pauli to F. Rasetti, October 1956, quoted by Hoddeson and Baym, 1980, p. 15.)

We know that in 1927 Pauli had other priorities than extending his free Fermi-gas model of alkaline metals to other problems; he considered it anyway to be 'only a very coarse approximation which had to be replaced by a more accurate model of the metal' (Pauli, 1927a, p. 85). He rather devoted his energy to incorporating electron spin into the wave-mechanical formalism and similar problems that he regarded as being fundamental, such as the proper representation of electrons in quantum field theory.$^{697}$ Sommerfeld, on the other hand, did not enter into the problem immediately either; maybe, he waited first for Pauli's response, but in any case he was quite busy in those days to learn wave mechanics and derive consequences from it. In particular, he took great interest in the diffraction phenomena with electrons, observed by Clinton Joseph Davisson and Lester Halbert Germer (1927a) and George Paget Thomson and Alexander Reid (1927) in spring 1927, and asked his student Hans Bethe to develop a wave-mechanical description of the experimental situation (Bethe, 1927, 1928a). As Bethe recalled:

> Very soon, after ... the Davisson-Germer experiment, Sommerfeld got interested in the theory of metals, and then I think almost the whole interest of Sommerfeld and the seminar concentrated on the theory of metals. (Bethe, AHQP Interview, 17 June 1964, p. 11)

Similarly, Carl Eckart mentioned 'he [Sommerfeld] got us all involved in ... the big project for the year ... to rework the Lorentz theory of electrons using the Fermi statistics' (AHQP Interview, quoted by Hoddeson and Baym, 1980, p. 15). However, Eckart came to Munich only at a later stage, i.e., in fall 1927, when the programme had already started. Still, one should note that there was a certain hiatus between February 1927, when Sommerfeld saw Pauli's paper and suggested the application of Fermi statistics 'to other parts of metal theory,' and the time when he actually began the enterprize.

$^{696}$ The meeting of the *Gauverein Niedersachsen* was held on 7 and 8 February 1927, with Sommerfeld in the chair on the first day. Sommerfeld also gave a talk at the University of Hamburg before that meeting, entitled 'Zum gegenwärtigen Stande der Atomphysik' ('On the Present Status of Atomic Physics'), in which he discussed the recent quantum- and wave-mechanical theory and its successes (Sommerfeld, 1927a).
$^{697}$ See Chapter II, especially Sections II.5 and II.7.
