584 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

Certainly, the preparation of the paper for the Como conference in September 1927 set a limit on the beginning of Sommerfeld’s theory of metal electrons, as well as the composition of the first paper ‘Zur Elektronentheorie der Metalle’ (‘On the Electron Theory of Metals’) for *Naturwissenschaften* (Sommerfeld, 1927b), which probably occurred in the same period.$^{698}$ In the *Naturwissenschaften* paper, Sommerfeld also indicated how his whole endeavour had begun with the observation that a degenerate gas possesses an internal energy that, in the first approximation, is independent *of the temperature; hence, a vanishing of the specific heat follows.*$^{699}$ He stated further:

> Following the removal of the first difficulty, the question arises whether the simple concept of the electron gas cannot be applied to the whole domain of galvanic and thermal conduction. I have tried this out in a lecture during the current summer semester, and I have arrived thus at remarkable results which I want to summarize here briefly. (Sommerfeld, 1927b, p. 827)

Sommerfeld then sketched in the *Naturwissenschaften* article an account of the following topics: electrical and thermal conductivity and Wiedemann–Franz law, contact potentials, and the Voltaic potential sequence; Thomson, Peltier, and thermoelectric effects. He finally added:

> Further problems which can be treated are: the emission of electrons from heated metals (Richardson effect); thermo-magnetic and galvano-magnetic phenomena, especially the Hall effect; perhaps even ferromagnetism, which occurs only in conducting substances and therefore must be determined by the statistics of free electrons. (Sommerfeld, *loc. cit.*, p. 831)

Sommerfeld commented on some of these additional topics already in his Como talk (1928a); he and his collaborators would work out more details in further papers submitted toward the end of the year 1927 and in the first half of 1928

$^{698}$ It seems that Sommerfeld first wrote the *Naturwissenschaften* paper (1927b) and a little later his Como talk (1928a), because he included in the latter a discussion of the Richardson effect that he had announced in the former (1927b, p. 831).
$^{699}$ See Sommerfeld’s statements in his *Naturwissenschaften* paper:

> Since the electron gas is degenerate, its internal energy will become independent of the temperature in the first approximation, therefore its specific heat would vanish. If one calculates in the second approximation, i.e., if one takes into account the weakly rising energy curve in the degenerate region, then a specific heat follows which grows slowly with $t$; however, when calculated at room temperature for a gram-molecule, it reaches a value of about $R/100$—while, according to the classical theory, it should be $\frac{3}{2} R$ (with $R$ the universal gas constant). The latter amount, however, contradicts the data, while the amount $R/100$ can be admitted. (Sommerfeld, 1927b, pp. 826–827)

We consider it possible that Sommerfeld recognized this result from Pauli’s paramagnetism theory of metal electrons already in February 1927.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0617 -->

III.6 The Metal Electrons and Solid State Theory 585

(Sommerfeld, 1928b, c, d, e; Houston, 1928a, b; Eckart, 1928). Full of admiration, Niels Bohr wrote in a congratulatory note for Sommerfeld's sixtieth birthday:

> With youthful enthusiasm he has turned to the application of the new statistics to the problem of electrical conductivity of metals, which despite the great hopes that one had once associated with classical statistics, has thus far resisted all attacks. As we know, he succeeded here in breaking all old barriers and opening a fruitful domain of work, in which already a host of successors has become active. (Bohr, 1928g, p. 1036)

Indeed, by the end of the year 1928, many fruits ripened from the work on metal electrons, which Sommerfeld had pioneered. In his Como talk, Sommerfeld emphasized that 'the main difference between the new [Fermi] and the classical [i.e., the old Maxwell–Boltzmann] statistics consists in the fact how the average velocity [of electrons] depends on temperature' (Sommerfeld, 1928a, p. 454). Although the square of this average velocity $v$ was formerly proportional to the absolute temperature $T$, it now become constant in Fermi's case of full degeneracy, or

$$v = \sqrt{\frac{3}{5} \frac{h}{m_e}} \left( \frac{3n}{4\pi} \right)^{1/3}, \tag{522}$$

where $n = \frac{1}{a^3} (= N/V)$ denoted the electron density that could be connected with the (average) de Broglie wavelength of the electron, $\lambda$, through the relation<sup>700</sup>

$$\lambda = \left( \frac{4\pi}{3n} \right)^{1/3} \tag{523}$$

Evidently, 'the de Broglie waves corresponding to the motion of the electron gas possess the character of $X$-waves and are temperature independent'; hence, the Fermi statistics of the electron gas must deviate fundamentally from the classical statistics. The same deviations showed up also for the electrical and thermal conductivity, as Sommerfeld showed by a comparative calculation (Sommerfeld, *loc. cit.*, Section II).<sup>701</sup> He started from the expression for the velocity distribution $f(\xi, \eta, \zeta)$, deviating from $f_0$ in the $x$-direction due to the action of an electric field $F$ or a temperature gradient in this direction,

$$f(\xi, \eta, \zeta) = f_0 + \xi\phi, \tag{524}$$

<sup>700</sup> Equation (522) followed from identifying the kinetic energy of the degenerate electron-gas molecules, $(m_e/2)v^2$, with the zero-point energy $\varepsilon_0$, Eq. (518).
<sup>701</sup> See also Sommerfeld, 1927b, Section II.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0618 -->

586 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

where (with $\varepsilon = \frac{m_e}{2}v^2$)

$$f_0 = A \exp\left( - \frac{\varepsilon}{kT} \right) \tag{525a}$$

for the classical (Maxwell–Boltzmann) statistics and

$$f_0 = \frac{1}{\left[ \frac{1}{A} \exp\left( \frac{\varepsilon}{kT} \right) + 1 \right]} \tag{525b}$$

for the quantum-mechanical Fermi statistics.<sup>702</sup> For the term $\xi\phi$ describing the collision between the free electron (velocity $\xi$ in $x$-direction) with the metal atoms (considered at rest), Sommerfeld proposed the usual *Ansatz* for $\phi$, namely,

$$\phi = - \frac{l}{v} \left( \frac{eF}{m_e v} \frac{\partial f_0}{\partial v} + \frac{\partial f_0}{\partial x} \right), \tag{526}$$

to obtain the following expressions for the electric current $J$ and the (thermal) energy current $W$, respectively,

$$J = e \int \xi f \, d\Omega \quad \text{and} \quad W = \frac{m_e}{2} \int \xi v^2 f \, d\Omega, \tag{527}$$

with the momentum-space element

$$d\Omega = 4\pi \left( \frac{m_e}{h} \right)^3 v^2 \, dv. \tag{527a}$$

Thus, he calculated the electrical conductivity $\sigma(= \frac{J}{F})$ and the thermal conductivity $\kappa$, both in the classical ($A \ll 1$) and extremely quantum-mechanical ($A \gg 1$) limits, obtaining<sup>703</sup>

$$\sigma = \frac{4}{3} \frac{e^2 l n}{\sqrt{2\pi m_e k T}} \quad \text{and} \quad \kappa = \frac{8}{3} \frac{l n k^2 T}{\sqrt{2\pi m_e k T}} \quad \text{for } A \ll 1 \tag{528a}$$

<sup>702</sup> Here, $A = \exp(-\alpha)$ in Pauli's notation; also, we have replaced Sommerfeld's $\chi$ in Eq. (524) by $\phi$ to avoid confusion with magnetic susceptibility.
<sup>703</sup> The temperature-dependent terms of the quantum-mechanical expressions were always second-order contributions.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0619 -->

III.6 The Metal Electrons and Solid State Theory 587

and

$$\sigma = \frac{4\pi e l}{3 h} \left( \frac{3n}{4\pi} \right)^{2/3} \quad \text{and} \quad \kappa = \frac{4\pi^3 l k T}{9 h} \left( \frac{3n}{4\pi} \right)^{2/3} \quad \text{for } A \gg 1. \tag{528b}$$

Consequently, Sommerfeld confirmed in all cases the Wiedemann–Franz law, namely,

$$\frac{\kappa}{\sigma} = \begin{cases} 2 \left( \frac{k}{e} \right)^2 T & \text{for } A \ll 1, \\ \frac{\pi^2}{3} \left( \frac{k}{e} \right)^2 T & \text{for } A \gg 1. \end{cases} \tag{529}$$

Sommerfeld concluded triumphantly: 'Our [quantum-mechanical] factor $\frac{\pi^2}{3}$ describes the observations still better than Drude's value 3 [and, of course, Lorentz' value 2]' (Sommerfeld, 1928, p. 459).

The next series of effects, also discussed in fall 1927, embraced the Thomson and Peltier effects, thermoelectricity, and the Hall effect, 'whose theoretical treatment shared with that of the Wiedemann-Franz law the specific property of being independent of the mean free path $l$' (Sommerfeld, *loc. cit.*, p. 460). The energy balance $Q$ now included a mixture of electric, magnetic, and caloric terms ($Q_1, Q_2, Q_3$). For instance, in the case of the Thomson effect—the change of the temperature gradient in a conductor carrying an electric current $\left( Q_2 = -\mu_{\text{Th}} J \frac{\partial T}{\partial x} \right)$—the coefficient $\mu_{\text{Th}}$ became in the classical and the quantum-theoretical limits, respectively,

$$\mu_{\text{Th}} = \begin{cases} \frac{3k}{2e} \left( 1 - \frac{2}{3} \frac{d \log n}{dT} \right) & \text{for } A \ll 1, \tag{530a} \\ \frac{2\pi^2 m_e k^2 \lambda^2}{3 eh} T \left( 1 - \frac{2}{3} \frac{d \log n}{dT} \right) & \text{for } A \gg 1. \tag{530b} \end{cases}$$

The result (530b) explained the smallness of the observed effect as compared with the classical calculation (530a)—except in the case of some substances (As, Sb, Bi). Also, the coefficients of the so-called Peltier effect (i.e., the heat production $\Pi$ per unit time at the soldering point of two metals) came out quite differently in quantum mechanics, namely,

$$\Pi_{q.m.} = \frac{2\pi^2 m_e k^2 T^2}{3 e^2 h^2} (\lambda_2^2 - \lambda_1^2). \tag{531}$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0620 -->

588 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

$\Pi_{q.m.}$ seemed to have the right order of magnitude and the right temperature dependence—the classical effect ($A \ll 1$) depended linearly on $T$. Sommerfeld obtained a similarly satisfactory result for the thermionic potential $\Phi$: the dependence on the difference of the temperature squares involved in $\Phi_{q.m.}$, rather than on the difference of the temperatures, as in the classical limit, and the order of magnitude (with the exception of Sb and Bi) spoke clearly in favour of the new theory. Only for the Hall effect, Sommerfeld failed to produce an essential correction of the classical, empirically quite unsatisfactory, result.

The set of physical effects to be treated included further the thermionic emission of electrons (the Richardson effect) and the Voltaic potentials. In the first case, the empirically discovered exponential dependence of the current was reproduced, but the formula contained, instead of one, two work functions $W_a$ and $W_i$, and the classical temperature-dependent factor $\sqrt{kT}$ had to be replaced by $(kT)^2$. For the Volta effect, the classical and the quantum-mechanical results were

$$\Phi_i^{cl} = \frac{kT}{e} \log \frac{n_1}{n_2} \quad \text{and} \quad \Phi_i^{q.m.} = \frac{h^2}{2 m_e e} \left( \frac{1}{\lambda_1^2} - \frac{1}{\lambda_2^2} \right), \tag{532}$$

respectively, but only the latter yielded the right order of magnitude and described the correct sequence of the observed voltages. 'Here we have treated only a small part of the vast field of metallic conduction,' Sommerfeld concluded his Como talk and stressed the general impression that 'by [means of] the new statistics the contradictions of the old theory have been removed and the facts of experience are represented [now] partly qualitatively and partly quantitatively,' especially, 'the agreement with the data of metallic conduction provides a firm empirical basis for this [Fermi] statistics' (Sommerfeld, *loc. cit.*, p. 469). At the same time, he admitted the weak points of the approach taken, namely, that it so far lacked a physical understanding of the concept of the mean free path $l$, which might be obtained perhaps by 'treating the scattering of de Broglie waves in a lattice of metal atoms and taking into account the thermal agitation of this lattice and the mutual collision of electrons' (Sommerfeld, *loc. cit.*).

The discussion at Como revealed certain problems in Sommerfeld's programme —e.g., Jakov Frenkel pointed out that the temperature dependence of electrical conductivity, Eq. (528b), contradicted experience—but, in general, the reactions were quite positive and encouraged Sommerfeld to proceed further. As Rudolf Peierls recalled, 'Sommerfeld certainly was interested in looking at all the various interactions of magnetic and electric fields and thermal gradients . . . and he had a long list of them' and:

> He was going around with a little book by Bädecker (1911), which was the reference book about the properties of metals and the definition of the various coefficients, and seeing how far things could be made to agree with the theory and how far they could not. (Peierls, AHQP Interview, 17 June 1963, p. 13)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0621 -->

III.6 The Metal Electrons and Solid State Theory 589

Indeed, Sommerfeld involved his collaborators and guest visitors at his Institute in the programme, especially the two Americans Carl Eckart and William V. Houston. Eckart investigated a detail of the Volta effect (Eckart, 1928), while the latter first improved on another aspect of the new theory and showed that in the Richardson effect the observed electron emission from cold metals could be explained ‘under the assumption that an external [electric] field reduces the work function of the electrons’ (Houston, 1928a, p. 33).<sup>704</sup> Both papers were submitted in December 1927 to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, simultaneously with a two-part memoir of Sommerfeld’s, ‘Zur Elektronentheorie der Metalle auf Grund der Fermischen Statistik’ (‘On the Electron Theory of Metals on the Basis of Fermi Statistics,’ Sommerfeld, 1928b, c). Sommerfeld discussed there systematically, with all of the technical details, the basis of his ingenious approach to metal electrons, emphasizing again ‘that no new physical hypotheses about the behaviour of metal atoms and their interaction with the electrons are proposed, but that the hypotheses of the old electron theory are just recalculated with the formulae of the new statistics’ (Sommerfeld, 1928b, p. 1). Beyond the aspects already treated earlier, the second part included in particular an investigation of the Hall effect, i.e., the action of a magnetic field on the motion of electrons in metals. Sommerfeld again followed the familiar classical approach, notably, that of Richard Gans (1906), and found a standard effect in a weak magnetic field having a constant \(R_0\),

\[
R_0 = \frac{1}{en},
\]
(533)

whose value deviated from the result of classical theory \(\left(\frac{2\pi}{8en}\right)\) only by a numerical factor of 0.85. Further, in the first approximation, \(R_0\) did not depend on the strength of the magnetic field, whereas in the second approximation a field-

<sup>704</sup> See also the criticism of Houston’s paper by A. T. Watermann (1928).
William Vermillion Houston was born on 19 January 1900, in Mt. Gilead, Ohio, and received his elementary and secondary school education in Columbus, Ohio, and received his baccalaureate degree from Ohio State University. He joined the graduate school at the University of Chicago, where he obtained a Master’s degree. He then returned to Ohio State University and received his Ph.D. in 1925. After completing his graduate study, he became a member of the faculty of the California Institute of Technology (1925–1927, National Research Fellow, 1927 assistant, 1929 associate professor, 1931 full professor) and later served as Chairman of the Division of Physics, Mathematics, and Electrical Engineering. In 1927–1928, he held a Guggenheim fellowship and studied with Sommerfeld and Heisenberg in Germany, taking part in the early development and application of quantum mechanics. The work he began there was continued on his return at Caltech, and it was during this period that he and his students undertook the pioneering work in precision spectroscopy that was to lead later to the discovery of the anomalies in the fine structure of hydrogen. During World War II, his efforts were devoted to undersea warfare research at Columbia University, for which he was awarded the Navy Medal of Merit. In 1946, he became the second president of Rice University. He served as president and professor of physics until 1961. Houston received many honours that were tributes to his dedication to science, to his skill as a teacher, and to his ability to inspire others. He was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 1943. He died in Edinburgh, Scotland, on 22 August 1968, at the age of 68.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0622 -->

590 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

dependent contribution arose, which was zero at the absolute zero temperature and rose quadratically with \(T\) (and linearly with \(H\) for \(T > 0\)). The numerical changes, however, were orders of magnitude below the observed ones, apart from the fact that the theory did not explain the anomalous Hall effects. Also, in the case of the Nernst effect, in which a temperature difference is created in a conductor carrying an electric current when it is placed in a transverse magnetic field, the new theory failed to a large extent: though the wrong classical result was corrected considerably (i.e., reduced by a factor of 1,000), the calculated value came out still off by a factor of \(\frac{1}{5}\) as compared with the observations (in Ag and Cu). Thus, Sommerfeld admitted a considerable limitation in his theory, which he ascribed to one weak point, namely: ‘The physical refinement of the concept of mean free path must be based on wave mechanics and the scattering of de Broglie waves by the atoms of the metal (in the lattice of the solid or the molten solid)’ (Sommerfeld, 1928c, p. 60). In addition, he emphasized the lack of a quantitative theory of the Volta effect.
In the first few months of the year 1928, the Sommerfeld school made considerable progress. In particular, Houston developed a wave-mechanical discussion of the mean free path by considering the scattering of electron waves by the ‘atmosphere’ of the atom (i.e., the electron cloud of the atomic ions in the metal); he thus derived the following formulae for the electrical resistance \(R\) (Houston denoted it by \(W\)),

\[
R = \begin{cases} \sim T/\theta & \text{for high temperatures}, \\ \sim (T/\theta)^2 & \text{for low temperatures}, \end{cases}
\]
(534)

with \(\theta\) the characteristic (Debye) temperature. Also, the pressure dependence of the resistance and the so-called Matthiessen rule—stating the influence of impurities—and, to a lesser extent, the dependence of the electrical conduction on the direction in single crystals came out essentially correctly.<sup>705</sup> Therefore, Sommerfeld concluded a second article on the new theory of metal electrons for the *Naturwissenschaften*, which appeared in the issue of 23 May 1928, with an optimistic remark concerning the defects mentioned earlier:<sup>706</sup>

I wish to withdraw this conclusion [stated earlier] now in view of the fine results of Houston’s paper, which in my opinion seems to satisfy everything that can be required from a general statistical theory of electrical conductivity. (Sommerfeld, 1928e, p. 381)

Besides his own associates, Sommerfeld also stimulated younger colleagues outside Munich. Thus, Lothar Nordheim recalled:

<sup>705</sup> See also the investigation of J. Frenkel and N. Mirolyubow (1928).
<sup>706</sup> In a similarly optimistic tone, he expounded the results at a meeting of the German Chemical Society, on 28 April 1928, entitled ‘Zur Elektronentheorie der Metalle nach der wellenmechanischen Statistik, insbesondere zur Frage des Volta-Effektes’ (‘On the Electron Theory of Metals Based on the Wave-Mechanical Statistics, in Particular on the Problem of the Volta Effect’ Sommerfeld, 1928d).

III.6 The Metal Electrons and Solid State Theory 591

I think I already started after the first communication by Sommerfeld [1927b]. And then it occurred to me that you should worry much more about the motion of electrons in solid metal than just the Fermi statistics. I worked out the theory of emission as an exercise without knowing anything that one had done classically. (Nordheim, AHQP Interview, 30 July 1962, p. 15)

In the fall of 1927, Nordheim had gone from Göttingen to Cambridge as an International Education Board fellow to work with Ralph Fowler. Fowler had listened to Sommerfeld’s talk at Como and argued that one could use the ‘Fermi-Dirac statistics’ also for ‘an application which Sommerfeld does not discuss ..., namely the calculation of the density of evaporated electrons in equilibrium with the heated metal’ (Fowler, 1928a, p. 549). For that purpose, he considered electrons in a large potential \(\phi_0\) inside and zero-potential outside the metal and calculated the thermionic electron density (outside the metal) of

\[
n_f = g \left(\frac{2\pi m_e k T}{h^2}\right)^{3/2} \exp\{-\phi/kT - \tau k T (\bar{n})^{2/3}\},
\]
(535)

with

\[
\phi = \phi_0 - \frac{h^2}{2m_e} \left(\frac{3\bar{n}}{4\pi g}\right)^{3/2} \quad \text{and} \quad \tau = \frac{\pi^2}{12} \frac{2m_e}{h^2} \left(\frac{4\pi g}{3}\right)^{2/3}
\]
(535a)

(\(g = 2, \bar{n}\) being the equilibrium concentration of electrons in the metal). Equation (535) deviated from the previous, semiempirical expressions by the Landé factor \(g\) and the second term in the exponential, and it gave rise to a thermionic saturation current of the form

\[
I = g(1 - r)(2\pi k^2 m_e e/h^3)T^2 \exp(-\phi/kT),
\]
(536)

with \(r\) denoting a reflection coefficient. Fowler announced in his paper, submitted in early December 1927 to the *Proceedings of the Royal Society of London*, that ‘Nordheim has shown how to derive formula [(536)] by considering the electrons incident on the discontinuity or sharp gradient of the potential at the boundary of the metal and their reflection coefficient there’ (Fowler, *loc. cit.*, p. 552). Nordheim indeed performed this quantum-mechanical calculation in a paper, entitled ‘Zur Theorie der thermischen Emission und der Reflexion von Elektronen an Metallen’ (‘On the Theory of the Thermal Emission and the Reflection of Electrons from Metals’) and received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 11 December 1927 (Nordheim, 1928a). He found, in particular, that the coefficient \(g(1 - r)\) assumed the value 1 for metals having a clean surface, i.e., a reflection coefficient of \(r = 1/2\) was obtained. Fowler then studied further conclusions from the Fermi statistics and determined the photoelectric threshold frequency and the thermionic work function (Fowler, 1928b), and afterward joined forces with Nordheim to work out the ‘Electron

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0624 -->

592 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

Emission in Intense Electric Fields’ (Fowler and Nordheim, 1928).<sup>707</sup> Nordheim had previously (1928a) calculated the reflection and transmission effects for various potential shapes, including those with barriers decreasing in height for larger distances. Since the action of an electric field \(F\) on the surface of the metal decreases the potential there, Fowler and Nordheim applied the result to derive the following formula for the emission current \(I\):

\[
I = \frac{e}{2\pi h} \frac{\psi^{1/2}}{(\phi + \psi)\phi^{1/2}} F^2 \exp\{-4K\phi^{3/2}/3F\},
\]
(537)

with \(\phi\) and \(\psi\) denoting the work function and the free energy of the electron, \(K = 8\pi m_e/h\), and \(F\) the electric field strength in volts per centimeter. This result fitted quite well with the recent empirical findings of Robert A. Millikan and his associates.
Nordheim had gone to Cambridge because of his interest in statistical mechanics, in which Fowler ‘was one of the foremost experts,’ but he soon realized that he was left there very much on his own:

I did not talk very often with [Fowler]. He was a very busy person. ... One paper, on the emission in strong fields, ... actually he wrote [Fowler and Nordheim, 1928]. We talked about it, and it was clear what was to be done, but then I went on vacations to visit my family in Germany, and when I came back he had already sent it off. ... He had worked out the mathematics, which was not very difficult, yet I was very much surprised when he had finished the paper after I came back after a few weeks. (Nordheim, AHQP Interview, 30 July 1962, p. 16)

In Cambridge, he observed in general a rather loose collaboration, because ‘everyone worked for himself,’ quite differently from what he had experienced before in Göttingen and would experience especially later in Copenhagen.<sup>708</sup> Yet Nordheim was quite productive there and submitted two more papers resulting from his work: the first, in May 1928, in which he reformulated the Maxwell–Boltzmann statistical mechanics with Fermi electrons for a theory of electrical conductivity (Nordheim, 1928b); the second, communicated by Fowler in early August, again to the *Proceedings of the Royal Society of London*, refined the previous mathe-

<sup>707</sup> In this context, Fowler and Nordheim referred to ‘some recent work by Oppenheimer [1928a] on the hydrogen atom in an external field’ (Fowler and Nordheim, 1928, p. 174). J. Robert Oppenheimer, in the third of his ‘Three Notes on the Quantum Theory of Aperiodic Effects,’ had treated this effect and obtained a very tiny rate (of \(1/10^{110}\) per second) for the electrons emitted or extracted by the electric field of 1 V from the metal; he had claimed that it might nevertheless help to understand the existence of free electrons in metals (Oppenheimer, 1928a, p. 81).
<sup>708</sup> Note the statements made by Nordheim:

I had occasionally talks with Fowler and I played chess with Kaptiza. Kaptiza had a kind of private seminar held sometimes in [L. H.] Thomas’ rooms, which was the only one where people got into contact with each other. ... Dirac was there, and I met him occasionally. But he worked by himself, and Fowler worked by himself, and Kaptiza worked by himself. (Nordheim, *loc. cit.*, p. 18)

matical evaluation of the strong-field problem with Fowler (Nordheim, 1928c).⁷⁰⁹ Later that year, he wrote a short note on the resistance in metal alloys, discussing the origin of Matthiesen’s rule on the basis of the scattering of electron waves from impurities in Sommerfeld’s theory (Nordheim, 1928d).

(c) Atomic Lattices in Leipzig: Heisenberg’s Ferromagnetism and  
Bloch’s Electrical Conductivity (1928)

Felix Bloch recalled his earliest encounter with Werner Heisenberg as follows:

> In the fall of 1927 I went to Leipzig. I had something written up about [the damping  
of wave packets]. When I came to Leipzig, Heisenberg wasn’t there yet.... Only  
Wentzel was there. He was extremely kind. I showed him that paper, and he looked  
at it and he said [that] he didn’t feel very competent about these matters, and he  
suggested that I show it to Heisenberg.... When I saw Heisenberg, I told him about  
it. He listened to me, and he immediately discarded it.... However, he did say that  
the problem would interest him, that it should be done more thoroughly, more gen-  
erally, not only for the harmonic oscillator.... I suppose he said to me that I should  
really use Dirac’s radiation theory, which was developed at that time.... I studied  
Dirac’s paper and published my first paper on radiation damping.... It showed  
something which pleased Heisenberg very much, namely if radiation damping does  
anything, ... it tends even to destroy phase relations, ... the wave packets run even  
slightly more apart. (Bloch, AHQP Interview, 15 May 1964, p. 18)

Bloch had just come from Zurich, where he had become interested in the problem  
of Schrödinger’s wave packets dissipating.⁷¹⁰ Now, the solution turned out to be  
against his original expectation (Bloch, 1928a), but Bloch had the pleasant feeling  
that Heisenberg ‘considered me ready to start a topic for my Ph.D. thesis’ (Bloch,  
1980, p. 24).  

Felix Bloch was born on 23 October 1925, in Zurich, the son of a Jewish busi-  
nessman, who had originated from the German-speaking part of Czechoslovakia,  
and Bloch’s mother was born in Austria. His parents moved in the late 1890s from  
Austria to Switzerland. Because his elder sister (born in 1902) died very young (in  
1914), Felix grew up alone, and attended a gymnasium where he was good in  
mathematics but also liked languages, especially Latin. He wanted to become an  
engineer. After the sudden death of his sister from blood poisoning, his parents  
showered all of their affection on him and protected him from any mishap that

by dealing with the diffraction of de Broglie waves in three-dimensional crystals (Witmer and Rosen-  
feld, 1928a, b).  

⁷¹⁰ This was an old problem noticed by Schrödinger already in the summer of 1926 (Schrödinger,  
1926g; see Volume 5, Part 2, pp. 629–638, for a discussion of this aspect). Before coming to Leipzig,  
Bloch had been with Schrödinger in Zurich.

might happen to him. He lived a very protected and secluded life, which allowed  
him much time for reading and study, especially languages and literature. At  
about the age of twelve or thirteen, he came across an old book on astronomy by  
Newcomb that fascinated him. He became very interested in Nature and ‘the Swiss  
mountains meant a great deal’ to him:  

> Since I wanted to go to the [Eidgenössische] Technische Hochschule [the Swiss Federal  
Institute of Technology in Zurich], which was the training [ground] for engineering,  
I decided I would go to the Realgymnasium, which was less humanistic and which  
essentially meant that I didn’t study any Greek, but I did have Latin.... Our math-  
ematics professor was [Emil] Beck, who worked with Pierre Weiss at that time ...  
actually a physicist; he redid the Einstein-de Haas experiment and found that the  
factor was twice as big, but he had no explanation for that. He was an excellent  
teacher, and it was really a joy to take mathematics with him. (Bloch, AHQP Inter-  
view, 14 May 1964, pp. 3–4)  

Analytic geometry was the most advanced topic to be taught in mathematics;  
however, when he was almost eighteen, Bloch got hold of a book on calculus.  
Physics, which was taught by an excellent teacher by the name of Seiler, included  
mechanics (without calculus), optics, a little bit of heat theory, some electricity—  
but no electromagnetic theory at all—and a laboratory course. After finishing  
high school with excellent grades, Block entered the ETH in 1924, where he  
studied engineering for a year, but he had some doubt whether he would even-  
tually like to end up as a businessman like many members of his family. Indeed,  
after getting some practical training in the summer vacations, he decided to  
change to physics.⁷¹¹ Peter Debye’s introductory course in physics stimulated great  
interest in the subject for Bloch, and he registered for the experimental lab-  
oratory with Richard Bär at the University of Zurich (in which he was the only  
student). Besides the obligatory courses, he also attended the advanced mathe-  
matics seminar of Hermann Weyl and George Polya, as well as the joint ETH–  
University physics colloquium, where he witnessed how Schrödinger arrived at  
wave mechanics.⁷¹² Thus, he learned the new atomic theory at its inception, ‘to a  
large extent by reading Schrödinger’s papers.’ As he recalled:  

> Then I got into personal contact with Schrödinger. Also what happened very much at  
that time was that Heitler and London came [to Zurich]. Although I was only a very  
young student, I established at that time a very close friendship [with them], and they  
took me on walks and sort of told me [that] they were working at that time on the  
covalent-bond theory.... Then I came to Schrödinger. I had heard, either through  
him or from London or from Heitler about this difficulty with the [dissipating] wave  
packets.... I went to Schrödinger and I said to him: “Maybe radiation damping will  
hold all the waves together.” And Schrödinger said: “That’s a very good idea. Why  
don’t you try it?” I did it for the harmonic oscillator. (Bloch, loc. cit., pp. 15–16)

III.6 The Metal Electrons and Solid State Theory 595

In fall 1927, there came ‘a great crisis in Zurich [physics], because at the same time  
Schrödinger [to Berlin], Debye [to Leipzig], and Weyl [to Göttingen] all left.’ (Bloch,  
loc. cit., p. 16)  

Felix Bloch did not regret the move away from home to Leipzig, where he knew  
at least one professor (Debye) in his field, who had advised him to work with Hei-  
senberg before he (Debye) left Zurich. He soon became acquainted with Heisenberg  
and, as he recalled: ‘I should say I had a tremendous impression of Heisenberg,  
right from the beginning’:  

> I was his first [doctoral] student, so I had a lot of [his] time. I participated immedi-  
ately in the seminars and established a very close and good connection with Heisen-  
berg and admired him tremendously ... Heisenberg himself was not too much inter-  
ested at that time in questions of epistemology.... He had a little bit this sort of  
aggressive way, like saying: “Well, now we have a new [theory]. Let’s try to under-  
stand metals and this and that.” (Bloch, loc. cit., p. 19)  

The Leipzig period in Heisenberg’s Institute started in quite a private way.  
‘Though my first seminar on atomic theory was attended only by one student, I  
was convinced that I would eventually make many fresh converts to the new  
atomic physics,’ Heisenberg himself noted rather optimistically (Heisenberg, 1971,  
p. 93). However, because that first student happened to be Felix Bloch, he indeed  
was lucky. Later on, both the lecture courses and the seminar filled very quickly.  
Already in summer 1928, when Heisenberg announced his lecture course on me-  
chanics, 150 students enrolled, and as many as 80 students attended the advanced  
course on atomic physics. The seminar, held jointly with Gregor Wentzel (who  
would soon leave for Zurich to replace Erwin Schrödinger at the University) grew  
to twelve participants, among them three researchers sent by Sommerfeld (who  
was preparing to leave on his world tour of India, China, Japan, and the United  
States in August 1928), namely, Rudolf Peierls, Carl Eckart, and William Hous-  
ton. Sommerfeld also provided Guido Beck as Heisenberg’s first assistant to Hei-  
senberg.⁷¹³ The earliest students included the Chinese Pei Yuan Chou and the  
Germans Bernhard Kockel and Rudolf Peierls (soon to be followed by many  
others); the earliest guest visitors, besides Eckart and Houston mentioned already,  
were the Austrian Otto Halpern, the Japanese Masazo Kuchi, and the Russian  
Gleb Wataghin. Already in June 1928, Debye and Heisenberg organized their first  
‘Leipziger Universitätswoche’ on the topic ‘Quantum Theory and Chemistry,’  
which attracted such illustrious speakers and visitors as Paul Dirac, Paul Ehren-  
fest, Arnold Eucken, Cyril Norman Hinshelwood (a well-known British chemist),  
Walther Kossel, and Erwin Schrödinger; further such meetings would follow in the  
next years. Leipzig soon became, certainly in Germany, the most actively growing  


⁷¹³ For Heisenberg’s early years in Leipzig, we refer to Lea and Wiemers, 1993, and Cassidy, 1992a.  
For Heisenberg’s students and auditors, see the articles: ‘Schüler und Gäste Werner Heisenbergs und  
Friedrich Hunds in Leipzig’ and ‘Verzeichnis der Studenten und Hörer bei Heisenberg’ in Kleint and  
Wiemers, 1993, pp. 136–143, 144–172.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0628 -->

596 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

centre of modern atomic physics. The work of Heisenberg and his first student  
Bloch contributed substantially to this increasing fame. Thus, when Peierls (after a  
semester in Leipzig) visited Cambridge in summer 1928, he found that Ralph  
Fowler ‘was delighted to hear that I came from Leipzig and said: “You must tell  
us about the work of Bloch”’ (Peierls, 1985, p. 35).  

Felix Bloch recalled that his work on metal electrons started in the following  
way:  

> After I had finished this paper and written it [Bloch, 1928a], I went home, and he  
[Heisenberg] said to me at that time [in winter 1927/28]: “Well, I think you ought to  
think about a thesis problem. Why don’t you think about some questions, what you  
might do?” I came back with some rather poor suggestions.... I thought, for exam-  
ple, that it might be of interest to follow Ehrenfest’s adiabatic theorem through, see  
how it goes in quantum mechanics. That question was apparently so clear to Hei-  
senberg that he said, “No, I don’t think that’s very interesting.” (Bloch, AHQP  
Interview, 15 May 1964, p. 20)  

Then Heisenberg, however, ‘suggested two problems that show very clearly what  
his interest was,’ namely:  

> One was: Sommerfeld had written before papers on the conduction of electrons and  
had pointed out that the Fermi statistics gives the right behaviour in experiments on  
specific heat and some other thermo-electric effects, and so it was clear that there was  
more to be done about that. Heisenberg said to me, sort of in a gentle way, “Well,  
maybe one should see what the electron theory of metals becomes like in quantum  
mechanics.” That was one possibility. And the other he mentioned to me was the idea  
of ferromagnetism.... He said, “Well, there is that Weiss field, and it strikes me as  
very similar to the problem of ortho- and para-helium.” That is to say that the para-  
position has really to do with symmetry, and therefore it’s an electric force. He  
sketched out to me briefly why the field is so very great because it’s not really of  
magnetic origin. (Bloch, loc. cit., pp. 20–21)  

Bloch knew very little about magnetism at that time; moreover, he felt that  
‘Heisenberg has it [i.e., the problem of ferromagnetism] already in a nutshell’;  
hence, he did ‘not want just simply to work it out.’ However:  

> I was then interested in this question of metal electrons, and very soon—in fact, I  
think only a week or two after he told me that—in some primitive way I had gotten  
the essential idea that a periodic arrangement is not really an obstacle for waves, but  
it’s only the thermal vibrations. Heisenberg was very pleased. I told it to him only in  
the one-dimensional case, in a very primitive way. And he said, “That’s explained  
now. Now I understand.” (Bloch, loc. cit., p. 21)  

So, while Bloch chose the conduction problem, Heisenberg was left with the  
problem of ferromagnetism.⁷¹⁴

netism. (See Pauli, 1979, p. 443.)

III.6 The Metal Electrons and Solid State Theory  
597

This problem consisted in explaining the origin of the strong magnetic interac‑
tion in certain metals and alloys, which belonged to the puzzles of classical elec‑
tron theory ever since Pierre Weiss had introduced what he called the ‘molecular
field’ to describe the situation phenomenologically (Weiss, 1907).<sup>715</sup> Could quan‑
tum mechanics with the spinning electron provide a solution? After his success
with the helium problem, in which he had been able to account for an apparently
large interaction of the spins of the valence electrons, Heisenberg had also hoped
to be able to attack also the Weiss field problem, as he informed Pauli:

> I have thought myself a little about the theory of ferromagnetism, conductivity and
> similar *S[chwein]ereien* (junk). The idea is the following. To apply Langevin’s theory
> [to] ferromagnetism, one has to assume a large coupling between the spinning elec‑
> trons (*only these* rotate). This force should, as in the case of helium, be supplied by
> the resonance indirectly. I believe that one can prove quite generally: the parallel
> position of the spin vectors yields always the smallest energy; the energy differences
> involved have the order of magnitude of electrical forces, but they decrease very
> rapidly with the distance. I feel, without even vaguely knowing the details, that this
> idea suffices in principle to understand ferromagnetism. In order to decide the ques‑
> tion why most substances are not ferromagnetic—while some are—one has to per‑
> form a quantitative calculation. One may then be able to derive that for Fe, Co and
> Ni the situation is most preferable. Similarly, for conductivity, one should take into
> account the resonance migration [of electrons] *à la* Hund. (Heisenberg to Pauli, 4
> November 1926, in Pauli, 1979, p. 353)

These ideas indeed contained the nucleus of the theories of ferromagnetism and
electrical conductivity that Heisenberg and his student Bloch developed more than
a year later in Leipzig.

From fall 1926 until far into 1927, Heisenberg took little time to pursue ferro‑
magnetism and the conductivity of metals, as there were more urgent problems of
a fundamental nature to consider, such as the physical interpretation of quantum
mechanics or it relativistic extension. Although he and Bohr finished the first
question by proposing the uncertainty relations and the complementarity princi‑
ple, respectively, the relativistic field theory was suddenly confronted in early 1928
with the serious difficulties of Dirac’s electron theory, as we have discussed in
Section II.7. At the instant, when progress in this fundamental problem stagnated,
Heisenberg returned to the problems of applying the established (nonrelativistic)
quantum mechanics. Thus, in spring 1928, he reported again to Pauli:

> Regarding the more important problems I do not know anything new. However, in
> order not to be forever irritated with Dirac, I have worked on something else, namely
> ferromagnetism, and I now wish to tell you about it. First a general remark on the
> problem of metals (see also Bloch’s work!). One can imagine three types of approxi‑
> mation to reality:
> 1. The “Pauli‑Sommerfeld” method, i.e., free electrons with Fermi statistics: the
> *mutual* interaction of electrons is suppressed.

715 See Volume 1, Part 2, p. 424.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0630 -->

598 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

2. The Bloch method: the action of the lattice is considered by taking corrugated‑iron
potentials (*Wellblechpotentiale*) but the interaction of electrons is neglected as well
against the other forces.
3. The—let’s call it so—London‑Heitler method, which I consider to consist in the
following procedure: the exchange of the valence electrons between any two atoms
in the lattice is taken into account according to London‑Heitler [in the hydrogen
molecule]. One considers, in the first place, only the states with all [valence] elec‑
trons assuming the ground state.

Evidently, the third method leads to a smaller term multiplicity than the other
two. For example, in the case of two hydrogen atoms (London‑Heitler), according to
the methods 1 and 2, the following *four* states would obtain the same energy in the
first approximation: (i) having electron 1 with nucleus *a* and electron 2 with nucleus
*b*; (ii) having electron 2 with nucleus *a* and electron 1 with nucleus *b*; (iii) having both
electrons with nucleus *a*; (iv) having both electrons with nucleus *b*.

In the case of method 3, one finds that only the energy terms (i) and (ii) are nearly
identical, and so are (iii) and (iv); but the latter lie much higher than (i) and (ii). It
seems plausible to apply this London‑Heitler treatment also to metals, that is, for the
moment only to those states in which every atom has only one electron (or several
valence electrons, according to the metal considered, i.e., an equal number per atom)
and to take into account their exchange possibilities. (Heisenberg to Pauli, 3 May
1928, *loc. cit.*, pp. 443–444)

After these guiding remarks concerning the Leipzig programme on metal elec‑
trons, Heisenberg sketched for Pauli the details of his new theory of ferromagnet‑
ism based on the ‘Heitler‑London method’ 3, because only in the case in which
electron interactions were not neglected could the phenomenon occur.<sup>716</sup> He
improved the preliminary treatment of his letter of 3 May quickly in further letters
to Pauli, dated 7, 10, 13, and 21 May, announcing in the last letter that he had
already submitted the finished paper to Karl Scheel, the editor of *Zeitschrift
für Physik*, and promised to send a copy of the proofs (of Heisenberg, 1928a) to
Zurich soon. On 16 June 1928, Pauli reported to Niels Bohr: ‘Heisenberg has
written to me about a very beautiful new theory of ferromagnetism, which he has
now found.’ (Pauli, 1979, p. 463)

In order to work out the details of his new theory, Heisenberg made full use of
the group‑theoretical results of Walter Heitler and Eugene Wigner in atomic and
molecular theory, and he referred to a model of the ferromagnet proposed earlier
by Ernst Ising in Hamburg (1925).<sup>717</sup> However, he did not refer to another source
of literature also connected with the problem of ferromagnetism, namely, the
papers written by Jakov Frenkel and published in spring 1928 (Frenkel, 1928a, b).
Actually, Frenkel in Leningrad, who had specialized in the theory of metal elec‑

That is, Frenkel guessed here, as Heisenberg had done in November 1926, that
‘Δ*U* actually represents an electrical (Coulomb) energy.’ He then outlined just a

phenomenological description of ferromagnetism (Frenkel, *loc. cit.*, pp. 36–37)
without developing an atomic (i.e., quantum‑mechanical) model, as Heisenberg
would do later.<sup>720</sup>

Supported by Pauli’s interest and constructive criticism, Heisenberg published
two papers in 1928 on his theory of ferromagnetism: besides the one submitted
in May (1928a), he wrote a second one for the *Festschrift* celebrating Arnold
Sommerfeld’s sixtieth birthday (Heisenberg, 1928b).<sup>721</sup> The theory started from
three fundamental observations: first, it was the valence electrons *with spin* that
created ferromagnetism (because of the observed *g* = 2 factor in the Einstein–de
Haas effect of ferromagnetic materials); second, the Pauli–Sommerfeld theory of
free electrons only provided para‑ or diamagnetism; and third, the exchange
mechanism (introduced for the case of the helium atom) produced the strong
forces behind the Weiss field. Heisenberg’s task now consisted in extending the
Heitler–London mechanism from a few (as in the case of molecules) to a large
number (2*n*, to simplify the evaluation) of interacting electrons and to calculate, at
least in a first‑order perturbation approximation, the energy of the metal. Heisen‑
berg wrote the perturbing potential as a sum of an exchange part *J*<sub>(kl)</sub> and a purely
static interaction *J*<sub>*E*</sub>, where

$$
J_{(kl)} = \frac{1}{2} \int \psi_k^\kappa \psi_k^\lambda \psi_l^\kappa \psi_l^\lambda \left( \frac{2e^2}{r_{kl}} + \frac{2e^2}{r_{\kappa\lambda}} - \frac{e^2}{r_{kk}} - \frac{e^2}{r_{kl}} - \frac{e^2}{r_{\lambda k}} - \frac{e^2}{r_{\lambda l}} \right) d\tau_k \, d\tau_l \tag{539}
$$

(where *k* and *l* denote the electrons, and *κ* and *λ* the atomic cores), and

$$
J_E = \int d\tau_1 \, d\tau_2 \, \dots \, d\tau_{2n} (\psi_1^1)^2 (\psi_2^2)^2 \, \dots \, (\psi_{2n}^{2n})^2 \cdot \left\{ \sum_{\kappa > k} \frac{e^2}{r_{kl}} + \sum_{\kappa > \lambda} \frac{e^2}{r_{\kappa\lambda}} - \sum_{k \neq \lambda} \frac{e^2}{r_{k\lambda}} \right\}. \tag{540}
$$

The additional magnetic interactions just ensured (as in the case of the helium
atom) that the electron spins are aligned parallel or antiparallel; however, their
contribution to the energy was neglected.

Evidently, Heisenberg characterized the energy eigenvalues of the ferromagnet
in his model by the (spin) angular moment $s\frac{h}{2\pi}$. The statistical treatment of the
system of 2*n* atoms (each having only one valence electron per atom in Heisen‑
berg, 1928a) required the knowledge of all energy values associated with the
quantum number *s*. For the energy of this term system *σ*, he took over Walter
Heitler’s formula for the ‘centre‑of‑mass energy’ [Heitler, 1927, see Eq. (466) in

to Peter Debye, the editor of the *Festschrift*.

601

Section III.4],

$$E_{\sigma} = \frac{1}{f_{\sigma}} \sum_{P} \chi_{\sigma}^{P} J_{P},$$ (541)

with $\chi_{\sigma}^{P}$ denoting the group character of the permutation $P$ and $f_{\sigma} = \chi_{\sigma}^{E}$ denoting the number of terms of the whole system. The perturbation energy $J_P$ could be obtained as the roots of an $f$-dimensional determinant. Further, Heisenberg derived for the energy fluctuation the compact expression

$$\overline{\Delta E_{\sigma}^2} = \frac{1}{f_{\sigma}} \left(\chi_{\sigma}^{E} \chi_{\sigma}^{P,P'} - \chi_{\sigma}^{P} \chi_{\sigma}^{P'}\right) J_P J_{P'},$$ (542)

which he simplified by assuming that only nearest neighbours have a nonzero exchange energy $J_P = J_0$ to

$$\overline{\Delta E_{\sigma}^2} = J_0 z \frac{(n^2 - s^2)(3n^2 - s^2)}{4n^3},$$ (543)

where $z$ denotes the number of nearest neighbours in the lattice. The partition function $S$ of this system in a magnetic field $H$ then became

$$S = F(2\cosh x)^{2n},$$ (544)

with $F$ denoting a function of $\alpha$ and $\beta$, having essentially the order of unity, and

$$x = \frac{1}{2} \left( \alpha + \beta \frac{m_0}{n} - \beta^2 \frac{m_0}{nz} + \beta^2 \frac{m_0^3}{2n^3 z} \right).$$ (544a)

Here, $\alpha$ and $\beta$ were given by the expressions

$$\alpha = \frac{1}{kT} \frac{e}{m_e c} H \frac{h}{2\pi} \quad \text{and} \quad \beta = \frac{zJ_0}{kT}.$$ (544b)

Finally, Heisenberg determined the most probable value for the 'magnetization' $m_0$ (which represents the average of the magnetic quantum numbers $m$ of the system, where $-s \leq m \leq +s$) by the equation

$$m_0 = \frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} \log S = n \tanh x.$$ (545)

Heisenberg noticed that Eq. (545) 'was essentially identical with the well-known Weiss formula for ferromagnetism,' except that here $\tanh x$ replaced the Weiss

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0634 -->

602  Chapter III  The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

function $coth x - \frac{1}{x}$, which however did not change the character of the solution.
When drawing the solution $y = \frac{m_0}{n}$ as a function of $x$ graphically, he found that the existence of ferromagnetism depended on the following condition to be satisfied,

$$\beta\left(1 - \frac{\beta}{z}\right) \geq 2 \quad \text{or} \quad z \geq 8.$$ (546)

He concluded with satisfaction: 'Ferromagnetism therefore occurs only for lattice types where one atom has at least eight neighbours,' because all known ferromagnetic substances obviously did so (Heisenberg, 1928a, p. 631). Yet, Heisenberg was aware that his theory had still to be improved at several points. Thus, for example, he had assumed a Gaussian distribution for the energy values, which could not really be justified; also, higher fluctuations $\Delta E^3$, $\Delta E^4$, etc., had to be calculated. Moreover, although the size of $J_0$ seemed to have the right order of magnitude (namely, $J_0 \sim kT_c$, where $T_c$ denotes the Curie transition temperature), the evaluation of its sign caused considerable trouble. However, a rough estimate for ferromagnetic substances seemed to suggest positive $J_0$ (in contrast to the negative value calculated in the Heitler–London hydrogen case).
In the paper for the Sommerfeld *Festschrift*, Heisenberg could not prove the desired positivity of $J_0$, but he generalized the theory to include several valence electrons per atom [in that case, the energy fluctuation formula, Eq. (543), had to be multiplied with the corresponding number]. Unfortunately, also the unrealistic assumption of a Gaussian distribution still had to be made—which only Pauli would succeed in removing in his Solvay report of 1930 [see Pauli, 1932a, Eqs. (64)–(66)].<sup>722</sup> We should further mention that John H. Van Vleck, in his book *The Theory of Electric and Magnetic Susceptibilities* (1932), replaced Heisenberg's tedious group-theoretical formulation by a simpler method involving Paul Dirac's spin Hamiltonian (Dirac, 1929b); he also wrote explicitly what he called 'Heisenberg's Hamiltonian,'

$$H_{\text{spin}} = \sum_{i,j} J_{ij} S_i \cdot S_j,$$ (547)

which Heisenberg in 1928 had described only in words. In spite of these improvements and limitations—the positivity of the exchange integral could still be doubted—Heisenberg had solved the problem of ferromagnetism in principle.
Even before Heisenberg finally attacked the calculations for the problem of ferromagnetism, Bloch was busy with his thesis work on the conductivity of metal

603

electrons. Heisenberg had stated the problem only vaguely: that somehow more must be put into the theory than just the Fermi statistics, in order to deal with metallic conduction and resistivity properly, and that especially the influence of the metallic ions had to be considered. When he thought more about the problem himself, Bloch soon arrived at the following conclusions:

> From the beginning I was convinced that the answer could be found, if at all, in the wave nature of the electron, especially since Heitler and London as well as Hund had shown before that the valence electrons in a molecule were not confined to stay in a single atom. The fact that the periodicity of a crystal would be essential was somehow suggested to me by recalling a demonstration in elementary physics where many equal and equally coupled pendula were hanging at constant spacing from a rod and the motion of one of them was seen to "migrate" along the rod from pendulum to pendulum. Returning to my rented room one evening in early January [1928], it was so vague in my mind that I began to use pencil and paper and treat the case of a single electron in a one-dimensional periodic potential. By means of straight Fourier analysis I found to my delight that the solutions of the Schrödinger equation differed from those of the de Broglie wave of a free particle only by a modulation with the period of the potential. The generalization to three dimensions was obvious and while it made me happy, the whole thing was so simple that I did not think that it amounted to much of a discovery; indeed, I saw later that Witmer and Rosenfeld had arrived [before the publication of Bloch’s results] at the same conclusion, and eventually I was even told by real scholars that something called "Floquet’s theorem" had been known for a long time. But my findings were news to Heisenberg, too, when I told him about them the next day, and in his usual optimism he thought that the problem was essentially in the bag. Actually, it took me a further half year before my thesis was finished and submitted for publication in the *Zeitschrift für Physik*. (Bloch, 1980, p. 25)

Thus began the story of Bloch’s method—called by Heisenberg method 2—which would play a decisive role in describing electronic phenomena in solids far beyond the solution of the thesis problem.
When he began, Bloch proceeded ‘in an extraordinarily primitive way’ by trying some Fourier analysis and: ‘In fact, by putting the Fourier coefficients together, I realized that it’s a wave which is modulated.’ As a ‘tribute to fashion’ also group theory got into the game, and further, as Bloch recalled:

> From then on I went pretty much on my own, with occasional help and correction from Heisenberg. I would say I saw Heisenberg regularly … often in the seminars … but also he occasionally asked, “Well, how is it going?” Sometimes I had difficulties, and Heisenberg made a suggestion to me. “Why don’t you try it this way?” And very often that was it. So I wrote this paper on the conduction of electrons in a very short time; I think that in about half a year it was finished. (Bloch, AHQP Interview, loc. cit., pp. 22–23)

Indeed, on 25 June 1928, Bloch signed the manuscript, and apparently Heisenberg kept it for a while before the *Zeitschrift für Physik* received the paper on 10 August (Bloch, 1928b).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0636 -->

604  Chapter III  The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

In considering the quantum mechanics of metal electrons for the problem of electrical conduction, Bloch neglected the exchange mechanism for strictly bound electrons, which had played the crucial role in the problem of ferromagnetism. As he had realized, one could just rely on the quantum-mechanical property of the electron (noticed especially by Friedrich Hund) to migrate through a potential wall; although in a strictly periodic potential it moved completely freely, the deviations from the periodicity because of the thermal motion of the metal ions created a finite conductivity (or the corresponding behaviour of the mean free path $l$ of the conduction electrons). In order to develop these ideas in detail and quantitatively, Bloch turned to the Schrödinger equation for an electron in a three-fold periodic potential,

$$V(\mathbf{r}) = V(\mathbf{r} + g_1 \mathbf{a} + g_2 \mathbf{b} + g_3 \mathbf{c}),$$ (548)

arriving at the solution

$$\psi_{klm} = \exp\left\{2\pi i \left(\frac{kx}{K} + \frac{ly}{L} + \frac{mz}{M}\right)\right\} u_{klm}(x, y, z).$$ (549)

Evidently, the result exhibited a periodic structure (with periods $a = |\mathbf{a}|$, $b = |\mathbf{b}|$, and $c = |\mathbf{c}|$); hence, Bloch concluded:

> The fact that from the eigenfunctions … always a factor $\exp\left\{2\pi i \left(\frac{kx}{K} + \frac{ly}{L} + \frac{mz}{M}\right)\right\}$ [with $k, l, m$ integers and $K, L, M$ periods] can be split off may be interpreted visually: we obtain *plane de Broglie waves*, which are modulated in the *rhythm* of the *lattice structure*. (Bloch, loc. cit., p. 559)

Bloch now studied two limiting cases. In the first, the case of free electrons, $\psi_{klm}$ reduced to the plane translational motion with the de Broglie wavelengths $K/k$, $L/l$, and $M/m$ through the crystal. For the second case of strongly bound electrons, on the other hand, the perturbation energy in the first-order calculation assumed the form

$$E_{klm} = E_0 + \alpha + 2\beta \left( \cos \frac{2\pi k}{G} + \cos \frac{2\pi l}{G} + \cos \frac{2\pi m}{G} \right),$$ (550)

with $G$ the third root of Avogadro’s number, and the triple $k, l, m$ denoting the state. The situation then deviated strongly from the free electron gas behaviour; for instance, the specific heat $c_v$ of the electrons decreased for $T \gg T_0 = \frac{2\beta}{k}$ proportional to $1/T^2$, whereas only for $T \ll T_0$ Sommerfeld’s behaviour followed with a linear increase in $T$.
The main task of Bloch’s thesis was, of course, to derive the electrical conduction behaviour by solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation of an electron

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0637 -->

III.6 The Metal Electrons and Solid State Theory 605

in a constant electric field of strength $F$ along the $x$-axis, in a crystal described by a periodic potential $V$,

$$\Delta \psi - \frac{8\pi^2 m_e}{h} (V - eFx)\psi + \frac{4\pi i m_e}{h} \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial t} = 0. \qquad (551)$$

Bloch then derived an equation for the distribution function $(\xi, \eta, \zeta)$, i.e.,

$$\frac{df(\xi, \eta, \zeta)}{dt} = - \frac{2\pi e F}{h} \frac{\partial f(\xi, \eta, \zeta)}{\partial \xi}, \qquad (552)$$

which closely resembled the classical Lorentz relation (used by Schrödinger also in the quantum-theoretical approach to free Fermi electrons)—except that the variables $\xi, \eta,$ and $\zeta$ did not represent velocity components, but different quantities describing the quantum states of the electron. The conductivity property then emerged from the interaction of the electrons with the elastic waves of the ionic lattice, especially:

> To account for the temperature dependence of the resistance, other deviations [than the defects in the crystal] from the strict periodicity must be decisive, namely those arising from the thermal vibrations of the crystal. Hence in what follows we are concerned with studying the interaction of two coupled systems—the electron gas and the lattice capable of performing elastic vibrations—by a perturbation calculation. If the temperature is sufficiently small, the wavelengths of the elastic waves may be assumed to be large with respect to the atomic distances, hence the crystal may be treated for them as a continuum; moreover, their amplitudes can be considered to be small, and thus the vibrations to be harmonic ones. (Bloch, *loc. cit.*, p. 578)

When Bloch carried out the corresponding perturbation procedure in a straightforward way through quite lengthy calculations, he arrived at a distribution function $f(\xi, \eta, \zeta)$ deviating only slightly from the field-free case $f_0(\xi, \eta, \zeta)$, i.e.,

$$f(\xi, \eta, \zeta) = f_0(\xi, \eta, \zeta) + \xi \phi(\rho), \qquad (553)$$

with $\phi(\rho)$ a small quantity depending only on $\rho = \sqrt{\xi^2 + \eta^2 + \zeta^2}$. Evaluating further, he found for high temperatures $T \gg \theta$ (with $\theta$ the characteristic Debye temperature of the crystal considered),

$$\phi(\rho) = -4Fe \text{ const.} \left( \frac{h \nu}{a k \theta} \right)^5 \frac{\partial f_0}{\partial \rho} \frac{\theta}{T}, \qquad (554)$$

and thence derived for the resistance $R = \frac{1}{\sigma}$ the result

$$R \sim T, \qquad (554a)$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0638 -->

606 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

as William Houston had obtained earlier (1928b) in Eq. (534). In the case of low temperatures, however, a result different from Houston's followed, namely,$^{723}$

$$R \sim T^3. \qquad (554b)$$

Though the empirical data rather spoke in favour of a $T^4$-law (Grüneisen's law), Bloch argued that more recent data tended to confirm the dependence given in Eq. (554b).

In a later study, submitted in November 1929 from Utrecht, Bloch corrected the low-temperature formula to

$$R \sim T^5, \qquad (555)$$

which even seemed to fit the data better than Eduard Grüneisen's rule (Bloch, 1930a). Theoretically, the new law came about by the fact that Bloch now managed to solve his complicated integral equation [given in Bloch, 1928b, Eq. (593), p. 598],

$$
\int_0^{\theta/T} \left\{ \frac{\exp(x) + 1}{\exp(\varepsilon) + \exp(-x)} \left[ c(\varepsilon) - \left( 1 - Q \left( \frac{T}{\theta} \right)^2 x^2 \right) c(\varepsilon + x) \right] \right. \\
\left. + \frac{\exp(-\varepsilon) + 1}{\exp(-\varepsilon) + \exp(-x)} \left[ c(\varepsilon) - \left( 1 - Q \left( \frac{T}{\theta} \right)^2 x^2 \right) c(\varepsilon - x) \right] \right\} \frac{x^2 dx}{\exp(x) - 1} \\
= P \left( \frac{\theta}{T} \right)^3, \qquad (556)
$$

without any approximations. [In Eq. (556), $\varepsilon$ denotes an energy, $c(\varepsilon) = kT[\exp(\varepsilon) + 1][\exp(-\varepsilon) + 1] \cdot \phi(\varepsilon)$, and $Q$ and $P$ are functions of atomic constants.]$^{724}$

Whatever refinements were applied later to the quantum-mechanical theory of conductivity, the Leipzig thesis of Heisenberg's first doctoral student provided a breakthrough in this important problem of the application of the new atomic theory. After an excellent oral examination—taken on 24 September 1928, with Heisenberg and Debye in physics, Leon Lichtenstein in mathematics, and Ernst Schiebold in mineralogy—Felix Bloch left Leipzig for a *Wanderjahr* with Wolfgang Pauli in Zurich, thus establishing a most active exchange on solid-state theory within the triangle of Munich–Leipzig–Zurich and even beyond. III.6 The Metal Electrons and Solid State Theory 607

came Wolfgang Pauli's assistant, Pauli proposed that he work on superconductivity, because in his opinion this was the only remaining problem of importance in solid-state physics. Bloch tried to explain persistent currents by the fact that they correspond to states of relative minimum energy, but under seemingly quite general conditions found that no such state carried current. This result has often been referred to as 'Bloch's theorem' and was jocularly summarized by the statement that 'any theory of superconductivity can be disproven.' [See Bloch's remark about the statement of this theory at the end of subsection III.6(e).] For a while Zurich even took a lead in the field of metallic conductivity, because Sommerfeld (in the second half of 1928) and Heisenberg (from March to October 1929) took long leaves of absence, but surely it is fair to say that the close cooperation between all three places provided the platform for the rapid development in the quantum-mechanical description of electrons in solids.

**(d) Band Theory of Solids and More on Magnetism in Munich, Leipzig, Zurich, and Elsewhere (1928–1932)**

Arnold Sommerfeld approached the age of 59 when he began to work out the new theory of metal electrons in 1927. In those days, great efforts were made to win him for the University of Berlin as the successor of Max Planck in the most prestigious chair of theoretical physics in Germany. The Bavarian Ministry of Education managed to keep Sommerfeld, the great master and teacher in his field, in Munich by offering him more favourable conditions.$^{725}$ Among the research students who attended his seminar at that time was a very talented young man, Hans Albrecht Bethe, who had come from Frankfurt-am-Main. Bethe hailed from the former German Alsace; he was born on 2 July 1906, in Strasbourg, the son of the physiologist Albrecht Theodor Bethe, who—as he recalled—'knew more about mathematics than was usual at that time for a physiologist; he knew calculus which was rare among physiologists.' (Bethe, AHQP Interview, 17 January 1964, p. 1) From the earliest times he could remember, Bethe was interested in numbers, in arithmetic, and:

> I used to play with numbers, finding prime numbers and making tables of squares and higher powers; I was fascinated with powers at an early age. I became fascinated with algebra as soon as I learned about it. The making of tables of power goes as far back as I can remember and farther . . . and that stayed with me all the time . . . When I was about 14 I found a textbook on calculus and analytic geometry which wasn't very good but which I stole and read on the sly . . . My parents did not like my spending so much time on these matters (Bethe, *loc. cit.*).

He went to the gymnasium in Frankfurt, where he 'disliked the classics,' but otherwise everything went very well and he learned a good deal of classical physics.

***

$^{725}$ See Eckert *et al.*, 1984, pp. 37–38.

608 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

Occasionally, he attended lectures on scientific topics at the University of Frankfurt, for instance, one by Erwin Madelung on the old quantum theory. He decided to become a physicist and began to study in 1924 at the University of Frankfurt, where Madelung, Richard Wachsmuth, Karl Wilhelm Meissner, and Walther Gerlach taught physics and Carl Ludwig Siegel taught mathematics at that time (Bethe liked number theory). Gerlach, whom his father knew, and Meissner advised him to go to Sommerfeld in Munich, where he arrived to begin the summer semester 1926 and immediately became involved in the theoretical physics seminar dealing with wave mechanics. In July 1927, Bethe submitted his first paper on a problem arising from one of Sommerfeld's lectures: he treated the scattering of electron waves in a single crystal (a phenomenon recently observed by Clinton J. Davisson and Lester H. Germer in the U.S.) with the help of the Schrödinger equation, finding especially that the so-called 'Davisson contraction' (i.e., the fact that the selectively reflected electron waves always have shorter wavelengths than the corresponding X-rays: Davisson and Germer, 1927a, p. 559) might be due to a change in the index of refraction (Bethe, 1927, p. 787). In the next note, dated 20 March 1928, and sent to *Naturwissenschaften*, he withdrew the previous result: the electron wave actually corresponded to a shorter X-ray wave (and did not have a refractive index smaller than 1: Bethe, 1928a). The important point was that Bethe became thoroughly acquainted with wave mechanics, and he then worked out the electron-diffraction problem in detail for his doctoral thesis, which he submitted in July 1928 to *Annalen der Physik*. (Bethe, 1928b). Sommerfeld, indeed, showed great interest in the topic and advised Bethe to treat it with Paul Ewald's dynamical theory of X-ray diffraction (Ewald, 1917). As Bethe recalled: 'I found rather quickly the refractive index and then much more slowly developed the dynamic theory which I couldn't solve, which also nobody has solved since then.' (Bethe, AHQP Interview, p. 14)

The extensive memoir on 'Theorie der Beugung von Elektronen in Kristallen' ('Theory of Electron Diffraction in Crystals') was published in the October issue of the *Annalen* (Bethe, 1928b). Notably, in §5 of the paper, Bethe discussed the wave-mechanical dispersion equations in the two practically important cases known from X-ray scattering:

1. *The Laue case*: Primary and secondary rays are both directed forward, away from the plane of incidence of the primary ray. Then both $\cos \theta_1$ and $\cos \theta_2$ are positive, hence the two solutions are real.
2. *The Bragg case*: The primary ray comes out again on the side of the incident ray, hence $\cos \theta_2$ is negative. . . . In this case the total intensity of the incident ray passes over into the reflected one. We shall call this case, which occurs for a certain domain $\zeta$ [Bethe named $\zeta$ the "Anregungsfehler" or "excitation error"], that of "selective reflection." (Bethe, *loc. cit.*, pp. 79–80)

In the case of X-rays, Ewald had baptized the latter as the domain of 'total reflection.' This phenomenon would later be associated (by Léon Brillouin and others, see below) with the energy gaps exhibited by electron bands in periodic crystals.

III.6 The Metal Electrons and Solid State Theory 609

Following a highly successful doctoral examination, Bethe spent a year (while Sommerfeld was mostly absent from Munich, having gone on his world tour) in Frankfurt with his family and then with Ewald in Stuttgart.⁷²⁶ After that period, he returned to Munich to get his *Habilitation*. Meanwhile, a former fellow research student in Munich, Rudolf Peierls, developed the theory of metal electrons further in Leipzig.

Peierls had arrived in Munich in October 1926, about half a year after Bethe, to continue his studies in physics that he had started in Berlin, the city where he was born.⁷²⁷ He immediately enrolled in Arnold Sommerfeld's mechanics course, followed by electrodynamics in the next semester, and he found these lectures excellent.⁷²⁸ Already in his first semester in Munich, Peierls 'made quite a stir' by working out a problem in relativistic mechanics and obtaining an answer different from the expected one (Hans Bethe was the assistant in charge of the problem session). In the second, spring semester 1927, he presented reports on the Dirac–Jordan papers on the quantum-mechanical transformation theory in two seminar sessions, which were also attended by Willy Wien, the professor of experimental physics (Peierls, AHQP Interview, p. 10). He learned about metal electrons as soon as Sommerfeld embarked upon his research on that topic. As Peierls recalled:

He had a sound understanding. . . . In those papers [of Sommerfeld] it was already indicated that the resistance of the metals might have something to do with the lattice vibrations, but it was not quite clear why first of all in the absence of lattice vibrations it would have an infinite conductivity. That was later done by Bloch. Or why you should have no resistance in a perfect metal at temperature zero because you still have the zero-point motion of the lattice vibration. (Peierls, *loc. cit.*, p. 12)

Before leaving for his world tour, Sommerfeld suggested to Peierls that Leipzig would be the best place for him to continue his work. Peierls arrived in Leipzig just

⁷²⁶ He recalled that 'When I was in Frankfurt, I studied a group-theory book by [Andreas] Speiser which is quite a good book, and then I found that the best way to go on was to solve the problem by group theory, so then I wrote the paper on the splitting of levels in a crystalline field'; this was the origin of his new scientific investigation (Bethe, 1929). In Stuttgart, Bethe served as assistant to Ewald. Later, in 1939, he would marry Ewald's daughter Rose.

⁷²⁷ Rudolf Ernst Peierls was born on 5 June 1907, the son of Heinrich Peierls from Silesia—a businessman 'who had a fairly important administrative job in industry; he was the managing director of a factory [the cable factory of A. E. G.] . . . later on he got a post in the board of his company' (Peierls, AHQP Interview, 17 June 1963, p. 1). Rudolf received a standard education at the *Humboldt-Gymnasium*, where he was very good in mathematics, but also showed an interest in physics. After completing his *Abitur* at Easter 1925, he spent six months in the research department of a factory before entering the University of Berlin in the fall of that year. Because he was not very good with his hands and had to wear glasses, he gave up the plan to study engineering and instead tried theoretical physics. In Berlin, Peierls attended the lectures of Max Planck (optics), Walther Bothe (X-rays), and Walther Nernst (general physics)—Nernst was a friend of his father—and took some philosophy courses.

⁷²⁸ At the University of Munich, Peierls also took a chemical laboratory course; he attended the lectures of Kasimir Fajans on physical chemistry, of Oskar Perron, and especially Konstantin Carathéodory on mathematics.

610 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

in time for the beginning of the summer semester 1928; he enrolled for lectures in pure mathematics and took advanced laboratory courses in physics (e.g., on radioactivity with Erich Marx and others). He also took Heisenberg's course on thermodynamics, but did not find it very inspiring. Peierls's first investigation for Heisenberg concerned an application of uncertainty relations to experiments made by Emil Rupp. As he recalled, it did not turn out to be very successful, but:

Then Heisenberg told me to look at the Hall effect in metals . . . specifically to look at the Hall effect, where the anomalous sign was unexplained at that time. I think Heisenberg must have had a fairly clear idea what he was after, because [he] had noticed that, if you have a complete shell minus one electron, you could really describe that in terms of a full shell and a positive hole. (Peierls, *loc. cit.*, p. 16)

Peierls claimed that, as early as 1928, Heisenberg mentioned to him the intuitive (*anschauliche*) idea of holes in order to understand the puzzle of the anomalous Hall effect. Consequently, Peierls worked out the problem in what he called:

the first paper of any importance I published . . . in a form which I would not allow my students to publish today. It was not then regarded as the responsibility of the professor to see that things were clearly written. He of course took enough interest in the work to satisfy himself that the results and the method were right. (Peierls, *loc. cit.*)

When Peierls arrived in Leipzig in the spring of 1928, Felix Bloch was just about to complete his doctoral dissertation containing the lattice model of electrical conductivity and Heisenberg was expounding the theory of ferromagnetism. He recalled that Heisenberg immediately suggested a problem for him to work on:

I should try to see whether one could get conductivity out of the Heitler-London model . . . taking into account the repulsion of the electrons. Each atom would tend to be neutral. It is now clear that you cannot get a conductivity out of that model, because electrons can't get past each other. They have to move bodily, for which there is not enough probability, but I spent some time trying to get something out of it, and it didn't work. (Peierls, *loc. cit.*, p. 21)

Then, Peierls became interested in Bloch's approach, apparently being the only person who got involved in it at Leipzig, because Heisenberg's official assistant Guido Beek investigated the regularities of radioactive elements and the visitors Isidor Rabi, Georg Placzek, and Otto Halpern worked on other topics.⁷²⁹ Thus,

⁷²⁹ In summer 1928, Peierls went on a vacation trip to England, where he also visited Paul Dirac in Cambridge, whom he had met before at the *Leipziger Universitätswoche*. He recalled that his hosts:

were obviously short of a speaker in the Kapitza Club, and they asked: "Can you give a talk in the Club?" Now in those days my English was still rather poor, and I really did not have very much to talk about except to give an outline of Bloch's theory . . . and to say a bit about my own attempts to get conductivity out of the Heitler-London model. (Peierls, AHQP Interview, p. 21)
