III.6 The Metal Electrons and Solid State Theory 611

when Bloch left for Zurich in fall 1928, Peierls developed the theory further by applying it to the Hall effect. Shortly before Christmas, he submitted a paper, entitled 'Zur Theorie der galvanomagnetischen Effekte' ('On the Theory of Galvano-Magnetic Effects'), to *Zeitschrift für Physik*. In particular, he showed in it 'that one can obtain from Bloch's calculations qualitatively correct results for galvano-magnetic effects, in particular both the signs of the Hall effect—which Sommerfeld's theory did not yet provide—as well as the order of magnitude of the change of [electrical] resistance' (Peierls, 1929a, p. 255).⁷³⁰
Peierls started the paper with a general remark on the properties of the electric current in Bloch's theory. In a metallic cube of length $K = aG$ (where $a$ denoted the atomic distance), $G^3$ translational states for each electron obviously existed there, characterized, say, by the energy values,

$$E_{k,l,m} = E_0 - 2\beta \left( \cos \frac{2\pi k}{G} + \cos \frac{2\pi l}{G} + \cos \frac{2\pi m}{G} \right), \quad (557)$$

and the current values in the $x$-direction,

$$s^x_{k,l,m} = \frac{eah\Phi^x}{\pi m_e} \sin \left( \frac{2\pi k}{G} \right), \quad (558)$$

with the constants $\beta$ and $\Phi^x$. The influence of an electric field (strength $F$) changed the eigenfunction of an electron to $\psi = \sum c_{klm} \psi_{klm}$, with the time-dependent coefficients satisfying the equation

$$\frac{d}{dt} |c_{klm}|^2 = - \frac{KeF}{h} \frac{\partial}{\partial k} |c_{klm}|^2. \quad (559)$$

Now, Peierls commented: 'The equation [(558)] has a strange consequence. For $k > \frac{G}{4}$ the current decreases . . . with increasing $k$, i.e., in a field such an electron will be decelerated rather than accelerated.' (Peierls, *loc. cit.*, p. 255) The question then arose whether this strange behaviour contradicted quantum mechanics, but Peierls demonstrated that it was fully consistent with Paul Dirac's formulation of wave mechanics (Dirac, 1926f) and yielded Louis de Broglie's relation (de Broglie, 1925, p. 61),

$$\frac{\partial E_{klm}}{\partial k} = - \frac{h}{m_e} p^x_{klm}. \quad (560)$$

Furthermore, he derived Eq. (559) without some of the restrictions that Bloch had assumed (concerning the wave packet used).

⁷³⁰ At the end of the paper, Peierls thanked Heisenberg for having stimulated the investigation and Bloch for many interesting discussions (Peierls, *loc. cit.*, p. 266).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0644 -->

612 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

In Section 2 of his paper, Peierls turned to the Hall effect. The action of a magnetic field of strength $H$ in the $z$-direction was represented in the Hamiltonian by the terms

$$\frac{eH}{m_e c}(xp_y - yp_x) + \left(\frac{eH}{m_e c}\right)^2 (x^2 + y^2), \quad (561)$$

with $p_x$ and $p_y$ denoting the quantum-mechanical momenta. Hence, the distribution function $f$ for electrons satisfied the equation—considered already by Sommerfeld as analogue to the corresponding classical equation—

$$\frac{df}{dt} = \frac{2\pi e a}{h} \left\{ -F_x \frac{\partial f}{\partial \xi} - F_y \frac{\partial f}{\partial \eta} + \frac{H}{m_e c} \left( p_y \frac{\partial f}{\partial \xi} - p_x \frac{\partial f}{\partial \eta} \right) \right\}, \quad (562)$$

if, in addition to the $H = H_z$-field, also the electric fields $F_x$ and $F_y$ acted upon the electron. (Note that $\xi$, $\eta$, and $\zeta$ are not to be interpreted as the classical momentum variables in Bloch's theory, but as quantum variables.) While Bloch solved the electric-field problem (based on the assumptions $s^x \sim \xi$ and $E \sim \xi^2 + \eta^2 + \zeta^2$) with the *Ansatz* (553)—i.e., $f = f_0 + \phi\xi$—Peierls rather chose [because of the general structure of Eqs. (557) and (558)],

$$f(\xi, \eta, \zeta) = f_0(\xi, \eta, \zeta) + \phi_1 \sin \xi + \phi_2 \sin \eta. \quad (563)$$

Then, he considered the generalization of Bloch's integral equation (556) to the situation including both electric and magnetic fields explicitly in two limiting cases: (1) the electrons are either free or have states $|k|$, $|l|$, $|m| \ll \frac{G}{4}$ (the case considered by Bloch); and (2) the electrons have states $\left| \frac{G}{2} - k \right| \ll 1$, $\left| \frac{G}{2} - l \right| \ll 1$, and $\left| \frac{G}{2} - m \right| \ll 1$. In those cases, the right-hand side of the generalized integral equation could be written as

$$2\beta \frac{\partial f_0}{\partial E} (F_x \bar{\xi} + f_y \bar{\eta}) + \frac{Hah\Phi^x}{\pi m_e c} (\bar{\xi} \phi_2 \cos \eta - \bar{\eta} \phi_1 \cos \xi), \quad (564)$$

where $\bar{\xi}$ and $\bar{\eta}$ took on the values

$$\left. \begin{array}{ll} \bar{\xi} = \xi, & \bar{\eta} = \eta \quad \text{in case (a),} \\ \bar{\xi} = \pi - \xi, & \bar{\eta} = \pi - \eta \quad \text{in case (b).} \end{array} \right\} \quad (565)$$

Peierls commented on this result as follows:

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0645 -->

### III.6 The Metal Electrons and Solid State Theory 613

In particular, for the vanishing magnetic field the difference between the cases (a) and (b) disappears, and the formula becomes identical with Bloch's [generalized to electric fields in $x$- and $y$-direction, of course].... In the approximation used here, the slope of the current values as function of $k$ essentially does not play a role for the conductivity. However, one recognizes from Eq. [(564)] that it does matter for the Hall effect, since in case (b) $\cos \xi$ and $\cos \eta$ are negative and in case (a) they are positive. Therefore $H$ appears to be multiplied in the second case by $-1$. (Peierls, 1929a, pp. 261–262)

The Hall effect followed from solving the full integral equation and taking the current in the $y$-direction equal to zero. Peierls thus calculated the Hall effect constant $R_0$ (with $I_x$ the current in the $x$-direction) to be

$$
R_0 = \frac{F_y}{H I_x} = \begin{cases} -\frac{2a^2}{ecx} & \text{for case (a)}, \\ +\frac{2a^2}{ec(1 - x)} & \text{for case (b)}, \end{cases} \quad (566)
$$

$x$ being the so-called occupation number (i.e., the ratio of the number of conduction electrons per atom over twice the number of quantum cells per atom). Peierls realized that the result, Eq. (566), agreed with Sommerfeld's, Eq. (533), as far as the order of magnitude was concerned. However, in contrast to the earlier result:

> The sign [of the effect] depends essentially on $x$. If $x$ is small, we have the case (a), hence negative Hall effect; if $x$ is nearly 1, we have the case (b) and the positive (anomalous) Hall effect. (Peierls, *loc. cit.*, p. 264)

He further realized that the deviations from the normal Hall effect were symmetric with respect to the occupation number $x = \frac{1}{2}$; therefore, no Hall effect at all should be observed for $x = \frac{1}{2}$. 'This fact is connected with the reciprocity law found by Pauli [1925b] between the free and the "occupied" places in the atom, although it applies here only for very low temperatures,' Peierls concluded.$^{731}$ Finally, for not too low temperatures, he evaluated the change of conductivity in a magnetic field, finding an effect in the second order of $H$, which seemed to have the right order of magnitude for normal metals (but not for Bi and ferromagnetic substances), though the predicted independence on temperature did not seem to fit the data in general.

Rudolf Peierls proudly presented these results at the next meeting of the *Gauverein Sachsen-Thüringen-Schlesien* on 20 January 1929, in Leipzig, where he also depicted a visualization of the cases (a) and (b) in a two-dimensional $\xi - \eta$

---

$^{731}$ This statement refers to what Peierls, in his AHQP interview, called Heisenberg's ideas of 'holes'; it is not clear that Heisenberg spoke explicitly about holes before Paul Dirac developed this concept in the relativistic electron theory a little later.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0646 -->

### 614 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

'momentum diagram' (Peierls, 1929b). Because Heisenberg left Leipzig on his world tour in the beginning of March, Peierls was transferred to Zurich to start work on a doctoral thesis under Wolfgang Pauli. Pauli had been installed at the *ETH* a year previously as the successor of Peter Debye and had begun to establish with his first assistant Ralph Kronig a programme of lecture courses, but had so far not taken any doctoral student. He immediately confronted Peierls with a problem that had bothered him for a while, as the latter recalled:

> Pauli was certainly exciting from the very beginning. Now he presented me with this problem and some handwritten notes where he had tried to work things out. This is, as far as I know, the only subject on which there is a wrong result published under Pauli's name. But it's only a summary; there is a report of a meeting of the German Physical Society where Pauli gave a talk about the damping of lattice waves in polar crystals [Pauli, 1925c],.... What he stated there was clearly nonsense. And I think he knew it wasn't right, and that's why he told me to look at it and gave me some help at the start. Then I could see that there were some very interesting aspects of that problem, and I wrote a Ph.D. thesis, which I typed myself with a typewriter [which he had received as a present from his parents who were visiting him in Zurich]. (Peierls, AHQP Interview, p. 21)

Besides publishing two short notes on the ionization potential of atoms (1929c) and the existence of stationary states in molecules (1929d), Peierls indeed concerned himself fully with Pauli's problem during the first half of 1929. In his thesis, submitted already in July, he worked out a kinetic quantum theory of heat conduction in crystals that involved nonharmonic forces and the question of the validity of a quantum-mechanical *H*-theorem. He showed in particular that only the *H*-theorem, applied to a three-dimensional lattice, yielded a *finite* value for the heat conductivity and obtained formulae for the heat resistance, e.g.,

$$
R_{\text{heat}} = \text{const. } T + \text{const.' } T^{\nu} \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2} \frac{\theta}{T} \right), \quad (567)
$$

for low temperatures $T \ll \theta$ ($\theta$ being the Debye temperature), where the exponential decrease in the second term arose from a detailed consideration of the lattice perturbations (Peierls, 1929e).$^{732}$ With the thesis work completed, Peierls returned to Leipzig and obtained his doctorate after an examination by Friedrich Hund (theoretical physics), Leon Lichtenstein (mathematics), and a professor of physical chemistry. Pauli then offered him the position of his assistant, as the successor of Felix Bloch who had held the position in summer 1929 (succeeding Kronig). During the following two-and-a-half years in Zurich, Peierls—as Pauli's new assistant—continued to work primarily on metal electrons.

---

$^{732}$ In a reminiscence of the old work, Peierls (who received the Max Planck Medal in September 1963 at the meeting of the German Physical Society in Hamburg) reviewed the further development of this problem (Peierls, 1964).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0647 -->

### III.6 The Metal Electrons and Solid State Theory 615

In fact, already in November 1929, Peierls submitted a substantial paper on the electrical and thermal conductivity of metals to *Annalen der Physik*, based again on Bloch's pioneering work (Peierls, 1930). He not only simplified the derivations of his predecessor, but also modified a particular point in the latter's treatment on the basis of his own experience from his doctoral thesis: in contrast to Bloch, who had assumed thermal equilibrium of the metal electrons independently of their velocity distribution, he now showed that only the lattice vibrations due to anharmonic forces would establish equilibrium. Thus, he developed a systematic perturbation scheme having the following orders: zeroth, free electrons; first, electrons in a lattice with harmonic forces; second, interaction with lattice vibrations, especially the anharmonic ones. Thus, he arrived at the following results: (1) by calculating the energy values in the first order, he found the dependence (later often reproduced) of $E$ on the component $\xi$ of the wave vector of the electron, consisting of parabola-like branches having gaps at $\xi = n\pi$, $n = 1, 2, 3 \ldots$; and (2) the interaction with the lattice vibration changed the wave vector $(\xi, \eta, \zeta)$ into $(\xi', \eta', \zeta')$; thus,

$$
\nu_1 + \xi - \xi' = k_1 \cdot 2\pi; \quad \nu_2 + \eta - \eta' = k_2 \cdot 2\pi; \quad \nu_3 + \zeta - \zeta' = k_3 \cdot 2\pi, \quad (568)
$$

where $\nu_1, \nu_2, \nu_3$ denoted the lattice mode and $k_i = 0, \pm 1$, and all three relations were satisfied by moduli $2\pi$. The discussion of the 'interference condition' revealed that the interaction with the lattice resulted in two effects that determined the finite electrical and thermal conductivity: first, the anharmonicity of the lattice vibrations (as considered in Peierls, 1929e) and, second, a new type of process that Peierls described as follows:

> Now this wave number also changes because of the collisions between the lattice and the electron if one considers the solutions of Eq. [(568)] not used so far. These contributions are the only ones at low temperatures, while at higher temperatures they have the same order of magnitude as the contributions due to anharmonicity. (Peierls, 1930, p. 130)

He called the new phenomena '*Umklapp* processes' (Peierls, *loc. cit.*, pp. 133–134), which resulted in the simplest case from the equation

$$
\xi + \nu_1 = \xi' \quad (\text{mod. } 2\pi) \quad (569)
$$

and implied two eigensolutions in the case of electrical conductivity. Thus, he obtained the following behaviour,

$$
\sigma \sim \frac{1}{T} \quad \text{for higher temperatures } T
$$

and

$$
\sigma \sim \frac{1}{T^4} \quad \text{for low temperatures } T \ll \theta. \quad (570)
$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0648 -->

### 616 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

The low-temperature formula agreed with Grüneisen's empirical result and slightly disagreed with Bloch's $T^{-5}$-law. Further, he remarked: 'For this result to emerge, it is necessary that the matrix elements vanish also for the *Umklapp* processes in the vicinity of $\nu_1 = \nu_2 = \nu_3 = 0$, otherwise one would obtain proportionality with $T^2$.' (Peierls, *loc. cit.*, p. 139) Because in the case of thermal conductivity, the *Umklapp* processes entered only in the next higher order approximation, the Wiedemann–Franz law (though remaining valid for high temperatures) failed at low temperatures (where $\kappa \sim T^{-2}$ and $\sigma \sim T^{-4}$). Peierls justified this conclusion as follows:

> The reason for this is that in the classical derivation of the Wiedemann-Franz law the classical *Stoßzahl Ansatz* has been used which, as Bloch has emphasized, does not apply at low temperatures where the Pauli principle plays an essential role. Hence it is not necessary to rescue the theoretical validity of this law by special assumptions. (Peierls, *loc. cit.*, p. 147)

While Peierls remained for a longer period in Zurich, Bloch—the previous messenger from Leipzig—stayed with Pauli for only a shorter stay. Besides trying to solve the final fundamental problem of metal electrons, i.e., superconductivity, Bloch worked out two consequences from his theory in notes submitted in December 1928 and June 1929 to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Bloch, 1929a, b). In the first note, he showed that the paramagnetic susceptibility $\chi$ exhibited the following behaviour: at high temperatures ($T \gg T_0$), Curie's law was valid, whereas at a certain $T_0$ ($= 2\beta/T$, with $\beta$ a characteristic energy determining the migration of the electron in the lattice), it assumed the value

$$
\chi(T_0) \approx \frac{\mu_0^2}{\beta} \frac{N}{V}, \quad (571)
$$

and then remained constant down to absolute zero ($\mu_0 = \frac{eh}{4\pi m_0 c}$, $\frac{N}{V}$ the electron density).$^{733}$ Furthermore, Bloch calculated the change of the electrical resistance, $\frac{\Delta R}{R}$, in a magnetic field $H$ as

$$
\frac{\Delta R}{R} = B H^2, \quad (572)
$$

with the constant $B$ ($\approx \mu_0^2/\omega^2$, with $\omega$ of the order of magnitude of the electronic zero-point energy) assuming a value of about $10^{-14}$ cgs units, in agreement with

---

$^{733}$ For alkali metals, $\beta$ is of the order of the ionization work, but for other metals it should be smaller (Bloch, 1929a, pp. 221–222).

# III.6 The Metal Electrons and Solid State Theory

617

observations.<sup>734</sup> In the second note, Bloch went on to connect the description of ferromagnetism with that of electrical conductivity. While Heisenberg’s original model, based on the exchange integral, allowed only for a poor conductivity (as Peierls had shown), Bloch’s model of electrons in periodic crystals, when combined with proper computational methods,<sup>735</sup> seemed to yield ferromagnetism, provided the electrostatic energy of the electrons surpassed their zero-point energy.<sup>736</sup> Bloch concluded his paper with the remark that, “in any case one recognizes that for deciding the question whether a metal is ferromagnetic, the zero-point energy plays a role, and further that the same electrons—which are responsible for electrical conduction—also give rise to ferromagnetism” (Bloch, 1929b, p. 555).

In fall 1929, Felix Bloch went from Zurich to Utrecht as a Lorentz Fellow, where he met Hendrik Kramers and Ralph Kronig, both of whom showed great interest in his work on metal electrons. In particular, Kronig had already introduced Bloch’s result on electrical conductivity into the dispersion formula in spring 1929 and concluded:

> One must expect therefore that the [old] phenomenological theory of dispersion in metallic conductors … will, for alternating field …, be in error by amounts of the order of \(\exp(-\beta\nu)\). These errors become serious at ordinary temperatures for frequencies \(\nu\) between \(10^{13}\) and \(10^{14}\) in agreement with experiment. (Kronig, 1929, p. 415)

A year and a half later—Kronig (after serving as a lecturer at the University of Cambridge and Imperial College, London, during the year 1929/30) had just moved as conservator at the University of Groningen—he contributed even a more substantial application of Bloch’s theory to an investigation with William George Penney. This work, entitled “Quantum Mechanics of Electrons in Crystals,” was intended “to obtain a clearer idea of the details of the behaviour … of electrons in periodic fields of potential somewhat similar to those met in practice and of such nature that the energy values \(W\) and eigenfunctions \(\psi\) of the wave equation can actually be computed” (Kronig and Penney, 1931, p. 500). Kronig and Penney indeed selected a most elementary model of a solid and arrived at a complete solution of the Schrödinger equation, which they summarized in four points:

1. It is shown that the wave equation representing the motion of an electron in a periodic potential can be interpreted in terms of elementary functions when the

<sup>734</sup> In contrast to Sommerfeld’s treatment, Bloch predicted a weak dependence of the effect on the relative direction between the magnetic field and the electric current (Bloch, 1929a, pp. 226–227).

<sup>735</sup> In this context, Bloch referred to the method of the “self-consistent field” (discussed in the previous section), which had been brought into a group-theoretical form by Max Delbrück (1928), and to the manuscript of John Slater’s paper (1929b).

<sup>736</sup> Bloch noted that in the case of alkali atoms, for instance, this condition was not satisfied (Bloch, 1929b, p. 554).

# Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

618

potential takes the form of a series of equidistant rectangular barriers. When the breadth \(b\) of these barriers is made infinitely small and their height \(V_0\) infinitely large, the results become particularly simple, the influence of the barriers depending only on the product \(bV_0\).

2. In the one-dimensional problem for this limiting case the spectrum of permissible energy values is found to consist of continuous regions separated by finite intervals. By varying the quantity \(bV_0\) from zero to infinity we pass from the case of free to that of bound electrons, and can thus study the changes in the allowed and forbidden ranges of energy and in the wave functions during the transition.

3. An investigation of the matrix elements of the linear momentum shows that the electrons can pass through the lattice and there exists for them the possibility of transition to other states under emission and absorption of radiation, the electrons thus having at the same time the characteristic properties of free and bound electrons.

4. An investigation of the reflection electrons by a crystal represented by the field of potential considered leads to results in qualitative agreement with experimental facts. (Kronig and Penney, *loc. cit.*, pp. 512–513)

Kronig and Penney indicated how their solution could be extended “to the case of a three-dimensional lattice, in which the potential is a sum of three terms, \(V(x)\), \(V(y)\), \(V(z)\), each of which depends on its coordinate in the same way as \(V(x)\) in the one-dimensional case” (Kronig and Penney, *loc. cit.*, p. 507). This general situation had been treated already with a different potential by Léon Brillouin in two notes, presented on 28 July and 11 August 1930, respectively, to the *Académie des Sciences* (Brillouin, 1930b, c) and a longer paper submitted at the same time to *Journal de Physique* (Brillouin, 1930d).

Léon Brillouin, since 1928 a professor at the Institut Henri Poincaré (and a colleague of Louis de Broglie there), had become interested in quantum theory quite early.<sup>737</sup> In his book on quantum statistics, published in 1930, he referred to Peierls’s treatment of the electrical conductivity problem in *Annalen der Physik* and suggested an alternative approach to the problem based on a detailed analysis of the behaviour of electron waves in crystals (Brillouin, 1930a).<sup>738</sup> In particular, he considered there the one-dimensional Schrödinger equation with a sinusoidal potential \(P\) given by

\[
P = P_0 - A \cos\left(\frac{2\pi x}{d}\right) \qquad (573)
\]

(\(d\) being the distance of atomic potentials) that transformed into the Mathieu-type equation,

\[
\frac{d^2u}{d\xi^2} + (\delta + \gamma \cos 2\xi)u = 0, \qquad (574)
\]

with \(\xi = \frac{\pi x}{d}\), and the constants \(\delta\) and \(\gamma\) depending on the energy parameters \(E, P_0,\)

<sup>737</sup> For a brief account of Louis Brillouin’s life, see Volume 1, Part 2, p. 579 ff.

<sup>738</sup> This idea was also recognized at other places, as, for instance, in Sommerfeld’s Institute in Munich—see Bethe’s work referred to above.

# III.6 The Metal Electrons and Solid State Theory

619

and \(A\).<sup>739</sup> The general solution

\[
u = \alpha \exp(\mu\xi)\Phi(\xi) + \beta \exp(-\mu\xi)\Phi(-\xi), \qquad (575)
\]

where \(\Phi\) denoted a periodic function in \(\xi\), remained finite for \(\mu\) (depending on \(\delta\) and \(\gamma\)) taking on imaginary values; this occurred—apart from a trivial constant potential \((\gamma = 0)\)—for \(\gamma > 0\) and \(\delta > -\gamma\). Because \(\delta\) physically corresponded to an energy and \(\gamma\) to a wavenumber, Brillouin concluded that \((\delta - \gamma)\)-curve represented simply Peierls’s first-order approximation (Peierls, 1930a, see the foregoing discussion). In the case of a more general potential, the Mathieu equation had to be replaced by the more general Hill equation, but quantitatively the same result followed.

In the two *Comptes Rendus* notes and the detailed paper, Brillouin (1930b, c, d) considered the three-dimensional crystal, observing that the propagation of the electron waves was determined by the well-known (from X-ray scattering) Bragg reflection condition, i.e.,

\[
\lambda = 2d \cos \theta \qquad (576)
\]

(\(d\) being the lattice constant). Brillouin then constructed the positions, where such Bragg reflection occurred in the reciprocal lattice, and thus obtained the “zones” (later called “Brillouin zones”), which he discussed in some detail in his paper in *Journal de physique* (Brillouin, 1930d, §7–§13). At the surfaces separating the zones (where the Bragg reflection occurs), the energy always exhibited a discontinuity (Brillouin, 1930b, p. 200). By comparing the behaviour of electrons in the crystal with that of a free electron, Brillouin wrote the energy relation for the different zones as

\[
E = E_0 + \frac{h^2}{2m^*}(a'^2 + b'^2 + c'^2), \qquad (577)
\]

with \(E_0\) an average energy different for each zone (corresponding to a level of the isolated atoms, and \(a', b', c'\) satisfying the condition \(-\frac{1}{2d} < a', b', c' < \frac{1}{2d}\)—see Brillouin, 1930c, p. 293). In particular, he noted that:

> It is not certain at all that \(m^*\) be equal to the real electron mass \(m_0\). According to Bloch, in the case of bound electrons … no simple relation between \(m\) and \(m^*\) follows at all. The coefficient \(m^*\) could even turn out to be *negative*, with the energy function assuming a maximum in the centre of the reciprocal zone \(a', b', c'\). (Brillouin, 1930 d, p. 397)

In the extended German edition of his book on quantum statistics (1930a), Brillouin discussed Bloch’s integral equation in greater detail (Brillouin, 1931, §22, pp. 349–357): in particular, he transformed it into a Volterra equation of the

\[
\frac{\sigma T_{\text{large}}}{\sigma T_{\text{small}}} = \left(\frac{T}{\theta}\right)^4 \times 497.72532. \qquad (578)

For the thermal conductivity \(\kappa\) at low temperatures, Brillouin, like Peierls, derived the \(T^{-2}\)-law. However, he emphasized:

> All these consequences are based on the hypotheses of Bloch, [namely]: 1. neglect of anomalous collisions (the *Umklapp* processes of Peierls); and 2. the assumption of a small mean free path of the elastic waves, and therefore the conservation of Planck’s distribution function. (Brillouin, *loc. cit.*, p. 382)

That is, Brillouin not only claimed that he did not need *Umklapp* processes, but that with Peierls’s method he would actually “finally arrive at a proportionality of the [electrical resistance] to \(T^2\), and not like the one he [Peierls] found with \(T^4\)”; hence, “it seems that one must conclude therefrom that Peierls’ *Umklapp* processes do not exist,” i.e., they just represented “a simple superposition of a Bragg reflection and a normal deflection” of an electron wave (Brillouin, *loc. cit.*, p. IV).

Peierls, while on a visit to Leningrad, got hold of the proofs of Brillouin’s new book, and he quickly sent a paper in reply, which was received by *Annalen der Physik* in September 1931 (Peierls, 1932a). He did not at all accept the criticism of his work, because Brillouin had used his method and should have arrived at the same result (Peierls, *loc. cit.*, footnote 3, p. 154). On the other hand, he now improved upon his previous, approximate method for solving Bloch’s integral equation and rediscovered, instead of his \(T^{-4}\)-law, the \(T^{-5}\)-law of Bloch’s original paper (Bloch, 1928b).<sup>740</sup> Still, the work on electrical conductivity went on and even turned into a different direction. In spring 1931, Alan H. Wilson from Emmanuel College, Cambridge, had visited Heisenberg and Bloch in Leipzig; a little later, in June of that year, he submitted a lengthy memoir (communicated by Paul Dirac) on “The Theory of Electronic Semi-Conductors” to the *Proceeding Royal Society of London* (Wilson, 1931a).<sup>741</sup> The problem Wilson attacked had not been

<sup>740</sup> The new result also changed certain details of a previous investigation concerning the influence of magnetic fields on the resistance in a single crystal, though the final result remained unchanged (Peierls, 1931).

<sup>741</sup> Alan Herris Wilson was born in Wallasey, England, on 2 July 1906, and studied at Cambridge University (Emmanuel College, 1923–1926), becoming a fellow of Emmanuel College and later John Richard Lecturer in Mathematics at Cambridge University (1933–1945). In 1945, he joined Courtaulds Ltd. (becoming managing director in 1954 and deputy chairman in 1957). He remained in industry until retirement.

Wilson’s interest in metal electrons had originated in Cambridge, where Peter Kapitza investigated the behaviour of the electrical resistance in strong magnetic fields, but most people around Rutherford at the Cavendish Laboratory showed no interest in a theoretical interpretation and preferred to work on nuclear phenomena. Hence, he went to Leipzig on an International Education Board Fellowship. More details concerning this visit may be found in Wilson, 1980, and in Hoddeson *et al.*, 1987, especially, pp. 298–300.

### III.6 The Metal Electrons and Solid State Theory 621

addressed either by Bloch and Peierls or their followers, namely, 'how to explain the non-conductivity of insulators and the temperature dependence of the electronic semi-conductors' (Wilson, *loc. cit.*, p. 459). Classical theory had answered this question simply by assuming two types of electron, free and bound ones, of which different fractions were contained in metals, semiconductors, or insulators. The quantum-mechanical theory, however, had removed the difference between free and bound electrons in crystal lattices and a new explanation had become necessary. After studying in detail the work of Bloch and Peierls, Wilson got the crucial idea: the new quantum theory of electrical conductivity would become, he argued, 'intuitively more plausible if one assumed that the quasi-free electrons, like valence electrons in single atoms, could form either open or closed shells' (Wilson, 1980, p. 45). He mentioned the idea to Heisenberg and Bloch, but the latter expressed doubts, because the divalent alkaline earths with their closed two-shells had then to be insulators. However, Wilson went ahead with his idea and eventually succeeded in solving the problem he had envisaged.

In those days, the effect of closed and open shells on atomic problems was eagerly discussed in Leipzig. Heisenberg, in particular, revived Pauli's old suggestion (in Pauli, 1925b), that some equivalence should exist between atomic systems having $n$ electrons and those having $n$ 'holes' with respect to closed shells, in a paper of June 1931 entitled '*Zum Paulischen Ausschließungsprinzip*' ('On Pauli's Exclusion Principle') (Heisenberg, 1931d). He demonstrated the validity of the suggestion with the help of the (nonrelativistic) quantum field theory, choosing two particular examples: the calculation of the lowest states of atomic spectra and the anomalous Hall effect. In the latter example, he confirmed Peierls's previous results (Peierls, 1929a) and showed 'that the holes move like electrons with positive charge under the influence of a perturbing external field' (Heisenberg, 1931d, p. 904). One might wonder why Heisenberg did not refer in his paper to Wilson's simultaneous (or even prior) work on semiconductors—but it seems that Heisenberg and Wilson worked quite independently during the latter's stay at Leipzig, for Wilson also did not mention Heisenberg's crucial concept of 'holes' in his publications.

While Heisenberg thus threw light on some previously treated problems with the help of the concept of 'holes' that would become fruitful far beyond solid-state physics, Wilson—with his simultaneous investigations—practically opened the new field of semiconductor physics. Before that time, not much was really known about semiconductors, except that certain metals and other substances seemed to be electronic conductors possessing a conductivity lying between that of normal conductors ($\sigma \sim 10^5$) and ionic conductors ($\sigma < 1$) with some unusual properties.$^{742}$ In his first paper, Wilson argued that 'it is not possible to maintain that the difference between good and bad conductors is one of degree only, the electrons in poor conductors being more tightly bound than in metals and giving rise to a smaller current,' and he just referred to the example of germanium, quite

$^{742}$ See, for example, Eduard Grüneisen's article on metallic conductivity in *Handbuch der Physik* (Grüneisen, 1928, pp. 60–64).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0654 -->

### 622 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

a bad conductor (in contrast to silver) in which impurities and higher temperatures rather decreased electrical resistance (Wilson, 1931c, p. 459). Now, in the theoretical models of metal electrons investigated so far, especially the one-dimensional ones (exhibiting a clear separation of the energy gaps with finite gaps in between), substances were either insulators—i.e., the closed atomic shells corresponded to filled electron bands in the crystal—or conductors—i.e., the electrons of nonclosed atomic shells could move freely among the partially unoccupied crystal bands.$^{743}$ Such a situation seemed to exist inevitably at zero temperature, but it could change for $T > 0$. For example, by considering a substance with a fully occupied first energy band, Wilson found:

> When the temperature is different from zero, there will be a few [excited] electrons in the second band and a few vacant places in the first band, and conduction can take place. The increase of the number of conduction electrons with the rise of temperature will tend to increase the conductivity, while the excitation of the thermal vibrations of the lattice will decrease it. At low temperatures the effect of the thermal vibrations will be more important, and the resistance will obey the normal law. This is what is observed for semiconductors (Grüneisen, 1928, p. 60). The problem has to be formulated a little differently when we deal with three dimensions, but it is possible to construct a model that reproduces the properties of semiconductors. (Wilson, 1931a, pp. 460–461)

Wilson elaborated upon these basic ideas quantitatively. He first summarized the previously proposed methods of treating (weakly or strongly) bound electrons in three-dimensional cubic crystals, which led in the case of alkaline earths either to conducting (when the electron were weakly bound such that $np$-levels overlapped with the $1s$-level) or to the semiconducting case (when the electrons were strongly-bound). In the latter case, a condition could be stated that made sure that all energies of the second Brillouin zone were higher than those of the first zone. Then he constructed the desired model of the semiconductor with the following properties: (1) at absolute zero temperature, the electrons occupy all $(2G^3)$ levels of the first Brillouin zone; and (2) for finite temperature $T$, $(2G^3/8\pi)n_0(\xi, \eta, \zeta) d\xi d\eta d\zeta$ electrons will be found in the upper levels, with $n_0(\xi, \eta, \zeta)$ denoting the Fermi distribution,

$$n_0(\xi, \eta, \zeta) = \frac{1}{1/A \exp(E/kT) + 1} \qquad (579)$$

(where $E$, of course, depended on $\xi$, $\eta$, and $\zeta$). The evaluation of the quantity $A$ or

$^{743}$ Bloch raised this argument against Wilson's original ideas, but Wilson replied that the situation would be quite different in three-dimensional models (Wilson, 1980, pp. 45–46).

### III.6 The Metal Electrons and Solid State Theory 623

$W_0$ ($= kT \log A$) yielded for low temperatures,

$$W_0 \approx \frac{1}{2}(W_1 + W_2) - \frac{1}{2}kT \log[3(\beta_1/\beta_2)^{3/2}], \qquad (580)$$

where $W_1$ and $W_2$, $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ denoted energy parameters of the first and second zone, respectively.$^{744}$ Finally, Wilson calculated three properties characterizing semiconductors in his model, i.e., the specific heat, the paramagnetic susceptibility, and the conductivity. He obtained expressions for the first two quantities, which at low temperatures, notably, $T \ll \theta_u$, contained the factor $\exp(-\theta_u/T)$ and further temperature-dependent factors; their order of magnitude agreed with the results previously obtained by Sommerfeld and Pauli. The low-temperature conductivity should obey the formula

$$\sigma = \sigma_0 \exp\left(-\frac{\theta_u}{T}\right) \quad \text{for } T \ll \theta_u = \frac{W_0 - W_1}{k} \approx \frac{W_2 - W_1}{2k}, \qquad (581)$$

where $\theta_u$ could be interpreted as a kind of excitation temperature. Wilson concluded: 'If $T \gg \theta_u \ldots$, the substance behaves as a metal and for sufficiently high temperatures must have a $\sigma$ inversely proportional to the temperature.' (Wilson, *loc. cit.*, pp. 489–490) Since a comparison of the results achieved with the available data even qualitatively revealed mixed conclusions, he added quite cautiously:

> From the experimental side, therefore, the existence or non-existence of semiconductors remains an open question, and neither the measurements of specific heat nor those of susceptibility are sufficiently accurate to supply additional evidence. Theoretically there is no reason why semi-conductors should not exist, the main difference between semi-conductors and insulators being that for the former $\theta_u$ is so small that the substance has a measurable conductivity, while for the latter $\theta_u$ is extremely large. Experimentally, however, the only substances which show undoubted semi-conducting properties are very impure, and it may be that they have no intrinsic conductivity. If this is so, the theory would have to be extended to take account of the effect of impurities in increasing the conductivity of poor conductors. (Wilson, 1931a, pp. 490–491)

A couple of months later, Wilson had a second paper ready, in which he removed certain invalid approximations of the earlier paper and then considered the effect of impurities in particular (Wilson, 1931b). He succeeded in describing the temperature dependence of the conductivity again by a relation of the type

$$\sigma = \text{const.} \exp\left(-\frac{W_2 - W_1}{kT}\right), \qquad (581')$$

$^{744}$ These energy parameters (i.e., $W_1$ and $W_2$ being the energy averages of the zones) occurred in the theories of Peierls and Brillouin. Note that in Eq. (580) the second term can be neglected unless $kT$ is of the order of $(W_2 - W_1)$.

but the constant now depended crucially on the ratio of the number of impurity atoms present to the number of atoms of the pure substance (i.e., it was proportional to the square root of that ratio). In addition, Wilson now treated the Hall effect of semiconductors and found that also the Hall effect constant $R_0$ assumed the characteristic factor $\exp\left(-\frac{W_2 - W_1}{2kT}\right)$, as compared with the case of a metal. Even the observation of such a complex substance as cuprous oxide seemed to follow from the new theory, provided its conduction was due to impurities and not intrinsic. Encouraged by the preliminary success, Wilson went ahead and applied his theory to describe the rectifying properties of the system copper-cuprous oxide (Wilson, 1932a), as well as to other questions of technical interest (Fowler and Wilson, 1932). Then, he turned to the theory of metals, getting involved in the Brillouin–Peierls debate about the necessity of *Umklapp* processes.$^{745}$

In the last part of this subsection, we now return to the problems of magnetism that started the entire quantum-mechanical theory of metal electrons. Late in 1929, a Russian visitor, the 21-year-old Lev Landau, arrived at Pauli's Institute in Zurich on a travel grant from the Soviet People's Commissariat of Education (which was later supplemented by an International Education Board fellowship).$^{746}$ He brought with him the manuscript of his ideas for a paper on '*Diamagnetismus der Metalle*' ('Diamagnetism of Metals'), which he worked out in Zurich and submitted in May 1930 from Cambridge to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Landau, 1930). With this investigation, Landau was finally able to answer a ques-

$^{745}$ Wilson, like Brillouin, claimed in a study on 'The Theory of Metals,' which Fowler communicated to the *Proceedings of the Royal Society of London* in July 1932, that there was no need to invoke such processes (Wilson, 1932b); however, Peierls replied by pointing out that the particular electron distribution used in Wilson's proof was nonstationary and therefore not applicable (Peierls, 1933c).

$^{746}$ Lev Davidovich Landau was born in Baku, on the Caspian Sea, on 22 January 1908, the son of a petroleum engineer and a physician. Being a child prodigy, he enrolled already in 1922 at Baku University to study physics, mathematics, and chemistry. Two years later, he transferred to the University of Leningrad, from where he graduated in 1927 and then enrolled at the Leningrad Physico-Technical Institute for postgraduate study. Even in these early years, he experienced the excitement of original scientific work, and, beginning in 1926, he published papers on quantum mechanics. In 1929, he obtained fellowships to travel to the centres of atomic physics in Berlin, Zurich, Copenhagen, Leyden, Leipzig, and other places. He worked in Copenhagen with Niels Bohr, in Cambridge with P. A. M. Dirac, and in Zurich with Wolfgang Pauli. The most important part of his education was his stay at Bohr's Institute of Theoretical Physics in Copenhagen. The scientific atmosphere of Bohr's Institute, intensified by the impact of Bohr's personality, had a decisive impact on Landau, and he subsequently always considered himself as Bohr's disciple. Upon his return home, he became in 1932 the Head of the Theory Division of the just established Ukrainian Physico-Technical Institute in Kharkov, where he developed intensive activities as teacher and researcher (notably, on the theory of phase transitions and superconductors). He visited Bohr's Institute in Copenhagen twice more, in 1933 and 1934. In the spring of 1937, Landau moved to Moscow, where he became Head of the Theoretical Division of the Institute of Physical Problems, which had been recently established under the direction of Peter L. Kapitza. During the Stalinist purges, he was arrested in the spring of 1938 (formally accused of being a German spy), but was released later in 1939 on the insistence of Peter Kapitza to Molotov himself. On 7 January 1962, Landau was involved in a very serious car accident; he never fully recovered and died on 1 April 1968, in Moscow. In 1961, he had been awarded the Max Planck Medal and the Fritz London Prize; in 1962, he received the Nobel Prize for his pioneering research in the theory of condensed mater, especially liquid helium. For details of Landau's life, see Mehra, 1990.

III.6  The Metal Electrons and Solid State Theory                                                                   625

tion that had hung around for two decades.$^{747}$ Although the motion of electrons in atoms must—due to Paul Langevin’s theory (1905)—give rise to diamagnetism, Niels Bohr (1911) and others had shown that the diamagnetic susceptibility of a free electron gas must vanish, because the effects of the orbital motion of electrons and those bounced off the boundary must cancel; hence, ultimately, the energy of an electron gas in a magnetic field becomes proportional to the square of the velocity and independent of the strength of the magnetic field, at least in the classical theory. Landau now argued that a quantum-mechanical treatment yielded a quite different result, which he demonstrated in two steps: First, he described—by means of a clever device—the motion of a free electron in a magnetic field by that of a harmonic oscillator of frequency $\nu_L \left( = \frac{eh/2\pi}{m_e c} \right)$ and the energy

$$E = (2n + 1)\mu_0 H,$$ (582)

with $\mu_0 \left( = \frac{eh/2\pi}{2m_0 c} \right)$ the Bohr magneton and $n$ a quantum number determining the translational motion; second, he evaluated the partition function, which turned out to be independent of a magnetic quantum number, and found for the magnetic susceptibility the result,

$$\chi = \frac{\mu_0}{3} \left( \frac{\partial^2 F}{\partial N^2} \right)^{-1},$$ (583)

where $F$ and $N$ denote the free energy and the number of electrons, respectively. With this, Landau concluded that, ‘we thus have in reality a diamagnetism which is equal to one-third of Pauli’s spin magnetism’ (Landau, 1930, English translation, p. 36).
    Landau added a few remarks about extending this result to the case of electrons in a periodic potential, i.e., in metals and insulating substances. More than two years later, Rudolf Peierls treated the situation in some detail and derived the result:

> The diamagnetic susceptibility is composed of three parts, of which the first stems from the binding and turns out—in our approximation—equal to the diamagnetism of single atoms. The last one corresponds to the diamagnetism of free electrons. [The second contribution] is a mixed term, which possesses no analogue in the case of a single atom or for free electrons. (Peierls, 1933a, pp. 786–787)

Peierls also generalized a criterion, which Landau had stated earlier, namely, that

While Landau had argued earlier that it might be impossible to observe this effect, Peierls drew attention to the observation of Wander Johannes de Haas and P. M. van Alphen, who had reported (in a paper submitted in December 1930) a field-dependence of the magnetic susceptibility of bismuth (de Haas and van Alphen, 1930). In a second paper of January 1933, Peierls then compared the calculated and the experimentally determined ‘de Haas–van Alphen effects’ (Peierls, 1933b).
    In the early 1930s, the theoretical description of ferromagnetic phenomena progressed considerably, particularly due to Felix Bloch’s investigations. As we have already mentioned, in 1929 Bloch had travelled to Holland as a Lorentz Fellow, where he spent six months with Kramers in Utrecht and a few months with A. D. Fokker in Haarlem. This was a fruitful time, during which he developed the $T^{-5}$-law for the temperature dependence of the electrical resistance (Bloch, 1930a), thus proving that the profound analysis of the electron–lattice interaction first introduced in his thesis was capable of explaining in detail the experimental results on the low-temperature resistance of metals. In a paper completed on 26 January 1930, he actually proposed a new approach to ferromagnetic phenomena, as reported in his abstract:

> In the exchange process of electrons in a crystal the eigenfunctions and eigenvalues of first order for the high-multiplicity term systems are determined with the coupling between spin and orbit being neglected. They make it possible to study the ferromagnetic behaviour at low temperatures, especially to answer the question under which conditions ferromagnetism may arise at all. It appears that this is possible only for special lattices; the saturation magnetization then assumes at low temperatures the form
>
> $$M(T) = M(0) \left[ 1 - \left( \frac{T}{\theta} \right)^{3/2} \right].$$ [(585)]
>
> (Bloch, 1930b, p. 206)

Bloch made use, as he had done already in a previous paper (1929b), of John Slater’s determinant method (1929b) to treat the exchange problem of complex atomic systems (and thus avoid the group-theoretical method used by Heisenberg and others). being bound in a periodic lattice, he then derived the eigenfunctions

$$a_{k_1\dots k_r}(f_1,\dots,f_r) = c_1 \exp\left\{ \frac{2\pi i}{N}(k_1 f_1 + k_2 f_2 + \dots k_r f_r) \right\} + c_2 \exp\left\{ \frac{2\pi i}{N}(k_2 f_1 + k_1 f_2 + \dots k_r f_r) \right\} + \dots$$ (586)

With these, the energy eigenvalues

$$\begin{aligned} \varepsilon_{k_1\dots k_r} &= 2J_1 \sum_{j=1}^r \left( 1 - \cos \frac{2\pi k_j}{N} \right), \\ k_1 \dots k_j \dots k_r &= 0, 1 \dots N-1, \end{aligned}$$ (587)

were associated, where $r$ spins were turned around against the remaining $n - r$ spins of the chain ($N = 2n$) and $J_1$ denoted the exchange energy of two electrons. The expression represented what Bloch would later call ‘spin waves’ (Bloch, 1930c). Similarly, Bloch obtained spin-wave solutions in a two- or three-dimensional lattice; e.g., in the latter case he wrote

$$\varepsilon_{k_1\dots k_r} = 2J_1 \left\{ \sum_{j=1}^r \left[ \left( 1 - \cos \frac{2\pi k_j}{G} \right) + \left( 1 - \cos \frac{2\pi l_j}{G} \right) + \left( 1 - \cos \frac{2\pi m_j}{G} \right) \right] \right\}$$ (588)

for a simple cubic lattice ($N = G^3$). With such solutions, he evaluated the partition function $S$ of the system in the presence of a magnetic field and derived the average magnetic moment $M \left( = kT \frac{\partial \log S}{\partial H} \right)$, arriving at the important conclusions: (1) in the cases of the linear chain and the two-dimensional lattice, the expressions obtained for $M$ diverged if the limit of vanishing magnetic field was taken; hence, no spontaneous magnetization resulted; (2) for the cubic lattice, however, $M$ remained finite and exhibited the temperature dependence given in Eq. (585). The $T^{3/2}$-law for low temperatures seemed to describe the observations reasonably well.
    Bloch presented his new theory, which (for $T$ larger than the transition temperature $\theta$) accounted for the paramagnetic behaviour of ferromagnetic substances, at the *Leipziger Universitätswoche* in June 1930 (Bloch, *loc. cit.*). Still, it contained some deficiencies; e.g., Bloch had not provided any reasons for the required positivity of the exchange integral.$^{748}$ On the other hand, Hans Bethe

$^{748}$ For example, John Slater would then argue that only the existence of outer ($3d$ and $4s$) electrons or incomplete shells guaranteed ferromagnetism (Slater, 1930b).

628     Chapter III  The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

(when in Rome the following year) succeeded in solving the problem of the one-dimensional Heisenberg ferromagnet, the linear chain, exactly: in this model, the atoms are supposed to have spin-$\frac{1}{2}$; only the nearest neighbours interact, and the interaction is supposed to be attractive if their spins are parallel, repulsive if opposite. The assumptions were thus similar to the Ising model, but the spins were treated properly by quantum mechanics. Bethe made an assumption about the eigenfunction and found the complete spectrum of the eigenfunctions with the help of the ingenious ‘Bethe Ansatz,’ which has since been much used in quantum statistics; he discovered a deviation of his result from the one given by Bloch in the paper ‘Zur Theorie der Metalle. I. Eigenwerte und Eigenfunktionen der Linearen Atomkette’ [‘Theory of Metals. Part I (Part II was never published): Eigenvalues and Eigenfunctions of the Linear Atomic Chain,’ Bethe, 1931]. Bloch, meanwhile, derived quite encouraging further conclusions from his approach (e.g., on the anisotropy of the magnetization in single crystals: Bloch and Gentile, 1931); he was not at all impressed by ‘Bethe’s tedious *Ixereien* (burdensome pickiness)’ (as he wrote to Peierls on 6 November 1931).
    Following his visit to Holland, Bloch returned to Leipzig, and after one year with Heisenberg, he was invited to Copenhagen for six months as an Oersted Fellow at Bohr’s Institute. He established a close friendship with Bohr during this period—a friendship that was to last through the trying years of the war and for the rest of Bohr’s life, and one that would be renewed by frequent visits. Bloch remained in continual contact with Bohr through the years, during which the same deep problems never ceased to occupy Bohr’s mind. As a result of conversations with him, Bloch became interested in the stopping power of matter for charged particles, a subject in which Bohr had had a long interest (see Chapter IV.5); however, Bloch never developed a passion for the epistemological problems that preoccupied Bohr throughout his life. In particular, he formulated in a lengthy memoir the spin-wave theory in all of the essential details, employing the language of nonrelativistic quantum fields and deriving a classically intuitive (*anschauliche*) description of the remanence and hysteresis phenomena, introducing what one would later call ‘Bloch walls’ (i.e., the boundaries between the domains of different magnetization). In 1932, Bloch returned to Leipzig, and with his new work on spin waves (Bloch, 1932), he obtained his *Habilitation* at the University of Leipzig; he became a *Privatdozent* and continued as Heisenberg’s assistant.
    In January 1933, Adolf Hitler was appointed Chancellor of Germany. This event was to have the same profound effect on Bloch’s career as it did on similar other great physicists (see Chapter IV). Bloch realized that he would have to leave Germany, and he spent the spring and summer semester in Switzerland and Paris (where he stayed at the home of Paul Langevin). He had applied for and was awarded a Rockefeller Fellowship for a year, which he intended to use partly in Rome with Enrico Fermi and partly at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge. On the way to Rome, he visited Bohr, where he received a letter from David L.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0661 -->

III.6 The Metal Electrons and Solid State Theory 629

Brewster, the Chairman of the Stanford Physics Department, offering him a position at Stanford University. Bohr had met Webster and knew that Stanford was a fine university. Bloch continued to Rome, but Bohr's advice persuaded him to accept Webster's offer and to abandon his planned visit to Cambridge.

Bloch was still in Leipzig. Heisenberg once told him his ideas about nuclei while they were walking together. The neutron had been discovered in 1932, and Heisenberg and Ettore Majorana had proposed that the elementary constituents of the nucleus were protons and neutrons, and he returned from a visit to Europe in 1935 with the resolve that Stanford should begin experimental work on neutron physics. This turned out to be a crucial point in Bloch's career: the neutron work combined with his earlier work on magnetism set him on the path leading to his discoveries in the field of nuclear magnetism, for which he and E. M. Purcell were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1952. Bloch pursued a most illustrious career at Stanford University. [See M. Chodorow *et al.*: 'Felix Bloch and Twentieth-Century Physics,' in *Rice University Studies*, Vol. 66, No. 3, Summer 1980, *Dedication to Felix Bloch's 75th Birthday*: (Published by William Marsh Rice University, Houston, Texas, 1980.)]

### (e) Conclusion: An Unsolved Problem (1928–1932)

Rudolf Peierls, one of the leading physicists in the field, summarized the results achieved in and the status of the theory of metal electrons in a review article for *Ergebnisse der exakten Naturwissenschaften* as follows:

> If one views the present status of the theory of metals, one obtains the impression that its goal, namely to explain the typical behaviour of metals from their molecular properties and to derive the existing quantitative laws, has been essentially reached, with certain exceptions to be mentioned presently. Still not solved, for instance, has been the problem of being able to compute, say, the material properties of all metals with the help of limited molecular data. But this [in my] opinion, is neither an interesting task of the theory—as the constants can be derived more simply in an empirical way—nor can it be carried out in practice because of the complex conditions existing in the interior of metals. (Peierls, 1932b, p. 320)

In the early 1930s, several such official reviews appeared in handbooks and similar publications, of which we may note especially those of Sommerfeld and Bethe (1933), Nordheim (1934), and Slater (1934). The most comprehensive of these was the Sommerfeld–Bethe treatise of nearly 300 pages, in which Sommerfeld himself wrote Chapter I, or the first 35 pages dealing with the initial free-electron approach, while his former student Hans Bethe worked out the later more realistic theory of metals, insulators, and semiconductors. Although Bethe, in comparison with the authors of other review articles on the subject, had played only a minor role in the results achieved, his treatment was the most thorough and critical, and

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0662 -->

630 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

it became the standard reference in the following decades.$^{749}$ Let us, however, return to Peierls, who also wrote in his concluding remarks:

> However, as we have seen in detail, the theory needs an extension in various directions. What is missing, in particular, is an investigation of the role played by the interaction of the electrons. One should expect that such an investigation might clarify, among other things, the origin of superconductivity. The impossibility to explain superconductivity constitutes the biggest defect of the existing theory. (Peierls, 1932b, p. 320)

The phenomenon of superconductivity had been discovered by Heike Kamerlingh Onnes in his low-temperature laboratory at Leyden, three years after the liquefaction of helium in 1908 (Kamerlingh Onnes, 1911). The very existence of superconductivity and the details of the phenomena associated with it had remained a puzzle, both experimentally and theoretically, although the physicists tried hard to understand the facts.$^{750}$ The experimental investigation suffered from the fact that, until 1922, when John C. McLennan installed the cryogenic laboratory in Toronto, no other place in the world reached the low temperatures obtained at Leyden; two years later, the work of Walther Meissner followed at the *Physikalisch-Technische Reichsanstalt* in Berlin, who soon extended the list of superconducting materials considerably, besides adding new metals (like tantalum and niobium) and compounds (like copper sulphate). Other important facts were discovered in Leyden, especially the observations that superconductivity disappeared in strong magnetic fields (Kamerlingh Onnes, 1913), that the impurities in a metal did not influence the superconducting effect (Sizoo, 1926), and that thermal conductivity—*unlike the electrical conductivity*—did not change at the transition point (de Haas and Bremmer, 1931).

With the advent of the new quantum-mechanical theory of metal electrons, the solution of the riddle of superconductivity also seemed to be close. Thus, Maximilian Strutt concluded his paper 'Zur Wellenmechanik des Atomgitters' ('On the Wave Mechanics of Atomic Lattice') by first showing the existence of energy gaps with the help of the Mathieu equation: 'It seems possible to me to get closer to an understanding of certain properties of metallic conductivity, especially superconductivity, by studying the spectra found above.' (Strutt, 1928, p. 324) Later that

year, on Christmas 1928, Niels Bohr wrote to Heisenberg: 'How have you been doing with superconductivity? Bloch's beautiful work, which you so kindly sent me and from which I derived much pleasure, taught me of course that the way out indicated [earlier] was not possible.' Even more seriously than Bohr, Heisenberg, and Strutt, Bloch then became involved in the problem, as he recalled half a century later:

> It started right after I had my Ph.D. and returned to Zurich as Pauli's assistant for the academic year 1928–29. Pauli thought that superconductivity was the only remaining matter of some interest in the theory of metals and that I should get on with it so as to be finally done with all these "dirt effects." Actually, I had already started to think about the problem and had realized that the explanation of persistent currents required a consideration of the previously neglected interaction between electrons. The idea, independently expressed by Landau, was that it should thus be possible at low temperatures to obtain a minimum of free energy in a state of the metal with finite current. My own confidence in the idea was supported by the analogy with ferromagnetism whereby I saw a parallelism between permanent magnetization below the Curie point and persistent current below the critical temperature. I therefore started industriously to consider various types of interaction, regardless of their possible origin, and to look whether the Schrödinger equation would allow stationary states of the electron with non-vanishing current and a minimum of the energy. Once in a while I thought that I had indeed found such states but it never took Pauli long to point to some error in the calculation. While he did not object to my approach, he became rather annoyed at my continuous failure to come out with desired answer to such a simple [!] question. (Bloch, 1980, p. 27)

The endeavor to find the superconducting solution continued incessantly from 1928 to 1933 (and beyond). The physicists mentioned already, notably, Bohr, Bloch, and Landau participated actively, and were joined later by Ralph Kronig. Only Kronig published anything about his ideas (Kronig, 1932, 1933). In particular, he proposed that the electron interactions eventually lead to a rigid electron lattice within the already existing ionic lattice; hence, no resistance would occur according to Bloch's theory. He discussed these matters with Bloch, Bohr, and Pauli, and many letters were exchanged between these people in 1932.$^{751}$ Bloch, in particular, developed into the most severe critic of all of these attempts at deriving a quantum-mechanical theory of superconductivity and thus became the most significant authority in this field, without himself developing a solution. Yet, Hans Bethe closed the discussion of the problem in his *Handbuch* article by saying: 'In spite of the failures so far, it should be safely believed that superconductivity must be explainable on the basis of our *present* knowledge of quantum mechanics.' (Sommerfeld and Bethe, 1933, p. 558) Like most of his colleagues, Bethe opti-

mistically thought that the solution was just around the corner, and only later was it discovered that the efforts made hitherto were misleading in two points. First, one did not think of the specific mechanism that creates ('Cooper') pairs; second, a mistaken assumption had crept into the proposals made at that time, as Bloch recalled:

> Assuming that a given state could be varied by letting the momentum of each electron increase by the same infinitesimal amount, I found that the corresponding differential change of the energy was proportional to the current with the consequence that an extremum of the former always led to a vanishing value of the latter. Now that one knows about the formation of Cooper pairs and long-range order, so clearly manifested in flux quantization, it is easy to see that the assumption was unjustified.... Indeed, I saw no further way to progress and for a considerable time there was for me only the dubious satisfaction to see that others, without noticing it, kept on falling in the same trap. This brought me to the facetious statement that all theories of superconductivity can be disproved, later quoted in the more radical form as "Bloch's theorem": "Superconductivity is impossible." (Bloch, 1980, p. 27)

### III.7 Aspects of Nuclear and 'High-Energy' Phenomena

#### (a) Introduction: The Experimental Facts (1908–1929)

The explanation of the constitution of molecules and the electronic properties in solids, as discussed in the last two sections, represented, together with the earlier explanation of atomic spectra (discussed in the previous volumes), an almost unlimited triumph of the quantum-mechanical theory. A quite different situation prevailed, however, in another domain of modern physics: i.e., nuclear phenomena. Although an immense wealth of data had been accumulated since the discovery of radioactivity in 1896, and a fairly good model had been proposed in 1911 to describe the role of the atomic nucleus in physics, the theoretical analysis of the observed properties progressed only very slowly. Thus, in a review of the problem of nuclear constitution, published as late as 1933, Eduard (Edward) Teller remarked:

> In the following sections, the status of the theory of nuclear structure would be discussed. One should rather say, the difficulties would be enumerated, which one has encountered in attempting to understand and explain the properties of nuclei. (Kirsch and Teller, 1933, p. 546)

These difficulties arose from two aspects: the diversity of the experimental facts and the problem of their respective reliability, and the obvious contradictions that arose from their theoretical analysis.

The first knowledge about atomic nuclei resulted from the phenomena of radioactivity, which were detected even before the details about the constitution

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0665 -->

III.7 Aspects of Nuclear and ‘High-Energy’ Phenomena  
633

of atoms were known. In spite of thorough physical investigations on the nature of the radioactive rays and decay products—the physicists developed great interest and devoted many publications to radioactivity [e.g., in the various principal journals in Great Britain, France, and Germany—including the newly-founded (1899) journal, the *Physikalische Zeitschrift*]—the exploration of chemical properties, like the transmutation of elements in the natural radioactive families, and the biological–physiological effects of radioactive rays dominated the research of this topic in the first decade. The new period in the physics connected with radioactive processes began in 1908, when Ernest Rutherford and Hans Geiger recognized the nature of $\alpha$-rays as doubly ionized helium atoms (Rutherford and Geiger, 1908). The following year, Geiger and Ernest Marsden used the scattering of $\alpha$-particles (and the new quantitative counting method with the scintillation screen) to discover an unexpected effect, namely, large deflections (by $90^\circ$ and more) in the case of scattering by thin layers of metal foils (Geiger and Marsden, 1909). Rutherford then interpreted these (and the results published later—Geiger and Marsden, 1913) to derive his model of the ‘nuclear atom’: the observed angular distribution of the scattered $\alpha$-particles could be understood if the atom (of the scattering metal foil) ‘consists of a central [positive] electric charge concentrated at a point [which Rutherford would call the ‘nucleus’] surrounded by a uniform spherical distribution of opposite electricity equal in amount [i.e., the negative electrons]’ (Rutherford, 1911a, p. 19). In August 1912, the young Niels Bohr, then working with Rutherford in Manchester, noticed in the course of developing a more detailed description of the passage of $\alpha$-particles through matter that:

> [By] adopting Professor Rutherford’s theory of the constitution of atoms, it seems that it can be concluded with great certainty, from the absorption of $\alpha$-rays, that a hydrogen atom contains only 1 electron outside the positively charged nucleus, and that a helium atom only contains 2 electrons outside the nucleus. (Bohr, 1913a, pp. 30–31)

Already during the following year, Bohr added quantum-theoretical conditions to Rutherford’s atomic model to establish his own model of atomic constitution, which formed the basis of the semiclassical theory of atoms (Bohr, 1913b).$^{752}$ While the electrons surrounding the atomic nucleus should give rise to the observed line spectra of atoms and molecules, Bohr concluded at the same time that the $\beta$-rays involved in radioactive transmutations (which were known to be fast electrons) emerged from the atomic nucleus.$^{753}$ In the fourth part of a memoir on the ‘Collision of $\alpha$-Particles with Light Atoms,’ published shortly after World War I (although most of the results had been obtained earlier), Rutherford announced the first observed artificial transmutation of a chemical substance,

$^{752}$ For details of this story, see Sections II.2 and II.3 of Volume 1, Part 1.  
$^{753}$ See Bohr, 1913c, §6, and also George de Hevesy, AHQP Interview, p. 3, quoted in Volume 1, Part 1, p. 184.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0666 -->

634 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

namely, the change of a nitrogen nucleus of the air into an oxygen nucleus plus a hydrogen nucleus (Rutherford, 1919). In his Bakerian Lecture of the following year, appropriately entitled ‘Nuclear Constitution of Atoms,’ he finally expounded that the nuclei of atoms consisted of hydrogen nuclei (now called ‘protons’) and electrons (Rutherford, 1920). He added that sometimes four protons and two electrons were strongly bound together in $\alpha$-particles, and he even speculated about the existence of ‘an atom of mass 1, which has zero nuclear charge’ that would arise from a very tight binding of a proton and an electron (Rutherford, *loc. cit.*, p. 396).

The Cavendish Laboratory, Rutherford’s new research institution after he succeeded Joseph John Thomson in 1919, soon became a great centre of nuclear physics, which engaged many talented students and collaborators, such as James Chadwick, Charles D. Ellis, and Patrick M. S. Blackett, who made fundamental contributions to nuclear research.$^{754}$ Thus, Chadwick and E. S. Bieler detected—in the scattering of $\alpha$-particles by hydrogen nuclei—possible deviations from Coulomb’s law (assumed thus far by Rutherford and Bohr) at small distances (Chadwick and Bieler, 1921) that would be ascribed (by Rutherford) to magnetic fields arising from the deformation of electrons and protons in the $\alpha$-particle.$^{755}$ On the subject of obtaining artificially transmuted atomic nuclei by collision processes with protons an $\alpha$-particles, a keen competition arose between the *Institut für Radiumforschung* in Vienna and the Cavendish Laboratory. Although the Cambridge people registered, in particular, transmutations of light elements (up to potassium), the Viennese researchers reported the smashing of nuclei (‘*Atomzerstümmerung*’) up to atomic number 53 (iodine).$^{756}$ Another valuable experimental source about nuclei was provided by the accurate measurement of the masses of isotopes, i.e., of the different masses of nuclei associated with the same element, notably, by Francis William Aston (see, e.g., Aston, 1924).$^{757}$ The results obtained in the 1920s established that the masses of nuclear isotopes are approximately multiples of the proton mass, thus supporting the nineteenth century hypothesis of William Prout, who claimed that all atoms are built from hydrogen

$^{754}$ We have described the atmosphere at the Cavendish Laboratory in the 1920s in Volume 4, pp. 31–37.

$^{756}$ See Pettersson, 1928, especially, p. 61. Later on, after the artificially accelerated nuclear particles became available, some of these results had to be withdrawn, because the transmutation required much higher energies than those of the protons used (especially in Vienna). In this context, one might also refer to various stories about a ‘low-energy’ transmutation of certain chemical elements, say, of lead into thallium and mercury, of mercury into gold (Davies and Horton, 1926), or of hydrogen into helium (Paneth, 1927). See the unsigned review article ‘The Present Position of the Transmutation Controversy’ in the *Nature* issue of 29 May 1926 (Vol. 117, pp. 758–760).  
$^{757}$ Aston had determined the first of such isotope masses together with J. J. Thomson already in 1913 (Thomson, 1913a). For a short discussion of isotopes and the physical consequences from the measurement of their masses, see Brown and Rechenberg, 1996, pp. 11–12.

atoms. The tables of isotope masses further exhibited, for moderate atomic numbers $Z$, preferred atomic weights $A$ (i.e., an accumulation of isotope masses): in particular, isotopes of even $Z = 2n$ were often associated with mass $A = 4n$ (times the proton mass), those with odd $Z = 2n + 1$ with $A = 4n + 1$. The deviation of atomic masses from integers in proton masses, the so-called ‘mass defect,’ evidently corresponded to the binding energy of nuclei, which assumed a considerable size (e.g., $\Delta m \approx 0.03$ for the helium nucleus) as compared with the binding energy of electrons in atoms. Having this information in hand, the physicists were ‘convinced that the building-up (*Aufbau*) of the nuclei from elementary constituents can be accomplished according to the same construction principles as the building-up of atoms from nuclei and electrons, namely by the rules of quantum theory’ (Sommerfeld, 1924d, p. 217).

Back in 1914, James Chadwick (then in Berlin) had studied the energy distribution of $\beta$-rays emitted radium B + C and concluded:

> The result is that the $\beta$-radiation yields a continuous spectrum, which is overlapped by a linear spectrum of relatively low intensity; only in the region of slow $\beta$-rays several more intense lines are existing. These results [obtained both with the counting and ionization methods] seemed first to contradict the results derived from photographic plates, which had led to the conception that $\beta$-radiation of most radioactive elements consists essentially of single homogeneous groups of rays. The difference between the electric and the photographic methods could be explained by the extraordinary sensitivity of the photographic plates for small intensity fluctuations. (Chadwick, 1914, p. 383)

In the 1920s, Chadwick and C. D. Ellis continued the study of $\beta$-spectra, confirming the view regarding a continuous spectrum. On the other hand, Lise Meitner of the *Kaiser Wilhelm-Institut für Chemie* in Berlin rather concluded from here experiments:

> For typical $\beta$-active substances, the nucleus is left by electrons of a homogeneous velocity. The $\beta$-rays will be transformed partially into $\gamma$-rays of the same energy, and these $\gamma$-rays stimulate in the different electron rings [of the atom] the emission of secondary $\beta$-rays, whose velocity is determined by the velocity of the primary $\beta$-radiation and the respective excitation energy. The largest possible velocity must correspond to the primary $\beta$-ray, and its determination provides at the same time the wavelength of the $\gamma$-radiation. (Meitner, 1922a, p. 143)

Hence, the continuous $\beta$-spectrum actually came about by secondary processes.$^{758}$ In the spring of 1927, C. D. Ellis and W. A. Wooster, at Rutherford’s Cavendish Laboratory, announced

$^{758}$ See also our discussion of the Auger effect in Section III.1 of the present volume.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0668 -->

636 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

a ready means of distinguishing between two views, since in one case [i.e., the discrete spectrum advocated by Meitner] a given quantity of energy would be emitted at each disintegration equal or greater than the maximum energy observed in the electrons escaping from the atom, whereas in the second case [i.e., that of a continuous primary spectrum advocated in Cambridge] the average energy per disintegration would be expected to equal the average energy of the particles emitted. (Ellis and Wooster, 1927a, p. 563)

Hence, they suggested:

> If we were to measure the total energy given out by a known amount of the [$\beta$-active] material, as, for example, by enclosing it in a thick-walled calorimeter, then in the first case the heating effect should lead to an average energy per disintegration equal to or greater than the fastest electron emitted, no matter in what way this energy was afterwards split up by secondary effects. Since on the second hypothesis no secondary effects are presumed to be present the heating effect should correspond simply to the average kinetic energy of the particles forming the continuous spectrum. (Ellis and Wooster, *loc. cit.*)

Upon carrying out the experiment, Ellis and Wooster found:

> a striking confirmation of the hypothesis that the continuous spectrum is emitted as such from the nucleus, since the average energy of the particles as determined by ionisation measurements gives a value of about 390,000 volts, whereas if the energy emitted per disintegration were equal to that of the fastest $\beta$-rays, the corresponding value of the heating would be three times as large—in fact, 1,050,000 volts. (Ellis and Wooster, *loc. cit.*, p. 564)$^{759}$

Evidently, the nature of the $\beta$-decay spectrum had a great impact on the detailed theoretical explanation of the rich data from radioactive decays available in those days. Thus, Lise Meitner attempted to formulate in a letter to *Naturwissenschaften*, dated June 1926, ‘a simple empirical relation between atomic weight, stability (lifetime) of an atom and the type of its transmutation,’ namely:$^{760}$

> If the most stable element [isotope] of a series of isotopes, that is, one which has the longest lifetime, possesses the highest atomic weight, then all members of the series decay with $\alpha$-radiation. However, if the most stable element possesses the smallest atomic weight, the transmutation occurs with $\beta$-emission. Quite naturally, then in the case that the most stable element possesses an average atomic weight the decay of the heavier isotopes occurs with $\beta$-particle and of the lighter isotopes with $\alpha$-particle emission. (Meitner, 1926, p. 719)

$^{759}$ For more details, see the full paper (Ellis and Wooster, 1927b).  
$^{760}$ For an analysis and discussion of these rules, we refer to Kasimir Fajans’s detailed letter in *Naturwissenschaften* (Fajans, 1926).
