III.7 Aspects of Nuclear and ‘High-Energy’ Phenomena 637

In those days, Meitner’s laboratory in Berlin clearly competed with the Cavendish and a few other institutions (such as the *Institut für Radiumforschung* in Vienna and Marie Curie’s laboratory in Paris) about the lead in nuclear science.<sup>761</sup>

On 7 February 1929, a meeting was held at the Royal Society of London to discuss the ‘Structure of Nuclei,’ which the chairman, Ernest Rutherford, opened by summarizing the accomplishments of the previous fifteen years of research; in particular, he emphasized ‘three new methods of attack on this problem,’ notably:

> The first, and in some respects the most important, has been the proof of the isotopic constitution of ordinary elements, and the accurate determination of the masses or weights of the individual isotopes mainly due to the work of Dr. Aston. . . .
>
> The next discovery was the proof of the artificial disintegration of elements by bombardment with alpha particles, in which I have been personally interested, as has also Dr. Chadwick, who will discuss the results obtained and their bearing on the structure of nuclei. . . . The evidence, as a whole, indicates that while the ultimate constituents of the nucleus are protons and electrons, secondary units in the form of helium nuclei are also present in heavier elements. . . .
>
> The third line of attack, which has proved of great interest, has been the study of wavelengths of the penetrating gamma-rays which arise during the disintegration of the radioactive nucleus. As the gamma-rays have their origin in the nucleus, the frequency of these rays, first determined by Dr. Ellis, gives us important evidence as to the modes of vibration . . . of the particles constituting the nucleus. (Rutherford *et al.*, 1929, pp. 373–374)

Rutherford went on to discuss his own work, done together with James Chadwick, to obtain information about the dimension of the nucleus and the law of force by scattering of $\alpha$-particles with nuclei, and finally pointed out the puzzling fact ‘that

<sup>761</sup> The role of eminent female scientists in nuclear science is rather remarkable, as Marie Curie and Lise Meitner were soon to be joined by Curie’s daughter Irène (see Rechenberg, 1997a).
Lise Meitner was born on 17 November 1878, in Vienna, the daughter of an attorney-at-law of Jewish descent. After being educated in Protestant high schools, Meitner studied at the University of Vienna (with Ludwig Boltzmann and Franz Exner) and received her doctorate in 1905. Already in Vienna, she started to work on problems in the field of radioactivity; after she moved to Berlin (to learn theoretical physics in greater depth under Max Planck), she collaborated further on radioactivity with Otto Hahn at the chemical institute of the University of Berlin, investigating—in particular—the $\beta$-spectra of radioactive substances. Hahn and Meitner continued their work from 1912 onward at the newly established *Kaiser Wilhelm-Institut für Chemie* in Berlin-Dahlem, where Hahn obtained the position of leading a laboratory for radioactivity, while Meitner served at the same time as assistant to Planck at the University. By combining physical (Meitner) and chemical (Hahn) methods, they studied many radioactive substances and discovered new ones, e.g., the radioactive protactinium in 1917. After World War I (during which Meitner spent a period as an X-ray assistant in Austrian Army Service), Hahn and Meitner headed their own respective departments at the *Kaiser Wilhelm-Institut* (namely, a chemical one and physical one in radioactivity). Meitner (like Hahn) was promoted to the position of *Wissenschaftliches Mitglied* (Scientific Member) at the Institute, and she obtained her *Habilitation* at the University of Berlin in 1922 (she was promoted to professor in 1926). Through her original and careful scientific work, she advanced in the 1920s to become a highly esteemed authority in the field of radioactivity—‘our Madame Curie,’ as Albert Einstein called her. Lise Meitner would continue to play a major role in the field of radioactivity and nuclear physics. (For the details of Lise Meitner’s biography, we refer to Frisch, 1969, and the book of Ruth Lewin Sime, 1996.)

This problem has been attacked by Mr. Gamow . . . and also by Gurney and Condon.’ (Rutherford *et al.*, *loc. cit.*, p. 378)
Finally, he interpreted Aston’s data on the isotope masses in the light of the electron–proton model of the atomic nucleus involving electric and magnetic forces and leading to a ‘tightly packed structure near its centre gradually becoming less dense toward the outside,’ yet ‘surrounded by a potential barrier which normally prevents the $\alpha$-particles from escaping’ (Rutherford *et al.*, *loc. cit.*, p. 381).<sup>762</sup>

Following this extended introduction by Rutherford, Francis Aston and James Chadwick furnished more details on the atomic weights and the ‘packing fraction’—i.e., the binding energies of nuclei as a percentage of the excess or deviation from a whole number of the oxygen scale—and the observed disintegration of nuclei by bombardment with $\alpha$-particles, respectively. Charles D. Ellis reported about the properties of nuclear $\gamma$-radiation that seemed to characterize the energy levels of the emitting nuclei (similar to the atomic spectra that characterize the energy levels of atoms). The last three speakers then turned to the theoretical discussion of nuclear phenomena. Thus, George Gamow added some remarks on a quantum-mechanical model, in which the nuclei are considered to consist essentially of $\alpha$-particles. Ralph Fowler, on the other hand, stressed the importance of the wave nature of atomic particles in explaining the properties of $\alpha$-decay. Finally, Owen W. Richardson of London said ‘a few words as to the evidence for the rotation of the nuclei,’ for which ‘good spectroscopic evidence of two kinds’ existed, first ‘the hyperfine structure of atomic spectral lines,’ and second ‘the alternation of intensity which is present in the lines and bands of symmetrical diatomic molecules, such as H<sub>2</sub>, He<sub>2</sub>, N<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub>’ (Rutherford *et al.*, *loc. cit.*). Rutherford closed the session in February 1929 by remarking that ‘Our knowledge of the nucleus is still in a very elementary state, although much greater progress has been made than I thought possible fifteen years ago.’ (Rutherford *et al.*, *loc. cit.*, p. 390)

Whereas the problems connected with $\alpha$-radioactivity and the transmutation of nuclei by $\alpha$-particles were addressed in detail at the 1929 London meeting, no reference was made by the speakers to the controversy involving, in particular, Ellis and Meitner on the nature of the primary $\beta$-decay spectra and, more generally, to the difficulties emerging from the assumption of electrons in the interior of nuclei. These difficulties would show up both in the theoretical description of $\beta$-decay and of the nuclear rotational momenta, to which Richardson called attention in the discussion at the Royal Society meeting as providing insight into the structure of atomic nuclei. In the following subsection, we shall first deal with the success story of the wave-mechanical theory of $\alpha$-decay, which will be contrasted by the unsuc-

### (b) The Wave-Mechanical Theory of $\alpha$-Decay and the $\alpha$-Particle Model of Atomic Nuclei (1928–1930)

In June 1928, a newcomer arrived from Soviet Russia at Max Born’s Institute in Göttingen, supported by a grant from *Narkompros* (The People’s Commissariat of Education). He was 24-year-old George Gamow, who had nearly completed his graduate studies at the University of Leningrad.<sup>764</sup> Instead of getting involved in problems that were popular in Born’s circle at that time, he rather looked for problems of his own and consulted the literature in the library. There, he hit upon the question of how the $\alpha$-particles were emitted from radioactive substances. This question had especially bothered Rutherford, who had assumed the potential in the interior of nuclei to consist qualitatively of two parts: an essentially non-coulombic part in the interior of the nucleus yielding attraction (for $r < 10^{-12}$ cm) and an electrostatic-repulsion part in the vicinity of $r_0$, about the rim of the nucleus (Rutherford, 1927). Because the height of the potential wall in between exceeded the energy of $\alpha$-particles in the nucleus, Rutherford had suggested the following process: in order to escape from the nucleus (and give rise to $\alpha$-decay), the $\alpha$-particle combined with two electrons and became a neutral object that could penetrate through the potential wall, leaving the electrons behind. ‘But,’ thought Gamow, ‘this assumption appears to be quite unnatural and hardly corresponds to

---

<sup>763</sup> For contemporary review articles, see: Mott, 1933; Meitner, 1933a; Kirsch and Teller, 1933; and Houtermans, 1930. The earliest review by Houtermans deals exclusively with the then successful $\alpha$-particle scheme.

<sup>764</sup> Georgii Antonovich (or George, a he would call himself later) Gamow was born on 4 March 1904, in Odessa; his family members were mainly teachers and military people. He received his early education in the city of his birth, finishing school (where his father taught literature) in 1921. Being interested in physics and mathematics, he entered the Novorossiik University (later named Odessa University), but moved already a year later to the University of Petrograd, where he also occupied positions at the meteorological station of the State Forestry University (1922–1923), the Field Meteorological Observatory at the 1st Artillery School (1923–1924), and the State Optical Institute (1924–1925). He came in contact with well-known teachers, such as the physicists Orestes Chwolson and Dmitri Roshdestwensky and the mathematician Alexander Friedmann, as well as the junior theoretical physicists (who would soon become famous) G. (Yuri A.) Krutkow and Vladmir Fock and his fellow students Dimitri Iwanenko, Lev Landau, and V. A. Ambartsumian. In September 1926, he submitted his first papers, especially the one on ‘*Zur Wellentheorie der Materie*’ (‘On the Wave Theory of Matter’), written with Iwanenko and dealing with the Klein(-Fock) equation in five dimensions, to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Gamow and Iwanenko, 1926). He also wrote a paper in Russian jointly with Iwanenko and Landau, entitled (in English translation) ‘Universal Constants and the Limiting Transition’; as the universal constants, the authors considered Planck’s constant $h$, the velocity of light $c$, and the gravitational constant $G$ (as Planck had suggested in 1899), and the limiting transitions characterized different theories like Newtonian mechanics ($h \rightarrow 0$). As a ‘candidate of physics,’ Gamow went abroad. (For the early life and work of Gamow, see the article by Victor Y. Frenkel, 1994.)

640 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

the actual facts’ (Gamow, 1928a, p. 205), and, therefore, he proposed to study the problem from the point of view of wave mechanics. The papers of Lothar Nordheim (1928a) and J. Robert Oppenheimer (1928a), which he quoted, taught Gamow how to overcome the difficulties. As he noted: ‘In wave mechanics there always exists a transition probability different from zero for a particle to get from one region to another which is separated from the first one by an arbitrary, but finitely high, potential barrier.’ (Gamow, 1928a, p. 205)

Gamow quickly carried out the necessary calculations in a simple, one-dimensional model, where he took the potential within the nucleus to be zero between the positions $-q_0$ and $+q_0$ (from the centre of the nucleus), then rising to two square-well potentials of height $U_0$ and width $l$, and becoming zero again to the left of $-(q_0 + l)$ and to the right of $(q_0 + l)$. Inserting this potential into the Schrödinger equation, he obtained a solution having the complex energy values

$$E = E_0 + i\frac{h\lambda}{4\pi}, \tag{589}$$

where $E$ denoted the usual energy value of the $\alpha$-particle (of mass $m$) and $\lambda$ an attenuation constant, expressed by the equation,

$$\lambda = \frac{4hk \sin^2\theta}{\pi m \left[ 1 + \left( \frac{k'}{k} \right)^2 \right] 2(l+q_0)\kappa} \exp \left( - \frac{4\pi l \sqrt{2m}}{h} \sqrt{U_0 - E} \right). \tag{590}$$

The symbols $k$ and $k'$ signified momentum quantities, i.e.,

$$k = \frac{2\pi\sqrt{2m}}{h} \sqrt{E} \quad \text{and} \quad k' = \frac{2\pi\sqrt{2m}}{h} \sqrt{U_0 - E}, \tag{590a}$$

and $\theta$ is an angle given by

$$\sin \theta = \left[ 1 + \left( \frac{k}{k'} \right)^2 \right]^{-1/2}, \tag{590b}$$

whereas $\kappa$ represented a constant of the order of 1. The wave function $\Psi$ then showed the following behaviour:

(1) Within the nucleus (essentially for $-q_0 \leq q \leq q_0$), a standing wave obtained from the superposition of an incoming and a reflected wave existed (at the square-well potentials).

(2) In the region of the square-well potentials [i.e., for $-(q_0 + l) \leq q \leq -q_0$ and $q_0 \leq q \leq (q_0 + l)$, respectively], the wave amplitude decreased.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0673 -->

III.7 Aspects of Nuclear and ‘High-Energy’ Phenomena 641

(3) Outside the nucleus [i.e., for \( q \leq - (q_0 + l) \) and \( q \geq (q_0 + l) \)], a decaying state existed, whose decay time \(\lambda^{-1}\) evidently depended strongly on the height of the barrier \(U_0\) and its width \(l\).

In a later section (§4), Gamow turned to a qualitative discussion of a more realistic three-dimensional spherical potential \(U\), having a negative part in the interior of the nucleus that turned positive (i.e., repulsive for the \(\alpha\)-particle) at \(r_1\) and rose rapidly to a maximum value, becoming zero again after a slow decrease at \(r_2\). The asymptotic solution of the corresponding Schrödinger equation (for large values of \(r\)) could then be written as

\[
\chi = \frac{A}{r} \exp\left\{i\left(\frac{2\pi E}{h}t - kr\right)\right\}. \tag{591}
\]

In the region of high positive potential, the wave function would decrease exponentially with an attenuation factor \(\lambda\) (which is essentially the inverse of the decay time) satisfying the equation,

\[
\lambda = D \exp\left\{ -\frac{2\pi\sqrt{2m}}{h} \int_{r_1}^{r_2} \sqrt{U - E} \, dr \right\} \tag{592}
\]

(with \(D\) a characteristic constant). An explicit evaluation of the integral yielded for \(\log \lambda\) roughly the simple relation,

\[
\log \lambda = \text{const.} + bE, \tag{593}
\]

where \(b\) represented a parameter common to all members of a given radioactive family. Evidently, Eq. (593) represented the well-known empirical Geiger–Nuttall rule, relating the range of \(\alpha\)-particles and the decay time. A rough theoretical estimate yielded \(b\) in the case of the uranium family,

\[
b_{\text{theor}} = 0.7 \times 10^7, \tag{594}
\]

as compared with the evaluation of experimental data according to Eq. (593),

\[
b_{\text{exp}} = 1.02 \times 10^7. \tag{594'}
\]

Gamow cautiously concluded:

> The agreement of the order of magnitude shows that the fundamental assumption of the theory might be correct. According to our theory there must be some deviations from the linear law [(593)]: with increasing \(E\) the quantity \(b\) should decrease, i.e., \(\log E\) must decrease a little more slowly than \(E\). (Gamow, *loc. cit.*, p. 212)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0674 -->

642 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

Indeed, some earlier observations in the case of RaC' (where the energy of the \(\alpha\)-radiation is very large) appeared to confirm this conclusion.
Gamow dated his paper 29 July 1928. The very next day, on 30 July, Ronald W. Gurney and Edward U. Condon from Princeton wrote a letter to *Nature*, in which they basically proposed the same explanation for \(\alpha\)-decay (Gurney and Condon, 1928). Then, on 28 November, they sent their complete paper, ‘Quantum Mechanics and Radioactive Disintegration,’ giving the details of their calculations to *Physical Review* (Gurney and Condon, 1929).\({}^{765}\) Gurney and Condon referred to the original idea of Friedrich Hund (1927c), as well as to its later application by Oppenheimer (1928a) and Fowler and Nordheim (1928), and then sketched the solution of the one-dimensional problem with one potential barrier \(U\), yielding the formula for the decay time,

\[
T = \frac{1}{\lambda} \sim a \sqrt{\frac{m}{2E}} \exp\left\{ \frac{4\pi}{h} \int \sqrt{2m(U - E)} \, dx \right\}. \tag{595}
\]

By assuming a reasonable qualitative behaviour of the potential \(U\) as a function of \(x\), they arrived at a satisfactory description of the empirical data and concluded:

> It was already clear that we should obtain for all elements some qualitative agreement with the Geiger-Nuttal relation: the higher the energy of the alpha-particle the greater the rapidity of the decay. But now we have found the unexpected result [from Eq. (595)] that the agreement is almost quantitative; that we do not have to choose a different potential energy inside the nucleus for each alpha-particle but having taken one potential curve for the whole series, it is the energy of the emitted alpha-particle which determines its own rate of decay. (Gurney and Condon, 1929, p. 136)

However, after having claimed that the new theory should apply as well to the \(\beta\)-decay, Gurney and Condon also mentioned possible limitations, because ‘the internal part [of the potential] is merely intended to represent the potential energy of a particular alpha-particle’ and ‘it must not be taken to represent a general central field common to many particles, such as we are accustomed to in atomic structure’ (Gurney and Condon, *loc. cit.*, p. 139).
Gamow did not take the appearance of the competing note (Gurney and Condon, 1928) too seriously. He immediately wrote a letter to *Nature* hinting at his previous work (Gamow, 1928b). He further presented, together with Fritz Houtermans, his theory in an improved version, submitted again to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Gamow and Houtermans, 1928). Two weeks after their submission, on 20 November 1928, the same journal received a ‘*Notiz zur Quantentheorie des Atom-*

---

III.7 Aspects of Nuclear and ‘High-Energy’ Phenomena 643

kerns’ (‘Note on the Quantum Theory of the Atomic Nucleus’), which the author, Max von Laue, introduced by saying:

> The quantum theory of atomic nuclei, as has been sketched by Gurney and Condon [1928] and carried out by Gamow [1928a] makes the first bridge from the physics of the electron shell of the atoms to the physics of the nucleus. The fundamental idea that wave mechanics admits in principle to surpass even the highest potential barriers appears so evident, and the derivation of the so far totally mysterious Geiger-Nuttal relation comes out so convincingly that one can count these papers among the most beautiful successes of the more recent physics. (von Laue, 1928, p. 727)

Because von Laue found the mathematics in Gamow’s paper to be ‘not totally correct,’ he went on to improve it at certain points. In particular, he repeated the calculation both in the case of one single square-well barrier and for the slightly modified, more realistic, model of the nuclear potential, consisting of a rectangular pit (with negative potential \(U''\) of length \(2q_0\)) to which square-well barriers (of height \(U_0 = U' - U''\) and width \(l\)) are added on the two sides. In the latter case, von Laue studied the scattering of waves in the following six regions: I (left of the first barrier), II (first barrier), III (left half of the pit), III' (right half of the pit), II' (second barrier), and I' (right of the second barrier).\({}^{766}\) The most crucial point in obtaining the scattering wave was represented by the centre of the pit; Gamow had joined these two solutions of the Schrödinger equation by assuming complex energy values, Eq. (589), and claimed that this could be done consistently by introducing two constants, particularly \(\lambda\) (Eq. 590) and a phase difference between the outgoing waves I and I'. ‘These limiting conditions must be satisfied *identically in time t*,’ von Laue now insisted, and added: ‘It would be strange if two quantities which are independent of time did accomplish this’ (von Laue, *loc. cit.*, p. 728). He then showed that one actually needed four such conditions. As a result a different relation followed for the quantity \(\lambda\), namely, for large values of \(k'l\),

\[
\lambda = \frac{8}{a} \frac{E^{3/2}}{(2m)^{1/2}} \frac{U_0 - E}{U_0^2} \exp\left( -\frac{4\pi}{h} \sqrt{2m(U' - E)l} \right), \tag{596}
\]

with \(a = 2q_0 - l\).
As the principal trick to derive Eq. (596), von Laue introduced two additional walls at a large distance \(L\) from the nuclear potential, which had the task of reflecting the outgoing spherical waves (in a more realistic three-dimensional model), thus avoiding the difficulties with boundary conditions at infinity. The physical process considered now was this: a wave of intensity \(I_0\) enters at a time \(t = 0\) from the left, passes through the nucleus of diameter \(a\) in the period of time \(\tau\), is reflected at the barrier on the right with intensity \(RI_0\), then returns to the left, and is reflected at the left barrier obtaining the intensity \(I_0 R^2\). By repeating the whole

---
\({}^{766}\) von Laue's calculations always employed one-dimensional models.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0676 -->

644 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

process again and again, the intensity of the wave can be written as a function of time

\[
I = I_0 \exp(-\lambda t), \quad \text{with} \quad \lambda = \frac{\log R}{\tau} \approx \frac{G}{\tau}, \tag{597}
\]

where \(G\) denoted the ‘transparency’ (\(= 1 - R \ll 1\)). The time \(\tau = \frac{a}{w}\), with \(w\) the group velocity of the \(\alpha\)-particles, then just represented the decay time for \(\alpha\)-decay. Hence, Gamow’s \(\lambda\) received a simple visualizable interpretation as the product of transparency \(G\) and the factor \(\frac{1}{\tau}\), which indicated the collision number. Still, von Laue had not yet arrived at his goal, because the result, Eq. (597), could be derived only for small wavelengths, or \(a \gg 2\pi/k\), which was not satisfied in the nuclear case. Upon carrying out the evaluation without the indicated limitation, he confirmed the validity of Eq. (597); thus finally, the two constants in Gamow’s Eq. (593) received a physical interpretation through Eq. (597).\({}^{767}\)
George Gamow, somewhat worried about such mathematical subtleties, proceeded to work out some details of his theory of \(\alpha\)-decay. With Fritz Houtermans, he tried to obtain a more accurate formula for the decay constant.\({}^{768}\) Gamow and Houtermans considered ‘the nucleus as the source of a damped \(\psi\)-wave, and the diminution of the \(\psi\bar{\psi}\)-amount of the \(\alpha\)-particle in the nucleus determining the radioactive decay’ (Gamow and Houtermans, 1928, p. 496). They solved the Schrödinger equation for the wave function \(\chi = \psi/r\) (with \(r\) the radial coordinate), i.e.,

\[
\frac{d^2\chi}{dr^2} + \frac{8\pi^2 m}{h^2} [E - U(r)]\chi = 0, \tag{598}
\]

and obtained the asymptotic solution

\[
\chi_{\infty} = A \exp\left( -\frac{\alpha}{2} ir \right) + B \exp\left( +\frac{\alpha}{2} ir \right), \tag{599}
\]

(596). Further, Theodor Sexl of Vienna got involved in the problem and worked out a quantitative, first-order solution of the problem of \(\alpha\)-decay (Sexl, 1929, and other papers by him). Finally, Ralph Fowler and Alan Wilson studied a resonance effect that should occur when \(\alpha\)-particles penetrate into atomic nuclei (Fowler and Wilson, 1929)
\({}^{768}\) Friedrich Georg Houtermans was born in Zappert near Danzig on 22 January 1903, as the son of a bank director; he grew up in Vienna, the hometown of his mother (who held a doctorate in chemistry from the University of Vienna). In 1921, he started his studies in Göttingen, but he had to interrupt to earn his living as a tourist guide in Rome. He completed his doctorate under James Franck in 1927 with a thesis on the resonance fluorescence of mercury. Then, he became interested in quantum mechanics and atomic and nuclear theory and entered into a collaboration with the Russian visitor Gamow in Göttingen.

where  

$$
\alpha = \frac{4\pi\sqrt{2mE}}{h} = \frac{4\pi mv}{h} . \tag{599a}
$$  

(*E*, *m*, *v* denoted the energy, mass, and velocity of the *α*-particle, *U* the nuclear potential.) The runaway solution, namely, *B* = 0, then exhibits a damping factor *λ*, which was calculated with the help of the conservation law for the quantity $\int \psi \bar{\psi} \, d\Omega$ and given by the equation  

$$
\lambda = \frac{h\alpha^2}{4\pi m} \left[ \int_0^{R\alpha} \chi(\rho) \bar{\chi}(\rho) \, d\rho \right]^{-1} , \tag{600}
$$  

with $\rho = \alpha r$. Here, *R* assumed the order of magnitude of the nuclear radius (i.e., about $10^{-12}$ cm), and the integral $\int \chi(\rho) \bar{\chi}(\rho) \, d\rho$ depended on the potential law *U*(*r*), which was taken to be Coulomb-like for larger distances (outside the atomic nucleus) and attractive for small distances (within the nucleus), or  

$$
U(r) = \frac{4Z^* e^2 \alpha}{\rho} - \frac{\beta}{\rho^n} , \tag{601}
$$  

where $Z^* = Z - 2$ denoted the effective nuclear charge, *β* and *n* being constants. Thus, Gamow and Houtermans eventually derived the relation  

$$
\log \lambda = \log \frac{64\pi^2 m^2 e^2}{h^2} + \log Z^* v + 2 \log \tan u_0 - \frac{8\pi e^2}{h} \frac{Z^*}{v} (2u_0 - \sin 2u_0) , \tag{602}
$$  

with  

$$
\cos u_0 = \frac{v}{\sqrt{Z^*}} \frac{1}{2e} \sqrt{m r_0} . \tag{602a}
$$  

(Here *r*₀ was the minimum distance from the centre of the nucleus, where the potential *U* could still be considered coulombic.) Eq. (602) explained to some extent the deviation of the experimental data from the original Geiger–Nuttall rule, although some difference still remained between theory and experiment, which Gamow and Houtermans explained as arising from some coarse assumptions made in their calculation.<sup>769</sup>

of *α*-particle physics, namely, ‘the quantum theory of smashing atoms’ or the description of the destruction of atomic nuclei when colliding with high-energy *α*-particles (see Gamow, ‘*Zur Quantentheorie der Atomzerstrümmerung*,’ 1928c). The experiments in Cambridge and Vienna had demonstrated indeed that the lighter nuclei could thus be transformed, a fact that now appeared theoretically quite probable on account of the possibility of an *α*-particle penetrating through the barrier of a nuclear potential. For making explicit calculations, Gamow assumed an appropriate potential of the form given by Eq. (601), determining *r_m* (i.e., the position of the maximum) from experiment (*r_m* became proportional to the third root of the atomic mass *A*). Then, he found the probability *W*₁ for smashing atoms (in the equivalent of 1 cm of air) to be given by the expression  

$$
W_1 = N \pi r_m^2 \exp \left\{ - \frac{16 e^2}{h} \frac{Z}{v_{\text{eff}}} J(k) \right\} , \tag{603}
$$  

where *Ze* was the atomic charge, *v*<sub>eff</sub> the effective velocity of *α*-particles *versus* the atomic nucleus, and *J*(*k*) denoted a function of the wavenumber *k*, which was defined as  

$$
k = \frac{m}{4\sqrt{3} e^2} \frac{r_m v_{\text{eff}}}{Z} . \tag{603a}
$$  

The experimental data obtained thus far (by Rutherford and collaborators, as well as by Walther Bothe and H. Fränz at the *Physikalisch-Technische Reichsanstalt* in Berlin) appeared to be quite consistent with Eq. (603), though not in all details.<sup>770</sup>  

Also, Fritz Houtermans, who moved in fall 1928 to Berlin (to join the *Technische Hochschule*), derived further consequences from Gamow’s theory, when he explored together with R. d’E. Atkinson the idea that in stars the elements heavier than hydrogen and helium (considered to exist already at an early stage) can be built up from protons penetrating into lighter nuclei (Atkinson and Houtermans, 1929). They chose the special nuclear potential  

$$
U(r) = \frac{Ze^2}{r} - \frac{a}{r^3} , \tag{604}
$$  

and calculated the probability for a proton (having the velocity *v*) to penetrate into the nucleus the simple expression  

$$
w_1 = \exp \left( - \frac{4\pi e^2 Z}{h v} \right) , \tag{605}
$$  

<sup>770</sup> Thus, the assumption of an angle-independent emission of protons from the collisions assumed by Gamow contradicted the experimental observations (see Gamow, 1928c, p. 515). One should note further that *W*₁, Eq. (603), did not describe the actual probability of the smashing, but rather the probability of the *α*-particles to penetrate into the nuclei; it still had to be multiplied by the probability *W*₂ that the nucleus becomes transmuted by emitting a proton.

\xi = \left( \frac{2\pi^2 e Z}{h v_0} \right)^{1/3} , \tag{606a}
$$  

where *v*₀ = 2*kT*/*m*. Although *w̄*₁ assumed for lead the very small value of $10^{-79}$, it went up quickly to $6.7 \times 10^{-24}$ for Ne$^{20}$, $6.2 \times 10^{-17}$ for C$^{12}$, $9.7 \times 10^{-11}$ for Li$^{6}$, and finally $2.7 \times 10^{-8}$ for He$^{4}$; that is, lighter elements would possess quite short lifetimes (of the order of seconds or minutes) under suitable conditions in stars. In the case of *α*-particles as projectiles, the *ξ* in Eq. (606) had to be multiplied by a factor of 2.5, which would already make the penetration of *α*-particles into lithium nuclei extremely improbable. On the other hand, Atkinson and Houtermans pointed out that the penetration of protons and electrons in nuclei might create *α*-particles in them, which serves as a powerful source of energy in stars as it sets free the large ‘packing energy’ of helium nuclei.<sup>771</sup> Though a number of difficulties remained—e.g., to arrive at the very heavy, say, radioactive, nuclei when the colliding particles have a Maxwellian distribution—Atkinson and Houtermans were confident to have brought the central problems of the energy production in stars, and their evolution in time, closer to a solution on the basis of the new quantum-mechanical theory of nuclei.  

Gamow, whom Atkinson and Houtermans thanked for fruitful discussions, presented in May 1929 (at the Conference on Theoretical Physics held at Kharkov) a new model of atomic nuclei, which he considered to consist mainly of an agglomeration of *α*-particles held together by a surface tension (compensating the inner pressure arising from the motion of the *α*-particles and other nuclear constituents) into the form of droplets (Gamow, 1929b).<sup>772</sup> He worked out the details of this model in a paper on ‘Mass Defect Curve and Nuclear Constitution,’ which Ernest Rutherford communicated to the *Proceedings of the Royal Society of London* in January 1930 from Cambridge, where Gamow spent some time on a  

<sup>771</sup> The six particles, four protons and two electrons forming the *α*-particle, could—according to that view—accumulate in nuclei; hence, no collisions of six free particles (which are extremely improbable) need to be involved.  

<sup>772</sup> Gamow sketched the *α*-particle model of nuclei already at the Royal Society discussion in February 1929 (see Rutherford *et al.*, 1929, especially, p. 386). In another note of spring 1929, a letter to *Nature*, Gamow discussed the consequence that his *α*-decay theory explained an observation in radioactive transformation series: the successive *α*-particles are shot forth with ever-increasing energy (Gamow, 1929a).

Rockefeller Foundation Fellowship (Gamow, 1930). In particular, he wrote there a formula for the energy of an atomic nucleus, consisting of two parts: the energy of the nuclear droplet *E*<sub>a</sub> and the Coulomb energy *E*<sub>r</sub> of the charged sphere (also represented by the nucleus), i.e.,  

$$
E = E_a + E_r \sim \frac{h^2}{4m R_0^2} N_a^{1/3} + \frac{(2e)^2}{R_0} N_a^{5/3} . \tag{607}
$$  

Here, *N*<sub>a</sub> denoted the number of *α*-particles in the nucleus (with *R*₀ a constant coefficient). Although Eq. (607) ‘fits more or less with the experimental points in the region of light elements’ (Gamow, *loc. cit.*, p. 637), it deviated considerably for heavier nuclei; hence Gamow suggested that the electrons in nuclei might cause the discrepancies and outlined an approximate scheme to explain the situation. Although such ideas would be abandoned after 1932, the *α*-particle aspect and the liquid-drop model derived from it remained a useful theoretical tool to understand atomic nuclei.<sup>773</sup>  

#### (c) The Difficulties with Electrons in Nuclei (1928–1932)  

To the ‘*Convegno di Fisica Nucleare*,’ held in Rome in October 1931, Niels Bohr contributed a few remarks that he later elaborated on for the proceedings of the congress under the title ‘Atomic Stability and Conservation Laws’ (Bohr, 1932b). After sketching (in Section 1) the great success of the quantum-mechanical theory of atoms, he addressed (in Section 2) the ‘Difficulties of Relativistic Quantum Mechanics,’ which were contained in Dirac’s electron theory (especially the negative-energy states) and showed up in the Klein–Nishina formula for the Compton effect and Klein’s paradox.<sup>774</sup> While these difficulties evidently did not play a role in atomic structure, they seemed to influence crucially the behaviour of electrons in atomic nuclei (Section 3). In particular, Bohr stated:  

> The experimental evidence regarding the charges and masses of atomic nuclei and their disintegration finds, as is well known, an immediate explanation on the view that all nuclei are built up of protons and electrons. The extent, to which these nuclear structures can be treated as independent mechanical entities is, however, far more limited than the possibility of considering the nuclei and electrons as separate particles in ordinary problems of atomic constitution. This point is most strikingly  

<sup>773</sup> In 1930, the first review on ‘*Neuere Arbeiten über Quantentheorie des Atomkerns*’ (‘Recent Works on the Quantum Theory of the Atomic Nucleus’) appeared in *Ergebnisse der exakten Naturwissenschaften*, written by Fritz Houtermans (1930). In this comprehensive account, the *α*-particle theory of Gamow constituted the central part. See, in particular, Houtermans’s discussion of *α*-decay in Chapters IV to VII—including also additional references to the work of Christian Møller (1929), which took into account relativistic effects in Gamow’s theory; he also discussed the detailed comparison of theory and experiment in Chapter VIII.  

<sup>774</sup> We have treated these questions in Section II.7 in some detail.

III.7 Aspects of Nuclear and ‘High-Energy’ Phenomena 649

exhibited by the failure of the fundamental quantum-mechanical rules of statistics when applied to nuclei. In fact, according to experimental evidence, the statistics of an ensemble of identical particles is determined solely by the number of protons contained in each nucleus, while the intra-nuclear electrons show in this respect a remarkable passivity, contrasting with the exclusion principle.
From the preceding remarks it will be also clear that a treatment of the intra-nuclear electronic constitution is far beyond the reach of present atomic mechanics. . . . Indeed, in the problem of the electronic constitution of nuclei, we are faced with entirely new aspects of atomic stability, and our only reliable guidance is so far afforded by the conservation of and the atomicity of electric charge. In this situation, we are led to consider the capture or the expulsion of an electron by a nucleus plainly as an extinction or creation, respectively, of the electron as a mechanical entity. We cannot therefore be surprised if these processes should be found not to obey such principles as the conservation laws of energy and momentum, the formulation of which is essentially based on the idea of material particles. (Bohr, *loc. cit.*, pp. 127–128)

The *idée fixe* of the breakdown of conservation laws expressed here had accompanied Bohr already for nearly ten years, and it had crucially entered into the formulation of the Bohr–Kramers–Slater radiation theory of 1924.775 It came up again in 1929, when Bohr, in a letter to Pauli, wrote about sending him two notes, one on the magnetic electron, and added:

> The other little piece about the $\beta$-ray spectra, which I have had in mind for a long time, and which has now been typed in the last few days, but I have not yet made up my mind to send it off, since it yields so few positive results and has been written very sketchily. (Bohr to Pauli, 1 July 1929; in Pauli, 1979, p. 507; English translation in Bohr, 1986, p. 5)

In the note (of which an incomplete copy still exists in the Bohr Archives), Bohr mentioned the failure to describe the experimental $\beta$-decay spectra by the usual quantum mechanics, and then drew attention to an idea of his associate Oskar Klein, claiming that ‘the conception of force is inherently bound up with the idea of mass’; hence, ‘the suggestion presents itself that the laws of interaction between particles of different mass may conflict with the simple identification of action and reaction, as that underlying the classical conservation principles.’ Consequently:

> While the quantum laws of propagation in free space offer no basis for a violation of the conservation principles, a departure from the laws might still result from the close interaction of the constituent particles of the nucleus. [Hence] we may be prepared for a disturbance of the energy balance also in certain large scale phenomena. . . . Perhaps in considerations of that kind we can find an explanation of the energy source which according to present astrophysical theory is wanting in the sun, and the origin of what is generally thought in the transformation of electric particles into radiation. (Bohr, 1986, p. 88)

775 See, especially, Volume 1, Part 2, Section V.2.

650 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

Wolfgang Pauli, the firm opponent of the violation of conservation laws since 1924 (when Bohr first broached it), was ‘little satisfied’ by the content of Bohr’s new tone and criticized it harshly. ‘In Zurich, Miss Meitner gave us a beautiful lecture about the experimental aspects of the question, and she *almost* convinced me that the continuous $\beta$-ray spectrum *cannot* be explained by secondary processes ($\gamma$-ray emission, etc.),’ he wrote back to Bohr and added:

> So we really *don’t* know what is the matter. You don’t know either. . . . In any case let this note rest for a good long time and let the stars shine in peace. (Pauli to Bohr, 17 July 1929; in Pauli, 1979, p. 513; English translation in Bohr, 1986, p. 6)

Bohr did not publish his note as he had had in mind, yet he continued to ponder about the continuous $\beta$-decay and conservation laws for several years.776
By the middle of December 1929, Lise Meitner and Wilhelm Orthmann submitted a decisive report, ‘*Über eine absolute Bestimmung der Energie der primären $\beta$-Strahlen von Radium E*’ (‘On an Absolute Determination of the Energy of Primary $\beta$-rays from Radium E’) to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Meitner and Orthmann, 1930). By using Orthmann’s calorimeter, especially designed ‘to measure the absolute value of small amounts of the heat produced without employing a needle galvanometer very sensitive to electric potentials, which is mostly unsuitable because of magnetic disturbances’ (Orthmann, 1930, p. 137), Meitner and Orthmann determined directly the energy of primary $\beta$-rays emitted from a source ‘whose radium equivalent, i.e., the number of decaying atoms per second, was obtained by a special investigation’ (Meitner and Orthmann, 1930, p. 143). They further demonstrated that their substance, radium E, ‘does not possess any continuous $\gamma$-ray spectrum within a large range of wavelengths.’ After this careful preparation of the methods, and the similar execution of the experimental determination, the following results were found: While the most probable average value for a $\beta$-particle measured (i.e., about 337,000 volts) agreed with the observation of Ellis and Wooster (1927b), the new experiment demonstrated beyond a doubt that:

> Since the magnetic spectrum of $\beta$-rays extends over an energy region of roughly from million volts down to 200,000 volts, and the energy derived from the heat measurements does not correspond to the maximal velocity but to a much smaller one, the primary $\beta$-rays must emerge from the atomic nuclei already with a continuous energy spectrum. Hence the assumption of Ellis is confirmed that the $\beta$-ray decay is not characterized by a definite value of the $\beta$-ray energy. (Meitner and Orthmann, 1930, p. 154)

776 See, e.g., the discussion at the Rome conference reported above, and his earlier correspondence with Paul Dirac. Dirac had learned about Bohr’s ideas through a talk of Gamow (who had visited Cambridge from Copenhagen) at the Kapitza Club; in a letter to Bohr, dated 26 November 1929, he wrote back that he preferred ‘to keep rigorous conservation of energy at all costs and would rather abandon even the concept of matter consisting of separate atoms and electrons than [violate] the conservation of energy’ (Dirac, in Bohr, 1986, p. 548). For the moment, Dirac proposed to explain the $\beta$-spectra on the basis of his new hole theory of relativistic electrons.

III.7 Aspects of Nuclear and ‘High-Energy’ Phenomena 651

As a consequence of the Meitner–Orthmann experiment, the following picture of nuclear constitution prevailed in the beginning of the 1930s. The atomic nucleus consisted of protons and electrons, forming as many $\alpha$-particles as possible and determining its mass and stability according to the conventional rules of quantum mechanics. However, the electrons in the nucleus exhibited a very strange behaviour inconsistent with any theory: their magnetic moments did not show up (as no Bohr magneton was observed at all), and they did not satisfy energy conservation when leaving the nucleus (in contrast to protons and $\alpha$-particles). The recent explanation of the continuous $\beta$-spectra by Heisenberg and Pauli (1929, pp. 60–61) as being due to a retardation effect also failed because then a continuous $\gamma$-spectrum should have been observed.777 Pauli now became the scientist and the theoretician most concerned about the unsatisfactory situation in nuclear physics. Previously, he had argued that the energy-determining experiments were ‘cheating’ (Pauli to Klein, 18 February 1929)—i.e., they did not take into account any possible contribution from $\gamma$-rays (Pauli to Bohr, 25 April 1929; Pauli to Ehrenfest, 15 May 1929)—and the experimentalist Lise Meitner had supported him enthusiastically. Now, in early 1930, Pauli became—again supported by Meitner’s experimentalist expertise—quite desperate, and he wrote to Oskar Klein: ‘In the present state of the theory, it seems to me quite impossible that anybody’s thoughts about $\beta$-spectra could have been clarified.’ (Pauli to Klein, 10 February 1930, in Pauli, 1985, p. 4)
The following months of that year turned out to be quite turbulent for Wolfgang Pauli. In late 1929, he had married Käthe Deppner, and then he spent a very busy time (mostly without his wife) travelling to Leyden, Copenhagen, and Como in spring, to the Soviet Union in summer, and to Brussels (to attend the sixth Solvay Conference) in fall; on 23 December 1930, exactly one year after it had taken place, his marriage was dissolved. Already three weeks earlier, Pauli had hit upon a new idea as to how to proceed with the $\beta$-decay difficulty: he proposed the existence of a new particle, which he called the ‘neutron.’778 Pauli wrote the details of his conception in an ‘Open Letter to the Group of Radioactive People Assembled at the *Gauvereinstagung* [of the German Physical Society] in Tübingen’:

> Because of the “wrong” statistics of N- and $\mathrm{Li}^6$-nuclei and the continuous $\beta$-spectrum, I have arrived at the desperate way out to rescue the “alternation rule” of statistics and energy conservation: namely, the possibility that there might exist elec—

777 Kudar (1931) criticized the suggestion of Heisenberg and Pauli from a purely theoretical point of view, as one could not understand how a retardation effect should influence an electron when passing through the static potential of a nucleus. He rather proposed a new law of force (including centrifugal forces) and a second-order relativistic equation to describe the behaviour of electrons in a nucleus (Kudar, 1931, pp. 35–37).
778 The first mention of the new object occurred in a letter to Pauli, dated 1 December 1930; in this letter, Heisenberg mentioned (evidently in response to a lost letter of Pauli): ‘I wish to make a remark on your neutrons: nuclei with even number of electrons and “wrong” statistics should also show up; these have not yet been observed. But perhaps the empirical data is not yet sufficient.’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, in Pauli, 1985, p. 37)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0684 -->

652 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

trically neutral particles, which I call neutrons, in the nuclei; they have spin 1/2 and obey the exclusion principle, and will—in addition—be distinguished from the light-quanta by not moving with the speed of light. The mass of neutrons should be of the order of magnitude of the electron mass and certainly not larger than 0.01 proton mass.—The continuous $\beta$-spectrum could then be understood under the assumption that in $\beta$-decay a neutron will always be emitted with the electron, such that the sum of the energies of neutron and electron becomes constant. (Pauli to Geiger and Meitner, 4 December 1930; in Pauli, 1985, p. 39)

What had convinced Pauli to try what he called ‘the desperate way out’?
By 1930, two methods for determining nuclear spins had become available: these were the intensity measurements of molecular band spectra and the determination of the hyperfine structure of atomic spectral lines. The story of the quantum-mechanical description of both of these phenomena had started with a theoretical observation reported by Heisenberg to Pauli in November 1926:

> Recently I have pondered about the change in intensity of band spectra according to resonance considerations and found out what it should be. . . . For two equal nuclei . . . the entire term spectrum separates into two groups of terms: *symmetrical* total eigenfunctions and *antisymmetrical* total eigenfunctions. . . . If both nuclei are really equal, according to Pauli there should be no first [i.e., symmetrical] group (see, e.g., for helium bands). . . . The occurrence of the symmetrical group . . . may happen in the case of two apparently identical nuclei because of two reasons: 1. Isotopes [representing different nuclei of the same element] . . . 2. The nuclei have angular momentum [spin]! In that case, the intensity ratio will be about the same as for ortho- and para-helium, namely 3:1, that is, like the ratio of statistical weights. This seems to be realized, for instance, for nitrogen. Hence [it provides] a new method for finding nuclear spin or isotopes, respectively. (Heisenberg to Pauli, 15 November 1926; in Pauli, 1979, pp. 355–356)

As we have mentioned earlier (in Section III.5), Heisenberg’s considerations were stimulated in fall 1926 by Friedrich Hund’s treatment of molecular theory, leading to the definite proposal of nuclear spin (Hund, 1927c, p. 112).
Now, Hund’s publication led Ralph Kronig in Utrecht to analyze in April 1928 certain results on the band spectra of nitrogen that had emerged from Leonard Ornstein’s spectroscopic laboratory on the band spectra of nitrogen (Kronig, 1928b). The $N_2$-band spectra indeed showed an ‘intensity change’ (‘*Intensitätswechsel*’), as predicted by Heisenberg. Kronig argued that ‘This behaviour of the statistical weights indicates, according to Hund, that to the nuclei there must be ascribed an angular momentum [spin] $s \frac{h}{2\pi}$,’ and concluded from the data (intensity ratio 2:1) for nitrogen bands that the nucleus $N^{14}$ possessed $s = 1$ (Kronig, 1928b, p. 335). However, he also noticed that the results contradicted the usual concept of the constitution of the nitrogen nucleus, which should consist of twenty-one Fermi particles (i.e., fourteen protons and seven electrons); hence, a spin $s = 1/2$ and a magnetic moment of the order of 1 Bohr magneton resulted, in

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0685 -->

III.7  Aspects of Nuclear and ‘High-Energy’ Phenomena                                                                    653

contrast to the Utrecht observations. In spite of the clear hint given there, Kronig’s note did not really alarm anybody, but on 28 July 1929 (after more than a year), Walter Heitler and Gerhard Herzberg wrote another letter to *Naturwissenschaften* with the title ‘*Gehorchen die Stickstoffkerne der Boseschen Statistik?*’ (‘Do Nitrogen Nuclei Obey Bose Statistics?’) (Heitler and Herzberg, 1929b). Heitler and Herzberg based their analysis on a different observation with N$_2$-molecules, namely, the recently obtained Raman spectrum (Rasetti, 1929), which yielded a symmetric total eigenfunction (orbital and spin parts); hence, nitrogen nuclei definitely obeyed Bose statistics.$^{779}$ Evidently, the electron lost its spin property when it became a nuclear electron, or as Heitler and Herzberg said: ‘The mechanical properties of electrons in the nucleus become modified much more fundamentally than those of protons and $\alpha$-particles; only their charge certainly remains conserved.’ (Heitler and Herzberg, 1929b, p. 674) In a further letter to *Naturwissenschaften*, dated 15 January 1930, Kronig emphasized that the anomalous behaviour of nitrogen nuclei, as revealed by band spectra, could not be ascribed to an isotope effect (Kronig, 1930).

The other determination of nuclear angular momenta arose from the detailed observation of what was called the ‘hyperfine structure’ of atomic lines. In early 1924, Hantaro Nagaoka, Yoshikatsu Sugiura, and T. Mishima wrote a note to *Nature* on ‘the accurate measurements of the position of satellites of mercury and bismuth lines,’ especially the ultraviolet ones, revealing a very complex structure; they associated these lines with nuclear vibrations that should cause an isotope effect (Nagaoka *et al.*, 1924). In August of the same year, Pauli became interested in this topic and composed a long communication for the *Naturwissenschaften*, entitled ‘*Zur Frage der theoretischen Deutung der Satelliten einiger Spectrallinien und ihrer Beeinflussung durch magnetische Felder*’ (‘On the Problem of the Theoretical Interpretation of Satellites of Some Spectral Lines and the Influence on Them of Magnetic Fields’), in which he explained the Japanese results as follows:

> Though we do not claim that the specific conceptions and particular views of these authors on the connection of the satellites with the different isotopes of an element, as well as their formal representation of the distances of certain satellites, are sufficiently [well-] founded, we wish to take over here the idea of Nagaoka and his collaborators into the general formulation that the satellites arise because of the composition of the nuclei and the deviation of the nuclear field of force from the Coulomb field. Moreover, as the only special assumption concerning nuclear structure to be introduced here, we assume that the nucleus possesses (apart from specific exceptional cases) a non-vanishing angular momentum. (Pauli, 1924c, pp. 741–742)

Both the nuclear system and the system of external electrons of an atom would take on quantized positions with respect to each other, Pauli noted, and continued: ‘The splitting of the spectral lines in satellites would then result energetically

through the *difference in interaction* energy between nuclear and external electrons in these different orientations.’ (Pauli, *loc. cit.*, p. 742)

Although the available data of the Japanese and some Tübingen experimentalists (who especially investigated the influence of magnetic fields on the satellites) seemed to agree with his interpretation, Pauli called his publication ‘my crazy satellite note’ (in a letter to Sommerfeld, dated 29 September 1924). The experimental work on satellites went on: thus, Hermann Schüler of Tübingen examined what he entitled ‘The Fine Structures of the First Lithium Arc Spectrum’ and detected many lines, which he could not connect with the usual multiplets; hence, he concluded: ‘Our present concepts on the atomic model, a positive nucleus and two electrons, do not yield any information about the unexpected manifold fine structure, and in attempts at the interpretation the idea forces itself upon us whether these phenomena arise immediately from nuclear structure.’ (Schüler, 1925, p. 297)$^{780}$ That is, besides the spectra of heavy elements, the arc spectra of light- and medium-light atoms provided further insight into the specific phenomenon. Thus, Derek Ainstlie Jackson of Oxford University explored the ‘Hyperfine Structure in the Arc Spectrum of Caesium and Nuclear Rotation’ (Jackson, 1928). He observed closed doublets and worked out a theory to explain their origin, ‘assuming a nuclear spin of one-half quantum’ and:

> By correlating the difference in the separation of the hyperfine structure doublets in the $1s – mp_{3/2}$ lines and the $1s – mp_{1/2}$ lines, it is shown that a ratio of the magnetic to the mechanical moment of the nucleus is about twice as large as the corresponding ratio for the electron would account for the observed frequency differences. . . .
> The results are compared with those found for the hyperfine structure of some of the bismuth lines by Back and Goudsmit, and are found to be in satisfactory agreement. A selection principle is found which applies both to the bismuth and caesium spectrum. (Jackson, *loc. cit.*, p. 433)

Already in 1927, Samuel Goudsmit and Ernst Back had confirmed the hypothesis of Pauli and Schüler that the nuclear properties, especially the nuclear spin, created the hyperfine splitting of atomic spectra (Goudsmit and Back, 1927; Back and Goudsmit, 1928). J. Hargreaves of Clare College, Cambridge, supported by Ralph Fowler and Paul Dirac, then attacked the quantum-mechanical calculation of the effect: he worked out in detail the case of a single electron in a Coulomb field created by a nucleus possessing one-half quantum spin and extended the

$^{780}$ It may be worth mentioning that, in contrast to Schüler’s observation, Pauli had earlier claimed that the satellites only occur for substances having high atomic numbers (close to those of radioactive substances).

Hermann Schüler, born on 24 July 1894, in Posen, arrived in Tübingen in 1920 and became, beginning in 1924, a leading expert on hyperfine structure. From 1924 to 1937, he worked at the Potsdam *Institut für Sonnenphysik* (‘*Einstein*turm’), and then joined the *Kaiser Wilhelm-Institut für Physik* in Berlin-Dahlem, moving to Hechingen toward the end of World War II. In 1950, he got his own *Forschungsstelle für Spektroskopie* of the *Max Planck-Gesellschaft* in Hechingen and was appointed a Scientific Member of the *Max Planck-Gesellschaft* (*Wissenschaftliches Mitglied*). He died on 5 July 1964, in Göttingen.

treatment to the case of any central field, which would include in principle any atom with nuclear spin $\frac{1}{2}(nh/2\pi)$ (Hargreaves, 1929; 1930a, b).

In a letter to *Nature*, dated 4 December 1929, Enrico Fermi announced ‘a more systematic and complete approach to the same problem, also removing a limitation of Hargreaves,’ who had ‘neglected the interaction between electronic and nuclear spins, which is of the same order of magnitude as the other terms’ (Fermi, 1930a, p. 16). He further announced:

> For the *s*-terms, which is the most important case, since they make the largest contribution to the separation, I have used Dirac’s theory of the electron, since the simpler Pauli theory gives a wrong result. For the *p*-terms, I have used Pauli’s method, taking into account the interaction of nuclear and electron spins. For the *p*-terms, it is not necessary to evaluate the eigenfunctions numerically, since the constants involved in the formulae can be derived from empirical data on the separation of the electronic spin doublets. For the *s*-terms, this method is of course impossible, and I have calculated the eigenfunctions by the statistical method. (Fermi, *loc. cit.*)

Fermi thus found the following expression for the two hyperfine structure components of the *s*-term sums $\Delta$,

$$ \Delta = \frac{2I + 1}{I} \frac{8\pi}{3} \mu\mu_0\psi^2(0), \tag{608} $$

where the mechanical momentum and the magnetic moments were given by $Ih/2\pi$ and $\mu$, respectively, and $\mu_0$ denoted Bohr’s magneton.$^{781}$ $\psi(0)$ represented the value of the normalized eigenfunction at the origin. For the splitting of the *p*-terms, Fermi derived

$$ \Delta = 146 \frac{\mu}{\mu_0} \frac{2I + 1}{I} \quad \text{for calcium,} \tag{609a} $$

$$ \Delta = 13.4 \frac{\mu}{\mu_0} \frac{2I + 1}{I} \quad \text{for sodium.} \tag{609b} $$

The comparison with observation suffered somewhat from the lack of precision of the data and the application of the statistical method to evaluate the eigenfunction $\psi(0)$—the latter amounted to errors within 20 to 30 percent; still, a value between $I = \frac{1}{2}$ and $I = 1$ seemed to follow. Fermi presented the details of his theory and certain improvements in two memoirs submitted in December and January to *Zeitschrift für Physik* and the *Memorie dell’Accademia d’Italia*, respectively (Fermi 1930b, c). Now, however, he made a consistent application of Dirac’s relativistic

$^{781}$ Actually, Fermi wrote $k$ for $I$ and $\mu_0$ for $\mu$, and $\mu$ for $\mu_0$, but we have adapted to later notations (also used in Fermi’s papers).

$$ \Delta = \frac{2I + 1}{I} \frac{8}{3} \mu\mu_0 \cdot \left\langle \frac{1}{r^3} \right\rangle \tag{610} $$

followed, and a similar expression for the $^2P_{3/2}$-terms. (The last factor denoted the average of the atomic radius, i.e., $\int \frac{1}{r^3} \bar{\psi}\psi \, d\tau$.)

Although Fermi’s theory, which he also presented at the sixth Solvay Conference in October 1930 (Fermi, 1932a), solved the problem of hyperfine structure from the theoretical point of view for atoms having one valence electron, the comparison with data to obtain information about the nuclear moments was not an easy task. Thus, Ralph Kronig and S. Frisch (a spectroscopist from the Optical Institute in Leningrad) listed in their comprehensive review of April 1931 the conclusions for the neutral atoms NaI, RbI, CsI, InI, TlI, and the doubly ionized TlIII, where clearly hyperfine structures had been obtained experimentally (Kronig and Frisch, 1931). After combining this information about nuclear angular momenta $I$ with those derived from the band spectra of diatomic molecules (the ‘alternation rule’ for intensity) and the specific heats (yielding the statistical weights also connected with $I$), they concluded:

> As one can see, in the large majority of cases the rule is valid that $I$ turns out to be integral or half-integral, according as the number of particles (protons and electrons) in the nucleus is even or odd. As exceptions one finds only Li$^6$ with $I = 0$, N$^{14}$ with $I = 1$, K$^{39}$ with $I = 0$ and In with $I = 1$. For Li$^6$ and K$^{39}$, the results are rather insecure, and also for the value of In [with atomic number 115] can still be doubted; however, for N the $I$-value is quite reliable and also the validity of Bose-Einstein statistics has been established. (Kronig and Frisch, *loc. cit.*, p. 471)

Wolfgang Pauli followed both the experimental and the theoretical debate of the nuclear-momentum problem with active interest. In the case of ionized lithium, he asked one of his students to examine theoretically the somewhat contradictory experimental information. Paul Güttinger performed the calculations for Li$^{++}$ (Li III) having only one electron—in which case, he arrived at Fermi’s results for the hyperfine splitting—as well as for Li$^+$ having two electrons (Güttinger, 1930). For the splitting of Li$^+$, he derived,

$$ \Delta = \frac{16\pi}{3} \mu_0 \frac{\mu}{I} \cdot \frac{(\boldsymbol{\sigma} \boldsymbol{j})(\boldsymbol{j} \boldsymbol{I})}{2j^2} \psi_1^2(0) \tag{611} $$

[the round brackets $(\boldsymbol{\sigma} \boldsymbol{j})$, etc., express the scalar products of the two enclosed vector quantities], where $\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ and $\boldsymbol{j}$ denote the spin momentum and the total angular

In a second investigation, Pauli joined Güttinger to improve on certain details of the calculation; especially, they now took into account the nondiagonal terms of ($I\sigma$) with respect to $j$, which had to be retained as the hyperfine structure was not small when compared with the triplet splitting of $\text{Li}^{7+}$ (Güttinger and Pauli, 1931). The calculated values fitted the new data of Hermann Schüler (1930) much better than Güttinger’s previous ones; hence, Güttinger and Pauli declared: ‘We would like to consider, because of the far-reaching agreement between theory and experiment, the value $I = 3/2$ for $\text{Li}^7$ as substantiated.’ (Güttinger and Pauli, 1931, p. 753) Finally, they turned to the situation in the case of the isotope $\text{Li}^6$, in which Schüler had observed not measurable hyperfine structure, or one that was less than 1/5 of that observed for $\text{Li}^7$. ‘It seems to us to be the most probable assumption that $\text{Li}^6$ possesses the momentum $I = 0$,’ Pauli and Güttinger concluded, and added:

> If this conclusion should turn out to be correct, then it would be very important due to the following reason. Starting from the mere assumption that the states of the nucleus can be described at all by eigenfunctions, and that they do not consist of any other elementary particles but electrons and protons, “the alternation theorem” (*Wechselsatz*) follows: nuclei with an odd (even) total number of particles have half-integer (integer) angular momentum and satisfy Fermi (Einstein-Bose) statistics. So far only one exception is known from this rule, namely the $N$-nucleus (odd particle number, but $I = 1$, Bose statistics). $\text{Li}^6$ has also an odd particle number (1 $\alpha$-particle, 2 protons, 1 electron); hence if for this nucleus $I$ were zero, this would be a second exception from the validity of the theorem. (Güttinger and Pauli, *loc. cit.*, p. 754)

In the beginning of December 1930, Pauli thus arrived at the conclusion that the *Wechselsatz* (‘alternation theorem’) was violated in at least two cases; hence, he had to introduce his ‘neutron’—which was later renamed as ‘neutrino’ by Fermi (see Chapter IV below for this story).<sup>782</sup> Kronig and Frisch, on the other hand, closed their review on nuclear momenta by stating the existing difficulties and further remarked: ‘A resolution of these contradictions should not be expected before one obtains a precise knowledge of the fundamental laws governing nuclei.’ (Kronig and Frisch, 1931, p. 471) They had not heard about or did not take seriously Pauli’s new hypothesis, as did not many other colleagues, including of course Niels Bohr, who would do so only in the following two or three years. Even in Zurich, during the *Physikalische Vortragswoche* from 20–24 May 1931, nothing about it was mentioned, and Eugen(e) Guth would remark in a summary report about the important items of concern as follows:

<sup>782</sup> For a derivation of the ‘alternation theorem,’ see Ehrenfest and Oppenheimer’s ‘Note on the Statistics of Nuclei,’ submitted to *Physical Review* (on 23 December 1930). There, the authors proved ‘that the clusters [of elementary particles forming the nuclei] satisfy the Einstein-Bose or Fermi-Dirac statistics according as to whether the number of particles in each cluster [i.e., nucleus] is even or add’ (Ehrenfest and Oppenheimer, 1931, p. 333).

(Bretscher and Guth, 1931, p. 673)

At any rate, at Pauli’s Institute, the theoretical discussions of consequences stemming from hyperfine structure remained a hot topic (see, e.g., Casimir, 1932).

**(d) Nuclear Particle Scattering at Low and High Energies (1928–1932)**

From the very beginning, the scattering of subatomic particles played a decisive role in the development of the young field of nuclear physics. Especially, the concept of the atomic nucleus was developed by Ernest Rutherford in 1911 on the basis of observations of the $\alpha$-particle scattering by atoms. The famous distribution law for the fraction of $\alpha$-particles—$nDI(\theta) d\omega$—scattered in a given direction $\theta$ and the spatial angle $d\omega$, where $I(\theta)$ assumed the form

$$
I(\theta) = \left( \frac{2Ze^2}{2mv^2} \right)^2 \frac{1}{\sin^4 \frac{1}{2}\theta}, \tag{612}
$$

provided the basis for interpreting the scattering data ($n$ denoting the number of atoms per unit volume in a metallic foil of width $D$, $Z$ the charge of the scattering nucleus, $m$ and $v$ the mass and the velocity of the $\alpha$-particles).<sup>783</sup> After quantum mechanics—and especially wave mechanics—became available, the derivation of a new scattering formula replacing Eq. (612) became an urgent task. The first step toward that goal was undertaken by Max Born in summer 1926. In a series of papers, he not ony arrived at the conceptually fundamental probabilty interpretation of the scattered wave function (first in Born, 1926a), but also established a systematic wave-mechanical scheme for describing the scattering of atomic particles, i.e., protons, $\alpha$-particles or even photons from atoms (Born, 1926b, f).<sup>784</sup> Then, in November 1926, Gregor Wentzel made a short remark on the scattering of corpuscular particles in Born’s theory; as a result of the first approximation, with a suitable potential screened off at the boundary of the atomic radius, he found ‘exactly Rutherford’s expression [(612)] for the directional distribution of scattered $\alpha$-particles’ (Wentzel, 1926e, p. 590). Five months later, J. Robert Oppenheimer derived the same result for fast charged particles even without any screening condition (Oppenheimer, 1927b).<sup>785</sup> The next studies were completed at two places,

<sup>783</sup> See Volume 1, Part 1, Section II.2.
<sup>784</sup> We have discussed Born’s scattering theory in Volume 5, Part 2, pp. 722–735.
<sup>785</sup> On the other hand, Oppenheimer also confirmed that the ‘anomalous scattering’ observed in the case of very fast particles ‘cannot be interpreted at all without assuming any further hypothesis about the structure of the particles’ (Oppenheimer, *loc. cit.*, p. 415).

Cambridge and Hamburg, and, in contrast to the previous investigations, they represented a complete solution of the wave-mechanical problem, and not just an approximation (i.e., the ‘Born approximation’ for small values of $ZZ'e^2/hv$, with $Z$ and $Z'$ the number of electric charges of the colliding particles).

On 4 March 1928, the *Zeitschrift für Physik* received Walter Gordon’s paper, entitled ‘*Über den Stoß zweier Punktladungen nach der Wellenmechanik*’ (‘On the Collision of Two Point Charges According to Wave Mechanics’) (Gordon, 1928b). Gordon evaluated the scattering according to two different methods, namely, the semiclassical scattering theory, or ‘ray optics and wave mechanics’ or ‘wave optics.’ In the former case, of course, Rutherford’s classical formula followed, whereas in the latter case Gordon derived the following expression for the scattered wave function

$$
\psi(r, \theta) = \exp\left\{ i \left[ kr \cos\theta + \frac{1}{ka} \log 2kr \sin^2 \frac{\theta}{2} \right] \right\} \times \left( 1 - \frac{i}{2k^3 a^2 r \sin^2 \frac{\theta}{2}} \right)
$$
$$
+ \frac{\exp\left\{ i \left[ kr - \frac{1}{ka} \log(2kr) \sin^2 \frac{\theta}{2} + \pi + 2\sigma(0, a) \right] \right\}}{2k^2 ar \sin^2 \frac{\theta}{2}}, \tag{613}
$$

with $a = \frac{h^2}{4\pi m e E}$ and $k = 2\pi m v / h^2$ ($e$, $m$, $v$ denoting the charge, mass, and initial velocity of the scattered nuclear particle, $E$ the charge of the scattering nucleus, and $\sigma(0, a)$ a phase constant). Now, Eq. (613) led again to the classical Rutherford scattering formula (612), and Gordon concluded: ‘This result can be viewed as corresponding to the fact that Coulomb’s law yields—also in ray optics (i.e., the old quantum theory)—*exactly* the same (i.e., not only for large quantum numbers) term values as the wave theory.’ (Gordon, *loc. cit.*, p. 190)

A little earlier than Gordon, Nevill Francis Mott of St. John’s College in Cambridge had submitted a theoretical investigation on ‘The Solution of the Wave Equation for the Scattering of Particles by a Coulombian Centre of Force’ to the *Proceedings of the Royal Society of London* (Mott, 1928).<sup>786</sup> Mott obtained

<sup>786</sup> Nevill Francis Mott was born on 30 September 1905, in Leeds, the son of Charles Francis and Lilian Mary Mott (*née* Reynolds), both of whom had studied at the Cavendish Laboratory under J. J. Thomson. Mott won a scholarship to St. John’s College and studied at Cambridge University from 1924 to 1928. He visited Niels Bohr’s Institute in Copenhagen in 1928, where he became friends with George Gamow; on his return to Cambridge, he turned his interest to $\alpha$-particle scattering. He spent the spring and summer months of 1929 at Göttingen, and in the fall of that year he became a lecturer at the University of Manchester, where he taught wave mechanics. Upon his return to Cambridge in spring 1930, he married Ruth Horder and collaborated with Charles D. Ellis at the Cavendish until 1933. Mott was then appointed Melville Wills Professor of Physics at the University of Bristol, where he completely changed the field of his research, turning then to solid-state physics. He soon became an expert and a very productive researcher in the new subject, as well as a gifted and successful teacher who attracted a large number of students and collaborators. After World War II (during which he

served as an advisor to the Royal Air Force), he returned to Bristol. In 1954, he was appointed Cavendish Professor in Cambridge (succeeding William Lawrence Bragg), where he served until 1971. In spite of many administrative duties (Master of Gonville and Caius College, 1959–1966), Mott continued active scientific work on solid-state problems, for which he received (jointly with J. H. Now, by solving the Dirac equation in the Coulomb potential of a nucleus, Mott arrived again at a scattering formula of the Rutherford type, Eq. (612). He further calculated the explicit expression for the asymmetry parameter $\delta$, i.e., for the scattering angle $\theta_1 = \theta_2 = 90^\circ$, obtaining

$$ \delta = 11.2 \times \frac{(1 - v^2/c^2)v^2/c^2}{2 - v^2/c^2} \left( \frac{2\pi Ze^2}{hc} \right)^2, \quad (618) $$

upon which he commented by saying:

> $\delta$ has a maximum when $v/c = 0.764$, so there is an optimum value of the velocity of the incident electrons [to produce polarization by double scattering]. With this value of $v/c$ we have $\delta = (Z/96)^2$, $Z$ being the atomic number of the nucleus. For light elements, therefore, the effect is very small. . . . For heavy elements, however, . . . the polarization effect increases with $Z^2$, and so it seems certain that the Dirac theory of the electron does predict a polarization on collision. (Mott, *loc. cit.*, p. 439)

Mott still doubted whether the calculated effect could really be observed in experiments; in addition, he noticed that the resulting formula ‘does not agree with the available experimental evidence, giving in all cases too little scattering’ (Mott, *loc. cit.*, p. 440).
Mott continued to work on the scattering of nuclear particles in 1929, turning to a specific quantum-mechanical aspect: if two identical microscopic objects collide, one cannot decide which one is the scattering particle and which the scatterer. This applied in particular to the scattering of electrons and $\alpha$-particles (Mott 1929a, b; 1930), because he expected that there were indeed deviations from the classical behaviour due to the symmetry and antisymmetry property of the two-particle wave functions in both cases. For a stream of electrons fired with velocity $v$ into a gas of electrons initially at rest, he thus derived by solving the two-particle nonrelativistic Schrödinger equation the expression

$$ \frac{e^4}{m^2 v^4} \left\{ \text{cosec}^4 \theta + \text{cosec}^4 \left( \frac{1}{2} \pi - \theta \right) - \text{cosec}^2 \theta \left( \frac{1}{2} \pi - \theta \right) \right\} $$

$$ \times \cos \left( \frac{e^2}{hv} \log \frac{1 + \cos 2\theta}{1 - \cos 2\theta} \right) \} \sin 2\theta \cdot d\theta d\phi, \quad (619) $$

giving the number of particles scattered into a solid angle $\sin \theta d\theta d\phi$. This ex-

which would still be valid quantum mechanically without taking into account the antisymmetry effect. On the other hand, for $\alpha$-particles obeying Bose–Einstein statistics (as derived from the band spectrum of the helium molecule) the corresponding expression

$$\frac{(2e^2)^2}{m^2v^4} \left\{ \operatorname{cosec}^4 \theta + \operatorname{cosec}^4 \left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta \right) + 2\operatorname{cosec}^2 \theta \operatorname{cosec}^2 \left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta \right) \right.$$

Although only scarce observations existed in the electron situation, the available $\alpha$-particle-helium scattering data were ‘obscured by the structure effect.’ Mott concluded: ‘To show the [symmetry effect], $\alpha$-particles would have to be used so slow that the structure effect was negligible’ (Mott 1930, p. 264). In the following year, the Cambridge experimentalists indeed confirmed the validity of Eq. (620) as predicted (Blackett and Champion, 1931).⁷⁸⁸ However, the scattering of $\alpha$-particles having high velocities should also exhibit deviations from the classical behaviour even without a symmetry effect, i.e., when the scatterer was assumed to be a light nucleus different from a helium nucleus. Again, the theory was developed by a Cambridge student, H. M. Taylor, who worked under the guidance of Mott and first dealt with the scattering of $\alpha$-particles with helium nuclei, because the data were available. Besides the symmetry effect existing in this case, he explained other ‘anomalies’ by assuming a breakdown of Coulomb's law in nuclei at very small distances, which are reached by very high-energy $\alpha$-particles (Taylor, 1931). In the next paper, Taylor derived formulae for the scattering of high energy $\alpha$-particles by hydrogen and helium nuclei, deviating fundamentally from the Rutherford scattering formula, Eq. (612) (Taylor, 1932).

Toward the end of the 1920s, Cambridge, England, had taken over a strong lead in nuclear physics, despite some competition from the European Continent. This development was substantially supported by the fact that new young theoreticians, like Mott and Taylor, succeeded in applying quantum mechanics to those collision processes that had been studied for more than a decade in Rutherford's Cavendish Laboratory. In the new ‘International Series of Monographs on Physics,’ published

> ⁷⁸⁸ Patrick Blackett and Frank Clive Champion observed the ratio of quantum mechanical over classical scattering for energies of the $\alpha$-particles in the electron-volt region and showed that it approached (for $\theta = 45^\circ$) the value 2, as derived from Eq. (620) and the corresponding classical relation.
