S. W. Massey’s *The Theory of Atomic Collisions* (1933). Moreover, Mott was invited to contribute the central theoretical review article, ‘Wellenmechanik und Kernphysik’ (‘Wave Mechanics and Nuclear Physics’) to the Geiger–Scheel *Handbuch der Physik*, which provided an excellent condensation of the results up to 1932 (Mott, 1933). Yet, interest in the theoretical problems of nuclear physics transcended Rutherford’s circle; besides various places in Central Europe (such as Berlin, Göttingen, Leipzig, Tübingen, and Zurich), especially Niels Bohr’s Institute in Copenhagen participated, where high-energy nuclear phenomena were considered as indicating the route to further revisions of the available quantum mechanics.<sup>789</sup> In Copenhagen in the late 1920s Christian Møller, a young Danish student began his career with theoretical studies on nuclear and high-energy phenomena.<sup>790</sup> His interest in nuclear phenomena was stimulated by visitors at Bohr’s Institute, especially George Gamow and Nevill Mott, and in high-energy physics by Yoshio Nishina, whom he helped in the calculations for the polarization of Compton scattering (Nishina, 1929, p. 877): the combination of the two fields of nuclear physics and relativity theory played a central role in all of his scientific work.<sup>791</sup> Thus, he began in 1929 to investigate the radioactive α-decay by describing the α-particle with the help of the Dirac equation (Møller, 1929).<sup>792</sup> Then, he directed his attention to the phenomena of α-particle scattering by light

<sup>789</sup> Of course, the close personal connections between the Copenhagen physicists and Werner Heisenberg, Wolfgang Pauli, and others propagated the general feeling that the quantum theory achieved thus far was only a preliminary step to further revolutionary changes. See our Section II.7 in this volume.

<sup>790</sup> Christian Møller was born on 22 December 1904, in Hunslev, Als (southern Jutland, which was a part of Germany until 1920). After his early education in German and Danish gymnasiums, Christian entered the University of Copenhagen in 1923 mainly to study mathematics; however, in 1926, he decided to become a theoretical physicist and joined Bohr’s Institute, where Werner Heisenberg and Oskar Klein taught courses on various topics of theoretical physics, and Hans Marius Hansen lectured on experimental topics. On two occasions during his student days in Copenhagen, he went abroad: in the summer semester of 1926 to Hamburg to attend Wolfgang Pauli’s lectures on relativity theory, and in summer 1928 to Berlin to learn from Schrödinger and Einstein. (For Møller’s early life and work, see Kragh, 1992, and Roqué, 1992.) After taking his doctorate with Bohr in 1933, Møller served as a lecturer at Bohr’s Institute in Copenhagen until 1940 (interrupted only by a Rockefeller Foundation Fellowship in 1934–1935, which he spent in Rome and Cambridge). In 1943, he was appointed Professor of Mathematical Physics at the University of Copenhagen, where he taught until retirement in 1975. Møller served as director of the Copenhagen theoretical study group of CERN (1954–1957) and as director of NORDITA (1951–1971). He died on 14 January 1980, in Copenhagen.

<sup>791</sup> During the 1930s, Møller worked on electron positron theory, and later on the meson theory of nuclear forces; from 1943 to 1947, he developed further Heisenberg’s *S*-matrix theory of nuclear forces.

<sup>792</sup> Møller was aware that the α-particles ‘probably possess no spin’; hence, the behaviour of α-particles ‘should be treated by the Klein-Gordon relativistic wave equation.’ Yet, he claimed: ‘For the problem of radioactivity it does not matter which of the two theories one uses, since the deviations—as will be shown in the course of our calculations—turn out to be meaningless.’ In the case of infinite velocity of light (i.e., in the nonrelativistic limit, the results of Gamow were obtained. (See Møller, 1929, pp. 451–452)

nuclei (Møller, 1930a, b), concerning himself especially with the higher Born approximations. By making use of Paul Dirac’s momentum-space method (Dirac, 1927d), he observed that ‘the second approximation for α-ray scattering ... becomes for all velocities occurring in nature of the same order of magnitude as [that of] the first order, hence Born’s method must be considered as not being suitable for α-rays’ (Møller, 1930b, p. 513). However, the situation appeared to be more favourable in the case of electron scattering from atoms, in which the condition,

$$
\frac{\pi Z e^2}{h v} \ll 1, \tag{621}
$$

made sure that the first Born approximation already described the observations.

In spring 1931, Møller began to work on his dissertation dealing with the passage of fast electrons through matter. This subject was an old acquaintance in the Copenhagen circle, although according to Møller it was the Russian visitor Lev Landau (who had arrived in Copenhagen in September 1930), ‘not Bohr,’ who brought Møller to work on the scattering problem (Møller, AHQP Interview, 29 July 1963, p. 15). Back in 1913, Bohr had treated the passage of charged particles through matter with the help of a perturbation theory involving their classical interaction with the atomic electrons (Bohr, 1913a). This approach (later extended relativistically: Bohr, 1915c) had described the data then available reasonably, and later attempts at a quantum-theoretical treatment did not essentially change Bohr’s results. However, by 1930, new experimental investigations had changed the situation that called for a new, quantum-mechanical treatment. Thus, Hans Bethe proposed a comprehensive ‘theory of the passage of fast corpuscular rays through matter’ in a lengthy memoir received on 3 April 1930, by *Annalen der Physik* (Bethe, 1930). In that memoir, he applied Born’s scattering theory to treat inelastic collisions of fast electrons, protons, and α-particles with atoms, giving rise to the emission of radiation, secondary electrons, and the occurrence of Compton effect. Bethe replaced the formula for the energy loss that Bohr had derived in 1915, namely,

$$
\Delta_s T = \frac{2\pi N e^4}{m v^2} \Delta x \log \left\{ \frac{k v^2 m v^2 S}{4\pi^2 v^2 2 e^4} \right\} \tag{622}
$$

(with $S = 2\pi N e^4 \Delta x / m v$, where $v$ and $m$ denoted the velocity and mass of the charged particles, and $\nu$ the eigenfrequency of the bound one-electron atoms), by the quantum-theoretical law

$$
\Delta_s T = \frac{2\pi N e^4}{m v^2} \Delta x \log \left\{ \frac{2 m v^2 S}{a R^2 h^2} \right\} \tag{622'}
$$

(with $a = 1.105$ and $R$ denoting Rydberg’s constant). The arguments of the logarithmic terms in Eqs. (622) and (622') did not agree fully, the differences being

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0697 -->

expressed by an extra factor $(4\pi^2 e^2 / h\nu)^2 = (2\alpha c/v)^2$ occurring in Eq. (622'), with $\alpha$ denoting the fine structure constant. For fast electrons ($v > c/70$), this factor became smaller than 1; hence, the quantum-mechanical result agreed much better with the data than the old classical one, as Evan J. Williams from Manchester showed later (1932).

Møller introduced his first paper on this subject with the following remarks:

> Born's collision theory, based on the Schrödinger equation in configuration space, does not apply, of course, to a situation where the velocity of the colliding particle assumes values of the order of magnitude of the velocity of light: first, because it does not take into account the variation of mass with velocity; and second, because it assumes an instantaneous interaction between the particles which cannot be valid in the situation under consideration. Now even today there exists no systematic relativistic quantum mechanics of the two-body system; nevertheless it seems to be possible to obtain—in the case where the first Born approximation suffices (i.e., for large velocities)—a suitable generalization for treating the problem satisfying all requirements of relativity theory. (Møller, 1931, p. 786)

Although Mott had carried out earlier the calculation of the two-electron scattering quite rigorously, he had used for the interaction simply the classical static Coulomb potential; hence, his approach failed to be a relativistic one. Several theoreticians, including J. A. Gaunt, Arthur S. Eddington, Werner Heisenberg, Wolfgang Pauli, and, in particular, Gregory Breit (1929), had attempted before to take retardation effects into account, suggesting to replace the Coulomb potential by the expressions,

$$V = \frac{e^2}{r} (1 - \mathbf{a}_1 \cdot \mathbf{a}_2) \quad \text{or} \quad \frac{e^2}{r} \left[ 1 - \frac{\mathbf{a}_1 \cdot \mathbf{a}_2}{2} - \frac{(\mathbf{a}_1 \cdot \mathbf{r})(\mathbf{a}_2 \cdot \mathbf{r})}{2r^2} \right], \tag{623}$$

where $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ denoted the Dirac vectors of the two colliding electrons. Now, Landau, in Copenhagen, had an idea, as Møller recalled:

> [He] mentioned that probably one could do such a calculation by a purely correspondence treatment. He mentioned also Bethe's treatment of the nonrelativistic case. Bethe had treated the collisions and stopping phenomena in the nonrelativistic case. He had written the matrix element for the transition in such a way that it looked as if one particle in its transition creates a charge distribution which acts on the other through the potential. And then the rather obvious idea came to do it relativistically, instead of using the Coulomb static potential, to introduce a retarded potential corresponding to the charge *and* current which corresponds to such a transition. (Møller, AHQP Interview, 29 July 1963, p. 15)

Further, Møller—the doctoral candidate—recalled that his teacher Oskar Klein had, in late 1926, tried to establish a theory of radiation emitted from perturbed atoms based on the correspondence approach (O. Klein, 1927a), and he had used this theory later with Nishina to derive the relativistic Klein–Nishina formula for

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v06_p01 p0698 -->

666  Chapter III  The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

the Compton effect (Klein and Nishina, 1929).$^{793}$ Thus, Møller combined Klein's correspondence treatment with Landau's suggestion to derive his scattering formula for the relativistic electron in his paper, entitled '*Über den Stoß zweier Teilchen unter Berücksichtigung der Retardation der Kräfte*' ('On the Collision of the Two Particles by Taking into Account the Retardation of Forces') and submitted in May 1931 (Møller, 1931).

In the interaction of two electrons described by two-component spinors—the negative-energy states of the Dirac equation were simply neglected—Møller used systematically the relations for the relativistic four-potential $(\mathbf{A}, \phi)$. The number of transitions per unit time of the charged-particle states (with charges $e_1$ and $e_2$ and initial momenta $\mathbf{p}_1^0$ and $\mathbf{p}_2^0$ and final momenta $\mathbf{p}_1'$ and $\mathbf{p}_2'$) could be written in the first Born approximation (and momentum representation) as

$$\frac{4\pi^2}{h} |\Phi|^2 \delta(E_1^0 + E_2^0 - E_1' - E_2') d^3 \mathbf{p}_1' d\mathbf{p}_2' \tag{624}$$

($E_i$ and $E_i'$ being the corresponding energies), with the matrix element

$$\Phi = \frac{e_1 e_2 h^2}{\pi} \frac{(\overline{\alpha_2' \alpha_2^0})(\overline{\alpha_1}, \alpha_1^0) - (\overline{\alpha_2' \alpha_2 \alpha_2^0}, \overline{\alpha_1' \alpha_1 \alpha_1^0})}{|\mathbf{p}_1 - \mathbf{p}_1'|^2 - \left( \frac{E_1^0 - E_1'}{c} \right)^2} \times h^3 \delta(\mathbf{p}_1^0 + \mathbf{p}_2^0 - \mathbf{p}_1' - \mathbf{p}_2'). \tag{624a}$$

[In Eq. (624a) $a_1^0$ and $a_i'$ denoted the wave functions of the particles, $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ their spin functions.] If the relativistic term $\left( \frac{E_1^0 - E_1'}{c} \right)^2$ in the denominator were dropped, $\Phi$ would assume the form

$$(s_1^0 \mathbf{p}_1^0 s_2^0 \mathbf{p}_2^0 | V | s_1' \mathbf{p}_1' s_2' \mathbf{p}_2') = \int \overline{\phi_1'(\mathbf{r}_1)} \overline{\phi_2'(\mathbf{r}_2)} V(\mathbf{r}_1, \mathbf{r}_2) \phi_1^{(0)}(\mathbf{r}_1) \phi_2^{(0)}(\mathbf{r}_2) d\tau_1 d\tau_2, \tag{625}$$

with

$$V = \frac{e_1 e_2}{|\mathbf{r}_1 - \mathbf{r}_2|} [1 - (\mathbf{a}_1 \cdot \mathbf{a}_2)]. \tag{625a}$$

This result agreed with Gaunt's nonrelativistic *Ansatz* for the interaction of two particles, in which the first term described the electrostatic interaction and the second the magnetic (spin) interaction (Gaunt, 1929). As Møller emphasized, however, the effect of retardation had the same order of magnitude as that of spin-interaction. By taking the retardation into account, Møller finally arrived at the expression for the differential cross section $dQ(\theta)$, giving the number of particles 1 scattered per unit time into the space angle $d\theta d\phi$ (the polar angles $\theta$ and $\phi$ are

$^{793}$ We have discussed this work earlier in Section II.7.

**III.7 Aspects of Nuclear and 'High-Energy' Phenomena**  
**667**

defined with respect to the initial momentum \( \boldsymbol{p_1^0} \), divided by the number of particles 2 (and the number of incident particles per unit area). In the case of not too large velocities \( v \) (where terms of higher order than \( v^2/c^2 \) could be neglected), he found for electron–electron scattering the expression  

\[
dQ(\theta) = \frac{e^4 \sin 2\theta \ 2 \, d\theta \, d\phi}{m^2 v^4} \left\{ \frac{1}{\sin^4\theta} + \frac{1}{\cos^4\theta} - \frac{1}{\sin^2\theta \cos^2\theta} - \frac{v^2/c^2}{4} \left[ \frac{4}{\sin^4\theta} + \frac{3}{\cos^4\theta} - \frac{2}{\sin^2\theta \cos^2\theta} - \frac{5}{\cos^4\theta} \right] \right\}
\tag{626}
\]

i.e., a generalization of Mott’s nonrelativistic formula (619), whereas in the case of close to relativistic velocities for scattering angles \( \sin^2\theta \gg 1/\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2} \) the result  

\[
dQ(\theta) = \frac{e^4 \sin 2\theta \, d\theta \, d\phi}{m^2 c^4 \cdot 4} (\tan^4\theta + \tan^2\theta)
\tag{627}
\]

followed.  

Møller’s theory was soon tested experimentally by Frank Clive Champion, a young experimentalist from Cambridge (a student of P. M. S. Blackett and the Cavendish Laboratory), with the cloud-chamber method (Champion, 1932).⁷⁹⁴ Between October 1931 and January 1932, letters were exchanged between Copenhagen and Cambridge, in which Møller finally reported an improved version of Eq. (627), in particular:  

I use the same notation as in my former letter. \( \theta^* \) is related to \( \theta \) by the equation  

\[
\cos \theta^* = \frac{2\cos^2\theta - (\gamma + 1)\sin^2\theta}{2\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta(\gamma + 1)}, \quad \sin^2\theta^* = \frac{\sin 2\theta\sqrt{(\gamma + 1)}}{2\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta(\gamma + 1)},
\]
\[
\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}
\tag{[(628)]}
\]

Then I get  

\[
dQ(\theta) = \frac{e^4 \sin \theta^* \, d\theta^* 8(\gamma + 1) \, d\phi}{m^2 v^4 \gamma^4 [(\gamma + 3)^2 - (\gamma - 1)^2 \cos^2\theta^*]} F.
\tag{[(629)]}
\]

F is the same factor as in [my] former letter,  

\[
F = 2\gamma^2(\gamma + 1) \left( \frac{4}{\sin^4\theta^*} - \frac{3}{\sin^2\theta^*} \right) + \frac{(\gamma - 1)^2}{4} \left\{ \frac{4[1 + (\gamma + 1)^2]}{\sin^2\theta^*} + 3 - 2\gamma^2 \right\} + \frac{(\gamma - 1)^4}{16} \sin^2\theta^*.
\tag{[(629a)]}
\]

---

668 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

You see it is rather an essential correction, since we must have symmetry about the angle $\theta^* = \frac{\pi}{2}$. Now I hope I have eliminated all faults. (Møller to Champion, 25 January 1932, in Kragh, 1992, p. 317)

Having compiled 131 events of electron–electron collisions with energies (of $\beta$-rays from radium E having velocities from 0.32 to 0.92c), Champion concluded: ‘Møller’s formula gives the best agreement with the experimentally observed scattering of electrons by electrons.’ (Champion, 1932, p. 103)

Mott also showed great interest in Møller’s results, especially when applied to the scattering of electrons by protons (Mott to Møller, 13 December 1931), and Møller replied: ‘The retardation of forces cannot be important if the velocity of the electron is not so large that the proton after the collision has a velocity of the same order of magnitude as that of light.’ (Møller to Mott, 25 January 1932) At any rate, in the nonrelativistic limit ($\gamma = 1$ and $\Theta = 2\theta$), Møller’s result passed over into Mott’s.

Encouraged by these successes, Christian Møller completed his thesis on the ‘Theory of the Passage of Fast Electrons through Matter.’$^{795}$ The task Møller accomplished in his thesis was that he—as in the electron–electron scattering—extended the earlier nonrelativistic treatment to include the effect of retardation. Thus, he arrived at a correction of Hans Bethe’s formula (622'), namely,

$$\Delta_s T = \frac{2\pi N e^4 \Delta x}{mv^2} \left\{ \log \frac{2mv^2 S}{a^2 R^2 h^2} - \log \left( 1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2} \right) - \frac{v^2}{c^2} \right\} \quad (630)$$

[see Møller, 1932, Eq. (92) on p. 536]. On 3 May 1932, *Annalen der Physik* received the paper ‘Zur Theorie des Durchgangs schneller Elektronen durch Materie’ (‘On the Theory of the Passage of Fast Electrons through Matter’) containing the principal results of the dissertation (Møller, 1932). On the following day, *Zeitschrift für Physik* received Bethe’s note on a ‘Bremsformel für Elektronen relativistischer Geschwindigkeit’ (‘The Breaking Formula for Electrons of Relativistic Velocity’), in which Bethe, based on Møller’s 1931 paper, improved his own theory of 1930 by adding the missing relativistic aspect (Bethe, 1932). One month later, Hans Bethe and Enrico Fermi submitted their investigation ‘Über die Wechselwirkung von zwei Elektronen’ (‘On the Interaction of Two Electrons’), again to *Zeitschrift für Physik*; they showed, in particular, that Møller’s scattering formula (624) could be derived in a systematic manner from the quantum electrodynamics of Fermi (Bethe and Fermi, 1932). Møller’s scattering theory thus became the prototype of a successful extension of quantum mechanics to the relativistic domain, similar to the Klein–Nishina formula.

Still, not every detail of the relativistic effects in these investigations turned out

III.7 Aspects of Nuclear and ‘High-Energy’ Phenomena 669

to be perfect. In particular, the just-mentioned Klein–Nishina formula, based like Møller’s electron scattering on the Dirac equation, was violated. By the end of the year 1929, the experimentalists were ready for a crucial check, as Carl Anderson recalled later:

> My thesis work as a graduate student at Caltech consisted of studying, by means of a Wilson cloud chamber, the space distribution in various gases of photoelectrons produced by X-rays. At the time (1927–30) that I was doing this work, Dr. Chung-yao Chao, working in a room close to mine, was using an electroscope to measure the absorption and scattering of groups from ThC''. His findings interested me greatly. At that time it was generally believed that the absorption of “high energy” γ-rays [2.6 MeV from ThC''] was almost wholly by Compton scattering as governed by the Klein–Nishina formula. Dr. Chao’s result showed clearly that both the absorption and scattering were substantially greater than calculated by the Klein–Nishina formula. . . .
> 
> My proposed experiment was to study the interaction of ThC'' γ-rays with matter in a cloud chamber operated in a magnetic field to study the secondary electrons produced in a thin lead plate inserted in the cloud chamber, to measure their energy distribution, and to see what further light could be thrown on Chao’s results. (C. Anderson and H. Anderson, 1983, pp. 135–136)

Anderson was not allowed by his professor, Robert A. Millikan, to carry out this proposed programme, but Chao’s results were eventually published (Chao, 1930a). Still, his paper was published with a delay as compared with his competitors in Europe, especially Lise Meitner and H. H. Hupfeld (1930); hence, the observed deviation of the anomalous absorption and scattering of high-energy γ-rays received the name of the ‘Meitner-Hupfeld effect.’796

The experimental investigation of this effect continued during the subsequent years: while Chao had worked with electroscopes, Meitner and Hupfeld employed Geiger–Müller counters. They explained the results as arising from the scattering with nuclear electrons. Whatever the cause, the results evidently contradicted the otherwise successful Klein–Nishina formula in the domain of high energies. In a paper on ‘Theoretische Überlegungen zur Höhenstrahlung’ (‘Theoretical Considerations on Cosmic Radiation’), in which he summarized the status of high-energy quantum mechanics, Heisenberg concluded the discussion of the subject by stating:

> The electrons of the atomic cloud can be considered in any case to be free for very energetic light-quanta ($h\nu \gg mc^2$), also the photo-effect will (except for very heavy elements) not have any influence on [the scattering coefficient] $\mu$. It is different for nuclear electrons. We have arbitrarily estimated their binding energies to be $2mc^2$ and $30mc^2$, respectively, hence we would expect that far above these binding energies the nuclear electrons should practically scatter like free electrons. . . . Perhaps the scattering for light-quanta of a medium-large penetration becomes particularly strong and might then again be fitted by the Klein–Nishina formula.

---

$^{796}$ We shall return to a discussion of this effect in Chapter IV in connection with the discovery of positrons. For a detailed historical account of the Meitner–Hupfeld effect, see Brown and Moyer, 1984.

670 Chapter III The Empirical and Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics

We need not emphasize that the considerations just mentioned on the scattering properties of nuclear electrons are hypothetical, and that perhaps the real behaviour of nuclear electrons does not show any similarity with what we have discussed here, because the electrons in nuclei cannot be treated according to the laws of quantum mechanics; therefore even a partial application of quantum mechanics, where it is possible, has to be doubted. (Heisenberg, 1932a, pp. 441–442)
